# PROLOGUE

## BY FRANCESCO GIORGIO THE VENETIAN, OF THE 
## FRANCISCAN ORDER, <note>original: "Minoritanae Familiae"; the "Minorite Family" refers to the Order of Friars Minor, or Franciscans.</note> FOR THE WORK ON THE 
## HARMONY OF THE WORLD, DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS

### PREFACE
### TO CLEMENT VII, SUPREME PONTIFF.

<insert>NATIONAL LIBRARY OF ROME, VITTORIO EMANUELE</insert>

**N**OT INDEED, MOST BLESSED FATHER, am I led by any pride, nor according to flesh and blood, but by a good spirit—indeed, by a better spirit—so that for those who are less enlightened, I might attempt to approach with this little torch, such as it is. It is certainly not a new light, but one that glows from that Light which illuminates all people. And from the most rich harvest of the Lord, I might bring into the Lord's barn to feed the poor at least some small sheaves, perhaps left behind for posterity by other reapers at the Lord's command. From these we have threshed the wheat—certainly not new wheat, but ancient wheat brought forth in a new form and worked in a new way. It is mixed with water, not from broken cisterns <note>A reference to Jeremiah 2:13, contrasting human-made systems with divine truth.</note> but from a better and saving wisdom, from which, for the one who drinks, it becomes a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. <note>A reference to John 4:14.</note> Those who first laid the foundations of Gospel teaching, having truly become children of God by drawing this water, considered the wisdom of this world to be foolishness. This worldly wisdom relies on its own strengths and those devised by human industry; it yields to no truth except that which its followers trust they can demonstrate through syllogistic reasoning. <term>Syllogistic reasoning: a form of logical argument (like "all men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal") which Giorgio argues is insufficient for understanding God.</term>

But those composite deductions, rooted as they are in the senses themselves, are unable to reach that solitary and intellectual nature of the Creator (as Proclus teaches).
<margin>Proclus</margin> <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Christian mysticism.</note>
Furthermore, they cannot teach the effects, properties, or "passions" (as they call them) of the lower world of nature, since the causes from which they think they can infer them by their arguments are (by the consensus of all of them) utterly unknown to mortals. Moreover, because they proceed from the senses, which are fallacious (as Pyrrho of Elis proves with many reasons), they can offer us no pure truth.
<margin>Pyrrho</margin> <note>Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BC) was the founder of Greek Skepticism, who taught that human senses and reason cannot reach certain truth.</note>
<margin>Plato</margin>
Hence, when dealing with divine matters, which ought to be compared to oracles (as Plato says), we must leave behind these types of composite reasons deduced from fallacious senses. They belong to those who occupy themselves only with sensible things, and who have established the "outermost boundaries" of their learning as those things which are subject to motion in the world of action. These people think they can combine and conclude everything through certain axioms which they believe it is impossible to refute. But such people mock the divine things hidden from them—things which are exalted all the more as a man presumes to ascend to a "higher heart." <note>A reference to Psalm 64:6 (Vulgate 63:7): "Accedet homo ad cor altum" (Man shall reach a deep heart).</note> For these sacred things are shown only by divine light; they hate contention and require silence...

<summary>In this dedication to Pope Clement VII, Francesco Giorgio argues that human logic and sensory observation (represented by syllogisms and Skepticism) are insufficient to reach divine truth. He positions his work as an "ancient wheat" presented in a new form, intended to synthesize mystical wisdom with Christian doctrine.</summary>

<keywords>Francesco Giorgio, Pope Clement VII, Neoplatonism, Proclus, Pyrrho of Elis, divine wisdom, Franciscan philosophy, syllogism, skepticism, harmony of the world</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the prologue addressed to Pope Clement VII. It transitions from a critique of purely human logic to the necessity of spiritual purification and the "harmonic kinship" between the visible and invisible worlds.</meta>

-># PROLOGUE<-

...desire <note>This sentence continues from the previous page, contrasting worldly logic with divine wisdom.</note>, the proud and the wise of the world they reject, while the little ones and the humble in heart they embrace and nourish. They utterly mock syllogisms and human deductions, since there is no prior principle of divinity, and nothing precedes it by which it could be proven otherwise. 

<margin>The Areopagite</margin> Hence, according to the witness of the Areopagite <note>original: "Areopagita"; refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian.</note>, it is only lawful to ascend to divine things as far as the ray of divine speech has suggested itself; for it offers itself to be perceived only by those whose minds have been purged. Therefore, if outsiders <note>referring to non-Christian philosophers.</note> studied with all care to remove the distractions that cloud the soul so that they might perceive even the smallest spark of divine things, how much more should those to whom divine utterances and the highest mysteries <term>sacramenta: in this context, "sacramenta" refers to hidden divine mysteries or sacred secrets rather than just the liturgical sacraments.</term> of things have been entrusted seek the purification of the soul with all zeal? 

<margin>The Brahmans</margin> For the Brahmans <note>original: "Brachmanae"; ancient Indian philosophers often cited by Renaissance writers as examples of ascetic wisdom.</note> admitted no one to their wisdom unless they abstained from wine and meat, and above all from vices, so that they might emulate God Himself—whom they desired to understand—through a divine way of life. <margin>Pharaotes</margin> <margin>Philostratus</margin> Likewise among the lower Indians, Pharaotes taught this, if we believe Philostratus <note>Philostratus authored the "Life of Apollonius of Tyana," which discusses Indian philosophy.</note>. 

<margin>Lysides</margin> Lysides the Pythagorean, also writing to Hipparchus, teaches that it is not at all pious to share the mysteries of true philosophy (which indeed savors of the divine) with those who have not even dreamed of the purification of the soul. <margin>Hierocles</margin> For neither can a bleary and unclean eye (as Hierocles <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist.</note> drew from the storehouses of the ancients who followed these paths) gaze upon things that are too bright. Nor can someone newly devoted to sacred things, if not well initiated, immediately perceive those divine illuminations; for one just awakened from sleep cannot immediately contemplate bright objects. 

The soul must therefore be accustomed to beautiful studies and gradually purified until the Divine light begins to shine through, and our intellect stands out within us (as <margin>Plotinus</margin> Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note> says), which may join the soul to the Father and to the true light, and place it unmixed within the understandings of the Creator. <margin>Proclus</margin> Let light also (says Proclus <note>A late Neoplatonist who emphasized the hierarchy of being.</note>) be joined to light—not of the sort they claim belongs to the sciences, but something more beautiful and more unified. 

Here, Abraham, the leaders of the chosen family, and the teachers of true wisdom were gathered with God; having been made "gods," <note>A reference to the concept of "theosis" or "deification," where the soul becomes like God through grace and contemplation.</note> they were powerfully elevated to receive 그 light. This light, which is most remote from mortals, the dark-minded Jews considered a scandal and the impious Gentiles considered foolishness; but to eyes that have been illuminated, it appeared as a most beautiful radiance and the true storehouse of all treasures and of the most perfect wisdom. 

Hence, with great constancy and even at the risk of their lives, they attempted to defend it with their whole soul. <margin>Paul</margin> To these treasures also (as Paul teaches) one arrives not through philosophy—that is, this empty fallacy handed down by men—but it is perceived by that light through which, ascending from glory to glory, we are finally transformed into the same image of Him who is the splendor of the Father and His true image. 

But since the number of the enlightened who can receive that glowing light is very small, I think that those who desire to be initiated in this way should be led through those paths by which they can more easily be prepared to perceive that supreme light. These paths, without doubt, lead through these visible things to the invisible things of God, based on their harmonic kinship...

<summary>The author argues that divine wisdom requires spiritual purification and asceticism, citing various ancient philosophers (Platonists and Brahmans) and the Apostle Paul. He proposes a path to enlightenment through the study of the "harmonic kinship" between the physical and spiritual worlds.</summary>
<keywords>purification of the soul, divine light, Neoplatonism, Brahmans, Plotinus, Proclus, spiritual hierarchy, harmony, sacred mysteries</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the prologue, moving from the necessity of spiritual purification to the specific methodology of the work: the study of "harmonic consonance" between the physical world and its divine archetype. It emphasizes mathematics and music as the primary tools for this ascent.</meta>

-># PROLOGUE<-

...which they have most harmoniously toward each other. Therefore, concerning the consonance of both the world and the Archetype <note>original: "Archetypi"; in Neoplatonic thought, the "Archetype" is the divine blueprint or the world of ideas from which the physical world is modeled.</note>, and concerning the state of all things and of all those elements which each world itself (insofar as it receives them from the Archetype) embraces in the greatest harmony, we have judged it appropriate to treat this for the sake of an easier guidance. For us who desire to do this, a journey must be taken through many paths, because we must encounter all the remedies of the technical disciplines: Natural Philosophy, Arithmetic, Astronomy, Geometry, Music, and Divinity.

If, therefore, our treatment concerns things subjected to the senses, then the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetici: followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on empirical observation and the physical world.</term> with their sensible doctrine will provide support. If we investigate celestial things, we shall rely on the demonstrations of the astronomers. If we search into the concord of natural things, we shall direct our journey toward the more secret philosophers. If a treatise is held concerning the variety of the stars, and regarding that harmony which arises from their diverse aspects, movements, and sounds, it will be immediately resolved by musical ratios. 

If we attempt to explain in any way the supreme intelligences and the super-celestial secrets, then—having set all these aside and left them at the entrance—we shall approach the prophets and the saints, to whom it was given by a special gift to know the secrets of the living God; or we shall implore that Light which illuminates all people and instructs them perfectly in such matters. 

If, however, by some reason we desire to be raised up from these visible things to the celestial and super-mundane inner chambers, there will be for us (once error is set behind) a single path through numbers. By these, these lower things are shown to be connected with the higher ones through their own harmonic proportion, appearing most sweet to those contemplating them, and providing the easiest path to those working through their mutual correspondence and the power implanted within them. 

For all things are arranged by numbers, and from this, they are so familiar to all things that nothing stands in their way. For, being related to the powers above, they ascend familiarly to celestial things; and again, they act in a home-like manner with sensible things. From this, they put on different natures and different modes. For Number, which (as <margin>Proclus</margin> Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who saw mathematics as a bridge between physical and divine realities.</note> says) always exists as the same, is nonetheless one thing in the voice, another in the proportion of things, another in the soul and reason, and another in divine things; and that which is bound in created things is found to be most absolute and familiar to God. 

<margin>Themistius, Boethius</margin> Speaking of lower things, Themistius and Boethius so prefer number that they believe no one can practice philosophy rightly without it. <margin>Pythagoreans, Academics</margin> Indeed, all the Pythagoreans together, and the Academics <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note>, but especially the <margin>Theologians</margin> more secret Theologians, everywhere celebrate and venerate numbers. And not without merit; for as <margin>Avenzoar</margin> Avenzoar the Babylonian <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-epigraphical source of "Chaldean" or Eastern wisdom, rather than the historical Andalusian physician.</note> proves, he knows all things rightly who knows well how to count. 

<margin>Plato</margin> Plato supports this, saying in the *Epinomis*: "If someone wishes to take away number from human nature, he leaves them in no way prudent or scientific." For the soul will perceive nothing without reason, nor can anyone give a reason for things who is ignorant of number. Also, if number is removed, the arts vanish entirely. And what is greatest of all: he asserts that number is the cause of all good things, but the cause of no evil. He who is to be blessed, who desires to search into celestial and divine things, must not be ignorant of number. Necessarily, therefore, we must proceed through the paths of numbers and the harmonic order, if we are to go rightly and appropriately through these lower things to the higher and supreme ones...

<summary>The author argues that mathematical numbers and musical harmony are the essential "paths" for a philosopher to ascend from the physical world to the understanding of divine secrets. He cites authorities like Plato, Proclus, and Boethius to prove that without number, true wisdom and science are impossible.</summary>
<keywords>Harmony, Numerology, Neoplatonism, Proclus, Plato, Boethius, Archetype, Quadrivium, Sacred Mathematics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the prologue's discussion on the "ascent" to divine knowledge, linking Classical philosophy (Pythagoras, Plato) with Judeo-Christian prophecy (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Moses). It introduces the central theme that the universe is structured according to mathematical and harmonic ratios.</meta>

-># PROLOGUE<-

<margin>
Orpheus
Pythagoras
Stoics
Plato
Porphyry
Iamblichus
Chalcidius
Proclus
Syrianus
</margin>
...if we ever wish to ascend. For all things correspond to each other in turn and through mutual harmonies, though with different and varying numbers. This is what Orpheus sang, after Pythagoras taught him, and which the Stoics likewise agree upon when they say the world was made by applying a certain "arranging art." Plato proposes this; Porphyry asserts it with many reasons; and Iamblichus, Chalcidius, Proclus, and his teacher Syrianus declare it. Indeed, as many as belong to the Pythagorean and Academic <note>The "Academic family" refers to the followers of Plato's Academy.</note> families interpret and affirm it with all their might, believing that nature possesses nothing older or more fitting, whether in things already produced or those yet to be produced, than harmony—by which all parts of this world-machine are made harmonious. But the divine prophets, leaving inferior numbers far behind and introduced into the divine and more secret inner chambers, contemplated many things not to be disclosed. Hiding the better parts in their hearts so as not to stumble, they provided some few things for us to contemplate, as much as was permitted to them.

<margin>
Isaiah
</margin>
Among these, Isaiah says: *I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne* <note>Isaiah 6:1</note>, above this entire worldly house, whose seat is heaven, and which is full of the glory of its Maker. This glory shines harmoniously in the distributed series of ranks alongside the divine patterns of the Maker himself. Hence, between the Craftsman and the creation, concord and mutual love are sung by two Seraphim calling to one another in alternating voices: *Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord God of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory*, shared with each thing in a fitting proportion through related numbers by which all things are arranged. Absorbed by these measures and most harmonious concerts, the celestial prophets, leaving vocal numbers <note>original: "numeros uocales"; likely referring to spoken language or audible music as opposed to the "silent" mathematical music of the spheres.</note> and their reasonings in the vestibules, philosophized in better and divine numbers, in the types and forms of nature—indeed, in the patterns themselves—proceeding through all classes of Ideas in a certain supreme order known to those who have seen them. Ezekiel, Isaiah’s colleague, applied himself to this as well, when 

<margin>
Ezekiel
The Hebrews
</margin>
he beheld the divine tribunal, which the Hebrews call the <term>Merkabah: the "Chariot" of God, a central concept in Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) involving the vision of the divine throne.</term>, composed of divine ministers—Seraphim, Ophanim <note>The Ophanim are a class of celestial beings described as "wheels" in Ezekiel's vision.</note>, and holy living creatures—leading into the harmony of all things. Concluding the whole matter, he said: *And their appearance was as it were a* <insert>wheel within a wheel</insert> <gloss>ha-ophan be-tok ha-ophan, that is, a wheel in the middle of a wheel</gloss>. To follow our own translation for now: this worldly house is spherical "in the middle of a wheel," and of that intelligible and supreme sphere—that is, in the Word, which holds the center in that super-mundane wheel, as John says: *That which was made was life in him* <note>John 1:3-4</note>.

<margin>
John
Moses
</margin>
In that Word, I say, by which the Father carries and sustains all things, and which John, the true prophet, saw on the twin-peaked Parnassus <note>Parnassus is a mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; here used metaphorically for the height of spiritual vision.</note>—namely, the breast of Christ—where the twin summits of divine and human nature stand out. Moses, the first revealer of these secrets, saw this same thing on the twin-peaked Sinai, from which that region achieved not just the name of "Arabia Felix" <note>original: "Arabia fœlicis"; meaning "Happy" or "Fertile" Arabia.</note> but the reality of it. There, he contemplated the summits of the Divine Face—before whom he spoke often—and the outcome of subsequent effects. But he enclosed these things in most hidden enigmas within his heavy and most fruitful description of the world's fabric, deeming the unrefined and unskilled common people unworthy of the secrets of both worlds. For the most sublime light was not to be placed before the dim eyes of a people so weak they could not endure...

<summary>This page argues that the universe is governed by a divine harmony or mathematical order, a concept shared by both ancient Greek philosophers and Biblical prophets. It specifically links the visions of Isaiah and Ezekiel (the "wheel within a wheel") to the idea of a structured, proportional creation centered on the Divine Word.</summary>

-># PROLOGUE<-

## PROLOGUE

[...shone] upon the face of Moses from his divine fellowship with that glowing light, unless he had suppressed that very splendor by drawing a veil (just as their blinking eyes required). He therefore handed down the highest mysteries to the unrefined people under the coverings of a narrated history, leaving a space in secret for the wise, so that they might approach the inner chambers of intimate wisdom and supreme doctrine with the curtain drawn back and the face revealed. Thus, they might at times openly contemplate that storehouse of truth, and at other times proceed from the lowest and visible things to the invisible ones through those related numbers and harmonic proportions. From these, both the wiser Hebrews and our own scholars have discovered the moral, allegorical, and anagogical <note>These represent the "four senses of Scripture": the literal, the moral (tropological), the allegorical (symbolic/christological), and the anagogical (mystical/heavenly).</note> meanings. Hence, these lower things are moved by the higher ones with a much greater efficacy, insofar as natural and divine things excel those which are prepared by human art.

<margin>
Pythagoras
Cicero
Boethius
Terpander
Arion
Ismenias
Dion
</margin>
Indeed, led by this art of music, Pythagoras—according to the reports of Cicero and Boethius—restrained a raging youth by changing the musical modes. Terpander and Arion of Methymna cured the Lesbians and Ionians of many very serious diseases with their concerts, as did Ismenias the Theban. Furthermore, the singing of trumpets and horns kindles the spirits of soldiers and horses. Regarding Alexander the Macedonian, Dion relates that he was sometimes so incited by the modes of Timotheus that he would leap up for his arms like a madman. So too, the madness of King Saul, as he climbed toward the sacred rites, was so tempered by David’s lyre that he was restored to his former peace once the evil spirit was put to flight; for that spirit, having fallen from harmony, could not endure any true concord, as it was hostile to itself. I believe these songs and harmonic sounds were introduced into the sacred rites by the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> himself, the restorer of the sacred ceremonies, and by those Fathers who perceived these mysteries of God and nature. What power and what delight, therefore, must we imagine exists in the concord of natural and divine things? For truth, which is the fittingness of things, is most effective even when explained in inferior matters, and brings a delight full of wonderful joy to those who perceive it. But in divine matters, it so cheers and moves the soul that it seems to change it entirely into something else—most especially in the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms</note>, which, though repeated so many times, are never tiresome to well-composed minds, but rather delight and favor them greatly. For in them, as if in a sort of rhythmic summary of the whole Law, the melodies of both worlds are sung together with the Archetype <note>The divine "blue-print" or original model of the universe.</note>, along with that harmony which has been restored to all things by the Messiah, and how his most perfect work returns to its Maker with a sweet step. Nor was it only this Royal Seer who did this, but all who contributed a symbol to the Sacred Page; they were such that we can admire in them both an ample knowledge of true harmony and divinity, and a profound study of all other doctrines. For who does not see that all the Prophets were instructed in true poetry? Who does not recognize the most exact geometric measurements in Moses, Ezekiel, and John? And again, in Moses, Ezekiel, Daniel, and John, the proportions of numbers? And in the Davidic hymns and the wedding song of Solomon <note>The Song of Solomon</note>, and indeed in the entire description of both Testaments, do we not hear—as if in a full wedding song—the sweetest concord of perfected music? A music, I say, more sublime than that of Orpheus, Amphion, and the like. Everywhere and throughout their works, you may drink the draughts of both philosophies <note>Likely referring to natural philosophy (science) and divine philosophy (theology).</note>, provided you have learned how to philosophize well. These, then, are the leaders we must follow; these are the teachers to be imitated, and whatever we strive to achieve must be formed according to their measure. For truly, [Most Blessed Father], as has been handed down to memory by many, it was from no other source that Mercury, Aglaophemus, Orpheus, and He[subsequent text missing]...

<meta>This page transitions from the historical power of music to the formal structure of the author's work. It establishes the "three diapasonic Canticles" that organize the text, moving from the general concept of harmony to its specific application in the relationship between God, Christ, and humanity.</meta>

-># PROLOGUE<-

# PROLOGUE

[...He]siod, Pythagoras, Archytas, Plato, Parmenides, Charondas, Zamolxis, Lycurgus, and whoever finally followed those who philosophized so excellently or gave laws, took what they handed down from him. We have deemed these men worthy of admission—insofar as we can make all things agree as is right—only to the extent that they appear in accord with the harmony we have determined to construct. Wherever they are out of tune, however, they must be rejected like useless strings. Following in the footsteps of those ancient fathers, we shall try to render other names of things—but especially those of the Craftsman <note>original: *opificis*, referring to God as the creator-architect</note>—into our Latin, just as they handed them down, or at least as close as possible. We do this to express more clearly their profound meanings and the sacred mysteries hidden within the symbols they wrote. Origen <margin>Origen</margin> even thought that these things, when translated into another language, lose their inherent power. Therefore, I should not be seen as a fickle or curious seeker of novelty if I use the original words themselves or those very close to them. Nor should you judge it superfluous or useless if we seem to repeat certain things often; for the same things must be repeated as many times as they are fitted to different contexts. Indeed, different things must be composed with different things, and the same things with many others, so that all parts may be shown to be in tune with one another, and the sweetest consensus of all the Lord’s works may be drawn from every side. This stands (we pray) by the Divine Spirit and the Architect of all things. We have judged that this all-encompassing concert can be contained within three diapasonic <term>diapasonic: relating to the "diapason," the musical interval of an octave, signifying completeness or a "full-sounding" harmony</term> Canticles. Thus, each Canticle will be completed by eight Tones <note>Referring to the eight notes of an octave scale</note>, namely a perfect octave. In the first Canticle, we shall sound the resonance of both worlds <note>likely the celestial/divine world and the material/human world</note> with each other, and both with the Archetype <term>Archetype: the original divine pattern or "blueprint" in the mind of God</term>. In the second, we deal with the agreement of all things with the Messiah as the head, and that concert which was restored through Christ himself to all things that were broken and out of tune because of sin. In the third, we treat the human being as the most harmonious bond of all things, who must be recalled to harmony with all that is bound within him, and with the Craftsman with whom it is innate for him to agree—indeed, to be unified. In these books (unless I am mistaken), the entire business of both worlds and the sum of many disciplines are contained.

Truly, Holy Father, even if according to the common proverb "all things new are pleasing," nevertheless new things often excite envy. They offend squinting eyes not accustomed to new light; thus, turning to hatred, people often begin to attack what they have not yet well perceived. Hence, I am not unaware that I am exposed to many sharp-nosed critics and easy detractors, both because of this new way of proceeding and because of certain sparks that have long been hidden under the ashes or newly struck from the flint. Therefore, Most Blessed Father, we have decided to submit this work (whatever it may be) and all other new things we attempt with God’s help—and everything that is within me—to your judgment and to that of your most sacred college of fathers, and of all those who, having left behind the dim light, have directed their vision toward the supreme and most splendid light (as far as is permitted). Nor would I consider this work of ours truly harmonious, Most Holy and Clement Clement <note>The author is punning on the name of Pope Clement VII</note>, unless by your virtue and authority it is rendered pleasant to all members of the ecclesiastical body, and a harmless food for those who partake of it. To you, therefore, I have dedicated it, you who act in the place of Christ (in whom are all things and through whom all things exist) in this Catholic body. Just as all things receive life and beauty from Christ, the Word of God, so may this work, which treats all things, live more happily through you, be beautiful, and be a safe and joyful banquet for all. FAREWELL. Holy Father, for a long time.

<summary>The author outlines the structure of his work into three "Canticles" based on musical octaves, exploring the harmony between God, the world, and humanity. He concludes by dedicating the work to Pope Clement VII, seeking his protection against critics of his "new" approach.</summary>

# INDEX OF THE HARMONIC VOLUME DIVIDED
# INTO THREE PARTS, ARRANGED ACCORDING 
# TO ITS OWN ORDER.

## INDEX OF THE TONES OF THE FIRST SONG.

[Q] <note>Historiated initial depicting the Creator or a philosopher.</note> Who is the progenitor of the world, and by what harmony he enjoys the most exalted unity. Tone I.
By what concord things, principles, and the descriptions of them agree or disagree. Tone II.
By what consonant number the supreme craftsman <note>original: *opifex*</note> descends into all created things. Tone III.
By what mutual harmonies <note>original: *concentibus*</note> the primary kinds of things agree with each other and with the Archetype. Tone IV.
By what consonantal intervals they are filled. Tone V.
By what concord all things are contained in man, as if in a small instrument <note>An allusion to the "microcosm," the idea that the human being contains the proportions of the entire universe.</note>. Tone VI.
By what sonority all things, even particulars existing in this soiled world, agree with the Archetype. Tone VII.
What is the ultimate thing, into which all diapasonic <term>diapasonic: pertaining to the "diapason" or octave, the most perfect musical interval that encompasses all other notes</term> harmonies are reduced. Tone VIII.

## INDEX OF THE FIRST TONE.

[Q] <note>Historiated initial depicting a scholar at study.</note> What we can learn about God from holy men enlightened by divine light, which we treat here. Chapter I.
That without such light, all who speak of God have wandered through many devious paths. Chapter II.
And though we cannot understand *what* God is, we are nevertheless taught *that* God exists by both oracles and reason, and by the consensus of all. Chapter III.
How, through the trace or image of created things and their harmony with the Archetype, we can arrive at a knowledge of His fecundity <note>original: *fecunditatis*, referring to God’s creative fruitfulness</note>. Chapter IV.
That God is full of the fecundity of all things and numbers, so that He can produce all things most harmoniously. Chapter V.
That God is one. Chapter VI.
That the most fecund first mind, which is called God, produced inward and outward. Chapter VII.

Christ and the Messiah is the Wisdom of God and the Word containing all things by ideal reason; and as a living man, he actually embraces all inferior things. **Tone I.**

->PREFACE TO THE FIRST SONG.<-

# THE FIRST SONG, BY WHICH DIVINE,
## HUMAN, CELESTIAL, SUPER-
## CELESTIAL, AND ALL LOWER
## THINGS ARE SHOWN TO BE
## DISTRIBUTED IN FITTING
## PROPORTION AND HARMONIC
## SWEETNESS.

<insert>NATIONAL LIBRARY ROME VITTORIO EMANUELE</insert>

### PREFACE TO THE FIRST SONG.

<margin>-></margin>
**A**s I am about to sing in concert <note>original: *concenturi*; the author uses a musical verb to describe his writing process.</note> regarding the sonority of the world, Most Blessed Father, it is only right that we take our path through those fitting steps by which that supreme **Master Musician** <term>Archimusicus</term> <note>A term for God as the cosmic composer and conductor who maintains the order of the universe.</note> entered upon His work: He who arranged each individual thing and the entire world itself according to sounding numbers. From this work the Artist himself did not release his hand until he had led the work into himself toward a perfect consonance through the appropriate numbers, so that a full **octave** <term>diapason</term> <note>From the Greek *dia pason*, meaning "through all [the notes]"; the fundamental interval of completion in music theory.</note> **harmony** <term>symphonia</term> might be completed. This harmony is finally fulfilled when, after the first [note] and the six intermediate ones have passed, he calls back the last one to himself—which is the same as the first, and yet not the same. Indeed, by this eighth [interval], the whole structure of the world is perfected; by this it is arranged; and by this it is finally brought to completion. For it is perfected when the supreme Creator <note>original: *opifex*; literally a craftsman or maker.</note> arranged this entire structure through six levels of things full of mysteries—unveiled by Moses under the veil of the six days [of Creation]—and rested on the seventh. If this [seventh day] is counted with the first, since it existed within Himself, it is the eighth. And the perfect work, arranged by this fitting sequence of days, continues: so that always after the seventh it returns to the eighth, which is the same as the first, and yet not the same <note>This refers to the musical octave where the eighth note begins the sequence again at a higher register.</note>. Thus finally the most harmonious work of God shall be brought to its conclusion, when in the perfect octave (about which we shall discuss in its proper place), all things shall be restored into that very same [One]. We also, following in the footsteps of the Creator, shall complete this harmonic work through that eighth, returning to the same point from which we take our beginning: so that both extremes may be of the Most High God. For the first **tone** <term>Tonus</term> shall be of Him, insofar as He is the beginning; the last shall be of the same, insofar as He is the end; while the intermediate ones concern the progress of the first into the last, in which (if I am not mistaken) are contained the elements of worldly and otherworldly contemplation.

A

->THE TONES OF THE FIRST SONG.<-

# THE TONES OF THE FIRST SONG.

The power belongs to the progenitor of the world, and in what harmony he rejoices in his super-excellent unity. **Tone I.**
By what concord the principles of things and their delineators <note>original: *descriptores*; those who define or map the nature of things</note> agree or disagree. **Tone II.**
By what consonant number the highest creator <note>original: *summus opifex*</note> descends into all created things. **Tone III.**
By what mutual harmonies <note>original: *concentibus*</note> the primary kinds of things agree with one another and with the Archetype <term>Archetypus</term> <note>The original divine pattern or model after which all things in the material world are shaped.</note>. **Tone IV.**
By what consonance their intervals are filled. **Tone V.**
By what concord all things are contained in man as if in a small instrument <note>original: *in paruo instro [instrumento]*; a reference to the "microcosm," the idea that the human being contains the structure of the entire universe.</note>. **Tone VI.**
By what sonority all things, even the particular things existing in this dross-filled <note>original: *feculento*; literally "full of dregs," referring to the impurity of the material world compared to the divine.</note> world, agree with the Archetype. **Tone VII.**
What the ultimate end is, into which all things return in an octave <term>dyapason</term> <note>The fundamental musical interval of the eighth, representing a return to the starting note at a higher register; here it signifies the completion and return of all creation to God.</note> of consonance. **Tone VIII.**

### CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST TONE.

What we can learn about God from holy men illuminated by divine light, which are the things we treat here. **Chapter I.**
That without such light, all those speaking about God have wandered through many bypasses. **Chapter II.**

### WHAT WE CAN LEARN ABOUT GOD FROM HOLY MEN ILLUMINATED BY DIVINE LIGHT, CONCERNING THE MATTERS WE ARE TREATING. CHAPTER I.

**AS WE DESIRE**, in accordance with the requirements of the work we have undertaken, to investigate who the progenitor of this world might be, there occurs to us, without a doubt, what Plato—inspired by some divine power—was accustomed to say: that it is as difficult to find the Maker <note>original: *Opificem*; a craftsman or artisan, here referring to the Creator</note> and father of the universe as it is to speak of him worthily once found, since he dwells in inaccessible light. <margin>Moses, the first writer.</margin>
Orpheus, with his sacred rites, preceded others—specifically in the time of Gideon <note>A judge of Israel; the author is establishing a timeline where Greek myth follows biblical history</note>—but he followed about three hundred years after Moses. Moses, therefore, was the first who committed to public writing those mysteries which he learned, illuminated by divine light and fellowship; in these mysteries, his ancestors had been partially instructed. But by wrapping these things in historical narratives for the unlearned common folk with whom he dealt, he made himself accessible <note>original: *domesticum*; suggesting he adapted high truths for "household" or common consumption</note>. He entrusted the more secret words to the wise, leaving behind for future sages in seclusion, under a veil <note>original: *sub cortina*; literally a tripod-cover or curtain, referring to hidden or oracular knowledge</note>, the most splendid light of divine and natural things to be peered into. This is just like that dove which the Prophets mention, simplest in appearance, but with its back parts shimmering with the gleam of gold <note>A reference to Psalm 68:13</note>. With this splendor, the eyes of the Wise—polluted neither by sensory things nor by any other filth—looked into the highest mysteries of God and nature. The first of these great men was Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure often equated with the Egyptian god Thoth</note>, who followed the intimate discipline of Moses so closely that he was called "the Mosaic one" by those ancient sages.

<margin>Artabanus, Plato, Cicero, Augustine, Apuleius, Proclus, Numenius.</margin>
Indeed, Artabanus <note>An ancient historian of Jewish history</note> shows that whatever is said of Trismegistus was likewise found in Moses. Plato also, the master of philosophers (as I agree with Cicero, Augustine, Apuleius, Proclus, and many other wise men, whatever others may say), so thoroughly agrees with Moses that Numenius the Pythagorean <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who sought the Eastern origins of Greek thought</note> says Plato is nothing other than Moses speaking in the Attic tongue <note>The dialect of Greek spoken in Athens</note>. Pythagoras, from whom the Academics <note>Followers of Plato's Academy</note> learned (according to the testimony of Hermippus the Pythagorean), transferred many things from the doctrine of Moses into his own

<margin>Plato, Hermippus, Iamblichus.</margin>
philosophy. Thus it is true what Iamblichus, the great priest of the Egyptians, says in the volume he compiled concerning their mysteries: Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato, Eudoxus, and many others went to the Egyptian priests; there, they learned a more secret philosophy from the pillars of Mercury <note>The "Hermetic" pillars said to contain the sum of all knowledge</note>, which were inscribed with every kind of doctrine. But Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, as we have said, drew his knowledge from Moses. He is therefore the teacher from whom all Syrian, Egyptian, and Greek wisdom emanated.

<margin>Augustine, Ambrose, Eusebius Pamphilus, Cyril.</margin>
In addition to Augustine, our own Ambrose, Eusebius Pamphilus, and Cyril testify to this. The last of these says word for word: "When Pythagoras and Plato were devoting themselves to their studies in the land of Egypt, they did not remain ignorant of the doctrine of many illustrious men, and especially that of Moses, because of their zeal. For at that time, the name of Moses was held in no small admiration among the Egyptians." From this, we do not doubt that they received the concept of God—that is, the First Cause. Following them, Numenius the Pythagorean

<margin>Basil, Clement, Atticus, Eusebius, Aristobulus.</margin>

For example, the story of Deucalion <note>The Greek "Noah" who survived a great flood</note> was drawn from the history of the Flood, and the fiction of Phaethon <note>Who drove the sun chariot and scorched the earth</note> from the retrogradation of the sun which occurred in the time of Hezekiah <note>Referring to the miracle in 2 Kings 20:11</note>. <margin>Ovid.</margin>

**"The seventh light had arrived, and all things were finished."** <note>A reference to the completion of Creation on the seventh day in Genesis</note> Others who followed have come to the same conclusion: and before them Orpheus, so that he might extol the Author of the universe with the highest praises, took this from his work on the Divine Word: for (as **Artabanus** <note>A historian who wrote about the history of the Jews, often identifying Moses with the Greek figure Musaeus</note> testifies) **Orpheus** learned many things from the teaching of **Moses**. After them, **Virgil** learned how the winds were restrained under Aeolus from the ark of **Noah**, in which animals of every kind were ruled by the command of Noah himself. Many also sang of the happy state of Adam, and wrote in prose about the "Golden Age of Saturn" <note>original: *Saturnia regna aurea*; a Roman mythological concept of a primeval paradise that the author equates with Eden</note>. It would be a long task to retrace how many kinds of secrets, regarding both lower nature and the world above, they learned to wrap in the veils of fables and enigmas; these were hidden by those who, instructed by sacred oracles, concealed the sacraments entrusted to them, lest they "cast holy things before swine" to be trampled <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6; the author argues that Greek myths are actually "hidden" versions of Bible stories meant to protect sacred knowledge from the unworthy</note>. But because some do not believe that Peripatetic <note>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle</note> philosophy can stand alongside the Hebrews—indeed, they take this as an occasion for mockery—let them say where they found, or rather fabricated, the saying attributed by their own **Aristotle** to **Moses**: "This man said many good things, but proved nothing." On the contrary, let the Peripatetic **Clearchus** <note>A disciple of Aristotle</note>, cited in the book *On Sleep*, say how much the prince of the Peripatetics deferred to the Hebrews.
<margin>Artabanus.</margin>
<margin>Clearchus.</margin>
For he says that when **Aristotle** was debating with **Hyperochides**, he said: "He was a Jew, who, descending from the higher places of Asia to the maritime cities, was Greek in both language and soul." And when it happened that we also were staying in the maritime places of Asia at that time, he came to us of his own accord out of a love for philosophy: he brought much more to us than he received. So says **Clearchus**. To these places, the same **Aristotle** sailed at the persuasion of a letter from **Plato**, written in commendation of the Israelite sages in Egypt, as we find in the records of the Hebrews. **Megasthenes**, indeed, in the third book of *Jewish Affairs*, declares not only **Aristotle** but all philosophers to be disciples of Hebraic wisdom. He says, "Everything that the ancient Greeks wrote about nature, others also handed down before them: for the **Brahmans** among the Indians (who are also called Jews) philosophized much earlier."
<margin>Megasthenes.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Nor should anyone wonder that the Jews were Indians, since even **Aristotle** says in **Clearchus**: "The Jews are **Calani** from India." <note>An ancient attempt to link the Jewish people with Indian priestly castes like the 'Kallianoi'</note> But they were called "Jews" primarily from the tribe of their father; "Israelites" from their divine Prince and progenitor **Jacob** (**Iahacob**); and "Hebrews" from the "crossing over" <note>The word 'Hebrew' (*Ivri*) is traditionally associated with the root *avar*, meaning to cross or pass through</note> to which they were always devoted as pilgrims. **Numenius** <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note> supports this in the first volume of *On the Good*. **Plato**, he says, and **Pythagoras** set forth in Greek what the Brahmans, Egyptians, and Jews had arrived at.
<margin>Numenius.</margin>
<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
There are also those who assert that the mysteries of **Numenius**, **Philo**, **Plotinus**, **Iamblichus**, and **Proculus** <note>Proclus</note> were received from **Paul**, **Dionysius**, **Hierotheus**, and **John**. Indeed, it would be troublesome to cite everyone who asserts that the Jews and our fathers (from whom we also received the beginnings of wisdom) were the first teachers of wisdom, from whose fountains all mortals have drunk. For not only do our own people believe this, but the most distinguished historians and famous philosophers testify to it. To these let us also add the oracles of the Gentiles, if they do not believe the witnesses brought forward: for **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was often critical of Christianity but respected ancient traditions</note> records that the oracle of **Apollo** handed down these things concerning the Jews.

Xenocrates says there are eight gods: five who are named among the wandering stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>; one who is composed of the other stars as if from dispersed limbs; the seventh is the Sun, and the eighth is the Moon.

Theophrastus, with a certain inconsistency, at one time attributes divine sovereignty to the mind, at another to the sky, and then to the signs and celestial constellations.
<margin>Strato</margin>
Strato the philosopher judges that all divine power is situated in nature: which contains the causes of giving birth, increasing, and diminishing, but lacks all sense and form.
<margin>Zeno</margin>
Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> judges that natural law is God: and that it possesses the power of commanding what is right and forbidding the contrary. Elsewhere he says the ether is God; and in other places, a certain reason diffused through the nature of all things, ruling them.
<margin>Aristo</margin>
His disciple Aristo says the form of God cannot be understood, doubting entirely whether God is a living being or not.
<margin>Cleanthes</margin>
Cleanthes, also a listener of Zeno, now says the world is God, now the mind; and he judges that the "utmost and highest heat" surrounding everything on all sides, embracing and encompassing all (which is called ether), is the most certain God.
<margin>Persæus</margin>
Persæus, another listener of his, says that useful and health-giving things were simply called by the names of gods.
<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato says that which is <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "Asomaton"; Greek for "bodiless" or "without matter".</note>, what kind of thing it could be, cannot be understood.
<margin>Xenophon</margin>
Xenophon, coming to almost the same conclusion, reported Socrates disputing that the form of God should not be sought.
<margin>Antisthenes</margin>
Antisthenes says the popular gods are many, but the natural God is one.
<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato also, when arguing with Hermogenes, says: "By Jove, Hermogenes (if we had in our minds a proper measure of rectitude), we should be led to admit that we know nothing of the Gods—neither about themselves, nor about the names by which they call themselves; for it is certain that they name themselves by their true names." Nevertheless, Plato admits an opinion along with his fellow Academics <note>Followers of the Academy, Plato’s school in Athens.</note> regarding the progenitor of the universe. And these (as
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine says) are closer to our own sages; they did not disdain to be watered by their springs <note>Augustine famously argued that Plato’s philosophy was the most compatible with Christianity.</note>. Others follow, though with much longer strides.
<margin>Speusippus</margin>
Speusippus, following his uncle Plato, says a certain power is God, by which all things are ruled, and that it is animate. From the same school,
<margin>Heraclides</margin>
Heraclides of Pontus sprinkled his books with childish fables, at one time saying the world, at another the mind is God, and attributing divinity to the wandering stars.
<margin>Chrysippus</margin>
Chrysippus, who is considered the oldest interpreter of the Stoic dreams, gathers a great crowd of unknown gods: and attempts in his second book, where he treats the nature of the gods, to adapt the fables of Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer to those things which he had said before about the immortal gods. Following him,

<margin>Cotta</margin>
Cotta <note>Caius Aurelius Cotta, a character in Cicero’s "On the Nature of the Gods" who represents the Academic Skeptic viewpoint.</note> fantasizes much concerning Minerva and the birth of Jove, and the origin of the Virgin. Cicero’s Cotta seems to refute and mock everyone speaking about the gods; his little boat sails through so many waves that, as if submerged after leaving the sea for dry land and despairing of the harbor, he struggles like a shipwrecked man. He concludes by holding that the natures of the gods are obscure and their explanations difficult. I shall omit those even more absurd things poured out by the voices of the poets, which did harm through their very sweetness: for they introduced gods inflamed by anger and raging with lust. They made us see their battles and wounds; furthermore, their hatreds, dissensions, births, deaths, complaints, and unrestrained lamentations, along with lusts in every form of excess, adulteries, chains, intercourse with the human race, quarrels, hatreds, and many such insanities.

<margin>Hermes
Assyrians
Moabites
Palestinians</margin>
But many reached such a point of insanity that they fashioned with their own hands the gods they would worship, as Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> says of the Egyptians. So did the Assyrians, for whom the statue of Belus—constructed by his son Ninus (as some prefer)—provided the cause for idolatry. Imitating him, the Moabites, Palestinians, and many other peoples fashioned their own statues according to their whim; they erected altars for themselves and named them with terms from their own languages.

And even if we cannot understand what God is, we are nonetheless taught that God exists by oracles, by reason, and by the consensus of all.

### Chapter III.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
**D**E Regarding God, therefore, we think that the saying of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works combined Christian doctrine with Neoplatonism.</note> should be observed, where he says: It is only lawful to ascend to higher things as much as the ray of the divine speeches deigns to instill itself. We must gather our strength to drink in those divine flashes. Moreover, we ought to revere divine things harmlessly, soberly, piously, and chastely, lest, if we wish to proceed by natural investigation, we fall into various errors—just like those "wise men of the age" whom we mentioned above. 

<margin>Simonides
Aristotle
Cicero
Hiero</margin>
Or let that happen which befell Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC), a Greek lyric poet.</note>, whom Aristotle and Cicero celebrate enough. When he was asked by the tyrant Hiero <note>Hiero I, the ruler of Syracuse.</note> what God was, he requested the space of one day to answer. Returning the next day, when he was questioned, Simonides asked for two days. Then, as the tyrant asked more frequently, Simonides always doubled the number of days. When Hiero asked why he did this, he replied: "Because the longer I consider it, the more obscure the matter seems," for He dwells in light inaccessible to human wits.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Hence the heavenly doctor protests in the Gospel titled according to Matthew, saying: *No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him.* <note>original: "Nemo nouit filiū nisi pater: neqz patrē qs nouit, nisi fili⁹: & cui uoluerit filius reuelare." — Matthew 11:27</note> Therefore, concerning this <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>A translation of the Greek "hyperousios," meaning "beyond being" or "above all essence," a key term in Dionysian theology.</note> and most sacred deity (as the Areopagite continues), one must not presume to say or think anything otherwise than what the sacred speeches have handed down piously and chastely. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
From these most sacred sermons we have certain truths to which some of the philosophers come with "unfettered feet" <note>An idiom meaning they arrive easily or readily at these conclusions through reason.</note>. There are other things, however, which they cannot reach; these they either do not admit, or they flee from them, or they leave them untouched as if they were doubtful. Treating each of these individually, we will propose them in such a way that the pious may admit them with fair ears, while the impious, even if they do not admit them, at least cannot reject them. These latter people are placed in the first category of impiety by Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus.

# OF THE FIRST SONG.

<margin>David
Aristotle
Avicenna
Plato
Cicero
Epicurus
Pythagoras
Eusebius</margin>
...those who deny that God exists. Having dismissed rather than refuted these men (for those who are unworthy of refutation cannot be considered wise by the learned), we shall proceed. First of all (as the divine oracles pass down to us), let us presuppose that God exists. No philosopher disagrees with this, nor does any mortal, unless they happen to fall into that state of which the Prophet [David] most wisely sings: **The fool (he says) has said in his heart, there is no God.** And they are very rightly called "fools" who deny God himself, since all reason dictates, and every light granted to mortals teaches, that God exists. For all created things, whose nature it is to depend on another, teach that there is something from which they themselves originate—and that this "something" comes from nothing else, lest the process go on into infinity. Furthermore, those things which are moved lead to the conclusion that there is one Being by whom all things are moved, but who is himself moved by no other; as Aristotle rightly proceeds at the end of his book on *Physics* <note>original: "Physico auditu"</note>. And that Being is perfect, lacking nothing: which is God—whether you call him the Principle, or the Fountain and Origin of all things, or the Supreme, or the Infinite, or that "than which nothing greater can be conceived" <note>A reference to St. Anselm’s famous ontological argument for the existence of God.</note>, or the First Mover, or the First Cause, or that which exists of itself, or the Archetype <term>Archetype|The original model or "blueprint" in the mind of God from which all created things are patterned.</term> who contains all things—by whatever name one calls him, he is God. He who denies Him (as Avicenna <note>A famous Persian philosopher and physician of the 11th century.</note> bears witness) is no less in need of reason than a man lacking his senses is in need of them to deny that snow is white. For as Plato says in his *Laws*: **The Earth, the Sun, the Stars—and the universe itself—as well as the most ornate variety of the seasons, distinguished by years and months, show that God exists.** Furthermore, the consensus of all Greeks and Barbarians agrees on this point. As Marcus Tullius [Cicero] says in passing: **For what can be so obvious and so clear, when we have looked up at the sky and contemplated the heavenly bodies, than that there exists some divinity of most excellent intelligence by whom these things are ruled?** For what nation is there, or what race of men, which does not have, even without being taught, a certain "anticipation" of God, which the common people call *prolepsis*? <term>Prolepsis|A Greek philosophical term (primarily Epicurean) meaning a "preconception" or innate idea that is naturally present in the human mind before formal learning.</term> Indeed, we have accepted from that heavenly volume of Epicurus regarding the rule and judgment that there is a certain "pre-information" of the soul's reason which we understand here: in which the nature of all men agrees that God exists and that He rules the world itself. To these points he connects the famous deed of the Athenians, who burned the book of the philosopher Pythagoras <note>While the text says Pythagoras, this historical anecdote usually refers to the sophist Protagoras, whose books were burned in Athens because he expressed doubt about the existence of the gods.</note>—at the beginning of which he seemed to doubt whether God exists—after he himself had been expelled from the city and the territory. But Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note>, going further, says: We cannot doubt God, since it is implanted in all things by nature, or rather by divinity, that God is the true creator of all things.

## How we can arrive at a knowledge of His fecundity through the trace or image of created things and their harmony with the Archetype. Chapter IV.

<margin>Mercury</margin>
**S**o that we might be able to grasp that most divine fecundity—which is found as a shadow in all His handiwork—from these familiar things we have at hand, each thing must at least be sketched out. For there is nothing in the nature of things (as Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage associated with the "Hermetic" writings.</note> bears witness) which does not bear within itself some image of divinity. For all living things produce offspring according to their own kind; and by producing in the open that which they conceived in their inner parts, they bring forth the praises of the Supreme Craftsman with a certain voice of their own. The children purified in the Babylonian furnace <note>A reference to the biblical story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who sang a hymn of praise (the "Benedicite") while in the fiery furnace, calling on all creation to praise God.</note> and David, when he would conclude his hymns, invite all things to these songs of praise. For even trees and plants, when they put forth their shoots or buds, bear seed as if it were the fruit in their bodies.

<page-num>VI</page-num>
<header>FIRST TONE.</header>

When the fruits of the earth are returned, they praise God with their own voice as if through a certain birth. Hail and snow are condensed in the air, and rains are prepared in the clouds; it is then that their conception occurs. But when they descend to the earth, like a completed birthing <note>original: "fœtura," referring to the bearing of offspring or a brood</note>, they themselves bless their Maker. Animals produce a more excellent offspring: but when they are brought forth into the light, they too burst forth in praise of God. Even the sensitive power <note>The "sensitive power" refers to the faculty of the soul responsible for sensory perception and mental imagery.</note> conceives within itself an image and an intention of things to be made; afterward, by applying its members to the task, it gives birth to what it had conceived. This offspring of the **Phantasy** <term>Phantasy|The "Phantasia," or the faculty of the mind that forms and stores mental images from sensory input.</term> is closer to the soul than to the vegetative power (which nevertheless exists in the body); therefore, it more clearly demonstrates the offspring of the divine mind. Thus, the rational soul, when it receives power from the phantasy—by which it measures all things with the necessary prudence—first produces a model of them in the mind as if it were an offspring in that same mind. Then it gives birth to this model externally, where that which was thought out in the mind is brought into its own proper figure or form. 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
This "thinking-out" <note>original: "excogitatio"</note>, as if it were a working life, expresses (according to Augustine) the creative divine life in which all things pre-existed before they were unfolded into their own proper forms. Furthermore, the work demonstrates the craftsmanship of the maker; when conducted in a harmonious order, it sings in praise of the maker himself, whom it resembles in the act of working. There is another offspring of the rational life similar to this: namely, reason and discourse, which, formed in the mind from that thing 

<margin>The same [Augustine]</margin>
which we know, is called a "Word" by the same Augustine. Both of these offspring are closer to the soul than the conceptions of the phantasy or the vegetative power, because the rational force is reflected back upon its own understanding, and through that, upon itself. Following these is a holy and free love—something which the Phantasy cannot produce. It gives birth to this progeny in the open when it manifests what it had conceived through a sounding word. But since the state of Angels is more perfect than that of those who still struggle in the stadium <note>A metaphor for human life as a race or athletic struggle on earth.</note>, they give birth to a more excellent conception, unchanged by any interval of time; in giving birth to this, they persevere continually in the praises of God through a certain proclamation. From all these things, we contemplate—in their various degrees—the Maker whose image they hold: both the conception of the Word and of creatures in the "Ideal Life" <note>The "Ideal Life" refers to the Platonic/Augustinian concept of the world of Ideas or archetypes existing within the mind of God.</note>. Moreover, He reveals the "Essential Word" when He manifests it in the Sacred Page [Scripture], and the "Ideal Word" when He causes those things which He had crafted in His mind to shine forth in His work. 

<margin>Moses David</margin>
This is a way of "speaking" and manifesting what has been conceived. Hence Moses and David—one of whom wrote the secrets of God, while the other sang them—both declared all things to have been produced by the Word.

Indeed, He is the true Sun—not this celestial one, but a supramundane and divine one. # OF THE FIRST SONG

-> symbolic imagery <-

In their symbolic depictions, they first placed horns on his head, denoting the kingdom which he holds in both the upper and lower worlds. For Jerome, in his long commentary on the Prayer of Habakkuk <note>original: "orōnē Abacuc"</note>, proves that a "horn" is accepted as a symbol for a kingdom even among those who wrote our sacred scriptures.
<margin>Jerome</margin>
Furthermore, his long beard represented the rays of light, or his divine power, extending down to the lowest depths. The lower part of his body was shaggy because of the trees, shrubs, mountains, rocks, and wild beasts; but the upper part was smooth. Hence, he is said to ride "upon the clouds" <note>original: "sup harauot," likely referring to the Hebrew 'aravot' (heavens/clouds)</note>, which our translation renders as "the setting sun" <note>original: "occasum"</note>. His pipe of seven reeds sounds the harmony of the seven planets, in which there are sevenfold sounds that complete the *diapason* <term>diapason: the full octave or perfect consonance</term>, the finished consonance. The rod in his hands is the power by which he moderates all things. They depicted him laughing, discovering in this his everlasting happiness. They asserted that he delights in the "Echo," which is the voice sent forth in hollow places, or resonating against any arranged obstacles. For the voice expresses the Word and the concept of the mind. Therefore, by His voice or command, God fashioned the world and all its members, and He governs them by imparting His voice. He also manifests His love toward us through many cries; and He delights in reciprocal love (which is the resonating Echo). And these are the delights which He has with the sons of men. He wore the *nebris* <term>nebris: a fawn-skin garment associated with Pan or Bacchus</term> of stars upon his breast, because he contains the gathering and force of all stars within a single skin, and by a single act or nod.
<margin>The Poet-Philosophers</margin>
But him whom the Poets called **Pan** (that is, the "All," containing all things), the Philosophers called the **First Cause** and the Principle of all causes, granting to all causes their ability to flow. For whatever a secondary cause does, it acts by the power of the First Cause, which flows into it more than the secondary one does, as Proclus says.
<margin>Proclus</margin>
And even if a secondary and universal cause should move away from a thing which it provided, the First Cause never leaves it. And he says below: all things have their essence from the One who is present, the First Cause; and they have life from the First Life; and they are immediate from the First and Supreme Intelligence. It is necessary that this Intelligence be the fertile source of all those things which others provide. And He is in Himself supremely happy and blessed. But Blessedness (as Speusippus defines it) is the Good accumulated from all goods.
<margin>What is Blessedness? Who is Blessed?</margin>
<margin>Speusippus, Augustine, Boethius, Plato, Hermes</margin>
Moreover, he is Blessed who lacks nothing and who has whatever he wants—if Augustine, Boethius, and Plato teach correctly. Therefore, nothing is lacking to Him who contains all things, like a true sphere of all things, as Hermes said. And since nothing exists outside the sphere of the world, so nothing is outside the divine circuit which embraces all things. To Him belongs that unexplainable Name <note>The Tetragrammaton (YHVH)</note>, where all the letters contain circular numbers: namely ten, five, and six <note>referring to the numerical values of the Hebrew letters: Yod=10, He=5, Vav=6</note>, each testifying that He is the most ancient Sphere, which they name as containing all things in its circuit. The meanings of these letters also indicate the same thing: for *Ioth* <note>Yod</note> is interpreted as "knowledge" or "principle"; *He* as "being"; and *Vau* as "that in which all things rest." Thus He is the Principle of all essences, granting to all things that they may be and exist. "Being" <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note> is the first of created things, as Proclus teaches. Therefore, it emanates from the First Cause, to whom alone the granting of "being" is attributed.
<margin>Proclus</margin>
Thus elsewhere he concludes with an open mouth that all things proceed from one Cause. It is necessary that this Cause be "pregnant" with all things; if the opinion of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle</term> is true: "No one gives what he does not have."
<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
Nor is anything produced by nature or fashioned by art unless it previously existed in the maker. An animal or a man is generated from a seminal power in which the offspring was contained; and a plant is generated from a seed, which is hoped for in the seed by potential (as the Peripatetics say) or by some virtue. <page-num>VII</page-num>

<margin>Moses</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
The most wise philosopher Moses, when dealing with the production of plants, said: "Whose seed—namely, of the plant—is in itself," <note>original: "Cuius, vʒ plantæ semẽ fit in ea"</note> that is, the seminal power for producing another plant. There also exists in the mind of the Craftsman <note>Referring to God as the Divine Architect or Demiurge</note> an ideal framework, from which He leads forth outward things: as Augustine discusses at great length when interpreting that passage of John, "That which was made, in him was life," <note>original: "qđ factum est, in ipso uita erat." This is a famous Neo-Platonic reading of John 1:3-4.</note> certainly a creative life, and the "idea" of all things to be made. For just as a craft lives in the mind of the craftsman before it is brought forth, so the world lived in that divine mind before it was led down into work. It contains, moreover, every number, existing itself as the True Unity: which is the principle and root of all numbers, granting to all things <margin>From number</margin> that they may be numbered. <margin>Proclus</margin> For every multitude (as the same Proclus says in his *Theological Elements*) <note>term: "theorematibus theologicis" - likely referring to Proclus's *Elements of Theology*, a foundational work of Neoplatonism</note> is from the One. Nor would anything be "one" while forming a multitude with others (as he follows up there) unless it obtained unity for itself through participation in the One. That this "One" and most ancient being is God, no one doubts; who, before communicating a particular unity to lower things, poured Himself into the first number: <margin>Hebrews</margin> And from here into the ten <note>term: "denarius" - the number ten, considered by Pythagoreans and Kabbalists as the number of perfection and universal completion</note> (if we admit the theology of the Hebrews) as if into ten "ideas," <margin>Aristotle</margin> and measures of all numbers and all things to be made. For this reason, a further number cannot be given, although Aristotle attempts to assign various other reasons. This "ten," when gathered into one, returns to that from which it took its beginning: so that the ten is the end and fulfillment of numbers, and the beginning of the decades. <margin>Proclus</margin> All things, by imitating this series of numbers as a true model, strive to return to that One from which they proceeded. As our Proclus adds a little further on, saying: that every order, beginning from unity, proceeds into a multitude co-essential with unity; and the multitude of the order itself is finally reduced back to unity. And all things that are beneath the lunar sphere <note>The "sublunary" world, or Earth, which in ancient cosmology was the realm of change and decay</note> return through Man (as if through their tenth genus) among those things subject to corruption; and the nine heavens through the tenth heaven (which they call the Empyrean); and the nine orders of Angels are restored through their own "ten" into the primary unity—matters which we shall discuss more extensively in their proper place.

### That God is One. Chapter VI.

<margin>Moses</margin>
**T**hat God is one, we have the lawgiver thundering by divine oracle:
> Hear, O Israel—you, namely, who have God as your prince (for so "Israel" is interpreted) <note>A traditional medieval etymology: *Ish* (man), *Ra'ah* (sees), *El* (God), or "Prince with God"</note>—the Lord your God is one God.

And again, he introduces God Himself protesting to the people: "See that I am alone, and there is no other besides me." <margin>David</margin> <margin>The leader of the choir ~ the arranger. Singer of power.</margin> With whom the singer of his law <note>Referring to King David as the author of the Psalms</note> agrees, saying: "There is no God besides the Lord, and there is no God besides our God." With which truth all wise men agree. Abraham, on account of his confession of one God, was cast into the "Ur" (that is, the furnace) <note>A common Jewish and Christian tradition that Abraham was cast into a fire by the Chaldeans for refusing to worship idols</note> by the Chaldeans and escaped unharmed; for which reason God followed him with the highest favor, for whose glory alone Abraham did not refuse to undergo death. <margin>Socrates: he suffered many things and death for the true God.</margin> For asserting this truth, Socrates endured both prisons and death, <margin>Apuleius</margin> <margin>Aulus Gellius</margin> as Apuleius and Aulus Gellius <note>Roman authors who wrote about the life and "daemon" of Socrates</note> attest. However, no grace was gained for him by this, because he brought death upon himself by willingly taking poison, contrary to the edict of that God whom he professed as the only one: who forbids anyone to bring death upon himself or others.

This is how <margin>☩ Jerome</margin> <margin>Jerome</margin> Jerome proceeds when discussing with his friend Rusticus: "Among bees," he says, "there is one leader; cranes all follow one in a letter-like formation; there is one Emperor, one judge of a province; in a ship, one pilot; and in the fabric of the world, one Creator, one Moderator." They add also concerning the power by which He can do all things: hence, if there were two, one could destroy what the other <margin>One omnipotent God</margin> built; and if he could not, he would not be God, who is omnipotent. And proceeding further, they reason that since both would be supremely "enjoyable," <note>In scholastic theology, "fructus" (fruit/enjoyment) refers to the final end or happiness found in God.</note> if they enjoyed each other, the one refusing to enjoy the other would sin; but the one enjoying the other would receive something from that other, as if he were imperfect. And thus the most perfect God would be imperfect—and so on. If there were two, which of them built this great machine of the world? And which of them governs it? And if the one who made it also rules it, what does the other do? If indeed one made it and the other governs it, how did the governor enter into <margin>Dionysius, Plato, Philosophers, Astronomers</margin> a house that was not his own? Therefore, from the order and governance of the world, let us conclude with Dionysius, <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> with Plato, and with all true philosophers and astronomers, that the Craftsman and Ruler of such great things, which agree so well with one another, is one and the same: who is the artisan of all things, possessing all power, and overseeing all. <margin>note.</margin>

### That first most fecund mind, which is called God, produced both inwardly and outwardly. Chapter VII.

<margin>John, Mercurius, Plato, Orpheus</margin>

Hence this is the most exact image of the parent, yet distinguished from the generator by a certain relation, or by some absolute intrinsic quality, as a thing begotten.
