...fruitful, and grants fecundity to His own works without offspring; as <margin>Isaiah</margin> through Isaiah He complains with a certain impatience regarding the unbelieving, saying: "Shall I, who grant generation to others, be myself sterile?" <note>A paraphrase of Isaiah 66:9: "Shall I who cause to bring forth, not give birth? says the Lord."</note>

There is indeed a seed and a fecundity in the Supreme Architect. Because even if He exists (says <margin>Richard</margin> Richard <note>Likely Richard of Saint Victor (d. 1173), a mystical theologian known for his works on the Trinity and contemplation.</note>) as most delightfully happy, nevertheless, out of His innate goodness, that most happy Mind wished to openly produce His offspring by constructing a world-fabric full of His own image. In this world, diffusing Himself in an ordered series of degrees, He made some beings capable of His propagation and happiness. Some of these He decreed should become partakers of His happiness through a momentary submission <note>A reference to the angels, whose "trial" was instantaneous.</note>, while others through a more prolonged struggle, assigning to each their due dwellings. 

But because those [angels] were soon after to oppose the King and Creator, He did not assign to them the lodgings of pilgrimage, or any other field for their instantaneous battle than the palace of triumph. To mortals, however (against whom He had declared a long war with diverse enemies), He gave broad spaces for the contest and suitable lodgings. And because they were joined with a changeable and deficient nature, He took care to provide the food and nourishment with which they might draw out the course of life to its due end. 

All of these things, to be prepared at the opportune time, He committed to the elements and the heavens as to most obedient servants, commanding that for the pleasure of the guest himself [mankind], the fields be spread out, the valleys sink down, the woods be covered with foliage, and the stony mountains rise—and other things of that kind, which we see ordained more for beauty and ornament than for necessity. He did this so that from these delights, which the guest might feel in these lodgings of service, he might ascend to contemplate those most exquisite banquets prepared in the triumphal hall. 

For He knew the unhappiness of this bodily prison, in which those most absolute goods—free from all degenerate matter—cannot be conceived except through sensible things, unless they are revealed by a particular light. Therefore, with the highest skill, He arranged harmonic images of those heavenly things, so that through these, once the veil of ignorance or sin was drawn away, we might easily be drawn toward those heavenly realms. Thus, from the beauty of the works and the elegance of the creatures (as <margin>Origen</margin> Origen writes in *On First Principles* <note>original: "Periarchon"</note>), we might understand the Parent of the universe. 

This is especially so since the proper principle of the image is found in man, who alone among mortals (as the <margin>Platonists</margin> Platonists say) possesses the likeness <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> of the divine mind. However, the animal holds the likeness of man; the <term>zoophyte</term> <note>A "plant-animal," a term used in historical natural history for organisms like coral or sea anemones that seemed to bridge the gap between plant and animal life.</note> that of the animal; the plant that of the zoophyte; the metals that of the plant; and stones that of the metals. 

And because things lower than man contain an imperfect image of God, the <margin>Catholics</margin> Catholic Sages say that all those things hold a "trace" <note>original: "vestigium"</note> of God, through which they represent His God-like form more imperfectly—each one more or less according to the perfection distributed to them. For the forms of the elements and mixed bodies are the most subtle likenesses of the highest good. But living things, the heavens, and the stars—especially the Sun—lead us toward the contemplation of more secret things. 

Rational minds, however, as the supreme level of images, entering into the innermost sanctuaries, arrive at that degree of contemplation by which they may eventually enter the prepared bridal chamber; indeed, they may establish themselves as the dwelling and temple of God, where a true banquet is celebrated with all musical harmonies.

### Chapter 8. That God Crafted the World.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**A**mong those things that lie hidden from human wits and transcend natural discourse is the birth of the world: whether it is, whether it was made anew, and whether it was by necessity or by a certain free abundance of the divine mind. Hence, the wise are divided into various factions. Aristotle, along with that crowd who admit nothing except what they can investigate by their own powers and wit, being unable to understand whence and why this birth occurred, scorns it. As an ungrateful disciple, he falsely accuses Plato <margin>Plato</margin> of being the only one who "generates" <note>In this context, to "generate" the world means to argue that it had a beginning in time or was created by a deity, rather than being eternal.</note> the world. But Plato himself, along with other wise men illuminated by a better light, professes the craftsmanship of the world; and he describes it as most harmonious and arranged with the fullest numbers <note>A reference to the Pythagorean and Platonic idea that the universe is built on mathematical proportions and musical intervals.</note>. Under the veil of these numbers and the obscure signs of the receding senses, he hid the mysteries of the world from those not yet well initiated, thinking it better to learnedly weave anew <note>original: "retexere"</note> what was received through divine oracles than to labor in vain with his own wit to grasp those things that escape the reach of rational discourse and are received only by a mind that is pure, joyful, and in festive harmony. <margin>Mercury</margin> Hence Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" writings, which the author treats as ancient wisdom compatible with Christianity.</note>, having embraced the Mind and entering into these inner shrines, hints in a few words in his *Pymander* <note>The *Poimandres*, the first and most famous book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*.</note> at the fabric of the world, its governors, the Composer of all things, and how the pure artifice of nature arose from the elements that tend downward, yet remain united to the mind of the Maker. He teaches that these "pre-thrown" elements exist in a lower state only by the will of God, for they pre-existed [perfectly] in the Maker. <margin>Empedocles Heraclitus</margin> Empedocles of Agrigento and Heraclitus of Ephesus assert that the world is not generated once, but is continually being born and decaying. This view, regarding parts of the world or a certain renewal hidden from those who are not illuminated, could be admitted into the bosom of truth. <margin>Democritus</margin> Democritus, however, teaches that the world was born once and will perish once, and will never again be restored. <margin>Hesiod</margin> Hesiod also, and <margin>Orpheus</margin> Orpheus, sing of the world being brought forth. <margin>Thales</margin> Thales, one of the seven sages, asserts that this orb is the handiwork of God. <margin>Pythagoras Hierocles</margin> Pythagoras and his interpreter Hierocles <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a commentary on the Golden Verses of Pythagoras.</note> profess God as the Maker and Father of things. <margin>Avicenna Algazel</margin> Avicenna the Arab, Algazel the Saracen, and Philo (no less famous for his learning than for his Greek eloquence) all agree. <margin>Philo Alcinous Plato</margin> So does Alcinous the Platonist, who says: "It is necessary that this whole universal world be the most beautiful handiwork of God." Many later thinkers follow, whom it would be tedious to list. Therefore, it is not Plato alone who "generates" the world, but he testifies to its birth alongside many others. Leaving aside these external thinkers, let us come to those who teach not what they imagine, but <margin>Moses</margin> what they have seen and received from divine oracles. For Moses, the father of theologians and the chief master of those who philosophize, says: "In the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth," and the rest that follows. One must believe this God—who is most full and quickened by holy divinity, and who proves what He said in many places—more than Aristotle, who confirms his own such trifles neither by reasons, nor by miracles, nor by oracles. The points by which Moses corroborates what he teaches are: miracles, portents, oracles, prophecies, the consensus of every part of his whole doctrine, and the grave authority of those who [upheld] his doctrine...

The Supreme Teacher—who was teaching both Moses and us through these events—provided these and many other such wonders to favor his doctrine. Even in his words, he calmed monsters, disasters ceased, and the poisoned were healed, so that by these sorts of wonders, the law, the wisdom of life, and the discipline he taught the people might be celebrated. And here I see His mighty hand: but to see Him as He truly is,
I am in no way able, for He sits upon the high clouds.
No one has seen Him, except for one born of Chaldean blood <note>original: "Caldeo de sanguine"; referring to Moses, though some ancients debated if it meant Abraham or Zoroaster</note>
Who was brought forth: whom the golden seat of the heavens
And the high place holds: whose right hand extends

The shaken mountains tremble: nor can they bear
His immense weight: He who dwells in the high
Summits of heaven: yet is never absent from the earth.
He is the beginning, the middle, and likewise the end.
The voices of the ancients have taught us all these things:
Which God once handed down to them on two tables.

<margin>Orpheus</margin>
Behold how Orpheus confesses with a clear voice that he learned from the Mosaic tables those things which he sings concerning the God known only to Moses, who was born of Chaldean blood. For some people imagine that Orpheus sang of Noah; others of Enoch; the Platonists of Zoroaster, who was the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, <margin>Didymus</margin> as Didymus himself attests—or even Ham the son of Noah, if Berosus <note>An ancient Babylonian writer and astronomer</note> is to be believed. But the tables were not given to those men, but to Moses, of whom alone it is read that he spoke face-to-face with God. Many, having been taught by his doctrine and emulating him, devoted themselves to a holy life: such as the prophets and those who, with enlightened eyes, strove to look up at wisdom. <margin>Solinus</margin> Regarding these men, Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer</note> says: "The interior parts of Judea, which look toward the West, are occupied by my Essenes <term>Essei: the Essenes, a Jewish sect known for their asceticism and communal living</term>, who are gifted with a remarkable discipline. They are separated from the rituals of all other nations, destined for this way of life by the providence of the Divine Majesty (as I believe). No women are there; they have utterly renounced sexual desire; they know nothing of money; they live on the fruit of palms. No one is born there, yet the number of men does not decrease. The place itself is devoted to modesty. Although many people hasten there from every nation, no one is admitted unless they are accompanied by a record of chastity and the merit of innocence. For he who is guilty of even a slight fault, even if he wishes to gain entry with the greatest effort, is kept away by divine power." For Solinus speaks here of the disciples of Moses, the sons of the prophets, and the prophets themselves. <margin>Paul the Apostle</margin> Regarding these men, our Paul also speaks when debating with the Hebrews, saying: "They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, being in want, distressed, afflicted: of whom the world was not worthy: wandering in solitudes, in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth." These were found worthy of that testimony, which is rightly judged to be believed. But what occurs as even more wonderful beyond measure is the consistent doctrine of Jesus, the heavenly and divine messenger, the true Messiah <note>original: "messiae"</note>, anointed with divine spiritual gifts <term>charismatibus: spiritual graces or gifts</term> above all his companions. He, approving and accepting the dogma of Moses, unlocked many secrets held by the Father for his disciples, which he proposed to the common people under parables, lest what is holy be given to dogs <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6</note>. <margin>Moses</margin> These disciples have so filled the entire world that...

<margin>Lactantius Firmianus</margin>
How many who call themselves wise men everywhere claim this name for themselves, yet they should embrace and venerate that doctrine in which there is such a splendor of divinity and divine light that it easily transcends all human inventions. Since nothing more sublime has yet appeared to mortals, nor ever will appear, let us all who care for wisdom look up to this doctrine. Nor should we wait (to speak with Firmianus <note>Lactantius Firmianus (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent defense of theology using classical rhetoric.</note>) until Socrates knows something, or Anaxagoras sees light in the darkness, or Democritus draws virtue out of a pit, or Empedocles widens the path of his own soul, or Arcesilaus and Carneades feel and perceive something—or even until Aristotle proves those things which escape the senses. For the <term>begetting of the world</term><note>original: "Mundi genitura"; referring to the act of creation.</note> is not to be numbered among the speculations of physics, for there we have God as the craftsman, who remains stable while fashioning or providing motion.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
But "whatever is not moved while moving others" (says your Aristotle) "transcends philosophical consideration and belongs to divine science."

<margin>Plato</margin>
"Which is to be obtained through prayers and oracles," says Plato; "natural things are to be sought by reason, and moral things are to be acquired by practice."

<margin>Solomon</margin>
And Solomon, the wisest of all, said: "I have found that the more one investigates these things, the less he will find; because man can find no explanation for the works of God." Therefore, philosophers have lost both their labor and their industry in such an endeavor, because the truth and the secret of the Most High God who made all things (Firmianus continues) cannot be comprehended by human wit or strength. Otherwise, there would be no difference between God and men if human thought could attain the counsels and arrangements of the Eternal Majesty.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Hence Aristotle himself celebrates the opinion of <margin>Simonides the poet</margin> Simonides in this regard, when he says: "God alone has this honor, to be a <term>metaphysician</term><note>In this context, one who understands things beyond the physical world.</note>." For the way of truth (as he confesses elsewhere) is closed even to the wise; and therefore, it must be awaited from the fountain of truth.

But (alas, it is too much to be lamented) it often happens as <margin>Iamblichus</margin> Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245 – c. 325) who focused on theurgy and divine rituals.</note> says: that the knowledge of things given by God is confounded over a long time by human opinions, retaining only a tiny bit of divinity and truth. This happens when one does not assent to those things which glide into the human senses; as that truth receded, darkness grew from beneath. Enveloped and blinded by this, those who trusted themselves too much became leaders of the blind; falling into the pit, they led many with them by false arguments and apparent reasons. I shall touch upon a few points concerning many of these men, so that others may recognize the path they are proceeding on.

### The nature of the world does not allow philosophers to draw conclusions against its creation. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**T**he <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for the "covered walkways" (peripatoi) of the Lyceum where they walked while teaching.</note>, who are numerous in these times, do not depart from their own senses. They believe that nothing can be established or known unless they prove it by reasoning from things perceived by the senses, using the same "demonstration" that Aristotle described—though he never actually followed it in his study of nature, since all his deductions proceed from principles he accepted beforehand. But leaving the others aside, let us come to those strongest arguments they put forward against the creation of the world...

<margin>Origen</margin>
But what can they bring against the truth itself (to speak with Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–c. 253), a prolific early Christian scholar and theologian whose works blended Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>) that cannot be proved foolish, weak, and false, since they propose certain ravings that are neither supported by reason nor worthy of even a prudent man? These we are certainly going to overthrow as easily (with God’s help) as they lightly objected to them. And to omit more frivolous things (since everything they bring forward is slippery), we will first bring forth the reasons they derive from the nature of the world itself against the <term>making of the world</term> <note>original: "mundi fabricam"; referring to the structural creation of the universe.</note>. They observed that the heavens were entirely removed from <term>contraries</term> <note>In ancient physics, "contraries" (like hot and cold) were the source of change and decay. Since the heavens seemed unchanging, philosophers argued they contained no contraries.</note>; from this, they concluded they were in no way <term>perishable</term> <note>original: "corrumpendum"</note>, and consequently, not <term>begotten</term> <note>original: "genitum"; created or born.</note>. They saw, moreover, that things which are generated acquire a new place for themselves; but because the heavens could not claim a new place for themselves, they argued they could not have been generated. They further observed that everything that moves migrates to a new place, or moves around something stable, just as all the spheres move around a center, so that every <term>irregularity</term> <note>original: "difformitas"</note> might be reduced to something uniform. In a similar way, they thought everything new is reduced to something old; thus, all <term>generation and corruption</term> <note>original: "generatio & corruptio"; the Aristotelian cycle of coming into being and passing away.</note> happens concerning ancient matter. And they argued all motion is regulated by the stable earth or an immobile center—foundations with which they did not see how the <term>novelty of the world</term> <note>original: "mundi nouitatem"; the concept that the world had a beginning in time.</note> could stand. And because the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, and nothing could precede the world that might be corrupted, they therefore asserted it was unbegotten. Proceeding further, they thought that every produced thing previously existed as a <term>potentiality in matter</term>, so much so that they thought it necessary that matter had always existed. They also bring forward their chief strength, admitted by everyone: that **nothing is made from nothing** <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fieri"; the foundational Greek philosophical axiom that existence cannot come from non-existence.</note>. Therefore, they inferred that the world, which nothing preceded, could not possibly have been made.

Whether all these arguments are conclusive or not, we will easily demonstrate by presupposing (as is the truth) three kinds of operations and three workers. For there is the **artisan**, who presupposes nature—namely, matter, form, and the whole composite. There is the **natural agent**, who requires the effect of God—namely, a subject or matter. And there is the **supreme builder, God**, needing nothing external, since He is perfect and contains every kind of power. These builders agree by a certain <term>analogy</term>, but they differ in <term>kind</term> <note>original: "equiuoco differunt"; they are distinct in their fundamental nature despite surface similarities.</note>. Nor is the power of one concluded from the mere way of operating of another. For it would be an error to proceed from art to nature; as if someone were to say: "Art requires a composite thing—the goldsmith requires gold, the blacksmith requires metal, the carpenter wood, and the architect stones and cement; therefore, the natural agent also requires a pre-existing composite." Thus do the "philosophers" err when they imagine that the Supreme Builder requires a subject or matter in His work, which is what a natural agent requires. Nor, because a natural agent works from one contrary to another, does it follow that the Supreme Builder proceeds in the same way. From where, I ask, did those men learn these inferences—those who taught that art is distinguished from nature, and that natural things belong to one kind of teaching, and eternal things, separated from motion, to another? For the artisan introduces an **artificial form** and presupposes a natural one. But the natural agent introduces a **form**...

...[is] substantial, and it presupposes matter, which is the effect of God. And if God, in his operating, required anything to exist beforehand, he would also seek out a prior God who had produced that thing: and thus there would be something prior to the first. What, then, are these monsters of arguments? They also use false logic [paralogize] when, because of the possession of a new place which a newly begotten thing acquires, they wish to exclude the world from being begotten, because it has acquired no place. But even if we grant that it prepared a place for itself, I would say it acquired that same place in which it now exists. For it is around the center either of the earth, or of the world, or of that intellectual sphere whose center <margin>Hermes</margin> (as Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed. The quote "God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere" was a favorite of Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note> says) is everywhere.

As for their stinging point that every new thing must be traced back to something ancient, we grant this to them. And that ancient thing is the **Divine Mind**, in which all things are contained before they are unfolded into their own forms: and once unfolded, it moderates and preserves them. As for what they add, that every natural transformation occurs from matter into matter, we admit it; but in the primeval production, and [one] absolute from all laws of nature—by which the Sovereign is not bound by right—this is not required.

Moreover, we grant that every product first pre-exists in a certain power: but natural things in matter, while the world itself and the species of things pre-exist in the **Ideas** or in those **Exemplars** <margin>Plato. John.</margin> in which the Platonists, together with our John <note>Saint John the Apostle. The author is linking the Platonic "Ideas" with the "Logos" or Word from the Gospel of John.</note>, transcend far above the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who generally argued for the eternity of the world and rejected Plato's Theory of Forms (Ideas).</note> and agree; for John says: *That which was made was life in him* <note>original: "Quod factum est in ipso uita erat"; a Latin rendering of John 1:3-4.</note>, where it had its being in power. Nor are the Ideas of Plato "monsters" to Aristotle; rather, his are the eyes of a bat (as you say) if he does not see those things which are most manifest in nature, or in the author of nature.

And so that we may untie the strongest knot of the naturalists—that <term>from nothing, nothing comes</term> <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fit"; the fundamental principle of ancient physics which argued that matter cannot be created or destroyed.</note>—I would wish them to be asked to explain this sentiment of theirs, since it is ambiguous. For if its meaning is that from nothing, through art or nature, nothing is made (which require a subject in which they work), we offer free hands [we agree]. But what is that to the Supreme Artisan, whom nature emulates with long strides, just as art emulates nature itself, as <margin>Aristo. Averrois.</margin> Aristotle agrees with his Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was a Spanish-Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational for Western Scholasticism.</note>? And just as in being, so too in work does a determined natural agent fall short—being subject to motion, time, and succession—compared to Him who is absolute from all laws of nature. 

But if they understand "from nothing" to mean that nothing is made *after* "not being," they have left this to be proved by posterity: whence a wide field is left to us for denying what is neither proved nor self-evident. But if they wish that "nothing" to exclude every kind of cause, we grant this too: But in the begetting of the world, we presuppose an operative and supreme cause; which contains within its own unending power the matter, the subject, the forms to be given, the instruments, the disposing qualities, and all things that are required to bring forth any work.

Nor does motion provide the same.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
...[if he] presided over the creation, they concluded that she <note>Likely referring to Nature or the "First Cause" in the context of the preceding sentence</note> was not there at all. Nor is it surprising if they erred, since they refused to depart from things perceived by the senses. From these (says Augustine), sincere truth is not to be expected. Nor from the senses themselves, or from arguments based upon them, can we (as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose works were often used by Renaissance theologians to reconcile Plato with Christian doctrine.</note> witnesses) arrive at the knowledge of divine things; for these are intellectual, removed from matter, motion, succession, and from all the senses. Thus, they strayed from those muddy and inferior generations toward the divine workmanship—which transcends every way of nature—by arguing.

They attach some frivolous and inept point, namely that straight motion cannot be made perpetual because it would have to traverse an infinite space, which nature cannot endure. But circular motion, because it does not traverse anything infinite, can be perpetual. Yet in eternal things (as they say), the deduction from "being possible" to "actually being" is valid. From this, they thought they could prove the eternity of the world. O, what a beautiful deduction, to presuppose the very eternity they pretend to prove!

<margin>Averroes</margin>
The blasphemous Arab <note>This refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university life, but whose views on the eternity of the world were often denounced as "blasphemous" by Christian writers.</note> adds that it would be impossible for the world to have any other disposition than it has now. Faithless dog! Who revealed this to you? By what measure have you measured the power of the Craftsman? By what authority do you presume to limit the power of the Infinite, as if He could not both destroy and build according to His will? This blasphemous beast should be hissed off the stage when he presumes to speak of divine things, rather than being listened to or deemed worthy of a satisfactory answer.

<margin>Albert the Great</margin>
Nevertheless, Albert, surnamed "the Great"—who was filled with a deeper philosophy than Averroes—responds to him. We shall say (he says) that the motion of the heavens is terminated at another state of the world, and at rest itself, toward which (as Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> teaches) all motion tends. Thus, the reasoning of Averroes falls, and his fiction is dissolved by its own weight.

But because motion gives birth to time, and time itself is the measure of motion and rest, they also use false logic regarding time. If the world (they say) did not exist before it took its beginning, since that "before" is a portion of time, then time preceded motion, which is its own cause and progenitor. They also add: at any given instant, that instant is the beginning of the future and the end of the past; therefore, time existed before that first instant, and consequently, so did motion and the world. 

All this error proceeds from a poor understanding of words, while they restrict that word **"before"** to signify only some part of time. For among our own people, and even among those outsiders most skilled in the art of speaking, we see that the word "before" signifies something other than a part of time. For sometimes it signifies **eternity**, as in the <margin>Proverbs</margin> Proverbs: *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything.* <note>original Latin: "Dominus possedit me in initio uiarum suarum, anteq̄ qcq̄ faceret." Quotes Proverbs 8:22.</note> And in <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Ecclesiasticus: *From the beginning, and before the ages, I was created.* <note>original Latin: "Ab initio, & ante sæcula creata sum." Quotes Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 24:9.</note>

<margin>Ovid</margin>
The man from Sulmo <note>Referring to the Roman poet Ovid, born in Sulmo, quoting the beginning of the "Metamorphoses."</note> also says: *Before the sea, and the lands, and the sky which covers all.* Nor was that most sagacious man ignorant that time flows from the circuit of the heavens; nevertheless, he says "before the sky," which covers all things. It also signifies the **prior part of a place**, from which we get the words for "those who walk before" <note>original Latin: "anteambulones"</note> and "to stand before." It also signifies a **higher rank**, from which we get the word "Overseer" <note>original Latin: "Antistes," usually referring to a bishop or high priest.</note> who is superior to others. And since that word [before] has so many meanings...

"Before": why do they want to restrict it to signifying only a part of time? Would they not also concede that matter is "before" form in a certain order, even if it did not precede it in time? Thus God was "before" the world in eternity, and in a certain order. 

<margin>Algazel</margin> 
Regarding what they add—that an "instant" is the end of the past and the beginning of the future—Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian who famously critiqued the Greek philosophical tradition in his work *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*.</note> solves this by saying: Just as a point is in continuous things (like a line), so is an instant in successive things (like time). For a point is sometimes the end of one part of a line and the beginning of another part; but sometimes it is the beginning of the whole line, and not the end of any preceding part. Thus that instant in which the world had its 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
beginning was the start of the time that followed, and not the end of a past time. The Arab <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> denies this comparison because time passes, while a line remains. O, what a ridiculous solution! Since the comparison is not about passing or remaining (in which they differ), but about the indivisible part (in which they agree). For all things which agree in one respect differ in another, as is trivial even to beginners in their doctrines. 

They add I know not what apparent truth: "That which flows," they say, "has something before it and after it." But (to bring forth something from the storehouses of nature and of God), we say more: namely, that everything that flows returns to that from which it also had the beginning of its flow. 

<margin>Solomon</margin>
For water returns to the sea, from which it drew its origin, as the most wise Solomon <note>Referring to Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea... unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."</note> teaches and experience proves. The 

<margin>Proclus</margin>
body returns to the earth from which it was taken. The spirit, and all things made by God, return to that same one from whom they were brought forth. "All produced things," says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a Neoplatonist whose philosophy focused on the "cycle" of reality: proceeding from a source and returning to it.</note>, "complete a circle, beginning from God and ending in God himself." So too time returns into that same eternity from which it flowed; which will remain when time ceases, just as it existed before time. 

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
Hence to Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose works blended Aristotelianism with Neoplatonism.</note> who asks how the Maker preceded the construction of the world, 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
we shall say with Augustine—a philosopher of the highest integrity—that He preceded it by that eternal 

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
duration. Plotinus also (who taught many things above the human level, which he 

<margin>Ammonius</margin>
drew from the fountains of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the legendary teacher of Plotinus in Alexandria.</note>, and he from those who were instructed by divine oracles) uses flawed reasoning regarding this duration of the world when he says: "That which is resolved into another is cut apart; but since there is nothing beyond the world into which it could be dissolved, it will last forever." 

To him we say: The world is resolved according to its parts, so that it might persist in a better condition; but we are not disputing about its dissolution at present, since the discussion is about its birth. Nor does it conflict 

<margin>Plato</margin>
with our religion that God's handiwork should last forever—so that we may agree with Plato and 

<margin>Plotinus</margin>

Hence we also assert the soul to be immortal, because it was produced and inspired by God. The body will also attain eternity if it puts on the nature of the soul, as we shall discuss elsewhere. Likewise, they attribute too little to its governors.

What Plotinus says when discussing the heaven and the world soul <note>original: "anima mundi," a concept where the universe itself possesses a soul that gives it life and order.</note> supports this view. He says: "It is surely absurd to imagine that the soul, which has held the heaven together for a time, would not also do so always, as if it held it together by force." And proceeding a little further, he asks: "What could be the cause for the world to eventually cease? For the elements of the world are not worn away like wood or other such things; and since these remain forever, the universe also remains." Here, speaking of a future permanence, he presupposes that the world has always existed. From this, he concludes it will last forever because the sovereignty of the soul itself cannot be dissolved, nor its nature weakened.

</margin>
Aristotle also holds this in high regard: because the prince of this worldly house, being eternal and receiving no change, his house also seems to be eternal. And since its governors <note>The "intelligences" or angelic beings believed to move the celestial spheres.</note> do not labor, nor grow weary from revolving, being devoted to eternal motion, they shall never rest. 

To resolve these points, we say there is an error of equivocation <note>A logical fallacy where the same term is used in different senses.</note> by arguing from the immediate end to the ultimate end. Almost all things are ordered toward various immediate purposes, but toward only one ultimate end. For animals, the immediate purpose is to live and feed, but the ultimate purpose is to serve man—who (in the opinion of many wise men) is the end of all inferior things. The immediate purpose of man, however, is to manage a house, a republic, or a family; to trade, to study, and the like; but his ultimate end is to reach God, or happiness—whether through Stoic virtue, or Peripatetic <note>Refers to the followers of Aristotle.</note> speculation, or Academic <note>Refers to the Platonic school.</note> purification, or through faith and grace, as our Catholics assert. 

For the Intelligences <note>Celestial beings/angels.</note> separated from God and corruptible matter, the immediate purpose is to rule the heavens, men, and other things committed to them; but their ultimate end is in the contemplation of the 
<margin>The same</margin>
First Substance <note>God.</note>, where they are made blessed, as Aristotle himself mentions in his *Ethics*. Therefore, granted that they may rest from motion and from their inferior purpose, they shall nonetheless not cease from their blessedness—just as a man will be no less happy if he does not govern a republic or inferior things. 

Indeed, it is a wonder that anyone would think those minds find their bliss in continual motion, since all motion (as they themselves teach) tends toward rest, and a greater perfection of wisdom is achieved in the lecture halls and in the seats by being still than in motion. They will not cease because they are tired, but because the work is perfected and completed, and the favor they owed to inferior things has been granted. 

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
Nor will the soul of which Plotinus speaks cease to provide life to the universe by ceasing from motion. We do not assert the annihilation of its elements or parts, but a rest from motion, so that it may finally be brought back, after many revolutions, into the Sabbatarian rest <note>A reference to the "Sabbath" of creation, a state of eternal divine rest.</note> which is closed off even to many wise men. 

<margin><warning>Faded marginal notes: Prophets, Ecclesiastes.</warning></margin>
Nor will the craftsman repent when he ceases with his work perfected; just as (with the Sacred Scriptures witnessing) God rested from all the work He had created when the fabric of the world was finished. Thus it is true, as the philosophers themselves teach, that all motion tends toward rest. Nor will the prince of this worldly court be weakened by reigning in quietude. Let all the wise men who perpetually investigate the end of the worldly machine fix their feet here, lest, running after an unceasing motion with an ineffable fantasy, they never find rest, nor be able to see their own peace with any light, being hindered by their continuous course.

<summary>The author argues that the universe and its celestial governors (intelligences) are not defined by eternal motion, but rather move toward an ultimate state of rest and blessedness in God. He refutes the Aristotelian idea that the cessation of motion implies decay, comparing the world's end to the "Sabbatarian rest" of the Creator.</summary>

### Nor do they prove their aim by proceeding from the Maker. Chapter XII.

<margin>Aristotle, Averroes, Moses the Egyptian, Cicero</margin>
**S**ince, once again, from this new birth of the world, a new relationship seems to be introduced to the Maker <note>original: "opificem," referring to God as the master craftsman of the universe</note> due to the novelty of the work, a certain change consequently follows in His nature or His will. This is something that cannot happen to a most perfect and immovable being. Such a change cannot come from within, because nothing can move itself; nor from without, because He would then be acted upon by something else, which contradicts the definition of the most perfect and infinite being. Many such arguments are brought forward by Aristotle, Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Mose ægyptio," referring to Maimonides, the Jewish philosopher who grappled with the conflict between Aristotelian eternity and Biblical creation.</note>, and those who follow them. Cicero, in his attack against Plato, wove these arguments together in one place with his eloquent speech: "With what eyes of the mind," he asks, "could your Plato have looked upon that workshop of such a great work, which he claims was constructed and built by God? What construction was there? What iron tools? What levers? What machines? Who were the ministers of such a great task? How could air, water, fire, and earth obey the Architect? From where did so many forms arise, so aptly suited to creating the soul and producing the senses?" And progressing a little further, he asks of them: "Why did these builders of the world suddenly appear after sleeping for countless ages? For even if there was no world, there were still ages—even if they were not those ages produced by the number of days and nights in their annual courses (for I admit those could not be made without the rotation of the world). There was, indeed, a certain eternity from infinite time which no marking of time measured. Yet, what kind of space that was cannot be understood, nor does it even fall within our knowledge, that there should be some time when no time existed. Therefore, in that so immense a space, why did Providence <note>original: "pronoea," from the Greek "pronoia," meaning divine forethought or providence.</note> cease? Was she fleeing from labor? What was it, moreover, that made God desire to decorate the world with signs and lights like an aedile <note>An "aedile" was a Roman official responsible for public buildings and organizing festivals/decorations. Cicero is using a mocking metaphor here.</note>? If it was so that God Himself might live better, then before that He was living in darkness as if in a hovel. If we think He delights in variety because we see He has adorned the heaven and earth, what kind of delight of God can this be, which He could have lacked for so long? Or were these things established by God for the sake of men, as you usually say? For the wise, or for the fools? If for the wise, then such a great construction was made for the sake of a few. If for the fools, there was first no reason to deserve well of the wicked; and secondly, what did He achieve, since all have been made fools? What can we call more wretched than foolishness?"

<margin>Alcinous</margin>
Thus far Cicero. Alcinous <note>A 2nd-century Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> adds: "Since nothing remains outside the world that could exert force upon it, it will suffer neither disease nor any dissolution. And since it will last forever, it therefore has also been eternal."

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> adds: "An agent acting by the power of another can produce now what he could not before, because he must wait for the favor of his co-agents. But the First Being, acting by His own power, ought not to wait; He should act continuously." Let the servants of the world say, for the dignity of their prince, that they are so devoted to continuous revolution that they never reach rest, in which true happiness lies. We, however, on behalf of the Supreme Maker, who is peace and rest... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "rest" (quies) on the next page.</note>

The central argument is that a perfect, eternal God would have no reason to "start" creating at a specific moment if He had not been creating eternally.</summary>

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
<margin>Scotus, Mi. Cas.</margin>
We grant to Aristotle that a new relationship arises, but it is one of reason <term>relationship of reason (relatio rationis): a connection that exists only in our minds to help us understand things, rather than a physical change in the object itself</term>, as Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval philosopher known for his complex "Subtle" arguments.</note>, a man of the sharpest judgment, thinks. And I wonder at this objection of a new relationship arising, since new things are continually produced: from which arises a new relationship, either to God as the builder or the governor, or at least (as they themselves say) as the beloved and desired end. Why then is the relationship of a new world against God's majesty, but not the relationship of new parts?
<margin>Algazel</margin>
Nor does that splendor of the Saracens, Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian who famously critiqued Greek philosophy in his "Incoherence of the Philosophers."</note>—who himself fights for the world's beginning and the Creator's rest—consider it an inconvenience that a most perfect agent, with all the necessary conditions for producing an effect, should delay as long as He wishes, and then produce it, with no new change accruing to Himself.
<margin>Philosophers</margin>
Nor do the Philosophers prove by their demonstration that once those conditions are set, the effect must follow in God, who acts freely—as we shall immediately declare, fortified by His support.
<margin>Averroes</margin>
Yet here and elsewhere that impious Arab <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the influential Islamic philosopher from Spain who argued for the eternity of the world.</note> rises up against him in vain, presupposing things that all wise men would deny: hence those Arabic fictions are indeed childish ravings; so much so that even his faithful interpreter, forced by the truth, considers him a fool and all his reasons to be such.
<margin>The same Algazel</margin>
Averroes claims that Algazel directed his war against the philosophers because he was hindered by a "frenetic disease" or by the error of religious laws. O insane and senseless man, that you strive with such labor to dissolve the reasons brought forward by one you claim is suffering from lethargy! Moreover, you accursed one, you blaspheme the most holy laws uttered by the divine mouth, and you dare to charge with error those things which are full of divinity: Now you shall see. I do not cry out for your sake, but for the youth and those not yet initiated, who—not perceiving the divine and most hidden reasons which are seen only after a long time, with the most exquisite diligence and a purified mind (as Plato and the wise men testify)—easily wander astray in such matters.
<margin>Plato Likewise</margin>
Therefore, with Plato, we exhort you young men not to rashly put forward an opinion about the divine mysteries and the secrets of the world: because at the first glance of things, nothing offers itself except what can be sensed. But those who rely on the senses, not perceiving the highest secrets of God and nature because their minds are darkened, either hiss at religion or cast it behind their backs; and these men think themselves the greatest of men if they claim for themselves the name of Averroists, or Aristotelians, or Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, often associated here with a focus on material atoms rather than divine providence.</note> (and would that it were falsely!), though they have not even caught a scent of the profound mysteries of religion. This is especially true of Averroes, into whose malevolent soul this wisdom has disdained to dwell or enter. And some ridiculous men think themselves great when they are thoroughly imbued with the discipline of Averroes: whose doctrine has something on its surface that attracts, which appears unshakable, probable, and useful. But when you look deeper within, you will see all things are false, unfaithful to his master [Aristotle], and impious toward all worship—with a few exceptions where he could not deviate from his teacher.

### Why the Philosophers strayed from the Catholic Truth. Chapter XIII.

<margin>Averroes</margin>
<margin>Porphyry</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>

**T**hese and similar strengths and siege-engines the philosophers directed in vain against the walls of celestial truth. Its discipline is not usurped by human pride, but is bathed in the clarity of the holy divinity: it mocks those who are wise in their own eyes and despise others, leaving them in the darkness of their own obscured arrogance; but those whom it illuminates, it leads to gaze upon the inner chambers of God and nature in a clear light. Certainly not univocal, if we follow their own principles, by which they teach that God and created things do not agree in any univocal definition of substance or being. Hence Porphyry, following their dogma, says: "If anyone calls all things beings, he will name them equivocally (so says Aristotle)." Many of the more recent followers follow him: although some, holding to a univocal concept of God and creature, substance and accident, try to interpret Aristotle’s mind to their own purpose, fearing perhaps to contradict so great a man without necessity. But if they are equivocal, it is no wonder if, by proceeding through these lower things, they wander in the knowledge of God. For what can they imagine about God through their motion, or through these sensible things—God who is utterly foreign to the senses and to motion? For he is (says Aristotle with his Averroes in the discourse *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de coelo"; Aristotle's treatise on the cosmos and the stars.</note>) utterly removed from the modes of creatures. Hence, that which is the First Mover, which is not moved...

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Dionysius</margin> Let them hear, I pray, what the great Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher whose works (now known as Pseudo-Dionysius) were highly influential in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for their blend of Neoplatonism and Christianity.</note> says of him—he who was first imbued with their discipline and later illuminated by the rays of the holy divinity. <term>God</term> (he says) is all things eminently. These men confess God to be the first and best of all, and other things to be inferior and serving him. These arguments are indeed subtle, yet they do not constrain him.

# OF THE FIRST SONG

->OF THE FIRST SONG<-

All things desire him, and for his sake they do everything—whatever they do according to nature. Yet they cannot imitate him continuously or in a perpetual way, because it is not possible for any corruptible thing <note>referring to physical things that decay or die</note> to remain identical and numerically one. Instead, each thing participates in that oneness as best as it can: some more, others less. Thus far speaks Aristotle. The sum of these words is this: that every member of this worldly body, the more perfect it is, the more it strives to emulate the Creator. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
But who is this faithless Arab <note>The author is referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century Spanish-Muslim philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle. Medieval and Renaissance Christian writers often engaged in harsh polemics against his views.</note> acting as an interpreter from heaven? For how is the heaven he presides over that eternal being which all things emulate, since He is eternal for whose sake the elements, the heaven itself, and all things act? 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Do not the dogmas of Aristotle resonate everywhere, stating that God is the end <note>The "Final Cause" or ultimate goal toward which all nature moves.</note> of all things, for whose sake—as the beloved and the desired—all things are moved? But these are among the smallest of the many points where that treacherous dog <note>original: "perfidus canis." A common, albeit harsh, period term for someone considered a heretic or opponent of the faith.</note> barks against the truth, distorting and destroying the meanings of his master <note>Aristotle</note>; in these matters, the name "Destroyer" rather than "Commentator" could be ascribed to him. Nor should anyone wonder if I burn with rage against this slanderer, for the zeal of the living God consumes me—the God whom that wretch dares to blaspheme and (alas, it is a painful thing) causes many others to blaspheme. 

Listen, I pray, to what that dog barks there concerning the best and greatest God. "Divine solicitude," <note>care or providence</note> he says, "since it could not make this individual thing remain permanent, took pity on it by giving it a power so that they might be able to remain permanent within their species." <note>Averroes argued that since God/Nature cannot make an individual animal live forever, He provided reproduction so the *type* of animal lives on.</note> 

Be silent, treacherous dog! Do not presume to speak of God, you who flee the light <note>original: "lucifuga."</note>. With what audacity do you dare to measure the power of the Almighty? Why could He not give permanence to man and other lower things—the same permanence He gave to Saturn and all the Planets and stars, as you yourself assert? How did He become powerless in lower things when He was so powerful in the highest? What sort of dignity is left to the supreme God if, when He could not provide one benefit to His lower creatures, He had to look for another way? 

If indeed you attribute this providence to the heaven itself, I am truly amazed that you assign the providence and work of the Supreme Prince to his ministers <note>the celestial bodies</note>. And if the heavens were unable to do this, why could the Supreme Prince not do it? 

But returning to where we digressed: those men admit that all things are divine and emulate perfection—the elements in their being, plants in their life and fruitfulness, and animals in a better life and whatever condition they have. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
But man, who enjoys the peculiar gift of liberty, emulates God in that very thing. From this, freedom in God is also proven, because He contains all things that He provides to others. 

The highest perfection does not fail in these lower levels, nor is His simplicity destroyed among many things, for He contains all things by His infinite power. For the intellectual soul is not debased if it exercises the power of sensing, growing, and moving according to its place—following their own dogmas. 

<margin>Porphyry, Aristotle</margin>
For God senses (to ascend to higher things) with His own senses, which the Holy Scriptures attribute to Him. 

<margin>Plato, Aristotle, Averroes</margin>
Remaining stable, He moves all other things; He nourishes and is fed by His own food of wisdom. But all these things exist in a mode and perfection that are hidden from human minds unless they are illuminated by His light. For freedom is not simply a choice according to nature (as some think), nor is it indifferent toward good or evil; rather, it is toward the good according to His will. However, in man—the most perfect of living things—this freedom has degenerated somewhat, so that it can even be carried toward evil. But in this, man does not emulate God in the least...

# THE FIRST TONE
<note>original: "TONVS PRIMVS." In this context, "Tone" refers to a musical or harmonic mode of the universe.</note>

->THE FIRST TONE<-

...it emulates: in a better way or perhaps above all things it carries His image. In God Himself, there is fecundity <note>the ability to produce offspring or new growth; fertility</note> without labor, as Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian-Greek figure associated with the Hermetic writings which Renaissance scholars believed contained ancient divine secrets.</note> says: 

<margin>Mercury</margin>
"God, fortified by the fecundity of both sexes, is the source of all sexes and all fecundities." And since He does not grow numb with idleness, He always produces inwardly; outwardly, however, He produces according to the choice of His will. Since this is the first rule of all things that can happen, it is neither within our power, nor is it right, to seek the cause of that first principle itself; when we reach that point, even Aristotle 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
commands us to rest. He requires no prior arrangement or approach, nor does He fear resistance, nor is He hindered by space—He who makes all things by commanding. However, these inferior causes and the subject matter beneath Him—which was fashioned by God Himself—require a prior arrangement: they demand an application beforehand, they wait for the passage of time, and they need aids of this kind, which they seek in an agent according to a determined power. Therefore, those who reason from these types of limited craftsmen to Him, who is most absolute and free from all these things, fall into various errors. If, however, they strive to arrive at a knowledge of the Archetype <note>The original pattern or model from which all things are made.</note> from those things they see in this workmanship, they should attribute all these things to Him in their appropriate and most perfect manner. But those things which denote weakness in a worker, they should remove; then they will see that the highest things of the Archetype correspond with the lower and middle things with that most sweet sonority and harmony which we have proposed. For singers, supporting singers, and counter-singers <note>original: "cantores, succentores, & occentores." These refer to the different voice parts (like soprano, tenor, and bass) in a musical arrangement.</note> do not enter into a concert <note>original: "concentum"</note> with the same key, even though they come together in the same consonance <note>A harmonious combination of sounds.</note>. So also the three worlds <note>In Renaissance thought, these were typically the Elemental (earthly), Celestial (stars/planets), and Intellectual (angelic/divine) worlds.</note>, which we claim are in accord, proceed with a different note yet produce the same concert. For all things are in the Maker as if in a certain model; things which are contemplated in these lower realms are like an image or a footprint. But the image, and much more the footprint, falls short of that which it represents. Nevertheless, from these things, through analogy and a certain symbol, we arrive at a knowledge of the Maker. These things do not correspond by a differing logic (as if they were unrelated), nor exactly the same (as if they were identical), but by representing that most perfect "note" of higher things through a certain similarity—each thing according to its own degree, however much more degraded or murky it may be.

We have already seen how weak the machines of the philosophers have been against the workmanship and newness <note>creation at a specific point in time</note> of the world; it remains for us, fighting from the opposite side, to draw ourselves up into a battle line and hurl their own darts back at them, seizing, where necessary, the broadsword <note>original: "rhomphea"</note> of the divine word. Among other weapons that the philosophers aimed was the perceived inconsistency of "newness" with the eternal God, as they did not perceive how newness could come to be. And (as Censorinus says) they ask whether eggs or birds were created first: since an egg cannot be produced without a bird, nor a bird without an egg. From this, they judged this world to be everlasting, and they believed the beginning and the end of every generated thing to be the same in its perpetual revolution. But I ask of you, O natural philosophers: from where does this "newness" come which we see continually? The Arab <note>Averroes</note> says this proceeds from new revolutions, which however...

<margin>Averroes</margin>

# PAGE XVII
### OF THE FIRST SONG.

<margin>**M. <unclear>Q.</unclear>**</margin>
<margin>**Aristotle**</margin>
Ancient things come from an everlasting succession, and stability is found where antiquity and novelty <note>In this context, "novelty" refers to the act of something new being created or beginning to exist in time.</note> are preserved together. Hence some have said that the heaven is partly new and partly ancient. But since these revolutions of the spheres are caused by the presiding "intelligences" <note>Medieval philosophers believed celestial bodies were moved by spiritual beings called Intelligences.</note>, there will be no true stability in heaven. I ask: from where do those things move anew, which are called the servants of the "Craftsman" or the "First Mover," as you call Him? They move anew in order to unfold those things which the First Mover commands to be made anew: He who, remaining stable Himself, grants all things their motion. Therefore, the principle of this novelty comes not from the heaven, nor from an intelligence, but from the First Mover: who commands these things to be renewed according to His will. He does this by a certain order hidden within Himself, compelled by no necessity, lest He seem to be bound to inferior things. Aristotle agrees with this when he asserts that God is happy without any external good.

<margin>**Aristotle**</margin>
Nor would there be any "contingency" <note>Contingency refers to things that can either happen or not happen—events that are not strictly determined by fate or necessity.</note> if everything proceeded into existence by necessity. Aristotle proves this contingency exists in the world by the fact that it would be useless to take counsel or conduct business unless outcomes were contingent. But this contingency is not something that has already been born into the thing; for once a thing exists, it is then "necessary" that it is what it is.

<margin>**The same, Solon, and Agathon**</margin>
Hence Aristotle commends the saying of Solon, or perhaps Agathon: "God is deprived of this one thing alone: the power to make what has been done, undone." <note>Aristotle quotes the poet Agathon in the Nicomachean Ethics to show that even God cannot change the past.</note> If, therefore, this contingency preceded the world, it existed in the producer—not in a secondary cause, which must follow the order of the first, but in the First Cause Himself. Nor is an individual thing "contingent" simply because it can be destroyed, while the "species" <note>The "species" refers to the universal category (e.g., "Humanity"), which philosophers often argued was eternal even if individual people died.</note> are eternal and cannot be dissolved. For if a thing can be destroyed after it is made, it was also possible for it not to have been made before it existed. They concede this regarding individuals, even though they claim species are necessary. For the act of production ends at the individual or the "suppositum" <note>A technical term for an individual substance or person.</note> from which the species results, as they themselves teach; therefore, let them solve this contradiction. Furthermore, by what measure do the supporters of the world's eternity wish this "machine" <note>A common Renaissance term for the structured universe.</note> of the world to be measured? If by time, it will not be eternal.

<margin>**Boethius**</margin>
If by "eternity," let them remember that eternity itself is "the whole and perfect possession of life all at once" (as the most upright philosopher **Boethius** writes), and it is removed from time and motion. How then shall this world be eternal, which is the same age as time and is utterly enslaved to motions? And if you contend it is eternal, tell me, I pray: does it endure by that same eternity by which God (Blessed be He) endures, or by another? If by another, there will be other "eternities" for the governors of the spheres and for the species, which would taste of the nature of the infinite; and thus many "infinites" would be contained in this world, which is so small. If it is by the same eternity as God, they are surely ridiculous; for they would be thinking that the celestial orbs and their movers are measured by God Himself, since eternal duration is not distinct from God.

<margin>**Albertus**</margin>
Nor can that which is changeable in its nature and operation (says **Albertus**) <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> be measured by the same measure as He who is entirely immutable. They will say: "The eternity of the world differs from that of the First Agent, because the latter is a possession of all at once, while the former is successive." But I say: if it is successive, it has part after part; and parts of this kind cannot be infinite.

<margin>**Raymond Lull**</margin>
<margin><unclear>**alonua**</unclear></margin>
It also has (to proceed with **Raymond Lull**) <note>original: "Raymundo Iulio." Referring to Ramon Llull, a Catalan polymath and mystic.</note> a successive beginning and end. If, therefore, it is enclosed by those boundaries, how can it agree with the Eternal, which is concluded by no end? Furthermore, how shall that be eternal...

# THE FIRST TONE
### XVIII

...to which something is always being added anew? How can something be added to the infinite? They will say that the infinite does not grow. We grant them this. What, then, will these new revolutions <note>The circular motions of the celestial spheres.</note> do? Are they joined with those first ones, or do they begin a new <margin>Averroes</margin> infinity? If the first, then there will be some things greater than the infinite. The Arab <note>original: "Arabs"; refers to the philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> says: This is not improper in successive things, just as it is not in numbers, where infinite tens would yield just as much from that infinite repetition as infinite hundreds. Nor would an added number make a greater increase to the former than to the latter. O good God, who, I ask, can hear such things with calm ears? Based on an impossible hypothesis imagined in numbers but never actually held, he wishes to solve those inconveniences that follow from the revolutions which he asserts have preceded infinitely. 

But lest a dispute arise over successions and numbers, let these supporters of the world speak honestly: Do the Intelligences <note>The spiritual beings or angels believed to move the planetary spheres.</note> who roll the spheres know these revolutions or not? If they do not know them, it is surely a great slander against them, to think they are ignorant of <margin>Astronomy</margin> their own motions, which many astronomers know. But if they know them all, and they are infinite, how can a finite, determined intellect grasp infinite things? If you say they know part of those revolutions and part not, which part, I ask, is not understood by the Intelligences, or what will be forgotten by those who do not suffer from forgetfulness? 

Furthermore, since generation ends at an individual, and the last generation of a horse ends at the last horse, at which first horse was the generation bounded? They will say: There is no first. And how, I ask, is there a last but no first? Where is the order that exists from the first to the last? Indeed, I wonder greatly, and I do not cease to wonder at the ancient wise men of the world and the more recent ones who agree with them, since they assert that all things are moved and ordered toward God as toward the ultimate loved and desired end, yet without an orderer. They say God is the First Mover but not the Orderer. But if He ordered all things, He also knew them in particular—the contrary of which they teach. 

They will say He ordered the higher things, but these lowest things [on Earth] are left to secondary causes. To whom I say: How do these lowest things correspond to the highest if there are different orderers? <margin>Aristotle</margin> Does not Aristotle say that there is only one Prince, lest things be poorly disposed? Again, if all things depend on that final cause so that by His grace they may make themselves great, how then do they have being from themselves when they seek to be <term>perfected</term> <note>original: "perfici"; in medieval philosophy, this means to reach completion or one's full potential.</note> in another? Why do they need a preserver if they did not need a generator? A son is preserved without a father, but he is by no means generated without one. Why then do they give a guardian to the members of the universe from whom they have taken away the parents? 

What trifles are these from those who accuse others of being triflers? For in one place they deny what they are forced to admit in another by the truth itself. <margin>Averroes, Aristotle, Plato</margin> The Arab denies that God is the Craftsman <note>original: "opifex"</note> of the world, yet in interpreting the discourse *On the Heavens*, he calls Him the Creator. Aristotle also, proceeding from sensory things, mocks Plato, who everywhere admits the world was born [created]. Yet in the book ascribed to him *On the World*, he asserts God is the Craftsman of the world itself; and in his Higher Philosophy <note>Refers to Aristotle's "Metaphysics."</note>, he teaches the same Prince of the universe. And how...

# THE FIRST TONE
### XVIII

...a Prince entered into a house, which (as they say) he neither built, nor acquired by hereditary right, nor bought for any price. They say again: He does not understand these particular things, lest that supreme mind be weary, or become base. <margin>Aristotle</margin> And in the discourse on good and bad fortune, they teach that he who is directed by God is "well-fortuned." But how does He direct those things which He does not understand? How does He return worthy rewards for deeds well or ill performed (as is asserted in that same place) if He does not examine individual actions? And in the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, a treatise on natural phenomena.</note> they teach that God placed pure fire beneath the sphere of the Moon. How did He arrange and ordain that which He neither made nor knows? It would indeed be troublesome to bring forward all the things which, by manifest contradiction, collapse, destroyed by their own weight. But I have brought forward these few out of many, so that they may understand that for the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> and <term>Averroists</term><note>Followers of the Islamic philosopher Averroes, known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> not all their dogmas are unshakable and solid. 

But to follow our purpose, I consider that we must weigh more heavily the judgment of <margin>Augustine, Macrobius</margin> Augustine, Macrobius, and many wise men, who do not think the eternity of the world can stand alongside such a small memory of deeds performed, and with the celebrated discovery of many arts and things by <margin>Eusebius Pamphilus, Clement of Alexandria, Berosus the Chaldean, Aristotle, Averroes, Theophrastus, Epigenes, Critodemus, Philostephanus, Suphanus, Hegesias, Archimochus, Damasthenes, Aulus Gellius, Pliny</margin> Eusebius Pamphilus, Clement of Alexandria, Berosus the Chaldean, Aristotle, Averroes, Theophrastus, Epigenes, Critodemus, Philostephanus, Suphanus, Hegesias, Archimochus, Damasthenes, Aulus Gellius, and very many others of various languages, but most extensively by Pliny in his *Natural History*, where he confesses to have collected many things from the aforementioned authors. 

<margin>Philosophers: Inventors of various things.</margin> The authority of the Sacred Scriptures favors these men, declaring the inventors of various things: although they may disagree about the inventors, just as the aforementioned authors disagree among themselves. This happens either through a variety of languages, or because historians, especially the Greeks, wished to claim things for themselves that were not theirs. If, therefore, the world existed from the beginning, or rather before the beginning (as the Philosophers assert), why, through the series of innumerable ages, had the culture we now use not been found? Not the use of letters, by which alone memory is made eternal; nor the experience of many things. Noah passed on the <margin>Moses, Berosus</margin> cultivation of the vine, as Moses relates; he was Janus, if we believe Berosus; but Bacchus, if it pleases one to borrow something from poetic fictions: by whom the true poets understood the solar power with which wine is filled. But only when Rome was already growing did the Gauls learn the cultivation of wine. Ceres, indeed, taught the cultivation and use of grain. 

The Greeks received letters from Cadmus shortly before the fall of Troy. The Egyptians (who <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> are called *Mizraimi* in Hebrew <note>original: "Mizraimi hebraice dicuntur"</note>) obtained medicine from Mizraim, the son of Ham and grandson of the great Noah (witnessed by Clement of Alexandria). Apollo and Aesculapius expanded it; Hippocrates of Cos organized it; Galen of Pergamum extended it; Avicenna the Arab (or Persian, as others say) increased it. Chiron, the son of Saturn and Philyra, found herbal medicines. Some hand down Pythagoras as the author of music; others, Amphion. But Tubal was the inventor and father of those playing the lyre, as we <margin>Genesis 4</margin> have in the Sacred Scriptures. Pythagoras, however, by the weight of hammers and the length of strings and pipes, arranged harmony under a numerical proportion. ### XVIII <note>The Roman numeral in the header is XIX, but the section continues from the previous page's theme. Note that the OCR identifies this as section XVIII.</note>

Mercury discovered it <note>Likely referring to the lyre or the art of speech, though the sentence starts abruptly due to the transition from the previous page.</note>. Copes [invented] the oar, Icarus the sails, Daedalus the mast and yardarm; the Salaminians the <term>horse-transport ship</term><note>original: "Hippagium"; a vessel specifically designed to carry horses.</note>, the Tyrrhenians the anchor, and Tiphis the steering aids. I omit the inventors of countless other things, whom the authors cited above describe. And to you, who assert that the world is eternal, I shall speak: What were those inhabitants of the world doing before these very brief times to which the inventors of things are assigned? What did they do without Ceres and Bacchus <note>Roman deities representing grain and wine; used here as metonyms for agriculture and viticulture.</note>, without the cultivation of the land? What did they do when they were not occupied by trade, nor the study of letters, nor academic disciplines, nor military service, nor navigation, nor the art of building, nor weaving, nor sewing, nor the loom, nor wool-working? On what did they feed? Where did they live? With what were they clothed? What did they do, being utterly ignorant of the arts? For it is truly ridiculous that those who assert the world is eternal also describe the inventors of the arts and of human sustenance, since these two positions cannot stand together <note>The author argues that if the world were eternal, human technology would not have such recent, identifiable starting points.</note>.

### Why God did not make the world before, or after, what Moses narrates. Chapter XV.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**H**ere, an imagination derived from the senses and domestic matters offends many—not only the common people, but even the wise. "What," they ask, "was God doing before he built the world? Why did he wait until then? Why did he not defer it for a bit longer?" These and similar questions entangle those who do not separate God's condition from our own. Augustine responds to the common folk with a wise joke when they ask what God was doing before the world's construction: "In the forest," he said, "he was cutting wood so that he might burn the reckless and the curious," who do not even remember what they did yesterday, yet presume to inquire into what God did before the birth of the world. But (to speak with the wise), let them say, I pray: What do they understand by that word "before" about which they ask? If they imagine a flow of time, they err, since time took its beginning simultaneously with the world. If, however, through that "before," they suppose something in eternity—since eternity is a total possession [of life] at once, having no succession—there is no "before" or "after" in it. Hence, no such question is valid. 

There was, however, before his work, an indivisible and simultaneously whole eternity, in which he always exercised a work co-eternal with himself—namely, by continuously producing his own intelligence and offspring <note>Referring to the generation of the Son in the Trinity.</note>, and his own <margin>The same [Augustine]</margin> love <note>The Holy Spirit.</note>. Just as the Sun (as Augustine says) would have always produced light and fire-breathing splendor if it had always existed. Nor does that infinite power terminate its work; having an infinite object, it produces infinite fruits measured by an eternity separated from all <term>successive duration</term><note>Duration that happens one moment after another; the linear experience of time.</note>. Therefore, things that are successive cannot be eternal, as the philosophers dream. For the "now" that stands signifies eternity, and the "now" that flows <margin>Boethius</margin> constitutes time, as the philosopher Boethius teaches—himself a most excellent man. Therefore, time does not agree with eternity, nor can it be eternal, nor can eternity have succession. Hence the question is foolish: why did God not make the world before temporal time? As if there were some successive duration before succession began; for time did not exist before the world. <margin>Aristotle, John Scotus</margin> Nor does Aristotle prove otherwise when he strives to demonstrate the eternity of the world (as John [Duns] Scotus, a man of the gravest judgment, determines), except that there was never time without the world.
