### Chapter XVI.

**N**ow that matters concerning the fabric of the world have been dispatched, another war remains for us to settle with the philosophers before we enter into the inner shrines of God and nature: whether God is led to His work by a certain necessity, or by a free and <term>contingent</term><note>In Scholastic philosophy, a contingent action is one that is not forced or inevitable, but happens by choice or chance.</note> choice. The philosophers were of the opinion that the condition of necessity was better than that of contingency, and for this reason they attributed the former to God. Reasons seem to support them, especially this: because He acts through His own substance and not through a borrowed virtue; also because many effects appear necessary, which seem in no way to come from a contingent cause; and the order of things appears invariable and necessary, so that the universe might not be confounded or disturbed. Nor could it be considered agreeable that the divine intellect should act by necessity while the will acts freely, since that divine mind and will are no less perfect than the intellect. We too could direct some arrows from the quiver of rational discourse against the philosophers, but since business of this kind pertains to God, it is not to be investigated by reasons, but learned from—

It challenges the Aristotelian idea that the world exists by "necessity," arguing instead that God remains a free "craftsman" who can alter the natural order without destroying its perfection.</meta>

# PAGE 19
## OF THE FIRST SONG

By necessity, which is seen in effects relative to the necessity of the cause, no one is convinced, since the necessity of effects depends on the order of the first cause. Indeed, they are not necessary, since all are particulars; for the work of nature is not terminated at the universal, but at the singular, which the very [philosophers] themselves prohibit from being more contingent than necessary. But because they contend that species are eternal, and that there is a necessary coherence of the subject to the predicate—in which the essential property, or <term>quiddity</term> <note>The "whatness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> (as they say), is spoken of the subject—another cause of necessity must be sought. This is (unless I am mistaken) the correspondence to those exemplars or eternal ideas <margin>Aristotle</margin> which were derided by Aristotle, who was immersed in his own senses, <margin>Plato</margin> but celebrated by Plato and our own wise men, and manfully defended by Syrianus. <margin>Syrianus</margin> I consider this correspondence to be supported by a better necessity than if that universal "sprouted" (as they think) from many particulars. Which (in my judgment) cannot stand, since that universal is a certain simple being which neither intelligence nor nature (according to the witness of Proclus and many wise men) <margin>Proclus</margin> <margin>Wise Men</margin> is able to produce; because even the universal (or the simple) is the first of all created things, produced before intelligence or the heavens or any other particular whatsoever. And although Proclus’s way of proceeding is criticized by some, they nevertheless agree in the conclusion. Having admitted this, let them untie the knot of the argument themselves. Therefore, the effect follows (to return to that from which we digressed) the immutable determination and order of the supreme cause, unless that same cause has decreed otherwise.

As for what they add—that God's will has an equal perfection with his intellect, which acts by necessity—we admit this, so long as it operates in the inner depths in conformity with that intellect; but he unfolds external effects (which the intellect depicted from eternity in the Word) according to his pleasure. Indeed, I marvel at those philosophizing who confess God to be most simple and perfect with all external things excluded, and then, immediately forgetting their own dogma, think that God has a necessary connection with inferior things, as if he could neither exist nor be blessed without them. How is he "most simple" if he has a necessary connection with others? How is he the "Prince of all" (as they say) if he is necessarily enslaved to the service of inferiors? What dignity or what condition would that be for the highest Prince? Nor should they fear that the order of the heavens and the universe would be destroyed if the Craftsman disposes and varies it according to his pleasure, since he knows how to reduce to order those things which he has skillfully made and ordained. Indeed, the destruction of the handiwork is not to be feared when the Craftsman applies his hand; by his touch, it is perfected rather than destroyed.

# XXII
## THE FIRST TONE

I would like for them to explain: from where do <term>monsters</term> <note>In a 16th-century philosophical context, 'monstra' (monsters) refers to biological abnormalities or "freaks of nature"—any birth or natural occurrence that deviates from the expected norm.</note> arise in nature? For they will surely say: because matter was lacking or was in excess; or because the qualities do not correspond in their due proportion; or because of the defect of the surrounding environment; and similar reasons, which they subdivide into various parts. But if these causes act by necessity, why do they not prepare everything properly, since nature (as they say) does not fail in necessary things? How, then, do they act by necessity if they fail? You wish to imply—they say—that natural causes operate <term>contingently</term> <note>To act 'contingently' means to happen by chance or in a way that could have been different, the opposite of acting by 'necessity.'</note>. And if I were to say so, what would follow? Nevertheless, so that superfluous argument may be removed, let them remember what is commonly taught in the schools: that "necessity" is held in a twofold way. One, indeed, is absolute; the other, however, is conditional. The one (unless the truth of the Holy Scriptures deceives me) is to be attributed to the blessed God alone. The other is attributed to lower things, so that they are "necessary" only according to the order given by the Craftsman.

But because the philosophers would perhaps deny this, let us come to the work of these causes. For if they "sin" and produce monsters, it is because the order fails—the order decreed for them by nature (as they say) or by the Supreme Craftsman, which is the truth. And if they fall away from that order, then that order was not simply necessary, but was given by the First Cause, under whose power the other subordinated causes act. If the First Cause withdraws itself from these, they not only fail, but they perform nothing at all. And if some things seem to lead by necessity, that <margin>David</margin> comes from the law given to them, as he who was full of God [David] sings: *You have set a limit which they shall not pass.* <note>The author is quoting Psalm 148:6, referring to God's authority over the natural elements.</note> Yet He who imposes the law on others is not Himself bound by the law.

But they will say: "Will science then be about things that can be otherwise—the opposite of what <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle teaches?" To whom we shall say: If your Aristotle understands those things which are known to be necessary *from the order of the universe*, then it will be impossible for them to be otherwise. But if he understands them to be *absolutely* necessary, let him remember what he taught at the end of his book *On Physics*: that it does not suffice for a wise man to speak unless he assigns a reason for what is said. Nor should he bring forward experience, because from that it is easily concluded that such necessity comes from the established order; if that order fails, those things fail. Therefore, they are not simply [absolutely] necessary. If they say, "Then they can be otherwise," what is that to me? Let them solve it themselves. For it is possible for fire not to burn—as has actually happened <note>A reference to the biblical miracle of the three youths in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3), where God suspended the natural property of fire.</note>—and it is possible for any effect to be removed from the cause that produced it, while the inherence (as we said) of the predicate to the subject remains, which is what their science is about.

But moving further, I would like to learn from the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The 'Peripatetics' were the followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle used to walk about the 'peripatos' (colonnade) of the Lyceum while teaching.</note>: from where do those things necessarily inhere? They will say: "They have it from nature, as we prove by experience." But what is this "nature" of theirs? Surely nothing but the Author of the universe, who is the true, non-erring intelligence; for (as they teach) the work of nature is the work of an intelligence that does not err. By His order all things follow, because all things serve Him, <margin>David</margin> as the Prophet says. And let them not say, "What are the Prophets to us?" since we do not think we know anything except what is proven by demonstration. But where, I ask, does demonstration have its origin? Does it not come from principles? We agree to these principles once the terms are known, or we prove them by experience. But if we believe in things demonstrated through principles and experiences, then those other things are better known than the things demonstrated. Oh exce...

->### OF THE FIRST SONG<-

...miserable vice which has grown among our people, who bear the Christian name, <margin>Aristotle</margin> that they do not accept anything as certain unless it is proven by "demonstration"—the kind Aristotle depicted. Yet he uses it very little in his own natural progression, where he always proceeds from presuppositions made by himself; so that what they believe to be a demonstration is actually a deduction based on authority, or on principles they have already accepted from him. If they are Catholics, let them believe the Sacred Page more than Aristotle. If they are <term>Academics</term> <note>Followers of the school of Plato, who emphasized that true knowledge comes from divine illumination or higher reasoning rather than just physical observation.</note>, let them know that many things—especially divine ones—are known through illuminating rays, or through the agreement of sayings with an intellect disposed toward the truth. If they are <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>, let them hear their own Aristotle say that things other than those "demonstrated" can be known with certainty. From where do they get the idea that "to know" means "to understand through demonstration"? Is it not from Aristotle saying so? But we have our dogmas from the <margin>Prophets</margin> Prophets, taught by divine oracle, who prove what they teach through miracles and the risk of their lives. 

And if we were to say that "to know" is a certain knowledge of any thing whatsoever, would we be sinning against the Holy Spirit, or against Aristotle? Certainly not against the Holy Spirit; and as for Aristotle, I care little for him, because he is not my lord, nor will I come before his tribunal to be judged if I do not adhere to him. But they will call me reckless or ignorant because I dare to depart from Aristotelian institutions, which so many brilliant minds follow. Hence this grief, hence these tears (alas, a horrendous crime!), since they fear more to deny Aristotle than to deny Paul—in whose breast Christ resounds—or even Christ himself, who is the Wisdom and Truth of God, who will judge all people. He will judge those especially who follow Aristotle—whom the Greeks call an "evil spirit" <note>original: "cacodaemonem"</note>—or the insane and impious Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle were often seen as conflicting with Christian doctrine.</note> in name, in doctrine, and in life. 

We consider it a small matter (to speak with <margin>John Scotus</margin> John Duns Scotus <note>A major medieval Franciscan theologian known for his critiques of Aristotelianism.</note>) to deny Aristotle in those things that are against the doctrine of truth which we defend. Though he was very shrewd, a studious reader of others' dogmas, and a diligent collector, he was nevertheless a cunning accuser of the ancients. He does not actually refute their poorly cited opinions, proceeding rather (as <margin>Simplicius</margin> Simplicius his listener <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> says) against their words than their intended meanings, and shutting many things away so that he alone might appear wise. 

What wonder then if he is most justly criticized, he who unjustly accused so many distinguished men? Parmenides, Melissus, Democritus, Pythagoras, and his divine teacher <margin>Plato</margin> Plato. His doctrine (in the judgment not only of myself but of many wise men) exceeds the Aristotelian as much as divine things—which Plato, along with Pythagoras, always breathes—excel the earthly things by which <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle is weighed down. 

As <margin>Proclus</margin> Proclus, a professor of Academic and Peripatetic dogma, says: he, along with <margin>Theophrastus</margin> Theophrastus and other Peripatetics, lit the light of their speculation only as far as the forms that move the universe. <margin>Plato</margin> Plato, however, takes his beginnings far from that which holds dignity among beings, and indeed from things more worthy; hence his progression is more sublime. Aristotle also accuses countless others whose sayings, if pondered, would perhaps not be judged worthy of punishment. For from these very people, he himself learned everything he wrote. Nor does he claim for himself—being forced by the truth—anything except the <term>elenchi</term> <note>original: "elenchos"; refers to Aristotle's 'Sophistical Refutations,' the study of logical fallacies used to win arguments.</note>. Accepting the rest from the ancients, he weaves them into his <term>syllogistic</term> <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> processes, so that he passed down an artificial craft and a lowly method of proceeding rather than true science—as he himself [confessed]...

# THE FIRST SONG

He tacitly admits this when he treats the *Posterior Analytics*, teaching that science is produced through "demonstration," and this through <term>quiddities</term> <note>original: *quidditates*; a scholastic term referring to the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note> (as they say) and the proper differences of things which are hidden from us. Hence, the principles of demonstration are proven to be unknown, and consequently, no demonstration—or at most very little—can be obtained from them. Moreover, he condemns "circular demonstration," yet he teaches that demonstration is made from those things which are "of the whole by itself" and "according to itself" <note>original: *de omni per se, & secundum quod ipsum*; these are technical Aristotelian terms for necessary, universal propositions</note>, to use his way of speaking. These statements are convertible and infer one another. He says that "circulation" <note>circular reasoning</note> is not allowed in demonstration from causes. But let them notice that just a little earlier he had said that circular demonstration is sometimes found. 

Setting these things aside, since he teaches nothing in his doctrines that he did not receive from the ancients, it is all the more striking that he is believed more than the ancients who passed knowledge down before him. They say: "We accept things weighed in the Aristotelian balance." And would that they were not distorted to the harm of the Christian religion and the truth! Yet some petulant men, novices in learning, dare to say with the most impudent mouths: "I do not cite Genesis, Jeremiah, or Isaiah to you; I bring forward Aristotle"—as if Moses and the prophets were not wise and skilled in letters! Yet Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was later raised up by the divine oracle to contemplate the innermost secrets of God and nature—things which neither Aristotle nor his most devoted followers ever imagined. And the Prophets, inspired by divine light—which those who flee the light and are in darkness cannot see—did more than just prophesy: they passed down many things from <margin>Prophets</margin> the inner storehouses of God and from the lower realm (though under their own riddles). 

Some more modest people say: "We honor the prophets and holy men in divine matters, but in natural matters, this man [Aristotle] is the rule we must follow." But I wonder, indeed, how they could have known divine and supreme things while the lower things, through which one reaches the supreme, were closed off to them? And since God is a mirror in which all things shine, how did they know Him without knowing the images that reflect in Him? They would not think that the prophets knew the <term>archetype</term> <note>The divine pattern or original model of the universe in God's mind</note> without knowing what is contained within it, if they had perceived the connection of the archetype with this <term>worldly machine</term> <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely designed mechanism</note> and the human world. 

Each of these holds the likeness and image of the other, and from the knowledge of one, the other is easily <margin>Hermes, Plato, Socrates, Zoroaster, Aristotle</margin> distinguished. Hence, self-knowledge is marvelously commended by the divine oracle and by many wise men—<term>Hermes</term> <note>Referencing Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with ancient wisdom and the "Hermetic" tradition</note>, Plato, Socrates, Zoroaster, and even Aristotle himself. For through self-knowledge, one more easily reaches the knowledge of God and the perfection of this "machine," which Aristotle himself teaches. It was certainly necessary for those seers to look upon divine and human things and their correspondence; they spoke of divine things through riddles and the "veils" of lower things, so that God's mysteries would be hidden from common people and from those with "night-owl" eyes <note>meaning those who can see only in the dark and are blinded by the light of truth</note>. But if anyone reads the prophets with the veil removed, he will see that they searched the secrets of nature and of God better than Aristotle. The Sun is not to be blamed if the eye does not see. As <margin>Jerome</margin> Jerome says: "When I was a devotee of Cicero, if I took any prophet into my hands..." <note>Jerome famously recounted a dream where he was beaten before the judgment seat of God for being a "Ciceronian" (valuing secular rhetoric) rather than a Christian.</note>

The speech was rough and unrefined; and I thought the defect was not of light, but of the sun. But once corrected, and with the veil lifted, he saw in the prophets what he had not previously read among the <term>gentiles</term> <note>original: *gentilibus*; here meaning non-Christian or pagan philosophers like the Greeks and Romans</note>. But let us return to the contingency of things. Here, <margin>Algazel</margin> **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian who argued against the eternal necessity of the universe in favor of God's free will</note> argues more sharply from the fact that the parts of this world-machine are arranged in such a way that they could have been situated differently without any logical contradiction; thus they are "contingent," arranged not by necessity, but by the will of the Creator. <margin>Averroes</margin> **The Arab** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), the "Commentator" on Aristotle, who argued the world’s structure is a necessary result of divine reason</note> responds: "We say that the parts of the world could not have been arranged otherwise, because the world is a living animal." From where, by your faith, did you learn this way of arguing from your Aristotle? You wish, indeed, for your own authority to stand as the starting point of a proof. From where else does this conclusion come? Are you dreaming, or are you suffering from a frenzy? If the world is an animal, is it a sensible one or an insensible one? If it is deprived of sense, then it is not an animal. If it is capable of sensation, does it see, hear, smell, taste, or eat? If it eats, who, I ask, prepares its food? From where does it obtain it? From within the world itself, or from outside? If from within the world, it eats itself; if from outside the world, then there must be another world. And there is a doubt that by eating itself, it would eventually destroy itself.

But leaving aside jokes in so grave a matter, even if it were granted that it is a "living animal" (as <margin>Plato Averroes</margin> **Plato**, **Aristotle**, and many wise men seem to have found), it is certainly not an animal contained under the standard genus of animals. For those things which are in this world-machine are divided by a prior division before they even arrive at the category of "animal." But even if it were called an "animal" according to a certain analogy or likeness, why could its arrangements not have been ordered differently? Why is it repugnant for a human to have only one eye in the forehead, as is said of certain people? Why could the upper jaw not be made movable and the lower jaw fixed in other living creatures, just as we see in the <term>crocodile</term> <note>Medieval naturalists often cited the crocodile as the only animal that moves its upper jaw instead of its lower one</note>? Why could other animals not have double knees, like the **Camel**? What contradiction would there be if a man had four arms and only one ear? These things were so coordinated by the **Supreme Moderator** <note>God</note> that they could have been arranged otherwise without any contradiction, were it not for the presupposed condition of a specific nature which that same Maker established.

But let us come to this "worldly animal." By what necessity is the sea and land so disposed that the ocean enters through the very narrow mouths of **Abyla** and the high promontory of **Calpe**—which antiquity called the **Pillars of Hercules** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note>? Why is it necessary that from there it immediately spreads far and wide, distending into the **Tuscan Sea** (which they call the **Tyrrhenian**), then narrowing into the **Adriatic Gulf**, then dilating into the **Syrian Sea**, then flowing around the **Aegean**—which is called the **Archipelago** because of the most beautiful multitude of islands lying within it? And from there, squeezed through the narrowest mouths, it becomes the **Hellespont** and the **Propontis** where it expands, and where it is pressed again it becomes the **Thracian Bosphorus**? When it pours out again, it becomes the **Euxine Sea**—that is, the "Hospitable Sea" <note>original: *Pontus euxinus*; the Black Sea</note>—its name changed because the customs of the wild nations there were softened, whereas it was first called **Axenus**—that is, "Inhospitable"—due to the truly savage nature of its inhabitants. And again, when it is mixed with the **Maeotian Marshes** <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, it is named the **Cimmerian Bosphorus**. What necessity is there, likewise, that the **Nile** reaches Egypt through the Ethiopians and Arabs, and the **Tanais** <note>The Don River</note> runs through both parts of **Scythia** and almost into the middle of the Maeotian...

### That God Knows Particulars. Chapter XVIII.

**N**ow other arrows must be turned back against the <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: *physicos*; referring here to those who study the physical world and natural laws, often from a strictly Aristotelian perspective</note> so that, protected by the shield of unshakable truth, we may proceed to other matters. They were of the opinion that God (blessed be He) looks only upon higher and <term>universal</term> <note>In philosophy, "universals" are general concepts or categories (like "humanity"), while "particulars" are individual, specific things (like "this specific person")</note> things, while individual <term>particulars</term> are either held in low esteem or entrusted to secondary causes. It is as if they thought the divine intellect would be lowered or perform a baser act if it were turned toward things of this sort. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle says: "To not see certain things is better and nobler than to see them." <margin>Averroes</margin> In interpreting him, the Arab [Averroes] says: "To be ignorant of base things is better than to know them." 

What, I ask, are those "base things" which it is better not to know than to know? Those things which do not exist cannot be known. Those things which *do* exist are certainly good. If they are good, how are they base? And if you contend that even some good things are base, what, I ask, are those "base goods"? If you mean an Angel, why not the heavens? And if the heavens, why not man? And if man, why not the elements where man dwells? Why not horses, and oxen, and all things serving man, and the specific traits included within man? Where shall we set the limits of His intelligence? In the heavens, or in the earth, the elements, the plants, or in living creatures? Where, I ask? 

<margin>Cicero</margin> And (to speak with Cicero) if God takes care for the heavens and the "island" which we call the world, He will also take care for its inhabitants, and the parts of the island—Europe, Asia, and Africa—and their dwellers. He cares for the great so that He may prefer them (for no one is great unless inspired by a divine breath) and for the small so that He may sustain them. For He made both the small and the great (as <margin>The Wise Man</margin> that Wise Man says <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom in the Bible, specifically Wisdom 6:7</note>). Since they themselves confess Him to be the Prince of the whole world, what will He do in His princedom if He is not granted the power of governance? And if He governs all things, how is it "better" that He be ignorant of even the lowest things which He governs than if He were to know them? Who forced Him into ignorance of physical, mathematical, and other things, even if they are the most minute? Who has measured His capacity? <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle, or <margin>Averroes</margin> Averroes? 

<margin>The Chaldeans</margin> Aristotle commends the opinion of the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Ancient Mesopotamian sages and astronomers often associated with early wisdom and star-knowledge</note> fathers, who investigated the knowledge of God with skillful wit; and yet he does not agree with them that God understands all things. The intellect of a wise man is not cheapened (good sirs) if he knows the grades, qualities, and powers of even the most minute herbs, juices, and stones. Nor is it cheapened if he knows the degrees, minutes, seconds, thirds, and hundredth parts of the heavenly bodies...

...of small things: let him know them. Solomon is commended by the voice of everyone, having the surname "the Wise" because he discoursed on everything from the <term>cedar of Lebanon</term> <note>A biblical metaphor for the grandest of trees</note> to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and because he spoke about cattle, birds, reptiles, and fish. Did his intellect and wisdom become cheap because of this? Did <margin>Aristotle</margin> <margin>Theophrastus</margin> **Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor, often called the "Father of Botany"</note> become cheap, who imitated him—one writing on the nature of animals, the other on the nature of plants? And if we wish to recall even more ancient figures: was not <margin>Hermes</margin> **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with secret wisdom and alchemy</note> the greatest in wisdom, who wrote of the singular harmony of certain animals, stones, and herbs? His grandfather <margin>Aesculapius</margin> **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine</note> (as some prefer) was held as a god along with <margin>Apollo</margin> **Apollo** because they were the first to apply the juices, leaves, and powders of herbs and roots to heal human bodies, having known their properties. I ask you, who are wiser: those ignorant of these things, or those who claimed the name of "wise" for themselves with such honor because of their knowledge of them? 

But they will say: They were wise not because of individual things, but because they contemplated the <term>species</term> <note>The general category or "kind" of a thing</note> and the universal nature of things. And how did they investigate the species of things, if not through experience gained from <term>particulars</term> <note>Individual, specific examples (e.g., this specific dog vs. the concept of "dog")</note> (as the teacher shows)? Nor could they know the species without the individuals, since the <term>universal</term> <note>A general concept that applies to many things</note> is nothing else (as they assert) but "one thing from many." How can this "one" be understood unless the "many" are also understood, from which that "one" is extracted by them—unless they use <margin>Plato</margin> **ideal reasons** <note>Plato’s Theory of Forms, which suggests abstract concepts have a higher reality; the author notes that his opponents do not accept this theory</note>, which they themselves do not uphold? 

And if it is not repugnant to a wise man to understand species, then it will not be <margin>Averroes</margin> <margin>ideas</margin> repugnant if he understands all species. He will be able, therefore, to know animals, little fish, worms, ants, and plants. But why, I ask, should he be ignorant of man, the overseer of the world? How shall he rule him like a prince, provide for his necessities, and judge him, unless he knows all his needs and his good and evil deeds? The wisdom of God thunders—and it is better to believe Him than <margin>CHRIST</margin> **Aristotle** or **Averroes**: *Your Father knows what you need.* <note>original: "Scit Pater ueſter quibus indigetis." (Matthew 6:8)</note> His <margin>David</margin> prophetic trumpet also thunders: *My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret; your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in your book all shall be written* <note>original: "Non eſt occultatũ os meũ a te... (Psalm 139:15-16)"</note>—so that they may receive worthy rewards for their good or ill deeds. 

They bring forward another point, which they consider their greatest strength: that the supreme mind cannot know these inferior things, lest it be moved by them, or lest its <margin><unclear>Hosea</unclear></margin> <note>The margin note likely references Hosea to contrast divine knowledge with human ignorance</note> simplicity be diminished by being perfected by them. I truly marvel how they equate the knowledge of the Most High God with our own, when <margin>Aristotle</margin> **Aristotle** says: "The intellect of God is simple, perfect, and from itself." And thus, from Himself, He understands all things that are in the world. Interpreting his words, <margin>Averroes</margin> **Averroes** puts a difference between God’s knowledge and ours: for ours is caused by being, but His is [the cause] of being. He does not wish to say openly that He is the *cause* of being, as Catholics freely profess, yet forced by the truth, he cannot remain silent. For earlier, through obscure words—which I know not whether a <margin><unclear>Averroes</unclear></margin> barbarian uttered barbarically, or whether he involved them studiously—he was forced to admit it unwillingly. 

Hear, I ask, these monstrous words: "The truth," he says, "is: first, that He knows all things; second, that He knows only Himself by a knowledge in being, which is the cause of their being." And to follow this barbarian in his barbaric speech: If knowledge in being in things is the cause of those things that exist, then by understanding He causes those things that exist. And if He understands them, is the understanding of them not in His intellect? Why then do you and your teacher mock **ideas**, which are nothing else...

<header>FIRST CANTICLE. XXV</header>

...they are nothing else but the knowledge of things and the patterns for making them in that **First Intellect**, which produces all things by knowing and commanding them. Nor does He take His knowledge from the object produced, nor is He moved, perfected, or forced to beg for understanding or stimulation by it, as our own intellect does. Nor does that Supreme Intellect fail by observing so many individual details. Rather, it is that "Unique Intellect" of <margin>Averroes</margin> **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Islamic philosopher who argued for a single, shared human intellect</note> that would fail in giving form to, directing, or illuminating so many individuals. 

O, what folly and madness! You imagine that the intellect you have manufactured is stronger than God, who manufactured all things—especially since God is the end of all things, toward whom all things are directed as toward one loved and desired, and by whom all these things are guided. 

"By Nature," they say. But what is this "Nature"? I have not yet found anyone who has explored what that "Nature" is of which they speak—whether it was manufactured by God, or whether it produced the world alongside Him as if it were God’s spouse. For they say: <note>original: "Deus, & nã nihil facit frustra"</note> **"God and Nature do nothing in vain,"** as if they were bringing forth the offspring of this world together. Nor can this "Nature" be matter or form, which do nothing and order nothing. Nor is it the underlying logic or the degrees of things, for they imply something universal through this "Nature" of theirs that acts alongside God. But they have never explained what that thing actually is. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
They profess, however, that God acts together with Nature and has disposed all things well; yet elsewhere they assert that God does nothing except as an attracting goal <note>Referring to the Aristotelian "Unmoved Mover" who draws things toward Him through desire rather than active intervention</note>. And if the secondary causes, with which He co-acts, are this "Nature," then who ordained them? Who established that they should cooperate? 

"Nature," they say, "is the principle of motion and rest." But what is this principle of motion and rest except an inclination implanted in things subject to motion by some agent? And whether they like it or not, they must come to an agreement on one source from which all motion and order proceed, as they themselves teach. And if I did not fear exposing myself to the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because he taught while walking (peripatos)</note> to be torn apart as a rash man, I would ask: what is this Nature, to which they say universals are "better known"? What is this mutual process from Nature to us, and vice versa? Who answers us in this <note>original: "pilarum ludo"</note> **game of ball**? <note>A metaphor for the exchange of cause and effect or intellectual debate</note> What is this Nature, again, which provides us with the first principles by which we might know conclusions? Is it some general active force? Or something aggregated from natural things? Or the order of those things itself? Is it something capable of reason, or is it an element, a stone, the heavens, or some such thing lacking in sense? 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Averroes</margin>
If it does not feel and does not understand, how are these principles "known" to it? But if it is an intellectual being, what is this Nature? Is it us, or the Intelligences, or God Himself? If it is us, how were these things "known" to Nature before us, from which we supposedly receive our knowledge? If the "Intelligences" <note>Celestial beings in medieval cosmology that move the spheres</note> are this Nature, how can they be outside the realm of natural and physical speculation (as they themselves teach), since they do not move while they are moving? And why do they not simply say: "these principles are known to the separate or joined Intelligences"? 

But if God is this Nature, why do they name it as something separate from Him when they say "God and Nature"? Is this Nature perhaps some intellect outside the universe, or a fifth or sixth essence? Perhaps the **Averroists** will say: Nature is a single, perfect intellect that understands all these things. But how will this intellect be the "principle of motion and rest" in that which is, according to what it is? This intellect would then have to be inside living creatures, fleas, flies, the smallest plants, and the elements.

...moving them by their own motions. Therefore, this <term>unique intellect</term> <note>The author is refuting the Averroistic idea that there is only one "active intellect" shared by all of humanity or the universe.</note> will belong not only to men, but also to all things: why, then, will all things not understand? Is this that blessed nature, which arranged the heavens, the members of bodies, and all the organs—of which you say: **that she does not fail in necessary things, nor does she do anything in vain**? <note>original: "non deficit in necessariis, nec aliqd frustra agit" — a classic Aristotelian principle.</note> For she admits no limb, nor heaven, nor the tiniest speck of dust, nor any motion that is superfluous, since she has arranged all things perfectly. But who is the one ordering all these things, if not He whom we profess to be God? Why, then, when speaking of nature, do you imply something separate from God himself? Perhaps it is so you do not have to confess that God made the world—which you impiously denied. Yet you have conceded that God acted together with nature, as if God could not achieve anything without nature. For what is the condition of this nature, that it should supply what is lacking in the most perfect God? Again, is this nature from itself, or produced by God? If from itself: then there will be two beings who exist of their own power, and two first causes—in short, two Gods. If it was produced by God: then God will be the architect of this universal nature; why then would He not also be the architect of particular things? What dreams are these? They will say: "In particular things, a particular cause runs together with the universal." If the first cause <note>God</note> runs together and acts with it, does He understand what He does? Or is He in a worse condition than the lower causes? If He understands those particulars in which He acts alongside nature, you speak foolishly when you say that He does not understand particulars.

<header>THE SECOND TONE.</header>

# HOW GREAT A DISSONANCE OF DISCORDANT SOUND
# THE WISE OF THE WORLD ARE FOUND TO HAVE IN
# THEIR TEACHINGS. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Aristippus</margin>
<margin>Ariston</margin>
<margin>Alexander</margin>
<margin>Averroes</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Al-Ghazali</margin>
<margin>Averroes</margin>
<margin>Lucretius</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
<margin>Iarchas</margin>
<margin>Apollonius of Tyana</margin>
<margin>Iamblichus</margin>
<margin>Porphyry</margin>
<margin>Proclus</margin>
<margin>Hermias</margin>
<margin>Syrianus</margin>
<margin>Timaeus</margin>
<margin>Thales</margin>
<margin>Anaximander</margin>
<margin>Anaximenes</margin>
<margin>Anaxagoras</margin>
<margin>Diogenes</margin>
**S**O GREAT a dissonance do those who are called the "wise of the world" strike and stir upon this earthly instrument <note>The "earthly instrument" refers to the world or the human understanding of it.</note>, that their schools cannot agree—neither in doctrine, nor in morals, nor in religion, nor even in the ultimate purpose for which they perform all things. They make a noise with such a horrid harshness that no one can listen to them sounding all at once without the harmony being utterly shattered. This harmony (as musicians define it) is a concord of strings or voices sounding together in perfect measures without any offense to the ear. Yet these men, though nurtured in the same family and taught under the same master, are utterly dissonant. The disciples of Socrates, Aristippus and Ariston, disagree so much regarding our ultimate purpose that one placed it in pleasure, while the other placed it in virtue. The chief followers of Aristotle, Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (c. 200 AD), a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> and Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher.</note>, split his teachings into a fork in the road, especially in the matter of the soul: for the former asserts the soul is mortal, while the latter asserts there is a <term>unique intellect</term> <note>The theory that all humans share a single, communal mind.</note> in all people. Thus they disagree not only with each other, but with the truth. Aristotle himself, a student of Plato for twenty-one years, disagreed so much with the doctrine and morals of his teacher that he pursued him with accusations and false slanders. The Saracen Al-Ghazali <note>Algazel (1058–1111), a Persian theologian who famously critiqued Greek philosophy.</note> rose up against all philosophers; and the Arab Averroes strove to attack him in turn, but like a snake, he was broken in the very attempt. Lucretius, the Epicurean, disagrees both with his fellow students and with himself—at one moment chanting that God has fellowship with mortals, and at another denying it; thus he pursues manifest dissonance in many other things. The Pythagoreans, moreover, are cut into many parts, being utterly dissonant regarding the transmigration of souls. Iarchas the Brahman and Apollonius of Tyana asserted that transformations even into beasts occur. From this source come those celebrated metamorphoses of which they sing: one changed into a wolf, that woman into a nightingale, another into a laurel tree, and other changes of this kind. But Iamblichus and Porphyry utterly rejected such transmigrations into beasts, not admitting that a soul can be torn from its center once it has been fixed there. Furthermore, Proclus, Hermias, and Syrianus thought it a horrifying crime that a celestial soul should be cast headlong into beasts. Timaeus of Locri, a most noble Pythagorean, asserts that these transformations were introduced merely to terrify men. Thales of Miletus thought that water was the principle of all things; but his student Anaximander believed the principles of things were infinite. His own student, Anaximenes, attributed the causes of all things to infinite air. Their disciples, Anaxagoras and Diogenes, then disagreed: the former persuaded himself that an infinite matter, woven from dissimilar particles, was the source and seed of all things according to its condition; while the latter thought that air (yet possessing divine reason) was the mother of all things. It would be superfluous and foolish to unravel all the points on which...

<header>OF THE FIRST SONG</header>

the wise of the world, disagreeing, strike a horrendous noise into the ears of their listeners. This happens to them because they have departed from the One, in whom all ought to meet, each one going his own way and following the figment of his own speculations. Hence their teachings (because they lack the One who grants to all things that they exist and harmoniously agree) are founded upon a confused multitude and are dissolved. "For everything exists for this reason," <note>original: "Omne .n. ideo eſt"</note> says Boethius, <margin>Boethius</margin> "because it is one in number." And all things, though they are very different, sound together within; for voices agree by that same proportion of numbers. For consonance (as the Musicians teach) is the concord <margin>Music</margin> of similar and dissimilar voices reduced into one. <margin>Different authors on consonance.</margin> Nor would they be dissonant if one man—like the divine Plato with his follower Plotinus, infused with a certain divine power—were to lift the mind; or if, with Pythagoras, he were to wrap the sacred mysteries of God and nature in numbers and enigmas; or if, with the sweetness of Ammonius, he were to equate truth with the mind; or if he were to delight the soul with the famous eloquence of Socrates; or if, with the sharpness and obscure speech of Heraclitus, he were to incite and inflame the powers of his listeners; or if, with the genius and most rapid speech of Carneades, he were to lead them into a state of wonder. There are others also, walking with various steps. Aristotle refreshes the mind with order, <margin>Aristotle</margin> yet he leaves it entangled by a crippled and ambiguous speech. <margin>Simplicius</margin> Simplicius expands the mind with an abundance of words. <margin>Porphyry</margin> Porphyry feeds wandering souls with a variety of doctrines. <margin>Themistius</margin> Themistius renders his listeners happy and attentive with concise speech. <margin>Alexander</margin> Alexander of Aphrodisias, with great constancy, expresses the very juices <note>A metaphor for the "essence" or "vitality" of philosophy.</note> of philosophy. Proclus <margin>Proclus</margin> flourishes with Attic fertility. And to turn myself toward the Saracens, Arabs, Egyptians, Persians, and Bactrians: <margin>Algazel</margin> Algazel the Saracen, taught by a due piety, intrepidly transcends the boundaries of common philosophy. <margin>Avempace</margin> Avempace and Al-Farabi, the Arabs, <margin>Al-Farabi</margin> solidify their feet with gravity. <margin>Averroes</margin> Averroes appears unshaken at first glance, but (in the judgment of many wise men) all his internal parts are dissolved by decay, so that he brings little concord to the divine and worldly harmony. Hermes Trismegistus the Egyptian (as it is commonly said), <margin>Mercury</margin> but a Madianite (as it pleases others), being united with his own mind, always smells of the divine and transcends human discourse. Iamblichus, devoted to numbers and mysteries, <margin>Iamblichus</margin> attempts to betray <note>In this context, "prodere" likely means to bring forth or reveal, rather than to act treacherously.</note> the Pythagorean and Egyptian secrets. Zoroaster, <margin>Zoroaster</margin> Orpheus, and Charondas the Persian, penetrating into the secrets of nature <margin>Orpheus</margin> so that they might marry the world to its own magic, sound the sweet <margin>Charondas</margin> epithalamia <note term="epithalamia">Wedding songs or poems, here used metaphorically to describe the mystical "marriage" of the physical and spiritual worlds.</note> of the Hymen of nature. But the wise men of the Hebrews <margin>Hebrews</margin> and Chaldeans, instructed by divine oracles, always sing of a more perfect Hymen: namely, <margin>Chaldeans</margin> of this cosmic machine with its archetype and the human world. I omit many later figures who, adhering to any one of these, produced their own songs and their own sounds. All of these (though with different instruments), as long as they sound by the same numbers, they too produce a sweet harmony. When, however, they depart from the proper numbers and from that consonance based on unity—from which all concord comes—they are like dissonant and offending strings, and must be cast out entirely from every harmonious consonance.

<margin>Wonderful harmony among the doctors.</margin>
...lay the foundations of the divine house. Moses, Job, David, Solomon, and all the Prophets, together with those who wrote the Gospels, and Paul with the entire Apostolic assembly, along with the super-heavenly intelligences, create a most sweet harmony in the assembly of God: indeed with diverse voices, yet with the same sound. For dissimilar voices do not create dissonance, but a concert, provided they meet in the One. For what consonance would there be if all the strings of a lyre rendered a low sound, or all a high one? Or if (to touch upon the principles of music) the <term>hypate</term> <note>The lowest string/note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note>, <term>perhypate</term> <note>The string next to the lowest.</note>, <term>lichanos</term> <note>The "indicator" string, played with the index finger.</note>, <term>mese</term> <note>The middle string, serving as the fundamental pitch.</note>, <term>paramese</term> <note>The string next to the middle.</note>, and all the following strings of the instruments—so named by musicians—all produced the <term>hypate</term>, the lowest tone representing Saturn? What would be the consonance of the planets if all marched with the heaviness of Saturn, or all ran with the velocity of the Moon? What beauty would there be in the body if all the members were eyes, or all were ears? For just as beauty (as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> teach) results from various members harmonizing with one another, so from various voices arises <term>diapentic</term> <note>original: "diapentica"; the interval of a fifth.</note>, <term>diapasonic</term> <note>original: "diapasonica"; the interval of an octave.</note>, <term>diatessaronic</term> <note>original: "diatessaronica"; the interval of a fourth.</note>, or <term>diatonic</term> <note>A scale proceeding by whole tones and semitones.</note> harmony. This harmony is not founded on various voices, but on the concordant sound that results from those diverse voices. Therefore, those sounding forth do not generate dissonance in the divine lyre: if John and Augustine lift themselves up toward the fervent and sharp Seraphim; if Ambrose and Matthew proffer the heavy voices of their judgments among the Thrones; if Luke and Gregory are delighted by Cherubic sweetness; if Jerome with Mark, with the more robust voice of the Powers and Virtues, compresses and suffocates the dissonant blasts of heretics; if Solomon and Bernard, with Gabriel, sing the wedding songs of the bridegroom and the bride for the heavenly nuptials. And coming to the Greeks: Basil with Ezekiel ever brings forth divine things with the superior minds. Gregory Nazianzenus with Jeremiah, with a tragic voice, compassionating the suffering bridegroom and bride, also deplores the slaughter of those invited to their nuptials. Isaiah and John (whose surname is Chrysostom) resound with the Archangels with marvelous eloquence. Daniel and that John of Damascus treat the sacraments of God with a clearer voice; but the latter describes the lower and domestic influences, while the former describes the super-heavenly source from which these lower things flow. Others followed as harmonious successors in this divine instrument. Duns Scotus and Francis correspond to the high-sounding Augustine; but the former, with slower motion, makes a heavier and more robust sound, while the latter, with swifter course, resounds more sharply. Albertus [Magnus], with his weighty judgment and skillful investigation of the secrets of both natures, emulates Ambrose. The angelic Thomas [Aquinas] follows Bernard in voice and doctrine and ineffable sweetness, but Augustine in his breadth. Bonaventure sings with Gregory in a modulation more devout than learned. Aegidius and Petrus Aureolus, with a certain Roman eloquence, savor of Jerome. Henry of Ghent refreshes elevated minds with the sublimity of his doctrine along with Origen. I omit the marvelous agreement of so many other various prophets and doctors, both ancient and more recent, with the various supreme minds: so that the latter resound harmoniously in the upper part of the instrument, and the former in the lower part, just like the musical birds...

...of various species. However, those who are called Philosophers and the wise of the world do not agree in voice or teaching any more than animals of different kinds do: of which some produce lowing, some neighing, others bleating, others roaring, others barking, or braying—emitting such great clashing dissonance that their concord seems impossible unless they are filled with the same spirit, which could lead them to unified character and sounds. 

<margin>Lactantius</margin>For, as Firmianus <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian advisor to Emperor Constantine, known as the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent Latin.</note> says, dissonance occurs for them because they have withdrawn (as we said) from that unique master of all truths and giver of consonance. Instead, they presumptuously attempt to scrutinize by their own strength things that God willed to be obstructed rather than hidden—namely, the nature of heavenly and inferior things. These things are far removed from us and can neither be touched by hand nor perceived by the senses; and yet they dispute the reasoning of all those things in such a way that they want what they assert to appear proven and known. From this, they have not only fallen into error themselves but, being blind, have led many others who cling to them into a pit of darkness and errors; and (alas, miserable to say) they continue to lead others day by day.

### How Great a Dissonance with which the Wise of the World Laid its Foundations. Chapter III.

<margin>Leucippus, Democritus, Diodorus</margin>**A**nd so that we may prove the truths we have spoken, let us again bring forward some of their foundations—but only a few, lest readers be affected by the weariness of their great dissonance or be disgusted by them, and lest we seem to have made a heap out of things with which others have filled many books. And let us pour out the outrages of Leucippus, Democritus, and Diodorus <note>These philosophers were proponents of Atomism, the theory that the world is made of tiny, indivisible particles.</note>, who claimed that certain light little bodies existed—some smooth, some rough, some round, some partly angular or pointed, others hooked—and from these, the heavens and earth were formed by a certain chance collision, with no governing nature. 

<margin>Thales</margin>Thales of Miletus <note>Often considered the first Greek philosopher (c. 624 – c. 546 BC).</note>, declared wise by the testimony of his own Apollo, believed that water was the principle of all things, since it seemed to him that all members of an animal are nourished by water. It resides, as it were, in the very center, just as in the center of animal bodies, the watery humor <note>The liquid components of the body.</note> provides food for all the members. The ancients called this water Tethys <note>A Greek sea goddess.</note> and the "fixed marsh," and they considered its power feminine, just as they considered Neptune's masculine; being stable, it would more perfectly receive the collision of all the stars. 

<margin>Anaximenes, Diogenes</margin>Anaximenes the Epicurean <note>Likely referring to Anaximenes of Miletus; the author may be following a tradition that links him to later atomists.</note> and Diogenes the Freedman agreed on a single principle, but they believed it was air, which is prior to water and the medium of respiration by which growth is received. For it is said that spirit and air are known by the same name among the Hebrews <note>The Hebrew word "Ruach" translates as spirit, wind, or breath.</note>. 

<margin>Hipparchus, Heraclitus</margin>Hipparchus of Metapontum and Heraclitus of Ephesus said that this one principle was fire, because it is the most subtle of all bodies and that from which the heavens are compacted. These, existing as a kind of light, send down their own all-moving light which is mixable with all things, so that from it all things are generated (with discord and friendship intervening). 

<margin>Empedocles, The Poets</margin>Empedocles, the son of Meton from Sicily, lest he should err, taught that all four elements together were that one principle. Following him, the poets said that Jupiter represented the ether, Pluto the earth, bounteous Juno the air, and "Mentis" <note>Probably referring to Nestis, the name Empedocles used for the element of water.</note>—which nourishes the rivers of men with wet tears—was the principle of water. 

<margin>Empedocles</margin>Empedocles continues, stating that earth is the matter and the primary subject of all things, which [gives] forms and figures...

<margin>Anaxagoras</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
<margin>Alcyon</margin>

<margin>Epicurus</margin>
<margin>Socrates</margin>

<margin>Diodorus Siculus</margin>
<margin>Anaximenes & Diogenes</margin>
<margin>Hippasus & Heraclitus</margin>
...might hold the essence of things; which water, air, and fire are unable to do. Anaxagoras of Clazomenae believed that all bodies were composed of similar parts, and that these "homoeomeries" <note>original: "homoeomorias" — Anaxagoras's theory that substances are made of tiny particles that contain the essence of the whole.</note> were subject to continuous division; when gathered together, they formed the underlying principle. Pythagoras, ascending higher than many might believe, judged that numbers and their underlying "measures" <note>original: "metras"</note>—that is, the adapted proportions which they call harmonies, concerts, and coherences—were the principles of things. He did not mean those numbers used by merchants, but formal or natural ones; the knowledge of these is hidden among those who have learned to philosophize and theologize through numbers. Pythagoras was followed by Alcyon of Croton, who spoke of one effective principle, but two (the "binary" or "dyad") for the material, subjective principle and the beginning of all multiplicity. But Anaximander of Miletus, going further, considered a certain infinity (which they call "indeterminate matter") to be the underlying principle. And because it lacks its own nature, quantity, and form, he thought it was the very substance of perpetual generation: so that infinite worlds are reborn and regenerated into infinity. Epicurus, the son of Neocles the Athenian, followed in the philosophical footsteps of Democritus and said the principles of things were bodily, solid, uncreated, perceived by the mind, and everlasting; they can neither be destroyed, nor crushed, nor changed in any way. To these principles—beyond the shape and size given to them by his teachers—he also attributed weight. Socrates, the son of Sophronicus, and Plato, the son of Ariston, both Athenians, posited three principles: God, Matter, and the Idea. Aristotle of Stagira, the son of Nicomachus, asserted the principles were Entelechy <note><term>Entelechy</term>: from the Greek 'entelecheia,' meaning the full realization or "form" of a thing as opposed to its mere potential.</note> (or Form), Matter, and Privation. He counted Privation among the principles despite having taught elsewhere that "equivocal" terms should not be counted. Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, placed God and Matter as the principles: so that the former is the active force, while the latter is the passive; with the four elements being intermediate. Diodorus Siculus, seeking deeper things, wished to describe this birth of the world; but after wandering through many words about his own investigation, he confuses the reader more than he teaches. Here I truly wonder greatly: for we have no explanation from any of these men who establish "matter" as the underlying principle as to whether it was fashioned by Blessed God, or whether that "makeable nature"—deprived of the beauty of all forms—fashioned the world alongside Him. Was it a companion lacking any shape, a co-eternal wife of Demogorgon <note>A primordial god in late Roman and medieval mythology, often associated with the underworld or the "creator" of the other gods.</note>, the father of gods (as the poets dream)? Or was it shaken out of the brain of Jupiter, like Pallas Athena? The mind cannot rest while we contemplate a nature lacking all virtue and all form without its Craftsman. Indeed, we have word from none of them as to who He actually was.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient philosophical opinions, shifting from the "principles" of the physical world to the nature of the human soul (anima). The author lists various conflicting definitions of the soul to demonstrate the "dissonance" of human reason before reaching a theological or Platonic conclusion.</meta>

<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
## OF THE FIRST SONG ##

<margin>Pythagoras, Dicearchus, Anaximenes, Xenophanes, Parmenides, Boetes, Epicurus, Diogenes the Cynic, Anaximander, Empedocles, Avempace, Anaxagoras, Crates of Thebes, Democritus, Leucippus, Critias, Virgil, Hippocrates, Asclepiades, Zeno, Galen, Hipparchus, Virgil, Heraclitus of Ephesus, Heraclides of Pontus, Critolaus, Posidonius, Chrysippus, Egyptians, Chaldeans, Aristotle, Alexander, Averroes, Pythagoras, Timaeus of Locri, Plato, and the same</margin>

...[regarded] the soul as similar to fire, and from this [it is given] to man. **Pythagoras** held this, while others thought it was the tiny particles found in the air; still others thought it was that which moves them. **Dicearchus** believed the soul to be a body moving of its own accord. **Anaximenes** believed it to be air; **Xenophanes** thought it was made of earth and water; **Parmenides** and **Boetes** from earth and fire. **Epicurus** believed it was a mixture of fire, air, and spirit proceeding through a similarity of atoms; <note>Epicurus’s theory of the soul involved four components, though the author here simplifies it to a blend of elements and atomic motion.</note> for this reason, when one is moved, the whole spirit is moved along with it. This is why it happens that when a man hears mention of snow, he sometimes recalls both its whiteness and its cold at the same time. Or when someone tastes something bitter, others are stunned; and others yawn along with those who yawn. In this, he followed the most ancient **Maurasphes the Arab**, who maintained that the soul consists of the entrance of this spirit; but as for its exit, they say it is resolved into nothing, as is set down in their theology.

**Diogenes the Cynic**, along with **Anaximenes**, believed the soul was air; **Empedocles** thought it was made of several elements; **Avempace** <note>original: "Auēdachis" — likely referring to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajja, known as Avempace.</note> thought it was from several elements, along with love and victory. <note>Empedocles’s forces of "Love" and "Strife."</note> **Anaxagoras**, the contemplator of the heavens, said it was something impassible <note>incapable of suffering or being changed by external forces</note> that does not receive passions. **Crates of Thebes** believed there was no soul at all, but that bodies were moved by nature. **Democritus** and his colleague **Leucippus** thought it was heat, or a round fiery shape, or a spirit made of infinite atoms with such ease of motion that every body is a path for it. **Critias** thought it was the blood poured from the heart; **Virgil** <note>original: "Maro"</note> emulated him when he sang: *He poured out his life along with his blood.* **Hippocrates of Cos** thought it was a thin spirit diffused through the body; **Asclepiades** believed it was the flesh with the exercise of the five senses acting in harmony with it.

**Zeno**, the leader of the Stoics, believed it was born from the support of divine fire—that is, providence. **Galen of Pergamum** believed it was the "complexion" <note>The specific balance of the four humors</note> of the body; **Hipparchus** thought it was the vigor of fire, of which the **Poet** <note>Virgil</note> says: *Fiery is their vigor and heavenly their origin.* **Heraclitus of Ephesus** thought it a spark of stellar essence; **Heraclides of Pontus** thought it was light. **Critolaus the Peripatetic** believed it was born from a fifth essence; <note>The "quintessence" or aether, distinct from the four terrestrial elements.</note> **Posidonius** believed it was an "Idea." **Chrysippus** thought the soul was spirit, because we breathe and live by one and the same thing: we breathe by spirit and live by the soul. The **Egyptians** saw it as a certain force passing through all bodies; the **Chaldeans** saw it as a power without a fixed form, yet capable of receiving all external forms.

**Aristotle**, after refuting many things the ancients said about the soul, decreed that it is the "perfection" <note>original: "p̄fectionē" — referring to the Greek "entelechy," the realization or full potential of a living thing.</note> of a natural organic body having the potential for life, or the principle of understanding, sensing, and of any movement whatsoever. In this (in my judgment), he declares the **effect** of the soul rather than its **essence** or **origin**. It is as if someone wanted to define who the Pope or the Emperor is, and said: "He is the one who moves the army, rules his horse, or commands in the kingdom." Concerning its nature and duration, however, he so restrained himself and obscured his opinions that no one to this day can clearly define what he felt. Hence his chief followers, **Alexander** and **Averroes**, reached a fork in the road; and how far each of them is removed from all piety, religion, and truth is now plain to see.

**Pythagoras** thought the soul was a certain divine genus existing within men, full of forms, but submerged and hindered by the "corporeal forest" <note>original: "corporea sylua" — a metaphor for physical matter (Greek: 'hyle').</note> so that it seems to have drunk from the river Lethe (that is, oblivion). **Timaeus of Locri** and **Plato**, with the rest of the Academics, imitate him. They studied to hide the essence and nature of this soul as if they were divine sacred rites, or perhaps they did not express what they did not even understand. As **Plato** testifies in the tenth book of the *Laws*: *What kind of thing the soul is, and what power it has, almost everyone seems to have been ignorant.* If they did hand down anything concerning it, they proceeded through numbers as things better known to them; whose nature is fourfold, and how from the vocal to the formal, and...

<summary>This page catalogs a vast array of conflicting ancient definitions of the human soul, ranging from elemental theories (fire, air, blood) to Aristotle's functional definition, which the author critiques for failing to capture the soul's true essence.</summary>
<keywords>soul, anima, Aristotle, Pythagoras, Plato, Greek philosophy, Epicurus, entelechy, quintessence, oblivion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient philosophical opinions regarding the soul (anima), moving from physical definitions to the specific locations of the soul within the body, and finally transitioning into Chapter V, which discusses the "ultimate end" or goal of human life.</meta>

<page-num>XXIX</page-num>

->**SECOND TONE.**<-

<margin>Anaxagoras, Aristotle, Severus, Plutarch, Atticus</margin>
From there, they fail to perceive how one must ascend toward the rational and then to the divine number; they either judged this progress through number to be a kind of raving, or, walking with longer and wandering strides after **Pythagoras** and **Plato**, they turned off into various paths. **Anaxagoras** <note>The text reads Anaxander, but the marginalia and context suggest Anaxagoras or a confusion of the two regarding the soul as a numerical principle.</note> said the soul is a number; **Aristoxenus** called it a self-moving number. Others thought the soul came from unity, as if from the indivisible, and from duality, as if from the divisible. **Severus** affirms it has a <term>geometric essence</term> <note>The belief that the soul's structure follows the laws of geometry.</note>, composing it from the "point" and "distance"—the latter being divisible, while the former is indivisible. **Plutarch** and **Atticus** say its divisible part is irrational, while the indivisible part is divine; the divine part emanates and composes, while the other takes the role of the subject. They add, of course, that the soul is unbegotten according to its substance, but begotten according to its form.

<margin>Plotinus, Amesius, Theodore, Porphyry, Proclus, Plato</margin>
**Plotinus**, speaking more as a physicist, places the soul midway between the intellect and the senses; it possesses the indivisibility of the former, but is divisible through bodies like the latter. **Amesius** and **Theodore** climb higher, drawing the origin of their opinion (according to **Porphyry**) from the <term>apsis</term> <note>original: "apside"; likely referring to the celestial vault or a specific Neoplatonic source.</note>; they posit two intellects above their soul: one containing the <term>ideas of universals</term> <note>The perfect forms of general concepts like "Beauty" or "Justice".</note>, and another of particulars, with the soul as the mediator between them. **Proclus** calls it one and many, indivisible and yet multiplied according to the number of subjects. Nor did he fully explain **Plato's** opinion on the soul, having emulated him closely; for in many places (especially when writing to **Dionysius**) Plato declares that the secrets of God are not to be made public. Nor do these "wise men of the world" set down any harmony regarding where the soul is located.

<margin>Hippocrates</margin>
**Hippocrates** asserts that the power of the soul primarily has its seat in the head. **Epicurus** denies this, because many animals live for a time even when the head is cut off—as if no damage were done to the whole—such as bees and drones.

<margin>Empedocles</margin>
**Empedocles** established the primary force of the soul in the heart. But **Epicurus** also denies this, because crocodiles live for some time and resist violence even when their hearts have been torn out.

<margin>Stoics, Chrysippus, Moses</margin>
The **Stoics** place it in the heart, not by means of the blood (as **Empedocles** said), but by spirit, so that it is located in the spirit rather than in the heart, as **Chrysippus** suggests. Others place it in the blood, a view which seems to be drawn from **Moses**, who (by divine command) forbade the eating of blood because the soul of the living creature is within it. Philosophers and doctors are still litigating this matter before the judge <note>A reference to Horace’s "adhuc sub iudice lis est," meaning the case is still undecided.</note>.

### That they disagree no less in describing the end which all things seek. Chapter V.

<margin>Augustine, M. Varro, Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Posidonius, Hecato, Dionysius the Babylonian, Stoics, Epicureans, Eudoxus of Cnidus, Cyrenaics, Plotinus</margin>
<insert>I</insert>t would be too long and tedious to bring forward all the many kinds of opinions regarding the <term>end</term> <note>The "telos" or ultimate purpose and highest good of human existence.</note> of this our life and condition. **Augustine** mentions two hundred and eighty-eight opinions collected by **Marcus Varro**. Six are also commemorated by **Plotinus** in his work *On Happiness*; omitting these, we shall more briefly run through those which are handled more frequently in the schools and in the streets. **Zeno of Citium**, **Cleanthes**, **Posidonius**, **Hecato**, and **Dionysius the Babylonian**—all Stoics—judged our end to be the laborious virtues; but **Antisthenes** expressed it as the virtue of the mind. The **Epicureans**, however, and especially **Aristippus**, **Eudoxus of Cnidus**, and the **Cyrenaics**, place it in pleasures, which are the opposite of labors. The **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> place it in speculation. The **Platonists**, always savoring of divine decrees, gave opinions close enough to the Christian religion; these decree the end of man to be union with the Highest Good, as **Plotinus** sets down at the end of his volume *On the One and the Good*. To reach this, they say one must recover the wings of a double philosophy, by which one flies out from this dark forest and mother of all evils toward the Mind through virtue.

It then introduces the various philosophical definitions of the "Highest Good," contrasting Stoic virtue and Epicurean pleasure with the Platonist ideal of union with God.</summary>

...through wisdom, however, toward God. These are the more famous opinions of the philosophical sects concerning the **end** <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the *summum bonum*, the highest good or ultimate purpose of human life.</note>, after which there are other more lowly ones. **Pyrrho of Elis**, **Eurycholus**, and **Xenophanes** take away all happiness <note>original: "fœlicitatē"</note> entirely; for which reason they are mocked by everyone. **Periander of Corinth** and **Lycophron** place it in honor and dignity. Others, however, place it in health; whence that wise man used to pray: *that there might be a sound mind in a sound body* <note>original: "ut eſſet mens ſana in corpore ſano," a famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal.</note>. **Herillus of Chalcedon** and many followers of **Socrates** place it in knowledge; **Orpheus**, under the fable of Narcissus, in beauty; **Epicharmus** and **Sphaerus** thought happiness was the "Idea." **Milo of Croton** and the greatest part of the athletes placed it in strength; **Bion of Borysthenes** in prudence; **Bias of Priene** in wisdom; **Thales of Miletus** in a heap composed of such effects; **Pittacus of Mitylene** in acting well. 

I omit what the more base sort feel, some of whom live just like **Sardanapalus** <note>An ancient Assyrian king who became a proverbial symbol of extreme luxury and decadence.</note>, having made no choice of life; others, indeed, labor in a continuous wind so that they might acquire what they never possess. But let us return to those who are held to be wise. For these, since they held to the closed boundary of man, were unable to teach the way. If, however, they handed down anything consistent with religion, they did so as if imitating **Moses** like apes, asserting through various fictions that they had learned it from oracles. For the legislator of the Egyptians, **Osiris**, claimed to learn from **Mercury**; **Zoroaster** for the Bactrians and Persians from **Oromasdes**; **Charondas** for the Carthaginians from **Saturn**; **Solon** for the Athenians from **Minerva**; **Zautrastes** among the Arimaspi from a good divinity; **Zamolxis** for the Scythians from **Vesta**; **Minos** for the Cretans from **Jove**; **Lycurgus** for the Lacedaemonians from **Apollo**; **Numa Pompilius** for the Romans from the nymph **Egeria**; **Muhammad** for the Arabs from the **Angel Gabriel**. In these you will find nothing harmonious, except what natural law, implanted in human minds by God, suggests—or what they stealthily received from the common teacher, **Moses**. But the last of these, having plucked parts from Moses and parts from the Christians, confuses both. Among these elements of the world's wisdom, therefore, the wise men fight with such great a contest that you would not know to which of them you should award the palm, until (as **Firmianus** <note>Lactantius, an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero."</note> says) someone should descend from heaven to pass judgment on the opinions of each one. But in the meantime, since we cannot endure their discords, let us leave them aside and return to our own people—to the source from which our people drew harmony, and those others drew dissonance.

# Chapter VI.

However many have handed down the institutions of music, they teach that the foundation of consonance is **One**, into which many similar and dissimilar things come together. And the poets and grammarians call that harmonic sound, which many singing together produce, **Polymnia** <note>Polyhymnia, the Muse of sacred poetry and many songs.</note>, as if it were a coming together of many songs into one. From this, it is necessary that this concord proceed from instruments, strings, pipes, or fitting voices, if harmonic sounds or voices are to come together into one. For no one can make the roaring of lions, the lowing of oxen, the neighing of a horse, or the braying of a donkey harmonize together. Nor can strings made from the guts of a **wolf** and a **lamb** (as we have learned from experience) be brought into any consonance, because their foundations are dissonant <note>A common medieval and Renaissance musical myth: it was believed that if a string made of wolf gut was placed on a lute with a string of sheep gut, they could never be tuned to one another and would produce a "jarring" sound.</note>. Nevertheless, the voices of men of different languages and nations come together in an easy meeting, because for them there is a single foundation according to their species. Many musical birds of different species also harmonize, because they have a single nearby genus and a sign from above. Artificial instruments also harmonize together and with natural voices, because in both cases...
