### THE SECOND TONE
<note>In this context, "Tone" refers to a mode of harmony or a specific division of the philosophical argument, blending musical theory with theological discourse.</note>

...similarity, whether true and expressed, or through a certain analogy. Our teachers also agree—for whom the sacred scriptures are sealed and the canon is defined (as <margin>Augustine</margin> **Augustine** says)—so that they disagree in no respect. This is because they laid their foundations with the one and true author of all wisdom. Upon these foundations, innumerable teachers, situated in various ways, in different climates and successive times, with manifold temperaments and multiple languages, have constructed diverse buildings in the greatest harmony. 

This could by no means have happened unless they were illuminated by the rays of the same divine intellect (as the <margin>Platonists</margin> **Platonists** say) or (as Catholics assert) were taught by the same Holy Spirit, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house <note>original: "inhabitare facit unanimes in domo," a reference to Psalm 68:6.</note>, and who easily provides one heart and one soul for all. Filled with this Spirit, the ancient prophets, Apostles, and divine instruments sounding the truth did not chatter in schools or gymnasiums with litigious disputes. Instead, they acted in the fields, in the cities, and among the thickest crowds, dealing with the learned and the unlearned, with princes and common people. They proposed those dogmas with such constancy that they confirmed those truths through the holiness and splendor of their lives, by many wonders, and by their own blood.

But those of the world—I will not call them "harmonizers" but "disharmonizers" (because they lacked faith in the foundation)—became utterly out of tune. These men, having become wise in their own eyes, either partially or entirely did away with religion. They despised the oracles; relying on their own strength and inventions, each echoing with his own voice, they became so discordant that some claim there is one world, while others claim innumerable worlds. And among those who admit there is only one, some say it had a beginning, others that it has no beginning, some that it will perish, others that it will exist forever. Some say it is guided by a divine mind, others by chance and accident. Some say souls are immortal, others mortal, some that they are reborn into beasts, others not at all. Of those who say the soul is mortal, some say it perishes immediately after the body, others that it lives afterward for a little while or longer, but not forever. Some placed the "end of the good" <note>The *summum bonum*, or the ultimate purpose of life.</note> in the body, others in the soul, others in both.

You will find these and almost innumerable other disagreements among the philosophers; thus, you may see that they have constructed not a harmonic consonance, but a "Babylonian confusion." The builder of this citadel was **Nimrod** <note>original: "Nebrot," a common Renaissance spelling of the biblical figure Nimrod, traditionally associated with the Tower of Babel.</note>, under whom the first confusion of languages occurred. Wishing to attempt higher things beyond his strength, he decided to build the tower all the way to the heavens, so that, removed from change, he might behold the sky and the supramundane things by his own strength, though still surrounded by a veil subject to change. 

Following him, these "wise men of the world" either became citizens of Babylon and confusion, or, flying higher than they should with **Icarus**, they were drowned in the waters. Thus the Supreme Craftsman brings to pass the oracle of <margin>Isaiah, Paul, Obadiah, Plato</margin> **Isaiah**, **Paul**, and **Obadiah**, which says: *I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject.* <note>original: "Perdā ſapiētiā ſapiētū, & prudētiā prudētū reprobabo." A citation of Isaiah 29:14, quoted in 1 Corinthians 1:19.</note>

If, however, they handed down any true things among the many false things they thought, they learned those without any doubt from divine voices; for the secrets of the Most High God cannot be grasped by our own strength. Therefore **Plato** often warns that the young, and those not yet initiated, should not rashly offer an opinion on divine matters, but should believe the laws, until with maturing age, through the proper steps of discipline and a certain separation of the soul, their eyes may be opened—which all possess, but very few use. Or (as <margin>Plotinus, Proclus</margin> **Plotinus** and **Proclus** say), a light from God may shine forth, more united to itself than the natural light, by which we know God himself and the father of all, and his primeval creation...

### Chapter VII.

<margin>Hebrew Authors / various preceding worlds.</margin>
**M**any Hebrew successors took part in these songs, and they followed a twin path. Some, declaring and explaining the scripture and the law insofar as it pertains to this sensible and lower world and the active life, were called Talmudists. Others, leaving the judicial cares of the world and every kind of use of both public and private affairs to the Talmudists, and devoting themselves to contemplation and the heavenly life, referred all things that were written to the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the divine, original pattern in the mind of God from which the material world is modeled.</note>. In that Archetype, they interpreted all things either through numbers, or through symbolic reasoning, or through the anagogical <note>Anagogical refers to the highest level of scriptural interpretation, dealing with spiritual or mystical meanings and the afterlife.</note> sense. And among both groups, there are those who proceed by both ways. For others, however, it is enough to be fed only by the shell <note>original: "cortice," literally "bark" or "shell," referring to the surface-level or literal meaning of the text.</note> of the letter, such as Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note>, David Kimhi, Levi ben Gerson <note>Also known as Gersonides or Ralbag (1288–1344).</note>, and Rebunachi. However, the Kabbalists—who received from a true oracle (for Kabbalah is called a "reception by mouth") or learned from those taught in this manner—pursued the more secret meanings of the law. <margin>Books by uncertain authors.</margin>
We do not have certain authors for some books, such as the *Gate of Light* <note>original: "Porta lucis," likely referring to Joseph Gikatilla’s *Sha’are Orah*</note>, the *Gate of Justice* <note>original: "Porta iustitiæ," likely the *Sha’are Tzedek*</note>, the *Book of Secrets*, the *Book of the Sabbath*, the *Book of Counsel*, *On the Order of Wills*, *The Knowledge of Finding*, *On the Gracious City*, *Against Errors*, the *Lamp of God*, the *Book of the Ten* (or *of the Decenary*), the *Treasure of Life*, the *Secret of Faith*, the *Light of the Eyes*, the *Crown of a Good Name*, the *Book of Figures* <note>original: "Sepher Temunot"</note>, *Ezekiel’s Chariot* <note>original: "Mercaua Ezechielis," referring to the *Ma'aseh Merkabah* or the mystical study of the divine chariot</note>, *On the Secrets of Prayers*, and *Words of the Book* <note>original: "Imre sepher," a play on the Hebrew phrase for "elegant words" from Genesis 49:21</note>, which is to say, of eloquent beauty. And many others have written, whose volumes have not yet been brought into our hands. There were also many who, even if they did not write, were nonetheless most skilled in that doctrine, having persevered in it for a long time. They earned a place in that most celebrated assembly of seventy sages (which they called the **Sanhedrin**), in which (as some assert) our **Paul** was educated at the feet of **Gamaliel**. For into this council they did not admit anyone unless they excelled in languages and the knowledge of secret matters. Among these (after those seventy upon whom **Moses**, by God’s command, imparted some of his own spirit, as we read in the Book of Numbers), there were many prophets and distinguished men.

<margin>Numerous Hebrew Authors.</margin>
But to omit the prophets and those most well-known to the whole world, **Ezra** was the first (as it is said) to commit these most sacred monuments to seventy volumes—things which previously were taught only by word of mouth. But he entrusted the understanding of those things which he wrote to **Simeon the Just**, the high priest and head of the Great Synagogue. From him, **Antigonus** and his colleagues received them. After him came **Jose ben Joezer** and **Jose ben Johanan** of Jerusalem; and from these, **Joshua ben Perachiah** and **Nittai of Arbela**; from whom came **Judah ben Tabbai** and **Simeon ben Shetach**; and from these, **Shemaiah** and **Abtalion**. From them came **Hillel** and **Shammai**, who had many thousands of disciples. And from those, a very great multitude grew: **Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai**, **Eliezer ben Hurcanus**, **Joshua ben Hananiah**, **Yose the Priest**, **Simeon ben Nathanael**, and **Eleazar ben Arach**, and almost infinite others whose opinions are celebrated partly in the **Talmud** and partly by those who wrote in the **Kabalistic** <note>The author uses "cabalistice" to refer to the mystical tradition of receiving divine secrets.</note> manner.

<margin>Christian Authors.</margin>
Among those, however, who followed the true Messiah, our **Paul** and **John** wrote more deeply than the rest, pursuing those magnificent insights everywhere. But of those who published commentaries (as I seem to see), no one caught the scent of those more secret sacraments except **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian mystic.</note> and **Origen**. But Origen—either because he strove, like the Prophet, to hide the divine utterances entrusted to him so that he might not sin, or because he was sworn by his teacher **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Saccas, the teacher of both Origen and Plotinus.</note> and did not dare to bring openly into the light those things which were boiling in his mind—always runs lightly over the "outer husk" <note>The "husk" (cortex) refers to the literal or surface meaning of a text, as opposed to the internal "marrow" or mystical meaning.</note>, yet in such a way that he hints at the more secret marrow to those who are experienced. Although, from certain words spoken against **Celsus**, some assert that he turned away from this kind of school and only reached those more secret nourishments by following **Platonic** dogmas. But (unless I am mistaken) in many places his doctrine—like that of Plato—smells of Hebrew Theology.

<margin>Foreign Authors.</margin>
Among the foreigners <note>The author refers to non-Hebrew and non-Christian philosophers as "externi."</note> who followed those paths, **Pythagoras** is the chief. After him came **Plato** with his Academics, **Eudoxus**, **Archytas of Tarentum**, **Philolaus**, and the **Brahmins** <note>The priestly caste of India, often cited in Renaissance texts as ancient keepers of wisdom.</note>, from whom **Apollonius of Tyana** learned, and as many as followed the Pythagorean family. These received the tradition either immediately from the Prophets or from those who had heard them.

<page-num>LXXX</page-num>
-># OF THE FIRST SONG<-

But all of these authors handed down their teachings <term>dogmata</term> hidden under veils and reclusive curtains, so much so that no one could understand them unless they themselves taught by living voice—just as the mysteries they treated and their own institutions required. For this reason, posterity—not understanding those most profound meanings pertaining to the super-excellent divinity—descended into other modes of interpretation; this includes the Greeks, the Latins, and many of the Hebrews.

### Why the ancients sought to hide the teachings which they handed down under metaphors and riddles. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Mercurius</margin>
**I**t has always been the pursuit of the ancients to wrap and cover the sacred mysteries <term>sacramēta</term> <note>original: "sacramēta"; here referring to "holy secrets" or "divine mysteries" rather than the church ritual</note> of God and nature, and to hide the divine words entrusted to them within their hearts, so as not to sin. This law was observed by the Indian Brahmans <term>Brachmanæ</term>, the Ethiopians, the Persians, and the Egyptians. Hence their splendor <note>or "guiding light"</note> Mercurius <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with secret wisdom</note> said: "To publish a treatise full of the entire majesty of the divinity to the consciousness of the masses is the mark of an irreligious mind." Orpheus and all the ancient seers, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Aristoxenus, and Ammonius kept this with inviolable faith. For this reason, Herennius, Plotinus, and Origen (as Porphyry writes in *On the Education and Discipline of Plotinus*) swore an oath not to publish the teachings of Ammonius. And because Plotinus violated the oath made to Ammonius and publicized the mysteries, he was consumed—as punishment for his transgression (as some assert)—by a horrific plague of lice <note>original: "pediculorū edulio," referring to Phthiriasis, a disease where the body was said to be eaten by lice, often cited in antiquity as a divine punishment for the impious</note>.

<margin>Aristotle, Themistius, JESUS</margin>
The leader of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle</note> (according to the report of Themistius) handed over his teachings on natural philosophy to Alexander the Great under the condition that no one should understand them unless the one who handed them down interpreted them himself. But leaving aside external matters, our Teacher and Redeemer of all, Jesus the Son of God, teaches his disciples not to give what is holy to dogs, nor to cast pearls before swine to be trampled. To ensure these monuments of the Master were preserved, the disciples either did not write them down, or they handed down only those things pertaining to miracles, the shaping of morals, and the statutes of the law, which are to be observed by everyone. All the Apostles and Evangelists did this, except for Paul and John. For John—after the three Gospels were already made public and many years had passed—spoke a few things, and obscurely, regarding the eternal generation of the Son of God and the union of man with God through Him (once our animal nature has been mortified), in order to uproot the heresy of the Ebionites <term>Ebionitarū</term> <note>An early sect that accepted Jesus as a prophet or Messiah but denied his divinity</note>, who asserted that Christ was a man but not God. Indeed, his *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> wraps so many mysteries in riddles that neither Oedipus (who alone solved the Sphinx’s riddle), nor Solomon (who solved the Queen of Sheba’s riddles), nor anyone else could untangle them unless they were steeped in the same Spirit that filled the one who wrote it.

<margin>Paul</margin>
But Paul, sensing that the fashion of this world was already passing away, chose some few disciples, of whom he said: "But we, beholding the glory of the Lord with an unveiled face." He grieved that he did not have many well-initiated followers to whom he could entrust these mysteries, and he specifically complained about the Hebrews, who were still unrefined and rustic, saying: "We have much to say that is difficult to explain, because you have become dull of hearing. For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic elements of the oracles of God. You have become those who need milk, not solid food. For solid food is for the perfect—those who, by constant practice, have their senses...

...used for the discernment of good and evil. But pay attention to what follows: "Therefore, leaving behind the talk of the elementary teaching of Christ, let us be carried toward more perfect things, not laying again a foundation of penance <note>or "repentance"</note> from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the Gifts <term>Charismatū</term> <note>spiritual graces or divine gifts</note>, of doctrine, and also of the imposition of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment." And these things indeed we shall do, if God permits. For it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to penance. In these words, two things must be noted. First, that the Apostle <note>Paul</note> here stores in the cabinet of his heart <note>original: "scrinio pectoris"; a metaphor for memory and internal wisdom</note> something beyond the doctrine of penance, baptism, the resurrection of the dead, judgment, and such things about which theologians write most fully. The second is to consider what kind of fall it is which he judges impossible to be relieved by penance—if one should reveal to the unworthy those things which ought to be kept hidden, or if someone, receiving them unworthily, should do injury to such a great mystery <term>sacramēto</term>. Therefore, the Apostle distinguishes the "more perfect" disciples; among them, he speaks of those things that pertain to a higher wisdom, having been made a disciple of the True Master <note>Christ</note>, who manifested the name of God the Father only to those whom the Father himself had given him; and he chose those to whom he spoke the mystery of the kingdom of God apart from those whom he taught in parables.

<margin>Ezra</margin> So to Ezra (as we read in his fourth book), God spoke with words of this kind: "Revealing, I was revealed upon the bush, and I spoke to Moses when my people were serving in Egypt; and I led him up onto Mount Sinai, and I kept him with me for many days; and I told him many wonders, and showed him the secrets of the times and the end; and I commanded him, saying: 'These words you shall make public, and these you shall hide.'" 
<margin>GOD</margin>
For in public, he made the precepts of the Law, the genealogy of Christ, and some very brief histories of the ancient fathers (though the mystery <term>sacramēto</term> within them was still enclosed). Likewise, the sacrifices, the ceremonies, the construction of the Ark, the war with the Amalekites, and with the other kings of various nations. And the wiser Hebrews call this the "Written Law," in which more sublime meanings are contained than many might think. The knowledge of these meanings the aforementioned wise men call "mouth to mouth" <note>the Oral Law or Kabbalah</note>, which, according to the command of the living God, Moses revealed by word of mouth to the seventy elders. Their succession lasted until the captivity made by Nebuchadnezzar <term>Nabucdonozor</term>, at which time it ceased or was diminished until the time of Cyrus. For then (at the suggestion of the divine spirit, with five thousand four hundred temple vessels assigned, the captivity ended, and the families sent back to the number of forty-two thousand, three hundred and seventy—excluding male and female servants), under the hand of Zerubbabel <term>Zorobabel</term>, Nehemiah <term>Neemiæ</term>, and Ezra, the temple of the Lord began to be rebuilt. When it was repaired and the sacred rites restored, Ezra (at the Lord’s command) reduced that doctrine into seventy volumes, according to the number of the elders, so that they would not be lost; yet with this law of the living God: that they should not be exposed to the unlearned. "For the first things," He said, "which you wrote"—namely the text of the Law—"you shall place in public, so that the worthy and unworthy may read them. But the last seventy books you shall preserve, so that you may hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge." These were, by a divine and unimaginable artifice, closed up beneath the "bark" <note>the outer surface or literal meaning</note>. And lest these things be despised as apocrypha <term>apocrypha</term> <note>texts of hidden or questionable authority</note>, let us see what Dionysius <margin>Diony.</margin> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite</note> puts forward in favor of this matter: "It was most fitting," he says, "that divine things..."

...and incomprehensible things are hidden through enigmas; and a sacred truth, hidden from the understanding of super-mundane <note>original: "supramundanorum"; referring to spiritual or celestial intellects</note> minds, is placed as a path for many. For not everyone is holy, nor (as the scriptures say) do all possess knowledge. And having progressed a little further, he <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> says: "O Timothy, made divine in divine doctrine, covering within the secret of the soul those things which are holy from the unclean multitude, guard these as unified things. We shall therefore philosophize about God (as Nazianzen <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father</note> teaches) for those, when, how, and as much as is necessary, committing to writing as much as the Lord permits and judges worthy of revelation, reserving those things which are to be communicated by mouth only among the wise.

### How those who are discordant could be brought into concord. Chapter VIII

<margin>Nazianzen</margin>
<margin>Lactantius</margin>
<margin>CHRIST. Luke</margin>
<margin>Jerome, Chrysostom, Gregory, Nazianzen</margin>

**L**est we admit anything harsh and discordant into our harmony—which is a sounding together of all strings <note>original: "neruorum"; literally 'nerves' but here meaning the strings of a musical instrument</note> into whole modes without the offense of clashing—we shall introduce the philosophers of the world themselves as choristers into this harmony, provided they wish to adapt their instruments or elementary strings. They will indeed do this if they wish to confess God (as nature teaches, religion persuades, and reason proves) as the author and craftsman of the universe: for the whole wisdom of man is placed in this alone (as Firmianus <note>Lactantius, often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> says), that he should know and worship God. Let us therefore accept this one true Principle of things, a free craftsman and supreme power, from whom all truth emanates. Then easily the sounds of all dissimilar voices will come into the same consonance, which results from similar and dissimilar voices: just as so many most diverse members, bound together by a single life, are in consonance in the same body; just as also the parts of the world-body agree in a most sweet concert, because they are bathed in and bound by a single life. For there is one spirit of life in them, rendering them all most harmonious. Moreover, all members of the mystical and ecclesiastical body agree in a most sweet melody when they live by that one life which says: *I am the way, the truth, and the life* <note>John 14:6</note>. Bathed in His spirit were the first fathers, and there was made for them all (as Luke says) *one heart and one soul* <note>Acts 4:32</note>. And all these, though of different languages, were instructed by the single voice of the Apostles, not without the wonder of those standing by. Bathed and illuminated by this same spirit, our Doctors <note>the Doctors of the Church</note>, although with different instruments and various songs, nonetheless sounded forth most harmoniously. And to begin with the foremost: four Greeks and four Latins sang in the assembly of God as the bases and foundations of our theology, together with those four who delivered the elements of the Gospel in four distinct yet consonant songs. For Jerome and Chrysostom explain the testament of Isaiah. Both Gregory the Roman <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> and Gregory of Nazianzus pursue the business of the soul enclosed beneath the bark <note>i.e., the literal surface of the text</note>. John of Damascus <note>OCR: Namaſcenus</note> with Ambrose fix the weightier sentences and allegorical meanings. Augustine flies forth with Basil...

<page-num>XXXIII</page-num>
# SECOND TONE.

<margin>Basil</margin>
<margin>Jerome</margin>

<margin>Damascene</margin>
According to Basil <note>Basil the Great, 4th-century Church Father</note>, in the anagogic <term>anagogic: a method of interpretation that finds spiritual or mystical meaning in a text, leading the soul toward divine things</term> song, the highest things are to be sounded. Jerome, moreover, commemorates those who preceded him up to his own time in his book *On Illustrious Men*, noting one hundred and thirty-seven known to him. To these, Gennadius, a priest of Marseille, adds ninety-one. Countless others followed these until the time of Peter Lombard; he, emulating [John] Damascene, reduced and organized theological doctrine into four volumes, providing the material for debate to those who followed. In this disputative genre, members of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> wrote up to the time of Bartholomew of Pisa, who commemorates one hundred of them, and even more. But they have increased so much from various professions, nations, and languages, sounding together in a wonderful harmony, that we can assign neither a limit to the sound nor a number to the strings. Of them it may be said: *I saw a great multitude, which no one could number* <note>original: "Vidi turbam magnam: quam dinumerare nemo poterat"; quoting Revelation 7:9</note>, except He who counts the multitude of the stars. Yet all agree in a wonderful consonance, because they are illuminated by the highest teacher and the supreme light, from whom all light and truth emanate.

Those, however, who lean on their own strength, find that prophetic saying proven in themselves: *Every man is a liar.* For God alone contains the fountain of truth, from which it is necessary to draw if we intend to hand down true and harmonious dogmas. For there is no knowledge concerning separate substances <note>i.e., angels or immaterial beings</note>, the secrets of nature, or concerning God the author of nature Himself, unless it be divinely revealed. For divine things are not touched [by human hands], and mundane things escape the senses at any moment. From this it follows: that what they call "wisdom" and "certain science," whether regarding celestial or natural things, is either the purest error or a thick darkness.

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Thus Isaiah, illuminated by light, reproaches the Chaldeans, the philosophers, and the wise men of the world, saying: *Your wisdom and your knowledge, it has deceived you* <note>Isaiah 47:10</note>. *Let the astrologers, the sky-gazers, and the diviners save you.* Therefore, we know only as much as the intellect—placed at the summit of the human soul—pure, bright, and clear, gazes upon in the mirror of eternity. Relying on this light, we come to the harmony of particular dogmas,

<margin>Augustine</margin>
proving what Augustine teaches in *On Genesis*: whatever philosophers have been able to demonstrate about the nature of things with true evidence is not contrary to our scriptures. But if they have said anything false, their cleverness must be cast aside. Let us therefore descend to these particular elements.

It is the doctrine of the wise: *He who remains for eternity created all things at once* <note>Sirach 18:1</note>.

<page-num>XXXIV</page-num>

# OF THE FIRST CANTICLE

God does not act with [manifestly] infinite power, because the work produced is not infinite. For He used His own boundless power in the building <term>fabricando: the act of "fabricating" or constructing the universe</term>, although He did not unfold that same infinity into the work itself; instead, He enclosed it within those limits He willed, which He also produced by His command. Since, therefore, He produced all things by His command and word—as the Prophet says: *He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created* <note>original: "Ipſe dixit/ & facta ſunt: mādauit, & creata ſunt"; quoting Psalm 33:9</note>—why, once the word was spoken, "let there be light," or "let there be a firmament," or the sphere of the heavens in the midst of the waters, or "let the earth produce green grass," was there such a delay for the light until the space of a day passed and evening came? And why was the sprouting of the earth delayed until the third day, and the production of the sun, moon, and stars until the fourth? And why was the spawning of the waters given only on the fifth? And why was the fashioning of man celebrated on the sixth? And why was the seventh set aside for rest? Let them speak if they have any answer.

<margin>David</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine rightly laughs at those who deserve laughter, who think that God requires time to act. We do not need to deal here with outsiders—those who say the world was uncreated, or those who, not seeing the cause of its novelty, assert it existed from eternity and was produced all at once—but rather with our own people. These are the ones who, not perceiving the mysteries <term>sacramenta: here meaning the hidden spiritual depths or "sacraments" of the text</term> of the Scriptures, strive to preserve the "killing letter" <note>original: "occidentem litteram"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life," suggesting that a strictly literal reading can miss the divine truth</note>. Hence they sometimes come to an unworthy conclusion (as the same Augustine says) if the meaning is always extracted according to the literal words. 

<margin>The same [Augustine]</margin>
<margin>Origen</margin>
Nor does Origen admit those among the sensible who imagine that the first, second, and third days (in which evening and morning are mentioned) happened without the sun, moon, and stars, or that the first day existed without the Heavens. Indeed, they do a great injury to the supreme and eternal Craftsman, before whom all things are present, while they suppose Him to work through time and succession. His measure is eternity, and His entire possession is held all at once. 

<margin>Hiarchas</margin>
<margin>The Ancients</margin>
<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Nor should the members of this "worldly animal" <note>This refers to the *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul," an ancient philosophical concept suggesting the universe is a single living organism</note> have been produced separately, says Hiarchas <note>Hiarchas was a legendary prince of the Indian Brahmans mentioned in the life of Apollonius of Tyana</note>, prince of the Brahmans, but all together. For almost all the ancients agree that the world is a living being, as do even some of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy</term>, and Augustine does not deny it. 

Concerning this entire structure made all at once, Moses himself—repeating that which he seemed to have distinguished by days—asserts it was produced together on one and the same day, saying: *These are the generations of the heaven and the earth when they were created, in the day that the Lord God made the earth and the heaven, and every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew* <note>Genesis 2:4–5</note>. 

<margin>Job</margin>

This most clearly implies that the evil angel—who is said by almost everyone to have been produced on the first day with the Angels of Light—was also fashioned at the same time as man. [John] Damascene, moreover, from the workshop of Gregory Nazianzen, asserts even more: namely, that the angelic powers were conceived in thought before corporeal things. That "thinking out" (as he says) is His work. To this is added what is subjoined in Job concerning the same: *He is the beginning of the ways of God* <note>Job 40:19</note>, by which ways He went out to produce His creatures. 

<margin>Job</margin>

# SECOND TONE XXXIV

...are said to have been spread out individually, it should be understood that this occurred according to that order in which man—for whose sake all things were made—is most fittingly introduced as the last
<margin>Peripatetics</margin> work of God, according to that common saying of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on logic and natural philosophy</note>: *That which is first in intention is last in execution.* <note>original: "Quod primum in intentione, est ultimum in executione." This implies God thought of man first, so He built everything else as a prerequisite before finally "executing" the creation of man.</note> Indeed, the intermediate things, following that same order, succeed one another from the first to the last. However, regarding this matter which seems to disturb many—the distinction of the seven days as it is narrated in the letter of the text—although it does not require much refutation because it collapses of its own accord, nevertheless, so that troubled minds may find rest, we shall say a few things. First, we must state that the three days which seem assigned to the building <term>fabricam: the structural creation of the universe</term> and the three assigned to the ornamenting <term>ornatum: the "furnishing" of the world with stars, plants, and animals</term>, and the seventh, which closes the circle of days and is said to be destined for rest, are not days defined by the circuit of the Sun. For it is not to be thought that the most wise man Moses—or rather God Himself speaking through Moses—was struck by such dullness that he would say the first three days, composed of evening and morning, preceded the Sun, which was only fabricated on the fourth day, and from whose motion evening and morning are caused. Nor should those ramblers be listened to who say that a certain "shining cloud" was created together with the heavens, by which the days and hours were divided. How, I ask, did a cloud illuminate, when it is the very nature of a cloud to darken and cover? How was it a "small cloud" that could illuminate the entire celestial and terrestrial machinery? Where, moreover, did they wish to place this cloud of theirs, since the ethereal region <note>The upper heavens</note>, being free from every foreign impression, would by no means admit it? Nor could a small cloud in the vicinity of the earth illuminate the whole hemisphere; for it is the great size of the Sun and its proper height that allow the whole hemisphere to be illuminated, while a pyramidal shadow <note>The cone-shaped shadow cast by the Earth into space</note> is caused in the other hemisphere, which causes night and darkness throughout the space of that pyramid. And because this pyramidal shadow does not cross the orbit of the Moon, the Stars—not being occupied by that shadow of the earth—suffer no eclipse, but continuously receive the light which they bend down toward us. Furthermore, how could this cloud, by illuminating the air, cause day from evening and morning, when the air was not yet distinct, nor was there a firmament, nor the globe of the heavens, nor were the waters above the heavens divided from those below? For you have it in the text that all things were in confusion until the second day. They even bring a no small reproach against the Supreme Craftsman <note>Artifex: God as the Divine Architect</note> when, by imagining this cloud of theirs, they think God fabricated an imperfect world and lit a "borrowed light" until He could kindle the proper light; just as our architects do, who sometimes build a wooden tower to house the bells until they can construct the actual tower of brick as they intended. All these things ascribe no small imperfection to the Creator. In the same way, those who dream that God fabricated the sun on the first day as something imperfect, and then gave it the form of light on the fourth day, are to be exploded <note>driven out or rejected</note>. Let them say, I ask: if the sun on the first day had been imperfect and not yet gifted with its own light, how did it cause day and night by illuminating the world, as they said just a moment ago? And if it was made without form at first, like raw matter, why did He not say—

Moses—the Sun—was "imperfect," as he had said regarding the earth: *The earth was formless and empty.* <note>original: "Terra autem erat inanis & vacua"</note> Afterward, concerning the perfection bestowed upon it, he added: *Let the earth produce green plants.* Furthermore, let them notice that on the fourth day God said: *Let there be two great lights;* <note>original: "Fiant, uel sint duo luminaria magna"</note> He did not say, "Let the two lights produce their own light," in the same way He had commanded the earth a little earlier to "produce." Those people imagined that God, in the manner of a painter, had first sketched a figure with a stylus so that he might later paint it by applying the appropriate marks and colors. This is surely unfitting for God; such things are what mortals seek out due to their own imperfect power. But because he says of matter that it was first unformed and later depicted with its own shapes, understand this: it signifies the order of nature, and not an order of time.

## Why the number six was assigned to the construction, and the seventh day to rest.

### Chapter XI.

<margin>Mathematicians. Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Peripatetics.</margin>
<margin>Simplicius.</margin>
**E**ven if it is said that all the works of the highest craftsman <note>The "highest craftsman" (summi opificis) refers to God as the Divine Architect or Demiurge, a common theme in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> were built with great mystery and great sacrament, this is no less true regarding the number six, by which the account of the entire construction is divided. For the number six (as the Mathematicians and **Augustine** teach) is the first "perfect number": because it results exactly from its combined aliquot parts <note>A "perfect number" in classical mathematics is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors. 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.</note>—one, two, and three. For this reason, it is also called *gamon* <note>original: "gamõ" from the Greek "gamos," meaning marriage or union.</note> by the followers of **Pythagoras**, because its parts, when placed next to one another, give birth to the number itself. Furthermore, any two aliquot parts combined constitute the number six: such as six times one, three times two, or twice three. Indeed, no number more harmonious than six could be found for the construction of the world, for it consists of the "double proportion" <note>The ratio of 2:1, which in music creates the interval of an octave.</note> which it contains most closely within itself. This is the ratio of four to two; these numbers, when joined together, return the number six. You would hardly find this in other numbers, unless in those that preserve the nature of six: such as its double, triple, quadruple, or its square, and similar forms. Therefore, the number six results from the double proportion, <margin>Pythagoras. Plato.</margin> which produces the "diapason" <note>term: <term>diapason</term> — The Greek term for an octave, considered the most perfect musical harmony.</note>, the most harmonious of all harmonies. For this reason, **Pythagoras** asserts that it is entirely suited to birth and marriage, and consequently to the construction of the world, in which the true marriages and unions of things are celebrated. The number six, being the first perfect number, also suits the highest craftsman, God, or His construction, in which nothing is lacking. Just as the number six, when distributed through its members, lacks nothing, has nothing in excess, does not fall short, does not exceed, does not flow out or in, and does not require outside help; rather, it is equal and balanced, standing and relying upon its own parts and strengths. Moreover, the parts that give birth return a product similar to the parent. Therefore, when God had brought His work to completion by dividing it according to this number, <margin>Moses</margin> **Moses** said: *Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.* <note>Genesis 2:1.</note> For this reason, **Orpheus** also commands that hymns be ended at the sixth generation, because nothing more can be sung concerning created things, since all perfection is terminated therein. Thus <margin>Augustine</margin> **Augustine** teaches that God perfected His works in six days; he believes that a mystery is signified by this number rather than literal parts of time. Therefore, we also require numbers to perceive the sacraments of God and nature—not merchant's numbers, but those distinct to their own purposes. Moving further, let us say that from the "triangular figure," this number best suits the construction: for the base of this figure is three, the summit is one, and the intermediate parts are two, as is clear in the figure shown here ∴ . For the entire construction emanates from three persons <note>The Holy Trinity.</note>, since their outward works are undivided. They also tend toward one end, toward which all things are directed. The transition, however, is through the "binary" <note>The number two.</note>, which is to say, "matter" <note>original: "materiã yʒ" (hyle). In this philosophical system, the number 2 often represents the duality or potentiality of raw matter.</note>. For the first principle of this departure was matter, which tastes of the binary; and it tends to be reduced to "one" through "form," which bears the image of the "ternary" <note>The number three.</note>. Just as in every part of the preceding figure the ternary tends toward the "monad" <note>The number one, symbolizing unity or God.</note> through the binary. Once all things have been led to this point, there follows the Sabbatical rest of the seventh day, closing and terminating the course of all days. This "six," therefore, is far more excellent than that which [marks the course] of days...

If it is admitted, therefore, that God, the highest craftsman <note>original: "opifex," a term used for God as the Divine Architect.</note>, proceeded in his perfect order into the work, the harmony of Catholic wise men with the philosophers—especially the Academics <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note>—will be easy. The Prince of these [Plato], in the *Timaeus*, said that God, the spreader of the world, after producing the twin matter of heaven and earth, immediately afterward produced the light by which things might be distinguished and, being distinct, might be known. Or rather, He commanded it to be within things. Therefore, it is pointedly said (as the literal truth holds), "let light be made" over matter, namely informing that matter itself. Thus, first the matter of heaven and earth is said to be fashioned, and simultaneously the light, through which that matter might be painted with the image or likeness of the Craftsman. And this was necessary; it is called the first emergence of the craftsman into the work, and the first illustration or light seen upon the darkened matter. Once the composite was made from the light and the matter together, the first day appeared, fashioned from the "evening" of matter and the "morning" of form. 

But because the total influx of divinity was by no means suitable for matter, on the second day He is said to have placed the *arachiah* <note>original: "arachiah," a Latinized form of the Hebrew "Raki’a," usually translated as "firmament" or "expanse."</note>—that is, the curtain or mass of the heavens—between the super-excellent fountain of light and waters and the darkened matter, and the few waters of goodness. This was done lest the influx of waters and goodness be greater than what was suitable for the matter itself. But this is said to have been done on the second day, which is "unlucky" <note>In various traditions, the second day was considered "inauspicious" because God does not say "it was good" after creating the firmament, which represents separation.</note>. Hence the Hebrews read of this separation with a groan, placing over it the accent which they call **אור** *Zarka* <note>The text identifies the word as "Or" (Light) but refers to the "Zarka" accent; the Zarka is a musical/grammatical mark in the Hebrew Bible that the author interprets here as a sign of sorrow or distance.</note>, as if grieving over the obstacle placed between the flowing goodness and the receptive matter. And this pertains to the primeval production. But we too must groan over this unlucky day, on which a tribunal was interposed between us and God, weighing how much grace and how much divine influx is to be allowed to each person. For the fountain of divine goodness is most exuberant; it would flow more than the recipients deserve, were it not for the obstacle placed in between to prevent it, just as ordering justice requires.

On the third day, however, according to the formal number of things, the forms are unfolded and said to be segregated from the interior and earthly things. Therefore it is said: *Let the waters that are under the heaven be gathered together into one place*—that is, let the generative powers be collected together—*and let the dry land appear*: which is to be made fruitful by the power of those collected forces. As it is added: *Let the earth bring forth green herbs, and the seed-bearing tree*, and those things which follow. 

Therefore, once the forms were produced and the earth was painted so that those pictures might appear and be seen, it was said in the fourth place: *Let there be two great lights* in the globe or mass of the heavens; and *let them divide*—that is, make a distinction—between the dark and the lucid, so that those things which are illuminated by their forms may be seen and distinguished from those which still lie in their own darkness and more obscure shapes. 

On the fifth day, the "vital" day, from the fifth character—namely **ה** <note>The Hebrew letter "He," which has the numerical value of 5 and is often associated with breath, spirit, and life.</note>, signifying life—the full communion of life is described, when He says: *Let the waters creep forth*, or *let them produce the creeping thing of a living soul, and the winged bird* flying both over the earth and over the face of the heavens. God also created on that same day great dragons, or great whales as our translation has it, and every living soul that crawls upon the earth; from which it may be understood that God is the author of all life, both higher and lower. ### Chapter XII: The Harmony of the Ancients regarding the Unity of All Things.

<margin>
Peripatetics.
Parmenides.
Simplicius.
</margin>

There is a controversy among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, who walked while they taught.</note> and the ancients—<term>Parmenides</term>, <term>Melissus</term>, and their followers—concerning the "unity of things." This dispute is almost entirely verbal, as <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note> and other wise men rightly perceive. Those who enter into this contest either do not understand, or pretend not to understand, in order to find an excuse for debate. Their quarrels are easily settled if one admits (as one should) that God is the author, the sustainer, and the "single thing" of all matters. Concerning this, **Plato**, speaking to Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus, says:

<margin>Plato</margin>
> You three who are present must read this letter, or at least two of you, and as frequently as possible: so that you may know God, the King of all things that were, are, and are to be; the Prince and Father and Lord of the principle and the crafting cause.

By philosophizing in this way, we can aptly reach the nature of a happy man: by knowing, namely, the King, the cause, the end, and the sustainer, or God continuously diffused within us. According to what that wise astronomer <margin>Manilius</margin> writes:

> For I shall sing of the Mind powerful over silent nature, and of God infused through the heavens, the earth, and the seas.

<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
Just as it says in Jeremiah:

> I fill heaven and earth. <note>Jeremiah 23:24.</note>

Unless He did this—giving life and sustaining all things—they would easily dissolve into nothingness. Thus, for all things, there is one "being" <note>original: "esse," the act of existing.</note> diffused within them, in which they exist and are preserved. We can provide an example of this even in sensible things. <margin>Iamblichus. Dionysius. The Academics.</margin> For the Sun (according to **Iamblichus**) is the visible image of divine intelligence; or a "visible statue" in this worldly temple (as **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> teaches along with the **Academics**). It is single in its essence and light, yet manifold in its rays. In the same way, the "First Being" is single in itself—divine, eternal, and immutable—yet manifold when diffused among creatures. And just as all things are darkness when the sun withdraws its rays, in the same way, when the Divine Sun turns His face away, all things are troubled and reduced to their dust, or to nothingness. <margin>Thales. Parmenides. Aristotle.</margin> **Thales**, therefore, contemplating this "being," asserted that it was infinite in its origin. **Parmenides**, however, thinking of it in its rays, said it was finite. Nor did such great men deny the diversity of the rays, as **Aristotle** used to charge against them. For as he himself admits, Parmenides proposed contrary principles of things; therefore, he conceded many things, since contrariety cannot exist in the same thing. And if he conceded principles, he certainly did not deny effects distinct from those principles; otherwise, they would not differ from the principles at all. <margin>The same regarding Melissus.</margin> Nor did Aristotle believe (as I think) that Parmenides and Melissus wished to...

<margin>Averroes</margin>
<margin>Plato</margin>
...generation, the principles of which they assigned as occurring only according to appearance; just as <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says in his rambling, along with some more recent followers wishing to defend Aristotle. For Aristotle lashes out against the words of the ancients, and not their intended meanings, so that from there he might find an opportunity for dispute, as <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian.</note> quite politely says:
<margin>Thomas</margin>
Aristotle rejects the words of Plato and other ancients, not indeed to refute what Plato wrote, but what the words appear to claim. He did this so that those hearing the metaphorical words of Plato—with which he used to hide a profound meaning—would not fall into error. For instance, when they hear the soul called a "circle" or a "number," they might believe these things were said according to material mathematics. Similarly, when all things are said to be "one," they might imagine that this "one" is some composite or a particular thing. Indeed, all things are understood to be "one" because they have their being from the One, just as all numbers have their existence from the unity diffused within them.
<margin>Heraclitus</margin>
Heraclitus does not differ much from these; he said that all things, on account of their mobility and instability, meet in a certain "One" that is permanent and unchangeable. This can be nothing other than that divine Being from which all things sparkle forth. But speaking quite obscurely (as <term>Jerome</term> <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> says), he is scarcely understood even by "sweating" philosophers <note>original: "a sudantibus Philosophis," meaning those who labor intensely over difficult texts.</note>. 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
<margin>Xenophanes</margin>
Xenophanes also agrees with these, if one carefully looks at those things recited by <term>Alexander the Greek</term> <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle around 200 AD.</note>, who was first a Peripatetic, but later, having been devoted to the school of Xenophanes, took up and wrote his dogma. 
<margin>Alexander</margin>
His arguments conclude that all things are one in the logic of the first and chief Being, not in the particular logic of existing. 
<margin>Albertus</margin>
Consenting to this, <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>The 13th-century teacher of Thomas Aquinas, known as "Great" for his vast knowledge.</note> adds: "There is no true 'being' except that of Him who said: 'He who is, sent me to you.'" <note>A reference to God's revelation to Moses in Exodus 3:14: "I AM THAT I AM."</note> 
<margin>GOD</margin>
For He exists of Himself and through Himself; but all other things exist neither of themselves nor through themselves, but only so far as they participate in His being.

<margin>Egyptians</margin>

For Pallas, who is said to have been born from the brain of Jove, signifies that Wisdom through which and in which all things were made, according to that prophetic word: *You have made all things in wisdom.* 
<margin>David</margin>
All things are also filled by her, as the same prophet follows: *The earth is filled with your possession.* 
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
Just as was recently said through Jeremiah, and many other wise men agree. The poets also sing of this, among whom <term>Lucan</term> <note>A Roman poet; the quote reflects Stoic pantheism.</note> says: *The seat of God is nothing but the earth, and sea, and air, and sky, and virtue; why do we seek the gods further? Jupiter is whatever you see; wherever you move.* 
<margin>Lucan</margin>
Perhaps he learned this from Isaiah, in whom God speaks, saying: 
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
*Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.*

And because all things are connected by love, <margin>Moses</margin> **Moses** introduces the spirit—which is love and the bond of things (as we shall explain, God willing, in its proper place)—hovering over and warming the waters; specifically those waters from which all living things are generated. For animals are commanded to be produced from the waters by the Artisan, and plants are not produced without water, even though it is said: "Let the earth bring forth green herbs." For the earth produces nothing at all without watery moisture.

### On the general concord of the Peripatetics, and of all others in essential matters.
### Chapter XIII.

<margin>Plato</margin>
**W**e establish that the Peripatetics and many others agree in a delightful harmony of wise men. This will certainly seem the more difficult as their leader [Aristotle], in order to be considered unique and more excellent, chose to disagree even when he was not in disagreement with others—most especially with **Plato**—by following an opposite process. For the process is twofold, just as nature is twofold, as **Plato** himself mentions. One nature is sensible [perceived by the senses], concerning which there is the reasoning of opinion, which they call "science." The other is the incorruptible nature of a better substance—immutable, constant, continuous, and always the same—which is not perceived by penetrable thought but is seen by the sharpness of the mind. This is called "divine science" because it treats of divine things and is divinely taught. The former, however, is called "daemonic" <note>In the Greek sense of *daimon*, referring to intermediate spirits or intelligences between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note> because it concerns earthly things and because it is suggested by those lower intelligences whom <margin>Tully, Cicero, Apuleius</margin> **Marcus Tullius** [Cicero] calls *lares* <note>Guardian deities of a location or household in Roman religion.</note>, **Apuleius** sometimes *lares* and sometimes *genii*, and others call *demons*...

...are contained below the lunar orb, revolving around the understanding of earthly things. Hence the Greeks, both **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for his focus on the physical world and logic.</note> and **Platonists**, called Plato himself "divine," but Aristotle a "demon" <note>In this context, 'demon' refers to a *daimon*, a powerful spirit or intermediate being of great intellect, rather than an evil entity.</note>. This is because it was always Plato’s care to treat divine matters and to learn from those who had received divine oracles. Aristotle, however, relying on his own strengths, wished to admit only those things which he judged he could prove by his own senses and reasons. For by this way, he hunted for manifold motions, fourfold qualities, the three principles of things, the four causes, and suchlike: which are easily perceived through the senses. Nor does the <margin>Aristotle</margin> sensible teacher <note>Referring to Aristotle’s focus on sensory experience.</note> proceed further, unless he oversteps (as he himself says) the boundaries of his sensory teaching. Which he sometimes does, confessing God as the maker of things; although, remaining within sensory limits, he asserts the world is unbegotten <note>i.e., that the world has existed eternally without a beginning.</note> and takes away from God the actual making of things.

If, however, we wish to bring him into the assembly of Platonists and divine wise men, <margin>The same, Plato, John</margin> this seems to me the only way: that (as musicians are sometimes accustomed to do) we observe that he seeks the highest things starting from the lowest; while Plato, together with **John** <note>The Apostle John, author of the fourth Gospel.</note>, descends from the highest progenitor to the lowest. For John, beginning from the **Word** <term>Logos: the divine Reason or Word of God</term>, says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" <note>original: "In principio erat uerbū: & uerbū erat apud Deum: & Deus erat uerbū."</note>. Afterward, he descends through the "idea" and the "light" provided to us for knowing divine things, down to the flesh assumed by the Word himself. We shall demonstrate such a twofold progress observed in the assembly when treating divine things along with elementary and inferior ones: for from God, one arrives at the heavens through the **ternary** <note>The number three, symbolizing the divine Trinity or the spiritual realm.</note>; and one ascends there from the elements through the **quaternary** <note>The number four, symbolizing the physical world and the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. Where these numbers, meeting and brought together, constitute through each other the **duodenary** <note>The number twelve (3 x 4), symbolizing the zodiac and the completion of the cosmic order.</note>, by which number the heaven is divided and manifoldly adorned, as we shall explain in its place (God favoring). This is the progress observed by these <margin>Plato.</margin> two principal leaders of philosophers. Plato, therefore, following the footsteps of the Pythagoreans and ancient wise men, wanting to describe the fabric of the world, began from the craftsman through the way of numbers. Concerning which, having found it with the greatest difficulty (as he himself confesses), he puts forward these things: "In the beginning, he took one portion from the universe; then a second, double the first," and the rest which <margin>Aristotle.</margin> follow. But Aristotle (especially in his book *On Physics* <note>Latin: *de physico auditu*, the standard title for Aristotle’s Physics.</note>) begins from the inferior and elementary principles, ascending through various <margin>Plato</margin> motions until investigating the **First Mover**, God. Plato, again, from the oracles and from those things he learned to "hunt" from the ancients, lays the foundations of his teaching upon numbers; since numbers are familiar to divine, earthly, and human things. It is clear, therefore, that if someone wisely leads Plato through the ternary of divine things, and Aristotle through the corporeal and sensible quaternary, arriving at the duodenary common to both, he will make them meet there. And (to speak more clearly) let the Peripatetic way proceed from the elements and the lowest principles of things up to the celestial machine that is seen; and the treatment will be of motion, generation, corruption, alteration, increase, decrease, and local motion up to the Pri[me Mover]...

<page-num>XXXIX</page-num>
->**THIRD TONE.**<-

# HOW THE ONE IS EXTENDED THROUGH TWENTY-SEVEN. CHAPTER ONE.

**[M]onad** <note>original: *Monas*, the indivisible unity or the "One" from which all numbers and things arise</note> diffused into a multitude is evident to all wise men. However, how the nature of unity corresponds with multitude, and dwells within it without discord, is the labor we must here exhaust. It cannot correspond in any other way except through the harmony of unity, which is found in the multitude. <margin>Plato</margin> Hence Plato, imitating the passage in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world</note>, describes the fabrication of the soul and the world by means of a received monad; and through doubled, tripled, and quadrupled proportions he arrives at twenty-seven, which is the **cube** <note>original: *cubus*, a number multiplied by itself twice, e.g., 3 x 3 x 3 = 27</note> of the first number, adding that all the intervals had been filled. So that his <margin>Proclus, Chalcidius</margin> interpreters, Proclus, Chalcidius, and their successors, might do this, they place the number six (the first "perfect number") in the place of unity; by doubling and tripling this in the same order, they arrive at 162. Then they fill the intervals with the harmony of **fifths** <note>original: *diapentica*</note>, **fourths** <note>original: *diatessaronica*</note>, and also with the tone, the semitone, and the **limma** <note>original: *lemma*, a small musical interval remaining when two whole tones are subtracted from a perfect fourth</note>, so that the whole soul and the whole world may be harmonic, containing every divine harmony. For the first and highest Monad is diffused into the first number, namely the **ternary** <note>the number three</note>; if this is squared, it completes the **nonary** <note>the number nine</note>. By this number, the orders of the separate intelligences, the heavens, and all elementary things are distributed in the highest harmony, as we intend to demonstrate below. If this number is reduced to a cube, it returns those twenty-seven mentioned above.

But before these harmonic steps and things are distributed, prime matter—which the Poets call **Chaos**, the Greeks **Hyle**, and the Hebrews <term>תהו</term> <note>Tohu</note>, that is, the "void" or "unformed"—was pre-required. This matter was not counted among the numbered things, just as the first agent and highest monad does not enter into the number of others, although by its unity it allows all things to be numbered. <margin>Moses</margin> Hence most-wise Moses, before the fabrication of things, placed the production of matter first, saying: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth*, meaning the matter of both, which were formed afterward. For He granted form to the one on the second day, when He said: *Let there be an **Arachiha** in the midst of the waters* <note>original: *Arachiha*, a transliteration of the Hebrew *Raqia*, usually translated as 'Firmament'</note>, that is, an extension or expansion of all the heavens. From which it follows: *and he called the **Arachiha** heavens*. For the *Arachiha* is not "the firmament" as our translation <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> has it, but the globe and mass of all the heavens. This is proven by what follows: *God made two great lights and the stars, and placed them in the **Arachiha***. For those lights were not placed in "the firmament"—that is, the starry heaven—but each in its own sphere; from which it is concluded that *Arachiha* signifies something gathered from all the spheres. He granted form to the earth on the third day, in that He said: *Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear*; which dry land He called "Earth." To express this more clearly, He had said above: *But the earth was **Tohu***, which is explained as chaos, or a certain crude mass, or matter. There follows <term>ובהו</term> <note>Vabohu</note>, the meaning of which is "And in that which" was to be formed;

<page-num>XIXXX</page-num>
->**OF THE FIRST SONG**<-

For in matter, all things (as is commonplace) pre-exist in potentiality before they are unfolded into their proper forms. The intermediate genera, therefore, are completed in the number twenty-seven; between these genera are many intervals, which must be filled by harmonic numbers or steps according to the genera and spheres. In the breadth of the sphere, individuals are arranged in that same order and by their own harmony. For species itself has a certain breadth, even though it may appear to consist of number, which seems to have no breadth. If, however, it is looked into more diligently, the unity of parts is divided: when the tone—which is generated from the excess of unity, namely of the nine to the eight—is divided into a semitone, and that into a **limma** <note>original: *lemma*, a small musical interval remaining when a perfect fourth is subtracted from two whole tones</note> (namely half a semitone), by changing smaller numbers into larger ones: 8 into 16 and 32, and 9 into 18 and 36, which is common practice among musicians.

Thus natural number, which is the proportion of things, is divided, even though the vocal sound may not be divided unless reduced to a higher number. For man differs so much from man, and horse from horse, and dog from dog, that there must be steps within the breadth of the species themselves. Therefore, there are twenty-seven primary genera of produced things, distinguished into three **nonads** <note>groups of nine; original: *nouenarios*</note>: namely, the **supercelestial** <note>the realm of angels and divine ideas</note>, the **celestial** <note>the realm of the stars and planets</note>, and the **elementary** <note>the physical world of earth, water, air, and fire</note>. Whose harmonic concord, infused by the most high God, we intend to declare (with His favor). For from the Archetype to the Angelic orb, from here to the spheres, and from there to the terrestrial volume, that Unity descends, rendering all things most consonant; so that whatever is in each one corresponds likewise in the others by a most sweet proportion, with voices of the energy of life in song. These voices of life the Spirit of life has provided since the primeval institution. <margin>Moses</margin> Hence Moses says: "And the Spirit of God <note>original: *Elohim*</note> hovered over the waters," namely over the primordial seeds of things, by warming them and providing a single, most sweet life.

<margin>Paul</margin> For "God," (says the Apostle <note>St. Paul in Acts 17:28</note>, following the sentiment of Aratus <note>a Greek poet</note>), "is he in whom we live, move, and have our being"—by the mediation of that Spirit which nourishes from within, and by the Mind which moves the entire mass of created things, as the ancient bards said. <margin>Virgil</margin> <note>original: *Maro*</note> But also God himself says through Jeremiah: <margin>Jeremiah</margin> "I fill heaven and earth." <margin>Platonists</margin> This Spirit, and this God infused into heaven, earth, and sea, the Platonists—as some of them clearly profess—called the **Soul of the World** <term>Anima Mundi</term> <note>the vital force that animates the universe as a single living organism</note>; which, by vivifying and binding the members of the world in harmonic concord, would make the harmonies of the world's instrument most consonant.

<margin>Pythagoras</margin> Pythagoras saw this; his study was centered on numbers and these consonances. <margin>Anaxagoras</margin> Anaxagoras signaled this when he contemplated "each thing in every other" or "anything in anything" (as the **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle</note> say mockingly). Not indeed asserting that there is a donkey in a fly, or an elephant in a goldfinch, or heaven in a flea: but that the species of each are represented in others through a marvelous affinity, living by the same universal life and united in a friendly society. Thus, a ready transition and **correspondence** <note>original: *symbolum*</note> is left for one into the other through the decay and generation of their own forms, since the same matter and life exists in all; from which a proportionate harmony results among them. But he did not explain it, for perhaps he did not clearly grasp it. <margin>Pythagoreans, Academics</margin> However, the Pythagoreans and the Academics <note>members of Plato's school</note>, illuminated by divine and prophetic light—because they had been taught by those who had drawn that Spirit from divine oracles—passed this on more aptly. These divine bards themselves [look] toward that deifying Banquet...

## Chapter II.

<margin>Of the number three <note>original: *ternario numero*</note>.</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras. Chaldeans. Assyrians.</margin>
**P**ythagoras—the Father of Philosophers and the most skillful seeker of natural order and concord, who had no predecessor in natural studies and saw no equal—drew his discipline not only from the Chaldeans and Assyrians, but was also imbued with the more hidden wisdom of the Hebrews. He attributed so much to the number three <term>the triad <gloss>the ternary number</gloss></term> (as we learn from his followers) that he asserted the entire nature of the Deity, and consequently the universe, is perfected by the triad. For every number grows by a threefold increase: namely, in length, breadth, and depth, beyond which no further progress is possible. Furthermore, perfect dimension in a physical body is completed by that same triple increase and by a triple intersection at a right angle. Indeed, no more than three right angles can be formed in any [solid] figure, though obtuse and acute angles may be numerous. Thus, there is a threefold production of numbers and of continuous quantity. For if a number is added to a single unit, it becomes linear; and if a point is drawn out in length, it constitutes a line. But if the number grows in breadth, it will be made a surface; and if width is added to the line, it is changed into a surface. If again the number is led into depth, it becomes corporeal, solid, and a cube. And if depth is joined to breadth, a body is constituted. To a body measured in three ways <note>original: *trimetro*</note>, and to a cubic number, nothing can be added, as all Pythagorean philosophers and mathematicians teach.

<margin>Pythagoras. Mathematicians. Aristotle.</margin>
Hence Aristotle celebrates this number at the beginning of his discourses *On the Heavens*, saying: "We have the number three from nature; and we uphold it as if it were a law, according to which all things are arranged." Hence, according to the same number, we are bound to magnify God, the artisan and creator of all things. All things, both spiritual and corporeal, consist of three parts: the beginning, the middle, and the end. This trinity they drink from that super-excellent Triad <note>The Holy Trinity</note> from whom are all things, in whom are all things, and through whom are all things, as Paul teaches.

<margin>Paul. Trismegistus.</margin>
Moreover (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with secret wisdom</note> says), the world is perfected by three things: destiny <note>original: *himarmene*, from the Greek *heimarmene*</note>, necessity, and order. These are the meeting of causes with one another, the execution or offspring, and the proper distribution of that offspring...

<margin>The wise man</margin> For as the wise man says: God arranged the world in three things: in **number**, **weight**, and **measure** <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight."</note>. In these, all things bear the footprint of the most high Trinity. For it holds its **Number** from that supreme unity and source of all numbers; its **Weight** from that wisdom which balances all things; and its **Measure** from that spirit of the Craftsman who assigns a fitting portion to each thing. Hence the Magi <note>Referring to the ancient Persian priest-philosophers</note> believed there were three 
<margin>The Magi</margin> princes over the world: **Oromasdes**, **Mithras**, and **Arimanius** <note>original: *Oromasim, Mitrim, & Araminim*; these are the Latinized names for Ahura Mazda, Mithras, and Ahriman</note>—that is: God, Mind, and Soul. For unity is the property of the high God; order or weight is the property of the Mind or wisdom; and measure and motion belong to the Soul or spirit. This is what 
<margin>Plato</margin> **Plato** touched upon through riddles to King Dionysius when he said: "All things are around the King of all; all things exist for his sake; he is the cause of all beautiful things" <note>A paraphrase of Plato’s *Second Letter*</note>. For all things are connected around the King by his unity; all things are weighted for his sake; all things are ordered toward him. And he, by numbering and proportioning all things, is the cause of all that is beautiful—acting as the efficient, final, governing, and sustaining cause. He is, namely, the beginning, the middle, and the end of all, as 
<margin>Orpheus</margin> **Orpheus** had sung before, and as **Plato** repeats again in his letters: "All things," he says, "proceed from him; they seek him again; and in him they rest and are sustained." For 
<margin>Plato</margin> all things proceed from the Father as from the first source; they reside in the Son as if in a house through the "Ideas" <note>The perfect patterns or forms of things</note>. The seal of this Son and of divine wisdom (as is held in the 
<margin>Hebrew Theology</margin> theology of the Hebrews) is **ב** <term>Bet or Bait<gloss>the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet</gloss></term>, which signifies a "house." And all things are unfolded into their proper forms through the Holy Spirit; hence the whole workmanship is described as being made by **Elohim** <note>A Hebrew name for God</note>. This name is not plural (as some think), as its punctuation indicates, but is a singular existing in **Binah** <note>original: *binā*; the Hebrew Sephira or emanation of "Understanding," which Christian Kabbalists associated with the Holy Spirit</note>—that is, the Intelligence which is attributed to the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said in 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Ecclesiasticus: "And he shall fill him with the spirit of understanding" <note>Sirach 39:6</note>. **Hermes** also teaches this 
<margin>Hermes</margin> Trinity under the riddle of a sphere when he says: "God is a sphere whose center—the Father—is everywhere through his power; but whose circumference—Wisdom and the Son of God—is nowhere, because he cannot be contained, and he encompasses all things." As we read in the same 
<margin>The same</margin> book of Ecclesiasticus: "I alone have encompassed the circuit of heaven, and have penetrated into the depth of the abyss" <note>Sirach 24:5</note>. The mutual relationship of both—namely the center and the circumference—signifies the Spirit and their reciprocal love. 

From this threefold Archetype, the fabric of the world could not emanate except as threefold, and in a triangular order and sonorous number, as the 
<margin>Pythagoras, Plato, Boethius</margin> **Pythagoreans**, **Platonists**, and **Boethius** discuss. For not every number is suited for harmony, but only that which is fitted by its consonant proportions. Thus, the **simple ternary** <note>the number three</note> is attributed to the most simple God, who, existing as the highest unity, nevertheless spreads himself into three "hypostases" <note>distinct persons or substances</note> in an inexplicable manner, though many try to explain it. To the **square ternary** or "surface" ternary <note>3 squared, which is 9</note> are distributed the three "Enneads" <note>groups of nine</note>, so that there are nine Intelligences <note>Angelic orders</note>, nine heavens, and nine kinds of things that can be born and perish. All these are completed by a tenth—not without a wondrous mystery (as we shall declare in its proper place). Finally, in the **cubic** or "solid" **ternary** <note>3 cubed, which is 27</note>, all the Enneads are completed together. In this number, all musical 
<margin>Plato, Proclus</margin> proportions are included, as **Plato** suggests and **Proclus** discusses in a long series of arguments.
