### How the Angels are distributed through our group of nine corresponding to a simple group of three. Chapter III.

<margin>
Dionysius
Iamblichus
Theologians
</margin>

**I**t is most certain among Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century mystic who wrote the definitive guide to the angelic hierarchy</note>, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Christian views on spiritual hierarchies</note>, and more modern theologians that there are nine orders or ranks of Angels. These are completed by the number nine—not indeed a simple nine, but one composed in a certain way. This is because the angels themselves, being separated from the most simple intellect <note>God is the "most simple intellect" because He is one and undivided; angels are "separate intellects" because they are distinct spirits</note> (wherefore they are called "separate intellects" by both philosophers and Hebrew sages), admit a certain degree of composition. For within them is an essence and a power that perfects them; or, as they say, "metaphysical matter" and "form." For they are not entirely stripped of matter as they recede from "pure act" <term>Pure Act: a philosophical term for God as absolute existence without any potential to change or be anything else; He is fully realized</term>; since it is evident in the broad spectrum of existence that whatever moves away from pure act necessarily declines toward matter.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Whence Dionysius, the primary teacher on Angels, asserts that they are "unmixed"—that is, unmixed with physical matter. However, because there are ranks of perfection within them, those closest to God are distributed in a group of three, bearing a more expressive image of the simple Trinity. Those following are concluded by a doubled group of three <note>the second hierarchy of three</note>, and the last are concluded by a tripled group of three <note>the third hierarchy of three, completing the nine</note>. Therefore, the first orders, rejoicing in a more expressive image of the triune God, represent that diffusion of the highest monad <term>Monad: the ultimate, indivisible unit of being; here referring to the oneness of God</term> into the Trinity. For God the Father of all, having His essence set before His own intellect (which is called "fruitful memory" by theologians), by understanding Himself, begets wisdom, or the Word, or the knowledge of Himself, which is called the Son. Hence He acquires the name of "Father" for Himself; for the produced wisdom, being most like the producer and emanating from Him by a natural progression, rightly receives the name of "Son." But the love budding from the knowledge of both—who are the highest good—is named the Spirit and the bond of both. The **Seraphic** order corresponds to this love, which connects the parent with the offspring. The **Cherubic** order, being full of wisdom and beauty, responds to the highest wisdom and to the Son, who is the Father's delight and the beauty of all things. The **Thrones** serve the Father Himself; in them He sits and is glorified in the continual production of the Word and the Spirit. In them He also judges the world, as it is read in the Psalm: *He has prepared His throne in judgment* <note>Psalm 9:7</note>. To this throne He also calls the Son, granting Him all power of judging, as the Son himself declares in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>: *I have overcome,* He says, *and I sit on the throne of my Father.*

<margin>Apocalypse</margin>
But since the highest good easily diffuses itself into others, He produced another threefold order regarding the production and governance of creatures. By these orders and ministers, like a magnificent craftsman and prince, He decided to work and rule. But one thing must be cautioned here: that God (as Augustine and the entire school of theologians agree) always works "externally" as triune and undivided, so that none of the Persons ever works without the others. This is also proven by examples: we have from the Father (says Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note>) that we exist; from the Son, or the Word, we have the sharing of reason and order; and we have life from the Spirit of life, who broods over the worldly and heavenly spheres. Because, therefore, God the Father gives to all that they exist, He is worthily called the Lord of all, of whom it is read in sacred speech:

### Chapter IV.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
**I**t is most well known in the writings of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels.</note> that not only the lower intelligences, but also we ourselves are illuminated, purged, and perfected by the higher ones. If we assent to these, we easily ascend to the grade and order of Angels nearest to us. From which, by acting rightly and being purified, we are deservedly preferred over others, and the Archangels (that is, the Angelic princes) have care over us. Between these prelates and subjects, the Principalities intervene, so that they may subject some and elevate others by a certain occult force. Though neither of them perceives this, the subject nevertheless feels a certain yoke of the one presiding, from which he cannot easily free himself; indeed, he fears and reveres that power which the Principalities pour into the prelates, just as they themselves draw it from the terrifying seat of the divine majesty, which is situated in the North <note>In biblical and medieval symbolism, the North was often associated with coldness, darkness, and the seat of judgment or evil.</note>, and which binds all minds—angelic as well as human—under the yoke of servitude with terrifying and fiery laws. The transgression of which
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
is the evil of guilt, and the punishment is the evil of penalty, as Jeremiah, carried away by the divine spirit, prophesies: <note>original: "Ab aquilone panditur omne malum."</note> "From the North all evil is spread abroad." Whence that murderer <note>The Devil.</note>, who from the beginning did not stand in the truth, broke forth with stubborn arrogance, saying: "I will set my seat in the North, and I will be like the Most High," namely the prince of the evil and confused forest <note>The "confused forest" (sylua) is a philosophical term for "hyle" or primordial, unformed matter, often associated with chaos and sin.</note>, just as He rules in the kingdom of peace and rest. For this reason, he is often called the "Prince of this world" (that is, of things separated from God) by the true Prince, 
<margin>John</margin>
as in the Gospel titled according to John: "The Prince of this world comes," he says, "and in me he has nothing." And again He says, when discussing the triumph He was to win over him: "Now shall the Prince of this world be cast out." And toward that same Northern region mortals turn, while they transgress the law...

...betake themselves there, so that they may bring back the punishment for their transgression. There, the trembling <note>original: "pauefacientes," literally those made to tremble with fear.</note> sons of *Elohim* <note>original: "filii elohim." In this context, it refers to the "sons of the judges" or divine beings who act as extensions of God's justice.</note>—that is, the sons of the just judge God—judge severely and execute judgment most sharply. They do this to strike into both demons and men that fear of God which the <margin>Jacob</margin> Hebrews call **Pahad** <note>Hebrew: פחד, meaning "Dread" or "Terror."</note>. Jacob, the master of these sacred mysteries, spoke of this when talking with his father-in-law Laban the Aramean, saying: "Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear <note>original: "timor"</note> of my father Isaac had been with me, perhaps you would have sent me away empty-handed." <margin>The same</margin> And again: Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac. God provided him with strength from that tribunal of vigor and justice, just as He did for his father Abraham from the south <note>The "south" traditionally represents the direction of warmth, light, and divine mercy in mystical geography.</note> of mercy and piety. Adorned with their symbol, Jacob sits in the middle of the throne of glory. From the north, therefore, proceeds all evil, transgression, and the severity of punishing justice, characterized by a certain terror by which the lower ranks are brought into a state of fear toward those presiding over them.

Is not a prince a man like other men? Why would others fear and revere him unless a Divine terror elevated him? By striking fear into the rest, it humbles them so that they might revere him as a prince. All of this is executed by our Supreme Prince through those "Principalities" <note>The order of angels known as Principalities (Principatus) was believed to oversee earthly kingdoms and provinces.</note>. However, any presidency is considered far too ugly unless ornament and beauty assist the one presiding, which is why a prince is rightly held above others. Therefore, the ministry of the higher orders is necessary for a leader, so that impediments—namely, vices and the pleasures of the physical world—may be shaken off. The order of "Virtues" <note>The Virtues (Virtutes) were the angelic order associated with strength, courage, and the performing of miracles.</note> effects this. By their favor, we acquire consistency and strength, and are made powerful against vices and effeminating pleasures.

But so that we may also prevail against these aerial powers <note>A reference to "the prince of the power of the air," or demonic forces believed to inhabit the atmosphere.</note> full of envy and malice, the protection of the "Powers" <note>The order of Powers (Potestates) was believed to guard the pathways between heaven and earth and restrain evil spirits.</note> is also necessary for us, so that <margin>Elisha</margin> we may say with Elisha: "There are more with us than against us." Furthermore, so that we are not hindered by worldly affections but instead dominate them all, those intelligences called "Dominions" <note>Dominions (Dominationes) regulate the duties of lower angels and represent the sovereignty of God over the material world.</note> assist with their own strength. By their favor, we are able to bring the body into servitude and "subdue the earth," according to the Imperial decree which says: "Fill the earth and subdue it."

Thus, once dominion over all lower things is obtained, it remains for us to turn toward God and attend to Him alone. This can happen if we retain the memory of super-celestial things through the aid of the "Thrones," contemplate them through Cherubic illumination, and—being fused by Seraphic heat—are united to our Kin and Supreme Parent. Hence, just as the Supreme Architect descends to us through the Angelic steps by His power and influence, so too through those same steps may we return to Him from whom we proceeded.

Nor shall I omit what Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-5th century theologian.</note> discusses concerning this return to God by these same steps. First, he counts four affections: namely fear, grief, joy, and hope. He believed these proceed from the "irascible" and "concupiscible" powers <note>These are the "spirited" (anger-driven) and "desiring" (pleasure-driven) parts of the soul in classical psychology.</note>. To these he adds sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence. By adapting this nine-fold set to the nine orders of Angels, he attempts to lead the whole man to God—though he leaves the completion of this to the prudent reader. However, as we can gather from him, he assigns "sense" to the Angels, who are called "messengers," just as the bodily senses are themselves messengers...

### On the Source of the Intelligences. Chapter V.

<margin>
Avicenna
</margin>
**I** have thought it appropriate, before we proceed further, to investigate who was the progenitor of the separate minds <note>original: "separatarum mentium." In medieval philosophy, angels were often called "separate intelligences" because they are intellects existing apart from physical matter.</note>. This is necessary because men of the weightiest authority, such as Avicenna <note>A 10th-century Persian philosopher whose works on medicine and metaphysics were foundational to European scholastic thought.</note> and others, have dared to assert that God, the parent of all, produced only a single intelligence first. They argued this because God is always the same and exists in the same way, and therefore (as natural reason indicates to them) He cannot produce diverse things directly. From this, they restricted God’s immediate offspring to only one intelligence. This intelligence, once produced by God, turned back toward the first mind, from which it produced a second intelligence. And by understanding itself, it generated the following one, namely the soul of the first sphere <note>In the ancient geocentric model, the "spheres" were the concentric shells carrying the planets and stars; each was thought to be moved by a specific soul or intelligence.</note>. Truly, by understanding its own operation, it proceeded into producing a further one. And thus, in succession, as the cause was varied in substance and operation, various effects were produced. 

We could easily surrender to this opinion if the first craftsman were restricted to producing only one effect. But it is most absurd even to imagine this regarding the Progenitor of the universe, since not a particular, but a universal effect corresponds to Him—namely, the unique world, and the unique "being" of all things. For "the first of created things is being," <note>original: "prima rerum pducta; eſt eſſe."</note> says Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Christian mysticism.</note>, as Parmenides and Melissus <note>Pre-Socratic Greek philosophers who studied the nature of existence.</note> rightly felt, and with them Plato in his works *Parmenides* and *Timaeus*; although Aristotle might labor in vain against the words, but not the meanings, of those wise men. 

<margin>
Proclus.
Parmenides.
Melissus.
Plato.
Aristotle.
Theologians.
</margin>
Therefore, this whole universe, like a certain animal—unique in itself but diverse in its members—was brought forth by a single parent and lives by a single universal life. Our Catholic sages, however, clash with these views using other weapons. They assert that the Supreme Craftsman enters into His work bound by no natural law, but is free to perform whatever work He wills, being most full of every kind of power and every kind of fertility. Nor did He enter into external work driven by any necessity, but by an innate benevolence. Although even these almost blasphemous philosophers rightly think that the first cause acts necessarily and always remains the same in the same way, it does not follow from this that He cannot produce more than a single effect.

# THE THIRD TONE.

Since by the same sun—which always remains the same—and by the same earth—which stands forever—various effects are produced without any change in the sources and without any cultivation; namely, herbs, flowers, and those things which the earth itself, having been decomposed, produces by solar power. And if they say: "Because other particular causes work together, various effects are brought about," they have left this to be proven: whether this variety proceeds from diverse causes, or from the same sun, which is fertile with a manifold power. 
<margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin>
How much more so for the first and true Sun, of whom **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, regarded as the "father of philosophers," who was believed to have authored the *Hermetica*, texts combining philosophy, magic, and theology.</note>—rightly called the father of philosophers—testifies in these words: "My God, being most full of the fecundity of both sexes, Life and Light, by His word brought forth a second crafting mind <note>original: "mentem alteram opificem." In Hermetic thought, this refers to the *Demiurge* or a secondary creative force acting on behalf of the Supreme Being.</note>, namely the Son, fertile with all ideas and patterns of things to be made, which pre-existed in Him as the life of all things." For all things (as 
<margin>Mercury</margin>
**Mercury** <note>Another name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note> follows up) are in God: not indeed as if placed in a location, but situated in the Mind, from which producing all things, He is called the parent of all. He alone, released from the laws of nature, with no presupposed subject and no matter, produced all things—and even matter itself—by His own most full fecundity. 

But a secondary or "natural" cause (as they say) requires a subject and matter produced by God upon which to act. And in these cases, the saying which the 
**Prince of the Peripatetics** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), whose followers were called Peripatetics because he supposedly taught while walking about.</note> lays down has its place: that it is agreeable to the common perception of the mind that "nothing is made from nothing" <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fieri." A fundamental principle of ancient Greek physics which the author is contrasting with the Christian doctrine of creation *ex nihilo*.</note>. Hence 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Augustine**, rightly the father of the Latin theologians, with that entire family [of thought] asserts with a clear voice that the **Angels** can create no nature at all; and that Angels are no more the creators of things than farmers are the creators of crops. This opinion the 
<margin>Giles of Rome</margin>
<margin>Henry of Ghent</margin>
<margin>Richard</margin>
<margin>John Scotus</margin>
more recent theologians have studied to fortify: **Giles of Rome**, **Henry of Ghent**, **Richard** <note>Likely Richard of St. Victor, a 12th-century mystical theologian.</note>, and most sharply **John Duns Scotus**; all of whose writings I leave to be read in their own books. 

At this point, I am struck with the greatest wonder that such great men would deny God is the maker of all things; and that secondary causes nonetheless produce things from nothing, contrary to the philosophy they profess. In that philosophy, the more famous thinkers assert that not even by the supreme Maker Himself was the world, or anything else, produced from nothing. Those, however, who have received the light of truth, profess God alone as the author of all things. 
<margin>Alcinous</margin>
Of the whole world (says **Alcinous the Platonist**), He is the author of gods and demons; and by the gift of the divine will, this entire universe shall never hereafter be dissolved. 
<margin>Plato</margin>
**Plato**, moreover, presupposing that the "Supreme Good" itself is the cause of the separated substances <note>A technical term for angels or immaterial intellects.</note> and of their duration, introduces Him speaking to them thus: "You are indeed not immortal, nor entirely indissoluble; yet you shall never be dissolved. For if all things that have been established can be destroyed and dissolved, to dissolve and destroy those things which have been rightly established and are faring well is the mark of a wicked and self-contradicting mind." 
<margin>Mercury</margin>
**Mercury** also, when he dealt with the presiding spirits of the planets, says: "Then He fashioned seven governors," and thus he enumerates all things produced by God. Nor should it be thought that in such great harmony of the universe there were many progenitors, or that there are many rulers, or that many things consist of themselves; because from that would come confusion, dissonance, and consequently an easy dissolution in the universe.

<header>OF THE FIRST SONG</header>

### How the Maker fashioned the heavens with the second square of three. Chapter VI.

<margin>Proclus, Aristotle, Astronomers, Ptolemy, Hermes, Aratus, Plato, Plotinus, Moses</margin>
**W**ith the same number and the same degrees, the Supreme Governor distributed the heavens, namely by a second nine-fold <note>original: "nouenario." This refers to the number nine (3x3), which the author views as a fundamental building block of the universe's structure.</note>: as the opinion of the ancients and the common view holds. However, some more modern writers assert a tenth heaven, not perceiving how the motion—which they call "trepidation" <note>An obsolete astronomical theory used to explain the precession of the equinoxes; it suggested the heavens "shook" or vibrated.</note>—can be maintained in the eighth sphere without a tenth circle. Nor does it seem consistent to them that the eighth sphere itself, which is turned by three motions, should be joined to the **First Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: In the old model of the universe, this was the outermost sphere that moved all the inner spheres.</term>, which is driven by only one rotation. For the eighth sphere has a daily motion from East to West above the poles of the world; it also has a motion from West to East above the poles of the zodiac (or the signs) by one degree every hundred years—as **Ptolemy** prefers—though others assert it happens in sixty years. It also has that asserted motion of trepidation. Because of this, they think there is a ninth heaven that moves with only a double motion between the eighth sphere and the First Mobile (which revolves with only a single motion), so that all things may be led back in due order to the **First Mover** <note>God, or the primary source of all motion.</note>, who, by whirling in a single motion, sweeps all other things with Him in a regular and ordered circuit. This preserves what **Aristotle** teaches in his higher philosophy: namely, that it is necessary for all things to be led back in due order to that which is their cause.

Truly, since eight orbs are visible and are proven distinct by the **armillary** <note>An armillary sphere: a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings.</note> and other instruments—and since there is a ninth beyond these (which astronomers call the **First Mobile**, but others, for I know not what reason, call the **Crystalline heaven**) —manifest reason concludes their existence. We admit these; but a tenth, since it has nothing to support it except to maintain that asserted motion of trepidation, we do not admit, as it can be maintained in another way. Indeed, I have seen through an instrument and proved by the clearest experience that all the motions of the eighth sphere itself are maintained under that ninth circle without a tenth. This tenth orb would not have escaped **Ptolemy**, **Hermes**, **Aratus**, and other most skillful ancient investigators of the heavens, motions, and their aspects, who were content with the number nine.

But because Theologians assert a tenth, which they call the **Empyrean** <note>In medieval cosmology, the highest heaven, occupied by the element of fire or the presence of God.</note>—vital, fiery, and divine—where they receive those who led a more divine life (just as **Plato** and his Academics, especially **Plotinus** in his work *On the World*, agree with our theologians), we therefore say: even if a tenth is spoken of, it is nevertheless strictly speaking not numbered with these nine. This is because these nine are mobile, but that one is stable; these are of one matter, but that of another. We can easily learn this from **Moses**, the prince of all philosophers, theologians, and prophets—indeed, from the Maker of things Himself. When Moses was asked to dwell with Him and be instructed by continuous oracles—which were required for leading such a numerous people and for delivering the Law—God said: "I will come; but make for me a wooden Ark which shall bear the type <note>A symbolic model or foreshadowing.</note> of the world in which I dwell. You shall complete it to a cubit and a half, namely, nine palms." For a **cubit** <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm; here defined as six "palms" or hand-breadths.</note> contains six palms, and half a cubit contains three palms, by which he might represent the nine heavens. But the tenth—the cover—He ordered to be made of gold, for the material differs greatly from wood. This tenth, along with those nine, is not fully joined...

is counted: but it is the beginning of another combination. For the number ten <note>original: "denarius"</note>, although it completes the first set of numbers, is nevertheless the beginning of the tens; just as the hundred completes the tens and is the starting point of the thousands. So also that covering (which they call the **Mercy Seat** <note>original: "propitiatorium"</note>) marking the boundary of the sanctuary, offered the beginning of a better thing. For above that sat the **Cherubim**, from which acts of atonement were received. But within the Ark, the Law, the Manna, and the Rod stood hidden in a profound mystery. In a similar way, the **Empyrean heaven**, although it completes the nine-fold number of the heavens, is nevertheless the beginning of spiritual and divine things, smelling of the angelic and divine nature, so that it is proportioned to those things placed within it. 

Thus also all **tithes** <term>tithes: "decima," literally "the tenth," a portion of one's goods dedicated to God.</term>—having something divine about them—are demanded by God as His own together with the firstfruits; so that the beginning of numbers, or the origins and ends of things, or the tenths may be returned to Him who is the beginning and end of all things. However, as we intend to treat of the "separated natures" <note>referring to angels or spirits existing apart from matter</note> and of those things which correspond to one another when counted together, we will omit those which, as their perfection, being connected with the more perfect, lead lower things into that perfect one. Concerning which union of any nine-fold set <term>ennead: A group or set of nine.</term> into its tenth, we shall (God willing) discourse on the perfect harmony of those enneads. 

There are therefore nine heavens: The **First Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: The outermost sphere of the universe in ancient astronomy, which imparts motion to all other spheres.</term>, through which the First Motor moves all things; afterwards the starry heaven, through which the Maker <note>original: "opifex"</note> spreads Himself into the numerous instruments for producing things. And He carries this out through seven chief ministers, upon whom those seven chief spirits or intelligences reside. Who, existing before the throne of God, enjoy His presence; and gazing upon all things to be completed in that divine face, as if in a mirror, they execute all those same things at the nod of the Prince. Their names (if we believe the Hebrew teachers) are these: **Zaphchiel** presides over Saturn; **Zadchiel** over Jupiter; **Camael** over Mars; **Raphael** over the Sun; **Haniel** <note>OCR: "Honiel"</note> over Venus; **Michael** over Mercury; and **Gabriel** over the Moon. Who, through the heavens as if through instruments, with the influences of all stars and signs gathered together, work in these lower things by concurring to produce metals, stones, plants, and animals—but most powerfully in all things which are in man and pertain to him, whether they seem good or evil. But how they work evil or good, I judge must be briefly run through.

### Chapter VII. By what means planets or stars work good or evil in lower things.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
**T**hat the stars flow in with good and evil, both **Ptolemy** and all those who treat of astrological matters assert. Through **Saturn** is given firm and unshaken prudence; from **Jupiter**, right justice; from **Mars**, constant strength and fortitude; from the **Sun**, fervent charity and love; from **Venus**, deliberative and most sweet hope; from **Mercury**, penetrating faith; from the **Moon** (which is most easy in motion, and stubborn in nothing), moderate temperance. Nor do these planets flow in as if they were the sources or lords of these virtues described above; but by disposing the body and its powers, they lead easily to the increases of the aforementioned virtues, provided that the mind, by moderating those powers, disposes them toward their attainment.

...by that which the giver of all good things decrees to flow down through his ministers or instruments. From Saturn, likewise, as if from a weightier and more sublime patron, we are drawn toward more secret things—namely theological and divine matters, a more hidden philosophy, and the mysteries of both natures. We are also led by a certain arrangement toward the accumulation of all things to be gathered—both temporal and divine—without which no one is truly great. For what is a teacher unless he has gathered many insights? What is an Emperor unless he has amassed wealth, forces, friendships, and the virtues by which he ought to be rightly perfected? What is a Saint unless he is surrounded by manifold merits and graces? 

Through Jupiter, led by a proper temperament, we establish and preserve law; we administer <margin>Prol...</margin> what is just; we govern our subjects in peaceful order and tranquil quiet through rightful leadership, so that we might not be worse than bees, cranes, camels, goats, and other such creatures that recognize their own leader. 

From Mars, we receive strength and the drive to complete our work, so that we might be successful in our endeavors. For the cause of fortune is the impulse of nature—if Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> is correct in what he wrote concerning good and bad fortune. 

Venus bestows charm, festivity, and love. Moved by this, we may complete even the most arduous tasks with delight, for delight perfects the work. Indeed, we could not endure the labor of investigating <margin>Aristotle</margin> things natural and divine <margin>Aristotle</margin> unless love were present; refreshed by it, we suppress the weariness that constant study brings. Neither would a merchant seeking to increase his wealth, nor those who aspire to high office, endure the hardships encountered in such pursuits were they not consoled by a love for the things they seek to acquire. 

Mercury <margin>Hermes</margin> renders men prompt, sharp, and skillful in every task, but most especially in tracking down the truth and in acquiring eloquence, music, and glory. 

In all these things, the Moon provides a closer and more varied motion, so that all the higher members might correspond to man—who is the end and the "type" <note>original: "typo," meaning a microcosm or symbolic representation</note> of both the celestial and super-celestial worlds. 

Of the Sun, I shall say nothing specific, for like the rooster—to whom the dying Plato <margin>Plato</margin> said he owed a debt <note>This refers to Socrates’ last words in Plato’s *Phaedo*, asking to sacrifice a cock to Asclepius, the god of healing, signifying death as a cure for the "sickness" of life.</note>—the Sun gives fertility, activity, and life. Just as charity—when we have made it our own—adorns all virtues as their life and form, so too do all things turn to evil for those who are poorly disposed. 

Hence, when Trismegistus <margin>Hermes</margin> dealt with those whom that divine spark (whatever it may have been) abandoned upon its departure—granting the sensible and animal remains to the demon—he says: "In these, the powers of anger and desire pass into a nature that lacks reason." 

He then left to the first zone <note>The "zones" refer to the seven planetary spheres the soul passes through.</note> the function of increasing and decreasing; to the second, the plotting of evils and idle guile; to the third, the deception of idle lust; to the fourth, impious and insatiable ambition; to the fifth, profane arrogance and reckless audacity; to the sixth, wicked and vain opportunities for wealth; and to the seventh, inherent falsehood. 

And thus the soul, having left behind these lower or animal conditions to the demon and to evil influences, and being stripped <margin>Plato</margin> of the motion of [celestial] harmony, returns as a divine thing to the "eighth nature" <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, the stage of spiritual return in Hermetic thought.</note>, reclaiming its own proper power. There, together with those who dwell in that place, it praises the Father. Solomon <margin>Plotinus</margin> <margin>Solomon</margin> also hinted at this when he said: *The spirit returns to Him who gave it.* All other things are left behind, subject to vanities. From these matters, we have sufficiently revealed the mysteries, as well as the influence of the spheres upon those who are ill-disposed...

### Whence Evils Arise: Whether from the Malice of the Celestial Influences, or from the Poor Disposition of the Recipient. Chapter VIII.

**W**hen the Supreme Craftsman <note>Referring to God as the Creator, following the language of Genesis</note> saw that everything He had made was "very good," we hear with no small wonder and distress of mind the many evils that some claim arise from the stars, who are the ministers of the Best and Greatest God. These writers designate certain planets as "malevolent," calling them "wicked" rather than "celestial." They claim that Saturn devours all his children except four; <note>A reference to the myth of Cronus/Saturn, who swallowed his children to prevent being overthrown; usually Jupiter, Neptune, Pluto, and Juno are cited as surviving</note> that he is a greedy, grasping, and difficult planet, plagued by misfortune, bringing about exile, danger, deceit, wickedness, and treachery. They say he further induces violence, imprisonment, damnation, perfidy, stubbornness, anger, a hatred of all that is good, fear, anguish, pain, funerals, mourning, and bereavement. Furthermore, they claim he creates sorceries, thefts, grave-robbers, <term>undertakers</term> <note>original: "vespillones, pollinctores," those who prepared bodies for burial</note>, and mages. <margin>Firmicus</margin> Regarding the significance of Mars, the famous Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the "Mathesis"</note> provides these details with his ready eloquence: that Mars represents betrayal, battle, slaughter, audacity, rashness, arrogance, sedition, controversy, plunder, treachery, robbery, wounds, imprisonment, flight, difficulties, perfidy, obscenity, reckless love, easy offense, wavering thoughts, a lack of counsel, and violent, fierce, and inhuman princes who are always hungry for the blood of others. He describes them as perjurers, deceitful, inconstant, foul-mouthed, disorganized, contaminating and polluting everything. He also signifies deformity, shamelessness, danger in childbirth, and the miscarriage of children. And in whatever part of the heavens he resides, he always threatens some evil. If he is in Aries, he makes men thieves, loud-mouths, and frauds. In Taurus, he makes them bold, reckless, and slanderers, for whom right and wrong are the same so long as they satisfy their lust. In Gemini, he makes them devoted to malice, seeking out hidden crimes with watchful sagacity. And he continues in this way through the other signs. He speaks similarly of the "houses": <note>In astrology, the twelve "houses" represent different areas of life, such as wealth, family, or health</note> if Mars is in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The 1st House, or the Rising Sign, which governs the self and physical body</note> he makes men cunning, bold, furious, and squanderers of their inheritance. If he is in the following house, <note>The 2nd House, governing finances and possessions</note> he decrees even greater evils, great misfortunes, alienation from parents, and making men forever wanderers from their own homes, leading to wounds and chains. Wherever he may be, they calumniate him with tireless speech. <margin>Ptolemy</margin> What Ptolemy had said previously supports this, <margin>Alcabitius</margin> followed by Alcabitius and Albumasar. <margin>Albumasar</margin> <note>Alcabitius and Albumasar were highly influential Arabic astrologers whose works were translated into Latin and became standard textbooks in the West</note> One of them asserts that even without "bad radiation" <note>An unfavorable aspect or angle between planets</note> Mars perpetrates malevolent oppressions, the shedding of blood, and many crimes. The other follows with calumnies that he cannot explain in few words. I will omit what the mathematicians and poets say about Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon: such as how Jupiter and Mars may meet in shameful and foul embraces with Venus, and perpetrate many unspeakable acts. Especially in the conjunction of Mars with Saturn, or with <term>Phaethon</term> <note>A poetic name for Jupiter</note>, or <term>Stilbon</term> <note>A poetic name for Mercury</note>, or <term>Phosphorus</term> <note>A poetic name for Venus, the "Light-Bringer"</note>, or the Moon; with any of these, some evil is always threatened—specifically, injuries from iron with the first, from brass with the second, from gold coins with the third, and so on. O good God, what have You done? How can all things be good?

...[divi]ne <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "divina" (divine things), completing a thought from the previous page</note> things which you have fashioned? Why have you set such evil governors over us? Who will be safe from so many crimes? Who will be exempt from these celestial ministers—or rather, these wicked ones? It is no wonder if those who profess a knowledge of the "hour" <note>A reference to "horoscopy," or the casting of birth charts based on the hour of birth</note> predict that so many evils will follow in the world every day, since the heavens, the stars, or the presiding Angels seem to lead us to commit them. <margin>Augustine</margin> But those who are not mere dabblers, but are instead lovers of true wisdom, feel quite differently. He says: "The newborn greatly imitates the seed and blood of the parents," as is common knowledge. He also attributes much to place, <margin>Porphyry, Ptolemy</margin> which Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says is the principle of generation, just like the father. Hence, even with Jupiter or Venus as the "significator," <note>The planet that rules a specific area of a person's life or appearance</note> Ptolemy continues, a person born in Ethiopia will not be born white, because the region and the place stand in the way. <margin>Haly</margin> Customs and diet are also added: because often, as his interpreter Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer and commentator</note> says, the children are drawn toward the nature of their customs and food. Little, therefore, is left to the stars. <margin>Virgil</margin> This was not hidden from the one <note>The Roman poet Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 129–131</note> who said:
> A few, whom impartial
> Jupiter has loved, or whom glowing virtue has carried to the heavens. The sons of gods were able to. 

By these words he suggests that not only the stars, but birth and character carry men to high things. <margin>Ptolemy *Apotelesmata*, *Alarba* <note>The *Alarba* or *Quadripartitum* refers to the four books of the Tetrabiblos</note></margin> Whence the "Prince of Astronomers" <note>Ptolemy</note> himself concludes: "Just as we praise physicians who inquire into the origin of an illness and its manifold causes, in the same way we should not be held in mockery if, in judging a birth, we inquire about the region, the nativity, the food, the customs, and other factors." And in that book called the *Alarba*, he concludes that these "accidents" <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like height or location</note> often occur in the newborn such that the child cannot receive the celestial influence—sometimes receiving a little, and sometimes a lot—which many are ignorant of. Hence, in his volume of the *Apotelesmata*, he complains about the many people who, because they do not have every cause for predicting in the stars, take their divinations from another source—namely, <term>necromancy</term> <note>Divination by communicating with the dead</note> and <term>geomancy</term> <note>Divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns of earth</note> (as his interpreter explains)—thereby leading men into sophistry and error. They wish to predict those things which a mortal cannot perceive, because nothing certain can be gathered in this art, but only an opinion drawn from many dissimilar things. And when they wish to assert something with "certain knowledge"...

<summary>This page refutes the idea that stars force humans to do evil, citing Saint Augustine and the astrologer Ptolemy to argue that heredity, environment, and character are equally significant. <margin>Mercury</margin>
...they make that doctrine abominable which is [in truth] good and useful. Thus says the Leader of Astronomers <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, regarded as the founder of the celestial sciences.</note> in various places. But I shall say more: if the heavens governed all things, they would certainly be very good, being moderated by good causes. Mercury Termaximus <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus ('Thrice-Greatest'), a legendary figure of late antiquity associated with wisdom, priesthood, and the hermetic sciences.</note>, so-called not only for his reign, priesthood, and learning, but as the supreme master of philosophy, meta-

<margin>Iamblichus</margin>
physics, and theology, left written on the pillars of Memphis (as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian theology and the soul's ascent.</note> reports in a long series) that all stellar influences are the best. If something evil follows, he commands that it be ascribed to an "indisposed subject" <note>An "indisposed subject" refers to a person or thing that is naturally or morally unfit to receive a positive influence, thereby corrupting it.</note>, and not to the stars. He demonstrates this by the example of solar light, which is certainly good; but if it

<margin>Plato</margin>
offends a bleary eye, that comes from the bad condition of the receiver. Plato supports this in the *Epinomis* <note>The text reads 'Epimenide,' likely a misreference to the *Epinomis*, a Platonic dialogue concerning astronomy and the order of the cosmos.</note> with these words: "God made the moon to wax and wane, and established the months and years, and taught that the whole number of these is brought together into a number by a certain happy fortune." From this, the earth, made more fertile, conceives and bears fruit for the nourishment of all living creatures, while the winds blow sweetly and the rains fall fortunately into the lap of the earth. But if any evil happens in these things, the divine and celestial nature is not to be blamed, but rather human nature, which distributes its life

<margin>Hierocles</margin>
unjustly. Thus far Plato. Hierocles the Stoic <note>A 5th-century commentator on the Pythagorean 'Golden Verses,' often grouped with the Neoplatonists.</note> also exclaims in his commentary on the verses of Pythagoras, saying: "That anyone is evil, he himself is the cause of his own malice." Nor do the

<margin>Plato</margin>
stains of an unjust mind emanate from the purest fountains above. Plato also in the sixth book of *The Laws*: from which Aristotle, drawing in the same way in his *Politics*, teaches: "That a man who has attained right discipline turns out to be the most divine and most gentle animal; but if he has been educated insufficiently or poorly, he is rendered the fiercest

<margin>Chrysippus</margin>
animal of all that are born on earth." And Chrysippus <note>A major Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) who argued that fate and human responsibility were compatible.</note>: "He certainly attributed the cause to madness, so that they might fall by their own doing." And again:

> How falsely mortals accuse the gods, and in their folly complain;
> For we ourselves are the cause of our own evils,
> And his own senselessness harms each man.
> <note>original: "Quã falſò accuſant ſuperos, ſtultiqʒ queruntur / Mortales: etenim noſtrorũ cauſa malorũ / Ipſi nos ſumus: & ſua quẽqʒ uecordia lædit." These lines are a Latin translation of a famous passage from Homer's Odyssey, Book 1, often quoted by Stoics to defend divine providence.</note>

Confirming by reasons what has already been decreed by the opinions of the wise.

### Chapter IX.

And even if some believe all influences to be good—based on the testimony of the wise—less than they ought, unless they are worthy of Hellebore <note>A plant used in ancient medicine to treat madness; to be "worthy of hellebore" was a common idiom for being insane.</note>, they will yield to the reasons which we shall bring forward as unexplainable [certainties]. Let those who assert evil influences say, I ask: Whence comes this malice? Is it from God commanding it, or from an Intelligence <note>In the medieval and Renaissance view, "Intelligences" were the angelic beings that moved the celestial spheres.</note> moving it, or from the heaven rotating? Certainly not from God, who is the primary rule of all things. And that is evil or sin which is done against the will of the prince [God], or by deviating from His balance. Nor can evil in

<margin>Psalms</margin>
nature proceed from the fountain of goodness. Hence, against those who cast the blame upon God, the Psalmist sings: *Because they turned evils against you, they devised counsels which they could not establish* <note>original: "Quoniã declinauerũt in te mala cogitauerunt conſilia, quæ non potuerũt ſtabilire" — a reference to Psalm 21:11 (20:12 in the Vulgate).</note>, because it is exceedingly foolish and absurd even to think that evils proceed from the best God, or a transgression of the law from the supreme Moderator, since His will is the law itself. Nor should it be said: "God always concurs in the motion, and consequently in the effect proceeding from it."

Chapter IX begins a rational defense of this position, asserting that evil cannot originate from God, who is the source of all order and goodness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into why "evil" effects appear in the world if the heavens and God are good. Building on the previous page's mention of the "indisposed subject," the author now uses the scholastic distinction between primary and secondary causes to shield God and the celestial "Intelligences" from blame for human sin.</meta>

->### OF THE FIRST CANTICLE<-

But the outcome is often harmful, whether due to the one influencing or the one receiving it; ultimately, God concurs in the evil act. However, even if He, as the **primary and universal cause**, concurs by providing the influence for the act, He does not cooperate in its *deformity* <note>In scholastic philosophy, "deformity" refers to the moral flaw or "misshapenness" of a sin, rather than the physical act itself.</note>, but only in the **underlying substance of the act**. As they say: the **secondary cause** <note>The "secondary cause" here refers to the individual person or the specific earthly conditions that channel God’s general power into a specific, flawed action.</note>, which introduces the deformity, is the one to be blamed. For it is a common principle that when several causes work together toward the same effect, the effect always follows the weaker and inferior cause. If the secondary cause were in harmony with the supreme cause, a good effect would always follow. Therefore, the fault lies not with the primary cause, but with the secondary one.

There are also those who presume to accuse the **presiding Intelligence** <note>The "Intelligence" refers to the angelic being or spirit believed to guide the motion of a specific planet or celestial sphere.</note>. But let such a person answer: does this Intelligence do this by the mandate of the supreme Prince, whom everyone acknowledges as the sole moderator of the universe, or does it act against His mind and command? If they fulfill something by His command, it is certainly not evil, because nothing is truly evil unless it is committed against the order of the supreme Moderator. If, however, they do these things in opposition to the Prince, there would be great confusion in the supreme Ruler if He allowed ministers of such rebellious insolence to go unpunished.

Nor should they look to "evil prelates" <note>A comparison to corrupt church officials on earth.</note>, who are merely travelers in this life and are granted their own free will so that they may earn merit by obeying the Prince’s command, or lose it as transgressors who must soon "render an account of their stewardship" <note>A biblical reference to Luke 16:2.</note>. This was also the case with the Angels before they were established in their permanent state. Whence many were punished and expelled from the ministry of God; this is taught not only by our most divine Theology, but is also confirmed by the dogmas of the Assyrians, Arabs, Egyptians, and Greeks.

<margin>Pherecydes</margin>
**Pherecydes the Syrian** <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek philosopher often cited as one of the first to write on the soul and the cosmos.</note> describes the fall of the demons, and identifies **Ophion** (that is, the demonic serpent) as the head of the rebellious army.
<margin>Ophion</margin>

<margin>Trismegistus</margin>
The splendor of the Egyptians, **Trismegistus**, touched upon this same fall, teaching that the Angel and Man (as is clear to an attentive observer) fell from the **octave** <note>original: "diapason." In the "music of the spheres," the diapason represents the perfect harmonic interval of the octave.</note> of divine consonance into a lower harmony, or rather a dissonance, and became a most miserable slave—indeed, an exile.

<margin>Homer</margin>
**Homer**, the foremost seer and painter of mysteries among the Greeks, sings in his poems of the fall of the first rebel under the name of **Ate** <note>In the Iliad, Ate is the goddess of mischief and delusion who was cast out of Olympus by Zeus.</note>. The theology of the Arabs likewise asserts the same, emulating the Hebrew tradition. Even the demons themselves have often unwillingly confessed their fall.

Once those others had fallen and been excluded, the remaining ministers were fortified with such stability that they cannot fall hereafter. But—to speak as we do with the wise and the well-initiated—do we not say that all those celestial movements are invariable and free from error in their continuous revolution? If, therefore, those orbs are turned with such diligence that no error ever occurs, why should they not be "faithful" in their signs and influences? And if they are obedient and faithful ministers, they will not influence toward evil, nor will they create a bad disposition while executing the mandate of the **Supreme Good**.

How, then, could ministers lead one to transgression against the King when they themselves never transgress the King’s orders? How could those causes, which never fail, propel anyone toward a defect? If someone were to contend that they *do* fail: since the Supreme Moderator leaves no evil unpunished in the universe, and none without a coordinating penalty, when would they be punished? Would they cease their motion, or would they be corrected of their error? If they were to cease, how could that motion be (as they say) perpetual? If they were corrected of their error, why are they not corrected quickly? For what reason would the correction be delayed? Why would God...

<header>THE THIRD TONE XLVII</header>
<sig>A</sig>

# THE THIRD TONE
## XLVII

<margin>Aristotle; Archimedes(?) on the source of evils.</margin>
...would he entrust the administration of his house forever to ministers who have remained uncorrected for so long, or rather, who are rebellious? How shall perpetuity coexist with error, since error is nearly nothing and tends toward nothingness? To those, however, who wish to blame the heavens themselves for malice, since they can no longer accuse God or the **Intelligence** <note>In medieval cosmology, "Intelligences" were the angelic beings believed to guide the movement of the planetary spheres.</note> that moves them, we shall say: If the heavens are evil, where does their malice come from? Were they produced as evil? Or were they depraved by bad habits? Or did they fall into evil because their nature failed them?
<margin>Avicenna, Basilides, <unclear>St. Isidore</unclear></margin> 
They were certainly not produced evil by the best of Makers. Nor were they depraved by habits, since they are not endowed with **free will**; for their movements and influences are natural and not free, as everyone asserts.
<margin>Lucretius, Orpheus, Ovid.</margin> 
But some will say: they are animate [have souls], and their souls can be depraved. What, I ask you, are these souls? Would they not be the moving Intelligences? But since we have just now absolved those from guilt, let us return to the heavens. Do the heavens influence things as **secondary causes**, or as **instruments**? <note>A secondary cause has its own power to act (like a person), whereas an instrument has no power except that given by the user (like a hammer).</note> If as instruments: since they are not moved nor do they work except by the will of the Craftsman who guides them, then the blame would be left with the Craftsman—an idea that has already been rejected. If, however, they act as secondary causes: since the work must come from a living thing, the error would be traced back to their souls, or the Intelligences moving them—which has also been excluded. Let us also add this: the heavens act either by nature or by choice. If by nature: since the order of nature itself is from God, that **Peripatetic** <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, who famously walked while teaching.</note> maxim is rightly celebrated:
<margin>Aristotle</margin> 
*In those things which are from nature, we are neither praised nor blamed.* For praise belongs to the one who sets things in order, and blame cannot exist in the order of the Supreme Good. If, however, they act freely, they do so led by the **irascible** or **concupiscible** <note>These are the two "appetites" of the soul in medieval psychology: the "irascible" (governing anger and courage) and the "concupiscible" (governing desire and pleasure).</note> appetites. If by the irascible: since some planet is always (as they say) decreeing violent influences, why is its eternal anger not consumed? Why, moreover, is it said to be more ignited in one **house** <note>A "house" refers to a specific sign of the Zodiac where a planet's influence was thought to be stronger or weaker.</note> than in another? What does it find in its own house, or in a foreign one, that moves it to decree evil? Furthermore, how can something be "ignited" which they assert is unchangeable? If, however, the heavens are led by concupiscence [desire]: what benefit or utility do they gain for themselves from the lower things of earth? For desire is only extended toward such things. And he who desires wrongly does so because he is overturned by **intoxicating matter** <note>The author argues that human sin often comes from the "heaviness" or "drunkenness" of our physical bodies; since the heavens are made of pure, unchanging matter, they cannot be "drunk" or "distracted" by physical urges.</note>. But since the matter of the heavens is so far removed from change, it neither intoxicates nor overturns. From what place, then, do they accuse the heavens? They are (they will say) evil by nature. Where, I ask, does evil come from in nature? The wise gather these reasons for the origins of evil in nature: either because the cause cannot moderate an excess of matter, or satisfy a deficiency, or dispose it properly, and the like. All of these proceed from a weaker power in the cause. But since the Builder of the heavens is of infinite power, how could He fail in His handiwork? No other deficient cause was involved, since He fabricated the heavens without any assistance—
<margin>Moses</margin> 
if one believes Moses, or rather, the truth. Furthermore, what could resist the Craftsman who was leading all things into being? Who resisted the Infinite, or who can resist Him?
<margin>Isaiah</margin> 
Hence the eloquent prophet Isaiah says:
> *The Lord of hosts has decreed: who can weaken it? And his hand is stretched out: who shall turn it away?* <note>original: "Dñs exercituū decreuit: quis potest infirmare? Et manus eius extenta: quis auertet eam?" — quoting Isaiah 14:27.</note>

<summary>This page argues that neither the physical heavens nor God can be the source of evil, as the heavens lack free will and God’s infinite power precludes any accidental defects in creation. It refutes astrological determinism by pointing out the logical contradictions in viewing planets as having human-like emotions or desires.</summary>

### That neither Saturn, nor Mars, nor any other star is evil: as was previously claimed. Chapter X.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
**L**et the accusers of the stars hear what the prince of astronomical doctrine <note>Referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose works defined the field for over a millennium.</note> first puts forward concerning Saturn in the third book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelesmatū"; this refers to Ptolemy's famous work, the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>. If Saturn, he says, is the sole significator of the state of the soul; and is the Lord of the place of Mercury and the Moon, and is positioned at the angles of the world with good irradiation, he will be a lover of good things, of great and firm counsel, and a seeker of secret and divine matters. Furthermore, Firmicus, following him with many praises, 
<margin>Julius Firmicus</margin>
says: that his leadership in deliberating matters provides the sharpest intellect, certain speech, stable friendship, long-lasting modesty, and royal counsel. It also signifies a high understanding and a profound knowledge of things. Even the younger writers <note>Meaning more recent or medieval astrologers.</note> testify concerning him: that while the common life is decreed by Jupiter, Saturn claims for himself a separate and divine life. To those, however, who merely feign this life, he is more hostile than to all others; Jupiter, having been spurned by them, abandons them, nor does Saturn recognize them as his own—for he loves those who are truly solitary and divine. Hence the ancients fashioned the story: that Jupiter usurped the kingdom for himself after Saturn was driven away, by those who are always hostile to the good Saturn. He, however, lay hidden in Italy, because he began to elevate the intellects of the Italians. He is said to have come then from Greece, because sublime and profound speculations reached the Italians from the Greeks. But long ago they came from the higher and more distant regions of the East, where, according to the Arabs and Persians, the most subtle spirits dwell, and where long and "Saturnian" lives are lived in those regions subject to Saturn. But (to speak more truly) these sublime speculations were taught by divine oracles.
<margin>Albumasar</margin>
Albumasar <note>An influential 9th-century Persian astrologer and philosopher known in the West as Albumasar.</note>, perhaps emulating the Arabs, says that in the regions of India subject to Saturn, men are long-lived and usually depart only in extreme old age, because Saturn does not harm his own household. The ancient philosophers and poets sang of Saturn as the best, and claimed that the **Golden Age** <note>The mythological first age of mankind, a period of peace and prosperity.</note> occurred under his rule. The man of Sulmo <note>original: "Sulmonensis"; referring to the poet Ovid, who was born in Sulmo.</note>, 
<margin>Ovid</margin>
imitating the Pythagoreans and Platonists, sang these things in his verses:

> The Golden Age was first sown, which with no avenger,
> Of its own will, without law, cherished faith and right. 
> <note>original: "Aurea prima sata est ætas, quę uindice nullo / Sponte sua sine lege fidem, rectumq; colebat." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, 1.89-90.</note>

And he recounts many good things that occurred under Saturn; and that mortals declined once they were released from his patronage, whence he continues as the cycle succeeded, saying:

> After Saturn was sent into dark Tartarus,
> The world was under Jupiter; and the silver race came in,
> Worse than gold, but more precious than yellow bronze.
> <note>original: "Postq/ Saturno tenebrosa in tartara misso / Sub Ioue mundus erat: subiitq; argentea proles / Auro deterior, fuluo pretiosior ære." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, 1.113-115.</note>

<margin>Virgil</margin>
To this another poet <note>Virgil, the famous Roman epic poet.</note> agrees, singing:

> Before Jupiter, no farmers tilled the fields.
> <note>original: "Ante Iouem nulli subigebant arua coloni." — Virgil, Georgics, 1.125.</note>

And to Pollio, as if prophesying something great, he says:

> Now the Virgin also returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return.
> <note>original: "Iam redit & uirgo, redeunt Saturnia regna." — Virgil, Eclogues, 4.6.</note>

<margin>Plato</margin>
Nor are the poets to be laughed at, who through their poetry (as Plato witnesses) penetrated to the depths of the mind and nature. Nor did they sing mere fables, as some believe—the kind that an old woman would not even tell to boys and girls. Those then called "Theologians" wrote of profound things...

The author argues that ancient poets and philosophers used myths as allegories for natural truths, particularly regarding Saturn’s role as "Time."</meta>

<page-num>XLVIII</page-num>
<header>THIRD TONE</header>

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
...and closing off secrets within the wrappings of fables. For this reason, they are celebrated by the wise who penetrate those mysteries. Aristotle, by the testimony of Simonides and Homer, reinforces the most serious points of philosophy. Arcesilaus <note>original: "Acheſillas"; referring to the Greek philosopher and founder of the Second or Middle Academy.</note>, the founder of the New Academy, granted so much to Homer that he would never retire to bed without first reading something from him; indeed, he used to say he was "going to his lover" when he went to read, so that he might be given a greater abundance of reading. Anaxagoras and our own Basil <note>St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father who wrote on the usefulness of Greek literature for Christians.</note> are admired for their extraordinary praise of virtue in Homer’s poetry. That Tuscan man <note>original: "Thuſcus ille uir"; the margin clarifies this is Dante Alighieri.</note>, a man gifted in all science and of the sharpest intellect, places Virgil <note>original: "Maronẽ"; referring to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note>—the imitator of Homer—above others as a teacher in all natural and moral philosophy. There are also those who reduce his entire fiction to allegory. Lucretius treats all the precepts of philosophy in his songs. Orpheus, reaching beyond human capacity, sings of the mysteries of Theology and sacred rites drawn from the Holy Scriptures (as he himself admits). Ovid also disclosed the secrets of Pythagoras in his *Metamorphoses*; but by corrupting them with a step that was far too lustful, he fell somewhat from that dignity. Others also declined, to the point that they perform the office of pimps rather than of prophets <term>vates: a term for a divinely inspired poet-prophet</term> and wise men, content only to weave poisons with the charms of words. Plato rightly commanded that these be banished from the Republic, even though they sing of the deeds of heroes, lest the tender minds of the young be corrupted by their portrayed lusts—stains which a more vigorous age would be unable to wash away.

But returning to those ancient philosophical and theological prophets, they attest that Saturn is happy and benevolent. They also wished him to signify "Time," which the Greeks call *Chronos* (with an 'h' sound), derived from *Cronos* (without the 'h' sound), which signifies the god Saturn. By this, they mean that Time devours all its children because it consumes all things, with the exception of the four elements; for while all things are transmuted out of them and into them, the elements themselves remain. Of these elements, the Poets called Jupiter "Fire," Juno "Air," Neptune "Water," and Pluto "Earth." However, those evils which some people claim to discern in Saturn actually proceed from his cold and dry power, by which he is seen to favor "black bile" <note>atrã bilem: the humor associated with melancholy and the "Saturnine" temperament.</note>. From this, the desiring power and natural love are suffocated and compressed, for their seat is in the moist and the warm. Therefore, they separate the Saturnine person from human society—not the planet itself, but the person born under it, whose "complexion" <note>The physical and psychological makeup of a person, determined by the balance of bodily humors.</note> the planet has disposed, partly by influence, partly by birth and diet, and partly by habits. Such a person is separated from human society, especially if they are supported by the dryness of Mars or the coldness of the Moon. But if such a man devotes himself to contemplation, study, and divine things—which are friends to one who leads a solitary life—he will feel that Saturn is not evil, but favors him with a good influence.

If, however, anyone feels himself to be sad because of a Saturnine complexion, let him hear Him who said: *Blessed are they who mourn.* If he finds himself excessively deep in thought, let him hear Him who said: *Mary has chosen the best part.* <note>A reference to the biblical story of Martha and Mary, where Mary represents the contemplative life.</note> If he labors under the desire for amassing wealth, let him gather for himself treasures in heaven. Let a person govern himself by these same laws if he is agitated by the inflammation of Mars. For if Martial "cholor" <note>The humor associated with anger and fire.</note> makes you impetuous and wrathful, do not use it against the poor and the weak, but to restrain your own vices. For as that "Golden-Mouthed" Chrysostom says: "Where there is no anger, knowledge does not profit, judgments do not stand, and crimes are not restrained."

<summary>The author argues that Saturn and Mars are not inherently evil, but represent natural forces like Time and Anger which can be directed toward virtue, contemplation, and the restraint of vice. He cites a wide array of authorities, from Homer and Dante to the Church Fathers and Christ himself, to prove that "Saturnine" traits like solitude and sadness can lead to a holy, contemplative life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s philosophical defense of planetary influences. Having previously discussed how ancient poets used myth as allegory, the author now addresses how human passions—traditionally associated with planets like Mars and Venus—can be directed toward virtuous ends through the governance of reason.</meta>

<page-num>XIIII</page-num>
<header>OF THE FIRST SONG</header>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Therefore, battles, slaughters, audacity, pride, plunder, captivities, flights, acts of violence, and whatever else of this kind exists, may be exercised against the enemies of the Lord; and this Mars <note>original: "Mauors"; an archaic name for the god Mars, here representing the drive for conflict.</note> will not be evil. Instead, such a man will be numbered among the saints and friends of God, like Phinehas the son of Eleazar <note>A biblical figure noted for his religious zeal (Numbers 25).</note> for his commended zeal, and like David fighting the battles of the Lord. If, however, deceit, perjury, frauds, rashness, furies, evil homicides, thefts, and similar things follow: all these come from the fact that the moderation of reason is warped. Once that gate is opened, the winds of the passions rush out and blow everything about in a whirlwind. But if they were under a pious Aeolus <note>The Greek god of the winds.</note>—that is, reason ruling as it ought—or (as it is held in the Sacred Scriptures) if the beasts introduced into the Ark stayed under a pious Noah, then all the impulses that arise from "martial" heat would certainly be moderate and good. We must judge no differently regarding Venus, who is said to lead one toward shameful intercourse. For if we were to duly moderate the concupiscence <note>The desire for physical or worldly pleasures.</note> associated with Venus, even with the Sun and Mars providing their heat, love will be good and fervent toward God himself and one's neighbor. And thus all shall prove that mortals falsely complain about their own nature or the influence of the stars (as Augustine says); and that sin is so voluntary that, if it were not voluntary, it would not be sin. From where the tilt of the ill-choosing will arises—and what should be ascribed to the stars, what to matter, what to concupiscence, or what to evil morals or bad habit—we have decided to declare elsewhere, God willing.

### Whether the stars act upon us or not, and if they act, whether by knowing or by disposing. Chapter XI.

<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
Some show and assert that we gain nothing from stellar inspirations <note>original: "afflatibus"; literally "breathings" or "blasts," referring to the subtle flow of influence from the heavens.</note>. For let them remember that, in favor of the dogmas they invented, they mentioned the commandment regarding the fields: in which it is commanded in Deuteronomy that no one should reap the whole field, but should leave an untouched portion for the poor, who might take the sheaves and bundles to take away their hunger. The wise do not condemn those things which you have devised as best by your own sharp intellect—even if they were not touched upon by others; likewise, no one ought to be condemned if he scrutinizes more deeply...

Therefore, the four elements result in four kinds of perfect compounds: **stones**, **metals**, **plants**, and **animals**. The first of these is founded upon the earthy corner of this worldly house: for **Stones** always imitate the earth by descending toward the center, unless they have been burnt, like pumice—spongy stones made with cavities full of air. However, when reduced to powder, they resume their proper stony nature and descend. Along with stones are numbered **crystal** and **beryl**; although these are born from water, they have become so frozen <note>The word "congelati" implies a medieval belief that crystals were water frozen so hard it could never melt.</note> that they have become earthy and descend. This does not happen with frost and snow. Even **calculi** <note>bladder stones or kidney stones</note> generated in the bladder descend by imitating an earthy nature, even though they are born from watery moisture. And all these are solidified by a certain astringency so that they cannot be melted like metals, even though they descend just like stones. Metals are constructed upon the second, watery corner; although they are composed of all elements (as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> testifies), they are mostly composed of water and share its nature, for they can be melted. In this, we have as witnesses **Timaeus of Locri**, **Plato**, **Plotinus**, **Aristotle**, **Avicenna**, and the more recent authors who follow them. **Democritus** does not disagree, though some falsely claim he taught that metals are generated from lye and lime; for that would be like cement and could not be melted. That great **Albertus Magnus** pursues this business with a long discourse, but **Abubacher** <note>Likely the Persian physician and alchemist Rhazes (Al-Razi)</note> does so more concisely. "We see," he says, "in mines, that because of the continuous heat of certain mountains, the thickness of the water is cooked and thickened to such an extent that over time it becomes <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; mercury</note>. And from the fatness of the earth, by that same cooking and heat, <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur and mercury were considered the two primary components of all metals.</note> is generated; and with continued heat, metals are produced." For **Gold**, having no defect, is born from quicksilver and pure, fixed, clear, and red sulfur. **Silver** is from the same mobile silver and fixed, pure, clear, and white sulfur, which lacks color, some fixation, and consequently weight. **Tin** is imperfect, made from the same parts but being imperfect through scant cooking and digestion. **Lead** is from the same earthy and dreg-filled silver, lacking purity and fixation, and from a coarse, somewhat red sulfur which lacks fixation, purity, and cooking; hence it is very imperfect. **Copper** is also from the same impure, non-fixed, earthy, and burning silver, and from a combustible sulfur of this kind which lacks fixation, purity, and weight; hence it is imperfect and unclean. Of Water to Air in the bases, [the proportion is] **double-sesquialter**: in the angles, however, **double**: <margin>Motions</margin> whence **diapason** and **diapente** arise in the bases: but in the angles, <margin>Paul</margin> likewise the **diapason** arises. However, the consonance and proportion of fire to water and air to earth—in which there is <margin>Man</margin> full contrariety in their qualities—falls somewhat short of that proportion which the elements have when placed in their own order: where two always meet through an intermediate that participates in both <note>This refers to the theory that elements link through shared qualities (e.g., Fire is hot/dry, Air is hot/moist; they share "heat").</note>: as the experts can calculate.

->OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.<-

# HOW THE ANGELS OF THE FIRST ORDER
# AGREE WITH THE FIRST HEAVEN
# WHICH IS CALLED THE 
# FIRST MOVER. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
**A**FTER we have discussed the generation of the three enneads <note>original: "enneadum." In Neoplatonic and Christian mystical thought, an ennead refers to a grouping of nine, specifically the nine choirs of angels arranged in three hierarchies of three.</note>, let us come to their concord—namely, the particular harmony of one structure with another. And starting from the highest spirits, so that we may presuppose something solid, we shall approach our Areopagite Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose work "The Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels for the Middle Ages.</note>, the true observer of secrets. He, bringing forth those mysteries which Paul (as some think) or rather 
<margin>Hierotheus</margin> 
Hierotheus (as he himself admits) had entrusted to him, says: that all lower intelligences are illuminated, taught, and purified by the higher ones, and finally sent to execute the works of God. The highest, however, are destined by God alone; and all are administrative spirits sent in service. But there is a difference: for the first are commanded by God alone; the following ones, however, are destined and impelled by God and the higher ones, yet still by the command of God. 
<margin>Paul</margin> 
Here Paul, teaching that all are sent, and 
<margin>Dionysius</margin> 
Dionysius, saying that the higher ones are not destined by others—namely, by other intelligences—but by God 
<margin>Isaiah</margin> 
alone, are in agreement. This we have in the heavenly oracle of Isaiah, in which it is said: "One of the Seraphim (that is, from the highest) flew to me," surely commanded by God, to whose gaze of throne and majesty he was subject; hence that Seraph was destined by Him. But because Dionysius teaches that "Seraph" is a name of office, not of person, then some, being deceived, 
<margin>Dionysius</margin> 
said that he was not from the highest order, but was merely performing the office of a higher one. Which (unless I am mistaken) is not according to the mind of Dionysius, since all Seraphim are named from <term>שָׂרַף</term> <note>Hebrew: *saraph*, meaning "to burn" or "to be on fire."</note>, which in Latin is said "to set on fire" <note>original: "accendere."</note>. And their office is to kindle not only themselves, but the lower ones to whom they are sent. Neither does an inferior perform their ministry, nor does a superior claim the name for himself. Therefore, since that Seraph came to kindle Isaiah and to purify his lips with a burning coal, he was a Seraph by office, name, and the highest order. These highest ones, therefore, who are destined by God alone, agree with the First Mover <note>original: "primum mobile," the outermost sphere in the geocentric model which imparts motion to all other spheres.</note>, which is moved and revolved by the First Mover alone. This is the First Mover, or the first intelligence, to whom the heavens are entrusted, or the first moderator of all things. 
<margin>Proclus, the Platonists, Trismegistus, Boethius</margin> 
Which Proclus and other Platonists, agreeing in like manner with [Hermes] Trismegistus, teach, as Boethius sings <note>A quote from Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III, Meter 9, a famous poem synthesizing Platonic cosmology with divine providence.</note>:

> You, binding the middle soul of threefold nature moving all things, 
> Spread it through harmonious members; 
> Which, when divided, gathered its motion into two circles, 
> Goes on to return into itself: and surrounds the profound 
> Mind: and at once turns the heaven in its image.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the celestial hierarchy, specifically exploring how the movement of the physical heavens mirrors the spiritual hierarchy of the angels.
