<page-num>LVI</page-num>

->FOURTH TONE<-

Other heavens are moved by a certain snatching impulse from the <term>First Mobile<note>The "Primum Mobile" in Ptolemaic astronomy was the outermost moving sphere of the universe, which carried all the inner spheres (the planets and stars) along with it in its daily rotation.</note></term>, or rather from the First Mover; but they are moved by lower intelligences through a particular motion and within their own proper space. And just as the first is moved by a single impulse, so it receives a single influx; but the others receive various influxes according to the variety of the movers and the motions.

<margin>Averroes</margin>
Hence the Arab <note>This refers to the philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science.</note>, though speaking roughly, truly declares: "The best has its perfection from itself; but that which is near to it reaches it through few operations, or only one operation and one motion; but that which is distant reaches it through many." For the higher someone is, the greater their motion is in power, but the fewer they are in number; and the lower someone is, the greater their motion is in number, but the smaller in power, all other things being equal. For although the Sun is in the middle of the planets, it is greatest in power and the king of the wandering stars <note>original: "erraticorum syderum," referring to the planets.</note>; hence, like a king, it holds the middle place.

That order is also evident in the civil Commonwealth and the super-celestial one. In the civil, ministers are agitated and troubled about many things so that they may fulfill the commands of the ruler; the <term>masters of the feast<note>original: "Architriclini," a term for those who manage a banquet or household, acting as intermediaries between the lord and the servants.</note></term>, being commanded, then command others and are moved by few things. But the lords, with a certain gravity, command almost immovably, not departing from their place or their purpose. 

In the super-celestial Commonwealth also, the lower intelligences are called *Malachim* in Hebrew <margin>Daniel</margin> <note>original: "מלאכים"</note>, *Angeli* in Greek, and in Latin *nuntii* or "those who are sent," because they are more frequently destined for us to carry the mandates of the Supreme. But the higher intelligences, because they are rarely sent, were called "those who stand by" <note>original: "assistentes"</note> by Daniel. They are sent sometimes, however, if Paul <margin>Paul</margin> speaks truly saying that "all are ministering spirits sent for the salvation of those who are capable of the eternal inheritance." The intermediate ones are sent more frequently than the higher and less often than the lower. 

So in the celestial Commonwealth, the higher circles move more slowly, and the lowest move more quickly. The Moon, the lowest of all circles, completes its own motion in twenty-eight or twenty-nine days. Saturn, being higher, in thirty years. The Sun and Venus, being intermediate, in one year. The <term>starry heaven<note>original: "Stelliferum," the sphere of the fixed stars, located just below the Primum Mobile.</note></term>, the supreme of all visible spheres, completes its revolution in many thousands of years; although all are snatched along by the First Mobile, whose motion comes immediately from the First Mover—hence it is single and simple, while the motions of the lower circles are multiple.

If it pleases us to run through the particular agreements which that First Mobile has with the supreme order of intelligences, which is that of the Seraphim, let us see what the great Dionysius <margin>Dionysius</margin> brings forth from the workshop of his teacher regarding those Seraphic minds. For he attributes sixteen things to them, saying:

> The name of the Seraphim signifies: always moving around the divine; unceasingly hot; sharp and super-fervid; of an always inflexible motion; leading back the lower ranks; an active exemplar; reheating those lower things; restoring them to a similar warmth from heaven with that fiery vigor provided, those things which it purges like whole burnt offerings <note>original: "holocausta"</note> by the greatest force of fire; not being veiled, but bright, inextinguishable, always illuminating, expelling all dark obscurity.

And let us see how much the First Mobile agrees with the Seraphim in these matters: For since it is the first thing that is moved, and immediately by the First Mover itself, it is rightly always borne toward that first one in its revolution, so that, receiving its commands, it may fulfill all things in others according to the will of the commander. It is necessary, secondly, that it move unceasingly...

[...thrives with inestimable] heat: by which it moves without pause, and draws all things with such force that they are at least not hindered by so great a machine. Moreover, it must be sharp in the power by which it penetrates all things and spreads its force even to the farthest spheres. And since it carries all along with it, it is more fervent than all of them. Therefore, as it is said, the order of the <term>Seraphim<note>The highest order of angels in the traditional Christian hierarchy, associated with fire and love.</note></term> is "super-fervid." For if they must move all lower things and make them glowing and God-like, that which makes all things glow for the sake of motion must itself be super-fervid. 

And since all lower things move at its command so that they may always fulfill what the Highest orders, both are forced to have an inflexible motion. And lest the labor of both in moving the things subject to them seem in vain: just as the Seraphim, by their fiery power, lead lower minds back to God, so this sphere, snatching everything in its fiery rush, so disposes them that they may return to the First. 

And because each not only pushes but, by proceeding, draws everything with it, they are called "active patterns." By the burning heat of the Seraphim, and by the swiftest motion and influence of this fiery sphere, they heat all things and thus lead them back into that fire by which they themselves are kindled. But the angels draw their power from God, whom they enjoy, while this sphere draws it from the twelve revolutions of the Great Name, which the Hebrews call <term>Havayah<note>original: "hauaiā". This refers to the Tetragrammaton (YHVH), the four-letter name of God in Hebrew, often associated with existence or "Being."</note></term>.

<margin>Hebrews, Greeks, Pythagoreans</margin>
Any one of these revolutions is placed over a sign of the Zodiac; and the whole name—which the Hebrews call the four-lettered name, the Greeks the <term>Tetragrammaton<note>A Greek term for the four-letter Hebrew name of God.</note></term>, and the Pythagoreans the <term>Tetractys<note>A triangular figure of ten points, sacred to the Pythagoreans, symbolizing the organization of the universe.</note></term>—is over all the signs. Their power is in the <term>Primum Mobile<note>The "First Moved" sphere, the outermost moving shell of the heavens.</note></term>, as the astronomers say; for although images appear in the starry heaven, they do so not only in the placement of the stars, but in true figures. This has been proven at certain times and with instruments by most esteemed men, who saw with their own eyes the figure of the Bull or the Ram in the circle of the signs. 

Therefore, by the power of that Holy of Holies and most holy Name, those angels are kindled, and this sphere—like a <term>fuller's wheel<note>original: "rota fallonū" (likely fullonum). A fuller's wheel was used in the process of cleaning and thickening cloth, here serving as a metaphor for spiritual purification.</note></term>—purifies those things which it moves, so that they are kindled like burnt offerings to ascend to the Highest. And just as the Seraphim know nothing higher by which they might be covered, since they are devoted to the first Light without a medium:

<margin>Plato</margin>
so this circle has no higher moving circle, since it is contiguous with the <term>Empyrean globe<note>The highest heaven, believed to be composed of pure light or fire and the dwelling place of God.</note></term> and the seat of God. That seat is so suffused with divine light that nothing obscures it, but rather it illuminates everything, having taken on the nature of what is above it—just like all <term>denaries<note>Groups of ten; likely referring to a mystical or mathematical grouping explained elsewhere in the text.</note></term>, about which we will discuss in the proper place. Hence, both are always brilliant. They also contain an inextinguishable light and fire by which they may always inflame and illuminate: so that the angels by their perpetual, clarifying fire, and this sphere by its snatching and its fiery power, may—after many circuits and with the dregs cast aside—return all things needing purification to the Creator, fully cleansed, so that they may make their destined return to the same source.

### Chapter II: On the harmony by which the Cherubim correspond to the starry heaven.

**W**e follow with the order of the **Cherubim**. Let us see how much they agree with the starry heaven. A "Cherub" (if the now-commonplace <term>Chaldean<note>A reference to Aramaic or Neo-Babylonian linguistic traditions often cited in Renaissance mysticism.</note></term> interpretations are true) is a "spotless picture." From this, a Cherub is called a <term>Phrygian work<note>In antiquity, "Phrygian work" (opus Phrygium) referred to exquisite embroidery or intricate needlework.</note></term> or something fashioned; or (as it pleases **Abraham ibn Ezra**<note>A famous 12th-century Spanish Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>) it is a picture or image of any separate form. But what more beautiful picture is there in the whole machine of the world than in the eighth heaven? There, many images exist, not made by Phrygians, Indians, or by **Arachne of Lydia**<note>A mythological weaver who challenged the goddess Minerva (Pallas) and was turned into a spider.</note>, but by **Pallas** herself and Divine Wisdom, who [decorated] the heaven...

# VOLUME FOUR

He painted that heaven with ever-living figures (as some prefer) and full of power: just as he had painted the species of Ideas in the Cherubic minds. Therefore, by another interpretation, the Cherub is called "multiplied knowledge," or "fullness of knowledge," or "many knowledges and orders," or "great order"; from <term>he ordered</term> <note>original Hebrew: *kara* כּרבּ</note> and <term>much</term> <note>original Hebrew: *rab* רבּ</note>. For in them, knowledge is multiplied, and the species of things are manifold, just as in the heavens there are many images. In both cases, however, the picture is spotless and indelible: it will be consumed by no decay of envious time, nor will it receive any foreign painting or impression, as both are filled with complete images from the fountain of Ideas. From these, as if from exemplary forms, this earth is composed with such a living ornament of flowers and herbs. For just as the earth is adorned with flowers and the heaven with stars, so the Cherubic mind is adorned with various scientific forms. Therefore it is called "multiplied knowledge," as its contemplation is extended to knowing the most diverse things. Likewise, the starry heaven is "multiplied light" for the sake of warming and nourishing the most diverse things. The Cherubim also nourish these lower things through that same heaven, the First Cause giving to them the source from which they may flow.

<margin>David</margin> Hence the Psalmist sings: *He ascended upon the cherubim, and flew* <note>Psalm 18:10</note>: so that all things might be arranged as quickly as possible through their all-encompassing knowledge and power. 
<margin>Dionysius</margin> And this is that first operative power (to use the words of <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical philosopher.</note>) with which the Cherubim are filled and disposed for the arrangement of lower things; as <margin>Hugh</margin> <term>Hugh</term> <note>Hugh of Saint Victor.</note> and <margin>Albert</margin> <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus.</note> agree in their expositions. 
<margin>Dionysius</margin> And what the Supreme Architect performs through the Cherubim, as if through ministers and secondary causes, He also brings about through the star-bearing orb, as if through an instrument; a point on which many agree with the Catholic Academics. Furthermore (says <term>Dionysius</term>), the Cherubic order is filled with divine beauty and the tradition of wisdom, and it communicates these to the secondary kinds. So too the eighth sphere <note>The firmament of fixed stars, which in ancient astronomy sat above the spheres of the planets.</note> is full of most beautiful stars and powers to be communicated to the second kind, namely the <margin>Pl...</margin> wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>. 
<margin>Astronomy</margin> It is common knowledge among astronomers how much power the constellations grant to the planets when they receive them into their "houses." The disposition they induce in the horoscope of someone being born is manifest; and no less so in the arrangement of other things in the lower world. They seem to moderate this "machine" <note>The physical universe.</note> beneath the globe of the moon, yet with favor drawn from the Supreme Parent and His holy name. 
<margin>David</margin> As it is sung in the Davidic hymn: *O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth!* For the earth draws life, beauty, and power through those starry figures and virtues imbibed from that Holy Name. Between these, the seven wandering stars <note>The sun, moon, and five visible planets.</note> intervene: which themselves receive the source of their influence from the "seven measures" or "circles of the fabric" (as <margin>Hebrew Theology</margin> the theology of the Hebrews teaches), regulated by their own seven intelligences. That star-bearing circle <note>The Zodiac.</note> is divided into twelve principal images, each of which disposes both a part of the earth subject to it and some member of the <term>lesser world</term> <note>The "microcosm," or the human body, which was believed to mirror the structure of the universe.</note>. Thus both worlds are regulated by the heaven itself; its middle circle is called the "Circle of Minerva" or "Circle of Justice" by the <margin>Egyptians</margin> people of Memphis, and the "King's Guide" by the <margin>Arabs</margin> Arabs. For by it, as if by a rod...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Cherubim, moving from their definition as "multiplied knowledge" to their role as mediators between the divine unity and the diversity of the created world. It reconciles Platonic philosophy with the angelology of Dionysius and the visions of the prophet Ezekiel.</meta>

<page-num>LVI</page-num>

## OF THE FIRST CANTICLE

<margin>Academics, Plato, Plotinus. Dionysius, Augustine. Dionysius, Psalms.</margin>
In a certain way, the supreme King governs the lower realms through the Cherubim, as if through ministers. In them, that singular knowledge of the King is multiplied, so that they may understand in repeated turns those things which the Supreme One encompasses in a single act. Likewise, the heaven explains through repeated revolutions those things which the Craftsman <note>Referring to God as the 'Opifex' or Demiurge, a term used in both Platonic and Christian thought.</note> grants in a single influx. And just as the starry heaven is rotated by the First Mover, so the Cherubim are stirred by the first order of Angels, namely the Seraphim. Thus, even among them, a place is found for that dogma of the Academics <note>The followers of Plato's Academy.</note>, or rather of divine men, which teaches that those who desire to become learned and wise must first become "amatory" <note>Filled with divine love or eros.</note>. Being moved toward the King through the love of beauty, they are then stirred to contemplate those very things. Plato writes most extensively on this in the *Symposium*, and Plotinus in his work on the *Triple Return of the Soul to God*. Hence, those things in Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential 5th-century Christian theologian and neoplatonist.</note> which seemed contradictory are easily reconciled. For he teaches that the lower Angels are taught, illuminated, and purified by the higher ones; yet he also says that the Cherubim receive immediately from God what is then communicated to those in the second rank. For all contemplate the divine essence without a medium, so that they may find bliss in the sole fountain of happiness. For if they were to draw from any channel short of the infinite, they could easily feel a defect in the influence and the influx alike, and such a defect cannot coexist with beatitude. That vision of the divine essence is called "midday" by Augustine; the vision of things in the Word is called "morning"; and the vision of things in their own nature is called "evening" <note>Augustine's famous distinction between *cognitio vespertina* (evening knowledge of creatures) and *cognitio matutina* (morning knowledge of things in God).</note>. Therefore, all angelic minds and the minds of the blessed are carried—with God as their guide—into that knowledge of the "right hand of the Most High," where all delights are found, which are said to be the Archetypes <note>The original divine blueprints or Ideas.</note> at His right hand; according to that saying of Dionysius: "All rejoice as the Father moves them" <note>original: *Gaudent omnes movente Patre*</note>. To carry out lower tasks, however, the lower ones are arranged by the command of the higher, whom they obey—while always keeping their eye directed toward God. As the Royal Prophet <note>King David, traditionally credited with the Psalms.</note> sings: *Set your hearts upon His power, and distribute His dwellings* <note>Psalm 48:13. The author interprets "dwellings" as the celestial and worldly spheres.</note>. This is the speech of the Prince commanding the angelic ministers: that they should always direct their hearts and affections toward God through the Seraphic fire. Being stirred by this, they distribute His dwellings—namely the celestial and the worldly. In this ministry, they are inflamed by the Seraphic fire, or rather by the fiery Spirit of God through the Seraphim. From them, they also receive the increase of illumination for handling lower matters; but so that they may fully enjoy God, they are illuminated by the infusion of the light of God Himself.

This is confirmed by the wondrous oracle of Ezekiel. <margin>Chapter 3.</margin>

Here I would wish the wise to be asked not to criticize me if I separate this passage of our Ezekiel from the common interpretation. All Catholics admit four senses in the Sacred Page: by which the truth of the letter, the business of the soul, the mystery of the Church, and the secret of heavenly glory shine forth. ...was given to Christ from the seraphim through the hands of the cherubim: for He did not give that fire to Him as to an inferior, but rather assigned it as a minister to the Artisan, by whose command the work was being carried out. For even if all things were made through the Word, He nevertheless executes many things through ministers, as a Supreme Prince. And after He received the fire, those serving Him went out to the work: because just as the Artisan, girded with love (as Dionysius, <margin>Dionysius</margin> <margin>Boethius</margin> Boethius, and other wise men testify), went out to bring the building to completion, so the ministers, kindled by love, execute what the Artisan commands. Yet these ministers themselves, because they cooperate with the Artisan, are not called the creators of things, but rather the executors of Him by whom all things are made. From this follows: *And there appeared among the cherubim the likeness of a man's hand*, namely His, who said: *My Father is working until now, and I am working.* <note>John 5:17</note> And lest anyone suspect from this interpretation that the Cherubim are in some <margin>Plato</margin> <margin>Plotinus</margin> <margin>Dionysius</margin> way the creators of things, we can also satisfy the critics by interpreting the passage differently: so that the "cherub" is the "ideal knowledge" <note>term: idealis scientia — the divine "blueprint" or world of ideas in the mind of God.</note>, or the knowledge of things to be made, which received the fire of love from the midst of the cherubim: that is, from the ideas and pictures <margin><unclear>sign/mark</unclear></margin> <margin><unclear>eye</unclear></margin> <margin><unclear>thing/deed</unclear></margin> which are in that most divine Word, by which He was moved before He unfolded them into their own proper forms. Therefore it is said that after the fire was accepted, He went out to the work. Indeed, He proceeded from nowhere else to go out into the building, except from love. Next follows the partitioning of the building along with the Cherubim themselves. *And I saw* (he says) *and behold, there were four Ophanim <note>original: "Ophanini," the Latinized Hebrew word for "wheels."</note> by the cherubim.* These Ophanim (if we wish to follow the literal letter) are the wedges or <margin>Jerome</margin> iron circles (as Jerome rightly feels) by which the spokes of the wooden wheels are tightened and bound, and they are not "wheels" as our translation <note>The Vulgate usually uses "rotae" (wheels).</note> has it. But if it pleases us to scrutinize the matter more deeply, the Ophanim (according to Abraham in the *Book of Formation*) <margin>Abraham</margin> <note>Abraham is the traditional attributed author of the "Sefer Yetzirah" (Book of Formation), a foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note> belong to the *Merkabah* <note>original: "mercaua," the Chariot-Throne of God in Ezekiel's vision.</note>, that is, the tribunal of the most high God, together with the seraphim, the angels of ministry, and the holy living creatures. For just as the intelligences correspond to the acting heavens and planets, so the intellectual virtues—which are called Ophanim—preside over the arranging of matter and elements. These Ophanim, next to the cherubim, arrange matter according to full knowledge or according to the "ideal pictures." And for every single thing to be arranged, there is one Ophaninus present next to one cherub: that is, according to the particular "idea" of the thing to be made. And since all the patterns of things are hidden like treasures of wisdom in the Word made flesh—as that great Paul says—therefore the likeness of a man is brought into the completion of the building. <margin>Paul</margin> With wondrous artistry, the heavenly prophet mentions now the supreme and uncreated cherub (that is, the fullest picture of the ideas), and now he commemorates many ministering ones, hinting that the God-like Cherub goes out through the produced cherubim and Ophanim to arrange the harmonious building. And because this work possesses not only consonance from the Master Musician <note>original: "Archimusæo," literally the "Chief of Muses," referring here to God as the cosmic conductor.</note>, but also beauty from the Beautiful itself, there follows: *Now the appearance of the Ophanim was like the vision of a Tarshish stone.* That which Aquila and our translation <margin>Aquila</margin> <margin>Symmachus</margin> <margin>Psalms</margin> have as "chrysolite," Symmachus translated as "hyacinth," and the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (Greek Old Testament).</note> translated as "carbuncle." But *Tharsis* [Tarshish] often signifies the sea, according to that verse of the Psalm: *Breaking the ships of Tarshish*, that is, of the sea. But returning to the interpretations of the stones...

...are uncertain, and vary among different Hebrew, Greek, and Latin authorities, yet each is moved by his own reasoning. Rabbi Bahya <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish kabbalist known for his commentary on the Torah</note> also interprets *tharshish* as chrysolite, which in Hebrew is called *cariolic* <note>original: קריאוליק. Likely a transliteration of the Greek 'chrysolite' into Hebrew script</note>. He claims this stone has the color of the sky or the deep sea, and that its power aids in digestion and "fattening" <note>This refers to the spiritual or physical enrichment of matter</note>. Thus, regarding the tribe of Asher (to whom this stone was assigned), it is said in the prophecy of Jacob: *Of Asher, his bread shall be fat; and he shall yield royal dainties.* <note>Genesis 49:20</note> And if we wish to reconcile all interpretations, we can indeed do so through the symbolism of everything contained within that one mysterious name of the Holy Tongue <note>Hebrew</note>. For if its meaning is "the sea"—since water, along with earth, is the nursery of all things—what fits the organization of matter better than the watery power supplied through the <term>Ophanim</term> <note>The "Wheels" from Ezekiel's vision, interpreted here as the angelic forces governing the physical elements</note>? For the Ophanim illuminate darkened matter by organizing it, disposing it to receive form and shape; hence their work is truly precious.

If, on the other hand, they interpret it correctly as chrysolite (as is common usage), it is itself like gold with a certain sea-like color, as Pliny, Arnold, and Bocchus <note>a legendary figure cited in medieval gemological texts</note> write. Ezekiel

The interpreter of sacred things adds that there were four Ophanim to organize the matter that was to receive the forms of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> before the composite whole was brought together. But because in composite things only one "face" is seen, it follows that *their appearance was as one likeness*, as if it were *an Ophan within an Ophan* <note>Ezekiel 1:16, "a wheel within a wheel"</note>. This is because in composite things, every single element is within the other; and if the joined whole is dissolved, it returns into those four elements. Therefore it follows: *When they went, they went toward their four sides* <note>Ezekiel 1:17</note>—meaning from the "friendship" or harmony of the composite body toward their own parts—*and they turned not as they went*. This is because elements, upon reaching dissolution, do not return into the composite whole unless led back by a higher cause. Thus he adds: *To the place whither the head looked, they followed*—that is, the leader—the elements themselves being obedient to a higher cause. As for the fact that the flesh, back, hands, and wings of the Ophanim are said to be *full of eyes*, it is a most beautiful image; for in the organization of the elements, as many "eyes" are required in the organizers as there are forms to be introduced into that subject matter.

### Chapter IV.
### The five properties of the Thrones.

<margin>Dionysius, Prologue</margin>
**H**ow great also the concord is between the Thrones and the third sphere—which is the first of the wandering stars <note>In the Ptolemaic system, Saturn is the first planet encountered when descending from the fixed stars</note>—we can judge from those things which <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational mystical theologian</note> hand down concerning the Thrones, and <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The famous astronomer and geographer</note> concerning his Saturn; each of them being easily the chief in his own teaching. For we have, in the ancient translation of Dionysius concerning the very seats of God, these words verbatim: *They are the highest and most compact of seats, diligently exalted above every ignominy of subjection; bearing upward to the highest point above the world, and ineffably into the most sublime at every extremity; and placed about the truly High with all their strength, incommunicably and stably; and receptive to the divine super-advent in all passibility and immateriality; and God-bearing, and familiarly open to divine receptions.* This indeed is the declaration of their names (as far as concerns us). Thus far Dionysius: but a little before he had said: that the name of the Thrones signifies an outpouring of wisdom, and a manifestation of their god-like dispositions. By which words, from the denomination rather than from the essence or reason, he touches upon the properties of the holy seats of God. The first is: that although they are seats, they are nevertheless exalted from all ignominy: because just as to serve God is a certain kingdom, so to be the footstool of God Himself is indeed not ignominious, but to be honored above all, and sublime. Therefore he prefaces that they are "highest." Next, the clarity with which these seats are illuminated is hinted at, because he says they are "compact," that is, joined in consonant truth (if <term>Hugh</term> <note>Hugh of Saint Victor, a 12th-century scholar</note> <margin>Hugh</margin> his faithful interpreter explains it well), because the one judging in them is truthful; indeed, He is truth itself. For the "joint" in the divine footstools is the agreement of judgments with that uncontaminable truth. Or they are "compacted" by love (as <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus, teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note> <margin>Albert</margin> prefers), just as our chairs are held together by nails or glue. Indeed, both interpret it well: because in those seats there is the power of Seraphic love and Cherubic illumination. And this is what the Lord commanded Aaron and the other priests who minister to God and judge in His place: that they should carry on their breast the <term>Urim and Thummim</term>; which our exposition holds as "doctrine" and "truth." But in interpreting the force of the words, *Urim* signifies "illuminations": from <note>original: אוֹר (*or*)</note> "light"; but the plural signifies manifold doctrine and collective illustration (with which a priest ought to be filled). *Thummim*, however, designates "perfections" and removals from any lower stain through the love of God. For priests ought to be perfect, so that they might worthily perform the office of the most perfect God. In the third place, so that their upright and faithful movement toward the Prince judging above them might be understood, he says: that they are raised up to the supra-mundane and most sublime, placed with all their strength in the truly High. Fourthly, so that they might draw from there...

### Chapter V.

->Let us see how this order of Thrones agrees with Saturn.<-

**T**he Thrones are said to be "exalted" above lower things: hence they are intimate with God, who through them judges all things contained within His workmanship. For anyone may obtain favor for himself from God through the celestial instruments and His ministers. ### OF THE FIRST CANTICLE

...divinity <note>The text likely completes the word "divinitatis" (divinity) or "trinitatis" (trinity) from the previous page</note>: which is called twofold: to which Saturn and the intelligence presiding over it corresponds. From this place flows rest, the remission of sins, and that abundance which is called the Jubilee, following the square of the number seven <note>Referring to the 49 years (7x7) that precede the 50th year Jubilee in Leviticus</note>: which agrees with Saturn, the seventh planet. It was said in the second place concerning the Thrones, that they are joined together by truth and love. <margin>Julius Firmicus</margin> And concerning Saturn, that famous Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman astrologer and author</note> says that he is tenacious: and he makes his "Saturnians" <note>Those born under the astrological influence of Saturn</note> well-joined together: hence he delights in silence and solitude (as <margin>Alchabitius, Ptolemy</margin> Alchabitius and Ptolemy bear witness). And they are of firm and solid counsel, as Ptolemy testifies: they are of a most tenacious nature from that joining together; therefore they gather greedily and dispense with difficulty; and being separated from society and collected within themselves, they investigate the secrets of God and nature more sharply through silence and an elevated mind: so that, along with the Thrones, they may become the living seats of God. Wherefore the above-mentioned astronomers—and with them <margin>Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, Avicenna</margin> Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and Avicenna—continue, saying: Saturn favors a high intellect, a profound knowledge of things, a more secret philosophy, and theology: of such a kind is that of the Hebrews, which tastes of the influence of the supramundane Saturn. And in this, he is most perfectly made equal to the Thrones: in which the sitting judge ought to shine with genius, knowledge of the laws, stable speech, long providence, and royal counsel: to which is added rectitude, unstained faith, and a harmony with the Prince who sits there. And of Saturn it is said, that if he rules alone, troubled by no impediment, he grants the firmest friendship. Furthermore, the Thrones are called <term>God-bearers</term> <note>Latin: "Deiferi." Those who are filled with or carry the presence of God</note>, pouring forth wisdom and God-like dispositions. And Saturn is a God-bearer, receiving divine inspirations <note>original: "afflatus"</note>: which he diffuses into his Saturnians. I shall not omit what antiquity reports of Saturn: <margin>Janus</margin> that he taught Janus wisdom, and yielded a part of his kingdom to him, finding in this that the outflow of wisdom proceeds from Saturn: filled with which, he has the greatest part in obtaining the kingdom: and he diffuses God-like dispositions in the times dedicated to him. Therefore, that age is preached as the most happy: and that there was then a Golden Age, in which neither theft nor anything done wrongly was committed: <margin>verses</margin> "There was no helmet, no sword, nor any use for the soldier: nor was it lawful under him to divide the field with a boundary: nor for anyone to be pressed into servitude: nor was anyone then troubled by the injury of war or famine." <note>These verses describe the mythical Golden Age of Saturn, a period of primordial peace and communal living</note> Therefore, as <margin>Macrobius</margin> Macrobius reports, solemnities and sacrifices were dedicated to him, which were called the *Saturnalia*: which were celebrated for seven days. In witness of this matter, <margin>Novius, Mumius, Masurius, Mallius</margin> Novius and Mumius are cited, although Masurius and Mallius felt otherwise: the former of whom consecrates only one day to him, the other three: for his solemnity was once a single day: but by <margin>Caesar, Augustus</margin> Caesar first, and later by the decree of Augustus, it was extended to a three-day holiday: however, the added celebration of the *Sigillaria* <note>A festival of gift-giving following the Saturnalia</note> extended the public discourse and religious joy to seven days. Indeed, the number seven is suitably dedicated to Saturn: who is the seventh planet: who suggests rest: to which the seventh day is ascribed: which indicates the seventh millennium: in which (as John testifies) the suggester of evils being held in chains, mortals shall rest, spending a tranquil life: which was sufficiently prefigured in <margin>Leviticus</margin> Leviticus through the seventh year of rest, and through the Great Year of Jubilee, after the squares of seven.

And this Law, pregnant with the divine birth of the Gospel, appears exhausted or cast out; yet it is held in the highest honor by those who think rightly, because the Gospel does not abolish the Law, but fulfills it down to the smallest "jot and tittle." <note>A reference to Matthew 5:18</note> Thus all the orders of Angels are joined with the <term>Thrones: the third-highest rank of angels, associated with divine justice</term> Thrones to complete the judgments of God, but the Thrones themselves are joined to none. <margin>Dionysius</margin>

...I believe this declares the revelatory name of the Dominations. It represents a certain absolute and free <term>anagoge: a spiritual or "upward" interpretation of text or reality</term> <note>original: "anagogen"</note>, liberated from all lowly, earth-bound degradation. In no way is it inclined toward any tyrannical lack of resemblance. It is a "freely severe" Dominion, placed above all demeaning servitude, superior to all subjection, and removed from all unlikeness to the Divine. It unceasingly desires the True Lordship and, as far as possible, conforms itself and those beneath it into the likeness of that naturally subsisting Power, doing so in an excellent and beautiful manner. It does not turn toward any of the vain things seen by the eyes, but toward the true, universal *Being* <note>The author uses "On," referring to the Greek "Ο Ων," meaning "The One Who Is" or "Being itself."</note>, and it is made a participant in the eternal, God-like form of the Lord, as far as is possible.

Thus far Dionysius. His intent (as he mentions beforehand) is to declare the names or designations of the holy Dominations, which are full of mysteries. The first of these is that they possess a certain absolute elevation, free from any trampling depression that might diminish the dignity of one who rules. Secondly, their mind is free from any tyrannical unlikeness, to the point that one finds no such inclination in them. Indeed, nothing can be more properly ascribed to tyranny than a "lack of resemblance" to true leadership; for the true leader rules by right, while the tyrant rules against it. The former strives to favor and lift up his subjects; the latter seeks to depress and plunder them. The former breathes truth, piety, generosity, justice, and mercy; the latter scatters everything with lies, deceits, impiety, greed, and cruelty. One acts through a divine image, the other through a diabolical one. The tyrant is therefore unlike a legitimate Prince—and much more unlike God, whose Dominations they represent.

Thirdly, true Dominion is liberal yet possesses a "severe equity." It is unencumbered by any menial or diminishing servitude. Nor should anyone think that severity is repugnant to liberality; for severity is a fair distribution without any biased affection, so that a judge, leaning upon the truth, may be able to restrain insolence and, with proper generosity, honor those who are deserving. This he cannot do unless he has a mind free from greed, hatred, personal gain, and similar things which lead the soul into a servitude that tips the right balance of justice. Hence, the Supreme Prince of all frequently cries out to, commands, and protests to judges and those holding his place, that they must keep their hands free from every gift; for gifts, once the eyes of the mind are plucked out, lead one into a most miserable servitude.

Hence, in the fourth place, it is inferred that a ruler must be superior to every kind of subjection—whether contracted through gifts, blood-relations, family ties, clientele, country, friendship, habit, ambition, or from any other source.

Fifthly, it is added that Dominion must be removed from any "unlikeness" to the Supreme Prince, who is Truth itself. Sin introduces this unlikeness, by which one deviates from the First Truth. Hence, the Greatest Teacher <note>referring to Christ in the Gospel of John 8:44</note> says of the first rebel: *He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.* But I think that "slayer" or "killer" <note>original: "occisor"</note> could be more aptly translated than "murderer" <note>original: "homicida"</note>; for at that time, he was not a killer of man, but a killer of himself. Furthermore, the word "murderer" is not in use among the Hebrews, in whose idiom John wrote his Gospel where those words are recited. Therefore, they are, and are to be...

# FOURTH TONE.

<margin>Exodus</margin> They ought to be so conformed to God that they may deservedly be called "Gods." As is said of them <margin>David</margin> in Exodus: *You shall not revile the gods* <note>original: "Diis non detrahes." The author clarifies that here "gods" refers to "judges" (iudicibus).</note>, meaning the judges. In the same place, it is commanded that the thief and the perjurer be brought before the "Gods," that is, the judges. And the Psalmist <note>Referring to King David</note>, when he sang of such beings, or of the Apostles who were set over the twelve tribes of Israel, said: *The strong gods of the earth are greatly exalted.* It follows sixthly that they must incessantly desire dominion. Here, the weak might be offended: asking how those beings of holy intelligence are said to aspire to dominion with unwearied desire, when in this Church—<margin>CHRIST</margin> of which that celestial one is the type and exemplar—those who burn for presidency are condemned by the supreme <term>hierarch: a leader of sacred rites or a high-ranking angel</term> Christ. For as He says in the Gospel titled according to Luke: *The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called "benefactors," but you are not to be so; instead, let him who would be greater among you become as a minister and a servant.* 

We shall satisfy these doubters by bringing forth the truth known to the wise: for the appetite for dominion and presidency, since it is innate to our nature, does not seem blameworthy. Nor can we immediately desire subjection and the lowest rank, just as we cannot extend our will toward pain; for <margin>Augustine</margin> pain (according to Augustine) happens from things we do not want. Thus, to desire the lowest things is against the instinct of nature, which is always carried toward greater and better things. Hence, one who desires great things should not be called proud, but <term>magnanimous: "great-souled," a virtue involving the pursuit of great honors through merit</term> <note>original: "magnanimus"</note>, if <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle teaches correctly in his *Ethics*. And if the appetite for presidency were a fault, the supreme <margin>CHRIST</margin> teacher, Christ, would not have proposed it as a reward to those renouncing earthly things, saying: *You shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* And <margin>Apocalypse</margin> again in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, to lead us toward the struggle and victory, He promises a high seat, saying: *To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on His throne.* 

Therefore, it is not the appetite that is to be blamed, but a "bad object"—namely, when we wish to be exalted in these momentary things of our pilgrimage at the loss of heavenly things, toward which we ought to aspire. The manner is also to be blamed, if one presumes to obtain by one's own power those things which ought to be recognized as coming from the Giver of all good things. 

This is where he <note>Referring to Lucifer/Satan</note> erred, who said: *I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of God; I will sit on the mount of the covenant on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; and I will be like the Most High.* He commits as many sins as he utters words. He claims a sublime seat for himself when no merits exist. Furthermore, he wished to climb to a more eminent throne without being called, when he should have sat in the lowest place until he heard the <margin>Jeremiah</margin> Prince saying: *Friend, move up higher.* And he had decided to sit on the mount of the covenant, on the northern side, from whence the law was given, where the stubborn are punished, and where falls and many crimes abound, according to that saying of Jeremiah: *Out of the north all evil shall break forth.* Hence, he deservedly felt the sentence and judgment of God, since he attempted to place himself (though in vain) in the seat of judgment. He likewise sought to climb above the height of the super-celestial clouds, from which all things are watered through the channels of God; and he wickedly thought to be made like the Most High, of whom he was not even worthy to be a servant.

## Chapter VII.

<margin>Julius Firmicus, Prologue</margin>
**I**t will be easy to judge how harmoniously Jupiter attains these attributes of the Dominations <note>The "Dominations" (or Lordship) are the fourth of the nine traditional ranks of angels</note>, if the things which astronomers testify about him are true. For that famous Julius Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman senator and astrologer</note>, from the school of Ptolemy, says: The significance of Jupiter is dignity of form, nobility of soul, sound wisdom, and intellect; then rights, laws, statutes, and religion; then piety, modesty, grace, faith, and whatever the soul of an excellent and well-ordered man can conceive. All of which he works most powerfully when he is in the Horoscope <note>The Ascendant or rising sign in a birth chart</note>, or in his own houses, or in his terms <note>specific degrees of a zodiac sign</note>, or in his exaltation, and in signs and places in which, rejoicing from a connatural property, he receives favor—so that he may dispose one toward those things which the Dominations influence by the command of the Prince. Positioned in places of this kind, he also makes men noble, illustrious, great, and distinguished presiding officers or governors of cities, and—according to the measure of their birth—good, modest, benevolent, joyful, and wealthy. And all these things (to speak physically) he works from a hot and moist nature, rendering the temperament manageable because of the moisture, friendly because of the blood, disposed toward wisdom because of the proportional heat, and noble because of the abundant influence. Hence in him is piety, benevolence, faith, modesty, grace, and whatever pertains to the just and the right; for a well-tempered complexion easily disposes one toward all good things. But if we wish to climb higher, this influence is drawn from the Dominations, which dispose the soul, while the star disposes only the body; but God, as the primary cause, provides both the influence and the growth to all. But let us come to the harmony. It has been said of the Dominations that they are free from all "pedestrian baseness" <note>original: "pedeſtri uilitate"; referring to crude, earth-bound, or common vulgarity</note>; and of Jupiter, that he disposes one toward nobility of form. Who, I ask, ascends to a more sublime place: man or beast? Man or woman? Angel or man? He, surely, who is more elegant in form is worthily placed before the others.

<margin>Genesis, Psalms, Paul</margin>
For among all living things, to man alone—who is more beautiful in form than all others—it was said: *Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and the beasts of the earth.* And of the Prince of all it is said: *Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men* <note>A reference to Psalm 45:2, often applied to Christ</note>. Nor is that form which merely charms the physical eyes sought in those who exercise dominion; but rather that which Paul desired for the Thessalonians—that they might deservedly be leaders and princes of others—saying: *You have been made imitators of us, so that you might be a form <note>In the sense of a model or pattern (original: "forma")</note> for all believers.* Of this form the Law boasted (as the Hebrews explain) or the Blessed Virgin, as our people assert, saying:

<margin>The Song of Songs</margin>
**I am black**, as far as outward appearance goes, **but beautiful** with an inner beauty. If indeed both types of beauty should coincide, a species even more worthy of the pious will result. He speaks in the second place of those who are subject to no tyranny, injustice, or robbery. And regarding these, he adds: **Nobility of soul is the sole and unique virtue**, as the <margin>Juvenal</margin> Satirist <note>The Roman poet Juvenal, known for his Satires; this quote is from Satire 8</note> says. Therefore, it is not the one who shines with bloodline, wealth, or power, but the one who glows with virtue who is deservedly called noble. Of this nobility, the <margin>Ecclesiastes</margin> wise man speaks when he says: *Blessed is the land whose King is noble.* So too Moses, who was instructed no less in moral discipline than in natural and divine matters, said in his repetition of the law: *I took from your tribes men who were wise and noble, and I appointed them as Princes, captains of thousands, of fifties, and of tens.* However, where we have "noble" in Deuteronomy, in the Hebrew it says <term>irduhim</term> <note>original: "ירדוחים" (yeduim); meaning those who are "known" or "recognized" for their reputation</note>, which is to say "those known" for their virtue and goodness. This is true nobility: a liberty removed from all tyranny and impiety. 

Regarding those minds, it is said in the third place that they have free dominion over themselves, trampling upon all things that lead them away from God. For what is this, if not the required moderation of all things by a ruler, which pertains to prudence and wisdom? And regarding the significance of this sixth heaven <note>The sphere of Jupiter</note>, it is said to be "sound wisdom and intellect." For who possesses sound wisdom and intellect except the one who moderates all that must be done, <margin>Lactantius</margin> admitting what is profitable and rejecting what is harmful? Hence Firmianus <note>Lactantius, often called the "Christian Cicero"</note>, defining wisdom, says: **Wisdom is the understanding directed toward the good, and the abstinence from sins and all wicked things.** <margin>Hierocles</margin> Hierocles the Stoic, moreover, put forth these thoughts regarding prudence and wisdom together: **Prudence and wisdom, the leaders of all divine and good things, when placed in a man's upright soul, support him so that he may counsel well concerning all matters.** This he does if he rules himself rightly and tramples underfoot all devious paths, so that he may be raised upward toward that sublime end for which he was destined. 

It follows in the fourth place that they should be free in their affections and minds from base subjection. And it is said of Phaethon <note>A poetic name for the planet Jupiter, meaning "The Radiant One"</note> that in the horoscope he makes those born under him great and leaders of the city. And if they are great, it is necessary that they be free in mind and heart. This liberty the Supreme Prince seeks not only in <margin>Paul</margin> princes, but in all his soldiers. Hence Paul glories with the Galatians: **We are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman; with this liberty Christ has gifted us**, snatching us from the slavery of sin and the tyranny of the devil. 

He adds in the fifth place that they should admit nothing treacherous into themselves that would render them degenerate or unlike the Supreme Hierarchy. And of our benign star <note>Jupiter</note>, <margin>Julius Firmicus, Alcabitius</margin> Firmicus and Alcabitius say: it leads one to the decreeing and observing of laws, rights, and statutes. Even the Hebrews call Jupiter <term>Zedec</term> <note>original: "צדק" (Tzedek); meaning "Justice" or "Righteousness"</note>, which signifies "the Just." For he is just <margin>Augustine</margin> who rightly observes the laws of truth and those eternal rules by which (according to Augustine) all things are moderated. 

It is subjoined in the sixth place that, out of a certain generosity of soul, they should serve no one except the Supreme Prince. And Jupiter always pursues his "Phaethontic" followers with justice and goodness, continually promoting them to sublime heights. From this it follows seventhly that, just as those people always labor to reach divine things to the best of their power, so Jupiter, by the influx of justice, continually leads his own people toward God.

In the eighth place follows love and charity toward others, so that they may lead them to the same goal toward which they themselves strive. The piety and justice of Jupiter <note>referring to "Jovian" qualities—characteristics associated with the planet Jupiter in Renaissance astrology, such as justice and benevolence</note> act in the same way. It is concluded in the last place that those minds, united with the Hierarch <note>The leader of a celestial or ecclesiastical hierarchy</note>, are one and the same, filled with all goodness and perfection. Hence, Pythagoras asserted that Jupiter was virtue, and harmony, and the temperament of the soul, health, and every good; and therefore, by his favor and help, all things stand firm.

### Chapter VIII. On the three equations of the fire of Mars with the Virtues.

<margin>Dionysius</margin> So that we may examine the harmony of the fifth order of the Enneads <note>The "Enneads" refers to the nine orders of angels described by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> themselves, let it please us to look at what our Dionysius, full of God, teaches concerning the holy Virtues. He says that the very "strong and unchangeable virility" <note>original: "virilitatem"; in this context, it implies spiritual strength or fortitude</note> of the holy Virtues indicates that in all their operations, according to their God-like form, they are not prone to any weakness in receiving divine illuminations. Rather, they are powerfully led back into the imitation of God, not abandoning their God-like movement through their own weakness, but bearing themselves firmly toward the super-essential and power-giving virtue; they are made as a similar image of that virtue (as far as is permitted) and are powerfully turned toward it as the principal virtue, while also giving to the secondary virtues in a God-like manner. 

These are the words of Dionysius. And before we proceed, we shall endeavor to declare why this fifth order is called by the specific name of "Virtues," even though all Angels are called "virtues" <note>In the general sense of "powers" or "strengths"</note> by the same Dionysius. This is rightfully so, since every operation requires an operative virtue. Therefore, since no order of Angels or particular intelligence languishes in idleness, but all execute the commands of the Prince, virtue is required in each of them, by which they might be named "virtues." To remove this difficulty, we shall remember what has been said about the Seraphim, Cherubim, and the other orders. For although the Seraphim understand, and all other spirits love, the Seraphim are nevertheless called "the burning ones" from the love with which they most intensely glow. And although all spirits understand, the Cherubim are nevertheless named from the fullness of their knowledge. 

In the same way, this order is called "Virtues" from the gift in which it most flourishes, although all angels rejoice in their own virtue and their own strength. <margin>Albertus</margin> The opinion of Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note> is also pleasing here: that since the higher orders are decorated with more noble titles, they yield this specific name to the lower ones. For Priests, although they hold the rank of Deacon <note>as they were ordained deacons before becoming priests</note>, nevertheless claim for themselves the more dignified name of Priest. The same is true of Bishops, Patriarchs, and the like. Therefore, the Virtues are named from the gift in which they most shine. This gift is described as being decorated with multiple properties—namely seven, which they receive from the highest virtue, and two by which they communicate themselves to the lower orders. For this is characteristic of all the ministers of God established in the Hierarchy: that they communicate to the lower orders those things which they receive from the higher. The first gift, therefore, is virility and unshakable fortitude for the overcoming of those things which belong to the highest...

### They war against the Prince [of darkness].

This mystery is wonderful: how that supreme and most blessed Emperor in the kingdom of peace—where he has broken the powers, the bow, the shield, the sword, and war—and being himself true peace and the blessedness of all, still contends and fights through his <term>Virtues</term> <note>The "Virtues" are the fifth order of angels, traditionally associated with performing miracles and, as described here, with divine strength and spiritual warfare</note>. To his favor, that warrior David prayed, saying: <margin>David</margin> *Fight against those who fight against me*, or *contend with those who contend with me*—as the <note>original: "veritas hebraica"</note> Hebrew truth has it—and *take up arms and shield, and rise up to help me.* For if his place is in peace, with all instruments of war broken, how can it be said that he fights? And if he fights, how does he rest in peace? Again, if he is almighty, what is a battle to him, since he could crush all things with a single nod? Let us open here something of the heavenly secrets. God most high is the supreme power, the perfect essence, lacking nothing, almighty, all-knowing, most blessed in himself, suffering nothing, susceptible to no contagion, no force, no trouble, and no external pleasure; for he does not need our goods, nor is he offended by any opposition. It is God himself working all things in all, and filling all things, so that he is able to rejoice, suffer, and fight in his members <note>The "members" refers to the "Body of Christ," the community of believers on earth</note>, as he himself testifies, saying: *I was hungry, I was thirsty,* and so on. He is, therefore, most blessed in himself and in the members reigning with him [in heaven], for whom he no longer takes up shield, sword, or war, since they all enjoy perfect peace in that triumphant court. He is also both fighting and suffering in the members of this <margin>JESUS</margin> <term>militant church</term> <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians on earth who are considered to be in a state of spiritual warfare against sin and the devil</note>. For he fought in the good angels against the bad; he fought in Moses, Joshua, David, and other soldiers who fought his battles, especially against <margin>Deuteronomy</margin> <margin>Exodus</margin> Amalek, against whom a perpetual war was declared, as is commanded in Deuteronomy and even more strongly in Exodus, where it says: *Because the hand is upon the throne of God to fight for the Lord against Amalek from generation to generation.* This battle was carried out most powerfully by Jesus Christ until he had utterly cast him out. Moses speaks of this battle <margin>Numbers</margin> in the book of Numbers, saying: *Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord.* Many, not paying attention, struggle to explain what that book was in which the wars of the Lord were written, and they mention many things that are not so; for Moses speaks of the future and of the book of the Gospel, as those with a sound understanding interpret it. For in that book are treated the wars of the Prince of Glory against the prince of darkness. Paul expressed this more <margin>Paul</margin> clearly when writing to the Colossians in these words: *Christ, taking away the <term>handwriting of the decree</term> <note>original: "chirographum decreti"; a legal metaphor for the record of human debt or sin</note> that was against us, and despoiling the principalities and powers, triumphing openly in himself, confidently brought over all the spoils and garments held tyrannically by the enemy.* He also fights daily in his militant members until they are led to true rest, of which it is said in Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah</margin> *My people shall rest in the beauty of peace, in the tents of confidence, and in wealthy rest.* The victors rest in the beauty of peace once the enemies have been defeated, and having put them to flight, they dwell in the tents of confidence, but they enjoy the "wealthy rest" while possessing the spoils. Since God carries out this battle in his members, he also commands his particular soldiers, who are called the "heavenly Virtues," to fight for us, lest we be overwhelmed by the mighty power of the enemies. And concerning the final battle, which will be the most bitter of all, it is said

<margin>Matthew</margin> It is said in the Gospel according to Matthew: *The powers of the heavens shall be moved* <note>original: "Virtutes cœlorum mouebunť"; Matthew 24:29. In Latin, "Virtutes" refers specifically to the angelic rank of Virtues</note>, namely to assist those who are then fighting. Therefore, those to whom battle is specifically committed are called <term>Virtues</term> <note>The Virtues are the fifth order of the celestial hierarchy, associated with the power to perform miracles and provide strength</note>; they are endowed with a virile and unshaken fortitude. And what the supreme Emperor <note>God</note> accomplishes through the Virtues, as if through ministers, he likewise accomplishes through Mars, as if through an instrument. It is common knowledge that Mars favors all who wage war, owing to his nature which is (to speak in physical terms) always ignited with a fiery favor, so that he makes his "Martial" followers choleric, wrathful, impetuous, brave, virile, and unshaken. Secondly, it follows concerning the holy Virtues that they undertake and perfect all their operations as beings that are Deific and Deiform <note>God-like in nature</note>, just as all other Intelligences <note>Angels</note> do; having been made Deiform, they do not deviate at all from that uniform and Deific beauty. This is what Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and every celestial instrument accomplishes, praising in this the supreme Craftsman, who fashioned all things to be "exceedingly good." Hence the Deiform harpist <margin>David</margin> sings: *Praise him sun and moon: praise him stars and light.* For the stars, both fixed and wandering <note>the planets</note>, and the light of them all, praise the Craftsman in this most resonant theater of the universe. Thirdly, it is required that they be in no way weak in drawing in the influence of divine power, lest they succumb if their own strength fails; for their strength tends toward nothingness unless favor is continually supplied from that supreme source, both for themselves and for those whom they favor. <margin>Moses</margin> Thus Moses came to the aid of the people fighting against the Amalekites by the power which he drew in by praying continually with his arms stretched out in the shape of a cross. <margin>Ptolemy, Hermes, Julius Firmicus, Alchabitius</margin> Mars also provides this by his fiery strength, as Ptolemy, Hermes, Firmicus, Alchabitius, and all the astronomers agree. Whence the <term>Empyrois</term> <note>Likely referring to a source or personification of the fiery Empyrean sphere</note> says: For the fiery power is never-failing and works without interruption. It is also always increasing and receiving growth according to the increase of matter. And so that it may always work upon that which is by nature defective, it is necessary that it always drinks [from the source]. Therefore, it is necessary for Mars, together with the present Virtues, to always drink from the superior power, so that they may always assist those fighters over whom they preside.

# XVI OF THE FIRST SONG.

The <term>Deiform</term> <note>Meaning "God-shaped" or "having the form of God"; a state of being perfectly aligned with the divine will</note> nature and the battle they have undertaken: lest they be driven out from the kingdom and the military service along with Saul, who did not fight with that faith which he ought to have had. In the sixth place, they are led firmly and incessantly into the most powerful and super-essential virtue, by which they may be compared to a perfect image of the Prince <note>God</note>. There is no trifle or repetition here; rather, it declares that they are always ascending to more sublime things:

First, they possess virile constancy. Second, they perform every work that is celestial and Deiform. Third, lest they grow weak, they always draw from the supreme source. Fourth, they have God before their eyes as a model. Fifth, they persevere in the work they have begun. Sixth, always tending toward the supreme Hierarch <note>The leader of the celestial order, God</note>, they acquire for themselves His complete likeness and image. To achieve this, they are turned toward God himself with all their affection and all their strength. Thus, like the most holy vessels filled with all spiritual gifts, they communicate, in the eighth place, virtue and strength to the inferiors entrusted to them. Last, they strive with all diligence to make those whom they favor Deiform. Toward all these things, <term>Pyrois</term> <note>A Greek name for the planet Mars, meaning "The Fiery One"</note> seems to dispose them by his fiery power. And since we have spoken of the first five stages, let us proceed with the sixth.

<margin>Dionysius. Plotinus.</margin>
Fire is (as our **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the orders of angels</note> bears witness) always tending upward, but **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> goes further and says: *Fire, reaching as far as heaven, since it cannot be sluggish, tends toward other things by its own expansion, seeking everywhere.* And since it cannot be carried to lower things—for it is very easy to lead when you are pushing it, and is led by a natural pull from the soul toward life—it makes a transition into the highest realms through communion with superior things, prepared by a single life. Whether Plotinus transcends the boundaries of philosophy or truth, let the readers judge. However, we hold this as a constant: that fire is always carried upward and seeks the highest rather than the lowest things.

What, I ask, could be said that is more suited to the sixth property of the **Virtues**, by which they are always carried upward, so that while serving the celestial beings they may strive to be transformed into their likeness? It is no different with the seventh property, by which they turn to God with all their strength to do the same, just as fire, which always strives to transform into the highest things whatever it can ignite, not only itself but everything else. But stones, earth, metals, and whatever things refuse to yield, it leaves behind in their lowliness.

And what has been said of fire, **Mars** likewise effects out of his own nature and fiery impetus. Regarding this, <margin>Ptolemy</margin> **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the famous 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note>, proceeding no less physically than mathematically in the first book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>Ptolemy’s foundational work on astrology, also known as the Tetrabiblos</note>, says: *The star of Mars dries and burns, and its heat is likened to fire.* Hence, through the fiery properties assigned to Mars, we have made him correspond with the most holy **Virtues**; thus, those whom Mars and the Virtues favor are rendered prompt and skillful for all things.

But since good happens in only one way, while evil happens in many ways, an impetus moderated by no bridle of reason and directed by no interior eye rushes, like a wild horse, into manifold precipices: tyranny, oppression, unjust homicides, thefts, robberies, immoderate lust, and other evils which the <term>sciolists</term> <note>People with superficial or "smattering" knowledge who pretend to be experts</note> are accustomed to predict with too much broad license through the significance of Mars. For this comes not from Mars, who only provides the impetus, but from the soul that directs that impetus poorly.

To achieve these things, the <term>choleric fervor</term> <note>In the theory of the four humors, the "choleric" temperament was associated with fire, ambition, and the planet Mars</note> seeks among natural gifts; among celestial gifts, it seeks Martian favor; among super-celestial gifts, the vigor of the Virtues; and among divine gifts, the grace of God or the inflammation of spiritual fire. By this fire, the saints were made strong in war: they conquered kingdoms; they performed justice; they obtained promises; they shut the mouths of lions; they extinguished the violence of fire; they escaped the edge of the sword; they grew strong out of weakness; they turned back the camps of foreigners, and other such things which Paul mentions when discussing the Hebrews.

<margin>Paul</margin>
These things Paul himself, as a true theologian, attributes to the fervor of faith; nonetheless, other correspondences also intervene. Nor is Mars alone the cause (as the pure <term>mathematicians</term> <note>In this period, "mathematicians" often referred to astrologers who calculated planetary positions</note> believe). For this reason, so many errors bubble up in their prognostications: namely, because they do not attend to the cooperating causes alongside the heavens, which their own leader, Ptolemy, teaches must be observed.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
And because the convergence of the stars and their virtues are not fully known by us—as is well known to all wise men—no certain judgment can be given regarding their effects. This is further complicated by the freedom of <term>will</term> <note>Free will was a crucial theological defense against "hard" astrology; humans could choose to resist planetary influences</note>, by which we are able to reject many things and undertake many things according to our desire. Nor should sharper minds be moved by the fact that the stars seem to provide a complete life and form to plants or to animals generated through putrefaction; nor should they conclude that because some of those forms seem good and others evil, that good and evil proceed from celestial influence. If they fall into this heresy, they will be easily removed from it if they observe (besides those things we brought up earlier) that it would be utterly absurd for anything turbid to emanate from those most limpid fountains of celestial or super-celestial waters.

<margin>The same</margin>
And regarding this Mars, Ptolemy decrees in the third book of the <term>Apotelesmata</term> <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology</note>: that if he alone presides over the disposition of the soul, the person born will be most brave and powerful. If, however, he is poorly disposed, this should be ascribed not to the stellar influence itself, but to repugnant qualities arising from a certain <term>antiparistasis</term> <note>A philosophical concept where a quality is heightened or altered by the presence of its opposite</note> of influences. But (to speak more accurately) this happens because the subject is poorly disposed: just as medicines, the best wines, and the most delicate foods harm those who are in poor health.

<margin>Iamblichus, Trismegistus</margin>
And regarding such things, <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work on theurgy and divine mysteries</note> draws these points from the pillars or storehouses of the great <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" wisdom tradition</note>: All celestial influences are good and beneficial, receiving only good itself. In doing this with an eternal gaze, they are immutable; although they may degenerate while working in this alterable nature, they are nonetheless always beneficial by a perpetual order. Therefore, from the flux of heaven into matter full of discords, something dissonant occasionally results, yet the celestial powers always remain good. Thus, the harmful quality on earth is distinct from the celestial influence, which, while it exists in itself and flows from the giver of goods, is good until it reaches the lowest depths.

### Chapter X.

<margin>Dionysius. Plato chapter 8.</margin>
**S**O THAT we may cause the most holy <term>Powers</term> <note>The "Powers" (Potestates) are the sixth rank of the nine angelic choirs, positioned between the Virtues and the Dominations</note> to agree with the planets under the King, we must see what Dionysius teaches about them. He says: "The well-ordered and unconfused arrangement of the holy Powers, equal in power to the divine <term>Dominations</term> <note>The rank above the Powers</note> and <term>Virtues</term> <note>The rank below the Powers</note> regarding divine receptions, and the arrangement of the super-mundane and intellectual power: not headlong or tyrannical toward those things which are inferior to the powerful Virtues, but powerfully led back to the divine after things well-ordered, and after that leading others back in a God-like way, and assimilated (as far as is lawful) to the power-making causal power, and revealing it (as is possible for Angels) in the well-ordered ranks through their powerful virtue." These are the words of Dionysius. Among the beginnings of this discourse, he includes the most worthy privilege of the holy Powers: that they are those which coerce all evils and the malignant together. Which Gregory and Bernard aptly report. Of whom the former [Gregory] says: "Those Angels are called Powers who received this more powerfully than the others in their order: so that the adverse powers are subjected to their command, by whose power they are restrained, so that they cannot crush or overshadow the hearts of men." Nor is there a confusion of celestial orders, because the gifts of one are shared with another: for just as all love and understand, so two...

->FOURTH TONE<-

<margin>Synesius</margin>
...the melodious harmonies of the universe and the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original divine model or "blueprint" of the world in the mind of God.</note>. Through the power of love, we are affected in the most beautiful ways. However, through philosophy—aided by the benefit of reason and discourse—we abstract universal principles or, as the Scholastics <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers who used a highly structured method of logic.</note> are accustomed to say, the "quiddities" <term>quiddities: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of things. The first of these stages occurs through a certain sensory reason, by which we perceive the consonance of things. The second occurs through the desiring reason, by which we are moved by that rhythmic harmony we have perceived. The third, however, occurs through the intellectual reason, which abstracts from all sensory things. Having been raised up through these steps and ascending to higher things, we lead the soul toward the ideas of total beauty and consonance, and finally to the Good and the Beautiful itself, toward which all its ministers and instruments invite and draw us. 

For Mercury impels us toward number, Venus toward love, but Phoebus <note>A name for the Sun, representing clarity and intellectual light.</note> toward abstract contemplation. And sometimes the Moon, being familiar with the Sun, performs his office and claims his name for herself, being called Phoebe. She—as 
<margin>Julius Firmicus, Mathematician</margin>
Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century lawyer and astrologer.</note> and other mathematicians <note>In this period, "mathematician" often referred to those who studied the movements of the stars, including astrologers.</note> assert—makes people cultivators of the fine arts and most diligent explorers of all sublime things. In the super-celestial causes and the ministers of the highest Prince, these same things occur through this final Hierarchy. For the **Angels** receive those who are released from sensory chains and are free for heavenly things. The **Archangels**, however, together with their own Mercury, set forth divine numbers <note>In the Pythagorean and Platonic tradition, "numbers" were seen as the divine building blocks of reality.</note> to be contemplated—numbers which follow the abstraction from the senses, just as sensory and vocal sounds precede it. Afterward, the **Principalities**, who care for all things with equal mind and arrange all things, may introduce us to that supreme Beauty to which we truly ought to be moved. 

This is where the thought of Iamblichus tends—or to put it better, 
<margin>Iamblichus, Trismegistus</margin>
the thought of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and hermetic writings were attributed.</note>, from whom Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</note> learned what he wrote: The **Angels** release us from the chains of matter; the **Archangels** call us upward by their sonority; the **Principalities** draw us toward Beauty itself by the power of love and unite us to it. And thus all the ministers of the Prince, most faithfully executing the duties entrusted to them, strive to lead all those under their care to the common Prince, unless those committed to them resist. 

Whence, to one asking why the Angels of the Persians, the Chaldeans, and other nations did not lead those entrusted to them to the knowledge of the true God, 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> responds, saying: "We cannot accuse the Dominations or the Archangels of being anything but upright and just. If the nations entrusted to them have slipped away into the worship of those who are falsely called gods, it must be blamed on the people themselves, who by their own habits strayed of their own accord from the right path tending toward God." The cause of such a pernicious error was self-love and pride. Whence the same crime is sometimes cast against the rebellious Hebrew people by the Prophet, saying: 
> You have rejected the knowledge of God, and you have walked after your own heart. <note>original: "Scientiam Dei repulisti: & post cor tuum ambulasti."</note>

Coming finally to the Angels, our teacher Dionysius says: For the Angels themselves (as we said before) fulfill and complete all the dispositions of the celestial minds, according to what must be completed.
