We call it a Planet, as it were, according to observation: because the decrees of the Moon are observed more than those of other planets. This is either due to the familiarity it has with us, or because it appears larger than the others besides the Sun; or because it is more varied in its motion, or because its harmful effects—being cold by its very nature—are more evident; or because it is the receptacle for all other celestial influences; or because its motion is <margin>Ptolemy</margin> more perceptible to common people (says Ptolemy) and even to the wise who claim this discipline for themselves. Hence, when I asked some people of this sort why they only observed the decrees of the Moon in giving medicines and administering other things, and not those of other planets, they responded: "Because the Moon is large, its motion is clearly perceived, and it is closer to us." I laughed, <margin>The Same</margin> remembering what Ptolemy states at the beginning of the *Apotelesmata* <note>original: "Apotelesmatū." Truly, because Galen—in forecasting illnesses and the death resulting from them—and Al-Kindi—in prescribing medicines, potions, and pills—seem to observe the decrees of the Moon, let those who only recognize the luminaries alongside irrational animals not rejoice. <margin>Al-Kindi</margin> For both of them, alongside the Moon as the <term>executrix</term> <note>One who carries out or performs a task; here, the Moon carries out the "orders" of higher celestial bodies.</note> of what the higher bodies decree, also observe the decrees of those higher stars. However, in a square aspect with the Sun, because it loses its strength, the rising and falling of the waters becomes weakest.

## Chapter XIV.

<margin>Solomon</margin>
**H**aving completed the harmony of the first and second <term>Enneads</term> <note>A grouping of nine; here referring to the hierarchies of angels.</note>, our pen must be turned to the correspondence of the elements with the heavens and the supracelestial minds. And first, the Earth corresponds to the Moon with a manifold harmony. First, because the Earth attracts and drinks in water: so much so that the wise man <note>King Solomon, traditionally the author of Proverbs.</note> numbers the Earth among the insatiable things which are never satisfied with water; so the Moon, by a perpetual attraction, draws the water, sometimes making it ascend—namely, when it rises from the eastern horizon to the mid-heaven—and descending from that same mid-heaven to the western horizon, it draws the water down with it with such force that it seems to flee from us. When it then proceeds from there to the opposite point of the mid-heaven, it draws the water with it: again returning to the eastern horizon, it leads the waters like its own handmaidens. It also draws the humors <note>The vital fluids of plants and animals.</note> upward in trees and human bodies by increasing [waxing], and drives them to the depths by decreasing [waning]. It agrees, secondly, in the primary qualities of cold and dryness: with which the Earth is filled in actuality, but the Moon in virtue.

<margin>Plato</margin>
From this nature, she [the Moon] is undeservedly blamed as harmful or malignant, though she is actually beneficial. For she drinks in, from her own earthy nature, those celestial waters and all the influxes of the heavens: which, because of her proximity to us, she communicates. Therefore, she receives from the other planets—especially the Sun—what she then imparts to earthly things. Hence Plato, in his *Symposium* <note>Original: "Convivio." A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of love and the origins of humanity.</note>, says the Moon is a participant in both the Sun and the Earth. She is, moreover, singular in her variety: for at one time she is curved into horns <note>The crescent moon.</note>, at another divided in equal proportion <note>The half moon.</note>, and at another curved into a full orb. She is sometimes sprinkled with spots, sometimes immense as a full circle, and suddenly she is nothing <note>The new moon.</note>. Now she is raised up toward the north, now cast down toward the south. Now, subject to conjunction <note>Coming together with the Sun in the sky.</note> in a short space of days, she is immediately full with pregnancy, and soon brings forth her "conception." Therefore, in this manifold variety, she likens the Earth to herself; for the Earth now appears dusky, stripped of its ornament, and now, painted with herbs and flowers, it is seen as most beautiful. One part is stony, another marshy; lean in one place, most fertile in another; depressed into valleys, raised into mountains; fertile here, and seen to be sterile there. One part is sprinkled with various spots, one part appears red, one part black, one part white, or somewhat dark. A portion of it is found to be firm, and another sandy and fluid. Now it is exhausted, and now it looks up to the conjunction of the stars, and in a short time, being pregnant, it brings forth its offspring. Therefore, the Moon among the stars and the Earth among the elements rejoice in a manifold variety, by which they are also made alike.

### Chapter XV.

**T**he nature of **Mercury** is as much more difficult to explain as the star itself is more hidden, so much so that it is scarcely and only rarely seen. Its power is concealed: for easily putting on the nature of the planet to which it is joined, or the astrological sign in which it resides, it is seen to operate not according to what is its own, but as the executor of another. Hence **Hermes**—that is, the "Interpreter" <note>The name Hermes was traditionally associated with the Greek word for interpreter (*hermeneus*).</note>—is said to be the offspring which other stars have conceived.

<margin>The same author</margin>

<margin>Antiquity</margin>
When mixed with Venus, he generates either an <term>Androgynous</term> <note>From the Greek *andros* (man) and *gyne* (woman).</note> or a <term>Hermaphrodite</term> (as the ancients fabled), named from **Hermes** and **Aphrodite** <note>Mercury and Venus.</note>. And this occurs when someone exercises the ingenuity provided by Mercury in the lust of "fertile"—that is, disordered—Venus. <margin>Plato</margin>
This is what Plato describes under another enigma: namely, that man is composed of the Sun, Moon, and Earth; and that he has from the Sun his nature as a male; from the Earth his feminine power; and from the Moon, which participates in both, a promiscuous nature, so that he becomes **Androgynous**. He is thus male and a man when, adhering to the Sun, he conceives from its face and brings forth a work worthy of God. But he is female when he only carries out the work of the animal or the earthly body. He is "promiscuous" [androgynous] when, having left the Sun and the supreme light, he combines his natural light with the earthly animal. 

<margin>The same author</margin>

> Two Loves made two cities: a regulated and good love of God, and a love of neighbors even to the contempt of oneself, made the City of God. But a perverted love of self even to the contempt of God made the city of the devil.

Indeed, by Love (says Boetius)

> the heavens are joined, and the elements agree in compounds. By love, animals live together; the City is preserved; and every Republic receives its growth. By Love, God fashioned and governs the world: and the summit of all things that He requires from us is Love itself.

Divine love (says Dionysius)

> did not permit the King of all to remain within Himself without offspring. And just as He poured Himself out into all things outside Himself through love, so He delights to draw all things to Himself through love, especially man, in whom all things are included. Therefore, when man is united to Him, all things will be united.

> Whether we call it divine, or angelic, or spiritual, or animal, or natural love, let us understand it as an indwelling and mixing power, which [moves] higher things...

**Semes** <note>Hebrew: *Shemesh*, meaning the Sun</note>, which can be interpreted as "one's own" or "private," because its light and its benefits are specifically its own. Other stars, however, receive both from it as a shared gift. It shines so much more excellently because that celestial fire is more sublime than this elementary <note>Earthly or physical</note> fire. Both provide heat, but this earthly fire does so by driving in moisture, while that celestial fire does so by drawing it out. This fire only provides its benefit to those nearby; that celestial fire benefits those farthest away, so that the power of its rays even penetrates into the bowels of the earth. There, it "cooks" and perfects metals, which this elementary fire later purifies. **Vulcan** was also named for his greater fiery force and violence, or because he flies "hoary"—that is, white—in the flame. But that celestial fire is called **Phoebus** because of its appearance and brightness, which is why the ancients imagined him as the most beautiful. Moreover, they called him the inventor of medicine because of his life-giving heat and beneficial power, perhaps imitating the more secret philosophers who say that **Raphael** (whose name is interpreted as the "medicine" or "physician of God") presides over him. This lower fire holds a likeness of him: by warming stiffened living creatures, it restores life to them in a way. The celestial fire puts to flight the princes of darkness and their troops, as is sung in the **Psalms**: *The Sun has risen, and they are gathered together, and they shall lie down in their dens.* And in **Job** it is said: *When they see the dawn, they think of the shadow of death.* This lower fire also puts the same to flight, so that it may act as an ally. 

For this reason, not without cause, the most wise founders of the budding Church ordered lights to be lit beside the bodies of the dead; they are not to be removed from them until, the sacred rites having been performed, they are buried in holy ground. They also taught that public prayers and the singing of psalms should be done with a light lit. And God, to whom these sacred things are offered, also requires this: namely, that all sacrifices be offered with fire, and that the fire should burn forever upon the altar. Hence **Pythagoras** said in his symbols: *Do not speak of God without light.* Yet others, and even we ourselves elsewhere, have interpreted this according to analogy. For this most sacred shining fire contributes to the celestial, the angelic, the intellectual, and the divine. 

But the dark fire is by no means so: it is not the infernal heat, nor the burning of evil lust, nor immoderate anger, nor the scorched intellect. For this dark fire consumes all things and fills all with sterility, so that no one can perform any work in that nocturnal flame. For this reason, some have wished to interpret "fire" <note>original: *ignis*</note> as that from which nothing is born. Nevertheless, there is a good and natural fire: the heat that grants life and fertility. For neither do eggs change into chicks, nor does the caterpillar or silkworm change into a pupa, nor do plants grow, nor are animals nourished and cherished, except by heat—whether superior, or vital, or elementary—which are of the same kind through a certain symbolic analogy. And fire is so fertile that it generates itself; and it provides for others so that they may generate, not by heat alone, but by the power of light, which it draws from Him who said: *I am the light of the world.* 

And so that **Moses** might declare that all things were produced by the benefit of light, after the creation of matter (which he calls "earth") covered in darkness, he said that light was immediately created; through it, life and form were given to all things, and by it (as **Plato** says) all things could be seen. That vigor of life is in that divine fire, which is called the **Spirit of Life** <note>The Holy Spirit</note> brooding over the face of the waters, providing life and forms to all, through which each thing was separated from the other and discerned by those who look upon them. For they are not distinguished from matter...

->Stones harmonize with the heavens. Chapter XVIII.<-

Since nature possesses mixed elements of many kinds, they do not easily harmonize with a single heaven. This is primarily because in every primary genus, many subordinate genera and species intervene, which savor of the nature of different stars. For in the genus of stones, there are diverse species, just as in metals, plants, and animals. And although stones are earthy, supported by a certain stability, and metals are fluid and liquefy by the power of fire so that they seem to pass into a watery nature, yet both contain very diverse species. They harmonize not only with different planets but also with the fixed stars: the Diamond with the head of Algol; the Garnet <note>original: "granata"</note> with the heart of the Lion <note>the star Regulus</note>; the Magnet harmonizes with the tail of the Bear <note>Ursa Major</note>; the Emerald and the *achamec* jasper <note>original: "achamec iaspis"</note> with the wings of the Raven <note>the constellation Corvus</note>; the *ardoniu s* <note>likely Sardonyx</note> with the heart of the Scorpion <note>the star Antares</note>; and Chrysolite with the falling vulture <note>the star Vega in the constellation Lyra</note>. Many such things are treated by Hermes <note>original: "Mercurio," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> and some more recent writers, perhaps to be explained more broadly in their proper place. 

There are also many kinds of Marble: there is Theban marble, more cheerful than the rest, green and spotted, appearing with the spots of serpents; hence it is called *Serpentinus* in Latin and *Ophites* <note>original: "Ophites," from the Greek for snake</note> in Greek. This is manifold: Lacedaemonian, Augustan, and Tiberian. Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrites"</note> is red with intervening white points, called *Leucoctictos* <note>Greek for "white-spotted"</note>. Basalt is of an iron color and hardness. Onyx <note>original: "Onychites"</note> was found in Arabia in ancient times, and later in Germany. Alabaster <note>original: "Alabastrites"</note> draws its origin from Thebes, Damascus, Carmania, India, and Asia; they hollow it out for ointment vessels and crush the burnt stone for plasters. There is also *Lygdinus* <note>a type of white marble</note> from Thebes of extraordinary whiteness, encircled with golden drops. Coral of black, white, and red color, which some call *Pyrites*. *Simires*, which they formerly called *Pyropaecilum* <note>meaning "varied with fire"</note> because it is varied with fiery flames. *Tasio*, flint, whetstones, tufa, and many other kinds which are recorded by Pliny, Albertus Magnus, and Vitruvius for the purpose of constructing buildings. ### Chapter XIX.

**M**etals are also of many kinds, but the seven more powerful ones are equated with the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the seven classical planets: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> (as is a most well-worn idea). And alone among metals, it does not take on rust, just as the sun admits nothing dark. Silver, and all silvery things like <term>marcasite</term> <note>A crystalline mineral, iron sulfide, often called "white pyrite"</note> and the like, are subjected to the Moon; and as far as she is distant from the Sun, so far is silver from gold. Tin is for Jupiter; yet there are some who attribute gold, silver, and all gilded things to him. Others, indeed, assign gold to Saturn because of its weight, but to the Sun because of its power. Nevertheless, tin is properly Jupiter’s; Copper belongs to Venus—specifically red copper, as some assert. Everything sulfurous, and iron, harmonize with Mars. Lead belongs to Saturn, as its weight and color indicate, for all dark things are his. Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, however, is with Mercury, who easily puts on the nature of the planet with which he is joined, or the sign in which he wanders—just as quicksilver itself, either by the operation of nature or the help of art (as they say), is easily transmuted into another metal. And although all the heavens concur in the production of metals, the Sun does so most powerfully; containing the power of all the planets, he penetrates with his rays into the bowels of the earth, ripening and perfecting all metals. Yet the specific planet assists its own particular kind. Let it also be that all metals savor of a watery nature, and each one corresponds to its planet by nature; yet they seem to be under the dominion of Mars, as we are taught from the secrets of the supreme Archetype <note>The "Archetype" here refers to the divine blueprint or the highest world in Kabbalistic thought</note>. -> Herbs respond with a livelier sound to the heavens, especially Jupiter. **Chapter XX.** <-

<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
**T**wo things occur both in herbs and metals that are worthy of no small investigation: namely, from where and how power is drawn by them. Not indeed from the hot, cold, moist, and dry, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who focused on the four physical qualities</note> assert—easily excusing themselves from assigning the cause of effects and operations...

...of things: For we prove in them a virtue that exceeds every physical quality, from which they either benefit or harm us. We are not content to depart from the theologians: who say, and truly so, that this power is implanted in them by God. It will be beautiful to run through, in some way, by what means that force—which the Hebrews call <term>כוח</term> *coah* <note>original: "coah"; a Hebrew word for strength, power, or potentiality</note>—is infused into things. The Academics <note>Followers of Plato's school of philosophy</note> teach this along with Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Hermetic philosophy and magic</note>, and Hiarchas, Prince of the Brahmans, invites this view in the writings of Philostratus <note>Referring to the life of the sage Apollonius of Tyana, who visited the gymnosophists of India</note>.

But in the more secret Theology of the Hebrews, it is everywhere asserted that all things which are beneath the lunar globe, and in this world subject to birth and decay, exist in a better state in the celestial world, in perfection among the Intelligences <note>Higher spiritual beings or angels that govern the spheres</note>, and in their most perfect form in the Archetype <note>The original divine "blueprint" in the mind of God</note>. In that same series, each thing corresponds to its superior and supreme counterpart according to its kind. From these they receive: from the heavens indeed that celestial force which they call the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The *quinta essentia* or ether, a substance distinct from the four earthly elements</note>; from the Intelligences a spiritual and living vigor transcending every physical quality; and from the Archetype, through these intermediaries according to its degree, the original power of all perfection. 

From here, every single thing can be aptly traced back to the planets and fixed stars, from there to the Intelligences, and from there to the Archetype. From the sequence of this arrangement emanates all <term>natural magic</term> <note>The study of the hidden properties of nature</note> and more secret, true philosophy. Hence comes the harmony of things in this manifold world, and the mystical understanding used in explaining that which is not explicitly stated through that which is written. Since it is our purpose to unlock this throughout our entire progression, for now we will only run through in a general sense how herbs agree with the heavens, just as we touched upon regarding metals.

Regarding metals, although each is led back to its own planet (as we said), they are nonetheless reduced to the Martian domain <note>Associated with the metal iron or forceful energy</note>, both in the heavens and in the Angels and the Archetype. In the same way, herbs, in which a more benign spirit of life exists, agree in general with the air and the "aerial" Jupiter <note>Jupiter was often associated with the temperate, life-giving air</note>; but in particular, each individual herb agrees with its own planet and fixed star. 

For since stones are of the earth and metals are of the water, plants are proven by a direct sequence to be of the air. The sign of this is that they sprout, come together, and grow under the air; but if deprived of air, they not only fail to grow, but they die. For herbs live and sprout under the open sky <note>original: "sub Dio"</note> by the benefit of Venus and Jupiter, with the Sun nonetheless infusing a certain seminal force. For lower things draw animal force from the Sun, generative force from Venus, and natural force from Jupiter—so named because he "always helps" <note>An ancient etymological play: "Iuppiter" was often derived from "Iuvans Pater," the Helping Father</note>. 

For any star—or rather all of them together, and especially Jupiter—fosters and strengthens the natural forces within us. Whence to receive influence from Jupiter is always auspicious; but to receive from the Sun perhaps (as some scholars prefer) is not always safe, because that immense vigor sometimes strikes against the weakness of the one receiving it. Therefore, because plants thrive most especially by the benefit of Venus and Jupiter, we say they are "aerial" and belong to Jupiter, although each individual herb may be subject to its own star. 

Hence, some plants, from an excessive influx of planetary power, may tend toward a harmful poison. For these, however, the good Jupiter—or rather the Highest Craftsman—has prepared antidotes. Therefore, herbs were never forbidden for human use, nor the fruits of trees, nor their cultivation: for man was placed in the garden of delight <note>The Garden of Eden</note> so that he might eat of the fruits of the trees and cultivate them; although the matter climbs higher than what it displays on the "bark of the letter" <note>A common metaphor for the literal meaning of a text (the bark) versus its hidden spiritual meaning (the pith)</note>.

## Zoophytes Sing in Harmony with Saturn. Chapter XXI.

**A**serting the views of those who investigate the more secret origins of nature, animals that are born through putrefaction <note>The historical theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter</note>—in water, in the earth, and in the ruins of houses—are generated by the favor of Saturn and are "Saturnine" in nature. And although some attribute this to the Sun (as the common parent of all among the stars due to its beneficial heat), it has nevertheless been investigated with more subtle diligence and asserted that this comes from Saturn. He, sensing the power of the higher and contiguous heaven, if he cannot arrange or lead "perfect" animals (as far as the nature of the star allows), at least the dregs and imperfect parts of animals coalesce by his power. This power is provided by the higher, indeed the supra-mundane heaven and by the presiding Intelligence. For each planet has its own Intelligence <note>A spiritual being or angel governing the planet's movement and influence</note> and its own measure in divine matters, according to the rule of which it is regulated; and these are called the "measures of the fabric." Saturn is therefore regulated by that measure 

<margin>Hebrew Theology <note>original: "The.he.", abbreviation for Theologia Hebraeorum</note></margin>

(as is taught in the theology of the Hebrews) where they say the <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: "Elohim"; a Hebrew name for God, here associated with the creative power of the seven days of creation</note> resides, who is introduced as the craftsman and commander in all the works of the six days. But since Saturn falls short of the primary craftsman and the all-encompassing instrument of the starry heaven, his power extends only as far as "imperfect" animals. Hence to him are attributed mice, worms, scorpions, and such things born from putrefaction; likewise oysters, sea sponges, shellfish, and this kind of thing, which are called <term>Zoophytes</term> <note>original: "Zoophyta"; from the Greek for 'animal-plants', referring to organisms like sponges that seem to exist between the plant and animal kingdoms</note> by the Platonists. 

<margin>Antiquity</margin>

From this, perhaps, antiquity (smelling of that primeval wisdom) fashioned the myth that Saturn was born from Heaven; and not that he generated as a father, but that after his genitals were cut off and thrown into the sea, Venus was generated from them; namely, the generative power arising from heated moisture.

These animals, although they are many and varied in nature, are rightly placed in the **eighth sphere** <note>In the Ptolemaic system, this is the firmament containing the fixed stars</note>: and true animals are subject to it: which is wandering in a threefold motion, and most diverse in the figures of its stars: whose number is known to God alone: just as their effects are upon the birds, animals, reptiles, fish, and herbs. Even if we make these agree with Jupiter, they are nevertheless not deprived of the benefit of the star-bearing heavens. For the planets carry out those things which the superior stars influence. Whence there is a great harmony of each thing with its own sign, house, or **triplicity** <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water)</note>, and particular stars: from which effects proceed no less than from the wandering stars [planets], although they are attributed to the latter as being closer, more distinct, and more manifest to mortals.

And if we wished to climb still higher, and scrutinize more deeply the causes, origins, and forms of animals: perhaps we would prove that these do not proceed from the "lap of matter," as the physicists dream, but from elsewhere.

Therefore, it was not without reason that we made animals agree with the superior heaven; for although they proceed from the Author of all things along with everything else, they are nonetheless manufactured through the starry heaven as through a principal instrument.

# They harmonize most especially with the supercelestial world. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>Prologue.</margin>
Since all things have proceeded from the first <note>original: "p'," shorthand for *principio* or *primo*, meaning the First Principle or Beginning</note> and the One, it is necessary that they depend upon the same and correspond to it. For it is written concerning the wisdom of the <term>Creator</term> <note>original: "Opificē," referring to God as the divine Artificer or Craftsman</note>, that by the spirit of his understanding he encompasses every power, looks upon all things, contains all the spirits of intelligence, and—remaining unique in himself—his power renews all things. With this same spirit he fills the entire circle of the earth, giving life, uniting, and making all things resonate together, reaching from one end to the other and disposing all things sweetly. We shall set aside these matters to be discussed more extensively in their proper place.

## Which things in particular correspond with Saturn. Chapter XXIIII.

Having established the absolute harmony of things in general, let us run through how the species themselves correspond with the higher powers, so that we may everywhere find means by which we are able to praise the Creator. And to begin with the lower compound things: From the elements, Saturn has **earth**. From the stones, those that are **black** correspond to Saturn: **Onyx** and **ziazaa** <note>a term found in Renaissance lapidaries for a dark, somber stone</note>, as the color indicates, which has a terrifying effect on the wearer, most especially when it puts the better spirits to sleep during dreams. Also **chalcedony** corresponds to Saturn, along with Mercury and the tail of the Scorpion, as its sub-sapphire, dark, and pale color suggests; it receives from a well-placed Saturn the power to expel phantastic illusions and to preserve and knit together the strengths of the body; but from Mercury it gains the power to prevent hoarseness and to clarify the voice, especially the darker variety. <margin>Hermes</margin> From the minerals, Saturn rules **lead**. It also claims for itself **jasper**, the **magnet**, and the **cameo** <note>original: "camoinū"</note>. <margin>Aaron</margin> From the herbs, the **serpent-root** corresponds to him and to the celestial Serpent-bearer <note>the constellation Ophiuchus</note>. He also rules over **rue**, **cumin**, **hellebore**, and **asafoetida**, which the Greeks call *Silphion*. Likewise **opium**, **mandrake**, and those things which are styptic <note>substances that contract tissues or stop bleeding</note>. From the animals, he possesses the **camel**, **pig**, **monkey**, **bear**, and the **cat** (especially a black one), the **mule**, and the **donkey**. Among birds, those which have long necks and coarse voices: **cranes**, **ostriches**, **peacocks**, and that sort; whence the <margin>Ovid</margin> Poet sings of Argus being turned into a peacock: "The Saturnian bird receives these eyes upon its feathers" <note>original: "Excipit hos oculos uolucris Saturnia pēnis" from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. The "eyes" of the giant Argus were placed on the peacock's tail</note>. Furthermore, he rules **serpents**, **scorpions**, and things that creep on the earth, in the waters, and in the ruins of walls or roofs, such as **mice**, **ants**, and various **worms**. Among the humors, he rules the moist **black bile** <note>the humor associated with melancholy</note>, both the natural and the acquired (except for the "burnt" kind). The colors **black**, **leaden**, and **livid** follow him. Also **sour**, **sharp**, and **heavy** tastes imitate his heavy nature. Similarly, those things which smell unpleasantly. In the seasons, he presides over **autumn** and **winter**, and over the stronger and heavy winds. Likewise, he rules the **Indians** and **Ethiopians**, as their color attests. So too with **obscure**, **subterranean**, and **solitary** places. Furthermore, he rules **fishponds**, **pools**, **marshes**, and **dreadful places**. Also **hidden treasures**, and those things which are acquired through long journeys and with great difficulty. What he possesses within man, we shall reserve for the discussion on the concord between the two worlds, the Macrocosm and the Microcosm.

Those things which receive strength from Mars.

### Chapter XXVI.

<margin>Hermes</margin>
**N**ow we have concluded that fire is dedicated to Mars; in the same way, all burnt and sharp things suit him: acrid and bitter flavors that burn the tongue, such as castoreum <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, euphorbia, radish, and the like. His colors are flame-red, violet, and purple. Among stones, the amethyst is dedicated to Mars along with Jupiter (according to Hermes). It possesses from Mars the quality of favoring the capture of wild beasts, making one victorious in battle with them, and making one watchful and experienced. From Jupiter, however, it increases good intellect and an equitable mind, as we can learn from Aaron and Artephius <note>Artephius was a famous medieval alchemist</note>. To the same planets is subjected the many-colored Jasper; it receives from Mars the power to make one potent, but from Jupiter the power to expel fevers and imbalances <note>original: "distēperamēta"</note> and to lead the body toward a balanced composition; in higher matters, it agrees with Alramet <note>likely the star Arcturus</note>. It also corresponds to Mars and the head of Algol <note>original: "Olgol"; the "Demon Star" in the constellation Perseus</note>. To both of these (as Hermes teaches), hellebore is equated. For Mars, again: euphorbia, armoniac, spurge laurel, monkshood, scammony, and generally hot poisons arising from an overabundance of heat. Likewise, cultivated or wild garlic (which Dioscorides calls *snake-garlic* or *deer-garlic* <note>original: "ophioscorodū, uel elaphoscorodum"</note>), onion, shallot, and all things of this sort whose flavor is said to be "tear-inducing." Among animals: horses, first of all, as they are most fit for war; mules, he-goats, kids, wolves (as even Augustine testifies), leopards, wild asses, and generally rapacious animals and those hostile to man, such as flies, fleas, and the like; also snakes and dragons that attack with venom. Among minerals: glass, yellow brass, and iron. Also masters of ovens, furnaces, and mills; bloodletters, surgeons, barbers, butchers, and all soldiers, who are everywhere called "Martial" after Mars. Among regions, Ptolemy subjects to him along with Scorpio: Syria, Cappadocia, Metagonitis, Commagene, Mauritania, and Gaetulia. With Aries, however: Britain, Galatia, Germany, Bastarnia, Coele-Syria, Idumea, and Judea. In particular, he governs lands and warlike peoples; also impetuous winds, especially those blowing from the northern region toward the west, and all impetuous and violent things. This is not indeed from the malice of the star so decreeing, but from an ill-moderated impulse: for the origin is from the celestial Mars.

...and super-celestial: the disorder truly comes from us who regulate poorly; hence people attribute to him [Mars] spoils, robbery, plunder, depopulation, deceptions, and all the nefarious deeds perpetrated by violence and impulse. But if that force and impulse were moderated by the bridle of reason and the laws, all these things would be conducted justly.

### Those things which harmonize with the Sun or Phoebus. Chapter XXVII.

**T**he Sun possesses the middle seat among the planets like a king of all, exceeding everyone in light, magnitude, power, and beauty. He illuminates all things and consequently intervenes in the arrangement of all lower things. But among the elements, the one that primarily follows his motion is fire; among metals, it is gold and all gilded things. Consequently, those things which shine with the same color—whether in flowers or small stones—belong to him: the Carbuncle <note>A legendary gemstone, often identified as a deep red garnet or ruby, said to glow in the dark</note> which glows at night; the stone called "Eye of the Sun," which has the shape of a pupil from which light flashes; the Chrysolite; the Topaz, which leans toward his golden color; the Hyacinth, Ruby, Balas <note>A pale red variety of spinel</note>, and others filled with golden or red color. The *Panthaura* or *Patheus* is so named because it resembles the Panther, a spotted animal; for they have certain black, red, pale, green, rosy, purple, and various small marks. Concerning this, <margin>Albertus</margin> Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> says it contains as many virtues as it has colors, and it especially makes the wearer a victor, or the one who looks upon it at sunrise. Aaron calls this stone *Evanthos* <note>original: "euanthũ", meaning "well-flowered"</note>; others call it *Pantheocreos*, because it seems to contain all colors. 

Many herbs are reduced to the Sun and through him to the star which is called "Canicular" by the Latins <note>The star Sirius, known as the Dog Star</note>; hence the "dog days" are hotter because of the Sun's conjunction with it. The Greeks call it *Sirion* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ σείριον", meaning "from the scorching"</note> from a word meaning "to dry up," because the greatest dryness occurs then; or from a word meaning "to gape" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ σαίρειν"</note> because it then makes men and especially dogs gape open-mouthed. It is placed in the middle of the sky, as <margin>Aratus Hyginus</margin> Aratus, Hyginus, and other mathematicians write. Among solar plants, the experts count Balsam, the Palm, the Cedar, and the Laurel, which repels poisons and lightning; because of its solar heat, it does not fear winter chills, and with it the Phoebean <note>Associated with Phoebus Apollo, the god of prophecy and the sun</note> prophets are crowned. Hence all the poets themselves declare it dedicated to the Sun. Also the Ash tree, which by the same Phoebean power keeps poisonous things at a distance. <margin>Dioscorides Romans Gauls Egyptians Greeks Theodore Ancient [writers] Theophrastus Cratinus</margin> The Peony too—as not only its power but its name indicates—not indeed that one which Dioscorides calls *Chelidonia* or *Cratea*, which the Romans call *Fabium*, the Gauls *Tona*, and the Egyptians *Mothon*; but rather that one which the Greeks call *Glyciside*, and Theodore among us calls *Dulcisida*, and the ancients called *Ephialtion* <note>derived from the Greek word for nightmare</note>, as being very powerful against nocturnal suppressions, incubi, and fauns <note>Historical terms for sleep paralysis or "nightmares," often attributed to oppressive spirits sitting on the sleeper's chest</note>. Also the Egyptian Lotus, which has round leaves and fruits. For (according to Theophrastus) there are many kinds of this plant, distinguished by flower, fruit, and stalk; but we speak of that which Cratinus calls *Stephane*, whose stalks close at sunset and open at sunrise. From its seed, bread is made by Egyptian shepherds, kneaded with water or milk; they say nothing is more healthful than this food, which is why they were called Lotus-eaters. To this also belong all the herbs and flowers called Heliotrope <note>literally "sun-turner"</note>, which close when the Sun departs and, in turn, open when he returns.

### Those things which delight with Venus. Chapter XXVIII.

<insert>V</insert>enus, the mistress of coupling, has a symbol with all well-composed things: and with those whose flavor is sweet and oily, whose scent is delightful, and whose color tends toward whiteness. She delights in moist things and increases their powers; hence she claims the waters for herself rather than any other element. From metals: saffron-colored brass and red copper. From stones: the <term>Beryl</term> <note>A transparent gemstone, often green or blue</note> is most particularly dedicated to her: which (says <margin>Aaron</margin> Aaron <note>Likely referring to a traditional authority on lapidaries/stones</note>) renders the wearer cheerful, wealthy, and magnificent; most prompt toward union and conjugal love. It consoles the desolate and favors pregnant women, lest their offspring be contaminated. And the water in which it lies takes away sighing and all infirmities of the liver. Mixed with silver, however, it frees one from leprosy and the "Martial contagion" <note>Illnesses associated with the planet Mars, such as inflammations or rashes</note>. In these things, it is very easy for one who knows her nature to judge how beautifully it suits Venus. Truly the <term>Chrysolite</term> <note>A yellowish-green gemstone</note>, favoring wisdom (as it is asserted) and resisting folly, is dedicated to Venus and Mercury: which (as it pleases <margin>Plotinus</margin> Plotinus and other <margin>Platonists</margin> Platonists) provides genius and the capacity for a kingly harmony, through which it also renders the affection...

<margin>The Poets</margin>

She also presides over lighter music, just as Mercury rules moderate music, and Jupiter and the Sun rule the more serious or "grave" kind. Likewise, she presides over all pleasures that are dissolved and dilated into the circumference, just as Saturn rules those contracted toward the center, and Jupiter and the Sun rule those mixed from both.

### Chapter XXIX.
### Which things sound in harmony with Mercury.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
**M**ercury moves the elements without distinction, and none in particular. For he is an assistant to whatever star he is joined with. Therefore, he regulates no specific complexion <note>The balance of bodily humors</note>, except insofar as he assists another when joined to it. Similarly, he has no specific flavors or colors, unless they are mixed, such as the Rainbow <note>original: *Iris*</note> and the tail of a Peacock and the like, or those which are ruled by the star to which he is connected. So also, he claims no sex for himself, but rather a mixed one: namely, the hermaphrodite or androgynous. Among the ages of man, he rules none specifically, but rather that which is apt to be changed into another. Among the climates, some ascribe the fifth to him; but <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy assigns to him—along with the sign of Virgo—Greece, Achaia, Crete, Babylon, Mesopotamia, and Assyria. Along with Gemini, however, he assigns Hyrcania, Armenia, Mantiana, Cyrenaica, Marmarica, and the lower region of Egypt. Among minerals, to him belong Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> and silver Marcasite. Among stones, those which are of diverse colors and varied shapes implanted by nature so that they appear painted: and of this kind are many, such as Agates, Porphyry, and similar stones.

### How all these things bring about a perfected harmony with the Moon.
## Chapter 30.

<margin>AnM</margin>
<margin>Iamblichus, Julian, Proclus</margin>
**T**he Moon is not incongruously called "another Sun" by some; for those things which the Sun generates above with masculine power, she receives—carrying the offspring of him and the other planets—and brings them forth into the lower world neighboring her. Therefore, her motion is observed above all others, as she is the one who gives birth to the concepts of all. For from <term>Mercury</term>, she receives the power to mix humors; from <term>Venus</term>, that which leads to forms suitable for birth; from <term>Mars</term>, strength and impulse; from <term>Jupiter</term>, the natural spirit and the nourishment of all things; from <term>Saturn</term>, structure and stability. But from the <term>Sun</term>, who contains every kind of virtue (as <term>Iamblichus</term>, <term>Julian</term>, <term>Proclus</term>, and many others assert), she receives every kind of offspring and light. All these she unfolds in various ways according to her varying temperament, her orbit, and her different aspects, both with the planets and with the other stars. For in her first quarter, the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> believe her to be hot and moist; in the second, hot and dry; in the third, cold and dry; in the fourth, cold and moist. Sometimes she is at her highest point <note>apogee</note>, sometimes low, sometimes at the furthest point of her epicircle; sometimes full of light...

We do not doubt that she does the same in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>original: *maiori mundo*; the "great world" or universe</note>, by ruling various things placed in different signs, so that by being ever-changing she produces various effects. Through her frequent conjunctions with the planets and other stars, having become the "wife of all," she receives from them those things which she—as the mother of all lower things and the mediator between both (that is, between the superior and the inferior realms)—communicates to all these earthly things.

Therefore, not without reason is she compared to that Mother full of all graces <note>the Virgin Mary</note>, who bestows upon lower beings those things which she draws from heavenly fountains through various channels, according to the capacity of those who receive them. But returning to the Moon: although she receives influence from all the stars, she does so most especially from the Sun. From her also begins the celestial series <margin>Plato</margin> which Plato calls the <term>chain</term> <note>The "Great Chain of Being," connecting the highest cause to the lowest matter</note>, in which every single thing or cause is linked to another and depends upon it, until it reaches the supreme Cause of all, from whom all things come. 

The lower things also follow this series. For stones correspond with herbs, and herbs with animals; these in turn with the heavens, and the heavens with the <term>separate intelligences</term> <note>pure spiritual beings or angels thought to move the celestial spheres</note>, and these with those divine properties or attributes, about which we shall discuss in their proper place.

But for the present, let us come to those things (if there be any) which are particularly ruled by the Moon. First, the water of the sea as well as of rivers, as is manifest, follows her motion. So too all moist things: the juices of trees and animals, and especially white fluids such as the whites of eggs, fats, sweats, and the superfluities of the body. Also those things whose flavor is somewhat salty and insipid, and white flowers whose temperament is cold and moist.

<margin>Varro</margin> Of gems, if any are attributed to her, the most prominent are <term>pearls</term> <note>original: *uniones*; large, singular pearls thought to be unique</note>, which (with Varro and experience as witnesses) are generated from water in shells. Regarding animals: although (as we have said) all follow the <term>eighth heaven</term> <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, nonetheless <margin>Mercury, Timaeus</margin> (as witnessed by Hermes Trismegistus, Timaeus of Locri, and other wise men), some are Saturnine, some Jovial, others Martial, Solar, Venereal, or Mercurial. Or, to speak more correctly, the soul is infused by the Giver of Forms through the favor or mediation of whichever star prepares the matter. ### Chapter XXXI. Which things resonate in particular with certain specific stars.

**N**OT content with the influence of the planets, those who desire to work in natural things have also endeavored to draw the influences of the stars—namely those stars of which they have been able to attain knowledge. For we find in a particular treatise attributed to <term>Mercury</term> <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, and among several more recent authors, that certain lower things correspond to certain major stars. And these stars seem to have a greater and more express power with lower things; and they study to connect all these things so that the power and the work may be more effective. For in the eighteenth degree of Taurus is <term>Caput Algol</term> <note>The 'Demon Star' in the constellation Perseus; its name comes from the Arabic *Ra's al-Ghūl*</note>, possessing the nature of Jupiter and Saturn, granting boldness and victory; under its power are the <term>Diamond</term> <note>original: *Adamas*</note>, <term>Black Hellebore</term>, and <term>Mugwort</term> <note>original: *Artemisia*</note>. In the twenty-second degree of the same sign are the <term>Pleiades</term> <note>the 'Seven Sisters' star cluster</note>, or the *Virgiliae*, of the nature of the Moon and the complexion of Mars, to which corresponds <term>Crystal</term>; but better is the <term>Diadochus</term> <note>a legendary gemstone used by water-diviners</note> which is similar in color to beryl, and the seed of <term>Fennel</term> with <term>Frankincense</term>. <term>The Goat</term> <note>the star Capella</note> is in the thirteenth degree of Gemini, to which they give <term>Sapphire</term>, <term>Prase</term> <note>a leek-green variety of quartz</note>, as well as <term>Mugwort</term> and <term>Mandrake</term>. <term>Aldebaran</term> is in the twenty-fifth degree

# OF THE FIRST SONG

Ruby, Spurge <note>original: *tithymallus*</note>, Mother of the Woods: the increase of riches and glory. In the sixth or seventh degree of Cancer is the **Greater Dog** <note>the star Sirius</note>, of the nature of Venus: it claims for itself the Beryl, Savin, Dragonwort, and the favor of grace. In the seventeenth degree of the same is the **Lesser Dog** <note>the star Procyon</note>, of a Mercurial nature and from the temperament of Mars; it presides over Agate, Heliotrope <note>original: *solsequia*; literally "sun-follower"</note>, Pennyroyal, and the gift of grace. In the twenty-first of Leo is the **Lion's Heart** <note>the star Regulus</note>, a royal star of Jupiter and Mars: this rules the Zircon <note>original: *gergonza*; likely a jacinth or zircon</note> or garnet, Celandine, and Mastic: it suppresses black bile <note>one of the four humors associated with melancholy</note> and renders one temperate. In the nineteenth of Virgo is the **Tail of the Great Bear**, of Venus and the Moon: to it belongs the Magnet <note>lodestone</note> and Chicory, whose leaves and flowers turn toward the North. Combined together, all these things protect against robbers, poisoners, and incantations: <margin>Hermes</margin> as **Hermes** writes. In the seventh of Libra is the right wing of the Crow, and in the twelfth the left wing, of Saturn and Mars: Black Onyx follows it, as does Four-leaf Dock, Henbane <note>original: *lusquiamum*</note>, and "Frog's-tongue" <note>original: *lingua rang*; likely *lingua ranina* or a similar herbal folk-name</note>. And these provide favor against evil men, demons, and wicked winds. In the fifteenth of the same is **Alaazel**, or the Ear of Grain <note>the star Spica</note>, of Venus and Mercury, to which they attribute the Emerald, Sage, Trefoil, and Mandrake. These indeed provide honesty, joy, the increase of riches, and victory. In the seventeenth of the same is **Alchameth** <note>the star Arcturus</note> of the nature of Jupiter and Mars: but it acts as Jupiter when the luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note> look upon it with a good aspect, and as Mars when, on the contrary, they look upon it poorly. To it they dedicate Jasper and Plantain, to stop blood and expel fevers. In the fourth of Scorpio is **Elpheia** <note>the star Alphecca</note> of Venus and Mars: to this belongs Topaz, Trefoil, Ivy, and Rosemary: which, however, pertains to more than is commonly believed. And these things render a man beloved by God and men for causes not known to many. Wherefore, not without reason, Rosemary was in frequent use for sacrifices in the Old Law; which they call in Hebrew **Ezob** <note>original: **אזוב**; Hyssop</note>: but because of the similarity to our word, they translated it as "hyssop." In the third of Sagittarius is the **Scorpion's Heart** <note>the star Antares</note> of the nature of Mars and standing with Jupiter, presiding over Sardonyx, Amethyst, Long Birthwort, Saffron, good complexion, a joyful mind, wisdom, and the flight of demons. In the seventh of Capricorn is the **Falling Vulture** <note>the star Vega</note> of the nature of Venus and Mercury, exceedingly temperate: which possesses Chrysolite, Savory, and Fumitory. In the sixteenth of Aquarius is the **Tail of the Goat** <note>the star Deneb Algedi</note> of Saturn and Mercury: to which belongs Chalcedony, Marjoram, and Catnip, which is called *Calamintha*, similar to Pennyroyal. Likewise, it grants grace in legal causes, the increase of riches, and the gift of safety. <margin>The same</margin> These are a few things from Hermes, which are almost nothing compared to those which could be brought forward in this matter. For there is virtue in every herb and stone: but a greater virtue is implanted by nature in the star. Moreover, every lower thing acquires many things for itself from its superior, but most of all from the presiding Intelligences: and most powerfully from the Supreme Cause, to whom all things respond in a single and perfect harmony, by which they always praise their Maker with their hymns and their chorus, just as they are invited to do.

# THE FOURTH TONE.

...by the holy youths singing in the Chaldean furnace: *Bless the Lord, mountains and hills / Bless the Lord, all things that grow on the earth: Bless the Lord, springs, seas, rivers, and all that move in the waters: all birds of the air / beasts and cattle, together with the sons of men, and let the Angels praise their Maker and Lord.* <note>This refers to the "Song of the Three Holy Children" from the Book of Daniel, a common liturgical text.</note>

How beautifully all these things are depicted in the Ark, which Moses constructed according to the heavenly oracle.

### Chapter XXXII.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a detailed woodcut of classical architectural ruins or a temple courtyard with columns and a tiled floor.</image-desc>

When the great burden was placed upon the shoulders of holy Moses by God, and because human weakness was not hidden from him, he refused to undergo it; but God, having decreed that he should lead the people out of Egypt, promised His Angel for his leadership and protection. Not content with this, Moses with great confidence protested to God, saying: *Unless you come yourself, I will not go.* <note>original: "Nisi ueneris tu / nō uadam"</note> For he knew that the presence of God was necessary for many things; wherefore, neither content with the promised Angel, nor with the power handed down for performing signs and portents, he demanded God Himself as his leader: *Unless you go before us,* he said, *do not make us go up from this place.* And again: *In what shall we know that I and your people have found grace in your eyes, unless you come with us?* Assenting to him, the Lord said: *Make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in the midst of you:* and this according to the entire likeness of the Tabernacle which I shall show you—namely, of this worldly house, which is the dwelling place of God himself; as he himself attests in open speech through the oracle of Isaiah, when he says: *Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.*

<margin>Exodus</margin>
When He showed this entire structure to Moses, He added: *See, and make it according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mountain.* But since it would be too long to recount everything shown which pertains to building the Ark in conformity with the world, we shall run through a few things. And first, the division, of which it is said: *Let its height and likewise its width have a cubit and a half*—that is, nine palms. For a cubit <term>cubitus: a unit of measurement based on the forearm</term> is divided into six palms, and a half into three. This division by nine represents the nine heavens, over which the Empyrean <note>The highest, most spiritual part of heaven in medieval cosmology.</note> presides, being of a different and more noble material. And this is denoted by the golden cover, which was of a more noble material than the whole frame of the Ark; which was ordered to be made of shittim wood, or cedar, which is the same thing according to the Hebrew doctors. And it is that wood (as some assert) which we call Larch, although our translation uses "Cedars" for Larch. There was also another three-fold division of the entire structure: one part of which, defended by no roof or shelter, was subject to rain, snow, sun, heat, and cold; this signifies that structure subject to all change, which not only the men of the world inhabit, but also the worldly, the profane, and all kinds of animals. And in it, because of the sacrifices and perpetual offerings, there was a constant cycle of life and death, just as in this world. The remaining two parts were both covered and free on all sides from any foreign injury, just as both the celestial and super-celestial worlds are capable of neither injury nor insult. Both were likewise honored with the name of holiness: the more secret part called the Holy of Holies, the other decorated only with the title of the Holy. And this represents the celestial world, where the Angels...

they inhabit, and it reveals: in which, after the fall of Lucifer <note>The author refers to the theological tradition that the highest heavens remained untainted by the rebellion of the fallen angels.</note> (as our theology teaches), neither sin nor any stain is found. Furthermore, the **super-celestial** realm is denoted by the interior and more secret place: into which those enter who, having been made true <term>priests</term> <note>Meaning those who have undergone spiritual transformation rather than just holding an office.</note>, have consecrated themselves as a **living and pleasing sacrifice to God**, so that they might deserve to be united with Him who is truly the **Holy of Holies**. And this (as I believe) is the true garden of delights, in which all the chosen trees of <term>Adonai</term> <note>original: "Adonai"; a Hebrew name for God meaning "The Lord."</note> are to be planted and made fruitful—those which the heavenly Father has planted, never to be uprooted by anyone again. Over this garden presides, not without mystery, the **cherubic power**, just as by God’s command they presided over the Ark which was placed in that location called the Holy of Holies. In that figurative place, they possessed remissions and intimate conversations with God; but there, in the true dwelling, those who enter having been purified possess perfect union with God Himself and full delight in every part.

It was also commanded that **seven golden lamps** be made, which represent the seven shining stars <note>In ancient and medieval astronomy, the "seven stars" or planets were the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> in their orbits. But the **lampstand** <note>The Menorah.</note> is named separately, with three branches on each side, along with its cups, spheres, and flowers. This represents the **Sun** in the midst of the planets, having three planets on each side in spherical form. These, like cups and receiving vessels for the influences that flow down from the higher realms, produce "flowers" by influencing the lower regions. And thus, that which was just now counted among the seven lamps—even when considered separately—is said to be fashioned together with the adjacent stars, so that it may be understood that these receive their light from the Sun and, in a certain way, arise from it.

He continues regarding the **four tents** situated at the four quarters of the world. These represent all the celestial and super-celestial mansions; and although there are many such dwellings in each "house," their total division is completed at the four cardinal directions. The eastern and western sections are divided by the number **fifty**, while the southern and northern are divided by the number **one hundred**. This is because retribution occurs through the "hundredfold"—which is a perfect number—whereas remission occurs through "fifty," a number signifying release, in the super-celestial tent, according to the pattern of which this earthly one was fashioned. There were also curtains in these tents with fifty openings, for which our translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> uses the word **loops** (*ansas*). Through these openings, as if through channels or vessels, the influx of remission is received.

There was also **one altar** in the middle of the Tabernacle for the <term>holocaust</term> <note>A "burnt offering" entirely consumed by fire, symbolizing total devotion.</note>, measuring fifteen cubits in both length and breadth. There was **another** for the burning of <term>incense</term>; this was completed by a single cubit on each side. Yet **another** was made of gold toward the north, from whence (as Job testifies) **gold comes** <note>A reference to Job 37:22: "Gold comes out of the north."</note>. Those two altars placed in the middle, where the **Tree of Life** is, are said to be made of wood, so that through the burnt offering, the life lost through sin might be recovered, and through the true incense, man might ascend back to where he returns. That first altar was completed by the number **fifteen**, which is the value yielded by the name <term>Yah</term> <note>original: "יה" (Iah/Yah); the shortened form of the Hebrew Divine Name.</note>. We are commanded to praise this name frequently when we say *Alleluia*, which means "Praise Yah." This name is composed of the letters for ten and five <note>In Hebrew numerology (Gematria), Yod = 10 and He = 5, totaling 15.</note>, from which comes remission, as is clear to those with knowledge. But the altar of incense was completed by a single cubit: for though the calculation may yield the Divine Name in whatever way it wishes to express His effects, nevertheless **God Himself is One**, to whom all prayers and offerings are presented, and who dwells in the true Tabernacle, to whom...

<margin>David</margin> Sighing as a prophet, David used to say: *Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?* And again: *I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle.* <note>These references are to Psalm 15:1 and Psalm 42:4, used here to show the soul's longing for a spiritual home.</note> Because it is divided into many mansions,
<margin>CHRIST</margin> Christ says there are several when he says: *Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal tabernacles.* <note>original: "Facite uobis amicos de mamona iniquitatis..." from Luke 16:9.</note> Yet it is one, embracing all things: its footstool and low seat is this worldly tabernacle in which we dwell. According to the image of both, with great mysteries, the one was built by Moses and the temple by Solomon; but this one was arranged and ordered by David. Likewise, this human tabernacle and temple—which according to the Apostle <note>Refers to St. Paul's statement that "you are the temple of the living God" (2 Corinthians 6:16).</note> we are—bears the same image.

But following further the hidden sacred mysteries <term>sacramenta</term> <note>In this context, "sacramenta" refers to hidden divine symbols or "mysteries" rather than the ritual sacraments of the church.</note> of this tabernacle, we must also consider the ten curtains of twenty-eight cubits. For this number contains three nines, exceeding them by one, and signifying that "one" toward which all nines are directed, as we shall soon say. Therefore, by the number ten, which embraces all lower numbers, the curtains are distributed: which veiled everything around, and were completed by the twenty-eighth measure, so that all those things distributed by the 
<margin>The Academics</margin> Academics <note>The author is likely referring to the Neoplatonic philosophers and their mathematical theories of the soul and the cosmos.</note> were contained within their twenty-seventh number. 

The planks, moreover, signified the elements from which all things consist, as both number and proportion indicate: for there were twenty, eight, and six. 
<margin>Timaeus</margin> And from the elements, water is described by Timaeus of Locri <note>A character in Plato's dialogues to whom a treatise on the nature of the universe was attributed.</note> in the shape of an icosahedron (that is, from twenty bases), and air as an octahedron (that is, of eight seats), earth from six, and fire from four. These were denoted by the planks of twenty, eight, and six, placed toward the four quarters of the world. In these is the proportion of a sesquialter, double, sesquitertial, quintuple, triple, sesquitertial, double, and sesquialter <note>These are technical terms for ratios: Sesquialter (3:2), Sesquitertial (4:3). The author is linking the architectural dimensions of the Tabernacle to the harmonic ratios that Greeks believed governed the physical elements.</note>, such as the proportion of the elements, as we touched upon before.

It must also be noted that each plank had two tenons [sockets] by which they were joined with the two planks adjacent to them: just as every element has two qualities by which it is connected with its two neighboring elements. For Earth is bound to Water by coldness, and to Fire by dryness. By the same sequence, the other elements agree. And just as each of the planks was secured by two bases, so every element resides in a twofold world—namely, the corruptible and the incorruptible or celestial. On both sides, however, the planks were connected by five bars or rods: because in every composite thing, the elements are gathered by a certain "fiveness," which they not ineptly call the **fifth essence** <term>quintessence</term>.

But if one wishes to climb higher: the more secret Hebrew theologians <note>A reference to practitioners of Kabbalah.</note> teach that all things are bound together by the letter **He** <note>original: "ה"; the fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>, which signifies five, and is the seal of the Holy Spirit, which is called the bond tying all things together. Therefore, all things pertaining to the tabernacle are said to be bound into one: yet they are dissolvable and can be reconnected by the ministers, the Levites; just as all things in this lower world are now dissolved through the angelic ministers and the heavens, and now, by a certain change, are composed again, yet by the power of the supreme bond, so that the worldly tabernacle remains always one. All other things pertaining to that tabernacle also represent some member of this worldly temple, and consequently the human temple, of which the Apostle speaks:

A tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. <note>original: "Tabernaculū nō manufactum.i.nō huius creationis." This is a reference to Hebrews 9:11, contrasting the earthly Tabernacle with the spiritual one.</note> To which we are invited through this one made with hands; many other things concerning this, which are touched upon there, we shall reserve to be explained when, God favoring us, we come to the interpretations of the sacred letters.

### With how great a mystery all enneads meet in their tenth. Chapter 33.

**N**on without a sacred mystery <term>sacramento</term> <note>The author uses "sacramentum" here to mean a hidden divine mystery or symbolic truth.</note> does the Maker of all things require from us the primary and tenth portions of all: namely, the first and the last. Since He Himself is the beginning and the end of all, we ought to offer the firstfruits to Him as the beginning, and the tenths to Him as the end. For the ten <term>denarius</term> <note>The Latin "denarius" here refers to the number ten or the "decade" as a complete unit, not the Roman coin.</note> is the end and the completion of all numbers; beyond which neither human wit nor any nation has devised a further number, for no number further than this is given. And because ten is the completion, He requires from us not only the tenth of our works and produced fruits, but in the natural series and genealogy of men, He willed to claim the tenth for Himself by a more celebrated election. For Noah was the tenth from Adam, and Abraham was the tenth from him.

Christ, however—the most pleasing of all—according to the legal genealogy composed by Luke, is the tenth of the seventh ten <note>The 70th generation.</note> starting from God, so that through the revolution of ten and seven, He might lead others back with Him by a more secret mystery returning into God. In the natural texture of Matthew, however, according to the flesh, He is the sixty-third from God, following nine groups of seven. <margin>Jerome, Augustine</margin> Thus indeed the Evangelists, who seem to disagree (as Jerome and Augustine teach), are in harmony: for Matthew describes the carnal genealogy, and Luke the legal one.

It must also be noted that the tenth always tastes of a double nature: both of the number of which it is the end, and of that of which it is the beginning. For ten is the end of numbers and the beginning of tens. For when you have reached ten, you say "one ten," "two tens," and so on, as the Hebrew characters indicate in their numerical significations. Thus the tenth in each of the primary kinds tastes of both natures. For the first group of nine <term>nouenarius</term> <note>An ennead; a group of nine things.</note>—namely, of corruptible things—ends in Man, who is joined together from the incorruptible and the corruptible. The group of nine of the heavens ends in the empyrean heaven; <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most spiritual part of the universe, composed of pure light or fire.</note> which, because it is material, agrees with the heavens, but in the dignity of its matter, it holds a symbol with the higher things. Therefore in the Ark, which represented the structure of the heavens, the tenth portion—namely the cover—was of gold, <note>The "mercy seat" or *kapporet*.</note> a material certainly different from that of the whole Ark, which was divided into nine parts (as we said a little before).

Even the nine Angelic orders end in Christ their King, who embraces both the nature of Angels and of God. In Him also all things end, as the Apostle says: "For it pleased God to make all fullness dwell in him," <margin>Paul</margin> and in Him to reconcile or "recapitulate" all things, as the Greek text has it. <note>Refers to Colossians 1:19 and Ephesians 1:10; the Greek term is *anakephalaiosis*.</note> These things we shall attempt to explain in the second volume (by the help of divine grace). And all things finally end in that truly tenth and first, of whom the Apostle again says, and Plato with him in his letters: <margin>The same Plato, Dionysius</margin> "From whom all things, in whom all things, and through whom all things." <note>A synthesis of Romans 11:36 and Platonic thought.</note> But the lower groups of nine are united with Him through the middle ones, and the middle through the highest (according to Dionysius), <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose "Celestial Hierarchy" describes how divine light filters down through ranks of angels.</note> to whom all praise and harmony is owed.

### Why this arrangement is reduced to larger numbers.
### Chapter III.

<margin>
Proclus
On the Timaeus:
chapter 19
Concerning chapter 19
On the Timaeus: chapter 2
Porphyry's
Sentences
</margin>
**E**ven if all the primary types of things and some intermediate ones are contained in the number 27, not all are; for the spaces are lacking in which those more significant intervening types might be placed. Therefore, another figure is assigned with the same boundaries and the same proportion, but in a broader field and with more ample intervals filled in. We must, therefore, take the number six <term>senarius</term> in place of unity, doubling it through 12, 24, and 48; and tripling it through 18, 54, and 162. In this figure, all intervals are filled with their specific types. For the means placed between 6 and 12 are 8 and 9, where 9 is exceeded and exceeds by an equal portion according to the number <note>This describes the arithmetic mean: 12 - 9 = 3, and 9 - 6 = 3.</note>. 8 itself, however, exceeds and is exceeded by the same part of the extremes <note>This describes the harmonic mean: the difference between 8 and 6 (which is 2) is 1/3 of 6, and the difference between 12 and 8 (which is 4) is 1/3 of 12.</note>. Hence, by multiplying the numbers for unity and duality by six, we find they take on the aforementioned means, which the previous number could not do.

Between 12 and 24 are 16 and 18; and between 24 and 48 are 32 and 36. Some of these are harmonic means, others arithmetic and geometric; yet they all pertain to harmony. For the ratio of the larger extreme to the smaller is a double proportion <term>proportio dupla</term>, which creates an octave <term>diapason</term>. From the smaller extreme to the larger mean is a ratio of one and a half <term>sesqualtera</term>, creating a perfect fifth <term>diapente</term>. But the ratio of that same extreme to the smaller mean is a ratio of four to three <term>sesquitertia</term>, and it yields a perfect fourth <term>diatessaron</term>. The same is true from the larger mean to the larger extreme. A perfect fifth, however, is made from the smaller mean to the larger extreme. From one mean to the other mean is a ratio of nine to eight <term>sesquioctava</term>, and it makes a whole tone <term>tonus</term>. From this, the whole harmony resulting from tones is obtained.

In the same way, on the other side multiplied by three, where the first extremes are 6 and 18, the means are 9 and 12. The other extremes are 18 and 54, between which are the intervening means 27 and 36. Again, there are 54 and 162, between which extremes the means 81 and 108 fall. These means correspond with the extremes and with each other in the same proportion as the means agreed between the doubled extremes. 

As for what the geometric, arithmetic, and harmonic means are, I will add these few points from the many things various authors have written. The arithmetic mean <term>medietas arithmetica</term> is essentially the proportion of differences; the geometric <term>geometrica</term> is the proportion of ratios; and from both of these, the harmonic <term>harmonica</term> results. To show how they behave, we will follow Proclus <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on Plato's *Timaeus* was a primary source for Renaissance music theory and cosmology.</note> as he derives them thus: Between 12 and 6, the mean is 9 according to the arithmetic mean; for the difference of three is found both from the larger to the middle and from the middle to the smaller. Again, I take the difference of the extremes, which is 6, and I multiply this by the smaller term; it becomes 36. I divide this by 18 (which is the sum of the extremes); the result of this comparison is two. I add this to the 6, and from this result, I have the harmonic mean, which is 8.

## OF THE FIRST SONG.

For by that same part of the larger term that it is exceeded by the larger, it exceeds the smaller term by that same part of the smaller. <note>This is the classic definition of the harmonic mean: the ratio of the differences between the terms is the same as the ratio of the terms themselves.</note> For instance, the number 8 is separated from 12 by a third <note>A third of 12 is 4; 12 minus 4 is 8.</note>, and it exceeds 6 by a third <note>A third of 6 is 2; 6 plus 2 is 8.</note>. Again, let us set an interval and its triple: such as 18 and 6. Combining these, I make 24; taking the half of this, namely 12, I have the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The simple average: (18+6)/2 = 12.</note>. Then, taking again the difference between 18 and 6, which is 12, I multiply it by the smaller term, 6, and the result is 72. This I divide by 24 (the sum of the extremes), and the result of the whole calculation is the width of three <term>ternarius</term>. I add this to the six, and I have found the <term>harmonic mean</term>, which is 9. It exceeds the smaller extreme by the same proportion that it is exceeded by the larger extreme. <note>9 is the harmonic mean of 18 and 6. The difference 18-9=9 (half of 18), and 9-6=3 (half of 6). The proportion is preserved.</note> By these rules, he teaches that all intervals are to be filled, except for <term>semitones</term> <note>half-steps</note> and <term>dieses</term> <note>microtonal intervals, often the difference between a major and minor semitone</note>. 

Others, however, calculate the harmonic mean in this way: they take two terms and a middle value between them such that the ratio of the larger term to the smaller is the same as the ratio of the difference between the larger and the middle to the difference between the middle and the smaller. For example, the numbers 3, 4, and 6. There, the ratio of 6 to 3 is a <term>double proportion</term> <note>2:1</note>. The difference between 6 and 4 is 2; the difference between 4 and 3 is 1. The ratio of 2 to 1 is also a double proportion. This gives me a double proportion, which is drawn from the difference as if from an arithmetic mean, and from the proportion as if from a <term>geometric mean</term>.
