### Why the arrangement should again be reduced to the largest numbers, from 384 up to 10,368. Chapter IV.

<margin>Proclus</margin>
**I**f indeed it were possible (says <term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Plato's Timaeus and its musical cosmology.</note>) for us to divide <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio, which in music corresponds to the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> proportions into <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>A 9:8 ratio, corresponding to a whole tone.</note> parts and <term>lemnas</term> <note>Also spelled "limma"; the small mathematical remainder (256:243) that functions as a semitone in the Pythagorean scale.</note> within the same terms we have already described, we would have no further trouble. But since that can in no way be done, we must investigate this by another rule. Since it was proposed from the beginning to fill the <term>duple</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio, or an octave.</note> proportion with the aforementioned means and sesquioctaves, it is necessary that the lower term of the double, along with two sesquioctaves, also possesses a sesquitertia. Therefore, let the third number from unity be taken, which according to an eightfold proportion makes 64. From this, it is possible to form three sesquioctaves: for every <term>multiple</term> number is considered to govern as many <term>submultiples</term> denominated by it as it is distant from unity; however, it does not have a sesquitertia <note>64 can be divided by 8, but it cannot be divided by 3 to create a clean 4:3 ratio.</note>. For which reason, tripling it again, we shall have 192. Its sesquitertia is 256; its sesquioctave is 216; and the sesquioctave of this is 243. Thus, the ratio of the limma itself remains after the removal of the two sesquioctaves, 243 and 256. For from every sesquitertia, when two sesquioctaves are removed, only the ratio of the limma remains. But the sesquioctave of 256 is 288, which preserves the <term>arithmetic mean</term> lying between 192 and 384: which has a duple proportion to 192, and a sesquitertia to 288. If, therefore, it were possible to form two sesquioctaves from 288, we would surely fill this sesquitertia with two sesquioctaves and a limma. But it does not happen: because its sesquioctave, 224 <note>This appears to be a calculation or transcription error in the original text; 288 divided by 8 is 36, and 288 plus 36 is 324. The author likely meant that the subsequent division leads to a fraction.</note>, does not have an eighth part; therefore, a sesquioctave proportion cannot be made from it, if we wish to keep the unit undivided: because its eighth portion is 40 and a half. Therefore, by doubling that same half, we shall make one whole; and then we will be able to take its eighth part. For which reason we are compelled to double all the numbers before it, and all those which come after it. Therefore, in place of 192, there will be 384; in place of 216, 432; for 243, 486; for 256, 512; for 288, 576. The sesquioctave of this is 648; and the sesquioctave of that is 729. Afterward, 768; being the double of 384. It holds the ratio of a limma to 729; and in this way, the duple interval of the proportion is filled and narrowed by <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, or a perfect fifth.</note>, sesquitertia, and sesquioctave ratios in these: 384 / 432, 486, 512 / 576 / 648 / 729 / 768. But if we wish to fill the whole figure and describe all the numbers in sequence: for the first part we ought to take 384; for its double, 768; for the triple of the first and the <term>sesquialter</term> of the second, 1152; for the quadruple of the first, 1536; in place of the fifth part, which is the triple of the third, 3456; for the sixth, which is eight times the first, 3072; and for the seventh, of which the first is the twenty-seventh part, 10368. If, therefore, we wish to fill these terms also and thicken them with <term>harmonic</term> and <term>arithmetic</term> means, which, placed between, create sesquialter and sesquitertia intervals, the intermediate values between 384 and 768 (which is its double) will be 512, which is the har-

<summary>This page explains why early music theorists, following Proclus, had to use large numbers starting at 384 to represent the musical scale. By increasing the scale's base number, they could divide intervals into tones and semitones (limmas) using only whole numbers, avoiding the "forty and a half" fraction encountered with smaller integers.</summary>

### Chapter V. Why in this kind of description Plato used the diatonic genus more than the chromatic and enharmonic.

<margin>Proclus</margin>
**M**any authors maintain that three genera of harmony were in use among the ancients: namely the <term>diatonic</term>, the <term>enharmonic</term>, and the <term>chromatic</term>. The diatonic consists of a semitone (or <term>limma</term> <note>original: lēma, the Pythagorean 'leftover' interval acting as a semitone</note>), a tone, and another tone. The enharmonic consists of a <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</note>, another diesis, and a <term>ditone</term> <note>An interval of two whole tones</note>. The chromatic, however, consists of a semitone, another semitone, and a <term>trisemitone</term> <note>An interval of three semitones, like a minor third</note>. A diesis is roughly a fourth part [of a tone], though not exactly; just as a limma is not a complete semitone, even though some ancients (as <margin>Plato</margin> Proclus testifies) called the semitone a diesis. Plato describes the matter of the World and the Soul through the diatonic genus; although <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist who disagreed with the Pythagoreans</note> says, to the astonishment of the wise, that the ancients did not know the diatonic figure. He asserted this not as the <term>truth</term> <note>original: ueꝝ (verum)</note>, but so that he might always seem to bring something new to light (as <margin>Adrastus</margin> Adrastus says) according to his custom. Plato therefore uses the diatonic genus in his <margin>Plato</margin> reasoning of the world and the soul, believing that it has taken up the rudders of rational life. He leaves the enharmonic to preside over all life that is shared with bodies, and the chromatic to the corporeal idea itself. For this [chromatic] genus is divided and not at all noble. The enharmonic is indeed suited for teaching and instructing; but the diatonic is fuller and simpler than the others, and more noble. Therefore, he describes the primary office of the soul and the universe through this genus as the one most suitable.

And these Hebrews say that he spoke with Moses and carried him up, so that he might speak with the Maker face to face. The letters of these words, when calculated <note>A reference to Gematria, the Jewish system of assigning numerical value to letters</note>, return (as is clear to those who know) 999. That is: nine hundreds, nine tens, and nine numbers, so that he may connect the power of all <term>creatures</term>. The simpler powers are explained through single numbers, the middle through tens, and...

### That from the unity of the First, consonance results in all things. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Boethius of Nicomedia</margin>
**A**ll created things, being spread out and divided into many portions, would remain discordant and out of tune unless they were brought back into one through proper harmony. For <term>consonance</term> (as **Boethius** and **Nicomachus** define it) is the concord of similar and dissimilar voices brought together into one. Hence, the consonance of this worldly instrument is the agreement of similar and dissimilar things into that first consonance: so much so that all things, rejoicing in that unity, are called "one." **Plato** disputes this learnedly and profoundly in the <margin>Plato, Aristotle, Simplicius</margin> *Parmenides*; **Aristotle**, contradicting him, argues more against the words (as **Simplicius** says) than against the sense. For (as **Orpheus** teaches) God is one through identity; whereas each of the other things is called one through diversity, and through dependence, participation, and binding together with the true One, who is God. He now shapes <term>matter</term> <note>original: "mām," an abbreviation for "materiam"</note> through manifold forms, and now gathers those many things (as he says) into one creative Idea. And finally, folding <term>all things</term> <note>original: "oia," an abbreviation for "omnia"</note> back together with their principle from which they <margin>Plato, Pythagoras</margin> emanated, He impels and draws them toward that same unity. Therefore **Plato** and other **Pythagoreans**, to demonstrate that this unique machine [of the world] is joined with that supreme unity through concord and agreement, collect the even and odd portions of things, and their harmonic proportions and agreements, saying that they all proceed from unity and tend toward unity. The desire for this unity is granted by He who, existing as the supreme One, grants to all things that they may be one and tend toward the One. <margin>Boethius, Proclus</margin> For everything that exists (says **Boethius**) exists because it is numerically one. And all these things (says **Proclus** in his *Theological Elements*) just as they proceeded from the One, so they hasten toward that One in a continuous course, agreeing with it with a greater concord the more they participate in that One, of which it is said: *Furthermore, one thing is necessary* <note>A reference to Luke 10:42</note>, namely as the goal and boundary in which all things are either made blessed or find rest. For the Creator himself (says <margin>Dionysius</margin> **Dionysius**), as the cause of all, turns all things back to himself, lest they fail or be disturbed if left to themselves.

<header>THE FIFTH TONE</header>

### By what mark the seven-stringed lyre befits the soul. Chapter IX.

<margin>Plato</margin>
**A**ND because Plato, through this his <term>heptachord</term> <note>original: "eptachordũ"; a seven-stringed musical scale or instrument, used by Plato in the *Timaeus* to describe the mathematical proportions of the soul</note>, seems to describe the workmanship of both the human and the world soul, we must also investigate how it is adapted to the human soul itself. Here, this is first presupposed: that the soul itself is not a quantity-based number when removed from all bodily laws; hence it is neither divided nor multiplied by parts. Rather, it is a substantial, uniform number, turning back toward itself, and a rational entity surpassing all bodily and material things by a long interval. Its division is not according to matter, nor does it proceed from lower and coarser things, but (says <margin>Proclus</margin> Proclus) it proceeds from an efficient cause. From these perfect measures of all things, looking upon which the <term>Maker</term> <note>original: "opifex"; referring to the Demiurge or Creator in Platonic thought</note> works, he divides the soul, just as he divides this universe according to the intelligible and divine patterns. 

Therefore, there is in the soul this mode of division: immaterial, intellectual, unmixed, perfecting the substance of the soul, generating the multitude which is within and beneath it, and collecting that same multitude into one order through harmony. It gathers different parts and, existing as the cause of unmixed purity, confers upon the soul itself a flowing communion of reasons—so that the soul itself (as <margin>Timaeus, Plato, Aristotle</margin> Timaeus and Plato teach) is both partible and impartible. For if (as Aristotle rightly feels) there is in divisible things themselves a certain indivisible thing which contains them, much more must there be something indivisible in those things which have not only a divisible but an indivisible nature, which always remains. For the eternal Maker himself, the builder (as they say), established the soul and other things as a certain whole unity before division. 

Nor does the eternal producer, when he produces one thing, destroy another in the whole; for the totality does not perish by the destruction or production of parts, but remains and presides over the parts themselves. For he did not produce the parts before the whole, but the whole itself before the parts—not indeed an integral whole <note>a whole made by adding parts together</note>, but an essential one. At once, therefore, the substance of the soul is a whole having parts: a unity and a multitude collected by a marvelous harmony. 

He who wishes to perceive this should not set the goal of his industry at mathematical speculations, but should raise himself, most greatly awakened, to the appropriate place of the soul's substance, and weigh with a just balance that there is a **triple totality**: one indeed before the parts themselves, another from the parts, and yet another in each of the parts. <margin>Plato</margin> But Plato taught concerning that which is before the parts, which is not at all consumed in the production of the parts, but remains. For he who delivers the parts is good, nor does he loosen the bond, which is the duty of the evil and the not-good. The whole itself, which precedes the parts, therefore remains; and he dissolves that which is said to be from the parts; and that which is fused together from the harmonic ratio of new parts perishes once the parts are loosened. For he dissolves what is in the parts, as indicated by Plato through those circles into which he divides the soul itself. The soul is therefore unique and multiple, having unity in the intellect itself, but tending toward quality and multitude as it stretches toward lower things. And that which, existing in itself, is unique, is divided when descending to the lowest things; returning to itself, it is composed again.

For there is (as they teach) in the Archetype a divine sun: from which all numerical beauty, all grace, fitting harmony, and life emanate. In its right hand is piety and beneficence, and in its left, severe punishment. But these gentile poets, either not perceiving the mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta"; here meaning hidden spiritual truths or mysteries</note> of God, or striving to hide them, sang all those things which flourish in the supreme sun as if they belonged to this sun which we see with our bodily eyes. And they called this sun Phoebus, Apollo, or the Sun, as we touched upon above. They said he carried the Graces in his right hand, but the bow and arrows in his left.

They also called him Bacchus and Father Liber <note>another name for Bacchus/Dionysus in Roman mythology</note>. But leaving these aside as far as the present business is concerned, they called him Dionysus by night, tearing apart and mangling, and even himself torn into seven parts; but Apollo by day, putting back together what had been torn apart; and he also was cut into seven parts. This occurs through the fitting <term>septenary</term> <note>the number seven, which the author views as the key to the soul's structure</note>, so that he always proceeds by the sevenfold. For this reason, they called him the leader of the septenary. And this results from the unity (1), the binary (2), and the quaternary (4) <note>1+2+4=7</note>; from which arises the <term>bisdiapason</term> <note>a double octave, which in ancient music theory represented the most complete and perfect range of harmony</note>, namely the most perfect harmony.

Wherefore he is deservedly said to carry the lyre and to be the leader of harmony. And rightly is the septenary attributed to the author of life and dissolution: for it is composed of the first odd number, namely the ternary (3), and the first even number, namely the quaternary (4). <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> For the binary (2) is not called a "number" by the Pythagoreans, but rather a certain confusion of unities <note>In Pythagorean thought, 1 was the Monad (source) and 2 was the Dyad (duality/matter); 3 was the first true "number" because it has a beginning, middle, and end</note>. From the even and the odd, then, as if from the active and the passive, all things are generated; and by the same way they are dissolved. But generation and life come from the supernal light and the uniting force, while dissolution comes from the infernal regions and the mangling night. 

Therefore, in the night he is called Dionysus the Tearer; but in the day, the Uniting Apollo, so named as if "driving away evils" <note>The author is using a Greek etymology: *Apollon* linked to *apellon* (to drive away)</note>. For this reason, the ancients said *Apollion* for Apollo. And the <margin>Ancients, Athenians, Homer</margin> Athenians called him *Alexiakos*, that is, the expeller of evils. By Homer, however, he was called *Oulios*, that is, the author of health. In him also resides that unity making all things most consonant: which, even if it seems to suffer division by indulging in lower things, is nevertheless not torn from its own state, but collects and reunites the dispersed. To this perhaps that prophetic saying tends: <margin>Psalm 104</margin>

> "You will take away their spirit (the spirit, I mean, of unity and the uniting force) and they will fail, and all things left to themselves will diminish. But if that spirit of life and unity is sent back, they are renewed and all those same things are recreated."

Since these things are performed by God the Blessed, it therefore follows: "Let the glory of the Lord be forever: the Lord shall rejoice in his works."

This occurs namely when he has led them to the proper temperament and union with their principle from which they had proceeded. Even though they are seen by him to depart from a divisible nature, they are not abandoned by him to remain dissolved forever; for that unity is always present, which both precedes and follows the parts, finally drawing all torn things back to itself by its own power.

# THE FIFTH TONE.

## How those three sets of nine are found in man. Chapter 10.

<margin>Plato</margin>
**M**an, being the most perfect image of the world, contains all those things which are gathered together in the great world, and in the same proportion. And first, there is a <term>novenary</term> <note>a set or grouping of nine</note> of hundreds in the lower part, which is the twofold body—as Plato asserts. Each of these parts is made of four elements: for the corruptible body is made of four changeable elements, and the incorruptible body created after the resurrection will be made of nobler elements, in no way subject to corruption. These two groups of four give me eight; and in these (so that the body may be joined together and live) there is a certain unique life. Let this be the soul, which the Hebrews call <term>nephes</term> <note>original: "nephes"; Hebrew *nefesh* (נֶפֶשׁ), referring to the "living soul" or breath of life</note>; or let it be the vital spirit or the rational soul fulfilling the roles of all lives, as more recent thinkers say. From this soul, together with those eight, results the first novenary, which terminates in the tenth—namely, the superior proportion.

In the soul, however, there is a second novenary collected from the five external senses and the four internal senses—namely the imagination, the cogitative faculty, the phantasy, and the common sense. This terminates at the intellect, as if at a tenth. And in this intellect is another, purer novenary in simple numbers, which corresponds with the nine orders of Angels and the superior enumerations, so that in it there is a full image of the Angels and of God, as we shall discuss in its proper place. This terminates in that tenth, namely the supreme source and parent of all, to whom all <margin>CHRIST</margin> works and prayers are owed, as the Son of God taught when he said: *When you pray, say Our Father.* And having finally turned toward Him, we ought to be united with Him.

Furthermore, the intervals of these <term>enneads</term> <note>groups of nine; from the Greek "enneas"</note> are completed through operations (which they call <term>second acts</term> <note>in philosophical terms, the "first act" is the capacity to do something, while the "second act" is the actual performance or exercise of that capacity</note>). For man has a triple operation, and this is consonant and harmonic: with this lower world in nature; with the heavens in the senses; and with the Angels in the superior part—namely the rational, intellectual, and voluntary part. Unless man had this consonance with all things, he could neither work in all things nor understand all things. And among all living creatures, man alone enjoys this honor: to act with all things and to be capable in all things, even reaching toward the supreme Creator through understanding and loving. But if we wish to precisely trace man according to the figure of Plato and the Pythagoreans, which is contained within seven <margin>Plato, Pythagoras, the Peripatetics</margin> principal terms collected from the first even number and the first odd number—as if from the active and the passive—we shall remember that most well-worn saying among the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>: that there is in man a <term>possible intellect</term> <note>the capacity of the mind to receive or become all things</note> receiving all things, and an <term>agent intellect</term> <note>the active power of the mind that produces thoughts or concepts</note> producing all concepts, which are received in that passive intellect. And in both of these—in the one receiving and the other producing—is a <term>septenary</term> <note>a set of seven</note> collected from a <term>ternary</term> <note>a set of three</note> and a <term>quaternary</term> <note>a set of four</note>. This is because there is a concept of higher things, to which the ternary is assigned, and of composite things, to which the quaternary is devoted. Moreover, man himself is fashioned from both parts: from the spiritual, namely the mind, and the thicker part, the body. From these, a certain mixture of both results, most especially the interior senses, which are partly animal and partly intellect...

### Caput VI.

<margin>Plato</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
<margin>Proclus</margin>
<margin>The same</margin>
<margin>Plato</margin>
**A**ristotle, in celebrating the number three, draws from the stores of the Pythagoreans, which we hold from nature; and we maintain it almost as a law. For from nature there is a progression of multitude from one, and a return to that same one, which occurs through the number three itself. For the <term>Maker</term> <note>original: "Opifex", referring to God as the Divine Architect or Demiurge</note>, content in himself and enclosed, is the supreme unity; but into the many things produced by him, which are called "the other," the <term>binary</term> <note>the number two, representing duality or division</note> spreads out; yet by calling all these same things back to himself, he completes the <term>ternary</term> <note>the number three</note>. And that unity is most perfect and most blessed; the binary, however, is <term>unlucky</term> <note>original: "infaustus"; in Pythagorean thought, the number two represented falling away from unity and was thus considered ill-omened</note>; but the ternary, converting the multitude back to unity, is itself a happy number, in which God rejoices—namely, when the work is led to its proper end with a perfect image of itself. For in Him is that most perfect generating unity, from which he obtains the name of Father. The second, which creates the binary in divine things, is the begotten Son—yet not "unlucky," because he is not contained outside that all-encompassing perfection of the divine essence, but is held within its circuit. Whence he is not entirely "other" or "second," except in person; for in essence he is inwardly the same. The third is Love <note>The Holy Spirit</note>, connecting the parent with the offspring, and vice versa. Hence (as the Pythagoreans say) wherever "one" is found, that thing is fruitful and generating; that which is "begotten" is the binary or second; but that which connects both makes the ternary. For the binary and "the other" do not rest until, through the ternary—that is, the form—they return to the first. Therefore, the identity of all existing things in the Maker is declared by <term>musical proportion</term> (says Proclus). The "otherness" of produced things is declared by <term>Arithmetical</term> proportion; but the union of those othernesses is <term>Geometrical</term>. By the same series, the business of the soul (as the same Proclus says) proceeds: existing as the same in itself, multiple in its powers and senses, and yet gathered back into itself; the same also in the Maker, yet multiple in itself, always tending toward union with that same Maker. For the Fabricator granted three containing unions to the soul itself and the world, which Plato called "means" <note>original: "medietates", mathematical or philosophical mediators that bridge different realms</note>, for the reason that they seem to bind the order of the universe. Geometry indeed encompasses the multitude of substances and unites substantial processes; for the principle of union is harmonic likeness, which contains all identities and their essences in one union.

<margin>Plato</margin>
**A**rithmetic proportion folds together and joins the differences—namely the first, middle, and last—into a single unity. Plato teaches in his *Republic* that cities are to be governed by these "mediations" <note>the Latin *medietas* refers to a mathematical mean or middle term</note>. For the **harmonic mean** is a likeness of justice, granting a greater ratio to the larger terms and a lesser ratio to the smaller ones. The **arithmetic mean**, by giving to each person that which is equal according to measure, brings about peace among peoples. The **geometric mean**, however, provides union by equating and binding things together. The ancient Greek poets (such as Hesiod and others, as Proclus himself recalls) imagined these proportions to be the daughters of <term>Themis</term> <note>Themis was the personification of divine law and order</note>, who contain the powers and strengths of all things; she is the divinity of those things which are <term>right</term> <note>Latin: *fas*, divine law</note>. 
<margin>Proclus Hesiod</margin>
For in Greek, "right" is called <term>Themis</term> <note>original: *θέμις*</note>, and her daughters are **Eunomia**, **Dice**, and **Irene**. The image of **Eunomia** (Good Order) is the **geometric mean**, which leads, as it were, to a good union. The image of **Irene** (Peace) is the **arithmetic mean**, which (as we have said) leads toward peace;
<margin>Martianus</margin>
for "peace" in Greek is called <term>Irene</term> <note>original: *εἰρήνη*</note>. For this reason, the jurist Martianus called those who were placed in charge of public discipline and the correction of morals "Irenarchs" <note>Lords of Peace</note>. **Dice** (Justice), however, is represented in **music** [the harmonic mean]; through it, identity and justice are declared, following what is equal according to worth. Each of these binds and conquers: Music in the identity of the beginning; Arithmetic in equal distribution; and Geometry in union with the principle from which things proceeded. Hence, Timaeus named these proportions "bonds." Therefore, these means penetrate through the whole world and the substance of the soul. They make the soul one out of many parts and endow it with various forms through their binding and uniting powers. Since there are three of these: the **Geometric** indeed binds everything that pertains to substance in souls and things themselves. For substance is a single ratio that passes through all things, containing and embracing all: the first, the middle, and the last—just as the geometric mean itself is one and the same ratio passing through three distinct terms. The **Harmonic**, however, grants to every divided identity of souls a community and a kindred coupling of the extreme ratios themselves. This identity is seen far more clearly in universal and more common things, but less so and more obscurely in particular things. **Arithmetic**, meanwhile, binds together <term>alterity</term> <note>the state of being different or "other"</note> and the varied progression of both soul and matter. This is present less in higher things according to their order, but more in lower things. For "alterity" dominates in particulars, just as "identity" dominates in universals and better things. These two have a relationship to each other like that of identity and alterity. And just as this unity is substance itself, so the **geometric mean** is unity. Therefore, the union and bond of all substances (which we wish to be understood in thirty-four terms) is the geometric mean itself; likewise, the harmonic mean is the bond of equal identities, just as the arithmetic is the bond of alterities—all of them, I say, extended through all the terms.

it becomes one with him: because all things pre-existing in the <term>Word</term> <note>original: *verbo*, referring to the Logos or Divine Reason</note> were identical with the Word itself, as our theologians say.
<margin>Orpheus</margin>
But following the example of Orpheus, we say that the soul places its "head" in the first intellect. The second limit, which contains a double proportion to the first, suggests the progress of that soul from God. The third limit, however, signifies the <term>egress</term> <note>here meaning a "return" or "going out toward" its source</note> toward the same. The fourth is its egress from itself, so that it may be occupied with the performance of other tasks. The fifth is a recession back to itself, so that its departure from itself is joined to the progress it makes from that which precedes it; thus, its return to itself depends upon its own return toward the Craftsman who precedes it. The final limits, indeed, which are composed of <term>solids</term> <note>mathematically, "solids" refer to cubic numbers like 8 and 27</note>, teach us the conversion of the bodies to which the soul itself is joined. I say "bodies," because the world consists of a twofold body: one incorruptible and celestial, the other corruptible and dross. In the same way—so that he may contain a perfect image of the world—
<margin>Plato</margin>
man is perfected by a twofold body according to the Platonists: the elementary and the celestial. The elementary body is denoted by the cube or solid of the <term>binary</term> <note>the number 2; 2 cubed is 8, symbolizing matter</note>, which signifies matter; while the celestial body is denoted by the cube of the <term>ternary</term> <note>the number 3; 3 cubed is 27, symbolizing spirit or the heavens</note>. Thus, the harmony of the world follows that which exists in the mind, the soul, and the whole of man.
<margin>The Academics. Proclus.</margin>
This is maintained in many places by the Academics, especially Proclus; but here he says that the world participates in ten modes of harmony, while the soul participates in four. And just as the unity of the <term>quaternary</term> <note>the number four</note> is the cause of the soul, so here the <term>denary</term> <note>the number ten</note> is the cause of the world. Thus, intellectual harmony produces the harmony of the soul, and the latter produces the harmony of the senses. Hence the Hebrews say—from their most hidden secrets—that the soul proceeds from the great four-letter name of God <note>the Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>, but the whole world proceeds from and is ruled by the ten <term>enumerations</term> <note>referring to the ten Sephirot of the Kabbalah</note>. However, it is ruled by the command of the three highest enumerations, and by the execution of the remaining seven; hence they call these seven the "enumerations of the fabric" <note>the Sephirot of Construction or Action</note>. Thus, according to
<margin>Syrianus</margin>
unity (as Syrianus prefers), the world is represented as perfect and whole. According to the <term>binary</term> <note>the number 2</note>, however, multitude and variety are suggested within it: through the division of even and odd, masculine and feminine, beginning from the gods themselves down to stems and plants. For that which is in the gods follows the binary and ternary; but that which is in the ranks better and higher than us follows the quaternary and the <term>nonary</term> <note>the number nine</note>. Finally, it proceeds through the cubes down to the terrestrial and the lowest species of life, leading those same things back to the first. 
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
Therefore, perfect harmony is completed through cubes, which the Pythagoreans were accustomed to call "harmony" because they are the only shapes whose angles are proportionally equal to their sides and surfaces. Thus, it also distributes larger and faster motions to the more subtle and thin elements, while giving smaller and slower motions—and consequently lower steps—to the thicker elements, in which those various harmonies result. The difference is 13, which pertains to matter, as Proclus says: because it is beyond the number twelve, which is surely a divine number and the one by which they measure the heavens. In this thirteen is founded the <term>lemma</term> <note>original: *lemma*; in music theory, a small interval or "remainder" left over after calculating larger intervals</note>, a proportion of the soul toward the material things themselves—the dregs, sediments, and disturbances—which nevertheless belong to the fulfillment of both worlds. Therefore, having removed this shapeless division, let us look at that in which all other proportions are found. "In the beginning," he says, "the Maker took one portion from the universe," which he doubled when he commanded matter to be formed: which had the proportion of the <term>lemma</term>. But he quadrupled it when he poured it out into the distinct elements: which he octupled when pouring out, and giving life to, composite things; but this is through the feminine power. But the <term>lemma</term> looks toward the bodily and the vegetative, reaching even to metals, stones, and all the lowest kinds.

## That those things which were said concerning those existing in the spheres seem to agree with Holy Scripture.

### Chapter XIV.

<margin>Pythagoreans, Academics</margin>
**N**OR should anyone wonder if the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in a mathematical and harmonious universe.</note> and the Academics <note>Followers of Plato’s school, the Academy.</note> say that the spheres are filled with intelligences and souls in those same places, since in the sacred word of Moses it is also said: "The heavens were completed, and all their host" <note>original: *exercitus eorum*; Gen 2:1</note>; in place of which we have the word "ornament" <note>original: *ornatus*; a common Latin translation for the Hebrew *tsava*, meaning host or array</note>. For the "hosts" and "celestial armies" are the intelligences and intellectual forms, which are <margin>Plato, Moses, Proclus, Euripides</margin> the most beautiful ornament of the heavens themselves. For through these forms, which Plato along with Moses calls the "heavenly host," the celestial spheres (as Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "souls" of the stars.</note> says) are adorned. For this reason, Euripides and many after him called them the dwellings and the halls of the Gods—that is, of the celestial minds. Moreover, what these forms are, and how many of them there are in the heavens, distinct from the highest God himself, only He knows, who "counts the <margin>Psalms</margin> multitude of the stars" (as the Psalmist sings) "and calls them all by their names" <note>Psalm 147:4</note>. Truly, He calls the names not of the physical stars, but of the presiding intelligences, as some wise men explain. For the entire school of the wise, even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on logic and natural science.</note>, assigns at least one intelligence to each individual orb. But since each individual star has its own power and influence over lower things, it is necessary that it also has its own presiding intelligence which bestows the power to act; for an action can by no means proceed from a purely physical body. Regarding our own souls, however, a difficulty remains; and among many it might be considered ridiculous that these souls should be placed within the spheres. Yet it does not seem strange to those who understand correctly. For even some Catholic thinkers of no small talent have sung of human souls being carried up to various spheres. This is not to be understood only of the physical spheres, but of those supramundane <note>Beyond the physical world.</note> wheels to which souls return as they first proceeded from them, as is most fully handed down in the more secret Theology of the Hebrews <note>likely a reference to the Kabbalah, which discusses the descent and ascent of souls.</note>. And these are, <margin>CHRIST, Pythagoras, Astronomy</margin> without a doubt, the "many and varied mansions in the Father's house," as the Supreme Truth <note>Referring to Christ, who calls himself "the Way, the Truth, and the Life."</note> proclaims <note>John 14:2</note>. Furthermore, the Pythagoreans believe that souls make their passage through them, descending through those intelligences and spheres, to which they return in a perfected course after a well-lived life. And from this, astronomers (if they possess any truth) determine by forecasting that one person is "Saturnine," another "Martian," another "Jovian," "Venerean," "Mercurial," "Phobean" <note>referring to Apollo/the Sun</note>, or "Lunar." Indeed, there are various dispositions, inclinations, and characters in men, which proceed not only from matter being variously arranged (as some believe), but from a varied influence and a diverse form—not indeed a diversity of species, but a particular and personal one. Though these grades are variously distributed <margin>Paul</margin> by Him who, remaining the same, "divides them to each one as He wills" (as the Apostle says <note>1 Corinthians 12:11</note>), the secondary angelic and celestial causes nevertheless work together, arranging the body and other things which God has committed to them. Nor let anyone say that the Apostle was speaking there only of the division of spiritual graces; because (as Gregory <note>St. Gregory the Great, an influential theologian and Pope.</note> rightly feels) both angelic and human minds are similar in their receiving of gifts, just as they agree in their participation in the levels of nature.

### What can be said concerning the completions of the intervals of the three enneads. Chapter XV.

<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
**A**fter we have forged <note>original: *cudimus*; literally "hammered out" or fashioned through study</note> the discussion regarding the filling of intervals, we must run through whatever can be said about the completions of the primary kinds—that is, the twenty-seven, or the three enneads <note>An "ennead" is a grouping of nine. Three enneads (27) represent the full cosmic hierarchy or scale of the universe in Platonic and Pythagorean thought.</note>. They are indeed filled according to <term>supparticular proportions <note>A mathematical ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number once, plus one aliquot part of it—for example, 3:2 or 4:3.</note></term>, as the Pythagoreans say. And this is according to a single portion imparted to things; yet that unique life is not divided. Rather, just as the sun is unique in itself, but in its rays and effects it is multiple and varied—flowing more effectively in one time and place than another—so too the soul, existing as a single unit in the body, has the most diverse effects. And to begin from the more noble parts: in the intellect, or in the head, it understands; in the heart, it wills; in the eyes, it sees; in the ears, it hears; in the hands, it works; in the feet, it walks; in the intestines, it digests, and it intervenes even unto the expelling of waste. In these places, the soul works as a whole, since it is not divisible; yet it does not act according to its whole self, but strikes <note>original: *pangit*; to fix or compose</note> according to a part of its power. For if the power were always the same, the resulting work would also be the same. Nor is the variety of organs alone sufficient to produce such varied effects, for if the soul were absolute <note>set free</note> from the body, it could only produce a single work. Nevertheless, even when removed from the body, it wills, understands, moves according to place, and uses the senses, which belong to the "inner man." Therefore, the soul is varied in its effects and one in itself; it restricts itself through its organs and instruments according to a part. From this results a supparticular proportion: namely, of the whole to some proportioned part. So too the life of the world is one, of which it is said: "God, for whom all things live." And Paul, celebrating the sentiment of Aratus <note>A Greek poet whom St. Paul quotes in Acts 17:28</note>, says: "In Him (that is, <margin>Paul, Aratus, Orpheus</margin> God) we live, move, and have our being." From the hiding places of this unity (says Orpheus), a numerous multitude proceeds. Thus the Tree of Life situated in the midst of Paradise, which provides life to all, is unique; and yet it is called <note>original: עץ חיים</note> *Etz Chaim*, that is, the Tree of Life <note>The author provides the Hebrew phrase *Etz Chaim* and its Latin equivalent *Arbor Vitae*</note>, because that unique tree diffuses diverse rays of life into others. Just as Paul says concerning the life of the mystical body: "One and the same Spirit <margin>Paul, Ezekiel</margin> divides to each one as He wills." This Spirit, being the spirit of life and the same as the Tree of Lives, gives life to all things, as we are taught by the oracle of Ezekiel, who says: "The Spirit of life was in the wheels." By "wheels" I mean the mundane, or celestial and terrestrial spheres. For all things, rejoicing in their spherical form, imitate that supreme and divine sphere. This life, therefore, existing whole in itself, communicates itself according to a certain portion (which is by no means cut off from it): to one indeed in a <term>sesquialtera proportion <note>A 3:2 ratio, which in music produces the interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note></term>, to another in a <term>sesquitertia proportion <note>A 4:3 ratio, which produces a Perfect Fourth.</note></term>, to another in a <term>sesquioctava <note>A 9:8 ratio, which produces a Whole Tone.</note></term>, and to another in a <term>sesquiextadecima <note>Likely a 16:15 ratio, which produces a semitone.</note></term>. From these result the <term>diapente <note>A musical fifth.</note></term>, the <term>diatessaron <note>A musical fourth.</note></term>, the tone, and the <term>lemma <note>A small melodic interval or semitone.</note></term>. However, as to which particular kinds and species the first life itself—diffusing and disposing all things by its numbers, weights, and measures—arranges with this or that proportion, no one has yet pointed out in detail. Nor do I think it can be expressed or perceived except by those who are purified and filled with wisdom, by which they are able to know all things and embrace all things; just as it says in the Book of Wisdom: <margin>Wisdom</margin> "He gave me true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the disposition of the world..."

VOICE OF THE FIRST SONG

## OF THE FIRST SONG

...or are judged as outsiders. For what the Wise Man <note>Referring to Solomon in the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight."</note> implies through number, weight, and measure, Plato <margin>Plato</margin> describes through numbers, figures, and solids. For by numbers he wished to signify the specific forms of things, which Aristotle <margin>Aristo.</margin> also compared to numbers. Through measures, indeed, he indicates the powers allotted to each thing, of which the Supreme Truth <note>Referring to Christ as the personification of Truth.</note> <margin>CHRIST.</margin> speaks in the Gospel, saying: "He gave to each according to their own measure," <note>original: *secundum propriam mensuram*. A paraphrase of the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25:15.</note> that is, according to what has been measured out to each from those Archetypal measures, which measure all things with the most just examination. By solids, however, the weights of things are understood, as well as the heavy elements which always lead us to the depths; or the inclinations of things, which like weights, pull and impel us toward either good or evil. Hence Augustine <margin>Augu.</margin> calls love a weight, saying: "My weight is my love; by it I am carried wherever I am carried." <note>original: *Pondus meum amor meus, illuc feror, ubi amo*. A famous quote from Augustine's Confessions, 13.9.10.</note>

Again, by numbers the arithmetic mean is designated. By dimensions and measures, the geometric mean. By weights, however, the musical mean <note>In ancient and medieval music theory, the "harmonic mean" was often linked to the weights used in experiments with strings or hammers to find consonant intervals.</note> is designated, which, in balanced proportion or likeness, comprehends the speed and slowness of motions, the sharpness <note>high pitch</note> and gravity <note>low pitch</note> of voices, and the heavier or lighter inclinations of things. And just as in strings, or pipes, or any sounding instruments, temperaments derived from weights are necessary, so in all things—and especially in man, who is the bond of all things—desires must be tempered <note>The author uses the metaphor of tuning an instrument.</note> like well-strung chords, and natural inclinations must be directed toward the goal of reason or the divine law implanted in human minds.

Foods must also be tempered, and all things we use, according to their proper weights; just as in this "great machine" <note>original: *maiori hac machina*. A common Renaissance term for the universe/macrocosm.</note>, the elements, the heavens, and all things rejoice in their proper temperaments, so that innumerable species and forms, balanced by their measures, harmonize together. Although their underlying bodies are all composed of the four elements, they are found to be innumerable. Nor is this a wonder: for if from a cube—which is made of three numbers (namely the linear, the plane, and the solid) and is formed from four surfaces—diverse and nearly infinite lines are led from the center to the circumference, how much more in the worldly cube <note>A reference to the Platonic cosmology where the cube represents the element of Earth, or more broadly, the stable structure of the physical world.</note> (as we wrote above), led from the number three to twenty-seven, will innumerable forms and innumerable composite subjects be found? 

This is true even though all things come from the four elements as if from four primary surfaces through their superior numbers, to which the multiplied forms correspond in their underlying bodies. These are led through the seven stars <note>The seven classical planets: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, through the seven intelligences presiding over them, and through the seven deities from whom the intelligences receive their influence. And most excellently that septenary [sevenfold] arrangement resulting from the four surfaces and three numbers is led into the composite world through the celestial, Angelic, and divine septenaries, with the twelve signs of the zodiac also intervening, which are led by the parts of the seven. For three times four and four times three constitute the twelve. From which such great harmony results that musical craftsmen, following nature as their guide, [produce] their...

**By what intervening causes these manifold kinds are brought together.**

### Chapter XVII.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
**A**ristotle, having scrutinized the causes of all things, found only four that are common to all: matter, form, the efficient cause, and the end. He described three of these quite copiously, but regarding the "acting" (efficient) cause in particular, he revealed little or nothing, saying only this: that God and Nature work in such things. But by what influx, by what instruments, and when He brings them together, Aristotle did not touch upon at all. And because he was unable to grasp the beginning of things, he contended to defend an eternal world. Other matters he passed over in silence as if they were foreign both to his doctrine and to human intellect.

They wish, moreover, for every compound thing to be named by those letters which designate the causes coming together to produce that compound. And so some assert that Adam knew how to bestow a name suited to each individual thing. Just as these points allow the letters to be uttered and, in a sense, to live, so by them they wish to designate the life of composite things. And because all things emanate and receive growth from supra-mundane fountains, and always depend upon them, they also wished to designate the fountains, channels, and influences proceeding from the ten divinities or fountains <note>The ten Sephirot or divine emanations in Kabbalah.</note> by means of accents placed above the letters. Behold, therefore, how 27 is found twice in that name: so that it denotes both that divine number which, never departing from unity, is the Idea and fountain of all numbers; and also that number of creatures, which is distinguished and counted among the various kinds of things. And it is not without mystery that the twin 27 is connected through that word *Asher* <note>meaning "that" or "which"</note>, which among us carries a relative meaning. Through this relation, or within it, those two numbers are joined and their conjunction is expressed; just as all operations which God performs, both internally and externally, are indicated through relations. 

For the highest teacher, Jesus Christ, when He wished to explain those most holy Persons—both the producing and the produced—expressed it in no other way than through certain relations, calling them Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the same way, in all things He does with us, He takes some relative name through which each of His works is indicated. 
<margin>Abraham</margin>
For while He fashioned the world, He took the name of "Maker" or "Creator," and this was in respect to the produced creature. Similarly, while He rules and orders the world itself, He is called "Ruler" and "Governor"; and through this act of ruling and governing He is joined with us, just as He was through creation when He first brought us forth.

It is no wonder, then, if even that twofold number, 27, is embraced by a relative term: which nevertheless in God is something most absolute, carrying much more and much greater significance. He indicated this as the greatest secret to Moses, to be reported to his fathers and brothers, when with a heavy hand and an outstretched arm and many wonders He wished to free them from Egyptian slavery.

->## THE FIFTH TONE<-

...the number nine, multiplied again by three, constitutes the perfect cube of the world <note>The "cube of the world" refers to the number 27 (3x3x3). In Renaissance Neoplatonism, this was seen as a foundational number for the structure of the universe.</note>. There is a manifold trinity in all things, since all things together possess a likeness or a footprint of the Triune God, at least in this: that all things have their exit and beginning from God, their progress through Him, and their end in Him from whom they proceeded. This beginning and end of things is God Himself, just as it is indicated through the letters of His supreme name. For there is the **Aleph** <term>א</term>, which is the beginning of the letters and signifies unity, which is the beginning of numbers. And there is the **Iod** <term>י</term>, which represents the number ten and the completion of numbers. Thus, these two letters denote that the Named One Himself is the beginning and the end of all things. 

Two **He's** <term>ה</term> also intervene: the first of which mediates between unity and the number ten, indicating the first "offspring" of created things which occurs in the mind of God, emanating from the first principle signified by the **Aleph** <term>א</term>, and tending toward the ultimate end indicated by the **Iod** <term>י</term>. <margin>The Hebrews</margin> Indeed, the other **He** <term>ה</term>, which is the last letter both of that supreme name <note>The name *Ehyeh* (I Am).</note> and of the **Tetragrammaton** <term>The four-letter name of God, YHVH</term>, suggests the "unfolding" of things into their own specific kinds. Therefore, the **Hebrews** say that God fabricated the world with the letter **He** <term>ה</term>. In the first instance, He produced it in His mind; in the second, He unfolded it into actual forms—yet by this law: that the things unfolded in the second production should follow and emulate the first production in likeness and harmony. 

It must also be observed that in both of the great names of God there is a quaternary <note>A grouping of four.</note> of letters, which nevertheless does not depart from the triad; for in both cases there are only three distinct letters, but one is doubled, which indicates both productions—in the mind and in the effect. Whence there is not strictly a quaternary in that divinity, which always "delights in the triad" <note>This is a common Pythagorean and Neoplatonic maxim: *Numero Deus impare gaudet* (God delights in an odd number/the triad).</note>. 

And so that it may denote all powers, attributes, properties, or measures, or whatever things in God seem to be numbered, all those numbers of the **Tetragrammaton** (which are 26) are reduced back to the **Aleph** <term>א</term>. This letter represents "one"; and it is shaped from a **Vav** <term>ו</term> (which gives the number 6) and from two **Iods** <term>י י</term> (each of which gives ten). These tens joined together return 20, which number together with that 6 constitutes 26 <note>The author is describing the visual composition of the Hebrew letter Aleph (א), which can be seen as a diagonal Vav with an Iod above and an Iod below. In Gematria, 10+10+6 = 26, the same value as Y-H-V-H.</note>. From this letter <note>Aleph.</note> almost all the most celebrated divine names begin, such as **God, My Lord, The Judge** <note>original: "אל אדני אלהים" (El, Adonai, Elohim)</note> and the like. Most powerfully, it begins that supreme name whose beginning is itself **Aleph**; which also signifies a "thousand," the end and limit of all numbers, decades, and hundreds. Thus you find that He who is the beginning and end of all is entirely One. 

God, therefore, exists as unique in Himself, and yet diffused into many-natured creatures, just as "one" is diffused into all numbers; He never departs from the unity proper and peculiar to Himself. Rather, gathering all the strings of the worldly **Enharmonic** <term>A system of musical tuning; here used as a metaphor for the harmony of the universe</term> from this unity into one, He renders them tempered and harmonious. For just as in vocal music (as <margin>Boethius</margin> **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" was the standard music theory text for a millennium.</note> teaches), harmony and consonance is a concord of equal and unequal voices reduced into one; in the same way, in the **Enharmonic** of this great machine <note>The universe.</note>, harmony and consonance is a fitness of equal and unequal genera, species, and individuals reduced into one. In that nearly "One" from which all multitude emanates, the world is sustained, ruled, and filled; just as all dwellings and unobstructed spaces of the hemisphere are illuminated by a single sun. And just as "one" collects all numbers after the square of the first number into a ten, and after as many tens as there are numbers.

In the square of the three-fold <note>original: "quadrato ternarii", referring to the numerical base of three</note>, it collects those very tens into one **hundred**; and finally, having counted as many hundreds as there are numbers and tens, it collects everything into a **thousand**: which is signified by **Aleph** <term>א</term>. Each of these letters, not without a great mystery, carries a **circular number** <note>Numbers like 5 and 6 are "circular" because their powers always end in the same digit (5x5=25, 6x6=36), symbolizing a return to the source.</note>, to the extent that all those numbers become circular, and all circular numbers are contained within those same letters. These are the five, the six, and the ten. The five is denoted by the letter **He** <term>ה</term>; the six by **Vau** <term>ו</term>; and the ten by **Iod** <term>י</term>. These individual numbers, and all of them together, properly signify God, that true **intelligible sphere** <note>A reference to the Hermetic definition of God as a sphere whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere.</note>. He gave His own likeness in a circle to all things produced by Him, so that they might strive to return, the course of the world being completed, to that from which they proceeded.

Another mystery contained in these same letters must be observed. For **He** <term>ה</term>, signifying the five, indicates the **quintessence** <term>the fifth element or "ether" that transcends the four earthly elements</term> implanted in all things composed of the four elements. **Vau** <term>ו</term>, carrying the perfect number six, denotes that life by which all things live. And **Iod** <term>י</term>, carrying the perfect number ten, represents divinity itself, by which all things are filled—as has often been said—and which all things represent, either through an image, a footprint, or a likeness. 

If we return to the supreme name <note>The name "Ehyeh" (I Am)</note>, in which **Aleph** <term>א</term> is placed instead of **Vau** <term>ו</term>, and that at the very front of the word: it is so understood that the Named One never departs from His circular property. **Aleph** <term>א</term> itself carries unity, which is the principle of all circular numbers. For it also returns into itself, and contains all numbers in potential, and leads them into action through multiplied unity; and finally, it leads back to the unity of the ten, the hundred, and the thousand, which is again signified by **Aleph** <term>א</term>. In this you most fittingly represent God: who, being supremely one, contains all numbered things in His power, and unfolds everything into particular and numbered forms; and finally recalls all those same things into Himself: so that the entire **worldly harmony** <note>original: "mundanū enharmoniū", a musical metaphor for the cosmic order</note>, proceeding from the One, most consonant in a single life and spirit, might tend toward and return to the One.

->**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.**<-

## OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.

## ON THE METHOD OF PROCEEDING, AND THE GENERAL HARMONY OF MAN WITH THE MACROCOSM AND THE ARCHETYPE. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Apollo</margin>
Painters, the most accurate rivals of nature, diligently imitate as much as they can the things they depict. For painting (says Apollonius the Pythagorean <note>Referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher often associated with Neo-Pythagoreanism</note>) is a kind of imitation of a natural thing, provided by nature; but the composition of colors is by art: though the greater power of painting is placed in the first sketch. And what they do with colors, likewise the true describers of things—whether they be Poets, Orators, or Historians—endeavor to do with their utmost effort. In all of these, imitation and a full description of things as nature provides them is more highly commended than a clever arrangement of characters. Therefore, since we are the describers of the works of the <term>Highest Artisan</term> <note>A common Renaissance term for God as the Creator</note>, it is right that the method of our writing should match the things we record as best we can. 

Of this matter, our Moses, filled with God, stands as the most famous example. In writing of the fabric of both worlds, he wove them together with fitting care as each required. For he relates that the parts of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe at large</note>—as the order of nature demanded—were brought forth by a single command. But coming to the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," referring to Man as a reflection of the universe</note> (which is nonetheless greater in virtue and mystery), he describes its workmanship with a craftsmanship as much more celebrated as the man himself was fashioned with a more excellent gift. This is manifest in those things done regarding him: for God had previously prepared a home for him, into which He led him once it was finished and ready. He then granted him dominion over all living creatures; He planted a place of pleasantness, sown with every delight for his pleasure; He gave him a most joyful companion. And He gave all things to his judgment, as if to a legitimate heir—excepting only a single tree, so that from it he might recognize his superior Lord. 

<margin>Mercury</margin>
For in this man, as if in his own form (say <term>Mercury</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and "Hermetic" texts were attributed</note> and Solomon), God took delight. Moreover, in fashioning him, He called together a most solemn council—either of the Holy Trinity, as Catholics say; or of the Holy Angels, as some of the Hebrews maintain; or of the <term>supramundane</term> divinities, or the measures of things to be made (which we may call <term>Ideas</term> <note>In the Platonic sense: the eternal, perfect blueprints of things in the mind of God</note> along with their attributes and persons), as the more secret Theologians assert. With a certain preamble, God formed him not by command alone, but with His own hands and power. Observing this, the most wise 

<margin>Moses</margin>
Moses narrates the workmanship of man in a longer and more celebrated discourse. For he repeats his formation twice: now "created," now "made," now the "breath of life" breathed into his nostrils. Not without mystery, he records distinctly everything done by the Artisan concerning him, and he sets forth other most solemn narrations pertaining to the same. Rightly, therefore, do both the creator and the writer pursue man with such great diligence, since in him the whole force of nature and the most sublime divinity [reside].

<summary>This chapter introduces the philosophical justification for studying Man as a reflection of the universe, arguing that while the universe was created by a simple command, Man was crafted with deliberate care and divine consultation.</summary>

# SIXTH TONE. C

<margin>N iiii</margin>
<meta>catchword: that</meta>

<margin>Algazel</margin> <note>original: Algazel; referring to Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> It is so established that the wise Saracen, Algazel, says: "Nature, coming to the composition of man, ceased, as if having nothing more honorable to compose in her hands." In him, indeed, is concluded (by the testimony of <margin>Galen.</margin> Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher (129 – c. 216 AD) whose views dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>) all wisdom, beyond which none is found, or—to speak more correctly—is not devised by us. He [the Creator] knew, moreover, that on earth man alone would cultivate virtue and heavenly things; therefore, he fabricated him with such diligence. Wherefore, since we have rightly preferred Moses in the description of both worlds <note>The Macrocosm (the universe) and the Microcosm (man).</note>, following in his footsteps, we also shall describe the craftsmanship of the <term>human world</term> <note>The Microcosm; the idea that the human body and soul reflect the structure of the entire universe.</note> with more industrious diligence. In him, the <term>Artisan</term> <note>God, envisioned as the Great Architect or Craftsman.</note> gathered all things with an inestimable art and incomprehensible wisdom, which He had distributed throughout so spacious a machine [of the universe]: so that, having been made the bond of all things, and gathering all things into one—just as all things themselves emanated from the One—they might be led back through the same [man] gathered into a globe toward that same One. This is necessary if the work is to imitate the Artisan: who is a certain sphere and circle, says <margin>Hermes</margin> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" tradition of philosophy and mysticism.</note>. In like manner, His fabric is a circle: of which one extreme is its exemplar or "idea" residing in that unique Mind or Word; the middle is all fabricated things; but the other extreme is man—who was produced last by the Artisan and is most similar to the Producer. Thus, that saying of <margin>Orige.</margin> Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> holds a place here: that the end in those who act rightly is always similar to the beginnings. The circle of created things stood open until, with man united to the Word <note>Referring to the Incarnation of Christ.</note>, those two extremes were closed: which was most especially done by Him who said: "I am the <term>Alpha and the Omega</term> <note>original: α & ω; the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end.</note>." And just as that divine Trinity is included in one essence, so these three worlds are concluded in a single circle. Concerning this, <margin>Plato</margin> writes most amply in the *Phaedrus*, and after him <margin>Procu.</margin> Proclus <note>Proclus Lycaeus (412–485 AD), a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> teaches summarily in his work *On Vows and Prayers*: for he says, "Created things, beginning from God and ending in God himself, effect a certain circuit of a circle." For all things remain in Him and are converted back to Him; which conversion they have according to the perfecting Trinity. <margin>Iohan.</margin> John <note>The Apostle John, referencing the prologue of the Gospel of John.</note> commemorates these three worlds, saying: "He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not." He calls them all "worlds" to declare that the same [essence] belongs to all. For all things are, and have their being communicated by Him who said: "I AM has sent me to you." Yet he distinguishes them so that he might demonstrate the difference between them: yet one is the image of the other. For the world in which we live contains the image of God; and man possesses the image of the world and of the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original model or the Divine Mind upon which all creation is based.</note>. Herein lies the concord of man with both. But let us begin from the agreement which he has through the body with this mundane fabric, so that we may ascend in due order from visible things to invisible things.

### OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.

It [creation] imitates the eternity of God and His simultaneous total fullness. Since things are unable to equal this, they decline from that total fullness into a sequence of time, and from immobility into motion. For this elemental fire imitates the solar light, and that [the sun] imitates the divine and inaccessible light. But as much as the Sun falls short of the supreme light, so much does this elemental light fall short of the solar—if a comparison with the infinite is permitted. Therefore, all lower things imitate the highest, even the supreme Creator, who is rightly called the <term>Archetype</term> <note>original: Archetypus; the primary pattern or "first type" from which all things are modeled.</note>, as it were the first type of all things, holding the first rank in everything. Indeed, He exists as the "idea" of all images seen in lower things; those which approach closer to Him, He assimilates more perfectly to Himself. 

Since, therefore, God is an "intelligible sphere," and this world presents itself to be seen in a spherical shape, it is necessary that man—who holds the middle ground between God and this world—be bounded by the same figure. He imitates that intellectual sphere in his soul, and the sensible [physical] sphere in his body, as this present picture can show: if a compass is drawn from the navel (according to some) or more truly from the pubic bone, that circle fits the body perfectly. From this, the entire measure of the body is recognized to arise from and tend toward roundness. For the <margin>Lactantius</margin> <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author who often wrote on the wonders of the human form.</note> head is round, like a globe or an orb, as Lactantius says. 

Also, the entire body is well-turned with the most proportionate measure. For from the end of the arm toward the hand, where the pulse beats, to the thumb, a <term>double-and-a-half proportion</term> <note>original: proportio dupla sesqualtera; a mathematical ratio of 5:2 used here to describe anatomical symmetry.</note> is found in circular measure. From the neck to the shins, the same proportion is found. From the thumb to the arm near the shoulder blade, the proportion is triple. The arm, in the same way, is triple in relation to the flesh of the hip. We could pursue many other things concerning the numbers and proportions of the human body, both the obvious and the hidden; but I fear that while we discuss numbers, we might exceed number and measure, and our weak strength might succumb to such a heavy burden. For these things lie hidden (though harmoniously arranged) in the veins, nerves, and internal organs. No one has ever found these, <margin>Augustine</margin> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). This likely refers to his writings on the "numbers" or ratios inherent in the soul and body.</note> says Augustine, nor even the cruel diligence of the anatomists, who tear apart the bodies of the dead to investigate all hidden things, and from there learn how and in what places to apply cures. Yet no one has been able to find the complete numbers by which this harmonic fitting-together of the whole body consists, both inside and out, like that of a musical instrument—which perhaps...

### Chapter III. On the proportion of measures in man.

<margin>Damascenus</margin>
**S**ince nothing in man was made at random or out of discord, but all things were guided by these numbers so that (as <term>Damascenus</term> <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and scholar who wrote on theology and science.</note> says) his members preserve a certain proportion to each other and to the parts of the world, just like the strings on a lyre: Therefore, regarding the care of the <term>Supreme Architect</term> <note>original: summi Opificis; a common Renaissance term for God as the master craftsman of the universe.</note> concerning the most harmonious arrangement and the measures of the limbs, we shall run through a few points out of many. In these, every melody and every perfected harmony will be seen, omitting those other parts by which the middle sections are completed like filled-in intervals. For the proportion of the entire body to the trunk is <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>A 9:8 ratio, which in music corresponds to a whole tone.</note>. From the trunk or chest to the legs all the way to the soles of the feet, a <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio, corresponding to the musical interval of a fourth (diatessaron).</note> follows. The proportion of the chest from the neck to the navel, and to the loins or the belly up to the end of the trunk, is <term>double</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio, corresponding to the octave (diapason).</note>. Indeed, the width of the hips to the width of the thigh is <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, corresponding to the musical interval of a fifth (diapente).</note>. In these proportions, the whole tone, the fourth, the fifth, and the octave result. There is also a <term>triple</term> <note>A 3:1 ratio, which is an octave plus a fifth.</note> proportion of the head to the neck, where there is an octave and a fifth combined. And again, the head to the knee is triple; and the same to the calf or the leg. And thus all members of the human body are proved to be guided by the most exact measures,

<margin>
Hippocrates
Boethius
Moses
</margin>
just as <term>Hippocrates</term> wisely teaches his son <term>Thessalus</term>; and <term>Boethius</term> discusses this in a longer discourse. It even pleased the Architect to explain this through <term>Moses</term> under the type of the <term>Ark</term> built by <term>Noah</term>. For he says: "The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth fifty cubits, and the height thirty cubits" [Genesis 6:15]. Thus, there is a sixfold proportion of length to width, and a tenfold proportion to height. By these measures, the structure of our body is taught—which is not only my opinion, but that of the divine 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
<term>Augustine</term>. Reading him after my own discoveries, I rejoiced in the testimony and favor of such a great man; but (to tell the truth) I felt a pang of grief that someone had voiced my discoveries before me. Therefore, the same proportion exists in that Ark as in the human body. But if we also desire to match the number, we must attend to the measures by which certain <term>microcosmographers</term> <note>Scholars or artists who map the human body as a "small world" (microcosm) that mirrors the "large world" (macrocosm).</note> measure the human body itself. For they divide it by six feet, which are slightly smaller than common feet; and they call the measure of one of these feet a <term>hexipeda</term> <note>A "six-foot" unit of measurement used here to scale human proportions.</note>. They divide this into ten degrees; thus from six hexipedas, sixty degrees result. Each degree is divided into ten, according to some—but better, as others say, into five "minutes"—so that all degrees together yield three hundred minutes. These are what Moses calls "cubits." If these were understood as common cubits, they could fit neither the Ark nor the human craftsmanship; for if they were applied to the Ark, it would have been very small by common standards...

# OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.

<margin>Augustine, Origen</margin> ...cubits: which are only two spans, having a foot and a half, or six palms. Therefore, Augustine and Origen prudently thought that those cubits were <term>Geometric</term> <note>original: Geometricos; a "geometric cubit" was a theoretical unit equal to six ordinary cubits, used by theologians to explain how all the world's animals could fit into the Ark.</note> (so that the ark would be large enough to hold all kinds of animals). For one Geometric cubit contains six common ones. And this was not unknown to him <note>A reference to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note> who was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, among whom this doctrine especially flourished. If we also wish to relate this to the craftsmanship of the human body, this kind of measurement <note>The common cubit.</note> can hardly be suitable. Therefore, the small units and the proportion resulting from their number agree, which is weighed by the wiser men in this manner. The human body is therefore three hundred units in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height, so that it matches the proportions of the ark. The <term>Supreme Architect</term> <note>original: summus Artifex; a common Renaissance name for God as the creator of the world's design.</note> took even greater care in the craftsmanship of this body than in the ark, which was to be constructed by art imitating nature. Furthermore, he mentions two windows: one above, as a breathing hole to take in air and other necessities; the other below, for evacuating superfluities. And what can be more aptly said of the human body, which has an upper window—though it is manifold—through which we receive both what is necessary for sustaining the body and the light to guide it? But this window is said to be completed at one cubit, a modest measure indeed, since the mouth is small in comparison to other living creatures. Out of a sense of decency, he describes neither the measure nor the function of the lower door; instead, he commemorates the unclean raven and the most pure dove sent out from the window: and how the raven sought out foul things, but the dove returned with an olive branch as a sign of peace. The mystery of these birds is clear: for from our upper window (the mouth, namely), there come out many things, both clean and unclean. Concerning the unclean things, the Heavenly Teacher 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> spoke in plain speech, saying: *Those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart, and they defile the man* <note>original: Quae de ore exeunt...; a quotation from the Gospel of Matthew 15:18-19.</note>—namely, evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies, and such things, which are rightly signified by the raven, who always delights in unclean things and is unlucky in its voice and omens. There also go out from that same window praises, hymns, prayers, confessions, instructions, and many kinds of good words, which are best described by the most simple dove. And this bird brings back the sign of peace to the ark: because good words (says the Wise Man) 
<margin>The Wise Man, Psalms</margin> multiply friends—namely, divine, angelic, and human ones. And how pleasing praise is to Him, God declares in the psalm, saying: *The sacrifice of praise shall honor me: and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God* <note>original: Sacrificium laudis...; a quotation from Psalm 50:23.</note>—and peace, and union with Himself.

### The harmony of the members and the features with one another. Chapter IV.

<insert>A</insert>nd unless we feared being accused of too much curiosity (which, however, would only happen among the common folk), we would also approach the very features of the face and hands. All these things the most wise Architect does not allow to occur by chance in so elegant a body, but He forms the soul and the body with an accurate seal; and in the same way, He signs and imprints all things that belong to the body, so that by that craftsmanship through which [the harmony] of the body and soul...
