And since man is led by his own free will, prognosticators err for a second reason if they wish to predict morals and outcomes themselves beyond the mere disposition of nature.

<margin>Zopyrus</margin>
This was proven in the judgment of Zopyrus, a story that has now become common in schools and on street corners. From his appearance, Zopyrus judged Socrates not to be prone to vices (as is commonly said), but to the <term>Venereal work</term> <note>Sexual activity or procreation; named after Venus, the goddess of love.</note> necessary for propagation, and therefore he judged him to be stained by those vices which usually arise from a lack of self-control. <margin>Socrates</margin>

Hence we are compelled to admire and praise the most accurate diligence of the Creator, who brought together even the features and colors of this corruptible body with such great artistry and such a great mystery. Hence men of the weightiest judgment have devoted themselves to this kind of doctrine.

Nor is it without reason that <term>Plautus</term> in his comedies, and <term>Martial</term> in his description of the wicked Zoilus, describe pimps and criminals based on a flawed <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging character from facial characteristics.</note>. And that <term>Satirist of Aquino</term> <note>Juvenal, the Roman satirist born in Aquino.</note> says of the common woman: "She offered her forehead and her hand to the seer." But lest anyone believe this is contrary to due piety, let us bring forward <term>Job</term>, confirmed by the testimony of God, who says: "He places a seal in the hands of men, so that each may know his own works" <note>Job 37:7. The author interprets the "seal" or "signs" in the hand as a biblical endorsement of chiromancy or palmistry.</note>. Although our doctors <note>Theologians and Church Fathers.</note>, attending more to the instruction of the soul's character than to the secrets of nature and the Artisan, have interpreted this in a different sense. It is also a trivial matter among physicians to judge the <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four humors in the body.</note> and the properties of nature through colors. For an earthy color, brought about by cold and dryness, promises a nature of <term>black bile</term> <note>Melancholy; the humor associated with the planet Saturn.</note> and a Saturnian disposition. A bluish color, or one tending toward whiteness, signifies <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita".</note>. 

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
For cold (according to <term>Avicenna</term>) makes wet matter white and turns dry matter black. A reddish color, like thick air glowing from the sun's rays, indicates <term>blood</term>. But a fiery color, burning like a flame, indicates <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note>. Although choler possesses a very sharp active power that dominates others, it is nevertheless easily mixed with other biles because of its subtlety—especially with blood and black bile. Hence, if it is mixed with an abundance of blood, it flourishes with redness. If, however, the choler is in excess, it produces a yellowish-red. If they are mixed in equal parts, it produces a pure red. But if the choler is "burnt" <note>Adusta; a medical term for humors that have become overheated and toxic.</note> with blood, it produces <term>canopus</term> <note>A dark, reddish-brown or grayish-red complexion.</note>—ruddy if the blood predominates, and sub-ruddy if the choler prevails. If bile is mixed with black bile, it is tinged with blackness; if mixed equally with black bile and phlegm, the color will be *canopus*. If phlegm is in excess, it is a pale yellow; if black bile conquers, it is a bluish-gray. If it is mixed with phlegm in equal portions, the color will be lemon-yellow. If one or the other predominates, it is pale or somewhat pale. Hence we speak of red, lemon, egg-yolk, or black choler, and the like. A man's nature is also conjectured from his actions and operations. For a slow and solid movement signifies earthy black bile. Fear, sluggishness, and slack work signify phlegm. Alacrity and friendly manners signify blood. A sharp impulse and fiery force signify choler. Many things of this kind are passed down by those instructed in the craftsmanship of nature; but we have touched upon these few so that we might show in what order and with what correspondence the Supreme Artisan constructed this <term>tabernacle</term> <note>The human body.</note> and the "husk" of the true man dwelling within it. From this, we may be raised up to contemplate the harmony of that better man who exists within, and his relationship with the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The divine model or plan.</note>, just as the exterior figure corresponds with the interior man.

### That all things are included in man: a general discourse. Chapter V.

<margin>Moses</margin>
<insert>W</insert>ith what fullness and what harmony all things were concluded in this man by the Supreme Artisan, our <term>Moses</term> <note>The author refers to Moses as a "perfect philosopher," a common view in Renaissance thought which saw the Pentateuch as a source of secret natural philosophy.</note>, that most perfect philosopher, indicated with a single and mysterious word, saying: "The Lord God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face (or his nostrils) the breath of life." He touches upon both extremes of all things so that every intermediate thing contained between those extremes might also be understood as included in man. In his craftsmanship, the highest and the lowest are described as reconciled. For the lowest element, diminished below all others, is the element of earth.

Therefore, there is in man the corruptible, the heavenly, and the divine, or a life of every kind.

For man lives the life of elements and stones: to which the vigor of being, increasing, and changeability is continually supplied. He lives with the metals a higher life: which possess a certain most secret spirit, which is therefore either never or very rarely discovered by craftsmen, though it is sought with much diligence. He lives with the plants a **vegetative** life; with the animals a **motive** life; with the separated minds a **rational or intellectual** life; and with the true God a **divine and eternal** life, of which <term>John</term> says: *The life was the light of men* <note>John 1:4.</note>. ### Chapter VI.

<insert>M</insert>AN is the most perfect and absolute work of God, and indeed the Lord of all things. He contains those elements that come together for his own composition as if they were choice portions for a "seasoning" of perfection and a sweeter consonance, surpassing those found in the creatures subject to him. Hence the elements, and all other things composing man, look up to him as their head with a certain more sublime dignity. Therefore, even if a consonance of the elements is found in all coarser things, it is found in man to a much greater degree, inasmuch as he himself is gifted with a better life. For he is (as we have said) the only one of all living beings who partakes of celestial and divine life. Therefore, the elements and all other things in this supreme piece of craftsmanship perhaps pursue a certain supreme quality. 

It is no wonder then if, beyond the common consonance which the corporeal portions and qualities have with one another in other composite things, some other kind of proportioned modulation is perceived in the <term>complexion</term><note>In pre-modern medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of humors in an individual's body.</note> of this man—in his colors, shapes, and well-drawn features. This is more clearly discerned by wise and experienced men as being far more pleasing than any harmony of the voice drawn in by the ears and by those who judge well. 

And since we touched above on the proportion of the elements and their qualities, we will now pass over those and run through the proportions they maintain in a well-ordered man. To ensure he is well-composed, the weights of the complexions and <term>humors</term><note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> have been assigned as follows: eight parts for Blood, four for Phlegm, two for Yellow Bile, and one for Black Bile. Thus, there is a "double" proportion <note>A 2:1 ratio, which in music forms the octave.</note> everywhere: the first to the third is a quadruple proportion <note>4:1 ratio, a double octave.</note>, and to the last, an octuple proportion <note>8:1 ratio.</note>.

<margin>Pietro d'Abano, Alexander of Aphrodisias</margin>
However, <term>Pietro d'Abano</term><note>A 13th-century physician and philosopher who sought to reconcile Greek/Arabic medicine with Latin philosophy.</note>, imitating <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term><note>A highly influential commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note>, assigns these proportions differently: namely, a "triple-super-tripartient-fourth," a "double-super-bipartient-third," and a "sesquialtera." Such is the proportion of fifteen to four, or thirty to eight, and eight to three, and three to two. But I do not know by what reasoning he was supported in doing this, since the ancients and the most skilled in the harmonic craft never admitted (on the testimony of <term>Proculus</term><note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on math and music.</note>) that harmony could result from <term>superpartient</term><note>A complex mathematical ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part of it (e.g., 5:3); these were often rejected by strict Pythagoreans as "unmusical."</note> proportions. 

<margin>Hippocrates, Galen, Haly Abbas, Avicenna, Pythagoras</margin>
Indeed, the body and its humors are most consonant; if even one of them disagrees with their harmony, it distempers the whole body. We can learn this most fully from <term>Hippocrates</term>, <term>Galen</term>, and <term>Haly Abbas</term>, as well as <term>Avicenna</term>, if we wish to read what the first wrote in *On the Nature of Man*, the second in his *Precepts on Complexions*, and the last in his *Theoretical Precepts*. <term>Pythagoras</term> also taught that man is formed by the thickening and joining of the humors within forty days, but according to the ratio of harmony, the infant is born as a finished and perfect child within seven, nine, or (most often) ten months.

<margin>Augustine</margin>

### Chapter VII. What things in man correspond to the elements.

**W**ith the elements, beyond those portions of them that are in the body, the more vital parts of man (says <term>Augustine</term><note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian philosopher who integrated Neoplatonic thought with theology.</note>) agree; namely, the external senses. For the **Eye** (because it sees by means of light) corresponds to fire; and without fire and light it perceives nothing. The **Ears** agree with the air, in which sound echoes, or by the striking of which sound is produced. **Smell** and **Taste**, however, correspond with water, in which flavor and odor reside. But smell is found in those moist exhalations with which this space is thickened, through which the birds fly; taste, truly, is found in those flowing and more corpulent humors. **Touch**, however, takes to itself the earth and coarser matter. <margin>Francis of Meyronnes</margin> From which the "very sharp" <term>Francis</term><note>Francis of Meyronnes (c. 1285–1328), a Scholastic theologian known as the "Doctor Acutus" (the Acute Doctor).</note>, deviating somewhat, says that Augustine spoke according to the minds of others regarding the watery object of taste itself. Nevertheless, proceeding further, Augustine gives the reason why taste corresponds to water: for he says: whatever things are tasted in the mouth are mixed with the humor of the mouth itself so that they may be tasted, even if they seemed to have been dry when they were taken in. Yet all these senses perceive by a certain **fiery power** <note>original: "ui quadam ignea"</note> by which the soul, which possesses the power of sensing, initiates movement in all the senses, though not in the same order. In sight, the heat is repressed even unto its light; in hearing, the fire penetrates by its heat as far as the clearer air; in smell, it passes through pure air reaching as far as the moist exhalation, where this thicker air subsists; but in taste, it passes and reaches as far as the corpulent humor; and even having penetrated and passed through this, when it reaches earthy gravity, it acts upon touch, the final sense.

### Chapter VIII. With what things from the composites do stones correspond.

<margin>Albertus, Avicenna</margin>

**A**fter the first elements, from which all things are composed, the mixtures follow; which, although they are mixed from all elements, nevertheless each one imitates the nature of some particular one. For **stones** possess an earthy property; although <term>Albertus</term><note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note>, supported by the testimony of <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician and philosopher whose work "The Canon of Medicine" was a standard text in Europe.</note>, attributed to them something of the watery, by which they might be composed and glued together, lest a prevailing dryness not permit them to be coagulated; nevertheless, the earthy force prevails. And since the members and parts of man follow the order of the mundane body <note>The macrocosm or the universe.</note>, **bones** possess the place of stones in man. <margin>Empedocles</margin> For even the stones themselves were called the "bones of the mundane body" by <term>Empedocles</term><note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the four-element theory.</note>; whom the <term>Poet</term><note>Ovid, in his *Metamorphoses*.</note> emulates, singing:
> The earth is the great mother; the stones in the body of the earth
> I believe are called bones; we are commanded to cast these behind our backs.
<note>original: "Magna parens terra est, lapides in corpore terræ: / Ossa reor dici / iacere hos post terga iubemur." This refers to the myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha, who repopulated the earth by throwing stones—the "bones" of Mother Earth—behind them.</note>
These stones also live in this mundane body, just as bones do in the human; whence some of the ancients even said that souls were present in stones: because they could put venom to flight, drive away phantoms, attract iron and straw, provide strength and audacity, and perform other things of that kind; which things look more toward life than toward mere qualities. <margin>Albertus</margin> Nevertheless, Albertus objects, since (in his judgment) the first work of the soul is to be "living," and also because stones lack porosity—through which life is penetrative—and because the soul performs many works, whereas stones have only one effect. But these reasons conclude regarding a "superior" life, but by no means regarding an "inferior" one. For the minds of the Angels live by one grade of life; [man lives by another...]

in one way humans, in another plants, in another metals, and in another stones. <margin>Albert</margin>
**H**umors follow next, which although they imitate the different natures of the elements, are nevertheless all watery; just as metals also possess a common watery nature. Yet each humor has a power corresponding to some element and some planet; in these, a more potent life resides than in bones and stones. Thus, humors are generated and dwell in the human body just as metals do in the earth, as if in the viscera of the world's body. Hence <term>Hermes Euates</term><note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many hermetic and alchemical texts were attributed; "Euates" may be a corruption of a title or name.</note>, the king of the Arabs, calls the earth herself the mother of metals, which are carried as if in a womb. They are nourished (as <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer.</note> pleases) from the concourse of the rays of all the stars, or (if we follow physical reasons with <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian polymath and physician.</note>) through a mineral power, or through a common force—as the same Hermes was of the opinion. This force, transcending physical boundaries, he located in Mars. Or they are generated by a parching heat, as <term>Empedocles</term><note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the four-element theory.</note> maintained; or by a fiery heat existing in mountains, as <term>Abubacher</term><note>Likely referring to Al-Razi (Rhazes), the Persian physician and alchemist.</note> asserts; or by the natural formative power of the stone, as <term>Albert</term><note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the medieval scholar who wrote extensively on minerals and nature.</note> holds. In the production of humors, there also intervenes the movement of the stars, the generative power, the presiding force of some planet, the natural heat by which they are cooked and purified, and their particular form. There is in metals (as we said) an imperfect life; there is also life in the humors, by which they are united with the whole body; and, preserved from rot, they serve the various operations of the body itself. The vigor of life resides more in bile and in blood: in the latter, so that the same life may be carried through it to all parts of the body; in the former, so that it may operate more vivaciously. And some have even believed that life is so inherent in the blood that they judged the blood to be the very seat of life; just as the sacred scriptures teach, with Moses speaking in the place of God:

->### CHAPTER X.###<-
->### Concerning how certain mixed minerals harmonize with these things through a wondrous artifice.###<-

Beyond the humors are their intestinal vessels, which hold the middle place between the bones and the flesh. This place in the great world <note>The macrocosm or the physical universe.</note> is possessed by <margin>Albertus</margin> marcasite <note>A mineral often identified as iron pyrite or "fool's gold," considered a "middle" substance in medieval alchemy.</note> and alum <note>A mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine, known for its astringent or "biting" properties.</note>, which (as <term>Albert</term><note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval science and philosophy who wrote extensively on minerals.</note> teaches) are intermediate between stones and metals. The intestines are also harder than flesh, but softer than bones; they feel and live less than flesh, but more than bones. Whence they are proven to be the middle between both. However, they are more subject to corruption than flesh because of the corrupting matter <note>Feces or waste products.</note> which they contain. 

But in the "better man," <note>The spiritual or interior person.</note> the vessels of the humors—that is, the vessels of the true spiritual influences—are the natural powers and strengths that receive them: namely, the <term>intellectual power</term>, the will, the <term>irascible faculty</term>, and the <term>concupiscible faculty</term> <note>These are standard medieval categories of the soul: the "irascible" deals with anger and courage, while the "concupiscible" deals with desire.</note>. All of these receive the illuminating and inflaming influences which lead to work through love or by command. These hold the middle place between the natural life and the divine virtues by which we are made like God Himself, just as those minerals exist between stones and metals, and the intestines between flesh and bones. 

But these powers are subject to corruption and to such great perversion that they are even said to be "taken away," just as it is written mystically in the book of Maccabees: that Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who desecrated the Temple in Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 1).</note> carried away from the great temple of God not only gold, silver, and all precious stones, but also the golden altar, the lampstand of light, and all the vessels. And what is understood by the golden altar carried away by Antiochus (who figures as the devil and sin), if not the will, in which golden charity resides? And what by the lampstand of light, if not the intellect, in which all light of the interior man shines, both natural and divine? 

By the other "vessels," the other receiving and operating powers are understood. Expressing these more particularly, the text adds: that he also took away the <gloss>mortariola</gloss> <note>Small mortars or grinding bowls.</note> and the vessels of desire. Of these, without any veil, the "vessels of desire" indicate the concupiscible power. Truly the mortars, with which hard things are crushed, suggest the irascible power; for when a man is angry against vices and his own sinning self, he grinds down hard affections, hard works, and crooked ways into dust. This is what alum and similar things achieve, being "biting" and corroding away superfluous and contaminated flesh—which signify bad actions and corrupt fruits. ->Chapter XI.<-

### With which things plants grow green and are invigorated.

<margin>Galen, Avicenna, Albertus, Aristotle, David</margin>
**A**fter metals, the primary kind of thing is plants. Their power in flesh and blood, along with the vital spirits <term>vital spirits: "spiritus vitalis," in medieval medicine, the subtle substance that carries life and motion through the body</term> passing through them, is clearly enough seen in this small world <note>The microcosm, or the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note>. For a plant is a vegetative nature of itself (by means of the vital spirit), nourishing and growing. There is also in the flesh a vegetative power providing manifest nourishment and growth; in both, what is lost is very easily repaired. For a cut plant sprouts again, even the somewhat hard bark; so too dried-out flesh and skin grow again, though often both skin in the flesh and bark in the plant remain with an eternal scar <note>Original: "uibice," referring to a mark or welt left by a wound.</note>. And both live by a certain most secret spirit; but by this the plant grows and produces various effects in those eating its leaves, fruit, or root. Flesh, however, not only grows but is moved by a manifold motion—by expanding, contracting, and moving from place to place—according to the diversity of the muscles existing within it. And if flesh does not grow in those who are already adults and have reached the limit of their growth, it is nevertheless continually nourished, as Galen, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, and others discuss at length.

Therefore, the powers of plants are present in man—not only those of the earthly ones, but also of the lofty ones. Concerning earthly plants, the master of the senses, Aristotle, speaking in his discourse *On the Soul*, says that man is an inverted tree <term>inverted tree: "arbor inversa," a classic philosophical metaphor where the brain/head is the root (drawing celestial nourishment) and the limbs are branches</term>, extending the hairs of his head like roots into the upper part; and existing in the heights, he takes nourishment through his mouth, just as a plant extends its roots into the earth and downward, and is nourished from below. And concerning the celestial trees, the celestial teacher <note>Referring to King David, traditionally the author of the Psalms.</note>, after he sang of celestial bread, wine, and oil, adds: "The trees of the Lord [Adonai] shall be filled," for which we have "the trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted." For he plants these trees, of whom it is said: "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up." 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
<margin>Moses</margin>
Moses wrote of this planting before, saying: "The Lord God planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning," which in Hebrew is <note>Original Hebrew: מקדם (Mi-qedem), which can mean "from the east" or "from ancient times/the beginning."</note> *michedem*. And if the force and mystery of this word is well weighed, *Chedem* will be seen to signify the Father, who is the beginning, source, and root of all plants. 

<margin>Song of Solomon, Psalms</margin>
Man was therefore planted in the garden of pleasure by his roots—his hair—of which it is said in the Song of Songs: "The hair of your head is like the king's purple bound in the channels" <note>Referring to Song of Solomon 7:5. The author interprets the "channels" (canales) as conduits for divine grace.</note>; namely, those celestial ones, through which flow all spiritual gifts <term>charismata: spiritual gifts or divine graces</term> from the fountain of all good things. And trees of this kind, planted beside the run-offs of waters, give their fruit in its season; and their leaf shall not fall away; and all things whatsoever they do shall prosper. For then the tree is good. If, however, it is separated from those celestial channels and fixes its roots in earthly and inferior things, then it is a bad tree, of which the Supreme Truth <note>Jesus Christ.</note> says: "A bad tree cannot produce good fruit," just as a good tree does not return bad fruit...

### That the animal conditions live in man is evident to all. Chapter XII.

**W**hatever qualities belong to animals, if they are contained within man—since they are manifest—we shall run through them more briefly than the subject might otherwise require. For man feels, moves, imagines, fears, grieves, desires, hates, eats, digests, expels waste, urinates, sleeps, sighs, cries out, howls, sings, chatters, walks, dances, swims, carries burdens, pulls, and feeds on the most diverse foods: herbs, fruits, meat, fish, roots, bread, wine, and water. Furthermore, he adopts all kinds of behaviors and produces the various effects of the most diverse animals. Hence, he seems to contain their natures either by power (as the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who famously walked about while teaching</term> say) <margin>Peripatetics, Aristotle</margin> or by virtue (as the more recent thinkers assert). Therefore, Aristotle, in his work *On Physiognomy*, judges the characters of men based on the similarity of their shapes and body parts to those of animals. And sometimes man imitates beasts to such an extent that <margin>Numenius, Harpocratius, Boethius, Plotinus, Empedocles, Pythagoras, Hermias, Syrianus, Proclus, Moses</margin> Numenius the Pythagorean, Harpocratius, Boethius, Plotinus, Empedocles, and before them Pythagoras, said that for the expiation of the soul, once the human garment is laid aside, it assumes the clothing of a beast whose behavior it had most closely mirrored. Or, as Hermias, Syrianus, and Proclus more politely put it, the soul becomes a "companion" to wild beasts. Though some think Pythagoras or even older figures were the authors of this idea of transformation or naming, our Moses (unless I am mistaken) and the writers of Holy Scripture were the true sources, whose monuments are the most ancient of all. For Moses writes of Lot’s wife being turned into a pillar of salt, and of Enoch being changed not into a beast but into something better: namely, into an Angel, or into God himself. Daniel describes Nebuchadnezzar turned into a beast, eating grass like an ox. Jeremiah, because of their cruelty, likens his people to ostriches <note>original: "structionibus," referring to the perceived cruelty of ostriches who were thought to abandon their eggs.</note>, and many such examples are found in the Prophets and in Solomon. <margin>CHRIST</margin> But Christ, the preeminent teacher of all, calls the greedy and bloodthirsty "wolves," saying: *But inwardly they are ravening wolves.* And he names Judas, insolent in his wickedness, a "devil" when he says: *Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?* And Pythagoras (as we said) received this from Moses; although Apuleius of Madaura asserts that Pythagoras himself was also imbued with these ideas by Zoroaster <margin>Apuleius, Zoroaster</margin>, the son of Oromasius and king of the Bactrians, who says in his oracles: *For the beasts of the earth shall inhabit your vessel* <note>original Greek: "σὸν γὰρ ἀγγεῖον θῆρες χθονὸς οἰκήσουσιν."</note>. That is, the beasts of the earth inhabit your vessel—meaning the powers of beasts are in your body—and it is not merely worms that shall eat your vessel, as Gemistus <margin>Gemistus</margin> <note>Gemistus Pletho, a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> explains. And if Pythagoras, as a diligent seeker of all teachings, was in some <margin>Archytas</margin> part taught by Zoroaster, nevertheless, setting aside all error, he learned much more from those who sucked at the divine breasts <note>A metaphor for the Hebrew prophets.</note>. And from him later Archytas...

### What the ancients thought about the transmigration of the human soul into beasts, and what the truth of the matter is. Chapter XIII.

**S**uch metamorphoses <note>original: *Metamorphoses*; here meaning the transformation of a human into an animal.</note> from the mind of Pythagoras and Plato are well-known even to boys in schools. But he received the idea of the transmigration of souls into beasts not as something he devised himself, but from the Egyptian priests—concocted, as they say, for the purification of souls. It was then sung in the poems of Orpheus, Empedocles, and Heraclitus. Those who judged rightly, however, and followed the true sentiment of Plato, utterly rejected the transmigration of the human soul into beasts. This was done by Iamblichus and Porphyry <note>Influential Neoplatonist philosophers who argued for a more allegorical interpretation of reincarnation.</note>, who do not allow the soul to be torn away from the center in which it is once fixed. Furthermore, Proclus, Hermias, and Syrianus considered it a horrendous crime for a celestial soul to be cast down into beasts: because the human body receives no other soul than a human one, nor does a human soul incline toward anything other than a human body. Nor is it right, they say, for a rational soul to fall into the body of a creature lacking reason, as divine law prohibits such a wicked generation. 

Hence Porphyry and Iamblichus, having refuted this error, conclude that a man depraved in 그의 morals should by no means be called an ass, but "ass-like," nor a lion, but "lion-like." ...rightly inflicted, namely that wicked souls should enter the fearful tents of women; and finally, given over to outrages, they are afflicted by entering the bodies of fierce beasts, bloodied with human gore. The souls of the lewd take on the forms of pigs or boars; those chasing light and lofty things take the shape of birds seeking the heights of the air; while the sluggish and idle take the form of aquatic creatures. Fate has assigned all these things for a second birth. Thus far Timaeus <note>Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean philosopher and a central character in Plato's dialogues, here credited with the theory that souls are reborn into bodies suited to their previous conduct.</note>.

Regarding these transmigrations, when understood sanely, these wise men held the correct opinion—indeed, they faithfully recounted what they had received from divine and prophetic teaching. In those teachings, they show such transformations without any veils: "In an image," says David, "man passes by" <note>Psalm 39:6 (Vulgate 38:7); original: *In imagine pertransit homo*. The author argues that "passing through an image" refers to the changing moral state of a person.</note>. 

<margin>Psalm.</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
Concerning the transition of the body for the better, the Apostle says when dealing with the Philippians: "We look for the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility, shaped to the body of his glory" <note>Philippians 3:20-21; original: *reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ*.</note>. Regarding the transmigration of the soul, he says writing to the Corinthians: "We are transformed into that same image" <note>2 Corinthians 3:18</note>, which is surely the Son of God; for power is given to us to become children of God. 

And concerning the transition into a worse condition, the Royal Prophet [David] sings again: "Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the foolish beasts and became like them" <note>Psalm 49:12 (Vulgate 48:13); original: *comparatus est iumentis insipientibus*.</note>—not indeed by nature, but by morals and habit. 

<margin>Psalm.</margin>
<margin>Pytha.</margin>
<margin>Plato</margin>
<margin>Boetius</margin>
With this view Pythagoras, Plato, and all their followers who judge correctly agree. Gathering their teachings scattered here and there about those changed for the worse, Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a Roman philosopher whose *Consolation of Philosophy* famously describes vices as animal transformations.</note>, their most faithful interpreter, says: "It happens, therefore, that when you see someone transformed by vices, you cannot consider him a man." 

Avarice boils, a violent robber of others' wealth; you would call him like a wolf. Fierce and restless in disputes, he exercises his tongue; he is comparable to a dog. The hidden schemer rejoices to have stolen by fraud; he is equal to little foxes. Intemperate in anger, he roars; let him be believed to carry the soul of a lion. The fearful one, who dreads things not to be feared, should be held as like a deer. The sluggish and stupid one is numb; he lives as a donkey. The light and inconstant one changes his pursuits; he differs not at all from birds. He is submerged in foul and filthy lusts; he is held by the dirty pleasure of a pig. Thus it happens that whoever deserts uprightness ceases to be a human; and since, enslaved to vices, he cannot pass into the divine condition, he is turned into a beast. 

Thus far Boethius, following Timaeus of Locri and other Pythagoreans. Therefore, this transformation occurs according to dispositions, habits, morals, and actions; by these, the nature of a thing is discerned no less than by its form and appearance. For I recognize an apple from a pear, and a peach from an almond tree more clearly by the fruit than by the trunk. Nor do I distinguish a wolf from a dog, or a donkey or mule from a horse, any less by their voice than by their skin. I also distinguish the Sun from the Moon more by light and color than by shape. 

Souls are said to "exit from the beasts" when they have overcome those animal dispositions, as Thespion <note>Thespion, described as a leader of the Gymnosophists (ancient Indian "naked philosophers"), appearing in the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.</note>, leader of the Gymnosophists, beautifully said when debating with Apollonius: "If you make your choice according to the judgment of Hercules, never despising frugality and embracing that parsimony which is according to nature, you will be said to have overcome many lions, and to have slain many hydras, and to have conquered the Geryons and Nessuses..."

<summary>This page argues that the Pythagorean doctrine of transmigration is actually a moral allegory, where humans "become" animals by succumbing to specific vices. The author supports this by citing both classical philosophers like Boethius and Timaeus, and biblical figures like King David and the Apostle Paul.</summary>

### What external writers have set down concerning particular transformations in wondrous harmony with our own teachings. Chapter XIV.

<margin>Heraclitus, the Chaldeans, Euantes, Aristotle, Plotinus, the Psalmist, Paul, Pythagoras, Malachi</margin>
**W**e have concordant witnesses to this transmigration <note>The author uses "transmigration" here to refer to both the soul's moral evolution and the ancient idea of reincarnation.</note> from every side. For Heraclitus said that the soul travels its path by a necessary succession from the highest to the lowest, and conversely, from the lowest to the highest. This confirms that celebrated opinion among the Chaldeans <note>Refers to ancient Babylonian or Neo-Platonic oracles often cited by Renaissance philosophers.</note> of which Euantes writes: namely, that man is an animal of a dissolvable nature, having no image of his own, but rather very many foreign and accidental ones. For both Aristotle in his *Ethics* and Plotinus in his book *On the Virtues* assert that man is transformed into a supreme and divine nature through the excellence of virtue. The whole crowd of poets follows them, singing of men being made into Gods. Our own David, eminent among the prophets, also sings: "I said, you are Gods" <note>original: *Ego dixi Dii estis*; Psalm 82:6.</note>. And Paul, discoursing with the Ephesians <note>The author attributes this to Ephesians, though it is a paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 6:17.</note>, says: "He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him." Pythagoras, half-theologian and half-philosopher, intercedes, saying: "If, having laid aside the body, you ascend to the ether, you shall be an immortal God." And Malachi clearly testifies that John was turned into an Angel, introducing God as saying: "Behold, I send my Angel before your face" <note>original: *Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum ante faciem tuam*; Malachi 3:1. The word for "messenger" in Hebrew and Greek is the same as "angel."</note>. The ancients used to call these Angels "Gods." The pagans themselves report that many were raised to this rank, and they even fell into such madness that they adored such men as Gods with a higher honor than that with which we venerate our own, whom we call "saints"—that is, those confirmed in union with God. For we only ask these to be intercessors with God, to whom they are united; but those [pagans] worshiped them as if they were Gods themselves.

<margin>Heraclitus, Empedocles, Ovid, Virgil, The Gospel, John the Baptist, Likewise Moses</margin>
However, far more fall toward the worse part; because (as Heraclitus adds) since it requires no small labor to live forever in the heavenly seats, to grow weary, and to converse with the Gods and be continually subject to them, he asserts that the soul easily falls to lower things—partly enticed by a desire for rest, and partly raised up by the hope of ruling. Having been cast down into these, it is sometimes (as Empedocles says) changed into a plant, just as Ovid sings of Daphne being turned into a laurel tree. The poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid* Book III.</note> also describes the soul of Polydorus crying out from a tree trunk. From Aristotle, but more clearly from the Gospel, we can learn in many places that men are called trees—sometimes good, sometimes bad. The good ones (as we touched upon before) are said to be planted in God’s little garden; but the bad ones in this lowly earth are indeed sterile and fruitless, awaiting the cutting down so that they may be cast into the fire to be burned. Concerning these, the Baptist cries out: "Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree" <note>original: *Iam securis ad radicem arboris posita est*; Matthew 3:10.</note>. And sometimes even the wicked are said to be changed into stones, as the same Baptist says: "God is able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones" <note>original: *Potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahæ*; Matthew 3:9.</note>. Moses also recounts that Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt. For he who is devoted only to nutrition and is sluggish by day and night, lives as a plant; but one who is hardened...

...if you never receive the word of God or the supernal gifts <note>original: "superna charismata"; these are divine graces or spiritual gifts believed to descend from heaven to soften the hardened heart.</note> to soften you, you are deservedly called a stone. Indeed, that woman <note>A reference to Lot's wife (Genesis 19), who was turned into a pillar of salt.</note> is described as having been turned into salt, who was given as an example and a seasoning <note>A play on the word "salt" as both a punishment and a "seasoning" or lesson for the faithful.</note> for those who obey. Almost countless authors on both sides agree that men are also changed into animals. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle writes in his *Politics* that a man depraved in his morals is not only changed into a beast, but becomes even worse than one. <margin>Plotinus</margin> Plotinus, in his discussion regarding the "proper daemon" <note>In Neo-Platonic thought, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or the highest level of one's own soul.</note> concerning the transformation into animals and plants, says: Whoever has preserved their human character is born again as a human. But whoever has lived by the senses alone returns as a brute animal; however, those who lived primarily by the senses but also with spirit will emerge as wild animals. Whoever uses the senses for the sake of lust and pleasure will return as lecherous and gluttonous animals. Truly, if they lived not so much by the senses as by a degeneration of the senses, they sprout again as plants; for in such people, only the vital power was vigorous, and their whole care was such that they might be changed into plants. But those who lived too much soothed by musical measures, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they were infected by some other wickedness. But he who has attained civic virtue returns as a human. Thus far Plotinus in that place, but in the work he published *On Providence*, he adds this: The "seed-reason" <note>original: "Ratio seminaria"; a Stoic and Neo-Platonic concept of the formative spiritual blueprints that govern the growth of specific living things.</note> of an ox is in no other matter than that of an ox; similarly, the seed-reason of a man exists in a human subject and is neither diminished nor increased from what nature granted from the beginning. It is not diminished according to the subject or the specific reason, but people are changed according to their affections. With this, all the Pythagoreans and Academics <note>Followers of Pythagoras and the school of Plato.</note> agree. <margin>Pythagoras, Academics, Sacred Scripture: Peter, Isaiah, Solomon</margin> But we find these same things written in many places in the sacred word, beyond those which were brought forward above. For the Apostle <note>Likely referring to 2 Peter 2:12.</note> says to those who are poorly initiated: "Like mute animals, you went as you were led." And the Lord, execrating the darkened and ungrateful people through Isaiah, says: "The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me" <note>Isaiah 1:3</note>—having been made worse, as it were, than the beasts. And in the proverbs of Solomon, he calls a man now a lion, a tiger, a bear, or a boar; now a hare, a greyhound, or a rabbit; now an ant, a hedgehog, a serpent, or a spider; now he names him an eagle, a lizard, a rooster, or some other bird. Discussing many such things in metaphors, he describes the characters of men through the beasts which they resemble. But lest we exceed our limits by explaining all the passages of external writers and sacred scripture of this kind, we shall bring forward what Moses summarized and perfectly concluded under the type <margin>Moses</margin> of the ark, which Noah is said to have built by the command of God with the highest mystery.

Moses describes everything contained in man through a sacred artifice in the Ark of Noah.

With a great figure and mystery, God said: **The end of all flesh has come before me, because the earth is filled with iniquity, or with robberies:** as the Hebrew truth has it. For man had seized the lots of lower things, whereby he had fallen from his own state. For his restoration, therefore, the supreme High Priest <note>A reference to God as the ultimate spiritual authority and architect of the soul's return.</note> said to him, who alone was found righteous in his generations: **Make for yourself an ark of planed woods:** for which in Hebrew it is given as woods of <gloss>גפר i.e., gopher</gloss> <note>original: "gopher"</note>, which signifies cypress, as <margin>Jerome</margin> it pleases some, and according to others, a pine dripping with pitch. Hence Jerome, in his commentary on Genesis, says: In place of "squared" or "planed," in the Hebrew we read "bituminized" <note>Meaning sealed with bitumen or pitch for waterproofing and preservation.</note>. 

<margin>Augustine; The Hebrews</margin> In which ark Augustine, the Hebrew sages, and all who judge rightly, believe that man is described in all his parts. Since we have already explained the divisions of this ark and of man a little earlier, let us come to those things which are contained within it, and consequently within man, to whom it is said: **Enter into the ark, you and all your household.** For a man ought to enter into himself if he wishes to provide for his salvation, just as it was said to Abraham: **Go to yourself,** <note>original: "Vade ad te"; this is a mystical reading of the command usually translated as "Go forth."</note> for which we have, **go out from your land.** 

And in the Gospel <margin>John</margin> of John it is said: **The disciples went away again to themselves,** namely, after knowing that Jesus was raised up. For they had withdrawn from themselves through the unbelief contracted from his death and passion. So also regarding that wayward <margin>Ambrose</margin> youth <note>The Prodigal Son (Luke 15).</note> who had gone away into a far-off country, Ambrose says: What is it to go further away, if not to go outside of oneself? Man therefore enters into himself when <margin>CHRIST</margin> he returns to the heart; gathered in that chamber, and with the door closed (according to the Savior's command), he prays to the Father, unhindered and prepared. 

He is also commanded to enter with his children and all his household; explaining this, He says: **Your wife, and your sons, and your sons' wives with you.** The sacrament of marriage is celebrated greatly in sacred scripture, and the kingdom of heaven is compared to it. Nor did Christ wish to reveal any sacrament to the Samaritan woman until her husband had been summoned: **Go,** He said, **and call your husband.** And to the husband the Wise Man says: **Enjoy life with the wife whom you love:** who should not be barren, but like a fruitful vine, producing appropriate fruits, of which it is said: **Produce worthy fruits of repentance, and the kingdom of heaven will draw near to you.** 

Perhaps <margin>Hermes Trismegistus; CHRIST; Revelation</margin> in this sense, Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure whom Renaissance scholars often viewed as a pagan prophet of Christian truths.</note> taught that one should beware of a man who has neither wife nor son. Hence also Christ, the leader and teacher of all, no less by deeds than by words, took a wife <note>In Christian theology, the Church is the "Bride of Christ."</note> by whom He fathered us all; and of whom it is said in the Apocalypse: **And his wife has made herself ready.** 

But what wife she may be, whom we ought to lead into the ark, is sufficiently expressed in the name of Noah's wife—if those things are true which are found in the records of the Scythians and Chaldeans—namely, that she was called Great Tythea, and Aretia, that is, <gloss>Earth</gloss>, which the Hebrews call <gloss>ארץ erez</gloss> and the Chaldeans call <gloss>ארעא arha</gloss>. With which earth, as if with the mother of all, our spirit and mind, being united, make us fruitful. Hence to man, as soon as he was brought forth with his wife, the divine oracle commands, saying: **Be fruitful and multiply,**

...and fill the earth, and subdue it, namely our animal nature <note>The author uses the Latin "animal vȝ" (animalitas) to refer to the lower, instinctual soul that focuses on physical survival, as opposed to the higher spiritual mind.</note>: once it has been reduced to servitude, we are made worthy to cling to that wife who descends from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband. The scripture continues by enumerating the sons whom a man ought to lead into the inner chambers of his mind: their names are Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The name Shem signifies that by which a thing is expressed and named, denoting that our fruits ought to be expressed, named, and known by God; for He calls all things by their names and counts the very hairs of the head. Following him is Ham, which the Hebrews write as <term>חם</term> <note>original: "Cham" (Ham), meaning heat or warmth.</note> and signifies "heat": with which our works ought to glow, so that they are not lukewarm or cold, but hot and fervent. And because works should not be presented to the Supreme Beauty unless they are themselves beautiful, the name of the third son is called Japheth, which is interpreted as "dilated" or "beautiful."

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
Our works are also said to be "married," because they must be joined with divine virtue—which they call "Grace" or "Charity" in common speech. Without this, our work is weak and useless, as the celestial Bridegroom says: 
> Without me you can do nothing. 
So too, our works cannot be perfected without his grace. Hence Isaiah says: 
> From your face, O Lord, we have conceived. <note>A reference to Isaiah 26:18, interpreted here as the soul conceiving spiritual fruit through God's presence.</note>

Thus the animals—meaning all the powers of the animal soul—are said to be brought into the ark under the command of Noah, namely the man ruling peacefully and resting in the ark of his own mind. This happens when, having subjugated the passions, the man knows how to tighten and loosen the reins according to necessity, just as the Poet <note>Virgil</note>, emulating Moses, sings of Aeolus <note>In the Aeneid, King Aeolus controls the winds in a cave, a common allegory for the intellect controlling the "winds" of passion.</note>.

<margin>Virgil</margin>
Furthermore, reason—or that higher portion, the intellect, to speak in the Platonic manner—is like a presiding priest in the entire human household, presiding over all things. There are also the powers of the beasts which must be ruled by the intellect or mind—namely, by the man who has already attained "mind" <note>Here "mind" (mens) refers to the highest intuitive faculty of the soul.</note>, of whom the sacred words intend to speak. But as to what these powers of the beasts are, Moses expresses it in a threefold way, saying: 
> From all the living things of all flesh, you shall bring with you into the ark, male and female: of the birds according to their kind, of the cattle in their kind, and from every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind. 
For a man "creeps" with the vegetative power along with the reptiles, which always crawl upon the earth; he "walks" with the animals through the estimative, imaginative, and cogitative powers <note>These are technical terms from medieval psychology describing how the brain processes sensory data and basic judgments.</note>; and he "flies" with the birds through the speculative and contemplative powers.

A man serves the first of these in his earliest age; the middle ones in his youth; and the last when he is already advanced in years and has attained that "mind" which (on the authority of Aristotle and proven by practice) arrives late in life. So it is also in the worldly animal...

There are, however, openings and pores in the human Ark, which the most wise Craftsman arranged for the purging of nature and for other necessities.

...takes its origin: For this reason, the ministers of the Gods (says **Alcinous**) established the <term>irascible part</term> <note>The "spirited" part of the soul associated with anger and courage.</note> in the heart, and the <term>concupiscible part</term> <note>The part of the soul associated with physical desires and lust.</note> in the place between the navel and the kidneys. They bound the latter there like a wild beast tied with a silver chain, so that **Free Will**, which is itself located in the heart, might moderate it and direct it at its pleasure. It keeps this part bound and imprisoned so that it can do nothing except what the "True Noah" <note>Here, Noah represents the rational mind or the soul's governing principle.</note> permits. And unless we moderated the impulses of both these "beasts" with these reins, they would rapidly carry everything away with them into the abyss. It is fitting that these impure affections are designated by the <term>binary</term> <note>The number two.</note>, a number which **Jerome** (discussing the matter *Against Jovinian*) says is unlucky and evil. 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
It pertains to "matter," which is the fount and origin of all evils. For this reason, on the **Second Day** of creation—and not without cause—that delightful phrase was omitted: *And God saw that it was good.* <note>In the Book of Genesis, the phrase "it was good" appears after every day of creation except the second, a point of much mystical speculation.</note> Hence also the "male and female" are said to be introduced <note>Referring to the pairs of impure animals entering the Ark in Genesis 7:2.</note> because in both parts of man there flourish those impure forces by which all things are propagated. In the "lower man," these are said to be infected by their material nature; in the "higher man," however, they are infected through their mingling with the lower. 

Yet the **Architect** <note>God.</note> acted with exceeding kindness toward us by implanting in us two of these impure affections that must be purified, but seven that are pure. This is because the pure are more numerous and are contained within a most celebrated number, which **Augustine** says implies the whole and the universe. 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
This is because it is composed of the "total odd" number, namely **three**, and the "total and first even" number, **four**. Or it is composed of the first masculine number and the first feminine number <note>In Pythagorean numerology, 3 is the first masculine and 4 (or 2) the feminine; here the author follows a tradition where 3 and 4 combine to make 7.</note>, which, when multiplied, yield **twelve**—a number truly divine and heavenly, as **Proclus** says. 
<margin>Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note></margin>
By this number twelve, the heavens, the signs of the zodiac, the presiding intelligences, the revolution of the **Great Name**, and many other things are partitioned (as we shall say shortly). Moreover, just as those parts yield twelve when multiplied, so when combined they constitute **seven**. This is the number by which purifications are distributed. Not without mystery did those ancient fathers ordain many things through this "septenary" for the purging of sins—namely, a seven-year penance for any sin, according to the sentiment of the **Wise Man** <note>Solomon.</note>, where it is said: *And sevenfold upon the sinner.* 
<margin>Solomon</margin>
The leper who was to be cleansed was also sprinkled seven times with the blood of a sparrow. Likewise, **Naaman the Syrian** was ordered by **Elisha** to wash seven times in the Jordan—a river whose name is interpreted as "judgment." 
<margin>Elisha</margin>
Remissions of debts were also made in the seventh year, and in the seventh month of every year, as the theology of the Hebrews teaches. And after a "square of seven" <note>7 x 7 = 49 years, leading into the 50th year, the Jubilee.</note>, a full remission was granted, as we read in **Leviticus**. 
<margin>Leviticus</margin>
With seven petitions, the **Heavenly Doctor** <note>Jesus Christ.</note> also completed the prayer ordained for our expiation <note>The Lord's Prayer (Our Father).</note>. By this same septenary, the words of the Lord are also purified (says the **Prophet**) like silver from the earth. 
<margin>David</margin>
And if we wish to climb higher and search for the fount and origin of remission, we shall find it in the "seventh place," or in the dwelling of the **Supreme Archetype**. There, having been purified through that very septenary, we may celebrate with a joyful soul the **True Sabbath**, which is granted in this sevenfold number. Hence, among the Hebrews, the names for "seven" and "Sabbath" are... <note>The text likely continues to explain that the Hebrew words for "seven" (sheva) and "Sabbath" (Shabbat) share a linguistic root or spiritual connection.</note>

### That all the heavens are also contained in man. Chapter 17.

<margin>David, Ptolemy</margin>
**P**ost after we have demonstrated that the first <term>Ennead</term> <note>original: "enneadem." A group or set of nine. In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the hierarchical structure of reality.</note> is concluded in man, we must declare that the second is also contained in him—namely, the heavens—which agree so closely with man that men are sometimes called "heavens." As **David** says: *The heavens declare the glory of God.* <note>Psalm 19:1. The author notes that theologians often interpret "the heavens" here as the Apostles who spread divine light.</note> Indeed, everyone thinks this should be interpreted as referring to the Apostles and preachers. For if the doctrine of **Ptolemy** is true—that the aspects of this terrestrial world are subject to the celestial countenances, so that the earthly Scorpion is under the celestial Scorpion, and the Bull or Ram living here is under the celestial images—how much more so does man, who is the "whole world" <note>The concept of the "Microcosm."</note>, agree with all aspects of the heavens? He does so to such an extent that he receives and contains all the powers of the heavens themselves and the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>Spiritual or angelic beings believed to govern the planets.</note> presiding over them.

<margin>Trismegistus</margin>
Wherefore **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings on magic, alchemy, and philosophy.</note> says: *And since man contained in himself the power of all things, he took notice of the works of the seven governors.* These, however, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a participant in their own order. But he speaks more deeply than what might appear on the surface of the letter.
<margin>Plato, Plotinus, Academics</margin>
How man draws from the planets themselves is taught by **Plato**, **Plotinus**, and the rest of the **Academics**. They say: *The soul, in its descent, receives from **Saturn** reasoning, intelligence, and the power of speculation; from **Jupiter** the powers of acting and the practical; from **Mars** the irascible part and the heat of spiritedness; from the **Sun** the imagination of knowing and the nature of forming opinions; from **Venus** the concupiscible part and the movement of desire; from **Mercury** the vigor of interpreting, pronouncing, and penetrating; and from the **Moon** that from which it can plant, generate, and grow.* The body itself, being tangible, is fashioned from the elements and the "lower ennead," and we have declared it to be similar to them.
<margin>Mercury</margin>
And so that he might receive from the universe, and that a certain "whole" might be completed, he draws even from the supreme sevenfold (as **Mercury** suggests)—indeed, from the entire **Archetype** <note>The divine "blueprint" or original model of the universe in the mind of God.</note>—those things which we shall declare in their place (God willing), at least in part.
<margin>Manilius</margin>
Now, however, let us follow those things in which man agrees with the twelve signs of the zodiac. Setting aside many things with which numerous authors have filled volumes, I will bring forward only what **Manilius**, the distinguished mathematician <note>Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century AD Roman poet who wrote "Astronomica." > Over the whole body: **Aries** is the head, the first prince of all:
> **Taurus** is allotted the most beautiful neck for its domain:
> And in **Gemini**, the arms are described as joined
> To the shoulders with an equal lot: and the chest is located...

### From where each of the signs of the zodiac has its name, and what those animals, from which they are named, do with the Sun. Chapter XVIII.

<margin>Macrobius</margin>
<insert>H</insert> Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and philosopher whose work on Cicero's "Dream of Scipio" was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance cosmology.</note> touched upon the reasons for these names from Academic sources, albeit lightly; to which we shall add those things which have been drawn from better streams. Therefore, the first sign is called Aries (The Ram), because <margin>Astronomy</margin> that animal lies upon its left side for the six winter months, but upon its right side from the vernal equinox. So too the Sun at that same time encompasses the right hemisphere, and for the remainder, the left. Moreover, the Ram is the head and leader of the sheep, and that sign named after it is the head of the signs and the leader of the months of the year. Whence by the astronomers, from the entry of the Sun into the first part of Aries, the events of the whole year are prognosticated. From the same also, those who philosophize on rural matters prophesy; who (as Isaac <note>Likely referring to Isaac Judaeus, a prominent 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note> reports) if they see the older rams more inclined to mating than the young ones at the appointed time, they argue from this a happy and favorable course of the year and the best temperament of the weather. Taurus (The Bull) follows, which Egyptian worship shows is referred to the Sun for multiple reasons; either because at Heliopolis they especially worship a Bull consecrated to the Sun (which they call Nerites), or because the Apis bull is received in the city of Memphis in the likeness of the Sun, or because in the town of Hermonthis, in a magnificent temple of Apollo, they worship a Bull consecrated to the Sun, calling him Pachim...

### THE SIXTH TONE <note>original: "TONVS SEXTVS." In this context, "Tone" or "Mode" likely refers to a specific section or chapter in a structured philosophical or musical work.</note>

->**TAURUS AND GEMINI**<-

...asserts that it changed colors every single hour, and is said to be hairy with bristles growing in the opposite direction, contrary to the nature of all animals; whereby it has, as it were, the image of the sun shining in the opposite part of the world. But since these things savor of the most unmixed fables, other reasons must be sought: for <term>Taurus</term> <note>The Bull.</note> is the king of the herds, just as <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram.</note> is of the flocks, the <term>Lion</term> of the wild beasts, and **Man** of all rational creatures. The Sun, the king of the planets, claims their images as his own dwellings. And from the Ram, whose power is in the head, he ascends to the Bull, who holds his power most especially in the neck; and from the king of the flocks he proceeds to the king of the herds, and from there to the king of those who use reason. 

From here they call the next sign the <term>Gemini</term> <note>The Twins.</note>, who are always succeeding one another in alternating deaths, as antiquity feigned concerning **Castor and Pollux** <note>In Greek and Roman mythology, these twin brothers shared immortality; when one was in the underworld, the other was in the heavens.</note>. For whether life follows them or death succeeds, man always lives in his better part, which remains for eternity, while the souls of cattle are dissolved into nothingness. Even in this mortal life, man himself lives by a perpetual succession of individuals. Furthermore, it is called the sign of the Twins either because when the Sun has arrived there, he "doubles" his strength, or because he then "doubles" his journey by descending just as he had ascended.

->**CANCER AND LEO**<-

The <term>Cancer</term> <note>The Crab.</note> follows, an animal that moves backward, because when the Sun has reached its first threshold, he begins to retreat toward the depths. Cancer is also, above all animals, "Lunar," and is rightly the home of the **Moon**; and this is, as it were, the chest of heaven, while the Twins are the arms. The **Lion** follows as the shoulder blades and the sides of that same heaven. In this sign, as if in his own proper home and in the image most especially dedicated to him, the Sun burns above all other times, although his rays are more bent than when he was traveling through Cancer and Gemini. For from there he receives strength, as if from a place named after the Lion, the foremost among the "solar" animals. For here he is seen to derive his nature from the very substance of the sun; wherefore, from the imbalance of the heat, he often grows faint, just as our own bodies do when the Sun is in that same sign. Therefore, at that time, **Physicians** <note>original: "Physici." Referring to medical practitioners of the time.</note> forbid **Medicines** <note>original: "Pharmaca."</note>, **bloodletting** <note>original: "flebotomiā." A common medical practice of the era to balance the body's humors.</note>, and the diminishing of blood, except insofar as necessity compels it.

->**VIRGO, LIBRA, AND SCORPIO**<-

The succeeding sign is rightly called the <term>Virgo</term> <note>The Virgin.</note>, because then the Sun—from whom the principal naming of the signs comes—seems to lose all power of producing, and to arrive at a certain sterility. For as he passes through there, the corn, the wine, and the fruits of the earth are already ripe, and the offspring of the earth are seen to be closed off. The sign which follows after is rightly called <term>Libra</term> <note>The Scales.</note>, because then the fruits collected begin to be divided by the scale or measure. The Solar course is partitioned into equal portions, both diurnal and nocturnal; the time also seems to be weighed on a balance, enjoying the greatest temperance, as a middle point between heat and cold. 

To this is added the <term>Scorpio</term> <note>The Scorpion.</note>, a venomous animal, more troublesome than the others by as much as it inflicts a heavier punishment. It has its poison in its tail and always strikes with an oblique blow. And this seems marvelous: that it never lacks venom, most especially at midday when the Sun glows with heat, even though **Phoebus** <note>original: "Phæbus." A name for Apollo, the god of both the Sun and of Healing.</note> is the Physician bringing a remedy to all. However, to those looking sanely, this ought by no means to seem discordant, since the more pernicious a poison things have, the more effective is their antidote. For the flesh of a **Viper** or a **Tyrus** <note>A specific type of venomous snake used in ancient medicine.</note>, from which **Theriac** <note>original: "tiriaca." An ancient "universal" medicine or antidote made from many ingredients, including viper flesh.</note> is made, provides a remedy for poisonous things, even though it boils with venomous gore itself. Likewise, the flesh of the scorpion itself is effective for those poisoned by the same. Thus, from wherever one extreme arises, the other also proceeds from it. For God Himself, the highest good, gave these testimonies of Himself...

### Why those signs and the principal joints in man are distributed in the number twelve. Chapter XIX.

<margin>Plato
Aristotle.</margin>
**I**N the archives of the wise, we find two progressions of things. One indeed is through the **ternary** <note>The number three, often associated by Neoplatonists with the divine triad or the soul.</note> seeking the lowest things from the highest; the other indeed is through the **quaternary** <note>The number four, associated with the material elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> ascending from the inferior things to the heavens. Plato followed the former path, from divine things to the lesser; but Aristotle, following the latter from the lowest to the highest, proceeded only as far as he could be led by his senses through these things. The **quaternary**, therefore, is the elemental number, and it is also found to be divine through a great mystery for the sake of the fitness of things, as **Orpheus** <margin>Orpheus.</margin> and the wiser men before him said. And this number brings forth the tireless (as the same Orpheus continues) and unchangeable number **ten** <note>The "denarius." In Pythagorean thought, 1+2+3+4 = 10 (the Tetractys), the perfect number encompassing all things.</note>, beyond which no number is given. But the **quaternary** itself, folded through the **ternary** number, leads to the **twelve** <note>The "duodenarium." 4 multiplied by 3.</note>, the first increasing number, more celestial and divine than earthly. Hence all growing things, and many divine things, are distributed by it. This number is also composed of two "first perfect" numbers, namely **sixes** <note>Six was considered a "perfect number" because it is the sum of its divisors (1, 2, 3).</note>; and it is the first "increasing" number, and in this it abounds in sixteen by four, whence that increase is happy, because it happens through a square of equal sides and the parent of the ten. Therefore, Plato deservedly <margin>Plato</margin> in the *Phaedo* and in many places venerates this number; and by it, he divides the upper world into twelve faces and as many colors, as a mark of perfection. For he asserts that stones, fruits, trees, flowers, and the like are found in the upper region with such perfection that they have neither come to our knowledge until now, nor can we even imagine them. For they received these things from those who were taught by divine oracles. Instructed by these, <margin>John.</margin> **John**, at the end of his **vision on Patmos** <note>The Book of Revelation (Apocalypse).</note>, relates that twelve fruits are produced by the **tree of life** every single month. He also describes that heavenly city as built upon twelve foundations of precious stones with the twelve names of the Apostles; twelve...

The princes <note>spiritual rulers or powers</note> are distributed into seventy-two through the duodenary <term>duodenarius: the number twelve</term> multiplied by its half—namely <note>original: videlicet</note> six. The poets, imitating this like apes, <margin>Poets</margin> invented twelve deities to preside over those signs: Pallas <note>Athena</note> over Aries, and consequently over the human head; Venus over Taurus, the neck, and the throat; Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> specifically over Gemini and the arms; Mercury over Cancer and the chest; Jupiter specifically over Leo, the shoulders, or the shoulder blades; Ceres over Virgo and the lower belly; Vulcan over Libra and the buttocks; Mars over Scorpio and the private parts; Diana over Sagittarius and the thigh; Vesta over Capricorn and the knees; Juno over Aquarius, as well as the shins; and Neptune over Pisces and the feet. <margin>Manilius</margin> Whence Manilius sings:

They assign some of these deities as masculine and some as feminine not without cause, so as to suggest that both forces descend from the heavens. I also think it should be observed that the heaven—the seat of divine things and the last of corporeal things—is divided by the number twelve. This number results from the elementary four <note>the four elements</note> and the divine three <note>the Trinity or divine triad</note> being brought together, and existing as a kind of bond, it connects corporeal things with divine things. Furthermore, this number contains (as the Pythagoreans say) <margin>Pythagoras</margin> a perfect diapasonic <term>diapason: an octave</term> harmony in the parts of which it is composed: namely 7 and 5. Of these, 7 contains the sesquitertia <term>sesquitertia: a 4:3 ratio</term> proportion from 4 to 3; and 5 the sesquialtera <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio</term> from 3 to 2. From these proportions the octave results, the extremes of which form a kind of circle back to the same note, but higher, ending one extreme where the other begins; thus the circular harmony matches the circular and harmonic heaven. Beyond this, it is almost by necessity that the heaven and its signs are distributed by the number twelve, so that within it could be found the aspects of opposition, trine, square, and sextile—which could by no means be had except in the duodenary.

### Correspondence of qualities with the planets and the eighth heaven. Chapter 20.

<margin>The same</margin>
**T**here exist in the human body qualities and temperaments <term>complexiones: the balance of humors in the body</term> having their own harmony with the planets and the starry heaven. Thus, those in whom this humor prevails are called "Saturnine," following his motion and influence so closely that Saturn seems to be present in all their operations. And attracted by him with a certain harmonious force, they always delight in Saturnine things: solitude, contemplation, profound imagination, and a desire for gathering resources arising from the fear brought on by the cold and dry nature of the earth, and in such decrees of Saturn. 
<margin>Jupiter</margin>
Jupiter, however, has his harmony with the blood and with the moist and hot air, and consequently with life, which resides most especially in such things. He, with his graceful expansion of equal force, renders his subjects <note>original: "phaetonteos," a poetic term for those influenced by planetary light</note> manageable, kind, and very ready for work; just as Saturn, by constricting, invites them to rest and inward-focused delight, yet Jupiter fortifies them with the strength and power of a well-joined structure. 
<margin>Mars</margin>
Mars, being entirely fiery, having a shared nature with bile <note>yellow bile</note> and all fiery things, impels his "Martial" subjects to all fiery impulses, both civil and spiritual: these indeed to fervent love, those however to wars and invasions. 
<margin>Sun</margin>

<margin>Venus</margin>

For she is like the dawn, in which for the greater part of the year the moist and lustful nature dominates, shedding dew, provoking sleep, and dissolving the limbs; but strengthened by the vigor of the succeeding Sun, or by his associated rays, she somewhat compresses these easy outpourings.

### That the intellect corresponds with the circle of signs. Chapter 21.

These hairs receive their influx and power from a supreme source, just as the stars do. But let us return to the intellect. <margin>CHRIST</margin>
Perhaps this is what the Highest Truth <note>original: "summae Veritatis," referring to Christ</note> intended by saying: *Your names are written in heaven.* For the Hebrews divide the twenty-two letters of their alphabet into three parts: three signify the three elements, seven signify the seven planets, and twelve signify the twelve signs of the zodiac, acting as their characters. They call those seven letters "double," both because they have a twofold pronunciation—soft and sharp—and because they represent the planets, which increase or decrease their power depending on the diversity of the signs in which they are found. The twelve, however, they call "simple," because they are always pronounced in a single way and because they represent the signs, whose power always remains the same. The [other] three they ascribe to the three elements: namely Fire, Water, and Earth. They do not hold Air as a separate element here, but rather as the "glue" or bond of the elements. Therefore, just as all bodies are composed from the aspects of the planets and signs together with the elements, so the names of things composed from them are formed from the letters and characters signifying those parts. This is hinted at with no small mystery in the *Book of Formation* <note>original: "libro de formatione," referring to the *Sefer Yetzirah*, a foundational text of Jewish mysticism</note> which is attributed to Abraham. Some assert that the spirit and soul of these composite bodies are signified by the points and accents <note>referring to the vowel points and cantillation marks in Hebrew script</note>.

->The first mover carries away the heart, or the freedom of the mind residing there.<-

## Chapter XXII.

<margin>The first mover is the leader of the heavens</margin>
**T**here is a ninth circle, which is called the <term>Primum Mobile: the "First Mover," the outermost sphere of the universe in Ptolemaic astronomy which sets all others in motion</term>. It is the leader of the heavens, carrying all the other heavens along with it by its own force. It is not led by any inner circle, but only by the intelligence that moves it, or by God’s command. Into it, as into the first mover, all motion is led so that the entire harmony of heaven is not thrown into confusion, as Aristotle proves at the end of his *Organon* <note>The author likely refers to the culmination of Aristotle’s logical or physical works regarding the Prime Mover</note>.
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
So in this "small world" of ours <note>the human microcosm</note>, the Will is the mistress of all other powers and their leader according to its pleasure. To it, the kingdom and sovereignty are rightly owed, because it always tends toward the Good as its proper object—even if someone occasionally chooses evil through error or the impulse of animal force, believing or pretending that it is good. In that case, the Will is not a mistress but is made a most wretched slave, as the Highest Truth says: *He who commits sin is a slave to sin.*
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Rightly, then, when tending toward the Good, it is lawfully preferred; just as in political systems, that which looks toward a better and greater good is deservedly placed first. This Will, or <term>Synderesis: the innate spark of conscience or the capacity to know the first principles of morality</term>, when joined with the higher part of the soul, leads all inferior powers with it toward its desire, like the First Mover. But the Will itself is led by nothing except the Highest Mover,
<margin>Theologians</margin>
or by that influence which theologians call grace, charity, or infused love.
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Regarding this, the Highest Truth says again: *No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him.*
<margin>David</margin>
And the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> says he then "runs through the way of God’s commandments" when his heart has been enlarged and moved by love. The progress of the rest of the inferior powers follows the orderly motion of this Will, just as all the motions of the spheres follow that of the First Mover.
