### SIXTH TONE ###

->P iiii<-

<margin>Augustine. Aristotle.</margin>
They regulate [all things] by the rotation of the <term>First Mover: the outermost sphere of the universe in medieval cosmology, which carries all other spheres in its daily rotation</term>. Nor should anyone say that the will, as if blind, is led by the intellect: for we can love nothing unless it is first known. The will is carried toward that thing alone which is first perceived, as Augustine and Aristotle agree. For just as light shows the way to the eye but does not actually lead it, so the intellect demonstrates the paths to the will, yet it does not lead the will along them; rather, the will remains the mistress of its own operation. In the same way, the <term>Stellar Heaven: the sphere of the fixed stars</term> corresponds in a certain manner to the First Mover; it receives the degrees and names of things to be produced through it and the planets, and the First Mover approaches to execute them, rolling all things in a daily

<margin>The same</margin>
motion. Therefore, there is in man the will and the heart (as Aristotle says) just as the first intelligence is in the orb—specifically the first [sphere]. Possessing the likeness of that first sphere, it rotates and draws all things along, just as the First Mover draws the other orbs. And just as sin in nature follows when the lower causes disagree with the first, or the lower orbs from the First Mover: so it is when the "law of the limbs" and the lower powers, fighting against the mind, lead the human captive into the "law of sin" <note>This is a reference to the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Romans 7:23</note>. Thus, the law of all the limbs ought to yield to the dictate of the mind, just as all the spheres yield to the First Mover, which snatches them all along in its daily motion. And although each of the lower orbs prepares its own course, they are much slower in their movements than the first. This beautifully instructs us that even if our lower powers perform some work according to what is proper to them, that work is slow or meager compared to the work of a well-regulated free will.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
However, the slowest of all motions is that of the stellar heaven, which moves one degree in a hundred years, as is pleasing to <term>Ptolemy: an ancient astronomer whose model of the universe was standard in the Middle Ages</term>. This is the number [one hundred] that is the square of ten, which is made up of the parts of the "quaternary" number of the elements. From this, it is suggested that this heaven represents the "elemental body," and also because it is integrated from a fourfold kind of signs, according to the nature of the four elements, just as the body is composed of the same. Nor should anyone carp at me because a little earlier we made the stellar heaven correspond with the intellect, but now we equate it with the body. For the serpent at one time represents the devil, and at another time acts as a type for Christ; and this is so because He himself said: *As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.* <note>Referring to John 3:14</note>. And any planet is at one time compared to an element, and at another to an order of Angels. Many such things are found compared to diverse things because of the "symbolic quality" which diverse known things have toward one another. For in respect to the higher minds, that heaven behaves as a body; but in respect to the lower things to be produced, it has the likeness of the intellect producing "ideas."

<margin>Porphyry. Aristotle.</margin>
So also in the coordination of things assigned by Porphyry and Aristotle, the same thing compared to a higher thing has the rationale of a "species," but toward a lower thing, the rationale of a "genus." Therefore, in our proposition, the motion of the First Mover is like the motion of the soul, and the motion of the stellar heaven bears the likeness of bodily motion; but the revolutions of the planets represent the motion of the powers existing between the body and the soul. But if we wish to equate these things with the lowest and the highest: in the heavens, the First Mover is the most fervent of all; in the <term>microcosm: the "small world," referring to the human being</term>, it is the heart and the will; in the Angelic hierarchy, it is the burning Seraphim. There is, furthermore, a fiery power in the Seraphim that inflames, in the First Mover that snatches away, and in our will and heart, it is a fervent virtue. Therefore, this virtue dwells in the heart, the hottest of all the limbs, possessing a heat that is both natural and of a higher kind; of which the Psalmist says: *My heart grew hot within me.*
<margin>David.</margin>

### What things are thickened and solidified with Saturn. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
The opinion of **Ptolemy** has been explained by his followers: that all the planets are destined to foster this human being, four of which serve to preserve the individual, and three serve for the performance of work. The four are
<margin>The same</margin>
the Moon, the Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn. The Sun, however, as the same author says word-for-word, is the origin of the vital power which is in the heart; Jupiter looks after the natural power in the liver; Saturn the receptive power; and the Moon the waxing and waning vigor. But the other three are required for character and operations: for the <term>phantastic power: the faculty of imagination and forming mental images</term> and the power of penetration in performing tasks must be sought from Mercury; appetite, concupiscence, and pleasure, which complete the work, from Venus; and the impulse along with anger and force, so that the work may be successful, from Mars. Saturn, therefore, governs the receptive power, and among the
<margin>Scotus</margin>

Presiding over this, Saturn renders his "Saturnians" <note>People born under the astrological influence of Saturn</note> good at remembering, since they possess that watery power so thickened <note>original: *constipatam*</note> that they can preserve the received images for a long time. And this is characteristic of Saturnians: that they hear, and ruminating in silence upon what they have heard, they enter into the more secret inner chambers, where through long and lasting consideration of many things and through experience, they are made prudent. But if he is well-disposed, he raises a person to the most profound and sublime things.

### What things are aligned with Jupiter. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>Galen. Moses</margin>
Jupiter, balancing all things, claims the left ear for himself to complete the wisdom already awakened by Saturn. And favoring love, he balances the liver as the seat of love and his own special home. For here love begins, which Venus (to whom love is ascribed) then unfolds; for it draws its origin from the liver, the seat of Jupiter. Thus, there is a proverb already common among medical authors: <note>original: "Splen ridere facit, cogit amare iecur"</note> *The spleen makes one laugh, the liver forces one to love.* This is supported by what **Galen** and **Moses of Cordoba** <note>Also known as Maimonides, the famous 12th-century Jewish physician and philosopher</note> derive from the ordinances of the ancients, who used to punish wrongdoers in the members with which they had sinned. For instance, those who entered the homes of others were beaten on their feet; slanderers and blasphemers had their tongues tormented, and many such things.

<margin>Poets</margin>
But the poets describe <term>Tityos: a giant in Greek mythology</term>, who was localized by excessive lust, being punished by the command of Apollo with his liver pierced by the beak of a vulture and a hawk. Therefore, Jupiter, considered in his power, being composed of heat and moisture, rightly presides over the liver; for the liver, enjoying the same quality, is nourished by thickened blood, as **Galen**, **Haliabas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, a famous Persian physician</note>, and the **Conciliator** <note>Pietro d'Abano, a medieval scholar who sought to reconcile philosophy and medicine</note> say. They provide this evidence: that blood clotted outside the veins resembles the liver itself. Hence, it is called by Galen the primary organ of blood. He also aligns the stomach to himself along with Saturn; but while Saturn dominates the nervous part, which is cold and dry, Jupiter dominates the fleshy part, which is hot and moist. And since the belly is also supported by moist heat, they subject it also to Jupiter. Many things could be discussed here concerning the muscles of the belly and other particulars, but since this might perhaps be too long and a superfluous labor, and would lead us away from our purpose by no short path, we shall omit those and speak only of the principal members.

The <term>dispositor: the planet ruling a person's physical form</term> of the body attributes a becoming figure, a moderate and handsome stature, eyes tending toward largeness and somewhat dark, yellow hair with a certain baldness, and two incisor teeth longer than the rest. But at sunrise he makes the skin quite white and the eyes average; yet at sunset, he provides a more subdued whiteness. In character, however, he makes men honorable, faithful, obedient to their parents, just, law-abiding, and many such things which are recorded by the astronomers. But these things occur only insofar as that heavenly power extends itself, whether it be the celestial star itself disposing the body, or the presiding <term>intelligence: the spiritual being or angel traditionally thought to move and govern a planet</term> operating further, by the command and cooperation of the First Cause.

### Chapter XXV. What things seethe with Mars.

<margin>Julius Firmicus. Avicenna. Galen. Avicenna. Galen.</margin>
**M**ars has his seats in the kidneys, the veins, the path of the sperm through the back, and in the <term>gallbladder: original: "chisti fellis"</term>. But these he holds alone; with Jupiter—according to the author Firmicus—he rules in the liver and the nostrils. Therefore, he appropriately "seethes" in the kidneys, since they themselves (according to Avicenna) are hot and dry, although others consider them hot and moist. But this is because a "radical" <note>Innate or fundamental to life</note> heat and moisture, shaped by life-giving warmth, flourishes in them, yet by their own simple nature they are dry and Martial <note>Pertaining to Mars</note>. 

A sign of this is provided by the <term>calculi: stones or gravel</term> which are generated in them: for they seethe most powerfully in those of a Martial temperament, and when Mars is favorable. These the disposer of nature combined, just as he did many members of the body, as Galen and Avicenna discuss. These <note>the kidneys</note> were given to cook the excess watery and bloody matter, just as the gallbladder serves as a receptacle for <term>yellow bile: original: "colere"</term>, and the spleen for the reception of the thick <term>melancholic humor</term>, as the same Galen determines. He is also set over the path of the sperm and the back through which it descends, so that the seed may be warmed by his heat and receive vigor for begetting offspring. Furthermore, those who treat such matters judge that he presides over the veins; although by their nervous, membranous, and ligamental nature they are cold and dry (regardless of the cold nature required to bind them tight), they are heated by him so that they may preserve the blood in its proper warmth. Indeed, all the veins, whether the portal vein of the liver or the <term>mesenteric veins: original: "maseraice," the veins of the digestive system</term> into which it is divided, have their origin from the hollow of the liver; at that point, like the "nail of a tent" <note>an anatomical metaphor for a central anchoring point</note>, they are gathered together (according to Galen), and many wise men agree with him. And just as blood flows between the liver and the heart through the life-carrying veins, so Mars is between Jupiter and the Sun, acting as a vehicle or <term>tinder: original: "fomentum"</term> of life, fostering it by its heat and impulse. And not only by position, but by its property and power—which is beyond the qualities themselves—it most appropriately presides over the veins and the <term>seminal duct: original: "canali spermatis"</term> in its own right; but most especially over the vessel of the <term>burning bile: original: "ferventis bilis," the gallbladder</term>, which is most characteristic of it. And if in such things the excess is so great that nature or art cannot restrain it, it brings about death. It also rules the nostrils, from which the heat of the bile, ignited in its vessel, might inflame the heart and exhale toward the brain in vapors.

<margin>Isaiah</margin>

In the exterior figure, it makes a person reddish: with shifting eyes tending toward yellow; the beard, hair, and other body hair red, dark, thick, and coarse; of middle stature; with a round face sprinkled with certain freckles and spots; wide and broad nostrils full of spirit; a fierce look; longer teeth; and a wide gait. In temperament, it makes one hot, and from this it confers impulse and the greatest force, rendering one ready for everything—and hence very powerful toward evil. And unless that impulse is moderated by the bridle of reason, it easily leads one into the precipice.

### Chapter XXVI. What things are quickened and made bright by the Sun.

<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
**S**ince the Sun (by the testimony of all the wise) is the father of life, and in which there resides (as the Pythagoreans believe) a certain power of life and the True Sun, they therefore assign it to the heart, as the primary seat of life. And just as the Sun itself in the <term>macrocosm: original: "maiori mundo," the greater world/universe</term> is the source of light and life, giving to all the planets so that they may shine; so the heart in the human world (according to

<margin>Galen. Aristotle.</margin>
Galen and other wise men) is the origin of life and heat, giving to all the members so that they may live and function. For the <term>soul: original: "anima"</term> (whose primary seat is the heart, as Aristotle says) is the principle of understanding, feeling, and movement from place to place. And just as the Sun itself corresponds to the heart by way of life, so by way of light it corresponds to the eyes, especially the right eye.

<margin>The same</margin>
The Sun responds to the Moon, leaving her on the left; it also takes charge of the **marrow**, which, as Aristotle says, should not be looked down upon as if it were a waste product, but is rather the very life of the bones and their <term>nourishment: original: "fomentum"</term> enclosed within them. For it is, in fact, another kind of blood, but one changed into whiteness through a process of "cooking" and heat, as said by 
<margin>Avicenna. Aristotle.</margin>
Avicenna and Aristotle with him. Providing evidence for this, he says that in animals that are still young, the marrow is quite bloody; however, as they advance in age and grow fat, it turns toward a fatty consistency. They also subject the **thighs** and **loins** to the Sun as the primary organs of generation—specifically the <term>seed vessels: original: "uasa seminaria"</term>. For this reason, not without cause, the wisest of the ancient fathers, Abraham, demanded an oath from his student <note>referring to his servant, Eliezer</note> upon the "thighs of the Messiah" <note>Abraham’s thigh was seen as the source of the holy lineage</note>, the vessel of seed, for whose pure and mysterious generation Abraham himself was concerned when he sent the servant, bound by the oath, to receive an Aramean wife for Isaac, from whose seed the Messiah was to be born. Furthermore, the Sun regulates the **vital spirit** as the instrument of life, as well as the **intellect** and **reason**. Hence, it is wonderfully favorable to learning, true philosophy, and knowledge set apart from the senses. According to its manly power, it makes a person magnanimous, composed in character, seeking high things and leadership, yet renowned for faith, *and of an excellent natural talent and virtue*. In external appearance,
it makes a person shapely and beautiful—and not without merit, since the Sun himself corresponds to super-worldly beauty and is its vessel, container, and instrument. He also provides various and very beautiful eyes, which are the primary indicators of the soul. Hence, concerning David, it is said (not without 
<margin>Kings</margin>
mystery) in the first book of Kings: that he was ruddy, with beauty of the eyes, *and of a good appearance*, for which we have "beautiful in appearance and of a graceful face." And the Sun favors these things most especially when it is at its rising; and if we wish to climb higher, the Sun does this when it receives the influence from the "High Sunrise," of whom it is said: *The just man shall come from the east.*
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Furthermore, the Sun grants a fitting stature, white in color with a certain duskiness or redness, *many* curly hairs, a round and lovely face, a becoming mouth, small lips, slender eyebrows, a sweet and grave voice, and a graceful gait. In temperament, he is moderately hot. If, however, the body is poorly disposed, the Sun stirs up various infirmities, most especially in the eyes. In the mouth, it causes <term>thrush: original: "alcolam," white mouth sores</term> and <term>gangrene: original: "cancrenam"</term>, and pustules on the body. It moves the limbs, each one according to the "house" of the zodiac in which it is found, but in a different way than the Moon does. For in **Aries**, it moves the thighs; in **Taurus**, the knees; in **Gemini**, the shins and ankles; in **Cancer**, the feet; in **Leo** and **Virgo**, the neck; in **Libra**, the arms and shoulders; in **Scorpio**, the chest and heart; in **Sagittarius**, the stomach and belly; in **Capricorn**, the back; in **Aquarius**, the hips *and the private parts*; and in **Pisces**, the thighs again, along with the succeeding Aries. But if the humor moved by the Sun boils over too much and the body becomes (as we said) poorly disposed, abusing the favor of its benefit, then burning heats occur, along with anxieties, restlessness, abscesses, powerful oppressions, or a flow of blood from that boiling; when these are increased too much, they become fatal. And thus Phoebus <note>a name for the Sun</note> the physician and healer, and his life-giving power, brings about even deadly injuries because of the bad disposition of the recipient. This is not surprising, for according to the different disposition of the receivers, the sun hardens mud but melts wax. So it was also said of the true and divine Sun: *He is set for the fall and the resurrection of many in Israel.*

### Of those things that are sharpened and penetrate with Mercury. Chapter 28.

<margin>The same author</margin>
**M**ercury claims the tongue in the head for himself, whose speech penetrates even to the inner parts of the mind; hence he is the patron of eloquence and Hermes—that is, the interpreter of nature. This tongue, the most hidden of all members, works most effectively and at a great distance, just as Mercury is so hidden that he is seen with difficulty and rarely; yet by penetrating most sharply, he acts with great efficacy. So too does the intelligence presiding over him, Michael, the Prince of Angels <note>In Christian Kabbalah and Neoplatonism, specific archangels were often associated with the seven planetary spheres</note>, as some assert. 
<margin>The same author</margin>
Because Mercury, by his effective subtlety and craft (as Ptolemy witnesses), also renders a person disposed and ready for work, he is therefore preferred for the hands as the necessary instrument of all works. They add the nerves, which some say—namely the passive ones—are of a cold and dry nature, while the motive <gloss>active</gloss> ones are warmer, both from movement and from the purer <term>spirit: original: "spũ"</term> existing in them.

</margin>

By his own nature, however, Mercury constricts, whence he renders his "Mercurials" slender and sinewy; for he presides over the nerves, which are the general instrument of works, just as the hand is a particular one. <margin>Albertus Magnus</margin>
From the heart again (as Albertus Magnus says) the nerves derive their hardness, but from the brain their softness, from which they are divided. Thus Mercury, whose power thrives in the nerves, receives his strength from the Sun—which is the heart of the world’s body. Like a son, Mercury always follows his father, obeying him so closely that he is separated from him by only a few degrees, or none at all. He is also connected to the Moon, which has an affinity with the brain; thus he receives power from both. In the brain, he also holds power over its <term>ventricles: original: "ventriculis"</term> <note>Cavities within the brain where "animal spirits" were thought to reside</note>, veins, and arteries. Finally, he presides over the shins and the feet, which are the helpers of the hands—so faithful, in fact, that if one fails, the other compensates. Indeed, some have been seen who, lacking hands, were able to write with their feet and perform many similar tasks of the hands. 

If Mercury's influence prevails in a man, it makes him of medium stature and slender, with a pale-white color, black and beautiful hair, beard, and eyes, a high forehead, a long face, straight nostrils, joined eyebrows, small teeth, and long, thin fingers. He is quite handsome in form, especially when supported by the rising Sun; but when the Sun is setting, Mercury makes the color blackish mixed with yellow, the body thin, and the <term>complexion: original: "complexione"</term> <note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) determining health and temperament</note> dry. 

However, in a poorly disposed subject, he induces madness, memory loss, restless diseases, various fears without cause, sluggishness in the limbs and nerves, and stuttering. Likewise, he brings on <term>frenzy: original: "frenesim"</term> <note>Severe inflammation or mental agitation</note>, apoplexy, epilepsy, colic, and diseases following from "raging" matter, the spitting of blood for no apparent reason, and hidden ailments. If these illnesses arise from an external cause, that cause is usually reading, writing, reasoning, measuring, excessive thinking about poetry, and things of this sort. And because he is so effective and swift in his operation, he leads his "mercurial" person to the end of life in a short space; so that in him, that word of sacred scripture finds a place:
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
*Being perfected in a short space, he fulfilled a long time.* <note>A quote from the biblical Book of Wisdom 4:13, suggesting a short but full life</note>

## What is governed by the Moon. Chap. XXIX.

Although the Moon disposes the whole body and individual members according to the variety of the signs and her <term>aspects: original: "aspectuum"</term> <note>The geometric angles between planets in astrology</note> with the Sun and other planets, she is nevertheless said to have the greatest power in moving certain members that correspond to her with a peculiar affinity. She presides over the left eye, just as the Sun presides over the right, so that the two lights in both worlds <note>The "two worlds" refers to the Macrocosm (the universe) and the Microcosm (the human body)</note> may harmonize with each other. 

She frequently predominates over all the humors which rise and fall in both worlds—and even in trees and animals—following the Moon herself. This is proven clearly enough in the "fluxes" of women, which are called "menstrual" because they follow the cycle of the Moon, which is completed in about a month. In other humors, it is likewise manifest to those who look closely, as they are more liquid when the Moon is in a watery sign than when she is in a fiery or earthy one. For this reason, those skilled in these matters command that this be observed when giving medicines. 

She is also judged to preside over the lungs, which, like a <term>fan: original: "flabellum"</term> <note>Medieval medicine taught that the lungs acted as a cooling fan for the heat generated by the heart</note>, cool and temper the heart and those things that are inflamed by the heart itself, just as the Moon cools those things that boil from the Sun's most burning vigor. 
<margin>Galen, Averroes</margin>
And just as the heart (according to Galen and Averroes) nourishes the lung by providing it with a digested and gentle heat, so the Sun, by his warming power, is the "nourisher" of the Moon. Furthermore, she presides over the marrow of the spine and the discharges that flow down through the strainers of the nose, mouth, and such; and also over the superfluous growth of nails and hair.

### Chapter XXX.

**S**aturn completes his motion in thirty years; Jupiter in twelve; from which results a ratio of velocity that is double sesquialter <note>original: "duplex fefqualtera"; a mathematical ratio of 5:2 or 2.5 to 1</note>. Moreover, the ratio of Jupiter to Mars—who completes his course in two years—is sextuple <note>6:1</note>. But the ratio of Mars to the Sun, Venus, and Mercury is double; since these complete the circuit of their sphere in about one year, though it varies slightly because of their epicycles <note>original: "epiciclos"; small circular orbits centered on a larger orbit, used in ancient astronomy to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward</note>. Hence the motion of each of them appears now faster, now slower, yet they equally complete the journey they began, producing this most sweet music of the heavens with the required modulations, now one preceding the other, now following. Again, the motion of Saturn is faster than the star-bearing heaven by a ratio of one thousand two hundred <note>1200:1</note>, if it is true that the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note> moves against the "first mobile" <note>the outermost sphere that carries the others</note> by only one degree every hundred years, as Ptolemy pleases <note>referring to Claudius Ptolemy's calculation of the precession of the equinoxes</note>. <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> For among us, neither is in doubt, nor false; but we presuppose that which is commonly held. Also the motion of Mars is faster than the motion of the eighth sphere by a ratio of one thousand; and thus the calculation of the remaining planetary motions relative to the revolution of the starry heaven and to one another is easy for those who know the limits of their revolutions. 

Hence, therefore, in the small world <note>the microcosm, or the human being</note>, the proportion of powers and operations can be conjectured. For the motion of the thinking faculty relative to the practical faculty should be as that of Saturn (who rules the former) is to Jupiter (who favors the latter). And the ratio of these should be to the impulse stirred by Mars. Life, moreover, and the concupiscible power <note>the faculty of desire or attraction</note>, and talent—of which the Sun rules the first, Venus the second, and Mercury the third—together produce the same melody, since one cannot stand without its companion. For the concupiscible power, and love, and the spirit of accomplishment follow most especially the rational life. <margin>Academics.</margin> Hence the Academics <note>referring to the Neoplatonist philosophers of the Platonic Academy</note> teach that through these three together, a return to God is given to man; but these are proportioned according to the numbers of their higher counterparts. And how excellently the concupiscible power and cleverness always accompany the soul and life; so that pleasure may sometimes remove the weariness that follows labor and work, and that all things may be performed properly through cleverness and skill. After all these is the Moon, unfolding all things, and she corresponds with the practical intellect, which directs every work like a pilot in a ship while he crosses the sea. Moreover, the proportion of the Moon and the planets to the sign-bearing heaven <note>the Zodiac</note> is according to the velocity of their motion; which proportion is followed by that of the practical intellect to all others.

...powers, both intellectual and animal <note>In this context, "animal" refers to the functions of the *anima* (soul) that govern movement and the senses</note>: and the relationship they have to one another, and of all of them to the body, which does not move except insofar as it is guided by the higher powers, just like the eighth heaven. To this eighth heaven, because of its fourfold triplicity <note>referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac divided into four "triplicities" or groups of three, each associated with an element</note>, the body composed of four elements is compared. Beyond the diurnal <note>daily</note> motion, by which it is guided by the *primum mobile* <note>the "first moved" sphere that drives the rotation of all other celestial spheres</note>, it has no motion of its own—neither that of trepidation <note>a theoretical oscillation of the equinoxes</note>, nor any other, as some assert. And that motion which it seems to have, they think comes from the variation of the Sun, whose motion is in a sense the rule and measure of the others. For the Sun traverses the Zodiac every year, and more: not only by the six hours which, calculated over any four years, return a full day—which is added every fourth year called **bissextile** <note>a leap year</note>—but also certain minutes, specifically about the hundredth part of a day. Collected over a hundred years, these constitute a full day. But since this extra day is not added as it is in a leap year, therefore every hundred years the Sun seems to anticipate its entry into Capricorn by one day. 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
Although Ptolemy <note>the famous 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> says that this occurs every three hundred years, we however have it proven from the year of Christ’s birth—when the Sun entered Capricorn on the twenty-fifth day of December—up to now, when it enters on the eleventh day, or thereabouts. 

<margin>Paul</margin>
In 1520 years <note>The margin likely refers to Paul of Middelburg, a contemporary astronomer and bishop who worked on calendar reform</note>, the Sun has anticipated its entry by about fourteen days. From this, it is proven by clear light that every hundred years it anticipates by a day, in which it is accustomed to move one degree. But this is estimated (as some assert) to come from the motion of the eighth sphere in the opposite circle, which results from this variation of the Sun. Having set this aside, along with the proportions by which our virtues and works are proportioned to each other, and with the motions of the spheres from which the sweetest harmony results—which pertains rather to the third volume—let us descend to the particular effects of those spheres regarding divine and human virtues. 

Therefore, seven principal virtues are counted everywhere, which are poured out into men from the supreme fountain of all good things through the seven planets, as if through instruments: 
* Through **Saturn**: hope and the contemplative life.
* Through **Jupiter**: justice and equity.
* Through **Mars**: fortitude.
* Through the **Sun**, king of all: charity, the queen of all virtues.
* Through **Venus**: piety and temperance.
* Through **Mercury**: prudence in action.
* Through the **Moon**—which now is hidden, now appears: faith. 

Faith, dealing with things fitting and hidden, provides leadership to those proceeding through the misty shadows of this night, until that supreme Sun shines forth with morning, evening, and midday light; which also illuminates those wandering in this valley of shadows, as much as the state of pilgrimage <note>a common metaphor for human life on Earth</note> requires, and as much as mortals are disposed to receive it through faith and purgative works.

Whether this corresponds with the human world is clear enough to one observing its arrangement: for in it is the supreme citadel <note>original: *arx*</note> of the brain, where the higher portion of reason—indeed, the divine portion—resides, governing all lower things. There is also a little heavenly dwelling <note>original: *mansiuncula*</note> in the front part of the head, where the obedient powers—namely the imaginative and cognitive ones and suchlike—dwell, like handmaidens <note>original: *ancillæ*</note> of the heaven and the superior king, carrying out what the Lord has commanded. There are also lower handmaidens <note>original: *pedisequæ*</note>—namely the sensitive powers—dwelling in the lower and perceptible house, which rightly should serve the higher ministers, but most especially the prince, as the supreme Emperor commanded, saying: *Thy desire shall be under thee.* <note>A reference to Genesis 4:7, often interpreted in this period as the mind's duty to control physical urges.</note> There is also the lowest place of the tomb <note>original: *busti locus*; the author uses "bustum" (tomb/pyre) as a metaphor for the physical body frame</note>, under which the feet are placed like columns: where there is the house of purging <note>original: *expurgatoria domus*</note> and the lower door of this human citadel, from which superfluous, dreg-filled, and filthy things are sent out, to be forever neglected. Of these another Prophet [Joel] says: *The beasts have rotted in their own dung.* Regarding whose confusion and corresponding disorder, we have touched upon these few things, so that no part of this mundane and human house remains untouched.

### That Man Harmonizes with the Angels by Containing Them. Cap. XXXII.

<margin>Mercury</margin>
**M**an is he (says the Sage) to whom the power of containing all things is given: Therefore, beyond lower and middle things—namely the changeable and the celestial—he also apprehends the Angels and God himself: so that he is in a way the bond <note>original: *uinculũ* (vinculum)</note> of all things, closest to everyone, and a true world containing all things, conversing with all: with the higher beings through faith and wisdom; with the middle through reason and discourse; with the lowest through sense and dominion. He is in harmony with all things through shared characteristics: with matter in his own subject; with the elements in his fourfold <note>original: *quadrifario*</note> body; with plants in his vegetative power <note>original: *uegeratiua uirtute*</note>; with the heavens in the influence of the higher parts upon the lower and in circular motion tending toward the same point from which he came; with the Angels in mind and wisdom; with God in the containment of all things—which man has by composition, but God by a certain simplicity. Hence Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with ancient wisdom and alchemy.</note> says: *Man is either more excellent than the celestial beings, or at least shares an equal lot: For whoever of the celestials descends to earth leaves the boundary of heaven; but man ascends into heaven and measures it: nor do those things which are lowest or highest escape him, nor all the rest: and what is greater, without leaving the earth he is raised to heaven; so vast is human power.*

# SIXTH TONE

Therefore, one must dare to say that a terrestrial man is a mortal God, and a celestial God is an immortal man. From this relationship, each individual thing is governed by their power; yet all things are subjected to one. That there are Angels is taught not only by the sacred scriptures, but even natural philosophers assert and prove it: <margin>Philo</margin> <margin>Plato</margin> Plato especially with all his Academics, Chrysippus, and Aristotle. <margin>Academic</margin> <margin>Chrysippus</margin> <margin>Aristotle</margin> For this latter philosopher says it would be absurd if that part of the universe which is most fit for producing living beings—such as the stars and the ethereal regions—were deprived of its own offspring. <margin>Chrysippus</margin> Whence he judged that births were necessary there, and that these beings are the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>original: *intelligentias*; in medieval philosophy, these are the spiritual beings that move the celestial spheres</note>. Chrysippus indeed asserted that perfection is found in each thing: for a puppy is imperfect, but a dog is perfect in its kind; likewise a foal becomes a perfect horse, and a boy a man. The same sequence occurs in the parts of the body, since a hand is more perfect than a foot, and an eye more so than a hand. Wherefore, since the parts of the lower world are imperfect—because the earth only brings forth life, beasts flourish in sense and motion, and man is ruled by reason yet drawn to the depths by appetite—there must therefore exist a reason not hindered by the senses, and this must reside in the Angels.

Hence Plato asserted that there are certain divine powers situated between Gods and men, intermediate in nature and location, and that these govern all divinations, miracles, and individual men. These are called <term>genii</term> <note>original: *genii*; protective spirits</note> by the gentiles <note>pagans</note>, but by our own people they are named Angels. But how they relate to us by influencing and conversing with us, from which a most sweet harmony results in their operation—because these things escape the sight of our eyes and our other senses—it is not easy to discuss them. <margin>Zeno</margin> <margin>Cleanthes</margin> <margin>Chrysippus</margin> <margin>Aristotle</margin> Therefore, we must consult not Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, or Aristotle, but our prophets and high priests, <margin>Dionysius</margin> Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, the traditional authority on the celestial hierarchy</note> and the other fathers illuminated by divine light in this matter; but especially that <term>Greatest High Priest</term> <note>referring to Christ</note> who says:
> **"All things, whatever I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you."** <note>John 15:15</note>
For He says:
> **"Their Angels—namely those of the little ones—always see the face of my Father"** <note>Matthew 18:10</note>
from whom they draw what they pour into us, so that like leaven added to our mass, by the power of the supreme craftsman they do not indeed <margin>CHRIST</margin> corrupt us, but change us into a divine lot. Whence, according to that prophetic saying: **"With the holy, you will be holy,"** <note>Psalm 18:25</note> it can also be said to us: **"With the Angel, you will be an Angel."**

While man receives their influence and vigor, he is called Seraphic, Cherubic, Angelic, and suchlike, according to the nature of the received influence. Thus man has an agreement with all of them, and receives from all (according to the <margin>Dionysius</margin> writings of Dionysius) purifications, illuminations, and perfections. But descending to particulars, man receives from the **Angels**, so that he may be a good messenger of God and interpreter of the divine mind; from the **Archangels**, so that he may rule all those over whom he is given to preside; from the **Principalities**, so that encompassing the strengths of all subjects, he may draw all to himself by a certain most hidden and super-celestial force; from the **Virtues** he receives the power by which he may be strengthened against the enemies of truth and the prize for which we fight; from the **Powers** he receives a defense against the enemies of this worldly house; from the **Dominions** he receives help by which we may subject the enemy...

**S**ufficiently, and more than enough, was it granted to man that he, having been made another world <note>The "microcosm" concept: man as a miniature version of the universe</note>, should embrace all parts of the world itself within himself; yet this seemed too little to the most munificent Giver, unless He also offered Himself to man as to a beloved son: Which I would least dare to assert, unless the wise, and the very Giver of all good things Himself, testified to the same. **Xistus the Pythagorean** <note>Likely referring to the "Sentences of Sextus," a collection of moral aphorisms popular in the early Church</note> judged that the soul of man is the temple of God, and therefore immortal like a guest, so that the place might be proportioned to that which is placed within it: But with a ringing voice **Paul** thunders this, saying: *You are the temple of God* <note>1 Corinthians 3:16</note>: Which could be proven by many passages of Holy Scripture: But let us first set forth how man is the likeness of God, made according to the image of God and with His similitude, as the Craftsman Himself reserved for Himself before He produced him: For he is the likeness and image of God containing all things that are in God: And in this an "image" differs from a "trace" <note>term: vestigium (trace). In Scholastic theology, a "trace" is a faint sign of God found in all creation, while an "image" is a fuller representation found only in rational beings</note>, because the latter represents a part, but the former represents the whole (as our theologians teach). Hence, those who have previously treated this image have attempted to investigate everything in God that a human being can represent: For the common thinkers, striving to fit all three powers of man with the three Persons, have said that in the **Memory** is the **Father**, who is called the "fruitful memory"; in the **Intellect** is the **Son**, the Word and Wisdom of God; and in the **Will** is the **Holy Spirit**, which is surely divine Love. But the more acute Theologians, proceeding further, teach that even in operations (which they call "secondary acts") those divine properties or actions are represented: whether they be called "notional" or "essential" <note>Technical terms in Trinitarian theology regarding the characteristics of the Divine Persons</note>, or by whatever other name the divine things can be called:

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>

For we do not know, nor is it permitted for those who know to speak of those secrets of God, who is removed from all modes of creatures: and who is (says **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic</note>) all things eminently: so much so that these words which we use cannot express those things which are in Him, except through a certain similitude and analogy: according to which, proceeding further, we shall say that even in our passions we represent certain things in God; for although there are no "passions" in God, we nevertheless call them by the name of passions by analogy: such as anger, fury, and desire.

<margin>David.</margin>

### On the Harmony of the Members of God and Man. Chapter 34. ###

<margin>The Ancients.</margin> **W**hich members are in God, to which man can be conformed, we shall run through by sketching rather than by painting, bringing forward a few things out of many which Sacred Scripture attests to this effect, and which the ancients described in the symbolic form of a most excellent tree. <margin>Moses.</margin> For all beings, both those using reason and the Redeemer, and God Himself, are called "trees," as **Moses** suggests in his garden of pleasure, which he describes as planted and established with various trees—that is, with many ranks and conditions of rational creatures. But in the middle, the **Tree of Life** is said to be placed, from which all life, whether Angelic or human or any other kind, emanates and flows. In this tree all things live, and were living before they were unfolded into their own specific forms, as **John** says: **That which was made, was life in Him.** In that same place, there is also said to have been a **Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil**, which (unless I am mistaken) is Christ as man, who alone, at one and the same time, tasted the good of blessedness and the evil of our passions. For (as all the **Theologians** <margin>Theologians.</margin> cry out) there was no one else who was simultaneously a "blessed one" and a "wayfarer" <note>In medieval theology, a 'comprehensor' (one who has reached the goal/blessedness) and a 'viator' (one still on the journey of life)</note> except **Jesus Christ**, whose rank was forbidden to Adam but granted to all others. Thus, man is a tree, Christ is a tree, and God Himself is a tree, who is described in the symbolism of a tree with such mystery that all the members of man correspond to Him. For its summit (which they call the **Crown** <note>A reference to "Keter," the highest point on the Kabbalistic Tree of Life</note>) is the head, upon which the crown itself is placed. On either side of the head is an eye: with the right eye He gazes most kindly upon those to be rewarded, and with the left eye He looks more severely upon those to be punished. Of these eyes, Scripture says: **The eyes of the Lord behold the good...**

But I think this should by no means be passed over, that the letter <term>ע</term> <note>The Hebrew letter Ayin</note>—that is, *Hain* in Hebrew—signifies both a **fountain** and an **eye**: so much so that the eye and the fountain of divine piety are the same thing, just as the eye and the fountain of piety are the same in us. If the eye is opened to pour out tears for the love of God, and out of grief for the suffering of Christ and one's afflicted neighbor, the fountain of divine piety is immediately opened to feel compassion for the one weeping. Therefore, the Savior said not without cause: **Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be blessed with consolation** <note>original: "Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur"; Matthew 5:4</note>, namely, by the abundance of divine piety received from that fountain, of which it is said in

But if our **head** is moved (that is, that highest part residing in the citadel of the soul) toward a divine object or some good, then the supreme Head of all things and the giver of all good things—
<margin>CHRIST</margin>

<margin>David. Joel.</margin>

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
He is moved then, He who was made the head of the body of the Church, as He Himself testifies to all when He says: **Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you**, coming kindly to you and making His dwelling with you. Beneath the eyes and the head are both **arms**, and the **right** and **left hands**. The right hand imparts mercy and all good things; the left, however, punishes the undeserving by the most severe law which proceeds from it. From the left comes the law and harsh justice; and from the right comes the law of mercy and grace through the Son of God, who is always said—not without reason—to be seated at the Father’s **right hand**. Hence, by a great mystery, the wicked who are to receive the harsh sentence of Christ are said to be placed at the Judge’s **left**, while those who will obtain mercy are placed at the **right**. Thus, the left arm was revealed to the ancestors under the 
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
harsher Law; but the right arm is disclosed to us through the Son of God, concerning whom **Isaiah**, wishing to prophesy, cried out: **Lord, who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?** Or "through whom has it been revealed," as the Hebrew truth has it. Certainly through Him, or upon Him, who grew up like a tender plant out of a thirsty land—namely, the Jewish people, who were then made dry by their crimes. He came, therefore, without outward appearance or the pomp of royal preparation, yet full of the **Treasures of wisdom and mercy**, which are placed at the right hand. Therefore, He poured out wisdom, clemency, and mercy upon His disciples and the people entrusted to Him, distributing all His own things—body, blood, and soul—judging it more blessed to give than to receive, and testifying and crying out to all: 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**Give, and it shall be given to you.** Move your hand toward your neighbor, and you will feel the right hand

of God most generously opened toward you. But in the midpoint, as if the **heart** and the whole **belly**, is the true, beautiful Socratic—indeed divine—thing from which all beautiful things come, about which the Psalmist...

# ALL THINGS ARE PROVEN BY REASONS AND AUTHORITIES TO HAVE SOMETHING IN THE ARCHETYPE TO WHICH THEY CORRESPOND. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**S**APIENTVM <note>The Latin text begins with a large decorative initial 'S'.</note> It is a most well-proven dogma of the wise, and no less well-worn, that all things manufactured pre-exist in the mind of a prudent craftsman, and are not fabricated by some fortuitous chance. In like manner, a house exists first in the architect; so also a speech pre-exists in the orator; nor is it otherwise for offspring in the one generating and pregnant. Thus, this machine of the universe was pre-eminent in the highest progenitor, God, like a creative life, as a goal toward which he might form all its members. For Number, Weight, and Measure, by which all things are counted, strengthened, and measured (as Augustine most wisely teaches), are not in the produced things themselves—just as the measure by which cloth is measured, or the weight by which heavier things are balanced, or the number by which all things are counted, is not found within the things measured, strengthened, or numbered, but is undoubtedly outside of them. Therefore, Number, Weight, and Measure, by which all things are measured and balanced, are necessarily outside of all those things. And since nothing exists outside of all produced things except God himself, it remains that Number, Weight, and Measure are in Him.

<margin>
Ancient
Theologians.
Abraham.
Abraham.
</margin>
Therefore, most excellently and elegantly did the Ancient Theologians <note>original: "Prisci Theologi," referring to a tradition of ancient wisdom-seekers like Hermes Trismegistus or Orpheus.</note> celebrate that most ancient dogma, first (as it is said) brought forth by the patriarch Abraham, by which we are taught that measures and countings exist in the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" is the divine world or the original ideal form in the mind of God.</note>, by which all things are arranged and numbered.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
And concerning these, Augustine follows up excellently, saying: In God there are numbers without number, since all things that are in Him are the one God Himself. And there is a weight without weight, by which the Craftsman himself is not burdened, but rather stabilized—He who grants all other things to move, while He remains stable at last.

<margin>Academics</margin>
Thus also our soul is a certain number and rational measure, as it was called by the Academics <note>Refers to the followers of Plato's Academy.</note>, by which we measure all things to be understood and performed by us, so that we may turn away from error, foolishness, and deformity in our works. Nor indeed would this harmonious fabric of the world, balanced by its due weights, subsist unless it were numbered and balanced by its Craftsman and Governor. Likewise, neither a house nor a Republic <note>original: "Resp." for "Res publica."</note> would enjoy its peace and tranquility unless it were moderated by the one who rules it: whose measure and balancing resides in the ruler, according to whose meter all things entrusted to him are arranged. Necessarily, therefore, measures and countings are understood to be in blessed God, by which He measures and numbers all things, as it is read in Ecclesiasticus <note>The Book of Sirach.</note>: The sand...

## To which majesty Prime Matter corresponds. Chapter II.

<margin>Eusebius Pamphilus</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras. Empedocles. Peripatetics. Plato.</margin>
To the one who makes all things, and to God the highest as the first act, it is fitting that almighty matter—the first receptive power—should correspond, so that between those two extremes all intermediate things may result. This arises from He who is almighty in bringing all things forth, and from she who is most disposed to receiving all things. Regarding the harmony of these two, Eusebius Pamphilus <note>A 4th-century bishop and scholar; the author refers to a lost or obscure work on Pythagorean numerology.</note> in his work *On the Triad and Monad* discusses elegantly. "Matter," he says, "is always opposite to the First Being; for He alone acts, while she only suffers <note>In the philosophical sense of 'undergoing' or receiving an action.</note>. He only moves, while she is only moved." Some physicists have named this receiver of all species *Pandochem* <term>Pandochem</term><note>From the Greek *pandocheus*, meaning "all-receiver" or "universal host."</note>. But Pythagoras and Empedocles, along with the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the Lyceum.</note>, called it *hyle* <note>original: "sylvam." The Latin *silva* (forest/wood) was the standard translation for the Greek *hyle*, meaning raw material or "timber."</note>. Plato indeed called it the formless womb, the mother of the world, the receptacle, the subject, the nurse of forms, and the power capable of them all. This is just as God is the one powerful to make all things, the shaper of all those same forms, the first cause acting in all things, the father of the world, and the fountain flowing in all things. And again they said that matter is the receiver and expeller of all species, just as the Craftsman distinguishes them according to the divine and causative examples. Matter is "non-being" and the passive principle of beings, just as God is the active principle of all, existing in all things and outside all things. From this, matter holds images and obscure manifestations and the requirements of the First Being. Whence every essence is led from potentiality to action, and that by right: for being placed diametrically opposite to each other, they project certain images of similarity.

The First Being, which is incomprehensible to the intellect, also constitutes an extreme that is incomprehensible to the intellect. And if anything of them can be apprehended, it will be grasped by negative reasoning. For the First is defined by the negative,
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic whose "negative theology" argued that we can only describe God by what He is NOT.</note> teaches: that He is nothing that exists among beings, but is the creative cause and better than them. The other extreme [matter] is also defined by negation: that it is nothing that exists among beings, but is worse than them. The first is most simple; the last is also most simple. But the latter wavers, leaping from form to form, while the former is always the same and always acting, just as the latter is always receiving as long as successive generation shall last. The middle intervals, participating in both extremes, are found to be more or less perfect, according as they [approach] one or the other extreme...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between divine principles and physical matter. It moves from defining matter as the "receptacle" of divine forms to establishing the correspondence between the element of Earth and the "Fatherly Mind" or the Archetype, bridging Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian and Jewish mystical traditions.</meta>

<header>THE SEVENTH TONE</header>
<page-num>CXXVIII</page-num>

<margin>Zeno. Plato. Socrates. Theologians.</margin>
...death approaches. Hence Zeno, the son of Mnaseas of Citium <note>Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BCE), the founder of Stoicism.</note>, established two principles of things: God and matter; of which he said the former was the cause of acting, and the latter the cause of suffering. But Plato and Socrates added a third, namely the **Idea** in the divine senses and visions of God, or in the divine mind, or the Word; as our Theologians are accustomed to hold, which is nonetheless the same thing. But here the sequence of the matter must be observed. Matter and its pure potentiality <term>potentiality</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "potentiality" is the capacity of matter to take on different forms.</note> correspond to the almighty Father: whence not without mystery does Moses introduce God as the creator and craftsman of this matter, which corresponds to Him without any intermediate cause. However, he describes other produced things through intermediate causes, yet by the command of the first parent and highest craftsman: so that the production of matter, and the produced matter itself, differs from the production of other things, and from the things themselves brought into the light. So much so, that Timaeus Locrus <note>A semi-legendary Pythagorean philosopher appearing in Plato's dialogues.</note> and Plato called the thinking of matter "spurious" <note>original: "spuriam" — often translated as "bastard reasoning," referring to how matter is difficult to grasp intellectually because it lacks form.</note> and alien to the thinking of other things.

<margin>Timaeus. Plato.</margin>
### With which the earth may be established. Chapter III.

<margin>Isaiah. Theologians. David. Plutarch. Physicists. Moses. CHRIST</margin>
**W**e have revealed through their fitting signs that all elements are found in the heavens, the angels, and in God: Now, however, it occurs to us to disclose by what harmony those same elements agree with the Archetype <term>Archetype</term><note>The original divine "blueprint" or master idea in the mind of God from which all creation is modeled.</note>. For the Fatherly mind is the most fertile of all, so that it might produce those two sprouts, namely the Son, and together with Him the Holy Spirit: through whom He produced all other things of this universe, and this entire globe. Which filial sprout He surely gave from Himself in the ordained course of time for the salvation of the nations. For which Isaiah, aware of these mysteries, prayed saying:
> Let the earth open, and sprout a Savior. <note>Isaiah 45:8.</note>
Our Theologians interpret this as the Blessed Virgin; the Hebrews interpret it as the last measure of the Archetype (which they call *Shekhinah* <note>original: "sachina"</note>, that is, the mediated and domestic dwelling of God in us). <margin>Earth is the Fatherly Mind.</margin> But (unless I am mistaken) it can rightly be understood as the Fatherly mind: which is the first budding-forth of the Son, and consequently of all other things. For concerning the Son, who is called the Word and the Truth of God, the Prophet [David] sings:
> Truth has sprung from the earth. <note>Psalm 85:11.</note>
Who also says that the water of salvation gushes from that same earth. This earth is therefore the receptive vessel of all fertilities, and consequently, like a first parent, it is the mother of all growth: so much so (on the authority of Plutarch) that the physicists believe God began the creation of the world from the earth as if from the center and the mother of all. Which Moses also implies when describing the production which God ordered to happen once the elemental foundations were cast, saying:
> Let the earth sprout green herbs, and fruit-bearing wood according to its kind. <note>Genesis 1:11.</note>
And just as these earthly trees do not live at all unless they are planted in the earthly element; so the Supreme Truth [Christ] says of the better and rational tree, that unless it is planted by the Father, the supreme farmer, namely in that supernal earth, it shall be uprooted. Also, this earth stands forever, never torn from its center, nor destined for another place, while all other elements and elemental things are agitated in a certain succession and seek diverse spaces. So too that first Mind is always stable in itself, neither sent anywhere, nor moved from its center, even if the Son, the Holy Spirit, and all intelligences are said to be sent forth to various ends.

<margin>David</margin>
Therefore, just as the earth is the center of the universe, so the Father is the center of the **intellectual sphere** <term>intellectual sphere</term><note>In Neoplatonic and mystical thought, this is the realm of pure divine thought and intelligence, where God's presence is most concentrated.</note>, existing everywhere through his essence and power; yet he appears in an open presence in the celestial palace, which serves as the earth and dwelling place of those citizens of heaven. Sighing for this place, the Prophet David used to say: *I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.*

### How the other elements resonate in the same way. Chapter 4.

<margin>John. Moses.</margin>
**A**s for Water, in which resides the **seed-bearing power** <note>original: "seminaria uirtus" — the inherent potential or "divine blueprints" within matter that allow life to sprout.</note> of animals (since their seed is of a watery nature), it corresponds to the Son. He, being the "True Water," contains the seed-bearing power of all things, as John says: *All things were made through the Word.* This is also what Moses said on behalf of the commanding Creator: *Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing, or the offspring of a living soul, and the winged creature flying above the earth, and over the face of the globe of the heavens.*

<margin>Thales.</margin>
For this reason, perhaps, Thales of Miletus <note>Thales (c. 624–545 BCE) is often called the first Greek philosopher; he famously proposed that water was the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>—from whom the Ionic school began—judged that water was the principle of all things. He believed that all things dissolve back into water, all are nourished by it, and all things wither if deprived of it.

<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>
And even though the seeds of fruits and herbs are of an earthy nature, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a fusion of Greek and Egyptian wisdom, central to the "Hermetic" tradition.</note> judged it necessary for them to **decay** <note>original: "tabescere" — in this context, it refers to the process where a seed must break down or "die" in the moist earth before it can germinate.</note> if they were to become fertile. For they were "decayed" from the beginning in the fountain of divine ideas. They likewise decay—either by the moisture of the earth, or by dew, or by rain, or by water added with intent—if they are to sprout.

<margin>Genesis.</margin>
Hence it is not without reason that in the description of the world's construction, it is said that the shrubs and plants had not yet germinated because God had not yet rained upon the earth.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Furthermore, even spiritual birth does not occur without water, which is the Son of God, as he himself said to Nicodemus: *Unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.* For from that "Divine Water," one receives the power of divine birth, but from that "Fiery Spirit," one receives the warmth of life and nourishment. Nor should one think that a man must be reborn from this common, elementary water to be fit for the kingdom of God; rather, it is from that Divine Water, of which this elementary water is but a sign and a **sacrament**.

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
Water is thus a necessary drink for sustaining the life of all plants and animals. Yet for man—as a royal living being—a more elegant drink has been prepared: specifically, the water which continually drips from that Vine which says: *I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener.* This water, soaking up a certain solar and beneficial power from that Vine, becomes a more profitable and celebrated cup for man, who is the overseer of all created things and the legitimate heir of the Creator himself.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus. CHRIST</margin>
The Wisdom of the Son of God is also the drink of the purified mind, as it is said in Ecclesiasticus: *And she gave him the water of wholesome wisdom to drink.* This Wisdom also cries out, saying: *If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.*

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
And again, speaking with the Samaritan woman, he said: *If anyone drinks of the water that I shall give him, it will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.* But even this water, once distilled through that super-mundane vine, is sometimes turned into the most healthful wine to be offered as a toast to his chosen family.

<margin>Solomon. CHRIST</margin>
To this, Wisdom invited us in the Song of Songs, saying: *Come and be drunk, my most beloved.* Regarding this wine, at the last banquet celebrated by the True Vine himself, he said: *Drink from this, all of you*—that is, from this earthly wine changed into the heavenly.

### Chapter V.
#### What stones signify to me.

<margin>CHRIST. Paul.</margin>
**C**oming to the elementary things, let us begin with stones, which are of the earth and, being suited for foundations and buildings, correspond to the Father and the Son. Hence, sometimes "rock" or "stone" is used for one, sometimes for the other, and sometimes for both. For the Son showed himself to be a rock when he said to Peter: *And upon this rock I will build my church*—that is, "upon myself," as everyone explains. Indeed, he himself is the foundational stone, as the Apostle says: *No man can lay another foundation, except that which is laid, Christ Jesus.* He is also called the "cornerstone," rejected indeed by those building according to the flesh and blood, but placed by the supreme architect at the head of the corner of the structure and building of that sacred Jerusalem, which is built from living stones. He was also that rock struck by Moses, from which waters flowed for the drink of the Israelite people, if Paul interprets it well when discussing it with the Corinthians. <margin>The same [Paul]</margin> *All our fathers,* he says, *were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock following them, and the rock was Christ.* 

But if we wish to understand the "water" as the wisdom of God, who is the Son (as we referenced above), then the rock from which that water of salvific wisdom flowed rightly signifies the Father. This is called *even* <note>original: אבן (Even)</note> in Hebrew, which we can perhaps interpret as "strength," "stony mountain," or "refuge." And who is strong, almighty, and the supreme refuge of all, but the eternal Father? Nor should anyone wonder that we take the "rock" now for the Father and now for the Son, because in the sacred scriptures it is sometimes used for both together. For even the Hebrew word *even* <note>אבן</note> signifies "stone"; if the first two letters of this word are taken, they make *Ab* <note>original: אב (Ab), meaning "Father"</note>, which signifies "Father." But if the middle letter is joined with the last, they constitute *Ben* <note>original: בן (Ben), meaning "Son"</note>, which is interpreted as "Son." Therefore, *even* <note>אבן</note>, which we call "rock," represents both the Father and the Son, who are one and the same. 

They were rejected by those building and constructing doctrines and statutes for the Hebrews or the Gentiles, who do not confess God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. He is called now the water flowing from the rock, and now that very same rock: because he proceeds from the Father, yet always existing as one with the Father. But how and why Moses struck this rock, and why God—angered by that striking—said to Moses and Aaron: *Because you did not believe me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, therefore you shall not lead this people into the land I have given them,* is a matter that requires a deeper investigation.

He struck it twice, namely with a double error: First, because he believed less than he ought; and second, because he transgressed the command. For the Lord had commanded that they should speak to the rock; but Moses, with Aaron consenting, struck it. Therefore, God complained that they did not believe—namely, that a word alone would be sufficient—and that they crossed the limits of the command by striking the rock, to which the Lord had ordered that they should only speak. And this was their sin; it was not, as many explain, because they claimed for themselves what they should have attributed to God. Nor was it a small transgression to carry out God’s work through severity (for that is what the striking implies) which God had determined to perform through piety, so that he might be more greatly sanctified among the people. Since they therefore wished to deal with the people with an "iron rod" (as they say), they deserved to feel the divine and "iron" sentence, by which it was said: *You shall not bring the people into the land which I have given them.* It would perhaps be too long and more mysterious than this place requires to uncover all the secrets that could be unlocked concerning the rock; and why

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
**M**etals, which are of a watery nature <note>original: "aquea sunt." Between these things, man holds a middle place, and it is necessary that he cling to one or the other. But let us hear the <margin>CHRIST.</margin> warnings of the Redeemer, saying: "Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven" <note>Matthew 6:20</note>. All other metals too, and everything necessary, have their place in the heavens, from whence they take the power and strength of whatever goodness is in them.

Heb.</margin> <note>This refers to Kabbalistic traditions where the four letters of the divine name are permuted to govern the months and astrological signs</note> And from this comes the fertility of all the signs and presiding intelligences, the primary spiritual influences, and the twelvefold fruits through the span of the entire year and time.

But not only are the "rational fruits"—that is, those well-initiated and soaked in that spiritual influence—healthful and beneficial; but even those who are unfruitful within themselves and not gifted with full grace (which theologians call "sanctifying grace") <note>original: "gratum facientem"; grace that makes a person pleasing to God</note> are useful to others. They impart doctrine and confer health through the sacraments and sacrifices, even though it may not benefit themselves. And these are the "leaves," of which it is said: *And the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.*

And this same tree is sometimes called the "knowledge of good and evil"—namely while, having emptied itself and been united with mortal flesh, it experiences also the evil of human suffering alongside the good, in which it most fully enjoys that divine portion. <margin>CHRIST</margin> <note>The author is identifying the Tree of Life/Knowledge with Christ, who experienced human "evil" (suffering) while remaining divine</note> This tree is in the middle of paradise, so that it might communicate its fruits in equal measure to everyone, according to the need of the recipients or the generosity of the giver. And from this, he sometimes names himself the vine, saying: *I am the vine, and you are the branches* <note>John 15:5</note>: so that in a mystical state, or in that true transformation which we sometimes undergo into God, we might be the same plant with the highest being—indeed, his very branches and sprouts.

Of this tree, or vine, and of the whole little garden with the other trees, the gardener is he of whom it is said: *And my Father is the gardener.* <note>John 15:1</note> For in that supreme garden, not only is that divine, exalted, and supramundane tree planted, but many others by which the whole little garden is filled, of which it is said in Genesis: <margin>Gen.</margin> *The Lord God produced from the earth*—namely the earth of the living—*every wood or tree beautiful to behold and sweet for eating.* <margin>Ibid.</margin> And again: *From every tree of paradise you may eat.* <margin>Ibid.</margin> For in that paradise these are not vegetative trees—the kind that are usually planted by us for a time, converted for use in buildings, or dried out to be burned—but those which have been planted from eternity by that gardener, of whom it is said in the same place: *The Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning.* <note>Genesis 2:8</note> He himself also says in Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah</margin> *I planted you as a chosen vineyard.* <note>Jeremiah 2:21 or Isaiah 5:2</note> And in a psalm it is said: <margin>Psalm</margin> *Perfect that which your right hand has planted.* <note>Psalm 80:15</note> But in another psalm nothing is more expressive than what is said: <margin>The same</margin> *The trees of Adonai shall be saturated*; <note>Psalm 104:16</note> where we [in the Latin Vulgate] have "the trees of the field" and "the cedars of Lebanon which he planted." These woods, or trees, are called <term>Adonai</term>, and <term>tetragrammi</term>, or <term>quadrilitteri</term> <note>meaning "four-lettered"</note>: so that it may be understood which trees he speaks of. <margin>Job</margin>
Job testifies concerning the angels, saying: *Behold, those who serve him are not stable*—or "they will not believe firmly"—*and in his angels he found changeability*, <note>original: "Ecce qui feruiunt ei, non sunt stabiles... in Angelis suis posuit mutationem"; see Job 4:18. <margin>CHRIST</margin>

<margin>Plato</margin>
Regarding that tree and other lofty trees, Plato—having been taught (in my opinion) by the prophets—speaks in the *Phaedrus* through the persona of Socrates beyond human paths, describing that higher and purer world, while at the same time separating all things that were produced for human use from this common condition. For he asserts that those [celestial] things are purer and more perfect: and that the true heaven is there, and the true light, and the true earth. From which, if anyone were to descend to this earth which we inhabit—to our stones, trees, flowers, fruits, and such things—everything would appear eaten away and corrupted by a certain saltiness of this [material] sea. 
<margin>Saturnian contemplatives</margin>
He also declares how great a difference there is between that contemplation held by the true "Saturnians"—divine men removed from the crowd—and that [vision] enjoyed by those who, entangled in these earthly cares, are contaminated by the saltiness, that is, the "wisdom" of this worldly sea. For he says there are trees, flowers, fruits, mountains, and stones there: sardius, jasper, emerald, and others of this kind, of which our [earthly] stones are merely certain deformed fragments. We arrive at the contemplation and clear intuition of these things when we are "dead"—as he revealed quite openly above—not indeed by the death of the body, but through a total sequestering of the senses and by the purifying virtues <note>In Neoplatonism, "purgatory" or "purifying" virtues are the first stage of spiritual ascent, where the soul detaches from bodily passions.</note> from everything foreign and alien. Until, however, all those things are offered to us to be looked upon with a clear gaze and contemplated with a revealed face, we must hold discourse among ourselves through these lower things, by which we may be able to hint at supramundane and divine things, and finally, under these auspices, be raised up to them, not unmindful of our lot.

The author is debating the translation of the Hebrew word "Aravot."</note> Regarding this, a faulty translation contains "the sunset" [or "the west"]: for <term>haravot</term> <note>Hebrew: עֲרָבוֹת (*aravot*), the name for the highest of the seven heavens in Jewish tradition.</note> signifies "pleasantness" or a "plain." But this [word for "plain"] is punctuated with two <term>segols</term>, whereas the other [the word for "evening"] is punctuated with <term>patah</term> and <term>qamets</term> <note>These are technical terms for the vowel markings used in Hebrew script.</note>; thus they differ entirely in meaning. When John (as Luke relates) <note>original: "Iohañes (ut narrat Lucas)"; see Luke 9:54-56</note> wished to call down fire from heaven to consume the Samaritans who had neglected to receive Christ with hospitality, He rebuked them, saying: "Do you not know of what spirit you are sons?" namely, of peace and charity. Wherefore He Himself, teaching better by deeds than by words, stood like a mute before the one shearing him, not opening His mouth, and like a lamb led to the slaughter. This was observed by the true Christians, who for three hundred years and more endured innumerable kinds of martyrdom with an undisturbed mind. Among them, neither murmur nor complaint resounded, for they had become imitators of that true Lamb seated at the right hand of God, who was led silent to the sacrifice, not opening His mouth in blasphemy, insults, or any complaints. 

But alas, these unhappy times! when only the name remains among Christians, all Israelite—nay, Christian—meekness and gentleness having been put to flight. The scythes and plowshares into which the swords had once been forged <note>A reference to Isaiah 2:4, reversing the prophecy of peace into a state of war.</note> they have forged again into spears and the sharpest, most harmful long-swords. They have become followers of Esau and Edomites <note>In biblical typology, Esau/Edom often represents the "earthly" or violent man as opposed to the spiritual Jacob/Israel.</note>: bristly, horrid, and more contentious than all other nations and peoples, so much so that they are never free from litigation in either temporal or spiritual matters. They are everywhere addicted to everlasting contentions, so that Christ may now least of all recognize them as His own, but may say to them: "I do not know you," and exclude from that most peaceful, gentle, and pleasant kingdom those who have always followed harsh paths and a bristly life. 

"We have possessed," (says Moses in his typical <term>typical: relating to "types" or prophetic symbols in the Bible</term> discourse) "all the cities situated in the plain," and he himself became their good possessor, of whom it is said in the book of Numbers that he was the gentlest man above all who dwelt on the earth.
