# OF THE FIRST CANTICLE

<margin>Psalm</margin>
<margin>Genesis</margin>
<margin>David</margin>
That supreme Zion speaks, to which this lower Zion—existing in the center of the world <note>original: "meditullio mundi." A common medieval geographical concept placing Jerusalem/Zion at the physical and spiritual center of the Earth.</note>—is perpendicularly subjected. Thus, from both, the true mediator and the celestial fountain may distribute manna, honey, milk, and the water of wisdom, and all good things to everyone. This is so that we may possess not only the level plain, but also the well-watered mountain country—that is, the eminence of glory and the degrees within that midday of grace—and Goshen <note>original: "Gessen."</note>, which is soaked and moistened by those heavenly channels and streams, or by that celestial rain spoken of in the **Psalm**: *You, O God, shall set aside a voluntary rain for your inheritance.* For "Goshen" is interpreted as "rain." Let us also possess the Plain, and the *Arabah* <note>original: "harauah." A Hebrew term for a desert plain or steppe.</note> of which we spoke above, and the flatlands, and the mountains of Israel—not indeed the woody and parched ones, but the fruitful and finest ones—and that part of the mountain which ascends toward Seir. For Mount Seir is the summit of worldly prosperity given to Esau, a portion of which was also given to Israel. Although a portion of divine matters was given to him as the cord of his inheritance, they were nevertheless not left destitute of those temporal goods which are called the gifts of fortune. The true Israelites did not possess these goods apart from their Patron, who is God, but rather together with Him, who said to Abraham: *I will be your exceeding great reward.* And of whom the Prophet said on behalf of himself and his fellow Israelites: *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.* Therefore, Joshua notably said that their portion extended as far as Baal-gad <note>original: "Bahalgad."</note>, which is interpreted as "the patron" or "the Lord of fortune." There are also arid and deserted mountains, which fall to one's lot along with the "dry land" of which we shall speak presently. Therefore, we shall pass over such dry mountains with a dry foot until we reach the uncultivated and barren wilderness, where we shall treat both.

->Chapter 10: What the desert and the dry land are.<-

<margin>Psalm</margin>
<margin>Leviticus</margin>
Since nothing exists in this lower world without its presiding intelligence (as many wise men agree) and without an "Idea" or measure in the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the divine mind or the original pattern in God's intellect from which all physical things are copied.</note> to which it responds and by which it is governed, it is fitting that even the desert and the arid places—having themselves been fashioned by the hand of the Lord—should have their own intelligences and something in the supramundane court, by whatever name it may be called. From this source they receive their dryness, or are secluded from the watering of the supreme fountain, which is the source of all true irrigation. Therefore, the desert is (to begin with the etymology of the word) a place destitute and abandoned by celestial favor, just as the Hebrew word sounds, which is *midbar* <gloss>Hebrew: מדבר</gloss>, and according to the etymology of that language, it is said to be "without anything." It is also called "the arid" or "the dry," as the Hebrew word sounds well when the waters are gathered into one place. Therefore, when the supramundane waters are gathered into one place, other places remain with a dry influence, neither watering nor moistening those things which they tend. Thus, all those places remain parched and dry, deprived of celestial benefit, as is sung in the **Psalm**: *When you turn away your face, they shall be troubled; you shall take away their spirit*—which is given through the heavenly watering—*and they shall fail, and return to their dust.* And in **Leviticus** the Lord says: *If you will not hear...*

But it must be noted that desert and arid places differ in many ways. For some are deprived only of the "heavenly irrigation"—not indeed entirely, for they would then vanish into nothingness, but rather more or less according to the worthiness of those receiving it, or according to the command of the one who irrigates. Others, however, are dried up not only by the absence of the supreme watering, but by the fire of that **Chaldean furnace** <note>The "Chaldean furnace" refers to the fiery furnace of Babylon mentioned in the Book of Daniel, here used as a symbol for intense spiritual trial or the fires of hell.</note>, whose flame ascended forty-nine cubits—a square number signifying both remission and punishment <note>Forty-nine is 7x7. In the biblical tradition, 7 is a number of perfection or completion, and 49 (the year before the Jubilee) often carries themes of debt-release and judgment.</note>. <margin>John</margin>

->What the fruitful earth is.<-

### Chapter XI.

<margin>Genesis</margin>
**N**o one doubts that the entire earth is dry by its own nature, as it says in Genesis: *The earth, however, was empty and void.* And again: *God called the dry land 'earth'.* This remains so until it is watered by its own springs, as follows in the same place: *A spring ascended, watering the entire face of the earth.* Therefore, made wet by this irrigation, the earth is made good. We have proven above that this "earth" is of many kinds: elemental, human, heavenly, angelic, divine, and internal. This internal earth is called by Job "the land of misery and darkness," where <margin>Job</margin> the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells. But setting aside this land—which is always dry and scorched by eternal fire—let us pursue that which is fertile and from where it is watered. For this elemental earth is only as fruitful as it is watered by heavenly springs—not indeed by common rain alone, which descends onto sterile mountains, rocks, dry ground, and completely infertile sand—but by the higher waters, both heavenly and super-heavenly. For the fruitful earth receives its natural fertility from nowhere else, as we can easily prove from many places in Sacred Scripture; I will bring forth a few out of many. Moses says in Deuteronomy: *If you listen to the voice of the Lord... <margin>Deuteronomy</margin> he will make you abound in all your works, in the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your cattle, and the fruit of your land, which the Lord swore to give to your fathers, so that he might give it to you. The Lord will open his best treasure, the heavens, to provide rain for your land in its season.* And through Ezekiel he says: <margin>Ezekiel</margin> *I will give a blessing around my hill, and I will bring down the shower in its season, and there shall be rains of blessing. And the tree of the field shall give its fruit, and the earth shall give its sprout.* In Zechariah also he says: <margin>Zechariah</margin> *These things I will do for the remnants of this people: the vine shall give its fruit, and the earth shall give its sprout, and the heavens shall give their dew.* And even if He does this, as in most cases, through secondary causes <note>Natural processes or intermediary forces</note>, sometimes He does it immediately; as the Lord speaks in the clearest language in <margin>Deuteronomy</margin> Deuteronomy, saying: *The land which you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt from which you came, where irrigation waters are led after the seed is cast, in the manner of gardens; but it is mountainous and level ground, awaiting rains from heaven, which the Lord your God always looks upon, and His eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year until the end. And if you obey my commands, which I command you today—to love the Lord your God and serve Him with all your heart and all your soul—He will give the early and late rain to your land.*

-># OF THE FIRST SONG<-

you gather grain, wine, oil, and hay from the fields to feed the cattle. This is a most beautiful doctrine, by which we are taught that Egypt—which signifies this world and worldly men—receives its watering from secondary causes <note>Natural processes like rain or irrigation, rather than direct divine miracles.</note> following the order given to them by Him who *makes His sun to rise upon the good and the bad, and rains upon the just and the unjust.* But special places and those who dwell in them receive an immediate increase from the very fountain of all goods. Beyond what the order of secondary causes requires, He opens the veins and channels of His goodness, pouring out and sending in grace whenever and wherever He pleases.

That which comes from ordered causes, acting unchangeably at the command of the Creator—or by an intelligence (as they say) that does not err in commanding or executing—is called the "work of nature." But in this particular case, the Creator works in a certain way according to the merits or crimes of the recipients. Thus, beyond the general and common care for all things (which they call "natural influence"), the Free Moderator <note>God, acting as a sovereign governor who can choose to give more or less.</note> grants abundance to those who deserve it, according to the promises brought forward, and withdraws it from those who deserve poorly. 

We can prove this from many places in Scripture. For He threatened in the same repetition of the Law <note>The book of Deuteronomy.</note>, saying: "If <margin>Deuter.</margin> you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God, cursed shall be the fruit of your womb, and the fruit of your land, the herds of your oxen, and the flocks of your sheep. And the Lord will strike you with poverty, fever, cold, burning, heat, and corrupted air. And the sky above you shall be as **brass**, and the earth you tread upon as **iron**. The Lord will give dust as rain for your land," and so forth. 

This has happened at various times. For in the time of Elisha, that most fertile land was dried up, so that the inhabitants of Jericho said to <margin>4 Kings</margin> him (as we read in the <term>Fourth Book of Kings</term><note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 2:19.</note>): "The waters here are very bad, and the land is sterile." And the whole plain around the <margin>Genesis</margin> <term>Asphaltites</term><note>The Dead Sea, often called Lake Asphaltites in antiquity due to its bitumen or asphalt.</note>—which, as we read in Genesis, was well-watered like the paradise of God before the Lord overthrew that <term>Pentapolis</term><note>The "Five Cities" of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah.</note>—is now (as we have seen) entirely dried up like the ash of a furnace. This matches the words of <margin>Jeremiah</margin> Jeremiah: "Because of a curse, the fields are dried up." This also happened because of the crimes of Ahab in the time of Elijah, when the rains were held back for three years. 

Regarding such matters, the <margin>David</margin> <term>Psalmist</term><note>The "Psalmographus" or writer of the Psalms, King David.</note> says: "He turned a fruitful land into a salt marsh because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it." Therefore, whatever land it may be, if it is to be fruitful, it must be irrigated by heavenly fountains through the mediation of that "land" of which the Prophet says: "I believe I shall see the goods of the Lord in the land of the living." That land, irrigated by the higher channels like a "superior pool," pours out into the interior earth and its inhabitants. 

And regarding that land, the same <margin>Ibid.</margin> Prophet says: "You have visited the earth and watered it; you have enriched it in many ways." For he does not speak of this <term>filthy earth</term><note>original: "feculenta," meaning dreg-filled or muddy.</note>, but of the divine earth, as he implies in what follows: "The River of God is filled with water." For the River of God is not suited to this lowest earth, but to that heavenly one, with its better hills and valleys, concerning which he adds: "The hills shall be girded with joy, and the valleys shall abound with grain; they shall cry out and sing a hymn." This, finally, is that earth of which we read in Genesis, which, before the Lord sent rain, a "fountain" or "vapor" (as the true text has it) [watered]...

It is also irrigated by that fountain which, divided into four rivers, moistens, hydrates, and makes fruitful the entire circuit of the lands. From <margin>Isaac</margin> which land, as if from a true reservoir <note>original: "piscina," literally a pool or cistern, here used as a source of grace.</note> of all spiritual gifts and blessings, Isaac—being well-instructed in such matters—wished to bless both of his sons, repeating this for both: *In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven shall your blessing be.* But in blessing Esau, he added that word **from above**, lest he—being a carnal and natural man—should seem to be excluded from the blessing of the heavenly reservoir from which every blessing descends. For by this the Angels are bedewed, who are called "earthly" <note>The author likely refers to angels who minister to the material world or are lower in the celestial hierarchy.</note>, as we discussed above. The regions of heaven are also bedewed, as are the earthly heavens themselves, and our own <margin>Psalm</margin> bodies, and whatever in us is parched, waiting for the heavenly watering, as it is said in the Psalm: *The Lord will give kindness, and our earth will yield its fruit.* For **kindness** or **goodness** (as the Hebrew text has it <note>Refers to the Hebrew word 'Tob' or 'Chesed' in Psalm 85:12.</note>) is the blessing and the watering flowing from that land of the living, bedewed and filled with the waters that are above the heavens. By these waterings, the earthly man, having been moistened, becomes capable of receiving the divine seed, <margin>CHRIST</margin> of which the heavenly farmer says: *A sower went out to sow his seed.* A portion of which, as he adds, fell into good soil. This soil (without a doubt) is the soul, or the mind infused or joined into this earthly and bodily vessel. Thus, having become in a certain way earthly itself, it must be bedewed by the super-celestial watering through that land of the living, of which it is likewise said: *Truth has sprung from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven.* Therefore, all our industry must be cultivated while the heavenly farmer waters and sows, so that it may yield fruits by which we may deserve to enter into His super-celestial land with the divine farmer, to dwell forever in the eternal mansions built upon that land; which may He, in His kindness, grant.

->### What the sea and the waters are. Chapter 12.<-

<margin>Genesis</margin> We are taught by the sacred utterances and by clear experience that the sea is a collection of waters, and that this is twofold: one which is under the heaven, and another which is above the heaven; between which is the globe or mass of the heavens. This lowest sea is therefore foul and salty from its agitation and heat; hence it is harmful to man for food and drink. It is, however, fertile for fish, producing also coral and pearls <note>original: "margaritas"</note>, and it is the origin of all sweet rivers and rains that fertilize the regions. Furthermore, its water, passing through subterranean passages to the springs, leaves behind its moisture and power, from which the earth—warmed by the sun’s rays—may produce metals. Yet it receives this fertility from those upper waters, of which it says: *Let the waters creep, or bring forth the creeping things of a living soul.* For not every living soul is produced from the sea, but from those waters which are above the heaven. If the intervening heaven did not stand in the way, those surpassing waters would make these lower ones, and the earth, and all lower things, even more fertile. For the intermediate heaven stands in the way—or rather, the ministers presiding therein...

Great indeed are the mysteries of the rivers: for the sea and the infinite deep is God himself, but the fountains are of a manifold kind. The rivers, however, are rational souls emanating from that same sea and returning to the same. But these elementary rivers flow and reflow in an eternal lapse and circuit; however, those better rivers—signified by these—tend toward their beginning once and in a single course, unless the opinion of the Pythagoreans regarding the circuit of souls <note>original: "circuitu animarum." A reference to metempsychosis or reincarnation, the belief that souls cycle through different bodies.</note> were true, which the <margin>Pythagoras</margin> Catholic faith does not admit. Concerning these rivers, it is sung in the <margin>Psalm</margin> Psalm: *The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice; the rivers have lifted up their waves.* <note>original: "Eleuauerunt flumina Domini, eleuauerunt flumina uocem suam: eleuauerunt flumina fractiones suas." Psalm 93:3 (Vulgate 92:3). The author interprets "fractiones" (breakings/waves) as the spiritual stirrings of the soul.</note> For neither the Eridanus, the Danube, the Tagus, the Nile, the Euphrates, nor the Indus are called the "rivers of the Lord," but rather the rivers of lands and regions; nor do they cry out or lift their voice. Therefore, these rivers of the Lord are those endowed with a mouth, tongue, ears, eyes, and hands, of whom it is said again: *The rivers shall clap their hands.* <note>Psalm 98:8 (Vulgate 97:8).</note> And the force of these rivers gladdens the city of God, while they pass through the earthy passages of this body from the eternal sea to the fountains; from which they still return to the sea itself through the earthy channels, but opening publicly by working in the body of the world, giving in their passage due fruits: irrigation to the earth, offspring to the fish, and passage to navigators—not suffocation, not the flooding of lands, not the ruin of buildings. Because those who do such things are not called rivers of peace gladdening the city of the Lord, but rather "Babylonians," <margin>Psalm</margin> about whom it is said in the psalm: *By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept.* <note>Psalm 137:1 (Vulgate 136:1). In this allegory, Babylon represents confusion and destructive, inordinate passions.</note> For they suffocate and destroy with an excessive or inordinate force, or they are dried up and become parched, according to that saying of <margin>Isaiah</margin> Isaiah: *And the water shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up, and the rivers shall fail. The streams of the embankments shall be diminished and dried up, and the channel of the stream from its fountain shall be laid bare; and every irrigated seed shall dry up.* <note>Isaiah 19:5–7. The author uses this prophecy of drought to represent the withdrawal of divine grace.</note> He pursues many other things as well, all of which would be tedious to re-examine and explain. 

But these dried-up channels are sometimes filled with the fire of punishing justice, which causes the rivers of mercy and piety to dry up—rivers which the impious do not deserve to receive. There are also "rivers of eloquence," as the adage is now common. There are also rivers of wisdom, as is said in plain speech in <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Ecclesiasticus: *I, Wisdom, have poured out rivers like a channel of immense water: I am like the rivers* <term>diorix</term><gloss>that is, a fishpond of a river, or a diversion</gloss>, and not the river "dorix" as faulty manuscripts have it; *and like an aqueduct I went out of Paradise, and said: I will water my garden of plantings, and I will inebriate the fruit of my offspring.* <note>original: "Ego sapientia effudi flumina quasi trames aquae immensae: Ego quasi fluuii diorix... sicut aquaeductus exiui de Paradiso." Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:41-42. The term "diorix" is a Latinization of the Greek word for a trench or canal.</note> And of <margin>Solomon</margin> Solomon it is said again: *He was filled as if with a river of wisdom.* <note>Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 47:16.</note> <margin>Job</margin> Job also says of the one seeking wisdom: *He has searched the depths of the rivers, and brought hidden things to light.* <note>Job 28:11.</note> These rivers flow most powerfully from the land flowing with milk and honey. They flow also from human <margin>CHRIST</margin> earth, if the supreme Truth <note>A common title for Christ (Veritas).</note> brings forth the truth...

when he says: "He who believes in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." <note>original: "Qui crediderit in me, flumina de uentre eius fluent aquæ uiuæ." The author distinguishes between the physical world and the "spiritual world" or Church.</note> For this world of foul earth, whose lord is the prince of darkness, was not founded upon the rivers; but the world of the church, and of the earth from which truth has sprung—the dwelling place of the Saints—is indeed founded upon the rivers, and upon those foundations of which the <margin>Paul</margin> Apostle says: "You are citizens of the saints, and the household of God, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets." These are the solid bases of the spiritual building and the rivers that irrigate all around. All these rivers, however, derive their power from that greatest river which (as we read in Genesis) went out from the place of pleasure to water paradise. And behold, it was divided into four heads. For that river first waters the paradise of pleasure through all the high channels, and was afterwards divided into four heads by a great mystery <note>original: "sacramento." In this context, it refers to a hidden spiritual meaning or sacred sign.</note> signified by the four letters of the most sacred name. <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH).</note> The full twelvefold revolution of this name gives (as we have said) fruitfulness to all the portions of the starry heavens and to those presiding intelligences, from whence they flow into the lower things contained under those portions. Thus, by drinking that water, and being moistened and washed, we may return to the very fountain and sea of all graces and pleasures, having completed the required course of our pilgrimage.

### What pools, lakes, and ponds are. Chapter XV.

<margin>pool.</margin>
From the sea, fountains, rivers, and waters gushing from the bowels of the earth—sometimes with the help of rain—there arise ponds, lakes, and pools; yet in the Sacred Scripture, these are held in very different regard. For the pool, which among the Hebrews has a name signifying blessing, is always auspicious. For <term>ברכה</term> <gloss>beraca</gloss> <note>The Hebrew word Berakhah (בְּרָכָה).</note> signifies both "blessing" and "pool." But the name for a lake, which is mostly translated from <term>בור</term> <gloss>bor</gloss> <note>The Hebrew word Bor (בּוֹר), meaning a pit, cistern, or the grave.</note>—which signifies a pit or a certain place of the underworld—is always inauspicious. A pond, however, which in Hebrew is called <term>אגם</term> <gloss>Agam</gloss>, is used sometimes in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense. But in ascending to the better things signified by these lower ones, it must be noted: that a pool, just as it receives water, so it pours it out, so that no putrefaction of the waters ever occurs within it. These are they who communicate the talents they have received and gain a profit unto a blessing by sharing themselves with others, according to the apostolic sentiment which says: <margin>The same [Paul]</margin> "I have become all things to all men, that I might win them for Christ." <note>1 Corinthians 9:22.</note> So also are those who communicate the <margin>CHRIST</margin> wisdom or doctrine granted to them, just as the Supreme Truth <note>A title for Christ.</note> teaches: <margin>Solomon</margin> "Freely you have received, freely give." And of these the Wise Man <note>Solomon, traditionally considered the author of Ecclesiastes.</note> speaks, who communicated that wisdom which he received as a divine gift by teaching and writing: "I made me," he said, "pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees." <note>Ecclesiastes 2:6.</note>

## Chapter XVI.
->What the Red Sea [signifies].<-

<margin>Exodus 14. The same. Jerome. Paul. Augustine. Jerome. [Saint]. Exodus. Psalm 104.</margin> **T**he Red Sea is not without cause so celebrated in sacred speech, because <term>ים סוף</term> <gloss>Yam Suph</gloss>—that is, the "finite sea" or "marshy sea" by its true interpretation—signifies this: For God alone is the infinite sea. All other seas, lakes, and pools are finite, limited, and disturbed; they are rendered marshy and filthy, filled either with saltiness or with earth and mud. And these are the seas we must cross together with the adjacent desert, so that finally, having passed through the hills and mountains, we may arrive at that clear and sweetest sea from which true milk and honey continuously flow. This happens once we have left behind Pharaoh—that is, the "destroyer" and "shaker"—along with his Egyptians, whose name is interpreted as "distress" or "those who cause distress." They are in that very marsh, which is formed by the mixing of water with earth; hence it is made swampy and, for the most part, filled with reeds. This is why we have that text well interpreted where the mother of Moses placed her son in the reeds of the river bank, where in Hebrew it is written <term>סוף</term> <note>Suph</note>, which elsewhere we find interpreted as "red," and together with <term>ים</term> <note>Yam</note>, which signifies "sea," it is interpreted as the Red Sea. Yet these "reeds" are not [limited to] that specific Red or marshy sea (called the Arabian Gulf) crossed by the Israelite people, since that is a long journey away from the royal city. Therefore, by <term>Zuph</term> it is well interpreted as "reeds" or "marshy," where (alas for us wretches) we are all placed together with Moses when, emanating from that most clear and immense sea, we enter into this bodily prison, <note>The author uses the term "ergastulum," a Roman work-house or prison, to describe the physical body.</note> only to return again to that same supreme ocean. We, therefore, must make the crossing through this narrow and marshy sea, but indeed a sea that is divided; so that we may obtain a free passage, leaving behind its inhabitants to be enveloped in that filth and to be overwhelmed by their own marsh along with their most stubborn leader, in whose mire they were rolled. Having crossed this sea, the true *phasce*—that is, the true "passing over"—must be celebrated by us with the greatest solemnity, with God as our leader, <margin>David</margin> and it must be said with the Psalmist: "We have sinned with our fa[thers]..." <note>Psalm 106:6 (Vulgate numbering). The text cuts off mid-word: "patribus."</note>

### What clouds and rain [signify]. Chapter XVII.

Two benefits are bestowed upon us from the clouds: one is shelter; the other is rain. And both mitigate the vigor of the sun. For its light is too excellent and strikes eyes that are poorly disposed or unaccustomed to such light; and its drying and burning heat sometimes parches. Yet both are necessary. For their tempering, the highest Governor commands clouds to be placed in between for a time, which may suppress the light and moisten and bedew the parched parts. No differently, those better clouds—of which these are but an image—are placed in between like veils, when the weak eyes of mortals cannot gaze upon the glory and splendor of the Maker, who is the true sun. Acknowledging this, David says: *You who make the cloud your ascent,* <note>Or "your chariot."</note> or your tribunal; or better yet, as the literal truth of the text holds. Thus His glory, or He Himself sitting in His glory, is like a cloud to those unable to look upon it because of the weakness of their sight, until it shall be granted to see Him face to face, just as He is.

### Chapter XVIII.
#### What dew and hoarfrost signify.

<margin>Plato</margin>
<margin>moving</margin>
<margin>benefit</margin>
**P**ouring down <note>The original Latin begins with a decorative 'P' for "Pluunt" (they rain down).</note> from the sky in clear weather are dew and hoarfrost, but there is a very great difference between them. For the former is pure, fertile, happy, and always beneficial. The latter, however, is ill-omened and harmful, descending with the greatest chill, and when it appears, the rivers are dried up and fail. And it is indeed a marvel that the moisture of the dew should nourish, while this wintry moisture <note>original: "brumalis"</note> dries up, burns the plants, and in a certain way consumes the earth itself. Thus from the same heaven comes both benefit and harm. For by the same sun, clay is hardened and wax is melted, according to the varying disposition of the receiver. From the most beneficent Christ, some receive a benefit and others harm, according to the prophecy of Simeon:

<margin>Simeon</margin>
> Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel.

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Finally, from the best God proceeds both good and evil, as Isaiah says: *I am the one making good and creating evil, making light and creating darkness.* Yet this stands alongside what Jeremiah says in Lamentations regarding the best God himself:

<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
> Out of the mouth of the most High proceed not evil and good. <note>Lamentations 3:38. This is presented as a paradox: God is the source of all, yet strictly speaking, "evil" is a human perception or a lack of good.</note>

And so that these words are not in conflict, we shall say that all things which proceed from God and from heaven are good in themselves, but are to us neither good nor evil except according to our own good or evil disposition: either in how much we use them well, or abuse them. Therefore, even if the first [hoarfrost] is counted among harmful things, it nevertheless favors the cabbage or kale, which it matures and perfects; it also kills worms so they do not gnaw the grain. But leaving this winter frost aside, let us come to the other thing figured by it: which is a certain effect of <term>punitive justice</term> <note>original: "iustitiæ punitiuæ"</note> descending when the earth is frozen and charity has grown cold, and when the rivers or channels of graces and divine <term>charisms</term> <note>spiritual gifts or favors</note> are dried up by men parched with fear and their own iniquity. This occurs to such an extent that even that bedewing is harmful, which would not harm those who are well-disposed at all; yet it still often profits them, as Gregory says:

<margin>Gregory</margin>
The evils that press upon us here compel us to go to God. Behold, therefore, how this winter frost, even if it destroys the wicked, nevertheless matures and perfects those who are well-disposed and receive it with patience. But dew is always beneficial; it is the virtue of the divine word bedewing those who hear it, soothing and cooling them. Therefore...

<margin>Hebrew Theology</margin>
...signifies, is the sheath of the most sacred four-letter name <note>original: "nominis quadrilitteri" refers to the Tetragrammaton, YHWH, the four-letter name of God</note>, so that we may reveal something of the secrets of hidden Hebrew theology. And although the word of God is published everywhere, even to rustics and the common folk, and the sounding voice reaches the ears of all, nevertheless its sense and taste—which are dew and manna—are diffused to very few, <margin>Haggai</margin> because it is denied to all who are unworthy, as the Lord says through the prophet Haggai:
> Because my house is deserted (that is, divine worship) and each man hastens to his own house seeking his own things and not those which are God’s, because of this the heavens were forbidden (that is, heavenly men) from giving dew, and the earth (the unworthy people) from giving its sprout. And I have called for a drought upon the earth, upon the mountains, and finally upon the works of the hands of those men who do not care for the things that are God’s.
<margin>David</margin> And acknowledging that dew is withheld by God’s severe justice, the Royal Prophet said of the mountains in which Saul was punished by it:
> Mountains of Gilboa <note>original: "Gelboe"</note>, let neither dew nor rain pass over you.
Thus, when we provoke that very justice of God against us by our wicked deeds, our earth becomes parched; and being unfruitful because dew and rain are withheld, it cannot give its fruit, because it does not receive that supreme blessing from the pool through rain and dew. <margin>Psalms</margin> May the Lord, in His kindness, send this down upon us, so that we may say with the Prophet:
> For the Lord will give His bounty, and our earth shall yield its fruit.

### What hail and snow signify. Chapter XIX.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin>
**T**he <note>The original Latin begins with a decorative woodcut 'S' for "Summus" (The highest).</note> highest and just judge, although He has prepared many good things for the favor of the good, has nevertheless also established some for the vengeance of evildoers, some of which are numbered in Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach</note>, where it is said:
> Fire, hail, famine, and death: all these were created for vengeance.
<margin>CHRIST</margin> And concerning fire—not the kind that warms but the kind that tortures—the Judge Himself threatens that He will say to those to be punished:
> Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels;
so that it may be for the vengeance and punishment of both. But since we have said enough about fire above, let us come to hail, which is water frozen in the air. It differs from snow and hoarfrost because hail is produced from rain frozen more firmly; snow from moisture more softly compressed; and hoarfrost from cold dew. And that frozen water, if it is packed together by a stronger cold, becomes hail itself; if by a lighter cold, however, it is generated as small grains which usually fall in springtime, such as in March and April. And it is not without wonder that water is frozen into hail in the summer season, and that in greater heat there is a greater freezing and larger amounts of water, whence it is called "grando" <note>hail</note> as if it were a "grandis aquæ gutta" <note>a large drop of water</note>. <margin>Job</margin> Therefore, not without cause, among the treasures of God (or of nature, which is His work and property), snow and hail are counted, as God Himself says in Job:
> Have you entered the treasuries of the snow, or have you beheld the treasuries of the hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?
From this we have proof that such things are not merely produced by lower and natural causes, as those whom they call "naturalists" or "physicists" strive to declare—fancifully and in vain—since they are ignorant of those things stored in the treasuries of the Creator.

Also, those Nazirites in 
<margin>Lamentations</margin>
Lamentations are said to be whiter than snow, since the brilliance of spiritual things is purer than the whiteness of snow, even though snow holds the highest rank of whiteness among physical things. To this whiteness, as if to something auspicious, 
<margin>Solomon</margin>
Solomon in the Book of Proverbs compares happy things, saying: *As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to him who sent him; he refreshes the soul of his master.* This was cited on behalf of the Eastern peoples, who are accustomed to preserve snow as a faithful guardian of the gift granted to them by the Supreme Provider, so that in summer and at harvest time it might slightly cool the fires of the sun and temper their burning limbs, so they may rest from that fiery agitation. In the same way, a faithful messenger tempers the anxious cares of his prince. This also has a place among the Gospel orators <note>The "orators" here refer to the preachers or Apostles.</note>, who were sent to that harvest of which the Lord said: *The harvest indeed is great, but the laborers are few.* Returning from this, the seventy-two faithful messengers (as 
<margin>Luke</margin>
Luke relates) with joy over the work done in the harvest, the Prince who had sent them also rejoiced; wherefore it follows: *In that hour he exulted in the Holy Spirit, saying: I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth,* and the rest that follows. Behold how much the Lord was refreshed by the faithful execution of the messengers He had sent. Furthermore, snow is cold, but its coldness—which is preserved in straw <note>Snow was historically packed in straw or "chaff" (*palea*) in pits to keep it from melting into the summer months.</note> filled with a good temperament, or rather tending toward warmth—is not a cold that expels the heat of charity, but rather one that restrains the heat of lust. And it is kept warm by the garment of double love, or charity: toward God and toward neighbor, according to that saying of the Wise Man in Proverbs: *She shall not fear for her house from the cold of snow, for all her household are clothed in double garments* <note>original: "uestiti sunt duplicibus"; Proverbs 31:21. While some translations say "scarlet," the Latin *duplicibus* implies "double-layered" or "twofold."</note>—namely, supported by both forms of charity, or by a good mind together with good works, as 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
Jerome mentions in his Commentaries. Yet if snow is dissolved into water that has not been boiled by fire, it causes harm. In the same way, if this coldness and the zeal for chastity is dissolved into the flowing water of worldly glory, and not "cooked" by the fire of the Holy Spirit and divine love, it harms and damns, and causes a return to a greater 
<margin>Job</margin>
heat of lust, according to that passage in Job: *They shall pass from the snow waters to excessive heat.* Snow, therefore, is the zeal for good works, which suppresses the heat of evil lust, serves God and neighbor, and shines with the brilliance of a good example and becomes white with purity. Hoarfrost, however, since it is frozen dew, represents those who receive the word of 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
God as hard as a rock, whereby the power of that divine word is frozen within them. And of such people it is said in the Gospel, where the seed of the word of God is discussed: *Other seed fell upon rock, and as soon as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture*—the power of the divine word being frozen by the hardness of the receiver, so much so that it brings forth no fruit in them.

# OF THE FIRST SONG

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
In the Book of Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientiæ"; referring to the Wisdom of Solomon.</note> it is said: *It was easily dissolved like ice.* <note>original: "glaties"; here referring to the temporary nature of the hope of the unrighteous.</note> But crystal is so compressed that, once the pores are completely emptied and removed, it can no longer admit heat into its interior to be dissolved. These things are also stored in the Lord’s treasury, and are commemorated in the sacred scriptures as a mysterious type <note>a "type" is a symbolic figure or foreshadowing.</note>; and they are invited into the praise of the Creator by those youths who were sprinkled with divine dew in the burning furnace: *Bless the ice and snow, the Lord:* because they also fulfill His word and carry out the command of the Prince. 

But let us come to man, for whose sake all things were made and all these things are commemorated. Ice holds the image of the sinner, for whom the water of divine kindness has been frozen by the cold of sin and by the north wind <note>In biblical symbolism, the north is often associated with the source of evil or spiritual coldness.</note>, from whence all evil is spread and opened, as it is said in Ecclesiasticus: *The cold north wind blew, and the crystal froze from the water.* But would that this frozen water, transcending the limits of ice, would not turn into crystal—so compact and compressed in itself that it can neither receive God as a guest nor the "foreign heat" <note>The "heat" of divine grace or the Holy Spirit is "foreign" to the cold state of sin.</note> of grace, nor be dissolved unless a power is present that exceeds every force of nature. 

Otherwise, human ice is dissolved by the heat of serene and pure love for God and neighbor, as we read in the same Ecclesiasticus: *As ice in the fair weather, so shall your sins melt.* <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Even if crystal requires a stronger force, yet—lest those frozen in the abyss of sins should despair—the Prophet, full of the Holy Spirit, consoles them by foretelling what the Word and the Holy Spirit itself, sent <margin>David</margin> by the Father, would do for the restoration of the heavenly Jerusalem, saying: *He sends His crystal like a morsel* <note>Referring to Psalm 147:17. A "morsel" or crumb is porous and absorbent, unlike solid crystal.</note>, which is very porous and receives the foreign moisture that softens it. And the Prophet himself, wondering how this could happen which nature cannot do, adds: *Who shall stand before the face of his cold*—namely, the crystal's—*able to dissolve it?* But immediately, illuminated by holy light, he added: *He shall send His word, and shall melt them; His spirit shall breathe, and the waters shall flow*—tears of repentance and floods of grace into the place of sin, according to that saying of the Apostle: *Where iniquity abounded, grace did superabound.* But let us pass on to better things.

### OF THE FIRST SONG
<margin>iii I</margin>

That name *Hêlēl* <note>original: "הילל", usually translated as Lucifer or "Shining One."</note> comes from *yālal* <note>original: "ילal", a Hebrew root meaning to wail or howl.</note>, which is an interjection or a word of lamenting; just as it was said a little before: *Howl, for the day of the Lord is near* <note>Isaiah 13:6.</note>, it is written there as *Hêlîlû* <note>original: "הילילו".</note>. And it was certainly right for him to howl, since he was cast out from every kind of delight into every kind of calamity. It follows: *You are cut down to the ground, you who wounded the nations.* <note>Isaiah 14:12.</note> For envy was the beginning of his sin; envying the human being who was to be exalted, he attempted to destroy him, as it is said in the Book of Wisdom: 
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
> By envy, death entered into the world. <note>Wisdom of Solomon 2:24.</note>

Therefore, a return to Paradise itself was granted to man, because he fell having been deceived by a certain ignorance and drawn away by fragility. But that one <note>Lucifer.</note>, shrouded in no ignorance and surrounded by no fragility of the flesh, sinned out of his own malice with an unpardonable sin—a sin entirely against the Holy Spirit. Yet a return is given to us through penance and a turning back to God, and to the place of delights. This is symbolized by that *land flowing with milk and honey*. ...to both [angels] and men: since both presumed to claim that rank for themselves from which they were cast out. Thus, Paradise is a place of delight and a dwelling established with every joy within the **Archetype** <term>Archetype: the original spiritual blueprint in the divine mind, of which the physical world is a shadow</term>, where the ranks of all creatures are found. In the midst of them all is **Christ**, serving as the tree and the fountain of life, most full of all good things, from whose fullness everyone receives. Into this place the "first-formed" <note>The "protoplast," referring to Adam as the first human.</note> was introduced, along with all the angels. After the rebels were expelled, some of the faithful were eventually brought in, to whom access was granted to the innermost chambers of the heavenly King—as is the common opinion regarding **Enoch** and **Elijah**.

Nor should we think differently of **Moses**, **Abraham**, and many prophets. To them, the secrets of the most high God were so revealed that some of them boast of having seen the King, God, face to face, and of having seen Christ, whose coming they preached in many various ways. No less should we consider the companions of Christ himself, already destined by the Father for the world, to whom he said: *I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved; and he will go in and go out* <note>John 10:9.</note> at will—namely, into that very Paradise of delight. This place is not terrestrial (as is commonly said), but was planted before the construction of the world, as **Jerome** rightly understands.

<margin>CHRIST.
Jerome.
Symmachus.

Symmachus.
Theodotion.</margin> Jerome, in his literal commentary on Genesis, says: *In place of "paradise," the text has [גן עדן] Gan Eden, that is, a garden of delights.* In place of this, **Symmachus** <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> translated it as "a blooming paradise." Furthermore, regarding the phrase "against the east" which follows, the Hebrew has [מקדם] *mi-kedem*. **Aquila** <note>Another early translator into Greek.</note> rendered this as *from the beginning* <note>original Greek: "από αρχής"</note>, and we can also say "from the outset." **Symmachus**, however, translates it as *from the part* <note>original Greek: "εκ μέρους τησ"</note>, and **Theodotion** <note>A Hellenistic Jewish scholar and translator.</note> as *among the first things* <note>original Greek: "εν πρώτοις"</note>, which also signifies not "the east," but the "beginning."

From this it is most clearly proven that before God made heaven and earth, He had established Paradise beforehand. Thus far Jerome; I have quoted him word for word so that no one, deceived by common errors, thinks I am dreaming when I say that Paradise is not terrestrial (as is said by those of little learning), but celestial—indeed divine. It is a place where entrance is granted when a person, having turned away from sin and created things, returns to God with a whole and pure heart. 

For then such a person sees God, attains the divine Mind, and possesses the Kingdom of Heaven, which is within us, and is in that very Paradise of delights. All these things (unless I am mistaken, and I do not think I am) are the same thing. This is the **whirling sword** <note>Genesis 3:24, the "flaming sword." The Latin "romphea uersatilis" allows the author to pun on "versio," meaning "turning."</note> held by the **Cherub** to guard Paradise—namely, a "turning." If this "turning" is away from God toward created things, then it has expelled the one thus turned away from the Tree of Life and the delights of Paradise. But if that turning is away from sins and creatures toward God, then through the Cherub one attains forgiveness and a return to that same Paradise from which they were expelled. 

And for this reason, the Cherubim were ordered to be placed over the cover of the **Ark of the Covenant**, which was called the **mercy seat** <note>propitiatorium</note>, because from there atonements and the remission of sins were made. This Cherub represents Christ in many ways, in whom the true atonement and remission of sins was achieved. The twin Cherubim of the Ark indicate the twin natures of that same Christ <note>the human and divine natures.</note>. I omit many things which could be brought forward to strengthen this opinion through the numerical values of the Hebrew letters and their mystical transpositions <note>likely referring to Kabbalistic methods like Gematria.</note>, lest they seem strange or fabricated to those not accustomed to them or lacking the basic elements of that study. But because the description of the rivers flowing out from there presses upon us—since they seem to flow through this habitable earth and have their origin in a physical place—let us see what those rivers themselves signify.

## What Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, and Euphrates are, flowing out of Paradise itself. Chapter 22.

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
**F**rom 그 fountain of paradise, water is said to emanate, or rather a river, which is immediately divided into four heads. If we wish to understand these according to their true <note>The "true sense" here refers to the allegorical or mystical meaning rather than a literal geographic one.</note> meaning, we will remember that from that divine fountain of life, water flows down—namely, the essence and the "being" of all things. This essence, in its first division, is partitioned into the four **elements** <term>Elements: in ancient science, these are Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, the four building blocks of the physical world</term> as the principal and primary material principles of things. This river of essence went out from "delight"—that is, from the most blessed Godhead—to irrigate and pour through the entire earth—that is, "matter," which was called "earth" when it was first produced. And it is well said that in its first course it is divided into four heads, namely into the four elements, with which the names of the rivers also agree.

For the name of the first is <note>original: פישון</note> **Pishon**, which some interpret as "the revolution of the mouth." But it would be better called "mouth" and "teething" from <note>original: שן</note> *shen*, which means "tooth," lest we think it is drawn from <note>original: פנה</note> *fana*, which means "he changed." From this, it also indicates the "earth," of which it is said that it circles all the land of **Havilah**. This name they interpret as "parturient" <note>Meaning "bringing forth" or "giving birth."</note>, because the land of Havilah—that is, the fertile and fruitful land—is surrounded by a dry shore; thus, by those words, both types of land are expressed: the dry and the fruitful. And it is fitting that the land is first expressed as "dry," since it is said in Genesis: "And
<margin>Genesis</margin> God called the dry land Earth." This earth would remain dry unless it were irrigated by that river coming out of the paradise of delight to water (as it says in the text) the entire earth. Therefore, having received fertility from God according to its capacity, it brings forth not only herbs and plants (as is obvious to everyone) but also metals and precious stones. Therefore it follows: "And there is gold, and the gold of that land is good; and there is born there <note>original: הבדולח ואבן השהם</note> **bdellium and the onyx stone**." Some interpret *Bedolach* as bdellium <note>A fragrant resin</note>, others as crystal or talc; and *Auen asoham* as the onyx stone.

Not without cause are these three said to be born in the earth: so that, in a few words, it may be indicated what good and evil we have from the earth itself. For we have gold and other metals, which all signify treasures that are failing and to be despised, yet granted for our use while we journey as pilgrims in this foul world, so that through them we may acquire heavenly things. 

**Bdellium**, however—that is, crystal or talc—is not dissolvable by any heat, as we have proven by clear experience. And the **onyx** stone is said to be "prestigious" <note>In this context, meaning "illusory" or "having remarkable properties."</note>: inside, around its center, it is of an earthy color, but on its circumference, it is heavenly. These two stones denote the "crossroads" of mortals proceeding or dwelling upon the earth. For there are those who savor earthly things to such an extent that their mind and their "watery" soul are hardened, like crystal or talc, against which no fire can prevail. I called the soul "watery," since it is not without reason said in Scripture: "Let the waters bring forth every living soul." But the **rational soul** <term>Rational soul: the part of the human soul capable of reason and understanding, distinct from the vegetative or animal soul</term> is especially "watery," so that it may be capable of receiving the "water" of saving wisdom. But sometimes it is so hardened by malice and sin that it cannot be dissolved by any natural heat. 

But lest mortals so hardened should despair, it is said through the Prophet: "He sends his 
<margin>David</margin> crystal <note>Usually translated as "hail" or "ice" in modern Bibles; see Psalm 147.</note> like morsels; before the face of his cold, who shall stand? He shall send out his word and melt them; his spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow." Others, however, are made like onyx stones; though they are "earthy" in their central nature, yet in mind and effect they contemplate the heavens and tend toward heaven. As for the etymology...

concerning the river, we said that it signifies a "toothed mouth": because while we are on earth, all food must be pressed, ground, and chewed with the teeth—that is, with certain powers of the soul—which we receive through the mouth for the sake of the soul. For unless someone does this, he is considered unclean in the law. <note>This refers to the biblical laws of kashrut/purity, where "chewing the cud" is a requirement for clean animals, here allegorized as the need for the soul to "digest" spiritual truths.</note>

The second river is called **Gihon** <note>original: גִיחֹון</note>, and it signifies the **chest**, which was commanded to perform the office of feet for the serpent. <note>In Genesis 3:14, the serpent is cursed to go "upon its belly" (or chest/pectus).</note> Water, flowing without feet or hands over a bed of earth, holds the likeness of this, moving as if on its chest upon the earth; and the water of the sea creeps over the shores in almost the same way. Moreover, this river circles the entire land of **Cush** <note>original: כוּשׁ</note>, which is interpreted as Ethiopia, and also as "covered." For Cush comes from *cassah* <note>original: כָּשָׁה</note>, which means "he covered." For water circles all the earth, covering and wrapping it round about, except for this small portion which we inhabit.

And the name of the third river is **Hidechel** <note>original: הִדֶּקֶל</note>, which is interpreted by our people as the **Tigris**. But it comes from *chad* <note>original: חַד</note>, which signifies "it sharpened," and *chal* <note>original: קַל</note>, which is interpreted as "light," so that its meaning is "sharp and light" [swift]. And it denotes the **air**, or the airy spirit, which is light and more penetrating than fire: because fire can more easily be excluded from entering somewhere than air. And this "precedes Assyria" [Assur], that is, the "rich man" who is inflated by wind and air. Or it "goes toward Assur," that is, against one who observes for himself. For *Assur* signifies both "rich" and "observer": for he who wishes to observe divine things by himself remains full of wind. And finally, that airy spirit will so sharpen the body—now made light through its spiritual gift—that it can penetrate the heavens and whatever is placed in its way better than this thick air.

Coming to the fourth river, Moses says: "The fourth river is **Perat**" <note>original: הוּא הַפְּרָת</note>, that is, *Perat itself*, for which we have "this is the **Euphrates**." For Euphrates is interpreted as "multiplying," or "fructifying," or "fruit-bearing," just as *perat* signifies "to bear fruit." Whence it encompasses the heat and fiery power which provides fertility to all things, as we prove by experience. For when heat arrives, all things begin to germinate, and they mature as it glows; and when that same heat recedes, the earth is stripped, and the trees drop their fruit and leaves. For the Sun, who is called the father of life, grants life to lower things by means of heat, and he accords with God, who, being **Fire**, gives fertility and fruit to all.

This God, containing not only the fiery power but that of all the elements, exists as the true fountain from which every elemental virtue emanates. And this is hinted (as the more secret theologians <note>Likely a reference to practitioners of Christian Kabbalah, who sought hidden meanings in Hebrew letters.</note> assert) through the four letters of His great name:
*   By the **first** [Yod], for many reasons which I keep silent, **Fire** is indicated.
*   By the **second** [He], which is a mark of breathing, **Air**.
*   By the **third** [Vav], **Water**.
*   By the **fourth** [He], **Earth** and all earthly things, with which that divine fiery power is united.

And this is hinted in the shape of that letter [He] in which *Yod* <note>original: י</note> (which is the first letter, indicating divine fiery power, as we said) is placed in the "belly" of that letter called *Resh* <note>original: ר</note>, which carries the value of two hundred <term>Gematria: a system where Hebrew letters have numerical values; Resh is 200</term>—that is, the number two [duality] led through the hundredth, which is the number of material things. But these things, being as if foreign to our Latin people and those not initiated into this kind of discipline...

<page-num>XLIX</page-num>

## OF THE FIRST SONG

We shall send forth. The fountain, therefore, and the super-exalted sea from which those four rivers <margin>The Hebrews</margin> flow, is the great four-letter name of God <note>This refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH).</note> (as the Hebrews say), or the power conveyed by that name, which the Pythagoreans <margin>Pythagoras</margin> call the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>The Tetractys is a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, which the Pythagoreans used to symbolize the organization of the universe.</note>. This indicates that the divine is the source of the fruitfulness of all things and that from which all things come. Orpheus and Homer <margin>Orpheus, Homer</margin> call this the Ocean, the origin of divine and human things: first as eternally existing; second as emanating in the generation of the Gods; thirdly as watering earthly things; and fourthly as trickling into all fluid matter. The emanation of this source is found through "form" in the angels; through "true participation and image" in rational souls; through "imagination" in those lacking reason; and through "shadow" in the shapes of physical bodies. 

This fourfold <margin>Ezekiel</margin> emanation is also hinted at by the four types of living creatures seen by Ezekiel <note>Ezekiel 1:5–10 describes the 'tetramorph': a lion, an eagle, a human, and an ox.</note>: of which the Lion is fiery; the Eagle is of the air; the Man is primarily in the soul (and in seed is watery, as we have declared elsewhere); and the Calf is truly of the earth, and always devoted to the cultivation of the earth. These elements, composed together, show a single face and power, which is why it is said: *There were four faces to one, and four wings to one.* We have spoken enough on this above. 

Because some truth is contained in the literal sense regarding the description of those rivers, we must also speak of where they arise <margin>Geography</margin> and where they flow, according to what we have received from the most diligent geographers. 

**Pishon** (as some assert, with whom Jerome agrees) is the **Ganges**, a river of India, the most principal among the rivers that bring forth gold. For these are counted as the gold-bearing rivers: the Tagus in Spain, the Eridanus in Italy, the Hebrus in Thrace, the Pactolus <margin>Artemidorus</margin> in Asia, and the Ganges in India, whose source is in the Modis mountains, according to Artemidorus. And of this, the text says: *And the gold of that land is the best.* 

**Gihon**, however, which is thought to be the **Nile**, passes through the entire land of Ethiopia and flows from the furthest reaches of the southern land toward the north in a marvelous and varied course. For although for a long time its origin was from uncertain springs, nevertheless, in the time of Nero <margin>Nero</margin>, its source is said to have been found in a mountain of Lower Mauritania, not far from the ocean, where a lake sits which they call Hilis. From there, it hides itself for a journey of several days, then bursts forth again in another larger lake in Mauritania Caesariensis. Reaching the sands again, it is carried through the deserts for twenty days until it reaches the nearest Ethiopians. Then it leaps forth into a spring which is called Black. From there, dividing Africa from Ethiopia, it cuts through the middle of the Ethiopians under the name **Astaplus**, which in the language of those nations signifies "water flowing from darkness." 

Here it creates many islands, the most famous of which is **Meroe**, named for the city of Meroe founded by Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, King of Persia, who conquered Egypt.</note> and called after his mother's name. Finally, reaching the Egyptian sea through many mouths, it makes Egypt itself an island in the shape of the Greek letter **Δ** (Delta). Thus, it rises in Africa, separated from Asia by the Arabian Sea, where the other rivers draw their origin. 

For the **Tigris**, which goes toward the Assyrians, rises in a conspicuous spring in the region of Lesser Armenia in a plain where it flows quite slowly; up to the borders of the Medes, it is called **Diglito**. Then it begins to be called Tigris because it seems to fly like an arrow; for the Medes call an arrow *tidrim*. It flows into Lake Arethissa, and from there, being carried along and meeting Mount Taurus, it is submerged in a cavern; having glided underneath, it bursts forth from the other side, a place they name Zeroanda.

<margin>Genesis 2</margin> The other <note>original: "Alterę"; likely referring to a branch of the Tigris or a related river discussed on the previous page.</note> then crosses the lake which is called Thesbitis <note>Likely Lake Thospitis, known today as Lake Van in eastern Turkey.</note>. Hence no conjecture remains as to how those four rivers could have the same origin, since they seem to rise in very distant places. Yet there are those who assert that there is a single primary source for all of them, but that they flow through subterranean passages to diverse places from which their courses seem to begin. But to the wiser authors, this does not seem consistent, as such distances of lands and seas are interposed that the sources of those rivers could not converge—unless it were said that the sea, from which all rivers arise, is also the source of those four named rivers. But then there will be no particular place which can be called by us the garden or paradise of delights, inaccessible to us. Whence that description of the rivers seems entirely symbolic <note>original: "typica"; here meaning allegorical or representational.</note>, through which are understood the four elements and the principles of all produced being. It indicates that fourfold power of the four-letter name <note>The Tetragrammaton (YHWH).</note>, or the fourfold principal emanation of the Archetype <note>The divine model or "First Mind" from which all creation flows.</note>. All of these things are described through those four rivers because they hold an image of them, just as higher sacraments are described through trees, fountains, the garden, and similar things.

## What the Jordan and the Ieor, the River of Egypt, Are. Chapter XXIII.

After those four elementary rivers from which all things consist, two other rivers are celebrated in Scripture: one in the holy Land of Promise, which is called the Jordan, and the other in the reprobate land of Egypt, named Ieor <note>The Hebrew word "Ye'or," used in the Bible specifically to refer to the Nile.</note>. These, by a great mystery, signify the auspicious and inauspicious emanations from the super-mundane tribunal. The sign of this thing is that everything performed in the Jordan was good and beneficial, while what was performed in the Ieor was, conversely, ill-fated and harmful. For in the Jordan were placed the memorial stones of the crossing of the children of Israel coming from Egypt and from the Moabites; in it Naaman the Syrian was healed by the command of Elisha; in it Christ was baptized, and John, who, preceding the baptism of Christ, had also baptized in it himself. Therefore, for this and other reasons, it is sung of in many places by the Prophets, and especially by the Psalmist. In the Ieor, however, many evils are remembered, performed to the destruction of various people: <margin>Exodus 7</margin> for there the infants of the Hebrews were seen to be submerged. Afterward those waters, at God's command through Moses, were <margin>The Psalms</margin> turned into blood so foul-smelling that the fish died and the Egyptians were afflicted when they wished to drink it, and that putrid gore was spread through the whole region. It also boiled over with frogs, which covered that Memphite land, and finally, being gathered dead into immense heaps, they infected the whole air round about. Therefore, the water of the Jordan is beneficial, while that of the Ieor...

For "Jordan" is written in its own Hebrew idiom as ירדן <note>original: "Ierden" (Yarden)</note> which, when the letters are turned around, makes נדרי <note>original: "nederi"</note>, that is, "my vow" or a spontaneous offering which each person makes of himself, wishing to serve God perfectly. Once this offering is made, all things succeed favorably and happily. However, the other river, which was previously called יאור <note>original: "iorah"; a Hebrew term for the Nile</note> in Scripture, was later called היאר <note>original: "haior"</note> with a letter transposed in a great mystery that must for now remain unspoken. But in the present, lest we pass over the meaning of the changed word in total silence, we will only bring forward this: for יאור <note>original: "Ior"</note> signifies "light," to which word the prefixed letter ה <note>original: "He"</note>, according to the properties of Hebrew grammar, has the power of an interrogation. Thus, the meaning of היאר <note>original: "haior"</note> is interpreted as: "Is there light?" This interrogative sentence implies a negative, so the sense is: "There is no light," and consequently, nothing good or divine is there, but it remains named as something destructive to those among whom it flows. Yet both these rivers flow from the heavenly tribunals: the Jordan from the Tribunal of Mercy, and the Nile <note>original: "haior"</note> from the Tribunal of Justice, so that the sheep to be placed on the right may be washed in the former, while in the latter, the goats who are to be condemned and punished may be submerged.

### What Wine, Milk, Butter, and Honey Signify. Chapter 23.

**W**ine, milk, butter, and honey, so often celebrated in Sacred Scripture, are not devoid of mystery. And so that we may come with ready hands to the interpretation of these words—which, like others, are used metaphorically in the sacred utterances—wine signifies the wisdom of lower things; milk and butter signify heavenly things; and honey signifies the taste and sweetness that is had from tasting them. For Solomon was filled with "wine," that is, the wisdom of lower things,
<margin>3 Kings 3</margin>
above all who were before and after him, just as he had requested from God when He offered and promised to give whatever he might ask. For he said: "Give to Your servant an understanding heart, that he may be able to judge Your people, and discern between good and evil; for who will be able to judge this, Your so great a people?" To him the Lord said: "Because you have asked for wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have done according to your words, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so much so that no one like you has been before you, nor shall any arise after you." Nevertheless, though he was full of that wisdom, he seems to still seek another, grieving that he could not attain it; as in his "sermon-book"—which in Greek is called *Ecclesiastes* and in Hebrew *Coelet* <note>Kohelet</note>—he says: "And I applied my heart to find wisdom." And again: "I thought in my heart to withdraw
<margin>Ecclesiastes</margin>
my flesh from wine, so that I might transfer my mind to wisdom." From what "wine," indeed, does he withdraw his flesh, if not from the wisdom of earthly things, which do not sit well with heavenly things, just as the wisdom of both does not agree? For this wisdom of lower things is signified by wine, being born from the earthly vine—that is, from human ingenuity—even if God sometimes bestows it, as we just said of Solomon. But that other wisdom of divine things is offered
<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
from those high breasts, of which it is said in the Song of Songs: "Your breasts are better than wine." And this teaches the true discretion between good and evil, as is said of Christ in Isaiah:
<margin>Isaiah 7</margin>

# THE SEVENTH TONE

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
**He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to refuse the evil and choose the good.** <note>Isaiah 7:15, a prophecy traditionally applied to the Messiah.</note> For no one will know how to make a distinction between good and evil by eating cow’s butter, but rather through that better wisdom, which is from above and is symbolized by the better part of milk, from which butter is made. And because attaining this wisdom requires the separation of the "better man" from the "animal man," <note>A common Renaissance distinction between the spiritual/intellectual self and the physical/instinctual self.</note> and indeed an ecstasy of the mind—which 
<margin>Theologians</margin>
is called "the death of the kiss" <note>original: "mors osculi"; a mystical term for the soul's union with God, where the soul "dies" to the world in a divine embrace.</note> by the more secret theologians—he therefore speaks of his aspiration toward it, saying: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* <note>Song of Songs 1:2.</note> Now, I believe I must explain why this better and divine wisdom is compared to milk, while the lower wisdom is compared to wine. For wine is drawn from a plant, but milk from an animal, which is superior. Likewise, wine inebriates, while milk does not, though both provide nourishment. Furthermore, wine, when stored and exposed, does not easily change or spoil; but milk, as long as it exists outside the breast, becomes worse and most easily suffers corruption. In the same way, the wisdom of divine things and the secrets of God suffer greater harm the more they are made public, just like blood outside the veins. Therefore, it is to be shared only among the "perfected," <note>A term for spiritually advanced practitioners.</note> or preserved in the heart according to that prophetic saying: *I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you.* <note>Psalm 119:11.</note> However, if milk is pressed into butter, it is preserved for a long time, and if boiled, it lasts even longer. Thus, divine wisdom—when "pressed" and well-fashioned in the mind of the possessor, and "boiled" by the fire of love—is preserved for a long time, even as a seasoning for other foods (namely, the records and monuments given by true teachers). But because both types of wisdom are good, provided that the "wine-like" wisdom is directed toward God and does not pervert a womanly heart <note>A reference to King Solomon's heart being turned toward idols by his wives in his old age.</note>—as was permitted in Solomon, lest anyone should place too much confidence in it:
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
And that both are given by God is testified by Isaiah, who speaks in the name of God himself: *All you who thirst, come to the waters*—namely, of saving wisdom—*and you who have no money, hurry, and buy wine and milk without any exchange:* <note>Isaiah 55:1.</note> because, indeed, they are given by God’s generosity without any fitting repayment. Although both wine and milk are good, when mixed together they spoil and rot. So it is with the lower and supreme wisdoms. Therefore, he who wishes to be wise in divine things must be stripped of 
<margin>Paul</margin>
lower wisdom, as God says through Paul and the prophet, when he deals with the 
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
sending of the higher wisdom: *I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.* <note>1 Corinthians 1:19 and Isaiah 29:14.</note> In the same way, when someone is too deeply immersed in the lower wisdom and cunning, he is stripped of the higher. Thus Adam was found naked, because he wished to be too wise by the persuasion of the serpent, who 
<margin>Solomon</margin>
is called ערום *arum* <note>original: "harū"; the Hebrew word means both "shrewd/cunning" and "naked."</note> which signifies both "naked" and "shrewd." This teaches us that the person who is always too shrewd is stripped of the wisdom of divine things. Hence, it did not turn out well for Solomon, who wished to mix both, according to the saying: *I drank my wine with my milk.* <note>Song of Songs 5:1.</note> But it turned out better and more happily for David, who was fed on milk and honey, just as it was commanded for all the elect: that they should be fed in a land flowing with milk and honey, as is repeated so often in Scripture. And if only Solomon had not mixed wine and milk, but had been content with butter and honey like the Messiah, or the honeycomb with honey 
<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
and milk—as is said of the true bride: *Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; milk and honey are under your tongue.* <note>Song of Songs 4:11.</note> This is what happens to all those who cultivate that true land of promise.

## What is the land flowing with milk and honey. Chapter XXV.

<margin>David</margin>
**A**fter we have explained what milk and honey are, it remains to be unraveled what that flowing land might be. For we must not think that God promised a land literally dripping with the milk of cows or sheep, or the honey of bees, to his most elect people after so many labors of wandering the desert, after the most burdensome observance of the Law, and after many wars fought in the name of the Lord. Instead, there is another land (unless I am mistaken) flowing with true divine milk and honey, which is celebrated with great frequency in many places by the Law and the Prophets. For it is the promised "land of the living" <note>A common biblical phrase (e.g., Psalm 27:13) interpreted by mystics as the spiritual realm or the state of grace.</note> which flows with true milk and honey; it is the land for which the divine harper <note>A poetic reference to King David, traditionally credited with the Psalms.</note> sighed when he said: *I believe I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.* The land to which the Israelite people were led after their long desert wandering was a type <note>In "typology," an Old Testament event or place is seen as a "type" or symbolic foreshadowing of a New Testament reality.</note> of this: a place where, above all other regions, the prophetic spirit flourished, along with the searching out of the Law's secrets, wisdom, and the "taste" of divine things. Indeed, that land was called by Daniel:

<margin>Daniel</margin>
<margin>Jerome</margin>
<margin>Symmachus</margin>
<term>Zebi</term> <note>original: "Zebi"; a Hebrew word often translated as "glory," "beauty," or "ornament."</note>, which means "glorious" according to our translation, or "renowned" as Jerome says, or the "land of strength" as it pleased Symmachus to translate it. It is pleasant and excellent above all others—not indeed in the fertility of corruptible things, because (according to 
<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
God's own witness in Deuteronomy) the land of Egypt is more fertile—nor does it exceed others in size or outward loveliness, for it is small and quite rugged. It is therefore excellent, glorious, and renowned because it was placed under the most abundant influence of prophecy, wisdom, and all divine matters. For there the Patriarchs were raised after Abraham was called from Mesopotamia of Syria. To the Israelite people traveling there, the Law was given, most full of all wisdom, so that the future inhabitants would be suited to the place. There, almost all prophecy was poured out; there were many prophets powerful in deed, word, and wisdom. There Christ—in whom are all the treasures of wisdom—was conceived, born, and raised. There he preached and filled many with wisdom. Nor did he ever depart from that place, except when he was led away as a small child into Egypt to escape the cruelty of Herod. There he suffered, rose again, and from there ascended into heaven. In that same place, he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples to fill their hearts with all wisdom and all skill in languages, and to feed them with milk and honey drawn from the land high above. There also was born, raised, and filled with the spirit 
<margin>David</margin>
that man who said: *How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!* To taste this sweetness, he invited others, saying: *Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.* But if we wish to ascend to the allegorical sense—which was perhaps more intended by the Holy Spirit—this land flowing with milk and honey is the flesh and body of Christ. From him flowed both water for the washing away of sins, and milk and honey for the true food of life and spirit; indeed, his very body was offered to us as bread, and his blood as wine. The milk offered by him is now given to beginners, according to that saying of the Apostle: 
<margin>Paul</margin>
*To you, as if to infants, we offer milk.* But now it is also given to the "perfected," as is said of the Apostles and the primary founders of the Church under the name of the Bride in the Song of Songs: *Honey and milk are under your tongue.* For then...

<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
