### ->What oil is.<- ### ->Chapter XXVI.<-

<margin>David, Joel</margin>
<margin>oil</margin>
Oil is also most highly celebrated in the sacred scriptures and is necessary for many things: namely, for the anointing of kings, priests, and prophets; for the smearing of those grain offerings which were offered; for the tending of lights; and for the healing of infirmities. Nor do I believe that 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
priests, kings, and prophets, as well as the sacrifices, are sanctified by the oil of the olive, but rather by a better virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" means a spiritual power or essence.</note>, of which that material oil was the physical sacrament. Therefore, the better and true oil is a certain divine power—indeed, it is divinity itself represented by the oil we 
<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
use. And regarding this "better oil," it says in the Song of Songs: *Your name is oil poured out* <note>Song of Solomon 1:3.</note>—that is, the divinity and power of divinity itself indicated by oil. Kings, prophets, and priests ought to be especially filled with this power. Kings, because they bear the specific role and image of God on earth. Prophets, because they perform miracles and foretell the future, which belongs to God alone, as Isaiah says: *Tell us the things that are to come, and we shall say that you are gods.* <note>Isaiah 41:23.</note> Priests, because they perform the office of God by judging souls and remitting sins, and because they stand as mediators between God and men. Now, a "middle" or mediator (as is common knowledge in the schools <note>A reference to Scholastic philosophy taught in universities.</note>) must participate in both extremes. And because JESUS was the King of kings, the supreme prophet, and the high priest, he had to be filled with divinity above all others, as the Psalmist sings: 
<margin>David</margin>
*God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.* <note>Psalm 45:7.</note> He rightly says "oil of gladness," because there is no true joy except where God resides; he who serves Him ought always to be joyful. Hence Christ says: 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
*When you fast*—that is, when you make yourselves empty for God through fasting—*do not become sad like the hypocrites. But rather, at that time, anoint your head,* <note>Matthew 6:16-17.</note> so that you may be joyful, 
<margin>David</margin>
according to that prophetic word: *That he may make the face cheerful with oil.* <note>Psalm 104:15.</note> And this is the "cheerful giver" whom God loves. Nor should that Gospel passage be brought up: *Blessed are they who mourn,* because that mourning pertains to the "animal man" <note>The "animal man" refers to the natural, unspiritual state of a person (from the Latin 'animalis').</note>, which must be taken up so that consolation may follow; therefore it is immediately added: *For they shall be comforted.* Just as, therefore, through the water of baptism that "water above the world" is indicated...

## What the Palm, Cedar, Shittim wood, Hyssop, and Willow are. Chapter XXVII.

Among plants, the palm, cedar, and hyssop are greatly celebrated; the first two as the most excellent of all trees, and the latter as the most excellent of all 
smaller plants. Indeed, the palm is so celebrated that it maintains a resemblance to animals in two ways. One is that it does not bear fruit without "intercourse," but its branches are impregnated by male buds, as if by a 
<margin>Hebrews</margin>
<margin>Arabs</margin>
female. The other is that in its upper part it has something like a brain, which the Hebrews call *halulab* <note>Hebrew: הלולב (*lulav*), referring to the palm branch or the heart of the palm.</note> and the Arabs call *chedar* or *Gemar*. If this is destroyed, the tree dies, just as the animal itself dies if the brain of an animal is destroyed; this indeed happens to this tree alone among plants. It is so celebrated that in the solemnity of the seventh month <note>The Jewish festival of Sukkot or Tabernacles.</note> its branches were commanded to be offered, which the Hebrews specifically call 
<margin>Hebrews</margin>
<margin>Jerome</margin>
*caphot* <note>Hebrew: כפות (*kappot*), meaning "palms" or "branches."</note>—that is, palms—together with willows of the brook and branches of the *habot* <note>Hebrew: עבות (*avot*), meaning "thick" or "intertwined" branches.</note> tree, which we have translated as "thick-leaved"; but Jerome translates it as "leafy," and others wish to interpret it as the myrtle. And all these are used together with the fruits 
<margin>Hebrews</margin>
of the most beautiful tree, which is the citrus or citron tree, which is ever-green and bears fruit at all hours, according to the common opinion of the Hebrews, who even to this day celebrate that solemnity with its fruit, which Galen calls "citrine," 
<margin>Spartans</margin>
along with the branches mentioned above. Emulating these Hebrews, the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedęmonii."</note> used to crown their gods with those fruits which they call *oximala persica* <note>Likely "Persian sour-apples," an early term for citrons or peaches.</note>, as 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
Aristophanes bears witness. Nor is it without mystery that this solemnity is celebrated with this fruit, which is effective against poison when placed in wine that is drunk, as Dioscorides writes. Neither are the other trees without mystery, which gave back a joyful day in that same solemnity. For the palm (as we said) maintains a sufficiently clear resemblance to an animal in its intercourse and its brain, and also in that it has a head of foliage at the summit spread all around, and branches stretched out in the manner of fingers, and fruit shaped almost in the figure of fingers, from which they are called *dactyli*—that is, "fingers" <note>From the Greek *daktylos*.</note>. The pulp of these fruits is also called "flesh," which is quite medicinal and of the highest nutrition, either from some almost animal-like power or from a solar nature. And it is of such great nourishment that certain anchorites <note>Hermits or religious recluses.</note> were content with that food alone, just as to this day many in Africa do not use other foods. Its fruit is of many kinds and more varied than all others. Furthermore, the tree is glorious and holds an express symbol of victory, because its branches never bend, 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Plutarch</margin>
but when burdened, they rise up against the weight, as Aristotle and Plutarch write, and as we have learned by experience. This, therefore, is a type, image, and sign of glory, just as it has its power from the seat of glory, as is known to those who are initiated into these matters...

<margin>Cedar.</margin>
...have been mentioned. But the Cedar (as those who treat plants—
<margin>Theophrastus</margin>
Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny—sufficiently agree) is that which is called *tya* <note>original: "tya," likely referring to the *Thuja* or a similar aromatic wood.</note>, providing a most 
<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
excellent resin, which is called *cedria* and *cedrium*. It is most useful for toothaches; when placed in 
<margin>Pliny</margin>
the cavities, it breaks them apart and settles the pains. It even brings life back to those breathing their last, because it takes up strength when joined with vital heat; but it preserves dead bodies from corruption by pressing out and consuming foul humors. Those who have written about plants also relate much about the cedar: that when applied with salt, it is a remedy for the bites of the horned viper <note>original: "cerastae," the Cerastes snake.</note>. It cures elephantiasis <note>A term often used historically for leprosy or severe skin diseases.</note>, and it is beneficial to sip a cup of it for ulcers of the lungs. Injected as a clyster <note>An enema.</note>, it is a protection against worms and mites, and against the mange of four-footed animals, dogs, and oxen; and it burns like a torch. The oil that is made from it is also much celebrated, perhaps indicating a fountain of true oil—namely, the place of mercy and divine piety, to which that tree corresponds. But 
<margin>Hebrews</margin>
whether this is the tree from which the Ark of the Covenant was fashioned, or whether it was the larch, as 
<margin>Pliny</margin>
many Hebrews assert, or a cedar of another kind from which (as Pliny and others relate) the precious tables of the nobles were made, we consider uncertain. But in this all the wise men of the Hebrews agree: that Shittim wood <note>original: "lignũ setim."</note> and the cedar, which they call in their own language *erez arezim* <note>original: ארזי ארזים, "Cedars of Cedars."</note>, are entirely the same thing. Indeed, it is the tree most famously sung of by the divine harper <note>A reference to King David and the Psalms.</note>, namely the tree of *Adonai* <note>The Lord.</note>, planted by him in 
<margin>David</margin>
Lebanon—that is, in the true super-worldly forest and garden of delights, or in that most eminent, bright divine mind. For Lebanon signifies both a 
<margin>Lebanon</margin>
forest and something bright or white. Therefore, this tree is sacramental, together with the palm and the myrtle, with which the feast days of the seventh month were celebrated by the command of God. For the more eminent Cedars signify those made great and the primary leaders of God, planted by Him; while the Palms signify the victories which they bring back in the warfare of God; and the Myrtle, providing for manifold infirmity, signifies the many kinds of healing grace which God bestows upon the victors. And those who are planted by the Father celebrate the feasts of God legitimately: for they conquer and bring back a triumph with the Son, and are beneficial, succoring the needs of others with the sevenfold spirit. Or (following the theology of the Hebrews) those celebrate the true feasts of God who are beautiful trees decorated by *tipheret* <note>Hebrew: "Beauty," one of the Sephirot in Kabbalah.</note> and the glory of God, and strengthened by the true heavenly strength which they call *gebura* <note>Hebrew: "Strength" or "Severity," another Sephirah.</note>, and anointed with the oil of piety and divine kindness for their own and others' health and salvation. To these are added the willows of the brook, not because (as I think) unfruitful trees belong to these—the trees on which the prophet says instruments were hung, lest they hear the songs and harmonies of God 
<margin>The same</margin>
above the unworthy rivers of Babylon. For he says: *On the willows in the midst of it we hung our instruments.* <note>Psalm 137:2.</note> But they can agree with those sacramental and festive trees in another significance: for where we have "willows of the brook," in Hebrew it says *u’erbe nachal* <note>original: וערבי נחל</note>, which can signify both the "delights of the inheritance." For *arab* means "willow," and is interpreted as "pleasant" or "lovely." And *nachal* signifies "brook" and "inheritance," so that both senses can exist: namely, the willows of the brook, and the delights...

<margin>David</margin>
> Rejoice to God our helper, shout for joy to the God of Jacob: take up a psalm, and bring the timbrel / the pleasant psaltery with the lyre: Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity. <note>original: "Exultate Deo adiutori nostro..." Psalm 81:1-3.</note>

If, however, the "willows of the brook" signified by the term <term>hirbe nachal</term> <note>original: "hirbe nachal," from the Hebrew *arvei nachal*, the willows mentioned in Leviticus 23:40 for the Feast of Tabernacles.</note> are understood in another sense, they indicate our bodies, which are fruitless; indeed, we ourselves are unfruitful unless we are irrigated by the waters from above and planted near the courses of waters, so that we may give fruit in its season. Therefore, not without reason are these called willows of the brook, which were used to celebrate the festivities of God. Nor is it without mystery that these celebrants are described now by willows, now by fruit-bearing trees: because each person is unfruitful when left to themselves, but fruitful when irrigated by that super-worldly water, which says:
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> Without me you can do nothing. <note>John 15:5.</note>

<margin>Rosemary.</margin>
That plant is also greatly celebrated which in Hebrew is called <term>ezob</term> <note>Hebrew: אֵזוֹב</note>, which by the similarity of the word was translated as hyssop, but in truth it is <term>libanotis</term> <note>A term used by ancient botanists for aromatic plants like rosemary or frankincense-herb.</note>, which the Romans formerly, but today all Italians call Rosemary. It is indeed the most noble among plants, and more excellent than is thought, although it is made common by its multitude and frequency. For it is evergreen, harmful to no one, and an enemy to many infirmities, especially the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "morbo comitiali," epilepsy, historically called the "comitial disease" because meetings of the Roman assembly (*comitia*) were abandoned if someone suffered a seizure.</note>, which is demonic. Also, its root with honey cleanses ulcers, heals griping pains <note>original: "torminibus," abdominal cramps or dysentery.</note>, and serpent bites if drunk with wine. It is also beneficial for the <term>royal disease</term> <note>original: "morbum regium," jaundice, so called because it was thought to require expensive, "royal" remedies.</note> in wine with pepper. And it prevails over greater evils to the extent that it enjoys greater protection and heavenly favor, from which all virtue is woven. Therefore, not without cause was it commanded in the Law to be used for making aspersions <note>Ritual sprinklings for purification.</note> with the blood of animals, according to what the Prophet sings:
<margin>David</margin>
> Sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed. <note>Psalm 51:7.</note>

For among the more secret theologians, it indicates that level of divinity, or that measure by which we are joined to God, and God to us: by whose pouring out we are cleansed from sins, expiated, and perfected. Hence, as a sacrament of this matter, aspersions were ordered to be made with that sacramental plant.

### What the vine and the vineyard are. Chapter XXVIII.

**E**qually celebrated among trees is the vine, first planted on the earth by Noah (as is clearly contained in the sacred utterances), from which the curse given through the sin of the first-parents and the fratricide <note>Cain</note> was removed, whose seed was entirely destroyed by the flood of waters. But Noah, not yet well initiated in the business of this vine and wine, being drunk, revealed his nakedness, so that he was held in derision by his son, who bound his father’s genitals (<margin>Berosus</margin> as Berosus <note>A 3rd-century BC Babylonian priest-historian; the author refers here to a legendary tradition where Ham castrates Noah.</note> writes, or cut them off, as others hand down) so that he might not complete what he had conceived while he had planted the vine. All these things are written in figure and under veils: for through this vine a better vine is understood: which our Redeemer taking up, so much so that he became it, says:
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> I am the vine. <note>John 15:1.</note>

<margin>THE SAME <note>original: "IDEM"; referring back to Christ, the subject of the previous page's final quote.</note></margin> [I am the] true [vine], and you are the branches. <note>original: "uera, & uos palmites." > From now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine, until I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom. <note>Matthew 26:29.</note>

Behold how clearly he explains both this vine, which provides our material wine, and that one, which produces a celestial and better wine. For through this is understood that supreme vine, which gives wine to gladden the heart of each 
<margin>David</margin>
person, according to that saying of the Prophet:
> And may wine gladden the heart of man. <note>Psalm 104:15.</note>

<margin>The same</margin>
<margin>*The true vine.*</margin>
For without that wine, there is no true joy. The true vine is thus the justice of God, which in distributing rewards and in punishing gladdens upright hearts, just as the Psalmodist sings:
> The just man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance. <note>Psalm 58:10.</note>

For even if the just man is sometimes troubled by apparent injustice when he sees the peace of sinners and the undeserved oppression of the righteous, once all things are weighed in a fair scale by the most just Governor and balanced by a correct examination, they finally rejoice in those things which, having not well understood shortly before, they were saddened by. He also calls this vine fruitful, so much so that it is compared to fertile things in many places, as it is written in the Psalm:
<margin>Psalm.</margin>
> Your wife like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house. <note>Psalm 128:3.</note>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin>
And in Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom says:
> Like a vine I caused the sweetness of scent to bud. <note>Sirach 24:17.</note>

This is because from there—that is, from that high strength denoted by the vine—a sharper virtue emanates, which, through the mediation of God’s grace, brings forth very many fruits. And what is marvelous is that the vine produces fruit when attached to any tree, but in different ways: for those leaning on willows are weaker than those on ash, elm, walnut, and the like. Not otherwise does that divine vine, and the strength poured into all "rational trees" <note>An allegorical term for human beings or souls.</note> (about which we have spoken elsewhere), nourish and produce fruit: but it produces better fruit when adhering to Peter, John, Paul, and such sturdier trees, than to weak and obscure ones. This vine also peacefully provides shade—though it is sharp by nature—while it clings to wood or columns. Thus that celestial strength, mixed with the grace and kindness of God himself, provides most pleasant shade, just as was 
<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
said to the Christ-bearing Virgin by the Angel:
> And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. <note>Luke 1:35.</note>

And in Solomon's Song of Songs:
> Under the shadow of him whom I had desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat. <note>Song of Songs 2:3.</note>

Which shadow even his Father desired, when he said:
> Protect me under the shadow of your wings. <note>Psalm 17:8.</note>

<margin>David</margin>
And what he calls "wings" here are called "shoots" elsewhere, as the Prophet, singing of that symbolic vineyard, says:
> Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God: it extended its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the river. <note>Psalm 80:10-11.</note>

But our vine differs from that higher one, because this material vine is supported by clinging to trees, whereas that divine one supports the trees and nourishes them, providing fertility, as the vine 
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
itself testifies, saying:
> He who remains in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit. <note>John 15:5.</note>

<margin>Jacob</margin>
And because Christ joined piety and mercy to this vine of justice, Jacob, when dealing with Judah—or rather with Christ himself, who descended from that tribe—said in his testamentary oracle:
> Binding his foal to the vineyard, and his she-ass to the vine of my son. <note>Genesis 49:11.</note>

For the ass and the foal represent piety and grace.

As has been explained elsewhere, those things which met in Christ with truth and justice, being bound together, prepared for Him a seat in the house of Jacob <note>original: "Iahacob"</note> forever.
<margin>THE SAME <note>original: "IDEM"; likely referring to the same author or authority previously cited.</note></margin>
And what is hinted at here through the vine and the donkey <note>A reference to Genesis 49:11, "Binding his foal to the vine, and his donkey's colt to the choice vine."</note>, is suggested elsewhere through the wine and the bread. These two He ordained for sacrifice in that house—namely, the Church—indicating by no small mystery that the donkey was tied to the vine, and that piety and mercy were kissed and connected together with justice and truth through Him. And so Noah <note>original: "Noe"</note> wished to plant and establish the vine of divine justice, so that He would no longer punish Noah's descendants, relying on the divine promise in which it was said:
<margin>GOD</margin>
> I will establish my covenant with you, and never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, nor shall there ever again be a flood to destroy the whole earth. <note>Genesis 9:11.</note>

<margin>Hebrew Doctors <note>original: "Doct. he." (Doctores Hebraei)</note></margin>
For he had decided (as the Hebrew doctors say) to place Canaan <note>original: "Canahan"</note>, the youngest son of Ham himself, in that place so that he would not feel divine justice upon himself, and even less so the other brothers who preceded him. > Canaan shall be a servant of servants to his brothers. <note>Genesis 9:25.</note>

However, if one plants the vine in its proper place and drinks of its fruit tempered with the water of wisdom and compressed into suitable bread, vapors do not rise, nor does it lead to drunkenness; rather, it strengthens one’s powers and grants the strength for acting. <margin>CHRIST</margin>

<margin>THE SAME</margin>

These things, therefore, must be eaten by us so that we may have life and be able to perform good works. To these the heavenly teacher again invites us, saying:
> Go you also into my vineyard. <note>Matthew 20:4.</note>
The vineyard, that is, of His Church, which He planted here below in the likeness of that celestial vineyard and court. For in both places a double tribunal has been erected: namely, of justice and mercy, prefigured by wine and bread, blood and flesh, right and left, and many such things; so that rewards may be given for good works, and a suitable punishment inflicted for evil ones.
<margin>THE SAME</margin>

<margin>CHRIST</margin>

# SEVENTH TONE. 155

<margin>Augustine</margin>
...and of piety: the use of these two is necessary, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christian theology.</note> has most excellently said: "Love and fear lead to every right action." Love, certainly, of the kind promise and the thing promised, and fear of punishing justice. These act like two spurs that drive one toward every good work, or like bread and wine that refresh the mind of the worker. However, if these two become disordered—if what should not be loved is loved, or what should not be feared is feared—they become spurs driving one toward every evil, and a lethal food and drink.

<margin>The same</margin>
Hence, Augustine brings forward a sentiment contrary to the first, saying: "Love and fear lead to every sin." For just as the love and fear of God draw one toward every good, so the love and fear of the world impel one toward every evil.

<margin>Paul</margin>
We can learn this from the Savior; for just as He promises life and reward to those who are fed by the bread and wine (or the flesh and blood signified by those two—namely, love and fear), so the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:27-29.</note> threatens those who abuse such things by loving and fearing what they should not, when he says: "He who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord." In that body, he had received both: justice, when He exposed that very body to punishments; and piety and mercy, when through those same wounds He obtained grace and pardon for us. So too, the "mystical body," <note>The Church or the collective body of believers.</note> having been led to its work through these two, He determined to finally render to each according to their works. And lest a person fear and love the world instead of the fear and love of God, He strove with all diligence to tear them away from that very world. And this is what the Prophet <note>The "Prophet" here is David, referring to Psalm 80:8.</note> sings under the figure of the vine: *You have brought a vine out of Egypt; you have cast out the nations and planted it.* For out of such darkness and narrow straits, He translated us into His wonderful light—the light from which those who were once called "Angels of Light" were cast out, though they are now the angels of darkness.

<margin>David</margin>
Or, following the literal truth—in which we find a "vine-stock" <note>original: "vitis"</note> rather than a "vineyard" <note>original: "vinea"</note>—this vine of Egypt is the human race, subject to sin and enclosed in the darkness and narrowness of this world (figured by Egypt). This vine He has shaken—or permitted to be shaken or trampled. For <term>תַּסִּיעַ</term> <gloss>tasiah</gloss> is a verb in the present of the third mode (or conjugation) and it signifies not "you transferred" (as we have it in our translation <note>The author is critiquing the standard Latin Vulgate translation "transtulisti."</note>), but "you permit to be shaken" or "trampled," or "you cause it to be." For the human race is greatly trodden down by the Adversary and his henchmen.

<margin>Job</margin>
And because when one generation or nation is depraved, God raises up and places another in its stead—according to that passage in Job: "God shall break many in pieces, and make others stand in their place" <note>Job 34:24.</note>—it follows: *You have cast out the nations* (that is, the bestial ones) *and planted it.* This was done, for instance, at the time of the Flood, when the human race was replanted. This is denoted in the present text by the vine, which we have said elsewhere signifies divine justice. And not without reason, for the Supreme Architect <note>original: "Opifex summus"</note> produced and arranged the entire fabric of the world, and the human race itself, by that distributive and regulating justice. Hence <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God</gloss>—in the sense that He is the Prince of that tribunal—is introduced as the builder and arranger of the world. It follows: *You looked before it,* namely, by preparing all things, so that all things were first rightly arranged.

<margin>John</margin>

Or he hints at the intelligences <note>Higher spiritual beings or angels that govern the natural world.</note> who preside over the animals themselves, just as they do over plants, stones, and all things which have some power here below. 

<margin>The same</margin>

<margin>Jerome</margin>

<margin>Hebrews</margin>

While often identifying a specific monster, the author here treats it as a general Hebrew term for great beasts or cattle.</note>, is the Ox; and among rational creatures, Man holds the sovereignty. All these things are joined by face and by power, as the Prophet says: **"Four faces to one, and four wings to one"** <note>Ezekiel 1:6</note>; because indeed God is one in all things, containing most diverse things by a better mark and power. 

To these four, therefore, all other animals are referred, because all things emanate either from the right, or from the left, or from the lower, or from the supreme divinity of the Archetype. To this, the Intelligences and the planets correspond, and we have explained above to some extent how these animals and other kinds of things agree with them. ### What are does, stags, and fawns. Chapter XXX.

<margin>Exodus</margin>
We see stags, fawns, does, and goats celebrated quite frequently in Holy Scripture, not only in the Songs, but in the Law and the Levitical hymns. <margin>Origen</margin>
...toward **better and hidden things**, just as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> agrees when he says: "The stag or the wild goat are animals which, according to the natural logic they carry in their bodies, are referred to certain causes of physical things. Yet that which is written: **The voice of the Lord preparing the stags** <note>original: "Vox Dñi præparãtis ceruos"; Psalm 29:9</note> seems to apply to those invisible stags." For what preparation is made by the voice of the Lord for these visible, physical stags? Or what doctrine ever descends to them from the voice of the Lord? By the voice of the Lord, it is disposed to hunt the race of serpents <note>A reference to the ancient belief that deer used their breath or water to draw snakes out of their holes to kill them.</note>. <margin>Psalm</margin>
**As the stag longs for the fountain of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.** <note>Psalm 42:1</note> Their offspring or fawns <note>original: "hinnuli"</note> are those who are newly initiated into the way of the Lord, so that they may run to the mountains, of which it is said: 
<margin>Psalm</margin>
**The high mountains are for the stags.** <note>Psalm 104:18</note> <margin>Mountains are the summits of virtues.</margin> For the mountains are the **summits of virtues**, toward which those run who are inflamed by the love of virtue, and those who have already reached the peak of virtue climb above them. In the **Archetype** <note>The divine "original model" in the mind of God.</note>, however, the stags and goats represent those divinities and influences from which the animals and the men signified by them receive their essence—the reason they are called stags or goats. Among the more secret theologians, the fawns of these "sublime stags" are said to be those lower measures which are beneath those fuller measures of <term>piety and justice<note>These are specific "measures" or attributes in the divine hierarchy, often associated with the Sephirot in Kabbalistic-influenced Christian thought.</note></term> designated by the stags and goats. Therefore, the most wise Solomon in his Song of Songs invokes these divinities or divine properties when he says: 
<margin>Solomon</margin>
**I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the goats and the stags of the fields, that you do not stir up nor awaken my beloved.** <note>Song of Solomon 2:7</note> The bond of this oath is through the **tribunal of grace**, by which the good are rewarded, and through the **tribunal of justice**, from which the wicked are punished. Hence, by swearing and calling upon these things, one submits and binds oneself to all the censures and sentences emanating from the celestial tribunals, so that the bond cannot be dissolved in any way; rather, one shall receive a reward for observing the oath, or punishment for its transgression. And because the lower measures, which are called fawns, are also called "breasts"—namely those which nursed all the prophets—it is said in the same Song: 
<margin>The same</margin>
**Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a goat.** <note>Song of Solomon 4:5</note>

## OF THE FIRST SONG.

**Jacob was a shepherd of sheep**, and his twelve sons were the princes of the twelve tribes. They were even taught by Joseph so that, when questioned by Pharaoh regarding their trade and industry, they would respond: "We are shepherds of sheep, both we and our fathers from our infancy even until the present." Nor is the passage that follows devoid of mystery: **The Egyptians loathe all shepherds of sheep.** For the worldly and the wicked have always loathed those who walk in all simplicity and in the straight way of the Lord, according to what the Supreme Truth says: *If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.* <note>John 15:18. The author links the biblical "Egypt" with worldliness and the persecution of the righteous.</note> For Egypt always signifies the worldly and those who cause distress to the good. Moses also tended sheep when he was called by God to perform better things. David too was a shepherd of sheep when, by the command of the Lord, he was anointed king of Israel by Samuel. But what is greater still, God himself is a shepherd of sheep, as is Christ and the Messiah, who says: **I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep.** <note>John 10:14</note> But concerning God himself, before he was clothed in flesh, the Psalmist says: <margin>CHRIST.</margin> <margin>THE SAME</margin> <margin>David</margin> <margin>Ezekiel</margin> *You led your people like sheep.* <note>Psalm 77:20</note> It is said more clearly in Ezekiel: *I myself (he says) will seek my sheep and visit them, just as a shepherd visits his flock; and I will deliver them from all the places in which they have been scattered. I will feed them in the richest pastures; their pastures shall be on the high mountains of Israel. There they shall rest in green grass, and they shall be fed in fat pastures upon the mountains of Israel. For I will feed my sheep, says the Lord God.* <note>Ezekiel 34:11–15</note> Indeed, sheep are pastured, as are oxen, goats, and kids; even pigs are pastured, but no mention is made of these in Holy Scripture because they are utterly unclean. However, sheep, oxen, kids, or goats contain their own mysteries. For sheep are the simplest of animals, always most useful, full of all gentleness, and removed from all harm. Therefore, <margin>Sheep signify divine Justice 2</margin> those who pasture sheep—that is, those who are mild and simple, harming no one and always doing good—are loved and exalted by God. But kids and goats do harm, provoking the vine itself. We recently said that this vine signifies **divine justice**, which is gathered and stirred up by those who offend God and sin. Therefore, just as petulant kids are said to be placed at the left hand of the Judge to receive the punishment for their outrages, so the gentle and beneficent sheep are said to be placed at the right hand. <note>A reference to the Last Judgment in Matthew 25:31–46.</note> Thus, to the shepherds of these sheep, as to men practiced in good things and as faithful ministers, God entrusts his "better" sheep, whom he himself—as the true and principal Shepherd—pastures and rules. Therefore, the true shepherds of sheep are those who, being simple, innocent, and always acting well, follow gentleness and piety. But if we must pasture kids, we must observe what is said <margin>Song of Songs</margin> in the **Song of Songs**: *Pasture your kids near the tents of the shepherds.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:8. The "kids" here are interpreted as our unruly passions.</note> We pasture our kids near these tents when we restrain our anger, our hot-headedness, and the raging impulses of lust, ruling them with sheep-like simplicity. For then, these kids, having been fed and initiated into the habits of sheep, can be placed with them at the right hand of the Judge to await the blessing and the reward of good works.

### Chapter XXXII. Which animals, fish, birds, and plants are clean and unclean.

<margin>GOD</margin>
**T**he Supreme Creator <note>original: "Opifex summus"</note> produced four kinds of living things for the food of man: plants and the fruits of plants, fish, birds, and four-legged animals. In each of these kinds He fashioned some as clean and others as unclean, just as among those who eat them, some are clean and some are unclean. For animals and men are fed by plants, but their foods are distinct, as God said: "Behold, I have given to you men every herb bearing seed which is upon the face of the earth, and every tree which has fruit, and the tree bearing seed; these shall be food for you. But to every beast of the earth, and to the birds of the heavens, and to everything that creeps upon the earth in which there is a living soul, I have given every green herb for food." <note>Genesis 1:29-30</note> And so it was established. He distinguishes the foods, therefore, although our translation speaks of these matters in a confused way: for He gave the seed-bearing plants and the fruit-bearing trees to man, who has the industry for sowing and gathering; but to the beasts, who do not know how to sow, He granted the green of the herb, which <term>vʒ</term> <note>that is</note> grows of its own accord, 
<margin>David</margin> as the Psalmist sings: "Bringing forth grass for the cattle," which comes from the herbs that grow naturally, "and plants <term>.s.</term> <note>namely</note> for the service of men." <note>Psalm 104:14</note> These plants, along with the fruit-bearing trees, He granted to man as clean and better; but those wild herbs He silently prohibited by giving them to the animals for food. These things, spoken enigmatically, indicate that fruitless works—which have no seed from which they can be sown and fruits gathered—are left to the beasts as if they were unclean; but those which have fruit, and the seed of the fruit for doing good, are assigned to man as clean. Regarding the animals, fish, and birds, He provided a clear distinction between the clean and the unclean, forbidding the latter and granting the former, <margin>Leviticus. Deuteronomy.</margin> as we read in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For He first separates the clean animals from the unclean by a twofold sign: one of which is to ruminate, or (as it is held in the Hebrew) to "lift the grain" <note>original: "levare granum." This refers to the process of chewing the cud, which was interpreted allegorically as meditating on scripture.</note>; the other is the cloven hoof. All these things said concerning animals are judged by Origen <margin>Origen</margin>—fortified by the authorities of the Apostles and of Christ—to pertain to men. For Paul, <margin>Paul</margin> <term>.n.</term> <note>indeed</note> when he was dealing with those fathers to whom this law was given, said: "All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." <note>1 Corinthians 10:3-4</note> And again: "Let no one judge you in food or drink, which are a shadow of things to come," <term>vʒ</term> <note>namely</note> of men to whom all those things refer. And to Peter, <margin>The same Peter</margin> who had gone up to pray and was seeking with Christ the things that are above, a vessel <note>The "vessel" refers to the great sheet let down from heaven in Peter's vision in Acts 10.</note> was shown in which were all four-legged animals, creeping things, and birds; and a voice was added, saying: "Rise, kill, and eat." And when Peter feared to do this lest he be contaminated, <margin>Origen</margin> it was said again: "What God has cleansed, you shall not call common." And this was repeated three times because they had been cleansed (as Origen himself says) by the power of the most holy Trinity, which Christ, the cleanser of those things, had taught.

Who also said: **What enters into the mouth does not defile a man.** <note>Matthew 15:11</note> Therefore, to lift up or bring back the grain, or to chew the cud <term>ruminare</term> <note>literally "to ruminate," used here as a metaphor for deep thought</note>, is to meditate upon the food of Holy Scripture which we take in, and the prayers which we pour out to God. These are brought forth in vain and to no purpose without the attention of the mind; likewise, the sacred words are read to no effect unless the one who reads them meditates upon them. <margin>David</margin> For this reason, the Prophet sings: **Blessed are they who search his testimonies.** <note>Psalm 119:2</note> And again: **Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.** <note>Psalm 1:1–2</note> In this passage, it is not the mere reading that is praised, but meditation, and in that meditation a man is declared blessed. Therefore, he "chews the cud" and "brings back the grain" who revolves what he reads with an attentive mind, so that he may fulfill in action what he understands and meditates upon. Furthermore, he "lifts the grain" when he makes his good works outweigh the debts contracted from his committed failings. He is said to have a "divided hoof" who, from the law he has studied, knows how to apply discernment <term>discretionem</term> between good and evil, rejecting the latter and embracing the former. Both are necessary, because knowledge and discernment are not enough unless the result is completed by action; nor can the choice of good be made unless a knowledge of the thing to be chosen comes first.

Moreover, those fish are judged clean which have wings and fins, by which they may be lifted from the mire, and scales to be cast off so that they may "put on the new man." <note>Ephesians 4:24</note> But those who wallow in the mire without scales or wings signify those who, rolled in the filth of lust or the mud of earthly things, never learn to depart from them. Truly, those are unclean birds which have strong talons and devouring beaks, living by prey. These signify those who always invade the property of others, never content with their own portion. Conversely, harmless birds are considered clean; these signify the mild, the gentle, and those who harm no one. That these foods to be eaten signify men, we can learn clearly enough from the Gospel, <margin>CHRIST</margin> where Christ says of the Samaritans coming to the faith: **I have another food to eat, which you do not know. My food is to do the will of my Father, who sent me.** <note>John 4:32–34</note> Just as the Samaritans beginning to be converted were the food of Christ, so each one of us, when we work well, is His food; and when one imparts doctrine or some useful thing to his neighbor, he is the food of that very person whom he serves. Thus Christ was made our food by giving Himself to us in many ways, <margin>THE SAME GOD</margin> so that He might fittingly say: **I am the living bread, who descended from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever.** <note>John 6:51</note> He was indeed the bread and food of life, administering to us the doctrine of life, the food of life, and the works of life. So we too, when we offer such things to our neighbors, are to them the food of life, and a food that is pure and clean. <note>In this context, "Tone" likely refers to a division of the book following a musical or liturgical structure.</note>

...do not take food of this kind. And these things [are said] concerning the mystical sense. Returning however to the literal sense, we must consider from where animals and plants take on purity or impurity. But this cannot happen without a higher and profound investigation. For they are not clean or unclean of themselves; nor does it seem that any evil proceeds from God, the good progenitor, or that anything unclean falls from the supremely pure, especially since it was said: <margin>Genesis</margin> **God saw everything that he had made, and they were very good.** <note>Genesis 1:31. The author is grappling with the paradox of how a perfect Creator could make "unclean" things.</note> On the other hand, it appears that hostile and evil things proceed from Him who says through Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah</margin> **I am the one making good, and creating evil, making light, and creating darkness.** <note>Isaiah 45:7. The author uses a specific Latin distinction here between "making" (facere) and "creating" (creare).</note> This can be understood in this way: since "to create" is to make from nothing and ends at the "subject" or "matter" (which has the nature of evil), He is therefore said to be "creating evil." And since "to make" ends at the "form" (which has the nature of good), He is therefore said to be "making good." <note>The author is using Scholastic philosophy: "Form" is the perfect idea of a thing, while "Matter" is the base substance that can lack perfection.</note> Therefore, as much as things decline toward matter, they have the nature of evil, and the more they approach the highest form, the more they have the nature of good. And this is what is said in Ecclesiasticus: <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> **Against evil is good, against life is death, and against the just man who devotes himself to God, the sinner always declines to the depths.** <note>Sirach 33:15</note> It follows: **So look upon all the works of the most High: two against two, and one against one,** because there is no good in the world without its opposite. For there are Angels of light and Angels of darkness; Angels of life and Angels of death; a dwelling of light and a dwelling of darkness; a vessel <term>crater</term> <note>original: "crater"; here referring to a Neoplatonic "mixing bowl" or receptacle of cosmic influences</note> of the clean and a vessel of the unclean. These were indeed made by God and are good in their own order, even if they are unclean to us. They draw this impurity either from a fierce and ravishing spirit influenced by Mars (as the astronomers say) or Samael <note>In Jewish tradition, Samael is an archangel often associated with severity or death; the author links him here to the planet Mars.</note>, his intelligence, as the Hebrews assert. Or they have it from Saturn, so that, infected by the evil melancholic humor <term>humore melancholico</term>, they are made into seats of impurity, just as good joy is the seat of a good spirit, or rather of God. Hence the Prophet: <margin>David</margin> **Restore to me the joy of your salvation,** <note>Psalm 51:12</note> and in many places he teaches us to serve the Lord in joy. Or perhaps this influence comes from a higher power, mediated by favorable or unfavorable secondary causes. Some things are said to be, and are, clean because they bring no stain to the one who eats them, but rather happy and good nourishment. Others, however, provide harm, being generated from much black bile <term>atra bili</term> <note>In the theory of the four humors, "black bile" was thought to cause melancholy and various physical ailments.</note> or infecting with poison, as is well known of many plants and all reptiles. Hence these are prohibited by Him who loves us, as things harmful by an open or hidden detriment known to God, while others are granted which bestow benefit to the body and spirit.

This ingratitude was a great lie and a sin all the greater because the influence of divine gifts was more effective upon that place, the temple, and the city, which was the chief city in the region "flowing with milk and honey." ...Christ the supreme High Priest. For this reason, it is asserted by the Hebrew doctors that a sin is greater when it is committed in Jerusalem, a temple fortified with such excellencies and enjoying the special sight of the prince. Hence, it was not without mystery that it was said to David as he ascended from Hebron to reign in Jerusalem: *You shall not enter here unless you take away the blind and the lame*—that is, ignorance and sin. <margin>The blind and the lame are ordered to be removed from Jerusalem.</margin> But the holy king himself did not only remove the blind and the lame who hated his soul and were hateful to him (as the common proverb says: *The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple*), but he inhabited (says our text) the citadel of Sion, or its fortification, as the "truth of the literal text" <note>original: "Veritas litterae," referring to the original Hebrew text</note> holds—that is, in a special outpouring by which he strengthened <margin>David</margin> and fortified himself so that he might not sin. Moreover, that Temple was built in the likeness of the Ark, or the Tabernacle of the Covenant, representing both worlds—namely, the greater and the lesser—according to whose exemplar (as we have said) the Ark and the Temple were built. In these figurative structures, figurative sacred rites were performed until the true sacred rites should succeed them, which would not be perfected in a temple made by hands, but in a better and more perfect one, of which the Apostle says: *You are the temple of God.* <margin>Paul says the same</margin> In this temple, if we perform the sacred rites well by purifying the temple itself, we shall ascend to another temple, of which the Apostle again says: *A tabernacle not made with hands, which is Christ himself*; into which an entrance is given to us through the door, which is He himself. Having entered into Him and been united with Him, <margin>Apocalypse</margin> we ascend to the super-mundane temple, of which it is said in the **Apocalypse**: *The Lord God Almighty is its temple*—that is, the temple of the heavenly city. Thus, by laboring so that we may deserve to reach the highest temple, we shall then be able to say joyfully and without falsehood: *It is the Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord.* May God, in His mercy, grant a happy entrance into these temples.

### What Egypt, Babylon, and Damascus signify. Chapter XXXIV. ###

<margin>Augustine</margin> Since the human race has always been divided into two—namely, the family of God and the family of the devil, as **Augustine** sets forth in the preface to his volume *On the City of God* and pursues throughout the entire context—it was fitting that in that mysterious and typical region, the sacred words should celebrate places that were the lodgings of each family. And just as Jerusalem, with all its surrounding places, was without any doubt ordained for the family of God (of which it would be a long task to tell of each one individually), so **Egypt**, **Babylon**, and **Damascus** always hosted the opposing family, by which the people of God were frequently troubled. Egypt had received a great benefit from the Israelite people, whence Pharaoh called Joseph **Zaphnat-Paaneah** <term>Zaphnat-Paaneah</term> <note>Hebrew: צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ. Traditionally interpreted as "revealer of secrets" or "savior of the world."</note>, which is a name...

It also begins a new chapter contrasting the holy geography of Jerusalem with the symbolic opposition of Egypt, Babylon, and Damascus.</summary>

...the Egyptian [name] is found nowhere else in scripture, as Rabbi Solomon <margin>Rabbi Solomon</margin> <note>Rabbi Solomon refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: for which our translation has, **Savior of the world**, but as others wish, it signifies **Revealer of secrets**: for <term>zaphan</term> <note>Hebrew: צָפַן (tsaphan)</note> in Hebrew carries the meaning of "to reveal," while <term>pahaneah</term> is entirely Egyptian and signifies "hidden" or "the unknown future." However, whatever the case may be regarding the words, Joseph the Israelite saved Egypt by revealing the secret of the vision, by which those evils were demonstrated to Pharaoh that were about to come upon his people, taking precautions against them. Nonetheless, Egypt itself for two hundred and ten years oppressed the people who had gone down there under Joseph’s guidance. Whence they rightly interpret Egypt, which in Hebrew is called <term>Mizraim</term> <margin>Mizraim</margin> <note>Hebrew: מִצְרַיִם. The author is playing on the word "meitzar," meaning a narrow strait or distress.</note> as **distresses**, although some—for what reason I do not know—add that it also signifies **darkness**. For the Egyptians were always the distresses and the distress-makers of good men. The Babylonians also, as if they were ministers of God, led captive all the best men from Jerusalem, and even their king, Jehoiachin, was transported into Babylon. Afterward, they again captured King Zedekiah while he was under siege, along with his entire army; his sons were slain, the temple was set on fire, and they held the people captive for seventy years. Damascus also many times afflicted God’s people, but did not lead them into captivity.

Please observe here the difference between these oppressors. Egypt received the people graciously, then later afflicted them, and finally dismissed them by force. Babylon led them away captive by force, yet acting ever more mildly, eventually dismissed them of its own accord. Damascus, however, without taking them into captivity, caused them trouble many times. For Egypt, the "distress-maker," is the **Devil**, who receives a man pleasantly and, once received, subjugates him and does not let go unless he is pulled away by divine power. Babylon is "confusion," representing the **Flesh**, which, taking the soul captive, immediately holds it in a state of confusion for seventy years—that is, the common course of human life. Yet it always acts more leniently as the days go by; the soul, which at first was so oppressed that it could understand nothing, is gradually released from the oppressing and darkening flesh so that it may act more freely. Finally, after the course of life, it is fully liberated, released from its bodily chains. Damascus, however, which is interpreted as **drinking blood**, is the **World**; it feeds on nothing except those things which are according to the flesh and blood; now it troubles a man, now it lets him go without trouble. Damascus is called the head of Syria, just as *Assur*—which is interpreted as **riches**—refers to the riches not of the heavens, but of lower things, of which this world is the head and storehouse.

Now, the "burdens," or divine sentences and sanctions regarding these places, are described by Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah</margin> which are briefly these: The burden <margin>CHRIST</margin> of Egypt—that is, of the **Devil**—is that his idols shall be moved and shall melt away at the arrival of Him who said: *Now the prince of this world shall be cast out.* The burden of Babylon—of the **Flesh**, which confuses the mind—is that every hand, and heart, and corruptible body shall be dissolved, and man shall be transformed for the better, more precious than pure gold. The burden of Damascus—that is, of this **World**—is that it shall cease to be a city and shall be like a heap of stones. For when the inhabitants are taken away, all the buildings of this worldly city shall be destroyed. Many other things that are said in that same place could be brought toward this meaning, which we omit, lest we proceed further than is proper.

### What Arabia, Mount Sinai, and Mesopotamia of Syria are. Chapter XXXV.

<margin>Paul</margin>
**I**t is not without reason that the law was given in Arabia, which rejoices in Mount Sinai <note>The author refers to the giving of the Ten Commandments to Moses.</note> and is blessed with incense and various gums. Nor is it without mystery that Abraham, filled with the Holy Spirit, demanded an oath from the senior servant of his house <note>This refers to Eliezer of Damascus in Genesis 24.</note> that he should by no means take a wife [for Isaac] except from his own kindred, who were in Mesopotamia of Syria. Following him, Isaac, himself filled with God, commanded Jacob while blessing him, saying: "Do not take a wife from the race of Canaan, but go and set out for Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's brother, and take for yourself a wife from there from the daughters of Laban, your uncle." Regarding the mystery of Arabia, the Apostle says: <note>original: "Abraham duos filios habuit..." Referring to Galatians 4:22–26.</note> Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. The one by the slave was born according to the flesh, but the one by the free woman was through the promise. These things are said through allegory: for these are the two covenants. One indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia which corresponds to the Jerusalem that now is, and is in slavery with her children. But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother.

<margin>Sinai is distant from Jerusalem by fifteen days' journey.</margin>
Here it must be noted how the Apostle says Mount Sinai is contiguous with Jerusalem, although it is distant from it by fifteen days' journey, with a vast desert placed in between. Therefore, he does not speak of a local connection (since they are separated by a great distance)—

<margin>David</margin>
—but of a connection of influence, just as the Psalmist <note>original: "Psalmographus"</note> speaks metaphorically of the dew of Hermon which descends upon Mount Zion, although those mountains are distant by eighty—

<margin>Hermon and Zion.</margin>
—thousand paces <note>Approximately 80 miles.</note>. Therefore, they are understood to be joined through an influence, which is the same on Mount Sinai, where the written law was given, and in Jerusalem, where it was kept with great favor by King David—who expanded the worship of God according to that same law—and by Solomon, who built the temple, and by many prophets who flourished in Jerusalem and the surrounding places. This law of slavery was prefigured by the son of the slave woman, who was cast out by Abraham at God's command into the wilderness of Beersheba, which joins with the desert of Arabia; nor is Sinai far from there, where Moses pastured the flock beyond the desert, as we explained a little while ago. On this mountain, therefore, the law of slavery was given to those who came out of Egypt, prefigured by those who descended from Hagar the Egyptian slave,

<margin>Paul</margin>
as the Apostle suggests in the words recently cited. And because the same law of slavery was kept in the lower Jerusalem, it is therefore said to be joined with Sinai: because both places were pressed by the same yoke of slavery,

<margin>Jerusalem joined with Sinai</margin>
until that new Jerusalem should descend from above, the free—

<margin>John</margin>
—one, who is our mother, of whom John speaks in the Apocalypse: <note>original: "Vidi civitatem sanctam..." Referring to Revelation 21:2.</note> I saw the holy city, the New Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband—that is, for our Father Christ, to whom she was a bride, but to us a mother. She is not made of stones squared by iron or of bricks, but of <term>living stones</term> <note>A reference to 1 Peter 2:5, describing believers as the components of a spiritual house.</note> raised up as children of Abraham, who are sometimes called children, and sometimes, when gathered together, are called the Bride, from whom the Father has begotten others. She appeared "new" because she was fashioned by a new influence from Him who, being a New Man and free, came to renew us all and free us from the slavery of the devil and sin, as the Apostle concludes: Therefore, brothers, we are not...

[We are not] <note>The word "non" (not) is implied from the preceding page's context of Galatians 4:31.</note> children of the slave woman, but of the free woman: by the liberty with which Christ has set us free. He who also gave new institutes, not indeed changing but renewing the ancient law, and transforming it into the law of liberty, which is according to the spirit, as he says elsewhere: *Where the spirit is, there is liberty* <note>original: "Vbi spiritus, ibi libertas"; a quote from 2 Corinthians 3:17.</note>. According to which law he regenerated us with a new seed, led down from that same place from which his prepared bride had descended. Therefore, Mount Sinai is drenched with the same influence as Jerusalem, although he says it is walled in by the desert. This is well explained in Exodus, where it says: *In the third month of the departure of Israel from the land of Egypt, they came into the desert of Sinai* <note>original: "In mēse tertio egreſsiōis Israel..." referring to Exodus 19:1.</note>. For having set out from Rephidim, they came into the desert of Sinai, and they camped in the desert; and there Israel camped over against the mountain, where many things are to be noticed.

First, that the place near Sinai (as we have said) was a desert. Another thing is that it is not without reason that it says Israel placed their camp opposite the mountain, so that from the well-watered mountain, at least by standing opposite it, they might receive those things which they were unable to receive upon the mountain itself. Indeed, access to the mountain was not granted—on the contrary, it was strictly forbidden, as it says a little further down: *Beware, lest you go up the mountain, nor touch its borders; for everyone who touches it shall die by death* <note>original: "Cauete, ne ascēdatis in mōtē..." quoting Exodus 19:12.</note>. This was because they were not yet capable of the power of the [celestial] influences, just as an infirm person is not capable of wine or solid food.

Therefore, thirdly, the order of the required progress is touched upon mysteriously when it says: that having set out from Rephidim they came into the desert, afterwards they camped next to Mount Sinai, and finally, having been purified by the required sacred rites, they came to the holy region. For <term>Rephidim</term> <note>The author uses a traditional etymology where Rephidim is linked to "pavements" or "supports."</note> signifies "pavements" which are produced by craftsmanship. From which place, not without mystery, the people are said to have come to the desert, and afterwards to Sinai, indicating a mysterious progress away from Egyptian or worldly craftsmanship. He who withdraws from such things and strips himself of them immediately finds the "desert," because he has been stripped of [worldly] favor. But he is immediately applied to Sinai, where he begins to receive the celestial influence; being well-saturated by this, he finally arrives at the land in which he can enjoy a fuller divine bedewing.

Lastly, it must be noted that by no small mystery, it first says in the plural, *and they camped* in the desert, and afterwards it says in the singular, *and Israel camped* <note>The author highlights the grammatical shift from the plural "castrametati sunt" to the singular "castrametatus est" in the Latin Vulgate of Exodus 19:2.</note> against Sinai. This was said so that we might be taught that no multitude can approach the celestial influence unless united in charity. The divine Harper <note>A poetic reference to King David.</note> recognized this and sang: *Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell as one* <note>original: "Ecce q bonū..." quoting Psalm 133:1.</note>. For upon them the celestial influence descends, just as the ointment flows from the head to the beard and down to the edge of the garment—that is, it is diffused through the whole body united in charity. And confirming this again, he says: *For there the Lord commanded blessing and life* <note>original: "Quoniā illic mādauit Dominus..."</note>, namely, where they are dwelling united in one heart and one soul.

And this Arabia is happy because of Mount Sinai and other good influences; that is, the region from which the Queen came, filled with wisdom and riches, to test the wisdom of Solomon. She is called <term>Saba</term> <note>The Queen of Sheba.</note> from the place where she came. For **שבא** <gloss>Sheba</gloss> in Hebrew is called "Arabia" in Latin, and it differs from "Seba," from which the Sabeans are named, because the latter is written with the letter **ס** <gloss>Samekh</gloss>, while Arabia [Sheba] is written with **ש** <gloss>Shin</gloss>. And both are found in the seventy-second Psalm, where we say: *The kings of the Arabs and Sheba* <note>Psalm 72:10.</note>. In Hebrew, it is written **מלכי שבא וסבא** <gloss>The kings of Sheba and Seba</gloss>. But when mention is made of that Queen, it is written with **ש** <gloss>Shin</gloss>.

Thus both were sent—one by Isaac and the other by Abraham—to the land and people of their own birth, which had descended from Shem, the son of Noah who was not cursed, so they might take wives from there. From these, they would produce a progeny that would expel the cursed ones and possess that entire region occupied by an unjust possessor. In which land, so that they might dwell worthily, that family was purified by law and sacrifices.

But when they had come to Haran, Terah the father of Abraham died there, unable to reach Canaan. But after his death, it was said to Abraham: *Go out from your land, and from your kindred or progeny, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I will show you.* <note>Genesis 12:1</note> By this context we are taught that in order to possess that beautiful region beloved by God, that family had first to depart from the confusion of sin and the fire of <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Strong desire or lust, often used in a theological sense for the inclination toward sin.</note>, and set out for Haran, which signifies "burning heat," "wrath," or "zeal," with which one ought to be armed against sin and evil. But one must be careful lest the burning heat be excessive and unrestrained, so that he does not die there with Terah. Rather, let him correct and bridle his anger with meekness, like Abraham, and with 

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>

Him [Christ] let him go out from the land of confusion, and from an impetuous lineage, and from the house of a father shattered by his own impulse, and come meekly to possess the blessed land, as it is said in the Gospel titled "according to Matthew": *Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.* <note>Matthew 5:5</note>

# What Amalek, Moab, Ammon, and Philistia Signify. Chapter XXXVI.

**B**ut since we have dealt to some extent with the regions, let us also run through the peoples beyond those, concerning what has been said of the nations of Egypt, Babylon, and Damascus: for Amalek, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines were exceedingly hostile to the people of God. Indeed, Amalek was so insolent that the most merciful God said in Deuteronomy:
<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, when you were coming out of Egypt: how he met you, and struck the rear of your company, those who were weary and lagging behind, when you were exhausted with hunger and labor, and they did not fear God. When, therefore, the Lord your God has given you rest, and has subjected all the nations around you in the land which He promised you, you shall blot out his name from under heaven: See that you do not forget. Truly, God’s severity against this Amalek seems great, which we believe was not done without a mystery <note>The author uses "mystery" in the sense of a hidden spiritual or allegorical meaning.</note>: for Amalek was a great nation, infected with the poison of the ancient serpent, and therefore an enemy to the family of God. For this reason, one must always fight against him, just as the heavenly rulers of the good family fought, as we read in Exodus:
<margin>Exodus</margin>
Because a hand is upon the throne of Jah, the Lord's war against Amalek from generation to generation. <note>original Hebrew: כִּי-יָד עַל-כֵּס יָהּ מִלְחָמָה לַיהוָה בַּעֲמָלֵק מִדֹּר דּוֹר. This verse (Exodus 17:16) is notoriously difficult; the author interprets "kes" as "throne."</note> Which, translated literally, says: Because a hand is upon the throne of Jah, that is, of God, fighting for the Lord against Amalek from generation to generation.
<margin>Saul</margin>
Therefore, Saul was cast out from the kingdom with heavy indignation: because he would not conform himself to the warring hand of the Lord, and fight against him upon whom the divine sentence had been passed and war declared, just as had been indicated to him through Samuel
<margin>Samuel</margin>
that he should strike and utterly destroy Amalek himself and all that he had, killing from man even to woman, from infant even to the suckling, from lamb even to sheep, from camel even to donkey: because all things were foul, and worthy of no preservation, and much less to be offered in sacrifice. Hence Saul’s sin was grave, because he wished to offer abominable things against the divine precept. But Moses, Joshua, David, and as many as were found faithful to God and zealous for divine honor, fought with all their might against this Amalek, though they did not destroy him completely, even as the divine sentence was passed upon him, as we read in the book of Numbers:
<margin>Numbers</margin>
Amalek was the beginning of nations, but his end shall perish. <note>Numbers 24:20</note> And this was because it was reserved for the Messiah to destroy him completely, as was indeed done: nor could it be done by another; rather, others prevailed against him by the power of the Christ who was to come, just as we read of Moses, who,
<margin>Moses</margin>
having sent soldiers to join the battle, fought against Amalek himself with prayers, his hands raised toward God. But his hands were heavy, because he did not have the full power of defeating Amalek. Therefore, those standing by took a stone upon which he sat, which—as the Apostle interprets—was Christ, upon whom he leaned:
<margin>Paul</margin>
And until Christ should arrive, who destroyed him completely, he was supported by Aaron and Hur—that is, by the priesthood prefiguring Christ, and by the burning of the fire which He Himself came to send upon the earth: for "Hur" is interpreted as a "burning" or a "furnace." <note>The author uses the Hebrew name Hur (אוּר) to link it to the word for light or fire (ur), creating an allegory for the "fire" of the Holy Spirit or Christ's passion.</note>

<margin>

is declared to us, with God saying: *I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.* Moab and Ammon, born of their father Lot (whose name is interpreted as "enclosed" or "veiled"), signify the flesh, which is generated from animal spirits and the seminal power enclosed in the paternal bowels. The Philistines, truly, signify the world, with which we play in continuous revolutions—now disentangled from it, now enveloped in it again. Hence, against Amalek and against Moab and Ammon (the first of whom portrays the devil, and the following the flesh), a continuous battle must be undertaken, and no peace, no concord, and no commerce should be held, as is commanded by the law. With the world, however, one must sometimes fight and sometimes converse: so that by drawing its lovers away from it, we may lead them into the service of God, just as Christ taught us—who ate and conversed with tax collectors and sinners so that He might call them back to repentance. We could bring forward many other examples from natural things—plants, stones, mountains, valleys, places, and particular peoples—through which, as if through enigmas, the sacred words indicate better things and those which pertain to the spirit. But lest we proceed further than is proper, let these few things out of many suffice.

THE EIGHTH TONE.

# THE EIGHTH TONE.

## GOD FILLS ALL THINGS WITH HIS BREATH, AND MOST SWEET LIFE. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Orpheus</margin>
<margin>Dorylaus</margin>
<margin>Alexander of Miletus</margin>
<margin>Gregory of Nazianzus</margin>
AFTER we have shown this worldly house arranged with its guest in the highest harmony, both in **enneads** <note>Groups of nine; likely referring here to the nine celestial spheres or the nine orders of angels</note> and in filled intervals, it remains that we make its melody heard, which results from the living and unfailing breath of its Creator filling all things with an inexplicable harmony. Concerning this, **Orpheus** says: *and you tune the whole world with a many-sounding lyre* <note>original Greek: σὺ δὲ πάντα κόσμον κινύρη πολυκρέκτω ἁρμοζία</note>, that is, you temper the whole heaven with a tuneful lyre. But proceeding further, **Dorylaus** the Pythagorean says the world is the **instrument** <note>original: "organum"; used here in the sense of a musical tool or machine</note> of God. Likewise **Alexander of Miletus** with **Gregory of Nazianzus**: "The world," he says, "is praiseworthy for each of its particular species, but much more praiseworthy for the harmony of all things and the structure of the universe, in which there is a supreme and stupendous concord arising from contrariety within the same life and sound; for while they are different among themselves, they all agree as a whole, just as the pipes or strings of an instrument come together into the same sound."

<margin>Timaeus Locrus</margin>
Hence the fabric of the world remains (as **Timaeus Locrus** <note>A legendary Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues</note> testifies) in that very harmony, most excellent by an indissoluble reason.

<margin>Apuleius</margin>
"There is also one single revolution," says **Apuleius** (emulating those wise men), "of the worldly sphere, one harmony, and one choir of the stars and other things resulting from their various settings and risings. For just as in dances the leader of the song sets the tone for the crowd of men and women singing the hymn, who resonate with one harmony through a mixture of deep and high voices—so the divine mind reveals the worldly varieties in the likeness of a single song."

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Which adaptation and harmony of all things men (says **Augustine** in his volume *On Order*) cannot embrace or consider with a weak mind; just as if someone were placed like a statue in the corner of a most vast and harmonious building, he would not perceive the beauty and harmony of its structure, even though he himself were a part of it; nor can a soldier standing in the battle line behold the order of the entire army. And this is because the soul, dwelling among the lowest things and polluted by the love of inferior beauty, has lost its own order and beauty: so much so that it cannot look into the beauty of the universe and the **Archetype** <note>The original divine model of the world in the mind of God</note>, unless it is again made beautiful and godlike, and resumes its former eye—now blinded by the thickness of this deadly and darkening mist. Thus, when the eye is purified or recovered, wherever the soul turns, it may perceive this worldly instrument as most harmonious; and as God modulates it, the soul finds His harmony so much sweeter than the sound proceeding from musical devices, as nature and the Creator of nature are more excellent than art itself. If, therefore, one turns to the first kind of formal music (which **Boethius** calls "mundane") and leans toward its base...

<margin>Exodus</margin> When God spoke to the people of Israel, they were seized by terror and said to Moses: "Speak you, and we will listen; let not God speak to us, lest we die" <note>Exodus 20:19</note>, for they were unable to endure with their weak ears the glory and majesty of the Speaker.
<margin>Job</margin> Hence also Job says: "Since we have heard barely a small spark of His word, who could look upon the thunder of His greatness?" <note>Job 26:14</note>. Just as He fills all things, He makes all things resound together; therefore it follows: *Under the whole heaven is His concert and modulation.* <note>A paraphrase of Job 37:3; "modulation" here refers to musical measurement or rhythm</note>
So that this might be perceived by a better eye rather than by ears, He spoke first, saying: "He extends His light over all the ends of the earth," so that these hidden mysteries might be seen by those who have been purified. Therefore, He resounds in this great **instrument** <note>original: "instrumento"; referring to the universe as a musical tool</note> of the universe with the voices of His greatness. But these wonderful harmonies cannot be grasped by weak minds; yet if a purified soul lifts its ears not just to these lower things, but to the highest **interstice** <note>gap or space between parts</note> of this worldly organ, it will sense the concord, the harmony, or the peace which God made (on the authority of Job) in His high places.
<margin>The same (Job)</margin> This should be interpreted not as referring to the physical heavens, but to the Angels (once error is set aside). Whence he adds: "Is there any number to His soldiers, or His ranks <note>original: "cuneis"; literally "wedges," referring to military formations</note>, upon whom His light does not rise?" Or His eye, searching all things, numbering all things, and fitting them together, so that they, along with the celestial circles, might complete a most tuneful course in most melodious succession and most orderly turns, with a unique variety.
He who, pouring over the earth now with heat, now with cold, now with moisture, now with dryness and many kinds of influences, makes it now stripped bare, now painted with flowers, herbs, and fruits according to the quality and opportunity of the seasons, always returning it to the same state (though in a continuous succession). Thus they clearly point to one single **Moderator** <note>original: "moderatorem"; in this context, a conductor or governor of a musical performance</note> of all things, at whose nod all things are disposed toward each other, just as the measures or strings <note>original: "fibrae"; literally fibers, used here for the strings of an instrument</note> moved in a certain succession by the same player create one harmony, indicating a single leader of the song.
If we turn our ears again to the counter-singers and those singing the inner parts in this psalmody, we will perceive that High-Sounding One making all things resound together in a certain **proportion** <note>original: "proportione"; a technical musical term for the mathematical relationship between notes</note> (as **Albert** says) discovered by the wisdom of the Creator.
<margin>Albert</margin> This proportion was not prepared by some intellect on its own, but was drawn from the fountain of super-mundane wisdom. For if health is the tempering of the parts of the body, does this not come from Him who arranged all things as "very good" and tempered from the beginning? And again, He sounds out by tempering together the dissonant things.
<margin>David</margin> Hence the **Psalmist** <note>original: "Psalmographus"; referring to King David</note> sings: "He sent His word and healed them" <note>Psalm 107:20</note>. And if the instincts of animals lacking reason agree with one another and with their necessary pasture, has not the Maker of nature instilled this, so that like things take delight in living with like? And having rejected harmful foods, they take for themselves those that are suitable, prepared by Him.
<margin>Job</margin> Concerning these things, Job continues, saying: "Who prepares for the raven its food, when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no meat?" <note>Job 38:41</note>.
<margin>David</margin> With which the Royal Prophet sings: "Who gives food to all flesh," namely, that which is appropriate for it. If, moreover, those using reason are fitted together in their customs, does not He do this, of whom it is sung again in the Psalms: "Who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house?" <note>Psalm 68:6</note>. If again they agree in harmony in a city or any republic, is not this—

Behold, therefore, the same [harmony] resounds in all things; flowing through all, he makes all things echo with his life-giving and deifying power.
