### Who is this one, who fills all things, and what we can know
### of him. Chapter II.

There is no doubt that there is One from whom all things have proceeded, who fills all things, and toward whom all these same things tend, as toward a beloved and preferred end. This same One is called **God** by all, though by different names according to the diversity of languages. This is he
<margin>Isaiah</margin> who says through Isaiah: *I am he, I am the first, and I am the last: My hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured*—or with its palm enclosed—*the heavens.* <note>Isaiah 48:12-13</note> Not without mystery (as the Hebrew text has it), the word "I" is repeated three times, to denote that a certain **Trinity** is contained within that supreme Unity. Therefore, he says, "I am he," which is to say he exists of himself; or "I am that which is," as the Hebrew words clearly sound. <note>A reference to the divine name revealed in Exodus 3:14</note> It follows: *And I am the first,* the origin of all things; *and I am the last,* the end toward which all things tend. And as the first efficient cause, *my hand founded the earth* (the stable foundation of the whole machine which was built upon or around it); *and my right hand measures, orders, directs, or with its palm encloses all things,* calling and drawing to me those very things from which all proceeded; whence it follows: *I call them, and they stand together,* namely, gathered into myself. But who, how great, or of what kind this God may be, since he escapes all human grasp,
<margin>Paul</margin> it will be difficult, indeed impossible, to investigate; because (as Paul witnesses) he *dwells in inaccessible light, whom no man has seen, nor can see.* <note>1 Timothy 6:16</note> This was not hidden from those ancient Fathers, who constantly asserted that the two supreme **measures** <note>likely referring to the Sefirot of Kabbalah, specifically Keter (Crown) and Chokhmah (Wisdom)</note> or divine dignities—the higher of which they call the source, the crown, the origin, from which all things emanate; and the other, Wisdom, the firstborn, and by many other appropriate names—are not known to mortals, not even to Moses himself. For they say that he did not enter even the fiftieth gate of the preceding measure. <note>In Jewish mysticism, there are "Fifty Gates of Understanding"; Moses is traditionally said to have reached only the forty-ninth</note> Therefore, no one could understand the Father or the Son, until he came who said: *No one knows the Son, except the Father, nor...* <note>Matthew 11:27</note>

<margin>John</margin> No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. Likewise, John also says: *No one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who is in the heart of the Father, he has made him known to us.* <note>original: "in sinu Patris"; literally "in the bosom of the Father," a metaphor for the closest possible intimacy</note>
<margin>Job</margin> Job also touched upon this under the name of light, saying: *Tell me, if you know, in what way does light dwell?*
<margin>James</margin> Surely that light is what is called by James the *Father of lights*,
<margin>John</margin> and that light which said: *I am the light of the world.* Concerning which John says again: *Life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it.*
<margin>Job</margin> Following which Job says: *Their light shall be taken away from the wicked.* This light is communicated to all, so that it may enlighten every person, provided they are not clouded by their own darkness and render themselves unworthy of such great light. By this light alone can God and divine things be perceived.

If, therefore, any knowledge of this **precentor** <note>the lead singer or director who sets the pitch for the cosmic choir</note>, and of the delightful **harmony** <note>original: "concentu"; a singing together or musical agreement</note>, and of the beatifying end and rest is to be had, it is necessary that it proceed from this light. Nor can we expect it from the wise men of the world, who are wrapped in the darkness of their own inventions, as Paul testifies when he says:
<margin>Paul</margin> *We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory; and which none of the princes of this age knew.* For neither the end, nor the means by which one arrives at that same end—or at the most sweet harmony between God and man, in which man himself is made blessed—did any of the philosophers or worldly wise men ever teach. Because the "natural man" <note>original: "animalis homo"; the person relying solely on human soul and reason rather than the Holy Spirit</note> or the wisdom of the world, which is carnal, does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, as the Apostle follows.
<margin>The same</margin> And adding the reason, he says: *For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so, no one has known the things of God, except the Spirit of God.* Therefore, we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God; we also speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

For there is a triple progression in science much celebrated among the **Peripatetic philosophers** <note>the followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on logic and categorization</note>: the resolutive (or defining), the dividing, and the composing. None of these pertain to God, who can neither be defined, nor divided, nor composed. Hence, **Peripatetic theology** <note>Scholastic theology based on Aristotelian logic</note> is far too diminished, and that doctrine is insufficient for divine matters, which are perceived by the pure intellect or the purified spirit.

Therefore, another way must be sought by us, by which we may receive divine things. For there is one and a sublime way, which is called **intuitive** <note>direct, immediate perception or "seeing" without the need for step-by-step logic</note>, when a person with a clean heart and eye gazes into those clear and eternal mirrors and spectacles to which all the prophets arrived; for this reason, they were rightly called "seers." Thus, Isaiah, wishing to explain what he had perceived, said:
<margin>Isaiah</margin> *The vision of Isaiah.* And again: *I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne.*
<margin>Ezekiel, Daniel</margin> So Ezekiel, indicating from where he had the things he announced, said: *The hand of the Lord was upon me, and I saw.* Likewise Daniel says: *I saw in my vision.* To which level all the Prophets arrived, though they saw different things; whom John, Paul, Stephen, and other apostolic men followed, of whom the first said:
<margin>John</margin> *We saw his glory.* And the last declared of himself...

"Behold, I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God." <note>Acts 7:56. The author refers to St. Stephen, the first martyr, who saw a vision of Christ.</note> Furthermore, he who is in the middle <note>Likely referring to St. Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven</note> testifies that he saw and heard the secrets of God, which it is not lawful for a man to speak. This is because words are not sufficient, nor are mortals—wallowing as they do in a slough of filth <note>original: "coeni uolutabro"</note>—deemed worthy to receive such precious pearls and splendor, by which eyes already stained are more likely to be offended than enlightened. Therefore, there is a progression and a middle way of knowing between this intuitive vision and those **Peripatetic modes** <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle; this refers to logical, earthly reasoning</note>. I would rightly count all these modes as one: namely, the agreement of the truths announced by those who saw them with our own intellect. Our intellect is capable of receiving all truths, which is why it is called the **receptive intellect** <note>original: "intellectus passibilis"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the part of the mind that receives sensory data and potential knowledge</note>, a dreamer of things understood—or rather, a seeker most greedy for all truths.

When this intellect is purified and assents to a declared truth, finding rest within it, it gains for itself a great judgment: that the thing is true because it fits so well with the intellect itself. This is just like a **key with a lock**; if it does not fit the craftsmanship of the lock, it is proven not to be the key for it. But if it matches, turns, opens, and closes, it is judged to be its own. In the same way, a meaning or interpretation of something announced by the Prophets is judged to be true if it fits a purified intellect without any conflict; but if it does not, it is judged false and not its own. 

Therefore, we must seek this way, since we cannot look upon divine things as the Prophets and Apostles did. We must strive for the understanding and interpretation of the scriptures produced by those who saw what they spoke of with a true eye. We shall judge such an interpretation to be true when it is balanced and harmonious with our own purified intellect. By this truth and doctrine, we have said that God is blessed, not only as the **artisan** of this great machine <note>the universe</note> and its **end** toward which all things tend (as we shall soon declare), but as the one who, filling all things, makes all things resound together, just as he professes with an open voice in Jeremiah, saying:

<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
"Do I not fill heaven and earth?" <note>Jeremiah 23:24</note> That is, he fills them with his spirit, his voice, his harmonious power, and his glory. As Isaiah testifies he saw when he said:

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
"I saw, and the house was full"—the heavenly house, that is—"with his majesty; and those things that were under him filled that high temple." <note>Isaiah 6:1</note>

<margin>Haggai</margin>
But the Artisan was not content with that filling; through the prophet Haggai, he promised that he would fill things even better at the coming of the Messiah, saying: "The Desired One of all nations shall come, and I will fill this house with glory." <note>Haggai 2:7</note>

<margin>Isaiah</margin>

...or by the name **Shaddai** <note>Hebrew: שדי; typically translated as "Almighty," though the author explores deeper etymological roots here</note>: Which we sometimes have interpreted as "Almighty," sometimes as "God of heaven," but here as "the Sublime God." Perhaps it could be better interpreted as "Sufficient Cause," or "God fully at work." For He is the one of whom <margin>David</margin> sings in the Psalm: *When you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness.* <note>Psalm 104:28</note> And again: *The earth is filled by your possession and your influence.* Therefore, when He is absent, all things are thrown into confusion and return to their dust. But if all things remain full, though they follow one another in a cycle of change, they do not fail in their harmony; rather, they follow their sequence just like the sound in a **pipe organ** <term>organum: the author uses the pipe organ as a metaphor for the universe, where different parts create a single harmony</term> when the fingers and hands take their turns on the touched keys. 
<margin>Wisdom</margin> As it is said in the Book of Wisdom: *For the elements, while they turn into one another, are like the sound of a quality changed in an organ, and all things keep their own sound.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 19:18. This refers to the idea that the basic building blocks of the world change form but maintain a cosmic musicality.</note> These things are found at the end of the book; but at the beginning it is also said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the orb of the earth; and this, which contains all things, has knowledge of the voice.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1:7</note> Here we are taught not only that the Spirit of God fills all things with a harmonious sound, but also that He gives it to the man who stands before Him, so that he may perceive that very concert. It says that the man who contains all things also has knowledge of that voice and harmony—provided, of course, that he is spiritual and has been made capable of receiving that Spirit. There are almost infinite places in Holy Scripture by which we could confirm our proposition, but let these suffice so that we may now come 
<margin>Pythagoras, Plato</margin> to the "outsiders" <note>Non-Christian or "pagan" philosophers</note> who, seeing these things, emulated the Fathers. The foremost of these, Pythagoras and Plato, having been taught by this same family of thought, teach with their Academics that a divine power is infused into all things. Some call this the **World Soul** <term>Anima mundi: a philosophical concept suggesting the world possesses a soul that connects all living things</term>, others the Spirit of God; the Poet <note>Virgil</note>, imitating them, sings:
<margin>Virgil</margin>
> A spirit within nourishes, and a Mind, infused through the limbs, 
> moves the entire mass and mingles with the great body. 
> From this comes the race of men and cattle, and the lives of flying things, 
> and the monsters the sea carries beneath its marble surface. 
> A fiery vigor is in them, and a celestial origin. <note>Virgil, Aeneid, VI.726-730</note>

<margin>Manilius</margin> Manilius sings with the same meaning, saying:
> For they sing of a nature powerful with a silent mind, 
> and a God infused into the earth, the sky, and the sea. <note>Manilius, Astronomica, 1.247-248</note>

<margin>Orpheus, Alexander, Dorylaus, Boethius</margin> Orpheus, Alexander of Miletus, and Dorylaus agree on this same point, as we touched upon above. From the workshop of all these, Boethius says:
> You, connecting the middle soul of a triple nature, 
> moving all things, release it through harmonious limbs. 
> Which, once composed, has gathered its motion into two circles; 
> it moves to return into itself, and circles the profound Mind, 
> and turns the heaven with a similar image. <note>Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book 3, Meter 9. This complex poem describes the soul of the world revolving in harmony with the mind of God.</note>

<margin>Aratus</margin> And Aratus sings under the name of Jove:
> The life of the elements, the heat of the world, the fire of the ether, 
> and the vigor of the stars; a perpetual substance of light, 
> and the number of heaven's modulation.

The highest God is said to be, to thrive, and to fill all things, and by shaking the heavens like a certain lyre, He creates a heavenly harmony. And Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of philosophical and "hermetic" writings that influenced Renaissance thinkers</note>, the splendor of philosophers, in that book titled *That <gloss>quod</gloss> God is both hidden and manifest at once*, says: "It is impossible for God to exist always, unless He always performs all things." That is: in heaven, in the air, the earth, the sea, in the whole world, and in every tiny part of the world, both in that which exists and in that which does not exist. There is nothing in all of nature that He Himself is not. For He is those things which exist; He is even those things which do not exist. Those things which exist, He leads into the light, and those which do not exist, He hides within Himself. This God is better than any name; He is hidden, yet again He is the most manifest of all; He is visible to the mind, yet present to the eyes; He is incorporeal, yet (so to speak) multi-corporeal. For there is nothing in bodies that is not He Himself. For He alone exists as all things <gloss>enim</gloss>, as even Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that all reality is one and unchanging</note> taught, whom Aristotle <margin>Parmenides</margin> <margin>Aristotle</margin> <margin>Mercury</margin> <margin>Orpheus</margin> <margin>Eusebius</margin> unjustly tries to refute. > Jupiter is the highest peak, and the lowest sole of the foot:
> He is the eternal one, existing all at once, and everywhere the whole 
> Foundation of the earth. And again:
> Jupiter is whatever you see, and wherever you are moved. <note>original: "Iupiter est quodcūq; uides, quocūq; moueris." Here, "Jupiter" is used by the Renaissance author as a poetic name for the supreme Divine Principle or God.</note>

And thus, filling all things, He makes all things sound together.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the divine return, moving from the Hermetic concept of God as "all things" to a Neoplatonic and Kabbalistic explanation of how all creation emanates from and returns to a single Divine Source, likened to a mathematical and spherical progression.</meta>

<page-num>CLXVIII</page-num>
<header>THE EIGHTH TONE</header>

# THE EIGHTH TONE

<margin>The same</margin>
...saying: "The dust returns to its earth, from whence it was, and the spirit returns to God, who made it." <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:7</note> For this spirit, which is from God, once released from the body, immediately returns to Him, unless it is held back by some violent impediment. However, the earthy part is brought back to the earth, from which it immediately proceeded. And since the earth is from God, who created it, and since it follows a due order along with everything sprouting from it, it must eventually return to God. He who moves all things and draws all things into Himself (says <term>Aristotle</term> <margin>Aristo.</margin> with his <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note>) acts as one desired and beloved by all through an innate love and longing. He who, proceeding by a mathematical way, had said before that all things are reduced to the One, just as they had proceeded from the One. This the <term>Academics</term> <note>Followers of the Platonic school</note> (especially <term>Proclus</term> in his *Theological Elements* <note>original: "Theorematibus Theologicis", a foundational work of Neoplatonism</note>) teach most clearly. 

In the same way, and with no small mystery, the Hebrew characters signifying numbers proceed in the same order. For **א** <note>The letter Aleph</note> is the character signifying "one," but having completed the discourse through all the characters—some of which signify units, some tens, and some hundreds—one arrives finally at the same **א**, which, when pronounced as **Aleph**, signifies a thousand, the completion of all numbers, and the cube of ten, the supreme number. Thus, just as the character itself signifies one, so when pronounced it signifies a thousand; and the character also signifies this same thing when a dot is added: **א̇**. 

But this **Aleph** also signifies a "leader," and it is the seal of the "highest crown" <note>likely referring to Keter, the highest emanation in Kabbalah</note>, or of the highest Father, containing within its shape two **י** <note>Yod</note> and one **ו** <note>Vav</note>. These letters, in their numerical values, yield 26 <note>Yod=10, Yod=10, Vav=6</note>, just like the great four-letter name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH, which also sums to 26</note>. Therefore, by a great mystery, that which represents the divine name through numbers hidden in a certain secret mystery, reveals God as the sole and first principle of all in the simple character itself, and as the end of numbers in its pronunciation. 

But another sacred secret is to be observed in that great name of God: in which all the letters signify <term>circular numbers</term> <note>Numbers that "return to themselves" when squared, such as 5x5=25 or 6x6=36</note>. For **י** <note>Yod</note> gives ten, **ה** <note>He</note> gives five, and **ו** <note>Vav</note> gives six. These are all—and the only—circular numbers. This is to suggest that God is a true sphere: and He proceeds in every progression by a spherical order, bringing all things back into Himself, just as they had proceeded from Him. This is testified through <margin>Isaiah</margin> Isaiah, who says: 

> I am the first and the last; my hands have founded all things, 

namely, by ordering these same things back into myself, so that they might follow a spherical order. Hence this mass of created things cannot strive toward anything else but Him, whose likeness it holds. Furthermore, all the lines of a circle going out from the center to the circumference, and from it back to the center, denote that all creatures emanating from the center of the highest sphere strive toward the circumference of that same sphere as their end. And just as these lines never leave the limits of the sphere or circle, so neither do creatures leave the boundaries of that divine sphere; so much so that they are from Him, remain in Him, and strive toward Him. Just as all <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are qualities (like color or size) that cannot exist on their own but must belong to a "substance"</note> rely on substance, which is their subject and support, so all created things—which are like accidents in respect to the first and supreme Being, which exists of itself...

<summary>This page synthesizes Aristotelian, Neoplatonic, and Kabbalistic thought to argue that all of creation follows a circular or spherical path, beginning with God as the "One" and returning to Him as the "Thousand." It uses the Hebrew letter Aleph and the mathematical properties of the Tetragrammaton to illustrate this divine symmetry.</summary>

### Chapter IV.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Boethius</margin>
**A**ll assert that there is a double <term>appetite</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, an "appetite" is a natural inclination or drive toward a goal.</note> in things: the natural and the free. But in man (if I am not mistaken) we could add a third, which is from without, and supernatural, and divine, drawing us to itself by its effect, and inducing us to perform meritorious divine works pleasing to God himself. And it is this which always prays for the best things—not indeed the natural discourse [of reason], as many think, but that higher portion which Plotinus calls the "intellect," distinct from the rational power: by which we understand God and divine things as a mediator: and we strive toward Him in mind and work: as he treats extensively in his book *On Man*. And this, residing in the citadel of the soul, always resists the law which is in our members, leading where natural virtue and affection can least go. This, therefore, is "I," but the other is "grace," according to the Apostle's doctrine, who said: "Not I, but the grace of God with me." <note>original: "Non ego, sed gratia Dei mecū." From 1 Corinthians 15:10.</note> This divine part, therefore, tends toward the best and divine things: but that other, the worse part and our "animal" side, always draws us to the depths, because matter is most distant from the supreme. Our soul, however, or the rational power, is in the middle, carried now here, now there: or adhering now to this one, now to that, either through laziness or by the choice of the will, although by its own nature it tends toward that principle from which it proceeded, unless matter, the mother of error, distracts it: as that common saying of Boethius is applied: "In the minds of men is implanted a certain desire for the true good, but wandering error leads them away toward false things." <note>original: "Inest mētibus hominum ueri boni certa cupiditas, sed ad falsa deuius error abducit." From Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*.</note> This is caused either by matter (as we said) drawing us to the depths, or by corporeal images and multiple objects distracting us from the present: for a present and sensible object moves more strongly a man who is still "animal," and one who does not have his senses trained for discernment...

Others run more easily toward dominion if their birth and virtue provide for it, and if the Sun, Mars, and similar stars favor them—if the things handed down by the Astronomers are true. Others run toward various virtues by a natural course according to the varying disposition of body and soul and the favoring heavens; yet they reach nothing of good unless the heavenly power favors them, from which all good comes. These things are not without a mystery: for he falls from the chariot of his own strength, in which he trusted; he is wounded between two pieces of craftsmanship woven by human skill, to denote that the "weaving" and every work devised by human cunning, or labored by one’s own skill and strength, is frustrated; and it is turned to the ruin of the one laboring without divine favor. Thus he was able to perform thereafter what he was not capable of before. <margin>Solomon</margin>

<margin>Peter</margin>

<margin>THE SAME</margin>

<margin>THE SAME</margin>

On the right side is charity, piety, love, mercy, kindness, and others of that kind; on the left, however, are fear, terror, threat, severe justice, punishment, and the like. Finding this, the divine preacher ought to draw souls more by soothing them than by terrifying them, and rather by the bonds of charity than of terror, as He himself...

...acted toward the adulteress, the sinner, the publican, and the tax collector, leading them with kindness and not by terrifying them with threats. And although the divine orator <note>A preacher or minister of the Word.</note> must sometimes announce the crimes of the people with a loud voice, he should nevertheless do so without casting insults, but by proposing with charitable admonition those things which are prepared by the rectitude of justice on account of those crimes. Casting their nets into this part, the Apostles were not able to draw them in for the multitude of fish, so that we may be taught what great profit is made in love and charity. Nor is it without cause that it is added: *And although there were so many, the net was not torn* <note>A reference to the miraculous catch of fish in John 21:11.</note>: because the virtue and the office of preaching performed in charity is made firm and strengthened, with God’s help, so that it cannot be broken or torn; rather, it accomplishes all things, according to that word of the Apostle: <margin>Paul</margin> **I can do all things in Him who strengthens me.** The Angels and ministering spirits also draw, so that they may carry out those things which the highest Moderator <note>God.</note> commands, as it is said of them in the Psalm: <margin>Psalm</margin> **Bless the Lord, all you his Angels, his ministers, who do his will**—not only among men, but by moving all things and influencing all things, even the smallest. Hence we see many things being stirred and worked beyond what their nature provides; and mortals, not knowing where these things come from, are filled with wonder. This happens in many ways: for sometimes they <note>The ministering spirits.</note> go before with a certain premonition and movement regarding things that are to come to a person, as we can prove through the clearest experience from the most serious authors, both secular and Catholic.

<margin>Cicero</margin> Cicero relates in the first book of *On Divination* that for the Spartans, shortly before the disaster at Leuctra <note>The Battle of Leuctra (371 BCE), where the Spartans suffered a major defeat against Thebes.</note>, the arms clashed in the temple of Hercules. At the same time in Thebes (as <margin>Callisthenes</margin> Callisthenes says), in the temple of Hercules, the doors which were closed with bars opened themselves; and the weapons which had been fixed to the walls were found on the ground. At that same time, many signs announced the disasters of the Leuctran battle to the Spartans. For the crown on the head of the statue of Lysander <note>A famous Spartan admiral and leader.</note>, which stood at Delphi, suddenly appeared to be made of wild and thorny herbs. Furthermore, the golden stars which had been placed at Delphi by the Spartans after that naval victory in which they crushed the Athenians fell down shortly before the Leuctran battle and were never found. Why should I mention those many portents recited by Josephus <margin>Josephus</margin> which preceded the destruction suffered by Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian? For many days, the moon seemed to suffer in an unusual eclipse, as if in sympathy with the coming ruin. For half an hour, a flash of light surrounded the temple as if it were midday. Its bronze gate, which could scarcely be moved by twenty men, opened of its own accord at the sixth hour of the night. Chariots and armies of armed men were seen being carried through the region with great force. All of these things are <margin>Eusebius</margin> confirmed by Eusebius of Caesarea in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*. And to dispatch the matter briefly, almost all notable disasters have been preceded by certain portents and wonders from the ministers of God. 

Signs have also preceded many at their birth, as Cicero relates in the same work regarding <margin>Midas according to Cicero</margin> the boy Midas: while he was sleeping, ants heaped grains of wheat into his mouth, an omen predicting great wealth, which indeed came to pass. As for <margin>Plato</margin> Plato, when bees had settled on his lip while he was sleeping in his cradle, the response was given that he would excel with a singular sweetness of speech...

<margin>Heraclitus</margin>
...of his speech, his future eloquence was foretold even in the child: a thing which we read in our histories happened to Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan <note>Legend says that as an infant, a swarm of bees settled on Ambrose's mouth, leaving behind a drop of honey—a portent of his future "honey-sweet" eloquence.</note>. To Hecuba, the wife of Priam, as she was about to give birth to Paris, it seemed in a vision that she gave birth to a burning torch which would set fire to Troy and all of Asia. To the mother of Phalaris <note>Phalaris was the infamously cruel tyrant of Akragas in Sicily, known for the "Brazen Bull" execution device.</note> (as Heraclitus of Pontus, a student of Plato, writes), it appeared that the statue of Mercury poured blood upon the earth, with which the entire house overflowed; this provided a sign of the immense cruelty in the son she was bearing.

<margin>Philistus</margin>
To the mother of Dionysius (as Philistus says), it appeared while she was pregnant that she gave birth to a little satyr. But to Ortolana, the mother of Clare of Assisi, it was not yet a vision, but it was signified by a clear voice that she should safely bring forth a certain most brilliant light <note>A play on the name Clara, which in Latin means "clear," "bright," or "shining."</note>. The portent that occurred at the birth of John the Baptist is known to everyone; by which it is proven that angels act with us both by anticipating and by celebrating a birth, even if among the gentiles <note>Non-Christians or pagans.</note> evil angels were at work. The angel Gabriel appeared to the father, Zechariah; because he did not believe, his speech was taken away; the sterile woman is made fertile; once the boy is born, speech is restored to the silenced father, so that the neighbors and those aware of the event were compelled to exclaim in wonder, "What, then, do you think this child will be?" 

And ascending to the more ancient ones, Isaac was anticipated by a most famous oracle: he was conceived by a sterile and aged woman and fathered by a man in decline. His son Jacob struggled with his brother in their mother’s womb, for which reason the parents were taught by a divine oracle that two nations were contained in that maternal womb. The ancient lawgiver <note>Moses.</note> was exposed to be killed in the river among the reeds; and he was taken up by the daughter of Pharaoh, not by chance, but by God’s disposition, who led her there by His angel so that the boy might be saved and called **Moses**, <note>original: "Moses .i. sumptus ex aqs"</note> that is, "taken from the waters," and so that by angelic favor he might continually be the leader of that most celebrated and much-sung crossing of the Israelite people out of Egypt. Samson, the strongest of the robust, was conceived by a sterile woman made fertile by an angelic oracle, and was established as a Nazirite—that is, "consecrated to the Lord"—before he was even born. 

It would be far too long to recount all the examples that could be brought from the Holy Scriptures and the many histories of the gentiles, by which it might be proven that the ministers of God anticipated many people either before or at their very birth, or favored them in war or other difficult matters, or acted familiarly with men in many ways. But let these few things be said so that the unbelieving—and those who refuse to admit anything except what they perceive with their animal senses—may learn that there are angelic ministers sent for our service. They do not only persuade us of what must be done in an imperceptible way, but they have presented themselves visibly and sensibly in many ways, drawing even those not yet born or not yet grown toward diverse ends, and forewarning of future destruction through various portents, or leading them to a strenuous work. These things we can still prove from the Holy Scriptures.

### Chapter VIII. How all things proceed from God through the number six.

<margin>Augustine</margin> **A**fter we have discussed a little about those things drawing us into God, even the numbers through which we have gone out and return again to God (to agree with Augustine) must not be despised. For <margin>Augustine</margin> in many places of Holy Scripture the logic of numbers is seen to be held in great esteem, and rightly so, since God made all things in number, weight, and measure. We read, therefore, not without mystery, that the supreme Creator set out to produce creatures through the <term>senary number</term> <note>The number six. In classical numerology, six is the first "perfect number" because its divisors (1, 2, and 3) add up to itself.</note>, which was indeed first perfected, and giving a triangle in a great sacrament, as we have explained above. This perfection it has from itself, and not merely because God created the world in it, as the same Augustine affirms elsewhere. <margin>The same</margin> Therefore, the most perfect Architect chose this first perfect number for the perfect fabrication of the world. And so that it might be harmonious, he chose that number which matches the intervals of the perfect <term>diapason</term> <note>The diapason is the musical interval of an octave. The author is linking the six days of creation to the mathematical structure of musical harmony.</note> consonance. For there are six, with seven intervals, after which one arrives at the eighth, which completes the octave itself. In this same order the weekly revolution proceeds, returning to the same eighth day from which it began: so that from Sabbath to Sabbath, and Sunday to Sunday, the intermediate days are always six. If this six is squared into 36, and at the same time reduced into a cube with the number ten, it completes the 360 degrees of the Zodiac. It would even complete the days of the year, were it not that the sun passes sparingly through one degree each day; for it prolongs its course up to 365 days, which is the number of joints <note>original: "artus"</note> in the human body. ...yields [to the twelve], and benefits the primary joints in our body, and brings many other things mentioned above, where we treated the number twelve. And furthermore, the <term>senary</term> <note>The number six (senarius), often regarded in Renaissance thought as a 'perfect' number because its factors—1, 2, and 3—sum to itself.</note> representing twice three, two triplets, by which the Creator went out into his work: For first he completed the structure, and second its decoration. For in the first three days he created all the elementary things, and the foundations of this worldly structure, and distinguished them: On the first [day], the super-celestial from the terrestrial by the sphere and mass of the heavens; afterwards the waters from the land, giving to the latter its fertility. Then in the remaining three days, he decorated the structure with its inhabitants, placing in the heavens two lights and stars; on the earth, four-footed animals; in the waters, fish and their creeping things; in the air, birds and winged things. And thus the triune God, acting with material things—of which the number two, or duality, is from matter—communicated himself in two ways: The Spirit in fire, light, and heat, with a life-giving mouth; the Son in the waters and the offspring proceeding from them; the Father, however, being the principle and origin of all in the primordial foundation and in the base upon which all things are fixed. On the sixth day, however, he produced man, the overseer of the entire world, embracing all those things: who also, growing through six ages, might progress, so that in the seventh and in the true Sabbath he might rest.

### How the human race is led into God himself through the six ages of time. Chapter 10.

<margin>John</margin>
**J**ust as the work of the world was completed in six days, so also the course of this world proceeds through six distinct times, as if through six ages, arriving at the millennial Sabbath <note>A "Sabbath of a thousand years," referring to the promised era of eternal rest or the kingdom of God.</note> described by John in the Apocalypse. For on the first day, the earth and the heavens are said to have been made along with a certain common light, and its division from the darkness, while the spirit of Elohim <note>The Hebrew name for God used in Genesis. The author uses it here to evoke the original scriptural language.</note> hovered over the waters. In the same way, man in the first age of the world is said to have been fashioned from soul and body, as if from heaven and earth, with a certain light of natural law and divinity shining upon him, especially while he was in the state of innocence. But light was divided from darkness when man was expelled from that paradise of pleasure, and when the shining and divine Enoch was snatched away from the dark crowd. And at the end of that age, it is said that the sons of Elohim approached the daughters of men, making them pregnant. Great indeed are the mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta." In this context, it refers to hidden spiritual meanings or allegorical truths rather than church rituals.</note> here regarding the correspondence of the sons of Elohim fertilizing the daughters of men, so that giants, or "falling ones" (as it is held in the literal text), might generate men of renown, powerful from of old with the spirit of Elohim; who, hovering over the face of the waters, rendered them fertile amidst the darkness that covered the face of the abyss.

The second age began in Noah, who was like a certain middle and firmament dividing that first long-lived age from the second, in which the confusion of tongues occurred, denoted by the "lower waters." And that middle was called "heaven," because Noah was heavenly and just in his generations—that is, as far as that circuit of time allowed. For at that season, the family of God was divided into Shem and Japheth, away from the family of the devil in Ham and his descendants. From him came Cush (that is, the Ethiopian), Mizraim (the Egyptians), and Canaan, from whom came the Canaanites—generations which were indeed inferior and rejected, signified by the "lower waters," and divided from those which were irrigated by the "higher waters." And this division remains even to this day, as Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> learnedly and well treats in his commentary on Genesis. 

<margin>Jerome</margin>

For to him first was given a sensible and distinctive sign between family and family, and he is called the "Father of Faith" (that is, of the faithful). Yet it was not said in this "day" or age "that it was good," because the whole period was surrendered to hardships and calamities. And from there he wandered as a pilgrim in Egypt and in Haran, and was oppressed exceedingly until a familiar hospitality might console him...

### How an individual human, living a regulated life, arrives in Christ through the six ages signified by those six days. Chapter XI.

It seems a difficult thing to investigate how this entire course corresponds in its parts to the six stages of a man's life leading into the seventh, unless we are illuminated by that light which shines its rays variously and appropriately upon every person throughout those ages. Therefore, bathed in that light, we shall attempt to match the stages of a human life with those six days of creation. For the infant, coming forth from the mother's womb where he lived in darkness, is said to "come into the light," so that the phrase applies to him most perfectly: "Let there be light," or let there be light also illuminating him. It should also be observed that this age passes in silence, performing no famous work; indeed, if there is anything, it is consumed by a "deluge of oblivion," because all those infantile things are laid aside. Only a few familiar things are saved and remembered, because few things remain in adolescents from their infancy—namely, the "seed-bearing" potential and the budding virtue of youth. This is indicated at the beginning of the seven-year period <term>septennium: a period of seven years used in classical and medieval medicine to mark developmental stages</term> by the changing of the teeth, which signify the strengths and virtues of a man, as we have explained elsewhere in a long discourse.

<margin>Chalcidius, Macrobius</margin> <note>Chalcidius (4th c.) and Macrobius (5th c.) were influential commentators whose works preserved Greek philosophical ideas about the soul and the significance of the number seven in human development.</note>
The second age follows after the course of seven years, in which (as Chalcidius and Macrobius extensively record) some change always occurs in a human being. In this stage, the boy, released from infantile bonds, begins to be taught various doctrines and divine worship, just as the world was then taught by Noah <note>The author is paralleling the "Second Day" of creation and the "Second Age" of the world (Noah) with the second stage of childhood (ages 7–14)</note>. And the boy receives a "dividing firmament"—that is, discretion—by which he distinguishes between "waters and waters": namely, rational actions from animal ones. And because the age is completed, but no specific work is finished—only begun—it therefore fits most appropriately with that day which the wise scribe Moses asserts was completed when he says: "And evening and morning were the second day." But he did not wish any work to be perfected in it, since he remains silent about what he says of the other days: "And God saw that it was good." Hence, a boy is neither rewarded nor punished for work performed in this age, since he is not considered legally responsible by any law, nor by God...

# OF THE FIRST SONG
<meta>image quality: good, some bleed-through; catchword: sterio (part of "mysterio")</meta>

...it seems to be counted among other works. Nor should it be insisted upon that on the first day it was said, "And God saw the light, that it was good," because light is not our own work, but was produced by God for our benefit and assistance. And although the firmament, or the sphere of the heavens, is said to have been made on the second day, the work was not yet perfect because it was not yet decorated with the sun, the moon, and its stars.

The third age follows, in which a person grows up, being fit for both kinds of seed, the bodily and the spiritual. For one becomes more fit for generating according to the flesh, and also according to the spirit; because then one begins to be watered by doctrine, by the law, and by the spirit, so much so that one is then judged by the wise to be fit for religion and for spiritual burdens. Hence it can deservedly be said to such a person: "Let the earth sprout," namely the green herb of your mind and the fruit-bearing tree. And this happens once the waters of one's powers have first been gathered into their proper place; for at first they were mixed together, so that the animal virtues <note>In medieval psychology, "virtues" or "powers" refer to the functions of the soul, such as movement and sensation (animal) versus reason (rational).</note> could not be distinguished from the rational ones. For then a better separation of powers occurs, and it becomes apparent to the person how the natural virtue is dry when left to itself. And here God sees in a twofold way that it is good: first, because the waters of the powers are gathered together; and afterwards, because the earth, moistened by super-celestial rains, produces fruit, so that one can say with the Prophet: <margin>David</margin> "For the Lord will give his blessing, and our earth shall yield her fruit." <note>Psalm 85:12</note>

The fourth age succeeds this, which is called the most flourishing youth; where one who walks rightly is perfectly illuminated in the mind, like the sun, and in the lower intellect, like the moon. For so <margin>Plato</margin> Plato teaches in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Symposio"</note>: that our intellect, when united with the divine light and made "mind," is called the sun; but when left to itself, it is the moon; however, when mixed with animal passions, it is the earth producing lower fruits.

After youth, however, manhood <note>original: "virilitas"</note> follows in the fifth place, in which a person ought to be a perfect man, adorned with the perfection of virtue and wisdom, which is called the "water of health" in <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach. Reference to Sirach 15:3.</note>. And because one produces better seeds in wisdom, it is therefore said, "Let the waters bring forth the living soul." Great and robust works are also produced, as are strenuous and most solid counsels, which fear no attacks of the sea. Thus they grow in strength, virtues, works, name, and fame; therefore it was said to those existing in this age: "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea," that is, may you have a complete watery wisdom, through which you may be permitted to run through all the bays of the sea.

But unless a person directs all these things toward God, he still lives somewhat like a beast, just as happened to Solomon (who was otherwise the wisest); therefore it is said that the beasts and cattle were made according to their kind. If, however, he lives for God, the sixth age immediately succeeds for him, along with that old age of which it is said in the <margin>Psalm</margin> Psalm: "My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn, and my old age shall be in plentiful mercy." <note>Psalm 92:10. The Latin uses "rhinoceros" in the next sentence to describe the same animal strength.</note> In a wondrous way, when he was believed to be failing in old age, he rejoices that he has received the strength of the rhinoceros; and when he was thought sterile, he is gladdened that it has been most fruitful. We read that this has happened to few—that they were made more robust in old age. There are some, however, who in old age do not fail in the strength of spiritual powers, as was written concerning Moses, of advanced and mature age, at the end of the Law, not without mystery, <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "mysterio" is completed by the catchword "sterio."</note>

The Spirit, who is called the Paraclete <term>Paraclete: A Greek-derived title for the Holy Spirit, meaning "Advocate" or "Comforter"</term> and the consoler of others, was not ignorant of any day or hour; for He is in the bosom of the Father, knowing all His secrets, and even all things that are hidden within man. But Scripture preserved the accustomed way of speaking that we use in our daily conversations. For we speak of a "joyful day" because it makes us joyful; a "polished tongue" <margin>Paul</margin> because it produces polished words; or a "quiet time" in which we ourselves are quiet; and many things of this sort. Thus is understood that saying of the Apostle <note>Paul, in Romans 8:26</note> that the Spirit intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be expressed, because He leads us back to the heart and to compunction, by which we ask for pardon with groans. So too is that saying of the Savior <margin>CHRIST</margin> concerning that day or hour: "No one knows, not even the Son" <note>Mark 13:32</note>, who is in the bosom of the Father. Augustine says <margin>Augustine</note> He said this in the sense of "not making the disciples know" <note>original: "ut scire faciat." Augustine famously argued that Christ "not knowing" was a figure of speech meaning He was not authorized to reveal it.</note>. Similarly, when it is said, "It repented me" <note>Genesis 6:6</note>, this is because He wished to punish the wicked; by which chastisement He made them repent, even if that repentance was fruitless for them. In like manner, it must be said that He "rested," that is, He reached the goal, which is Christ; in whom we ought to rest and pause. How Moses touched upon and wrote this in a wonderful and hidden way in that narrative of the world's construction, we shall declare in its proper place, God willing. Hence <margin>CHRIST</margin> Christ himself, the true Sabbath, says: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you: and you will find rest for your souls" <note>Matthew 11:28-29</note>.

<margin>Augustine</margin> **N**ot without diligence (to agree with Augustine) was it said on the sixth day: "God saw everything that He had made, and they were very good." Because if each individual thing has its own measures, numbers, and orders in its own kind, how much more so all things together, and the universe itself, which is completed by these individual things collected into one? For all beauty is much more praiseworthy in the whole than in the part. For the beauty of the whole body is greater than that of the nose, or the mouth, or the cheeks. And a speech composed of its words and clauses is more beautiful than the words themselves or particular sentences; and a song from all voices and the harmony of many is more pleasant than a single voice, however sonorous. So the universe of the world is more beautiful and better than its own parts and members; therefore, when the structure was complete, it was said that all things were "very good," namely, perfect in their whole. This sense is indeed beautiful, but more beautiful (if I am not mistaken) is the interpretation in the most beautiful Jesus: if the wise teach truly, things are only so much real, so much good, and finally so much beautiful (as the Academics <margin>Academics</margin> <note>The "Academics" refers to the Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophers who taught that all beauty participates in a supreme "One."</note> add) as they participate in the supreme being, the supreme good, and the supreme beauty from which all beautiful things come. Hence our theologians <margin>Theologians</margin> have said that human nature is more perfect after the Fall than before; because, united to Christ God, it is adorned like a royal necklace; and is decorated with a divine lineage and ancestry from its own regeneration in Christ himself, and by a greater communion with God. Since therefore everything [is] so much [beautiful]... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the word "beautiful" on the next page.</note>

### That the heavens in their revolution lead to a kind of octave. Chapter XV.

Two things are to be considered in the <term>diapason</term> <note>The octave</note>: One, that it always returns to the same tone from which it departs; the other, that it is not that tone of the same key and nature. <meta>This page continues the discussion of cosmic and musical harmony, specifically how the physical motions of the heavens and the mathematical distances between planets mirror the divine order and the "Eighth Tone" mentioned on the previous page. <page-num>LXXXIX</page-num>
->OF THE FIRST SONG<-

...responding: Thus the heavens, in their daily circuit, always return to the same place from which they had departed through the point of the circuit. However, it is not the same revolution, nor are the degrees or minutes of that day the same, because any heaven or planet changes its degree on any given day, or at least its minute—such as Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which do not traverse a full degree every day, but only some minutes. The star-bearing heaven (if many are right in their opinion) is moved from its place by a certain space, and it too completes its own revolution every day, returning to the same place through the point from which it had departed. All these heavens, by these revolutions of theirs, not only signify but favor the idea that all things into which they flow <note>referring to astrological influence or "influx" upon the earthly realm</note> follow this circular motion and return to that from which they had proceeded. Some indeed return through corruption to the earth, or the matter from which they were composed; but other incorruptible things return, through sequestration from this thick matter, to that principle from which they emanated, though under a different reasoning. For they proceeded from Him insofar as He is the principle, and they tend toward Him in that He is the end. Yet the same God is the principle and the boundary.

They also make their daily revolution in 24 hours, which yield three eighths, or octonaries; these, when compared to each other, give a triple proportion. For 24 contains eight three times. And this proportion constitutes the <term>diapason</term> <note>the interval of an octave, traditionally a 2:1 ratio, but here part of a larger harmonic complex</note> and the <term>diapente</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fifth, a 3:2 ratio</note>, so that the circuit of the heavens may be harmonious, just as is the distance and correspondence of their motions to one another.

### On the concord of the heavens, both from distance and from the harmony of motions, Chapter XVI.

<margin>
Censorinus
Pliny
Eratosthenes
</margin>
That the heavens are most harmonious, not only from motion but from distance and their mutual agreement, almost all antiquity testifies. Censorinus, Pliny, and Eratosthenes, assigning the distances of the heavens from the Pythagorean workshop <note>referring to the Pythagorean school of thought which first linked musical ratios to planetary distances</note>, conclude that the circuit of the earth is 252,000 <term>stadia</term> <note>a Greek unit of distance; the author later specifies which type of stadium he means</note>. And they judged that there are as many stadia in each star as there are on earth, which are said to be of various magnitudes. But leaving aside this controversy as less opportune, we say that these stadia are Italian ones of 125 feet, not Olympic ones which are 600 feet, nor Pythic ones which are 1,000 feet. From the Earth, therefore, to the Moon there are 126,000 stadia, and they make the interval of a tone. From the Moon to the star of Mercury, which is called <term>Stilbon</term> <note>original Greek: "the gleaming one"</note>, it is half of that, like a semitone. From here to <term>Phosphorus</term> <note>original Greek: "light-bringer"</note>, which is the star of Venus, almost as much—that is, another semitone. From here to the star of Jupiter, which is called <term>Phaeton</term> <note>original Greek: "the shining one"</note>, half of that, which makes a semitone. ### Concerning the Fruitful Harmony in the Sevenfold Number of the Planets. Chapter XVII. ###

<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
<margin>Chalcidius, Macrobius, Galen</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
**M**oreover, it seems truly wondrous that the planets, through which fruitfulness is supplied to all things, are distributed in the number seven. This is called an <term>infœcundus|unfruitful or barren</term> number by those skilled in formal arithmetic, and most especially by the Pythagoreans, because within the number ten, it neither generates another number nor is it generated by any number. Therefore it is called sterile, and for that reason is judged unhappy and ill-omened. If, however, one weighs this number on a true scale, he will find it fruitful and most auspicious. For it is generated from the first even <note>original: "pari"</note> number, four, as if from a female; and from the first odd <note>original: "impari"</note> number, three, as if from a male. From this arises every fruitfulness, beyond which no other is given. Hence, after reaching the sevenfold number, there is no further progress, but always some change for the better until the required growth is achieved. Concerning these changes—which occur in humans through every seven-year cycle—Chalcidius, Macrobius, Galen, and others write most extensively. This is most thoroughly proven in the fabric of the world, in which, when the Creator arrived at the seventh day, He rested, not proceeding further but leaving it to all things He had crafted to produce through their own seven-fold cycles. Thus it was not necessary for the number itself to be composed of certain parts to give birth, because it had drawn perfect fruitfulness from the first male and female numbers.

Yet it is called sterile by the Mathematicians because it does not give birth to a number within the limits of ten, nor is it born from equal parts. But by more secret <note>likely referring to esoteric or mystical traditions</note> wise men, it is considered most fruitful, since from the female and male power it contains, it bestows fruitfulness and fruits upon things. Therefore the planets and the signs grant fruitfulness to lower things from the numbers twelve and seven; each of which is composed of the first even and first odd, as if from masculine and feminine, but in different ways, as we shall say presently. And hence every planet and every sign tastes of either a masculine or feminine nature—except Mercury, which is both <note>Mercury was traditionally considered androgynous or "common" in astrology, taking on the nature of the planets it associated with</note>. Furthermore, in the sevenfold number itself, perfect rest occurs with perfect fruitfulness. For this number contains the first perfect six, in which all things were made, and the seventh day of rest, which corresponds with both Saturns—namely, the celestial and the supramundane. From both comes a Sabbath <note>original: "sabbatum"</note> that is not unfruitful, but is the boundary of the preceding cycle, after which another immediately follows, in which operations are performed again. And Christ, containing this sevenfold number most perfectly, as our true Sabbath, introduces us (as we have said) to the eighth <note>referring to the "eighth day" or the state of eternal resurrection beyond the seven days of the week</note>. Hence, by no small mystery <note>original: "sacramento"</note>, John, being carried away in the Spirit, saw seven golden candlesticks—that is, the seven planets...

### On the harmonic agreement of the sevenfold number of planets with the twelve signs. Chapter XVIII. ###

<margin>John</margin>
**A**nd although a discrepancy may seem to exist in the numbers of the planets and the signs, there is nevertheless the greatest agreement in the root of each, which is the numbers four and three. If these are joined, they constitute seven; but if one is squared by the other—that is, saying "three times four" or "four times three"—they yield twelve. Furthermore, the planets agree with the signs in their qualitative and elemental virtues and their better powers; hence, any of the planets has its own <term>domicilium|home or ruling sign</term> in a certain sign, and its <term>exaltationem|exaltation or position of greatest influence</term> in another, receiving some power and nourishment from each of them. Nor do the seven intelligences presiding over the planets have any less agreement with those twelve minds who preside over the twelve signs. John mentions each of these in the <note>The Book of Revelation</note> Apocalypse, at the beginning of which he says:
> And from the seven spirits, who are in the presence of the throne of God: whom I have found to also preside over the planets. <note>original: "Et a septem spiritibus, qui in conspectu throni Dei sunt"</note>

At the end of the volume, however, where he describes the structure of the heavenly city, he testifies that at its twelve gates were twelve Angels. For this reason, we have touched upon the agreement of those Angels, planets, and signs: so that it may be understood how much harmony both the ministers and the instruments of the Creator bring to us. Indeed, the signs themselves are made and called the gates of the heavenly city—those twelve, perhaps, of which John writes in that same place.

<margin>Plato</margin>
How these signs are the gates of the heavenly city is touched upon in some way by Plato, who says:
> That Cancer is the gate through which the soul descends to the body: and Capricorn is the gate through which it ascends again to God.

Hence they called the former the gate of men, but the latter the gate of the gods.

<margin>John</margin>
But if there are twelve gates (as John asserts) equated with the twelve signs, or those things signifying them, each of them will be called a gate; we shall run through how this is briefly. For the gates are Aries and Taurus, which are offered for sin, without the purging of which no one can enter there. From here one arrives at Gemini, the two acts of charity: namely, of God and of neighbor. This dual charity is strengthened in the very strong arms of Cancer, with which a person embraces every object worthy of love. Afterward, in a wondrous way, it is made most powerful in Leo, the most potent of animals. Arriving there, a person weakens his animal nature, reducing it to servitude, and makes it sterile through Virgo. But in Libra, he weighs the strengths and actions of each, reflecting daily on which are the greater and more powerful works: those according to the spirit, or those according to the flesh.

### On the true harmony of the heavens, which some, not understanding, falsely deny. Chapter XIX. ###

<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
<margin>Academics</margin>
<margin>Pythagoreans</margin>
<margin>Plotinus</margin>
**S**ome men of the gravest authority consider the musical modulations of the heavenly orbits to be utterly ridiculous; this is because that sound is not heard, nor perceived by any sense, they being in no way able to persuade themselves how a heavenly chorus should not resonate, or a harmony not be heard, from that triple and most rapid motion in thick air or fire. Hence, they took away harmony from natural motion along with **Pythagoras**; and against all the **Pythagoreans** and **Academics** <note>Followers of Plato's Academy</note>, they clung to their own **Aristotle**, the chief enemy of this harmony, regarding violent and daily motion. But lest there be a discrepancy and disagreement among the supreme observers of this most consonant universe, we shall easily make them agree by attending to that in which they differ. The **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> deny a vocal sound perceptible to these physical ears; this we grant them. The Academics and Pythagoreans pass from vocal number to natural or formal number, and they arrange the feet and rhythms of the universe in the innermost sense of reason. Leaving behind the vocal harmony that itches the ears with the drum, lyre, organ, and human voices, they have embraced the better harmony which is in the numbers by which the Craftsman <note>original: "opifex" — the Creator or Demiurge</note> disposed the universe. **Plotinus** expresses this clearly when he teaches us to return to God through music, saying: "Wherefore after sensible sounds of this kind, numbers, and figures, it is necessary to lead a person in such a way that the matter in which the sensible proportions and their comparisons exist..."

### On the harmony of the heavens with the celestial minds. Ch. 20.

Beyond those things which were said above regarding the agreement of the stars with the Angels, I judge that this also should be touched upon: that the Angels themselves are moved by the Father, who is the source, the origin, and the first mover of all. <margin>Dionysius</margin> Hence Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings on celestial hierarchies were highly influential.</note> says: *All things rejoice when the Father moves them.* <note>original: "Gaudent omnes movente Patre."</note> Therefore, they, being moved by God, move the sphere; and these beings dispose our bodies and other lower things toward that consonance which the first mover of all Himself commands. So that those motions and influences might be harmonious, He placed appropriate <term>intelligences: spiritual beings or angels assigned to govern celestial bodies</term> over each sphere and each individual star: those seven supreme spirits over the seven planets (as we said), and twelve over the twelve signs of the zodiac; and over that entire sphere and the planets, the Queen of the Heavens <note>In this context, the Virgin Mary is depicted as the cosmic ruler who embodies the harmony of the spheres.</note>, who is said to be crowned with twelve stars for the number of the signs, and decorated with many groups of seven, and full of innumerable <term>charisms: divine gifts or graces</term>, just as the starry heaven is full of innumerable stars. And because they contain the power of all the heavens and of the Angels presiding over them, she is therefore rightly said to be exalted above all the choirs of Angels. 

Furthermore, the <term>prime mobile: the outermost moving sphere in the ancient model of the universe</term> must be ruled by the first mover; and through it, the other spheres, to which particular ministers are nonetheless assigned. Through these ministers and through the heavenly instruments, that highest Moderator disposes all lower and particular things, yet by this law: that the higher ministers and those closer to the highest King are moved by fewer motions, while those more distant are moved by more. Consequently, those are more blessed who adhere more closely to the highest "One" than these others, as <margin>Aristotle, Albert, Ptolemy, Mestalac</margin> Aristotle, Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note>, Ptolemy, and Mestalac <note>Likely referring to Mashallah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a prominent Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note> teach; but most especially <margin>Academics, Dionysius</margin> the Academics <note>Followers of the Platonic school of philosophy.</note> with our Saint Dionysius. And although the lower things are agitated by more motions, they nevertheless arrive at the same consonance by the power of the first, unique, and uniform motion from the same single mover. Hence, the Queen of Heaven herself, adhering more closely to the first and only One, is agitated by fewer motions, yet she gathers the power of all within herself, and diffuses that which she has gathered—first into the twelve Apostolic princes, and consequently descending to particular things in great numbers, just as that power of the starry heaven is divided into the twelve signs, and consequently into innumerable stars; and as the power of the soul is gathered first in the brain...

For just as an individual human is a single person directed toward a single end, although distinguished by various limbs and movements, so this unique fabric and mundane body, distinguished by diverse and fitted members, is a single thing, moved by one Mover, and set apart for that same end, although it may seem divided into very many parts. Therefore, all things tend toward God: and they direct us toward Him, although they may seem to direct their steps toward different things. And finally, they will lead us there, unless we ourselves, by the free will of the soul, resist them all as they invite, lead, and draw us.

All things lead back to the same [source], because they receive from the same [source] that from which they flow, although the influx may appear diverse. 

->CHAPTER XXI.<-

**H**owever, it will be more difficult to explain than to assert how all things receive the same influx from the same source through different channels, so that they proceed into the same [end], although by different paths. For the truth of the matter is one where the 
<margin>Plato</margin> Philosophers walk with ready feet alongside our divine wise men: that all good things proceed from above, from the <term>Father of Lights: a biblical title for God from James 1:17</term> and the Highest Good. But how this is so is indeed difficult to explain, as Plato prohibits descending into particulars; yet, with the Father of Lights himself illuminating us, we shall explain some things according to our strength, just as Plato himself and the most ancient Theologians teach: namely, that all things are bound together by a certain chain, so that the lower always receives from the superior, and the superior from the Supreme, just as we have related in some detail in the preceding pages. For a herb or a stone has its power 
<margin>Exodus</margin> supplied by the heaven; the heaven by an intelligence; and the intelligence from the Creator, in whom all things exist in the greatest power. And always in that same order, each thing corresponds to another. This is hinted at by the Supreme Architect in Exodus, when He commands that each curtain of the Tabernacle—which bore the most expressive type of this <term>cosmic machine: the "machina mundana," or the structured mechanism of the universe</term>—should be joined with its sister or companion. For the elements are joined, and all mixed things with the heavens, the stars, and the intelligences...

This is sometimes called the **land of the living**, sometimes the **tabernacle**, sometimes the **moon**, sometimes the **receptacle and bosom of all influences**, and now it is called the **kingdom**. 
<margin>David</margin> 
Regarding this, it is sung in the Psalm: <note>original: "Regnum tuum regnum omnium saeculorum"</note> *Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages.* And again: *His kingdom shall rule over all.* In this mansion, He who is always everywhere is called **Adonai** <note>original Hebrew: אדני</note> or **Melec** <note>original Hebrew: מלך</note>, that is, **Lord** or **King**. <margin>Psalm</margin>

For from there, or through Him, the life of all things proceeds from a higher source (or from a super-mundane sun), just as the favor of life is poured out from the sun through the moon.

**Mercury** corresponds to the second particular numbering named **Hod** <note>original Hebrew: הוד</note>, which among us sounds like **ornament**, **glory**, or **renown**.

There, the flowing God is called **Elohim Zenaot** <note>original Hebrew: אלהים צבאות; God of Hosts</note>, which is the name of God the Ordainer...

# OF THE FIRST SONG

We find that Saturn receives whatever it possesses from **Binah** <term>Binah: The third Sephirah on the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing Understanding and the receptive, maternal aspect of the divine</term>, which signifies "Understanding." It is here that the Holy Spirit is said to reside primarily, concerning which it says 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> 
in **Ecclesiasticus**: *The spirit of understanding shall fill him*. <note>A reference to Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 39:6.</note> This Spirit also gave the Prophets and Apostles an understanding of secret matters. From this place, the Hebrews received their Sabbath, and the seventh day is dedicated to both the celestial and the "supramundane" Saturn. From this also come the remissions, years of rest, and jubilees through the simple or squared number seven. God is said to perform all these things through the letter **He** <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> along with the Ineffable and four-lettered Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHVH</note>, of which the magnitude of the mystery forbids us to speak.

The Starry Heaven is subject to **Chokmah** <term>Chokmah: The second Sephirah, representing Wisdom and the primordial point of creation</term>, which is that supreme Wisdom. This is the Son of God, full of the **Ideas** <term>Ideas: In the Platonic sense, the eternal forms or blueprints of all things</term> and forms of all things to be produced and already produced, just as that heaven is full of stars containing the power of all things within themselves, as we said a little while ago. On this throne, the Son sits at the right hand of the Father and is himself named **YHVH** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>, which is the very **Shem HaMephorash** <term>Shem HaMephorash: The "Explicit Name" of God, often associated with the 72-fold name or the Tetragrammaton</term>, and the four letters together with the letter **Yod** <note>The Hebrew letter י</note>, a letter indeed signifying the most simple divinity itself.

Truly, the **Primum Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: The "First Moved" sphere in classical astronomy, which carries all other spheres with it</term> corresponds to the First Mover and the source of all things. Moving all things, He draws all things to Himself, just as a center leads all lines of a circumference into itself. For He is the Center, the Circle, and the Sphere, embracing and filling all things and conducting all lines into Himself. I would not dare to ascribe this "attraction" 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> 
to the Supreme Father, unless His Son taught me, saying: *No one comes to me, unless my Father draws him.* Since the Son has this attractive power from the Father, He therefore said: *When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.* Residing in this supreme seat, the Highest Father is called **Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh** <note>original Hebrew: אהיה אשר אהיה</note>, which we have translated as "I am who I am," but according to the sense of the letters, it would be better said as "I shall be who I shall be." Or, according to another way, His name is simply **Ehyeh** <note>original Hebrew: אהיה</note>, which speaks of the most simple essence of divinity, of which one must not speak. From this, He is nicknamed by the experts **Ayin Lo Roeh** <note>original Hebrew: אין לא ראה</note>, that is, "the eye has not seen," because no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him. 
<margin>James</margin> 
Therefore, I will say only this: when He who "is," or "I am who I am," is named, he is understood as the **Father of Lights**, from whom (witnessed by James) every best gift and every perfect gift emanates. Yet, flowing through various channels into all lower things, He grants that all things cooperate with Him, so that all beneficial things may be gathered into Him. Hence, all prayers ought to be directed to Him, 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> 
as He taught who alone knew Him, saying: *When you pray, say: Our Father.* And repeating this often, He urged that we ask from the Father, the giver of all good things, who by His mercy may direct us toward that same end for which, and for the beholding of which, we were established.

<margin>David</margin>
**S**ince in many places in the Psalms <note>original: "P.S."</note> and quite frequently we see repeated by the Royal Prophet in his hymns that joyful (so to speak) refrain <term>refrain: The original "celeuma" refers to a rhythmic chant or call used by sailors or rowers to keep time, here applied to the repetitive call of the Psalms</term>, *Sing to the Lord a new song*, I was inquiring whether any new things have been made to be sung in a new song; since we see no other heaven, nor stars twinkling with a new brightness; nor do we see the sun complete different circuits by day, or the moon by night; nor is the day distinguished by different hours, nor does the summer season advance by new increases, nor fail with fresh decreases in the winter storm; nor do we perceive any new living creatures, or any new species of things; and, to conclude briefly with the Wise Man <note>A reference to Solomon and the book of Ecclesiastes 1:9</note>, *there is nothing new under the sun*. # TONES OF THE SECOND SONG.

**C**hrist and the Messiah is the wisdom of God and the Word <note>original: "uerbum," referring to the Logos</note> containing all things by ideal reason <note>original: "ratione ideali." This refers to the Platonic and Neoplatonic concept that all created things exist first as perfect "Ideas" or blueprints in the mind of God.</note>, and as a human being, he actually encompasses all lower things. **First Tone.**

Christ is the life and the support of all, giving life to all things and drawing all things to himself. **Tone II.**

Christ is the true priest, the true bread, the victim <note>original: "hostia," the sacrificial offering</note>, and the sacrifice, purifying all things and bringing peace to all. **Tone III.**

Christ is the highest truth and the light teaching everyone and illuminating all things. **Tone IIII.**

Christ, having become the father of all through true regeneration <note>spiritual rebirth</note>, and as the head of the mystical body <note>original: "corpus mystici," the collective community of believers</note>, flows into all its members. **Tone V.**

Christ is the end and the fulfillment of all works, giving to all the power to act. **Tone VI.**

Christ is the King of kings and the highest Emperor, ruling and governing all things. **Tone VII.**

Christ is the mediator: through whom passage is given to everyone so that they may reach their ultimate end. **Tone VIII.**
