# THE DEITY OF THE MESSIAH IS PROVED BY REASONS.
## CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Theodore, Proclus</margin>
**W**e can prove that the Messiah, Christ our Anointed One <note>The terms Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) both mean "The Anointed One."</note>, was and is God, not only through witnesses and oracles <note>referring to biblical prophecies</note>, but by the strongest logical reasons. For we see a ready and unanimous consensus that the Blessed God, existing of himself, possesses all things from himself and nothing from another. All other things, however, have from him their existence and their power to act. Therefore, the great Theodore said (as witnessed by Proclus): "All things pray, except for the First <note>God</note>, and they draw something from him who exists of himself; he is the fountain and origin of all things; otherwise, they would flow away into nothingness." Since, therefore, all things have their being, their natural power, their beauty, and their adornment from God, all things participate in that very divinity, though in different ways. All things (says Origen) have from God the Father the fact that
<margin>Origen</margin>
they exist; from the spirit of life, the fact that they live; from the Son, the fact that they understand and have a portion of reason; and from the Holy Spirit (who is nevertheless the same as the spirit of life), the fact that they are holy. Therefore, something divine is in all things: in one thing, it is simply being, whether simple or composite; in another, it is being and acting; in yet another, it is being, acting, and understanding. But leaving others aside, let us speak of man, to whom all things have been communicated so that he might bear the most perfect image of God and the Father. Hence, he can rightly be called a "Son of God," as the royal prophet sings: *I have said, you are gods, and
<margin>David</margin>
all of you are sons of the Most High.* <note>original: "Ego dixi dii estis, & filii excelsi omnes," quoting Psalm 82:6.</note> And since God communicates himself more to the one whom he pleases to make more excellent and perfect, it was fitting that he should more greatly adorn with divinity this one whom he appointed as the head of others, the redeemer, the king, and the eternal priest. This divinity is called "oil" in Holy Scripture, as the prophet sings again: *God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your
<margin>The same [David]</margin>
companions* <note>original: "Vnxit te Deus Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis," quoting Psalm 45:7.</note>—so much so, that he made him more excellent than all others in that communicated divinity itself. Hence, through a certain <term>antonomasia</term> <note>A rhetorical term for substituting a title or epithet for a proper name, or vice versa—here, calling a man "God."</note> and <term>hyperbole</term> <note>Rhetorical exaggeration for emphasis.</note>, he is called God. Another reason is also at hand: since man was made capable of divinity—in which alone he can find rest and blessedness—he must at some point arrive at divinity itself and be united with it. By this union, God is not merely brought down into man, but rather man is drawn into God himself, since he becomes a participant in every kind of virtue and efficacy. And the more this God is united with someone, the more he renders that person divine. It is no wonder, then, if he rendered this Messiah and Christ—to whom he offered himself in that fullness which a man can receive—such that we can rightly call him God himself, who also gave to others the power to become sons of God. Let us add another reason: that just as all things contain...

...and is recapitulated in man, so all things ought much more to be recapitulated <note>To "recapitulate" is a theological term meaning to sum up or bring all parts of creation together under a single head or source.</note> and united in God through man: specifically through that man who ought to hold, and indeed does hold, the first place among all others, and who drew all things to himself so that he might lead those same things back to God. Nor should some contend, saying

<margin>
The Apostle
Christ
**CHRIST**
Paul
</margin>
that this union does not prove divinity in the one united, but only a conjunction. For the Supreme Truth itself declares what kind of union this is when he says: "I pray, Father, that just as you and I are one, so they may be one in you" <note>John 17:21</note>. Furthermore, he expresses what their union is like elsewhere, saying: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me" <note>John 14:10</note>. And again: "I and the Father are one" <note>John 10:30</note>. Paul also reminds us of this with a clear voice: "He who adheres to God," he says, "is made one spirit with him" <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note>. If all people, therefore, can become one spirit with God, why shall he not be united with Him who, by <term>antonomasia</term> <note>A rhetorical term where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name, such as "The Philosopher" for Aristotle.</note>, is called <term>Messiah</term> <note>Hebrew for "Anointed."</note>, <term>Christ</term> <note>Greek for "Anointed."</note>, and <term>The Anointed One</term>? Namely <note>original: "vʒ," an abbreviation for *videlicet*.</note> by that divinity with which he was so filled that we all receive from his fullness.

For (to proceed further), man—a creature made of every kind of substance—ought not to have been restored by any other than the one by whom he had been established. But all things were established and made through the Word, which was made flesh; therefore, all things ought to have been restored through that same Word. And so that the redeemed—angels, men, and everything contained within them—might owe their debt to a most honorable liberator, it was fitting that the liberator to whom all things would be subject should be the most excellent of all. This could not happen except through a greater participation in divinity. Furthermore, the restoration and repair, which is esteemed as a greater work than the original creation, ought not to have been done by an inferior to the one who performed the creation itself. Since creation was performed through the Word of God, it was necessary that restoration be performed through the same, as there was no greater means through which it could have been accomplished.

Moreover, since the entire human creation had failed, such a fall could not be repaired by one who was himself a transgressor. Nor should it have been done by an Angel, who is considered by the wise to be lesser than man, to whom it is given to transcend all the angelic choirs. This could not be achieved unless there pre-existed in man a power greater than the angels themselves. Nor was an Angel or any other creature—except for a man of every kind <note>implying a man who contains the nature of all creation</note>—unitable with the Creator of every kind. Therefore the Apostle said: "He never took on the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham" <note>Hebrews 2:16</note>.

Also, since the sin itself was against God, it could not be repaired except by God. For ignorance was not the cause, as ignorance is given as a punishment for sin and ought not to precede the fault. Nor was it mere fragility, because the senses had not yet rebelled. Rather, pride was present, which caused both Angels and man to apostatize from their Maker; for each had presumed to claim for himself a higher rank than was fitting. For while man was permitted to emulate the condition of all other creatures, he was by no means permitted to emulate the coming Christ. Hence all the better and rational trees, or those of virtues, were permitted to him for food, except for the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is Christ: who was meant to experience at once, and did experience, both the good of blessedness and the evil of our sufferings.

### How the Deity and the Word are in Christ himself. Chapter III.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>Although the manner in which the Deity was and is in our Redeemer is difficult and almost impossible to explain—indeed, it is not even perceptible to the intellect, as <term>Damascenus<gloss>John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and theologian who wrote extensively on the nature of Christ</gloss></term> says that the incarnation of the Word was unknown even to the highest <term>seraphim<gloss>the highest rank of angels, traditionally said to be closest to God</gloss></term>, not only regarding the time but also the manner—nevertheless, so far as God allows us to speak, we shall attempt to explain how the Deity and the Word are in this Man-Redeemer. Thus, in many children, there appears not only the fatherly spirit, but his speech, voice, manners, appearance, facial features, physical stature, and such. <margin>Aratus</margin> Therefore, man perceives and contains something of divinity more excellently than other created things, because we are his own peculiar offspring, as the wise Aratus says. <note>Aratus was a Greek poet (c. 315–240 BC) quoted by St. Paul in Acts 17:28: "For we are also his offspring."</note> And before 
<margin>Pythagoras</margin> him, Pythagoras says: "A divine race is within men." With these, that "semi-Pythagorean" <note>Referring to Ovid, who incorporated Pythagorean themes into his poetry.</note> 
<margin>Ovid</margin> hesitatingly says: "Man was born: whether that Architect of things made him from divine seed..." <note>original: "siue hunc diuino semine fecit ille opifex rerum" — a quote from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* regarding the creation of man.</note> And much more, an incomparably greater gift of the deity ought to be in him who is called the <term>Son of God</term> <note>original: "antonomatice dicitur Filius Dei"; to speak antonomatically is to use a title as a proper name because of the subject's excellence.</note> by way of excellence, and through whom all other sons of God are made. Not only is the originating power <note>original: "seminaria uirtus"</note> of God in all produced things, and most especially in man, but there is a continuous outflow of that divinity, just as the continuous spreading of the sun's rays illuminates and warms all places. It reaches them as a benefactor, always providing life and fruitfulness. This we prove by the clear light of experience: when the sun approaches us, the earth is made fertile, plants sprout, animals burn with the desire for generation and offspring, birds hasten to produce and warm their eggs, and fish, by scattering their eggs, provide the greatest increase to their kind. Conversely, when the sun recedes, the season of birth seems closed, and plants shed what they had previously produced in their fertility. Hence, if the flow of the sun itself were uniform, the fertility in all things would always be equal. However, the <term>Supreme and Supramundane Sun</term> <note>The "Supramundane Sun" is a Neoplatonic and Christian metaphor for God, who exists beyond the physical world.</note> neither approaches nor recedes, because he is always everywhere; he is poured out into all things according to their capacity. By always flowing into all things, he preserves their being, continually granting and suggesting the power of fruitfulness and action, unless the weakness of the recipient stands in the way. Thus, the more one is disposed toward him, the more one feels the abundance of divinity. Recognizing this, 
<margin>Jeremiah</margin> Jeremiah said: *But you are in us, O Lord, and your name is called upon us* <note>Quoting Jeremiah 14:9.</note>—that is, the power of the name and of the one named is felt within us. For the Name of God is the same as God himself, and the power of the divine name is the same as the power of God, if the 
<margin>Hebrew Sages</margin> Hebrew Sages speak rightly in their interpretations. As the Lord testifies concerning the angel sent for the protection and guidance of Moses: 
<margin>GOD</margin> *Behold, I send my Angel, who shall go before you: observe him and hear his voice, because my name is in him* <note>Quoting Exodus 23:20-21.</note>—that is, the power of my name and my divinity, as those cited above explain. And the power of the Name of God had passed to Christ to such an extent that he himself attained that Name in which all knees should bow, and in which all wonders are performed. These wonders used to be done in ancient times in the name <term>El Shaddai</term> <note>original: "אל שדי" — a Hebrew name for God often translated as "God Almighty."</note> until the time of Moses, and from Moses until Christ in that great four-lettered name <term>Yahweh</term> <note>original: "יהוה" — the Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in the Hebrew Bible.</note>. Christ, feeling the power of these names combined in himself and in his own name, said with great authority: 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> *In my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.* <note>Quoting Mark 16:17-18.</note> Therefore, God flows into all things, filling everything according to its capacity, just as air fills every space not occupied by another body; for all things [are full of Jove]. <note>The text ends with the start of a quote from Virgil: "Iovis omnia plena" (All things are full of Jove/God).</note>

These supreme things are the Angels and man, whom he fills as if they were the heart and brain—not merely with a common life, but with a rational, intellectual, free, and loving life. Nor does God fill these worldly members with any less power than the sun fills the spaces of the world, or the soul fills all the members of the human body. <margin>Theologians</margin>

<margin>James</margin>

But Christ himself said that he was united with us by a certain 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
continuation, saying: "I am the vine, and you are the branches." So too his assumed nature is united with the vine of divinity by a certain better-known continuation. Other examples could also be brought forward of this union of divinity with that assumed human nature, but let these suffice for the present.

<margin>David</margin>

<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
they are granted to prepared matter. Not perceiving this, the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, especially the more recent ones, argue with great controversy about the "introduction" or "beginning" of forms. But if we wish to review the more ancient thinkers, they are of many kinds; 
<margin>Averroes, Anaxagoras, Alpetragius</margin>
although Averroes says they are divided into three groups. For the followers of Anaxagoras believed that nothing was made anew, but rather that those forms which were hidden were brought out into the light, thinking that "anything is in anything." <note>Anaxagoras's theory of *panspermia*, where every substance contains the seeds of all other substances.</note> In what sense they meant this, we have explained elsewhere. Alpetragius <note>An Arabic astronomer and philosopher.</note> thought that forms came from the substance of heaven, and that essential dispositions were not in things through their own particular being, but from the influence of the first heaven.
<margin>Mathematicians, Themistius</margin>
The Mathematicians held that the form itself is given by the stars. Themistius, and several others with him, determined this matter in various ways according to the diversity of the things generated. For they thought inanimate things, such as the elements, were generated from a single form of matter. But animate things, which are produced by "equivocal generation" <note>The obsolete theory that life arises from non-living matter.</note>—such as wasps from the carcasses of horses, bees from the rotting of a cow, gnats from spoiled wine, and frogs and mice from the decaying of the earth—they thought these and similar things were produced by a "form abstracted from matter." They presupposed that everything which comes to be must necessarily be made by something similar to itself; and since there is nothing similar in lower things from which such things could be generated, they therefore believed in 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
abstract forms, from which, or according to whose likeness, they were generated. But the leader of the Peripatetics [Aristotle], teaching with his school that the producer does nothing else in the logic of a composite thing except by moving the matter and transforming it, draws out <note>The technical term is "educes."</note> the form from the "bosom" of that matter, where it previously pre-existed in potentiality.
<margin>Averroes, Anaxagoras, Empedocles, Avicenna, Algazel</margin>
And here the Arab [Averroes] says that this opinion has a certain similarity to the sentiment of the followers of Anaxagoras and Empedocles, since both say the agent "sequesters" the form from the subject. But they differ because those others separate what pre-existed in "actuality," <note>That is, the form was already fully present but hidden.</note> while the Peripatetics separate what was only in "potentiality." <note>That is, the matter had the *capacity* to become the form, but the form wasn't there yet.</note> However, Avicenna and his summarizer Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali.</note> gave decrees quite close to our John, saying that according to how matter is prepared by the heavens and secondary causes, forms are infused by God, the "Giver of Forms." And this indeed happens in particular and successive productions. But in the primordial production, they thought that first matter, and then the forms that define it, flowed from the same source: namely, the Divine Word. To these is added that 
<margin>Cinesius</margin>
illustrious philosopher Cinesius of Cyrene <note>Likely referring to Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop.</note>, who philosophizes in this way, saying: "The first beings are simple; but nature, descending from them, is varied in a manifold way. But the first being is the simplest, from whom the middle things..."

### OF THE SECOND SONG.

...and last things come forth: But that most simple thing is God, containing all things through his Word. <margin>Proclus</margin> Indeed, Proclus Diadochus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who sought to synthesize Greek philosophy into a grand system.</note> in his theological and philosophical *Theorems*, proves that just as every number proceeds from unity, so every multitude proceeds from the One, in which it was contained by power. This "One" is present in all things in actuality: for in the number three there are three unities, in the number four there are four, and so on for the rest, as Rabbi Samuel <note>Possibly a reference to Samuel ibn Tibbon or a source from the Jewish mystical tradition such as the *Sefer Yezirah* (Book of Formation).</note> treats more copiously in his commentaries on the book titled *On the Formation of Things*. <margin>Ra. Sa.</margin> Thus also that supreme "One" is "One" in actuality in all things, sustaining all, as we have from Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist writer.</note> in his *On the Divine Names*: where he says: <margin>Dionysius</margin> The Monad <note>term: Monad—The ultimate, indivisible 'One' from which all numbers and things originate.</note> holds every number within itself uniquely, and every number is indeed folded within the monad: but as much as it proceeds from the monad, so much is it distinguished and multiplied. This must be understood regarding number and formal, essential unity. <margin>Hermes</margin> And to revisit the more ancient thinkers—who confess that all things pre-existed in the divine Word before they were unfolded into their own forms—let us hear what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the *Hermetica*, viewed by Renaissance scholars as a contemporary of Moses.</note> discusses with his son Tat: "O son," he says, "the holy word of the holy and only Lord of all is a secret of wisdom, which is beyond man to speak: because from Him comes man, and all things, and in Him are all things." <margin>Plato</margin> Plato in the *Epinomis*, when he argued concerning the fellowship and equal dignity of divine things, says: "And let us render honors, not assigning a month to one, a year to another, and perhaps nothing to some other, nor excluding any time: but let all be attributed to Him in whom He makes the world run its course; He who ordained the most divine Word of all." <note>original: "uerbum omniū diuiniſſimū"</note> Nothing is more fitting with what our John says: <margin>John</margin> *All things were made through the Word*; and with what the Prophet sings: <margin>David</margin> *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note>

---

->In the same place all things are in number, weight, and measure. Cap. V.<-

<margin>Proclus</margin>
**AND** just as all things are arranged by the Creator by number, weight, and measure, in the same way they pre-existed in that most holy Word: in Number indeed, because the multiplicity of things requires the universality of their patterns in the Archetype, <note>term: Archetype—The original 'blueprint' or divine idea of a thing existing in the mind of God.</note> as we discussed more broadly above. Yet they exist in that multitude in such a way that they never depart from the unity of the storehouse. This is also what Proclus teaches in his theological theorems: "Everything," he says, "that participates in the One, is both one and not one." <margin>Parmenides</margin> Thus also the divine persons (as we are taught by our Theologians) are one in the root of the essence they share, and three as distinct in themselves. Moreover, all creatures are one in the fountain from which they flow (as Parmenides most wisely said, though he was falsely accused of error by Aristotle), <margin>Academics</margin> but distinct in their particular forms: yet they are to be united again with that One, toward whose union the Academics (especially Plotinus) <margin>Plotinus</margin> persuade us with such great renown. Therefore, the numerous mass of stars is in God, and in the Word by which the heavens were made firm: so too the numerous multitude of animals, trees, stones, and all things that have been created. Not only is there the number of species there, but even of individual beings, <margin>CHRIST</margin> as the Word Himself says to particular men: *Your names are written in heaven.* <note>Luke 10:20</note> And what is greater, even of those things that seem superfluous...

### The exemplary cognitions in the mind of the Craftsman are called Ideas, and they truly exist. Chapter VI.

**W**e have learned from many wise men that there are twofold rules in the Mind and the Divine Word. Some of these are the rules for things to be made by Him, and these are properly called <term>Ideas<gloss>From the Greek word ἀπὸ τοῦ εἴδεος (apo tou eideos), meaning "from the form" or "from the appearance"</gloss></term>, which signifies a species or a shape. Others, however, are <term>exemplars<gloss>models or patterns to be copied</gloss></term> toward whose boundaries our own works must be directed; these too are called "Ideas" by a certain analogy. Therefore, Ideas are the forms, species, and eternal models of things always existing in the Divine Mind, even before the things themselves were made, so that each individual subject might be imprinted by them as if by its own proper seals. And even now, they persevere in their own existence, so that the species themselves are always preserved and remain eternal; they are neither corrupted nor changed by the corruption or transformation of the individual person or thing. And by a certain analogy, even the thoughts of things to be made by us through art <margin>Augustine</margin> are called "ideas" and "exemplars," as Augustine discusses at great length in his work *On John*. But because these are not the models of the species and the essential things themselves, they are not strictly "Ideas," but are called so by analogy, through which we can catch a glimpse of those divine ones.

<margin>Plato</margin> These Ideas (as Plato teaches) are a single, simple Idea in the Paternal Intellect <note>The "Paternal Intellect" refers to the first person of the Trinity or the highest level of divine thought.</note>, universal in its power and causality, containing all forms within itself in a certain more excellent way. This Idea, proceeding forth, shines and is multiplied in Him <note>the Son or the Word</note> who holds all things from the Father. It is then spread further, divided in some way into different "places" or "mansions" of the <term>archetype<gloss>the original pattern or first model</gloss></term>. Afterward, it descends to the <term>movers of the orbs<gloss>The celestial intelligences or angels believed to move the planets and stars</gloss></term> and other Intelligences, to whom God committed the arrangement of lower things, providing them with a kind of "seed" and commanding them to carry out and lead these things according to the infusion given to them. These beings then unfold the Ideas through the heavens as if through instruments, using various radiations and favorable <term>aspects<gloss>The geometric angles between planets, such as trines or squares</gloss></term>—trigons, hexagons, and tetragonals—sometimes approaching and sometimes receding. Finally, the forms are infused according to the disposition of the subjects, which always yearn to be formed and perfected, just as a woman desires a man so that she may receive offspring and lineage from him, or so that she may rejoice in his nature. All these things are arranged by the power of the light of the First Cause, which was commanded from the beginning to illuminate and make all things fruitful, like the seed, form, and life of all. Hence John said: *And the life was the light of men* <note>John 1:4</note>, because that supreme light is the life of them and of all things. This life and light is led into matter through secondary causes...

**L**et Aristotle, Proclus, Porphyry, and other wise men say how much authority the easy agreement of many sages on the same opinion provides, and how much truth it demonstrates that opinion to possess; for they prove the truth of a matter many times over from the common consensus of the wise. Therefore, in this business of the "ideas," not only do all Catholics or Christians agree, but so many and such great external <note>In this context, "external" refers to non-Christian or pagan philosophers.</note> wise men agree that all suspicion could rightly be removed that our people affirm them more by law than by truth. <margin>Zeno</margin> Zeno, the ancient philosopher, proclaims God as the prince and disposer of nature: whom he names <term>Logos<gloss>original: "logon"; the Greek term for "Word" or "Reason"</gloss></term>—that is, the Word—which is the intelligence of Himself and of the things to be made, and consequently the "Idea." This God of fire and spirit then fashioned seven governors in succession, who encompass the sensible world in circles; and their arrangement is called <term>Fate<gloss>fatum</gloss></term>. From there, the Word of God joined together the pure artifice of nature from the downward-tending elements of God, united with the craftsman mind; for it was consubstantial. See how piously, learnedly, and clearly he teaches that all things existed beforehand in that most fertile mind or intelligence of <margin>John</margin> God, which he calls the Word, according to the doctrine of our John <note>Referring to the Gospel of John: "In the beginning was the Word."</note>. Moreover, the Mind which He brought forth is another person but the same essence, in which craftsman mind—that is, the Word produced—He fashioned all things. First, indeed, those seven minds were fashioned, which are called the first separate intellects, according to that supramundane <note>Existing beyond the physical world.</note> seven-fold group which the <margin>Hebrews</margin> Hebrews call the "Seven of the Fabric," with which we have declared both these intelligences and their orbs to agree. These seven intelligences or Spirits (as we read in the <margin>Revelation
Tobit</margin> Revelation and Tobit) are always in the sight of the throne of the highest Prince: who, arranging the lower things, carry out what the Most High commands; hence their arrangement is called Fate. Afterwards, he speaks clearly of how the Word of God—that is, the thinking-out of things to be made, or that in which the thinking itself exists—fashioned this worldly work to be united with its maker.

# SECOND CANTICLE

...in the first place. And just as the Word itself is of the same substance <note>The author uses "consubstantial," a theological term meaning of the same essence, usually referring to the relationship between Christ and God the Father.</note> and united to the first—that is, the highest Father—so it leads back to union all things that were crafted through it. And from these sources, or from the higher workshop revealed to prophets and holy men, Socrates and Plato learned.
<margin>Socrates, Plato, Peripatetics, Plato, Theophrastus, Stoics, Zeno</margin>
It was they who said that the Ideas exist separated from matter in the secret depths of God, not among the clouds or in the hollow of the moon—as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who often mocked the Platonic theory of Forms as being too abstract or misplaced.</note> or other mocking critics <term>nasuti</term> <note>literally "big-nosed," a Latin idiom for those who are overly critical or prone to mockery.</note> falsely claim. Let the Ideas therefore be in the mind or Word of the supreme Architect as the causes of things. Proceeding from these, Plato is rightly said by Theophrastus to have assigned causes from divine providence above all other philosophers. The Stoics, imitating their Zeno, said that the "pre-conceived notions" in our souls are the Ideas; but these are so only by analogy, whereas those in the divine mind are truly Ideas, because unformed matters are shaped into specific species according to their likeness, as Plutarch says in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*.
<margin>Plutarch, Timaeus of Locri</margin>
And before these, Timaeus of Locri teaches that the Idea is unbegotten, serving as an external pattern and a helping cause or form of all things that undergo change.
<margin>Epicharmus, Sphaerus, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Plotinus, Hermias, Numenius, Proclus, Syrianus, Alcinous</margin>
With him Epicharmus, Sphaerus, and many other ancients agree. The more recent Platonists—Iamblichus, Porphyry, Plotinus, Hermias, Numenius, Proclus, and his teacher Syrianus—expanded this doctrine. The last of these spread himself so far in his *Apology for Plato* that he produced a most voluminous book. Alcinous also, explaining the master’s dogma in the book titled *On the Doctrine of Plato* and in his *Summaries*, says: It pleased Plato that there be Ideas—not indeed of man-made things, such as a shield or a lyre; nor of things against nature, such as fever or bile; nor of individuals, such as Socrates or Plato; nor of tiny things, such as dust or straw—but they are the immutable and ever-abiding notions of perfect beings. They exist as certain immaterial measures, because the world was not made by chance, but by the highest order according to the likeness of those patterns which were crafted in the Workman. These Ideas in the Workman are a single and universal cause, possessing and pre-possessing all things by their power, but multiplied in respect to the things formed by the Ideas <note>original: *ideata*</note>, because the cause belongs to many. Hence, in origin the cause is one, but it becomes many from the things determined by it.

This opinion, supported by so many wise men and divine oracles, is judged worthy of greater assertion than the "heresy" or mockery of Aristotle—even if the clouded minds of Alexander and Averroes
<margin>Aristotle, Alexander, Averroes</margin>
felt the contrary. And it is a beautiful thing (if Aristotle is well-considered) that although he seems to differ in words—by I know not what spirit—in reality he does not feel otherwise. For he concedes that active power and art preside in the craftsman before he comes to his work. Nor is there less reason in the Architect of the world's structure; because they did not know Him, nor when, nor why, nor how He built this "world-house," Aristotle sometimes denies the structure itself and its manner and order—yet elsewhere, forced by the truth, he confesses it. Perhaps he denied the Ideas and the world's construction while professing and teaching contentedly within physical limits. For he asserts in that treatise *On the Universe* <note>original: *de mundo*</note>, which is ascribed to him...

...it will be seen that this machine was crafted by the highest artisan; and in the higher philosophy, released from physical laws, he speaks quite well as a theologian, saying that just as our intelligence is caused by things and known objects, so the science and knowledge of God is the cause of those things that exist. <margin>Paul</margin> 
Paul, when discussing the incarnate Word with the Colossians, brings this forth from the treasury of the third heaven: "He is the firstborn of every creature, in whom all things in heaven and on earth were established." <margin>Moses</margin>

<margin>Solomon</margin> 
Solomon, judged most wise by the judgment of God and men, when speaking of the Wisdom of God in which all things were made, places her production before the earth, the mountains, hills, abysses, or unformed matter, before the rivers, seas, and whatever is contained in them; and he says she was present at the crafting of the heavens and lower things, saying: "When He prepared the heavens, I was there: when with His decree and a circle He enclosed the abyss," namely forming all things and imprinting His measures and order upon them. From which follows: "When He strengthened the ether above," or as the truth of the letter has it: "When He brought down the clouds from above, and strengthened the fountains of waters, and set a law for the waters lest they cross their boundaries: and when He ordered the foundations of the earth, I was with him as *amon* <gloss>אמון: Hebrew for a master craftsman or architect</gloss>," which is interpreted as a master in any art, or a craftsman and shaper. Behold how clearly he professes that in divine wisdom there is a craftsmanship by which all things are formed and moderated; and that is the exemplar and "Idea" of things to be made.

### Those who rejected the Ideas, and by what arguments. Cap. VIII.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**P**recipuous among those who cast away the Ideas is Aristotle with his Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school, named for his habit of walking about while teaching</note>. And this man is indeed of the gravest authority among those who follow only sensible doctrine <note>meaning knowledge derived only from the physical senses</note> and lower philosophy. Like an ungrateful disciple, neither piously nor justly, but by mocking his master [Plato], he says: "Farewell to Plato's Ideas, for they are nothing, or they are monsters," deeming it superfluous, ridiculous, inconvenient, and false to admit the Ideas themselves. He thought it superfluous, since his own object—which is his essence, through which he works all things and in which he contains all things—is sufficient for the first agent <note>God, or the primary cause of all action</note>. Indeed, he thought it ridiculous because God does not need a likeness or a paradigm <term>paradigma</term> <note>a model or pattern used by an artist</note> through which to know something else, just as [a human craftsman] needs...

->## SECOND SONG<-

<page-num>CXCI</page-num>
<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: Orpheus</meta>

<margin>Aristotle was a student of Plato for twenty-one years.</margin>
...a human being through a sensible or intelligible species <note>original: "specie sensibili, aut intelligibilis," referring to the way we perceive things through the senses versus the intellect</note>. It also seemed inconvenient and absurd to them that corruptible and temporary things should be generated from those eternal forms. And since Ideas are relative—because they refer to the "ideated" things <note>original: "ideata," the physical things modeled after the divine archetypes</note>—they cannot exist in that most simple Substance which is foreign to all imperfection. They even say it is absurd to contribute them to number, since they exist as "equivocals" <note>terms that have the same name but different definitions</note> of a different nature from the things being numbered. Furthermore, they thought it was false that things produced through those exemplars were made like the Artisan <note>referring to God as the Creator</note>, as the supporters of the Ideas seem to assert; for produced things are not made like the First Cause except through attributes, whose meanings are found in produced things at a much lower level and through a certain analogy. From this, even those who are Christians in name only—but are actually followers of the evil demon <note>original: "cacodaemonis," likely a harsh polemical reference to Aristotle's influence</note>—stagger, thinking it erroneous and ridiculous that their most skillful Aristotle, the searcher of causes and things, did not imagine these Ideas; especially since he was a student of Plato for twenty-one years. Hence, it is a wonder to them that if he had perceived anything good from him regarding these Ideas, he would not have approved and committed it to writing. And going further, they judge it trivial—even if asserted in Christian doctrine—if it is not bolstered by the authority of Holy Scripture. This is especially true when they believe that everything said regarding God, our knowledge, and the eternity of things can be preserved without the need for Ideas. For our knowledge (as they say) is most sufficient through the "genus" in a universal sense and through the "proper difference" in a particular sense, provided it is known. This determines the species and the proper specific form, which is not an exemplar in another thing, but as it exists in act within a composite, it is the very thing providing the form <note>the Aristotelian view that "form" exists within the object, not as a separate archetype</note>. Nor does God seem to them to need those figures as if they were an impressing seal, because by His own power He can do all things, and He acts without an instrument. Yet if He commands some instrument to concur, it is outside of Himself and not in Himself, as is said of the Ideas. Nor (they say) can those exemplars cause the motion of generation and corruption, because they are not in a subject like the power in a seed; nor do they move by contact, like the power of the stars reaching down to the qualities of the elements, because these Ideas are said to be entirely separate. These are the strongest monuments and strengths of those who deny the Ideas.
These are errors, and not reasons, which seem to act against them.

### Chapter IX.

**W**hether or not we should battle against the enemies of the Ideas, the mind is in doubt: because holy things are not to be set before dogs, nor are lamps and lights to be lit for bats, nor are pearls to be cast before swine to be trampled underfoot <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6, suggesting that divine mysteries should not be shared with those who cannot appreciate them</note>. This is what we would have to do if we were to explain the secrets of the Ideas while debating with such people (as would be necessary). Lest we send our readers away entirely hungry, however, we shall run through something lightly, yet by that law by which Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet, seen by Renaissance thinkers as a source of "ancient theology" that prefigured Christian truths</note> was accustomed to sing of divine secrets—with this protestation first sent ahead according to custom.

Nor was he an inventor in the field of physics, but merely a collector, as he himself admits in the *Sophistical Refutations* <note>original: "Elenchis," a work by Aristotle on logical fallacies</note> saying: "If praise is given to anyone for things discovered, it is owed to me for the *Refutations*." There, compelled by the truth, he did not wish to claim for himself what he had not done. Therefore, having occupied himself with those rules of arguing and with things perceived by the senses, he voluntarily departed from the **divine banquet**. 

<margin>Simplicius</margin>
In that banquet (says Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle who tried to harmonize his work with Plato</note>), Plato was nourished and always venerates divine things.
<margin>Plato always venerated divine things.</margin>
<margin>Plato</margin>
Beginning from those eternal species and **ideas**, he descended all the way to the lowest things. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle, however, proceeding from sensible things <note>things perceived by the physical senses</note>, climbed only as far as his reasonings—formed from those sensible things—could lead him. For there are "varieties of graces," as our **Paul** says. 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Therefore, to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another various kinds of tongues, and so forth. Thus, to one it is given to know human things; to another to be wise in divine things. 

<margin>Cicero</margin>
To others also (as Cicero says), an abundance of speaking was given; to others, entrance into the inner shrines of learning. But he had seen it happen to none of the Greeks (as he says) to achieve both. What he may have thought of himself, I will keep silent; but let us come to the arguments. They think it is enough for God to be His own object of thought. We grant them this, but we say that in Him—or in the **Word** <note>The "Verbum" or Logos</note> produced by Him, which is the same as the object itself—there are the **ideas** of things. This is not the object under the category of the "Son," or the "Word produced," or of "ideas," but under the category of the **deity** or the **essence**. 

Nor do the supporters of the **ideas** propose anything ridiculous when they say that God does not "need" a likeness, since He Himself established Himself as the **exemplar** <note>The perfect original pattern or model</note> of things to be made. Nor is it a wonder if corruptible and temporary things are generated from eternal exemplars, since a work always falls short of a voluntary and free craftsman—and often falls short because of the instrument. For a silver or gold seal leaves its mark in wax or mud, which is much more ignoble than the gold itself. 

Nor are the **ideas** "relations" in any way other than the relation by which God is related to His creatures. Let them be "reasons" <note>original: "rationes," used here in the sense of the underlying logic or blueprints of creation</note>, or whatever name they are called by. For just as a creature depends on God, so it depends on the **ideas**, which are one and the same with God Himself. To relate the ideas to **number** is also not absurd, since there are as many species as there are ideas of them. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>

<margin>Albert</margin>
deservedly scorns him. He was in error because the discussion does not concern **mathematical number** when the principles and ideas of things are assigned, but rather a **higher number**, which the Arab did not reach. Afterward, he [Albert] excuses him (if he is worthy of excuse), attributing the error to a "corrupt opinion"—though it should rather be attributed to a **corrupt mind**, which was always an enemy to divine things. 

To the other point, however: It is true that "assimilation" <note>becoming like God</note> in the journey toward God occurs through attributes and virtues. By climbing through these toward the **Supreme Truth** and the exemplar of virtues, we draw nearer and nearer. In the "exit" <note>the process of creation</note> from God Himself, however, we proceed as likenesses through the **ideas**, by which we are shaped in His image. <margin>Johannes Scotus</margin>
...refused to admit them out of envy, or because it did not harmonize with the progress he made starting from the senses, or because Plato did not explain divine things to that "evil genius" <note>original: "cacodaemoni"; likely a harsh Renaissance rhetorical jab at Aristotle's perceived spiritual blindness</note> nor did he believe in them—what is that to us? Nor are the sacred scriptures <note>original: "sacra eloquia"</note> lacking in testimony regarding the **Ideas**, provided they are understood soundly, as we touched upon above. And we do not admit them as necessary for that method of doctrine which Aristotle teaches (through definition by genus and specific difference), but for that method which proceeds from a **superior cause**. Even Aristotle, while grieving, praises reaching this point (if the faculty were present), mourning that our eye is toward those things which are most manifest in nature—and in God, the author of nature itself and of natural things—just as the eye of the **night-owl** <note>original: "nycticoracis"; a famous Aristotelian metaphor for the human mind's struggle with divine light</note> is to the light of the sun. He further grieves that our discourse concerning **divine substance** is very meager and weak in us. Hence, those men must be venerated to whom God entrusted His words and mysteries, which we cannot investigate by our own strength. And it is true that God does not need any instrument or external thing in His working, being content and sufficient in Himself; but the Ideas in Him are one and the same with Him, even when imparted to things, and are not external. Nor is it inconsistent, according to the Platonists and divine sages, that what emanates from the **supreme being** and participates in it is in some way one and in some way not one; in some way the same and in some way not the same, just as the sun is one in itself but manifold in its rays. The heat proceeding from it is the same with the sun at its source, but in the recipient, it is not the same. Likewise, a tree is one in itself, but manifold in its branches; it is the same as its fruit, yet not the same in flavor, taste, and nature. This is learnedly and wisely discussed by **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his commentary on the *Timaeus* and in his *Theological Elements*. So too does **Johannes Scotus** <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena, a 9th-century Irish theologian who integrated Neoplatonism into Christian thought</note> teach that an object, as it exists in the one who knows it, is the same as that person, but different in its own proper being. The **Craftsman** <note>original: "opifex"; God as the Great Architect</note> does not use these Ideas as an instrument, but as a power—so to speak—that is **seminal** and expressive of essential forms, by which an image is left in the recipient, just as a **specific form** is imprinted by a natural generator. For from a horse comes a horse and not an ape, and from an eagle comes an eagle and not a donkey. And indeed, I wonder why they doubted how that power of the Ideas—since it is like a **seminal virtue**—moves everywhere to receive form; for the same doubt would exist concerning any agent, since there is no less application (whether called "virtual contact") in the primary cause than in the secondary causes. We could pursue many arguments with such men, but we judge it superfluous, as these matters should not be brought into controversy, but rather received with all reverence, giving thanks to God who illuminates our intellect to receive His secrets and treasures.

...since, so that we may be preserved and understand, we have, finally, our own weight and measure. And as for the first part, many people dispute the origin and the beginning of forms—where they proceed from. The <margin>Peripatetics</margin> <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, known for walking about while discussing.</note> agree with a common step that corruptible and mortal souls emerge from the "womb of matter," to use their words. Regarding the **intellective soul**, however, since it is still a matter of doubt among them whether it is mortal or immortal, they have not determined where it comes from. <margin>Aristotle</margin> But their Leader <note>Aristotle</note>, speaking with hesitation, says: "If there is any form coming from the outside, it is the intellective soul." But I truly do not know how anyone could imagine that a form is drawn out of matter, unless the opinion ascribed to <margin>Anaxagoras</margin> <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything."</note> is true: that anything can be in anything.

But they say that there is a **potentiality** within matter that is eventually led into **actuality**. But, oh Peripatetics, who gave that potentiality to matter, and who leads it into actuality? "Nature," they say, "grants this to matter and the subject, and a particular agent, by means of **seminal power** <note>original: "uirtute seminaria"; the internal life-force or "seed" that allows a thing to develop its specific form</note>, leads it into act." However, they do not determine what this nature actually is (as we have said elsewhere); but it can be nothing else except the **First Architect** <note>original: "primus Opifex"; referring to God as the Creator</note> performing all things in all things, or secondary causes acting at His command and by His power.

He is, therefore, the first agent and the **first giver of forms**, from whom comes all life, form, and order. But since no one gives what they do not have (as the Peripatetics themselves teach), it is therefore necessary that every form exists within the Architect from whom it proceeded. And the forms existing there are **Ideas**, according to whose limits we have our particular forms and our being. And since that being continuously flows from Him who gave it, we have from the **Ideas**—according to which He grants it—the source by which we are sustained, lest we flow away into nothingness.

For our being flows continuously; and that which flows must be sustained in something permanent. For time and motion flow, and they are sustained in the permanent heavens. Natural heat flows, and is sustained by food. Water flows in a river, and is sustained by the channel. Finally, every creature flows toward nothingness, and is sustained by the **Divine Word**, in which all things were established. <margin>Paul</margin> This is what Paul says of the Father, the fountain of all good: *Bearing up all things by the word of his power* <note>original: "Portans omnia uerbo uirtutis suæ"; a quote from Hebrews 1:3</note>. 

From this we have the means to understand, by those things which remain unchanged and immutable. For from these things which are continuously flowing and never <margin>Heraclitus</margin> remaining in the same state, nothing can be known, as was the opinion of Heraclitus of <margin>Paron</margin> Ephesus, <margin>Cyrillus</margin> Cyrillus, Paron, and many others. Because the form of transmutable things flows continuously, they thought it was not always the same, nor did it have a determined being—so much so that not even a definition (which belongs to permanent and necessary things) could be had of them. <margin>Parmenides</margin> For this reason, Parmenides also asserted that nothing could be known of lower things, except insofar as they depend on the Supreme, of whom there is true knowledge. After he sang of divine matters, he adds concerning lower things:

> *Thus far you have heard the mind of truth and its pure words.*
> *Now hear also the deceptive song of mortal affairs.*
> <note>original: "Hactenus & ueri mentem... Nunc res mortales carmen quoq; sumite fallax"; these lines are from Parmenides’ poem "On Nature," marking the transition from the Way of Truth to the Way of Opinion.</note>

Behold how piously, how justly, and with how elevated a mind he calls the knowledge of divine things "true science," and the discourse concerning them "undefiled," because they are stable and firm. These Ideas also necessarily contribute to **number**, because in changeable things subject to continuous variation, enumeration cannot be verified or established. Nor did the Creator <note>original: "Opifex," meaning the Craftsman or Architect of the universe.</note> arrange all things otherwise than in "number, weight, and measure," except insofar as they were enumerated in the Word, balanced by its weights, and measured. "Seventy weeks" <note>original: "hebdomades"; a reference to the prophecy in Daniel 9:24.</note> (Gabriel said to Daniel) "are determined for this people," for which we have "abbreviated." For not only were those weeks determined there, but all things which happen and have happened in this world; they are weighed so that they might be harmonious. For (as Pythagoras <note>The Greek philosopher often credited with discovering the mathematical basis of musical intervals.</note> first proved, and many after him confirmed) the true ratio of harmony is perceived from **weights**, yet it is founded upon **numbers**. And these vocal numbers, together with natural, formal, and rational ones, proceed from divine things, without which—as primary foundations—those other numbers would be nothing at all.

...receive [all things] from a single word, and by its power they tend toward the unity of the first, and are led by its attraction. From this was taken that portion about which 
<margin>Plato</margin>
**Plato** says in the *Timaeus*: "The creator took one portion from the whole in the beginning." For from the source of the universe and of all being, one portion was received, which is (unless I am mistaken) the very "being" of all things communicated by Him who said: 
<margin>GOD</margin>

Since this communication was made to the first matter produced from Him externally, it follows, according to **Plato**, that from that first One emanates the <term>binary</term> <note>The number two or the "dyad," representing the first step away from perfect unity into multiplicity.</note> attributed to matter itself, because it first attained duality. **Aristotle** teaches this from that "workshop of Plato" at the beginning of his book *On the Heavens* <note>original: *de cœlo*</note>. Through this form, matter is reduced into "act" <note>In Aristotelian terms, "act" or "actuality" is the fulfillment of a potential; form makes matter a specific, real thing.</note> and returns to the first. Hence, form stands as a middle ground between the most perfect and the most imperfect, familiar to both and holding a certain symbol with the highest and the lowest, so that it may lead the latter back to the former. In this ternary, form and the Giver of Forms Himself rejoice; therefore here, according to our most divine Theology, it is diffused into it, communicating it to us in some measure.

Our theologians say that it differs by a real relation, yet not in essence or substance; although some think that they are distinguished by certain absolute qualities. But having set these things aside, let us return to our business. Now from **Plotinus** we have two things in divine matters: the generator and the begotten—not indeed by animal generation, which he commands to stand far off when eternal things are discussed. <margin>Plotinus</margin>
**Plotinus** descends to the soul, which he says is the word of the divine mind, bearing its image. For the soul and all other things were produced by the Word of God, existing as such; and the soul itself is a "word"—not indeed that essential Word and Son of God, but a certain expressive word of an ideal concept. For just as the word we utter with the voice manifests the thought we have conceived in the mind, so the produced creature, like a kind of word, manifests what God had conceived in His mind. And although any created thing could be called God’s "word" in this way, none possesses the "image" except the soul. Therefore, the soul also rejoices in the <term>ternary</term> <note>The number three, symbolizing the Trinity and the structure of the soul (memory, intellect, and will).</note>, as does its progenitor. And whatever Trinity of things exists, it comes from the first ternary, from which all multiplicity flows through the Word. In which multiplicity, since there is similarity and dissimilarity, parity and disparity, from this results harmony—which is (according to 
<margin>Boethius, Nicomachus</margin>
**Boethius** and **Nicomachus**) the concord of like and unlike, or similar and dissimilar voices brought together into one. See, therefore, how all harmony proceeds from the Word itself.

## How these ideas are understood by us. Chapter 12.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**I**t is a Platonic dogma that natural things are to be learned and moral things are to be acquired through use, but divine things are to be received with reverence from oracles; for we cannot reach them unless the supreme light itself illuminates our eyes. Hence not even an Angel, whose intellect is not hindered by matter, is able to understand God’s handiwork without that divine light. Therefore **Moses** (as **Augustine** feels) hints with wonderful craftsmanship how all things being produced were made manifest to the angelic minds through a certain succession of that flashing light, saying: Just as the "reason" by which a creature is established is prior in the Word of God than in the creature itself which is established, so the knowledge of that reason happens first in the intellectual creature not subject to sin through the light of the Word, and afterward in its own kind of existence. From these two types of knowledge, by the same light—as if from morning and evening—the "day" is completed <note>Augustine’s "Morning Knowledge" (*cognitio matutina*) is the angel's knowledge of things in the Word/God, while "Evening Knowledge" (*cognitio vespertina*) is the knowledge of things in their own created nature.</note>. ### The necessity of things, and all being depends on the ideas. Chapter XIII.

<margin>David Aristotle</margin>
**F**rom the workshop, therefore, of the Supreme Architect, we hold that we receive from the <term>ideas</term> <note>In this context, "Ideas" are the eternal forms or blueprints in the mind of God according to which all things are created.</note> themselves not only our forms and a continually flowing existence, but also our knowledge, the number of things, their weight, and their measure, and consequently that all things are harmonious. Furthermore, they have from this source the reason for why they exist and why they are necessary, which we can prove. For we consider it known to all that no one possesses those things which he busies himself to acquire and preserve. For we seek truth and wisdom because we do not have them from ourselves. We seek goodness and pleasure, and to profit and be perfected in virtue, since these things are not in us but must be obtained from elsewhere. We labor even to preserve our very existence, since we draw it continually from another; and finally, whatever good there is, we take care to acquire it as something proceeding from elsewhere. God, however, seeks nothing, since he does not stand in need of our goods, as the **Prophet** <note>Referring to King David in the Psalms.</note> says. Along with whom **Aristotle** says in the *Politics*: God being witness, happiness does not consist in external things, because He is happy without anything outside of Himself. Since God, therefore, has all things from Himself, while we have nothing, we wait to receive all things from Him, who distributes them according to those most just measures which are in the <term>Archetype</term> <note original: "Archetypo">The "Archetype" is the original model or divine pattern from which all created things are copied.</note>. Some of the Hebrew sages teach that these measures are the "ideas," just as the names harmonize: for an Idea is a pattern...

### Christ is true man full of divinity. Chapter XVI.

**[S]**ince it is widely confessed by everyone that Christ was a true man, it is superfluous to argue the point. Instead, what remains for us to run through is why he wished to redeem the human race by assuming a human nature. The first reason for this is that since the entire human race <term>fell into sin</term> <note>original: "praevaricatum"; refers to the transgression of a law or duty, specifically Adam's original sin</note> in the <term>first man</term> <note>original: "primo homine," referring to Adam</note>, it was only just that satisfaction be made before the tribunal of God's supreme justice by a man. 
<margin>Exodus Deuteronomy</margin>
This stands according to the law of God himself, which dictates that each person must be punished through the very things by which he sinned. Satisfaction must be made by an equivalent, just as we read repeated in Exodus and Deuteronomy: that whoever harms another must give a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot, a burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, and a bruise for a bruise. Therefore, a man had to be offered up for man—but a heavenly man, innocent and free from sin, for the earthly man, the transgressor and criminal. This was so that he might not only take up the required penalty, but that a lawful redemption might be made by one who was not 
<margin>Paul</margin>
obligated to pay for himself. Paul thunders this with his echoing words, saying: *For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection <term>of the dead</term>. And just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.* For that satisfaction which exacts a penalty could not be made except by one who was subject to suffering. Furthermore, it was necessary for the one placed in charge of any work to have experience in it. Hence, for a fragile man subject to many sufferings, it was fitting to have a Leader instructed and 
<margin>The Same (Paul)</margin>
accustomed to such things, as our Paul says when discussing matters with the Hebrews: *For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities, but one tempted in all things according to our <term>likeness</term>, yet without sin.* This was so he might rule with due mercy and with sorrow for the misfortunes of others, judging piously because he had experienced the weakness of those being judged. Christ himself indicated this with these words: 
<margin>CHRIST. Lucretius.</margin>
*The Father gave the Son of Man the power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man*—meaning he is conscious through experience of the condition <term>of those</term> who are to be judged. He also had to be established as the head of a body that was of the same nature as the body itself, lest he become a <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythological hybrid monster; used here to mean an unnatural or incoherent mixture of species.</note>, of which it is said: *A lion in front, a dragon behind, and in the middle the chimera itself.* <note>original: "Prima leo, postrema draco, media ipsa chimæra." This is a quote from the Roman poet Lucretius (De Rerum Natura 5.905).</note> For the collection of all those serving God is a certain body of which Christ is the head, as the 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Apostle says: *He is the head of the body of the church;* and elsewhere: *Just as in one body we have many members, but all members do not have the same function, so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another.* Moreover, since a heavenly kingdom has been prepared for us from the foundation of the world, and we were created to obtain it so that we might acquire it by hereditary right, the Father raised up a man so full of God and filial divinity that he might not only make him the <term>firstborn</term>, but through him give the power to all who wish to live piously—not according to flesh and blood—to also become children of God. And this <term>firstborn</term> had to be a brother to the others by a shared and 
<margin>The Same (Paul)</margin>
kindred nature, if he was to be counted as the first among them. Paul, being conscious of these mysteries, did not remain silent but said: *Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the <term>firstborn</term> among many brothers.* 
<margin>The Same (Paul)</margin>
And again: *If children, then heirs; heirs of God indeed, and joint-heirs with Christ.* Furthermore, he came into this man in whom all things had been contaminated by his rebellion...

# VOLUME ONE

[The text] recapitulates and embraces those things which had been treated diffusely and individually throughout the whole discourse. Just as the <term>Supreme Craftsman</term> <note>original: "summus opifex"; a common Renaissance term for God as the divine architect or builder</note>, having produced all creatures distinctly, produced man on the sixth and final day—in whom all things are contained—so also in this final time and age, He raised up and showed to the world His Son, Jesus Christ. In Him, all these same things are contained with much greater excellence than in other men. For in Him, insofar as He is God,
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
is contained the eternal Father himself: "The Father," He says, "is in me, and I in him." <note>original: "Pater... in me est, & ego in eo"; see John 10:38</note> He contains the Holy Spirit, of whom He says: "He shall receive of mine." <note>original: "Ille de me accipiet"; see John 16:14</note> And again: "I will send Him to you." But He does not send unless He is the one who produces [the Spirit], as our theologians say; nor does He produce unless He first contains that within Himself. He contains all divine perfections, as He himself professes with a clear voice,
<margin>THE SAME</margin>
saying: "The Father has given all things to me." <note>original: "Omnia dedit mihi Pater"; see Matthew 11:27</note> And again: "All yours are mine." Just as these things are infinite and immense, so the explanation of them is impossible. For He contains piety, justice, mercy, strength, beauty, command, kingship, all attributes, and every gift of craftsmanship. Whence He is also called the <term>maker of the world</term> <note>original: "fabricator mundi"</note>, and the one through whom all things were made and are made. Hence He says: "My Father
<margin>THE SAME</margin>
works even until now, and I work." <note>original: "Pater meus usque modo operatur, & ego operor"; see John 5:17</note> Furthermore, insofar as He is man, He contains all things that are joined together in man, but of a more perfect quality; just as man himself, united to God, is more perfect—indeed, the most perfect of all. Hence He is called the "firstborn of every creature," <note>original: "primogenitus omnis creaturae"; see Colossians 1:15</note> not however in time, but in dignity and perfection. And through the symbol of all things which He took upon Himself, He perfected and purified all things, just as Peter, while staying with Simon the Tanner, was instructed by a vision of four-footed animals and birds existing in a vessel. These, before Christ, were considered
unclean in the Ancient Law, but by a heavenly oracle they were declared purified—specifically in the time of Christ, who cleansed all things. For even if this was demonstrated as a <term>type</term> <note>original: "typum"; a biblical event or person serving as a prophetic symbol of something to come</note> of the Gentiles being purified, it does not fall away from the truth of the matter. Hence, foods are permitted to Christians which were said to be, and were, unclean before the coming of Christ. This He Himself
<margin>THE SAME</margin>
declared when He said: "Not what enters into the mouth defiles a man," <note>original: "Non quod intrat in os coinquinat hominem"; see Matthew 15:11</note> because, you see, they were already being cleansed through Him. For if the earth, which was cursed in the sin of Adam, was purified through Noah—
<margin>Lamech</margin>
as Lamech is brought in by Holy Scripture, saying after he fathered Noah: "This one shall comfort us from the works and labors of our hands, from the earth which the Lord has cursed" <note>original: "Iste consolabitur nos..."; see Genesis 5:29</note>—it was so much so that just as the fruit of the cursed earth was offensive and hateful to God before the flood (whence the offerings and gifts of Cain from the fruits of the cursed and unpurified earth were rejected), so after Noah, the Lord accepted, and indeed required in the Law, the firstfruits of all the fruits of the earth, from which the curse had been removed through Noah, as the
<margin>Wise Hebrews</margin>
wise Hebrews treat more diffusely. <note>This likely refers to Rabbinic commentaries or Midrash that link Noah's name (meaning "rest" or "comfort") to the restoration of the soil's fertility after Adam's curse.</note> Therefore, much more and more perfectly ought the fruits of the earth and all things to be purified and cleansed through Him, of whom
<margin>Paul</margin>
the Apostle says: "He has pacified through the blood of His cross both the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth." <note>original: "Pacificavit per sanguinem crucis eius..."; see Colossians 1:20</note> Nor would He have pacified them unless they were first purified from every uncleanness, because of which they were rendered hateful to God. To this, that saying of John bears witness: "God sent His Son, not to judge the world"—that is, as guilty and unclean—"but that the world might be saved
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
through Him," namely, by Him purifying and cleansing it. Which the Redeemer Himself hinted at when He said: "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into His hand," <note>see John 3:35</note> so that He might contain all things.

## THE LIFE OF ALL THINGS IS BOTH MANIFOLD AND ONE. CHAPTER ONE.

UNLESS the Sun / which God kindled to declare His majesty, and the soul, which He fashioned with such excellence, taught me how one thing can be manifold or many, I would not truly dare to say that life is at once single and manifold. For the sun is unique in itself, but manifold in its rays / single in essence, yet all-encompassing in power. The soul is also single in itself, but manifold in its operation: for it hears in the ears; it sees in the eyes; it smells in the nostrils; it tastes in the mouth; it touches and acts in the hands; it understands in the brain; it loves in the heart; it walks in the feet; it digests in the stomach / liver / and other digestive organs; it generates in the instruments designated for this / so much so that it appears manifold, though it remains single. Nor because it seems to suffer a defect in some member is it diminished: For if the eye or the hand were weak / it is not therefore lesser in the brain or heart. From these things, it is easily discerned how that single life would be manifold in its members / if we were to admit the world is a living being <note>original: "animal"; in this context, it refers to a "living creature" or "animated being," supporting the Platonic idea of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul.</note>, as many wise men agree, even those who venerate the sacred words / since they seem not to oppose it at all:

<margin>Augustine, Origen</margin>
as Augustine, a man of most sharp intellect and excellent learning, decrees; wherefore he also seems to assent to this opinion. Origen, however, runs toward this same opinion with swift feet; which he strives to prove both by reason and the testimony of sacred scripture, saying in his *On First Principles*: "Although the world is ordered with diverse functions: its state must not be understood as discordant or discrepant: but just as our body is fitted together from many members and is held by one soul, so I think the whole world must be considered as a certain immense and vast animal <note>original: "animal... immane"; here meaning a living entity of gargantuan proportions.</note>: which is held as if by one soul through the power of God and reason." Which I also think is judged by sacred scripture through

<margin>
Jeremiah
Isaiah
CHRIST
Paul
Aratus
</margin>
that which is said by the Prophet: "Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord." <note>Jeremiah 23:24</note> And again by another Seer: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." <note>Isaiah 66:1</note> Which the Savior also confirms when He says: "Do not swear, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God: nor by the earth, for it is His footstool." <note>Matthew 5:34-35</note> But also that which the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> / while preaching among the Athenians and approving the sentiment of Aratus <note>A Greek Cilician poet (c. 315–240 BCE); Paul quotes his poem *Phaenomena* in Acts 17:28.</note>, said: "Since in Him we live, move, and have our being." And how is that possible, unless because God by His power constrains, contains, and gives life to the whole world? How also is heaven the throne of God, and earth His footstool,

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
unless because He fills all things in heaven and on earth? Thus far Origen / With whom Eusebius Pamphilus <note>A 4th-century historian and exegete; the "Pamphilus" was added in honor of his teacher.</note>, reasoning about the supreme craftsman in his *Theological Solutions* regarding the supreme craftsman, says: "Life is there, and mind, so that for life itself it remains an eternal being, but for the mind..."

## OF THE SECOND SONG.

It fashions and contains those things which exist. Hence the first being must be vital and intellectual: From which all essence, life, and intellect are named more by participation than by species: For that being itself is life through itself, and intellect through itself. Whatever is besides this is more "non-being" than "being," because there was a time when it was not a being. And through this perpetuity, it remains a being, lives, and understands: For it is a participant in life to the extent that the first being provided it, and it understands to the degree that the first being granted it. Many things follow in this matter, from which he concludes that there is one life of all living things, just as there is a single soul in all members of the body. This soul is not only diffused within its own proper members, but is in some way diffused even to extraneous things. For from sweat flowing from a human, condensed and arranged, a certain weaker life is infused—weaker than the life of the human—and lice are produced. Moreover, from the accumulation created by breath, the life of bedbugs and fleas is filled. This happens either from the disposition of the matter, or from a spark of life falling from the human, 
<margin>
Cardinal 
Cusa
</margin>
which, being less perfect than life itself in its essence, gives life to those lower subjects with a coarser mark. And from among those who are called the "hinges" <note>original: "cardines"; a pun on the title of Cardinal</note> of the Christian house, a most skillful and singular investigator <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a philosopher and cardinal known for his work on the "coincidence of opposites."</note>, when he compared the microcosm <note>the "small world," referring to man</note> to the macrocosm <note>the "large world," referring to the universe</note>, said: That life of the world, which moves itself and all things, is perpetual, because its motion is round and circular, containing all motion, just as a circular figure enfolds every other figure within itself. Toward this soul, the entire corporeal world relates just as the human body relates to its own soul. Furthermore, the soul is in the world like a king in a kingdom, by whose governance the inhabitants are led; by whom diverse princes and leaders are assigned, under whose leadership particular peoples are ruled, yet not secluded from the king of the entire domain. Thus every single creature—which first pre-existed in that life of the universe—lives with its determined leadership, species, and form, whether as an angel, a man, a lion, an eagle, or a plant. Yet it is not secluded from that single-born life, but when that particular life departs, or that particular leadership is removed, the body returns to the more universal kingdom—namely, the element of earth—while the soul returns to the universal kingdom of life. For "the spirit returns," (says the wise man) "to God who made it." <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 12:7.</note> If any, however, are thrust down into Tartarean <note>original: "tartareis"; referring to the ancient Greek underworld, here used for Hell</note> prisons, they are bound there by force. If we wish to bring forward external authorities, we have many at hand: For Aristotle, who at this time is most celebrated among the philosophers, along with his pupil Theophrastus, and Averroes, professes that the world is a living creature <note>original: "animal"; in this context, it means an "animated being" or "living thing" rather than a beast.</note>.

Democritus says that God is the soul of the animal world. The Indians (as Iarchas teaches in Philostratus) said the world is a living creature, and specifically an androgynous <note>original: "androgynum"; having both male and female characteristics</note> one, because it fulfills the role of both father and mother in the generation, education, and love of living things. Zeno proves the world is animated and perceptive from the fact that it generates animated things from itself. And wisely, Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings.</note> says in that book titled *That God is Hidden and Manifest at Once*: "There is nothing even in bodies which is not God himself: For he alone exists as all things, bringing into light the things that are, and enclosing within himself the things that are not. He is the hidden one, he is the most manifest of all: He is visible to the mind, he is present to the eyes."

<margin>Orpheus</margin> Along with these, Orpheus in his theology chants at length that God exists and is perceived
<margin>Manilius</margin> in all the members of the world; whom Manilius, following precisely <note>original: "ad unguem" – literally "to the fingernail," meaning perfectly</note>, sings:

*so that neither the waters nor the stars would fail us,*
*nor would the heaven fly either greater or smaller than is just:*
