<margin>The Platonists</margin> All the Platonists affirm this same thing with one voice, for it is their peculiar doctrine. And out of many reasons by which they likewise asserted it, let us draw out only this one from Plato: 
<margin><insert>That which moves from itself of its own accord is more divine.</insert></margin> 
For it pleased him [Plato] that there are two motions: one proper, the other external. He held that what moves from itself of its own accord is more divine than what is agitated by an outside impulse. Moreover, he placed this motion in souls alone, and believed that the principle of the other motion was derived from them. Therefore, since every motion arises from the heat of the world, and this heat is moved not by an external impulse but by its own accord, it is necessary that it be a soul. From this we understand that the world is a living being; and from this it can also be understood that intelligence exists within it. But one might rightly wonder, since the world is a living creature, why it is not altered, or becomes sick, or fails, like other living beings. Here the

<margin>Moses</margin>
...through secondary causes, are narrated by the most wise philosopher, Moses. Nor is this wrongly said concerning man, who was fashioned by the hands of God; for man was not formed without dust or the intervening subject of earth. This is unlike the heavens and the whole machine of the world, which was made immediately by God out of nothing. Therefore, the world—in regards to its underlying parts which were immediately fabricated by God—is perpetual and unfailing; just as the soul of man was produced by God himself without any intermediary. There is also another reason: the world consists of all its parts in such a way that no part of any body, however small, is left outside the world's embrace. Thus, nothing approaching from the outside, whether hot or cold, can cause sickness in the world; for the world is most perfectly proportioned within itself, even if its parts sometimes seem altered, they are nonetheless harmonious in relation to the whole. Furthermore, the world is a total body, such that it lets nothing flow out of itself, nor does it diminish or suffer loss, which would otherwise happen from the wasting away of parts that dissolve into something else. For all things live within the world; hence the parts flow and yet do not flow away, since there is nothing outside its boundaries into which they could leak. Therefore, its parts, which sometimes flow out when weary, eventually return to the nature of the universe, having been refreshed.

**S**ince there is a unique source of a double life—he who says in Jeremiah: *They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, the Lord* <note>Jeremiah 2:13</note>—it is necessary that all people draw both natural and spiritual life, and whatever other life there may be, from that fountain. From him proceeds the river of which it is said in Genesis: *And a river went out of the place of pleasure* <note>The Garden of Eden, interpreted here as the "Archetype"</note>—which is God—to water first the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original "blueprint" or divine model of the universe in Platonic and mystical thought</note> itself through various channels of things to be communicated. And these are the "waters above the world," which Moses and David say are above the heavens. Afterward, the divided river waters the entire earth in four heads. These waters of life are first in the primary fountain, and afterward in the Son, who is himself the fountain existing with the Father, as is sung in the Psalm: *For with thee is the fountain of life.* <note>Psalm 36:9</note> For the Son is with the Father, to whom the Father, giving all things, also established him as the fountain, so that he might rightly say: *I am the life,* <note>John 14:6</note> granting both natural and spiritual life to all. For when we say *all things that were made were life in him,* <note>John 1:3-4</note> this is understood as natural life. But when he says, *I am the resurrection and the life,* <note>John 11:25</note> it is understood as spiritual life, which is made perpetual as eternal life; this we also have from the Son of God himself, as he himself testifies in many places, saying: *I give them eternal life.* And again: *If anyone drinks of the water that I shall give him, it will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.* <note>John 4:14</note> There is also another fountain of life in that most holy Archetype, which is the Holy Spirit; and he is sometimes called the Spirit of Life, just as we read in Ezekiel: *And the spirit of life was in the wheels.* <note>Ezekiel 1:20</note> Concerning which it is also sung in the Psalm: *Send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created,* <note>Psalm 104:30</note> even those things which were dead and destroyed. Yet these three fountains are one in that fountain of life and divine essence, without which nothing lives and nothing exists. As Apuleius of Madaura <note>A 2nd-century Latin philosopher and rhetorician</note> most beautifully and piously brings forth those things which he had gathered from the Platonic workshop, saying: "Concerning the ruler of all things, as much as it is lawful to say (for ancient opinion prohibits speaking much about him, since he escapes all human grasp), these things..."

...we determine: That it enters into the thoughts of all men that God exists, and that he has no author of his own origin. Finally, that he is the salvation and perseverance of those things which he has made. Nor is any thing of such outstanding strength that, deprived of God's help, it would be content with its own nature. But since we believe that God permeates through all things, and extends to us and beyond the power of his name—as much as he is absent or imminent—so much it must be thought that he gives more or less utility to things. Nor does this doctrine differ <margin>Paul</margin> from that which the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> hands down, when he both describes the degrees in the church and likens the whole congregation to a body; whose soul and life diffuses itself more or less into the members according to their requirement and proximity—not indeed of location, but of power and symbol.

### What the Tree of Life is. Chapter III.

**I**t is commonplace to all that Christ, our Messiah, is celebrated in many kinds of mysteries and called by many names: for he is called the Lamb, the Lion, the Cornerstone, Christ, the Word, Truth, Life, and such things. So he is also called the Tree of Life, which was placed in the middle of the garden of delights <note>the Garden of Eden</note>, so that he might impart life to all, as we have revealed above. But why he is called a tree must now be explained. A tree is rooted in the earth, from which it receives the increases of life. And Christ is the tree having his root in the land of the living, from which he drew his first origin; although he drew the body and instrument of his divinity from a <margin>Isaiah</margin> people now dry and parched, as Isaiah says: "He grew up like a sapling from the earth, and like a root from thirsty ground." A tree is divided first into larger and fewer branches, afterwards into very many smaller ones. And the most full power and grace of Christ was first diffused into the few Apostles—but they were great and robust in virtue—and through them into very many others, to whom those [Apostles] are therefore worthily to be preferred. A tree draws from the earth continuous increases of life to be communicated to the shoots, twigs, flowers, and fruits. Christ also lives in that land of divinity and of the father <margin>CHRIST</margin>, as he himself testifies, saying: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father." Having received this life from the Father, he imparts it to others that they might live; whence he adds: "And he who eats me, by taking food as a branch does from the trunk and root, he shall live because of me." And again: "If anyone does not remain in me"—namely, by drawing life from me—"he will be cast out like a branch and will wither." Flowers live and grow beautiful on a tree, but once cut off, they immediately wither or rot. So too live the flowers of our thoughts in that tree which says: "Without me you can do nothing." <margin>Paul</margin> "Nor are we able to think anything from ourselves, as if from ourselves," says the Apostle. Fruits also ripen on a tree, receiving continuous <margin>CHRIST</margin> nourishment from it, just as the tree itself speaks, saying: "He who remains in me and I in him, this one bears much fruit."

#### Where this tree is planted. Chapter 4.

**W**here this life-giving tree has its roots, we have two records from the divine storehouses <note>The author refers to the Holy Scriptures as "divine storehouses" or treasuries of knowledge.</note>. One is that paradise, or that garden of delights, was planted by the Lord God <term>from of old</term> <note>original Hebrew: mi-qedem</note>, which signifies either "from the beginning" or "from ancient times." This is because the whole garden and all true pleasure is rooted in that most ancient Eternal Father, the first origin of all good things; or, the garden is planted in that divine essence which is the true land of the living, from which all life and all delights and pleasures sprout. The second record is that the tree of life was in the middle of paradise. This is because the divine Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to Christ.</note>, who is the true tree of life, is the middle person in that most holy Trinity. Furthermore, having put on human flesh and lived among men, he always held the middle place: for he was found being born in the middle of animals, disputing in the middle of the doctors, dying in the middle of thieves, and rising again in the middle of his disciples. And although he himself, as the Word, as the Son, and as the Wisdom of God, sits at the right hand of the Father, nevertheless as teacher, as redeemer, as Messiah, and as the tree of life, he stands in the middle of the archetype <note>The "archetype" refers to the original divine pattern or world of ideas.</note>. Just as the life of a human being, which is made in his image, has its seat in the heart—which occupies the middle of the human body—and from which life flows into all the limbs. And although God is entirely everywhere, not divided into parts or members (and consequently there is no "right," "left," "middle," or "extreme" in him according to our physical laws), there is nonetheless a certain disposition in a divine and excellent way that we cannot fully perceive. This is not a disposition of his essence, which is most simple, but rather an "influence" or "flow" in relation to us, according to which we hold his image. It is of this that the Scripture speaks when it repeatedly mentions the right hand, the left, the middle, the east, the west, the south, the north, and such arrangements of the divine influence, according to which that tree of life is said to be placed in the middle.

#### How the tree itself is formed. Chapter 5.

<margin>Wisdom of Jerusalem</margin>
**T**he wise Hebrews depict this tree of life in an even better way, as far as they are able, through the shaft of the letter <term>Vav</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ו (Vav), which is shaped like a vertical line or a hook.</note>, which is straight like the trunk of a tree. They show it with that upper part, which is like the letter <term>Yod</term> <note>The small letter י (Yod).</note>, united to that shaft, signifying the highest fountain of life—the Eternal Father—flowing into the Son. The Hebrews themselves call this the "upper crown" <note>likely referring to Keter, the highest Sephirah in Kabbalah</note>, to which they wish the letters <term>Aleph</term> and <term>Yod</term> to be dedicated. One of these signifies "one" and the "beginning" <note>Aleph, א</note>, and the other signifies "ten" and the "completion of numbers" <note>Yod, י</note>, to suggest that the Eternal Father is the beginning and the end of all things. And through the continuation and union with that shaft which represents the tree of life, the union he has with the Son is denoted, into whom all things flow, so that he himself can also be called the beginning and the end; thus the whole <term>Vav</term> is attributed to the Son. By a great mystery <note>original: "sacramento"</note>, God commanded in the book of Exodus that there be carved into the pillars of the tabernacle <term>the hooks of the pillars</term> <note>original Hebrew: vavei ha-ammudim</note>, that is, "their silver hooks" <note>original: vavim eorum argentea</note>. In place of this, our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has "with silver heads" or capitals. This is either because the translator did not know what the word implied, or he did not wish to reveal the mystery. For the Pillar of the Tabernacle—and of the whole world, according to whose example the tabernacle was built—is Christ, the Word made human. By him the heavens were made firm, and the Father carries and sustains all things. Therefore, by God's command, there was carved upon this pillar the letter that signifies life, to denote that the principle of life was placed in him by the Eternal Father: so that he might [bring] the same...

<header>FIRST TONE</header>

<margin>CHRIST.</margin> [The Tree of Life] imparts to others, just as Christ himself deigned to reveal, saying: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me will live because of me." <note>A quotation from the Gospel of John 6:57.</note> And this tree is divided into root, trunk, branches, flowers, and fruits: For the **Root** is the budding Godhead <term>Godhead</term> <note>The essential nature or essence of God, often distinguished from the personhood of the Trinity.</note> itself; the **Trunk** is the Word produced within it by the Father; the **Branches** are the attributes communicated to it by Him who gave all things to it; the **Leaves** and **flowers** are the living Ideas <term>Ideas</term> <note>In this context, the Platonic "Ideas" or eternal patterns of all things existing in the mind of God.</note> existing within it. But the leaves are the ideas of irrational things, which were produced for the service of intellectual creatures, just as leaves are established to cover flowers and fruits, and as it were, for their service. But the **Flowers** are the ideas of intellectual things <note>Meaning angels and humans, who possess intellect.</note>, from which the owed fruits are expected: But just as many flowers fall without fruit, so many Angels and men have fallen and fall continually without fruit; and being dead, they wither away from that tree of life, destined to be burned in unquenchable fire. Indeed, the **Fruits** are the rules for our good actions, and the gifts and graces <term>charismata</term> with which we are continually endowed, so that living according to those rules, we too may present the fruits of our works to Him who planted the tree of life itself, and us as little shrubs, so that from that tree of life we may
<margin>Paul.</margin> receive [sustenance], from which we may produce the due fruits according to the Spirit; which Paul mentions, saying: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, etc." <note>Galatians 5:22.</note> which follow. Nor shall we proceed further concerning the figure of Him who is shaped by no figure, yet gives to all things their form; nor is He enclosed by any limit, although He encloses all things in Himself. But let these few things be said, according to what we have been able to learn from the sacred scriptures.

->To whom, and in what way life is communicated. Chapter 6.<-

**W**ithout any doubt we hold that all things which enjoy life draw it from the fountain of life, or receive it and eat of the fruits of the tree of life. But it comes into controversy which things are living, and whether all things live. To be sure, Angels, men, animals, and plants live, each with its own life, as all agree; but regarding metals, stones, elements, and the heavens, a difficulty exists among some: because since their life is not apparent, they judge that these do not live at all and call them inanimate. But if the world is a living creature <term>animal</term> <note>This refers to the concept of the *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul," the idea that the entire universe is a single, living organism.</note>, as we have discussed above, and as many wise men agree, there is no doubt that all these things live, just as all members—flesh, intestines, nerves, blood, and bones—live in a human or animal body, even though bones and such might seem removed from private life. For in the body, bones grow, move, and sustain the body itself, as if they were living columns. Flesh thrives and is restored, so that it does not fear wounds or incisions; and broken bones are knit together, which does not happen at all to dead things. So too the members of the great and worldly living creature live, each
<margin>Hermes.</margin> <note>original: "Mercu." referring to Mercurius/Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom ancient philosophical texts were attributed.</note> with its own life, as Hermes says in that treatise which he calls "On the Common [Mind]": "Everything that is in the world is moved either by increasing or decreasing; but that which is moved, lives for that reason." And since all things are moved, even the earth—especially by generative and transformative motion—it also lives. But let us come to the higher members, about which it is doubted whether they live: and these are the heavens, which he who
<margin>Theophrastus.</margin> doubts they live (says Theophrastus), is not considered a philosopher. Nor were there lacking those who would say that the heavens are living animals: which from [their] rational and co[ntinuous] motion...

...they strive to prove by a continuous influx, because they could not provide a living force unless they themselves were living. But descending to lower things, Stones are said to be alive for the reason that they live: for they grow, condense, harden, and possess various effects which many believe cannot proceed except from a living being. Metals live (as we have said) with a higher life, into which a certain most hidden spirit is infused by the luminaries and the heavens. This is what some rivals of nature <note>A reference to alchemists, who were often described as "apes" or "rivals" of nature for attempting to replicate natural processes in the laboratory.</note> strive to achieve, thinking they can transmute tin, bronze, or quicksilver <note>original: "argentũ uiuũ"</note> into gold or silver by instilling into them the spirit and life of gold or silver, as they say. Water lives, to which the germ of animals is especially attributed, in that which was said: *Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing, or the offspring of a living soul.* <note>A paraphrase of Genesis 1:20.</note> The earth also lives, as we have said; we easily prove its life when we see it most fertile with living plants. And one part is more fruitful than another, which could not be unless it were more full of life. The life of this earth is also recognized by a certain thickness and richness which increases from the waste of living animals falling from a living creature; whence, carrying life with it in some way, it imparts it to the earth with which it mixes, favoring the generation of living plants, which could least of all come from a non-living thing.

<margin>Ancient Hebrews</margin> But the Air contains so much of life that the Hebrews more often call it "spirit" <note>The Hebrew word "Ruach" means both air/wind and spirit.</note>, a spirit, I say, containing and coupling the other elements. Regarding fire, I shall say nothing, since all the ancients admit that life is a certain kind of fire, and that life itself proceeds from fire and light. And all these things, together with those that live with a visible life, receive life according to their capacity from the Author of Life: who is called now a fountain, now a river, now the tree of life. This life spreads itself into the whole body of the world, just as a particular soul spreads into all the members of its body, so that all operations which occur through any member of that body proceed from the soul giving it life and movement. For just as a man speaks in his mouth, sees in his eyes, hears in his ears, walks with his feet, and other such things, so God—the first life of all—shines and warms in the sun, flows in various ways in the diverse stars, rains in the clouds, breathes in the air, germinates in the earth, and works various things in the waters, fish, and animals. So also He works in different men (as Paul says) *all things in all.* <note>1 Corinthians 12:6.</note> And here God is also life;

<margin>Aristotle</margin> for that common "Nature" which operates, and which Aristotle seems to distinguish from God when he says: *God and Nature*, is as if she were the companion and spouse of God. Nor is "Nature" anything else but God, who, diffused into all things, gives to all the power to act.

<margin>Socrates</margin>
<margin>Anaxagoras</margin> This is what (as Socrates reports in the *Phaedo* <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, depicting the final hours of Socrates.</note>) Anaxagoras, the contemplator of the heavens, teaches in the beginning of the book he published about the world, saying: *Mind is the cause of all things, the maker and moderator, adorning and filling all things.* And Socrates grieves that Anaxagoras does not declare the reason and the manner of those things which are done by that first Mind.

<margin>Academics</margin>
<margin>Porphyry</margin>
<margin>Cyril</margin> Indeed, all the Academics <note>The followers of Plato's school.</note> profess with one voice a "Soul of the World" <term>Anima Mundi</term> by which all things live: and the greater part of them believe this Soul to be God. For Porphyry (as Cyril reports in *Against Julian* <note>A polemical work by Cyril of Alexandria against the Emperor Julian the Apostate.</note>) said that God was first the Supreme Good, second the Creator, and third the Soul of the World; so that first He might be in Himself, second He might create things, and third He might fill and give life to all.

<margin>Numenius</margin> Numenius, however, perhaps proceeding further than is expedient, says: The first God is subsisting in Himself, but the second and third...

He is one with the first: But that second <note>Referring to the Second Person of the Trinity, the Word or Son.</note>, adhering to matter—which is binary <note>In the philosophical tradition the author follows, the number one represents unity and God, while the number two (the "binary") represents the first step away from unity into the multiplicity of the material world.</note>—is divided by it: Yet he himself, together with the third, infuses life into things: These things (rightly understood) agree with our Theology: in which we say the Father is the first principle of all, and from him comes—not indeed a second God, but speaking in our human way—a second person, who adhered to matter when he took up human flesh, or when he went forth into the work of imprinting forms into things according to the exemplars <note>The divine "blueprints" or "Ideas" in the mind of God.</note> existing within him. By forming these diverse things, he is, as it were, divided into them; yet he is not diminished, nor does anything fall away from him. And these, together with the third—that is, with the third person—who are nevertheless all one God, infuse life into things. For the Son is called "Life" and the "Tree of Life," and the third person is called the "Spirit of Life," because both infuse life into lower things. But the Word and the Son give life to things so that they may *be* alive:

<margin>David</margin>
But the Spirit gives life so that they may perform the *works* of life. This is what the Prophet <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> implies when he says: "By the Word the heavens"—and consequently all things—"were formed and established, but by the spirit of his mouth is all their power" <note>original: "uerbo cœli... spiritu oris eius est omnis uirtus eorū"; a reference to Psalm 33:6.</note>: namely, in their operation. 

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
Just so, we read in the Book of Wisdom: "The holy spirit of intelligence is mobile" <note>original: "Spūs intelligentiæ sanctus mobilis est"; a reference to Wisdom of Solomon 7:22.</note>, that is, causing others to be moved to work. To express this better, he adds: "Having all power." 

<margin>Paul</margin>
So also Paul divides the works of various people according to the spirit, concluding: "But one and the same spirit works all these things, dividing to each one as he wills." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:11.</note>

-> When and why the tree was forbidden. Chapter VII. <-

**E**xplicit doctrine is found in the sacred words, that God, after Adam’s transgression, said: "Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil: And now, lest perhaps he should stretch out his hand, and take also from the tree of life, so that he might live forever, let us cast him out." And this was done. Nor should anyone wonder why God seemed to take it poorly that Adam had become a knower of good and evil. For he did not take vengeance upon Adam's progress, but upon his arrogance: since he wished to discern good and evil for himself, and to decree what is just and unjust—which belongs to <term>Elohim</term> <note>A Hebrew name for God; here the author uses it to refer to divine judges or the "assembly of the gods" mentioned in the Psalms.</note> and to judges, in whose congregation and assembly God stands, judging among them. A man cannot do this without God himself. Or perhaps it was because he wished to assume the rank and place of the <term>Messiah</term> <note>The "Anointed One." The author links the Messiah to the true source of wisdom and life.</note>, who (as we have said elsewhere) is the true tree of the knowledge of good and evil. He had forbidden it, therefore, lest anyone should claim for himself the dignity of the Son of God and of the Messiah by emulating him who is the trunk of true life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. 

But this is a deeper mystery than may be spoken. Therefore, let us assign another reason that may be understood by everyone: and that is, lest man, infected by sin, should unworthily receive the nourishment of life to his own destruction. For if he had entered into impurity, he would have remained so forever, and would stand impure, if indeed impurity can exist alongside that life. Or, lest receiving the nourishment of life while unprepared, it should turn to his harm—just as the best wine harms a man with a fever, and the most delicious meat, however 

<margin>The same [Paul]</margin>
well prepared, harms one with pleurisy. And this is what Paul says regarding those who would eat the bread of life: "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself." <note>1 Corinthians 11:28-29.</note>

For just as the tree of life was to our first parents, so to us is the bread of life: which is forbidden to the unworthy, just as that tree was forbidden to the transgressor Adam; and it is forbidden to anyone unworthy and defiled by some crime: because since crime and sin are the work of death, they can in no way be compatible with life.

### How all things live in that tree, and consequently in Christ. Chapter VIII.

<margin>John</margin>
**I**t has been repeated quite often, that most famous sentiment of John, that all things, before they were made, were life in the Word. <note>Referring to John 1:3-4: "All things were made through him... in him was life."</note> Nor should it be thought that things, once unfolded into their own proper forms, are abandoned by that creative life by which they lived in the mind of the Maker: but beyond this, they acquire other lives according to their capacity. For life is manifold; therefore this tree is called by the famous name <term>עץ החיים</term> <note>original: "ez haijim"</note> *Etz ha-Chayyim*, that is, the "tree of lives," and not "life" in the singular. <note>The author points out that the Hebrew word for life, "Chayyim," is plural, suggesting a plurality of ways in which God animates the world.</note> Therefore, all things live by that creative life; they also live by their own natural life, which nevertheless depends on that highest life and is a ray or spark of it, in which we live, move, and have our being. Man also lives, beyond his manifold natural life, by a certain life of the spirit, concerning which it is said: *It is the Spirit that gives life.* And here <margin>Christ. Ezekiel. Paul.</margin> he favors a twofold life: the Natural, according to that saying of Ezekiel: *And the spirit of life was in the wheels, giving life to all things*; and the Spiritual, of which the same Prophet says: *Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, and let them live again.* For they were dead in sin and stood in need of the life of the spirit; concerning which Paul says: *If by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live.* Both of these lives, even if they are supplied by the spirit of life, nevertheless proceed from the tree of life, which is the very Word of God made human, who says: *He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life.* And again: <margin>Christ.</margin> *For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself.* And repeating this often, he affirms that he is the life, to be communicated to others also according to their degrees: through which degrees he intends to lead us into 그 blessed and eternal life, beyond which there is no other: *I* (he says) *give eternal life to my sheep.* And again: <margin>The same [Christ]</margin> *It is necessary for the Son of Man to be exalted, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.* Of which life the Father is the fountain, who says: <margin>Jeremiah</margin> *They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters.* The Son, however, is the river of life proceeding from the Paternal fountain, or the tree of life planted in the land of the living. <note>A common mystical and biblical phrase referring to the heavenly realm or the state of grace.</note> But the Spirit is like a pool, receiving the water of life from the fountain and the river of life, and diffusing it into us also: which Origen discusses at length in his commentary on Matthew. <margin>Origen</margin>

### Christ is the support of all things. Chapter IX.

<margin>Paul. The same. Isaiah.</margin>

### Why all are not supported by him. Chapter X.

# THE SECOND TONE.

...salvation: For just as the crown of the kingdom has been prepared for us from the foundation of the world, yet no one will be crowned unless he has competed according to the rules; <note>The author uses a common biblical metaphor of the "crown" awarded to athletes who compete fairly, referring to 2 Timothy 2:5.</note> in the same way, not everyone receives life from the tree or the river of life existing or flowing in the middle of paradise—though it is shared with all—except for those who have prepared themselves to receive that life. <margin>Revelation, in the same place</margin> For this reason, the voice cries out at the end of the Book of Revelation: "Let him who is thirsty come; and let him who wishes take the water of life freely." <note>original: "Qui sitit, ueniat: & qui uult, accipiat aquã vitæ gratis." See Revelation 22:17.</note> He does not only seek our consent and our desire from us, but also our vigor, by which we might overcome through fighting, just as it is described at the beginning of that same revelation: "To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God." And while he lived in mortal flesh, he cried out in the temple: <margin>CHRIST.</margin> "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." <note>John 7:37.</note> It is certainly enough that he has procured life for us, and is ready to give it, and that he has borne the iniquities of us all; yet he seeks consent from us, so that we might be co-workers in our own business. Therefore, he who does not want to hear the one calling, nor yield to the one drawing him, nor receive the gift from the giver, is deservedly excluded from such a great benefit. As Paul and Barnabas frankly and constantly said to the Jews, just as we read <margin>Paul, Barnabas</margin> in the Acts of the Apostles: "It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first, but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles." <note>Acts 13:46.</note> And the Lord himself, in the Gospels recorded by Matthew and Luke, when he proposed the parable of the wedding, the lunch, <margin>Matthew, Luke</margin> or the supper, added that many judged themselves unworthy of such a great feast, namely by despising the messenger who called them, and therefore they were excluded. And wherever there is talk of acquiring the heavenly kingdom, or having Christ’s support and protection, our consent is required. Whence Augustine wisely and learnedly says in <margin>Augustine</margin> the volume titled *On Church Dogmas*: <note>Though attributed here to Augustine, this work is now generally attributed to Gennadius of Massilia.</note> "We have the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy; but that we yield to the saving inspiration is within our own power." For in every place, province, and region, God invites each of us by the voice of the prophets, the preaching of the Apostles, the published Gospel, the suggestion of Angels, and by internal inspiration. As Paul says when discussing with the Romans: <margin>Paul</margin> "There is no distinction between Jew and Greek: for the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone, whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? How shall they hear without a preacher? And indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." <note>Romans 10:12–18.</note> These are the words of the Apostles and preachers, the words of Angels speaking internally and providing guidance, and the words of Christ and the Holy Spirit speaking and inspiring from within. For Christ—our support—tries everything so that he may have our consent for receiving the grace and salvation which he intends to confer upon his chosen people. With an open voice, and consequently to <margin>CHRIST</margin> all, he says: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wing, and you were not willing." <note>Matthew 23:37.</note> For his word is to all, he who wants all men to be saved.

### How He was lifted up from the earth. Chapter 11.

<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
<margin>THE SAME</margin>
"It is necessary," (says God the Son himself) "that the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." <note>original: "Oportet... exaltari Filium hominis, ut omnis qui credit in illum non pereat/sed habeat vitam æternam." See John 3:14-15.</note> How great a mystery <term>sacramentum (mystery)</term> is here: that eternal life depends on the lifting up of the Son of Man, and that he says he is lifted up "from the earth," just like the serpent in the desert. I do not think this should be understood only as the lifting up of his body when it hung upon the wood above the ground, or the mountain upon which the cross was fixed and raised. Nor do I think it refers only to that exaltation by which he is forever exalted with the Father, sitting at his right hand. Rather, it refers to that lifting up which takes place in our sight, when the excellence of his divinity becomes clear to men; so that seeing him for who he is, they might venerate, exalt, and magnify him. This happened at his death when the Centurion <note>The Roman officer supervising the crucifixion who, according to the Gospels, recognized Jesus's divinity after seeing the earthquake and the darkness.</note> and those who were with him, seeing the air darkened against the order of nature, the earth trembling, the rocks splitting, and the dead rising, cried out saying: "Truly this was the Son of God." Or, it refers to that lifting up by which, through the cross itself, Christ as a man earned the right to be set above every creature, just as the Apostle speaks in plain language, saying: "Christ became for us obedient even unto death, even death on a cross; because of which God has exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father." <note>A translation of Philippians 2:8-11.</note> The Savior himself confirms this, saying: "It was necessary for Christ to suffer, and so enter into his glory." <note>Luke 24:26.</note> By these words he aptly demonstrates that, insofar as he is a man, he acquired glory and a kingdom through the work completed in his passion and the cross. But he is said to be "lifted up from the earth" because both the work he performed and the sublime and exalted kingdom he obtained were not earthly, but heavenly, sublime, and high. "My kingdom," he said, "is not of this world," <note>John 18:36.</note> but it is that which the Father prepared from the foundation of the world; the possession of this he obtained for us, and the rule of it for himself, upon the cross.

<margin>Numbers.</margin>
As for why the lifting up of Christ on the cross is compared to the lifting up of the serpent which Moses raised up at the Lord's command, the text in the Book of Numbers <note>Referencing Numbers 21:4-9.</note> is clear enough. There we read that when the people had sinned by complaining about the food brought down from heaven <note>The manna.</note>, God sent fiery serpents among the people. Struck and plagued by them, the people came to Moses as suppliants, asking that the serpents be taken away. Therefore, when Moses prayed for the people, the Lord said: "Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign: whoever is bitten and looks upon it shall live." And so it was done. In the same way, those struck by any kind of sin—with which the ancient serpent <note>A traditional reference to the Devil or Satan.</note> and his followers are accustomed to wound mortals—are healed if they look upon Christ hanging on the wood, where he obtained health and salvation for all, and if they beg for his help. But here a mystery lies hidden: why did God want a serpent to be lifted up, which is the image of the enemy of the human race? And why is Christ likened to it? For what does a serpent contribute to health? What is the agreement between the image of the Prince of Darkness and the Prince of Light? What symbol does Christ share with that unclean and diabolical reptile? There is no agreement or symbol here except in the "lifting up." Yet health is granted in a different, indeed entirely opposite, way: for those who look are healed...

But let us move on to other things.

# Whereby the virtues and divinities seemed to be spread into many forms. Chapter XIV.

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
<margin>Eusebius</margin>
**G**od, as we have proven, works in all the members of the world's body, providing for all things so that they might cooperate with Him, lest the parts of the world, if cut off, should fail without a uniting power, or resist one another so much that they could not stand. But the ancients, not perceiving this mystery of unity, believed in a multitude of divinities multiplied according to the plurality of things, as Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who often interpreted traditional myths as allegories for natural or spiritual forces.</note> gathers, and after him Eusebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century Christian historian who often cited pagan philosophers to show how they glimpsed—but ultimately missed—the full truth of monotheism.</note>, from those things which the ancient prophets sang in various places. We shall touch upon these briefly. Indeed, they called the power of the entire air Juno (because she "helps mortals" <note>An etymological play on the Latin 'iuvare' (to help) and 'Iuno'.</note>). But they called the lower, more feminine air "the inferior Juno," since nothing is softer. Furthermore, they called the power of this lower air, which is illuminated by the light of the moon, Latona—from the word for "hiding" <note>original: "a latendo."</note>—because she causes the souls of those for whom they were intended to hide and forget before they descended through the lunar sphere, so that they might appear to enter this lower air like blank slates.

They call the power of the Earth "Vesta," because she produces herbs and flowers, which are like the "garments" and ornaments of the Earth itself <note>Another etymological play: "Vesta" linked to "vestes" (clothing/garments).</note>. And because this power is fertile, they chose to represent her in the form of a woman. They considered Rhea (whom the Latins called Ops) to be the power of the stony and mountainous earth; Ceres, however, they called the power of the fertile plains. But the power of seeds they called Persephone. They called the power of all plants Dionysius, which is of a mixed nature because herbs are always combined with both sexes. This same power the Egyptians named Iris and Osiris. There is also (as Plato says in the *Cratylus*) a Dionysius <margin>Plato</margin> who is, as it were, "the giver of wine" <note>original: "didus inon."</note>, and consequently the giver of other fruits, ripening them by his fiery power—not indeed an elemental fire, but a solar one. For the elemental power of fire they named Vulcan. But the power of devouring fire they called Vesta, and they said she was barren. Whence the Poet <note>Ovid, in his work *Fasti*.</note> says:

> Think of Vesta as nothing other than a living flame;
> And you see no bodies born from flame.
> Rightly, therefore, is she a virgin, who leaves no seeds behind.
> <note>original: "Nec tu aliud Vestam/q̄ uiuam intellige flammam: / Nataq; de flamma corpora nulla uides. / Iure igitur uirgo/ quæ semina nulla reliquit."</note>

But as Plato perceives, they called Vesta (whom they also call Vestia) the <term>ουσιᾶν</term> <note>ousian</note>—that is, the "essence" of things—because all things are "clothed" by it. And she is sterile because essence itself does not generate, nor is it generated; rather, the individual generates and is generated, not by reason of its essence, but by reason of the generative power existing in the generator, to which a passive potentiality in the offspring corresponds. 

But let us continue. In the Sun, therefore, this fiery power is called Apollo, from the motion of his rays, or from a fourfold etymology (as Plato prefers) according to the fourfold power <margin>The same (Plato)</margin> dedicated to him: music, medicine, prophecy, and skill in archery. Hence Apollo is said to be from *homopolon*, that is, "turning all things together," and leading them to a proper temperament by a certain harmony; or from *apolyon*, which means "washing away" and "purifying," and consequently "healing," which is the task of the physician; or from *aplon* <note>Meaning "simple" or "unified."</note>...

It argues that these myths were fragmented attempts to understand a divine unity that "clothes" and sustains all of creation.</summary>

This is not because the moon alone does these things, but because she immediately pours out the influences which she receives from the higher heavens, like a womb <note>original: "matrix"</note>, to be poured forth. They attributed the power of **Saturn** to **Time**, since it is cold and slow, painting him as an old man because all things grow old with time. They placed the fiery **Mars** over war, because of the impulse he provides in the bile. **Venus** with her **Cupid** they assigned to generation and love. The power of speech and interpretation they named **Mercury**.

It would be a long task to bring all these forward, nor do I think it entirely necessary or very fitting, as they are applied somewhat harshly. For **Plato** wished to imitate the etymology of the first language, in which the first-formed man <note>Adam, the "protoplast."</note> gave the most appropriate names to things. But the correspondence of names with things in the **Hebrew** language differs from that in the **Greek** and **Latin** tongues just as much as the **Hebrew** language itself is more sacred and divine than those that follow it—though they follow at a great distance, and Latin at a greater distance than Greek, because the latter was derived immediately from Hebrew, while Latin was derived from Greek. But let us continue. They called the symbol of the **Universe** **Pan**, which means "the whole" <note>In Greek, *Pan* means "All" or "Everything."</note>. ->CANTICI SECUNDI<-

## OF THE SECOND SONG

They believed in diverse deities and pleaded with them through various prayers, many kinds of sacrifices, and incense. For they demanded Wisdom from **Minerva**, whom they believed to be the favoring deity of wisdom, born from the brain of **Jupiter**. They asked to conquer in war from the deity **Victory**, whom they believed to be the offspring of **Acheron** and the **Styx**, that is, from affliction and sadness. For *Acheron* means "without joy" or "without gladness," and *Styx* signifies "sadness." This is for the reason <term>p</term> <note>abbreviation for 'quod,' meaning 'because' or 'that'</note> that those who desire to conquer must necessarily abstain from many things and exert the greatest force upon themselves, from which sadness arises. But in punishing the wicked, they implored the power of victorious **Justice**, whom they call **Nemesis**. They believed that obtaining a kingdom came from **Jupiter**, the lord of all; and a happy marriage bond from **Hymenaeus**. Moreover, they sought prosperous navigation from the winds, the sons of **Astraeus** the Titan and **Aurora** <note>the Dawn</note>, as if they were born from the heat of the sun thinning the air, especially at dawn when the sun begins to spread its rays over the earth.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Which **Aristotle** follows when he says in his *Meteorology* that winds are produced by the heat of the sun. They are nevertheless said to hold their command from **Juno**, because they blow only in the air (which is called Juno). But regarding where the winds come from, although the wanderings of poets and philosophers are long, the truth remains one:

<margin>David</margin>
concerning which the Prophet <note>King David in the Psalms</note> says: *He who brings forth the winds from his treasuries.* But let us proceed. They believed they obtained grace from **Venus**, who is so named as if "beautifying all things" or "coming to all things,"

<margin>Cicero</margin>
as it pleases **Cicero**. And if they hoped to receive any other benefit from the earth, sea, sky, plants, trees, heavens, and such things, they invoked those deities who they believed presided over them. However, the common people, whose concern is always to lean toward the many, were not content with these deities and divided them into even more: for they believed in five **Suns** based on various effects; four **Vulcans**; five **Mercuries**; four **Apollos**; three **Aesculapiuses**; three **Dianas**; five **Dionysiuses**; five **Minervas**; four **Venuses**; and three **Cupids**. And wandering through many such things—even through ruinous things sent by evil angels—they not only gave them the names of gods but also established sacred rites for them. For they publicly dedicated a temple to **Fever** on the Palatine Hill in Rome;

<margin>Pliny</margin>
and an altar to **Bad Fortune** on the Esquiline Hill, as **Pliny** reports. And they reached such a point of madness that they even wished to assign deities to thefts and crimes. Creating images of all these, they instituted sacred rites for them, having despised the one God from whom all things come. From this, everyone took up the cause of idolatry, fashioning for themselves

<margin>The same</margin>
(to jest with **Pliny**) **Junos**, **Jupiters**, **Genii**, **Lares**, **Penates** <note>various types of Roman household and guardian spirits</note>, and whatever gods they wished. Led to the extreme of madness and darkness by the Prince of Darkness, they were not even ashamed to find gods to worship in the underworld, venerating the most miserable and lowest of all under three names: him whom they called **Dis** and **Pluto** from the word for "enriching." ### Christ, liberating the human race from this calamity, cast down that three-headed beast.

->Chapter XIV.<-

<margin>Revelation</margin>
**P**itying therefore such great error, wickedness, and unhappiness, the Eternal Father sent down his son Jesus Christ, who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the son of his love <note>original: "filii dilectionis suæ"; a reference to Colossians 1:13</note>. He, therefore, having taken up the battle against the prompter of all evil, utterly defeated him; and having stripped away his power, he bound him in Tartarean <term>Tartarean: related to Tartarus, the deepest abyss of suffering in classical mythology, here used for Hell</term> prisons, having (as is said in the Book of Revelation) the keys of the abyss and of hell. And by his command, an Angel descending from heaven bound with a great chain (as is said in the same place) the great serpent, who is the devil: whom He, exalted on the cross, had already defeated, just as he had promised, saying: *Now the prince of this world shall be cast out.*

<margin>CHRIST. Paul</margin>
For which cause Paul, exulting with the Corinthians, says: *Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?* Indeed, "death" is the angel of death himself and the prince of darkness, as all who think rightly explain. The sting and arrow of death is sin: with which the angel of death himself strikes and kills us, like a poisoned arrow. But the power of sin and its strength is the law, the transgression of which is sin; if there were no law, sin would not be imputed. But thanks be to God the Father, who gave us victory through Jesus Christ our Lord. Yet we do not attain this victory unless we cooperate with the Victor, as is required by our status on the way and in the struggle <note>original: "status uiæ, & pugnæ"; refers to the concept of the 'wayfarer' (viator) who must still fight spiritual battles during earthly life</note>.

But at last (by God’s command), death itself and the angel of death shall be utterly destroyed, every power of doing harm having been taken from him, as the Apostle had said a little earlier: *He must reign until he puts his enemies under his feet; and the last enemy to be destroyed is death.* As he says more clearly when disputing with the Hebrews:

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
*That through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil; and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to servitude.* And so that he might destroy the desire for possession <note>greed</note>, he taught by word and deed to detest riches, protesting that we cannot serve God and Mammon <note>original: "Mammonæ"; a term for personified wealth or greed</note>. And so that he might suppress the ambition for ruling, he taught us to be mild and humble of heart: and when invited to a kingdom, he refused and fled. And so that he might remove from us all desires of the flesh, he commanded us to gird our loins, and exhorted us to be chaste <note>original: "castrari"; literally 'made eunuchs,' referring to Matthew 19:12</note> for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

<margin>Matthew 4, Luke 4</margin>
Nor was he content to have instructed mortals by word alone; he wished to teach by deed also, so that as a true leader he might go before us into battle, saying: *Follow me.* For being led by the Spirit into the desert, he endured those three battles: in which, always striking the enemy with the sword of the spirit—which is the word of God—he brought back a glorious triumph. For what is understood by the "bread," the primary nourishment of the animal man <note>original: "animalis hominis"; the natural or unspiritual person</note>, if not concupiscence and the allurements of the flesh, and everything that pertains to it? And what is denoted by the suggestion of acquiring glory in the casting down from the pinnacle of the temple, if not ambition and the haughtiness of pride? ### How he called to himself all other deities. Chapter XV.

Indeed, so that he might remove idolatry and the worship of many deities from mortals, he called to himself (at the command of the Father) the whole divine power which had been scattered among many. Truly, making this mystery known to those who understand, he said:
<margin>CHRIST. Paul</margin>
*All things have been handed over to me by my Father,* <note>original: "Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo"; a reference to Matthew 11:27</note> that is, the strengths of all, the virtues of all, the divine powers of all; just as Paul admonishes us with a clear voice, saying: *Stripping the principalities and powers, triumphing over them openly in himself, he confidently transferred all the power of the others to himself.* <note>original: "Expolians principatus, & potestates..." paraphrasing Colossians 2:15</note> And again: *He did away with every principality, and power, and virtue,* so that we should no longer seek what is necessary and opportune from others, but from him, to whom the Father gave all things. Hence he taught everyone that for the rest of time they should ask the Father in his name: *Whatever* (he said) *you ask the Father in my name, he will give to you.* And this is the "principality" or government which (according to the testimony of Isaiah's oracle) *was placed upon his shoulders*:

<margin>Paul</margin>

Even the princes of the world, seeing these things with their own eyes and unable to deny them, attributed the works and miracles of those men to magic arts—men who were actually striving with all their might to destroy magic, necromancy, divination, deception, and whatever else the Gentiles were laboring at through the art of demons. Nor should the truth of the Scripture be doubted, since so many witnesses agree in diverse parts of the world, making it impossible for their assembly to be false—especially since even their adversaries confess that such deeds were done by them.

Truly, why do we need witnesses? We already see for ourselves the temples of the gods destroyed and the oracles extinguished. These began to yield immediately upon the death, or rather the triumph, of Christ, as even the enemies of the Crucified One have voluntarily confessed, and as we read most extensively in our own books. Indeed, when Bartholomew entered Albana <note>Modern-day Baku or Derbent; a major city in ancient Great Armenia where tradition says the Apostle Bartholomew was martyred.</note>, a city of Greater Armenia, and entered the temple where 
<margin>Bartholomew</margin>
Astaroth <note>Astaroth was a major deity in the Ancient Near East, here described as a demon inhabiting a temple statue.</note> was worshipped, the demons were no longer able to give responses. The inhabitants, wondering at this, traveled to a neighboring city to which the Apostle had not yet journeyed, and inquired of the idol existing there why they could not have responses in Albana. The evil demon, compelled by the power of Christ, confessed the truth: that the God of the Albanians—or rather the evil demon—had been bound in chains because of Bartholomew’s entry into the city and the temple, so that he was no longer able to speak. The evil demons also confessed to Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian of Antioch, a legendary figure said to have been a powerful sorcerer and necromancer before converting to Christianity.</note>, who was then a magician or necromancer, that Christ had prevailed against them. <margin>Isaiah</margin>

For the Sun, in its original design, was filled with that light which is most sufficient for illuminating all parts of the world; yet it does not shine upon all parts at once. The **Sun of Justice**, Christ, has also risen with perfect light, by which He could illuminate every person. But there is a darkness that cannot comprehend it, either never or only for a time. ...and famous hymns dictated: Or let it be speech pure and clear, not according to a specific dialect, but proceeding from a pure and singular heart in all people out of a binding charity. And then men shall be led back from the multiplicity of rites and ceremonies, in which they are often confused, to a single worship; which then shall be clearly explained according to the pleasure of God, all discord and disagreement ceasing. Whether these discords proceed from minds naturally distrustful, or from bodies composed of contrary qualities, or from many-natured forms, or are fostered by varied worship, multiple influences, and diverse nourishments—to discern this would indeed require a most profound investigation. Indeed, contrary qualities are present in man, mixed in the most diverse ways; from which arise diverse temperaments <term>complexions; the physical and psychological makeup of a person based on the balance of bodily fluids</term>. Various influences also intervene, disposing our bodies in most diverse ways. There are also diverse regions, varied foods, and manifold social interactions, from all of which (as Ptolemy <margin>Ptolemy</margin> holds) man is led to diverse effects.

Nor does it proceed any less from minds, which, even if they proceed from the same source, yet passing through diverse media (as the Pythagoreans <margin>Pythagoreans, Academics</margin> and Academics assert) take on diverse natures and inclinations, from which dissension arises. But since that which is supremely One, from which all multiplicity emanates, intends to lead all multiplicity back into itself as one by a due course, it is necessary that by gathering the multiplicity it should prune and remove all things that distract from unity. Hence (which is wonderful to say) He will also at last remove the Intelligences <note>original: "intelligentias"; here referring to the angelic beings believed to govern the nations and the movements of the celestial spheres.</note> from those whom they protect. ## That he will finally draw all who are to be drawn.
### Chapter XIX.

<margin>Paul</margin>
**A**ll impediments having been removed, and his protection gathered, he will at last lead all who are to be drawn to himself without any resistance or error, according to what he says: I give eternal life to my sheep, and no one shall snatch them out of my hands. And again: All those whom you gave to me, I have not lost any of them. And once more: All those whom you gave to me, I have guarded, and none of them has perished, except the son of perdition <note>original: "filius perditionis"; referring to Judas Iscariot</note>, so that the scripture might be fulfilled, which had predicted many things concerning the traitor. For just as God has chosen, so he has devised a way and a path by which he might lead them to himself, just as Paul teaches us when discussing with the Romans: Those whom he foreknew and predestined <term>predestined; the theological concept that God has ordained an individual's destiny from the beginning</term> to become conformed to the image of his Son, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified <term>justified; to be declared righteous or made right in the eyes of God</term>; and those whom he justified, those he also glorified. What then shall we say? If God is for us—namely, drawing and leading us—who is against us, distracting and leading us astray? He says this as if to say "no one." And concerning this most powerful drawing, Paul continues, saying: Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword? For in all these things we overcome because of him who loved us, and who draws and holds us. Therefore that wise man prayed, saying: Draw me after you, and we shall run <note>original: "Trahe me post te curremus"; a quote from the Song of Songs 1:4</note>. Indeed, the Eternal Father drew and draws with divine cords, but God-made-man draws with the cords of men, just as he predicted through Hosea: In the bonds of men I will draw them, in the bonds of charity <note>or "love"</note>; or in the servitude of love, as the truth of the letter <note>the literal text of the scripture</note> has it. By these bonds of man, extended by him who was found in appearance as a man, he drew a much greater multitude because they are perceptible to the senses, familiar, and the greatest pledges of love; he drew them in far greater numbers than those he had ensnared with those invisible bonds, not perceived by the senses, upon which the dense crowd of common people relies. But here arises a significant dispute among many wise men: which crowd is greater, those who are drawn, or those who are cast away by Christ? Wishing to determine this, Simeon said: Behold, this child is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many in Israel <note>Luke 2:34</note>, not weighing one multitude more than the other. Some are also moved by that word which this "Drawer" <note>Christ, who draws souls</note> had spoken: Many are called, but few are chosen, thinking that only a few chosen ones out of many called are saved. But what shall we say to Paul, who speaks not against Christ but for Christ, saying: Those whom he called, these he also justified. Therefore, all who are called are in the number of the chosen...

...are considered to come. Nor indeed is it foreign to the truth: For those few elect are not set apart from the called as if from the rejected, but are selected as if marked out from that great multitude which no one could count <note>A reference to Revelation 7:9</note>, so that by that order and the number twelve <note>The number twelve often signifies the tribes of Israel or the Apostles, representing a "fullness" or sacred order</note>—which is full of sacred mystery—they might be preferred over others. In that supper also, to which many were called, we read that only one was expelled and cast out, while the others remained in those nuptials of eternal happiness. From this we are taught that of those called, not a few, but almost all are saved. 

Nor can that word <margin>CHRIST. Jerome.</margin> of Christ, where he says: *Many are called, but few are chosen* <note>original: "Multi sunt uocati, pauci uero electi"; Matthew 22:14</note>, be understood only in reference to that one expelled person, but rather to those many who were invited. Although Jerome says that by that one person we should understand all who are united together in wickedness, along with the Jews <margin>The same</margin> who were called through the Law, and of whom only a few were made participants in the wedding. Nevertheless, so that the seats would not remain empty, messengers were sent to the crossroads <note>original: "exitus uiarum"</note>, that is, to the Gentile peoples who were outside the way of the Law, so that they might bring in <margin>Isaiah</margin> to the wedding whomever they found, just as Jerome well interprets. 

Thus, therefore, few of those called through the Law become elect until the time is given for the remnant of Israel to be converted, as we are taught by the oracle of Isaiah saying: *In truth the remnant shall be converted, the remnant, I say, of Jacob to the mighty God. For if your people Israel were as the sand of the sea, only a remnant shall be converted from it* <note>Isaiah 10:21–22</note>. This is what Paul also brings forward when discussing with the Romans. But from the greatest multitude of the Gentiles, all are called, and all who are found wherever they are, are brought in. Therefore, there are few chosen from the many Jews called, to whom Christ’s speech was directed; or there are a few chosen so that they may be preferred over others. For the crowd of those saved is a great multitude from all languages, peoples, and nations. Their names, even if obscure to the common people, are nevertheless known and most manifest to God, recorded in the book of life, which is always open <margin>CHRIST.</margin> to God. 

Moreover, those who diminish the number of the saved in favor of the things they had said, bring forward another word of the Savior, who said: *Narrow is the gate, and cramped is the way that leads to life, and there are few who find it* <note>Matthew 7:14</note>. From this, it seems manifest enough that few enter or are drawn to life, compared to the many who walk the path of death and damnation. 

But let them attend, I pray, only to the manner of speaking of the highest Truth, who says: *And there are few who find it.* <margin>Baruch</margin> For if we say that no one finds it, we shall not depart from the truth, as Baruch proclaims: *There is none that can know her way, nor that can search out her paths* <note>Baruch 3:23</note>. And if we cannot search it out, much less can we find it, unless he shows us and leads us—he who knows all things; who knew her and gave her to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. Afterward appearing on earth, he taught it with his own mouth; indeed, <margin>CHRIST.</margin> he made himself the way and the door <note>original: "hostium" (likely a variant for "ostium", meaning door)</note>, saying: *I am the way; I am the door; through me alone is entrance given to life.* 

He alone, therefore, found the way and the door, without whom we can do or think nothing. Yet many followed him as he taught, led, and passed through—a great multitude that no one can count. Nor do I think that he, who wishes all men to be saved, was of such small power that for the salvation of a few...

# THE SECOND TONE.

...being content, he should cease from the care of others. Nor was the virtue of the leader <note>The "leader" here refers to Christ as the head of the faithful.</note> so meager that it would seem extinguished by the attraction of only a few, for <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says to the Romans: *If by the transgression of one man many died, much more has the grace of God and the gift in the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, abounded unto many.* And again: *If by the transgression of one man death reigned through that one, much more will those receiving the abundance of grace, and of the gift, and of justice, reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.* Therefore, just as through the transgression of one it resulted in condemnation for all men, so also through the justice of one it results in the justification of life for all men. And just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one many shall be made just. <note>This entire section paraphrases Romans 5:15–19, contrasting the "fall" of Adam with the "grace" of Christ.</note> If, therefore, they are "many," how can they be "few"? Paul—in whose breast Christ resounds—is not against Christ, but with Christ, who says: <margin>CHRIST.</margin> *I came to save and to seek those who had perished.* <note>Luke 19:10</note> And who said again: *Of all those whom the Father gave to me, I have not lost any of them.* <note>John 17:12</note> Therefore, he saves all who were given by the Father.

But it must not be thought that the most generous giver of all good things gave only a few out of a vast multitude to his Son, to whom he gave all things. Nor does it suit the goodness and mercy of God that he should allow more to perish than he saves, since he is able and willing to save all, except those who refuse salvation. Indeed, a time will be given (God willing) when the remnants, when the dispersed shall be gathered, when all shall serve <margin>Zechariah.</margin> God with one shoulder <note>original: "humero uno"; a biblical idiom meaning to serve with one accord or in total unity (Zephaniah 3:9).</note>, and when (as Zechariah says) *the Lord shall be one in all, and his name one.* <note>Zechariah 14:9</note> This will be (as he said above) on a day known to the Lord, in which the waters that are above the heavens shall go out—namely from the heavenly Jerusalem—and half of them shall go toward the eastern sea: toward that East, indeed, of which Isaiah says: <margin>Isaiah David</margin> *You call the just man from the East.* <note>Isaiah 41:2</note> And of which the Psalmist says: *He ascends above the heavens of heavens to the East.* <note>Psalm 68:33</note> 

But the other half shall go to the sea—not indeed that Syrian sea which makes the shores of Palestine, as some interpret—but to Christ, who in the latest times was filled with that divine and super-celestial water, so that, having become a sea in his own fullness, he might irrigate everyone. He offers this water with such a willing spirit that he cries out publicly in the temple and says: <margin>CHRIST.</margin> *If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.* <note>John 7:37</note> And these waters (as the Prophet continues) shall never fail, but shall always be refreshing souls in winter and summer. And then the Lord shall be King over all the earth—not indeed having acquired a new kingdom at that time, because he has already been made King of kings and Lord of lords—but because all those whom he allowed for a time to wander by their own will shall then have him as Lord. Or the Lord shall be Lord of all because the dominions and princedoms of others shall cease, as we said a little while ago. This shall take its effect either at the second coming of Christ, <margin>Jerome.</margin> as Jerome feels, or when He has decreed it, to whom alone this day is known. Since it is not for us to know the times or the moments, which <margin>CHRIST.</margin> (as Christ openly reported when calling back his disciples from such an inquiry) the Father has placed in his own power. <note>Acts 1:7</note>

<page-num>220</page-num>
->THIRD TONE.<-
E iv

# WHAT A PRIEST IS, AND HIS OFFICE. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Leviticus</margin>
**W**e enter into a very wide field, one that rises above our eyes by its sheer magnitude, when we wish to treat the subject of the priest. He is one who holds the middle ground between God and man, and is, as it were, a visible god. This is especially true of the supreme and true priest, Christ, whose priesthood we intend to explain according to our ability. A priest <note>Latin: *Sacerdos*</note> is so named as if "giving holy things" <note>The author uses a popular medieval etymology: *sacer-dos* from *sacra dans* (giving sacred things).</note>. For he administers to the people those things that come from the celestial sanctuary. From this, let wise men judge how pure, how clean, and how divine he ought to be. For even if he must administer all holy things to us, we will presently run through seven duties that are most necessary to him. First, therefore, he must pray for the people as a mediator, just as in Leviticus, when dealing with the unfaithful and the perjurer, it is twice repeated: *And the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him*; or, *he shall be propitiated for him*, or *he shall pray over him for remission*, as the truth of the letter sounds, which is held thus: <term>וְכִפֶּר עָלָיו הַכֹּהֵן</term> <note>Hebrew: *ve-kipper alav ha-kohen*</note> "And the priest shall make atonement for him." So too, where it treats the purification of a woman after childbirth, it is said: *And the priest shall pray for her, and she shall be cleansed.* And in whatever expiation or propitiation the law commands, it is required that the priest intervene as a middleman and as one who obtains favor and remission.

<margin>James, Paul</margin>
So also James says: *Is any among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him.* In the second place, he ought to offer sacred things, as Paul reminds us when discussing with the Hebrews, saying: *Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices*; and a little before: *Priests have need to offer sacrifices first for their own sins, and then for the sins of the people.* Regarding this, we are most fully taught in the Law. In the third place, he is appointed as a teacher of the people—not indeed of vain and curious doctrine, but of the Law and of those things which are of God, as

<margin>Haggai, Malachi</margin>
it is said in Haggai: *Ask the priest the law.* And through Malachi: *The lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the Angel of hosts* <note>The Latin *Angelus* here means "messenger."</note>, that is, the leader of the Lord's army. Whence, consequently, in the fourth place, he is appointed as the leader of the divine army, so that he may direct and strengthen the weaker

<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
people, and be the first to withstand the onslaught of the enemies. We are taught this in plain speech in Deuteronomy: *If you go out to war* (it says) *against your enemies, and you see cavalry and chariots, and a multitude of the adversary's army greater than you have, you shall not fear them, because the Lord your God is with you in your midst.* and this occurs with the priest intervening. Whence it follows: *The priest shall approach the people and say to you: Let not your heart be afraid; do not yield, do not fear them, because the Lord your God goes with you, and he will fight for you against your adversaries, and he will save you.*

<summary>This page defines the nature and office of a priest as a mediator between God and humanity, specifically detailing the first four of seven primary duties: prayer, sacrifice, teaching, and spiritual leadership.</summary>

<page-num>230</page-num>
<header>OF THE SECOND SONG.</header>

# OF THE SECOND SONG.

Which was also done in the case of Phinehas, that most zealous priest, who at God's command was appointed leader of an army of twelve thousand chosen men from every tribe of Israel against a great multitude of Midianites, over whom they reported a glorious triumph. Every priest ought to do the same against all visible enemies or the powers of the air <note>A reference to demons, often called "powers of the air" in Pauline theology (Ephesians 2:2).</note> whenever danger threatens the people and divine worship. They ought to fight with zeal, prayer, and the sword of the Spirit—which is the word of God—rather than with physical arms. This is how Samuel, Elisha, Moses, and Aaron acted under the Old Law. For while the people fought against Amalek, Moses prayed for the people with uplifted hands; Aaron and Hur, who prayed with him, supported his wavering hands. And as prayer prevailed, the people of God prevailed against their enemies. 

<margin>Paul</margin>
Concerning these and others fighting in such a way, Paul says: *They were made strong in war, they turned back the camps of foreigners, they put to flight the edge of the sword.* <note>Original: "Fortes facti sūt in bello, castra uerterunt exterorū, effugauerunt aciē gladii" (Hebrews 11:34).</note> And after the time of Christ, Martin—not yet appointed as a priest, but a future one—offered himself securely under the banner of Christ himself to charge the enemy ranks. Leo the First, the Supreme Pontiff, taking pity on the people invaded by Attila, King of the Huns, approached him fearlessly, comforted by the Spirit of God. As he prayed in the king’s presence, he so softened the savage mind of the barbarian that he promised to leave Italy and return to his own lands. When his entire army wondered and asked why he did so, he replied (as the story goes): "I did not do it because I was won over by the priest's prayer, but two men standing by him, holding drawn swords, terrified me and threatened death to me and my army." These are believed to have been Peter and Paul. Or perhaps they were Angels, just as they stood by Elisha when he was surrounded in Dothan by Assyrian soldiers intended to capture him. To his terrified servant, who cried out, "Alas, alas, alas, my lord, what shall we do?" he said: "Do not fear, for there are more with us than against us." And as the man of God prayed that the servant's eyes might be opened, he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire all around. Furthermore, as the prophet prayed that the Lord would strike them with blindness, they were blinded, so that they were led by Elisha into Samaria—the very land of their enemies. Most recently, the famous Capistranus <note>John of Capistrano (1386–1456), a friar and preacher who led a crusade against the Ottoman Empire at the Siege of Belgrade.</note>, rushing against the enemies on behalf of the Pannonians <note>The people of the Kingdom of Hungary.</note> with the banner of the cross, turned them to such a great flight that an eternal terror of him remained among those who had seen and heard of the event.

In the fifth place, a priest ought to lead the people to the end destined for them, just as we read figuratively in the book of Joshua. 

<margin>Joshua</margin>
Namely, while the Israelites were crossing the Jordan to proceed to the Promised Land, the priests went before the people, dividing the Jordan. One part of the waters surged backward, while the other part fled in a rapid flow into the Salt Sea. In the same way, the true priest, under the high priest **JESUS** <note>In Latin, the names Joshua and Jesus are identical (*Iesus*). The author is making a typological connection between the biblical Joshua and Christ.</note>, wishing to introduce the people into the true land of promise, goes before them through the Jordan—that is, the water in which (as the Apostle says) 

<margin>Paul</margin>
we have all been baptized—making a division of the waters in the administration of baptism. For one part remains firm and constant in its sweetness, namely in those who fulfill in deed what they promised in baptism; but the other part, which is in bitterness...
