<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD TONE</header>

...is turned; it belongs to those (let us speak with sorrow) who, defiled by the enticements of the flesh and the vices of the world, turn the sweetest gift of grace into bitter damnation.

<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
Sixthly, it is the duty of priests to judge: as it says in Deuteronomy: "If you perceive a judgment to be difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and non-leprosy, and you see that judgment within your gates is varied, arise—as if for the final remedy—and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose. And you shall come to the priests of the Levitical race, and you shall ask of them: who shall judge for you the truth of judgment. From there, you shall do whatever they shall say: And they shall teach you according to the law of the Lord, and you shall follow their sentence, and you shall not decline to the right nor to the left." <note>A paraphrase of Deuteronomy 17:8-11. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, this passage was frequently used to justify the legal authority of the Church hierarchy.</note> But in those days, none were admitted to the priesthood except those most skilled in the law and in all judgments. But alas, these unhappy times! In which, many times, the dregs of ignorance and the sewers of filth are chosen for the priesthood; men who have neither the cloven hoof <note>In medieval allegory, the "cloven hoof" of clean animals (Leviticus 11) symbolized the ability to discern between good and evil, or between the literal and spiritual senses of Scripture.</note>, nor ever eat butter and honey <note>A reference to Isaiah 7:15, "Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good."</note> so that they might know how to refuse evil and choose good, nor ruminating on even a tiny bit [iota] of the law, nor meditating on its true sense.

<margin>Exodus</margin>
In Exodus also, God holds priests and true judges in such high regard that he calls them "Gods," saying that those who harm their neighbor must be brought to the Gods—that is, the judges—who were chosen primarily from the priests, as we have already proven from the testimony of Deuteronomy. <note>original: "Deos" (Exodus 22:8). In older translations, the Hebrew word 'Elohim' was sometimes rendered as 'judges' or 'gods'.</note> In the final place, a priest, like a good shepherd, ought to have care for his sheep, to minister the sacraments, to watch over the flock, and to lay out everything for the salvation of the people committed to him—even his life, if there were need: because the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. These are the things which most especially pertain to the office of a priest.

### That Christ was a true priest, and filled with everything that pertains to a true priest and supreme pontiff. Chapter II.

**C** <note>The letter C is printed as a large decorative woodcut initial.</note> hrist JESUS, anointed as king, prophet, and priest above all his companions, was deservedly King of kings, Prophet of prophets, Priest of priests, or Pontiff of pontiffs. But leaving the first two roles to be explained in their proper place, let us see how well he performed the office of priest. First, for he prayed for the people, not only once but many times, and throughout the entire time of his life—now on the mountain, now in a cave, now publicly, now secretly—as is recounted by the evangelists in many places.

<margin>Paul</margin>

Concerning this offering, after Paul had discussed many things with the Hebrews, he finally added: <margin>The Same</margin> "But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God." <note>A reference to Hebrews 10:12.</note> Through the power of this sacrifice, offered once and for all, it is granted that we may offer a daily and perpetual sacrifice. <margin>Peter</margin> And Peter indicates what He achieved by this offering of His, saying: "Christ died once for our sins, offering Himself—the just for the unjust—to the eternal Father, so that He might offer us to God, mortified indeed in the flesh, but brought to life in the spirit." <note>A paraphrase of 1 Peter 3:18.</note> Furthermore, He showed Himself to be a Teacher <term>Doctor: This title implies more than a modern teacher; it signifies a master of doctrine and theology.</term>, teaching that doctrine which was hidden from the wise of this world, which He had received from the Father of lights. <margin>CHRIST</margin> "My doctrine," He says, "is not mine, but the Father's who sent me." Behold, I have given him as a witness to the people, a leader and a teacher to the nations." Through "David," everyone interprets Christ to be signified and denoted in many places as the son of Jesse, and rightly so: for the historical David did not rule, nor was he a leader or teacher among the Gentiles, but only among the Israelite people. Finally, the true Priest of priests, the Pontiff <note>High Priest</note> of pontiffs, and Prince of the princes of priests, had such a care for souls that, as the good and best Shepherd, He gave His life for His sheep...

### To Christ as the True Priest, All Priestly Honors are Owed. Chapter III.

<margin>Numbers</margin>
**S**o the Priest (by the command of the Law) was given the firstfruits <term>Primitiæ: The first and best portion of a harvest or livestock, dedicated to God in the Temple.</term> along with everything offered in the sanctuary. Likewise, all sacrificial victims were his, and the people were commanded to honor and revere him. Regarding the first of these, it is said to Aaron in the book of Numbers:
> All the firstfruits which the children of Israel offer belong to the priest; and whatever is brought into the sanctuary by anyone and delivered into the hands of the priest is his own.

<margin>In the same place</margin>
But later, in the eighteenth chapter, the Lord says:
> Behold, I have given you the custody of my firstfruits.

<margin>Origen</margin>
It is as if He were saying: "I have handed over my firstfruits to be guarded," as Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian who often sought the "spiritual" or allegorical meaning behind the literal text of the Bible.</note> rightly perceives. This can hardly be applied to the literal letter of the law, because these items were consumed as food and, having been digested <margin>Gospel</margin> (as it says in the Gospel), they passed into the sewer. Therefore, we must necessarily refer this to the law of the spirit, according to which firstfruits can be preserved forever. These are certainly the ones of which the Apostle says to the Romans:
<margin>Paul</margin>
> But we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit.

This can be understood in two ways: either the firstfruits that the Holy Spirit gave to the Apostles in the primitive Church—namely, manifold gifts and <term>charismata: Spiritual gifts or extraordinary powers granted by the Holy Spirit, such as healing or prophecy.</term>—or, by these "firstfruits," we understand the good beginnings of our works or our holy inspirations. We ought to preserve these and offer them to Christ, the Great High Priest, so that they may be kept by His grace and increased by His merits, so that He may present them as most pleasing to the Father. These offerings are said to be made only by the "sanctified of Israel"—that is, by those who, having become princes of God, begin to fight against the enemy whom our own Jesus, the High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex Maximus"</note>, also fought. They are offered by those who have been initiated and consecrated to God through baptism and the other sacraments. Furthermore, the firstfruits of the fruits of our works are the beginnings of love and charity <note>original: "dilectionis, & charitatis"</note> by which we embrace God and our neighbor. 

<margin>The same</margin>
Indeed, among the fruits of the spirit, charity is placed first by Paul. Our Great High Priest seeks this charity above all other things, as the true firstfruits and tithes. He concludes everything within it, as if it were the primary foundation and the goal that beautifies all other commandments, the entire Law, and the Prophets. He commands with a specific precept that it be observed with all diligence, saying:
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> This I command you: that you love one another.

And again:
> By this shall men know that you are my disciples, and the sheep entrusted to me as the Good High Priest, if you have love for one another.

<margin>Paul</margin>
But so that all works may be done in charity and be pleasing to God, their beginnings must be consecrated to Christ, just as Paul teaches us in the letter to the Colossians:
> Whatever you do (he says), do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

We ought, therefore, to present the firstfruits and all things brought into the sanctuary to this Supreme Pontiff, so that He Himself may sprinkle them...

...with his own blood, and seasoned with his own merits, he might present them as a pleasing gift to the eternal Father in an everlasting presentation. And this is what is said: *These things were for the priestly office, by an everlasting statute.* But since such things have ceased in the priesthood of the Law, so that the scripture might not be broken, it is necessary that they be fulfilled in our true priest, Christ, in whom and in his successors—namely, the presbyters or priests—all the priesthood of the Law has been transferred. There is also owed to this High Priest <term>Antistiti: A Latin term for a high-ranking priest or overseer who stands before others.</term> not only the firstfruits, which the Hebrews call *terumah* <note>original: "תרומה terumah"</note>, but the *terumah* of the *terumah*—that is, the firstfruits of the firstfruits. These were chosen in this way: out of one hundred, the people offered ten to the priests.

<margin>Numbers</margin>
But the priests offered one out of ten to God, as we read in the book of Numbers. Therefore, to the most simple God was given one; to the people, as the material portion, one hundred; but to the priest, who holds the middle place between God and the people, ten. Ten is the end of the [single] numbers and the beginning of the tens, and it is the middle point between one and one hundred. To our Christ, however, the High Priest, both one and ten are owed: ten as to a human priest, and one as to God. For he is the mediator and the end that brings rest and refreshment. Furthermore, to our Priest are owed not only the firstfruits of virtues, but of men. These were the first Innocents killed for his sake, of whom John says: *These were purchased from among all, the firstfruits to God and the Lamb.* <note>Referencing the "Holy Innocents" killed by Herod and the imagery in the Book of Revelation 14:4.</note> Nor does he reject others because of this, provided they are willing to offer him firstfruits and tithes—that is, the beginnings and the completions of their works. Thus he says: *He who perseveres until the end, he shall be saved.* For perseverance is the offering of true tithes. He also seeks the firstfruits of days. In the ancient Law, God was content that the last and seventh day of the week be sanctified. To Christ, however, together with God the Father, we give the first day, which is called the "Lord's Day" <note>original: "dies dominica"</note> because it is consecrated to the Lord. On this day he gave the beginning to the world as well as to spiritual life, with Christ himself rising on that day so that he might give the start of the blessed life in it, just as he began his handiwork in it. From this, some say this will be the last day, on which God will close the state of our pilgrimage, just as in a perfect octave <note>original: "diapason"</note> drawn from many eight-fold cycles. It was for this "eighth" that David celebrated several hymns, as is evident from their titles.

<margin>David Leviticus</margin>
Sacrificial victims are also owed to the Priest, as we are taught from the book of Leviticus, where it says: "As for the sin offering, so for the guilt offering"—or for the offense, as our translation has it—the victim belongs to the priest. The text mentions two victims here: one is for a sin of commission—namely, where there is some measure of voluntary fault—the other is for a trespass—that is, a sin of omission—as Origen <term>Origen: An early Christian scholar (c. 185–253 AD) famous for his allegorical and multi-layered interpretations of the Bible.</term> feels.

<margin>Origen</margin>
But if the truth of the letter is well-considered, it is for a fault committed through error. This sacrifice the Hebrews call *asham* <note>original: "אשם asham"</note>, as appears in the fifth chapter of the same Leviticus, where it says: "If he has erred, and he himself did not know, and it shall be forgiven him, he shall offer a guilt-offering as a guilt-offering to the Lord" <note>original Hebrew: "אֲשֶׁר שָׁגָג וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע וְנָסְלַח לוֹ : אָשָׁם הוּא אָשָׁם אָשָׁם לַיהוָה"</note>, which translated word-for-word says: "Because he erred, and he did not know, and he will be atoned for, or spared, he himself shall offer a guilt-offering as a guilt-offering to the Lord"—that is, as a sacrifice for a fault committed through error. Such and other victims belonged to the priest, so that in receiving them into himself, he might also take upon himself the trespass, the sin, and whatever fault there may be.

...for which they were offered: and he would intercede with God for those making the offering. In this was fully prefigured **Christ the Great High Priest**; in him the Father placed, and he himself took up, the iniquities of us all. Having become the **Lamb** and the true <margin>Paul</margin> victim, he bore the sins of the whole world, just as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: *Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many.* And again: *We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once.* And once more, <margin>The same</margin> speaking to the Ephesians, he says: *Christ loved us, and handed himself over for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling aroma.* And in many places, we read of the offering made by Christ, the true Priest, for us—so much so that we no longer have a necessity to offer animals or other sacrifices, but rather ourselves, in recognition of such a great benefit. We do this so that he, the true Priest, might sanctify, cleanse, and present those offered to the eternal Father. Regarding this first kind of offering, the Apostle, <margin>The same</margin> dealing with the Hebrews, says: *Through the spirit let us offer a sacrifice of praise always to God,* that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name; for with such sacrifices is God won over. Regarding this, God also says in the <margin>David</margin> Psalter: *The sacrifice of praise shall honor me.* And this applies as much to the confession and praise of his name as it does to the giving of thanks. Regarding the second kind of offering, the same Apostle, teaching us in the letter to the Romans, says: *I beseech you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, which is your rational service.*

If we wish to descend even to the particulars, we read in <margin>Leviticus</margin> Leviticus that the breast of the peace offerings and the right shoulder were given to the priest. In the breast sits the heart; and the "shoulder" in Hebrew is called שׁוֹק <note>original: "שׁוֹק" (shoq), usually referring to the thigh or leg of the animal sacrifice.</note>, which among us signifies the shoulder and desire. Therefore the heart, which resides in the breast, and the shoulder, in which there is desire and appetite, are given to the priest to be judged and cleansed. From this, we also expose our thoughts and affections to the priest in <margin>CHRIST</margin> confession, along with all those evils which (as Christ says) come out of the heart and become evil desires. This is done so that he may judge them and, through the imposition of penance and absolution, purge and cleanse them. Indeed, it is very profitable that everyone should keep their heart and affection in the hand of a good and wise priest, by whom they may always be cleansed and directed toward the good. For (as we said above) the judgment of difficult cases—and distinguishing between leprosy and leprosy <note>The author uses "leprosy" as a metaphor for different types of sin or spiritual impurity that require a priest's discernment.</note>, and purging it (which is most difficult)—belongs to the priest. He can by no means judge the case of the heart unless we present it openly to him. And because the priest holds the place of God on earth, judging hidden things and those matters that belong to divine judgment, therefore by divine command, honor is also <margin>Deuteronomy</margin> owed to him, as is said in Deuteronomy: *He who acts proudly and refuses to obey the command of the priest who ministers at that time to the Lord your God, shall die by the decree of the judge, and you shall take away the evil from Israel. And all the people, hearing this, shall fear, so that no one thereafter shall swell with pride.* Summarizing this, I say that God commands this because the priest is His minister...

<margin>David</margin> To this, that saying of the Royal Prophet <note>David</note> bears witness: *Touch not my anointed ones, and do no harm to my prophets.* <note>original Latin: "Nolite tangere Christos meos & in prophetis meis nolite malignari"</note> And this is because whatever the priest does on earth while performing his priestly office, he does acting in the place of God; as Christ protested with a clear voice, saying: *Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven: and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.* <note>Matthew 18:18</note> There is, 
<margin>Theologians</margin> moreover, in the priest either a certain <term>character<note>In Catholic theology, a "character" is an indelible spiritual mark or seal impressed on the soul through certain sacraments, like ordination, which can never be removed.</note></term> (as our theologians say), or a certain divine power, or an awe impressed upon him, which others might fear, just as in princes and earthly kings there is something which the people, out of fear, revere. There is also, or ought to be, a certain badge of virtue in the priest, and consequently divine favor, so that all should revere him. Hence Alexander 
<margin>Origen</margin> <note>Alexander the Great</note> (as Origen reports in *Against Celsus*) <note>A famous work of early Christian apologetics</note> when he was waging war against Darius, showed reverence to the Jewish High Priest of God, just as he had been instructed by a nocturnal oracle. The Emperor Theodosius revered Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, who famously compelled the Emperor to do penance</note> when he rebuked him. Attila (as we have said) was terrified by Pope Leo. <note>Pope Leo I, who famously met Attila the Hun and persuaded him not to sack Rome</note> But it would be too long to bring forward everything we find written about these and similar things. 

Truly, we must grieve over the calamity of these times, in which (I speak with shame and resentment) priests have so mixed themselves with base and shameful things—serving the wicked and not the heavenly—that they are now a mockery to God, angels, and men. However, to Christ—the true and greatest Priest, marked not with a common priestly character, but with that of the supreme high-priesthood and rule over all, shining with doctrine, wisdom, and holiness above all others—is due honor and glory beyond the rest. Whence not only in his name does every knee bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, but even insensible things revere him, and all things tremble at his nod. For he commands the sea and the winds, and they obey him; he blesses the bread, and in a wondrous way it is immediately multiplied; he orders the water jars to be filled, and it is made into wine; he calls souls back from the underworld, and they are reunited with their bodies; he commands fevers, and they cease to trouble. And to conclude briefly, all things revere him; all things obey him. Indeed, he has even given us power over every strength of the enemy, provided we wish to follow in his footsteps and become true priests, consecrating ourselves to God as a sweet-smelling aroma.

### Chapter IV.

So that we may see what a <gloss>true</gloss> legitimate and true priest and High Priest our Christ was, we have thought it appropriate to bring forward what garments were ordained by God for the priests and high priests of the ancient law; all of which bore the figure and type of our high priest JESUS, and of those things which he established in the gospel priesthood. The garments, therefore (as we have gathered from various places of scripture), are eightfold: four of which belong to the priests and high priests alike; while the other four were used only by...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the priesthood, moving from the general dignity of the office to a detailed description of the High Priest's sacred vestments, as interpreted through the writings of Josephus and Jerome.</meta>

<page-num>224</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD TONE</header>

<margin>Josephus</margin> The High Priest. The first [garment] is *micnece* <note>original Hebrew: מכנסי</note>, in Greek *periskeles*, or in Latin *feminalia* <note>original: "fœminalia," meaning breeches or undergarments</note>, which are breeches reaching down to the knees: these (says Josephus) were woven from twisted <term>byssus<note>A fine, costly fabric of linen, cotton, or silk used in antiquity.</note></term> so that they would be strong. Another is *cetonet* <note>original Hebrew: כתונת</note>, in Greek *chiton*, and in Latin it is called a tunic or a tight-fitting shirt without a fold. The third is *abnet* <note>original Hebrew: אבנט</note>, which we can call a belt, a strap, or a sash. It is like the skin of a snake when it sheds its old age <note>a metaphor for renewal</note>; it is woven with a weft of scarlet, purple, and <term>hyacinth-blue<note>original: "hyacinthi," referring to a blue or violet dye derived from sea-snails</note></term>, and with a warp of fine linen for beauty and strength. It is distinguished by such <term>intricate art<note>original: "polymira arte"</note></term> (says 
<margin>Jerome</margin> Jerome) that you would think the various flowers and gems were not woven by the hand of the craftsman, but added on afterward. By this belt, which is four fingers in width, the linen tunic was bound between the navel and the chest. The fourth kind of garment is a round little cap, like a half-sphere, which the Greeks and our own people call a *tiara*, and others call a skullcap, but the Hebrews call it *miznephet* <note>original Hebrew: מצנפת</note>. It does not have a point at the top, nor does it cover the whole head, leaving a third part of the forehead uncovered. It is bound at the back of the head with a ribbon so that it does not easily slip off the head; it is made of fine linen and is so skillfully covered with a linen cloth that no traces of a needle appear. Of the remaining garments, which belong specifically to the High Priests, the first is the *mahil* <note>original Hebrew: מעיל</note>, that is, a floor-length tunic entirely of hyacinth-blue, having sleeves of the same color sewn on at the sides. It is open at the top where it is put over the neck—what is commonly called a hood—with very strong borders woven into it so that it is not easily torn. On the hem, however, toward the feet, there are seventy-two bells and as many pomegranates, alternating with each other, so that the priest would enter the temple with a full sound, lest he should die. The sixth is the *ephod* <note>original Hebrew: אפוד</note>, which the 
<margin>The Same [Jerome]</margin> <term>Septuagint<note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> call the *epomida* (the shoulder-piece). <term>Aquila<note>A 2nd-century translator of the Bible into Greek.</note></term> calls it an *epigramma*; but Jerome calls it by its own name, the *ephod*. It is of two types: one belongs to the [ordinary] priests, and this is simple linen, which Samuel the Levite and priest used. 
<margin>David</margin> King David also used it when he wished to consult the Lord as to whether he should pursue the raiders who had burned Ziklag and plundered it. Then he said to Abiathar the priest: "Bring the ephod to me." Clothed in this, he consulted the Lord and received a clear response. The other is the [High Priest's] ephod, woven from the four colors often repeated in the Law—hyacinth-blue, fine linen, scarlet, and purple—interwoven with gold. It has a weft of hyacinth, scarlet, and purple, and a warp of fine linen. It is of marvelous beauty, having on each shoulder two 
<margin>Septuagint, Josephus, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion</margin> gemstones enclosed and set in gold, which in Hebrew are called *soham* <note>original Hebrew: שהם</note>. The Septuagint translated this as "emerald," Josephus as "Sardonyx," but Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion called it "Onyx"—and rightly so, as we shall declare in its proper place. On each of these were inscribed six names of the Patriarchs: on the right shoulder the elder sons of Jacob, and on the left the younger. The seventh garment is small in size but more celebrated than all those previously mentioned: in Hebrew it is called *hossen* <note>original Hebrew: חושן</note>, in Greek *logion*. From this, it has been translated into Latin as the *rationale* <note>The Breastplate of Judgment</note>.

->OF THE SECOND SONG<-

A small cloth indeed, woven from the four aforementioned colors <note>Fine linen, purple, hyacinth-blue, and scarlet</note>, having the size of a span <note>A 'spithame' or span is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger</note> in a square, and it was doubled so that it would not easily tear. It had four rows, or lines, in each of which were three precious stones: In the first, sard, topaz, and emerald; In the second, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; In the third, ligure, agate, and amethyst; In the fourth indeed, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl. In these were engraved the twelve names of the twelve sons of Israel. On the four corners of this <term>Breastplate<note>original: "rationalis," the Breastplate of Judgment worn by the High Priest</note></term> were four golden rings corresponding to four rings that were on the <term>ephod<note>original: "superhumerali," the shoulder-garment</note></term>, joined by hyacinth-blue ribbons and golden chains, so that the binding would be firm and it would appear to be a single fabric. There was also (which is of greatest importance) placed in that same Breastplate of Judgment, by the command of God, the <note>original Hebrew: האורים והתמים</note> *Urim and Thummim*, which we have translated as "Doctrine" and "Truth." And these were over the heart of Aaron—for which we have "upon the breast of Aaron"—whenever he entered into the temple before the Lord, so that Aaron might carry the judgment of the sons of Israel upon his heart whenever he entered before the Lord forever. The eighth ornament was a certain golden plate, which in Hebrew is called <note>original Hebrew: ציץ זהב</note> *ziz zahab* <note>meaning "flower of gold"</note>, on which was inscribed the great four-letter name of God, <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note> the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred name YHWH</note>. And this was upon the linen cap common to all the priests. But for the High Priest, it was fastened to his forehead with a hyacinth-blue ribbon. And with all these things, the head of the priest was crowned and protected with a marvelous visible beauty, 
<margin>Plato</margin>
and an intrinsic, virtuous, and divine beauty, which according to the Platonists is the participation in divine beauty. These things have been excerpted from many sources concerning the priestly vestments; now let us see what they signify.

## What these garments conferred upon the priests and the Great High Priest.

### Chapter V.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
<margin>Hebrew Sages</margin>
Wishing to discuss by what mystery or what figure these garments were ordered to be made by the Greatest God, we shall not despise those things which the Hebrew doctors set forth to declare the mystical sense. Even Jerome did not blush to imitate them, as they were the most skilled in this matter. Afterward, having removed the veil and being illustrated by divine light, we shall declare in a mystical sense what they represent in our own priests, and what they represent in our Supreme Pontiff, Christ, toward whom all things tend. Therefore, the Hebrew sages say that the four colors refer to the four elements from which the universe consists. <term>Fine linen<note>original: "byssus"</note></term>, which is produced from the earth, is assigned to the earth. Purple to the sea, since it is dyed from its shellfish. Hyacinth-blue to the air, because of the similarity of color. Scarlet as if burning with fire and ether. For they judged it right that the High Priest should give thanks to the Supreme Architect, who produced the elements themselves and whatever has been fabricated from them; and that he should represent the elements themselves, and consequently all things made of elements, to their Architect. Therefore, the first garment, by which the private parts were covered, was of linen, signifying that [earth] from which we are drawn, whence our genitals must be covered: because from there we feel pleasure, to which we ought by no means to descend...

the priest must have: nor should he act with his own limbs except insofar as necessity, which we have drawn from the earth, compels. But being gradually raised from earthly things to high things, they were covered from head to ankles with a **hyacinth-blue garment** <note>original: "veste hyacinthina," a deep blue or violet robe symbolizing the sky or air</note>: which indicates the air diffused from the heavens even to the earth. To this were hung **bells and pomegranates**. The noise of these represented the thunders and lightnings that occur in the air, or perhaps their sound terrified the aerial powers; or (to put it better) they represented the harmony and consonance of the elements, and of all things that are composed of them. This is also signified by the composition and wonderful order of the pomegranates.

Ascending even higher, they say that by those **seventy-two bells** and just as many pomegranates, they also summoned the seventy-two princes of languages <note>A reference to the seventy-two nations or languages traditional in mystical geography</note>—six for each sign of the zodiac—with all those entrusted to them, so that they might be present at the sacrifice which was performed by the High Priest <note>original: "summo Pontifice"</note> to the Lord of the universe. But if this opinion of theirs is true, that summoning was figurative, through the bells sounding as a kind of prelude to indicate those things which were fulfilled at the advent of the true High Priest, as we shall soon declare. 

Truly the **gold** with which the colors were interwoven, or that colored gold, represents the vital bond by which the elements are connected in composite things. The **ephod** <term>shoulder-garment<note>original: "Superhumerale"</note></term> indeed represents the upper hemisphere, in which there are two **Onyx stones**—that is, the two great luminaries <note>The sun and the moon</note> glowing from above. Regarding the **sash** <note>original: "Zonam"</note> by which the priest's breast is bound, and the linen tunic, some wish them to signify the ocean, and others the zodiac; but we can say both. For in that the linen garment (that is, the earth) is girded, it is the ocean surrounding the earth; but in that it is wrapped around the priest's breast, which is the center of the "lesser world" <note>The "microcosm," or the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>, the **Zodiac** is understood, encircling all the central parts of the "greater world" <note>The "macrocosm" or the universe at large</note>. 

The **Breastplate** <term>judgment-piece<note>original: "Rationale," also meaning "the thing pertaining to reason"</note></term> placed in the middle of the breast explains the earth and its adornment, clothed with flowers, herbs, and fruits. Holding the center of this worldly body, it receives the powers of the **twelve signs**; these are represented by the twelve stones fixed in that Breastplate. Indeed, they are distinguished by four rows, in each of which are three stones, representing the **four seasons of the year** by which the earth is variously disposed, giving three months to each season. Alternatively, through the four rows, they represent the four natures of the signs, since three are found in the property of each element <note>In astrology, each element (fire, earth, air, water) governs three signs of the zodiac</note>. 

And so that they may apply everything in the pectoral to the earth, they even wish that through the <term>Urim and Thummim<note>original: "urim ue tumim," Hebrew terms for "Lights and Perfections"</note></term> they might signify clarities and perfections; these are recognized everywhere on earth, where the effects of secondary causes appear. For here we comprehend in some measure how clear and perfect are the works of God and His ministers. Beautifully, therefore, is this very thing which is in the middle called "Rationale" <note>The Breastplate of Reason/Judgment</note>, because on this central earth, the purified mind perceives the "reason" <note>The underlying logic or plan</note> of secondary causes and the effects of the Most High God. For all things here are full of **Reason**, with earthly things corresponding and bound to heavenly things. Hence the Breastplate is said to be bound with the ephod (the shoulder-garment). And explaining that *Urim* and *Thummim* more clearly, they say it signifies the **truth and perfection** of things; truth indeed, because everything that exists...

## THE SECOND SONG ##

<margin>Metaphysics Genesis</margin>
That is also true which the **Metaphysicians** <term>Metaphysicians</term>—scholars who study the nature of existence and reality—say: In like manner, Scripture says that everything that exists is good: *God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good* <note>Genesis 1:31</note>, that is, perfect in their kind. Not without reason, in the High Priest performing the sacrifice for the Supreme Architect <note>original: "Opifici," referring to God the Creator</note>, the very handiwork of the architect is represented. To this is added truth—or clarity—and goodness in the priest, who ought to instruct the people through the brilliance of doctrine and the perfection of good works.
<margin>Jerome</margin>
This is so to such an extent that even his steps (as **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> says), his movements, and everything he does should be "vocal" <note>meaning his every action should speak as a testimony of faith</note>. Thus, he should receive truth and divine brilliance in his mind and reflect it in his whole manner and dress, so that whatever he does and whatever he speaks may be a lesson for the people. 

The **turban** <note>original: "Cidaris"</note> and the **blue band** <note>original: "vitta hyacinthina," a violet or sky-blue ribbon</note> represent heaven beyond all controversy. This should always be above the priest's head and set before his eyes, never to be laid aside. On it is the **golden plate** inscribed with the great name of God <note>the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God</note>. From this we learn that the great name of God is engraved in heaven, presiding over and sealing all the **twelve signs** of the zodiac and all the corners of the world, just as we are taught in the *Book of Formation* <term>Book of Formation</term> (the *Sefer Yetzirah*, an ancient mystical text of Jewish tradition) which is attributed to 
<margin>Abraham</margin>
**Abraham**. From this name, all things receive power and nourishment. 

But the name is said to be inscribed on a plate of **gold**, which we find signifies both natural and spiritual life. This is quite fitting because gold is solar in nature, corresponding with the celestial sun—which is called the giver of natural life—and with the "supramundane" <note>beyond the physical world</note> sun, which bestows spiritual life. Therefore, the High Priest, carrying the imprint of all creatures and of the whole world, indicated when he sacrificed to God that all things stand in need of His mercy and favor, by which they must be purified and cherished. And so he prayed, not only for children, parents, and kinsmen, but for **every creature**, both by voice and by his garments. 
<margin>Exodus Leviticus</margin>
The garments of this high priest are ordered to be made in the Book of **Exodus**, but in **Leviticus**, Aaron is dressed in them by Moses (at God's command). This is because these things must be learned from the Law and assumed at God's command. For no one should take this honor upon himself, as the 
<margin>Paul</margin>
**Apostle** <note>St. Paul, in Hebrews 5:4</note> says, unless he is called by God like **Aaron**; nor should he presume to judge what is pleasing to God unless God Himself dictates it.

### What these figurative garments pertain to regarding the priests of Christ. Chapter VI. ###

Since all these things happened to those fathers <note>the patriarchs and figures of the Old Testament</note> in a figurative way, and all these sacred matters (as **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note> says) refer to **Christ the High Priest** and to those things which He commands to be done by His followers, we shall see first how all these things come into use for Christian priests; afterward, we shall discuss how all these same things are concluded and resolved in Christ. 

But here I think it should be mentioned first that the priests and high priests were washed before they put on any of those garments, 
<margin>Leviticus</margin>
as we read in **Leviticus**. There it is recorded that, by the Lord's command, Aaron and his sons were called to the door of the tabernacle with a calf for sin and two rams and a basket of unleavened bread. When the assembly of the sons of Israel was gathered before the doors of the tabernacle, Moses said: *This is the word which the Lord commanded to be done.* And immediately...

<margin>Jerome</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
Moses offered Aaron and his sons, washed them, and dressed the High Priest in a linen under-tunic <note>original: "subucula linea"</note>, girding him with a belt. He then clothed him in a blue-violet tunic <note>original: "tunica hyacinthina," often interpreted as the color of the sky or a sapphire</note> and placed the ephod <term>ephod</term>—a decorative vestment worn over the shoulders—upon him. This he fastened with a waistband and fitted with the breastpiece <note>original: "rationali"</note> containing the **Urim and Thummim** <term>Urim and Thummim</term>—sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will. He also covered his head with a turban <note>original: "cidare"</note> and, upon the front of it, placed the consecrated golden plate for sanctification, just as the Lord had commanded. Thus, the priest was washed before he put on any garment. This washing, however, was performed by the power and judgment of the Law which the Lord gave through Moses; therefore, it is said he was washed by Moses. Nevertheless (as **Jerome** says), this prefigured the cleansing of the world and the **sacrament of baptism** or penance, in which we are washed before we put on that sacred garment of which **Paul** says: *Put on our Lord Jesus Christ.* Indeed, Christ himself wished to be washed in the Jordan and to be clothed and filled with the Holy Spirit—who descended upon him in the likeness of a dove as he emerged from the water—before he entered into sacred mysteries and the atonement of the human race. Having been baptized, he immediately began this work by engaging in battle in the desert against the enemy of mankind, thereafter continuing by teaching and healing, and finally offering himself as a sacrifice.

<margin>The Same (Jerome)</margin>
Once washed, the priest first put on the linen under-tunic or breeches. One who is about to perform a sacrifice must observe this first: he must "gird his loins." When a man is serving his wife by the right of marriage, he cannot properly devote himself to God and sacred things unless he abstains from the marital act. Hence the **Apostle Paul**, teaching married people that each should grant the other their "due" (since neither has power over their own body, but rather the spouse does), adds: *Unless you devote yourselves to prayer for a time.* This would mean nothing if it did not presuppose that one cannot serve the requirements of marriage and prayer—or other sacred duties—at the same time. For just as we cannot serve both God and Mammon <note>wealth or worldly gain</note>, we cannot serve both the spirit and the flesh, or the ambitions of the world and the yoke of Christ simultaneously.

Afterward, he was girded with a belt made of four colors. Through these colors (as we have said), the **four primary elements** <term>four elements</term>—earth, water, air, and fire—and everything composed of them are understood. This denotes that all these things, which are said to belong to this world and are made of corruptible elements, ought to be bound and tightened at the thigh and the lower parts of the body. In this way, being left behind there, they do not hinder the upper part of the priest when he is performing sacred rites and is about to sacrifice to God.

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
Afterward, he is clothed in the blue-violet tunic, so that from its color he may learn to become entirely heavenly. For this color, reaching toward the sapphire sky, invites the priest to the heavenly dwelling which **Ezekiel** saw was the color of sapphire. This contains a great mystery to be declared in its proper place. The ephod <note>original: "superhumerale"</note> was then placed over him, made of the same colors as the belt but interwoven. This signifies that once these changeable elements and their compounds are relegated to the animalistic part of the self, the priest should lift his mind toward the better elements, the celestial and divine. This is also signified by the **Shoham** stone <note>Hebrew: שׁהם</note>—that is, the **onyx**—fastened with gold on each shoulder. Indeed, this stone is earthy near its center but sapphire-like on its surface. By this, the priest is taught that while earthly things are enclosed at the center and the bottom, he should appear heavenly in all his outward actions. And because it is the priest’s role, as a middle-ranking **Hierarch** <term>Hierarch</term>—a sacred leader who mediates between different levels of reality—to lead the lowest to the highest, and the people entrusted to him into...

God, it is therefore said, because the names of the sons of Israel were inscribed on those stones, and consequently the names of all the tribes descending from them, so that by presenting the whole people to God in sacrifice, the priest might reconcile them with Him. However, as for the fact that the names of the elders are said to be placed on the right, and the younger on the left, I believe this signifies that greater things are given to the greater—not merely in age, but in virtues and merits—and lesser things are given to the lesser and those of less merit. Much could be said about the individual sons and tribes: how, by God's command, they were positioned figuratively in the camps, and what is signified by the right and the left. But these are not matters for our present meditation; therefore, let us come to those things which the priests of our own time <note>The author is likely referring to the Christian priesthood as a fulfillment of the Jewish Levitical priesthood.</note> ought to carry. They do not carry the names of the sons of Israel and the four-lettered names, but the names of the Apostles, who stand for the sons of Israel in the Church, and the name of **JESUS**, in which resides the power of the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton</term><note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH), considered most holy.</note>. In the foundations of the holy and new city descending from heaven (says John),

<margin>John</margin>

the names of the Apostles and the Lamb were written <note>original: "scripta erant nomina Apostolorum, & Agni"</note>. Hence, any priest of this city, performing the office of a true priest, ought to have these names—that is, the virtue and favor of those who laid the primary foundations of that city. For this reason, the priest who is about to celebrate, in the Canon of the Mass, names the Apostles and others who laid at least the secondary foundations, after God the Father and Jesus Christ His Son, imploring their prayers <note>A reference to the *Communicantes* prayer in the Roman Canon of the Mass.</note>. Afterwards, the most sacred breastpiece <note>original: "rationale"</note> was hung with twelve precious stones, and the **Urim and Thummim**. This breastpiece was joined to the shoulder-piece <term>ephod</term>, both featuring the number twelve. For on the shoulder-piece were inscribed the twelve names of the sons of Israel upon two onyx stones; whereas on the pectoral <note>another term for the breastpiece</note> or breastpiece, there were twelve precious stones in four rows with twelve names engraved, corresponding by a great mystery to the twelve names located on the back. We do not doubt that this was done for a great sacrament <note>The word "sacramentum" here refers to a hidden sacred meaning or mystery.</note>. For the earthly twelve corresponds to the heavenly twelve, which we have shown elsewhere to be most celebrated. So too, the twelve of the Gospel, figured in the precious stones of the breastpiece, is equated with the twelve of the Law, which was contained in the two stones of the shoulder-piece. Therefore, the twelve precious stones in the breastpiece of the ephod represent the twelve Apostolic leaders with the twelvefold family of twelve thousand chosen ones, each having the twelve fruits which the Tree of Life produces. These are called by Paul "the fruits of the Spirit." For life 

<margin>Paul</margin>

and spirit are the same, since the spirit is life and provides life to others. But some are the fruits which we produce on earth by the grace of God, and others are those which we shall gather in eternal blessedness. Those we produce on earth ought to correspond to those heavenly ones: the earthly twelve to the heavenly twelve, and the evangelical twelvefold family to the figurative twelvefold family. They should be bound together, just as the breastpiece was to the shoulder-piece, because Christ our High Priest made one out of both. We leave this to be explained in its proper place. Furthermore, in that breastpiece or rationale were the **Urim and Thummim**, which, I know not in what manner, they have interpreted as "Doctrine and Truth." For *Urim* <note>original: אורים</note> comes from *Or* <note>original: אור</note>, which signifies "Light." Thus, *Urim* means "clarities" or "illuminations of doctrine."

and they seem to signify the spirit to me: which the priest ought to possess, who performs the office of mediator between God and man, and provides guidance to the people toward God. For a leader will not know, nor be able to direct anyone on a path which he himself does not know: nor can a blind man provide good leadership to another: nor will he find favor with God who is not illuminated by the light of His grace; for we can know neither God nor divine things without His light. Therefore, the high priest <term>pontifex</term><note>The author uses 'pontifex,' a Roman term for a high priest, here applied to both the Jewish High Priest and Christian bishops.</note> must be illustrious and illuminated in doctrine, in the knowledge of both Testaments, and in spirit, so that he may know what he does, understand by what path he leads the people, and recognize what God requires of us for our purification and sanctification. By this mystery, our bishops are said to wear that **bipartite miter** <note>The traditional two-pointed hat of a bishop.</note> so that it may denote the knowledge which the bishops themselves must have in both Testaments; although in many cases in our time, the reality falls far short of the sacred sign. The priest must also be pure, clean, and perfect, lest being hateful to God, he place a stumbling block between God and the people rather than a means of reconciliation. And this is signified by that word תמים <term>tumim</term>, which we can interpret as <term>immaculate, perfect, complete, simple, and without defect</term>. Hence, such great diligence is commanded so that a priest might not only beware of sins, but also be unpolluted by a dead body, or by a woman who has given her body to another man. Likewise, he must be free from leprosy, from a flux of blood, and from a hernia; he must be whole in all his limbs, not blind, not lame, not hunchbacked, nor with a nose too large and deformed—all of which things are tolerated in others, but in a priest not at all: because he must be complete in every intrinsic and extrinsic perfection.

<margin>Leviticus</margin>
Concerning the first point, it says in Leviticus word-for-word: "The high priest among his brothers, upon whose head the oil of unction was poured, and whose hands are filled" <gloss>that is, with good works for the purpose of clothing him</gloss> "specifically in the priestly garments / shall not uncover his head, and shall not tear his clothes, and shall by no means come near any dead soul / nor shall he be polluted even for his father or his mother: And he shall not go out of the sanctuary, and shall not profane the sanctuary of his God: because נזר <term>nezer</term>, that is <term>a Nazirite, which means separated (specifically from the crowd), or crowned (with the crown of holiness)</term> / the oil of the chrism of his God is upon him: I am the Lord." These words are full of sacred mysteries: but let us briefly run through what they signify. The **oil** which is poured upon the head of the priest is divinity, with which the priest ought to be drenched more than the crowd—especially in the head, where resides that supreme portion of the soul which is divine, and by which we understand God and perform those works which are pleasing to God, provided it is bedewed with His grace. In the High Priests, Kings, and Prophets who were anointed, it ought to be sprinkled by a particular outpouring. The **filling of the hands** signifies a multitude of good works, with which a priest ought to be filled. Therefore, drenched in divinity and made divine, and full of good works, he should also take up the habit of the divine ministry which is pontifical or priestly. He shall not uncover his head by removing the **miter** <term>cidarim</term><note>The cidaris or mitznephet was the Hebrew priestly turban.</note>, which (as we said) signifies the upper hemisphere: by which the head of the priest ought to be covered. And to speak more clearly, he should never lay aside heavenly things, but always attend to them with his mind and soul: for if it is commanded by Christ to all people to always pray and never fail, then it is always

And each one ought to have his soul and mind in heaven, since he does not truly pray with a mind that he does not have raised toward God:

<margin>Damascene</margin>
> Prayer (says Damascene <note>St. John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and theologian.</note>) is the lifting up of the mind to God.

Much more, therefore, should the priest, who prays for himself and for the people, always have his mind and head turned upward toward heaven and overshadowed by divine protection. Furthermore, he should not tear his garment. There are two kinds of garments that every Christian ought to wear:

<margin>Jerome</margin>
One is of baptism, of which Jerome says: *I received the garment of Christ at Rome* <note>original: "Vestem Christi Romae suscepi"</note>: for he was speaking of baptism. God clothed the first-formed man <term>protoplasten</term><note>A Greek-derived term for Adam, the "first-formed" human.</note> with this, as well as all those who are saved after falling into sin:

<margin>David</margin>
of whom the Prophet says: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.* And our Great High Priest, Christ, used this double kind of garment—not for Himself, but for all whose sins He bore. One was the **seamless tunic** <note>original: "tunica inconfutilis," the garment of Christ mentioned in John 19:23.</note>, which signifies the garment of baptism, which is indivisible and never to be repeated. The other was divisible, part by part; and this signifies the garment of penance, to be put on again as often as a person sins, as Christ Himself said to Peter, to whom He especially gave the power of putting on this garment:

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven <note>original: "septuagies septies"</note>, that is, as many times as necessary, as everyone explains it.

Certainly, both use the number seven for forgiveness, but Christ multiplies it by ten, and by that seven derived from the complete ten, He squares it—not without a mystery to be explained in its proper place. From all these repeated instances of penance, only one garment is fashioned, which is unique, even though it is divisible in the manner we have described. However, the priest and high priest must tear neither of these, but must keep both untorn, lest his shameful nakedness ever appear through a garment torn by sin; for it is his role to clothe those who are naked. He must therefore be undefiled, holy, and clean. Nor is it an obstacle that he first offers for his own sin a calf, two rams, and a basket of unleavened bread, since no one is said to be clean from filth, not even an infant of one day; for we are all born children of wrath and subject to sin. Indeed, there are sins called "venial," which do not tear the garments and are worthy of easy pardon; nevertheless, the priest ought to be clean even from these, if he wishes to deal with a God who is holy, clean, and pure.

Hence it follows that he should not approach any dead soul, lest he be polluted and defiled by the dead, even if it were his own father or mother. From this, one sees how much greater purity is required in a high priest than in a regular priest: for the latter, at the beginning of the chapter, is permitted access to the funeral of a father, mother, son, daughter, brother, and even an unmarried sister. But for the Supreme High Priest, access to any funeral whatsoever is forbidden. What foulness a funeral may contain, such that it could defile one approaching it, is not the subject of the present treatise. However, I will say this: the ancient Fathers, who were more skilled in spiritual matters than those today who hallucinate while trying to discover "relations" and "quiddities" <term>quiddities</term><note>A scholastic term referring to the "what-ness" or essence of a thing. The author is critiquing overly abstract contemporary theologians.</note> which they never find, did not without reason ordain that a corpse be buried in a sacred place and accompanied by light,

...as long as it <note>The corpse of the deceased.</note> remains on earth, let it be sprinkled with holy water and censed with incense.
<margin>Leviticus, Numbers</margin> All these things are ordained—not in vain, as the common people think—but for the expiation of the corpse, which is exceedingly unclean. And who would not be weighed down by this foulness, being defiled by a mortal body? Indeed, such defilement is contracted even when one merits grace by committing a dead person to the grave out of charity. Nevertheless, God commands the priest to be immune even from this foulness. He also commands that the priest should never go out of the sanctuary, but always (if it can be done) remain holy, as he is to minister to the Holy of Holies. For he is a **Nazarene**, that is, one "separated" from the contaminated crowd and from the common works that defile his dignity. Or he is a **Nazarene**, meaning "crowned" with the diadem of holiness and anointed with the oil of divinity. After all this, God adds: *I am the Lord*, that is, I am **Adonai**, or the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: "quadrilitterus," referring to the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, who am indeed the most holy and most pure; therefore, I require my ministers to be pure and holy, just as He says elsewhere with a clear voice: *Be holy, because I am holy.* Nor does He wish a priest to be defiled with a woman who is a widow, divorced, sordid, or a prostitute; instead, he should have a virgin as a wife. Being joined with her, he may hold the <term>sacramentum</term> <note>In this context, a "sacred sign" or "mystery."</note> of a single union, such as we ought to have with God in the marriage to which we are invited in many places in Holy Scripture. This rule is also observed among our priests; those who have been joined to two women, or to a woman who has been known by another man, are called **irregular** because of <term>digamy</term> <note>The state of being married twice; in canon law, this often barred a man from the priesthood.</note>, lest the sacrament be violated by a double marriage.

But alas, these are unhappy times and ruined morals! For now, the words of the statute and the precepts of the law are kept only "on the bark," while the trunk is depraved and the root is rotten. Men of such double-marriage are not admitted to the priesthood unless a dispensation is granted by the Pope, who acts as the representative of God on earth, even though it goes against the Lord's statute. And yet,
<margin>CHRIST</margin> prostitutes and effeminate men are admitted everywhere by the priests. Moreover, there are the hunchbacked, the lame, those with hernias, the illegitimate, and those with crooked or oversized noses—every kind of monstrosity. According to the mystical sense, these signify vices and defects in the soul. Those who are diminished by such things cannot carry the **Thummim**, which signifies perfections and completions, both in natural and spiritual matters. ...the clarity of the gospel. It is said in Leviticus <margin>Leviticus</margin> that when the multitude had been gathered at the door of the tabernacle, Aaron was appointed priest by Moses. Moses had summoned him there with his sons, along with a calf for sin, two rams, and a basket of unleavened bread. Was it not also Christ—wishing to offer a single sacrifice for the sins of the whole world—who presented himself as a victim for sin, for guilt, for error, for iniquity, for transgression, for rebellion, and for every crime that was not purged by the sacrifice of the Law? Accompanied by a great crowd of Hebrews, Romans, and all nations, he went "outside the gate" <note>A reference to Hebrews 13:12, "Jesus also suffered outside the city gate."</note>, appointed as a priest not indeed by Moses or the Law, but by God the Father, who "has sworn and will not repent" <note>Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:21.</note> that he should be a priest forever. He finally offered himself as a victim pleasing to God the Father, calling into himself the power, the mysteries, and the meanings of the calves, goats, unleavened bread, and all the things that were offered by the priests of the Law. <margin>CHRIST</margin>

<margin>John</margin>

As John says: "He has washed us from our sins" through true baptism.

Thus, after the washing, he took up garments; or rather, he made himself the garment with which to cover our nakedness, just as he had made himself the water with which we are washed, the victim he would offer for us, the bread with which he would feed us, and the door through which we would enter.

# THIRD PART #

But these names are said to be written on <term>onyx</term> <note>original: "onychinis"; a layered stone, here described as having an earthy core and a heavenly surface</note> stones, which are earthy below toward the center, but heavenly on the surface; by this, it is suggested that he intends to make that entire family, which was earthly and animal-like, into a heavenly one. He also took up the <term>Chossen</term> <note>original Hebrew: חושן; the "Breastplate of Judgment" worn by the High Priest</note>, which the Greeks call the <term>Logion</term> <note>original Greek: λόγιον; meaning "oracle" or "rationale"</note>: this is the pectoral ornament in which there were twelve precious stones with the twelve names of the sons of Israel. However, those names were carried engraved upon the two stones of the shoulder-pieces and upon the twelve stones of the breastplate. From this, our High Priest **Christ** is expressly shown: who ascended the altar of the cross to pray *and to sacrifice for both* twelve-fold families. Of these, the figurative one was contained on the back by the two onyx stones, but the true one was inscribed upon the twelve precious and varied stones. This is because the family of the Patriarchs was not gathered from every nation that is contained under the twelve heavenly signs <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac, used here as a metaphor for the whole world</note>, but was born from one race and from one father, Jacob. Yet it is called "two-parted" because from that same family are those who were to be placed on the right and those who were to be placed on the left. But this new family, and the new bride descending from heaven, was gathered by our supreme priest **JESUS** from every tribe, language, people, and nation which is under heaven, divided chiefly into twelve parts contained under the twelve heavenly signs. Therefore, she is said to be inscribed upon twelve precious stones, because everything that has been done in this family can deservedly be called "precious." Indeed, we could apply a twelfth part of this new family, with its twelve leaders, to each of the stones; but (God willing) we shall reserve this to be done in its proper place.

Now, as to why the breastplate itself is said to be woven from the four colors often mentioned before, we can easily explain if we remember that we said those four colors signify the four elements from which all things are composed, and into which even the heaven itself is said to be divided and composed—not indeed from these decaying elements, but from the better ones. Hence, three of its signs are called "earthy," three "watery," just as many "airy," and the rest "fiery." All things corresponding to them agree with these, so that all things, both heavenly and earthly, are distributed among those elements signified by the four colors. Therefore, the "type" <note>A prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> of both families is distinguished by those four colors.

Furthermore, those two sacred objects called <term>Urim and Thummim</term> <note>Ancient Hebrew oracular devices kept in the breastplate; traditionally translated as "Lights and Perfections" or "Doctrine and Truth"</note> so belong to Christ our High Priest that he does not merely carry them, but is inwardly the very thing they signify, however they may be interpreted.

<margin>**CHRIST**.</margin>

For if they are translated as "doctrine and truth," he already cries out publicly: **"I am the truth"**; and "my doctrine is not mine by origin, but His who sent me," yet it is so communicated to me that I am doctrine for the people in both word and deed: for every action of Christ was our instruction. But if they are interpreted as "clarity and perfection," he himself was the light illuminating every man, and so immaculate *and perfect, that he represents us as immaculate to God the Father through his grace and* merits. And if the whole breastplate is called the <term>Logion</term> <note>meaning "verbal" or "rational"</note>, is he not the Word <note>The "Logos" or eternal Word of God</note> in whom are all the rules both of created things and of those things which we ought to do? He also provides the very reason for understanding and acting. And it is called "double" because there were two natures there: in each of which...

...we find a rich pasture of reason and understanding. The breastplate and the shoulder-piece were also bound with blue ribbons and small golden chains in pairs of four rings—four on one side and four on the other—corresponding to each other. But what better blue and heavenly ribbon is there than He who is entirely heavenly, who descended from heaven to make us heavenly? And what is this golden chain if not charity and love, with which our High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex maximus"</note> came to bind us, striving toward this with every word and deed? And so He bound both families, the ancient and the new; He bound the heavenly and the earthly; He bound the creature with God, just as two natures were bound in Him, and one was made from both. Finally, He Himself, as the head and the connection of the sinews, bound all the members together. 

There remains the golden plate <note>The "Tzitz," a thin gold plate worn on the High Priest's forehead</note>, on which was written the great four-letter name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>; which is explained in a name of forty-two letters <note>A complex divine name used in Kabbalistic tradition</note>, through which God fashioned the world, as all those who treat such names agree. This name is fitting and combined with the name of our greatest Bishop **JESUS** <note>Hebrew: ישו</note>, whose letters all together yield the number 316 <term>gematria</term> <note>A system where Hebrew letters represent numbers: Yod=10, Shin=300, Vav=6</note>. If forty-two is added to this, they rise to 358, which is the value of the name of this "Rational" <note>The "Rationale" or Breastplate</note>, which is **MESSIAH** <note>Hebrew: משיח</note>. For *Shin* (ש) gives 300, *Mem* (מ) gives 40, *Yod* (י) gives 10, and *Het* (ח) gives 8; which, when calculated, give me 358. 

From these things, those most skilled in this sacred art—namely, the divine arithmetic of letters—conclude that this most mysterious breastplate, in which the twelve precious stones were inscribed with the names of the chosen family, along with the most sacred *Urim* and *Thummim* <note>Sacred objects stored in the breastplate used to determine God's will; their names mean "Lights and Perfections"</note> (in which all things to be understood and done shone forth), truly represented Christ. In Him is the power of the created world, as John says:

<margin>John</margin>
> All things were made through the word <note>original: "Omnia per uerbum facta sunt"</note>.

Behold, therefore, how well that name of forty-two letters, in which the world was fashioned, fits with **JESUS**. But we are entering into so many and such great mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta"</note> that if we wished to explain everything that occurs here, my strength would not suffice to speak, nor would readers grasp what might be written. Nor is it fitting that those things which should be communicated by mouth among a few wise men be committed to public writing:

<margin>David</margin>
> I have hidden (says the prophet) your words in my heart, so that I might not sin against you <note>Psalm 119:11</note>.

Lest, however, the readers be sent away entirely hungry, we shall touch upon a few points. If all those chosen and sealed ones are said to have the name of the Lamb and the name of His Father written on their foreheads, it is no wonder if we say that the Son of God Himself—the firstborn among many brothers, to whom the Father gave all things—has the name of God Himself within Him. And here, I pray, let the readers notice why our High Priest himself, in the days of His flesh, said:

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give to you.

While later, rising again, He says:

> In my name they shall cast out demons <note>Mark 16:17</note>, and the other things that follow.

Where, with careful investigation, one must notice why He remains silent about the great name of God, by which Moses, the Fathers, and all the Prophets from then until Christ performed whatever wonders they did; and though this name is sung with such great celebration in many places by the divine harper <note>King David, author of the Psalms</note>, our Jesus nevertheless passes it over in silence and puts forward only His own name, in which He teaches us to pray to the Father and ask for whatever we desire to have. Did He wish to claim for Himself what He should not? Far from it! For He did not think it robbery to be equal to God. But He did this because...

->### THE THIRD VOLUME ###<-

<margin>Paul</margin>
**Paul** perceived the power of the great name given to him by the Father, and enclosed within his own proper name. Thus he gave power to men, who would perform miracles, speak in tongues, and such things, which were done by the power of the great four-lettered name <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>. But in this current course of our time, from Jesus onward, we ought to carry the name of Jesus himself, and consequently the great name of God included within the very name of Jesus: and this should be bound on our foreheads with a blue and heavenly ribbon—that is, with a heavenly and spiritual life, conversation, and mind. For (as the Apostle says) "No one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit." Therefore, it is not by naming Jesus with a polluted mouth, or as if it were the name of just some man, or even of an individual assumed by divinity, merely uttering it with the mouth and understanding it according to the doctrines of men, that we can perform miracles in the power of that name. Rather, by calling upon it in the Holy Spirit with a purified mind and a fervent soul, we shall achieve those things promised in that name, especially through preceding knowledge, according to that prophetic word: "I will protect him, because he has known my name." Now, therefore, in the name of Jesus wonders are performed and salvation is given, because there is (as Peter says) no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved, except this one. Concerning this name, its power, and how
<margin>Peter</margin> 
other names are enclosed within it—to whom the Father gave all things—we, wishing to speak, might bring forward that saying of Paul: "We have much to say, and it is difficult to explain in words," since many have become weak in understanding. These are primarily those who, in the most sacred secrets of God, wish to have **Aristotle** and **Averroes** <note>Aristotle (Greek philosopher) and Averroes (Islamic scholar); the author critiques those who rely on secular philosophy to understand divine mysteries</note> as their guides. For these things are not learned in the schools or gymnasiums of the Gentiles, but from the Holy Spirit; and they receive these things from the divine light only if they have been chosen for such things by the eternal Father, as the Son says: "Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me."
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
He said "your name" while speaking with the Father, yet the Son who was speaking manifested His own name. This is because the name of the Father was included in His own. How this name, and how one is included in the other, not even the whole world together could understand unless He Himself revealed it; for these things are hidden from the wise and the prudent, and revealed to the little ones, and to those who are of a pure and clean heart.

### Christ is a priest forever. Chapter VIII. ###

<margin>Paul</margin>
Therefore, our Christ is the true Priest and High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex maximus"</note>, performing an eternal priesthood, as Paul says to the Hebrews: "There were indeed many priests made according to the law, because they were prevented by death from continuing; but this man, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood." Wherefore He is able to save forever those who approach God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for us. Hence
<margin>David</margin>
David predicted in a prophetic spirit: "You are a priest forever." Nor is He hindered by death from performing a perpetual priesthood; indeed, in death He offered Himself as a sacrifice consecrated to God the Father, and through the resurrection, it was changed for the better. Therefore, remaining and having been made unfailing, He always and perseveringly stands before God, so that He may be an eternal propitiation for our sins: through which, having been presented to the eternal Father and the divine tri...

Therefore, Christ performs an eternal priesthood in heaven, a better one than Michael, of whom it is said that he is a priest and prince over all souls to be received, and no less over bodies. For he even disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, as Thaddeus <note>Saint Jude, often called Thaddeus, whose epistle mentions Michael the Archangel disputing with the devil over Moses' body (Jude 1:9).</note> reports in his canonical epistle. For the devil wanted to carry it away as if it were subject to sin; but Michael, on the contrary, wanted to present it to God as if purged by the law and purified by divine fellowship. For this reason, he had brought his face to such brightness that the children of Israel could not gaze upon it because of the splendor of his countenance. We believe this was done through the merit of our eternal priest, about whom Moses himself said many things, so that both that soul and body, now purged, could be presented to God. Thus Michael fought as a true priest, and the angels (that is, his ministers) with him for the souls of all, against the ancient serpent, who continually seeks them out to devour them. But Michael prevailed, and the dragon was cast out. No less now and continually is he an aid to the people of God, as we read in Daniel: <margin>Daniel</margin> "Michael, the great Prince, who stands for the children of your people," that is, for the elect. Concerning this, the Church sings that he has been appointed prince over all the elect souls to be received by God. If, therefore, Michael performs a perpetual priesthood, having continual care for souls, how much more the Son of God and High Priest Christ, to whom has been given every kind of redemption for those souls, and who, by his offered sacrifice, continually and perpetually found eternal redemption for us, ought to perform an eternal priesthood, interceding continually before the face of God for all souls for whom he offered himself as a sacrifice and a victim. And this is what **John** says: <margin>John</margin> "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation <term>propitiation: an act of atoning for sin to appease divine justice</term> for our sins, and not for ours only, but for those of the whole world."

### Why Christ Was a Priest by an Oath. Chapter IX.

<margin>Paul</margin> Our Paul, educated at the feet of Gamaliel <note>A renowned Jewish teacher of the law; Paul mentions studying under him in Acts 22:3.</note> and instructed in the third heaven <note>A reference to Paul’s mystical vision in 2 Corinthians 12:2, where he was caught up to paradise.</note>, was not silent about how Christ was appointed a priest by an oath, saying to the Hebrews: "Others indeed were made priests without an oath, but this one with an oath by him who said to him: <margin>David</margin> The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent, 'You are a priest forever.'" But what this oath implies, and how it binds all those who swear it so that they cannot depart from the oath without cause, is a hidden mystery. The more secret Hebrews <note>Likely a reference to practitioners of Kabbalah or esoteric Jewish scholarship.</note> say that an oath connects many things, especially that exalted seven-fold nature from which all things come, just as the words for "oath" and "seven" are the same in their language; so much so that *hashba* <note>original: "השבע", meaning 'he swore'</note>, which signifies "he swore," comes from *sheba* <note>original: "שבע", the number seven</note>.
