->### THE THIRD TONE<-

...which signifies seven, so that according to their sense it means: *He swore*, that is, he "seven-ed" <note>In Hebrew, the verb "to swear" (*shava*) is etymologically derived from the word for "seven" (*sheva*), likely from the custom of swearing an oath by seven witnesses or sacrifices.</note>, or he swore an oath by seven, and brought those seven into witness. Abraham, wishing to signify this <margin>Abraham</margin> when he made a covenant with Abimelech, set out seven ewe lambs as a witness: through which seven lambs he intended to represent that high **septenary** <note>The "septenary" refers to the number seven and specifically the Seven Spirits of God mentioned in the Book of Revelation.</note>, according to which stand the seven spirits who are in the sight of the throne of God. Hence, the transgression of an oath is, in a certain way, to wish to make those spirits false witnesses, and to deprive oneself of the influence of those from whom all good comes. The Lord therefore swore to Christ, entreating him through that septenary, and communicating every kind of its sevenfold influence to him, according to that oracle of **Isaiah** <margin>Isaiah</margin>, in which he speaks of Christ having been made a priest by this oath: *A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety: and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall rest upon him.* <note>Isaiah 11:1–2. These are the classic "Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit."</note> It is as if he said, according to that septenary, there shall rest in him the spirit of intelligence, and the one who remits faults; likewise grace or piety, justice and terror, beauty and rectitude, victory and perpetuity, honor and ornament, life and the <margin>CHRIST</margin> kingdom, so that not without cause did he say: *The Father has given all things to me.* Weighing this, **Origen** <margin>Origen</margin> writing on that passage of Isaiah, *Seven women shall take hold of one man*, says: <margin>Isaiah</margin> "The Holy Spirit with his gifts was over many, but he rested in none, except upon **JESUS**." He is that unique bridegroom whom seven women—that is, that high septenary—have taken hold of with an indissoluble bond. For the spirit of wisdom with the other gifts came into **Moses** <margin>Moses</margin>, but it did not rest, especially when he erred in the striking of the rock <note>A reference to Numbers 20, where Moses struck the rock twice in anger, leading to his exclusion from the Promised Land.</note>, on account of which the leadership of the people to the promised land was taken from him. It came upon **Aaron** <margin>Aaron</margin>, but in the sin of the [golden] calf it withdrew. It came also upon **Isaiah** <margin>Isaiah</margin>, but because he said: *I am a man of unclean lips.* It came also upon **David** <margin>David</margin>, but feeling that he had earned the right to be deprived of it, he cried out saying: *Take not your holy spirit from me.* And since there is no one who does not sin, there is no one from whom the spirit of the Lord does not withdraw for a time, except Jesus alone, of whom it was said to **John**: *Upon whom you shall see the spirit descending and remaining on him, this is the Son of God; this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit*, being able to impart the spirit itself, which he firmly possesses, to others as well. <margin>John</margin> "And because I saw," says John, "the Spirit descending and remaining, I have borne witness that this is the Son of God." Therefore the spirit remained; that septenary also remained firmly upon Jesus, without any gap and without any withdrawal. But why this? Because *the Lord has sworn, and he will not repent:* He swore that he might be a priest forever; he swore that he might be the Greatest Pontiff <note>High Priest</note>; he swore that he might be holy, pure, clean, and separated from sinners, so that he might be able to take away the sins of all. And because he swore, therefore the spirit rested upon him, and that thing which is greater than all, which the Father gave to him. From this, that third thing is equated, namely <term>שבת</term> <note>original: "שבת" (Shabbat)</note> **Sabbath**, which the **Hebrews** <margin>Hebrews</margin> say corresponds with an oath and the septenary; and it signifies rest. Therefore the sevenfold spirit rested in him, as did that high septenary, because the Almighty Father swore to him, so that remaining always holy and divine, he might sanctify others and make them divine.

### Chapter 10: How he was a priest according to the order of Melchizedech.

<margin>Paul</margin>
He who established our Christ as the High Priest <term>Pontifex Maximus; literally 'Greatest Bridge-builder', the title for the supreme priest</term> by an oath, ordained him according to the order of Melchizedech. Since this is known to all, let us therefore see what the "order of Melchizedech" is, according to which Christ was ordained.

<margin>Genesis, Paul</margin>
Having discussed those things which we read in **Genesis** and those which are treated by **Paul** in the Letter to the Hebrews concerning this Melchizedech, we find five points in which our Christ corresponds with him. Four are touched upon by Paul, the first of which is that Melchizedech is introduced in Scripture without father, without mother, and having neither beginning of days nor end; thus the Son of God was ordained a priest without beginning or end of days, since he is eternal. Nor are a father or mother assigned to him in his priesthood <note>original: "nec in eius sacerdotio assignatur pr̃, aut mãter". This refers to the theological idea that Christ's priesthood comes from his divinity, not his earthly lineage.</note>. Therefore, Paul says: *In this, Melchizedech was made like the Son of God.*

<margin>The same: Rabbi Solomon, The Hebrews, Jerome</margin>
However, **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says, and with him many wise men of the Hebrews—with whom **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> agrees—that "Melchizedech" is an appellative name meaning "Just King," and his proper name is **Shem**, the son of Noah.
<margin>Shem</margin>
Thus, we do have his father, although not expressly mentioned by the Scripture. Likewise, we have the Father of our Christ, although he is not expressly mentioned where his priesthood is discussed.

The second point is that he was King of **Salem**, that is, "of Peace," signifying our Christ as the High Priest and King of true peace, who came to give and leave that true peace to us, which the world <margin>CHRIST</margin> cannot give. Therefore, as he entered the world, his ministers sang: *And on earth peace to men of good will.* And when leaving the world, he himself said to his disciples: <margin>Isaiah</margin> *My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you; not as the world gives, do I give to you.*

The third point is the interpretation of his name, which is "King of Justice," fitting our Christ, of whom **Isaiah** says: *And a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and he shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.*

The fourth point, which is inferred from this, is that just as Melchizedech was both king and priest, so also was Christ. He therefore came from the royal tribe of **Judah** <note>original: "Ichuda"</note> so that he might assume the kingdom by hereditary right according to the flesh, just as he received it from the Heavenly Father, so that he might give it to us together with the priesthood.
<margin>John, Peter</margin>
Hence **John** says in the **Revelation**: *And he has made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father.* With this, **Peter** agrees, writing to the strangers dispersed in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia: *You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood.*

The fifth point, which I weigh more heavily, is the offering which is found to have been made by this Melchizedech in bread and wine alone, with no mention made of animals or any other things. This rite is most suitable for our High Priest, Jesus Christ, who enclosed every sacrifice in bread and wine alone, as if in the primary substance of human food. To this sacrifice, all the blood and the slaughter of animals, and whatever else was offered under the Law, has yielded. For now we do not lack blood in which we may be cleansed, because the human race has already been perfectly cleansed in the blood of Christ; and all things which were then unclean [are now clean]. Because our law is one of grace and of water <note>A reference to the transition from the "bloody" sacrifices of the Old Testament to the "watery" rite of Baptism and the "unbloody" sacrifice of the Eucharist.</note>, we no longer enter into this law or into the Christian family through the blood of circumcision, but through the water of baptism; and also because nothing more expressively figures the mystical body of the universal church...

...of which Christ is the head, as of bread: For this [bread] is made from many grains, and is the common and universal food of all nations: just as this mystical body <note>The "mystical body" refers to the Church as a collective of believers.</note> is made from many individuals from every nation under heaven. <margin>The same</margin>
tithes from Abraham, and consequently from Levi—who (as Paul says) was still in his loins <note>A biblical way of saying Levi was a future descendant of Abraham.</note>—and blessed him, he was greater than Abraham and Levi; and his priesthood was greater

<margin>The same</margin>
than the Levitical and legal priesthood: most especially because (as the Apostle was able to show) the legal priesthood had to be transferred into that of Melchizedech, that is, into the priesthood of Christ, who was appointed a priest according to the order of Melchizedech. Therefore, Christ himself was not of the priesthood of Aaron, nor of the tribe of Levi, but of the royal tribe of Judah: so that it may be understood that the priesthood of Christ was royal and according to the true order of the Just King <note>The name Melchizedech literally translates to 'King of Righteousness' or 'Just King'.</note>. Hence this witness: *You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedech*; this was indeed a setting aside of the former commandment and priesthood, as being weak and useless, since the Law leads to no perfection. Therefore, the priest who was made according to the law of a fleshly commandment had to cease, and he had to arise who was according to the power of an indestructible life. We have derived these things from Paul. But why was Christ’s eternal priesthood prefigured in the priesthood of Melchizedech? To this, I shall respond with Jerome:

<margin>Jerome</margin>
If the "chosen vessel" <note>A traditional epithet for St. Paul, from Acts 9:15.</note> is stunned by the mystery, and confesses that what he discusses is inexpressible, how much more should we little worms and gnats confess only a knowledge of our ignorance, and that we have seen an immense house through a tiny hole, as it were. For it is a grand discourse and difficult to explain <note>original: "interpretabilis" - here used in the sense of requiring extensive explanation.</note>, why Melchizedech is introduced without a genealogy. And if the Hebrews speak truly, that he was Shem <note>Referring to the Jewish tradition that Melchizedech was Shem, the son of Noah, who survived long after the Flood.</note>—what does this name "Shem" mean, which translated into Latin signifies "Name"? Perhaps that Name which is above every name; just as when "Virgin" is said, the Virgin who is above all virgins is understood; and "Apostle" above all apostles; and "Father" above all fathers. And to conclude briefly from all this: in Melchizedech there was something divine and permanent, in which the eternal priesthood of Christ was represented; about which (as Paul says) it is not permitted to speak; therefore, let us move on to other things.

<margin>Paul</margin>
How much greater and better a priest Christ was than Aaron and all the legal priests.

<header>OF THE SECOND SONG</header>

## SECOND SONG

A High Priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation: Neither by the blood of goats, or calves, but by his own blood he entered once into the holy place, having found eternal redemption. <note>original: "Pontifex futurorũ bonorum... æterna redemptione inuenta." This is a paraphrase of Hebrews 9:11-12.</note> Six points are touched upon by Paul in which Christ was a more perfect and excellent High Priest than the legal and symbolic priests: First, because those priests obtained propitiation <term>propitiation; the act of regaining the favor of God through a sacrifice</term> from God, by which, being appeased, He might favor them with temporal goods. This is evident in the whole promise of the Law, where it is said: *If you listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the earth:* <note>original: "Si audieritis me, bona terræ comedetis"</note> And: *Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies:* and *One of you shall chase a thousand, and two shall chase ten thousand,* and things of this sort. All of these were temporal things, although they were figures of eternal things. Toward those eternal things, the wiser men occasionally moved, speaking of the future age, of the blessed life, and of the true paradise of delights. To that state one did not arrive through sacrifice, but through a better lot and the precious death of the saints, just as the Prophets arrived. But let us speak of the sacrifice through which only some sins were expiated, and not all: hence, those purified by them did not merit an eternal reward, but only those things which

<margin>Paul</margin>
the present age promised, according to Paul. But our High Priest has become (says Paul) a priest of the good things to come, and therefore through a greater and more perfect way. In the second place, the Levite priest entered a handmade tabernacle—indeed, one made of wood, and later of stone when the Temple was erected—but our High Priest entered a tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. By this "tabernacle," Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> understands "heaven." This can be confirmed by the testimony of Paul saying: *We have a great High Priest, Jesus the Son of God, who has passed into the heavens.* And again: *We have such a high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens; a minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man.* Origen himself strengthens his statement

<margin>David</margin>
with the testimony of the divine Lyre-player <note>The "Citharędi" or Lyre-player refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> saying: *I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me: for I shall go into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.* And again in another psalm: *Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? Or who shall rest on your holy mountain? He who walks without blemish and works justice.* And what is the place of the wonderful tabernacle from which one arrives even at the house of God? And what is that tabernacle, the memory of which caused the prophet’s soul to be poured out within him, as if dissolved by a certain unbearable desire? Truly, it was not that one made of goat skins and curtains of fine linen, purple, hyacinth, and scarlet; nor that which was captured by the Philistines; <note>original: "Allophylis." In Latin biblical texts, this term refers to the Philistines as "the foreigners."</note> nor that which was to be built by the son <note>Referring to Solomon, the son of David, who built the First Temple in Jerusalem.</note>; but it is the Father's Tabernacle, which, being divided into many

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
mansions, is named in the plural by Christ when he says: *Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of iniquity, that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal tabernacles.* <note>original: "mammona iniqtatis... ęterna tabernacula." Quoting Luke 16:9.</note> And by the Royal prophet in the psalm: *How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord.* This tabernacle not made with hands is therefore heaven, which was built not by the hands of men, but by the power and command of God. There is also another tabernacle in which God delights to dwell...

<margin>Paul</margin> That which is called the temple of God by Paul, who says: *The temple of God, which you are.* <note>original: "Templū Dei, qđ estis uos." A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:17.</note> Therefore, the soul of each person, once cleansed and purified, is a temple and a tabernacle of God. And this is *not made with hands*, <note>Hebrews 9:11</note> and not of this creation or workmanship by which all these material things were manufactured, but it was breathed into existence by the mouth of God in a unique way. Thirdly, because the legal high priest <note>The "legal" priest refers to those operating under the Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note> approached the holy places with the blood of goats, calves, rams, lambs, sparrows, and doves, or with the sprinkling of the ashes of a heifer, and things of this sort. All of these are animal things, and they pertain to the cleansing of the natural man. <term>natural man; in Latin "animalis homo," referring to a person living by physical nature rather than by the Holy Spirit.</term> Christ, however, entered through his own blood into the holy place, so that he might cleanse all things—so much better as the blood (I will not say of a man, but of the most holy Son of God) is more precious than the blood of animals, by which the natural man was cleansed. And consequently, the priesthood of Christ, cleansing through his own blood, is so much more perfect than the legal priesthood, which cleanses through the blood of animals.

<margin>The same (Paul)</margin> But why is almost everything (as the Apostle says) cleansed in blood? (He says "almost" because metal vessels were purified by fire, and other vessels and garments were cleansed with water, as we read in the Book of Numbers.) <note>Numbers 31:22-23</note> I believe the reason is this: because sin takes its origin from blood and flesh, therefore the expiation <term>expiation; the act of making amends or reparation for guilt.</term> had to be made through blood. For the tribunal of God's justice, seeking punishment where the sin occurred, wills that blood be shed and the flesh be restrained, which were the kindling for sin. But in the legal and symbolic sacrifice, which did not fully expiate, the purifications were made in the symbolic blood of animals. Christ, however, coming and promising and giving heavenly things, having become the head of all the members of this mystical body, shed blood—not human blood subject to sin, and not the blood of animals, but blood most precious above all other blood that was in this mystical body—for the expiation of all.

<margin>The same (Paul)</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
<margin>The Apocalypse</margin> Hence our Paul says: *It was necessary that the copies of heavenly things should be cleansed with those animal sacrifices; but these heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than those,* <note>Hebrews 9:23</note> that is, by the blood of the Redeemer. As John says in his epistle: *The blood of Jesus Christ has cleansed us from all sin.* <note>1 John 1:7</note> And in the Apocalypse: <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> *Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood.* <note>Revelation 1:5</note> And it is already known to all that Christ, in his suffering, satisfied the tribunal of divine justice not with the symbolic blood of animals, but with his own blood. Fourthly, because the legal priests entered the holy places to seek propitiation as often as people came to them for their sins, and they slaughtered animals. Our High Priest Christ, however, entered once into the holy place; for he ascended the cross once, offering himself to God the Father and satisfying for all—not with a symbolic satisfaction, but a true one—even for the fathers who came before. For this offering that was to be made had already been accepted by the Father before the foundation of the world, 
<margin>John</margin> and in it were expiated as many as were saved, as John expressly says in the Apocalypse: *All worshipped the beast whose names are not written in 
<margin>Peter</margin> the book of life of the Lamb, who was slain from the beginning of the world.* <note>Revelation 13:8</note> And Peter says: *You were redeemed from your vain way of life of paternal tradition, not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an unspotted and undefiled lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but manifested in these last times.* <note>1 Peter 1:18-20</note>

<margin>Paul</margin>
...in those times. By these words, it is declared without any ambiguity that the sacrifice of our High Priest <term>High Priest; in Latin "Pontifex," referring here to Jesus as the supreme mediator between God and humanity.</term> Jesus, made of himself, was preordained from eternity, so that by it even the Hebrew people might be cleansed from the defilements from which they could not be purified through the sacrifices of animals. Fifthly, in that which he says: *Eternal redemption having been found.* <note>original: "Aeterna redẽptiõe inuenta," from Hebrews 9:12.</note> These words can have a double sense: One is that we are redeemed from sin and led to eternal glory; the other is that our High Priest Jesus discovered a redemption which is unique and eternal, so much so that we do not need another, just as those Fathers of the ancient law needed, who awaited this redemption. And in the meantime they made many redemptions: they redeemed the firstborn at a certain price—for they redeemed the firstborn of a donkey with a sheep—and they redeemed sold properties and freedom in the year of jubilee. <note>The Year of Jubilee was a Jewish sabbatical year occurring every 50 years, during which slaves were set free and debts were forgiven.</note> But also the entire people was redeemed from Egyptian servitude, only to be taken captive again. And many times they were redeemed, sometimes generally, sometimes particularly, now from one servitude, now from another, now from sin, now from obligation. Christ, however, redeemed us once, having found an eternal redemption. He redeemed, I say, properly, and did not [merely] buy: because we were already his by nature, even though we were turned away from him by our sins. Since all are indeed redeemed, nothing is lacking except that we obtain the effect of this redemption; which we can obtain, if only we wish, because the fountain of baptism, where we obtain that effect, is now open to all. The grace of grace and remission is also open: for after the redemption was made, he left behind his ministers and executors, granting to them every kind of power to distribute that same redemption, saying: *Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them.* <note>John 20:23</note> And again: *Whatever you loose on earth, shall be loosed also in heaven.* <note>Matthew 16:19</note>

<margin>Paul</margin>
From all these things in the text, it is most importantly to be weighed that a person was not justified by the sacrifices of the law, but through Christ, as Paul, writing to the Romans, testifies with a fitting voice, saying: *By the works of the law—namely, both the natural and the written law—no flesh is justified before him.* <note>Romans 3:20</note> But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe in him. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus: whom God set forth as a propitiator <term>propitiator; one who reconciles or makes atonement, specifically through a sacrifice to satisfy divine justice.</term> through faith in his blood, for the demonstration of his justice because of the remission of previous sins: which he had decreed to punish, unless the mediator had redeemed them by satisfying the tribunal of justice. This satisfaction the just and merciful God accepted, justifying those who are of the faith of Jesus Christ, and not through the natural or written law.

<margin>CHRIST Paul</margin>
For the knowledge of sin comes through the law—the natural law, that is, as Jerome and Origen <note>Saint Jerome and Origen were influential early Christian scholars and theologians.</note> concordantly interpret—because from it anyone can judge what is just and what is unjust, as the same Paul had said a little earlier: *For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature those things which are of the law, not having such a law, they are a law unto themselves, who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or defending one another.* <note>Romans 2:14-15</note> And by this law [the mouth] is stopped...

...every mouth [may be closed], and all the world may become subject to God. <note>original: "omne os, & ſubditus ſit omnis mūdus Deo," referencing Romans 3:19.</note> This cannot be understood as referring to the written law <note>The Mosaic Law or Torah.</note>, since it did not bind everyone, nor did it close the mouths of all, as it was given only to the Israelites. Furthermore, that law did not grant justification except for sins committed through error <note>Sins of ignorance or accidental ritual impurity.</note> and a few other secret faults which did not carry the penalty of death. However, crimes, rebellions, and iniquities—which are more severe sins—were not forgiven under the law, neither through sacrifices nor through the prayer of a priest, but were expiated by the sinner's own death. This is evident in the cases of the blasphemer, the murderer, the adulterer, and those who commit acts with beasts or against nature: all of whom were ordered to be stoned or burned, as we read in various places in the books of the Law.

<margin>Paul</margin>
Therefore, the Apostle says to the Hebrews: *It is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls and goats.* <note>Hebrews 10:4.</note> For this reason, entering the world, our <term>High Priest; the Latin "Pontifex maximus" here identifies Jesus as the supreme mediator, contrasting him with the Jewish High Priests.</term> and Son of the living God says: *Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me,* in which, clearly, I might offer a sacrifice for all. *Burnt offerings and sin offerings did not please you. He takes away the first <note>The animal sacrifices of the Old Testament.</note> in order to establish the second: namely, the offering of Christ. From this it follows: *By which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.*

And indeed, every priest stood daily ministering and offering the same sacrifices repeatedly, which can never take away sins. But this man, after offering one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, waiting from then on until his enemies are made his footstool. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. These things are so clear that they do not require further explanation.

<margin>David</margin>

...he himself sustained the aforementioned things: for he was expelled by his son while his wives were violated; he saw the death of Amnon and Absalom, his sons; and Adonijah, immediately after his death, was delivered to execution by the order of Solomon. <note>The author is listing the tragedies of King David to show that even a "man after God's own heart" suffered the earthly consequences of sin, unlike Christ.</note> But this High Priest of ours <term>Pontifex maximus; traditionally the title of the Roman chief priest, here applied to Christ as the supreme mediator.</term> purged all crimes and bore all sins through the sacrifice which he offered, as had been predicted by the beautiful oracle of Isaiah: <note>Isaiah 53:5</note> וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵינוּ מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ <note>original: "Et ipſe infirmatus eſt propter impietates noſtras, & attritus eſt propter iniquitates noſtras" — He was weakened because of our impieties and crushed because of our iniquities.</note> This impiety and iniquity, called in Hebrew <gloss>havon</gloss> (עָוֹן) and <gloss>passah</gloss> (פֶּשַׁע), were not forgiven through the legal sacrifices <note>The animal sacrifices mandated by the Law of Moses.</note>. Therefore, the most merciful Father placed all these things upon the shoulders of His Son, so that by offering himself as a sacrifice, he might take them all away. And because not all wish to obtain the benefit of this expiation, it follows: *And he bore the sins of many,* namely of those who wish to be saved. *And he prayed for the transgressors,* doing what was in his power for everyone. If they do not attain salvation, it should be imputed to themselves, because they do not wish to embrace the salvation acquired for them.

### Christ was the true victim, and the original sacrifice, and offering. Chapter XII.

<margin>Ovid</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Also Paul</margin>
<margin>Origen</margin>

**H**aving been offered for us, he was therefore made the true <term>hostia; a sacrificial victim, often associated with a peace offering or a sacrifice after victory.</term>, burnt offering, sacrifice, sin-offering, guilt-offering, peace-offering, and <gloss>cherbona</gloss> (קרבן)—that is, an offering or gift—and whatever else was offered under the Law. For a "hostia" and a "victima" (victim) is that which is offered (as the authors of our language teach) when someone attacks enemies or brings back a victory or triumph over them. As the Poet, most skilled in such matters, sings: *The victim is so named because it falls by a victorious right hand; the hostia takes its name from the defeated enemies.* <note>original: "Victima, quæ dextra cecidit uictice uocatur: Hoſtibus a domitis hoſtia nomē habet." Quoted from Ovid's *Fasti*.</note> Thus Christ, having attacked the enemy of the human race, offered himself to the Father as a living "hostia," and while casting down and warring against that enemy, he slaughtered himself as a "victima," so that he might simultaneously report a victory and offer himself as a hostia from the defeated enemies. Therefore Paul says to the Ephesians: *Christ loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling aroma,* <note>Ephesians 5:2</note> so that he might snatch us from the hands of our enemies once they were defeated. And again, he says to the Hebrews: *But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the destruction of sin through his own sacrifice.* <note>Hebrews 9:26</note> Concerning this sacrifice, Origen discusses many things in his letter to the Romans.

Christ was also a "holocaustum," which among the Latins signifies "entirely burned." In Hebrew, it is called <gloss>haholah</gloss> (הָעֹלָה), which is properly interpreted as "ascending." For he was entirely burned by the fire of love, consumed, and transformed into a spiritual nature. Demonstrating what he was to become, he was transfigured before them, his body changed from being passible <note>Subject to suffering and change.</note>, obscure, and heavy into a body that was agile, luminous, and impassible. But this state did not remain, because he had not yet been offered as a burnt offering, truly burned and transformed. However, after the burnt offering was made on the cross, in rising he showed himself to be (as he truly was) utterly transformed, entering through closed doors, appearing when he wished, and hiding himself at will. And finally, having become most light, he ascended gloriously while many were watching. Whence he is fittingly called <gloss>olah</gloss> (עֹלָה), that is, "ascending." Having been burned, therefore, and transformed by the power of divine fire into the very nature of fire and spirit...

CCXXXVI

-> VOLUME THREE <-

B iiii

...transformed, he ascended to the Father, having first demonstrated the truth of his resurrection to his disciples over forty days. And "ascending on high," <margin>David</margin> he wished for many to ascend with him, according to that word of the Prophet: *Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.* <note>Psalm 68:18, also quoted in Ephesians 4:8. The "captivity" refers to those souls held in Limbo whom Christ liberated.</note> There was also a sacrifice offered for sin, which the Hebrews call <term>hatat <note>Hebrew: חטאת (chatat); a purification offering usually translated as "sin offering."</note></term>, and in translating it properly we can say nothing more fitting than <term>peccatarium <note>A Latin term coined by the author to mean "sin-bearer" or "sin-remedy," distinguishing the offering from the sin itself.</note></term>, from <term>hata <note>Hebrew: חטא (chata); the root verb meaning "to sin" or "to miss the mark."</note></term>, which is "sin." Concerning this sacrifice, <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says to the Corinthians: *He who knew no sin, for our sake he made him a sin-offering* <note>original: "peccatarium." This refers to 2 Corinthians 5:21.</note>. For this, faulty manuscripts have, *for us he made him sin.* For how could he, who knew no sin, be made sin? And what fruit would it have brought us if he had committed sin? Nor does that explanation given by some please me: "he made him sin," that is, "he offered himself for sin"; because even if they agree in the general sense, that interpretation cannot truly fit the wording. It was therefore a "sin-offering," that is, an offering for the sins of all. There was also a "guilt-offering," a sacrifice offered for a specific fault or, to speak properly, for an error. This sacrifice in the Law is called <term>asham <note>Hebrew: אשם (asham); a "guilt" or "reparation" offering required when someone had deprived another of their rights or desecrated something holy.</note></term>, which we have translated as "for a trespass." In this ritual, a bull was offered by a priest or an anointed one who had sinned, and by the crowd; however, a goat was offered by a prince. But an ordinary person offered a female goat or a sheep, as we read in <margin>Leviticus</margin> Leviticus. And with some of the blood dipped on the priest's finger, the horn of the altar was sprinkled, and the rest was poured out at the base of the altar itself. All these things are full of <term>sacraments <note>In this context, the author uses "sacraments" to mean "holy mysteries" or "hidden spiritual meanings."</note></term>. For by the bull, the goat, and the female goat, the tribunal of divine justice was appeased, to which all those animals correspond. These animals also signify that part in man in which the <term>kindling of sin <note>original: "fomes peccati"; a theological term referring to the tendency toward sin or "tinder" that allows the flame of temptation to catch.</note></term> resides. It is not without reason that those about to receive judgment and the punishing justice of God are compared by the Savior to kids, which are of the goat and buck kind. Through these animals being slain and sacrificed, God was easily appeased, with the error of the sinner partially excusing them. And the priest sprinkled the horn of the altar erected before the tribunal with the blood of the offered animal to appease the celestial powers, who demand blood from those who sin according to the flesh and blood—so that according to the rectitude of justice, each might be punished through the very things by which he sinned. This was done by the finger of the priest, who intervened as a mediator to appease God on behalf of the sinning human. Christ, however, was not only the Priest and High Priest, but also became the goat, the bull, the sheep, the lamb, and every kind of sacrifice, as we shall immediately declare. He himself, pouring his own blood upon every horn of the altar of the cross, more extensively and perfectly appeased the eternal Father and the tribunal of His justice than was ever done by the blood of animals. Nor is there a lack of mystery in the blood that was poured at the base of the altar in much greater quantity than that which was sprinkled on the horn of the altar. This is because there is much more blood—and merit acquired through that shed blood—which overflows and is held in reserve, than that blood or merit applied to the horn of the altar by the finger of the true Priest for the purification of a sin. For the blood of Christ and his merit would have been sufficient, and is sufficient, for thousands and thousands of thousands of worlds, as our theologians say. Therefore, the part that overflows and is reserved is greater than that which is applied for our actual cleansing. But this too must be noticed...

<summary>The author explains the Hebrew sacrificial system of 'hatat' (sin offering) and 'asham' (guilt offering), arguing that Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of these types. He emphasizes that Christ's merit is so vast that the blood shed on the cross far exceeds the requirements for human salvation, being sufficient for infinite worlds.</summary>

<margin>The same from the Acts of the Apostles</margin>
Why is this part, by which we are cleansed, sprinkled by the finger of the priest? It is because the merits of Christ are dispensed to us through <term>the hands of the priest <note>The author is linking the ritual sprinkling of blood in Leviticus with the Christian sacrament of Ordination and the "laying on of hands."</note></term>, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles:
> Through the hands of the Apostles, many signs and wonders were done, given to them indeed by the power through the blood and merit of Christ. <note>original: "Per manus autem Apostolorum fiebant signa..." Refers to Acts 5:12.</note>

Hence Paul writes to Timothy:
> I admonish you to stir up the grace of God which is in you through the imposition of my hands. <note>original: "per impositionem manuum mearum." Refers to 2 Timothy 1:6.</note>

And in the first Epistle to the same:
> Do not neglect the grace that was given to you through the imposition of the hands of the priesthood. <note>original: "per impositionem manuum presbyteri." Refers to 1 Timothy 4:14.</note>

And again in the Acts of the Apostles it says:
> Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. <note>original: "Tunc imponebant manus super illos." Refers to Acts 8:17.</note>

All these things are said to denote that the merits and gifts of Christ are dispensed through the hands of priests and his ministers, far and wide and openly, just as the symbolic blood was sprinkled sparingly by the finger of the priest of the Law. > All we like sheep have gone astray, every one has turned aside into his own way: and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before his shearer, he does not open his mouth. <note>original: "Omnes nos sicut oves erravimus..." This is the famous "Suffering Servant" passage from Isaiah 53:6–7.</note>

Behold how he is called now a sheep, now a lamb offered for the purging away of sins. There was also the peace offering, which in the Law is called <term>זבח השלמים</term> <gloss>sacrifices of peace offerings <note>original: "zebah aselamin," from the Hebrew "Zevakhim Shelamim."</note></gloss>:

For (as we have said quite often) he wishes us to be his co-workers, so that the reward may be more precious to us, and more just for him, since he gives it with our own efforts intervening. ## How Christ Was the True Lamb. Chapter XIII.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
<margin>Exodus</margin>
**T**he first sacrifice which the children of Israel slaughtered was a lamb, which they prepared by God's command for the <term>Passover <note>Original: "pascate," from the Hebrew "Pesach," meaning "to pass over."</note></term>, that is, for the celebration of the passage out of Egypt. Its preparation was this, as we read in Exodus: *This month of March, which the Hebrews call **Nisan** <note>Hebrew: ניסן</note>, shall be for you the first among the months of the year.* <note>Refers to Exodus 12:2.</note> Indeed, it is rightly the first, since in it the beginning of a new life was given; it is not the first because the world was created in it, for from the Law—and more clearly from the wise Hebrews—it is held that the creation of the world occurred in the month of September—namely, at that time when the crops ripen and trees return their fruit, so that just as man was introduced into a house with the building already complete, so he might find mature and prepared those things which belong to human sustenance. The Hebrews hold this time as most celebrated and venerate it as the days of remission; just as God was munificent in building the world, so he would be in forgiving. Hence this month of September is appropriately named from the number seven <note>In the Roman calendar, September was the seventh month (septem), a number associated with rest and forgiveness in biblical tradition.</note>; but by the Hebrews it is called **Tishrei** <note>Hebrew: תשרי</note>, as if "directing" and "balancing" all things. They also celebrate the feast of Tabernacles in the same month, but of these things elsewhere. That month [March/Nisan] was therefore called the first, not in respect to creation, but to the renewal of the world itself. God's edict follows: *On the tenth day of the month, let everyone take a lamb according to their families and houses.* This number ten, being complete, denotes the full course of life and the consummated work which the Author of life then fulfilled; as a type of this, the legal lamb was commanded to be sacrificed and eaten. Nor is the material number considered here, but the formal reason of completion which is in the number ten; it is to this that those who philosophize and theologize through numbers primarily look. It was commanded, therefore, that a lamb be taken for families and houses in such number and distribution that it would suffice for those eating, and they could eat the whole thing so that nothing remained to be discarded, nor would it be lacking for those wishing to eat. Now the <term>sacraments <note>Used here in the sense of "sacred mysteries" or "foreshadowings."</note></term> of spiritual things begin, which suffice for all who receive them, however many they may be, and nothing remains to be cast away; it was in the figure of these things that the precept concerning the typical lamb was given. And let the lamb be a year old, which has experienced the months and the total revolution of the heavens, so that as one full, without blemish, and perfect with merit, it might represent Him who did no sin, nor was deceit or error or defect found in his mouth or his works. According to this rite, you shall also take a kid...

It emphasizes that the sacrificial lamb must be perfect and fully consumed, foreshadowing Christ's complete and sufficient sacrifice for all humanity.</summary>

Thus two leaders prefigured that full moon, namely David and Solomon: under whose reigns the fullest worship of the Mosaic and figurative law was held; and both of them prefigured Christ, but in different ways. ### Chapter XIV: On the Rod of Moses and the Cross

Beyond the typical lamb <note>A "type" is a person or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament; here, the Passover lamb foreshadows Christ.</note> there was present in that transition of the Israelite people the sacramental rod. At first, it was quite wondrous in the sight of Pharaoh, and afterward in all the miracles performed in the sea, the desert, and all places, until the people entered the land of promise. Although it was called the rod of Moses, it was without doubt the power of God, upon which Moses leaned, trusting in no power of his own. Among other things performed under the guidance of this rod, there was this remarkable wonder: that when cast upon the ground, it raised itself up as a serpent. When its tail was grasped by the one who threw it, it appeared as a rod again. From this we are taught that when one is cast out from the power of God, one does not act except by the favor of the serpent <note>The devil.</note>, who, as a master of deceptions, easily slips in to favor illusions in place of the rod, since he cannot agree to true miracles. A wise man ought to look toward the end of such deceptive outcomes, which is always evil, so that, despising them and their author, he may cling to God, the true worker. Therefore, Moses was commanded to catch it by the tail—that is, to look to the end and the outcome of poisonous and deadly <term>deceptions (praestigia): illusions or magical tricks intended to mislead.</term>—and putting them to flight, he should lean on God alone. This is also indicated by the removal of shoes from the feet and the pasturing of flocks beyond the desert. For God had commanded that he should remove the shoes of his affections, which he wore shod in the doctrines of the Egyptians; because the place, the land, or the state to which he had come was holy. For he no longer lingered in a desert place empty of divine influence, but had moved beyond the "desert" of magic and Egyptian art. For this, we have "to the further parts of the desert": for he was not then in the heart of the desert, but was staying beyond the desert itself, namely in Arabia Felix on Mount Sinai, which is watered by much divine influence. For on the summit of that mountain, which is called Horeb, God spoke familiarly with Elijah; and on the other peak...

On that same mountain named Sinai, He gave the law to Moses, dealing with him most familiarly and showing many wonders, so that it was not a desert, but a most well-watered place. That rod of divine power, when cast before Pharaoh, appeared as a serpent, especially to Pharaoh and his wise men who were accustomed to magic arts; for they performed all their deceptions by the power of the "ancient serpent." <note>A reference to the Devil, often called the "ancient serpent" in biblical commentary.</note> These men, thinking that the power displayed by Moses proceeded from that same ancient serpent, opposed him with the powers they had truly received from the evil serpent, and their rods were likewise turned into serpents. But the rod of Moses—that is, the true divine power—although it appeared as a serpent, devoured those rods and their <term>necromantic (necrománticas)</term> powers. This was to indicate that by the rod—that is, the divine power which overcomes every demonic force—He performed miracles in Egypt, the Red Sea, and the desert. 

However, the true and universal redeemer, Christ, performed more sublime and excellent wonders through the "rod" of the Cross than the lawmaker Moses did. For the power of Christ was not merely a rod consisting of a single extension, but it also passed across, creating a certain strong and wide <term>texture (texturam)</term> from the <term>warp and woof (stamine & subtegmine)</term>. <note>The author uses a weaving metaphor to describe the horizontal and vertical beams of the Cross.</note> For the rod of Jacob and Moses was only erected vertically, but this rod of Christ was extended in every direction: in length, breadth, height, and depth. Therefore, it did not prevail only to liberate the single people of Israel, but the whole human race, even warring against the "powers of the air" <note>Demons or fallen angels, following the language of Ephesians 2:2.</note> and sustaining the people, so that nothing remained over which His power did not prevail.

<margin>Paul</margin> 
And of this the Apostle speaks, saying: *That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth*—namely, of the surpassing knowledge of the charity and power of Christ fixed to the cross. <note>original: "Vt possitis coprehédere... quæ sit latitudo, lógitudo, sublimitas, atq; profundú." See Ephesians 3:18.</note> Its extension and intensity are indicated by its branches and their angles. For the branches extend high, deep, and across, so that by stretching into the different and all-encompassing parts of the world, they signify that His power is diffused everywhere. 

Furthermore, the sixteen angles—that is, four at each end of the timber—indicate how intense His power is. For sixteen is the first number increased from the first growing twelve, by which (as we said above) all growing things are distributed. <note>This refers to sacred geometry and numerology, where 12 represents the created order/zodiac and 16 represents a further perfection or "intensity."</note> But it must also be observed that one set of four is hidden in the earth, where the timber is fixed into the ground or stone, and twelve angles appear in the three exposed branches. This number twelve—arising through three being led by four, or four multiplied by three (the former being divine and the latter elementary)—expressly indicates that all things, both divine and earthly, are reconciled in the cross itself, since in the number twelve one is led by the other, and both are connected within it.

<margin>The same</margin> 
And this is what the Apostle says: *For it pleased the Father that in Him all fullness should dwell, and through Him to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of His cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.* <note>original: "Cóplacuit. f. Patri omnem plenitudiné in ipso habitare... per sanguinem crucis eius." See Colossians 1:19-20.</note> Thus, even in the divided heavens, spiritual and bodily things are reconciled by this number twelve, with the "intelligences" <note>Celestial beings or angels that were thought to move the heavenly spheres.</note> assisting there, influencing through those twelve corporeal signs. <note>A reference to the twelve signs of the Zodiac as the "corporeal signs" of the heavens.</note> The number four, representing growth...

### THE THIRD TONE ###

<margin>CHRIST.</margin> The hidden Christ signifies the fruit of the cross itself, which is concealed from our senses and judgments; yet He is nonetheless the root and foundation of all fruits and merits, just as the <term>quaternary (the number four)</term> is the root of all numbers. That <term>duodenary (the number twelve)</term> is also brought together by another significant mystery: namely, from the four points of the cross itself, the three nails, and the five wounds of the one suffering upon it. Here, the number twelve results from the material four, the divine three, and the bonding five. For this number five is denoted among the Hebrews by the letter <note>original: "ה" (He)</note> in which they say the world was fabricated and joined together, and which is the seal of that craftsman-spirit who is called the "bond." And this cross was seen at one time as a serpent—not indeed a deceptive and lethal one, but a saving one. Of this it is said: *Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up*—specifically on the cross, and stretched out in the manner of a cross, so that He Himself was crucified. Thus, the cross and the serpent were displayed not for destruction, but for salvation; whence it follows: *That everyone who believes in Him may not perish, but may have eternal life.* For just as the flesh of a serpent brings a cure to a poisonous wound—from which **theriac** is made, which is the antidote to poison, derived from the flesh of the viper—so the flesh of Christ provides health and life to all whom the evil serpent, and not Christ Himself, has bitten. Therefore, against the poisons of this serpent, we must eat that very flesh.

<margin>THE SAME</margin> And because He appeared to Himself as wounded, leprous, and a "spotted serpent," He began to fear, to feel weariness, and to be sorrowful, and finally to say: *Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.* Indeed, it was possible, and He knew it; hence that "if" can be understood as "since" (as they say). For He greatly desired (unless I am mistaken) another, more useful order for coming to our aid. Nor was He failing in His supreme love by yielding to His physical feelings, as some believe, since He was always ready to lay down His body and soul for His sheep; rather, He was content to draw out a longer delay with us, so that He might complete a more excellent work. Hence He did not say that the cup should be *removed*, but that it should *pass*, and be deferred until that time when He might fulfill what the Apostle <margin>Paul</margin> said (being conscious of these <term>sacraments</term>): *Lastly, however, the enemy death shall be destroyed*—that is, the Angel of Death. As he explains more clearly elsewhere, saying: *That through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil; and might deliver those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives.* Yet the Father did not wish to grant this—not indeed scorning the prayer of the suppliant, whom He always heard, but so that all things might be balanced by their own weights and distributed in their proper times and moments. The Father holds these in His own power as a great mystery, so that it is not for us, nor even for the Apostles, to know them. But what He did not complete in His first coming, He will complete without any doubt in His second. But to return to where we digressed: although He felt horror at the terrifying passion and death offered to Him, nevertheless, "grabbing it by the tail"—that is, looking toward the glorious end—it appeared again as a distinguished and most celebrated rod. Which again...

CXXI
# OF THE SECOND SONG.

<margin>The Pharisees</margin>
This serpent <note>referring to the previous page's discussion of the rod turning into a serpent</note> appeared as a snake to the Pharisees and the malevolent ones who said: *He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.* But he demonstrated that divine power which would devour every diabolical force, proving that a demon is not cast out by a demon, but by the **finger and power of God**. By this power, many miracles were performed in the "Egypt" of this world: in the granting of health, the raising of the dead, the multiplication of bread, the transformation of water into wine, and countless others of this kind—not for the destruction of the "Egyptians," but always for benefit and profit. Finally, he sanctified the sea—namely, the **water of baptism**—through which a passage is given to us into divine fellowship at Sinai. There we hear the law and sense God acting familiarly with us, and we are fed with a better bread than that <term>dewy bread</term> <note>manna, which fell with the dew</note>; namely, the living bread which descended from heaven, offered and baked in the **oven of the cross**. By this rod, finally, our teacher Christ introduced us into the true Promised Land, flowing with true milk and honey. This, Moses was unable to do; for he could not lead the people into the figurative land with that rod, which he had misused by striking where and when he should not have. <note>A reference to Numbers 20:11, where Moses struck the rock twice in anger, leading to his exclusion from the Promised Land.</note> We must, therefore, lean more happily upon the rod of the cross and of Christ than upon those of Moses and Jacob; for if we rely on those, we will either fail on the journey or reach only a land of shadows. But supported by this rod, we shall arrive at the land and the true dwellings of the living, following a leader who cannot go astray. <margin>Jacob</margin> Hence Jacob, while setting forth his final words—in which he predicted in summary almost all the affairs of both the figurative and the true family—leaned no longer upon his own staff, with which he had crossed the Jordan, but upon this better rod, in whose power he foresaw all those things were to be accomplished. For it is said in the text: *And he gathered his feet*—that is, his affections—<note>original: "המטה EL hamitah"</note> <term>toward the bed/rod</term>. Although we have this well translated as "toward the bed," it can also be understood as "toward the rod." For <note>original: "מטה" (mitah/matteh)</note> signifies both **rod** and **bed** if the vowel points are changed. In the literal sense, therefore, it refers to the bed, but in the allegorical sense, it is more aptly translated as the **rod**, which is the cross. He sensed the power of this no less than some of the ancients who venerated the sign of the cross before Christ, as men of no small authority write. This was either by nature, or by the dictate of the Spirit, or taught by wiser intelligences who knew how great the things were that were to be achieved through the cross.

And in this way, they are given those things in us which are animalistic and defiled—either because God permits the devil to take what is "diabolical," just as it is said of the betrayer: *One of you is a devil*; or because we voluntarily leave behind and give to the devil what is his, so that we may render to God what is God’s, according to the edict of the <margin>CHRIST</margin>Savior saying: *Render the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God.* But we are taught with clear light from Holy Scripture which things belong to the <margin>John</margin>devil; for the Supreme Teacher calls the devil the "prince of this world." Those things which belong to the world, John briefly reduces to three: the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life. But leaving aside the spiritual aspect for the moment, let us come to the other two, which are flesh and riches: from these, those who intend to be entirely free for God vow to abstain, or they strive with all diligence to be stripped of them. <margin>CHRIST</margin>First, regarding riches, as Christ says: *No one can serve God and <term>mammon</term>* <note>original: "mamona"; a Semitic term for wealth or profit</note>. CXXIII

->### OF THE SECOND SONG.<-

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
Therefore, the riches which belong to <term>Mammon</term> <note>original: "mamonae"; a biblical term for wealth or property, often personified as a false god</note> are distributed, and the flesh is crucified, tamed, and sacrificed (which, regarding its itching desires and the resistant force we must overcome, belongs to <term>Azazel</term>, whom the wise consider to be the same as Mammon) so that what belongs to God may be returned to Him purified. Then (unless I am mistaken) that reminder of Christ is preserved, in which he says: *Be in agreement with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps he deliver you to the judge.* <note>Matthew 5:25</note> This agreement consists in giving out or relinquishing what belongs to the adversary’s jurisdiction, or in sacrificing our "animal" nature—which is the chief seat of the adversary himself—so that once it is sanctified and cleansed, he may find no entrance into it. Thus, satisfaction is made to the tribunal of divine justice, and the animal nature itself is sanctified so that it is no longer the devil’s, but God’s. That which was subject to itching, pleasure, or corruption is left to the devil and is completely uprooted from us. We read this prefigured in a great mystery in <margin>Leviticus</margin> Leviticus, where God commanded two young goats to be chosen, and once lots were cast over them, one would be sacrificed to God, but the other would be sent away into the desert to Azazel, the prince of all deserters. This goat, buck, or he-goat destined for Azazel is called the <term>scapegoat</term> <note>original: "emissarius"; literally "the one sent out"</note> in our translation—not indeed because it is given like a horse to impregnate females, but perhaps because "emissary" is used somewhat loosely since it was "emitted" or sent out. And this he-goat, before being sent into the wilderness, was set alive before the Lord so that, after prayers were first poured out over it, it might be sent into the solitude to the accuser of the human race, so that the mouth of that accuser might be stopped. And to reveal something of the sacrament hidden here, that animal which was sent is called in the Hebrew language <term>שעיר</term> <gloss>sahir</gloss>, which signifies a buck, a young goat, a hairy one, a devil, a bad thought, foulness, a bad mind, or a whirlwind. We are to understand by this that whatever is evil, diabolical, crafty, foul, hairy, and shaggy is destined for the desert and the devil. Hence <term>Jacob</term>, the smooth one, was beloved by the Lord; he took the birthright from his brother, received the blessing, and obtained dominion over his brothers, being supported always and everywhere by divine favor. But <term>Esau</term>, the hairy and shaggy one, was cast out with all his leaders and the family proceeding from him to Mount <term>Seir</term> <note>original: "Sehir"</note>—a place named in the mysterious language by the very word used for everything destined for that place. For there are two things in man: one is spiritual, and the other is animal. And in the animal part there are again two things: one which is left to the <margin>Paul</margin> devil, and another which is transformed into something better and spiritual, as Paul says: *What is sown is animal, and what rises is spiritual.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:44; original: "Seminatur quod animale, & surgit, quod spirituale"</note> We have an image of this thing in the seed of plants, in which something is changed into a greening plant that produces fruit, but something else is soon corrupted and resolved back into the earth. These two are signified by these goats, one of which is offered to the <margin>Origen</margin> Lord, while the other is thrown to the Prince of corruption and death. Or these two he-goats (as Origen feels) are the two families of God and the devil: one of which, offered to the Lord, is sacrificed as a spotless, living, and holy victim.

# THE THIRD TONE. CCXLII

One [goat] is pleasing to God; the other indeed is sent away to the devil, for whom he lived: just as we read concerning the rich man and Lazarus the beggar <note>original: "mendico"; the OCR reads "medico" (doctor), but the context of Dives and Lazarus confirms the biblical beggar</note>: that the Angels carried the latter before the Lord, while the former was buried in hell, signified by the wilderness, which is a place deserted by virtues, deserted by God, deserted by justice, deserted by Christ, and deserted by every good thing. It should also be noted that the animals which are offered in sacrifices here and everywhere are not "unclean" but "clean." Although one of them is seen to be cast out as if it were unclean, this is done so that they may be understood to hold the form of those who are not merely outside the faith, but who have been offered to God through baptism. Some of these are reserved for God Himself, while others, having become unclean again, are handed over to the devil to be further tormented. To any of these it can be said, since they were once offered to God: *Sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.* <note>original: "Iam amplius noli peccare"; John 5:14</note> Therefore, when the goat is commanded to be given for sin, the command is to return the dross, the dregs, and what belongs to the devil back to him, so that what belongs to God may be returned to Him pure and clean. For that offering, like the others, was figurative. Or let us say that for the "goat-like" nature <note>original: "re capraria"; referring to unruly, lustful, or stubborn impulses traditionally associated with goats</note> which is poorly 

<margin>Song of Songs, Paul</margin>
governed within us, and which is commanded to be fed in the Song of Songs <note>original: "Canticis"; Song of Songs 1:8</note>—not without reason—beside the tents of the shepherds, a buck is given. <margin>John, <unclear>Matthew, Baptist</unclear></margin>
expiation, would utterly drive out our accuser. As John says in the <term>Apocalypse</term> <note>The Book of Revelation</note>: *Now salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ have come: because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the sight of our God day and night.* <note>Revelation 12:10</note> Therefore, all things must be left to the devil which agree with him in both fact and name: namely, evil thoughts, foulness, and whatever is "hairy" and rough within us. All these are called <term>sahir</term> <note>Hebrew for "he-goat" or "shaggy demon"</note>, just like the devil and the animal which was commanded to be offered for this kind of expiation. If, however, we wish (as we ought) to refer these things to Christ—who is the storehouse, the connection, the virtue, and the truth of all sacrifices—we certainly can. For in Him was the divinity, which neither sacrificed nor was sacrificed. There was also his humanity resulting from two things: namely, soul and body, or the animal and the spiritual. And both of these were offered for sin, as is said of those two goats. For his soul was offered to God for the sins of the people, according to that 

<margin>Isaiah, CHRIST, Luke</margin>
saying of Isaiah: *If he makes his soul an offering for sin.* <note>Isaiah 53:10</note> He did indeed lay it down, as he himself testifies, saying: *I lay down my life for my sheep.* <note>John 10:15</note> The body, also offered, was handed over to the will—I will not say of the devil—but of his members, as Luke says: *But he delivered Jesus to their will,* <note>Luke 23:25</note> specifically as far as the body was to be crucified. And just as he who carried the goat into the wilderness and handed it over to the power of the desert washed his clothes upon returning, so Pilate, bearing a certain likeness to that man, washed his hands when he had handed Jesus over to the power of darkness. Or let that goat be that which Jesus himself handed over to be crucified, crushed, and put to death, placing upon it—at the Father's command—our iniquities.

<margin>THE SAME John</margin> since He Himself is (as John says) the faithful witness. For we offer our prayers and oblations at this door when we say to the Father: "Through Jesus Christ our Lord," as if through the medium by which we are introduced and obtain whatever we seek. And because it is said that the Lord "smelled" those sacrifices as a "sweet odor," as if they were offered to Him and as if He were delighted by the scent of thick things <note>referring to the physical smoke and fat of burnt offerings</note>, we say for some measure of explanation that all those sacrifices were offered primarily to the honor of God, so that a portion might be given to various virtues as necessity required. And the Lord Himself "smelled"—not indeed those thick plumes of smoke—but was delighted by the sweetness resulting from the order by which everything was distributed to each, as was fitting.

### Why a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, were commanded to be offered for the purification of childbirth, and for the woman who has given birth. Chapter XVI. ###

IN the matter of purification after birth, it is a beautiful thing to examine why, by divine command, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons were offered. The reason for this (as I have learned from those more learned than I) is that even though marriage was ordained by God, it is nevertheless practiced without fault only with the greatest difficulty, given the current fallen state of human nature. This [faultless state] occurs when spouses live together specifically to generate offspring for the honor of God and the increase of the human race. But this happens very rarely, as each person yields to **concupiscence** <term>concupiscence: the persistent inclination toward worldly or carnal desires that theologians believe remained in humans after the Fall of Adam and Eve</term>, to itching desire, and to the fulfillment of lust. Consequently, the devil infects these means through which impurity is contracted. 

Therefore, to expel this [impurity] and to purify the seed received from both parents—that is, from both the father and the mother, who are both infected—a pair of turtledoves is offered. These birds are the most faithful of mates and rejoice in great purity. Alternatively, two young pigeons may be offered; these birds are themselves most simple and full of all purity, harming no one—especially the young ones, which are commanded to be offered. These birds are endowed with such purity that the Savior, the Wisdom of God, indicated the cleanliness and simplicity He requires from us through the simplicity of these animals, as if He possessed nothing simpler. He said: 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
*Be simple as doves.* <note>original: "Estote simplices, sicut columbæ"; Matthew 10:16</note> 
<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
And in the Song of Songs, the most pure bride is compared by the groom to a dove, when he says: *My friend, my dove, my beautiful one.* <note>Song of Songs 2:10-14</note>
<margin>David</margin>
The dove also flies with such simplicity and directness that the prophet <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms</note> desired to be carried to God on its wings, saying: *Who will give me wings like a dove? And I will fly away and be at rest.* <note>Psalm 55:6</note> 

And what is greater still, the Holy Spirit wished to be likened to no other animal except the dove alone, as we read in Matthew: 
<margin>Matthew</margin>
*And behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.* 
<margin>The Baptist</margin>
And the Baptist, in the Gospel of John, says: *I saw the Spirit descending, and it remained upon him.* For it descends just like a dove, which flies toward the depths with a steady and great impetus. Or it appeared in the form of a dove, as some say, supported by the words of Luke, who says: 
<margin>Luke</margin>
*The heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form like a dove upon him.* But even so, it is not concluded that it was [actually] in the shape of a dove, since a dove descending upon a man does not enter into him. It seems, therefore, that the comparison refers more to the flight or the characteristic [of the bird] than to its physical form. Or, if it is insisted that it actually took the shape of a dove, we would say that the figure, although bodily, was not thick or heavy, but subtle—so that nothing would hinder its entry into a man, just as a breath or fire descended and entered into the Apostles. Thus, He who purifies all things was compared to the most simple and pure dove, as is said in the Acts of the Apostles: 
<margin>Acts</margin>
*God sent the Holy Spirit to them, who [purified] by faith...*

This animal, therefore, being consistent with the purifying Holy Spirit, is appropriately offered for the purification of birth, prefiguring the purification to be performed by the power of the Holy Spirit himself, who is called the purifier of all outrages. And because the turtledove and the pigeon agree in the same purity, either of them is commanded to be offered indifferently by the poor, who do not have the means to offer a lamb; for the lamb, filled with that same purity as those birds, was commanded by the law to be offered by the wealthier. And because by the purification of one, the other is also purified, a pair of these animals is commanded to be offered without distinction.

But why this purification is appointed at the end of forty days is not without a mystery. For just as in forty days the seed, having become an embryo, is vitalized and transformed until it is brought into an organic body perfected in its due and harmonious measures, so that it is disposed to receive the masculine soul—which is the most powerful reason <note>or "essence"</note> of man—so the woman passes through forty days after the birth is produced, so that the female parts moved in birth may be restored before she is purified. <note>The author is referencing a common medieval belief, rooted in Aristotelian biology, that a male fetus was fully formed and received its soul at 40 days.</note> In the pigeon, therefore, or the turtledove, God (through a certain figure) purified the offspring and the woman giving birth through the priest, so that the whole newborn might be holy, hinting at the true purification to be performed through the High Priest Christ in the Holy Spirit—who came like a dove, and to whom it belongs (as we have said) to purify mankind. For when he gave us the power of purifying men from the defilement of sin, he said: *Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them.* <note>John 20:22-23</note> For God sends this spirit through his Son, as Paul says: 

<margin>Paul</margin>

->THIRD TONE. 244<-

it was commanded to be expiated with other birds / or indifferent ones: although in our translation <note>likely referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> those birds are expressed as **sparrows** which were commanded to be offered for the purification of lepers. For <margin>*Tzipporim* <note>original Hebrew: צפרים</note></margin> ***Tzipporim*** signifies birds indifferently, as we can understand from many places in Holy Scripture, and particularly from the present text, where it is said: "Command the priest, that he take two live, clean *zipurim*," for which our translation says "from those which can be clean." For if ***Tzipporim*** meant sparrows <margin>Origen</margin> specifically, it would not have been necessary to add "clean," or "from those which can be clean." In common, therefore, birds are commanded to be taken, which **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> thought were hens. But because the Scripture does not express more clearly what they are, let us therefore admit they were birds in general and come to the explanation of other mysteries. Two birds were commanded to be offered, of which one was sacrificed, or slaughtered, in an earthenware vessel over living waters. The other, however, [remaining] alive, was dipped with cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop into the blood of the sacrificed sparrow, with which he who was to be cleansed from leprosy was sprinkled seven times; and the live bird was released over the face of the field. Indeed, these two birds in the leper indicate two conditions of the flesh: for a certain part of the flesh lives, but the other part is so dead that if someone should prick it, the leper does not feel it. Therefore, the bird that is released alive indicates the purification or the sign of the living flesh that is not fully infected. But the other was killed for the purification and the revival of that pre-dead flesh. This also was done over waters—the first and most important wash for all filth—and "living" waters, because dead waters are commonly putrid, polluting rather than washing. Moreover, it was slaughtered in an earthenware and earthly vessel, which signifies the body, in which that volatile, animal spirit infecting the flesh itself (which we call pre-dead) must be purged through mortification. However, the live bird that was released into the field signifies that stronger flesh, or the spirits not yet infected, or the better soul. 

But ascending to the allegorical sense, the two birds indicate two pledges which that supreme purifier, **Christ Jesus**, offered for our expiation: namely, the spiritual man and the natural <term>animal man<gloss>the "soul-led" or physical aspect of human life, from the Latin *animalis*</gloss></term>. And this one was slain so that he might purge our concupiscence <note>strong desire or lust</note>. He is said to have been slaughtered in an earthenware vessel because he was sacrificed in his own body fashioned from the earth. And this [happened] over the watery power of mercy, the sign of which—together with the blood, which is the sign of justice—came out from his side as he was dying. Thus, the slain bird is the body, or his natural power extinguished in the vessel of his body. But the live bird is his spirit, or his soul, also offered for our <margin>CHRIST</margin> expiation, according to that which he said: *And I lay down my life for my sheep* <note>original Latin: "Et animam meam pono pro ouibus meis"; quoting John 10:15</note>. But since it could not be killed, it was released alive into the field.

Both of these were sprinkled with the blood of that true bird slaughtered for human salvation. But the divine nature was sprinkled in the garment of the human nature: concerning which Paul says: <margin>Paul</margin> *Found in appearance as a man.* Therefore the Angels said: *Why is your garment red and splattered?* Hyssop, or *libanotis* (as we have explained elsewhere), is a plant most excellent of all, as is known to the wise, and most fit for sprinkling, since it has woody little branches with very thick and tiny leaves. For this reason, the sprinklings themselves were commanded to be performed with it, representing the true sprinkling to be done by that plant or sprout, the best of all shrubs: of which Isaiah says: <margin>Isaiah</margin> *And he grew up like a sprout, or a plant before him.* Therefore, with the blood of the killed bird, the one to be cleansed was sprinkled seven times—a number indeed (as we have said elsewhere) most fit for forgiveness and atonement. Nor is it added in the text in vain: *And he himself shall be clean:* because many washings for cleansing and many medicines for healing are spent in vain; but this one was not empty, especially in the prefigured leprous human race, which without doubt was entirely cleansed by the blood of that true bird, Christ. Just as he flew from heaven to us, so, once we were purified, he flew back again to heaven. John, seeing that cleanser there <margin>John</margin> at the forefront of his most famous vision, says: *Christ loved us, and washed us from our sins in his blood*—cleansing us better and more effectively than the first-created man <note>protoplastes; referring to Adam as the first-formed human.</note> had infected us.
