### Why a calf, or an ox, was offered for sin at the same time as a goat. Chapter XVIII.

<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
**F**or sin, a goat is commanded to be offered—namely the father of the kids who will be placed on the left hand to be judged <note>A reference to the Last Judgment in Matthew 25, where the "sheep" are placed on the right and the "goats" on the left.</note>—so that through the offered goat, the goat-like or kid-like part that is within man might be expiated. For there is a lascivious portion in man similar to a goat, or a kid, or its mother goat, frisking about and destroying vineyards. Therefore, it must be expiated, restrained, bound, and led into the service of the better portion, just as it is said of another animal similar to this in the Song of Songs: <note>original: "Cantica," referring to the Song of Solomon.</note> *Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.* Regarding the kids, it is also said there: *Feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds*—those shepherds, namely, who are said in scripture to feed the sheep well. Their prince is he who says:
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
*I am the good shepherd, and I give my life for my sheep.* Therefore, these kinds of appetites must be offered and
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
chastened—those which destroy the vineyard, that vineyard which (as Isaiah says) is the house of Israel, the assembly of the elect, and the inheritance of the Lord. Speaking of this in parables, Christ
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
says: *Go you also into my vineyard,* into which flesh and blood cannot enter, nor that lascivious portion. Therefore, it was to be offered and expiated in the goat, in which there is a greater and more ingrained lasciviousness than in a kid—so much so that it reeks strongly, just as the flesh of those living too lasciviously reeks much more than the flesh of those living chastely. Nor is the beard, which this animal offered for sin possesses, devoid of mystery. For a beard signifies strength <note>original: "robur," meaning physical strength, hardiness, or power.</note>, which is manifold: sometimes good and to be preserved, and sometimes evil and entirely to be cut away. For there is the strength and virtue of the Greeks (says
<margin>Origen</margin>
Origen) <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> in wisdom acquired by human wit; and there is the strength of the Assyrians and Chaldeans in the knowledge of the stars and in the influence received from them; there is also the strength and virtue of the Persians and Egyptians in a more secret philosophy, even extending to pacts with evil spirits; there is also the strength of temporal lords in money, soldiers, and instruments of war; finally, there is the strength of carnal men, the generative power itself. And many similar things are all signified by the beard—not indeed that of the Nazarenes, <note>The Nazirites (Numbers 6) were Israelites who took a vow to remain consecrated to God, which included never cutting their hair.</note> which must never be shaved, nor diminished, nor cast down, but that beard which signifies the strength of those who are outside the bosom of the good, and beyond the river that divides those gathered in the bosom of Abraham from those who are buried (or to be buried) in hell, just as we are taught by the oracle of the prescient Isaiah. Who, when he prophesies concerning the birth of the Maiden <note>original: "Halmę," from the Hebrew 'Almah' (עַלְמָה), meaning a young woman or virgin.</note> and of Immanuel <note>original: "Himanuel," from 'Immanuel' (עִמָּנוּאֵל), meaning "God with us."</note> who will eat butter and honey so that he may learn to discern between evil and good, adds: *In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor those who are across the river, by the king of the Assyrians...*

## What the Sheep and the Lamb Signify. Chapter 19.

**A**lthough the Law commands that the goat, the calf, the sheep, the lamb, the cow, sparrows, turtledoves, and such things be offered, there is one reason for offering some and a different reason for others. For the purification of a birth, a lamb or turtledoves—or even two young pigeons—were offered. For the purification of lepers, sparrows were used. For sin, however, a calf and a goat were offered. But the red heifer <note>original: "vacca rubea," referring to the ritual of the Red Heifer in Numbers 19.</note> was offered for the universal and enormous crime of our first parents, and for the worship of the [golden] calf. Yet, I find that sheep and lambs are to be offered nowhere except for the purification of birth and for the establishing of peace between man and God. The reason for a mystery so sublime is so high and elevated beyond our view that we scarcely dare to speak of it. But I have considered it appropriate to first mention that <term>צאן</term> <gloss>zon</gloss> signifies the entire ovine family, namely sheep, rams, and lambs (both male and female); while <term>כבש</term> <gloss>chebes</gloss> or <term>כשב</term> <gloss>chesseb</gloss> (which is the same thing) signifies a very tender lamb. Sometimes—though always with a mystery—the word <gloss>zon</gloss> is placed in the Scripture, and sometimes one of those other two. Keeping silent for now about the sacred secret of this matter, let us state another: that the lambs or sheep, which shall be placed at the right hand of the Judge to receive blessing and life, have their origin from a higher place. Thus, it is not without mystery that our Redeemer, who proceeded from the Father, was called now a lamb and now a sheep.

<margin>John the Baptist, Isaiah</margin>
Of the latter, he than whom no greater has arisen <note>A reference to Matthew 11:11, identifying John the Baptist.</note> said, speaking of Christ: *Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.* <note>original: "Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi," from John 1:29.</note> But of both, Isaiah says: *He shall be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer.* <note>original: "Tanquam ouis ad occisionem ducetur, & quasi agnus coram tondente se," from Isaiah 53:7.</note> And because he took care to make us all sheep, he himself—out of a sheep and a lamb—was made the Good Shepherd, even to the point of laying down his life for his sheep. Therefore, the sheep is rightly a true "type" <note>In theology, a "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of him who made peace for all things through the blood of his cross; it is offered for the making of peace between man and God. For no one was equally able to reconcile us with the Highest Father as he who is in the bosom of the Father and proceeds from him. He is most expressly portrayed by the sheep and the lamb, both because they harm no one and are always beneficial with many kinds of kindness, and also because of an intrinsic property and origin of which it is not permitted to speak at present. For this reason, the sheep is not unworthily held in such high esteem that the greatest men and the shepherds most pleasing to God were keepers of sheep: such as Abel, the first to be honored with the name of justice and by the testimony of the Son of God; Abraham, the Father of Faith and of many nations; Jacob, the father of the chosen family and a prince and heir of God; Moses the lawgiver, who was more intimate with God than all the prophets; and David, chosen according to the Lord’s heart, the first King from the tribe of Judah, the singer of the Holy Spirit, and the restorer and supporter of the most sacred worship.

It concludes by highlighting the high status of shepherding through biblical figures like Abel, Abraham, Moses, and David.</summary>

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
And finally, he himself is the Redeemer of all and the Son of the most high God: who also declares that he came only to seek the lost sheep of the Israelite and chosen family. For whose leading out from Egypt—that is, from the narrowness and darkening of sin—he was offered like a sheep and a lamb, just as that symbolic lamb was sacrificed by the command of the Law. While it would be most difficult to explain every detail of this mystery, we shall nevertheless run through a few points by way of a sketch. It is commanded in the Law that every family take a lamb to be sacrificed and entirely eaten, so much so that if a single family is too small to be sufficient for eating it, they should take in a neighbor as a guest. For every family must take a lamb, lest any remain deprived of the favor of the true Lamb, of whom that one carried the symbolic type. It is also commanded to be eaten in its entirety, lest anything remain to be wasted, according to the word of that same true Lamb: <note>John 6:12</note> "Gather up the fragments, so they do not perish" <note>original: "Colligite fragmenta, ne pereant"</note>: because nothing of precious things ought to perish through our neglect. Indeed, Bread and the Lamb are esteemed at the same value by those who know; therefore the Redeemer specifically wished to be named both "Bread" and "Lamb." The lamb had to be a male, in whom a more noble and stronger virtue might flourish. It had to be a year old—that is, perfect throughout the whole course of the sun—which itself signifies the Redeemer who makes fertile the twelve princes <note>The twelve Apostles</note>, whom he established over the twelve tribes of the chosen, just as the sun in a year makes fertile the twelve celestial signs <note>The Zodiac</note>. It also had to be without blemish, to signify divine things, which are all whole and perfect, according to the word of the prophet: "The works of the Great God are perfect." And our Lamb says: "I have made the whole man healthy."

<margin>Moses</margin>
It is added that a goat should be taken with the same rite, which (as we said recently) was offered for the expiation of the <term>animal man</term> <gloss>the physical or sensory nature of a human being</gloss>, just as the lamb and the sheep were offered to reconcile the "better man" <note>The spirit or higher soul</note> with God, so that the whole man might make a perfect passage to the true land of promise. But while the lamb is ordered to be sacrificed on the tenth day, the goat was kept until the fourteenth, not without a <term>sacrament</term> <gloss>a sacred mystery or hidden meaning</gloss>. For when the course of life designated by the complete number ten is finished, the perfect expiation of the animal and <term>quadrielemental</term> <gloss>composed of the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</gloss> man is still drawn out. Because once the spirit is blessed and restored to God (who gave it at a certain curriculum of time determined by the Father), the relief of the animal man and the fourfold body from corruption is extended, as is its passage into a heavenly and blessed nature. Therefore, to indicate that the whole man is to pass from "Egypt" to the true promised fatherland of the heavens, the whole man is expiated: first the better part through the lamb, and afterwards the remaining fourfold part through the goat, which is why the goat is reserved to be sacrificed after the fourth day <note>The four days represent the four elements of the physical body being purified after the spirit (the 10th day)</note>. Truly, the lamb is commanded to be sacrificed and eaten with greater observance and more celebrated ceremonies, because more diligent care must be had for the sanctification of the "heavenly man"; and from his sanctification follows the sanctification of the "earthly man." And so that a wide entrance may be granted to both types of man, it is commanded that from the blood of the sacrificed lamb...

<margin>Paul</margin>

<margin>The Law</margin>
> You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
And since the head ought to be loved and received above all members, therefore mention is first made of the head, and it is said:
> You shall eat the head with the feet and the intestines:
And so that we may observe diligently, lest we exclude anyone from our love and communion, it is commanded that nothing remain uneaten. If indeed anything remains, let it be given to the fire, so that it may eat it and offer it, transformed, to God: because if there is anyone to whom we cannot bestow the benefit of love and actual service, let us offer him to God, cooked by the fire of love and commended by prayer. However, we must eat with unleavened bread, that is, with sincere charity; in which there is not even a little leaven of wickedness, and malice, or hypocrisy corrupting the bread of love. And though such spoiled bread might seem sweeter to the taste, it nonetheless contains the malice of corruption: which, like all other things, was commanded to those fathers in a symbolic figure.
<margin>Paul</margin>

<margin>Peter</margin>
it may be eaten with affection and appetite: which contributes to good digestion and the transformation of the one eaten into the one eating: or with bitterness and the mortification of the animalistic man, so that the spiritual man may become stronger and more fit for digestion. This is expressed more clearly in the things which follow: for it is added
<margin>Leviticus</margin>
> You shall gird your loins,
namely, so that nothing carnal may be felt or thought during this eating. ### fine flour smeared with oil. Chapter XX.

But since enough has been said regarding the offering of the flesh of various animals, it remains for us to run through something concerning the breads: which are commanded to be offered under various figures and manners, not without a profound mystery perceived by very few. <header>THE THIRD TONE.</header>

# THE THIRD TONE.

...it is commanded to be offered <gloss>Hebrew: *solet murbebet halot*, that is, fine flour added with a cake</gloss> and that whole thing kneaded together and wrapped in oil. Our translation <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> is so entangled and confused in this passage that neither the action, nor the mystery, nor the sacrament—which is a great thing—can be perceived. For these things, together with what is said concerning the **bread of the faces** <note>original: *panis facierum*, traditionally known as Showbread</note>, are the most deeply hidden secrets. They serve as a symbol for that sacrifice which our High Priest, Jesus Christ, commanded to be offered for our food and our life, and in remembrance of Himself. It is a sacrament, moreover, because through that single bread compacted from diverse grains and transformed into His own body, He suggests that all of us, who are His members, are to be fashioned into one body through charity and love, and afterward offered to God as a holy **offering** <term>hostia: a sacrificial victim or bread used in the liturgy</term>, pleasing to God Himself, so that we may finally be transformed into Christ, so that we may say: *I live now, not I, but Christ lives in me* <note>Galatians 2:20</note>. This High Priest, just as He was seen on earth, enclosed the whole sacrifice in flesh and bread—as if expressing, above all else, that our body is to be joined with our head, Christ, and our soul is to be transformed into God—likewise when He once spoke to His beloved Israel, He enclosed the figurative sacrifice in this way: namely, in flesh and bread. And He ordained certain loaves to be placed upon the table in the Tabernacle before the face of the Lord who was present there; hence it was called the **bread of the faces**, that is, placed before the Lord. It was not lawful for anyone to eat of this bread except the priests and those who were clean from women and from the union of the body for the previous three days, just as Ahimelech made clear to David when David was demanding that bread in a moment of extreme necessity—a condition for which alone it was permitted for those who were not priests to eat it. That holy bread expressly signified that bread which descends from heaven, which is the true bread of the faces, because it leads us into the life in which we shall see God face to face. And just as that bread was not handled except by priests alone, nor given except to the clean, so this bread is not handled except by priests, and it is forbidden to be given to the unclean under the greatest threat, 
<margin>Paul</margin> 
as Paul says: *He who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment unto himself* <note>1 Corinthians 11:29</note>. Indeed, if we weigh the matter well, it is not given except to priests, because it is given only to Christians, 
<margin>Peter</margin> 
to whom Peter says: *You are a royal priesthood* <note>1 Peter 2:9</note>. For we are members of Him who was appointed a priest according to the order of **Melchizedek** <note>Hebrew: *Malki-tzedeq*, meaning King of Justice</note>; because we have all offered ourselves in baptism, having been put to death in the flesh, but made a living offering to God. And so that God might perfect the mystery of the bread, 
<margin>Leviticus</margin> 
He commands in Leviticus that oil be added, which (as we have said elsewhere) signifies the divinity with which kings, prophets, and priests offering sacrifices were anointed and drenched. The loaves were also anointed, signifying those things in us which are to be drenched with divinity, namely our souls. For that flesh signified another body of Christ, which He drew from the purest blood of the Virgin, and afterward our own bodies which are to be offered together with Him whose members we are. But the bread represents that soul of our Priest which descended from heaven, and consequently our souls which are to be drenched with the fullness of His divinity; therefore those loaves signifying these things were commanded to be [anointed] with oil...

# Page 218
## OF THE SECOND SONG

->of the deep.<- But observe, I pray you, the order of this pouring out: For first, there was offered an unleavened cake kneaded with oil; afterward, wafers only smeared with oil; and finally, fine flour was added to the cake, which was kneaded together with the cake in oil, along with unleavened bread. By these things is denoted the departure of the soul (signified by the bread) from God, its progress in life, and its rightful return into God himself. For our soul, while it departs from God, feels the nature of its parent and of God breathing into it; whence it is said to be enveloped and kneaded with divinity. The sign of this is that it knows not how to do harm, it gladly performs divine deeds, and it seems to aspire toward God, whose seed it still retains while fresh, until it becomes darkened and puts to flight God its guest by admitting the delights of inferior things and of sin; when these enter, God withdraws. 

But because the soul is not utterly forsaken, even if it be in sin and full of earthly affections, it is still "Christian"—that is, "anointed" <note>The author plays on the Greek etymology of *Christos* meaning "Anointed."</note>—and therefore it is designated by the wafer only smeared with oil. If, however, a person labors to return to God and to become his son, according to the power delivered to him by God, then he is again anointed with the oil of divinity and is filled from the fullness of Christ, just as happened to those ancient fathers of whom it is said: *They were all filled with the Holy Spirit* <note>Acts 2:4</note>. And then the person returns to that state and covenant with God in which we were when we first came forth from him. 

To this state the heavenly teacher desires us to arrive; indeed, he exhorts us even with threats that we might arrive there, when he says: *Unless you become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven* <note>Matthew 18:3</note>. This is invited by the cake or the roll which is commanded to be offered, kneaded with oil, in the third place. 

Furthermore, the fine flour <term>simila: the finest, whitest wheat flour</term>—that is, the "deflowered" flour, whiter than the rest, from which the Easterners are accustomed to make very white coils—indicates that better portion of divinity which we acquire in the pure, clean, and faithful service of God, through the gift of divine grace. This is signified by the five or two talents acquired beyond those originally delivered to the good merchant <note>Reference to the Parable of the Talents, Matthew 25</note>. For we ought not to remain content with the talent provided, lest we be rebuked as sluggish and ungrateful by him who delivered it. 

There is added yet to this cake and fine flour a leavened bread with a sacrifice of praise, namely in the peace-offering of the one sacrificing. This leaven is not that of wickedness and malice which corrupts the whole mass, but a better leaven transforming the person into a stronger and higher degree, and into that same image which is the Son of God—being the true stone, not that of the philosophers or physicians, but the heavenly and divine stone, which is Christ. Therefore he enters into us, so that he may make us divine and heavenly, of whom Peter says: 

<margin>Peter</margin>
*Coming to him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen and honored by God* <note>1 Peter 2:4</note>. He who is now our foundation is also a certain sanctifying and transforming power; therefore Peter follows with: 

<margin>The same</margin>
*And you yourselves, like living stones, are built up into spiritual houses*—behold the first part. Afterward, concerning the second, he follows saying: *Into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ* <note>1 Peter 2:5</note>, who namely by his power transforms us into true priests and sons of God, so that we may be co-heirs of his kingdom and glory. This power and authority he bestowed upon us, just as he delivered himself to be eaten: so that we, having been made ungrateful <note>The text likely intends "ingrafted" or "transformed," though the Latin *ingrati* literally means ungrateful; it may be a printer's error for *ingratiati* (graced) or *ingrafti*</note> into him, might be transformed into the bread of heavenly divinity, kneaded with oil and leavened by his grace and power.

### What is incense-burning, or the censer, incense, and the act of perfuming? Chapter 21.

<margin>A lie has <unclear>all its</unclear> feet.</margin> <note>original: "Mendaciū totus pedes habet." This is likely a variation of the common proverb "a lie has no feet," meaning it cannot stand up to scrutiny.</note>
<margin>David</margin>
**N**or is the act of perfuming with incense, which He commands to be done in sacred rites, void of mystery: for it is just that both God be worshipped and the interior man <note>The "interior man" is a traditional term for the human soul or spiritual nature.</note> be nourished in all possible ways. For God is worshipped through hearing, when we fill Him, as much as we are able, with prayers and praises. The man is nourished through his ears by the food of all the words that proceed from the mouth of God, and by those internal speeches of which the Prophet says: <note>original: "Audiā qd loquat in me dominus Deus"</note> *I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me.* God is worshipped by the food that we set before Him, when He Himself enters to sup with us: and this food is the conversion and the attraction of our souls, just as 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Christ himself testifies when speaking to his disciples about the converted Samaritans, saying: <note>original: "Aliū cibū habeo māducare, quē uos nescitis"</note> *I have another food to eat, which you do not know.* And the man is nourished through the mouth by that bread which descended from heaven, and by the flesh of the lamb offered for us—He, surely, who took away the sins of the world. 
<margin>David</margin>
God is worshipped by our knowledge and meditation, of which the royal Bard <note>King David.</note> sings: <note>original: "Beati q scrutant̃ testimonia eius, in toto corde exqrunt eū"</note> *Blessed are they who search His testimonies; they seek Him with their whole heart.* And again: <note>original: "Et meditabor in mādatis tuis, quę dilexi"</note> *And I will meditate on Your commandments, which I have loved.* Our "better eye" <note>The eye of the soul or intellect.</note> is also nourished by that light which illuminates every man coming into this world. God is worshipped by a manifold burning of incense, so that in many places the Scripture says: <note>original: "Odoratus est Dñs odorē suauitatis"</note> *The Lord smelled an odor of sweetness.* And the "better man" is nourished through the nostrils, through which was infused that better soul which is the breath of life <note>A reference to Genesis 2:7.</note>; but it is certainly said in the literal truth that this same perfuming with frankincense and aromatic herbs comes from that place from which the breath of life itself was infused. Thus, the food is of the same kind as the one who is fed: and he who worships may harmonize with the medium by which he worships, and both together with Him who is worshipped. For the soul proceeds from the supreme 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
fountain of all good things, and the true giver of forms, through Him by whom all things were made, just as He Himself testifies, saying: <note>original: "Pater meus usqz modo opatur, & ego opor"</note> *My Father is working until now, and I am working,* either by creating anew, as our theologians say, or by infusing that which emanates from the fountain itself, as others assert. From that same place, both frankincense and perfumes of this kind—which are commanded to be burned in the Law—receive their origin and power, as the more secret <term>Theologians</term> <note>Likely referring to mystical or esoteric scholars, such as those of the Kabbalah or Neoplatonism.</note> say. For every single thing, as they teach, has a particular place in the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The divine blueprint or world of original ideas in God's mind.</note> from which it draws its power and origin. Hence the Lord receives a most sweet odor of this kind from those things which are returned to Him by a purified soul, now prepared to depart together with that incense-smoke. It was with such smoke that the divine Lyre-player <note>King David.</note> wished at least his prayer would ascend, when he sang, saying: <note>original: "Dirigatur Dñe oratio mea, sicut incēsum in cōspectu tuo"</note> *Let my prayer be directed, O Lord, like incense in Your sight.* Our soul also, the very offspring of God, delights in perfumes of this kind, receiving them through those nostrils through which it first entered into the "lower man" <note>The physical body.</note>; through which also, at times, are emitted those most <term>lively spirits</term> <note>In early medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried life and emotion through the body.</note> which cannot be held back in the heart when bile or labor is boiling over. From this, some believe that the sense of smell itself is more vivid and spiritual than the other senses. Furthermore, the incense which is commanded to be burned in the Law was composed of various spices and gums, gathered with such great art and <term>sacrament</term> <note>In this sense, a "sacrament" refers to a holy mystery or symbolic ritual.</note> that God commanded with a great threat that this composition should not be turned to other uses, nor burned for anyone other than God Himself, as is held at the end of the thr[ee]—

<margin>Paul</margin>
...[thirti]eth chapter of the book of Exodus, where it is said: *That incense shall be to you the Holy of Holies; which you shall by no means make for your own use, because it shall be holy to the Lord.* <note>original: "Sanctum sanctorum erit uobis thymiana illud... sanctum tibi erit Domino"</note> *Whoever makes such incense for its sensual scent shall be cut off from his people.* What exactly went into that composition and how it was prepared, I do not yet have perfectly explored, although some boast of their knowledge of that composition, and of the gum and the aromatic ingredients used to produce that incense. I find various opinions and interpretations regarding the gums and spices that make it up: <term>Nataph</term> <note>Hebrew: נטף</note> in our translation we have rendered as *stacte* <note>A precious oil of myrrh</note>, but others, not ignorant of the matter, assert that it is balsam, and others opobalsam. <term>Sachelet</term> <note>Hebrew: שחלת</note>, which our translation calls *onycha* <note>A shell-like ingredient from the Red Sea</note>, is held by others to be *ambraca* <note>Ambergris</note>. <term>Helbena</term> <note>Hebrew: חלבנה</note>, which our translator interpreted as galbanum of good odor, others assert is mastic. Likewise, though the text says all these are taken in equal weight along with the clearest or most transparent frankincense, nothing is said about the method of compounding them, except that it is to be done by the art of the <term>perfumer</term> <note>original: "pigmentarius" — a specialist in spices, pigments, and medicinal ointments</note>. What that art might be, God knows. Those ancient fathers also knew that they were accustomed to burn such perfumes for God; but for us, in whom the symbolic figure has given way to the truth, we must most diligently take care—instead of animal sacrifices and delicate incense—to offer ourselves to God as a holy victim, pleasing to Him, and as incense composed of various virtues by the grace and art of our supreme perfumer, Jesus Christ. Thus we may say with the Apostle: *We are the good odor of Christ to God and to men.* <note>original: "Christi bonus odor sumus," referencing 2 Corinthians 2:15</note>

->### THE FOURTH TONE<-

->J ii<-

### WHAT TRUTH IS, CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Truth</margin>
**S**O GREAT IS THE SPLENDOR OF TRUTH, that it overwhelms all weak eyes, and, exceeding the capacity of small strength, it causes offense. Hence the minds of the common people, and those not yet well purified, are more delighted by a thick lie than by a subtle truth. <margin>Wisdom</margin> For truth is a rectitude perceivable by the mind alone, as the Wise define it by common consensus. And if it is perceived by the mind alone, it is therefore not grasped by those who do not possess a mind in any sense, who do not savor the things which are of God, who is the source of all truth: whose proper power is harmony, and the agreement of the middle with the beginning and the end. 

Hence, by no small mystery, in the most ancient language (which is called holy), truth is described thus: אמת <note>Hebrew: *Emet*</note>. In which word the first letter of the alphabet, the middle, and the last are joined in agreement. For א <note>Aleph</note> is the first, ת <note>Tau</note> is the last, and מ <note>Mem</note> is truly the middle; and with their vowel points, it is pronounced *emet*. By these letters the entire texture of things is indicated—namely, the proceeding from the beginning into the thing itself, and the return at the end. And this is properly truth, and the rectitude that pertains to truth. 

Furthermore, to denote the firmness and stability of truth, its name is composed of letters that are "quadrate" <note>Square or solid</note> in two ways: in shape and in numbers. For the shape of these letters is such that they have firm feet and bases upon which each of them stands separately, and even more strongly all together; just as, on the contrary, the name signifying a lie is written with those letters which have no stability, and can stand neither separately nor joined together. Thus the proverb is true: a lie has short <margin>A lie has short feet.</margin> feet—indeed, it is lame and weak. For that name is written שקר <note>Hebrew: *Sheqer*</note>, which, pronouncing it in our tongue, we call *shecher* <note>original: "secher"</note>. 

In numbers also, all the letters from which the name of truth is composed signify a firm and solid <term>quaternary number</term> <note>The number four, which the author considers a foundation of stability</note>. For א <note>Aleph</note> signifies one and a thousand: one is the solid principle and essence of all numbers; a thousand is also the cube of the complete number ten. מ <note>Mem</note> moreover signifies 40, which is a number derived through the complete number ten and through the radical quaternary number, the solid foundation of all numbers. ת <note>Tau</note> truly signifies 400, a number derived through the ten and the forty, or through the four and the hundred, which is the square of ten. For ten times forty, or four times one hundred, makes 400. Thus the numbers, as well as the shapes of the letters contained in the name of truth, are always solid. However, in the letters which compose the name of a lie, neither the shapes (as we have said) nor the numbers represented by them contain any solidity; whence it is implied that a lie easily collapses of its own accord. Furthermore, it should be noted that the numbers of the letters of a lie differ greatly from the numbers denoted...

<summary>This page defines truth through a Kabbalistic lens, analyzing the Hebrew word for truth (Emet) as a symbol of stability, containing the beginning, middle, and end of the alphabet. It contrasts this with the linguistic and numerical instability of the Hebrew word for a lie (Sheqer).</summary>

## Christ is the Truth.
### Cap. II.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**F**rom the aforementioned things, it is easily perceived how Christ is the truth, who not only makes the middle agree with the beginning and the end, but is himself the middle, the beginning, and the end, just as he himself testifies when speaking to John in the vision on Patmos, saying: I am <margin>α & ω</margin> alpha and omega, the beginning and the end <note>Revelation 21:6</note>. For he was speaking in the Greek language, just as the revelation itself was written entirely in the Greek idiom, and it is the same as if he had said in the Hebrew tongue: I am א <note>aleph</note> and ת <note>tau</note>. For of these, one is the first and the other is the last letter, just as in the Greek alphabet alpha is the first and omega the last. Therefore, no doubt remains that Christ is the first and the last, the beginning and the end: Who said again: "I am the beginning": And again: "I will draw all things to myself," as if to an end. This indeed was the only thing that remained: that he should also be established as the middle. Hence (as we shall explain in its proper place), he was made the middle and the mediator in many ways. Behold, therefore, the most elegant reason why the Word of God assumed humanity, a body, and the whole man as a creature of every kind: so that, existing as the beginning and assuming the middle—that is, man, who is the middle between God and other creatures and contains them all—he might lead him and all things in him to their proper end. And in this way, making the extremes and the middle agree with each other, he deservedly claimed the name of Truth for himself and said: "I am the truth." Moreover, he is allotted the name of Truth because <margin>THE SAME</margin> within him are the eternal rules to which all ought to be conformed in life and morals. Whence he himself is made the moderator of all things: the way, the door, the vine, the trunk, the rule, the teacher, the master, the regulator, directing all and filling them with truth, because he himself is most full, according to that saying of John: "We have seen him full of grace and <margin>John</margin> truth, from whose fullness we have all received" <note>John 1:14–16</note>.

## Christ is the truth of the law.
### Cap. III.

<margin>The same</margin>
**I**n this Christ, not only is every creature gathered, but the whole law and the prophets tend toward him to such an extent that he is the truth of the law itself: because through him and in him the whole law is verified. And this is what John says: "The law was given through Moses, but grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ" <note>John 1:17</note>, by fulfilling, namely, those things which were written of him in the law.

<margin>Philip.</margin>
And in this sense Philip says of him—who had not yet fulfilled the scriptures—"We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets: Jesus the son of <margin>CHRIST.</margin> Joseph of Nazareth." <note>John 1:45</note> And Truth itself <note>referring to Christ</note> says: "Moses wrote of me," wishing to imply that those things which were written in the law are verified in him. This is indeed true, but in various ways: for sometimes his genealogy is unrolled; sometimes the scripture speaks of him typically and figuratively; elsewhere it is through the effects shown by the power of the coming Christ; in other places it truly prophesies by promising his coming; and in many locations it records his dignity, glory, power, and most noble works of many kinds. And all these things are hidden by that veil, so that unless it is removed, it can nowhere be clearly perceived where Moses wrote of Christ. But with the face revealed, we will be able to gaze upon something of the glory of the Lord. May he, by his kindness, grant this, who—as <margin>SAME Luke</margin> Luke tells it—beginning from Moses and the Prophets, so interpreted the scriptures to his two companions that they said: "Was not our heart burning within us, while he opened the scriptures to us on the way?" <note>Luke 24:32; the story of the Road to Emmaus</note> For the unweaving of the genealogy begins from the first-formed man <note>Adam</note>, proceeding through the whole Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>, and through the books of the leaders, judges, and kings, and through the books of the days, which they call *Paralipomenon* <note>The Books of Chronicles</note>. From these, Matthew and Luke took what they would briefly review regarding his genealogy. And although those two may sometimes seem discordant, they nevertheless do not relate false things; for one describes the natural lineage and the other the legal lineage, <margin>Jerome.</margin> <margin>Augustine.</margin> as Jerome and Augustine discuss at great length. Truly, through figures and likenesses, we have our Christ depicted in almost innumerable places: for in the entire sequence of the tabernacle, the sacrifices, and the priesthood of Melchizedek and Aaron (as Paul interprets), he himself is described in great sacraments <note>or "sacred mysteries"</note>, as we have somewhat shadowed forth above. It is no different regarding Jonah sent to the Ninevites, who, fleeing into Tarshish, is cast into the sea, and finally by his preaching impels the Assyrians to repentance; just as Truth itself reported that matter to have been shown as a type and sign of himself. Likewise also in the whole history of Abraham, who (as <margin>Paul</margin> Paul interprets when discussing with the Galatians) fathered two sons, signifying two testaments: one indeed in the servitude of the law, the other truly in the liberty of the spirit. And the son of the handmaid was first by birth, just as the testament of servitude was; but the later son and heir was the son of the free woman, just as the testament of liberty in the spirit promises a true and everlasting inheritance. And just as the son of the handmaid then persecuted the son of the free woman, so also for a long time since, those descending from the son of the handmaid—who are called Ishmaelites—have persecuted and do persecute the co-heirs of Christ, until the time is given when there shall be one fold and one shepherd. And then all things will be seen fulfilled in clear light. This time (unless I am mistaken) is very near. Moreover, the effects which are said to be shown in the law by the power of Christ are almost infinite, yet all proceeding from one root: which root is redemption, or liberation, clemency, piety, mercy, and the forgiveness <margin>The same</margin> of sin, according to that word of the Apostle: "When you were dead in your sins, he brought you to life together with him..." <note>Colossians 2:13</note>

### How one iota, or one dot of the law, shall not pass away without being
### completed and verified in Christ. Chapter IV.

<margin>Simeon Elchana</margin>
The **I**ota is the smallest letter of the alphabet, while the dot is a point or an accent. All these things have been placed in the Scripture with their due number, weight, and sacred mystery <note>original: *sacramento*; implies a hidden, holy meaning or "sacrament" within the text's structure.</note>, so much so that Rabbi Simeon Ben Jochai <note>A 2nd-century tannaitic sage to whom the *Zohar*, the foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), is traditionally attributed.</note> and after him Elchana <note>likely referring to a medieval Kabbalistic author such as Elkanah ben Jeroham.</note>, and others, attempted not only to interpret the sentences and words, but also to give an account of the letters and their very shapes, along with the dots placed below and above them. And to bring something forward as an example, when interpreting the first word of the Law, which is <term>בְּרֵאשִׁית</term> <note>Hebrew: *Beresit*, meaning "In the beginning."</note>, they first ask why the Law and the description of the creation of the world begin with the letter <term>בּ</term> <note>Hebrew: *Bet*, the second letter of the alphabet.</note>. They respond: Because <term>בּ</term> (Bet) signifies a house, and it indicates the "higher wisdom" in which all things were placed before they were led forth into their own forms, and through this wisdom all things were produced, according to that saying of the Psalmist: *You have made all things in wisdom.* <margin>David John</margin> John supports this, saying that all things existed beforehand in the Word <note>original: *verbo*; referring to the *Logos* in the Gospel of John 1:1.</note> as a kind of creative life, and afterwards all things were made through that same Word. Secondly, it is asked why the following letter is <term>ר</term> <note>Hebrew: *Resh*, the letter corresponding to the number 200.</note>. And to omit many of the things that Elchana touches upon, some say that since the *Bet*—carrying the number two—denotes the first "product" in divine matters (which is the Son and the second person of the Trinity), <margin>Elchana</margin> the <term>ר</term> (Resh)—carrying the value of two hundred—hints at the first thing produced in the coarsest of things, namely matter, which among the <margin>Pythagoras</margin> Pythagoreans is denoted by duality. See, therefore, how the Hebrew doctors, by referring to the mysteries of the letters, confess the Father and the Son, and consequently the entire Trinity. Hence, in a wondrous order, three other words follow, the first letters of which, placed in the proper order, constitute the name **Iesu** <note>ישו</note>. Therefore, because this new name has been raised up, which the mouth of the Lord has named, this prophetic hymn begins: "Sing to the Lord a New Song." Hence the heavens, the sea, the lands, and the fields are invited...

### Christ perfected the Law. Chapter V.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**N**or did he only verify the law by completing all things contained in it, as he himself testified saying: "I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it," <note>Matthew 5:17</note> but he also perfected it, and led it to a better degree through the Gospel, which signifies "good news." It is just as if someone were to take lead characters <note>A very early reference to movable type in the printing press</note> impressed and arranged in a tray to express harsh things, and then rearranged those same characters to express sweeter and more sublime words, while the shape of the characters remains the same. In the same way Christ did not invent another law, but perfected the same law, and led it into a better lot, so that it may seem like another, when it is nevertheless not, but the same—just as a cloth when it is dyed with kermes <note>original: *uermiculo*; a brilliant scarlet dye derived from insects</note> or some precious color, is perfected and not changed. The law was therefore perfected, dyed and colored by the blood of Christ much more happily than it was [previously] sprinkled [with the blood of animal sacrifices].

### What the red heifer and its ashes signify in sacred rites, and in the expiation of the defiled. ###
<margin>Chapter VI</margin>

<margin>CHRIST. <unclear>Exod. 32</unclear></margin>
**E**ven though all the expiations <note>rituals for the removal of guilt</note> were established by the Supreme Lawgiver in a wonderful order, the mystery of the **red heifer** <term>red heifer (vaccæ rubeæ) — An Old Testament sacrifice (Numbers 19) whose ashes were used for ritual purification, seen by Christians as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ's cleansing power.</term> was esteemed as the most excellent and the most celebrated above all other sacrifices. Let us see, then, if it was ordained for the expiation of the crime of the erected calf: for the children of Israel, having been led out of Egypt and released from the yoke of that dominion (which was ruled by the Ram), yet still fearing that influence...

Deprived of their leader <note>referring to Moses, who was atop Mount Sinai at the time</note> (as they believed), they wished to adopt a power stronger than that of the Egyptian bull—namely, the one which sits in the celestial circle after Aries <note>The author is using astrological symbolism here: Taurus (the Bull) follows Aries (the Ram) in the zodiac</note>. Therefore, by a certain more secret art, after things were arranged and the metal was melted according to custom, a calf was fashioned. Raising it up, and still ignorant of divine matters, they thought they could draw out a power superior to Aries, and from there prevail (if need be) against those who were ruled by Aries. But this was a mistake and a very great sin, as they wished to attribute to the celestial bull the favor they ought to have looked for from the living God, just as they had received it until then. The error was also increased because they raised up an image of a beast against the commandment of God, their helper. 

For this crime and wound, by God’s own command, two remedies were applied. One: many were ordered to be expiated in their own blood. This was carried out by the sons of Levi, by which they earned the blessing of which that family had been deprived because of the crime committed against the people of Shechem <note>Referring to the massacre in Genesis 34, for which Levi was originally rebuked by Jacob; their zeal against the idolaters in Exodus 32 restored their standing</note>. The second remedy was this red heifer. Let us briefly run through its mystery: Observe, I pray, the order. A cow (or heifer) is chosen to counter the sin of the worshipped calf, so that purification might be made through the very thing by which one sinned. 

However, the weaker sex <note>the female heifer vs. the male calf</note> is chosen, so that we do not believe the expiation comes from the power of the animal itself. For it was not from the animal, but from the divine power that the purification flowed. Hence, not the "worthier" animal, but the weaker in sex is set apart. And so that it might be proved that the favor was to be drawn not from the animal itself, but from heaven, God commanded it to be burned with all its entrails—specifically with that fire which was administered from heaven for receiving burnt offerings, as we can learn from many places in Scripture and as is widely known by famous report among the Hebrews. This fire (as they say) was given from heaven throughout the entire time of the First House <note>The First Temple of Solomon</note>, but was also sometimes supplied in the Second, as we have from the second volume of the <margin>Nehemiah</margin> Maccabees. There it is read that Nehemiah, coming from Persia to sacrifice, sought the hidden heavenly fire and did not find it, but found a thick water instead. He ordered the sacrifices to be sprinkled with this, since he did not have fire administered from heaven <note>A reference to 2 Maccabees 1:19-22, where the "thick water" miraculously ignited</note>. 

Furthermore, Elijah, in the time of the First House, in order to prove that the worship of his God was better than the worship of the prophets of Baal, exposed his sacrifice to fire to be supplied from heaven, demanding that the prophets of Baal do the same. And when the fire by no means consumed the sacrifice of those false prophets, but did burn Elijah’s sacrifice—presenting it to heaven transformed into fire—Elijah’s worship was proved true and good, as is held in the third volume of Kings <note>Known today as 1 Kings 18</note>. Therefore, when the cow had been burned by this fire along with all its intestines, the defiled were sprinkled with <margin>Paul</margin> those ashes, according to that saying of Paul: *For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, being sprinkled, sanctifies the defiled for the cleansing of the flesh* <note>original: "Si enim sanguis hircorum, et taurorum et cinis vitulae aspersus inquinatos sanctificat ad emundationem carnis"; Hebrews 9:13</note>. This refers to the flesh and blood through which sin comes into man; therefore sin tastes of the nature of red blood. Hence the sinner Esau was called Edom (that is, "Red") and is said to have sold his birthright for something red. The first parent also, through whom sin was introduced to all, was named Adam, because from the earth... <note>The name Adam is etymologically linked to "adama," meaning red earth or ground</note>

"red" (as they say) in our language. But if we carefully weigh those characters, that name signifies that which is "blood-stained with divinity." For it is composed of <term>א Aleph</term> <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often used by mystical writers to represent God or the Divine unity</note>, which is the letter indicating divinity, and <term>דם dam</term>, which signifies blood. For this reason, for the expiation of sin, it is most especially a red heifer that is chosen—not only because of the adored calf <note>The Golden Calf of the Exodus</note>, but also on account of the first-formed man <note>protoplasti; referring to Adam</note>. This signifies not the redness of flesh and blood, but a better redness, of which it is said in the 
<margin>Canticles</margin> **Canticles**:
> **My beloved is white and ruddy: white indeed in his innocence, ruddy in his charity and fiery fervor.** <note>original: "Dilectus meus candidus, & rubicundus: candidus quidem innocentia, rubicundus caritate, & igneo feruore." This refers to Song of Solomon 5:10, interpreted here as a description of Christ.</note>
And just as Adam, through whom sin was brought into the lower world, was called "red" or "red earth"—because he was drawn from <term>אדמה adama</term> <note>the Hebrew word for earth or ground</note>, which signifies red earth—so too David, chosen according to the heart of the Lord, was called <term>אדמוני Admoni</term>, that is, red or ruddy, as we 
<margin>Kings</margin> have in the first volume of **Kings** <note>1 Samuel 16:12</note>. And Christ, descending from him—the heavenly man from heaven, the repairer of the sin brought in by the first earthly man—was red, if painting teaches us the truth, and those who describe his physiognomy <note>the practice of judging character or nature from physical features</note>. His redness was so effective that, just as the brightness of his transfigured body overflowed into his garments so that they appeared white as snow, so too the fervor of his suffering was diffused into his garments, so much so that (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian and philosopher</note> witnesses) the wondering Angels said that line of 
<margin>Isaiah</margin> **Isaiah**:
> **Why has your garment become red?** <note>original: "Quare rubeum factum est uestimentum tuum?" From Isaiah 63:2.</note>
It is no wonder, then, if a red heifer is commanded to be chosen to prefigure the expiation to be made by the ruddy heavenly man for the sin contracted through the red earthly man. But this heifer had to be perfect, defiled by no blemish, and having carried no yoke of inferior servitude, so that it might fully indicate the purging which was to be done in the law of liberty, and most perfectly by Him who freed us from all servitude. And so that it might more easily receive the heavenly influence (if any was then given), which turns away from the defiled and those corrupted by any blemish, as we are more clearly taught in the Law. The heifer was also slaughtered outside the camp, as the 
<margin>Paul</margin> Apostle says to the Hebrews regarding this and the true burnt offering:
> **The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary for sin were burned outside the camp. For which reason Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his blood, suffered outside the gate**, <note>original: "Quorum animalium infertur sanguis pro peccato in sancta, horum corpora cremabantur extra castra: Propter quod & Iesus, ut sanctificaret per sanguinem eius populum, extra castra passus est". From Hebrews 13:11-12.</note>
so that he might expiate even those who had been excluded from the assembly of the 
<margin>CHRIST.</margin> righteous through sin, according to what the supreme Redeemer says:
> **I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.** <note>original: "Non ueni uocare iustos, sed peccatores". From Matthew 9:13.</note>
And again through another Evangelist:
> **The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.** <note>original: "Venit Filius hominis quærere, & saluum facere, quod pierat." From Luke 19:10.</note>
From the blood of the slaughtered heifer, the priest, with his finger dipped in it, sprinkled seven times toward the front of the tabernacle—certainly a number of remission <note>The number seven was associated with the Sabbath, completion, and the forgiveness of debts/sins</note>—to indicate the remission to be made in the blood of the true burnt offering, who alone is the door through which we enter into salvation and life. Afterward, it was burned with that fire administered from heaven, so that it might be a suitable remedy, or at least a figure of the remedy, against the stain derived from the inferior and red fire. Finally, from the ashes of the burned animal, the defiled person was sprinkled (not without mystery), because nothing sanctifies our "red animal" <note>our fleshly or earthly nature</note> more than its mortification,

<header>### SECOND CANTO ###</header>
->SECOND CANTO<-

...and the burning was performed by that holy fire which the Redeemer came to send into the earth. <note>Refers to Luke 12:49: "I have come to bring fire on the earth."</note> 
But a wondrous <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "sacramentum"; here meaning a hidden spiritual truth</note> occurs: For if those ashes sanctified and cleansed the defiled, why did they defile the priest who carried those same ashes outside the camp, or the one who burned the heifer? For it was said of these ashes that they "purged the defiled and fouled the clean." From this I infer that since the mystery of this heifer and of the other sacrifices is manifold and profound—more so than almost anything else found in Holy Scripture—the question is therefore resolved in multiple ways and through various senses. <margin>Others</margin> Some, therefore, say that this defilement and purity were contracted by the priest burning it because the matter was more sacred than his priestly rank—just as happens to a layman or a woman touching the sacred vessels or the **Body of Christ**, which is to be handled only by those in holy orders. <margin>Others</margin> Others say it is because sacred things received with devotion and reverence cleanse, but when handled irreverently or investigated with curiosity, they defile. <margin>Others</margin> Still others say that, according to the literal sense, the one burning it was "unclean"—that is, in a state of ritual contact—until that animal was expiated through fire. And anyone who handled those ashes outside the camp, or in whatever manner, handled them as if they were a carcass <note>original: "morticinum"; the body of an animal that died of itself, which was ritually polluting</note>. Whence it immediately follows: *Whoever touches the corpse of a man shall be unclean for seven days; but if sprinkled with water containing those ashes on the third and seventh day, he shall be clean.* Others say that the proper place for those ashes was inside the camp; therefore, anyone touching them outside the camp was unclean, just as with consecrated things kept in an unsuitable place. 

If, however, we wish to scrutinize this matter further and reveal something of the hidden mysteries, we shall say that this **red heifer** is the **Blessed Virgin**, of the lineage of the "ruddy" David. Through her, a blessing was brought in that expelled the curse and the infection spread by Eve into the human race. <margin>The Name of Mary</margin> And lest we blush to assert this without reason, let us see briefly how all things agree in this sense: Eve was the "red one" of the earth <note>referring to the name "Adam," which means red earth</note>; Mary is the "red one" of heaven, full of the fiery Spirit, and full of grace and virtues. As the heavenly oracle proclaims— <margin>The Church</margin> or as the Book of **Ecclesiasticus** might say: **"My resting place is in the fullness of the saints."** <note>original: "In plenitudine sanctorum detentio mea." Sirach 24:16</note> Therefore, it says that this heifer was to be chosen perfect, whole, and without any blemish: one that had never been pressed by any yoke. This is just as the Virgin protested to the heavenly messenger, saying: **"Since I know not man."** <note>Luke 1:34. The "yoke" is interpreted allegorically as the yoke of marriage or sexual union.</note> Furthermore, the sacrifice of this heifer and all its mysteries were celebrated "outside the camp" and apart from the common assembly of even the chosen people. In the same way, all of Mary’s mysteries were celebrated outside the common law of nature: for she was announced by an Angel, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, made pregnant by divine power, and filled with a grace that was not common, but which was found with God, the primary fountain of all good things. She gave birth to a son without pain, the enclosure of her virginity remaining preserved, always proceeding beyond the laws of nature. <margin>Solomon</margin> Hence **Solomon**, seeking and investigating her in the book of **Proverbs**, says: **"A valiant woman, who shall find?"** And lest he seem to have searched in despair, he adds prophetically: **"From afar and from the furthest ends"**—or "from the inner chambers," as the literal truth has it—**"is her price."** <note>Proverbs 31:10</note>

And so that we may relate something of the mysteries of a more secret Theology,

This is the same amount yielded by the name of **Mary**, who was full of every virtue and strength, so that she might give birth without a man through a most hidden mystery—one which I have not yet seen explained by anyone in writing. There was also present in that most high ritual of expiation the larch, or the "cedar" as our translation has it, and the smallest of all, the hyssop. This is either rosemary itself or a species of it (as we have said elsewhere according to the minds of some), which is a very small tree or a larger plant, and perhaps participates in the nature of both, as happens in other cases we have touched upon elsewhere. Thus, the highest and the lowest trees were present: the former to denote the most eminent peak of Mary's excellence, according to what was said: *Blessed art thou among women*; the latter, however, to suggest her profound humility, of which she herself says: *Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.* <note>Quotes from Luke 1:42 and 1:48, the "Magnificat."</note>

<margin>Paul</margin>
With these things, the people were sprinkled, as if by a certain prelude to the true and perfected expiation that was to happen in **Christ**. <margin>Angel in Matthew</margin>

If, therefore, the law gives the knowledge of sin and does not justify, but the gospel truly justifies—and does so without the law—even though it was predicted in the law, the gospel is altogether something other than the law. CCLVIII

# OF THE SECOND SONG

...it is credited to him as righteousness: For this word (as Paul testifies) was brought forth not only for Abraham’s sake, but for all of us, to whom it is credited as righteousness as we believe in him who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, who was handed over because of our sins, and rose again for our justification <note>original: "iustificationem"; this follows the argument in Romans 4:23-25</note>. Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we boast in the hope of the glory of the sons of God. This glory and consolation we have in Christ, who is the fruit of the law and the true interpretation of the law itself, as well as its true perfection. For from that wisdom we have the means to be justified from the sins contracted through the law, the means to be liberated from the slavery of the law, and the means to obtain mercy and grace, which are the antidotes to the infecting law. For from the law we contract guilt, but from the gospel we receive medicine. From the law we feel punishing justice, but from Christ and the gospel we feel grace and mercy. From the law comes the offense; from the gospel comes the means by which the offense is forgiven. Through the law we all, like sheep, have gone astray; through Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life, our feet are directed into the way of peace. From the law, our iniquities weigh upon us like a heavy burden; but in Christ, the Father has placed the iniquities of us all. By the law the soul is wounded and made weak, but by Christ’s stripes <note>original: "liuore"; literally the 'livid bruise' or 'welt' of a wound, referencing Isaiah 53:5</note> we are healed.

## By what Rectitude of Truth Christ as God Governs the World. Chapter IX.

**B**ut before we come to those particulars which he taught according to the truth, let us see with what rectitude he governs the world—he to whom the Father gave all judgment and all power in heaven and on earth—even though it may seem contrary to those who do not fully perceive the things of God. Let us see with what hidden wisdom the supreme Moderator himself permits many evils, so that he may extract a greater good from them, and so that the wisdom and goodness of him who governs may appear. Just as in the beginning, in the construction of the world, he placed evil against good, the crooked against the straight, darkness against light, the passive against the active, cold against heat, and many things of this kind; in the same way, in the members of the true and mystical body, he has placed one against the other. In the world, he placed the right against the left; in the mystical body, he placed the angel of darkness against the Angel of light, and the wicked against the good. <margin>Clement</margin> From these, several are elegantly listed by Clement <note>referring to the *Recognitions of Peter*, a 4th-century text attributed to Clement of Rome</note> in the *Recognitions of Peter*: namely, Cain against Abel, the Giants against Noah, Pharaoh against Abraham and against his family chosen by God, the Philistines and Gerarites against Isaac, Esau against Jacob, the Magicians against Moses, the Tempter against the Redeemer, Simon Magus against Peter, the Gentiles against the believers, and the son of iniquity against Christ. Therefore, he is now called Antichrist by everyone, as if "against Christ." And so all things have their opposites, so that as if through a certain <term>antiparistasis: the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite (e.g., a light appearing brighter in total darkness)</term>, the harmony of the world and of the human body is held to be sweeter. <margin>Dionysius</margin> Wherefore Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian mystic and philosopher</note>, in the place where he treats of...

It then introduces Chapter IX, which argues that God governs the world through a balance of opposites (antiparistasis), allowing evil to exist so that the beauty of the good might be more clearly seen.</summary>

...concerning the divine names, he discusses evil, as if it were something pertaining to Divine providence and to the harmonious arrangement of things.

<margin>Amos</margin>
Hence also Amos broke out with great confidence:
> Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done? <note>Amos 3:6. In this context, "evil" refers to calamity or punishment rather than moral wickedness.</note>

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
And Isaiah, speaking in the person of God, says:
> I am the one creating evil: <note>Isaiah 45:7.</note>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Yet God does not create punishment, as some explain it, because the evil man generates it for himself from his own discordant habits and a disturbed mind: since every disordered mind (as Augustine rightly perceives) is a punishment unto itself. Therefore, God is "creating evil" in the sense that he created matter, which by its own nature is "evil" <note>original: "mala"; the author is likely using "evil" here in a Neoplatonic sense, meaning matter is the furthest point from divine perfection and lacks inherent form or goodness.</note>, and everything leaning upon it and adhering to it is drawn toward evil, because it causes one to recede from the first and highest act, which is the very rule of goodness and truth. He also "makes" every evil who made a nature that is changeable and joined to matter, from which it is made prone to evil. Nor should the Maker himself be judged evil for this, since he prepared and offers a much greater remedy of goodness to the one who desires it than is the natural proneness to evil. Nor could any creature be produced which, by its own nature, did not differ from the first rule—and by diverging from that rule in habits and will, the creature sins.

<margin>Anselm</margin>
Hence Anselm, and others following him, say that God could not have made a nature that was "impeccable" <note>term: <term>impeccable</term> (incapable of sinning)</note>: because he could not make another God who would be the first rule of all things. But since I would not wish to be a censor of divine power, nor to assert whether God could have done this or that, or not—since he himself can do many things which we are unable to understand—let us therefore abstain from such judgment and say that in the primordial distribution of things, it was absolutely required that a fitting limitation and measure of goods be given to each, lest anyone should presume to claim for themselves what had been granted by the highest Giver. For this reason, because the first apostate <note>Refers to Lucifer/Satan.</note> had been gifted more than was equal, he swelled with great pride, saying:
> I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God—that is, above all the elect—I will exalt my throne: I will sit on the mount of the covenant, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the height of the clouds—above those highest ones in which the Lord is accustomed to dwell—and I will be like the Most High. <note>Isaiah 14:13-14.</note>

And while he presumed to be made like God by his own strength, he receded from God as a sinner, and was made utterly unlike him. Therefore, to crush and punish his pride, it is added:
> Nevertheless, you shall be dragged down to hell, into the depths of the pit.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Moreover, it was fitting that every rational creature, knowing itself, should say with Augustine:
> When I stood, I stood through you; when I fell, I fell through myself; and when I had fallen, I would have always lain in the mud unless you had raised me up.

Finally, it was likewise appropriate for each thing to be so governed that their Moderator <note>The author uses "Moderator" as a title for God as the governor or director of the universe.</note> allowed them to carry out their own movements. Yet, if they should fall, they would be led back to the proper order by the Moderator's providence. In the first case, the most wise Maker is seen as a Distributor; in the second, as a kind and free Sustainer; and in the third, from the abundance of his goodness, as the best Restorer. Thus God made all things "very good" and ordered: and yet there is no evil which he does not "make" by granting a nature that is changeable and inclined toward falling by its own weight, unless it be sustained by the highest good itself—by whom things are created so that all might learn that the Creator is the same as the Sustainer and the Helper.

## OF THE SECOND CANTICLE.

...was: and thus we would be bound to Him in two ways, both because He is the Creator <term>opifex: literally 'artisan' or 'maker'</term>, and because He is the one preserving and perfecting us. Therefore, there is no evil, properly or formally speaking (as they say), that comes from the highest good; rather, that in which evil is grounded is nature—namely, a changeable nature—and that by which we are drawn toward evil is matter, which is utterly distant from the good, especially when the most wicked tempter <note>Referring to the Devil or Satan</note> drives us. He, who is utterly removed from God, seeks to gather everyone with him into the center of his own wickedness, and to tear them away from the sphere of goodness and happiness. Between these two (namely, the highest good and the most wicked perverter), man is placed in such liberty that God does not wish to be judged the perpetrator of good or evil,
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
according to that saying of Jeremiah in the Lamentations: *From the mouth of the Most High shall not come forth good or evil*, <note>Lamentations 3:38. The author interprets this to mean God does not "author" the specific act of sin, but grants the freedom of choice.</note> so that one might be the sole perpetrator of either, although He is the co-operator with anyone doing good. Nor is any evil found to be produced by God such that a man lusting after it commits a sin: because nothing exists outside the universe, and the things found within it are "very good," yet they are contained by their own limits and distributed by their own ranks. But evil is perpetrated when, having despised a greater good, we cling to a lesser one. Hence Dionysius
<margin>Dionysius, Hugh, Wisdom</margin>
<note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian philosopher; Hugh refers to Hugh of St. Victor, a medieval theologian.</note> and Hugh his interpreter, and all truly wise men agree that sin, both in angels and in men, was and is when someone, departing from the highest good, wishes to take delight in a lesser one. Hence God Himself encompasses the whole sum of sin while
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
saying through Jeremiah: *My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, the Lord; and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.* <note>Jeremiah 2:13</note> Nor is it only sin when a created good is preferred to the highest good, but also when, there being two created goods, the lesser is preferred—such as when one puts their own private advantage before the public good or the utility of many. 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Avoiding this error, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> said: *Not seeking what is profitable for me, but for the many.* In the same way, sin occurs when bodily pleasure is put before spiritual delight. It is (as we may finally conclude) sin and error when the due order is perverted, so that the saying of 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> is true: *Evil is the privation of order, or of due rectitude.* But this 
<margin>The Savior</margin>
error, or perversion of order, is not from any power granted by God, but from our own weakness or the darkness contracted by our laziness—which the Savior, 
<margin>Dionysius, Damascene</margin>
and with Him Dionysius and Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian</note>, call "night" or "darkness," saying: *He who is in darkness knows not where he goes.* And again: *He who follows me* (namely, the supreme director) *does not walk in darkness* (namely, as a sinner). This darkness is followed by the eternal night of hell, of which he says again: *The night will come when no one can work.* And just as night or obscurity is the privation of light, so error is the privation of rectitude. From this it is concluded that the very essence of sin is the privation of good: into which man runs either by perverting order in his choice, or by presuming for himself what he ought to acknowledge as from the supreme Teacher. Thus, the fault is not from God, but from a will choosing poorly or presuming too much. But that which is poorly chosen is indeed from God, as is the will itself, which by its own fault errs in choosing. It remains, therefore...

### Chapter 10: What Christ taught in truth concerning those things which must be believed.

<margin>No one before Christ expressly revealed the Trinity.</margin>
But concerning those things which our Teacher has handed down to us to be believed, all agree on those points which are called the "articles of faith." In these, the Trinity is expressly contained, having been explained by Christ. For no one before him had openly unlocked the Trinity, clearly expressing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and the <term>circumincession: the theological concept (also called perichoresis) that the three persons of the Trinity dwell within one another</term> of the persons themselves (as they say), just as Christ taught, saying: *I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.*
<margin>No one spoke a word regarding the production of the persons.</margin>
And regarding the production <note>The theological term for the "origin" or "coming forth" of the Son from the Father and the Spirit from both</note> of these persons, no one before him spoke a word, but Christ aptly explained it, saying: *I came forth from the Father*, just as a son truly begotten by him. And concerning the Holy Spirit, that he proceeds from the Father, he said: *The Spirit who proceeds from the Father.* Because he also proceeds from the Son himself—contrary to what certain Greek <term>scioli: literally "know-it-alls," a dismissive term for those with superficial or false knowledge</term> who, misunderstanding the words of their own fathers, falsely assert—he says: *He shall receive from me.* He did not merely receive the doctrine as a disciple of the Word itself, like a little boy instructed in schools, but he received his very being along with the understanding with which he had previously instructed the Apostles and the prophets.
<margin>The Holy Spirit received being and understanding from the Son.</margin>
For the wisdom and understanding of the divine persons, and their other properties or attributes (as they say), are not distinguished from one another, nor are they infused like <term>accidents: in classical philosophy, qualities that can change without changing the essential nature of a thing</term> starting anew. Hence, whatever one person is said to have received from another, it is immediately concluded that he received the whole of what that person is, and all the attributes belonging to him; since these can neither be separated nor received one after another. Therefore, just as the Son confesses that he came forth from the Father, and received doctrine from him in such a way that he calls it the Father’s doctrine and not his own, in the same way let us confess that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son together with the doctrine, and that he received the doctrine together with his personal being.
<margin>The Holy Spirit received doctrine together with personal being from the Father and the Son.</margin>
And since we have learned with sufficiently clear light from the words of our teacher Christ those things which are attributed to each person, and those things which Christ himself had come to accomplish, we can easily profess or chant the articles of faith with the Apostles. For when we have learned that the Father is the first fountain from whom the Son and the Spirit proceeded, we can attribute the construction of the world's fabric to him as the primary craftsman, saying: *I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.* And when we have learned that wisdom is attributed to the Son—in whom both the world and we ourselves were created, and through whom we are all enlightened, and who is called the true water, not only celestial but supra-mundane <note>original: "supramundana"; meaning "above the physical world"</note>—to him is rightly attributed the restoration of the whole fabric, and most especially the restoration of man. This was done so that all things might be restored by the same wisdom by which they were created; and that he might wash the human race with that washing flowing from the supra-mundane source, since it could not be cleansed by any earthly source, because this whole world was thoroughly infected. We profess this restoration while we recount the primary deeds of the Redeemer: namely his conception by the Holy Spirit, his birth, passion, burial, descent into hell to lead out the captives, resurrection, and ascension, and his return to the Father from whom he had come forth, so that he might happily carry all his followers there. And when we are taught regarding the Holy Spirit...

Nor was the Holy Spirit a stranger, by whose power the Virgin was made fertile and the Word was united with that assumed nature, through which he might repair the entire mass of the human race. 

These things, having been taught by our teacher, we lawfully profess. <margin>The nakedness of man was to be protected by the skin of Christ.</margin>

Afterwards, by our eating the flesh of that same better serpent, we would be healed from the wound inflicted by that most wicked serpent. <margin>The flesh of the serpent against the venom of the serpent.</margin>

<margin>Our redeemer and heavenly teacher Christ came with great power.</margin>
