<margin>No one can know of the secrets of the prince except those who are in his secrets.</margin>

These indeed are the things our teacher Christ taught us to profess, provided that we fulfill by our works what we profess and believe. And because some, not only in our own turbulent time but also in times past, have stubbornly attempted to assert that faith alone is sufficient for salvation, we shall attempt to briefly extract from the sacred words what is to be held firmly on this matter; for we cannot express it from any other source, since human reasons are less than sufficient, nor should others be believed concerning those things which are handled in the secret court of the Prince <note>God</note>, except those who are in the secrets of the Prince himself. Such were, in our business, the Apostles, Evangelists, Prophets, and the Prince Christ himself, our supreme teacher, to whom all owe indubitable faith.

## Why faith alone, which is pure belief, is by no means sufficient for salvation. Chapter XI.

<margin>Faith alone [is] pure belief.</margin>

Truly indeed, not only in this time, but much earlier ones—even among the Hebrews—wished to assert that faith alone is sufficient for salvation. And those were called Rabbis: because they followed the opinions of certain masters. Against them, on the opposite side, arose another sect called the <term>Caricni: likely the Karaites, a Jewish sect that rejected oral Rabbinic tradition in favor of the written text of the Tanakh alone</term>, because they followed only the reading and text of the sacred scripture, admitting no human opinions nor the sophisticated reasons of the masters. 

<margin><insert>The newer ones.</insert></margin>

Omitting their reasons and their inventions of ignorance, we shall come to our contemporaries, who, leaning on many authorities of the Gospel and the Apostles which seem to assert the same, have dared to attribute so much to faith that they somehow condemn works. Indeed, they seem to assert that faith cannot exist alongside works, because if anyone presumed to be <term>justified: made righteous in the eyes of God</term> through works, this would be *to limp in two directions*, *to worship Baal*, and *to kiss the hand* <note>Job 31:27. This refers to the ancient practice of throwing a kiss to the sun or moon as an act of idolatry.</note>—which is a very great iniquity, as Job says. Further adding, they say: "When you begin to believe, you simultaneously learn all things that are in you..."

<margin>When you begin to believe, you simultaneously learn that everything in you is blameworthy.</margin>
...to be entirely blameworthy, sinful, and damnable, according to that saying of the Apostle: *All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.* <note>original: "Oēs peccauerunt, & egēt glia Dei" — Romans 3:23.</note> <margin>The Apostle and the Psalm</margin> And again: *There is none righteous, there is no one who does good; all have turned aside, together they have become useless.* <note>original: "Nō est iustus... oēs declinauerūt" — quoting Psalm 14 and Romans 3:10-12.</note> Following many such passages, they finally infer this: Therefore, the first care of any Christian ought to be that, having set aside any reliance on works, faith alone may be more and more strengthened, and through that same faith, one may grow in the knowledge not of works, but of Christ Jesus, who suffered and was raised for him. In him, as Peter says, *believing, you will exult with inexpressible joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls.* <note>1 Peter 1:8-9.</note> So also Christ, who (as John narrates) when he was asked by the Jews what they should do to perform the "works of God," rejected the multitude of works with which he saw them swollen and prescribed a single one to them, saying: *This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.* <note>John 6:28-29.</note> For faith carries universal salvation with it, preserving one from every evil, just as the Author of faith himself explains in a brief speech at the conclusion of the Gospel titled "According to Mark," where he says: *He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned.* <note>Mark 16:16.</note> Paul agrees, who, when debating with the Romans, says: *If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.* <note>Romans 10:9.</note> And again: *Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.* <note>Romans 10:4.</note> And earlier, bringing forward the opinion of the prophet and the oracle, he says: *The righteous lives by faith.* <note>Habakkuk 2:4, cited in Romans 1:17.</note> Many other opinions of the Gospel and the Apostles could be brought forward that seem to sound the same, which even they did not cite; but let these suffice for the moment. Let us now bring into the open how he attempts to sophistically <note>The author uses "sophistice" here to mean with clever or intricate reasoning, likely summarizing a Reformist argument.</note> explain how satisfaction is made for so many demanded works, ceremonies of the law, and all affirmative commands through faith alone.

<margin>Faith pertains to the inner man, works to the outer man.</margin>
For they say that nothing else pertains to the **inner man** except faith, but that **works** are useful for the **outer man**, so that through them he may be mortified and made subject to the inner man who believes.

<margin>Scripture is divided into precepts and promises.</margin>
Finally, they also divide Scripture into two parts: **precepts** and **promises**. They say the precepts teach certain things we must do, which nonetheless *cannot* be done; they are truly intended to make a man recognize his own impotence and despair of his own strength. For the Law says: *You shall not covet.* <note>Exodus 20:17.</note> Yet there is no one who is able not to covet; and it is the same for the other precepts. Whence, since he is moved by his own impotence to observe the Law—of which not even the smallest <term>iota or tittle</term><note>The "iota" (the smallest Greek letter) and "tittle" (a small stroke in Hebrew writing) refer to the absolute precision required by Divine Law, as mentioned in Matthew 5:18.</note> ought to be passed over unobserved—he should therefore despair and be reduced to nothing in his own eyes. Nor should he dare to approach the other part of Scripture, which are the **promises**, by which the glory of God is announced, until he hears this: "If you wish to fulfill the Law as it requires, go to Jesus, in whom grace, peace, righteousness, and liberty are promised to you." All these things you shall have if you believe; if you do not believe, you will lack them. Hence, God’s promises give what the precepts demand, and fulfill what the Law commands. Just as the sick were healed by the touch of Christ, so by faith and the word of Christ, the person most tender in faith is justified, sanctified, made true, pacified, liberated, filled with every good, and is made a son of God by believing in his name. And they pursue this opinion with a long discourse, repeating and affirming it with persuasions, asserting in various words what they had often said: for even to Abraham, as they argue, *faith was credited as righteousness*, not any work. They judge that the same should be believed concerning others. I think it superfluous to repeat all these things, since we can address all the points brought forward (and those yet to be brought) based on this same foundation.

<summary>This page explains the theological distinction between the Law (precepts) and the Gospel (promises), arguing that while the Law reveals human inability, faith alone in Christ fulfills the Law's requirements. It also introduces the concept of the "inner man" who is justified by faith and the "outer man" who performs works to remain disciplined.</summary>

# The Removal of Those Foundations. Ch. XII.

<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Peter</margin>
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
**T**o uproot all poorly placed foundations, we advise reflecting upon that sentiment of James: *Faith without works is dead.* <note>original: "Fides sine opibus mortua est" — James 2:26.</note> And again: *The demons believe, and they tremble* <note>James 2:19.</note>; in which he concludes that faith without works is utterly extinguished. But if they do not wish to stand by these words, as if they were from a doubtful author <note>A reference to the fact that some early Reformers, like Luther, questioned the apostolic authority of the Epistle of James, calling it an "epistle of straw."</note>, let us come to the Gospel and to the judgment of Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness. For what did he say here? *He who believes and is baptized will be saved.* <note>Mark 16:16.</note> Elsewhere he also said: *If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.* <note>Matthew 19:17.</note> And what is more, he concluded the entire business of achieving salvation and blessedness in works, saying: *On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.* <note>Matthew 22:40.</note> For indeed, he did not say that the Law and the Prophets depend on faith, but on the love of God and neighbor, which consist in action and not in pure belief.

What, then, will the "new dogmatists" say to this? For, being defeated by this and similar sentiments of the Highest Truth <note>Christ</note> and his disciples, they praise works when they cannot exclude them, but immediately, having applied their poison, they suggest that a work is to be done only so that it may mortify the rebellious body and subject it to the spirit, but that the work has no power toward salvation. In this, they think they magnify the service of Christ the Redeemer, to whom they attribute all things. <margin>The offering and prayer of Christ were of the greatest efficacy.</margin> That offering and the prayer made for us were indeed of the greatest efficacy and were most sufficient for the salvation of all; nevertheless, it was such that the Offerer himself wants us to be his co-workers, according to that saying of the Apostle: *For we are God's helpers.* <note>original: "Dei. n. adiutores sumus" — 1 Corinthians 3:9.</note> 

Hence the Redeemer himself, having distributed the wealth acquired in the work of redemption (which in Matthew he calls <term>talents</term><gloss>a large unit of currency or weight</gloss>, but in Luke <term>minas</term><gloss>a smaller unit of currency, about 100 drachmas</gloss>), adds: <margin>Do business</margin> *Do business until I come.* <note>original: "Negotiamini dū uenio" — Luke 19:13.</note> Here two things occur that must be attended to: First, the money or gifts provided from the treasury of his clemency and the fullness acquired in the work of redemption; Second, our cooperation is invited when it is said: *Do business.* And what is even more to be observed: unless we return a profit by doing business, he threatens punishment—specifically for him who, having hidden the talent, reports no profit through cooperation. 

If, therefore, work is not necessary, why is so much demanded of us under such great threat? Why does he command that the one who neglects to cooperate with the talent provided be cast into the outer darkness? Tell me, I pray, new theologians: by what justice are those punished who omit things to which they are in no way bound? How does your opinion stand with the opinion of the Truth? The Highest Truth says: *He who does not work according to the grace provided shall be cast into the outer darkness*—that is, he will be damned and deprived of salvation. But you say: *Faith saves without works.* 

Without a doubt, one of the two is in error. Certainly not the Highest Truth. Therefore, you are the ones in error, you who presume too much, interpreting the senses of the Gospel against and above so many wise men. Nor is it a wonder if you rush into fitful error, since that decree was remembered by the Highest Truth speaking familiarly with the Father: *You have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent* <note>Matthew 11:25.</note>—namely, those who are wise in their own eyes and who despise others—*and you have revealed them to little ones*, who prefer to humbly agree with others rather than to appear unique; while those elated by pride and arrogance, together with negligent workers, are led away to the inner and outer darkness. If, again, our Redeemer does not require our works...

...as if necessary for salvation: why does his herald <note>Referring to John the Baptist</note>, already instructed in the evangelical doctrine, cry out and protest, saying: *Produce worthy fruits of repentance*? <note>original: "Facite dignos fructus pœnitentiæ" — Matthew 3:8</note> And granted that repentance is a "return to God" (as you assert, and as the Hebrew term <term>תשובה</term> <note>Teshuvah: the Hebrew word for "return" or "repentance"</note> indicates), why are "fruits" required beyond repentance? For what are these fruits, if not good works performed by those who, having already turned back to God, follow the perfect path of repentance? Into those who are thus aligned with God, the Spirit of God enters, making the soul pregnant so that it may produce the fruits of even better works. The Apostle Paul commemorates these when speaking to the Galatians, saying: *But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, modesty, continence, chastity, etc.* <note>Galatians 5:22-23</note> If, therefore, faith is listed here as a single fruit and a part of those things which the Spirit requires of us, how is faith alone sufficient as a medium to fulfill the things that belong to the Spirit? 

Hear this and understand, you who—despising all others—claim for yourselves alone the knowledge of the Spirit and the Gospel; see how far you have strayed from the spiritual paths. Nor do you only wander aimlessly here, but you also exalt marriage 
<margin>Paul</margin> 
which Paul exhorts those who intend to devote themselves to prayer to abstain from. <note>1 Corinthians 7:5</note> You despise continence, chastity, and abstinence from carnal fuels; you commend such things with only a few words, merely so that you are not held in contempt by everyone. Indeed, by using a single word of Paul, you commend marriage and the raising of children to such an extent that you consider those who observe celibacy and abstinence from food to be utterly damned—even when they do so only at certain times so that, with carnal fuels removed for a while, they might more freely devote themselves to God during the fast days and periods of abstinence following the solemnities. 

Why, I ask, are you so led by one word of the Apostle that you despise a thousand other sayings that assert the contrary? Does not the same Apostle count carnal luxury and "revelries"—even within marriage—among the works of the flesh which always oppose the Spirit? *Now the works of the flesh are manifest,* he says when speaking to the Galatians, *which are: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, luxury, dissensions, sects, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; of which I tell you, as I have told you before, that those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.* <note>Galatians 5:19-21</note> 

The "kingdom" to come is not to be given to those who will be on the right hand in the Final Judgment; nor is the present kingdom—which by Christ's testimony is within us—to be obtained and increased except by doing violence to ourselves <note>A reference to Matthew 11:12, "the kingdom of heaven suffers violence"</note> while we restrain ourselves from the delights and pleasures of the flesh. This kingdom of heaven and of God is, without doubt, God dwelling in us: whether through grace, as many are accustomed to have it; or through light which (as John says) illuminates every man; or through a certain power and anointing, which is God himself pouring into us and soothing us with his mercy and goodness. He who was called "The Anointed" was drenched in this—called *Unctus* in Latin, *Christos* in Greek, and *Messiah* in Hebrew. <note>The author provides the etymology of "Christ" across the three "sacred languages" of the Renaissance: Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.</note> By whatever other name or metaphor it is described, the kingdom of God is God himself dwelling in those who not only believe in his name, but who work according to the faith they have received. As the Teacher of the Church himself testifies, saying: *If anyone keeps my word, my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.* <note>John 14:23</note> For his "word" is not only about having faith in him, but about love and the observance of his commandments.

# FOURTH TONE

...of the commandments, which belongs to works, and not to faith alone. Therefore, we receive this kingdom of God—with God dwelling within us—all the better and more fully the more we distance ourselves from the works of the flesh and preserve **celibacy**, which you shamelessly despise. 

<margin>Paul</margin>
Hence Paul says to the Romans: *Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurities, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires* <note>original: "Non in comessationibus, & ebrietatibus..." — Romans 13:13-14. This is a classic passage used to support asceticism.</note>, by delighting yourselves in such things; for these delights and fleshly 

<margin>Peter</margin>

There are innumerable sayings of the Apostles of this kind, by which we are persuaded to fight against the flesh and blood that resist the spirit. This is done through abstinence from food and all luxury, and through true celibacy, which you despise. But let us return to where we digressed: Come and hear, all you who, despising works, extol faith alone: what does Christ, appointed as the judge of all, promise to reward and threaten to damn? Is it faith alone or unbelief, or is it works themselves? 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
For he stands ready to say: *Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you.* And he adds the reason for this reward, saying: *I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink,* etc., and what follows. Conversely, however, he threatens that he will punish not a defect of faith, but a defect of works, subjoining: *Go, you cursed, into eternal fire, for you did not feed me, nor did you give me drink, you did not visit me, you did not clothe me, you did not care for me, and finally, you did not do the works of charity* <note>Matthew 25:34-43. The author uses the "Sheep and the Goats" parable to argue that the final judgment is based on "corporal works of mercy."</note>. Where will those owls <note>The author likely refers to his opponents as "noctuae" (owls or night-birds) because they are perceived as being blind to the light of the Gospel or preferring the "darkness" of their own interpretations.</note> flee from this glowing and most clear sentence of the judge and true light of the world? Indeed, I do not see with what face anyone would dare to exclude works, and testify that they are not required by the judge, and will not be necessary for obtaining salvation and the kingdom. Is this not to presume rashly against the judge’s edict? Why, I ask, do you wish to attribute so much to faith that you push aside works? For those already introduced into the house of Christ through the door of faith, works are sought by Christ himself with such affection that he seems to conclude everything in them—especially in charity, the root of all good works—saying: *This I command you, that you love one another.* And again, as if having forgotten all other things, he repeats: *This is my commandment, that you love one another.* 

<margin>John, Paul</margin>
That disciple whom Jesus loved <note>The Apostle John</note> repeats and confirms this very often in his epistles; he who, above all others, was privy to His secrets. And Paul, in whose breast Christ himself also echoed, prefers charity to faith, saying: *And now these three remain: Faith, Hope, and Charity; but the greatest of these is charity* <note>1 Corinthians 13:13</note>. And proceeding further, he asserts that even the highest faith—so great that even mountains might be moved by it—is nothing without charity. What will you say to these things, you who dogmatize new things? Perhaps you will say that charity *is* faith? But this is not according to the teaching of the Apostle, who, numbering those virtues, distinguishes one from another completely—so much so that at some point, when faith ceases, charity remains, which never fails. Since, therefore, charity is distinguished from faith, it is counted among works—this being especially true according to the common distinction of all, that those things pertaining to the Law and the Gospel, and our whole business, are divided between things to be believed <term>credenda</term> <note>Matters of faith or doctrine</note> and things to be done <term>operanda</term> <note>Matters of practice or ethics</note>. Charity, therefore, which is placed before faith, is a work, along with everything done in that same charity. And charity itself, together with contemplative love and all works performed in charity, [leads to] that most happy...

CCLXIII

->OF THE SECOND CANTICLE.<-

...there are pastures which everyone finds who enters through the door of faith toward those divine pastures, and who also goes out toward the pastures of love and the work to be shown toward one’s neighbor. Those who linger only at the door of faith will hardly taste these feedings.

### How the authorities that seem to attribute everything to faith should be understood. Chapter XIII.

**A**uthorities <note>In this context, "authorities" refers to specific passages from the Bible or Church Fathers used to support a legal or theological argument.</note>, therefore—all those which I know the teachers of the new dogmas have brought forward in excessive favor of faith—do not stand in the way of the true doctrine that all who think rightly profess, nor do they favor the heresy of those men. We could prove this with a single solution, by saying that all those passages testify that faith is necessary as a door and a beginning of salvation, and like a seed of good works and their root. Hence the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> asserts that all meritorious works, pleasing to God, were performed in faith. <margin>Paul</margin> But that greatest of teachers warns us with a clear voice that the word of God, which we must believe, is the seed of good works. How then, O **Northern Theologians** <note>original: "Aquilonares Theologi." This refers to the Protestant Reformers in Germany and Northern Europe.</note>, does faith exclude works? For what is a door to us without a house, or a root and a trunk without fruit? Again, why does he limp who desires to be justified <note>To be "justified" means to be made righteous or right in the eyes of God.</note> and to show himself pleasing to God from the fruits along with the root and the seed? You are the ones who limp, and falling everywhere, you collapse, because you are content with only one foot and you despise the other, which is supremely necessary. For we wish to walk with both feet—namely, of faith and of charity—with a firmer step than you "one-footed" men. Nor do we delight in "kissing our own hand" <note>An idiom suggesting self-reliance or pride in one's own power.</note>, but rather the hand of God, relying on whose help we trust to undertake whatever work is assigned to us. For it is not we alone, but the grace of God with us, through which we strive to do good like the Apostle, while we have the time. And this is what we learn as believers: because we are all born children of wrath, we need not only the glory but also the grace of God, so that we may perform good in the faith we have received. We recognize, moreover, our downward-leaning nature, our frequent falls, and our weakness, and therefore that we need favor so that we can do good. Nor should the opinion of works be cast aside; rather, we should aspire to them through the grace of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: "xp̄i," a common abbreviation for the Greek "Christos."</note> who suffered for us, was raised, and who is always favoring us by his merit. In this we exult with unspeakable joy, bringing back the goal of our faith: the salvation of our souls. And this is provided that faith itself is perfected through charity, with which the fruits of good works are produced, for which a reward is promised. O good God, with what face, with what daring, with what (to speak truly) rashness do those boastful recent theologians presume to exclude works? For the royal Prophet <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms.</note> denounces it, the Apostle proclaims it, and the Judge of all himself declares that when he comes with his Angels to put an end to human business, he will render to each according to his works. Fall silent, therefore, and do not submit to the spirit of error, but yield to the prophet, yield to the Apostle, yield to <term>Christ</term>, and to the Holy Spirit, inspired by whom the holy men of God have spoken. For even if they extolled faith, they did not entirely exclude works, except those which we do without the favor of him who said: *Without me you can do nothing.* <margin>CHRIST</margin> He said this to the Jews who were not yet initiated, and who had not yet received the seed of faith nor planted the root of good works: that it was the work of God that they should believe in him whom he had sent, who also sows the good seed of faith in the field of our soul, so that we may produce the fruit of good works. He is the door through which we enter into the vineyard and the field of the Lord...

CCLXIIII

->FOURTH VOLUME.<-

...bearing fruit from there. And in this way, faith holds all salvation within itself, like a <margin>Peter</margin> door and a seed through which (as Peter says) we are born in Christ himself. He suggests this when he says: 
> He who believes and is baptized shall be saved: 

This refers to the one who, like good and well-watered soil, has received the word of God, which is the seed of faith. For there are those who, like dry rock, receive it, believing for a time and falling away in the time of temptation, because they do not have the moisture of grace—that is, the watering grace—through which we work for the good. Behold, therefore, that from this Gospel word, which you value so highly, something else besides faith is required by Christ. For, by his own interpretation, the seed is the word of God, which we must believe. But beyond this, good soil is also required; and watering is required, which is done through the true water of baptism. This water is salvific wisdom; it is also grace and the favor of working well, obtained from Christ, who cries out to everyone in the temple, saying: 
> If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. 

And again to the Samaritan woman: 
> Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, there will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. 

And let them not say that faith and baptism are the same thing; for he first separates these two, and then joins them together, testifying that both are necessary, because it is a compound sentence <note>A "compound sentence" (original: "copulata sententia") refers to the grammatical structure of "He who believes AND is baptized," implying both conditions must be met.</note>. Along this path runs that saying of Paul: 
> If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved: 

for you already have the pledge of salvation and have received the seed of faith—not on rock without moisture (for such people are excluded by Christ), but in well-watered soil that produces fruit in its own time. And this is what it means to believe in Christ raised, and the one who raises us up to perform good and heavenly works, according to that saying of the Apostle: 
<margin>Paul</margin> 
> If you have risen with Christ—believing, that is, that he himself was raised—seek those things which are above, savor those things which are above. 

Seek indeed with affection, and savor with taste, when you perform those things which look upward. Therefore, works are not excluded here, but included. We confess, moreover, with the Apostle, that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes—the end, certainly, which the law and the precepts of the law itself, proven by works, desire, and are received from him so that those works performed according to the law might be alive. These works, without doubt, were dead without the tree of life, without the bread of life, and finally without life itself, which is Christ. In this, ceremonies and the works demanded in the law and affirmative precepts cannot be satisfied by faith alone. For by faith in Christ, satisfaction is made for all those things which prefigured Christ himself and were completed—nay, perfected—in him: such as the sacrifices, <term>sacraments</term><note>In this context, the author uses "sacraments" to refer to the various holy rites and signs of the Old Testament, not just the seven sacraments of the Catholic Church.</note>, garments, ornaments, the entire structure of the tabernacle and temple, and finally all the ceremonies which happened to them as a figure of Christ. But the commandments are by no means fulfilled by faith alone; otherwise, Christ would not have said: 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> 
> If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: 

but would have said instead: 
> If you wish to enter into life, believe in me. 

If, therefore, the observation of the commandments is a condition so necessary for salvation that salvation is promised to us by the author of salvation through it, how is it that work belongs only to the "outer man"? <note>The "outer man" refers to the physical or worldly self, as opposed to the "inner man" or soul. The author is arguing that good deeds affect the salvation of the whole person, not just the body.</note> Is it only the outer or lower man who is saved? Indeed, these dogmas are fit only for raving old women and the common rabble, but should be persuasive to no one of sense.

CCXIII

### OF THE SECOND SONG

But perhaps they will say: That it is necessary to mortify the outer man <note>To "mortify the outer man" (original: *mortificare exteriorem hominem*) refers to subduing physical desires and the ego through self-discipline and asceticism</note> so that one may enter into life. We grant this. This work is therefore necessary, as is the hand working together with the heart. But we say more: it does not seem sufficient for the heart to believe while the tongue confesses, when Truth itself and our Judge says: *Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord"*—even if believing and confessing—*shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.* He likewise shows that the "useless servant," who neglects to work with the money received from his Lord, is to be cast into the outer darkness and cursed by God and salvation. And what profit He seeks, He immediately declares by adding: that the least of His members be fed, clothed, and the like—which are works, and not faith alone. And as for their presupposition that God commanded the impossible, this, according to Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father and translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>, is anathema <note>A formal curse or denunciation by the Church</note>. 

But I will say <margin>Paul</margin> more: It is impious, the worst blasphemy, and a condemnation of God, if He commands and demands from us the impossible, since it can be supported by no order, no equity, and no reason that a Lord should demand and want from a servant what is impossible. But they will say: Christ supplies this by His merit and His grace. Now, everyone knows this—even raving old women. Why then do you propose these things as if they were your own inventions? For this was already declared <margin>CHRIST, Paul</margin> by Christ saying: *Without me you can do nothing.* This is confirmed by Paul, who says: *Not I, but the grace of God with me.* Nor can you find anything else through these premises, as you claim; for you use new terminology so that you may appear new, and be able to push for novelty in what you intend. But I trust in the righteous Spirit of Jesus, who will lead to a better fate that which perhaps you build up with a distorted mind. For what is it to say "no one can fulfill the law <margin>Paul</margin> without Christ," except "without the help of Christ"? This we have already conceded. 

And when they say, "No one can approach Christ without faith, therefore faith is sufficient," the conclusion is false and inconsistent, and the premise is a doubtful sentiment, since Christ himself says: *No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him.* Whether this "attraction" is faith itself or something else, these new dogmatists <note>The author uses "new dogmatists" to mock the Protestant reformers for introducing what he considers theological innovations</note> have not yet explained. For we do not doubt whether faith is necessary to approach God, because that is the clear opinion of Paul, if the Epistle to the Hebrews was written by him, where he says: *Without faith it is impossible to please God.* For it is necessary for one approaching God to believe. 

But we deny that this alone is sought. For someone drawn by the Father and introduced into the house and family of Christ through the door of faith immediately receives talents or minas <note>Ancient units of currency used in Jesus’ parables to represent spiritual gifts or responsibilities</note> (or whatever other name that gift is called), so that they may immediately begin to work and return a profit on the gift received. Nor was there any need, O novice theologians, to obscure the truth (already manifest and accepted by all) with many words, either so that you might seem to have brought something new into the open, or to stir up some scandal that you have not yet vomited out from your heart. For what is it to condemn works, if not to pervert the entire Gospel life and to prepare oneself—along with Sardanapalus <note>A legendary Assyrian king often cited as a symbol of extreme luxury and decadence</note> and other most filthy, I will not say Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, often characterized in this period as mere seekers of physical pleasure</note>, but beasts—for every kind of pleasure? For that undoubtedly follows if they trust in faith alone, lest they not condemn vigils, fasts, chastity, austerity of life, works of charity, and all celibacy, as you do. Nor should you lean on those words which were said:

CCLXV

->THE FOURTH TONE<-

<margin>Genesis 26</margin>
Abraham [believed] God, and it was credited to him as righteousness <note>original: "reputatū eſt ei ad iustitiā." A central biblical phrase from Genesis 15:6, frequently cited in debates about how a person is made right with God.</note>. For although that faith was a work of righteousness, it was nonetheless not only righteousness through which he was so pleasing to God that such many and such great promises were made to him. Read (if you please) the book of Genesis, chapter 26, and you will find these things said word-for-word to Isaac, the son of Abraham himself: *For to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, fulfilling the oath which I swore to Abraham your father; and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven; and I will give to your descendants all these lands, and in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed; because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my precepts, and my mandates, and my ceremonies, and served the law*—or as the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>The term "Hebrew truth" (original: *veritas hebraica*) was used by scholars like St. Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament as opposed to later translations.</note> has it, *and kept my charge*, namely those things which I handed over to be kept: *my precepts, my statutes, and my law.* If, therefore, faith was sufficient, why was the observance of the law added? Why is Abraham commended now for faith, and now for the observance of the law, and why is such a beautiful promise made to him? Not, indeed, because faith and work are the same thing, but because each presupposes or draws the other, nor can one be perfect without the other. For faith, in order to live, leads to work; while work truly presupposes faith. Abraham, therefore, is commended as perfect in both: sometimes specifically regarding faith, and sometimes regarding the observance of the mandates. These mandates had been revealed by God to Abraham himself no less than to Moses, even though Moses, at God’s command, handed them over to the people and committed them to writing. And so Abraham kept the law, the precepts, and the statutes; therefore, these things can be observed. Why then do you chatter <note>original: "garritis." The author uses a dismissive tone, accusing his opponents of empty talk.</note>, saying that the law cannot be observed, and that Abraham was justified by faith alone and not by works? Search the scriptures, and let one passage be fitted to another if you wish to perceive the truth. Abraham's faith was indeed credited to him as righteousness, but his works were also credited, on account of which the blessing of all nations was promised in his offspring—most especially when he offered his son Isaac as a sacrifice. And even if he offered him in faith (as the Apostle says), that offering was not faith itself, but a work founded on faith, which is the foundation of the spiritual building.

## ON THE SECOND CANTICLE

...sins: *Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin* <note>original: "Beatus uir, cui non imputauit Dominus peccatū." A quote from Psalm 32:2, famously cited by St. Paul in Romans 4:8 to discuss how God forgives sins.</note>. And a little later: *For the promise to Abraham or his offspring, that he should be the heir of the world, was not through the law.* For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is abolished. Although these words seem to favor the **new dogma** <note>A likely reference to the Protestant Reformation's doctrine of "Justification by Faith Alone" (Sola Fide), which the author is here trying to nuance.</note>, they are nonetheless not foreign to that which the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul.</note> preaches as contrary in many other places. For he in whose heart Christ resounds is not so delirious that he would assert one thing now and immediately begin to **change his tune** <note>original: "palinodiā canere," literally "to sing a palinode," a poem or song retracting a previous statement.</note>. 

For his speech was aimed at calming the Hebrews and the Romans: the former placed their trust in circumcision and the law, while the latter placed theirs in **uncircumcision** <note>original: "præputio," referring to the state of the Gentiles.</note> and baptism. Hence he shows himself as a most pious defender now for the one group, and now for the other. And he most fiercely opposes those in whom either the former or the latter swelled with excessive pride and confidence. He places himself between them as an arbiter of these same questions, as Jerome best understands. 

He also attempts to demonstrate that the salvation brought by the **Messiah** is conferred neither from circumcision, nor from the law, nor from the works which we have done, but from the grace and munificence of God, who through his mercy and clemency sent a Savior to us. For we had done nothing by which we could extort or dispose the clemency of God toward giving a Redeemer and toward obtaining the lamb who takes away our sins. Who was slain by the decree of the Father <margin>John</margin> (as John says) from the beginning of the world for the universal salvation of all, but this was done out of pure grace of God. 

But so that anyone might receive a portion of the water and blessing from this universal abundance of salvation for their own particular salvation, it is necessary that they cling through faith to the one offering and bringing the salvific water, so that they may drink, and by means of this very work grow immensely, and that there might become in them *a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.* 

Hence one must not stand in faith alone, but must proceed further to the works which the faith received demands. But if someone is unable to work, the will is counted for the deed, and in this sense he understands that word of the Apostle: *But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness* according to the purpose of the grace of God, who accepts the will when the impossibility of working is present. 

And this is a singular grace and a certain blessedness, according to what follows: David calls the man blessed to whom God grants righteousness without works: *Blessed also are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.* God, who wants all men to be saved, could certainly save everyone even without works, but he does not save everyone because not everyone obeys him, nor does everyone want to work according to the faith received, of whom <margin>Paul</margin> the same Apostle says: *He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.* And again: *While we have time, let us work good, for in due time we shall reap.* 

Hear, O despisers of works, what the Apostle says: He does not say, "let us believe and we shall reap," but he says, "**let us work** and we shall reap." And this is according to the measure of the works, <margin>The same</margin> just as he says elsewhere: *He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings*—in the blessings of grace, indeed, provided for cooperation, as he adds: For God is powerful...

<summary>The author argues that St. Paul's emphasis on faith was a rhetorical strategy to mediate between Jews and Gentiles, rather than a dismissal of good works. He maintains that while salvation is a gift of grace, individual salvation requires active cooperation and the performance of good deeds.</summary>

### FOURTH TONE
<note>original: "TONVS QVARTVS." This likely refers to the "tone" or volume of a larger collection of musical or theological works.</note>

...make grace abound in you, so that having all sufficiency in all things, you may abound in every good work. And for what purpose is this good work? Certainly not merely so the body may sustain the spirit, but so that we may receive a reward, <margin>Paul</margin> if the work which we have built upon remains, as **Paul** teaches in his first epistle to the Corinthians. But returning to the earlier words of the Apostle, we confess that no one is justified by the **works of the law**, nor has ever been justified, because the sin of our first parent—and consequently of the entire human race—was such that it could be pulled out by no human powers, nor purged by any natural or legal remedy, nor could that ignominy be veiled by any garment made of lower things. Here, a fig leaf was not sufficient to cover the nakedness of the **first-formed** <term>protoplasts</term> <note>original: "protoplastorū," a common Renaissance term for Adam and Eve as the first-created beings.</note>, although Isaiah healed King Hezekiah <margin>the fig healed Hezekiah</margin> of a specific plague with a fig. Hence, the most merciful God, having pity on the human fall, removed the covering sewn from fig leaves and, taking a **tunic of skin**, clothed them; a tunic surely fashioned from the hide of **that lamb** who took away the sins of the world. By this garment, divine mercy not only covers the nakedness of our first parents, but of all <margin>from the skin of the lamb he covered the nakedness of Adam and Eve</margin> whom He had judged worthy of that covering. This work, and this garment, neither the law could provide, nor sacrifice, nor any priest, except for Him who, being both priest, victim, and lamb, was slain for all from the beginning of the world so that He might benefit all. Since, therefore, the law or the observation of the law could by no means confer this, for that reason no one was justified by the works of the law. Neither Abraham, nor any other of the fathers, was justified by the works of the law so as to have glory before God, who commanded justification and purification to be done through Him who bore the sins of all, and through His own blood, and not through the blood of animals. In this Redeemer Abraham believed, and it was credited to him as righteousness, because he trusted not in his own merits, nor in himself, nor in the works of the law, but in the true Purifier in whose coming he believed. And so it happens to all who worked and continue to work according to the law: to whom a reward is given according to the merit of that rule which says, *He will render to each according to his works.* But since those <margin>The same</margin> works, whatever they may be, are not sufficient for salvation—which is given through the grace obtained <margin>our works are not sufficient for salvation, which is given through grace</margin> by Christ—therefore the Apostle says that it is not imputed to him according to grace, but according to debt, in accordance with that Gospel pronouncement to the servants who fulfill by their work <margin>CHRIST.</margin> those things commanded in the law: *When you have done all these things, say: we are useless servants; we have done what we ought to do.* Nor do we acquire the grace of the children of God from that, unless we are aided by Him who obtained it and gave us the power to be made children of God. In whose name it is right that we believe; and let us not follow the birth which is according to the flesh and blood, but 그하나 that which is according to God and the spirit, according to which we should also work. For we cannot stand idle, nor should we, having been established as children of God, work according to the flesh and blood. To that level and to the reward according to it, we are unable to arrive by **condignity** (as they say) <note>original: "de condigno," a scholastic term for merit that is equal in value to the reward.</note>, or according to an **arithmetic proportion** of equality, but through grace and in a **geometric proportion**: so that if for one thing, a hundred are given; for...

# CCLXXI

-> ### OF THE SECOND SONG <-
<note>original: "CANTICI SECVNDI." This may refer to a specific section of a commentary on the Song of Songs or a liturgical division.</note>

...two hundred should be given for two, and a thousand returned for ten. Here, several things are preserved that at first glance seemed to fit poorly. For here it is saved <note>In this context, "saved" means the theological logic is preserved or reconciled.</note> how the sufferings of this time are not worthy of our future glory: because those sufferings are carried out in simple numbers, but the glory is returned in hundreds. It is also saved how the **grace of God** is **eternal life**; since through a work that we perform in the weight or measure of "one," we cannot by that single unit reach the point of making a hundredfold reward, unless the grace of Him who is rich toward all who call upon Him favors us. 

Here it is also explained how we are saved **through faith**, since we must adhere to Him who brought it about that our works, offered as units, are rewarded in hundreds. Here, finally, it is related that if we are saved through grace and faith—and even if our works are not worthy of future glory—the **Just Judge** in rewarding will nonetheless render to each according to their works. This is because this reward is made in an equal proportion, through the grace of the Redeemer (which He promised in the Law and the Prophets) always intervening. 

<margin>Paul</margin> 
And in this sense, those words of **Paul** are understood: *If those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is abolished.* <note>A reference to Romans 4:14. The author is arguing that the law alone cannot save, but faith makes human effort meaningful.</note> For it is most clear to everyone that salvation was not given through the law, or the blood of animals, but through **Christ** and the **Messiah**, to whom the sacrifices, the prophets, and the whole law correspond. In Him, it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell, and through Him all things are reconciled. 

<margin>In the same place</margin> 
And this is true, provided that we take up our cross, laboring, struggling, working, and exerting force upon ourselves so that we may abstain from vices and perform good according to our strength. The rest, however, He—the one most full of all good things—will supply, so that from His fullness we all receive. This is the true doctrine preached by Christ and the Apostles in many places, sincerely proclaimed to all, which makes all the declarations uttered by the same Spirit through the mouths of various people in many places agree as one. Therefore, this dogma—at other times persuaded by the **cunning of the devil**, and now put to rest by the providence of God—is being stirred up again so that a ruinous scandal and **schism** may emerge, and so that the faithful may be drawn away from **good works**, for which life and salvation are promised.

## HOW GOD IS THE FATHER OF ALL.

**H**OW the eternal Father first, and afterwards Christ, was also called the father of all, if we wish to explain, it will not be out of place to repeat those things said by the natural philosophers <note>The "naturalists" or scientists of the classical and medieval periods who studied the physical world.</note> concerning the generation of every animal, and of man most especially, since in these lower things there are likenesses and images of divine matters.

<margin>Hippocrates</margin>
Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE.</note> therefore thought that the frothy and fleshy part of the seed emanates from the brain;

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle from the heart, which is the principal seat of the soul;

<margin>Galen</margin>
Galen from the liver, since the natural power of digestion and generation is situated within it;

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
But Avicenna <note>The 11th-century Persian polymath and physician.</note> professes that it flows from the three principal members—namely the heart, brain, and liver—so that he might admit the opinions and reasons of all.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Some indeed (as Aristotle mentions) are of the opinion that the seed itself falls from every member of both sides <note>The left and right sides of the body.</note>, because delight is then felt in all the members; also because from every mark of any member of the father, something similar is generated in the son; and also because in many cases every part of the one begotten is formed in the likeness of the father. Whence it is conjectured that from every part of the one generating, the seed flows down according to the "idol" <note>original: "idolum". In this context, it refers to a formal "image" or "template" of the body part.</note> existing within it. Some have wished to attribute all of this to a strong imagination, but they did so falsely: both because this happens without the imagination of the one generating, and also because from the excessive shedding of the seed, every member of the generator himself is weakened. Therefore, let others say whatever they wish for the exercise of their wit; to me, it seems that a portion of the seed falls from every member, from which the son is formed with the image of the generator, which represents the whole and all the members. And thus the heart of the begotten is from the heart of the generator, the brain from the brain, the eye from the eye, the hand from the hand, and so on for each thing; even though the power and spirit are principally from the brain, heart, and liver, as from the principal and more spiritual members. Thus, descending from the brain, it draws the rational power, and passing through the veins which are behind both ears, it proceeds to the *mica* <note>original: "micam". This likely refers to the "nucha" or spinal marrow, thought to be the conduit for the generative seed.</note> to which it is joined, through the kidneys all the way to the seminal vessels and the testes. But proceeding from the heart and from the liver, it draws out power and the spirit of love and affection.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
So also Christ, the Son of God, the perfect image and wisdom of the Father, emanated from all things that are in the Father, drawing all things with Him; therefore He said: *All things have been handed over to me by my Father* <note>original: "Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo" (Matthew 11:27).</note>, just as He proceeded from all things: for He emanated and emanates from the essence, piety, mercy, justice, goodness, infinity, and from the entire fountain of all goods; but especially in that He is Wisdom, He proceeded from the brain—that is, from the paternal mind.

<margin>Orpheus</margin>
As Orpheus <note>The legendary Greek hero and "theologian" of the Orphic mysteries.</note> (and after him the theologians of the Gentiles) said not unsuitably, Pallas <note>Pallas Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, who famously sprang fully formed from the head of Zeus (Jove).</note>—that is, true wisdom—was born from the brain of Jove. But from the heart and the innermost paternal sanctuary He drew that from which He might produce, together with the Father, the spirit of love. According to whose model we also were first begotten by the eternal Father, yet through the Son, into whom the seed of Ideas <note>In Platonic and Scholastic thought, the "Ideas" are the eternal forms or patterns of all created things existing in the mind of God.</note> had been poured; and afterwards we were regenerated again through the Son made man. For this our seminal power first...

[it] comes from the brain of the fatherly mind, from which [comes] the Word and the storehouse <note>The original Latin *armarium* literally means a cupboard or chest, here used as a metaphor for a divine repository of forms.</note> of all things created <note>Original: "creag," likely a contraction of *creatarum*.</note>. For in Him all things are formed as ideas, like seeds in potential; all things, whether they are in the heavens or on the earth, visible and invisible. Hence, since man possesses the image of the Father so that he may represent everything that is in the Father, he is formed from all things that are in the generating parent, though not with that perfection which the Son <note>Referring to Christ as the Logos or Eternal Son.</note> possesses, but in a more distant and obscure image, which is nonetheless sufficient for him to be called a son, who <margin>Aristotle</margin> must be like the one generating him, as Aristotle teaches in the second discourse on the soul <note>Referring to Aristotle's *De Anima*, a foundational text on the nature of life and the soul.</note>. To Him also He teaches us to approach with great confidence when we pray, saying: When you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven. Paul also calls Him the Father not only of rational creatures, but of all things, when he says: <margin>Paul</margin> From whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named <note>Ephesians 3:15.</note>.

### Chapter II. How Christ, regenerating us again in human nature, was made a true father.

<margin>CHRIST. Nicodemus.</margin> **W**e have spoken of the Son, who is like the one generating and producing Him. Therefore, since we were made in the image and likeness of God, the supreme craftsman of all, we are called children of God above all things produced by Him. But with the image defiled and the likeness utterly lost, we were not worthily called children of the supreme Father unless, being regenerated, we should reform that dishonored image and recover the likeness that was completely destroyed. But not understanding the mystery, Nicodemus said: How can these things be? # OF THE SECOND SONG
### PAGE 277

The best philosopher <note>The author likely refers to Christ as the ultimate "Philosopher" or "Lover of Wisdom" who understands the true nature of reality.</note>, and the Son of God who is well-acquainted with the ancient generation, spoke regarding the second [rebirth] as if conforming to the first, saying that it is necessary for us to be born again of water. He meant that just as the first creation emanated from the supramundane and heavenly waters, so too should our regeneration proceed from those same waters. Therefore, in the Son of God—who is the true **supramundane water**—all things were established, and in Him all things are regenerated. 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>

For He was not speaking of common, physical water when He said: *Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit* <note>A reference to John 3:5.</note>. For what has this murky <note>Original: "feculenta," meaning dreggy or filled with the impurities of the material world.</note> water to do with that holy and divine Spirit? How can these utterly different things agree, so as to become a single principle of rebirth? He speaks, therefore, of the water which is the Son of God, who together with the Holy Spirit regenerates mankind. 

The sacrament of these [divine agents] is this physical element of water, which is applied externally to the head of the one being reborn, along with the spoken word sounding outwardly. One of these signifies the **semen** <term>semen: used here in the philosophical sense of a "generative seed" or the potential for new life</term>, and the other signifies the power of propagating that life. 

And because this rebirth from the Spirit requires the fiery, warming, and preparatory power of the Holy Spirit, the person is marked through the audible voice—as if through a sacrament—by the minister. Faith and the renunciation of the devil’s and the world’s obstacles are required and promised when the priest asks the one to be baptized: *What do you seek from the Church?* and *Do you renounce the devil, the world, and its pomps?* 

The one being reborn professes to renounce all those things, so that by setting aside the love of lower things, he may be gathered entirely through the Holy Spirit into the love of God. This process also demands faith and the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that the person may firmly cling to Him by whom they are begotten, and be joined to Him by that same Spirit, which is called the **bond and link of love**. 

We are therefore regenerated by the Son and the Holy Spirit in baptism. The signs and sacraments of these regenerators are the water, the words, and the external rituals. These do not merely signify the effect and the grace to be given, but represent the Regenerator Himself as the true efficient cause. 

But because in natural birth we look for a father who begets, a seed that is infused, and a mother who receives it, one might rightly say here: "I have a Father, who is the regenerating Christ; and I have a seed, which is His aqueous power and effective nursery; but I do not recognize a **mother** who receives the seed." 

It does not satisfy me when people commonly say that the Church is the spouse formed from the side of Christ as He slept on the cross. For "the Church" is nothing more than a term for a gathering, or the assembly of the faithful themselves. Since these people are the ones being born, they cannot be both the mother who gives birth and the children being born. Even less can a mere "gathering" or "relationship" conceive and give birth to men, whether according to the flesh or the spirit. 

We can address this double difficulty in two ways: First, just as the Eternal Father did not require a mother in the eternal and divine generation of the Son, nor in the original creation of the world and man, so too Christ, who regenerates us in a spiritual and divine birth, does not require a mother. But if it is argued that by the voice of all, the Church is called the spouse...

The author challenges the common trope of the "Church as Mother," seeking a more philosophically rigorous explanation for spiritual generation.</summary>

# THE FIFTH TONE
### PAGE 269

<margin>Paul</margin>
Regarding the [union] of Christ and our mother [the Church], we shall speak so that there may be no contention where there ought not be: The first marriage, which was between Adam and Eve—a great sacrament <note>original: "magnum sacramentum"; in this context, it refers to a sacred mystery or symbolic sign</note> indeed, as Paul says—teaches us how these things stand regarding Christ and the Church. For there, the woman was first a daughter, because she was taken from the rib of Adam, as if from a material proportioned to him by a great mystery. Afterward, truly, having been formed from his rib, she became a wife and bore children. So also was Christ’s first spouse, the Church—that is, the assembly of the Apostles—formed into spiritual life from his "rib," which is to say, from his heartfelt love, because he chose them out of the world. <margin>Water of grace.</margin> This formation also came from the water of grace and baptismal power flowing from the side and the heart of Christ, especially while he "slept" on the cross. Once they were formed and instructed, he sent them through all the regions of the world, pregnant with the seed and the power of generating children, which <margin>CHRIST</margin> provided to them when he said:
> Go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

And so from them—whom he had first established as foundations, and as the Church, and consequently as the mother of all who were to be generated—he begot the rest of the children of the Church. <margin>Paul.</margin> Therefore the Apostle, like a tender mother coaxing the Galatians, said:
> My little children, for whom I am again in labor, until Christ be formed in you, so that you yourselves might also be able to be pregnant with grace and power from Christ himself and labor to bring forth others.

Again he says, according to that word of Christ:
> It is necessary for you to be born again.

The Apostles, therefore, were the first foundations of the spiritual building; they were the firstborn, and the first bride of Christ, from whom we have been reborn.

<margin>Seminal power infused into the Apostles.</margin>
For it is not read that Christ baptized anyone, except perhaps John; yet it is believed he also baptized the Apostles and his mother, into whom (and all those holding their place) he infused a **seminal power** <term>seminal power: "seminaria uirtus," a philosophical concept describing the inherent potential or "seed" within a cause to produce a specific effect</term>, by which they might labor to bring forth others anew throughout the entire world, providing the sensible signs of regeneration and new birth which are called "sacraments." That is, they are signs of sacred things and of those things which are not seen. Whether these sacraments are merely signs, or also instruments, or whether they work effectively, is a matter debated quite seriously by our theologians. But, unless I am mistaken, the difficulty is solved and all ambiguity removed if we pay attention <margin>The whole of it is granted by our Father Christ, who generates us.</margin> to the source from which all power proceeds: for this power comes from our Father who generates us, the Son of God, just as a seed has power from the one from whom it falls. But this power is contained or signaled through extrinsic and sensible signs, so that those who rely only on their outer senses—not yet having their inner senses trained for the discernment of spiritual things—might perceive the mystery in some small way.

<margin>Isaiah</margin> <margin>Christ our Father, the redeemer.</margin>
Therefore, because the Son of God and our Redeemer regenerates us in this way as a true Father, Isaiah addresses him in prophecy, saying:
> For you are our Father, our Redeemer; your name is from everlasting.

<margin>The same</margin> Speaking again of this child, he says:
> And he shall be called Mighty God, Prince of Peace, and Father of the age to come—that is, the father of regeneration, through which we are able to enjoy the future age.

For with his seed, which falls from him, the generative spirits also descend; these savor of the divine nature and make those who are reborn capable of the age to come.

### Why faith is required of us in this spiritual rebirth. Chapter III.

<margin>
Aristotle
Avicenna
Aristotle
Algazel
Galen
Galen
Moses
Jacob
Paul
</margin>
**E**ven though faith is required in any earthly marriage as one of its primary virtues—so that the spouses are faithful to one another and the legitimacy of the children to come is trusted—faith is also required in this spiritual marriage and rebirth. It is demanded not only from the Church (the "formed spouse") but also from those about to be reborn, as the very starting point and preparation for approaching God. Indeed (to draw something out from the most secret depths), the minister demands faith from the person being baptized with such care so that, by a firm clinging and a mind focused on what is happening within us, we might be better shaped through a strong "imagination" <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, 'imagination' was thought to be a physical power that could shape the body or the soul during formation, a theory known as 'maternal impression.'</note> to resemble the one who begets us during that rebirth. 

For faith—which is a firm clinging and a fixed intention—accomplishes much in any person who is cooperating in a task, or who is receiving the "seed" of teaching and instruction, or even the biological seed of life. Aristotle believed that a child is made to resemble the parent because of the strong imagination of both the mother and the father. Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037) whose medical texts were standard in European universities for centuries.</note> attributed so much power to the imagination that he believed it could affect not only the person's own body and fetus, but even external objects if the thought was intense. Aristotle elsewhere agrees with this opinion, as do Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a major Islamic theologian and philosopher known in the West as Algazel.</note>—the wisest of the Saracens—and Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>. 

The first of these proves his opinion by a common story: a woman gave birth to a child with dark skin <note>original: "ethiopem"</note> because she had a strong imagination of a painting of an Ethiopian that was in her bedroom. Galen, moreover, urges that the eyes of the mother be kept fixed on such an image, and consequently her mind on the figure she desires her child to be like. For if she desires a beautiful child, she should keep Polycleitus <note>A renowned Greek sculptor of the 5th century BC, famous for creating the "Canon," a statue representing the perfect proportions of the human body.</note> or Absalom <note>The son of King David, described in the Bible as the most handsome man in all of Israel.</note> before her mind, and a statue of them before her eyes. If she wants a brave soldier, she should fix her thoughts on Caesar, Alexander, Hannibal, or someone of that kind. If she desires a philosopher, she should consider Aristotle or Plato. 

These wise men perhaps learned this from our most upright philosopher, Moses, who relates that Jacob placed rods in the watering troughs where the sheep drank, so that they would produce the kind of offspring he desired—white, black, or speckled. Firm and certain faith, which Christ our parent requires of us not only in baptism but in every work we perform, is nothing other than this stable clinging and powerful application of ourselves to Him (who works with us and gives us strength) and to the work we intend to do. It is so powerful that a kind of "image" <term>idolum</term> <note>original: "idolum"; here used in the philosophical sense of a mental blueprint or "ideal form" that guides the creation of a virtue or an action.</note> of the virtue to be received—or of the thing to be done by us or in us—is formed within us. 

And because this faith cannot exist in a tiny infant, faith is required of the godparents during the baptism of a child. They act upon that tender infant by preparing and cooperating with the "mother"—that is, the minister who conceives and gives birth—and with the primary parent, Christ, by whose power the infant is reborn. Therefore, this firm clinging to the parent (or to the chief cooperator, God or Christ Jesus) is so beneficial that Paul attributes all the great deeds performed by famous men to faith, as is clear in the long series of examples he recites to the Hebrews. But especially this...

Faith is sought in those receiving the divine seed in the field of the soul and of their mind, so that being entirely occupied with God through a firm clinging of faith to him, the enemy of man <note>original: "inimicus hoĩs," referring to the devil</note> upon arriving may find no empty space where he might sow weeds <note>original: "zizania," often translated as "tares" or "darnel" in the Parable of the Weeds</note> over the crop. Therefore, not without cause is faith sought, which ought not only to be in pure belief, but a firm and strong clinging of the mind, and a total application of the soul toward the one who sows and regenerates.

### *From what source the male, female, or androgynous is generated. Chapter IV.*

**C**lear experience proves that in natural generation, some offspring are male, some female, and some (though rarely) of a mixed sex. But from what source this occurs, there are various opinions among the wise. Some attribute it to celestial influences; others to the vessel of the womb, saying that if the seed is received while residing in the cavity to the right, the offspring will be male; but if to the left, a female is conceived. But 
<margin>Galen</margin>
<margin>Hali Abbas</margin>
the opinion of Galen and Hali Abbas <note>Hali Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi) was a 10th-century Persian physician whose works were foundational to European medicine.</note> is preferred here: that this results from the seed itself. For if the male seed should be overabundant, the offspring will be more like the father and male; but if the female seed should prevail, a female will be conceived more like the mother. If, however, they are mixed equally as a consequence, the conception will be androgynous <note>term: <term>androgynus</term> (an individual possessing both male and female characteristics; a hermaphrodite)</note>. 
<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato discusses this most beautifully according to our mystical sense in the *Symposium*: "When," he says, "a man clings to the light of the sun—that is, to the divine seed—he generates a male; if to the earth, a female; but an androgynous being when he is mingled with the moon." For at evening a man looks up to the sun and generates with it when he receives the light that illuminates every man; he receives the seed of the one who best impregnates all rational minds, just as this sun which we see shining above the earth impregnates the stars like a "rooster of the heavens." <note>This striking metaphor suggests the sun "awakens" or fertilizes the stars.</note> Therefore, by clinging to the higher Sun, we are made two in one spirit, 
<margin>Paul</margin>
as Paul says: *He who clings to God is made one spirit with him.* <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note> And then, having received His seed, we generate an excellent and "masculine" <note>In this context, "masculine" refers to spiritually strong, active, and virtuous deeds.</note> work. But if one clings to the earthly animal, finding delight in the same, he conceives an "animal" and lowest work, which is called "feminine," and he himself is made effeminate, as it is said in Holy Scripture: *Those who are even commanded to be exterminated from the earth as defilers and despisers of their own dignity.* If, however, he leans upon the natural light, which is called "lunar," mingling himself with civil life and content with natural and moral philosophy, he gives birth to an "androgynous" work, a middle ground between the divine and the animal. Therefore, since we have at hand the Father who generates us, Christ who feeds and instructs us; and we have our animal nature which coaxes us so that it may drag us to the lowest things and defile us; and we have the "civil middle" which agitates and disturbs us concerning many things and distracts us from the better; and since a free choice has been given to us so that we might be able to cling to whomsoever we wish: we must take care that we choose well. For if we should prefer to cling to the animal and its allurements, having become effeminate, we shall conceive a "feminine" work, which, deceiving the man, causes him to transgress...

### Whence comes the likeness that completes the image of the begetter in the begotten. Chapter 5.

<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
<margin>First and second generation</margin>
**I**t is indeed beautiful when a son is like his good father in every kind of likeness, which is manifold: For a son is fashioned according to the form of the parent, first in his specific nature <term>ratione specifica; the essential characteristics that define a species</term> proceeding from nature itself in univocal generation <note>A philosophical term for reproduction where the offspring is the same species as the parent.</note>, in which the one begotten is said to be a son most like the begetter according to his species. A son is also fashioned with the likeness of the father in features, outward appearance, voice, speech, gesture, and such, which can proceed from a strong imagination and the image <term>idolo; here used in the Platonic sense of a mental archetype or "idea" rather than a physical idol</term> existing in the heart of the begetter (as we have said); or from the powerful force of the seed and the spirit emanating from the begetter through that very seed; or it is (as some believe) from the influence of the heavens, which favor the begetter and the begotten by some symbolic connection. Furthermore, a son is made like his parents in character when he strives to emulate them: in all these ways, the child of Christ can and should be made like his father. First, therefore, he is like Him in spiritual generation, nature itself requiring it, as the Apostle <note>Paul</note> says: *The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly man, so are the earthly; as is the heavenly man, so are the heavenly.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:47-48</note> *Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.* In this image <note>effigie</note> also, the Christian is made like the Father, while he is formed by the seed separated from the Father, Christ, full of the Holy Spirit and the divinity with which the begotten is filled. Therefore, the preeminent teacher of this rebirth said: *Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit* <note>John 3:5</note>, namely, from a seed full of the divine spirit. Nor indeed does the image fail in our regenerating Father, who, with perfect foreknowledge and full affection, has begotten and regenerates us in both cases from the most perfect image <term>idolo</term>. For in the first generation <note>The Creation of humanity</note> He fashioned us according to the ideal image; but in the second <note>Spiritual rebirth in Christ</note>, he regenerates us in the Word—in whom all are written—according to that image which is painted in the book of predestination and life.

### How Christ feeds all those whom he begets. Chapter VI.

<margin>N</margin>
## N
or would it have been enough for our most pious Father to have begotten us into the spiritual man, unless he had also prepared foods suitable for him. For his care for feeding the spiritual man was no less than for the animal man <term>homo animalis; the natural or physical human being, as opposed to the "spiritual man"</term>, for whom he prepared such a great abundance of things. For he filled the air, the sea, and the earth with animals for his food; and he made these fertile with the multiple influences of the heavens, adding the nourishment of the winds, the dew, and the rains, so that he might produce grasses and multiple, most abundant fruits for the food of the same. It remained to prepare foods for the better man as well. Hence he prepared a paradise of pleasure planted with many kinds of trees, most fertile with all fruits. Furthermore, he placed the Tree of Life in its very center, not for the animal man, but for the better man; and near it the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil—good indeed for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to the sight. And to irrigate all the trees, there was a river flowing out of the place of pleasure, which, afterward divided into four heads, would also water all the lower parts. All these trees, fruits, and waters were granted to man, except for the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, which is Christ, as we have said elsewhere. Man ought not to have vied for his rank, nor fed upon him, or the Tree of Life (which is the same thing), until the time predefined by the Father arrived, when the ripened fruit would be offered to us.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin> as food. This truly happened when he said: *Take and eat, this is my body* <note>original: "Accipite, & manducate, hoc eft corpus meũ"</note>; he offered not only the fruit, but the entire tree, yet without any lessening of himself. Nor, however, from the time of the first-created man <term>protoplast; from the Greek "protoplastos," referring to Adam as the first human formed</term> until Christ was the spiritual man left without food; for he gave sacrifices and prayers, which we read that <margin>Abel</margin> Abel first offered. Then all his descendants did the same by God's command, as all those who are truly wise rightly conclude: for no one would have attempted to offer sacrifices and gifts to God that were not required by God.
