Moreover, when the divine family went out from Egyptian servitude, manna was added—the food of Angels, or of the strong, as it is contained in the literal truth of the scripture. Sacrifice was also increased, the law was given, and hymns were celebrated: all of which are true foods for the spiritual and better man. From this family, as it degenerated and became entangled in many crimes, these foods were withdrawn when it was destined for the Babylonian captivity. Released from that captivity, but not fully restored, it arrived quite weak at the time of Christ. In those times, the most pious and generous Father regenerated it and the entire mass of the human race, preparing a better food than that shadowy <note>original: "umbraticus"; referring to the "shadows" or types of the Old Testament that foreshadowed the New</note> food, as he himself said when relating the secret mystery: <margin>CHRIST.</margin> *Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you bread from heaven... For I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died... but I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.* <note>John 6:32-51</note> Therefore, the tree and the fruit of life have been granted to us—which the first man was expelled from that place of pleasure <note>Eden</note> so that he might not touch it—and it has been offered for us to eat under the threat of death <note>referring to spiritual death or the requirement of the sacrament for life</note>, when it is said: <margin>THE SAME</margin> *Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man*—which is the same as the bread of life—*and drink his blood, you will not have life in you.* <note>John 6:53</note> Thus, each Father was most concerned with feeding both natures of man: both he who first begot us, and he sent by him who regenerated us. For this one said concerning the animal man <note>the "animal" or "natural" man refers to the physical body and its needs</note>: *Be not anxious for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on. Look at the birds of the sky, which neither sow nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. <margin>THE SAME</margin> Are you not worth much more than they?* <note>Matthew 6:25-26</note> Why then do you distrust the Father? Why do you doubt his providence to his injury? When did you see him neglect the care of his children? If he cares with such providence for all those things produced for the service of man, so that nothing is lacking to them, why do you doubt the provision for his children? Not only has he prepared food and clothing for animals, but he even descends to the humbler flowers of the field, saying: <margin>THE SAME</margin> *See the lilies of the field, or the roses, how they grow: they do not labor, nor do they spin, and yet they are clothed more precious than Solomon in all his glory.* <note>Matthew 6:28-29</note> For Solomon used garments woven by craft and painted with artificial colors; but the flowers, which nature prepared, put on garments and are painted with colors provided by nature, which is more noble than art. If God clothes [the grass of the field] in this way, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith? <note>A reference to Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28.</note> Having been taught by this Teacher, we are also able to argue: If He feeds the body—which is destined to be handed over to worms—with so many and such exquisite banquets, how much more will He feed the spiritual man? This is the man whom He brought forth from His own innermost being to be taken up as a co-heir to the paternal inheritance and to be joined to Him in perpetual fellowship. For this "better man," He has prepared special foods sent down from heaven—celestial and divine—so that by eating them, the man himself might be made entirely divine. He enclosed these foods under the forms of bread, meat, and wine, just as if they were the primary foods and drink of human life.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Truly, just as blood is "cooked" within a mother’s womb and transformed by a marvelous change <term>metamorphosis; the author uses the Greek-derived term to describe the biological belief that breast milk was actually processed blood</term> into milk to be given to infants and tender little ones, so for adults and those more mature, that same blood—in which celestial life resides—is changed into a celestial wine and offered to be drunk. This is according to the words of the Apostle:

<margin>Paul CHRIST</margin>
*We offer milk to you as if to infants; but solid food is for the perfect—for those who, by constant use, have their senses trained to distinguish between good and evil.* <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:14.</note>

<margin>Peter</margin>
Peter supports this, saying: *As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk [of the word] without guile, so that you may grow by it toward salvation; for then you will be able to taste how sweet the Lord is.* <note>Refers to 1 Peter 2:2-3.</note>

And thus, the very same drink that is given to infants in the form of milk for food and drink is given to adults under the form of wine and blood. This is certainly not the kind of blood in which a beast-like soul resides and which cannot possess the kingdom of God, but the blood in which divine life resides, by which the spiritual and divine man must live.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
And this was prepared as a special gift at the Last Supper, when He said: *Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new and eternal testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.* <note>original: "Bibite ex hoc oēs: Hic est .n. sanguis meus noui, & æterni testamēti, qui pro uobis, & pro multis effundetur in remissionē peccatop̄"</note> By this blood, being cleansed, you may live a divine life.

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
From this it is concluded that this blood was both a bath [for cleansing] and a drink. To accompany this drink, He gave matching bread and meat, and these were "cooked by fire" so as to prevent any revulsion <note>A theological metaphor suggesting that the "fire" of the Holy Spirit or divine love makes the idea of consuming "flesh and blood" palatable and spiritual rather than literal or "raw."</note>, as we shall soon discuss. This bread He elsewhere called the "Word" which proceeds from the mouth of God, in which He also said that man lives, and not by bread alone. For the animalistic man lives by physical bread, but the spiritual man lives by the Word.

Now, if by this bread we mean the "Bread of Life" and the spiritual bread, then we can say that the spiritual life of man is sustained by this bread. However, insofar as it is the "Word" and "Wisdom," that intellectual part of the soul is fed.

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
Nevertheless, it is the same Being taking on different properties: for the same Christ is bread in His body, the Word in His divinity, and blood and wine in His soul. Yet in each part, the power of every other part is present. Therefore, whoever receives the bread also receives the power of the blood and the divinity. This is what we are taught by the common rite of the Church, which judges that the laity are spiritually fed by receiving only the bread and the body, as if the power of the blood and the divinity were contained within it. <note>This refers to the doctrine of "concomitance," the Catholic teaching that the whole Christ—Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity—is present in either the bread or the wine alone.</note>

<margin>CHRIST THE SAME</margin>
Our Parent, declaring what this multi-faceted food is, said: *I am the living bread who came down from heaven.* <note>original: "Ego sum panis uiuus, qui de cœlo descendi"</note> And again: *My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.* He also adds the effect of eating this food, saying: *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.* He teaches that He is not only the wine, but the vine from which it is born, saying:

### Chapter VII. How He cooked these foods to remove nausea.

But lest it cause indigestion in those receiving it, the most pious Father took care to cook these foods, just as was observed with a happy omen in the figurative foods [of the Old Testament]. For when the Israelites were about to make their symbolic passage, God commanded that they roast the figurative lamb with fire. And to those offering bread, it was ordained in the Law that they should by no means present it raw, but baked in an oven. <margin>JESUS</margin> Therefore, the Father and our greatest high priest, Christ—observing everything set forth in the Law down to the smallest stroke <note>original: "apicem," referring to the smallest mark in Hebrew script</note> and fulfilling it—cooked every food He prepared in the "oven of the cross" by that fire of which He said: *I have come to send fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it burn?* <note>Luke 12:49</note> Indeed, it burns not to consume, but to cook the prepared foods; to fuse us into one; to instruct and transform us, <margin>Jeremiah</margin> according to that saying of Jeremiah in Lamentations: *From on high he sent fire into my bones and instructed me*—or "dissolved me by melting," as the literal truth has it, or "acquired me," having been transformed from a natural being into a spiritual one. <note>original: וירדנה *vairdenah*; a Hebrew grammatical form the author interprets as "and he acquired" or "and he dissolved."</note> This fire thus dissolves us so that it may fuse and transform us into something better. 

It is not unfitting, therefore, for <margin>Guido of Châtres</margin> <note>original: "Gui.La." referring to Guido II, the Carthusian author of the *Scala Claustralium*</note> Guido of Châtres to exclaim toward this fire, saying: "O happy flame, burning and not withering, illuminating and not turning to ash; thus you transform all who love you into yourself, so they are rightly called by the name of the living God. You warmed the Apostles, and by leaving everything except you, they were made sons of God. You warmed the martyrs, and they shed their blood so that theirs, mixed with your blood, might become one thing. You warmed the virgins, and by the fire of love they extinguished the fire of foulness, so that they might be made lawful brides to be joined to you. You warmed the confessors, and they gave themselves up to harsh prisons so that, being free for you alone, they might easily be united with you." 

Every creature, therefore, lives by the benefit of this fire, so that there is nothing that can hide from its heat if it desires to have fellowship with God. He kindles this divine fire in cooking the prepared foods by adding the fuel of wood appropriate to it. These were prefigured by the wood of the cross, the true oven where these foods are cooked. And these woods were cedar, cypress, olive, and palm, as is commonly asserted. The first is the cedar, which knows no corruption and lasts forever, denoting an unfailing affection and effect, and the everlasting fuel of fiery love; for the good man always burns with love. The fragrant cypress signifies the scent of His virtues, always fragrant to cleansed nostrils, so that one sensing it says: *We run in the scent of your ointments.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:3-4</note> Indeed, <margin>Origen</margin> Origen says that God the Father, anointing Him with various ointments, made Him the Christ <term>Christ; from the Greek 'Christos', meaning 'Anointed One'</term> and a physician. He also made Him a pillar of smoke from the aromatics of myrrh and frankincense, and every powder of the perfumer.

Delighted by these scents, He was set on fire with the desire that He might sprinkle us with them and make us fragrant, according to that saying of the Apostle: <margin>Paul</margin> *We are the good odor of Christ.* <note>original: "Christi bonus odor sumus" from 2 Corinthians 2:15</note> Indeed, we are fragrant with this odor when we offer our works to God, and offer ourselves as a *living sacrifice, pleasing to God,* which He receives as an *odor of sweetness.* <note>original: "hostiam vivam... in odorem suavitatis," referencing Romans 12:1 and Ephesians 5:2</note> This was the fuel of that warming love with which He was ignited to carry out the work of our redemption. The olive tree represents mercy and kindness, which is always directed toward us as a benefit of His burning love. The palm tree, however, signifies the triumph to be won over the ancient enemy, by whose love He was also set on fire. For martyrs carry the palm as a sign of constancy and triumph, because the more its branch is loaded with fruit, the more it rises up and is never bent down. <note>A common medieval and early modern belief held that the palm tree grew stronger under the pressure of weight, making it a symbol of resilience.</note> These, then, are the four woods <note>In Christian legend, the Cross was often said to be composed of four types of wood: palm, cedar, cypress, and olive.</note> that provided fuel for that divine fire, by which our Redeemer—perfected, cooked, and seasoned—was brought forth as the finest bread and flesh to be provided for us as food.

Furthermore, with that same fire spread within us, like a good baker and bread-maker, He cooks us and prepares us into bread and food to be eaten by Him. <margin>CHRIST</margin> "I will enter," He says in the Apocalypse, to the one who opens for me, "and I will dine with him, and he with me." <note>Revelation 3:20</note> For He became man so that He might make man God; He also made Himself the food of man, so that He might make man His own food, and both might eat lunch and dinner together in that last and eternal supper. In that place, cooked and forever warmed by that divine fire, the foods set before them never fail. There also is that new wine produced from that vine which says: *I am the true vine.* <note>John 15:1</note> <margin>THE SAME</margin> And it was squeezed in the winepress of the cross by the same one who said: *I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.* <note>Isaiah 63:3</note> He alone, indeed, trod the wine of merit, because He alone earned the grace by which we might work well, and the prize of glory which is given to us.

Therefore, He prepared these foods cooked by divine fire for the feeding of the sons born from those divine and most sacred loins <note>A metaphor for those spiritually begotten by Christ.</note>, so that they might not faint. Just as the "natural man" <note>original: "animalis homo," the unspiritual or worldly person</note> lives on bread of rye, barley, or wheat—whether it be a primary or secondary loaf, or a cake baked under ashes <note>original: "subcineritio," bread cooked directly in the embers</note>—along with various kinds of meat, fish, fruit, and vegetables, and drinks diverse wines and various waters, so too should the spiritual man be fed by bread provided from heaven, having all delight within itself and filled with the power of every food, kneaded with the sweet blood of the true Lamb. He should be fed with flesh in which the most excellent power of all flesh is enclosed by a certain mark—not only because it is the flesh of a man exceeding all others, but because it is the flesh of the Prince, because it is immaculate flesh, being the ark of divinity, and the flesh of Him who is the bond of all creatures. He is also fed with milk or butter; he who eats this knows how to refuse evil and choose good. <note>Isaiah 7:15</note> This milk is pressed from those lofty breasts of which it is said in the Canticles: <margin>Canticles</margin> *Your breasts are better than wine.* <note>Song of Songs 1:2</note> And again: *There I will give you my breasts.* <note>Song of Songs 7:12</note> He also drinks the water of saving wisdom, offered by that host who, wandering as a pilgrim with us, cried out saying: <margin>CHRIST</margin> *If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.* <note>John 7:37</note> And again: *He who drinks of this water which I [shall give him]...*

### He Who Begot and Feeds Us Also Instructs Us Like a Good Father. Chapter 8.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin>
**I**f you have sons <note>The Latin text begins with a decorative initial 'F' for "Filii" (Sons), but the translator has adjusted for the English 'I'.</note> (says that wise man), educate them. <note>original: "Filli tibi sunt... erudi illos" from Sirach 7:25. "The wise man" refers to Jesus ben Sirach, the traditionally attributed author of this book.</note> Hence, Jesus, the wisest and best of all fathers, after our birth and nourishment, has taken the greatest care to instruct us in every kind of doctrine, taught not only by words but by deeds and examples. All the Gospels are full of the doctrine conveyed by word, where it frequently records how He opened His mouth and taught and preached in the synagogues of Galilee and Judea, so that the doctrine, sown in the very center of the world, might more easily be carried to all the ends of the earth. He also drenched the Apostles and disciples with the promised Holy Spirit, who, by suggesting all things to them, taught them everything, so that they might spread the doctrine they had received throughout the whole world and bring all things to the goal of the Gospel and divine wisdom, as the divine
<margin>David</margin>
Lyre-player <note>The author uses "Citharoedus" (one who plays the cithara or lyre) as a poetic title for King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> sang beforehand, saying: *Their sound has gone out into all the earth*—or "their line," as the true text has it, meaning the rules for all things—*and their words to the ends of the world*; <note>original: "In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum... in fines orbis terræ uerba eorum" from Psalm 19:4</note> or, even better according to the literal sense, their discourses. Nor were there any languages in which their words were not heard, for they were given the power to speak in the tongues of all peoples in the name of Jesus, our parent and teacher, so that this doctrine might be understood by all. This was a confirmation that the doctrine was from the Holy Spirit, just as the gift of tongues was, and consequently from our teacher Christ, who had sent Him. He also taught by deeds and examples, according to what He said:
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
*For I have given you an example, that as I have done, you should also do.* <note>original: "Exemplum enim dedi uobis, ut quemadmodum ego feci, & uos faciatis" from John 13:15</note> And He taught so much by His deeds that our wise men say that His every action was our doctrine and instruction. <margin>David</margin>
subjected to the spirit, into God, as is sung in the Psalm: *The law of the Lord is immaculate,* <note>original: "Lex Domini immaculata" from Psalm 19:7</note> that is...

# A brief epilogue regarding those things which Christ taught concerning the nature and purpose of man. Chapter X.

<margin>Peripatetics, Academics, Plotinus, Pythagoras</margin>
**V**arious things have been established regarding man by the wise of the world; these matters were mostly touched upon, though not settled, by those whose works we now have at hand, but they were most clearly defined by Christ: Who are we? Where do we come from? Where do we live? To what end do we strive? By what path? Who man is, we have determined from the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their scientific and categorical approach to philosophy.</note> only so far as that he is an animal, and specifically a rational one produced by man and by the sun. <note>This refers to the Aristotelian idea that "man and the sun generate man," meaning that biological life depends on both human parents and the celestial heat of the sun.</note> However, by the <term>Academics</term> <note>Followers of the school of Plato.</note> (as they had drawn from the prophetic workshop), it is added that beyond animal nature and reason, there is something divine in man, which **Plotinus** calls the "intellect" or "intellectual light." By means of this light, we are able to know God and perform good works pleasing to God himself. **Pythagoras** also drew from that same workshop, saying in his "Golden Verses": *Have confidence, for a divine race is within men.* <note>original: "Confide, quoniam diuinum genus hominibus inest"</note> But Christ, transcending even further, taught that we are the children of God, while He commends the <margin>David</margin> Prophet who had said: *I have said, you are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.* <note>original: "Ego dixi dii estis, et filii excelsi oēs" from Psalm 82:6</note> But because we fell from this dignity to such an extent that no trace of it remained in us, nor could anyone be found who was able to teach or know anything about it, **JESUS** <margin>John</margin> our teacher not only taught us, but (as John says) gave us the power so that we might be children of God, once the flesh and blood that had torn us away from 그 dignity were put to death. <margin>The same</margin> And elsewhere, exulting, he says: *See what kind of love God has given us, namely through Christ, that we should be named and indeed be the children of God.* <note>1 John 3:1</note> He taught again that we are made children of God through a sweet harmony with Him, saying: *Blessed are the peacemakers, <margin>CHRIST</margin> for they shall be called children of God.* <note>original: "Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei uocabunt" from Matthew 5:9</note> This peace is certainly not that of **Octavian**, <note>A reference to the "Pax Romana" established by Augustus Caesar (Octavian), which was a political and military peace.</note> nor that which the world desires—where each person might enjoy his own goods more securely without fear of robbers or assassins—but rather that peace which we ought to have with God. This consists in an all-encompassing consonance and harmony with Him: so that we desire nothing and accomplish nothing except insofar as it is pleasing to Him, with vices and lusts utterly suppressed, enemies conquered, and the passions set at peace. We neither knew how to do this, nor were we able, except through JESUS Christ our father and teacher, as <margin>Paul</margin> **Paul** says: *But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through JESUS Christ our Lord.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:57</note> This peace and victory stand firm amidst every kind of external war, <margin>Vincent</margin> persecution, and martyrdom. While being tortured, **Vincent** <note>St. Vincent of Saragossa, a famous early Christian martyr.</note> said: *I am led in the highest places, therefore I do not fear your torments.* <note>original: "In sublimibus agor, ideo tormẽta tua non timeo"</note> He taught, moreover, that the human <margin>CHRIST</margin> condition is finally to be made like that of the angels, when He says: *And they shall be in heaven, like the Angels of God,* <note>Matthew 22:30</note> perhaps with a greater identity than a mere likeness. He also declared the value of the soul, placing it above the whole world, saying: *What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his own soul?* <note>original: "Quid prodest homini, si uniuersum mũdũ lucret, animæ uero suę detrimentũ patiatur?" from Matthew 16:26</note> If anyone well considers all these things and those similar to them, he will understand those things defined concerning the condition of man which the wise of this world have least of all explained. The second point is: <margin>Aristotle</margin> **Where do we come from?** This we are unable to learn from **Aristotle**, since he does not determine from where the rational soul emerges—whether from the lap of matter itself, or whether it comes...

...for in the world there is nothing but what is hostile to us: the **lust of the flesh**, the **lust of the eyes**, and the **pride of life**. <note>A reference to 1 John 2:16, a standard biblical summary of worldly temptations.</note> Furthermore, our teacher and Father showed by His deeds more than by His words that this is not our homeland, but a temporary lodging-place of pilgrimage, while He presented Himself as a pilgrim to His disciples. <margin>Plato</margin> 
**Plato**, imbued with the same teaching, says in the *Phaedo*: *Those who are found to have lived more piously than others are released from these earthly places as if from a prison, and they ascend to higher things, dwelling in a pure region above the earth, where the reward is beautiful and the hope is great.*

<margin>CHRIST</margin> 
knowledge cannot be fully possessed in this pilgrimage, He declared when it would be obtained, saying: *When the Son of Man comes in the seat of His majesty, all nations shall be gathered before Him.* Once they are separated, He will say to those on His right hand: *Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.* In that kingdom, there will be the open vision of the Father and the Maker; there will be the enjoyment of all good things; and finally, there will be a state made perfect by the gathering of every good, which is the state of true <term>blessedness</term> <note>original: "beatitudo," referring to the ultimate state of happiness in God's presence.</note>.

Which of the philosophers, however, ever declared that a kingdom was prepared for us? Who would have dared to ask for it, or hope for it, unless the Lord of that kingdom Himself had declared and promised it? Again, who declared that we are invited to that kingdom as if to a wedding feast, except our teacher, as is clear in the parable of the wedding?

The final point, which is the most difficult of all, is 
<margin>Baruch</margin> 
by what way one must travel to that end. *There is no one,* says **Baruch**, *who can know the way of that kingdom, nor is there anyone who can think out its paths.* <note>Reference to Baruch 3:23.</note> Neither the giants, who were of great stature and famous men from the beginning; nor any of the princes of this age, who are destroyed; nor any of the philosophers, who consumed their lifetimes and years in searching—and as 
<margin>Lactantius</margin> 
**Lactantius** discourses at great length—lost both their time and their labor. This continued until our teacher and Father was seen on earth and lived among men. He not only taught the way, but He *made Himself* the way—not, I say, merely that way of the commandments in which **David** ran with an enlarged heart, nor only the way of the virtues (though He taught those most fully in every form), but He made Himself the way and the staff upon which we might lean as we travel to the Father. He does not merely sustain us, but leads us, draws us, and carries us, as in the parable of the lost sheep carried upon the shoulders of the shepherd.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
...we are taught; in whose person **Augustine** says when disputing against five heresies: "When you were an enemy to my Father, I reconciled you; when you wandered among mountains and woods, I sought you; among the stones and wooden idols <note>original: "lapides & ligna"</note> which you adored, I found you; on my shoulders I carried you all the way back to the Father, to whom I returned you." He also took upon Himself the entire weight of our sins, so that, having been unburdened, we might proceed or be carried more easily. He also taught how we ought to be renewed and transformed, so that having been made lighter, we might not falter on this most high and difficult journey. He taught us this so that we would not appear in the image of the beast—which we had taken on through sin—and be expelled from that court of minds and intellectual spirits <note>This refers to the assembly of angels and perfected souls in heaven.</note> much more severely than that man who was said to be cast out from the wedding feast because he did not have a wedding garment. The beginning of this transformation occurs through the **sacramental seed**, by which we are conceived in baptism and reborn according to the spirit. But through the resurrection, we receive the completion of this perfect regeneration, of which it is said: *In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty with his angels, you—namely the Apostles—shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* Moreover, all others who have left home, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children, or fields, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life. For who had ever spoken or even thought of this regeneration before Him? Of this regeneration, which happens in the resurrection, He Himself was the beginning and the way, 
<margin>Paul</margin>
as **Paul** says: *Christ is risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep, for since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.* And this is the true way of life which our teacher Christ taught, just as the 
<margin>David</margin>
Prophet **David** had foretold: *You have made known to me the ways of life*, which (as 
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
**Ambrose** says) were previously considered unknown. Foreseeing Him in the spirit, 
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
**Isaiah** joyfully said: *Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord*, namely to that mountain raised above the peak of mountains and above all hills—that is, above all those who are sublime in power, wisdom, and holiness—and to the house of the God of Jacob, from which our teacher **JESUS** came forth according to the flesh; *and He will teach us His ways, and we will walk in His paths: because the law shall go forth from Sion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.* Indeed, the Law was recently brought low (as we said), and the Word of the Lord, which was made flesh, taught us most powerfully in the Temple which is in Jerusalem, and on the cross fixed before its gate.

### In what school of training, and from what teaching chair He instructed us. Chapter XI.

**A**LTHOUGH this Father and our Teacher taught us in the Temple, on the mountains, in the synagogues of Galilee, and in various places, He nevertheless delivered the entire sum and effectiveness of His doctrine on the Cross, so that 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Augustine** rightly says: *The Cross of the suffering Christ was the teaching chair <term>cathedra</term> <note>The 'cathedra' is the official seat of a bishop or teacher, signifying authority.</note> of the master.* 
<margin>Paul</margin>
This was also recognized by **Paul**, who said to the Corinthians: *I decided to know nothing...*

# OF THE SECOND CANTICLE

### OF THE SECOND CANTICLE

I decided to know nothing among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified: because being placed on the cross, he gave us every kind of teaching. Running through this teaching on the surface <note>The author suggests he is providing an introductory overview before diving deeper.</note>, we say that, beginning from the elements of a better and **mystical grammar**, he led us all the way to the highest peaks of the deepest theology, leaving no intermediate doctrine untouched. For first, he taught that the eternal **Word** <note>original: "verbum," which in Latin means both "the Word of God" and the grammatical "verb."</note> agrees with that **Noun** <note>original: "nomine," meaning "name" or grammatical "noun."</note> which is above every name,
<margin>Paul</margin>
granted to him indeed through the power of the cross—if Paul teaches truly. For Paul says of this incarnate Word, who is surnamed Christ: *He was made obedient for us even unto death, even the death of the cross: because of which God also has exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, so that at the name of JESUS every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.* The power of this name, though given on the cross, is nevertheless given in view of the divine Word united to it, pouring through this name JESUS and the one named, so much so that by <term>antonomasia</term> <note>A rhetorical figure where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name.</note> he is surnamed the **Messiah** <note>Hebrew for "Anointed One."</note> and **Christ** <note>Greek for "Anointed One."</note>, that is, the "Anointed One" above all his companions. From here he also taught the **Participle** <note>In grammar, a participle "shares" the nature of both a verb and an adjective; here, it represents Christ's two natures.</note>, that is, the portion taken from both natures by which Christ himself is constituted. He also explained another "participation" on the cross, when he shared with us the grace, glory, and merit which he acquired upon it, so that he might make us sharers of himself and unite us with him. The **Pronoun** is truly that surname "Christ" which we use in place of the name JESUS; thus we are called "Christians" from Christ, just as we ought to be called "Jesuans" from Jesus. Or let us say that even if Jesus is a noun, it can nevertheless be a pronoun, because it stands for us in place of the great name of God <note>This refers to the Tetragrammaton, the unpronounceable name of God in the Hebrew tradition.</note>, which could not be expressed until the work of the cross was demanded. On the cross (as we said), power was given to this name, which we invoke in place of the great name of God, as we declared above.
<margin>The same</margin>
Furthermore, he taught the **Preposition** when he handed down his name to be "placed before" all our works, just as Paul expressed, saying:
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
*Whatever you do, do in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.* He also taught us to "put before" us the cross which must be followed, saying: *He who wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.* I, who am to be fixed to the cross, offer it to you as a staff and a sign going before you, to be set forward in all your works.
<margin>The same</margin>
He also explained the **Adverb** <note>In Latin, "ad-verbium" literally means "beside the word/verb."</note>, namely the Mother standing "beside the Word," when he said to the disciple, and consequently to all of us: *Behold your mother.* I leave her in my place so that through her mediation—she who stands continually beside me and before the face of the Father—you may be able to obtain from the Father and from me whatever you wish. Therefore, the disciple then, in his own name and in the name of all of us, received her into his protection and as a refuge in place of Christ, and simultaneously along with Him. But he also taught us to make the greatest **Interjections**, providing the source from which we might emit sighs and all the utterances of a grieving person. Lastly, he taught that **Conjunction**, for which we were all established: the union with God that brings us bliss. For sensing what he was shortly to do on the cross, so that he might work more effectively, [he...]

He also provided two most pleasing ways to reconcile the "Auditor," the Father, in whose presence we must always pray. One is the diligent care we must have so that a pure and clean soul is represented to God the Father, from whom we received it; this he taught us to do by his own action when he said: <note>original: "Pater in manus tuas cōmendo spiritum meū"</note> *Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.* The other is the love of enemies, in which he offered himself as a singular example to be

<margin>Arithmetic</margin> 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>

But he also taught us how to **multiply**, when he instructed us to join our few merits with his own most abundant ones, so that a proper account might be found. He also taught us how to **divide** the soul from the spirit by the spiritual sword, which is the Word of God entrusted to us, having its power most especially through the cross and Christ crucified. He also demonstrated how to **subtract** debts <note>In a theological sense, "debts" refers to sins or spiritual failings.</note> from our merits, so that it might be seen what fruit remained from our works. In **Geometry**, however, he taught

<margin>Matthew</margin>

Here it is a metaphor for joining the infinite/divine (the circle) with the finite/material (the square).</note> And he did this while he "squared" the intellectual sphere and the divine nature within the body of the fourfold element, <note>Refers to the four classical elements—earth, air, fire, water—which make up the physical body.</note> providing for us, from those same squared elements, a way that we might be able to meet with that divine sphere. For the sphere of a square or a cube cannot be rightly produced unless 그 square shape is dissolved and reduced back into a circle. Therefore, it is necessary for this corruptible and rectangular (or fourfold) body to be dissolved and mortified through the cross, if it is to become spherical and divine.

## Chapter XII. With what treasures, like a good father, Christ enriches us.

<margin>Marcus Varro</margin>
<gloss>N</gloss> <note>The letter N refers to the decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting foliated patterns.</note> it would not have been enough for our parent to have fathered us, and to continually feed and instruct us, unless he also made us rich and provided for us in all things. For "riches" <note>original: "diuitiæ"</note> are so named (as Marcus Varro <note>A celebrated Roman scholar and writer (116–27 BC).</note> and other grammarians teach) because they make us "god-like" <note>original: "diuos"; the author is following a traditional but folk etymology linking *divitiae* (riches) to *divus* (divine/god).</note> and lacking in nothing, just as God is. True riches lead us to this state. But such a great error has grown among men that they think they make themselves rich in those things which are dedicated to the lower kingdoms like dregs and refuse. For Pluto, the anti-god, also has his riches dug out of the earth, wherefore he is called *Dis* <note>A Latin name for the god of the underworld, often associated with *dives* (rich).</note> because he is always rich in these earthly things, as Pluto himself says in the poet Claudian: *And we always hold what the gods above once held.* <note>Claudian, *De Raptu Proserpinae*. Pluto argues that the underworld contains the "wealth" of everything that has died or fallen from the upper world.</note> This Pluto (as we have said) is named Mammon by the Savior, as are the riches he possesses. These riches are opposed to the true ones, just as their prince Mammon is opposed to our Father, who is truly rich—not only for 
<margin>Paul</margin>
himself, but for all others, as the Apostle says: *Rich toward all who call upon him.* <note>Romans 10:12.</note> And so great is the discrepancy between them that no one can serve both, as he testifies...

### To whom and how much he has bequeathed. Chapter 15.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
**S**ince these things which take place in civil matters are consistent with divine and heavenly ones, and one Republic is an image of the other, we can most aptly learn about divine things from those which are familiar to us at home. A civil testator can bequeath many things to many people, provided that some heir is appointed from whom the hereditary legacies (as the legal experts <term>Iureconsulti</term> <note>referring to experts in Roman Law</note> assert) are owed. In like manner, Christ brought this about, as Ambrose discusses well, saying: The Author of Piety, hanging on the cross, established a testament, distributing works of piety to each: To the Father his spirit, to the Virgin a bridegroom-attendant <term>Paranymphum</term> <note>original: "Paranymphum"; here referring to the Apostle John, whom Christ appointed as a guardian for Mary.</note>, to Nicodemus his body to be committed to the earth, to the Apostles persecution, to the Sinner hell, to penitent Christians the cross, to the Thief paradise, and to all faithful children the inheritance of eternal life. Of which inheritance it is not granted to speak, since they themselves who saw it testify that it is not lawful for man to speak <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:4</note>, and the Testator himself says: "No one knows the manna and the banquet I have prepared to be given, and the delights to be distributed, except he who receives them." Hence, to the striving Augustine, inquiring what glory and joy is prepared for the blessed, a light shone and a voice sounded saying: "Augustine, Augustine, what do you seek? Do you think to put the whole sea into a small vessel? To enclose the globe of the earth in a brief fist? To fix the heaven so it does not exercise its usual motions? What no eye of man could see, yours shall see; what no ear has drawn in, yours shall draw in; what the human heart has in no way understood, yours shall understand." <note>This refers to a famous legend where Augustine, walking on a beach while contemplating the Trinity, saw a child trying to pour the ocean into a small hole, illustrating the impossibility of the finite human mind grasping the infinite God.</note> What shall be the end of an infinite thing? By what measure will you measure the immense? For the object which those citizens enjoy is indeed infinite: the duration for those blessed ones will be infinite through succession: their progress will be infinite, because it will never be terminated; nor shall they find an end to those goods in which they take delight, or to that Good which contains all things with such excellence that, in comparison to its own form, all others might be called shadowy <note>original: "umbratica"</note> by reason of the singular excellence which they have in the fountain of all goods.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
[Stephen], filled with the Holy Spirit, looking into heaven, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God, having already, as it were, entered into possession both for us and for himself. <note>A reference to the martyrdom of St. Stephen in Acts 7:55-56.</note> Regarding this possession, he had said with certainty to the thief: "Today you will be with me in paradise." And lest anyone should hold those witnesses as suspect—as if they were merely kinsmen or close friends—he also took as a witness Paul, who had been a persecutor and an enemy, a man of the sharpest intellect, so that no one could accuse him of "credulous simplicity." <note>The author argues that Paul's conversion proves the truth of Christ's glory because he was originally a hostile intellectual, not a gullible follower.</note> Him he raised up even to the third heaven, where according to the Hebrews, the beauty and glory of God's theology shines, and where the "breasts" are which used to nurse the prophets; and there he showed and entrusted to him that glory and those secrets which it is not lawful for a man to speak. Yet, to attest to the truth of this matter, Paul laid down his life and his head. So too, for the truth of this glory (just as they felt it with a perfect definition in their minds and hearts, illuminated by divine light), many others gave up their lives, who are called <term>martyrs</term> <note>original: "martyres"; from the Greek word for "witnesses."</note>. And so great was the abundance of these that, up to the time of Constantine, they are calculated to have been thirty-two million <note>original: "triginta duo millia milliũ"; literally "thirty-two thousand thousands." This reflects a traditional medieval pious exaggeration of the number of early Christian martyrs.</note> who gave their lives to attest to the truth of the glory prepared for our soul, and for the whole composite body after the resurrection. They would by no means have done this unless they had been taught by the Holy Spirit and had been made certain in some way of those things which they were proving at such great risk to their lives. Moreover, he appointed all those as heirs of this kind of glory and of the kingdom of heaven who are willing to become his and to be reborn of his seed. But those who wish to live according to the flesh and blood are disinherited, for they cannot possess the kingdom of God. Nor does the <term>Prince of Tartarus</term> <note>original: "tartareus princeps"; a classical reference to the ruler of the underworld or Hell.</note> claim them against their will; of them our Testator once said: "You are of your father the devil, and <margin>THE SAME</margin> you wish to do the desires of your father." This is because, by adopting his ways, they do his works, all of which are founded on a lie, since he himself is a liar and the father of lies, instructing his children in falsehood and deception. For he can neither promise nor act toward us except in lies and deceit, since he can give nothing but punishment, mourning, horror, darkness, and such things which man by his very nature abhors. Therefore, it is necessary that he entice those whom he draws to himself with some falsehood. He offers pleasures, therefore, as the "baits" of his fraud, so that by those allurements (which cannot possess the kingdom of God), enticed mortals might be torn away and diverted from that kingdom and inheritance from which he himself was expelled. This inheritance has been prepared for us from the foundation of the world, and bequeathed in the most celebrated testament of the Son of God.

### On the Solemnity with which He Celebrated this Testament. Chapter 16.

**I**n the solemn celebration of a testament, there is required (as the <term>Jurists</term> <note>original: "Iureconsulti"; experts in Roman and civil law.</note> say, or as is customary) a capable testator of sound and healthy mind, a <term>notary</term> <note>original: "tabellio"; a public scribe or official who drafted legal documents.</note> having authority, witnesses, and heirs. The Testator was Christ, the Son of the eternal Father, long ago appointed heir of all things with the fullest authority for making a will, leaving legacies, and appointing heirs, with that division of the estate which (by the judgment of the best Father) shall seem fitting to each. Concerning this <margin>Baruch</margin> testament, it had been predicted long ago in the oracle of the prophet Baruch in this manner:

...with these words: "I will establish for them another everlasting testament, that I may be to them a God, and they to me a people." <note>A reference to Ezekiel 37:26 or Jeremiah 31.</note> Concerning this, it is also said in Jeremiah: "Behold, the days will come, says the Lord, and I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the pact which I made with your fathers—a pact which they rendered void." For this will be a pact, and a new and eternal testament, no longer to be removed nor made obsolete. "By saying 'new,'" <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says, "he has made the first one old. And that which is made ancient and grows old is close to vanishing." <note>Quoting Hebrews 8:13.</note> Therefore, since that ancient testament had existed, it had to be changed into a new one, <margin>The same <gloss>Paul</gloss></margin> and it was changed into that which no further change is expected. Nor should it trouble anyone that Jeremiah says "covenant" or "pact," because "covenant," "pact," and "testament" are accepted as the same thing, as we can learn from Paul’s progress with the Hebrews. <note>In the Latin Vulgate, the word *testamentum* translates both the legal "will" and the theological "covenant."</note> So too it was called the "Ark of the Covenant" and the "Ark of the Testament"; and everywhere that promise made in the law, and confirmed by the death of animals, is called the "Old Testament." 

Therefore, this testator <note>Christ</note> was capable, and he testified to such great things while in a most excellent and sound state of mind, so that no equal to him has ever existed. This is clear from his most celebrated teaching and from the things he most prudently did when he founded this testament. There was also not just one, but four notaries <term>tabelliones</term> <note>original: "tabelliones"; these were public officials or scribes in Roman law who drafted legal documents.</note> beyond all reproach—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—appointed by the supreme Emperor <note>God</note>, who wrote down the life, teaching, deeds, and the testament of this Father of ours. The witnesses were innumerable, from every nation that is under heaven; for to this spectacle had gathered Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamians, Cappadocians, Phrygians, Egyptians, Arabs, Cretans, and the rest who are named in the <margin>Acts</margin> Acts of the Apostles. But these witnesses spoke especially from the three most famous languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—in each of which the cause of the testator himself was written above him. <note>Refers to the *Titulus* or sign placed on the Cross above Jesus' head.</note> All of these heard what the great man JESUS ordained in his testament before his death, and they saw those signs and wonders which <margin>Consequently in blood.</margin> were performed for its corroboration, both then and afterward. 

The heirs are all those who are born of God and are reborn, refusing to live according to flesh and blood. "For if anyone is not a son, he is not an heir; but if a son, then an heir," says <margin>Paul</margin> Paul. Since we are sons—not of the slave woman or illegitimate, but of the free woman and legitimate—we are consequently heirs. And a little before: "You are all sons of God through faith in Jesus Christ, as many of you as have been baptized in Christ." And again to the Romans: "If children, then heirs; heirs of God and co-heirs with <margin>Peter</margin> Christ." And Peter says: "The baptism of Jesus Christ saves you; he is at the right hand of God, swallowing up death, so that we might be made heirs of eternal life." For he swallowed up and destroyed the death that hinders us and removes us from that inheritance.

<sig>II</sig>

...it is, it is necessary that the death of the testator intervene: <note>The author is quoting Hebrews 9:16.</note> for a testament is confirmed upon death; otherwise it is not valid while the one who made the testament is still living. This is because a human’s will is changeable <note>original: "deambulatoria," literally "walking about" or shifting.</note> right up until death, and can be altered in any direction. No one can impose a law upon themselves from which they cannot later withdraw. And since a testator can change or even destroy a testament they have already made as long as they live, it has no legal force unless the testator reaches the point of death, after which it can no longer be changed. 

Nor should anyone say that the ancient testament—in which he bequeathed a land flowing with milk and honey—was the "true" testament and yet was confirmed by no death. For <margin>Paul</margin> Paul has already satisfied this objection, saying: "Even the first testament was not dedicated without death and blood." After the mandate of the law was read by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: "This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded to you." <note>Quoting Hebrews 9:18-20.</note> That figurative testament was confirmed by the death of animals, which prefigured the death of the one who was also represented by those animals. Thus the Apostle follows: "It was necessary therefore that the copies of heavenly things be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these," <note>Hebrews 9:23.</note> namely, by the own death of the true testator himself. Therefore, at the Last Supper he said: "This cup is the new and eternal testament in my blood." It is "eternal" indeed, because no other shall be given beyond it, since it is sufficient and unchangeable, promising a heritage that is not a mere figure—which only points toward and ends in the truth—but the truth itself, beyond which we expect no other.

<margin>John</margin>
I also believe we should not overlook why both testaments are said to be confirmed not only by death, but by blood, when the death of the testator would seem sufficient on its own, as was presupposed. This was done (if I am not mistaken) so that the heirs might be made fit and capable of receiving the left heritage. For those who are defiled and stained cannot possess it, as <margin>The same <gloss>John</gloss></margin> John says: "Nothing defiled shall enter there." <note>Revelation 21:27.</note> Nor can those living according to flesh and blood reach that inheritance. Therefore, so that he might cleanse us from defiling blood, the testator wished to pour out his own most pure blood, by which we might be cleansed from the stain of our own defiling blood, as John says again: "He who washed us from our sins in his blood." <note>Revelation 1:5.</note> Nor was there any other way, according to divine justice, by which he might establish us as sons and make us capable of such a great inheritance. 

But some are troubled when it is said that a spiritual person is cleansed by blood, which is corporeal; and that even angelic minds are cleansed by it, as <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says: "Making peace through the blood of his cross, both as to things on earth and things in heaven." <note>Colossians 1:20.</note> To these we respond by saying that since "life is in the blood" (as Scripture teaches), the life of Christ existing in the blood purges the angelic spirits and souls. Yet that blood had to be shed as the occasion for all sin. For blood and that earthy matter is the <term>kindling of all sins</term> <note>original: "fomes omnium peccatorum." The term "fomes" (tinder) refers to the innate tendency toward sin in human nature.</note> as Dionysius defines in *On the Divine Names*. For <margin>Blood had to be shed as the kindling of all sins.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Christ’s role, moving from the legal concept of his "Last Will and Testament" (discussed on the previous page) to his biological and spiritual role as the "Head" of the human "Body." It transitions from discussing how sin affects the blood to how Christ’s blood purifies humanity.</meta>

<sig>n iii</sig>

Sin arises from one’s own self-complacency <note>original: "complacentia," referring here to an excessive self-satisfaction or "egoism" that prioritizes the self over God.</note> even to the point of contempt for God, as <margin>Augustine</margin> Augustine most excellently judged. However, the complacency that separates us from God belongs to the realm of "matter"—that is, the sensory appetite <note>The physical desires and instincts of the body.</note> which a person wishes to satisfy. Because of this, one is bound by the "law of the members." <margin>Paul</margin> Sighing for this state, Paul says: *I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive into the law of sin, so that I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want.* <note>Quoting Romans 7:23.</note> So too in the Angels, the "weight" that turned them away from God is matter—whatever its nature may be <note>A reference to the scholastic debate on whether angels have a form of "spiritual matter."</note>—according to which, wishing to please themselves, they withdrew from that purest Act, which is God. And in those who possess an organized body and <margin>Concupiscence in the blood.</margin> blood, concupiscence <note>The inclination toward sin or worldly desire.</note> resides most powerfully in the blood. This blood cannot possess an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God until our stained blood has been purged through the most pure blood of Christ, according to the law decreed <margin>Wisdom</margin> in the Book of Wisdom: *By those things through which a person has sinned, by those same things shall he be punished.* <note>Quoting Wisdom 11:16.</note> Therefore, our blood is purged in the blood of Christ, since we have all been made one body, and he is the head of all. Hence, just as medicine taken by the head through the mouth purges the whole body, so too the medicine taken from Christ the head has healed all the members. For he drew to himself all our iniquities to be purged through his own blood, so that the <margin>Isaiah</margin> oracle of Isaiah might be fulfilled, which says: *By his bruises we are healed.* <note>original: "liuore eius sanati sumus," from Isaiah 53:5. "Liuor" refers to the dark bruising or welts from a lashing.</note>

->How Christ was made not only the Father, but the Head of all.<-

### Chapter XVIII.

## How Christ, as the True Head, Flows into All the Members. Chapter XIX.

<margin>Galen, Haly Abbas <note>Haly Abbas was a famous 10th-century Persian physician whose works were standard in medieval universities</note>.</margin>
<margin>Life and motion are in the Heart.</margin>
<margin>The motive, sensitive, and rational power is in the head.</margin>
**W**e have already proven that Christ is the head of the whole mystical body; it remains for us to see how the nourishment of life, governance, motion, and whatever pertains to the support and fostering of the body itself flows into all the joints and limbs. And although life and motion (as some wise men think) may be principally in the heart, nevertheless, according to the opinion of **Galen**, **Haly Abbas**, and others who have written on the nature and condition of the human body, every motive, sensitive, and rational power is in the head. For the motive power descends from the head itself through the nerves, which have their origin in the back part of the brain and are spread through the various members. Nor would motion be regulated and rational unless it proceeded from the place where reason, or the "image of reason," resides—I say "image," because this exists in place of reason in beasts. The sensitive power is evident in the eyes, ears, mouth, and nostrils, all situated in the head. And although the sense of touch is principally in the hands, it is nonetheless not absent from the head and the whole body. And for there to be a rational judgment concerning things handled, it is necessary that everything be referred back to the head, where the judgment of reason resides.

There are also in the head all the internal senses: the **common sense**, the **phantastic** power, the **imaginative**, the **cogitative**, and the leader of them all, the **intellect** and **reason**. Hence the members are said to be ruled by the head as if by a leader, and to be filled with power just as streams and channels are filled from a spring. There is no doubt that all these things, according to a spiritual "flow," come from our head, Christ. For in Him are—and by Him are filled—all the senses of the interior man, since we can neither taste, nor see, nor smell, nor hear the things that are of God, except through the power of this head, Christ, as Paul says:

<margin>Paul</margin>
> By the grace of God I am what I am <note>original: "Gratia Dei sum id, quod sum" (1 Corinthians 15:10)</note>;

Which grace flows into us through Jesus Christ. Hence he says to the Philippians:

> Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ <note>original: "Gratia uobis, & pax a Deo Patre, & Dnõ nostro Iesu Christo" (Philippians 1:2)</note>;

He recognizes it from both: the Eternal Father and Christ, because it flows from both. But neither reason, nor intellect, nor light for knowing divine things exists in us unless it is supplied by our head, who is the **True Light** illuminating everyone. Nor can we be moved to any work unless He provides it, who says:

> Without me you can do nothing <note>original: "Sine me nihil potestis facere" (John 15:5)</note>.

For just as when the head is cut off, nothing that remains in the torso...

### How much care Christ our parent has for us his children, whom he begot, in the provision of temporal things.

### Chapter XX.

**S**o that he might make us entirely divine, he wished to remove all worry <note>original: "solicitudinem"</note> of temporal things from us, taking upon himself the burden and the duty <note>original: "provinciam"</note> of providing whatever is necessary, bringing the Father into the faith as the guarantor of this liberality, as he says in the Gospel titled according to <margin>Matthew</margin> Matthew: *Do not be anxious, saying, what shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed? The first reason is that this belongs to the Gentiles—those, clearly, who do not admit the providence of God, but ascribe all events to chance, or to their own wit and prudence. Second: because the best Father, caring for all, is concerned for us and knows our need; hence if he provides for the birds and other living creatures, it is right that he provides more happily for us. The last reason is because the order and rectitude of justice requires that we seek the kingdom of God and his justice, so that we may find all these following things ready. <margin>Plato</margin> Which also Plato teaches from the prophetic symposium in the first book of the *Laws*, saying: *if anyone takes up greater things, they will also possess the lesser; but if they lack those, they are deprived of both.* The greater and divine goods are justice, piety, and the other virtues which lead into God; human goods are strength, beauty, health, riches, and also civil virtues. <margin>Cicero</margin> Following him, Cicero in his *On Duties* says: *Those who prefer advantages to virtues pervert the order and foundation of nature.* <margin>Macrobius</margin> These are supported by those things which Macrobius brings forward in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*. Looking at the nature of all things and actions, Plato noticed in all his discourse proposed concerning the institution of the Republic that the love of justice must be infused, without which not only a republic, but not even a tiny gathering of men, nor even a small house will stand. And before Plato, having drunk from the same fountain, <margin>Pythagoras</margin> Pythagoras said in his symbols words sufficiently close to the sacred Gospel: *Do not sit* (he says) *upon a bushel*, or *upon a choenix* <note>A choenix was a Greek unit of measure for a daily ration of grain</note> (as is the truth of the matter). # CHRIST IS THE AUTHOR AND END OF FAITH.
## CHAPTER I.

**H**ow many things appear to be matters of belief <note>original: "Credenda"</note> which are not Jesus Christ himself? Indeed, I would by no means dare to call him the author and end of faith, unless <margin>Paul</margin> Paul—in whose breast Christ resounds—taught me so. Paul, while debating with the Hebrews, exhorts everyone among them, saying: *Let us run the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith* <note>original: "Occurramus in oppositum nobis certamen suspicientes in authorem fidei, & consummatorem Iesum" — a citation of Hebrews 12:1-2</note>.

Now, I believe this was said for the following reason: while we might be able to bring forward some logical reasons for other articles of faith, for those which treat of Jesus Christ, we can bring forward absolutely none, except for "fitting" reasons, and even these only insofar as we are taught by divine oracles. For we can investigate through natural reasoning that God exists, and that he was the maker of all things. What <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle, as a physicist proceeding through the senses, would not admit this? Once awakened by the senses themselves, he does not differ from the other wise men, such as <margin>Plato</margin> Plato, who confess God to be the maker of the entire world.

However, that He made all these things through the Word Incarnate, who is Jesus Christ, is something we hold only from holy scripture, along with the other articles pertaining to Him. This is so true that some of the more recent theologians have asserted that Christ is the "subject" around which our entire theology revolves, since all articles of faith seem to refer back to Christ himself. 

For in the first article it is said: *I believe in God the Father* <margin>I believe</margin>. Yet a father cannot be a father without a son, who is Jesus Christ. The second is: *And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.* The third: *Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.* The fourth: *Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.* The fifth: *He descended into hell.* The sixth: *On the third day he rose again from the dead.* The seventh: *And ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father.* The eighth: *From there he shall come to judge the living and the dead.* The ninth: *I believe in the Holy Spirit.* And because the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he can neither be possessed nor understood without the Son. The tenth: *The holy catholic church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins.* Since all these things pertain to the "mystical body" <note>A theological term for the collective body of believers or the Church</note> whose head is Christ, they cannot exist or be held at all without Christ himself; this is especially true since the grace that unites us, the life which all members share, and the merit by which they obtain forgiveness, all come from the same Jesus Christ. The eleventh: *The resurrection of the body.* This cannot be, unless Christ had risen, who is the "firstfruits of those who fall asleep" <note>original: "primitiæ dormientium" — a reference to 1 Corinthians 15:20</note>. The twelfth:

speaks through Jeremiah: *I fill heaven and earth* <note>original: "Cœlum, & terram ego impleo," from Jeremiah 23:24</note>. But they fill things in different ways according to the different roles appropriate to them. We spoke above 
<margin>Origen</margin>
concerning the mind of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar who attempted to synthesize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine</note>, that from the Father we have our being; from the Son, our understanding; and for other things to be ordered: but from the Holy Spirit, that we might be holy; yet from the spirit of life, that all things might live. If, however, we wish to follow the
<margin>Ancient Theologians</margin>
ancient theologians, who say that "The One" precedes "Being" itself, we shall attribute that "One" to the first person, who is the Father, the first origin of all. "Being," however, we attribute to the Son, as is expressly held in their theology—namely, that Being belongs to the Supreme Wisdom, which is the Son. That Being is certainly communicable <note>In this context, "communicable" means a quality that can be shared or imparted from God to his creation</note>, just as the wisdom to be communicated to us is attributed to the Son; which, as it exists in the Father, is to be given only to the Son himself. And this is what he said: *No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him* <note>Matthew 11:27</note>. See how clearly we have it that wisdom is first in the Father, then in the Son, and thereafter communicated to others through him. So also Being, before it is communicated to others, is in the Son and in the Supreme Wisdom as if in a
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
storehouse <note>original: "armario," literally a chest or cabinet; here used metaphorically as a treasury of divine ideas</note>, where all things exist through an "ideal reason" <note>The "ideal reason" or "ratio idealis" refers to the Platonic idea that the perfect blueprints of all created things exist eternally in the mind of God</note> according to simple Being, before they have a determined existence in their own forms. Therefore, Unity emanating from the Father fills all things so that each thing may be "one," and by means of that unity they may be counted. But Being is communicated to all from the Son and through the Son, so that they may be made and exist; because *all things were made through the Word*, as 
<margin>John</margin>
John says; and as 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Paul says, *in him all things were created*. Moreover, all things are filled
<margin>David</margin>
with goodness by the Spirit, according to that word of the Prophet: *When you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness* <note>original: "Aperiente te manum tuam omnia implebuntur bonitate," from Psalm 104 (103 in the Vulgate)</note>. For the "Hand" is the Spirit of God, through whom—as if through the craftsman of all things, or the working hand—He performs all things in us. And just as "The One," "Being," and "The Good" are the same thing (as those who teach the elements of logic say), so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in essence, although distinct in their relations. But let us proceed concerning the Son, who fills all things with Being and Truth, just as the Father fills them with Unity and the Holy Spirit with goodness; and each of them, and all together, fill them by the power of divinity. But concerning
<margin>Hierotheus Dionysius</margin>
our Jesus, Hierotheus <note>A legendary teacher of Pseudo-Dionysius; his works are often cited in mystical theology as a primary source of wisdom</note> says in Dionysius's *On the Divine Names*: "The Deity of Jesus is the cause and the fulfillment of all things." And He is the cause, the being, and the life of those things which exist (as was said above); and He is the restoration and resurrection of those who have fallen away from God; but for those who, by a certain lapse, have lost the divine image within themselves...

...renovation and reformation; again, for those shaken by a certain profane agitation, he is a sacred strengthening, lest they be dashed together; for those who remain, a safe security; for those proceeding toward him, a leading forth with an outstretched hand; the brilliance of the enlightened; for those being perfected, the very leadership of perfection; or for those who are deified, the divine-source <note>original: "thearchia," a term from mystical theology referring to God as the principle of divinity and the source of all authority</note>; of those who are simple, simplicity itself; of those who come together into one, likewise unity; and the beneficial distribution of the most sacred hidden things, as far as is divinely permitted <note>original: "quantum fas est," a phrase used to denote the boundaries of human understanding when approaching divine mysteries</note>. <margin>Paul</margin>
And again to the Colossians: *Christ is all in all*, because he completes all things with a fullness suitable to each <note>original: "Omnia in omnibus Christus," from Colossians 3:11</note>. How, however, this Christ may be something separate from all, and yet all in all, let us see.

### Christ is neither a part, nor the whole, and yet he is the whole and a part. Chapter III.

<margin>
Dionysius
Hierotheus
</margin>
**S**ince, therefore, Christ is all in all, it might rightly be asked whether he exists as a part of each thing, or as the whole in all the parts, or as some divine power <note>original: "numen," referring here to a spiritual presence filling a space</note> filling all things. The venerable Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose mystical writings deeply influenced medieval thought</note>, following the opinion of Hierotheus <note>Dionysius’s mentor, a semi-legendary figure mentioned in the Dionysian texts</note>, says: Jesus is neither a part nor the whole; and yet he is the whole and a part, receiving and possessing in himself the part and the whole of all things. Explaining this, he says: The deity of Jesus is indeed perfect in imperfect things, just as a perfect gem might be in a rotten wooden box, which ought to be set in gold. It does not, however, shine equally well, nor does it work so perfectly as if it were bound in metal or in something proportioned to itself. But in perfect things, he is not perfect by that perfection by which they are perfect, but by a supra-perfect and pre-perfect perfection—exceeding, namely, every lower perfection. And he is the form-making agent, inducing form in those things which lack it, as the true giver of forms and the prince of form—not existing as a form himself (specifically a determined one), but above all forms; just as the sun favors the production of all herbs and animals without being an animal or plant himself, but having a superexcellent power to produce all those things. And he is the substance supporting all substances, illuminating all of them without any defilement of himself; because he is set apart from every substance, just as solar rays are in no way defiled when bathing filth, mud, or anything base, because they are separate from them. And he is the one ordering all principles, determining all orders, yet placed above every order and every principle and every sovereignty <note>original: "principatum," referring to the rank of 'Principalities' in the celestial hierarchy of angels</note>, just as an Emperor must order all his generals while being above every generalship; and just as the Pope orders all bishops while being himself a bishop, yet above every bishopric. And this is what the Apostle says to the Colossians: *He is before*...

<summary>This page explores Christ's dual nature as both the "all in all" and a transcendent being separate from his creation. Using the philosophy of Dionysius the Areopagite, the author argues that Christ provides form and substance to all things without being limited or defiled by them.</summary>

...all things and all people consist in him, since he is the head of the body of the church. Thus, by his kindness, he came down to our nature, and truly became a human substance and a man, and the highest man, yet he was called God. And although he took on what belongs to our nature, he always remained something supernatural and supersubstantial <note>a term from mystical theology meaning "above all essence" or "beyond being"</note>, suffering no injury at all in his dignity from that ineffable emptying <note>original: "exanitione," referring to the *kenosis* or self-emptying of Christ described in Philippians 2:7</note>, which communicated itself to us invariably and without confusion. Therefore, he was a novelty surpassing all novelties, existing in our natural qualities supernaturally and in our substances supersubstantially, holding all our things above us, containing all things, and perfecting all things, as we said above. And he is (as the Apostle says) the bond, the foundation, and the support of every creature, binding all things, connecting all things, embracing all things, vivifying and filling all things.

### From the sacred utterances we hold that Christ is all things. Chapter IV.

**W**e have demonstrated in a certain general way that Christ is a kind of "whole" in all parts, but we shall briefly run through what testimonies the sacred scriptures provide regarding this in particular. Beginning from the lowest of all formed things, we say that God is the earth—indeed, that true earth flowing with the milk of higher wisdom and the honey of divinity, or the taste of divine things, of which the Prophet sang: **For indeed the Lord will give his goodness, and our earth will yield its fruit.** <note>Psalm 85:12</note> He is also water, as we have explained more extensively above. He is also air and breath, for blowing upon his disciples he said: **Receive the Holy Spirit.** <note>John 20:22</note> For he would not give it unless he possessed it. He is the fire which he came to send upon the earth so that it might burn. <note>Luke 12:49</note> He is the grain of wheat and the sprout of the earth, saying of himself: **Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it brings forth no fruit; but if it dies [it brings forth much].** <note>John 12:24</note> From this wheat was made that living bread descending from heaven for our salvation. He is the tree (as we have said) of the knowledge of good and evil, and the tree of life, providing timber for the framing and joining of the whole true building to be constructed by us. He is also the stone and the rock, as Paul says: **But the rock was Christ.** <note>1 Corinthians 10:4</note> Upon which the church is founded, and also placed as the cornerstone <note>original: "in angulo," in the corner</note> it joined the whole building together; and he is the rock that provided us with water for washing and for drink.

This Christ, therefore, because he is of every kind and contains all things, has been allotted names of every kind, not only in natural, infernal, and celestial things, but even in artificial and divine things.**
