## What the fivefold group placed between others signifies in the camping around the Tabernacle of the Covenant. Chapter 22.

<margin>Numbers</margin>
**A**fter the arrangement of the camp, around the **Tabernacle of the Covenant**—or of meeting, where the people were called to the divine oracle—we read in the book of Numbers that five tents were placed between the Tabernacle and those twelve tribes surrounding it. Two of these belonged to **Moses** and **Aaron**, of whom it is said in that same place: *They shall camp before the Tabernacle of the Covenant, that is, on the eastern side: Moses and Aaron with his sons, having custody of the sanctuary in the midst of the children of Israel; whosoever of a stranger comes near it, shall die.* <note>original: "Castrametabuntur ante tabernaculum fœderis, idest ad orientalem plagam Moses, & Aaron cū filiis suis... quo quisquis alienus accesserit, morietur." — Numbers 3:38</note> The other three tents of the sons of **Levi** were ordered to be pitched by three families, which are:
*   The **Kohathites** <note>original: "Caatitæ"</note> to the south
*   The **Merarites** to the north
*   The **Gershonites** to the west

And all these had their assigned cares, over whom **Eleazar**, son of Aaron, was the prince of princes. Now, the leader of the Kohathites was **Elisaphan**, and these took care of the vessels: the table, the bowls, the cups, the lampstands, the lamps, the oil vessels, the fire pans, the flesh-hooks, the tridents, the hooks, the jars, and such things; and moreover, the oil for dressing the lamps, as well as the incense and the sacrifices. The Gershonites, whose leader was **Eliasaph**, guarded the curtains of the Tabernacle, the roof, and the other covering, and especially the **violet-colored veil** <note>original: "uelamen hyacinthinū"</note> of the tent which hung at the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Covenant. They also cared for the curtains of the court and the veil that was before the Tabernacle itself, as well as the cords, the vessels of ministry, and everything that pertained to the altar. But the Merarites, whose leader was **Suriel**, took charge of the joined boards, the bars of the Tabernacle, the columns of the court round about with their bases, pegs, and cords, and all the equipment of the altar, just as the Gershonites cared for those things that pertained to the erecting of the altar itself. And they were chosen from their thirtieth year of age until their fiftieth. This Tabernacle without doubt prefigured that **true tabernacle not made with hands**, just as the
<margin>Paul</margin>
**Apostle**, discoursing at length with the Hebrews, follows through, saying: *For the first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, and the table, and the setting forth of loaves, which is called the Holy place. And after the second veil, the tabernacle which is called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the Ark of the Testament covered on every part with gold, in which was a golden urn containing manna, and the rod of Aaron that had blossomed, and the tablets of the testament; and over it were the Cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, of which things it is not now necessary to speak one by one.* <note>original: "Tabernaculum enim factum est primum... de qbus nō ē dicēdū ꝑ singula." — Hebrews 9:2-5</note> Now when these things were thus arranged, the priests always entered into the first tabernacle, completing the duties of the sacrifices; but into the second, the **High Priest** entered alone once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own and the people's ignorance. By this the **Holy Spirit** signified that the way into the sanctuary was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle was still standing. This is a parable of the present time, according to which gifts and victims were offered, which could not make him that served perfect according to conscience, standing only in foods and drinks...

...and in various washings <note>original: "baptismatibus"</note>, and regulations for the flesh, imposed on them until the time of reformation. But Christ, being present as a High Priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption. Regarding this tabernacle, it might perhaps be considered rash to discuss it in detail, and rightly so, since the Apostle [Paul] did not dare to do so; or perhaps he was unwilling, because he did not have disciples who were initiated and perfected to whom he could reveal the secrets of wisdom. But since, with an unveiled face, it is granted to us to behold the glory of the Lord, we shall not think it rash in the least (with the Holy Spirit as our guide) to at least shadow forth something of this kind.

That typical tabernacle was therefore in the middle of the camp, signifying as a figure of the tribes the true tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation, but produced by a more blessed birth—which is Jesus Christ, erected in the middle of the true tribes and the camps of the whole of this world-machine <term>world-machine: a common Renaissance term for the universe as a complex, divinely engineered system</term>,
<margin>David</margin>
according to that prophetic word: *He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.* <note>Psalm 74:12</note> For Jerusalem, where He found propitiation, is in the center of the world, near the super-celestial temple, as the more secret theologians assert. And it is (if we follow the astronomers) in the corner of the southern triangle, near that true south, of which
<margin>Habakkuk</margin>
Habakkuk says: *God shall come from the south.* <note>Habakkuk 3:3</note> To which region God is also said to have walked when he wished to help our first parent [Adam] and cover his sin with a garment made of skin—the skin of that Lamb who took away the sins of the world. For from that region He bestowed all spiritual gifts upon us: for there He was born, there He taught, there He suffered, and in that same place He rose, and from there He ascended to that true south and heavenly temple, from whence He gave gifts to men, and from whence comes all mercy, grace, and salvation. Toward this direction the whole troop and all the camps must direct their banner and their face, so that the countenance and prayer may be directed to that place from which one hopes to receive rewards.

This tabernacle was therefore erected in the center of both worlds <note>meaning the physical world and the spiritual/heavenly world</note>, so that He might reign in both places in the house of Jacob, He who is said to hold the center on the supramundane throne; and here below, He received the center of the habitable earth as His possession. Thus also Christ, the true tabernacle—in His birth, His teaching, His appearing, and His death—always held the center. Just as He reigns in the midst of the house of Jacob, the true Israel—that is, the heir, or prince of God—sits. Toward this true heir and prince of God, who conquered the princedom of the world by the trophy of the cross erected in the middle of the world, all the tribes and families fighting for God look, being led into that sacred group of twelve, three for each part of the heaven: for which
<margin>John</margin>
(as John testifies) three gates stand open to the heavenly kingdom. And most beautifully and most mysteriously, that typical tabernacle is described as being in two parts, to signify that the true tabernacle is two-fold: where the first part receives human nature, and
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
is itself called "holy" because it is anointed with the holy oil of divinity above all its participants, and illuminated by the light of that lampstand, which says: *I am the light of the world.*

# VOLUME SEVEN
### CCCXXVII

And there also are found the loaves of the face <note>original: "panes faciei", traditionally called the "shewbread" or "bread of the presence"</note>, as Christ also testified, saying: *He shall go in, and go out, and shall find pasture.* <note>John 10:9</note> For Christ himself, as man, is the true prince of faces, through whom we are introduced to the face of divinity. Into these holy places, therefore, all those who sacrifice and meditate enter at will, because meditation on man and his work is easy. 

But into the Holy of Holies—which is the divine nature enclosed within the human, and from which propitiation and salvation are properly expected—the great and extraordinary priest enters. For no one enters the divine inner sanctum unless he is perfect and has consecrated himself most excellently to God. Indeed, he enters once a year, specifically when, being renewed and transformed for the better, he gathers new and annual fruits like another well-cultivated world. And he always gathers these the more excellently the more he is separated from the tamed flesh and almost extinguished blood. Therefore, he is said to enter "not without blood," by which he, progressing, is always purged, until the blood is entirely extinguished and he deserves to be made a son of God according to the power handed down by the Word <note>original: "a uerbo traditam", referring to the Logos or Christ</note>. 

But there is a great difference between the symbolic and the true tabernacle. For in the symbolic one, the blood of animals expiated only the ignorance of the priest and the people; here, however, in the blood of Christ, all crimes are purged, provided they are not committed against the Holy Spirit, which are forgiven neither in this world nor in the future. 

And entering there, he finds the golden censer—that is, the vessel of prayer enriched by perfect charity. There he finds the ark of the testament, perfect as the understanding of scripture, which is given to true priests and to those who, having attained a well-purged mind, have earned the right to see God. They also look upon that most sweet and hidden Manna, which no one knows except he who receives it. Furthermore, he finds the Rod—that is, the priestly virtue, blossoming and always progressing for the better. He may also gaze at will upon the Tables of the Testament, engraved by the finger of God <term>finger of God: a biblical metaphor for the Holy Spirit or direct divine action</term>, because he finds the love of God and neighbor carved in his heart; to which, as if to two primary engravings, the whole law and the prophets are reduced. Finally, he gazes there upon the cherubim of glory, through whom all created things shine (as we touched on above), divided into the heavenly and earthly machine <term>world-machine: a common Renaissance term for the universe as a complex, divinely engineered system</term>, above which sits He from whom all propitiation emanates. 

Between this tabernacle and the twelve tribes surrounding it—which encompass the whole assembly of God's soldiers—it is said that five particular and separate troops lie between, in just as many tents, not without a sacred mystery. These (to leave aside the anagogical sense <term>anagogical sense: the spiritual or mystical interpretation of a text leading toward heaven or the afterlife</term> for now) signify, if I am not mistaken, five approved ranks of priests, leaders, Levites, and mediators in the Church of God, between God Himself, who was said to reside in the tabernacle, and the people of God collected and described through those twelve troops. 

And these are the colleges of Peter, Augustine, Benedict, Basil, and Francis <note>The author identifies the five "tents" with the major founders of Christian monastic and ecclesiastical rules: St. Peter (the secular clergy/papacy), St. Augustine, St. Benedict, St. Basil, and St. Francis.</note>. To these, all other troops of God's particular ministers are reduced, or they sprout from them as if from the principal trunks like certain small branches. The first two tents belonged to Moses and Aaron together, to which those of Peter and Augustine correspond...

...communities, both of which are called Canons. But these are the "regular" ones <note>The "Canons Regular" followed a specific Rule (regula), unlike "secular" canons who lived in the world</note>, and they are more ready to handle those sacred matters, provided they observe the institutes handed down by their father Augustine himself. I say "handed down" not as if he were perfecting the religion of Peter—or rather, of Christ—but so that he might lead these men back to those ancient customs in which that apostolic assembly had been educated. Among them, the authority of judging always remained, just as it did with Moses, who held the first place in that **group of five**. 

But the three following crowds of Levites—who are the Kohathites, the Merarites, and the Gershonites—signify three other groups of those under a Rule. For the **Kohathites**, whose name is interpreted as "the grieving," <note>The author uses a traditional medieval etymology linking the Hebrew name Kohath to sorrow or mourning</note> symbolize the ranks of the **Benedictines**. These appear obscure and always weathered by the continuous mourning for sins and the death of Christ to which they are devoted. For this reason, the small mortars were entrusted to them—vessels in which sins are crushed—along with the censers of fragrant prayers, and the bowls from which heavenly things are poured out. In addition, they hold the lampstands and the lamps of the readings and of the lights from above; also the vessels for the oil of mercy, with which they are always compassionate toward others, and the receptacles for the fires and flames of the Holy Spirit. Even the flesh-hooks, tridents, hooks, and dishes are theirs, by which the fire of fervor and love is stirred up. But all these things were believed to be clothed for them in a **blue** <note>original: "hyacinthino", referring to the celestial blue or violet color of the Tabernacle cloths</note> and heavenly color, since they ought to be always intent upon the things above, whether in active continuous contemplation or by virtue, so that they may observe that Gospel saying: *One ought always to pray, and never give up.* <note>Luke 18:1</note>

<margin>THE STATE OF CHRIST</margin> The **Merarites**, whose name signifies "those embittered" or "those observing watches," represent the family of **Basil** and the **Anchorites** <note>Hermits or monks living in seclusion</note>. With a certain sharp austerity in their solitary life, intent on continuous vigils, they made themselves hard and bitter toward themselves so that they might be an example of "Gospel mourning" to others. To them, as to most robust men, all the strong things were rightly entrusted: the pillars, the bases, the bars, the planks, and similar monuments of the Tabernacle. But alas, it is a cause for grief, though no wonder, if we have seen the Tabernacle for the most part in ruins, because it no longer has its Pauls, nor its Peters, nor its Macariuses, nor its Anthonys, nor its Hilarions <note>A list of the great Desert Fathers and early monastic pioneers</note>, nor others of that kind who might sustain the Tabernacle itself with holiness, doctrine, miracles, and example.

The **Gershonites**, however, whom they interpret as "sojourners" or "the cast out," represent the poor men of the Gospel. It is commanded of them that they lead their lives exactly according to the goal of the Gospel, and that they be sojourners and pilgrims in this world. They live entirely removed and expelled from it, so that they can say with the Apostle: *The world is crucified to me, and I to the world.* <note>Galatians 6:14</note> To these were entrusted the curtains of the Tabernacle, the curtains of the court, the veils, the roofs, the coverings, and everything that pertained to the concealing of sacred things, so that they might nonetheless reveal and uncover the secrets at the time appointed by the Father on high. In the meantime, some have come forward from this group who have given off certain flashes of the immense light hidden in the Tabernacle, as can be seen by those who have read the **Scotists**, the **Meyronnists**, the **Halesians**, the **Ockhamists**, the **Bibracensians**, and others of that kind <note>This list refers to major schools of Scholastic theology: followers of Duns Scotus, Francis of Meyronnes, Alexander of Hales, and William of Ockham</note>. To them also was committed the blue and heavenly veil through which the entrance to the Tabernacle lay open; and the cords were also committed to them. And even if I cannot explain these things without the envy of many, I shall not nevertheless cease from expounding them at least in part.

Through these celestial men, indeed—to as many as the entrance to the true tabernacle was open—they bind others with the cords of Seraphic love <note>The "Seraphic" rank refers to the highest order of angels, associated with burning love; it is also a common epithet for the Franciscan order</note> and charity, in which the Supreme Inhabitant of the tabernacle draws to Himself those He has chosen, as is plain to see. ## What is signified by the seventy-two disciples, whom our prince JESUS is said in the Gospel to have chosen. Chapter XXIII.

**B**eyond the group of twelve and five, of which we have already spoken, those who were privy to the divine secrets claim that Christ JESUS, the Lord of all things and nations, chose seventy-two disciples. This was done so that each family—both the symbolic one <note>The "typical" or symbolic family refers to the Old Testament Israelites</note> and the Gospel one—might correspond in part with the entire higher world, and no less with our own tabernacle, which itself bears the image of the world. For in the figurative and legal family <note>The "legal" family refers to those under the Old Covenant Law</note>, not only are the twelve and the five found, but seventy-two leaders were also commanded by the Lord to be chosen, so that it might bear a perfect image of heavenly things. There, one finds the twelve signs <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>, the seventy-two princes, and that sacred group of five, at whose limit God deals familiarly with us. (And in that very limit, denoted by the last letter of the Great Name of four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton (YHWH). The "four letters" are Yod, He, Vav, He. Christian Kabbalists often analyzed the mathematical and symbolic properties of these letters</note>, as the more secret theologians assert, the Supreme Artisan fashioned the world). 

Furthermore, those seventy-two princes are distributed in the heavens in such a way that six are said to preside over each sign, and over seventy-two languages; from these is gathered that greatest multitude of the elect, which no one can number. And it is very beautifully gathered from the seventy-two, because the number is derived from six—the first perfect number—and from twelve, the first increasing number. Thus, this family gathered from every nation under heaven is understood to be perfect and overflowing. This most full mystery is found more happily in the kingdom and family of Christ (to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth) than in the heavens or in the figurative world. This mystical body is perfected under the perfect head, Christ, with every fullness, just as this natural body and human tabernacle is composed of seventy-two articles and just as many joints. 

Twelve of these are primary, in the arms and legs: for in each arm there are three joints—one at the shoulder, the second at the elbow, the third at the hands—which, when combined, yield six. There are likewise three in each leg—one at the hip, the second at the knee, the third at the ankle—which are as many as in the arms, and when calculated together, they constitute twelve. Again, there are three joints in each finger of the hands, from which thirty joints result from the ten fingers; and just as many in the ten toes of the feet, which all together...

combined they make sixty, and together with those twelve greater ones <note>The twelve Apostles</note> they complete seventy-two. Nor should anyone object on the grounds that in the Book of <margin>Numbers</margin> Numbers it was commanded that only seventy should be gathered to whom the spirit of Moses would be delivered: for even there the number of seventy-two is found, if those two are counted who, filled with the same spirit (as we read in the same place), were prophesying in the <margin>Rabbi Solomon</margin> camps. These two had not been numbered with the others because (as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar whose commentaries were often cited by Christian Hebraists</note> says) they did not receive a written slip by lot. Nor is it a wonder if Moses and Aaron were sometimes numbered with the rest, and at other times not at all, since this occurred with Paul in the "new family" <note>The New Testament Church</note> and with Ephraim, Manasseh, and others in the "ancient one" <note>The Old Testament tribes</note>, not without mystery. The Craftsman of the universe joined this together with no less diligence than he used at the beginning to fabricate man’s "tabernacle," which is so quickly dissolved <note>A metaphor for the mortal human body</note>; for he loves this spiritual body, glued together by his own blood, far more than that which was fabricated from the dust of the earth.

->### That Christ rules and governs the whole mystical and mundane body. Chapter XXIII.<-

**F**ormed thus, the mystical body itself—made of all those chosen for life as if from members great and small—it is fitting that he, who is the life and resurrection of all, should quicken his whole body and all its members, just as a particular soul quickens the body which it informs and all its members. It must also be observed that the soul does not only quicken the body, but rules and moderates the whole of it and all its parts. No less is Christ the moderator and <margin>Paul</margin> rector <note>The director or governor</note> of his body. Therefore, Paul calls him not only the life, but also the head of this universal body, saying to the Colossians: *He is the head of the body of the church* <note>original Latin: "Ipse est caput corporis ecclesiae" — Colossians 1:18</note>. And he is the rector not only of this mystical body, but also of the entire mundane <note>The physical or worldly</note> body, just as it too was fabricated through the Word which lies hidden in Christ. Thus, not without cause does he protest and say: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth* <note>original Latin: "Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & in terra" — Matthew 28:18</note>. It was certainly given by him to whom it is said in the Book of <margin>CHRIST the Wisdom</margin> Wisdom: *But you, Father, by your providence, govern all things from the beginning.* And this is done with the sweetest harmony, as was promised above: *But you judge all things with tranquility*, although sometimes the governance of the world may seem null or even horrid to us who are blind. For he leaves nothing disordered, but binds all things to their own orders, just as he knows even the <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> most minute things, as that Wise Man, whoever he was, declares, saying: *The sand of the sea, the [drops] of rain...* <note>original Latin: "Arenam maris, pluviae" — from Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 1:2</note>

### OF THE SECOND SONG

...that all things were present, before they were made, and not see how those same things are preserved in their proper places? Therefore, He who knows all is not ignorant; nor is He powerless to rule, He who was able to make all things; nor does He refuse or disdain to govern those things which He manufactured, whatever they may be, whether noble or base. And so, no doubt regarding this providence remains for the wise, who know the divine nature to be wise, most good, and most powerful. Nor does the Moderator of the universe Himself possess providence only through some general rule of governance—as some claim—for if He protects and cares for the whole, He must also look after the parts. For it is so arranged by nature that well-being cannot exist in the whole unless the parts are also rightly disposed. For no doctor, no ship’s captain, no leader of an army, no <term>head of a household</term> <note>original: "paterfamilias" — the male head of a Roman family or estate</note>, no ruler or governor of a Republic, no craftsman, whoever he may be, cares for his work in such a way that he manages the weightier matters and despises the lighter ones; rather, each is judged to have performed his duty when he applies himself to every individual detail with zeal and diligence, as the nature of each requires. Since if men do not pass over even the lighter matters, surely God must not be thought to neglect any small things; and much less does He despise man, whom He set over all living creatures.

Therefore, that highest Father is He who knows all, numbers all, measures all, and cares for all with special governance: which governance He also entrusted to the Son, as to a legitimate heir after the triumph held over the <term>tyrant</term> <note>In this context, the "tyrant" refers to the devil or death, defeated by Christ.</note>. This Son, therefore, rules all these same things by the wisdom and power handed down by the Father. 

But many things disturb people—things which seem to happen outside of the natural order and seem unworthy of such great governance. For those evils rise up on every side which, under God's rule, ought not to happen, since evil cannot proceed from God; this is something not only our own <note>i.e., Christian theologians</note> assert, but as <margin>Plato</margin> shows in the third book of *The Republic*. And leaving aside other things that seem to decline from the order of nature and good governance, we shall run through a few points regarding the Overseer of the world and whether He governs poorly. For these questions have struck even the wise and the most eminent heroes in the kingdom of God so forcefully that, out of a certain impatience, they seem to break out in complaint even against God the Moderator Himself. 

<margin>Habakkuk</margin>
"I will cry out," says Habakkuk, "suffering violence, and You will not save? Why have You shown me iniquity and toil, to see plunder and injustice against me? Why do You look upon the scornful, and remain silent while the wicked man tramples one more righteous than himself?" <note>Habakkuk 1:2–3, 13.</note> 

<margin>David</margin>
And the <term>Royal Prophet</term> <note>original: "regius Vates" — King David</note> says: "But my feet were almost moved, my steps were nearly poured out, because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners; because there is no regard for their death, nor strength in their suffering. They are not in the labor of men, and they shall not be scourged with other men. Therefore pride held them," <note>Psalm 73:2–6 (Vulgate 72).</note> by which pride they burst out against God and men because of their unmerited success. 

<margin>Jeremiah, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine</margin>
No less do Jeremiah, Augustine, Jerome, and many other members of God's household complain about such things. To them we could always say that sentiment revered among the Greeks, and highly celebrated by Augustine in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul*: "Seek not the things that are above you." <note>A common Latin rendering of a Greek proverb: "Quæ supra nos, nihil ad nos" (What is above us is nothing to us), often attributed to Socrates or found in Ecclesiasticus 3:22.</note>

It also introduces the "problem of evil," citing the frustrations of biblical figures like Habakkuk and David regarding the prosperity of the wicked.</summary>

# CHRIST IS THE MIDDLE PERSON IN THE MOST HOLY TRINITY.

## CHAPTER ONE.

ALL who speak of the Trinity easily agree that the Son and the Word—who was made flesh and named Jesus, titled Christ in Greek, Messiah in Hebrew, and "Anointed" in Latin—holds the middle position among the persons of that most holy Trinity. In this Trinity, the Father is the first root of all blossomings, both in divine and in created things. The Holy Spirit is produced by the Father and the Son, and produces nothing further within that most holy Trinity. The Son is also the middle person, produced indeed by the Father, and together with Him producing the Holy Spirit in an eternal outflowing <gloss>an eternal emanation</gloss>. 

Not only do all Christians profess this doctrine, but even the more secret Hebrew theologians <margin>Hebrew Theology</margin> teach that <term>Hochma</term> <note>Hebrew: חכמה; "Wisdom." In Kabbalistic thought, this is the second Sephirah or emanation.</note>—which signifies wisdom—emanates from the supreme source, or blossoms from the super-excellent root which they call <term>Keter Elyon</term> <note>Hebrew: כתר עליון; "The Supreme Crown," the first and highest emanation of the Divine.</note>. From these two sources—or rather from the first source and the river proceeding from it—is produced that third thing which they call <term>Bina</term> <note>Hebrew: בינה; "Understanding" or "Intelligence."</note>, which we, interpreting it properly, can call "prudence" or "intelligence." 

It is certainly that "Intelligence" of which it is said in the book of Ecclesiasticus: *And he shall fill him with the spirit of intelligence.* <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Indeed, intelligence is a level of cognition closer to us than wisdom (which is attributed to the Son), and therefore it is more easily received by us. For this reason, the Son said: *I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,* <margin>CHRIST.</margin> because, clearly, you are not strong enough to endure the splendor of my wisdom. *But when that Spirit of Truth comes, he will teach you all things, and will suggest to you everything I have said to you*—at a level somewhat lower than those things are taught in me. For no one knows the Son—that is, in a proper sense—except the Father. 

However, at a somewhat lower level, he also offers himself to us to be seen, according to what he said: *He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.* And also, sometimes he manifests the Father through himself, according to what he says: *He who sees me, sees also my Father*—a person who is surely more sublime than all of us, since he is further removed from our grasp. The Holy Spirit, however, is more "domestic" <note>original: "domesticus," meaning familiar or closer to home.</note> to us; but the Son is the middle between both. 

And although God is a circle and a kind of intellectual sphere whose center (that is, every created thing) is everywhere, nevertheless, by the reasoning of the "Persons," we do not express them through a circle, but through number, saying: the First, the Second, and the Third (or final) person.

<summary>This chapter establishes Christ’s position as the "Middle Person" of the Trinity, bridging the gap between the "remote" Father and the "domestic" Holy Spirit, while drawing parallels to the Hebrew Kabbalistic concepts of Keter, Hochma, and Bina.</summary>

beyond which there is no further production of persons in divine matters. In that middle person, however, as if in a certain house, all things are placed through vital ideas. Whence just as the middle person himself was the medium through which all things emanated from the Father, so he is also the medium through which we know the Father. For no one can arrive at the knowledge of the Father except he to whom the Son wishes to reveal him <note>A reference to Matthew 11:27.</note>. That the outgoing from the Father happens through the Son, who is the second person in divine matters, <margin>Iamblichus</margin> Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Christian mystical theology regarding the nature of the "One" and the "Many."</note> hints at when he treats these matters through numbers, saying: "Unity exists as the cause of identity and union; the binary <note>The number two.</note> is the provider of distinction and progress; but the ternary <note>The number three.</note> is the leader of the return of those things that have proceeded." <note>original: "Vnitas identitatis, unionisq; causa existit: binarius uero discretionis, progressusq; præbitor: sed ternarius regressus eorum, quæ processerunt dux."</note> Referring these things to what has been said: the first and unique is the Father; the second, or the Binary, is the Son, through whom all things were made, and from whom comes the cause of distinction and progress. The third, however, which completes that trinity, is the Holy Spirit, who, hovering over the waters, provides forms to all things and grants his favor so that they may be led back to the First, yet through that same medium through which they had been dispersed.

### Christ is the true tree placed in the middle of paradise. Chapter II.

**A**nd so that it may be clearly signified that the Son, who is Christ, claims the "middle" as something peculiar to himself, when the series of intellectual things was treated by Moses under the metaphor of a garden and trees, he describes the tree of life planted in the middle of that garden. There is no doubt that this is Christ, who is called the bread of life, the wood of life, and life itself. He was planted in the middle so that each person might more easily receive from the fullness of his life according to their own capacity. Hence also, when the fullness of time came, this tree was grafted into the tree of the nature he assumed in the very center of the world, so that he might distribute his fruits to all those round about in due proportion. Regarding this grafting, James says: 
> Receive the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls. 
<margin>James. <br/> Dionysius.</margin> <note>James 1:21 and likely a reference to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> And this tree of life, namely the divine person grafted into human nature, is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; because he alone (as we have said elsewhere) being a wayfarer, experienced the good of blessedness and the evil of human passions. He is, moreover, the tree of good and evil <margin>Isaiah</margin> because he, more than others, knew how to discern good from evil, according to that prophecy of Isaiah: "He shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know to reject evil and choose good." <note>Isaiah 7:15.</note> Nor did he alone know this, but he also taught us to know the true goods which we ought to love, and the true evils to be feared and avoided by us. Finally, he is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil to whom judgment is given, and the knowledge of discerning the good from the bad. Whence, as he himself attests in the Gospel, when he comes to the universal trial, he will place the good on his right and the bad on his left, standing himself in the middle, separating these from those by a perpetual segregation. ### Why this middle divine person joined with the human nature he assumed. Chapter III.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
**N**or is it without mystery that that middle person in the most holy Trinity assumed human nature. This is because human nature itself is the "middle" between heaven and earth; the middle between God and other creatures, tasting of the nature of both, so that through this middle nature he might unite all extremes. For human nature itself, possessing the <term>center-point</term> <note>meditulium: a technical term for the exact middle or heart of all things</note> of all things, exists as their bond; and having a part with all things, it delights with all. For the "Good," in which there is delight, encompasses the entire breadth of things; no creature is drawn toward this whole except for man. For the supreme Moderator grants to each creature its own specific food, but to man he grants every kind.
<margin>Moses</margin>

For while the beasts are left with their greenery of herbs, to man are granted not only sown herbs, but eventually even living creatures. And once placed in the paradise of pleasure, "every tree"—that is, every vigor and delight of rational creatures—is granted for food, and even the tree of life, which was in the center of paradise. The middle creature <note>original: "creatura media"; this refers to humanity, positioned between the purely spiritual angels and the purely material animals.</note> between God and the rest of creation is able to take delight both in God Himself and in all created things. For we were brought forth for the purpose of enjoying God <margin>Augustine</margin>—if Augustine and the whole crowd of theologians judge correctly—and until we reach that enjoyment of God and union with Him, we are permitted to possess all creatures according to a rightful law. For we possess the earth, which we tread upon, and which provides us with food and a stable foundation for constructing buildings. We sail upon the water, we wash things to be cleaned in it, and we use it for many necessary purposes. We also possess the air, which we breathe and through which we enjoy the benefit of sight. We also live by the power of fire and its heat, and through it we complete the tasks of cooking and refining. We feed upon plants and the flesh of animals; we are clothed in their wool and skins; with their help, we cultivate the land, carry heavy loads, and even when weak, we travel long journeys with ease. We also receive great benefits from the heavens, and even greater ones from the Angels and from other men, with whom we are delighted in a wonderful way by honorable pleasure, whether conversing in spirit or in bodily presence. But from the **tree of life**, which is in the center of all these things, we receive every kind of perfect delight, both of life and of all true pleasures. Therefore, it was fitting that the Middle Person of the Divine Persons <note>The Son/Christ, as the second person of the Trinity.</note> was united with the human being, the middle creature, and with that creature which is the bond of all things, so that through Him as the middle, all extremes might be united together.

### Chapter IV. How sin and evil were brought into the world from that tree.

<margin>The same, Dionysius, Simeon</margin>
For just as every justice, every right, and every good proceeds from that tree when it is rightly and dutifully received, so we do not doubt that every evil has proceeded into the human race—and even into the Angels—from that tree being violated. Nor should anyone wonder if we say that evil arises from good, since it cannot proceed from anywhere else, as Augustine clearly defines in his *Enchiridion*, and as Dionysius <note>referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian Neoplatonist.</note> said before him: **The beginning and end of all evils is good.** Assigning a reason for this, he says: "Nothing acts with a view toward evil, but toward a good which it either neglects or desires inordinately." Therefore, this tree is the principle of all goods and evils: because if anyone honors and observes it, they perform good; but if anyone neglects it and presumes to devour or trample it, they perform evil. This was testified by that most holy old man Simeon, speaking of that tree grafted into the human branch: <note>original: "humano furculo insita"; a metaphorical reference to the Incarnation where the divine nature is grafted onto the human.</note> **Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many in Israel**, and among all people, both Angelic and human. For the Angel sinned by refusing to receive Him as the true Lord and true Lawgiver, and by refusing to obey the rules described in Him, and by being unwilling to revere Him as the mediator through whom we are made co-heirs...

This seems to be a matter of the greatest difficulty to decide, since evil is not a being, nor pure nothingness, nor some cause (since every cause is something existing in reality). Nor does it seem to be an effect, because every effect proceeds from a cause, and a cause of this kind is such that in its working it always looks toward the good and always performs good—though in a free agent, the imagination often fails by thinking or imagining that something is good which is not. Nor is it clear how evil could arise from good, as the highest Truth proclaims: *A good tree cannot produce bad fruit.* <note>Matthew 7:18</note> And also, because nothing is made from contraries, except as from a starting point, as the <margin>Peripatetics</margin> <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, known for walking while they taught.</note> are accustomed to say. Nor can evil be produced by evil, since evil is the cause of nothing (for then it would have the character of a good). All these things, though they seem very difficult at first glance, are very easily resolved when considering what has been said about the tree. For evil is a lack of rectitude, good, or order which is required in a work. Rectitude and order, however, consist of conformity with those rules existing in the tree itself, from which good and evil are discerned. When this rectitude is present, the work is good; but when it is absent, it becomes evil. This is so even if the law prohibiting a good object (toward which the will is carried) is good; even if the will which chooses a good body is good; even if our animal nature to which we consent is good; even if the <term>concupiscible appetite</term> <note>The natural desire for sensory pleasures.</note> and the <term>irascible power</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that deals with anger, courage, and overcoming obstacles.</note> by which we either desire or refuse are good—since all these things were granted by a good author for our benefit. Furthermore, the external act is good (which is called the "underlying substance of the deformity"). Only that disorder and lack of harmony, or the lack of order and conformity with the rules existing in that tree, is evil. From this it is most clearly inferred that evil comes from that tree—not indeed produced by it—but because the one performing the act turns away from it, as the <margin>Paul</margin> Apostle clearly proclaims: *When the law is removed, sin is taken away.* And again: *If the law did not exist, sin would not be imputed.* <note>References to Romans 4:15 and 5:13.</note> Therefore, let the <term>Manichaean</term> <note>A follower of Manichaeism, an ancient religion that taught a dualistic struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> lie defeated here, who dreamed that there were two principles: one of good things (which is good) and another of evil things (which is evil). For there cannot be a producing principle unless it is good. Nor can there be a pair [of principles] unless it draws its origin from one. Thus, there must be one primary thing from which these two principles would emanate. Nor could God be happy if anything were to oppose Him, the invincible...

### Christ in this life was always delighted by the middle. Chapter V.

<margin>Theology</margin> **A**nd so that he might show by his deeds that he is the perfect mediator, in his entrance, in his state, in his departure, and in his kingdom, he always took care to hold the middle place: For when he was born, he was placed between two animals, the ox and the ass, not without a great mystery. For the ass (as the more secret theologians say) corresponds in the <term>archetype</term> <note>The "archetype" refers to the original divine pattern or ideal world in God's mind.</note> to the right hand, where there is mercy, and the ox to the left, where there is justice: since our Mediator, making these meet each other at his coming, stood in their midst: which he wished to be signified by the placement between the ox and the ass from the beginning. He also wished to perform his first celebrated work in the middle: for while still a young boy, he disputed in the midst of the teachers. And when he had received the perfect increase of life and virtues, wishing to impart those spiritual gifts with which he was filled, he placed himself in the middle, just as he himself testifies, saying: *I am in your midst as one who serves* <note>original: "Ego ſum in medio ueſtrum, tanq̃ qui miniſtrat." See Luke 22:27.</note>, so that he might distribute the received gifts to all in one equal distribution—at least a geometric one. <note>A "geometric distribution" refers to a form of justice where rewards are given according to the merit or proportion of the recipient, rather than a simple equal split.</note> And when he had come to the goal of his life and the mysteries entrusted to him, he also took care to hold the middle: For when he was fastened to the cross, he was placed in the middle of two hanging thieves, one on the right and the other on the left, so that, having been established as their judge, he might render to each their due reward according to the merits of both; and by a certain omen of the great and final judgment, he had the one to be rewarded on his right, and the one to be punished on his left. By dividing them, he also hinted at that final division which he is to make. In his kingdom also he always held, and will hold, the middle place between the Father and us, existing as advocate and mediator, and continually interceding for us. For he is, as John declares, in that heavenly kingdom *in the middle of the throne, in the middle of the four animals, and in the middle of the elders.* <note>original: "in medio throni, in medio quatuor animaliū, & in medio ſeniorum." See Revelation 5:6.</note> <margin>Abraham</margin> Finally, he holds the middle in that divine Archetype, in which Abraham, full of piety...

### Christ was the best mediator. Chapter VI.

<margin>Paul</margin>
Rightly, therefore, he who is the center in divine matters—and was planted in the middle of paradise like a tree in the middle of a garden, and who always held the middle path in life—became the true and best mediator between God and man, according to that word of the Apostle: *There is one mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus* <note>original: "Vnus est mediator Dei, & hominum Christus Iesus." See 1 Timothy 2:5.</note>. He is the true mediator for many reasons, but most especially (as some believe) because of the flesh and human nature he assumed. Because he shares in both extremes <note>The "extremes" refer to the infinite nature of God and the finite nature of humanity.</note>, he was a good middle point, a bond and a "glue" binding, connecting, and uniting man with God. Because true priests also perform this office, any of them may be called a mediator—not the primary one, of course, but a secondary one, holding the place of the true and first mediator. He is, moreover, the best medium and mediator, and like a certain channel through which the living waters flow to us from the living and supreme fountain—waters which he offers us freely in many places. Thus, a person possesses as much of the heavenly influence as they receive from the fullness of this mediator. Finally, the creature could not return to God, from whom it proceeded, except through this middle way, which participates in both extremes.

### Through Christ the man we ascend to God and the Father. Chapter VII.

<margin>John</margin>
This Christ of ours is, therefore, the middle way and the ladder through which we ascend to God the Father, as he himself plainly declares in the Gospel titled "according to John," saying: *I am the way... no one comes to the Father except through me* <note>original: "Ego sum uia, nemo uenit ad Patrem, nisi per me." See John 14:6.</note>. He also showed himself in the <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a symbolic figure or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a future reality in the New Testament.</note> of a ladder to the ancient father Jacob, in whose house he was to reign, by which the chosen descendants of that visionary might ascend to God. For the lower end of this ladder was fixed on the earth, because the mediator’s soul—which was given as the price for human redemption and prepared the way by which we might ascend to God—was fixed, just like other souls, in earthly flesh.

See John 10:9.</note>. <margin>Paul</margin> And it is that "house" in which all things were placed from the beginning, and into which he receives those of his household so that he may grant them pastures—specifically those things which people standing in the vestibule, or even entering the atrium or porch of his humanity, are unable to taste. <margin>Jacob</margin> Nor should it be doubted that the Redeemer was shown in advance to Jacob in this most celebrated vision, since God, leaning above the ladder, clearly expressed it with that most beautiful blessing: *In you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth will be blessed* <note>original: "Benedicetur in te, & in semine tuo cunctæ tribus terræ." See Genesis 28:14.</note>. <margin>God</margin> Wherever these words were shown to the patriarchs, everyone asserts by common consent that they were spoken concerning Christ. Our patriarch Jacob even made a vow and swore an oath to him, first demanding a sign confirming those things which the oracle had promised in the passage where it is said: *He also vowed a vow, saying: If the Lord will be with me,* confirming namely those things which he promised I would obtain in this life; from which follows: *And if he will keep me in the way in which I walk, and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and I return prosperously to the house of my father, the Lord shall be my God, and this stone which I have raised as a monument shall be called the house of God; and of all that you give to me, I will offer tithes to you.* Broad indeed and wide is the spirit of the prophets—rather, the Holy Spirit filling the prophets and speaking through their mouths—and therefore, while speaking of one thing, it is verified in many. But leaving other matters aside, let us pursue those things which concerning Christ...

-># OF THE SECOND CANTICLE #<-

<note>original: "CANTICI SECVNDI"</note>

<warning>There is significant bleed-through from the reverse side of the page. The first word of the first line is partially obscured.</warning>

...the father Jacob, full of God, touches upon [this] through the mediator. He requires three things in the proof of the Messiah, about whom he prophesies: First is the pre-showing of the way, the leadership, and the protection. The Messiah provided all these to all the sheep of the house of Israel who had perished. He did not merely show the way, but made himself the way, providing light and leadership to all. He also maintained such guardianship that he could say: *No one shall snatch my sheep from my hand* <note>original: "Non rapiet quisq̃ oues meas de manu mea." See John 10:28.</note>, for I clearly guard them as the Good Shepherd. Furthermore, he provided as food the living bread which descended from heaven. Finally, having become the Lamb himself, he granted his own skin as a covering for our nakedness and shame; indeed, he alone was able to cover our sins, because we were all children of wrath and stripped bare. Therefore, the <margin>Paul</margin> Apostle says: *Put on our Lord Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Induimini Dominum nostrum IESVM Christum." See Romans 13:14.</note>. Thus, once the way is possessed and shown, along with protection for the journey and the best <term>travel-provisions</term> <note>Latin: "viatico." In a religious context, this often refers to the Eucharist as food for the journey to the afterlife.</note> for one traveling to the appointed region, he then confesses him as true Parent and Lord.

He also accepts him as God, since he holds from him all things that pertain to eternal life. No one could lead human nature—especially fallen nature—to that life, unless he was above human nature itself, untainted by it, and yet a participant in both extremes. And this alone is Christ, the Messiah: God-man and man-God. Then, therefore, he recognized him as the true mediator and the ladder through which access into heaven is granted to us. No one from the tainted mass of humanity could ever approach there until our mediator opened the doors, of whom Paul says: *Let us hold fast the firm confession of our hope* <margin>The same [Paul]</margin> *having a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God* <note>original: "Teneamus spei nostræ firmam cõfessionem habentes Pontificem magnum, qui penetrauit cœlos, IESVM filium Dei." See Hebrews 4:14.</note>, so that he might also introduce us there and present us to the Father. 

Here we must not overlook a most beautiful lesson: that one should not believe every spirit, every oracle, or every revelation. Instead, the truth must be sought from those things which precede what is predicted. Or, sometimes, confirming signs must be demanded, as our Patriarch <margin>Jacob</margin> Jacob did here. Such signs are also occasionally offered by the predicting spirit, just as it was said to Hezekiah through Isaiah: *Ask for a sign for yourself from the Lord your God* <note>original: "Pete tibi signum a Domino Deo tuo." See Isaiah 7:11.</note>. <margin>Isaiah</margin> The Prophet also granted this to the one willing to ask, saying: *The Lord himself will give you a sign* <note>original: "Dominus dabit ipse uobis signum." See Isaiah 7:14.</note>. Moreover, the <margin>Apostles</margin> Apostles asked, saying: *What will be the sign of your coming?* <note>original: "Quod signum aduentus tui?" See Matthew 24:3.</note>. 

Nor should it disturb anyone that the Lord calls that generation "unbelieving and perverse" which seeks a sign; for they already had many signs proving that he was from God, to which he sometimes directed them, saying: <margin>CHRIST</margin> *If you do not want to believe me, believe the works; for the works that I do, they bear witness of me* <note>original: "Si non uultis mihi credere, operibus credite: Opera enim, quæ ego facio, illa testimonium perhibent de me." See John 10:25, 38.</note>. Those people, therefore, were seeking a "sign of signs," not so they would have a reason to believe, but so they might mock him; for this reason, they deserved to be rebuked by the Knower of Hearts.

->TONE EIGHT. 335<-

## How, according to the opinion of the Apostle, Christ is the mediator of the new testament. Chapter 8.

<margin>
Genesis
Moses
Paul
</margin>
**A**nd beyond those things which have been explained concerning our mediator, it remains to be declared why he is called by the Apostle the "mediator of a new testament." To explain this, it must be noted that in a <term>testament</term> <note>While we usually think of a "testament" as a will, in this biblical context it refers to the Covenant or legal agreement between God and humanity.</note> there is one person who testifies (the testator), another who is the beneficiary (the legatee), another who is the witness, and another who is the trustee or executor of the testament. This last person is properly called the "mediator," just as Moses was named by the Apostle as the mediator of the old testament. *The law* (he says to the Galatians) *was given through angels by the hand of a mediator* <note>original: "Lex data est per Angelos in manu mediatoris." See Galatians 3:19.</note>, that is, Moses, who was the executor of that testament—though not entirely, on account of the sin of the <note>original: "percussi lapidis." Referring to the incident in Numbers 20 where Moses struck the rock twice in anger rather than speaking to it as commanded, leading to his exclusion from the Promised Land.</note> struck stone.

<margin>Joshua</margin>
Therefore, Joshua stood in his place to fulfill it, leading the people into the land promised in that old testament.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
But JESUS, truly perfect and failing in nothing, was the full executor of the new testament. This testament was promulgated by the Son and committed to execution; however, it was ordained by the Father, as the Son himself testifies in the Gospel according to Luke, saying: *Behold, I appoint to you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one to me* <note>original: "Ecce ego dispono uobis regnum, sicut disposuit mihi Pater." See Luke 22:29.</note>. And again, as the faithful executor of the Father’s will, he promised he would say: *Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you* <note>original: "Venite Benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum uobis regnum." See Matthew 25:34.</note>—prepared, certainly, by the Father, by whom you are also blessed. Behold, therefore, from these and many other places, that those things pertaining to the new testament were arranged by the Eternal Father, but committed to execution by the Son. To the Son He gave such great power that He was even able to draw up the testament. Therefore, JESUS Christ was the testator by the power handed to Him by the Father; He was also the executor of this better testament, just as Moses was of the former.

<margin>Paul</margin>
Now, as to why this new testament is better than the old, Paul, assigning the reason to the Hebrews, says: *Because it is established on better promises* <note>original: "Quoniam in melioribus promissionibus sancitum est." See Hebrews 8:6.</note>. For in the former testament, this lower land was promised—namely the land of Canaan, yet flowing with that milk and honey of which much has often been said. But in the second, a land was promised and given which is the flesh, the tabernacle of the soul, and the divinity of the Messiah. From this "land" flowed a milk and honey more perfect than that from the land of Canaan. For from His very fleshly body, that wisdom was communicated to us which none of the wise of this world had known before; and that honey-sweet taste was given to the human race, so that an innumerable multitude of men and women, enticed by that sweetness, exposed their bodies and souls to various and most cruel kinds of death. They could by no means have suffered these with such great eagerness unless they were comforted and anointed by the sweetness of the honey flowing from the divinity through the earthly flesh and humanity of Christ.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
Finally, that "land of the living" was promised, as the testator himself clearly promises in the Gospel according to Matthew, saying: *Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land* <note>original: "Beati mites, quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram." See Matthew 5:5.</note>. Again, in the former testament, length of life upon that lower land was frequently promised...

<summary>This page explains Christ's role as the "Mediator" and "Executor" of the New Testament, comparing his perfect fulfillment of God's promises to Moses' incomplete leadership of the Old Testament. It highlights that the New Covenant is superior because its "milk and honey" represents spiritual wisdom and the presence of Christ's divinity, which empowered martyrs to endure suffering.</summary>

EIGHTH TONE. 338

->ON THE SONG OF SONGS<-

<margin>Exodus</margin>
Regarding the other matter, we read in Exodus how a hand is said to fight against Amalek himself upon the throne of God from generation to generation. <note>See Exodus 17:16. Amalek was a traditional enemy of the Israelites, here interpreted as a symbol of spiritual evil.</note> Indeed, these Amalekites, along with the Assyrians, Philistines, Moabites, and Ammonites, signify certain powers of darkness against whom a most bitter war has been declared upon us, and perpetual enmities established, as is said in <margin>Genesis</margin> Genesis: *I will put enmities between you and the seed of the woman* <note>original: "Ponā inimicitias inter te & semē mulieris." Genesis 3:15.</note>, because that ancient serpent—of whom Amalek was a member and a certain power—presumed to oppose the first man, and consequently his posterity as they set out toward the true land of promise and a place truly (not just figuratively) destined for them, just as here, following their father and leader, he presumed to oppose the people traveling to a figurative place. <margin>David</margin> Hence, a perpetual war without any peace or truce has been declared against both, and against all things that belong to them, because all those things are hindrances to us as we strive toward our fatherland. For this reason, those of us about to serve as soldiers for Christ vow to renounce the devil, the world, and its pomps. Concerning these peoples, beyond what we discussed above, we judge it worthy of every observation that we have victory against these enemies only from God through Jesus Christ <margin>Paul</margin> our mediator; which Paul also proclaims with a raised voice, saying: *But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:57.</note>

<margin>Moses</margin>
And Moses indicated this same thing by his own symbolic progress: for the people who were fighting against Amalek only won when Moses prayed with his arms extended in the manner of a cross, so that he might implore help from God through Him who was to be fixed to a cross. <note>This refers to the battle in Exodus 17, where Israel prevailed only as long as Moses held up his hands.</note> Also, after the victory was gained, Moses built an altar and invoked: **The Lord is my standard-bearer.** <note>original: "Adonai uexillifer meus." From the Hebrew "Adonai Nissi."</note> For which a faulty translation has: *And he called its name, The Lord is my exaltation.* <note>The author is criticizing the standard Latin Vulgate translation of Exodus 17:15, "Dominus exaltatio mea."</note> He appropriately called the mediator himself, through whom he had the victory, **Adonai**, or the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH). The text uses "quadriliterum" to refer to this.</note>, just as in Scripture our Messiah and mediator is often called by that name. He also rightly added, **my standard-bearer**, because He is the standard-bearer of every person fighting against the powers of darkness and their prince, whom our standard-bearer, raised on the cross, defeated and cast out. But because the eternal Father always favors the Son, fighting also for him against his enemies, according to that prophetic saying: *Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool* <note>Psalm 110:1.</note>, therefore <margin>The same (Moses)</margin> Moses added: *Because a hand upon the throne of Jah* <note>original: "Iah." A shortened form of the name of God (Yahweh).</note>, fighting for **The Lord** (or the Tetragrammaton) from generation to generation. Truly, the "hand" is power—not a created power, but divine—because this alone can be upon the throne of **Jah**. This word signifies divinity, or rather the pure essence of God, which no one can fittingly praise unless they are purged and transformed into something better and purer. Hence the Church forbade anyone from saying **Alleluia**—which translated means "Praise Jah"—during the time of penance <note>Lent</note>, before a person has been fully purified. And this <margin>The same (Moses)</margin> those ancient and good Fathers had learned from David, who was full of God, and who never wished to sing **Alleluia** until he had first, through many psalms, removed whatever...

<margin>David</margin> *May sinners vanish from the earth, and the wicked, so that they are no more: bless the Lord, O my soul, alleluia.* <note>original: "Deficiant peccatores a terra & iniqui, ita ut non sint: benedic anima mea Dominū, alleluia." ->Whether we require a medium so that we may come to this Christ the mediator.<-
->Chapter 10.<-

**A**ND because it may be doubted whether another medium is necessary for us through which we might come to this mediator, I say—resolving this briefly—that there is no "mediator of a mediator," lest we proceed into infinity. <note>The author is using a logical argument: if you needed a middleman to reach the Middleman (Christ), you would eventually need an infinite chain of middlemen. Therefore, Christ must be directly accessible.</note> But rather, two means or prior dispositions are required through which we may receive him and be united to him. One of these is emanating from above: namely, the election <note>election: In this context, the divine "choosing" or grace of God that calls a person to faith.</note> of divine mercy and piety, placing us among the sheep who had perished from the true house of Israel, for whose redemption he came. The other is that we labor faithfully for the talents entrusted to us, so that this election may be effective in us according to the purpose of the one choosing, and that we follow the footsteps of the mediator himself, who said: *I have given you an example, so that just as I have done, you also should do.* <note>original: "Exemplum dedi uobis, ut quēadmodum ego feci, ita & uos faciatis." John 13:15.</note> Who again exhorts and invites us to follow him, saying: 
<margin>CHRIST.</margin> *Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life*—namely, that light which illuminates every person, provided that no one, rolled in the darkness of sins, voluntarily refuses that light itself. <note>original: "Qui sequitur me non ambulat in tenebris, sed habebit lumen uitæ." John 8:12.</note> Through this, without any other medium—the divine election standing firm—we can be united with the mediator and receive, according to our capacity, all those things which we have explained in this song to be communicated from the <term>supramundane: originating beyond or above the physical world</term> source to all members of the Christian body through the head and our mediator, Christ, from whose fullness each person receives the part appropriate to them.

# PREFACE TO THE THIRD AND LAST 
# SONG.

<margin>David.</margin>
**S**INCE WE have already completed two songs—the first of which, the ancient one, concerns the harmony of the greater world <note>original: "maioris mundi," referring to the Macrocosm or the universe at large.</note> with the lesser world and the Archetype <note>original: "Archetypo," the divine blueprint or the mind of God from which all things are modeled.</note>; and the second, the new one, concerns the agreement of all the members with Christ the head—it remains for us to approach the last song. In this, we shall fulfill the harmonious progress and state toward the destined end of the lesser world <note>original: "mundi minoris," referring to the Microcosm, or the individual human being.</note>, for whose sake all things were made. We believe this will be all the more pleasing to the Supreme Prince [God] because He fashioned man himself more precisely than the other things we have already discussed. Concerning this song (if I am not mistaken), the Prophet—bathed in full light for the understanding of all things—sang in advance when he said: *O God, I will sing a new song to you.* <note>original: "Deus, canticum nouum cantabo tibi." Psalm 144:9.</note> I will surely sing about man, who is God’s latest work, who must be brought into harmony with the Maker through the observation of the law and the ten commandments. These are symbolized by the ten-stringed psaltery <note>original: "psalterium decachordum," a musical instrument with ten strings, often used by medieval and Renaissance writers to represent the Decalogue or Ten Commandments.</note> upon which the Prophet played. The sacred mystery of these commandments is entirely included within the Gospel lyre, and the praise of both is fulfilled by a well-stringed body, a harmonious spirit, and a soul singing well. Therefore, in another hymn he sings: *Rejoice in God our helper, O you well-stringed men* <note>original: "Exultate o bene chordati uiri Deo adiutori nostro." The author uses the metaphor of a "well-stringed" person to mean someone whose physical and spiritual life are in perfect tune with God's law.</note>—from whom comes every perfect symphony and praise. *Shout for joy to the God of Jacob*, you who have brought under foot
<margin>The same [David].</margin>
and trampled all obstacles to the due praise. Take up the psalm with which you may praise God in mind and soul, and give for His praise the well-composed tambourine <note>original: "tympanū," often interpreted in this period as the physical body.</note> of the body; then you shall take up the delightful psaltery with the lyre. For the delightful psaltery of the law is taken up when it is perfected in the Gospel lyre, in which (as is clear to one who understands well) even the smallest *jot* and the tiniest *tittle* of the law itself is fulfilled. <note>original: "minimū iod, & minutissimū apex." A reference to Matthew 5:18, emphasizing that even the smallest Hebrew letter (Yod) or stroke of a pen in the Law is significant.</note> For all those things contain their own sacred mysteries. And then they perform harmonious songs when, with the well-stringed instruments of the body, spirit, and soul, we return to God our due praises and harmonious works according to our strength. But we perform more full songs when, having overcome and subdued our enemies, we arrive at the true praises of *Jah* <note>original: "iah," a shortened form of the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh.</note>, just as the prophet teaches in the previously mentioned hundred and third psalm,
<margin>The same [David].</margin>
when he says: *Let sinners fail from the earth and the wicked, so that they are no more; bless the Lord, O my soul, Alleluia*—that is, "praise Jah." <note>original: "Deficiant peccatores a terra & iniqui... Alleluia. i. laudate iah." Psalm 104:35 (Vulgate 103). The author explains that "Alleluia" literally means "Praise the Lord (Jah)."</note> This, no one can do unless the enemies have been put to flight, as we are taught in the preceding psalms. However, we shall perform the most perfect and fullest songs (God willing) when we praise Him in the heights together with the Angels sounding in that choir of the blessed—not only with the tongue, but with the spirit, soul, body, and all members—to the praise of the Maker, to whom all things owe glory and honor forever. And this we shall perform with the diapasonic <note term="Diapasonica">Refers to the interval of an octave, which in musical theory represents the most perfect consonance and a return to the beginning at a higher level.</note> harmony of the eight Tones, just as we completed in the two preceding songs.

<sig>e</sig>

On the manifold concord of the soul, the body, and the virtues. Tone I.

On the consonance <term>consonantia|A pleasing agreement between sounds or parts, used here to describe the harmony of the soul's inner workings.</term> of the soul through the understanding of things. Tone II.

On the agreement of man with the heavenly and sacred intelligences <note>original: "intelligentiis cælis," referring to angelic beings or divine minds that govern the celestial spheres.</note>. Tone III.

On the agreement of all things with a well-tuned man <note>original: "homine bene chordato." This is a musical metaphor suggesting a person whose internal "strings"—reason, spirit, and body—are in perfect tension and harmony.</note>, so that he may be able to operate in all things and command all. Tone IV.

On the consonance of the soul with its own spirit and all other spirits. Tone V.

On the most sweet harmony which well-tuned men make with God. Tone VI.

On the harmony of the body and the soul changed for the better through the resurrection. Tone VII.

On the most sweet harmonies and that eternal rest <note>original: "pausa illa æterna," literally "that eternal pause," a musical rest representing the soul's final peace in God.</note> in the attainment of blessedness. Tone VIII.

# CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST TONE.

Chapter I. On that agreement and symmetry which exists in the body.

Chapter II. On that consonance which exists between the body and the soul.

Chapter III. From whence dissonance arises in the body.

Chapter IV. From whence and what consonance or dissonance exists between the body and the soul.

Chapter V. On tempering the body and the arrangement of the "tent" <note>original: "tentorii," a metaphor for the physical body as a temporary tabernacle or dwelling for the soul.</note> through natural remedies.

Chapter VI. How much prudence and proper regimen <term>regimen|A systematic way of life, including diet and exercise, intended to maintain health or produce a specific physical state.</term> contribute to achieving such temperaments.

Chapter VII. How much true self-knowledge avails each person in achieving these things.

Chapter VIII. That the body, and consequently the whole man, is tempered and strengthened by heavenly favor.

Chapter IX. By what short path we may draw favor from heaven, the angels, and God.

Chapter X. How man, the little world <note>original: "homo paruus mundus," or the Microcosm.</note>, is able to receive nourishment from all the members of the greater world <note>original: "maioris mundi," or the Macrocosm (the universe).</note>, which he most resembles.

Chapter XI. On the agreement of the soul with itself.

Chapter XII. On bringing about a harmony of the virtues, so that the soul may be healed and delighted by them.

Chapter XIII. On the consonance of the virtues with the soul.

# ON THE AGREEMENT AND SYMMETRY WHICH EXISTS IN THE BODY. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Vitruvius</margin> The commensuration <term>commensuratio|The measurement of parts in relation to each other to create a harmonious whole.</term> of the body is so great that skilled architects have divided temples, shrines, houses, columns, architraves, bases, and all manner of crafted members—however small they may be—according to the measure of the human body. This includes even the smallest parts: the rounded moldings <note>original: "toris"</note>, squares, concave moldings <note>original: "trochilis"</note>, plinths, lintels, bead-moldings <note>original: "astragalis"</note>, modules, column bases, pedestals, and whatever pertains to architraves, bases, columns, and pillars <note>original: "antes," referring to the pier-like ends of walls in a temple</note>, or to any kind of building. As Vitruvius, the undisputed leader of this teaching, interjects while discussing the matter at length: "No temple can have a rational plan of composition through any symmetry and proportion, unless it possesses an exact ratio of the members of a well-formed man." For the proportion of architecture (as he says) is the modulation of a fixed part of the members in every work, and of the whole, from which the ratio of symmetry is produced. 

And progressing further, he strives to prove that every number—and specifically those numbers called decimal or "six-part" <note>original: "sextertii," referring to the perfect number six or the sestertius system</note>—was discovered from the joints of the body. For the ancients counted with their fingers and indicated numbers with those same fingers; thus, they divided all buildings according to the measure of the body. God, the Supreme Architect, greatly favors this view, for He taught Noah to build the Ark according to the measure of the human body, as we explained above. Furthermore, I have seen skilled men derive the measurements of ships from the human body. Indeed, the Supreme Craftsman Himself made the entire machine of the world symmetrical to the human body and fashioned it entirely as a symbol of it; hence, the former is not undeservedly called the "Great World" <term>Macrocosmus|The universe seen as a large-scale reflection of humanity.</term> and the latter the "Small World" <term>Microcosmus|Man seen as a miniature map or reflection of the entire universe.</term>. 

We have demonstrated their consonance and symbolism in part, as we revealed all the elements and things made of elements, the heavens, the Angels, and even God Himself (if it be permitted) to be contained within man. We have also explained with what proportion the elements, qualities, and temperaments <note>original: "complexiones," the balance of bodily humors</note> agree within the human body, and with what consonance the circumference of the members harmonizes. But others add that the measurements of the length of the body's members are also proportioned. 

For the face of the head, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part of the body's height. Likewise, the palm of the hand to the tip of the middle finger is the same. The head, from the chin to the very top of the crown, is an eighth part. From the top of the chest to the roots of the hair is a sixth. To the top of the crown, a fourth. Of the face or countenance itself, the height is divided into three: the first part is from the bottom of the chin to the bottom of the nostrils; the nose, from the bottom of the nostrils to the middle point between the eyebrows, is the same; and from that point to the roots of the hair where the forehead ends, is likewise a third part. The foot, however, is a sixth of the body's height; the cubit <note>the length of the forearm</note>, a fourth; and the chest likewise, a fourth. Thus, all the remaining members have their own proportions.

For a tenfold proportion makes a <term>tridiapason & diapente|A musical interval spanning three octaves and a perfect fifth.</term>. An eightfold proportion [makes] a triple octave. A fourfold, a double octave. A sixfold, a double octave and a fifth. A triple, an octave and a fifth. In the same way, all the commensurations of the other members are proportioned and consonant: and what is greater, they are most fittingly in agreement with the members of the world, the joints of the heavens, and the measures of the Archetype, which is the highest.
