<margin>Ancient Theologians</margin> to some sign <note>referring to the signs of the Zodiac</note>, to some planet, and to some measure which exists in the Archetype, as the Ancient Theologians teach. There are, moreover, in him (as we explained above) elements and humors mixed in due and harmonic proportions: from whose temperament health, and from whose distemperament <note>an imbalance of the bodily fluids or humors</note> infirmity proceeds. And all—I will not say parts of the body, but the portions of the whole man—agree in one and the same soul giving life to all, just as the strings of instruments, or various melodies, come together in one consonance. And although the life of man appears to be of many kinds—vegetative, animal, spiritual, intellectual, or whatever else it may be—yet there is one single reason of life in all of them. Hence, not without mystery, Scripture says that God, when he gave life to man, breathed into his face the breath or soul of life, which the Hebrews call <term>nishmat chayyim|Hebrew: נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים</term>: it says "lives" <note>the Hebrew noun is plural</note> to hint that in that breathing, or soul, which was infused, every kind of life was contained which pertains to the whole man.

### ON THE CONSONANCE WHICH EXISTS BETWEEN THE BODY AND THE SOUL. CHAPTER II.

**W**hat kind of harmony there is, however, between the body and the soul—which seem entirely different—the Pythagoreans, the foremost investigators of consonances, have tried to conjecture from that most quiet and sweet union which is seen by everyone. Among whom, Timaeus of Locri, a distinguished Pythagorean, shadowed it forth in his usual manner, saying: "For the soul to be well, it is expedient for the body to have its strengths, health, ready senses, vigor, and beauty." The beginning of this exterior beauty is commensurability, which they call <term>symmetry|From the Greek 'symmetria', meaning the proportional agreement between the parts and the whole.</term>. Nature prepares a tent for the members themselves and the soul, as if it were an instrument: and it is compliant, like a certain tunable thing, to the reasons of living and subjection. Proclus agrees with this in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, saying: "The soul from the beginning was constituted according to harmonic ratios: and the entire body is said to be joined to it according to proportions: the universe itself also is bound together harmoniously and fittingly." And regarding where these harmonic joints proceed from, he says next: "Their principles are from nature, or from the highest work[master]..."

### Why dissonance arises in the body. Chapter III.

**C**orpus <note>The letter 'C' is a decorative woodcut initial in the original manuscript.</note> However, although the body is most well-tempered, it sometimes feels the most violent dissonance. We do not doubt that this happens primarily from a twofold cause. One is the distemperament of the <term>humors|The four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to control health and temperament in pre-modern medicine.</term>, arising either from excess, or from deficiency, or from an internal or external alteration. The other is because it falls out of harmony with the celestial bodies, so that influences that are otherwise good may harm it. It falls out of harmony, indeed, when the soul turns away from that which the celestial influence requires. Many other disorders follow this lack of order, because (as Proclus says) the soul that is out of harmony is immediately subjected <margin>Proclus.</margin> to an evil demon <note>Proclus was a 5th-century Neoplatonist. In this context, a 'demon' refers to a spiritual force or internal disorder that plagues the soul.</note> until it is purified by due expiations. But as to what the distemperaments of the humors are—since this belongs to the physicians—leaving to them what is theirs, we shall run through those things which pertain to our subject and to the proper training of the "better man" <note>Referring to the cultivation of the spiritual or inner self.</note>. For the humors are distempered (from which infirmities arise) not only from superfluous, diminished, or altered matter, but more often because the body is poorly ruled by the soul. For if it is fed with superfluous food, from which superfluous humors are generated, is this not the fault of the soul not restraining its gluttony? And if harmful foods are eaten, is the soul's imprudence not to be blamed? And if there is excessive labor, from which comes exhaustion and various alterations of the humors, is our lack of skill not to be condemned? And if a man commits something from which sadness arises and <term>black bile|Also known as 'atra bilis,' the humor associated with melancholy and depression.</term> is increased, by which the humors are infected, or if he grieves and is saddened by occurrences more than is proper, so that he boils with bile or is weighed down by <term>melancholy|A state of deep sadness or depression once thought to be caused by an excess of black bile.</term>, is this not from a soul in a bad state? This is the "Aristotelian sadness" <note>Refers to Aristotle's famous observation in 'Problemata' that great men of genius are often prone to melancholy.</note> which absorbs and corrupts the power of the one who possesses it. But if the soul, like a leader in the whole human army, agreeing with the commander or king, [directs] all inferior...

### Whence and what is the consonance or dissonance between the body and the soul. Chapter IV.

**T**here exists also an agreement between the body and the soul, worthy of all the greater admiration the more those things which are connected seem to be diverse; so much so that this craftsmanship transcends all human understanding. For so great is their binding together that man, regarding their dissolution as the most terrible of all things, flees from it as much as he can, desiring rather, as the Apostle says, <margin>Paul, and...</margin> to be "clothed upon" rather than "unclothed." And in this hope we live happily. Nor was war ever declared between these two: but rather between the "spiritual man" and the <term>animal man</term> <note>original: "homine animali," meaning the natural or soul-led man who lacks spiritual grace, a concept from 1 Corinthians 2:14.</note>; which differ by much reason from "body" and "soul," though sometimes "spirit" is taken for the soul, and "body" or "flesh" for the animal man. However, concerning the peace, concord, and union of these, the Scripture says: "God breathed into the face of man the breath of life, and man was made a single thing, namely into a living soul." But concerning their battle, Paul says: "The flesh lusts <margin>The same (Paul).</margin> against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another"; and again, "I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive into the law of sin; so that I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want." Whence there is no discord between the body and the soul, which are natural things, desiring no fight but peace; just as the supreme Maker bound them together in a firm and continuous covenant. Hence many err, who, while they think they are reducing the body into the slavery of the spirit with Paul—that is, the "animal" appetites—they instead destroy nature or natural gifts, which ought to be exercised with full and undebilitated strength for the praise of God, one's own benefit, and the advantage of one's neighbor. Therefore, discord among natural things is not to be procured, nor are they to be destroyed, but rather preserved. Hence the same Apostle <margin>The same (Paul).</margin> teaches his Timothy to use wine for the sake of comforting his stomach; and as [was mentioned] a little before...

<note>original: "Tonus Primus." In this context, "Tone" likely refers to the first part or volume of a larger work on harmony or spiritual order.</note>

<margin>Jerome</margin> We have said that Jerome commands all our service to be reasonable <note>original: "rationabile obsequium," a reference to Romans 12:1, often translated as "spiritual worship" or "reasonable service."</note>. Consenting to this, Jerome himself also prescribes that our fasts should be moderate: since God is not delighted by the emptiness of our bellies, nor by us needing to support our wavering steps with a staff or a wall. Instead, those fasts, abstinences, and mortifications are to be undertaken by which the spirit may grow strong and become mightier and more agile in the service of God—not by destroying the body, but by bringing it into servitude. There must be a continuous discrepancy and struggle between the **celestial man** and the **sensual man**, until the former has reduced the latter into perfect servitude: so that, being together in agreement and peaceful, they may be blessed in the very kingdom of peace. Indeed, the concord of the body and the soul must be preserved, by which the <term>Maker</term> <note>original: "opifex," referring to God as the divine craftsman.</note> bound them together, until (at His command) that dissolution occurs by which we are set free from this body—in which we live as pilgrims away from the Lord—and the soul may attain possession of the promised kingdom. Once this is obtained, it shall again take up the body, now clothed in incorruption, immortality, and a spiritual nature: so that, united together, they may never again be dissolved from that place, nor ever admit any dissonance from which any sorrow might be generated.

### Chapter V. On tempering the body, and the arrangement of the tent through natural remedies.
<note>The "tent" or tabernacle is a common Renaissance metaphor for the physical body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> Since, indeed, when the <term>humors</term> <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed in ancient and medieval medicine to govern health and temperament.</note> are discordant, the **animal spirits** <note>original: "spiritus animales." In pre-modern medicine, these were not "animalistic" but "soul-spirits" (from *anima*) that acted as the bridge between the physical organs and the mind.</note> that reside in those very humors also fall into disagreement; the senses, the **imaginative power**, and all the organs of the higher soul are disturbed. Since the soul follows the passions of the body, it becomes distempered itself. Hence, remedies and physicians are not to be despised, as the Scripture says: *Honor the physician because of necessity; the Most High created him.* <margin>David</margin> And again: *The Most High has produced medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not abhor it.* And because (as is inferred below) all healing is from God, therefore the Prophet says: *Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed.* For health and medicine are conferred by Him for both parts of man. For the virtue of **herbs, roots, stones, words**, and all things which pertain to the medicines of both parts of man, has been implanted by God: who sometimes works those things which regard the health and nourishment of the body directly by Himself, and sometimes through the <term>intelligences</term> <note>Celestial beings or spirits believed to move the planetary spheres and influence earthly health.</note> and the heavens. And He does this most especially for the sake of the soul, for which He cares most. The soul, so that it may be perfectly healthy, requires a healthy body: therefore that wise man used to pray that there might be a *sound mind in a sound body.* <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano," a famous phrase from the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> For both, therefore, the Most High has prepared medicines and physicians. For the healing of the body (by God's arrangement), great was the labor of the wise: <margin>Apollo, Aesculapius, Hippocrates, Paul, Galen, Damascene, Dioscorides, Avicenna. Theologians. John.</margin> **Apollo, Aesculapius, Hippocrates, Paul, Galen, John Damascene, Dioscorides, Avicenna**, and many of the Arabs, Persians, Greeks, and various nations. Some were most diligent in investigating the natures and virtues of things, others in composing and applying them according to the quality of bodies and illnesses. But concerning the medicines of the soul (beyond those which are spoken of most fully by our Theologians in the fourth volume of the *Theological Sentences* regarding the sacraments and sacrifices, which were instituted as healings for souls), **John** says that in the super-celestial region he saw the **Tree of Life**, whose leaves were for the healing of the nations. Having recovered this health, the nations themselves—now having become men—would eat of the fruits of life, which are called the **food of the strong**, not to be taken by any who are infirm. Concerning the physician, the **Psalmist** sings: *He sent his word...*

### OF THE THIRD CANTICLE

...and he healed them. From this, the Word itself, sent from the Father and made flesh, said of himself <margin>CHRIST</margin>: "Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick do" <note>Matthew 9:12. The author uses this to establish Christ's identity as a healer.</note>. And Origen <margin>Origen</margin>, explaining that sacramental song, says: "We will run in the fragrance of your ointments" <note>original: "In odore curremus unguentorum tuorum," from the Song of Songs 1:3-4. Origen was a prominent early Christian theologian known for allegorical interpretation.</note>. For God the Father, anointing him with various ointments, made him Christ <note>The name "Christ" literally means "The Anointed One."</note> and Physician. For it was fitting for God the Father to destine such a bridegroom for a sick bride <note>The "bride" is a common metaphor for the Church or the individual soul.</note>. This bridegroom, so that he might fulfill the office of a good physician by healing the whole man, also gave power and a command to the Apostles regarding the healing of both parts of man: as it is written in the Gospel titled "according to Matthew." Having handed over this power, he said <margin>Matthew</margin>: "Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons." Afterward, he commands <margin>CHRIST</margin> that, being unburdened of gold, silver, money of all kinds, traveling bags, extra tunics, shoes of vain things, and the staff of human or worldly power, they should announce peace in whatever house they entered.

Observe, I pray, the order of the Supreme Physician: for he commands those whom he sends as guides for men on the path of salvation to first heal bodies, raise those who are dead, and cure those possessed by demons; afterwards, once unburdened from all earthly things, they are to announce and grant peace—which is truly the <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperamentum." In Renaissance medicine, health was defined as the perfect "temperament" or balance of the four bodily humors.</note> and true health, or rather, the tranquility of the soul. Neither can one provide nor possess this peace unless they are wise of heart and entirely free from earthly impediments and troubling cares; therefore, he orders that those who were to announce it should be unburdened of such things.

Therefore, bodies must be cared for first, so that from the harmony of a healthy body we may arrive at the harmony of the spirit, of virtues, and of better things, and finally at divine harmony, just as Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras</margin> teaches. And just as in outward matters these things lead by the favor of Phoebus <note>Apollo, often called Phoebus, was the classical god of both music (harmony) and medicine.</note>, who provides the greatest power for health and harmony, so in the inner man—indeed in both—it leads by the favor of the **True Sun** <note>A common metaphor for Christ.</note>, achieving both effects: health and harmony. Thus, when bodies are tempered, the spirits, senses, all operations, and the mind are tempered, so that they might taste heavenly and divine food. For this to happen perfectly, it is completed in the perfect state of blessedness, where the body itself is tempered and changed into the nature of spirit, so that, weighted down by no imbalance, it may always be able to receive that food together with the spirit.

Nor should anyone be terrified by that Apostolic sentiment <margin>Paul</margin>: "When I am weak, then I am strong" <note>2 Corinthians 12:10.</note>; because there, the divine man speaks not of physical weakness or the imbalance of the body—from which many evils follow—but of that surrender which the "animal man" <note>The "animalis homo" refers to the lower, sensory nature of a human, as opposed to the "spiritualis homo" or spiritual nature.</note> must make to the spirit in the continuous struggle where one of the two must succumb. In this case, it is not physical weakness that is sought, but the subjection of the animal man, which occurs not through a distemper of physical qualities, but through a harmonious surrender and a certain transformation of animal powers into spiritual powers. However, for a body suffering from discord, a cure is achieved through medicines, exercises, a pure and sparse diet, and celestial favor. Medicines are many: partly from the nature of <term>simples</term> <note>Herbs or minerals used on their own for healing, believed to derive their power from the stars or "intelligences."</note> drawn from the heavens and the intelligences, but primarily from God; partly from the harmonic composition of medicines among themselves, suited to the receiving body. This works greatly, though it is little known to the wise men of our time, who, following their Aristotle, attribute everything to primary and secondary qualities...

Due exercise and joyful, honorable occupations also benefit the temperament of the body and, consequently, the soul. There are also many aids for recovering and preserving strength. ...perceive the French poison <note>original: "toxico gallico"; likely referring to a specific herbal poison or disease known in the late medieval period</note>, they seek out the oak (as some claim) but Croatia (as pleases others) for a cure. Barbarian panthers (as <margin>Cicero</margin> Cicero reports) have a certain remedy in poisoned meat, which they use to avoid death. Stags also, after a fight with serpents, hasten to springs of water to extinguish their thirst, which has been stirred by the serpents' poisonous breath. The wise man sends the lazy back to the ant, which builds its granary with such care—sensing the coming winter—that it seems to flourish with the greatest prudence. The stork (it is said) purges its intestines with its own beak. The camel, when properly loaded, rises, but refuses to be loaded further because it knows it cannot carry the weight. Since there are infinite examples of this kind among animals, such wisdom should be found much more in a human endowed with a mind. 

But some have judged such a prudent regime so effective that they have refused external medicines; <margin>Asclepiades, Pliny</margin> just as Pliny tells of Asclepiades <note>Asclepiades of Bithynia (c. 124–40 BCE) was a Greek physician who rejected the theory of humors and championed diet, massage, and exercise.</note>, who, having cast aside all drugs and reduced the whole of medicine to chance, professed five things as the most common aids: **abstinence from food**, at other times **from wine**, **friction** (massage) of the body, **walking**, and **being carried** <note>original: "gestationesque"; refers to passive motion, like riding in a carriage or litter, thought to aid digestion</note>; these are things anyone can provide for themselves. Others praise sweats induced by exercise for those who are healthy, and by multiple layers of clothing for the sick. Many things of this kind are commended by some, which we can bring about through a certain prudence alongside the favor of nature. 

This is also what Plato teaches in the *Timaeus*. Diseases, he says (unless they are very dangerous), should not be provoked with drugs, but corrected and managed with diligence, as far as leisure is granted to each. He also highly praises **motion** for preserving health and curing the body of sickness. But, he says, in healing the body, let one imitate that nature which we call the "nourisher of the universe": so that it never allows the body to become sluggish, but always moves it. By constant agitation, with internal and external motions, resisting everywhere according to nature, let it—through a certain moderate commotion—bring the wandering passions of the body and its related parts back into order, keeping reason in command. Of all motions, he believes the best is that which comes from within oneself, because it is most closely related to the mind. That which is caused by another is worse. Therefore, of all purgings and strengthening of the body, that which is done through **gymnastics** is the healthiest. Next to this comes easy transport, whether by ship or any other vehicle. 

Prudence, therefore, seeks not only such very useful aids—easily obtained by a prudent person—but also ensures that one curbs gluttony and avoids superfluous and harmful foods. It would be best (though very difficult) if everyone knew exactly how much was enough for them and took no more, so as to avoid <term>superfluous humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). An excess or "superfluity" was thought to cause disease.</note>. <margin>CHRIST</margin> This is what some assert concerning Christ: that he took food in such specific measure that he did not generate the waste of the <term>fourth digestion</term> <note>The final stage of the metabolic process in Galenic medicine, where nutrients are assimilated into the tissues.</note>. 

Many others also have enjoyed a certain thinness of food along with health and agility of the body. <margin>Moses, Elijah</margin> **Moses** and **Elijah** extended their fasting until the fortieth day; hence the former’s face shone, his body now purified, and the latter was carried up in a light and fiery chariot; he led his body as easily as a spirit at his command. <margin>Jerome</margin> **Jerome** boasted of having learned to endure a week-long fast, yet remained robust in mind and body. And many others, observing great abstinences, were content...

Thus, food serves for sustenance and not for pleasure. 

Because it is most difficult to know the limits of this, some, afflicting their bodies with more fasting than is proper, have suffered clear and various harms. Indeed, a great search for prudence is required here, so that, like a good musician, one may draw and fit all the strings with a just rhythm, lest by being tighter or looser than is fitting, they drive away harmonies rather than creating them. For no less skill and sharpness is required in judging the harmony of the members of the body and in moderating them—so that all are tempered with the spirit and soul—than a musician requires in tuning his instruments. But since perfect knowledge of such a matter cannot be had except by the most perfect, everyone should consult those more experienced. They teach at least some things to be guarded against until, with a mind attained, one arrives at the perfect knowledge of one's own <insert>body as a</insert> "tent" <note>A common biblical metaphor (the tabernacle) for the physical body housing the eternal soul.</note> that houses the soul, the intelligence that guards it, and of all things pertaining to the perfection of the soul itself, as well as the perfect temperament of the body and its complete harmony with the soul.

### How much true self-knowledge avails each person in achieving these things. Chapter VII.

There exists a most celebrated <term>monument</term> <note>original: "monumentum"; here meaning a precept or famous maxim.</note> of the wise, by which a person is able to moderate their own body, everything within the body, and everything adjacent to it. That maxim is: **"Know Thyself."** This does not merely mean knowing that you are made of earth, or born of vile matter, or soon to be resolved back into earth, or that you live amidst countless troubles—as some interpret that maxim. Rather, it requires that one know what the soul itself is, from whence it proceeds, with how many and how great degrees of perfection it is filled, with what intelligence it is fortified, by what means it is diffused into the body, by what harmony it is joined to it, and what affinity it has with God, the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>Celestial or angelic beings.</note>, the heavens, the elements, and all things, of which it holds the image and likeness. It asks by what influences the body is assembled, and by what course of life it is to be bounded, beyond which no further progress is allowed. For these and such things are sought by that maxim which Greece boasts to have received before all others from the <margin>Oracle.</margin> Delphic oracle upon the ancient tripod. Yet praise should not be given to the one speaking in the oracle as if they were the inventor of that teaching, since before the oracle of Apollo, those who were taught by the Holy Spirit had already delivered it; for <margin>Job.</margin> Job says: *visiting your form* <note>original: "visitans speciem tuam"; reference to Job 5:24, often interpreted in this period as an exhortation to self-examination.</note>...

Concerning this, the **divine Harpist** <note>original: *diuus Citharista*; a common poetic name for King David, referring to his playing the harp and composing the Psalms</note> thunders with a clear voice, saying: <margin>David</margin> *Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the foolish beasts and made like them.* <note>Psalm 49:20. Explaining this, <margin>Macrobius</margin> **Macrobius** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher famous for his commentary on the "Dream of Scipio."</note> in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, says: *We say that souls have fallen from heaven into bodies, and this is the perfect wisdom of the soul while it uses the body: to recognize from whence it arose.* For thus all who think rightly desire that such knowledge be required through which, once impediments are excluded, a straight path to God may be taken. Hence, they judged that the oracle emanated from heaven rather than from a demon, as the **Satirist** sings: <margin>Juvenal</margin> *From heaven descended the command: "Know Thyself."* <note>original Greek: *γνῶθι σεαυτὸν* (Gnothi seauton). Juvenal, Satire 11.27. The author attributes this famous Delphic maxim to divine inspiration.</note> Indeed, this instruction sprang from heaven and from the Holy Spirit, as we have said, even if it was brought forth to the Greeks by a demon through an oracle. 

Therefore, by having this knowledge of ourselves, we know God, in whose image we were made; we know the world, whose likeness <note>original: *simulachrum*; the concept of the human as a "microcosm" or miniature world</note> we carry; we know all creatures, whom we embrace and with whom we have a shared symbol and **harmonic proportion**. We know what nourishment we can draw from stones, what from herbs, what from the heavens, and finally what we can draw from every single thing. We know, moreover, how we are able to fit each string of our bodily instrument into its proper place.

# OF THE THIRD SONG

->That the body is tempered and strengthened, and consequently the whole man, by celestial favor.<-

## Chapter VIII.

<margin>Mercury. Jeremiah.</margin>
**And** because diseases are sometimes fatal (as <term>Plato</term> asserted in the *Timaeus*) <note>In the Timaeus, Plato discusses how the physical constitution is linked to the mathematical order of the universe.</note>, reaching their end at certain cycles of time from the very beginning of their generation and following the great movements of the living universe: therefore, the disease must be tempered and virtue must be strengthened by celestial favor. This must be sought even by those who, having fallen into the lower harmony, have become (as <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus.</note> says) the most wretched servants of the heavens and other lower things. For there were, and are still found, some to whom it is said through <term>Jeremiah</term>: *Do not fear the signs of heaven, as the nations fear them* <note>original: "A signis caeli, ne timueritis/ sicut gentes timent"; Jeremiah 10:2.</note> because neither the sky, nor the earth, nor any corporeal thing, but the Lord Himself is the immediate part and the measuring-line of the inheritance of those to whom the same Prophet says again: *Do not fear these things, because they can do neither evil nor good.* We shall speak with those people in the proper place; but for now, we speak with those who are subject to the heavens. To them we say that, until they are freed from the governance of the stars, they should take care like wise <term>Astronomers</term> to guard against not only the many evils that the heavens threaten (as <term>Ptolemy</term> teaches) but should continually draw favor and protection until they are released from that celestial governance.

<margin>Ptolemy. Plotinus.</margin>
This drawing down of favor occurs (as <term>Plotinus</term> <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, who taught that the physical world is a reflection of a higher spiritual reality.</note> teaches) by means of the <term>World Soul</term>, which, containing as many <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rones [rationes] seminales"; the formative principles or "seeds" of all things in the natural world.</note> as there are ideas in the divine mind, grants to each thing its own particular power according to the virtues of the ideas received, just as it also grants life. For there is no member in this "worldly animal" <note>Referring to the Platonic concept of the universe as a single living organism.</note> so deformed that (as the Platonists assert) it does not possess the gift of both soul and life.

<margin>Plato. Zoroaster. Synesius.</margin>
These connections of life <term>Zoroaster</term> calls "divine lures," and <term>Synesius</term> <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop who wrote on dreams and the soul's descent.</note> calls "symbolic attractions." According to these, not all good things arise from heaven at once, but according to the cycles of time and opportunity, and according to the aptitude and disposition of each individual. When this disposition is brought about, the person who is properly prepared receives the favor of the stars and the governing intelligences suited to them, just as an organized body, brought to its final disposition, receives life and a soul. For we see, in the succession of time and through the many and various revolutions of the heavens, that men profit greatly in the increase and expansion of life, soul, reason, and many gifts which cannot be achieved by the tools of art and industry alone; so much so that we are forced to confess to celestial favor. This has often been proven by diligent observation, even though those who predict the future are sometimes deceived: either because they do not fully know all the influences and where they come from, or because a man, by his own judgment and freedom of soul, tends elsewhere than the celestial influence itself dictates.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
For (as the prince of Astronomers, <term>Ptolemy</term>, teaches in the beginning of his <term>Apotelesmata</term> <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>), it is not enough for someone to be chaste and just to have <term>Jupiter</term> favoring them in their horoscope, unless they also avoid pimps and harlots, whose conversation blocks the celestial influence. For habits, morals, blood, place of birth, the freedom of the soul, and very many occasions stand in the way, since those influences do not compel, but rather dispose <note>original: "influxus illi nõ cogant, sed disponant"; a famous phrase in Renaissance astrology meaning the stars suggest or incline the path but do not force human will.</note>.

<summary>This chapter explains that while the devout may transcend celestial influence through God, most people are subject to the stars and must use "celestial favor" to maintain health and virtue. It argues that the World Soul mediates these influences, which "incline" human nature without overriding free will.</summary>

# THE FIRST TONE.

And may they favor us. And this (as we have said) happens through the **World Soul** <term>anima mundi</term> <note>A Neoplatonic concept suggesting the entire universe is a single, living, breathing organism endowed with a soul that connects all things.</note>, yet through the particular power of images and the presiding **intelligences** <term>intelligentiarum</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, these are non-physical beings or "angels" that guide the movements and influences of the planets.</note>, as well as through the gathering of rays and astrological aspects when those stars and images align in a certain peculiar and harmonious assembly. And the power of all these things is nurtured by the Sun as if by the true **rooster of heaven** <note>original: "uerum celi gallum"; a metaphor for the Sun as the herald of light and the awakener of life.</note>, who pours out both the common force of life and the seeds of particular virtues. The stars, being made pregnant by the power of his seed—especially the Moon—pour out the offspring into us in her own time, acting as a womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> not only for the Sun but for the other planets. From all of these, she receives the seed and the influences sent down from the higher spheres, and like a mother of the household, she bestows them upon us. Hence, she is observed by almost everyone with the most diligent care. We can learn and prove this within the **microcosm** <term>minori mundo</term> <note>The "small world"—the human being—which was believed to be a perfect miniature map of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note> and within ourselves. For in the heart of man, which holds the image and power of the Sun, is the source of common life and the virtue of all the members of the entire body. For everything in the body receives nourishment from the heart, along with the force of life and motion. This force passes from the heart to the brain—which is of a lunar nature—and from there it is spread to all the members of the body through the veins and the nerves descending from it.

<margin>Plato.</margin> Following the **Platonists** <note>Philosophers following the traditions of Plato, who viewed the universe as an organic, interconnected whole.</note> therefore, who agree in the common opinion that the world is a living animal—more "one" than any other thing that exists—we say that the universal and particular members are bound together in the same way. They are equal and very similar in their influence, mutual communication, motion, quality, and every kind of correspondence. For in both cases, the principal member exerts the greatest influence: which is the Sun in the "world-animal," and the heart in the individual. The other higher members of both flow into the lower ones, according to the disposition of those receiving the influence. This disposition is both implanted by nature and aided by the tools of wisdom and art. But even a small amount of this preparation, acquired through industry, is enough to grasp the gifts of heaven; therefore, it should not be despised, as it contributes much to the natural disposition (so that it may be full) and to the soul's ability to arrange things, since the soul itself favors the process of arrangement, just as the celestial influences do. And though a man may receive favor from the whole sky, he nevertheless drinks most powerfully from the "heart of heaven," which is the Sun, since man is a "solar being" <margin>The Arabs. Hebrew theology.</margin> (as the **Arabian astronomers** <note>Medieval Islamic scholars whose works on astrology and astronomy were foundational to European Renaissance science.</note> say). He is decorated by a certain peculiar gift of both suns—namely the celestial sun and the one above the world—as we have gathered from the **theology of the Hebrews** <note>A likely reference to the Kabbalah or Jewish mystical traditions which discuss spiritual "suns" or emanations of divine light.</note>. This is also taught by his beautiful and upright stature, his subtle humor, his clear spirit, his keen imagination, his pursuit of truth and glory, and many other things in which man possesses a symbol of both suns and a peculiar image of them—an image that is more expressive the more perfect the man is. For this reason, Christ Jesus, the prince and head of men, is called the Sun in many places; from the fullness of whose light, life, and all good things (as John says), we have all received. 

<margin>John.</margin> We also draw influence from other planets and stars, but by the power of the Sun, who nurtures them with his own seed or virtue. Just as in the **mystical body** <term>corpus mysticum</term> <note>A theological term for the collective unity of believers, traditionally viewed as a single body with Christ as the head.</note> (where we receive primarily from Christ the heart or head), we nevertheless also receive, through his virtue, from the other members, which are like stars in the great mystical body.

The Sun itself is the foremost giver of life among the celestial members through a certain vital spirit. By this spirit (as Timaeus the Pythagorean says) <note>Referring to the character Timaeus in Plato’s dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the world.</note> the whole world lives, continually drawing it in, together with the spirit and power of the other stars. This is especially true for man, who—through his own spirit being of the same nature as theirs—is made more closely related to them by art and prudence, and by many rules and aids. True sages discuss these matters by word of mouth rather than in volumes of books. And a person receives a more frequent soul <note>original: "celebriorem animam"; implying a soul more active or attuned to higher frequencies.</note> not only from the stars and **intelligences** <term>intelligentiis</term> <note>The angelic beings believed to move the planetary spheres.</note>, but from the very fountain of all good things, the more one is made celestial, angelic, and divine. 

One turns out celestial, moreover, when—trampling and scorning corruptible things—one embraces the incorruptible, and conducts their mind and works into a circle like a sort of heaven, reflecting their path and work back toward the heaven from which they proceeded. This cannot happen unless there is a prior separation from the clouding vapors and from all those things that make a human being unlike heaven. One is also made angelic while serving God with a clean and pure mind, always delighting in clean things: in the bowels, on the skin, in clothes, in dwellings, and in utensils. The uncleanness of all these things frequently infects the air; it disturbs that most pure influx of celestial and divine things and puts the clean ministers of God to flight. Yet sometimes unclean angels—acting as apes of God and His ministers <note>The "Apes of God" is a traditional term for demons who mimic divine rituals to deceive people.</note>—seek out this kind of cleanliness either so that they may be worshipped or to deceive. Indeed, He requires the former first, saying through Isaiah: *Wash yourselves, be clean; take away the evil of your thoughts.* <note>Isaiah 1:16.</note> He also requires the latter, since in sacred matters He always demands that all things be clean: the vessels, the gifts, the victims, and the sacrifices. <margin>Paul. Deuteronomy. Achinas.</margin>

Often translated as 'soothsayers' or 'observers of times' who practiced divination by clouds or seasons.</note>," which our people call "augurs," but they are "calculators," as Achinas <note>Likely a reference to a Jewish commentator or a specific scholar known to the author's circle.</note> says.

<margin>CHRIST. John.</margin>

He deemed it sufficient to have obtained for them an oracle and a "domestic God" <note>A resident divine presence within the home or soul.</note>, from whom, through due and most sacred worship, they could opportunely draw all things. This was even better perfected by the true discloser of the law, Jesus Christ, teaching how we might draw God into ourselves—not into a tabernacle made by hands, but into ourselves, who are made temples of the living God and palaces of the heavenly kingdom—and how he might lodge in them, saying: "We will come to him and make our dwelling with him." <note>John 14:23.</note> He taught, moreover, and gave the faculty by which we can rouse the God who is within us to favor us; indeed, to change us into Himself, as John says: "He gave them power to become children of God." <note>John 1:12.</note>

This, the Christians of our time neither do nor know, because the evangelical monuments have been so obliterated and cast behind their backs that their tracks and outlines are scarcely seen. Behold, therefore, how you may receive favor from God, from the Angels as His ministers, and from the heavens as His instruments. Now, receive how you may do this by a short and easy journey.

### By what short way we may draw favor from heaven, the Angels, and God. Chapter IX.

<margin>Porphyry. Julius Firmicus. Chaldeans.</margin>
**I**t would indeed be a long, arduous, and overly doubtful journey if we wished to hunt for all the stars, influences, and favorable aspects, and through them to know who or what kind of guardian or **genius** <term>genius</term> <note>A personal tutelary spirit or guiding deity assigned to a person at birth.</note> is ours. For the professors of that doctrine have handed down long, most difficult, doubtful, and sometimes conflicting instructions. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note> seeks the genius from the planet that is the lord of one's birth. Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Latin author of the 'Mathesis,' a major work on astrology.</note> seeks it either from there, or from that planet which has the most dignities in that place, or from the one whose house the Moon is about to enter immediately after the sign which holds the person at birth. The Chaldeans <note>A term often used generally for ancient Babylonian astrologers and magicians.</note> begin the search for the genius rather from the Sun or the Moon. Others teach how to seek it from some cardinal point of the sky. And so through...

The professors of this doctrine wander through many things, either because they do not fully know the secrets and order of the heavens, or because they refuse to disclose and make common those things which ought to be shared only among a few wise men. Since, therefore, that path is long and most hidden, a short journey must be seized by inquiring of ourselves what we cannot do from the heavens. This indeed we shall do if, with impediments removed, we submit ourselves to our spirit as our guide; if we do not resist him, he will show us the way to heaven, to our <term>genius</term> <note>A personal guardian spirit or guiding light believed to be assigned to every person at birth.</note>, and indeed to where the Moderator <note>God, as the governor of the universe.</note> leads us. And this happens if we attend to those things which nature suggests to us from our earliest age, distracted by no contagions; or what we feel, imagine, imitate, and attempt more frequently when the mind is purged of vain care and distorted affection by the dictation of nature itself or the spirit. For nature and our spirit feel the instinct and favor of heaven; they feel the persuasions of one's own <term>genius</term>, which is given to each from the beginning of his birth.

<margin>Platonists. Our Doctors. CHRIST.</margin>
As not only the Platonists assert together with our own doctors <note>Theologians or Church Fathers.</note>, but as Infallible Truth <note>Christ.</note> professes in a fitting discourse when He says: *Their Angels always see the face of the Father.* For these [Angels] favor their little clients, leading them where their star inclines—always indeed toward the good—unless a man turns aside his path, deceived by allurements or the persuasions of an evil demon. For he who walks through devious ways does not truly have a guide for his journey, since the duty of the stars and of our guardians is always to act rightly, and to dispose us toward right and more excellent things. Therefore, by assenting to the persuasions of the heavens and the <term>genius</term>, or one's own Angel (to speak in a Catholic manner), one will act prosperously and live happily. Otherwise, he will feel that heaven and the powers above are his enemies, and find fortune adverse (which is the guidance of the divine) in everything he performs, having become a stranger to his celestial patrons. To this, perhaps, that adage tends: *Do nothing in life against Minerva.* <note>original: "Nihil agas in uita Minerva." A Roman proverb meaning one should not attempt something against one's own natural bent or talent.</note>

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
And if (as Zoroaster teaches) fate is not to be increased, it is even less to be changed. For if, by your own talent, you profess something against your <term>genius</term> and the voice of the celestials continually inviting you, you will labor in vain.

<margin>David.</margin>
As the Prophet says: *Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain. And unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it.* <note>Psalm 127:1-2.</note> For it is vain for us to rise up early, or to act before or against the light that shines from heaven, which leads and conducts a man where he ought to go. Therefore, those seeking a favorable omen for the things they must do must observe with all diligence so that we may hear what God speaks within us, or in His holy scripture and law; what the good guardian persuades, what the spirit suggests, and toward what end the faithful [spirit] gives favor. We must also attend to where they lead you. For "place" confers much, since not without reason did God (or the good guardian in His stead and name) say to Abraham:

<margin>GOD</margin>
*Come into the land that I will show you, and I will make you a great nation, and I will bless you and magnify your name.* <note>Genesis 12:1-2.</note> Here it is clearly perceived how much a place contributes to favor. And a little later it follows: *Abraham went forth, proceeding and progressing toward the south.* There he felt the most ample favor of the super-celestials.

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
Just as did Isaac in the north, of whom it is said: *Isaac came into Gerar, where he sowed and gathered a hundredfold*—or a hundred measures of barley, as the literal truth of the text has it. <note>Genesis 26:12.</note>

# How the Human Being, as a <term>Microcosm</term> <note>literally "Little World"</note>, can receive nourishment from all members of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>the "Greater World" or universe</note> (to which he is most similar). Chapter X.

<margin>Aristotle.
Plato.
David.</margin>
**W**e receive no small favor and protection not only from heaven, the Angels, and the intelligences, but from every member of the worldly body. For the human being is divided by some wise men into five parts: the intellectual, the rational, the irascible <note>The faculty of the soul associated with "spirit," courage, and anger.</note>, the desiring, and the senses, with all their instruments. The Intellect, placed in the highest citadel and alone a member of the household of the Supreme Prince, draws from Him things that neither reason nor sense can grasp. For God Himself and His ministers do not submit to the judgment of our senses, except insofar as they themselves wish to show themselves through sensible images by their own will. Nor does Reason perceive them, except as the movers of the spheres through their motion, as Aristotle and other natural philosophers "hunt" for them. Much less is God perceived by sense or reason, except only that He exists. If, however, we perceive any secrets concerning God and His ministers, we do so through that supreme portion which the Platonists call the Intellect, as distinct from Reason. And this is done by means of a certain divine light with which the intellect itself, or 그 that higher portion, is flooded. Concerning this light, the Prophet says: "In your light, we shall see light" <note>original: "In lumine tuo, uidebimus lumē" — Psalm 36:9.</note>. The Rational faculty, also placed on a higher throne, midway between the intellect and the imagination, receives growth from all things it moves through: from celestial, earthly, and human things. It is especially expanded and sharpened by the presence of other humans, "just as iron is sharpened by iron," as the common proverb says. The Irascible faculty, dwelling in the home of the heart, does not need much external favor, being sufficiently inflamed by the heart and the bile itself, except insofar as it receives an external object at which to be angry. But Desire and appetite are twofold: one is in the heart, supported by reason...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the human being as a "Microcosm" (a little world). The previous page began describing the faculties of the soul; here, the text explains how the higher and lower appetites are fed, and how the five senses act as bridges between the internal mind and the external universe.</meta>

<page-num>IIII</page-num>
<header>### THE THIRD CANTICLE ###</header>

...the **intellect** is carried into all things through which reason wanders, and from these things it receives that by which it may be expanded and increased. But it receives this most powerfully from the supreme object of love, **God**, provided that it leads into Him through the understanding, illuminated by His light. The other <note>The lower appetite or part of the soul</note> is bound to the lower regions, established far from wisdom and reason, so that its troublesome proximity might not disturb reason, which is set above all else. This lower part receives the growth of a true man from material things, to the extent that it obeys the higher faculties and is conquered by them. 

The **means**, however, by which the higher appetite is nourished, are the institutions and teachings contained in upright laws and doctrines, especially in **sacred eloquence** <note>The Scriptures</note>, where all things are contained that pertain to directing and nurturing the soul. There are also sacred rites by which the soul is purified so that it may grow more strongly. 

Finally, the **senses**, acting as the ministers of reason and will, receive from all sensible things that which brings them delight and favors their presiding masters. 

**Hearing**, for instance—a partaker of the air and of the "choir" <note>original: "corę", likely referring to the rhythmic dances or "chorae" of sound and celestial movements</note> which cannot be grasped by other senses—is a most accurate organ and a magnificent minister of higher things. For the sake of acquiring wisdom, it serves above all other senses. For it measures the **rhythms of speech** and of all harmony, as well as the modes of things and of the whole discourse. From this, a man can become a composer and a **Musician**, and even "semi-rational," since hearing alone among the senses can perceive the flow of reason. From complex and man-made instruments, and from the **harmony of the world** <note>The "musica mundana," an ancient belief that the movement of celestial bodies creates a perfect, though inaudible, musical harmony</note> which it perceives through a refined sense of hearing, it receives 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
wonderful delights and instructions. By these, a man may "compose" himself, as the 
<margin>Pyth.</margin>
**Platonists** and **Pythagoreans** assert. 

With the **eyes**, likewise, man measures the heavens, the stars, and the most harmonious circuits of the constellations—their settings and their risings—as well as the beautiful painting of the earth, the fertility of the waters, and the composition of all visible things. From these, he drinks from the most abundant **fountain of philosophy**, through which he arrives at a higher wisdom. From there, no less than from doctrine, is gathered the food for both parts of man <note>The inner spiritual man and the outer physical man</note>. 

Between the eyes and the ears, in the middle region of the face, nature has placed the **nostrils**, through whose harmony scent travels with the breath. Receiving solace from things that are sweet-smelling and well-composed, they provide no small benefit to the human being. 

The **mouth** also, in the center of the face, fortified by teeth, the palate, and the tongue, grants many kinds of gain to man. For it receives all the nourishment of the body to be carried into the belly—as if into a storehouse—and thus to the whole body. But these things are first committed to the judgment of the **palate**, so that it may reject what is harmful and admit what is profitable. And these the teeth chew, so that the food, already ground, may be offered to the **cauldron of the stomach** <note>original: "lebeti stomachi"</note> to be easily digested. 

For the turning of this food, the **tongue** was given, which serves the spirit and the soul no less than the body, bringing forth in speech what the heart and prudence conceive. Thus, it may provide a benefit to one's neighbor and report back advantages from the same—indeed, from the powers above and from God Himself—and through much discussion, it may acquire wisdom. 

What remains, therefore, in the whole **machine of the world** <note>The universe viewed as a complex, divinely-ordered system</note>, from which man does not receive a benefit through his ears, eyes, nostrils, mouth, tongue, or mind? Nothing escapes; everything is subjected to the judgment of one of these. For those things which the touch, sight, smell, and taste reject are at least perceived by the ears and discussed by the tongue; since the latter can speak of all things, and the former can hear of all things, whether they be physical or intellectual.

<page-num>XII</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST TONE</header>

Therefore, hearing is the sense that, above all others, serves the intellect and is its peculiar minister. Following this are three other senses <note>likely sight, smell, and taste</note>, established in the royal hall of the head in the sight of reason: so that every judgment of theirs may be weighed by reason's balance. Touch, indeed, is left to the animal parts <note>the rest of the body</note>: so that while it perceives those things which are more solid and more material, it leaves nothing that might escape human judgment, and from which man himself does not receive nourishment. And if there is anything that the senses do not perceive, the mind at least contemplates it. 
<margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin>
For Hermes proposed these things for the consideration of his son Tat, saying: "Observe this, my son, that each genus of living beings inhabits its own province of the world. Damp things inhabit the water; terrestrial things, the earth; flying things, the air; but man uses all of these—earth, water, air, fire, and whatever is contained within them." Furthermore, he looks up at the heavens and reaches them with his sense; but God himself, he reaches with mind and intellect. And because he holds a proportion and "symbol" <note>a shared essence or link</note> with all things, he therefore understands all things, and draws from all things a symbolic power, by which he may be nourished and grow. He receives growth in two ways: from God the craftsman and progenitor—as if from a father providing all nourishment—and from other things, as if from fodder prepared by the father for his support and nutrition. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
In this, the Leader of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle</note> agrees when he says: "We are, in a way, the end <note>the goal or purpose</note> of all things." 
<margin>Simplicius and Thomas Aquinas</margin>
Nor does the opinion of Simplicius and Thomas please me, which holds that this statement should be understood only regarding artificial things <note>man-made objects</note>, as if he made us the end of artificial things alone and not others. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
For Aristotle explains himself at the beginning of the *Politics*, saying: "It must be considered that plants are for the sake of animals, and animals themselves for the sake of man." For tame animals—that is, gentle animals which the Hebrews call <term>behemoth</term> <note>original: "בהמות behemot", here referring generally to livestock or beasts of burden</note>—are for use and sustenance; while wild beasts, if not all, then many are held for the sake of our sustenance and convenience, and most of these supply other gains. If nature makes nothing either imperfect or in vain, no one is ignorant that these things were made for the sake of man. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
And even if Aristotle himself would not admit that the heavens were made for man—since he prefers the heavens to man in his *Ethics*—nevertheless, as far as we can learn from Sacred Scripture and from those who think rightly, they too were created for the service of man; even if they receive the influence of God more immediately. For they influence lower things so that they may favor man without any other medium; or they influence plants and animals, which it is already granted are ordered for the service of man. Man therefore receives increments of his own perfection from all things, provided he knows how to use all things and to rule over all things, just as it was instilled in him by the Creator, as we shall discuss in its proper place (God himself favoring us).

Whence, the structure of its rational movements being dissolved, it inflicts upon itself punishment and torment. And of these gods...

<margin>Chalcidius</margin>
<margin>Proclus</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory, Seneca, Cicero, Isaiah</margin>
...punishment of disorder <note>original: "deordinationis"; the text begins mid-word from the previous page</note>, all senses and all limbs, which ought to be ruled by the soul, feel themselves destitute or disordered. Therefore, the soul must be cared for through true philosophy and the study of truth—which is indeed hidden from the common crowd—through sacrifices and all fitting expiations: so that, restored to health, strengthened by truth, and protected by such safeguards, it may fear nothing of the "shocks arising from below" (as Chalcidius <note>a 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato's Timaeus</note> discusses at length in his discourse). Instead, being in harmony with itself, it may agree with all other things from that point, and like a friend, take from all things the safeguards for its own growth. For one who is at odds with himself cannot agree with others, nor can he perceive the "harmonic symbol" <note>the underlying musical or mathematical resonance</note> of others. For he who (as Proclus says) fights against himself is also unable to agree with others, nor can he truly take delight in others or receive nourishment from them. Rather, from this discord, he has that which causes him to always pay the penalty for his error, as Augustine says: *You have commanded, O Lord, and so it is: that every disordered mind should be its own punishment.* 
<margin>David</margin>
<margin>The Same</margin>
<margin>Plato</margin>
To this, Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory, Seneca, Cicero, and all who think rightly agree and confirm with various words but the same sentiment. We can also learn this from the sacred utterances. *The wicked* (says Isaiah) *are like the tossing sea, never at rest, but their waves overflow into trampling and mourning: for there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.* And there is a reason: for when uprightness is put to flight, order is disturbed, and true peace—which is the "tranquillity of order" <note>a famous definition by St. Augustine: *tranquillitas ordinis*</note>—is exiled. From this arises distemper, perturbation, restlessness, inconstancy, affliction, and various kinds of torments. Many of these are recounted by David in the thirty-seventh Psalm <note>Psalm 38 in modern Bibles; the author uses the Vulgate numbering</note>, where, beginning from the infirmity of the soul and its discord, he commemorates the many evils that follow from it. *There is no health in my flesh,* he says, *and there is no peace in my bones, in the face of my sin.* For the Prophet does not speak of material bones, but of the virtues and powers of the soul, signified by "bones." He follows with: *For my iniquities have grown heavy over me like a heavy burden.* Afterward, he mentions decay, misery, being bowed down, illusions, and afflictions, even unto the roaring groan of the heart. From this, the Platonists rightly judged that the temperance of the soul is the best harmony of all the virtues, which the others follow and imitate. Therefore, before all things, the soul's consensus with itself must be procured, if anyone desires to be delighted by the harmony of others, to obtain from them the power by which he may be perfected, and to be liberated from all the calamities that proceed from a disturbed soul.

### On Bringing Together the Harmony of the Virtues, so that the Soul may be Healed and Delighted by them. Chapter XII.

**E** AND because the virtues are the soul's delights and medicines, it is necessary that they be harmonious; for both health and delight proceed from things that sound together, and are themselves certain kinds of harmonies. For the health of the body is the temperament (as we have said) of the humors and of those things that pertain to the substance of the body. So too, the health of the soul is the concert of the virtues and their operations. And delight arises from the proportion of the power with its object. And the greater the proportion, the greater the pleasure. And thus the same thing is made both delightful and healing...

...drawing power from Apollo, who is celebrated as the inventor of the lyre <note>original: *cithara*</note> and of medicine—not only for the body, but truly for the soul as well. But much better is this achieved by the truer and supramundane <note>existing beyond the physical world</note> Apollo, resonating with a better harmony—compared to which this artificial or natural harmony is far inferior and even a dim image. For He himself <note>referring to Christ as the divine physician</note> excelled and taught how to give perfect health and temperament to both parts of man [soul and body], through those things which He, as the most experienced and wisest physician, judged to suit our infirmity and to temper all our parts. Indeed, every effort—whether decided or devised by any other doctrine, way, or rule for instructing and perfecting the human race—can be considered vain compared to that most perfect way handed down by Christ. 

But just as in healing bodies, harmony is so beneficial that not only natural <note>biological or elemental</note> but even vocal harmony brings a remedy—as Democritus and Theophrastus seem to affirm, and Pythagoras and Empedocles, along with Asclepiades, demonstrate in words, which David and others proved by deeds.

For he [David] cured Saul, who was raging with an evil spirit, through song and the lyre. Many others also, as recorded by Boethius and others, were healed by perceptible harmony. Rightly, therefore, natural harmony—which is surely stronger and more excellent than artificial [musical] harmony—ought to do the same. 

For that [natural harmony] consists in the proportion and tempering of medicines with one another, and with the qualities of the body to which they are given. Therefore, medicines must be tempered with one another and with the body if they are to bring soothing and the balances of health. 
<margin>Damascene
The Ancients</margin> 
Hence, Damascene <note>referring to either John of Damascus or the medical author Mesue the Elder</note> and other ancients who treat such matters took the most diligent care in proportioning and tempering medicines, assigning just and harmonic weights in their mixing, leaving to the physicians who administer them the care of proportioning them to the bodies they intend to heal. Many ignorant people in this time, despising this, more often introduce dissonance into the intestines: so that they shudder, grieve, and are tortured by the dissonance of the drug <note>original: *pharmaci*</note>, when a consonant temperament should have brought health. 

In the same way, the virtues—which are the medicines of the soul—must be tempered among themselves and with the soul if they are to bring health and delight to the soul itself. Our theologians dispute in long sermons about the connection and joining of the virtues: namely Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, Henry <note>Henry of Ghent</note>, John Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>, and others.

For just as vocal harmony (as Boethius defines it) is a concord of like and unlike voices reduced into one, so the harmony that perfects the soul is a "concert" <note>original: *concentus*</note> of like and unlike virtues reduced into one. For the virtues are "unlike," such as Liberality and Faith, Parsimony <note>frugality</note> and Hope, Contemplation and the busy work of Charity in frequent service, and many of this kind. ...they agree in one accord; otherwise they cannot be considered virtues, but vices. However, that point in which all must meet is charity and the love of God and neighbor. In this—as if in the root, foundation, life, and soul of all virtues—are founded and depend all things contained in the Law and the Prophets, as the Highest Truth <note>referring to Christ</note> teaches. 
<margin>CHRIST. Paul.</margin>Paul also warns of this with a clear voice, saying: "If I speak with the tongues of men and angels; and if I should have faith so as to move mountains, and the gift of prophecy, and piety in distributing my wealth, and all other virtues; but have not charity (in which, clearly, all others ought to meet), I am nothing but a clanging cymbal," <note>original: *cymbalum tinniens*</note> that is, useful only for the benefit and delight of others. Indeed, there is no progress in the virtues unless they are anchored in the root and foundation of charity. Nor is there true delight unless all things agree in one—which Plato in his *Epinomis* calls "piety," <note>an ancient Greek philosophical dialogue attributed to Plato or his circle</note> 
<margin>Plato. Paul.</margin>but our Paul and his teacher Christ call "charity." And should one see that same common point in which all virtues must meet, Plato himself in his *Republic* (whom 
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>Macrobius follows, as do Ambrose and Lactantius) asserts that it is 
<margin>Plato.</margin>justice—or, as others say, temperance—which imposes a limit upon all virtues. 
<margin>Macrobius.</margin>Nevertheless, they do not contradict what has been said concerning 
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>charity. For just as in a musical sound, the harmony is twofold: one is of 
<margin>Lactantius.</margin>the strings, melodies, or pipes individually; the other is with other strings, melodies, or pipes, so that from the whole instrument—and even from many instruments—a single harmony resounds. So too in the concert of virtues, the modulation is twofold: one is of each virtue within itself, and this is justice—which (as Ambrose says) is a "common virtue" by which we measure each individual virtue so that it neither exceeds nor falls short, but is stretched as far as is fitting. This balance others have called temperance. But the second modulation is of all virtues agreeing with one another in that same harmony of charity and the love of God or neighbor (or both together). Thus, the virtues do not merely delight the listeners, but bring benefit to the one playing them. Indeed, by this charity, we temper and moderate all virtues; furthermore, every good work is directed toward God, from whom comes all true symphony. This is taught not only by our fellow Catholics in agreement, but also by many of the wise among the Pagans. 
<margin>Hierocles.</margin>Among them, Hierocles <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says: "The rational race, if it desires to obtain its own splendor, should wish for those same things which the divine law determines. For the mind is not well-disposed in any other way except according to God. And falling away from God, it falls also from the intellect; and from the rule of good things, it is banished into darkness." 
<margin>The same author.</margin>And again, more clearly: "The mind, led by the divine spirit, is joined to God; for it is necessary that like approach its like. Nor can anyone be a good priest of God unless, offering himself as a sacrificial victim, he builds up his own soul like a certain image and constructs his mind and intellect into a temple in which he can receive the divine light." Moreover, this union with God and the arrangement of the temple is achieved through true love, which is the fullness of the law and the progress of the entire mind—provided, however, that the necessary knowledge comes first. ## On the Harmony of Virtues with the Soul. Chapter XIII.

AND because (as we have said) a <term>proportion</term> <note>the balanced relationship between different parts</note> of antidotes is not only sought relative to one another for healing bodies, but also for tempering them in accordance with the body and the qualities of that specific body. For us, beyond the proportion of the virtues to each other, the proportion of the virtues with the soul must also be sought. And although every virtue benefits any soul, yet one virtue benefits one soul better than another, regardless of the category. For singing is so proportioned and proper to one person that (so to speak) he sings without a teacher or error, and penetrates the whole power of music most easily; yet another person, even with the most diligent industry over a long time, cannot arrive at this, and by his own nature is so dissonant that even if he excels in the technical art, he cannot harmonize with his voice. One person, through a brief study of the art but with much natural power, will produce a perfect painting or engraving, which another cannot do despite great diligence. Another, by his <term>genius</term> <note>referring to a person's natural temperament or guiding spirit</note> or innate talent, knows gems most easily; another, however, does not. One person makes progress in the sciences in a short time and with little labor, while another labors in vain with much sweat and study. One is most devoted to contemplation, but very little to physical exercise. Another, however, performs services and ministries with great delight and ease. From these things one easily discerns that there is one God and Spirit, the craftsman, working all things in all people, yet he does not instill all things into one and the same person, but distributes to each according to his will. These various ministries and virtues also follow the stars, and the "geniuses," and God himself the distributor, as we said a little before. Hence, while no virtue is to be despised, yet each person should strive to adopt that one toward which his star, his genius, nature, or rather the Supreme Distributor himself leads him. He it is who enriched Peter with faith, John with charity, James with devotion, Thomas with prudence, Abraham with piety, Moses with meekness, <margin>Phinehas and Elijah.</margin> Phinehas and Elijah with Zeal, and David with religion and strength. See, therefore, in which virtue you may more easily make progress, and occupy yourself in that, and care to climb to its summit, so that you may excel in one, since you cannot excel in all. As for other virtues, however, progress as much...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter XIII, exploring the Neoplatonic classification of virtues as defined by Plotinus and their relationship to musical harmony and spiritual ascent.</meta>

...you may be strong, and not despise them. In these matters, no single rule can be given by which everyone <margin>Plotinus</margin> measures where he might feel the soul’s progress more easily. This progress is reached through that threefold kind of virtues, first described by Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; his works, the *Enneads*, deeply influenced Renaissance thought</note> and celebrated by all wise men, namely: the **Civic**, the **Purifying**, and the **Heroic**. To these is added the **Exemplary**, but this is not properly within us; rather, it is like a rule directing and measuring the virtues that are within us. That threefold kind, therefore, produces in us a most perfect harmony of virtues.

For the **Civic** is like the <term>hypate</term> <note>The lowest-pitched string in the ancient Greek lyre</note> or the <term>proslambanomenos</term> <note>The "added note," the lowest note in the Greek musical system</note> on an instrument, or the deeper and lower voice in a song. The **Heroic** is like the <term>nete hyperboleon</term> <note>The highest string/note of the highest tetrachord</note> or the elevated and highest voice. And the **Purifying** kind is like the <term>mese</term> <note>The "middle" note, serving as the harmonic center</note>—that is, the middle string on an instrument or the middle voices in a song. And (as musicians teach) from the *proslambanomenos* to the *mese* is an <term>octave</term> <note>original: *diapason*</note>, and from there to the *nete hyperboleon* is another octave; and in both, there is perfect harmony. 

Thus, a person climbing from the civic virtues is raised to the purifying ones, as if by the first octave-harmony; but when carried up from the purifying to the heroic virtues, another octave produces a truly most consummate harmony. <margin>The same [Plotinus].</margin> And how virtues make the soul harmonic, Plotinus—rightly the prince of this doctrine among philosophers—explains clearly enough, saying: In man, two motions occur that disturb the soul. One consists of certain unthinking animal impulses, whether they are inciting or terrifying. The other occurs when we follow those motions with deliberate effort and purpose. 

The **Civic** virtues, therefore, temper these second motions with prudence and deliberation, so that one does not admit what reason judges to be evil. By introducing this tempering, they begin to harmonize the soul. The true **Purifying** virtues do not merely restrain those motions but uproot and eradicate them; they suppress the first impulses to such an extent that the mere presence of reason—the mistress of the appetites—is sufficient to suppress them. When these Purifying virtues have thoroughly freed the soul from those disturbances, they render the "instrument" of the soul most temperate, so that nothing remains except to begin the song and the harmonic, distinguished work. When the soul achieves this, leaning into the greatest progress, it emerges as **Heroic**. 

Again, the **Civic** virtues compose our "animal" or outer man. The **Purifying** virtues, as if through the first octave, purge the spirit and render it harmonious, so that a person may be called (and truly be) spiritual. But the **Heroic** virtues elevate the mind to the supreme concord, uniting man with the <term>intelligences</term> <note>Celestial or angelic beings</note>, and indeed with <margin>Aristotle</margin> God himself. Aristotle agrees with this, saying that men become gods through the excellence of virtue. <margin>Plotinus</margin> But our Plotinus continues, saying that the pursuit and <margin>CHRIST</margin> vow of the Hero is not only to be without sin, but to be God, and to return to where he proceeded from—just as He said: "I came forth from the Father, and have come into the world; again, I leave the world, and go to the Father." <note>original: *Exivi a Patre, & veni in mundum: itez relinq̃ mūdum, & vado ad Patrē* — John 16:28</note> And since we are his brothers, having proceeded from the same Father, we must return to the same—though at a lower level. When we return to where we came from, we complete a perfect octave, in which the tone returns to the same point from which it departed, though on a different key, as musicians say. So we also emanated...
