XV

# FIRST TONE #

...from God, as if from a productive beginning: and we return to Him, yet under a different aspect—namely, as our beatifying end <note>The "beatifying end" refers to the ultimate state of happiness found in union with the Divine</note>. Thus, man is (following the thought of Plotinus) a "twin being," both God and spirit <margin>Plotinus</margin> <margin>Plato</margin> <margin>Chrysostom</margin> <note>original: *demon*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to an intermediate spirit or a "guardian" intelligence rather than an evil entity</note>, if he accidentally admits something erroneous by following those first impulses. This is because even spirits—that is, wise intelligences (as the Platonists say)—are touched by certain affections. These are the ones of whom Chrysostom says:

> Even if they are holy, they are only men; and though they cannot be conquered by evil, they can still be struck by it.

If, however, a man feels nothing of these first impulses while in this state, he is God alone. He is "God," I say, from the number of those who follow the First—namely, the sons of God, <margin>John</margin> of whom John said:

> He gave them power to become sons of God.

<margin>Plotinus</margin> But proceeding further, Plotinus carries men up even to the **exemplary virtues**, which he says are of two kinds. <margin>Plotinus</margin> Some are in the **Intellect**, while others are in the **Soul**. Within the Intellect <note>In this context, *Intellect* refers to the Divine Mind, the second "hypostasis" in Neoplatonism, which contains the perfect forms of all things</note>, they are not properly called virtues, but the *models* (exemplars) of virtues. However, in the Soul—which is (as he teaches elsewhere) the proper form of man—they are properly called virtues. Indeed, in the Intellect they are as if in God, and for that reason are called "models." For in God, and in the Intellect (which is a certain divine thing infused within us), there are the actions of that which Truly Is. But in the soul, they are the virtues that bring perfection.

There [in the Intellect], justice, temperance, and the like are not properly virtues, but directing rules; whereas while they are in the soul, they are properly virtues. For there, **Justice** is the turning of the one toward himself—namely, a conversion—and nothing is different from that in which it exists. But in the soul, it is that which directs the soul toward God. **Temperance** is also there the Intellect's inward turning toward itself, as far as is fitting; but in the soul, it is the tempering of its passions. **Fortitude** is there established entirely outside of passion, prevailing over all things; but in the soul, it is a participant in passion, fashioned after the likeness of that from which it was received. **Prudence** is there a full intuition, moderating all things; but here [in the soul], it is a habit acquired from many experiences.

There too is **Charity**—to treat also of our theological virtues—a delight and love embracing all things and pouring out all things through their fitting degrees; but in the soul, it is a gift distributed part by part. And the **Faith** which in the soul is instructive—a knowledge of certain things granted by divine light, from which a solid argument is made for the "truth of things not seen"—is, in the Intellect, the most certain knowledge of divine and all other things. <margin>Plotinus</margin> And those things which the soul holds through **Hope**, the Intellect possesses through firm apprehension. The soul also strives toward that which the Intellect reaches through "touch." For the Intellect (as Plotinus himself says) possesses through a certain touch that which the soul desires and hopes for.

<margin>John</margin> Lest Plotinus seem to have dreamed this up, let us hear what our John testifies, who had climbed to that level:

<margin>Plotinus</margin> 
> That which we have heard, and seen, and touched with our hands concerning the Word of Life, this we announce to you.

Now, one "touches" divine things who confirms them by a certain experience, or who adheres to God through that higher portion (which Plotinus calls the *Intellect*), resting upon Him and united by a certain contact. <margin>Proclus</margin> Proclus says:

> We touch the divine essence, and leaning toward it, we rest upon it with the supreme "head" of the soul.

<margin>Paul</margin> And Paul says: 

> He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him.

This unity of spirit follows the union of the Intellect itself.

-> SECOND TONE <-
XVI

# WHAT THE SOUL IS. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
After we have investigated the soul's harmony with the body—of which it is the form—and with the virtues—in which it is the subject—it remains for us to see what agreement it has with all the things that it understands. For this purpose, I judge it appropriate to see what the soul is, which holds such a proportion with so many things that it is able to understand them all. And setting aside the many opinions we brought forward in the first volume, we shall see what it is specifically regarding this capacity for understanding. Here, I am by no means satisfied by that very famous definition given by Aristotle, stating that the soul is "the actuality <note>original: *actus*; here referring to the Aristotelian 'entelechy' or the realization of a potentiality</note> of a physical, organic body having life in potentiality." This only explains that the soul is the mover of the body itself; it does not explain how it is able to understand all things. Nor is the other definition he handed down sufficient, saying: "The soul is the principle of sensing, understanding, and moving according to place." From this we only gather that it *is* the principle of understanding, but not *how* it understands all things. Nor is it surprising if he fell short, since the knowledge of the soul—

<margin>The same. Plato.</margin>
(by his own testimony) is profoundly difficult. We have no doubt that this was drawn from Plato, who says in the tenth book of the *Laws*: "Almost everyone seems to have been ignorant of what kind the soul is and what power it has." Nonetheless, he handed down a doctrine of the soul from which we can more easily investigate its symbol and proportion with all things. But because he himself did not wish to speak of the soul’s business in plain speech—considering it a most difficult matter and hidden from almost everyone—his disciples defined it in various

<margin>Proclus</margin>
ways, as we cited in that same place. And though Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who provided massive commentaries on Plato.</note> rejects many who tried to explain Plato's mind regarding the soul, even he did not wish to fully reveal what Plato felt.

<margin>Theologians. Plato.</margin>
But (unless I am mistaken) he left it to readers to gather from many signs, just as the more "secret theologians" <note>This likely refers to Hermetic or mystical traditions that influenced Renaissance thought.</note> are accustomed to doing in any arduous matters; there is no doubt that Plato followed their footsteps and doctrine. We can therefore hunt for this definition of the soul from him: that it is a certain divine substance, emanating from divine springs, bringing with it a number—not indeed that divine number by which the Creator <note>original: *opifex*; literally 'the craftsman' or 'maker'</note> disposed all things, but a **rational number**. By having a proportion with all things through this number, the soul is able to understand all things. Nor should anyone be disturbed because we said the soul is something divine and emanates from divine springs:

<margin>Pythagoras. Paul.</margin>
since even Pythagoras, the father of philosophers, asserts this, saying in the *Golden Verses*: "Consider that a divine race is in men." And what is more, Paul in the *Acts of the Apostles* cites and approves the opinion of Aratus <note>A Greek poet; Paul quotes him in Acts 17:28.</note>, saying: "For we are also His offspring." Therefore, since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think the Divine is like gold, silver, or stone—the product of human art and industry. See how clearly he concedes that the human race is divine. And this is on account of that

<margin>Aristotle. Xenocrates.</margin>
higher portion which the Platonists always venerate as divine. Furthermore, Aristoxenus and Xenocrates <note>Xenocrates was a student of Plato; Aristoxenus was a student of Aristotle who famously argued the soul was a 'harmony' of the body.</note> said that the number which is the soul is "self-moving."

<summary>This page critiques Aristotle's definitions of the soul as being too focused on physical motion, proposing instead a Platonic view of the soul as a 'divine substance.' The author argues the soul contains a 'rational number' that allows it to resonate with and understand the entire created universe.</summary>

<header>OF THE THIRD SONG.</header>

## OF THE THIRD SONG.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
And this is because the soul itself is the principle of movement for the body (as Aristotle proves) and also of itself; although here he might seem to oppose this opinion, as well as all those who say the soul is a number. And I believe Aristotle did this rather to provide material for debate than to destroy the truth. This is especially true since they <note>The Platonists and Pythagoreans</note> speak of a rational and formal number, while he speaks here of material number and the vocal counting used by merchants. And they speak of the motion that belongs to the soul, whereas he speaks here of the motion of the body, which gains its position through the succession of one part after another. Hence, Aristotle's entire argument in both cases is based on an equivocation <note>original: *aequivoco*; a logical fallacy where the same term is used with different meanings in different contexts</note>.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
For according to the doctrine of Augustine, which all theologians venerate, the soul—that is, free will or the will, which is a power of the soul itself—moves itself toward whatever it chooses. 
<margin>Theology.</margin>
"Nothing," he says, "is so much in the power of the will as the will itself." <note>original: *Nihil est... tam in potestate uoluntatis, quam ipsa uoluntas*; a famous quote from Augustine's *On Free Choice of the Will*</note> Which also, according to the common opinion of these men, can command the intellect to understand, and itself to will or not to will, carrying itself toward anything. Even though this motion is not according to a divisible partition <note>meaning it cannot be broken down into physical stages</note> (as Aristotle presupposes), it is nevertheless a true change and motion, which those who say the soul moves itself are speaking of.

<margin>Job.</margin>
And this motion also belongs to the Angels and Intelligences <note>spiritual beings that move the celestial spheres</note>, of whom Job says: "Behold, those who serve him are not stable (or are not faithful), and in his Angels he placed change" <note>original: *Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles... et in Angelis suis posuit mutationem*; a variation of Job 4:18</note>, as the literal truth of the text holds, in place of which we erroneously have "he found wickedness." This change, though it does not occur through the succession of one part after another, is nonetheless a certain kind of motion. The soul also moves while it moves the body; if it did not do so, Aristotle, as a natural philosopher <note>term: *physicus*; one who studies the physical world (physics)</note>, would not be able to treat it according to what he presupposes in the *Physics*, saying: 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
"Whatever things are moved while they move fall under physical consideration; but those things that are not moved while they move do not pertain to physical speculation." 
Since he himself treats the soul moving the body as a natural philosopher, it follows from his doctrine that the soul is moved while moving. And though this motion is said to be "by accident" <note>term: *per accidens*; secondary or incidental rather than essential to its nature</note>, it is nevertheless true motion, since it has the principle of movement within itself and is not moved by another. Nor do the arguments by which he strives to prove that the soul is neither a number nor a harmony carry weight; for they are undoubtedly founded on material and sensible numbers, whereas the soul consists of formal numbers and harmony, drawn away from the senses—which Aristotle, being unwilling to learn from them, does not wish to admit into his sensible doctrine. "There is not," he says, "in the soul a harmonic proportion of things composed with one another, because the soul itself has no parts from which it might be composed."

<margin>The same.</margin>
We grant this: but we say that there is a higher and rational harmony, having within itself the "species" <note>term: *species*; the mental forms or essential images of things</note> of things by which it understands them, and the numbers of things by which it counts them. These numbers and species are not merely adventitious <note>external or arriving from outside</note> and newly acquired, but are innate to the soul itself, existing in it with a better quality than they do in the things themselves; just as all agree concerning the "exemplars" or "Ideas"—that they have a more perfect existence in God, who produces and understands them, than they do in their own kind. As John says: "What was made was life in Him." <note>original: *Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat*; John 1:3-4</note> Life indeed, created— 
<margin>John.</margin>

<summary>This page argues that the soul is a self-moving principle, reconciling Aristotle's physical observations with Augustinian theology. It posits that the soul contains innate "rational numbers" and "higher harmony," allowing it to understand the world through divine exemplars.</summary>
<keywords>self-motion, free will, Augustine, Aristotle, numerus rationalis, formal harmony, celestial intelligences, innate ideas</keywords>

<header>SECOND TONE XVII</header>

[...] creatress, and divine: because nothing can be in God unless it is divine. 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
And Augustine judges the same regarding the models of artificial things existing in the mind of the craftsman, which evidently have a more perfect existence there than do the forms of manufactured objects: because here those forms are accidents and a certain craft, but there they live, and participate in the nature of the intelligent soul. 
<margin>Theology</margin>
Because the object, as it is known (as some theologians say), has that being which the cognition itself has. It also has that being which the cognitive virtue or power itself has: if the <term>species</term> <note>original: *speties*; in this context, the mental forms or images that allow the mind to recognize objects</note> are produced together with it, 
<margin>Academics</margin>
as the Academics assert: because they do not see how the soul could measure those things which it understands unless it has within itself the measures by which it may measure them. Nor do I see how the intellect could perceive that it understands the truth unless it has something within itself to which what it understands conforms. Nor is that intellectual power sufficient on its own: but something particular is sought out, to which that which it perceives may be equaled. 
<margin>Plato</margin>
These, however, are the species existing there in act, but hindered, 
<margin>The Ancients</margin>
as was pleasing to Plato and the ancients. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
To which Aristotle also consents when he says: "The soul is, in a certain way, all things." <note>original: *Anima est quodammodo omnia*; a foundational concept in Aristotelian psychology meaning the mind can take on the form of any object it contemplates</note> 
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
And I do not understand this otherwise, except that it contains all things in the mode of understanding, or has a proportion with all things: 
<margin>Plato</margin>
and that is the **rational harmony** about which we speak, along with the Pythagoreans and Platonists. Nevertheless, the soul falls far short of the first and supreme intellect <note>meaning God</note>, because that intellect understands all things at once. 
<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
For this soul—although it contains the forms and likenesses of all things to be understood, and to be made by it through art, whether equally by some power or in act or in potentiality (as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> say)—yet it does not understand all things at once in act and by a single act of understanding, like the first intellect; 
<margin>The Same</margin>
but by many and successive acts. The soul is, therefore, something intellectual, containing all things in a certain harmony, so that it can understand all things that are to be understood by it.

## Whether the Creator created all souls equal. Chapter II.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**T**he Peripatetics said that all souls were produced in equal degrees, and continue to be so produced: led by the opinion of their teacher, who says in his "higher philosophy" <note>likely referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>: "Species are like numbers, in which the species is changed by the variation of a single unit." For if one is added to three, it becomes four, and so with the others. 
<margin>Theology</margin>
Yet the more recent Parisian theologians, in their articles, have decreed that souls differ, not only by accidents <note>external circumstances or traits</note>, but by certain intrinsic degrees rooted in their essence: by which each thing is *this* specific thing, differing from another by that which is proper to itself. They decreed this, stating that whoever says the soul of Peter is not more perfect in its own intrinsic degree than the soul of Judas, is in error. 
<margin>John Scotus</margin>
Which they pluck, not without wit, from their own John Duns Scotus <note>a major medieval Franciscan theologian</note>. Who, in the second volume of his theological questions, says that everything is distinguished first by its own nature—which is *this*—before it is distinguished by a principle of operation, or by work, or by some arriving accident. 
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
To which that saying from the Book of Wisdom strongly agrees: "I was a clever child, and I received a good soul," <note>Wisdom 8:19</note> better, evidently, than many others. So great is...

<summary>This page discusses the soul as a "rational harmony" that contains the forms of all things, contrasting human discursive thought with God's simultaneous understanding. It also introduces a debate on whether souls are created essentially equal or if some (like St. Peter's) are inherently more "perfect" than others (like Judas').</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s exploration into the nature of the soul. <page-num>XVII</page-num>
<header>OF THE THIRD SONG</header>

Indeed, the distance of one soul from another—in wisdom, goodness, strength, power, and disposition toward different things—is such that I do not see how they could possibly be of equal rank. Nor should some say that they differ only in the gifts they receive, for the Supreme Truth <note>The "Supreme Truth" refers to Christ speaking in the Gospels.</note> stands in opposition, saying: *To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own virtue.* <note>original: "Uni dedit qnq; talenta, alii duo, alii uero unū, unicu iq; secundū propriā uirtutē." A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25:15.</note>
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Since, therefore, these talents are gifts received by each person according to their "own virtue," what (I ask) is that "proper virtue" belonging to each individual? It is certainly not a freely given gift <note>The author distinguishes between *gratuitous grace* (the talents) and *natural capacity* (the virtue).</note> itself, because that gift is distributed *according* to the virtue. This virtue, then, is a certain natural power, determined at a specific level, according to which a soul is capable of its duty and receives it. 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Nor should anyone object by saying that, according to the Apostle's <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> sentiment, God distributes gifts to individuals just as he wills. Is it not true (I ask) that justice is preserved in the distribution of gifts, so that the gifts correspond to the virtue of each person? Otherwise, neither order, nor beauty, nor fitness would be maintained by Him who is supreme justice, beauty itself, and the very harmony of all things. Observe, I pray, the Apostle's
<margin>The same [Paul]</margin>
words. *He gave,* Paul says, *some to be Apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.* <note>Ephesians 4:11-12.</note> For if He gave some to be Apostles, does He not distinguish the gift of the Apostolate from the intrinsic disposition by which He allowed them to be fittingly chosen for that role? If He had not given that disposition, they would have been less suitably chosen for that rank. 
<margin>Gregory</margin>
Gregory speaks most excellently on this matter: *Angels,* he says, *and likewise men, meet in their duties just as they do in the gifts or ranks assigned to them by nature.* <note>Referring to Pope Gregory the Great.</note>
<margin>Origen</margin>
Origen agrees, saying: *There are certain invisible powers to whom the management of things on earth has been entrusted; among them, we must believe there is no small difference, just as is found among men.* And just as the members of the human body differ by a great distance—though they all live by one single life—not otherwise do the members of the mystical body differ, just as the eye, the shin, or the knee differ in the human body. Nor does the fundamental principle and the comparison with numbers stand in the way, since the infallible Gospel and infallible Truth do not lie. 

But lest we seem to despise so great a force, we shall say that even in musical or formal unity there are certain hidden degrees, such that it can be divided into unequal parts. Let us provide an example in musical unity, as it is more manifest. A whole tone consists of a "sesquioctave" proportion <note>original: "pportione sexquioctaua"; the 9:8 ratio used in Pythagorean music theory to define a whole tone.</note>, such as 9 to 8, where 9 exceeds 8 by a single unit, which creates that tone. However, the tone is divided into semitones, <term>lemmas</term> <note>original: "lemata"; the "leimma" or "leftover" interval in Greek music theory, often used for a semitone.</note>, and <term>dieses</term> <note>original: "dieses"; plural of "diesis," the smallest interval in ancient music, often a quarter-tone.</note>—that is, into a half-tone, a quarter-part, and into more if need be. For this division, it is necessary that the unit be divided—not, of course, a material unit, but a musical one. For example, let 18 be put in the place of nine, and 16 in the place of eight; between 18 and 16 there is the same sesquioctave proportion. In this, there are now two numbers and two distances making two semitones: for there is a distance from 18 to 17, and from there to 16. And again, the semitone is divided into four parts of a tone, which are called *dieses*; and this is done by taking larger numbers, namely 36 in place of...

nine-fold, and 32 in place of eight-fold: And from 32 to 36 there are four numbers making four <term>dieses</term> <note>A *diesis* is a very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone, used in ancient Greek music theory.</note>. And thus by multiplying the numbers, that musical unit can be divided until it is no longer divisible. The same reasoning applies to natural number—which is the natural proportion of things—where the unit can be divided in that same order. Therefore, let the unit be the specific ratio of the tone, and let the ratio and individual degree of the semitone, the <term>lemma</term> <note>A *lemma* (or limma) is the "remainder" interval, often the ancient Greek version of a minor semitone.</note>, or the <term>diesis</term> be the individual degree. These ratios agree in their species, just as those parts of the tone agree in the unit.
<margin>Jerome</margin>
Jerome calls these individual degrees "powers," saying in his commentary on the five talents given to each according to their own virtue: "He did not bestow more to one and less to another out of generosity or stinginess, but according to the powers of those receiving them." <note>original: "Non pro largitate, & parcitate alteri plus, & alteri minus tribuit: sed pro accipientium uiribus." Jerome was a 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note>

***

->### Why the most just Judge used this inequality in the primordial distribution. Chapter III.<-

And because (as I know) there is no shortage of followers of Marcion, Valentinus, and Basilides <note>These were early Christian Gnostics who often argued that the material world was flawed or that the God of the Old Testament was unjust.</note> and their like, who might ask why souls were distributed with such great inequality that one reaches the highest peak of wisdom while another is barely removed from the beasts; one is full of virtues, while another has either none or very little; one is taken into a kingdom and empire and so much is handed to him that he is intoxicated and overflowing, while from another even the little he has is taken away and given to the one who has much. One is led to the Apostolate and the highest peak, and another, having become half-beast, feeds the beasts. Who could consider these things without wonder? Who would not desire to understand this distribution of God, and by what scale it is balanced?

Truly, to ask this is nothing other than to ask why the Creator himself did not make all animals Angels; or all planets the Sun; or all limbs eyes. For if all limbs were eyes, where would be the hands, the feet, the mouth, the stomach, and the other members necessary for the body? And if all planets were the Sun, where would be the Moon, looking up at the starry birth to bring forth offspring for us? Where would be Mars who strengthens, Jupiter who balances, Mercury who sharpens the mind, Saturn who firms, and Venus who connects through love? And if all animals were Angels, where would be man, the particular image of God? Where would be the horses to carry him? Where the oxen, the servants of human sustenance? Where the other animals which were produced for the adornment of the world and the service of man?

For just as there is no consonance if every string of the instrument were a <term>nete</term> <note>The highest-pitched string in the ancient Greek lyre.</note>, or a <term>paranete</term> <note>The string next to the highest note.</note>, or a <term>mese</term> <note>The central or middle string of the scale.</note>, or any such uniform thing—since consonance is generated from equal and unequal chords or voices (for the harmony and beauty of the universe shines forth from things of equal and unequal degrees)—so the beauty of the entire human race consists in the variety of individuals. These most diverse things the Supreme Moderator (as <margin>Origen</margin> Origen <note>A 3rd-century theologian who theorized about the pre-existence of souls and the cosmic order.</note> says) has drawn into the consonance of one mystical body under the head of Christ. This consonance, of both the world and this mystical body, although known to very few, is nevertheless conducted with such great elegance and sweetness that no...
<meta>catchword: nulla (no)</meta>

<sig>c ii</sig>

<summary>The author explains that human inequality is a divine necessity for cosmic harmony, comparing the variety of human souls to the different strings of a lyre or the different roles of the planets and bodily organs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from Chapter III, moving from the specific musical intervals discussed on the previous page to a broader defense of cosmic and social inequality as a form of "harmonic" justice. <header>OF THE THIRD SONG</header>

...could be found more perfect. From this, the opinion of Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BC) was a leading Stoic philosopher who argued that the universe is a rational and providential system.</note> is fitting:
<margin>Chrysippus</margin>
Let someone teach that things could have been done better; certainly no one will. And if anyone wished to correct something, they would either make it worse, or desire that which could not be done, or which is not fitting. Therefore, all parts of the world are so established that they could not have been made better for use, nor more beautiful for appearance. So also individuals are distributed within the breadth of their species by a certain unequal equality and consonant variety, especially human beings: any one of whom, and all together, bear the image of the mundane body <note>The "mundane body" refers to the physical universe viewed as a single, organized structure.</note>. To these things, differing by nature, various gifts are assigned, to each according to their own virtue and disposition. To these also rewards are rendered according to their works, yet by <term>geometric proportion</term> <note>In this context, geometric proportion refers to "distributive justice," where rewards are proportional to merit rather than everyone receiving the exact same amount.</note>, which is not based on number, but on the proportion of proportions: so that whatever the proportion of gifts to gifts, and of merits to merits, the same is the proportion of rewards to rewards. And by this proportion not only does God render rewards to all, but the civil Commonwealth is also governed, as Plato,
<margin>Plato, Iamblichus, Proculus</margin>
Iamblichus, and Proculus <note>These are influential Greek philosophers; Iamblichus and Proclus were Neoplatonists who saw mathematical laws as the foundation of reality.</note> write. They add, however, for the good governing of the Commonwealth, the necessary <term>arithmetic proportion</term> as well: by which, as if by a certain justice in moderate things, peace may be preserved. Nor is Musical proportion lacking, which is justice granting a greater ratio to the greater, and a lesser to the lesser, as Proculus says.
<margin>The same [Proculus]</margin>
And this is founded upon both, taking from arithmetic that which follows number to number, and from geometry that which compares proportion to proportion. From all these proportions (as we said in the first volume) this harmonic machine of the world is composed. Therefore it is ruled and arranged by these same, not only by those who hold the image of the highest Prince, but by the supreme Governor himself: who fashioned the human race with these same proportions, which holds the likeness both of God himself and of this great machine. Just as, therefore, in all this massive workmanship there are unequal and equal degrees of things from which all those proportions result, so in the human Commonwealth there are equal and unequal degrees and ratios of individuals, from which—and equally from their duties and operations—all those proportions result: so that each commonwealth, the mundane and the human, is harmonic and conforming.

<margin>Peter</margin>

# THE SECOND TONE

<margin>
Peter.
Acts.
Theology.
</margin>
...of them <note>The text likely continues from a word like "Apostolorum" (of the Apostles) on the previous page.</note> in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter gives thanks to God when he most certainly proved that there is no partiality of persons <note>original: "acceptationem personarum." This is a traditional biblical phrase meaning "favouritism" or "respect of persons," where a judge is swayed by status rather than facts.</note> with Him. For a "respecter of persons" (as our theologians teach) is one who, for some reason, owes something to others, and yet when their merits and crimes are equal, does not render equal rewards or equal punishments. For a judge appointed to administer justice, finding two people equal in the crime of homicide, is rightly called a "respecter of persons" if he orders one to pay the penalty for his guilt but absolves the other either entirely or partially from the deserved punishment. It is no different if he has two people who have served the Republic equally well, and he gives rewards to one according to his works, but to the other, not at all. If, however, someone by his own liberality gives to one what he does not wish to give to another, he is not a "respecter of persons" for that, because he is a debtor to no one. Hence, in the original distribution—where no merit was foreseen and no obligation intervened, whether natural or by law or by contract—if God grants to one that he should become an Apostle, to another that he should be a teacher or a prophet, and to others that they should be peasants or butchers, who shall accuse Him of injustice or of partiality?

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Does the thing formed (says the Apostle) <note>Referring to St. Paul in Romans 9:20-21.</note> say to him who formed it, "Why have you made me like this?" Or does the potter not have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? Can an ant or a flea say to its maker, "Why did you not fashion me as a horse or an elephant?" Indeed, the Supreme Governor <note>original: "Moderator." A term for God as the one who regulates or "tunes" the universe.</note> willed that in His worldly house there should be sheep, oxen, donkeys, goats, camels, and many such kinds of animals—not only terrestrial ones, but also those in the water or the air—to be most diverse species. So also in the human Republic, which bears the image of the heavenly court, He willed there to be Kings and the counselors who assist them; and then soldiers, craftsmen, officers, peasants, and such like who serve. He also commanded that in spiritual matters there be Popes, various Prelates, preachers, and teachers to be the leaders of others. To these He subjected those who were to be ruled and those who would hear the words of the preachers. For there are (says the Apostle) in the great house of God vessels of gold, silver, wood, and clay, as the order and beauty of the universe requires. Therefore, the Supreme Governor willed that there be various kinds of men and granted diverse gifts, intending to render diverse rewards for the "many mansions" that are in His house. And sometimes (as the Rewarder Himself says) He will render a reward beyond all correspondence to the work, yet with no violation of justice.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
For He says in the Gospel titled "According to Matthew," that the Father of the Family <note>original: "Paterfamilias." Referring to the master of the house in the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20).</note> rewarded with a daily denarius <note>A silver coin representing a standard day's wage.</note> both the one who had entered the vineyard at evening and those who had borne the burden and heat of the whole day. And when these men complained about the pay—that an equal portion was not distributed compared to the one who had come last—the Just Rewarder replied: "Did you not agree with me for a daily denarius?"

# THE THIRD SONG

"Take what is yours, and go. I wish to give to this last person just as I give to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish, since I am a free employer? Or is your eye evil because I am good?" <note>A quotation from the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20), where laborers who worked only one hour received the same pay as those who worked all day.</note> These things were spoken either concerning the Jewish people and the Gentiles—of whom the former came in the early morning to the Lord's vineyard, but the latter in the evening—whence arose an argument between them, just as Paul <margin>Paul, Jerome.</margin> runs through this theme throughout the entire Epistle to the Romans (as Jerome testifies in his preface). Or, if this is understood regarding individual men, we have this one fact: that the promised reward is at the pleasure of the one promising, without any injustice, since no prior obligation exists.

Where, however, some reason or agreement <term>pactum: a formal covenant or contract</term> intervenes, God always deals with us in equal measure. For there is in Him a certain obligation, either of a dictating nature—as in having care for all His children, providing salvation and a kingdom for them, in whom He also sees His own image and loves them greatly as His own work, making it rain upon both the good and the bad, and making His sun rise—or it is an obligation <margin>The same (Jerome).</margin> freely undertaken from a covenant entered into regarding the granting of life and the eternal kingdom to those keeping His commandments. He enjoined these commandments so that He might have (according to Jerome's opinion) a reason for rewarding us; or so that He might purify and perfect man through those very commands and sacrifices.

Therefore, not content even with these, so that He might perfect His children even more, He gave "counsels of perfection" <note>In Catholic theology, these are the evangelical counsels—poverty, chastity, and obedience—which go beyond the basic requirements of the commandments.</note> with an express agreement of reward, saying: <margin>CHRIST.</margin> "Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life." And because He is the Father of all, He calls all as children to His kingdom. Hence, when Peter <margin>Peter</margin> saw that God had care for the salvation of Cornelius the Gentile just as He did for the Jews, he said: "Now I know that there is no partiality of persons with God." <note>Acts 10:34. This was a pivotal moment in early Christianity when the mission expanded beyond the Jewish community to include everyone.</note> 

But once an agreement has been made to reward each person according to their works: if He failed in anything, He could be accused of partiality. However, if He grants something out of His own generosity beyond what was promised, He incurs no mark of partiality.

### Solution of some difficulties. Chapter V.

<margin>Malachi.</margin>

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Now indeed, before we proceed, we must explain to the best of our ability some things which seem to trouble us exceedingly. These are the primary issues: Why, concerning two brothers born of the same parents, when they had done nothing good or evil, was it said through Malachi: "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated"? No less does it trouble us what the scripture says regarding Pharaoh: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." Recalling these things, Paul adds: "Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens." This is indeed a hard saying, and one that seems greatly at odds with the character that God has previously put forth. <note>The author is identifying the central tension in Christian theology between God's universal love as a "Father" and the biblical passages that suggest predestination or the "hardening" of certain individuals.</note>

For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.”* <note>Romans 5:18–19</note> He repeats this often to make us attentive that the justifying and cleansing power of Christ is no less than the polluting sin of Adam. For in Christ, and through Christ, who is the true washing water (of which this elementary water is the sign), we are reborn and purified. And although the sign is never without the thing signified (provided the recipient does not present an obstacle), the reality of the sacrament which is signified can well exist without the sign. There is (say the <term>Theologians</term> <note>Scholars who study the nature of God and religious belief.</note>) a threefold <term>baptism</term>: of the river, of the spirit, and of blood. <note>original: "fluminis, flaminis, & sanguinis." This refers to the traditional Catholic doctrine of the three ways to receive the grace of baptism: by water (river), by deep desire or the Holy Spirit (flaminis), or by martyrdom (blood).</note> And it is sufficient (as they say) to have the baptism of the spirit without the baptism of the river, but not the latter without the former. For God is able to raise up children of
<margin>Paul</margin> Abraham from these stones—namely, those who seemed to be rejected. And God is able (says Paul) to graft in those who were cut off because of unbelief, unless they remain in that same unbelief. And through grafting, both the wild olive shoot and the fruitful branch of the good olive tree may bear fruit. For each is grafted here to be 
<margin>James</margin> fruitful. The divine word is also grafted in us (as James says); and we are grafted into him when we cling to him through faith: and in him we lay the foundation of our works: and then the vessels which were formed for dishonor are made into vessels of honor, and worthy of the royal table. Nor were only some vessels for 
<margin>Paul</margin> dishonor (as the Apostle touches upon elsewhere), but all, as he himself says in another place. We are all born children of wrath, subject namely to sin, and vessels of dishonor: though some may be ordained for honor. And who? Let Paul himself say, discussing this with Timothy: *“If anyone,”* he says, *“shall cleanse himself, from a vessel of dishonor he shall become a vessel of honor.”* <note>2 Timothy 2:21</note>

<summary>The author argues that God's grace is more powerful than original sin and can save those outside the visible Church. He explains that "baptism of the spirit" allows for salvation even without the physical ritual of water baptism.</summary>

### Chapter VI: How the soul is naked in the beginning, or how it appears so.

<margin>GOD</margin>
<margin>The Wise Man</margin>
**A**lthough souls are distinguished into various degrees by the Maker, there is nevertheless one common origin for them all, and the same beginning. "All souls," says the heavenly Father and giver of all forms, "are mine," <note>Ezekiel 18:4</note> and were clearly begotten by me and diffused into bodies. Furthermore, as for my birth, I am indeed (says the wise man) a mortal man, like all others, conceived from the seed of man and the pleasure of the flesh coming together. And when I was born, I took in the common air, and fell upon the earth made like it, and like everyone else, my first sound was a cry of weeping. Nor did any king have any other beginning of birth. Therefore, there is one entrance into life for all, and a similar exit—namely, without knowledge or any power. <note>Referencing the Book of Wisdom 7:1–6, traditionally attributed to Solomon.</note>

<margin>The Peripatetics</margin>
Hence comes that now trivial opinion among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for his empirical approach to knowledge.</note>, <term>that the soul from the beginning is like a blank slate</term> <note>original: "tabula rasa"</note>, on which nothing is yet depicted. This seems to be supported by what that wise man, whoever he was, adds: "Because of this (namely, that I came out of my mother's womb naked and ignorant) I prayed, and understanding was given to me; I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came into me." <note>Wisdom 7:7</note>

<margin>Plato</margin>
But Plato, whom many from his Academy follow, when he saw many people learning without difficulty—or rather, often knowing things they had not been taught—opined that the species and forms of things, and consequently doctrines, are created together with the soul, but are hindered by the senses and bodily bonds, so that through study, time, and exercise, the species that were within are shaken loose. 

<margin>The Ancients</margin>
Hence some of the ancients said that the soul, entering the body, drinks from the whirlpool called Lethe <gloss>from the Greek word "lethe," meaning "forgetfulness"</gloss>. Although others say this is a river of the underworld, to which those descending drink from it so that they forget all the pleasures with which they were delighted in the world. 

<margin>Seneca</margin>
Whence Seneca says: *Within an immense fold, the quiet Lethe glides with a peaceful stream; it takes away cares, so that the ability to return no longer lies open. It winds its heavy river with many bends.* <note>Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher; this quote is from his play Hercules Furens.</note> And truly, the soul suffers a great lethargy in both cases: both when it is immersed and bound in the body, and when, deprived of divine light, it is delivered to the murky shadows of the pit. 

<margin>Plato and ancient theologians</margin>
Nor was this opinion first published by Plato, but was accepted from the ancient theologians, who believe that all souls were produced by their Progenitor, perfected in all their forms, just as the soul of the first-formed man <note>original: "protoplastis", referring to Adam.</note> had been produced. Which he, through transgression...

## To what degree of understanding the soul can reach.
## Chapter VII.

<margin>Adam. Abraham. Moses. Solomon.</margin>
**T**HERE are very many things to be understood, all of which the divine intellect alone perceives; others, however, perceive only as much as is granted to them. Nor is it fitting that all should be equal to the First [God], because there would be no distance between God and the creature if the thought of others could attain everything that God knows. There are likewise many things that the Angels (especially the higher ones) understand—for which reason they are called <term>Intelligences</term><note>In medieval philosophy, "Intelligences" were celestial beings or angels who governed the movements of the heavens and possessed direct, non-sensory knowledge.</note> or understanding beings—which we are unable to understand, being hindered by our corporeal bonds. Among men also, distinct levels of cognition are most clearly discerned. For Adam, Abraham, Moses, Solomon, and the other prophets knew many things which the common people, and even many who claim the name of teacher and wise man for themselves, do not know at all. I found in that most celebrated <term>Ancient Theology</term><note>This likely refers to the *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Formation), a foundational text of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) which describes the creation of the world through 32 paths of wisdom.</note> ascribed to the patriarch Abraham, that there are thirty-two paths of wisdom, or thirty-two degrees of understanding, corresponding to the thirty-two numbers contained in the Hebrew word for "heart," which is written thus: **לב**. These letters are **ל** <note>Lamed</note>, which gives 30, and **ב** <note>Beth</note>, which gives 2; joined together, they return the number 32, which is indeed the number of justice, because it is always divisible into equal parts all the way down to unity. This number is gathered, not without a great <term>sacrament</term><note>In this context, "sacrament" means a sacred mystery or hidden symbolic meaning.</note>, from the 22 letters of the alphabet and the 10 divine enumerations or measures by which God measures all things. From these are constituted those thirty-two degrees of understanding which a well-disposed and pure heart is granted to ascend, according to what is said in the Davidic song: <margin>David.</margin> *He has set ascensions in his heart* <note>original: "Ascensiones in corde suo disposuit." Referring to Psalm 84:5.</note>. *They shall go from virtue to virtue* <note>original: "Ibunt de uurtute in uirtuté." From Psalm 84:7, often translated as "from strength to strength."</note>, or from fortitude to fortitude, or from degree to degree, and the God of Gods shall be seen in Sion. This vision is given through the disposition and purity of the heart, according to that saying of the <margin>CHRIST.</margin> Supreme Truth: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God* <note>original: "Beati mundo corde, quoniā ipsi Deū uidebunt." Matthew 5:8.</note>.

Now, the first of these degrees is: The **Ancient Intellect**, without beginning, and the first glory of all intelligences, whose being no creature can reach. 

The second is the **Illuminating Intellect**, the glory of created things and a unique splendor, placed at the head and existing as the light of all things, illuminating all. 

The third is the **Holy Intellect**, existing as the foundation of ancient wisdom, called the true and faithful teacher; its root is faithful, suggesting all truth to us. 

The fourth is the **Deep Intellect**, so called because from it go forth all virtues or spiritual powers, which they produce by the power of ancient production. 

The fifth is the **Rooted Intellect**, equating and uniting in the property of intelligence, produced or separated from the hedge or boundary of ancient wisdom. 

The sixth is called the **Magnified Influence**, or the amplified influence: because in it the produced influence is increased: and it is itself flowing into and over all blessings or uniting pools.

<summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of divine knowledge, explaining that while God's intellect is infinite, humans can ascend through thirty-two "degrees of understanding." These degrees are linked to the Hebrew word for "heart" (Lev) and represent a mystical path toward perceiving the divine.</summary>

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>

And the remaining levels that follow: whose depth allows for no explanation. For these are the levels of most secret wisdom, which are only hinted at among the perfected, without being fully explained. Since there are so many levels, there is no doubt that a lower intellect cannot reach those things which are open to higher ones; rather, every intellect is ordered according to its capacity to the level appropriate to it. Truly,

<margin>The Peripatetics, Aristotle</margin>
the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle used to walk about while teaching.</note> will object, along with their Aristotle, saying: The <term>possible intellect</term> is that which is able to become all things, and the <term>agent intellect</term> is that which is able to make all things—that is, it is powerful in every intelligible matter. To them we shall say that Aristotle speaks of the agent and possible intellect in a general sense—which some of them thought was a single entity shared by all people—but not of this or that particular intellect, which some of them denied. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
Averroes especially held this, judging it sufficient for the constitution of a human being to have that universal intellect joined with this or that particular animal. 

<margin>The Ancients</margin>
In this, he corrupted the opinion of the ancients, who spoke of that single and universal intellect. And that error was fixed—and remains fixed—which subverts the true and ancient natural philosophy: it destroys moral philosophy and theology; it takes away justice and every virtue; and it is so distant from all reason that it is worthy of neither calculation nor memory, but should be carried away into eternal silence by total oblivion. We could also say that even if the intellect 

<margin>Theologians</margin>
apprehends all things, it does not however comprehend them (as some <term>theologians</term> say), or at least does not apprehend them fully. For regarding God, everyone perceives *that* He is; but *what* He is, no one knows. Even the most simple confess the Father, but who He is, no one knows except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him. Many also speak much concerning the Son, yet no one knows Him. Concerning these matters, therefore—both the secrets and the mysteries which surround the 

<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin>
most holy Trinity and God Himself—we can say that word of <term>Ecclesiasticus</term><note>Also known as the Book of Sirach. This quote is from Ecclesiasticus 43:30-32.</note>: "Glorify Him as much as you can, for He will still exceed it; and His magnificence is wonderful. Exalt Him as much as you can, for He is greater than all praise. When you exalt Him, be filled with strength; do not grow weary, for you will never fully comprehend. For there are many hidden things greater than these, and we see but a few of His many works."

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle also agrees when he says: "Our speech concerning the divine substance 

<margin>Simonides</margin>
is very meager and weak." And he praises that sentiment of <term>Simonides</term><note>A Greek lyric poet. Aristotle cites him in the *Metaphysics* to discuss whether the "highest science" belongs only to God.</note> that God alone possesses this honor: to be a <term>metaphysician</term><note>In this context, someone who possesses direct, perfect knowledge of the ultimate reality and the divine nature.</note>, namely, understanding Himself, all divine things, the separate substances, the essences, the properties, the numbers, the proportions, and the universal proportion of all things. Behold, therefore, how many things there are which 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
our intellect cannot reach. Even when released from the body, it will not perfectly understand all things which that divine and infinite intellect comprehends. Nor is it a contradiction that the Supreme Truth spoke regarding the Spirit which the believers were to receive: "He will suggest all things to you, and will teach you all things." For this is understood 

<margin>The same John</margin>
not as "all things" in an absolute sense, but concerning those things which they were meant to understand, and especially those things which He desired to manifest to the disciples while He lived, saying: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." Thus also is that saying of John understood: "You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things"—namely, all things that are meant to be understood by you.

### Whether the Intellect Always Attains That Which It Is Able to Attain. Chapter VIII.

[N]<note>The original text begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'E', though contextually it forms the word 'Nec' (No/Nor).</note>o small difficulty arises here: whether the intellect always reaches every intelligible thing to which it could ascend by its own nature. Here we say briefly that (unless I am mistaken) understanding and living run at the same pace. For there is a fixed limit of life for each person, which they cannot pass, yet to which few arrive, since death prevents it for many reasons. 

<margin>Wisdom.</margin>
Sometimes, it is because violence is inflicted, or because through bad management, infirmity and death itself are hastened. Or (to speak with the Wise Man) because being "perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long years" <note>original: "consumatus in brevi explevit tempora multa" from Wisdom 4:13.</note>: For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore, He hurried to lead him out from the midst of iniquity. It happens no differently for one destined for some degree of learning and some grace. For to proceed there, he sometimes—and even often—neglects, either entangled in other cares, or fearing the labor, or clouded by his own malice. Whence **Wisdom** and the knowledge of divine and human things disdain to enter into that malevolent and sluggish soul: just as she is disdained by it, as is said in the prophet Hosea: 

<margin>Hosea.</margin>
<margin>David.</margin>
"But you have rejected knowledge" <note>Hosea 4:6.</note>. And in the Davidic hymn: "He would not understand, so that he might act well" <note>Psalm 36:3.</note>. And many times a person falls short of the degree of cognition prepared for them, because they despise the fountain of all science and light: 

<margin>Jeremiah.</margin>
<margin>David.</margin>
as Jeremiah says: "They did not seek the Lord, therefore they did not understand" <note>Jeremiah 10:21.</note>. Because just as the sun is not seen except in the light of the sun, so God is not seen except in that light of which the Psalmist says: "In your light we shall see light." Light, I say, not only of divine things, but also of natural ones.

<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
Those wise men illustrated by this light perceived the natures and properties of things much more clearly than those who relied only on natural light. Hence Eusebius of Caesarea <note>An early Christian historian and bishop.</note> offers an excellent judgment concerning both lights, saying: "When I compare the philosophers among themselves or with others, I would not easily deny that they were illustrious men. But when I compare them to the Hebrew theologians and philosophers, and compare their teaching to the teaching of the former, all things which the philosophers devised seem to me fleeting and frivolous. Nor is it a wonder: those [Hebrew] things were published divinely, these [pagan] things humanly. 

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Those things, I say, were seen (to speak with Plato) by solar light, while these were seen by lunar light." For Plato calls that "solar light" which is poured out from God; and "lunar light" that which is gained by the powers of nature. 

But let us pursue the business. In the Gospel, many are said to be invited to the wedding, but because they despised coming, others were substituted in their place. 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Many were called to the heavenly kingdom, to whom it was also said: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing fruit." Twelve were chosen as **Apostles**, to whom the most hidden secrets of God were entrusted; yet one of them became a devil and a horrific cavern of darkness. Many others again were called to the discipleship of Christ, to whom He was going to give grace, the kingdom, and the true doctrine of things, if they had stood fast. For to the disciples who followed Him, He daily suggested many things by His light; but some, obscured and enveloped in the darkness of their own obstinacy or evil works, being unable to bear that light, "went back" (as John says) and departed day by day. Taking pity on them, the most merciful Father and Teacher says: "Hold fast to what you have, so that no one else may take your crown" <note>Revelation 3:11.</note>.

<summary>This page argues that while the human intellect has the potential to reach high levels of understanding, it is often limited by moral failings, lack of effort, or the absence of divine light. It distinguishes between the "lunar light" of natural philosophy and the "solar light" of divine revelation.</summary>

## By what means we may be able to reach the degree of knowledge prepared for us. Chapter IX.

LEST anyone should labor in vain regarding many things in order to arrive at that very level of knowledge which he is able to reach according to his own disposition, we shall approach the highest master of all wisdom and learning, **Jesus Christ**, and we shall see from whence he drew his own teaching. "My doctrine," he says, "is not mine, but His who sent me, the Father's" <note>original: "Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius qui misit me Patris"; John 7:16.</note>. And making his disciples sharers in this instruction, he said: "All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you" <note>original: "Omnia quæcumq; audiui a Patre meo, nota feci uobis"; John 15:15</note>—namely, according to your capacity. For he reserved many things which, although they had been baptized and washed with the water of saving wisdom, they were nevertheless neither able to grasp nor to carry at that time; because, being not yet well-cleansed and strengthened, they were struck by the superior light. Therefore he says: "But when that Spirit of truth comes, whom the Father will send in my name, he—being, as it were, more familiar <note>The author uses "domesticus" to suggest the Holy Spirit dwells within the believer.</note> to you—will stir up and sharpen your minds by his fiery power. And dwelling with you, and poured out within you, he will suggest all things to you, and he will teach you all things, whatsoever I have said to you." 

Nor should this be said only of the twelve Apostles. For that Spirit was poured out upon all who were together in the same place; the total of whom <margin>Luke.</margin> (as **Luke** had said shortly before) was nearly one hundred and twenty people. This Spirit had also poured into many others, as **Luke** follows up regarding the Samaritans. When the Apostles who were in Jerusalem heard (he says) that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. And then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. This was given through the laying on of hands <margin>The same.</margin> <note>Referring to Luke, the author of the Acts of the Apostles.</note> by the Apostles, and sometimes through their speeches, as is said below. While **Peter** was speaking with the Centurion, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who had heard the word of God. Whence many were amazed that the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out even upon the Gentiles. And when **Paul** had baptized certain Ephesians and had laid hands upon them, <margin>Paul</margin> the Holy Spirit came into them. 

And what this Spirit worked is immediately declared when it is said: "And they spoke in tongues and prophesied." For they immediately attained from that sacred <term>chrism</term> <note>Chrism (unctio) usually refers to anointing oil, but here the author uses it to describe the internal "anointing" or empowering of the soul by the Holy Spirit.</note> the gift of knowledge and different kinds of languages, so that they might be able to express to everyone the things they knew. And this is the true chrism with which those of old were anointed who immediately turned out to be prophets; and the first evangelical fathers were anointed so that they might know all things and speak in tongues. Of which chrism (alas, unhappy times!) we now have only the outward sign or the name, so that we are called "Christians" and "anointed ones." For these (says <margin>CHRIST</margin> the Supreme Truth) shall be the signs of those who believe in me and who have been anointed, namely, with my chrism: "In my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak in new tongues," and the rest that follows. 

Forgetting the power of this name and the gift of the Holy Spirit, those who are called "wise men" in this time of ours labor to learn from the **perfidious Arab** <note>A reference to Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and other Islamic philosophers whose commentaries on Aristotle dominated medieval universities.</note> or from a **Greek demon** <note>A polemical reference to Aristotle or pagan Greek philosophy.</note> those things which come from heaven and from the Holy Spirit.

<margin>Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure often associated with the Egyptian god Thoth, seen here as a pagan prophet of Christian truths.</note></margin>
And the Mind must be sought, which having attained (says Trismegistus), men are held to be immortal instead of mortal, having embraced in their understanding all things that are on the earth, in the sea, and whatever else exists above the heavens. And they raise themselves up so far that they even behold the Good itself. When they clearly perceive this, they consider this air which we breathe here <note>The atmosphere of the material world.</note> to be a kind of misery; and holding all bodies in neglect, they are carried toward the One alone. For this is the knowledge of the Mind: namely, the contemplation of divine things and the understanding of God, there being a divine mixing bowl <term>crater: a vessel used in the ancient world for mixing wine and water, here used as a metaphor for the container of divine intellect</term>—that is, the intellect—and that divine part communicated to us. 

When wisdom had filled this vessel, it sent a herald—surely good conscience <term>synderesis: the innate spark of moral consciousness that directs us toward the good</term>, or a "good guardian spirit" <note>original: "bonum genium"</note>—commanding such things to be announced to the souls of men: "Let whoever can, immerse himself in this bowl!" Believing that the soul will return to the God who sent down the mixing bowl, and knowing the purpose for which it was born. Therefore, whoever hears the herald and immerses themselves in the Mind, they become partakers of knowledge and, looking up toward the Mind, they emerge as perfected human beings. 

And to a son asking in what way he might be washed in the liquid of this bowl, he said: "Unless, O son, you hate your body, you will not be able to love yourself. As soon as you love not yourself, but God, you will immediately attain the Mind." Having finally obtained this, you will obtain knowledge in its footsteps. Do not believe you can attend to both at once—to mortal and to divine things. For we have two: the corruptible and the incorruptible; by the choice of one, we lose the other. 

<margin>The same <note>Referring again to Hermes Trismegistus.</note></margin>
And whenever care for the one is relaxed, it is intensified for the other. And so that Mercury himself might apply his soul to wisdom, having let go of all care for lower things, he labored (as we have learned from a good author) for twenty-six years before he attained the Mind, in order to achieve it. 

This [Mind] the true disciples of Christ attained immediately, although each source handed down similar precepts for attaining it. Did not Christ also teach us to hate the body and this soul—namely, the lower and animal soul? Did he not declare with a full voice <note>original: "ore rotundo," a Latin idiom meaning eloquently or clearly</note> that we can by no means serve two masters: God and **Mammon** <note>Wealth or earthly greed</note>; the spirit and the flesh; divine things and earthly things—all of which run along the same path. Did he not teach us to first seek the kingdom of God, which once obtained, all other things follow? 

But you will say, "I am not able either to acquire this Mind, nor to be filled with the light of Christ or the Holy Spirit, since now in this unhappy season of ours, the divine powers no longer seem to dwell with us, perhaps (though I hope I am wrong) driven away by our shameful acts." They must, therefore, be called back with all our strength. But if that cannot be done, hear what Jerome says against Rufinus <note>A reference to the famous theological dispute between Saint Jerome and Rufinus of Aquileia in the late 4th century.</note>: "What the Holy Spirit suggested to the Apostles, I must acquire through the study of letters." Specifically, letters which set down those things which flow from divine oracles...

<margin>Lactantius. Socrates. Anaxagoras. Democritus. Empedocles. Arcesilaus. Carneades. Origen. Paul.</margin>
...things were received, not those devised by human wits: for these do not illuminate, but rather cause the intellect to grow dark. For whom do they teach and instruct (says Firmianus <note>Lactantius, a 4th-century advisor to Constantine, known as the "Christian Cicero" for his elegant Latin defense of the faith.</note>) who have not yet instructed themselves? Whom can the sick heal, or the blind lead? Let us all, therefore, who have a care for life, gather here. Shall we wait until Socrates knows something? <note>A reference to Socrates' famous claim: "I only know that I know nothing."</note> Or until Anaxagoras sees light in the darkness? Or until Democritus pulls virtue out of a well? <note>Democritus famously remarked that "truth lies at the bottom of a well."</note> Or until Empedocles widens the path of his own soul? Or until Arcesilaus and Carneades <note>Leaders of the Academic Skeptics who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> see, feel, and perceive? Behold, a voice teaching from heaven, and showing us a light clearer than the sun: why are we unfair to ourselves, and why do we hesitate to receive the wisdom which learned men, having worn out their lives in searching, could never find? Therefore, whoever wishes to be wise and blessed, let him hear the voice of God, who speaks in all the Holy Scriptures that truth which He alone has known, offering the path which He alone has taught: showing the light, upon which the sharpest edge of the human mind cannot be fixed, unless it be cleansed and awakened by Him who pours out the light. For all the secrets of nature and of God are handed down in the sacred words: yet by this law, that only the truly wise and enlightened may perceive them; others, however, are fed in the vestibule <note>The entrance or porch of a temple.</note> with parables and enigmas. For this was the custom (as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar who pioneered the allegorical interpretation of the Bible.</note> says) not only of Christian and prophetic teaching, but also of those studying philosophy: that some things were put forth openly, while others, less common, were suppressed in silence. For there were those who heard Pythagoras teaching publicly: and those who were instructed privately in those things which (as he was as accustomed to say) were in no way worthy to reach profane and not yet purified ears. The Apostle Paul also had "perfect" <term>perfecti: fully initiated or spiritually mature</term> disciples, among whom he spoke wisdom: and there were the common ones, not yet initiated, to whom he set forth public sermons and letters. There were, moreover, friends more secret to Christ, to whom he handed over the sacred things and most precious pearls: and there was the crowd of disciples, to whom he spoke in parables. Therefore, let him who desires to learn the secrets of nature and of God remove the veil from his eyes and enter into the inner shrines of Scripture: and let him arrive at 그at limit of perfection to which he was destined by his own nature or by divine gift.

### Whether one must proceed through the external senses so that we may arrive at that very goal. Chapter X.

**A**ND because many are addicted to the bodily senses, the secrets of nature and the sacraments of God were given to them under veils and sensible signs. ## SECOND VOLUME.
XXVI

<margin>Origen.</margin>
...they changed into a better state: namely, by using the internal senses, as Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian theologian who defended Christianity against the pagan philosopher Celsus.</note> excellently discusses in his work *Against Celsus*. But this would seem too harsh and foreign to the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, so named because they often taught while walking about in the Lyceum.</note>, who have this principle repeated in many places by their master Aristotle:

<margin>Peripatetics. Aristotle.</margin>
> **Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.** <note>original: "Nihil est in intellectu: quin prius fuerit in sensu." This is the foundational maxim of Aristotelian empiricism, suggesting all knowledge begins with physical perception.</note>

We grant this to those who have only tasted knowledge derived from the senses and are content with their triple method of knowing: through definition, division, and composition. But it is clear to us that there are two other modes of understanding, untouched by the teacher of sensible doctrine <note>Aristotle.</note>. One of these is vision—a clear contemplation, or rather an intuition and a direct contact with divine and natural things. The other is the harmonizing of the truth itself, as explained by others, with our own intellect.

<margin>Moses</margin>
Moses had attained the first of these regarding natural things, according to what the Lord had promised him, saying: "You shall see my back" <note>Exodus 33:23.</note>—namely, the creatures, which

<margin>Peripatetics.</margin>
in respect to the Craftsman <note>God as the creator of the universe.</note>, are the "back" or the "posterior" parts and His effects. From this comes the usual way of speaking among the Peripatetics: <term>those who argue from the effect are said to argue "a posteriori."</term> <note>Literally "from what comes after." Reasoning from a visible result back to its invisible cause.</note> According to this way of knowing the Craftsman of all things,

<margin>Wisdom. Moses</margin>
we are taught to proceed in the Book of Wisdom, where it is said: "From the greatness of the beauty and the creature, the Creator of these can be known" <note>Wisdom of Solomon 13:5.</note>. And if Moses had not known the nature and harmony of things, he would not have skillfully ordered the Ark and the Tabernacle of the Lord, in which a perfect image of the triple world <note>The "triple world" in Renaissance thought usually refers to the three nested realms of the universe: the elemental world (Earth), the celestial world (stars and planets), and the super-celestial world (the realm of angels and God).</note> was contained. Nor would he have rightly applied the sacrifices which are required to appease God and the heavenly powers, and to purify man, who himself bears the image of God and the world.

<margin>Rabbi Simeon</margin>
Regarding the sacred mysteries of these sacrifices, Rabbi Simeon Ben Jochai <note>A 2nd-century sage traditionally credited with the authorship of the *Zohar*, the foundational work of Jewish mysticism or Kabbalah.</note> published a most famous and extensive volume on Leviticus. In it, he discusses the natures of almost all things. That same God who said, "I will show you all good," also revealed divine matters to Moses himself.

<margin>GOD</margin>
Nor is "all good" anything other than that from which all good things come. And although He once denied His face, and further protested <term>that no one shall see His face and live</term>, nevertheless, a little earlier it is said: "The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend." This speaking face to face seems to presuppose a vision of that very face. And (as the Hebrews say)

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
the Angel who spoke with him was named <term>Metatron</term>, the Prince of Faces, because his office is to introduce others to the face of the Prince <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition who serves as a celestial mediator and scribe.</note>.

<margin>Jacob. David</margin>
Jacob also testifies that he saw this face when he says: "I have seen the Lord face to face." Nor was the divine Harper <note>King David, who was believed to have composed the Psalms while playing the harp.</note>, full of the Holy Spirit, ignorant of whether this face of God could be seen, for he repeats so often in his hymns the desire for it to be shown: "Show your face," he says, "and we shall be saved." And again: "Seek His face always." And once more: "Illuminate"—that is, make your face shine—"upon your servants."

<margin>Isaiah.</margin>

<margin>CHRIST</margin> Truth <note>original: "Veritas." But if it dies and yields to the spiritual and interior person, it brings forth much fruit by working, seeing, and tasting divine things.
<margin>Paul</margin>

<margin>Paul</margin>

For then there occurs a separation of the soul from the body, but not of the body from the soul; because the body is vivified by the soul itself, which neither works in the body nor lives in it, except insofar as it gives it life. To this mode of knowing the Apostles had also arrived, as had all those who were filled with that divine light and the Spirit that suggests all things, and they too departed by this precious death. The sign of this was that they feared neither death, nor suffering, nor the insults inflicted upon the body and the animal part that was already dead. Truly, those mysteries were shown to some less and to others more, according to their capacity, even though they were seized by the same death.

The second mode of knowing is through truth being equalized with our intellect, just as a key is fitted to its lock. And even if we do not perceive with full light those things which those who witnessed the mysteries themselves set down, the gate is nevertheless opened to us. By the conformity of the perceived truth and the light that illuminates us from those opened sanctuaries, we are made more certain than by the "apparent" demonstrations of the philosophers. I call them "apparent" because they have made either no, or very few, true demonstrations in natural matters; rather, they are deduced from things previously accepted from Aristotle, or whoever it might be who spoke them before.
<margin>Philosophers</margin>
Therefore, I judge this mode of understanding assigned by the philosophers to be the lowest of all and the least certain.

The highest mode is that which is held in that clear contemplation. The middle mode, however, is when it is given to us not only to read and understand with external ears, but to perceive with better senses those things which are hidden within what those who saw them with true intuition handed down under veils. For there are many of whom the supreme Truth says that hearing they do not hear, and understanding they do not understand.
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
For to us it is sometimes given that we may clearly perceive the truth emanating from the marrow <note>meaning the core or essential depth</note> of sacred letters, and that, with the veil removed...

SECOND TONE. XXVII

...[illu]mine <note>This is the conclusion of a word from the previous page, likely "illumine."</note>, and with revealed face we may inspect those things which are hidden from the common folk and the wise of the world: and with such certainty, that all perplexity is removed, since we perceive them with better senses than the exterior ones.
