## That there are true and necessary internal senses, by which more and more certain things can be perceived than through the exterior ones. Chapter XI.

<margin>Peripatetics</margin>
**C**oncerning these interior senses, then, as being superior, we must discourse. This is especially necessary since the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who emphasized knowledge gained through the physical senses</term>, who are the most prominent school in this time, have written most fully and minutely about the exterior senses, but of the interior senses they have written nothing, except that there is a certain "common sense" and "phantasy"—or imagination—which they located in the front cavity of the brain. They held that it receives the sensed forms <note>original: "species"</note>, judges between them, and, having stripped them of their material conditions, represents them as purified images to the intellect. And (as Algazel <note>Algazel: the Latinized name for Al-Ghazali, a famous Persian philosopher and theologian</note> says) <margin>Algazel</margin> all senses are joined in this "common sense," and they emanate from it and depend upon it just as parts depend on their whole. Or (as others say) this sense results from the parts, as a kind of integral whole. Or it is (as held by others) a virtue or power more spiritual than the particular senses. They proceeded no further regarding these internal senses. 

But Plato, agreeing with Mercury <note>Mercurius Termaximus, or Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure representing ancient esoteric wisdom</note> and Moses, <margin>Plato, Mercury, Moses</margin> asserts in the *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio," referring to Plato's dialogue on love and the soul</note> that man is twofold, and each version of man has his own senses. Thus, a man has four eyes: two belonging to the exterior man, and the others to the interior man; and as many ears, nostrils, hands, and feet. Likewise, he has two mouths and a double taste, and finally all things are doubled. These concepts are both presupposed and discussed in the first Homily on the Song of Songs by Jerome, or by Origen, <margin>Jerome, Origen</margin> or by whoever published it (for its author is uncertain). In that work, we are reminded through many passages of Holy Scripture that man is double. For thus Moses wrote in the beginning of Genesis: <margin>Moses</margin>

> male and female he created them. <note>Genesis 1:27</note>

Yet the woman was not actually produced at that time, but only later, after many other things had been produced in that interval. Therefore, that writing concerns the twofold man, of whom the exterior and animal man is called "feminine" and inferior; but the interior and better man is named "masculine." Concerning these, Paul <margin>Paul</margin> often repeats and teaches much about the interior man, separating him from the exterior man which is corrupted. Of that interior man also is the entire singing of the divine wedding song <term>epithalamium: a song or poem in honor of a bride and groom, here referring to the biblical "Song of Songs"</term>. For it is not sung concerning the eyes, nostrils, mouth, teeth, breasts, chest, belly, legs, and other members of the animal man, but of the better and archetypal <note>The "archetypal man" refers to the spiritual blueprint or perfect form of humanity</note> man, as we have discussed more diffusely elsewhere. 

Proceeding with the senses, we say that the worldly wise do not know these interior senses, <margin>The same</margin> nor can they perceive any better things through them, except for those who have their senses (as the Apostle says) "exercised for the discernment of good and evil" <note>Hebrews 5:14</note>. This discernment is by no means accomplished through the exterior senses. For the boundaries of the sense of touch are hot and cold, hard and soft...

<page-num>XVII</page-num>
->### OF THE THIRD CANTICLE.<-
<sig>iii b</sig>

...rough and smooth. Sight, indeed, extends as far as color, light, and darkness. Smell distinguishes between scents and stenches. Taste [distinguishes] between sweet and bitter, sharp and fatty, salty and pungent, harsh and pleasant, tart and acidic; but hearing only perceives sound. 

None of these, therefore, makes a distinction between good and evil; rather, it is the better senses—through which we can perceive not only moral matters but God Himself—that do so, according to <margin>David</margin> that verse of the Davidic song: *Taste and see that the Lord is sweet* <note>original: "suavis," often translated in English Bibles as "good," but "sweet" or "pleasant" captures the sensory metaphor used here</note>. And again: *I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me*. The interior man, also perceiving His fragrance, cries out in the <margin>Canticles</margin> Canticles: *We run in the fragrance of your perfumes* <note>Song of Solomon 1:3</note>. 

<margin>Peripatetics</margin> Perhaps the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, known for their focus on the physical world and empirical observation</term> will hiss at this and say: "With all zeal and diligence we have investigated the lot of human nature, yet we have not perceived whether these interior senses exist; indeed, we have not even heard of them." 

I am not at all surprised, since divine and spiritual things are of such a nature that they mock the proud and those who presume upon themselves, and are hidden entirely from them. Regarding which <margin>Plato</margin> Plato [says] in his letter to Dionysius: "Whoever hears these things rejects them at first sight; but after they have been well-discussed and tested, they find those who agree with us." For there is nothing that seems more ridiculous to the common people and those devoted solely to the exterior senses, nor anything more to be looked up to and divine among the noble and well-practiced. For there have been very many people, indeed of brilliant wit and endowed with the best judgment, who at first glance would judge these things to be utter nonsense <note>original: "nenias," meaning trifles or children's songs</note>; but later they not only agreed, but longed for these things in a wonderful way, so that what then seemed entirely improbable now seemed the opposite to them. 

Chief among these [errors] is the idea that the principle of all truth arises through the exterior senses. Rather, all those [sensory principles] are to be scorned when we have arrived (as Origen teaches against Celsus) at the exercise of the interior senses which we use when we deal with God, who escapes all grasp of the exterior senses. 

For I do not believe it suffices for complete <margin>Aristotle</margin> happiness <term>beatitudo: the ultimate state of blessedness or fulfillment found in the vision of God</term> that the soul merely understands and loves God, although intellect and reason are called "the whole man" according to Aristotle. For the complete man results as a certain whole from the soul and the body, having all the operations of both senses even while existing in the body. But the operation of the exterior senses is in the body and through the body, which is subject to corruption; while the operation of the interior senses is in the better body into which this natural body will be changed, as the <margin>Paul</margin> Apostle says: *What is sown as a natural body rises as a spiritual body; it is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power* <note>1 Corinthians 15:42-44</note>. 

But you will say: "Since we are in this valley of misery, clothed in this corruptible body, we cannot use the interior senses." I pray you, hear what <margin>The same</margin> Paul adds: "If there is," he says, "a natural body, there is also a spiritual body; just as it is written: The first man, Adam, was made into a living soul..."

...the last, or the later Adam became a life-giving spirit. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. You will say he speaks of Christ. <margin>Paul</margin> Listen to what follows: *As was the man of dust, so are those who are of the dust; and as is the man of heaven, so are those who are of heaven*. Therefore, if we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly. Both, therefore, according to Paul's opinion, seem to be within us—something I would hardly dare to say unless taught by the Apostle. <margin>The same</margin> You will say: "We have only one body, which is now corruptible, and it will become incorruptible through the resurrection," according to that word of the Apostle himself: *We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humble state, conformed to the body of His glory* <note>original: "claritatis," often translated as "glory" or "brightness" in a divine context</note>. For is not the grain eventually to become a plant, unless it contains the living body of the plant at least in potential—as all the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, who emphasize physical observation and the "potential" within matter</term> agree? <margin>The same</margin> For this rises from the deadened <note>original: "mortificato," referring to the process of a seed "dying" in the earth to grow</note> grain, and our spiritual body, in which we bear the image of the heavenly, rises from the natural <note>original: "animali," literally "animal-like" or "souled," referring to the physical life-force shared with animals</note> and corruptible body being deadened. This happens either by that common death which everyone undergoes and accepts, or by that death of which the same Apostle speaks: <margin>The same</margin> <margin>Psalm</margin> *Mortify your members* <note>original: "Mortificate membra uestra," meaning to put to death earthly desires or physical impulses</note>. <margin>Paul</margin> And again: *It is written, For your sake we are being put to death all day long*. And as he says more clearly to the Corinthians: *Always carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death for the sake of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh*, concerning which we have discussed at length just a little while ago. <margin>The same</margin> Paul is not raving here, although these things seem like delusions to those who have neither accepted Christ, nor a better life, nor a spiritual body. Look how clearly he speaks, saying *that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal body*. <margin>The same</margin> And lest they quibble that this manifestation will only happen after the resurrection, listen to what he says when debating with the Romans: *We were buried with Christ through baptism into death. And if we have been planted together in the likeness of His death, we shall be also in the likeness of His resurrection: knowing this, that our old man was crucified with Him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and we should no longer serve sin*. Look how the Apostle asserts both men: the "old man" who must be crucified, and the "new man" who must live with Christ. <margin>The same</margin> For he asserts a body of sin and death, and immediately adds a mention of a body of life and grace. *Let not sin reign*, he says, *in your mortal body, so that you obey its lusts. Neither yield your members as instruments of iniquity to sin, but yield yourselves to God as those who are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of justice to God*. This cannot happen unless the carnal members themselves, having been deadened, give way to the members of the better man. <margin>The same</margin> To which state our Paul, living in this life and a pilgrim in this body, had come when he said: *But now we are released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter*. He called the written law the "law of death," which purified the natural man, and...

# WHAT SYMBOL AND WHAT CORRESPONDENCE MAN HAS WITH THE ANGELS. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Paul</margin>
**H**aving arranged and tempered man, and having assigned the manner of his progress and the reason for it—at least regarding the steps and gifts distributed to him—we must now traverse the correspondence he has with created beings: and especially with the Angels, from whom, as if from individual companions of his whole journey, he may receive increases in his progress. First, therefore, they agree in their natural disposition, since both are partakers of reason, capable of intelligence, and tend toward the same end, being immediate servants of the same Lord. Likewise, both are incorruptible and perpetual; however, the Angels exist in an equal and continuous succession, while man, according to his better part <note>The soul.</note>, exists in the same way; yet according to his other part <note>The body.</note>, he exists through a certain transformation, of which it is said: *This corruptible must put on incorruption.* <note>original: "Corruptibile hoc induet incorruptionem." A quote from 1 Corinthians 15:53.</note> Both also drink from the same Fountain and Rock, of which it is again said: *For they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ:* <note>original: "Bibebant autem de spirituali consequenti eos Petra, Petra autem erat Christus." A quote from 1 Corinthians 10:4.</note> for them, indeed, He was foreseen, but for us He is sculpted, upright, and filled with immense water, so that from His fullness we may all fully receive. For not only men, but even Angels draw from Him, as Augustine says: *The Angels themselves consult Him as the fountain of life.* <note>original: "Ipsum consulunt Angeli tanq̃ vitæ fontem."</note>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Peter</margin>
Into Him also (as Peter says) the Angels desire to look: <note>A reference to 1 Peter 1:12.</note> namely, that they might always draw for themselves and for us, over whom they have care, so long as we are thrust down in this corporeal prison. <note>A common philosophical metaphor for the physical body.</note> And although they are said to differ in species from men, they nevertheless correspond to them no less than men do to the horses they sit upon, whom they lead at their pleasure with a small bit, and urge on with a slight touch of the spurs or a gesture of the body; they instruct them, instilling a certain prudence for making the journey. Nor do they have less correspondence with men than men have with birds, which they instruct either for hunting, or for song, and for imitating human speech. Thus they, presiding over us, rule, impel, and instruct us, so that we may capture the prey of heavenly things, and that we may bring back divine eloquence, more or less according to our capacity and the diligence we show in listening to them and making them our familiars. Hence the ancient fathers studied with all diligence to adhere to them and to have a domestic fellowship with them.

## Whether man is higher than the Angels, or the reverse. Chapter II.

<margin>David</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
**A**ND because we said man is led to God through an Angel as if he were an inferior, I judge that the discussion should by no means be omitted here as to whether the Angel presiding over or ministering to us is more noble, or the man guarded by him and receiving the ministry. For that sentence known to all in the Davidic song <note>The Psalms.</note> seems to narrow the matter, which the prophet sings when treating man: *You have made him a little lower than the Angels.* <note>original: "Minuisti eũ paulominus ab Angelis." A quote from Psalm 8:5.</note> Likewise, those things which are said by Augustine: that He made the Angel near to Himself, as if more worthy and excellent than the other things performed by Him. For those things which approach closer to the first and most perfect cause <note>God.</note> seem to be more perfect. And since, furthermore, Angels are above time, and produced in a certain eternity, and set apart from burdensome matter, they seem more noble. Some add that the Angel, because he is intellectual <note>term: "intellectualis" — In medieval philosophy, this refers to direct, intuitive understanding, whereas "rationalis" refers to step-by-step logical reasoning.</note>, is considered worthier than man, who is rational. And they attempt to prove this by the oracle of Ezekiel, in which it is said: *You are the seal of resemblance.* <note>original: "Tu signaculum similitudinis." From Ezekiel 28:12.</note> By which words (as some explain) something more seems to be attributed to the Angel than to man, who was made in the image of God. For they judge that something more perfect is hinted at through the "seal of resemblance" than through "image." Standing in opposition to these, we take from the infallible Truth <note>Christ.</note> that he who reclines at the table is greater than he who serves. But of the Angels, Paul says: *They are all ministering spirits,* <note>original: "administratorii Spiritus." From Hebrews 1:14.</note> yet not indeed of God...

<page-num>XXXI</page-num>

### ->THE THIRD TONE. XXXI<-

but also of men: from which it follows: *They are sent for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation.* <note>original: "Missi propter eos, qui hereditatem capiunt salutis." A reference to Hebrews 1:14, describing angels as ministering spirits.</note> Some say that Angels serve us, not as if we were nobler than they, but as if we were weak and in need of their protection. To them we say that the Angels carried the soul of Lazarus into the **bosom of Abraham**, not as one who was weak, but as one released from the body and enlightened. And although a child sometimes requires the guidance of a tutor <term>pedagogue|In the ancient world, a 'pedagogus' was a guardian or tutor who supervised a child; the author argues that while the tutor has authority, the child—as the heir—is higher in status.</term>, yet the child is greater than the tutor, being soon to possess the kingdom. We, however, whom the Angels serve, are to possess the kingdom prepared for us—not for the Angels—from the foundation of the world. From this, it is concluded that our condition is better than the condition of the Angels. This is also shown by the order of creation: for man was the final work of God, who was first and more excellent in the divine mind, according to the common opinion of the Philosophers, which says: *What is first in intention is last in execution.* <note>A standard scholastic axiom: God intended humanity as the pinnacle, so humanity was created last after the 'house' (the world) was prepared.</note> Man was the final work of God, brought into this world as its <margin>Philo</margin> overseer <term>antistes|A Latin term for a presiding officer or high priest; Philo of Alexandria often described man as the 'priest' of the temple of the world.</term>, as if into a house already built and prepared. Furthermore, since Christ the man is held to be nobler than the Angels, we can conclude that human nature is nobler, through that **Aristotelian** principle admitted by all: *When the best of one kind is better than the best of another kind, then this kind is nobler than that one.* And unless Christ and the Blessed Virgin were nobler than the Angels, they never could have transcended their choirs and <margin>Paul</margin> ranks. But of Christ, Paul says: *Having become so much better than the Angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.* <note>Hebrews 1:4.</note> But setting aside many other points that are brought forward by some to save their opinion regarding the nobility of Angels, I will resolve one of their strongest arguments: namely, that the soul of Christ was nobler through **grace**, even if it were inferior by **nature**. If this is carefully weighed, it will be seen to be far from the truth: since freely given gifts (as we explained above) are given according to the dispositions of nature. And let that saying of the Apostle be considered (I pray): that he is so much better than the Angels, as he has obtained a more worthy name. Which name, certainly, was not imposed by chance or improperly, as our names are daily imposed, but was most fitting to the one named, and crafted in the council of the **Most Holy Trinity**: where both the ranks of things and all properties, even individual ones, are known. And if Adam, with only a small light bestowed upon him, knew how to give names to things according to their properties, does not the Most Holy Trinity, the source of all light, know it even better? For by this Trinity, Gabriel was destined to announce the birth to the Virgin, with a command regarding the name to be given to the Son whose conception he was announcing. God also took care to add a single character to the name of Abraham, so that it might be more fitting for the one named. <note>In Genesis 17:5, God changes 'Abram' to 'Abraham' by adding a letter, signifying a change in destiny.</note> What do we believe concerning the name given to the Son and to Christ the man, whom he loved and honored above all? If, therefore, he gave him a more honorable name than the Angels, he also made the one named more honorable. I do not mean according to his divinity, because the Angels could not worthily be compared to that, since it exceeds them by infinity and an immense interval. To the extent that, according to that nature, no comparison is possible.

### ->OF THE THIRD CANTICLE<-

<meta>catchword: by itself</meta>

no comparison can be made. It remains, therefore, that Christ as man is more honored, just as he has inherited a more excellent name. I will add one more thing which greatly explains the nobility of man: because he contains within himself the machine of the world, the Angels, and the Archetype <term>Archetype|The original "blueprint" or divine model in the mind of God after which all creation is patterned.</term>, as we explained above; for this reason, he possesses a more expressive image of God, in whom all the most beautiful marks of God shine forth. 

<margin>Ficino
Coelius
Augustine</margin>

Nor does that prophetic sentence weigh against us, in which it is said that man was made *a little lower than the Angels*, when in the truth of the letter it is written: <note>original Hebrew: וַתְּחַסְּרֵהוּ מְּעַט מֵאֱלֹהִים (vate chasrehu mehat meelohim)</note>. If this is translated word-for-word, it says: *You have diminished him a little*, or *a little less than God*; for *Elohim* signifies God, although sometimes it refers to Angels and sometimes to judges. But in this place (as the wise Hebrews commonly feel), it signifies God. This is hinted at by the words that immediately follow: *And you have set him over the works of your hands.* Therefore, man is not inferior to the Angels, because they too are the works of God's hands.

<margin>Paul</margin>

And how much God himself valued man, Paul hints when he says: *He nowhere takes hold of Angels, but of the seed of Abraham* <note>original: "Nusquam Angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ." A reference to Hebrews 2:16, arguing that Christ took on human nature, not angelic nature.</note>, as being more capable of union than the Angels.

The more secret Theologians <term>secretiores Theologi|A reference to scholars, often Christian Kabbalists, who looked for hidden meanings in the numerical values of Hebrew letters.</term> go further, explaining that word *me'at* <note>original: מְּעַט meaning "a little".</note> through numbers. For those letters yield 119:

Therefore, the enemy fights against us, and our genius <note>original: *genius*; here referring to a tutelary or guardian spirit assigned to a person from birth.</note> and guardian fights for us against that very enemy. For this reason, in that great contest, Michael fought for the Prince, and his Angels for his soldiers. But the Dragon fought against the Prince of the human race himself, and against the Prince of Angels who was fighting for him. His henchmen fought against the soldiers of the Prince and their Angels, so that the battle is always equal: Prince against Prince, and soldiers against soldiers.

Man, therefore, stands in the middle of these combatants; he grants victory to whichever side he wishes, and he follows that victor. Unless a man gives himself up voluntarily, the Angels of life and light prevail against the Angels of death and darkness.

The Angel of light strives to lead us through the former, while the Angel of obscurity and Satan strives to lead us through the latter. These are the things called "life and death," "evil and good" in the book of Ecclesiasticus. Indeed, God left man "in the hand of his own counsel," <note>Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 15:14, a key verse regarding free will.</note> even though he has leaders and prompters for both directions. But the Angel of light must be listened to, with whom we share a natural bond and friendship. We must reject that other one, between whom and us implacable and most bitter enmities were placed from the beginning. Our soul and spirit should always shudder, and all that is within us should be disturbed when we sense him—especially in the dark, where he assumes no small amount of power.

# OF THE THIRD SONG

...shining down, it flows a certain virtue into the heavens and through them into the lower things. For from the Father of lights, from whom every best gift comes, both being and movement and generation and every working power proceed, as much in the heavens as in the elements, plants, animals, and men. But all these things are received through the heavens as if through mediums and instruments, like certain nourishments, which are called natural gifts. Men, however, beyond these, receive that from which they compose various characters and a manifold life; as all astronomers everywhere assert, <margin>Astronomy</margin> deciding that this man is benign from Jupiter, that one impetuous from Mars, another splendid from the Sun, and many things of this kind, some of which we touched upon above, and the astronomers themselves have filled immense volumes. This happens either through the arrangement of the canopy <note>original: *tentorii*; likely referring to the celestial vault or the specific layout of a horoscope.</note>, or through a certain power which, proceeding from the intelligences <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, "intelligences" were the angelic beings responsible for moving the celestial spheres.</note> and penetrating through the heavens, reaches not only our bodies but the inner parts of the spirit, proceeding from spirits. We also receive the greatest power from the harmony <note>original: *concentu*; literally a singing together or concord.</note> of the heavens, which disposes us to harmonize our morals, unless by our own bad disposition we block it and turn the harmony into a clattering noise.

<margin>Pythagoras, Plato, Cicero, Macrobius</margin> Pythagoras and Plato speak of this harmony of the heavens flowing most melodious influences into us, especially in the *Republic*. Cicero follows them in the book under the same title <note>Referencing Cicero's *De Re Publica*, specifically the final section known as the "Dream of Scipio."</note>; but Macrobius, in the first book on the *Dream of Scipio*, resuming their words, says: 
> When I looked at the heaven in amazement, "What is that," I said, "which fills my ears with such a great and sweet sound?" "This," he said, "is that sound which is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves, at unequal intervals, yet nonetheless distinguished by a proportional logic; and tempering high notes with low, it produces various harmonies equally." 

For the star-bearing heaven, whose rotation is more excited, makes a higher sound, while the lunar sound is the deepest—namely by a violent motion, for the higher sphere is moved more swiftly. But by its own motion, the lower sphere is swifter and higher, while the higher is slower and deeper. This harmony is indeed most beautiful, and most sweet in its reciprocation, so much so that no song is sweeter than this, which is drawn from numbers and measures in the likeness of the motions of the spheres, as we have clearly proven. 
<margin>Plato</margin> Nor is there less harmony in the signs of the star-bearing heaven, over which (as Plato says) the Sirens are placed, who are called "songs" because, presiding over those signs, they render harmonious influences.

### What Man Shares with the Sacraments
### Chapter VIII.

<margin>Theology</margin>
<margin>Hebrew</margin>
<margin>John</margin>

**A**lthough the Supreme Moderator <note>God, as the one who governs the universe.</note> is most simple, unique, and almighty, he nevertheless acts with us many times through the intervention of Angels, the heavens, and other suitable means which share a symbolic connection with both sides. For the heavens, which are distributed by twelve and seven <note>Referring to the 12 signs of the Zodiac and the 7 classical planets.</note> (derived from three and four), participate in divinity through the number three, and in the nature of lower things through the number four. <note>In this system of numerology, 3 represents the spiritual/divine (the Trinity) and 4 represents the material (the four elements).</note> Angels also have many things in common with God, and many with man in his earthly pilgrimage; therefore they are mediating ministers, until that better fate is given to man himself which does not require angelic favor. Yet, not content with these, the most pious Father established other means through which he might deal with us more familiarly. These are the sacraments and sacrifices, which savor of the nature of both worlds, or represent those divine things through analogy.

For human filth is washed away by that super-worldly water which is the Son of God, the Wisdom of God, and the Word of God, which sustains and heals all things; he is also the one who alone bore the sins of the world, performing the purging of sins. Hence, as a sign of this washing, this elementary water was ordained, whose nature is to wash away the impurities of bodies and to signify that water which washes all stains of the soul and spirit. For these pollutions could not be washed away except by that water which is the piety, clemency, grace, and mercy of God. This is so true that even the Hebrew theologians are forced to confess that the Messiah must purge man through water, who under the "fiery law" was purged through blood. Thus, seeking justice—which Christ did not omit but rather perfected—he came (as John says) not in water alone, but in water and blood. And since, beyond washing, we also need to be strengthened, anointing and corroborating oil was ordained. This oil has such a correspondence with the divine name—from which comes every delighting and strengthening power—that the name itself is said in the Song of Songs to be...

Furthermore, man has a meeting with these same things by divine institution, since God's will has no less power and efficacy in instituting anew than it had from the beginning, when He bestowed law and order along with being upon things. Yet He instituted those sacramental signs which would suit the things signified and those receiving them. ### What Man has to do with the words and prayers that assist him. Chapter X.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**A**nd because Man is purged and perfected not only by words expressed in the sacraments, but also in hymns, prayers, and however they may be duly expressed, we must therefore examine what man has to do with these words. For words are intermediaries between the speaker and the listener, conveying not only a concept but the power of the speaker, through a certain <term>energy</term> <note>original: "energia"; here used in the Aristotelian or theological sense of "active power" or "actualization."</note> acting upon those who hear and receive them. Whence they change not only the listeners, but often many other things as well. For Christ would not have said, *In my name they shall cast out demons*, unless there were some power in that spoken name over demons, the sick, and such things. The words of those who chant wisely also move [things] in their own ways. And this happens either from a force inherent in the words themselves, or by the power of the things explained through words, which are like vehicles for the power of the thing expressed. Furthermore, words (especially Hebrew ones) are certain signs and sacraments of heavenly things; hence they have a force like that of sacraments. This arises either from the power of the one who instituted them, or from that representation of sacred things, as is said concerning the more famous sacraments. And because Hebrew words represent things—whether divine, heavenly, or even natural—more expressly and mysteriously, <margin>Orpheus</margin> Orpheus therefore commands that <term>barbarous names</term> <note>original: "nomina barbara"; a term used in ancient magic and Neoplatonism to refer to foreign, untranslatable names (often Hebrew or Egyptian) believed to hold innate sacred power.</note> (that is, Hebrew ones) must not be changed in sacred rites if we wish to work effectively. And beyond the efficacy which words possess—whether from a certain force inherent in them, or from the divine and sacred things they represent, or from whatever source—another power is also found in complex prayers. This comes from the truth contained within them, which has the greatest power for impressing, changing, and stabilizing, so much so that when stirred up it shines more brightly, and when attacked it is further strengthened and consolidated. This truth is not found in simple words,

# ON A CERTAIN HIDDEN HARMONY OF THINGS AMONG THEMSELVES, FROM WHICH ONE WORKS UPON ANOTHER IN A WONDROUS WAY. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Trismegistus</margin>
**T**he most exalted craftsman, God, fashioned (as **Trismegistus** <note>original: "Trismegistus." Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational texts of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy are attributed.</note> says) two images of Himself: namely the world and man, so that in one He might play, and in the other He might truly enjoy delights. For in the world He plays with certain wondrous operations—not only through qualitative, or elementary, or stellar power—but by a certain force hidden from the minds of men, except insofar as He deigns to manifest it to His friends. For it is known to everyone that a certain power exists in the magnet <note>original: "magneti." The lodestone.</note> by which it attracts iron; and in amber <note>original: "electro."</note> and jet <note>original: "balagio."</note> so that, when warmed by rubbing, they draw up straw. But from where this comes, or what it is, no one has yet declared from among those who fill vast volumes concerning the properties of things. So too it is not known from where the <term>Eagle-stone</term> <note>original: "Aetites." A hollow stone believed to be found in eagles' nests, traditionally used as a charm to prevent miscarriage or ease labor.</note> derives its power to strengthen the fetus of women and plants when placed beneath them, or to draw it out when positioned elsewhere. Nor is it known how <term>jasper</term> <note>original: "iaspis."</note> restrains blood, or how the <term>Echneis</term> <note>original: "Echneis." From the Greek for "holding back ships."</note> (which is also called the **remora**) stays a ship. Nor why coral, when hung about a person, bestows a certain power of joy, or why the <term>hyacinth</term> <note>original: "hiacynthus." Likely the gemstone zircon or a similar blue stone, rather than the flower.</note> is the best companion for those traveling. Nor why <term>Rhubarb</term> <note>original: "Rheu barbarum," which the Arabs call "Ravend."</note> expels bile from the human body; and many medicinal substances draw out and drive away the most diverse humors. There are many things of this kind which would take a long time to discuss individually. We also see many animals that, by a certain power implanted in them, are deceptive and prophetic. The rooster, by its song and chatter, and flies, by their sharp stinging, announce coming rain; and dolphins, with their frequent leaps above the <margin>Cicero</margin> water, precede a storm. And (to touch upon specific details) roosters (as **Cicero** writes) among the people of the Thebaid, by crowing through entire nights, foretold for the Boeotians that <margin>The Augurs</margin> victory against the Lacedaemonians. From this, the **Augurs** <note>Priests in ancient Rome who interpreted omens based on the behavior of birds.</note> interpreted that this bird, if conquered, remains silent, but sings if it is the victor. The monkey which the King of the Molossians kept as a pet showed a very great portent to the Spartans. For when they had sought an answer from <term>Dodonean Jove</term> <note>The oracle of Zeus at Dodona, where the god's will was interpreted through the rustling of oak leaves or lots.</note> regarding victory, and the legates had placed the lots in which they were to cast their fates, the monkey disturbed the lots themselves and the other things prepared for the drawing, scattering one thing from another. Then she who presided over the oracle, the priestess, is said to have spoken: "The Lacedaemonians must think of safety, not of victory." The liver of a chameleon <margin>Democritus</margin> (as **Democritus** <note>original: "Democritus." A Greek philosopher often cited in early natural magic for his purported experiments with animal properties.</note> attests), when burnt upon the highest roof tiles, excites rain and thunder. The <term>Ligurian stone</term> <note>original: "Ligurus." Often identified with amber or a stone formed from lynx urine in ancient lapidaries.</note> (as has been proven) takes away deceptive veils from the eyes. It would be a long task to recount all the prophecies which the Phrygians, Pisidians, Cilicians, Arabs, Umbrians, Tuscans, and other peoples learned from birds, following the auguries...

And even though Panaetius and Carneades might mock them, since these auspices often fail—whom Cicero follows after many examples brought forward concerning divination through birds and the entrails of animals—it has nonetheless been more often proven true. And what is more, certain birds prophesy from the right, like the raven; others from the left, like the crow. Furthermore, even inanimate things have been seen to prognosticate. Which we read was also done at other times at the death of certain Kings. For the Sun foretells in many ways: for sometimes it has seemed to shine with a dim light <margin>Virgil</margin> as it did at Caesar's fall, as the Poet writes: *The Sun will give you signs; who would dare to call the Sun false? Ille etiam extincto miseratus Caesare Romam, cum caput obscura nitidum ferrugine texit." A famous passage from Virgil's Georgics I, 463-467, describing the omens following the assassination of Julius Caesar.</note> And concerning the lower elements another Prophet sings, saying: *And he often foretells coming winds, the inflated sea, when it suddenly and deeply swells, and the curved rocks foamed with snowy salt water,* etc., as is said there. The Supreme Truth <margin>CHRIST</margin> also testifies that the terrifying day of the universal judgment is to be announced by great earthquakes, which will occur in various places, and at the same time by other unusual and wonderful portents: whence it is proven that earthquakes are brought forth, just as winds are, from the storehouses of God. But the former are more often for the utility of men, the latter however to warn them of evil outcomes, as Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras</margin> rightly feels; although many who play the philosopher say <margin>Seeking the cause of earthquakes.</margin> they proceed from a natural cause. But since this is not the case, they are unable to discover it for themselves. Hence they have wandered through many theories. For Anaxagoras said the cause of earthquakes was the ether; Empedocles, fire; Democritus and Thales of Miletus, water; Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the medieval polymath.</note>, wind or subterranean vapor; Asclepiades, a fall or collapse. Thus Posidonius, Metrodorus, Callisthenes, Parcas, Seneca, and others, distracted in different directions, never discovered the cause of that effect: which is from the Supreme Moderator, either by immediate command, or through commanded ministers, or by some force infused into things, to be unfolded into effect at will, to foretell slaughters, which commonly follow an earthquake: as even Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> confesses in the *Meteorology*. This prophetic power is also implanted in other things. For the Marsic war was preceded by the sweat and blood of statues, and by voices. Moreover, the collapse of the territory of Privernum was preceded by a roar heard from heaven, and perceived globes, three moons, and torches seen in the night. Before the destruction of Jerusalem, there were raging swords in the sky, the clatter of temple gates with no visible mover, and many other wonders. And in our own time in the territory of Modena, before the very recent surrender of that city...

## Those things which agree among themselves meet much more happily in man, who is the most perfect bond of all things and is supported by divinity above all. Chapter II.

<margin>
Paul
Plato
Hermes
Sextus
</margin>
**F**ROM the mutual correspondence of things (as we have explained), one thing works upon another by a certain wonderful and hidden power. Therefore, it is no wonder if man—since he possesses both the image and the symbol of all things—is able to operate in all things. This he achieves provided that he enjoys his proper temperament and governs himself, so that he may rightly rule among all other things. For in the man who governs himself well, God is present and indwelling, performing all things—as not only Paul and our own scriptures assert, but also foreign sages. For Plato teaches this in his *Ion* and in the *Parmenides*; <note>Plato’s *Ion* discusses divine inspiration, while the *Parmenides* deals with the nature of the One.</note> so does Hermes <note>original: *Mercurius*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> in the *Poimandres*, and Sextus the Pythagorean, who says that man is the temple of God, and God is his guest. This is also what the Poet <note>The Roman poet Ovid, from *Fasti* VI.5.</note> celebrates in these verses: *There is a God within us, and there is commerce with heaven; that spirit comes from ethereal seats.* <note>original: "Est Deus in nobis, sunt & cōmercia cœli: Sedibus ęthereis spiritus ille uenit."</note> For God Himself transfers Himself into holy souls; He establishes His prophets and friends as powerful in deed and in word.

<margin>
Paul
Aristotle
</margin>
Sensing this, Paul said: *I can do all things in Him who strengthens me.* For God is our mind, our total virtue, without whom (as He Himself declares) we can do nothing. Aristotle also confesses this in his *Meteorology* <note>original: *Methauris*</note> and at the end of the *Ethics*, saying that there is no virtue, whether natural or moral, except through God. And in his more secret dogmas <note>Refers to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a text widely attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance that dealt with occult properties.</note>, he asserts that a good and healthy intellect can penetrate the secrets of nature, provided that the influence of divine power is present; otherwise, not at all. We receive this influence more copiously the more we are released from the impediments of the heavy flesh, from earthly occupations, and from ambition or a mind unduly agitated toward one's neighbor or any other thing. This we have not only from our own <margin>Hermes Cicero</margin> dogmas, but also Hermes and Cicero attest to it. For the latter, in his work *On Divination*, says: *The soul of man never divines, except when it is so released that it has clearly nothing or little to do with the body.* <note>original: "Nec aliquādo animus hōis diuinat, nisi cū ita solutus est, ut ei plane nihil sit cū corpore, aut parū."</note> The former [Hermes], moreover, says to Tat <note>Tat was the disciple and son of Hermes in the Hermetic dialogues.</note>: *Let them certainly despise both bodies and all bodily things; and let them be carried toward the One alone, if they wish to attain the Mind and God. For it is impossible, O son, to attend to both at once: things mortal and things divine.* The more we leave behind the animal and human life, the more we live as Angels or as God. Joined to them, and restored to our own better lot, we have power over all things, ruling over all. And this is the honor in which man existed before sin...

## That a Wise-Hearted Man is Sometimes Made a Seer through the Multiple Assistance of Lower Things.
### Chapter III.

<margin>Isaiah, Peter</margin> **E**ften a man who governs himself is made a sharer of the divine mind, so that he may predict future things—which is a power proper to God, according to that saying of <margin>Stoics, Cicero</margin> Isaiah: *Tell us the things that are to come, and we shall say that you are gods.* <note>Isaiah 41:23</note> To this Peter agrees, saying: *For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will, but the holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit.* <note>2 Peter 1:21</note> The Stoics also confess this, whom Cicero follows in the first book of *On Divination*, saying that the "pre-sensing" of the future belongs only to the Gods, because there is no determined truth concerning future contingencies <note>Events that may or may not happen.</note> through the <margin>Ptolemy</margin> pure judgment of mortals. Ptolemy, agreeing with them, says in his *Fruit* <note>The *Centiloquium* or *Karpos*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy.</note>: *Only those inspired by the divine predict particulars.* Yet that there have been many seers <term>vates</term> <note>original: *vates*; a term for a divinely inspired poet or prophet.</note> and many true "pre-sensings" (to leave aside our own people) is testified by Cratippus, <margin>Zeno, Pythagoras, Certain Fore-signs</margin> who was considered equal to the greatest Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> by the testimony of Cicero. Zeno also testifies to this, as do many who came after him from the Old Academy. But before them, Pythagoras, and the Stoics who followed them, assert the same. For Calanus the Indian predicted the death of Alexander, and the Asiatic Magi predicted that the birth of Alexander himself would be the ruin of Asia. Socrates divined that death was imminent for Crito on the third light <note>The third day.</note>; the priestess Diotima, a woman gifted with prophecy, predicted a plague. Anaximander announced an impending earthquake to the Spartans and warned them to leave the city and their homes—which then entirely collapsed, and the furthest part [of the city] from Mount Taygetus...

### THE THIRD TONE.

<margin>Epimenides</margin> ...the part was torn away, as if the stern of a ship. <note>This fragment likely concludes a metaphor from the missing portion of the previous page regarding the soul's journey or the loss of divine grace.</note> Epimenides of Crete, a man of divine character, arrived in Athens ten years before the Persian War, having been warned by an oracle. He performed certain sacrifices prescribed by the oracle. To the Athenians, who were terrified of the Persian fleet, he predicted that the Persians would not come for ten years, and that once they did arrive, they would depart having failed in their mission. Why should I recount the prophecies of Cassandra, Helenus, Calchas, Amphiaraus, Tiresias, Mopsus, Amphilochus, or Polybius of Corinth? <note>These are all famous legendary or historical seers from Greek mythology and history.</note> A single volume could not possibly hold the oracles of the <margin>Diverse Prophets</margin> Druids of Gaul, the Magi of the Persians, the Chaldeans, the prophets of Memphis in Egypt, the Sibyls, and others—some of whom I have heard and confirmed to have predicted the truth.

But setting aside the memory of countless examples, let us see where this foreknowledge comes from. For there is a certain divine category of knowledge that is developed through skill and experience in various affairs. In the Athenian Republic, Solon foresaw the rising <margin>Solon Cato</margin> tyranny long in advance; and Cato used to say of Caesar with a prophetic mind: "Beware of the boy who is poorly girdled." <note>original: "male præcincto." This refers to Julius Caesar’s habit of wearing his belt loosely, which was seen as a sign of an effeminate or untrustworthy character.</note> Countless examples of this kind could be brought forward. 

Even in domestic matters, many wise men have prophesied natural events. <margin>Pherecydes Thales</margin> Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras, predicted that an earthquake was coming after he saw water drawn from a deep well. Thales of Miletus, in order to convince his critics and show what a philosopher could do, bought up the entire olive harvest in the region of Miletus before it had even flowered, noticing by a learned conjecture of nature that there would be an abundance of oil. This came to pass, and he gained a great profit of money—not for the sake of the money itself, but to spite his detractors. <note>Thales used his knowledge of meteorology to predict a bumper crop and cornered the market on oil presses.</note> Doctors, farmers, and sailors also foresee many things, each by his own art and through probable signs, which we usually disregard as if they were common knowledge. 

And because significant things to be foreseen come from those who are in command, which cannot be anticipated by mere prudence or skill, it was therefore a matter of the most diligent care for many ancient nations—Barbarians, Greeks, and Romans, but most especially the Hebrews—to consult prophets or God himself. <margin>Athens Lacedaemon</margin> The Athenians always employed certain divine priests in their public councils, whom they called <term>Mantes</term> <note>From the Greek 'manteis', meaning diviners or soothsayers.</note>. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans.</note> gave their kings an augur as an assistant and wished him to be present at public councils. These same people always consulted either the Delphic oracle, or the oracle of Ammon, or Dodona regarding matters of greater importance. The Romans, in difficult senate business, would order the "Ten Men" to consult the Sibylline books. <margin>Rome Hebrews</margin> The kings of the Hebrews were accustomed to always employ their own prophets, of whom there were very many; and if they themselves were prophets, they consulted God <margin>David</margin> immediately, as we often read concerning David. 

But these diviners were of many kinds. For there were Astronomers, who divined through the appearance of the heavens; Augurs, who observed birds guided either by the influence of the heavens or by those spirits who preside over them; <margin>Haruspices Pyromancy Hydromancy Geomancy Necromancy</margin> Haruspices (or "gut-examiners"), who predicted the future by inspecting entrails; Pyromancers, who did so through fire; Hydromancers through water; and Geomancers through points, either cast by chance or drawn by a certain force of the arm or hand (as the ancients used to do), from which they constructed celestial figures by art to divine the future. Then there are the Necromancers (who are also commonly called Magi)...

But these people proceeded in two ways. Some, most wicked (even in our own time), submit themselves to these unclean intelligences and offer sacrifices. They are guilty of a double and most monstrous crime: first, they commit idolatry; and second, they show themselves to be more base than the basest things, dragging down their own noble and excellent nature. Others, however, call upon them and compel them—chiefly through the power of divine names—to reveal what secrets they have gathered from the higher moderators. We see all these kinds expressed in the sacred scriptures.

If, however, this happens to someone who is fully awake, it occurs either during prayer or in some higher state of mind than to one resting in bed and about to yield to sleep. <margin>Democritus</margin> We also read that prophecy <term>vaticinium</term> through frenzy <note>original: "furorem"; often referring to the 'divine madness' or inspiration described by Plato.</note> has happened to both pagan and our own divine prophets. This frenzy the Greeks call *Mantia* <note>original: "Mantiā", from the Greek word for divination or prophecy.</note> after Manto, the founder of Mantua; although *Mantia* is more often used for every kind of lower divination. Num & Saul inter prophetas?"</note>. This change, however, was brought about by the Spirit of the Lord seizing him; this is the true "frenzy" <term>furor</term> <note>In this context, 'furor' does not mean anger, but a state of divine possession or inspired madness where the mind is elevated above its normal state.</note> that sometimes seizes a person, even one subject to sin, when there is a legitimate cause. As the Evangelist says of Caiaphas: *And he prophesied, being the high priest of that year* <note>original: "Et prophetauit, cum esset pontifex anni illius." Referring to John 11:51.</note>. Thus many poets, either out of a love for study or being filled with some virtue—or for some good reason known to God—have sometimes, when filled with frenzy, brought forth hidden things and occasionally prophesied. <margin>John</margin> Cicero mentions this frenzy and sleep in his book *On Divination*, <margin>Cicero</margin> saying: "There is another kind of divining in those who do not act by reason or by some conjecture from observed and noted signs, but by a certain agitation of the mind, or by a loose and free movement, they foresee future things." <note>original: "Est aliud diuinandi genus... sed cocitatione quadam animi." From Cicero’s 'De Divinatione'.</note> This happens quite often to those who dream, and sometimes to those prophesying through frenzy, <margin>Bacchus, Epime., Sybilla, Cicero</margin> like Bacchus among the Boeotians, Epimenides among the people of Cos, and the Erythraean Sibyl among the Trojans. But Cicero is mistaken regarding the Sibyl, because her kind of divining fits neither with dreaming nor with frenzy. For there is a certain "particular influx" <note>A technical theological term implying a direct, specific infusion of divine knowledge rather than a general state of madness.</note> in them, about which it is not permitted to speak at present. Cicero continues: "For there is a certain foreboding of the mind instilled from without and enclosed by divine power. If this burns more fiercely, it is called frenzy, when the soul, abstracted from the body, is incited by divine frenzy," <margin>Democ., Plato, Plotinus, Porphy.</margin> as Democritus and Plato assert. This frenzy is followed by a certain departure of the mind and an "ecstasy" <term>extasis</term> <note>literally "standing outside oneself"</note>, as Porphyry writes of Plotinus: who often released himself from the body and changed in his countenance, from which he then discovered certain wondrous things to write down; Porphyry asserts that he himself was present for these miracles four times. He affirms that he himself, when he was passing through his sixty-eighth year of age, experienced this from the divine power once while in contemplation. <margin>Heracli., Democ.</margin> But we read that many years before these men, Heraclitus and Democritus did the same; for this reason, they delighted in solitude. One of them, through the intensity of his study, was somewhat gloomy; the other, however, raised above all lower things, laughed at every individual thing. For this reason, he was judged a fool by the Abderites (as Hippocrates writes). <margin>Hippo., Pythag., Zoroa., Harmo., Semtoph, Aristo., Diome.</margin> Seized by this ecstatic delight, Pythagoras and Zoroaster remained hidden, the former for ten years and the latter for twenty. The soul of Harmonius of Clazomenae used to wander, having left the body (as he said)—yet it was not truly "left" by the body, as the truth of the matter is. We also read that Diomedes of Syracuse, intent upon geometric figures, did not perceive the tumultuous destruction of his perishing fatherland or the enemy looming over his head. <note>The author likely conflates Diomedes with Archimedes, who famously died during the Siege of Syracuse while focused on his diagrams.</note> This happens either through the excessive concentration of the one Speculating, or because of a man's vigorous virtues, <margin>Cornel., Aul.Ge.</margin> as Aulus Gellius wrote of the most chaste priest Cornelius. At Padua, at the time when Caesar and Pompey were clashing in Thessaly <note>The Battle of Pharsalus, 48 BCE.</note>, Cornelius was carried away in his mind...

->## FOURTH TONE<-

<margin>Socrates</margin> he foresaw the time, order, and outcome of the battle. Socrates (as Plato writes) <margin>Plato</margin> stood from the rising of the sun until the next sun rose, without food, and without any sensation or movement of the body, with his face and eyes directed toward the same spot, deep in thought and abstracted from his body. Plato, having frequently withdrawn far from his body through the intensity of contemplation, finally departed entirely from his bodily bonds during that very state of abstraction. <margin>The same [Plato].</margin> His disciple Xenocrates was abstracted from his body for a full hour every single day. <margin>Xenocrates</margin> And what happened to the philosophers by the force of most intense speculation, the men and women of the Gospel achieved much more happily by the power of the Holy Spirit, which was poured out most abundantly in many of them—and even more so as they were found to be more purified. 

Francis (to begin with our own) <margin>Francis</margin> was many times suspended in such an excess of mind that, snatched outside of himself and sensing something beyond human feeling, he was entirely unaware of what was being done around him externally. For while passing through the town of Sansepolcro <note>original: "burgum Sancti sepulchri." A town in Tuscany famous for its association with the Holy Sepulchre.</note>, he was so collected within himself—or rather, joined to God—that he did not see the place, nor did he recognize the many things that those townsfolk displayed around him. 

Augustine, <margin>Augustine</margin> when he was intent on meditation, did not notice a woman who had approached him to consult with him while she was speaking. Consequently, she left without her consultation, somewhat indignant at the bishop, believing she had been snubbed by such a great man. But on the following day, receiving a kind response, she realized she had not been neglected but simply unnoticed. 

Thomas Aquinas (as it is told), <margin>Thomas</margin> intent on higher things, was seen to be lifted from the earth by a cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly 18 inches, the length of a forearm from elbow to fingertip.</note> in both mind and body. Mary Magdalene, <margin>Mary Magdalene</margin> instructed and supported by the Good Master, while living in the solitude of Marseille, used to be lifted on high at set hours by the ministry of angels. Mary of Egypt <margin>Mary of Egypt</margin> followed her; having been purged of her former softness by the harshness of the desert, she was seen hanging high above the earth at a cubit's altitude while praying. 

Clare of Assisi, <margin>Clare</margin> lying from the Lord’s Supper <note>Holy Thursday.</note> until the day of the Resurrection, contemplating the trophy of the Cross on high, seemed to herself to have not even rested for an hour when she returned. I have confirmed this in another woman, similar in name and life, who, after receiving the sacrament at the twilight of that same Thursday, stood motionless on her knees until Sunday; rising then as if with Christ, she related many things to me which she had seen. 

We could bring forward innumerable examples of this kind, both of Paul <margin>Paul</margin> and of those later ones down to our own times—people I have either seen or known through worthy reports—who were seized by frenzy, or rather by a holy divinity, and led to a place where the human mind, relying on its own strengths, cannot reach. 

But let us come to another kind of divination, which happens through clear vision. Here, man (as Proclus says) <margin>Proculus</margin> "feasting on the truth," lives in pure splendor, having been initiated into perfect, stable, and sincere spiritual images <term>phantasmata</term> <note>In this Neoplatonic context, 'phantasmata' refers not to "ghosts" or "illusions," but to divine forms or spiritual realities perceived by the soul's eye.</note>—not at all these things drawn from the senses, but those better "sacraments" which the prophets foresaw in the archetype; having first been purified through sacrifices and by some peculiar gift of God, with the mediation also of the virtues, which Plotinus... <margin>Plotinus</margin>

<page-num>XIII</page-num>
->ON THE THIRD SONG<-

## THE THIRD SONG

...using the borrowed name of "purgatorial" <note>original: "purgatorias." In this context, it refers to the "purgative way," a stage in mystical theology where the soul is cleansed of worldly attachments to prepare for union with God.</note> virtues. By these he teaches that we should scrape, polish, and wipe ourselves clean until each person has formed themselves into a beautiful statue. He says a "statue" and an "image" through which we might perfectly reflect the most perfect Craftsman <note>original: "Opificem." A common philosophical term for God as the Creator or Architect of the universe.</note>. For, he says, let everyone be made beautiful and God-like <term>Deiformis: the state of being "god-shaped" or restored to the image of God</term>, if they are to look upon divine beauty. For it is necessary for the one seeing to become like the thing seen. And he pursues many points, all of which the Supreme Truth <margin>CHRIST</margin> <note>A common title for Christ in medieval and Renaissance theology.</note> encompasses in a single word, saying: **Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.** In this God all things are seen, and all things are known, more or less, according to how that vision requires a suitable disposition in the one seeing. And these are the true seers, who learn those things which they predict by seeing them in the mirror of that eternal light. Hence, according to custom, the Scripture calls the oracles uttered by the prophets "visions," when it says: *The vision of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel*, or of other seers; and the prophets themselves were called "seers." But since the fullest mirror of light was opened to <margin>Moses</margin> Moses more than to the others, so much so that he was said to speak face to face with God, the Holy Scripture places him before the other prophets. We have this in those words which <margin>Joshua</margin> Joshua (at the Lord's command) added at the end of Deuteronomy, saying: *And there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and wonders which he sent him to perform in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and all his servants, and before all Israel.*

There is a final kind of prophecy which is produced through an articulate and expressed voice, <margin>John</margin> the most excellent of all. Hence John [the Baptist], who was called "the voice," is also held by the Supreme Truth to be even "more than a prophet." For this <margin>Abraham</margin> voice is first read to have been brought down to Abraham by an Angel crying out from heaven, "Abraham, Abraham!" By this voice, both the liberation of his son and the blessing which was poured out through his seed upon the whole human race were announced. To <margin>Moses</margin> Moses also, while he was pasturing his flock on Mount Sinai, that divine voice thundered, saying: "Moses, Moses!" Once called, he immediately believed in the task of liberating the people from Egypt, publishing the Law, and committing the Scripture to writing. Furthermore, a <margin>Samuel</margin> voice came to Samuel, calling twice and saying: "Samuel, Samuel!" establishing him as a priest, director, and leader of the people of Israel. 

Nor do I think we should overlook the sacred mystery of why the voice always calls someone twice by name. For the wise believe this was done because the voice always raises the one who is called to a higher rank. Therefore, the double voice indicates both the rank in which he was and the rank to which he ascended when called. Thus, purified and well-hearted men reach this point: having more frequently been made participants in the Spirit of God and the holy divinity, they prophesy, discern hidden things, and predict the future—which belongs to God alone, and to those with whom God has decided to communicate and make Himself familiar. This He never grants except to well-purified and composed men.

->THE FOURTH TONE<-

### Defense of Prophecy. Chapter V.

<margin>Cicero</margin>
**A**lthough it should be clear to everyone that there have been prophets and many prophecies, there are nonetheless those who attempt to attack them. For this reason, I judge it appropriate to briefly dismantle their arguments. For they say (as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator whose work *On Divination* provides the primary skeptical framework for this chapter.</note> gathers in the second book of *On Divination*): Of what does divination consist? Is it of fortuitous things, or of things determined by fate? It cannot be of fortuitous <term>Fortuita: random events that happen by "chance" rather than by a predictable cause</term> things, because there can be no foreknowledge of those things which have no rational cause for why they should happen. But what is "chance," or a "fortuitous event," except when something falls out or happens in such a way that it could just as easily have not happened, or happened differently? How, therefore, can that which occurs at random, by blind chance and the instability of fortune, be foreseen and predicted? Nor is divination concerned with fatal things; for since they must happen by necessity, foreknowledge of them is of no use—indeed, it is a torment—if the future outcome is to be a bad one. Nor can those things which are fated be avoided. Nor should it even be said that the impact of events will fall more lightly if divine matters are performed <note>original: "rebus divinis procuratis." This refers to the Roman practice of performing rituals or sacrifices to "expiate" an omen and lessen its impact.</note>, because (as they say) since nothing exists outside of fate, nothing can be lightened by a divine act. They conclude, therefore: if nothing can be foreseen of those things which happen by chance because they cannot be certain, then divination is nothing. If, however, they can be foreseen because they are certain and 
<margin>
Chrysippus
Diogenes
Antipater
</margin>
fated, then divination will be of no use. Chrysippus, Diogenes, and Antipater <note>These are Stoic philosophers. While the Stoics generally defended divination, the author is here using their complex arguments about the nature of the gods to highlight skeptical challenges.</note> add: If there are Gods by whose patronage (as it is said) divination occurs, why do they not openly explain what future things ought to be avoided or embraced? This is especially pressing since they are said to be beneficent and friends to the human race—unless the Gods think it makes no difference to humans whether they know or are ignorant of what is to come. And why do they hide so many and such great things from humans, so that the things they do know or foresee are nothing in comparison to those that remain hidden? From this, they seem to conclude that the Gods reveal nothing; rather, if anything is foreseen, it is due to natural talent, art, or luck. Some also rail against the signs which seem to be given from heaven, relying chiefly on this reasoning: that winds, lightning, thunder, comets, earthquakes, and vapors seen battling in the air and such things are natural phenomena, not prognostications. A supporting proof of this is lightning cast into the middle of the sea, or sent down elsewhere to no purpose; and because comets and earthquakes are not always followed by those events they are said to signify. Many people, pursuing such points, scheme greatly against divination; yet these arguments, in fact, collapse entirely under their own weight. 
<margin>Cicero</margin>
Nevertheless, we shall respond to the points that have been brought forward. For there is (to turn myself toward Cicero and those who follow him) a divination of both fortuitous and fatal things. And although fortuitous things seem to have no rational cause, that is only the case for those people to whom these things happen. For in the Supreme Moderator <note>original: "summo Moderatore." A reference to God as the governor or pilot of the universe.</note> from whom they proceed, they are not without reason. For all fortuitous things are disposed by God according to His own reason. We, however (as Aristotle <note>The author refers to a work attributed to Aristotle regarding luck and divine providence.</note> rightly perceives in *On Good and Evil Fortune*), since we do not see the cause of these things, which is God, we attribute them...

OF THE THIRD CANTICLE.

## OF THE THIRD CANTICLE.

...[we attribute it] to fortune, that is, to an unknown cause. Therefore, these things do not happen outside the intention of the **Supreme Governor** <note>original: "summi moderantis," a term for God as the pilot or ruler of the universe</note>, just as an iron axe-head might fall into the water beyond the intention of the woodcutter. For the lot seemed to have fallen upon **Saul** by chance when he was chosen as king; yet he had already been indicated to **Samuel** as king by the Lord. And by Him who had indicated it, the lots were so arranged that they would fall upon Saul—though to those who did not understand God's own arrangement, they appeared to have fallen by chance. 

<margin>Saul</margin>

So it happens in many cases that things are judged to be accidental which in fact proceed from a divine decree with the highest reason. In God, these are called **divine provisions**; if they are arranged through the heavens, they take on the name of **fateful things** <term>Fatalium: events dictated by Fate or the stars</term>; however, in the lives of those to whom they occur, they are judged to be fortuitous events. And prophecies of these things are often sent beforehand so that mortals may know that such things are foreseen and destined by God. From this, they may prepare themselves to receive these spiritual influences <note>original: "influxus," the celestial or divine "flow" into the material world</note> well and be grateful to the Giver. 

Sometimes, however, things are arranged in such a sequence that their outcome depends on the disposition of the recipient, such as the grace given to one who works well, and manifold favor. These are even promised under certain conditions, as the **Supreme Governor** often repeats in Holy Scripture, saying: *If you listen to me, if you do this or that, I will be a generous rewarder.* And although the Supreme Governor knows what a man is going to do, that vision does not pass into the past; it is not as if, because it has been seen and concluded, the thing must follow as an infallible event. 

How, moreover, the same event can be a "contingent" <term>Contingens: an event that is possible but not certain; it might happen or not</term> event and yet be "infallible providence" in God, and "fate" in the heavens (as **Plato** rightly feels), is among the most difficult of all matters. And although we see and approve of these things, no one has yet fully explained how they fit together. 

<margin>Plato</margin>

Yet we can offer an example to lead us toward an explanation of this matter. A river flows by God’s eternal command, and with an unfailing glide it passes through various regions for the benefit of all inhabitants. One person takes care to receive the flow of water, admitting as much as is sufficient to irrigate his fields. Another, having fortified his embankments, admits no water for either benefit or harm. Yet another, through his own laziness, builds no embankments and allows all his lands to be drowned and all his crops <note>original: "fata," here used to mean the potential harvest or the "destiny" of the seeds</note> to be overwhelmed. 

Therefore, the course of the river is from God’s providence and His unvariable command—or from the order of the heavens, which is fate; however, the benefit or the harm is contingent, depending on the industry or laziness of the recipient. If someone had prophesied about that flood, perhaps one of the inhabitants would have better fortified his dikes to avoid the harm, and another would have prepared himself to receive a more bounteous benefit. Behold, then, how even those things that are fateful are mitigated—or (to speak in our own way) those things that come down from the infallible providence of God. 

To **Chrysippus** <note>A Stoic philosopher who argued for a strict chain of cause and effect</note> and his colleagues, we shall say: the **Gods** (that is, the **Angels**) reveal certain things to us by the command of the Supreme Governor, as both the honor of the Prince and our own merits require. And from these oracles...

<margin>Chrysippus</margin>

XLIIII

# THE FOURTH TONE. #

<margin>Deuteronomy</margin> Having been declared by the eye <note>original: "oculo"; likely referring to the visual nature of the examples or signs previously discussed</note>, we can hunt for many other similar things, because "God speaks once" (as **Job** says) in the same cause, namely, that we may direct our efforts in similar matters toward the goals of His unique speech. And this is what the prophet **Amos** says: "The Lord God does nothing unless He has revealed His secret to His servants the prophets," <margin>Amos</margin> either explicitly or through something similar. Truly, many things are hidden from the unworthy, just as much knowledge of things that ought to be known is hidden from us. Nor is it fitting that a Prince reveal his secrets to the common people, but rather to a few who are in his secret council <note>original: "a secretis," referring to private secretaries or confidants</note>, and to those who are most faithful; nevertheless, their execution is entrusted to the people in due time. And then all come to know those things which were hidden among the few. This is the order for arranging affairs—not indeed for the harm, but for the benefit of the entire Commonwealth. Moreover, the claim that some celestial effects are not signs of a future event is nothing; while some effects are natural, others occur by the immediate command of God. Therefore, those that are natural are not signs; but those that are commanded by God to terrify or punish peoples—such as those wonders sent through **Moses** <margin>Moses</margin> against the **Egyptians**, and many similar things—can rightly be called signs, and they are: from which a man can guess the outcome of events. Therefore, the reasons brought forward do not press us so narrowly that the corner of a true escape (as those arguing supposed) is closed off to us. Nor should anyone wonder if prognostications are obscure and require interpreters, since in a way nothing is accomplished in natural things that does not require the help of man. For gold and silver and other metals are dug up and excavated full of slag and mud, but they are purified by human industry. The grape is born and matures by the protection of nature; but the same grape withers unless, by human diligence, it is gathered and pressed into wine. Grains also, harvested with much labor, are threshed, ground, and handled many times before bread is prepared for food. Flax requires innumerable labors (if I may say so) before cloth is woven for human use. And just as the works of nature are completed by art, so too the divine oracles are offered to us to be explained: so that, having been made co-workers of nature and of God, we may have something in both wherein we can exercise ourselves. Truly, at times one must practice divination so that we may understand what the divine prophets foresaw. From this, error frequently occurs—not indeed from a vice or defect in the prophecy, because those things which proceed from the mouth of God do not become void—but it happens through the fault of the one who understands poorly. Nor is prophecy to be denied because an interpreter is ignorant or errs in interpreting; for medicine is not to be denied even though doctors are deceived in many things. Farmers and ship-pilots are also deceived, even though they are considered good **Haruspices** <term>Haruspices: ancient diviners who interpreted signs, originally from the entrails of sacrificial animals, but here used generally for those who read natural signs</term> from proven signs. Nor is prudence and reason lacking for governing the Commonwealth, although **Gnaeus Pompey**, **Marcus Cato**, **Hannibal**, <margin>Pompey</margin> and many most prudent senators and most illustrious leaders were sometimes deceived. So it also happens in the art of divining, which is either...

...prudence, or conjecture, whether it is brought about by the agitation of the spirit or by a vision, so that diviners are sometimes deceived: either because what the spirit suggests or the vision indicates is not well perceived; or because there is some change in that which was the subject of the prophecy; whence <margin>Jonah</margin> the sentence of the oracle may either be changed, if it was intended for punishment, or if for a benefit, it may be delayed.
