->Well-ordered men draw all things to themselves.<- ### Chap. VI.

**N**ot by meager experience has it been proven that well-ordered strings <note>original: *nervos*, implying both musical strings and the fibers of the human body</note> on a lute, when some are struck, cause others to resonate. It also happens to oysters and all shellfish that they grow with the moon and likewise decrease with it. Trees also in the winter time age together with the Moon and the Sun, and let down their humors, for which reason they are thought to be cut down at the appropriate time. All things sprout and flower in the spring, and joyfully follow the course of the sun. Many things of this kind also occur, in which the connection and correspondence of things is perceived. Since, therefore, man is the bond <note>term: *vinculum* — the central link or "glue" connecting the material and spiritual worlds</note> of all things, the well-ordered man easily moves all things, and draws and leads them to himself: no less than a magnet draws iron, or rubbed amber <note>original: *electrum*</note> draws straw. Hence He, who is the most perfect bond of all, and rejoices in full harmony, said: <margin>THE SAME <note>Referring to Christ</note></margin> "When I am lifted up from the earth"—namely, most perfectly stretched out on the wood of the cross, and in harmony with all things that are in the length, breadth, height, and depth of this worldly machine—"I will draw all things to myself," to dispose of all at my will. He who is made more similar to Him and is united with Him, attains a greater power of attraction, and is more strengthened by it, fortifying that power which is implanted in man by nature for drawing things through the symbol <note>original: *symbolum*; in this context, a shared essence or "tally" that allows one thing to influence another</note> that he has with all. This is inferred from the fact that while every animal has its own specific foods—some hay or barley, others herbs, others legumes or seeds, others meats and the like—man alone feeds on all foods, receiving growth and support for life from all. Likewise, some among living creatures possess the land, some the sea, some the air, and the more worthy ones the heavens. But man, using every element for his own benefit, draws pleasure and advantage from everywhere. Not content with those, he strives to ascend into heaven, indeed into God Himself, so that there is no place that he does not claim for his use and...

XLV

# THE FOURTH TONE #

<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>...rightly, so that the sentence of the Supreme Prince may be true: "Every place where your foot treads shall be yours" <note>Deuteronomy 11:24</note>: namely, until you return to me, bringing all things with you. And just as all things bring profit to a man who is in a good state with God, as <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says: "For those who love God, all things work together for good" <note>Romans 8:28</note>: so for one who is out of harmony with God, all things turn toward destruction, for he has become the son of that rebel <note>referring to Adam after the Fall</note> to whom it is said: "Cursed is the ground because of your work" <note>Genesis 3:17</note>. Following the curse of this earth—which is the primary element and foundation of all bodily things—comes the curse of all things which are made from it or are attached to it. From here, evil and dissonant demons lead away these rebels, about whom <margin>Porphyry</margin> Porphyry says in *On Good and Evil Daemons*: "The bodies of good spirits consist of proper proportion; but the bodies of the wicked are unbalanced and, through passive affection <note>original: *affectione passiva*; referring to being easily swayed by physical sensations or emotions rather than reason</note>, they inhabit a place near the earth, or rather, within the earth itself. There is no evil they do not dare to commit. They have a completely violent and unhealthy character, being deserted by the protection of better spirits. And therefore, they plot and labor at many violent and sudden traps. While they carry out their raids, they are accustomed partly to hide, and partly to inflict violence. For this reason, the sufferings inflicted by them are sharp and swift. However, cures and corrections from better spirits occur more slowly." And <margin>The same</margin> after he has listed many evils that they commit, he adds: "For they take great delight in all things done so wickedly and discordantly." Therefore, those who live out of harmony with God, with conscience, and with good spirits—having commerce with discordant spirits—perform all things in a dissonant, disordered, and shivering manner; so much so that, being out of harmony with themselves, they agree with no one, but approve of all things that are dissenting and disordered. But those who are in agreement with themselves and with God, being placed in their proper station, feel all things corresponding to them and easily guided: because (as <margin>The same</margin> Porphyry says in the same place), "every good thing is easy to govern and steady, because it proceeds from order; from which follows agreement, tranquility, and the easy consensus of all things."

->Men placed in their proper station and well-ordered easily rule over all things.<-

### Chap. VII. ###

**I**t is spread by celebrated fame (as we have already often said) that man, by the testimony of Holy Scripture, is preferred and set over all the works of the hands of God. Imitating these doctrines, the poet of Sulmo <note>original: *Sulmo*; referring to Ovid, who was born in the town of Sulmo. This quote is from *Metamorphoses* I.76-78</note> sings: "A holier animal than these, and more capable of high mind, was still lacking, one that could rule over the rest; man was born." Nevertheless, we see most people, and almost the whole crowd of men, being enslaved rather than ruling. We do not doubt that this has happened because man, rebellious against God (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical texts were attributed</note> says), has fallen from the contemplation of the Father and from His fellowship—from which he used to receive the power of ruling—into the sphere of generation <note>the material world of birth, decay, and physical change</note>, and has been made the most wretched servant of all...

->### OF THE THIRD CANTICLE ###<-

...it is. And (with the Supreme Truth as witness <note>original: *summa Veritate teste*; a reference to Christ or divine revelation</note>) by sin man is made a slave of sin—that is, a slave of Satan who leads him into sin, or of lust, which is the parent of sin itself. 
<margin>James</margin>
For lust (as James says), when it has conceived, gives birth to sin <note>James 1:15</note>. For this reason, all things resist man when he has fallen from his dignity, nor do they deign to hold as their master one who has now been made such a vile slave. And they refuse to obey him until he is restored to his former honor from which he had fallen, and becomes of one mind with God, from whom he may resume the power of ruling, just as he had received it from the beginning. Then he will not fear 
<margin>First Kings</margin>
poisons and enemies; then he will not dread wild beasts, but will strike them with terror, just as we read concerning David in the first volume of Kings <note>modern Bibles call this 1 Samuel; see 17:34-35</note>: who said to King Saul—who was terrified and trying to call him back from the contest with the giant: "Your servant followed a lion and a bear, and I struck them, rescuing the prey from their mouths. And when they rose up against me, I caught them by the chin and choked them." Daniel killed the dragon and stood fearless among the hungry lions. Paul shook off the viper clinging to his hand as if it were chaff, fearing nothing of its bite or its harms, for he had obtained full dominion over it. For Paul did not lack the one who said to the other Apostles: 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
"Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you" <note>Luke 10:19</note>. John drank poison, joyful and steadfast, and escaped unharmed from the boiling oil. For (as 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine, in my judgment, rightly determines in the third book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*) poisonous, hostile, and troublesome animals were not produced in this way at the beginning for the human race; but after sin, they were made hostile and rebellious. This was delivered by the sentence of the Lord as a punishment for the unjust rebellion of our first parents. For to the serpent, the most hostile of all animals to man (so that we may understand what was said to the other hostile animals from that starting point), he said: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring." And having barely uttered the sentence, providing also for the remedy, he said: "He—namely the offspring of the woman—shall crush your head," so that you may be able to harm neither him nor his true followers. For this reason, not only the Apostles but also their successors prevailed against hostile animals. For Jerome led a most fierce lion into his own service <note>referring to the legend of St. Jerome removing a thorn from a lion's paw</note>. And many Anchorites <note>early Christian hermits who lived in total seclusion</note> stayed in caves and caverns of the earth, fearing neither lions, nor bears, nor serpents, nor the most powerful harassing demons. And what is more, the friends of God prevailed against the most bitter natural force of the most impetuous fire. For the three youths in the Chaldean furnace <note>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the book of Daniel</note>, and Thomas in India, extinguished the force of fire, and Francis extinguished the vigor of the glowing iron <note>A reference to St. Francis of Assisi undergoing a cauterization procedure without pain through divine grace</note>. And to 
<margin>Paul</margin>
conclude with Paul (for time would fail me in the telling), the Saints through faith—that is, through a faithful and firm clinging to God—conquered kingdoms, performed justice, obtained the promises, and shut the mouths of lions...

### Where the Power of Ruling Comes From, How It Was Lost, and How It Was Restored. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Pliny</margin>
**W**e have said long ago that the power of ruling <note>original: *dominandi uim*</note> was implanted in man by the Supreme Architect <note>original: *Opifice summo*; a term for God as the creator</note>. But what this power is, and how we possess it, I think must be examined. Pliny <note>referring to Pliny the Elder, author of the 1st-century *Natural History*</note> examines this with subtle investigation, saying: "An elephant, happening upon a man in the wilderness who is simply wandering, is said to be merciful and gentle, even showing him the way." The same elephant, noticing a man's footprints before seeing the man himself, trembles for fear of an ambush, stops to sniff the air, looks around, and huffs in anger. By these and other signs which the natural historian adds in the same place, it is clear that man is greatly feared; but from where that fear comes, we could hardly understand. 

But lest we seem to claim spring from "only one rose" (as they say) <note>a variation of the proverb "one swallow does not make a summer," meaning one shouldn't generalize from a single example</note>, in this same way the tiger is terrified—she who is more savage than other beasts and even scorns the footprints of elephants—is said to move her cubs immediately upon seeing a man. How is he recognized, when he had never been seen before by the one who fears him? For it is certain that forests of this kind are rarely frequented. Truly, they marvel at the rarity of the footprint itself. But how do they know they should be feared? Or rather, why do they fear those seen more often, though they [the beasts] are so much superior in strength, size, and speed? 

Surely this is the nature of things, this is its power: that the swiftest and largest of beasts, who have never seen what they should fear, immediately understand why it is to be feared. However, what this nature of man is that strikes fear into 
<margin>Apollo.</margin>
beasts, Pliny does not declare for whoever might inquire and suggest it. But Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, while being led by the elephants of Phraotes, King of the Bactrians, to the Brahmans <note>a high-caste group in India known to the Greeks as philosophers</note>, when he saw a small boy leading that huge animal with a hook fixed in the elephant's neck, he tested Damis—his inseparable companion—as to where this great obedience of such a vast animal toward a boy came from. And to the ignorant Damis, who longed to be taught, he said: "It is from a certain active terror, instilled in man by the Architect, which the lower creatures sensing, all animals fear and revere man himself." This terror the 
<margin>Hebrews</margin>
Hebrews call <term>pahad</term> <note>Hebrew: פחד, meaning "dread" or "terror"</note>. And this is stronger in one person and less in another.

<summary>This page discusses the inherent "power of ruling" granted to humans by God, citing Pliny the Elder and Apollonius of Tyana to show how even the largest wild animals instinctively fear and obey humans. It identifies this supernatural dread as the Hebrew concept of "pahad."</summary>

But this power was greatest in Isaac: therefore Jacob, to whom the father had granted it by hereditary right, said to Laban the Aramean, his uncle and father-in-law: *Unless the Lord God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac had been with me, perhaps you would have sent me away empty-handed.* <note>Quoting Genesis 31:42. In this context, "the Fear of Isaac" is a title for God.</note> Where in Hebrew, for "fear," that word <term>pachad</term> <note>Hebrew *pachad* (פַּחַד) refers to a deep, trembling dread or awe, distinct from ordinary fear.</note> is used. And in the same place Jacob swore again by the fear, that is <term>pachad</term>, of his father Isaac. For this is like a terrifying sign that subjects anything to man—whether it becomes a servant or an animal. Otherwise, a boy would not rule over oxen, horses, and elephants, nor would a king strike terror into the people of a whole region. Nor does man possess only a sign by which he is feared, but another by which he is loved: in this also he is an image of God, who is hedged in by both tribunals: of love and of fear. In this way, he also becomes an imitator of Christ, of whom it is said: *He shall reign in the house of Jacob.* Participating in both the kindness of Abraham and the terror of Isaac, he possessed a balanced center. And the first-formed man <note>original: *protoplastes*; a Greek-derived term for Adam as the first created being.</note> was decorated with both these royal insignias. Hence
<margin>Adam</margin>

And the more sin weighs down upon a man, the more he falls from that dignity that inspires terror and that kindness that attracts, falling instead into fear and the servitude of others. <margin>Francis</margin> Francis, however, having again embraced the Apostolic life, stripped entirely of money and vices at once, commands all creatures, and they obey him: He turned water into wine; he crossed the fluid element with dry feet; he rendered the rabid wolf most gentle and domestic; <note>A reference to the famous story of Saint Francis and the Wolf of Gubbio.</note> to the chattering swallows, he imposed silence by a single command; he commands the falcon, and it becomes like a rooster that wakes him; he made hares and rabbits domestic; he speaks to the burning fire, and the fire, forgetting its power, provides warmth to the man of God without a horrible burning. He performed many wonderful things of this kind, having been restored to his pristine dignity. Nor is the hand of the Lord shortened for all who offer faithful obedience to Him. Nor indeed do all those show this who say, "Lord, Lord," or who wear the outward sign of Christ or his imitators, behaving more like **apes** than leading the true life of Christ and the Saints.

...to exhibit, many things have been attempted in which man appeared as an emulator of God and nature. Archytas of Tarentum (as it is said) made a fiery dove <note>original: *columbā igneā*. Most historical accounts describe Archytas's mechanical pigeon as wooden (*lignea*); "fiery" here may be an OCR error or refer to the steam/air propulsion used to make it fly.</note> flying through the air. Certain people of our own time also glory in doing such things. The Egyptians (as Mercury <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the beginning of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note> relates) constructed such statues of the Gods that they could speak. Albert, surnamed the Great, is also said to have done this—namely, making a speaking bronze head. And I have found those who boast that they can make all sorts of bodies speak, yet these bodies do not possess vital spirits <note>original: *uirtutes animales*. These are the "powers of the soul" that animate a living being.</note>, nor do they last for long. To bring these things about, they say they summon the powers of the heavens by observing certain celestial alignments.

<margin>
Daedalus.
Roger Bacon.
</margin>
But perhaps another cause is at work. Daedalus is said to have flown with skillfully made wings. In this our own time, a certain man did the same for a short distance. Roger Bacon boasts that he performed many things through pure and natural magic: namely, thunders in the air, clouds and rains, and very many transformations of things.

<margin>
Athenian.
Plato.
</margin>
A good many people, through art, have also been found to be most shrewd emulators of nature; regarding this, the Athenian <note>The "Athenian Stranger," the primary speaker in Plato's *Laws*.</note> says in Plato's tenth book of the *Laws*: art was given to mortals so that they might generate certain later things, not indeed participating in truth and divinity, but producing certain "likenesses" <note>original: *simulachra*.</note> known to themselves. Some, not content with art, became most diligent investigators of nature and strove to bring together those things which had been prepared by nature, applying active agents to passive subjects <note>original: *applicātes actiua passiuis*. This is a fundamental principle in medieval science/magic: "Natural Magic" consists of speeding up natural processes by bringing the right materials together.</note> before the time ordained by nature itself. Whence they commonly seemed to perform miracles, which are nevertheless natural works, occurring solely through the acceleration of time.

<margin>Magi</margin>
Furthermore, those who used to perform these things were called by the Persian name "Magi," that is, "wise men"—although that name is accepted by many as a term for a "necromancer" through a certain misuse. For they were wise and knowledgeable in hidden things. Among them were those who, seeing the star at the birth of the Redeemer of the human race—an event beyond and outside the order of nature, which was otherwise very well known and familiar to them—suspected (as was right) that someone had been born who would transcend the order and limits of nature. Moved by this, they came from Persia and the regions of the East (namely, to the city of Jerusalem and then Bethlehem) to adore the boy pointed out by a marvelous and supernatural sign. For those who are called Magi first studied medicine, so that they might know what was suitable for expelling choler, what for phlegm, and what for black bile <note>These are the "humors" of ancient medicine; health was believed to depend on their balance.</note>; and what was needed to temper the heart, liver, or stomach, and such things. So that they might do this better, they added astronomy, believing that the natures of illnesses, herbs, roots, and other medicinal things could be easily judged from the planets and stars with which they correspond. We prove that Hermes did this, and with him Zoroaster, Charundas, Ostanes, Zamolxis, the Brahmans, the Gymnosophists <note>The "naked philosophers" of India encountered by Alexander the Great.</note>, and many in the middle and later ages whose fame (even though they excelled) is obscure. However, for many reasons to be kept silent here (lest we digress more than is proper), the knowledge of that natural order and the application of things has been lost. Whence others, by the names of evil demons...

### Chapter X.

<margin><unclear>Motes</unclear></margin>
**S**ince therefore (as we have said) some are content to marry the world <note>a Hermetic metaphor for connecting heavenly influences to earthly materials</note> and to apply active things to passive as far as art, genius, and our nature allow, these are called wise men, true philosophers, or magi, searching into the secrets of nature and the symbols of things. They are not to be held worthy of any rebuke or injury, but of all veneration; for the Lord of the universe willed to have them as witnesses and supporters of his most happy birth <note>referring to the Three Magi at the Nativity</note>. But when they consult evil demons, imploring their help to bring about those things which neither art nor human genius allows: then whatever is perpetrated by their favor, those are not miracles, but illusions <note>original: *prestigia*, meaning deceptive tricks or "glamours"</note>; because they either occur only according to appearance, or they are done for the harm of those who receive them or those who perform them. For they appear as donkeys, or horses, or any other animals, seen as transformed only by eyes that are fascinated and deceived. Hence that woman, who was judged by the common people to be a mare, appeared to Hilarion <note>Saint Hilarion, a 4th-century desert hermit known for his spiritual discernment</note> as a woman, as she truly was. We indeed acknowledge many obstacles brought about or removed by God, Angels, and demons: for sometimes they disturb the eyes of the onlookers, and sometimes the medium through which they look. For demons stand present (as we have learned by clear experience) before ten or twenty people, but are seen by only one or two, and by the others not at all. And this is because they hide themselves at will, and at will make themselves visible. Likewise, many will judge that a donkey, a lion, a rooster, a goat, or a man is standing there. Others, however, see nothing at all: and that happens through the art and illusion of evil demons. But let us come to the heavenly beings.

XLIX
# THIRD SONG

...their eyes, they saw themselves to be in Samaria. This the holy man <note>referring to the prophet Elisha in 2 Kings 6</note> sought not at all for the harm of the Assyrians, but for the glory of his God. For when the King of Israel wanted to strike them, he said: "By no means; for you did not capture them with your sword. Instead, set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master." Behold how, at the prayer of a <term>well-attuned man</term> <note>original: *bene chordati*, literally "well-stringed," describing a soul in harmonious resonance with God</note>, the power of vision was increased beyond natural limits in the boy, and diminished in the Assyrians, and then restored again. But let us return to where we digressed. Thus, some wonders were performed by soothsayers and illusionists—by whatever name they may be called—according to appearance, which are rightly called <term>illusions</term> <note>original: *prestigia*, referring to deceptive tricks or "glamours" that fool the senses</note>. Some also were done by the art of demons, either by transferring things—as we already mentioned regarding crops moved to other fields—or by applying active agents to passive ones. Just as when Pharaoh’s magicians were chanting, frogs and flies were brought forth, produced by demons through a rapid gathering in a short time of things that would naturally take a long time to develop; or by transmutation, just as they did by turning water into blood. And much has been said about soothsaying women who transform many things. But these people neither confer any benefit, nor are they capable of things that are truly above nature. For the frogs, flies, and blood served only as a <term>curse</term> <note>original: *maleficium*</note> upon their own Egyptians. However, those things performed above nature and for a beneficial purpose are called true miracles. Moses, therefore, at God's command, performed a miracle by bringing forth lice, for which there was no nearby material to be gathered. Furthermore, by bringing water from the rock, manna from heaven, and preserving the <margin>David</margin> people from sickness, as the <term>Psalmist</term> <note>original: *Psalmographus*, likely referring to David</note> sings: *And there was not one feeble person among their tribes.* The preservation of their clothes so they would not wear out, and many things of this sort, were true miracles. Some of these, even if performed as a curse—or rather as a punishment for the Egyptians' unbelief and insolence—nevertheless resulted in the benefit of the liberated people. But the illusions of the Egyptians were of no use to anyone. Elijah and Elisha performed miracles, raising the dead, multiplying oil and flour, healing the sick, and such like. But above all, <margin>CHRIST</margin> Christ performed miracles, commanding as the true Lord of kings; and always for a benefit, but never for a curse. And what his followers have done in his name is now spread by celebrated fame throughout the whole world, as we touched upon above. From this, it was seen in those immediate or close disciples of his that the true Kingdom of God existed, which he had promised to give; or rather, which he had already given, when he said: "The Kingdom of God is within you." And again: "Behold, I have given you power over every hostile and resisting force"; namely, for you will easily have friendly power at your command. He, therefore, has restored the lost kingdom to us, provided that we, being well-attuned, follow his footsteps with a straight and perfect stride.

<margin>Origen</margin> This agreement is not merely between two or three men; rather (as Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian</note> rightly understands), it is the harmony of the <term>natural man</term> <note>original: *animalis hominis*, referring to the soul-led or earthly nature of a human being</note> with the spiritual man. The harmony of three is when both of these are in accord with God. And this is that <term>tempering</term> <note>original: *temperamentum*, meaning a proper blending or tuning</note> which we express—or rather, which God Himself expects from everyone—if He is to receive grateful and sweet prayers. For then a man is like a <term>tuned lyre</term> <note>original: *temperata cithara*</note>, rendering every voice and sound of his work pleasant and most sweet to God, so much so that God Himself, sounding in their midst, provides force and energy, so that the prayers are pleasing and effective to the Fatherly source of all good things, from whom all goods are drawn and whatever is asked is obtained.

<margin>Moses</margin> Here the prayer of Moses (or rather, Moses praying) prevailed so greatly that it changed the divine sentence. Even when God said, "Let me be, that the fury of my wrath may be kindled against them and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation," Moses did not care for the promised exaltation—being already in harmony and united with God—but cared instead for God’s own glory. From this place he prayed, saying: "Let not (I beseech you) your wrath be kindled against this people, lest the Egyptians say: 'With cunning he led them out to kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth.' Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: 'I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and all this land of which I spoke I will give to your seed, and you shall possess it.'" Because of this, the Lord was appeased, hearing the one praying, Moses, as a truly faithful and <term>well-harmonized</term> <note>original: *bene consonum*</note> servant. Zealous for the honor of the Lord, Moses set forth those things which the nations might use to bring insult to the Lord, and he brought up the oath already sworn, lest the malevolent should mark Him for unfaithfulness to His promise. And this man, being so <term>well-stringed</term> <note>original: *bene chordatus*</note> with God, had such power with Him that he overcame Him, so that God could not punish the rebels against Moses' judgment and consent. Hence He said: "Let me be." And what is wonderful is that God came into agreement with Moses’ judgment, so as not to disagree with him who was so well-tuned with Him.

Hezekiah prayed for himself, yet he obtained the request not only for himself but for the city and the people to be freed from the Assyrians. And by what virtue (I ask) did he rely, or by what reason was he fortified? Surely because he felt himself to be <term>well-stringed</term> <note>original: *bene chordatum*</note> with God. In this place he said: "Remember (I beseech you) how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes."

### THE FOURTH TONE

My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns <note>original: *cisternas dissipatas*; quoting Jeremiah 2:13. In this context, it refers to leaky or ruined vessels that cannot hold the "water" of spiritual grace</note> that are unable to hold water. They have also changed their glory into an idol; for the glory of man—his goodness and happiness—consists in clinging to God. But he creates an idol who, having neglected God, worships himself or something even baser, with great **dissonance** and a ruined order. And since tranquility arises from order, one who lacks order also lacks tranquility. Therefore, by making an idol of himself or of inferior things in an inverted order, he digs for himself broken cisterns that can hold no water of true delight. Thus, when a man is restored to his glory and dignity and returns to the fountain of living water and true refreshment—from which he may always draw that which allows him to rejoice—only then does he live joyful and happy.

# WHAT THE SPIRIT IS: CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>The Hebrews</margin>
**S**ince the entire law of the Gospel deals with the perfecting of man according to the spirit, always concerning itself with spiritual matters, it is therefore right and timely that we should briefly examine the spirit. This term is used so variously in Holy Scripture that it is understood with no small difficulty. For it is among the most hidden things of nature; nothing can be discussed concerning it except what we can gather from the Holy Scripture—issued by that first and principal Spirit—or what we can forge from the characters of the words in that language <note>The author refers to Hebrew, which Renaissance scholars believed was the "natural language" where names perfectly matched the essence of things</note> in which all names were given to things according to their properties. For the Hebrews call the spirit *Ruah* <note>original: רוח (*Ruach*)</note>. In this word there are three letters. One is *Vav* <note>original: ו</note>, which is the letter of divinity, signifying the number six <note>In Hebrew numerology, Vav has the value of 6</note>. According to this number, the supreme Spirit himself, the craftsman of all things, first brooding over the fertile waters, arranged (as was fitting) this entire machine of the world. For the principle of all things is threefold—going forth into work, adorning, and nourishing—and each of these acts through an intermediary spirit, from which the number six results in the greatest unity.

<margin>Hebrew Theologians</margin>
For this reason, the most profound Hebrew theologians have said that this letter of divinity, *Vav* <note>original: ו</note>—which signifies the beginning and the end, since it is the end of the single digits and the beginning of the tens—has six "thorns" <note>original: *spinulas*; likely referring to the decorative strokes or "tittles" in Hebrew calligraphy</note>. In that respect, as God himself is the beginning marked by that letter, he is a trinity: from whom, in whom, and through whom all things exist. But in that respect where he is the director, nourisher, and bringer-back, he enjoys another spiritual trinity. This is not because there are three spirits of God (even though

<margin>Abraham</margin>
Abraham, in the *Book of Formation* <note>original: *Sefer Yetzirah*, an ancient Jewish mystical text traditionally attributed to the patriarch Abraham</note>, speaks of "spirit from spirit"), but because his operation is threefold. According to this operation,

<margin>David</margin>
the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> in the fiftieth Psalm calls him the "principal spirit," the "right spirit," and the "holy spirit" <note>Referring to Psalm 51:10-12 (Psalm 50 in the Vulgate)</note>. There is, therefore, in that word and name the letter of divinity, which is *Vav* <note>ו</note>. There is also another letter of life, which is *Chet* <note>original: ח</note>. For life is called *Hai* <note>original: חי</note>. The third is *Resh* <note>original: ר</note>, which signifies two hundreds, and matter, or a certain corporeality. For the number two <term>Binary</term> <note>The number two was often associated in Pythagorean and Hermetic thought with division, matter, and the "falling away" from the unity of the number one</note> implies matter; hence,

<margin>Jerome</margin>
(according to Jerome) it is always unlucky unless it is made happy by being joined with another number. For that which is material is happy only when associated with life and divinity.

<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
The "two hundred" <note>The numerical value of the letter *Resh* is 200</note> imported by the letter *Resh* are those things dealt with in the Song of Songs. There, after *Aleph* <note>א</note>, and "one," and "a thousand" have been attributed to divinity, it is added: *And two hundred to those who keep its fruit.* <note>Quoting Song of Solomon 8:12</note>. For we are placed as "keepers" in the vineyard of the Lord with a binary corporeality <note>A reference to the dual nature of man, composed of body and soul</note>. If we keep the fruitful commandments of the Lord there, we shall at last be united with that *Aleph* <note>The letter Aleph signifies 1 or 1,000, representing God's unity or "the thousand" belonging to Solomon</note> prepared for every truly peaceful person, and for him who has peace within himself. The spirit, therefore, is a certain bond, binding and connecting two extremes together: quickening and strengthening them according to the condition of the uniting spirit. Hence it tastes of the nature of the two extremes which are being united, and of its own nature as the connecting medium, as in...

<margin>Paul</margin>
Apostle teaches we are separated by the power of the word of God, saying:

> The word of God is living, and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit. <note>original: "Viuus est sermo Dei, & efficax, & penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti ptingens usq; ad diuisionẽ animæ, & spūs." From Hebrews 4:12.</note>

For the word of God teaches us to remove all rational affection, which pertains to the spirit, from animal desire and pleasure, and to lead it back to God through that supreme and divine part which is in us by the grace of God. The spirit ought to be united with this higher part not only in affection, but in reality. Nor can it be fully united with the higher part unless it is separated from the lower, just as fire proceeding from wood is not united with the higher, ethereal fire unless it is separated from the denser material. That which is separated is also distinguished. And if it be said that the spirit is the rational soul, we grant it. For it is
<margin>Plotinus
The Academics</margin>
a certain medium (as pleases Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> and the Academics <note>Followers of Plato's school of philosophy</note>) between the lower animal nature and the divine, which is higher, connecting both and able to be united with both. But lest readers be offended when they hear that the soul is something corporeal, we say that it possesses or tastes of something of corporeality while it is in the body and uses the body as its necessary instrument. But if it is separated entirely from the body, it is united with that higher divine part—indeed, with God Himself—being entirely removed from all corporeality. Finally, it draws with it the body, which is glorified, and for which the soul stood as the immediate form. And since the soul is the medium leading the body into a better fate, it must necessarily participate in the nature of both. This is as much as we can say regarding our spirit at present.

***

### Of how many kinds the spirit is. Chapter II.

**A**nd because spirits are found not only in man, but also in other things, let us explain the various natures of spirits. For there is a natural spirit, a celestial one, a demonic one, a human one, an angelic one, and a divine one. The natural spirit is that medium, in both the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>the universe</note> and the <term>microcosm</term> <note>the individual human</note>, by which one member acts upon another. In man, it is the imaginative or "phantastic" power.

<summary>This page defines the spirit as a "nexus" or mediating substance that connects the physical body and animal soul to the divine intellect. It uses biblical examples of strength and philosophical concepts from Plotinus to argue that the spirit must separate from lower desires to unite with God.</summary>

->OF THE THIRD CANTICLE<-

...in the head, so that it may move a hand or a foot, and immediately it moves; although the limb is quite distant from the head, where that thinking power resides. This happens through the mediation of manifold <term>spirits</term><note>In Renaissance thought, "spirits" were subtle substances that carried signals between the soul and the body.</note> that exist between the head and the hand or foot. Concerning these natural or vital spirits, medical authors have written much; we leave those details to be read in their own books. For it is through these spirits that the soul is united with the flesh and the body, from which it draws life; and through the body, with these spirits acting as mediators, the soul performs its work. In the same way, there is a manifold spirit in this lower "world-body" through which one thing acts upon another: just as the magnet acts upon iron, attracting it; and as various stones act upon humans, bringing joy, strength, and inducing manifold dispositions. Whatever acts upon another does so not only through its primary qualities <note>Primary qualities refers to the basic physical properties like hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note> but through what they call a "hidden virtue." Since this is the medium that allows one thing to act upon another, it can rightly be called a spirit. There is also a celestial spirit, by which lower things are bound to the heavens, so that they may draw from them and receive heavenly <term>influences</term><note>The "inflowing" of power from the stars and planets into the earthly realm.</note> through that very spirit. There is also an evil demonic spirit and a good angelic spirit, both of which are given to every human being. Their duty is to seek union with our own spirit, so that each might call out and draw our spirit to itself. The evil one strives to make us like himself and united to him through evil works, as the Supreme Truth <note>A common title for Christ.</note> says of the betrayer:

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> I have chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil,

meaning he had turned toward the diabolical spirit through his own wickedness, becoming united with it and made the same. For these spirits mix together just like water and wine, or two wines, or two waters poured together. But the good spirit strives to lead us into the nature of Angels through good works and things symbolic of them, as God testifies concerning John in the book of Malachi:

<margin>Malachi</margin>
> Behold, he says, I send my messenger <note>original: "Angelum"</note> before your face.

Finally, there is the divine spirit, which is called the <term>nexus</term> <note>A bond or connection</note> by holy and true teachers; it binds our soul with God himself, having first been made one with that spirit, according to that saying of the Apostle:

<margin>Paul</margin>
> He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him. <note>original: "Qui adhæret Deo unus spiritus efficitur cū eo." From 1 Corinthians 6:17.</note>

And this is the perfected union which we ultimately hope to attain. And because all things must finally be led back to their beginning from which they proceeded—since all things exist through him from whom all things emanated (as the Apostle teaches)—

<margin>The same</margin>
therefore that spirit, which by "brooding over the waters" brought all things into the light, is required so that through that same spirit they may be led back to that from which they came. Hence it is said of him:

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
> The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world:

And again: *And by the spirit of his mouth all their power.* For by him not only the heavens, but this entire universal machine is sustained, lives, is strengthened, is bound together, and is finally led back to where all things tend. Moreover, this divine spirit is entirely free from all corporeality; it is like a fire that consumes, melts, transforms, and leads those it touches into its own nature, making them divine. Until he fully deifies them, he is always flowing into them and soaking through them, existing as both the fire and the channel through which it flows.

**spirit:** a subtle substance; **soul:** the animating principle; **body:** the physical frame; **magnet:** a natural attractor; **celestial influence:** power from the stars; **demonic:** pertaining to evil spirits; **angelic:** pertaining to good messengers; **deification:** the process of becoming god-like; **divine nexus:** the holy bond.

<page-num>LIII</page-num>
<header>FIFTH TONE</header>

## What the spirit does in man beyond the soul. Chapter III.

<margin>
Plato.
Hebrews.
Plotinus.
Paul.
</margin>

**T**ruly, if we wish to follow the Peripatetic <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who generally taught that a human being is a composite of only two parts: a physical body and a rational soul.</note> doctrine, from which we hold that man is composed only of soul and body, it will be difficult to explain what the spirit is and what it does in man beyond the soul, since each of these is considered by them to be the same thing. But if we listen to the Platonists and the Hebrews, who distinguish between them and place more parts in man: for Plotinus <note>A major Greek philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, who lived in the 3rd century AD.</note> posits three things in man: the highest, the lowest, and the middle. The highest is that divine part, which our writers call the "superior portion" <note>In mystical theology, the 'superior portion' of the soul is the part that remains in constant contemplation of God and is incapable of sinning.</note>. The lowest is what Paul calls the "animal man" <note>original: "animalem hominem"; a reference to the "natural man" or "fleshly man" mentioned in 1 Corinthians 2:14.</note>. The middle is the soul or spirit, connecting both.

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
These three things all the Hebrews call <term>nephesh, ruach, neshamah</term> <note>Hebrew: נפש רוח נשמה. These terms represent a hierarchy of the soul: the vital/animal breath, the spirit/ego, and the divine spark.</note>. Which we, in translation, call the soul, the spirit, and a certain divine thing, for which we have no more suitable word than the "superior portion"—or as we have it translated in Genesis as the "breath of life" <note>original: "spiraculum"; the breath of God mentioned in Genesis 2:7.</note>, breathed into us by God, or by His spirit.
<margin>Genesis</margin>
Which, when united with the lower soul through the mediation of our spirit, the whole is called by the common name <term>soul</term> <note>Hebrew: "nephesh" (נפש)</note>.
<margin>Plotinus</margin>
Therefore, that intermediate part is what Plotinus calls "rational" and the Hebrews call "spirit," but our own writers call it "soul" because of the mixture it has with it. That highest part also always prays for the best things, never sinning, but murmuring against sin and error.
<margin>Paul</margin>
The lowest part is always immersed in evil and lust, according to what the Apostle says:
> I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive into the law of sin: so that I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want. <note>A combination of Romans 7:19 and 7:23, where Paul describes the internal conflict between the spirit and the flesh.</note>

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
But the middle spirit, which is also called the "rational soul" by Plotinus, can adhere to either at will. It earns merit by adhering to the higher, but by clinging to the lower, it turns away from God. That higher part, since it never consents to sin, in no way sins, and therefore is not condemned; but when its companions are to be punished, it departs unharmed, just as when a window is closed, the solar light departs, the space remaining dark. So, when that light departs, the soul remains, and the spirit must be thrust into the inner darkness, to which the outer ones will be added,
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
according to that testimony of the Highest Truth regarding the damned:
> Go into the outer darkness. <note>Matthew 25:30.</note>

And because man performs a twofold work through the mediation of that higher part—namely, he understands God and earns merit by working well—hence, when that part departs, he can neither understand God nor earn any merit. Thus he is rendered impenitent, never to return to God. But the middle soul, which I believe to be the same as the spirit, either consents to that higher part and earns merit, eventually being united with it and made blessed; or it consents to the lower part, which pulls toward evil and is agitated by an evil demon, and then it earns punishment; and it becomes so depraved that it becomes one with that evil demon itself. Therefore, the spirit differs from the lot of the superior and inferior soul, though it can be united with either at will: but walking in the proper path, it must be separated from the lower and united with the higher.

It argues that the spirit's salvation or damnation depends on whether it chooses to align itself with the divine spark or with lower fleshly desires.</summary>

<header>THIRD SONG.</header>

### What agreement man has with the spirit of God. Chapter 4.

**S**ince we have said that the spirit is a medium connecting both extremes, it follows that it shares the nature of both. Therefore, the Spirit of God, by whose mediation man is united with God, shares the divine nature: indeed, it is God Himself. It also has a very great <term>correspondence</term><note>original: "symbolum"; in this context, it refers to a mystical link or shared characteristic between the divine spirit and the human spirit.</note> with that divine element which exists in man. For this reason, the disciples were better suited to be taught by the Holy Spirit, as by a closer person who possessed a more expressive correspondence with man, than by Him <margin>CHRIST</margin> who said: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now" <note>original: "Multa habeo uobis dicere, ſed non poteſtis portare modo"; quoting Jesus in John 16:12.</note>, meaning me, in my role as teacher. But when that Spirit of Truth comes, he will suggest all things to you and teach you all things, as one who is more familiar to you. For this reason, and not without cause, <margin>Stephen and the Apostles</margin> Stephen, the Apostles, and others are said to be filled with the Holy Spirit rather than with the Son of God. This is because the spirit is more capable of uniting with us than the Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to the second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ.</note>; hence, not even the Word was united with man without the spirit, as the oracle said to the Virgin when she was to conceive: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you" <note>original: "Spũs ſanctus ſupueniet in te"; from the Annunciation in Luke 1:35.</note>, by which medium you shall conceive, and the union of two natures <note>The "two natures" refers to the theological doctrine of Christ being both fully divine and fully human.</note> will occur.

Thus, while our spirit is in the body, it possesses something of a bodily nature; but when united with God, it separates from the body—especially from this corruptible and heavy one. For according to the <margin>Platonists</margin> Platonists, the spirit carries with it an <term>ethereal body</term> composed of the "fifth essence" (as they call it), which they name the "vehicle of the soul." In this vehicle, the soul can suffer the torment of fire, feel sorrow or joy regarding many bodily things, and appear visible at will. There are also those among them who assert that the soul is eventually separated even from that ethereal body and is united inwardly with God. This occurs when the soul has been thoroughly purified, not only in the first but in the second <term>purgatory</term>. For they believe in a double purgatory: in the first, souls are cleansed of filth, if there be any; in the second, they are more perfectly purified so that they may become more divine and be able to say <margin>David</margin> with the divine Harpist: "In peace I will sleep in that very place, and find holy rest" <note>original: "In pace in idipſum dormiã, & reqẽ ſcã"; a reference to Psalm 4:8.</note>. But since we hold from the sacred scriptures that our bodies are to be glorified along with the soul, this shall happen when, according to the Apostolic teaching, the body puts on the nature of the spirit; leaving behind the animal and corruptible, our bodies shall rise incorruptible and spiritual.

---

### What relationship man has with the Angelic spirit. Chapter 5.

**E**ven as the Angels are also called spirits according to that prophetic saying: <margin>The same (David)</margin> "Who makes your Angels spirits" <note>original: "Qui facis Angelos tuos ſpiritus"; Psalm 104:4.</note>, we must examine what particular correspondence or relationship man has with the angelic spirit. For we receive ministry from them, because (as the Apostle says) <margin>Paul</margin> "all are made ministering spirits" <note>original: "adminiſtratorii ſpiritus"; Hebrews 1:14.</note>. In this ministry they labor to lead us back to God as intermediate and true spirits; thus they share the nature of both God and ourselves. And since the lowest things are led to the higher by intermediaries, and the middle is led to the highest by the superior, there are innumerable intermediate spirits between the Supreme Being and the lowest beings who are to be led to Him. These spirits successively care for man, who procures for himself one guardian after another day by day as he ascends from virtue to virtue.

->What man has in common with the diabolical spirit. Chapter VI.<-

<margin>Mercurius</margin>
**H**umanity (*according to Mercurius* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical "Hermetic" writings are attributed.</note>), consisting of all powers, has commerce with all things: through the intellect with the high and good; through
<margin>Michael</margin>

I have confirmed this in certain people who confessed with their own mouths that they felt within themselves not a soul, but an evil demon, always leading them toward blasphemies against God and toward every kind of crime. There are also those who have commerce and a conjugal mixture with evil demons; these are entirely carnal and earthly, made into food for those demons, just as the divine sentence thundered as a punishment for the first sinner: You shall eat the earth all the days of your life <note>original: "terrā comedes omnibus diebus uitæ tuæ"; from Genesis 3:14.</note>. And to the sinner: You are earth, or dust, and to dust you shall return <note>original: "Terra, uel puluis es, & in puluerē reuertēris"; from Genesis 3:19.</note>. From this, it is gathered that the evil man is given as food to the evil demon.

->How the spirit of one is understood to enter into the body of another. Chapter VII.<-

**F**ollowing the mixing of two spirits—the human and the evil demon—when the latter enters into a body, the other also enters, having now been made an evil demon. Both enter, having become the same, not to
connect the living creature with the higher portion, but so that they may also lead the spirit of the one whom they enter into their own lot (if they can). If not, then they enter so that they may torment him by the power granted by God through a judgment hidden from us; and so that the evil demon may take pleasure in that seat which had been prepared for the Supreme Lord. Indeed, he delights too much in dwelling in a house ordered for the Highest Guest, who commanded and urged with great diligence that it be prepared.

<margin>Isaiah</margin>

A lodging must be prepared no less than a path, and both must be arranged with uprightness, since the guest who is to dwell there is the supreme Truth and righteousness. But the evil demon, being by nature a liar and crooked, ensures that a place is prepared for himself through error and falsehood. Nor is the dwelling-place of our heart ever left empty: for when one guest departs, another immediately enters. As it is said of <margin>Saul</margin> Saul in the first book of Kings: *The Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him* <note>original: "Spiritus Dñi recesserat a Saul, & exagitabat eū spūs neq̃, a Dño"; 1 Samuel 16:14. In the older Latin tradition, the books of Samuel were often called 1 and 2 Kings.</note>, being sent out as the order of things required. So it is also held in the Gospel <margin>Luke</margin> titled according to Luke, concerning that man possessed by an unclean spirit; once the spirit was expelled, the house was made clean. The expelled one, returning so that he might re-enter, was not able to do so until the good guest was put to flight by the impurity brought in by seven more wicked spirits. Once the good guest was driven away, the evil ones entered. For neither God, nor an Angel, nor a demon dwells in anyone, nor acts with them, except through a mediating spiritual power. Here <margin>Paul</margin> Paul, after he had mentioned many things which God bestows and works within us, adds: *But one and the same spirit works all these things* <note>original: "Hæc autē opatur unus atq̃ idē spiritus"; 1 Corinthians 12:11.</note>. Yet this is sometimes (as we touched upon above) called the Spirit of the Father, according to that word of the Savior: *But the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you* <note>original: "Sed spiritus Patris uestri q̃ loquitur in uobis"; Matthew 10:20.</note>. Sometimes it is called the Spirit of the Son, of which the Apostle says <margin>Christ, Paul, Acts of the Apostles</margin> when dealing with the Galatians: *God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts* <note>original: "Misit Deus spiritū filii sui in corda nostra"; Galatians 4:6.</note>. Sometimes it is a spirit from a spirit: as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: *They were all filled with the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Repleti sunt omnes spiritu sancto"; Acts 2:4.</note>. This Spirit, however, did not depart from its own dignity and deity, but by a certain spiritual power it sanctified and deified the spirit of the Apostles upon whom it was poured out.

### What harmony may be brought about between the spirit and the soul. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Philosopher</margin> **S**o that the good spirit, whether angelic or divine, may be introduced into us, harmony must be brought about between our spirit and our soul—not necessarily that soul which is the same as the spirit, but with the "better" part. From this harmony, the soul may finally come to a union with the spirit, and lead the lower part along with it as a medium, transforming it into spirit for a better fate. For just as in the <term>transmutative art</term><note>A reference to alchemy, the medieval forerunner of chemistry focused on transforming base metals into gold and achieving spiritual perfection.</note> (as the more secret Philosophers say), there is a medium, like a certain "spirit" that is clothed in and first drinks in the nature of gold, and afterward, by a mighty and very swift power, leads all other <margin>Chaldeans</margin> metals into gold. And because the spirit of man is transformable into different natures, hence the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages often associated with magic, astrology, and early philosophy.</note> said that man is an animal of a "dissolvable" nature, having no fixed image, but many foreign and external ones. For the spirit is transformed not only into the higher and lower natures that are within man, but into a demon, an Angel, or God, as we have mentioned. And when, having been transformed into a better state, it leads the lower part with it, it makes itself more refined, just as gold is refined when drawn through a very narrow opening: so that like a silken or linen thread it may be led at will, and from a "living" or animal being it becomes a "spiritual" one. Hence, not without mystery, the word <term>Ruach</term><note>Hebrew: רוח, meaning "spirit" or "breath."</note> which is "spirit," when its letters are reversed according to the Kabbalistic method of <term>Siruph</term><note>Also spelled "Tsiruf"; a Kabbalistic technique of permuting or rearranging letters to find hidden meanings.</note>, yields <term>Hur</term><note>Hebrew: חור, meaning "hole" or "cavern."</note>, which signifies a "hole" or "opening," through which the passing animal body becomes spiritual, so that, united with the higher, it may be made blessed. And this happens when the spirit first unites with that...

### On the Sweetest Harmony of Man with God, so that he may begin to enjoy Him here.
### The Sixth Tone.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **M**an emulates God by nature. | Chapter I. |
| Man mirrors the Archetype <note>The divine blueprint or original model in God's mind.</note> in form. | Chapter II. |

CANTICLE THE THIRD

-># MAN EMULATES GOD BY NATURE<-
->## CHAPTER ONE<-

Since it is our purpose to explain the way in which Man corresponds to God and is made like Him—as we are urged and invited to do in many places—we have thought it appropriate to revisit the image of Himself with which the Supreme <term>Artisan: Latin 'Opifex', referring to God as the master craftsman of the universe</term> produced man. For it is already a commonplace to everyone that man was made in the image of God and brought forth in His likeness. 

However, since it has not yet been clearly explained <note>original: 'enucleatum', literally 'to take the kernel out of the nut'</note> exactly what this image consists of (if I may say so with the kind permission of those who have written on this), let us investigate it. For by common and old-fashioned teaching, it is said that the three divine persons are represented in the three powers of the soul: memory, intellect, and will. Yet this cannot truly be called an "image"—the nature of which is to represent the whole and the total form—as is best determined by our more keen-sighted theologians. It is rather a <term>vestige: or 'trace', a faint mark or footprint (Latin 'vestigium') that hints at something but does not fully represent it</term>, representing not the full subject but some aspect or part of it. And although the entire divinity is contained within the three persons, and even within the very nature of the deity, there are many more things that can be explained in God which man represents most fully in other parts of himself than in those aforementioned three powers. 

<margin>The Scotists</margin> Hence, some of the more acute among the newer theologians, not content with that simple assigned reason for the image, say that it consists not only in those three powers or (to speak in their fashion) in "primary acts" alone, but also in "secondary" ones. For there is in us intellect, memory, and will; and these represent the same three in God. There is, moreover, the "word" produced by our intellect and the "love" emanating from our will—one of which signifies the Divine Word, and the other the Holy Spirit, who is a certain kind of Love. 

Truly, the intellect, having an object present and producing it, portrays the Father. But this image in man falls no less short of the God it portrays than a painted image of a man falls short of the true man himself. For the "word" produced within us, and likewise the "love"—which they call "secondary acts"—are <term>accidents: in scholastic philosophy, qualities or properties that exist in a subject but are not essential to its nature</term> in us; but in God, they are substance and are one and the same with God Himself. And memory, which in us is the recollection of past things, is in God the most full contemplation of all things past, present, and future. 

But we can hunt for an even more expressive image of God in man by comparing to God not only the soul, but the whole man, in whom the complete image of God Himself shines back. God is, therefore, full life, giving life to all members of the worldly body. There is also in the soul a certain fountain of life, emanating however from the supreme and divine sea, [flowing] to all the body's own members according to its...

<meta>Catchword: con/ (likely 'constitutionem' or 'concordiam')</meta>

The author suggests that the true likeness to God is found in the whole human person, body and soul, emulating God's role as the life-giver to the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how man serves as an image of God. ->### THE SIXTH TONE<-

<margin>Solomon</margin>...granting life by His decree. Hence it is said in the sacred page: *And he breathed into his nostrils the breath, or the soul of lives* <note>original: 'spiraculum, aut animam uitarum'. This refers to Genesis 2:7, using a phrasing that suggests multiple "levels" of life.</note>: so that He might provide the body with a life that is vegetative, sensitive, rational, intellectual, and divine. God is the one who contains all things by His power; and the wise man [Solomon] says of man in his sermon: *God made man from the dust of the earth, and gave him the power of containing all things.* God knew all things. Man also can know all knowable things, since he has as his <term>adequate object: a technical term in Scholastic philosophy meaning the full range of what a faculty, like the mind, is capable of perceiving</term> (as the Theologians and Philosophers say) the True, or Being in general. But the image differs from the one imagined: God understands all things in a single act, while man understands through a certain succession.

Furthermore, God is a certain circle, drawing His origin from no other place but Himself, and tending toward Himself, He brings all things there with Him. Man is also a circle proceeding from God and tending toward Him: leading all things there since he contains all things. Nor does he ever rest until he reaches God Himself, from whom he proceeded. He also emulates God as much as he can in duration. But since he cannot possess his whole duration all at once <note>referring to the idea that God lives in an eternal "now," while humans experience time second-by-second</note>, he lasts at least through a perpetual succession. And he is so similar and (if I may say so) of the same nature as God, that eventually he is united with Him; as we shall declare in the proper place, God willing.

Finally, God is free from <term>passions: in this context, 'passions' (Latin: passiones) refers to any emotion or physical state that involves being "acted upon" or changed, such as anger or pain</term>, except insofar as He suffered in the body He assumed [as Christ]: no passion indeed passes over to God Himself. Just as He does not receive passion when (as Jeremiah says) filling heaven and earth, He is changed in the members of the worldly body which He fills. 

<margin>Jeremiah</margin> In this sense, perhaps not foolishly, all those scriptural sentences can be understood in which God is said to be angry, to repent, to grieve, to desire, and the like. For He does not "repent" except insofar as it appears in the members or things which He fills: from which, if He withdraws Himself and turns away His face, all things are troubled; and being void of the life-giving God, they return to their dust. Thus those members—nay, God in them—seem to grieve, be saddened, be indignant, and repent: namely, by ceasing from His customary influence. But when His spirit returns, which fills the whole circle of the lands, everything is recreated and all things seem to rejoice. 

<margin>Aristotle. Plotinus.</margin> Our soul is no different, of which Aristotle and Plotinus say: "He who says the soul is saddened or rejoices, says that it weaves or spins." Thus, the soul itself does not rejoice or grow sad—just as it neither weaves nor spins—except insofar as it is joined to the body. For it belongs to the animal part (as Plotinus follows) to suffer and to act, but not to the rational soul, nor the intellect. Rather, it is the role of these higher powers to direct the animal which acts: just as it is God's role to moderate the world, whose members are secondary causes operating with such agitations and passions. Nor is there found any disposition in man in which something of divinity does not shine forth; nor is there anything in God that is not represented in man. But let us come to the diagram.

## Man Portrays the Archetype in His Form. Chapter II.

<margin>David</margin>
**I**f, however, Man is to contain the true image of God, it is necessary that he enjoys a form very similar to His. But alas, where are we entering? What form shall we assign to Him who is closed in by no boundaries, shaped by no lines, and painted by no colors? For this reason, divine law provides with such great diligence that no image should be made at all, neither of God Himself nor of any heavenly things: both so that visible creatures should not be adored through those idols, and also so that what cannot be portrayed might not be falsely expressed. Yet, even if no figure can be drawn, and nothing is found among inferior things in which the likeness or image of God may be discerned, we shall nonetheless—supported by the testimony of God—hunt for His likeness and figure in man, at least through a certain <term>analogy: a comparison between two things that are otherwise unlike, used here to bridge the gap between the physical man and the spiritual God</term> by which the supreme <term>Artisan: "Opifex," a common term for God as the creator-craftsman of the universe</term> Himself deigned to ascribe these things to Himself, such as the divisions and all the members of the human body. For He said that He has a right hand, just as is chanted in the Davidic song:
> The Lord said to my lord: sit at my right hand.

He also has a left hand, at which the wicked who are to be condemned will be placed in the final examination. He is also said at times to sit like a man, as He says in Isaiah:
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
> Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.

He is also said in Genesis to walk at midday, or in the breeze of the day. And regarding the paths of His eternity, the <term>Psalmist: "Psalmographus," referring to David as the writer of the Psalms</term> says:
<margin>David</margin>
> They have seen your entries, O God; the entries of my God and my King who is in the sanctuary.

These steps and paths sometimes strike terror, so that by them (according to the testimony of Habakkuk) the mountains of the age are crushed and the hills of the world are bowed down: because (as Jerome rightly explains) when He came to us, He destroyed the demonic powers and reduced the heights of the age to nothing. Sacred Scripture is a most wealthy witness concerning the members ascribed to God Himself. For He has eyes and ears, concerning which it says in the Davidic hymn:

There is taste and a throat, of which it says in the Song of Songs:

> And it was given to her—that is, to the Lamb and to his bride the Church, whom mercy has betrothed—that she should clothe herself in fine linen, shining and white. For fine linen <note>original: "byssinum," a high-quality ancient flax fabric often associated with purity and priesthood</note> represents the justifications of the saints, which are communicated to us through God's grace and mercy (with Christ as the mediator).

Therefore, by imparting good things to us, He is clothed in this garment as if in fine linen. And because His mercy and immense piety are tempered by the balance of justice, He therefore assumes another garment of justice: which in Scripture is sometimes called blood-stained, and sometimes linen.
<margin>The same</margin>
For He was clothed (says <margin>John</margin>) in a garment sprinkled with blood, and His name was called the Word of God: that very Word through which all things were made and restored. Human nature, united to Him, shed blood to appease divine justice, which requires blood where sin was contracted through flesh and blood. At this garment the Angels marveled (as <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century mystic who wrote extensively on the celestial hierarchy and the nature of God.</note> suggests), saying:
> Why has your garment become red, like those who tread in the winepress?

In the book of Daniel, however, Gabriel—who announced to the Virgin that Christ was to be conceived at that moment and sometimes (not without mystery) represents His very person—was seen clothed in linen, a mystery perhaps to be explained elsewhere. And since He is the supreme beauty making all things beautiful—especially human nature, to which He granted His all-encompassing image—He therefore assumes another garment, which in many places of Holy Scripture, especially in the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms, attributed to King David.</note>, is called **Tipheret** <term>tipheret</term> <note>A Hebrew word meaning "Beauty," "Splendor," or "Glory"; it is one of the ten attributes (Sefirot) of God in Jewish mysticism.</note>. This we have translated sometimes as comeliness, sometimes as beauty, and sometimes as magnificence. But it is properly the name of divine glory and beauty. Communicating this to us in various ways, He says in Ezekiel:
<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
> And I clothed you with diverse colors, and fine linen, and embroidery:

and concluding after many things commemorated there:
> These things I gave to you, so that you might be perfect in comeliness and beauty.

<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
Hence in the Song of Songs, human creation is called the "most beautiful of women," that is, of all creatures. After these, the supreme Governor is clothed in two other garments, by which He shows Himself more familiar to us, and through which many spiritual gifts <note>original: "charismata," divine gifts or graces</note> flow into us. Concerning these garments, it is sung in the Davidic ode:
<margin>David</margin>
> You have clothed Yourself with confession (or celebration) and beauty:

because clearly through these God makes men celebrated and beautiful. These garments are sometimes called "breasts," which indeed suckled the prophets and suckle all those who are familiar with God, just as it is said in the Song of Songs:
> I will give you my breasts.

<margin>Paul</margin>
These are also sometimes named the "third heaven," to which <margin>Paul</margin> was lifted up. And because the Creator Himself also grants us life, a foundation, and the stability of every good work, He is therefore called Life, the Tree of Life, and the Land of the Living. In this land He also shows Himself clothed for us, as the divine Harper <note>A common medieval epithet for King David, author of the Psalms.</note> sings:
<margin>David</margin>
> The abyss is like a garment of His covering:

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Certainly of that land—not indeed this corruptible one which will pass away along with the material heaven, as the Supreme Truth <note>Referring to Christ's words in the Gospels.</note> says—but of that which is never changed, concerning which the prophet follows:
> It shall not be moved for ever and ever.

Finally, this supreme divine majesty takes up a final cloth/ <note>Catchword "ami/" likely for "amictus" (clothed or garment).</note>

These are called "members" for one reason; for another reason, they are called "garments"; and for yet another, they are called "measures" by which God himself measures and moderates all things: but He moderates man especially toward his perfect goal.

### Why the soul is placed in the body as in a casting vessel to be purged: before it returns to him, from whom it came. Chap. V.

**B**efore the soul returns to this unity with God, it is enclosed in the body, so that it may perfect the body: and be perfected by it. And I do not know whether it perfects first, or is rather perfected, or whether both happen at the same time. And perhaps both are perfected simultaneously in those who proceed well and rightly. The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, known for walking while they taught.</note> and our theologians say: the soul is in the body like a "form" perfecting the body itself: not only giving movement, and the power of sensing, growing, and understanding: but perfecting and purging the body: so that it might be transformed into a better lot <note>Or "state of being."</note>. Nor does the soul prepare the body to be transformed, unless the soul itself has been purged. 

<margin>Paul</margin>
"Not all of us shall be transformed" (says the Apostle), although we shall all rise again: but only the bodies of those whose souls are found purged will be transformed. The soul, therefore, is placed in this body, as if in a casting vessel <note>Latin: *vas fusorium*; a crucible or vessel used in metallurgy for melting and refining metal.</note> to be strained and purged by the fire of charity <note>In a theological sense, "charity" (Latin: *caritas*) refers to divine, selfless love.</note>, and by the divine grace poured into the whole man—poured in according to the capacity of the receiver, through the intervention especially of sacrifices and sacraments. Hence, when that supreme sacrifice was offered, to which all others assist and yield, by the high priest Jesus, the redeemer of the human race, that fiery spirit <note>The Holy Spirit, specifically referring to the event of Pentecost.</note> was sent to melt, purge, and fuse together <note>Latin: *conflada*; a term from metalworking meaning to blow together or forge into one.</note> the hearts of the disciples, and of those who would believe through them. Nor did any space of time intervene after that supreme sacrifice was presented, except for the number of fifty days, a number suitable for the sending of that fiery spirit. He would not have been sent unless the Son of God had been offered as a sacrifice, as He Himself testifies, saying: "Unless I go away"—that is, offered to the Father as a <term>holocaust</term> <note>A "burnt offering" in which the entire sacrifice is consumed by fire, symbolizing total devotion.</note>—"the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>From the Greek *parakletos*, meaning an advocate, comforter, or helper; used to refer to the Holy Spirit.</note> will not come to you." 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
This victim was often prefigured in the ancient law: namely, when after the sacrifice was offered, fire was expected from heaven, which, coming and finding the sacrifice already lit and changed into fire, would lead it back with a great mystery to the sublime height from which it had come: and would spread among those offering it that fire of which it is said in Deuteronomy: "God is a devouring, or eating, and consuming fire." 

<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
For just as one who eats consumes food and changes its substance into himself: so God, looking upon the true sacrifice of one who offers rightly, feeds upon both the sacrifice and the offerer, translating both into Himself. The true sacrifice, however, which we ought to offer together with the sacrifice offered by the high priest Christ Jesus, is that each person, according to the Apostolic teaching, should offer himself as a living victim, immaculate, holy, pleasing to God with rational service. And thus not only will the soul ascend into God Himself: but also the mortal and corruptible body, putting on (as the same Apostle says) 

<margin>Paul</margin>
incorruption and immortality: and then it will be a true holocaust, that is, totally burned-

The Hebrews, moreover, call this sacrifice *עולה* (holah) <note>original: "עולה holah" meaning a burnt offering or "that which goes up."</note>, that is, "ascending": because the whole sacrifice, once burned and now changed into fire, ascended before God.
