### Chapter VI. Why God placed the soul and the changeable mind here.

**A**nd since the soul is in this casting vessel <term>casting vessel</term> <note>Latin: *vas fusorium*; a crucible used in metallurgy to melt and refine metals. Here, it represents the human body.</note> for the sake of being purged and perfected, some people—even those of lower rank, whose habit it is to always strike at their superiors with their own judgments and words—wonder why God sent the soul down here not only in a changeable state, but to be continually attacked by a most fierce enemy. And as if appointing themselves God's counselors with reckless audacity, these bats <note>A traditional metaphor for people who are "blinded" by the light of truth or who cannot see the obvious brilliance of divine wisdom.</note> dare to accuse the highest light and supreme wisdom. 

But let dust and ashes blush even to name Him whose beauty of form shines from the rising of the sun to its setting. And if (according to the monument of the wise) young men ought to be silent in the midst of the great and the elderly: what should we do in the sight of the Ancient of Days, and Him in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden? We may nevertheless ask—not to accuse, but to be enlightened—why the most wise Craftsman did not make man stable, and continually proceeding on the right path. 

<margin>Anselm</margin>
Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note> responds here: because He could not. But (to speak more accurately), it was not fitting to make another God: who alone is by nature impeccable and immutable <note>Meaning God alone is incapable of sin and unchanging.</note>. 

<margin>Alexander, John Scotus</margin>
Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Hales, a 13th-century theologian.</note> tries to bring forth the reasons for this saying: which John Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a major medieval Scholastic philosopher.</note> decided to support as if they were weak, yielding however more to the opinions of the saints than to his own reasons. Therefore, leaving these arguments—since they are weak according to the judgment of their own author—to be read in his books, 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
we shall confess with Augustine to Volusian, that God can do many things which we are not able to understand, since the whole reason for the deed is the power of the Doer: which is infinite, and transcends every human and Angelic intellect. 

Therefore, for the discussion of this matter (as the Lord shall enlighten our eyes), we shall say something, presupposing what the order of things requires: which 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
(as Aristotle also teaches) is twofold in every army: namely, the order of the soldiers among themselves, and the order of all of them toward the Prince and head: if they harmonize with him, all things proceed rightly; but if they disagree, they become discordant and confused. 

Just as all soldiers can fall away from a good Emperor, so can all creatures fall from God: for many distracting objects are before us, by which we are carried now to the highest, now to the mediocre, now to the lowest. Now also we are distracted by a lower good, now by an apparent one, now (as they say) by a fixed one: and we are mocked by these continuous games: until our heart, always restless and always unstable, is fixed in the Prince: who alone is stable. Whence if we are ever made stable, it is not of nature (says 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine) but by the grace of Him whose nature it is to stabilize all things. 

How fittingly, moreover, it was done that man should be placed in the field of battle in a doubtful fight, 

<margin>Gregory</margin>
Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note>, inspired by the divine spirit, declares: "In the labors," (he says) "of the scourges, and the struggle against vices..."

<page-num>XI</page-num>
->**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**<-

...trials, not only is our own weakness made known to us, but we also recognize by how much virtue we advance. For no one knows their own strength in time of peace. Indeed, if wars are absent, the proofs of virtues are of no use. He is a shiftless soldier who boasts of his bravery in peace; for no one knows how much they have progressed except in the midst of adversity and uncertainty. To this
<margin>Firmianus</margin>
**Firmianus** <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> agrees, saying: "Before all things, God willed that there are opposites within us, and He did not open the <term>mystery</term> <note>Latin: *sacramentum*; here referring to the hidden divine plan of creation.</note> to the common people, but revealed it to very few. This diversity, however, contains every secret of the world. For this makes virtue: without which it could not only not exist, but could not even be sought after. For virtue cannot exist unless there is some adversary in overcoming whom the soul may either exercise or show its strength. Just as victory cannot exist without a contest, so neither can virtue exist without an enemy. Therefore, when He gave virtue to man, He set an enemy against him from the opposite side, lest virtue, growing sluggish in idleness, should lose its nature. The reason for this is that virtue may be strengthened when it is shaken and undermined. Nor could it otherwise reach the highest peak, unless, always stirred by an opposing hand, it establishes itself for its own salvation through a zeal for fighting. For the Lord did not wish that blessedness and reward to be reached by a path of luxury. Therefore, being about to give virtue, He also gave an enemy who would instill desires and vices into the minds of men, and hold them in uncertainty—he who is the author of evils and the plotter of all errors—so that while God calls man to life, the enemy, on the contrary, may seize and lead him toward death. This has left our journey in doubt, with an uncertain battle and many chances. For that enemy leads away or deceives those who are eager for the truth. Or, if he cannot prevail by trickery and effort, he carries out a manly spirit <note>original: "virilem gerit animam"; here used ironically to mean a vigorous or aggressive assault by the tempter.</note> by which he tries to undermine the vigor of the sublime; plotting things foul to speak of and accursed, he harasses and kills. And yet, as he strikes down many, so he departs conquered and prostrated by many. For great is the power of man, great is his reason, and great is his mystery." **Origen** <note>A prominent and controversial early Christian scholar from Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253).</note> also follows this matter in his *On First Principles*, saying: "For if God had granted that we could be conquered in no way, what cause for struggle would remain for him who cannot win? Or what merit would there be in the palm of victory, where the reason and ability to resist do not allow for winning? From this, the things that oppose a person are good enough for him; when he has conquered them, they exist as a cause for greater glory. For **Job** received double after his victory over the enemy, who had received the power of fighting against him. Indeed, a crown is not owed to us unless a contest precedes it first. For what is the glory and what is the praise of one who is crowned, unless he has earned it through some race or battle? For the condition of earning is such that one prevails from the very place where one could have been shipwrecked. And it is the praise of victory that one wins from the very place where one could have been defeated." Hence the Wise Man praises him who could have
<margin>The Wise Man</margin>
transgressed and did not, or who could have done evil and did not. At last, the good things of such a man shall be established in the Lord, so that he may never again depart from order, peace, and quiet."

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological discourse from the previous section. While page XI discussed the necessity of trials, page LXI (61) focuses on the ontological nature of evil as a "lack" or "disorder" and the process of returning to God through repentance.</meta>

<page-num>LXI</page-num>

# THE SIXTH TONE

...to God, or outside of God, are disordered. And consequently, guilt is disorder, dissension, a lack of righteousness, a defect, sin, and <term>nothingness</term> <note>The author uses the philosophical concept of "privation," arguing that evil has no independent existence but is merely the absence of good.</note>. But alas, we enter a most foul and horrendous forest when describing that which is nothing; and when discerning that evil is a disorder in that workmanship which is ruled by the Supreme Moderator who orders all things. Truly, evil is a disorder and a falling away from that which is, and from that which is good. Nor is evil a <term>substance</term> <note>In philosophy, a substance is something that exists in itself; the author argues evil cannot exist on its own.</note>, because its "being" is to exist within another thing. Nor is it an <term>accident</term> <note>A quality or attribute; the author argues that because evil is the opposite of good, it must be categorized differently than a simple physical property.</note>, because it is contrary to good, and consequently belongs to the category of good—since opposites belong to the same category—and true good is a substance in itself. Nor is it an existing thing, because whatever is of this kind possesses the quality of goodness. Nor is it above all existing things, because that is God, the highest good. Nor is it entirely nothing, because evil is the opposite of good, and vice is the opposite of virtue. Yet "nothing" cannot be the opposite of anything, because things that are opposites must be *something*. Nor is good the opposite of itself. Therefore, evil is a middle point between being and nothingness; it is a "being" in which the defect itself is founded, existing as a departure from the righteousness that ought to have been present in that which exists. This defect is a certain <term>privation</term> <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness is the absence of sight.</note> founded in being, but tending toward nothingness. Therefore, just as the good is above all being—where whatever tends toward it is perfected—so evil is below all being, and that which tends toward it
<margin>The Academics</margin>
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
falls away. And just as by contemplating the good, which is above all being (as pleases the <term>Academics</term> <note>Followers of the Platonic school of philosophy.</note> and **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who wrote about the "Good" being beyond all names.</note>), we are ultimately resolved into being; so also by contemplating evil, we arrive at a certain privation. Therefore, evil is a defect in
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
nature, and a privation of natural order and perfection. From this, a woman is an evil (as **Pythagoras** <note>The author cites the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who associated the "limitless" or "disordered" with the feminine in his table of opposites. The text reflects the era's patriarchal views, framing the female as a "defect" of the male "perfection."</note> used to say), because she falls short of the perfection of a man; so too is darkness, because it falls short of light; and so is every deprived thing or "monster," because it falls short of the order established by nature. And evil in morals is a defect of righteousness which ought to be in the acts and operations we perform, or a disagreement with the highest good to which we ought to cling. It is caught in privation, a fugitive from the region of light and being, weak, wretched, tearing, destroying—and not only disagreeing with the good, but leading away from it.

### Just as Man falls away from God through sin and disagrees with Him, so he is brought back and tempered through repentance. Chapter VIII.

**T**herefore, the man who falls away from God and disagrees with Him through sin has only one antidote: that he should return and come into agreement with God Himself. And this is true <term>repentance</term> <note>Latin: *poenitentia*.</note>, which is not (as some assert) "the holding of punishment" <note>A common medieval folk-etymology: *poenae tenentia* (holding onto pain/punishment).</note>, or a sorrow for sins voluntarily assumed, but a **return** to God from whom he had departed. This is indicated by the etymology of the "more perfect language" <note>The author refers to Hebrew, which many Renaissance scholars considered the original, perfect language of humanity.</note>: for he says repentance in Hebrew is <term>Teshuba</term> <note>original: "תשובה" (Teshuvah); literally meaning "returning."</note>, which signifies a "return." For many indeed feel sorrow and are tortured by the greatest punishments because of a crime committed, yet they are neither freed nor justified; for they do not have the antidote for sin, which is to return to God from whom they departed, and to agree with God with whom they disagree. Hence, always the oracle...

<margin>Zechariah</margin>
The voice thunders to the sinner: Return, or be converted. "Turn to me" (He says in Zechariah) "and I will turn to you." And through another Prophet: "But you
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>

<margin>CHRIST</margin>

While often translated as 'Repent,' the author emphasizes the active 'doing' or 'turning' involved in the process.</note>: and the kingdom of heaven will draw near." For what is the kingdom of heaven but God, who turns toward us when we turn toward Him? And because at that time He dwelt with us in a special way, and now, in the human nature He assumed, He offered us an easier way of returning to God Himself, therefore He said: "because the kingdom of heaven"—and God Himself, toward whom we strive through true repentance—was drawing near to us. However, if sorrow and affliction follow this conversion (which presupposes a withdrawal and a "fasting" from all unlawful pleasure), this is by accident and not of the essence of repentance or of that conversion. For many afflictions follow sin, from which a person is nonetheless not called "repentant." Nor should anyone think someone is repentant just because they take on voluntary sorrow, for that is sometimes found in sin; for just as sorrow follows the act of conversion, so it follows sin: since all disorder pulls affliction and punishment along with it.
<margin>Augustine</margin>
For no one can directly will sorrow: because sadness (as Augustine says) is what happens from things we do not want. Yet the occasion of the sorrow differs: for in the repentant person, there is a progression toward the good; in the sinner, however, there is a fall and a headlong rush, or evil. Therefore, the true <term>temperament</term> <note>Here, 'temperament' refers to a state of being properly balanced or 'tuned' like a musical instrument.</note> of the soul is the returning, the application, and the adaptation to God in truth and affection; just as the Lord requires through Joel, saying:
<margin>Joel</margin>
"Return to me with all your heart," that is, with full affection: "in fasting" from things that lead away from God himself: "in weeping and mourning": so that by tears drawn from your eyes, you may move the divine eyes and the fountain of His mercy to drip grace down to water you. For our eye moves the fountain of divine piety; which in the <term>mysterious language</term> <note>A common reference to Hebrew, which Renaissance scholars believed held hidden, primordial truths.</note> is called by the same name as "eye." For both are called <term>Ayin</term> <term>ע</term> <note>The Hebrew letter 'Ayin' (ע) means both 'eye' and 'spring' or 'fountain.' The author uses this linguistic pun to show a spiritual connection between human tears and divine mercy.</note>. Wherefore, as in name, so also in reality they have a <term>Symbol</term> <note>A 'symbol' here is a mystical correspondence where one thing naturally affects another.</note>: and from this, the movement of one easily leads to the movement of the other, as we have said elsewhere regarding the strings of a well-tuned <term>cithara</term> <note>An ancient stringed instrument; the author uses the 'sympathetic resonance' of strings—where plucking one makes another vibrate—to describe how human prayer affects God.</note>.

...they agree, and are made harmonious. From this, the sacraments were ordained as signs of sacred and divine things and, in a way, as effective causes. For they are effective signs of divine grace and favor, which is granted to man within them, so that it may lead to the required <term>harmony<note>original: 'concentum.' A musical term meaning a singing together or concord, here used to describe the soul’s alignment with God.</note></term> with God. Because man is born a "child of wrath" and is dissonant due to sin, the sacrament of baptism was given for his <term>tempering<note>original: 'temperamento.' In both music and medicine, this refers to the proper mixing or tuning of elements to reach a balanced state.</note></term>; in which he is washed and tuned to God, not only by the power and efficacy of the sacrament itself, but by the favor of the one who instituted it—provided the recipient is well-disposed. 

Man also falls out of tune and fails in his daily works, in which neither his whole mind, nor his whole soul, nor all his strength agree as the law commands; thus, there is a daily failure and dissonance. For the tempering of this, the sacrament of penance was given: by which—both through the reason of "turning back" to God (as we have said) and by the efficacy of the sacrament and absolution—discordant things are fitted back together. And because we are infected and "distempered" by the food we continually consume, the sacrament of the Eucharist was ordained: by which we repair that which was infected by other foods, and we prepare the "body of our humility" so that it may be fitted and shaped to the "body of His glory." <note>A reference to Philippians 3:21: "Who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body."</note> 

And that which is made foul and out of tune in the generation of offspring by the allurements of the flesh is repaired by the sacrament of matrimony, when it is duly observed. Two other sacraments were judged quite opportune: one of which is confirmation, or the strengthening of that which was done in baptism; especially in those who received it with weak virtue and no active disposition—namely, in the first and infantile stage of life. The other is called extreme unction, in which we intend to abolish and perfectly wipe away a man from every contagion and from all distrust (if any remains). 

There exists also another sacrament by which the hierarchy in this mystical body is established, and the "beard" is raised up toward the head: from which, and through which, the sacred <term>chrism<note>Anointing oil used in the sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders.</note></term>—anointing all things and tempering all things—descends even to the hem of the garment of the body itself. As it is said in the 
<margin>David</margin> 
song of David: *It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments.* <note>Psalm 133:2 (Psalm 132 in the Vulgate). The author uses this biblical image to describe how divine grace flows from the "head" (Christ/Church leadership) down through the entire "body" (the faithful).</note> This chrism, or this influence, is called by another metaphor the "dew of Hermon"—that is, of that place from which sadness has been banned; for "Hermon" is interpreted as "the banishment of sorrow." This dew first descends upon Mount Zion—that is, upon those who are placed in the <term>watchtower<note>original: 'specula.' Refers to those in positions of oversight, such as bishops or clergy.</note></term> over others—and from there it is spread to the whole city and the gathering of the faithful. Whence, through that chrism or dew, blessing and life are commanded even forevermore.

<margin>Proclus</margin>
...established: For an evil demon possesses a person (says <term>Proclus<note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher. The author here uses his ideas to explain how spiritual purification drives out negative influences.</note></term>) until they are purified through sacrifices. And then, once the evil demon has been put to flight, the person returns to God. Truly, the sacrifice that cleanses, tempers, and unites is twofold. One is that which the high priest, Christ, offered for the remission of all sins, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether for things in heaven or things on earth. This peacemaking returns the person, now purified, to a state of being in <term>concord<note>original: 'concordem.' Staying with the musical theme, this implies the soul is "in tune" with the divine.</note></term> with God in the highest harmony, and modulating most sweetly. The second sacrifice is to offer oneself as a clean, unblemished, and perfect <term>living victim<note>original: 'hostiam uiuentem.' Often translated as "living sacrifice," based on Romans 12:1.</note></term> to God, holy and pleasing to Him. <margin>Porphyry</margin> Regarding this, <term>Porphyry<note>Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305 AD) was a student of Plotinus. His work "On Abstinence from Animal Food" is cited here to support the idea of a "silent" spiritual sacrifice.</note></term> also says in his work *On Abstinence from Living Beings*: "Let us worship God with silence, care, and reverence, with pure and true thoughts about Him, laboring to become like Him and to be joined with Him; and let us offer the sanctity of our lives as a sacrifice, and adapt ourselves to sacred things." <margin>CHRIST</margin> Our Christ hinted that he expected this when he spoke with the Samaritan woman, saying: "There will be true worshipers who will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For God is spirit: and he seeks worshipers conformed to himself." However, so that we might be conformed to Him by being made spiritual—indeed, converted into a better spirit—Christ willed to mortify himself, offered as the highest <term>burnt offering<note>original: 'holocaustum.' Literally a "whole-burnt offering," the most complete form of sacrifice in antiquity.</note></term>: so that he might offer us to God, mortified in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. Therefore, so that we may be conformed to and united with God, <term>our animal nature<note>original: 'animal nostrum.' In this context, it refers to the lower, sensory, and biological impulses of a human being as opposed to the higher rational spirit.</note></term> must be mortified, so that the spiritual nature may rise and grow strong. <margin>The same</margin> And this is what he said, as John reports: "Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies—namely according to the flesh and blood—it brings forth much fruit." And again: "It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing." Hence the high priest Christ offered himself, and taught us that we are to be offered together with him, when he said: "Do this in my commemoration and imitation"—namely, offering yourselves just as I have been offered. For he commanded the mystery of his body to be commemorated, which was already offered in sacrifice, mortified through his passion, and now made alive in the spirit: so that the teaching concerning the sacrament of his body to be eaten by us, and offered by him on the cross, and the commemoration to be made of it, might be applied. "The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life." Into which spirit and into which life all our affairs must be led back, if we wish to follow God.

### Washed by Almsgiving. Chapter XI.

**A**fter tempering penance, harmonious sacraments, and purifying sacrifices—so that a person is not led away from their fellowship and union with God by any defilement—there follows the "washing" which, after that of baptism, is performed through almsgiving. I would hardly dare to assert this, unless the Supreme Truth itself taught me, saying: "Give alms, and all things are clean for you." For there is a certain water flowing from super-mundane springs, <margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin> according to what is said in <term>Ecclesiasticus<note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach. The quote "As water extinguishes fire, so alms [extinguishes sin]" is from Sirach 3:30.</note></term>: "As water extinguishes fire, so alms..."

Hence the Munificent Rewarder himself said: *You shall receive a hundredfold for one, and you shall possess eternal life.*

## Man Resounds with Virtues.

### Chapter XII.

<margin>Plato</margin> **A** man who is thus washed and tempered, and whose <term>instruments<note>The "instruments" here are the faculties of the soul and the body, continuing the book's metaphor of the human being as a musical device.</note></term> are composed, desires to produce harmonious melodies. But at first glance, he perceives a difficulty: because (as <term>Plato<note>Plato (c. 427–347 BC) argued in the 'Timaeus' that the soul has a mathematical and harmonic structure.</note></term> says) our soul, proceeding from God and enclosed in a body, suffers a "dissonance." To settle this, harmony was given by the Muses, which renders the motions of our soul harmonious and <term>akin<note>original: "cognatas." Meaning the soul's movements become related to the divine order.</note></term> to the divine, provided that a man uses them well by embracing the appropriate virtues. <margin>Chalcidius</margin> Explaining this, <term>Chalcidius<note>Chalcidius (4th century AD) was a philosopher whose Latin translation and commentary on Plato’s 'Timaeus' was the primary way the Middle Ages knew Plato’s thought.</note></term> says: Since the Creator fashioned the soul in higher realms according to harmonic principles, He ordered all its actions to consist of rhythms and modes. However, these usually fade away due to the soul's association with the body, which it necessarily maintains; for this reason, the souls of many people become "un-musical." <margin>Plato</margin> Therefore, as a remedy for this vice, He established music: not that kind in which the common crowd delights—which incites one to pleasure and often to vice—but that divine music which is never separated from intelligence. For Plato believes that this music recalls souls that have wandered from the right path back to their <term>ancient symphony<note>original: "ueterem symphoniam." The state of perfect internal and external harmony the soul possessed before being "distuned" by physical existence.</note></term>. Furthermore, the best symphony is found in our morals and in <term>justice<note>Justice is presented here as the "master tuner" that balances all other virtues.</note></term>, which is the tempering of all virtues, through which every other virtue carries out its duty and work: so that reason may be the leader, and that inner vigor (which is like righteous anger) may offer itself as an ally to reason. Moreover, these things cannot occur without <term>modulation<note>In this context, modulation refers to the "measuring" or "tuning" of one's actions.</note></term>. And there is no modulation without symphony. For symphony itself is intelligence and the "concert" of virtues, adorning the soul and rationally leading it back to its ancient nature, finally making it such as God the Creator had made it from the beginning: namely, so that it might "resound" with virtues. Although these virtues are fourfold <note>Referring to the four cardinal virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>, they are all found to be harmonious, just like the strings of a <term>cithara<note>An ancient Greek musical instrument similar to a lyre or harp.</note></term>, of which some are lowest and deeper, some are in the middle, and some are higher and shrill. For virtues are all the "works" coming forth from a well-stringed instrument. They are indeed named from the word for "man" <note>original: "dictae quidẽ a uiro." The author is using the Latin etymology: 'virtus' (virtue) comes from 'vir' (man).</note>, or because they are harmonious, as the grammarians <term>define<note>Catchword "diffi/" completed as "diffiniunt" (they define).</note></term>...

...is defined. Virtue is a habit of the mind consistent with the way of nature. According to the reasoning by which it is derived from the word "man" <note>original: "uiro." The Latin *virtus* (virtue) comes from *vir* (man/hero).</note>, they describe it thus: Virtue is a constant and fitting affection of the mind, making those in whom it dwells praiseworthy. Or: Virtue is a brave and unconquered patience in enduring things; for "man," as they say, implies bravery or fortitude. 

If, however, we approach the sacred and proper <term>idiom<note>Refers to the Hebrew language, considered the "sacred tongue" by Renaissance scholars.</note></term> and wish to name it there, we must observe by what words a "human" is called and a "man" is called in that language. For a human is called אָדָם **Adam**, אֱנוֹשׁ **Enos**, and גֶבֶר **Geuer** <note>These represent different aspects: Adam (earthly), Enos (frail/mortal), and Geuer (mighty/strong).</note>, for various reasons that must remain unspoken for now. This much only should be noted: in any of those names, there is either one letter of the divinity, or none at all. 

But a "man" is called אִישׁ **Ais** <note>Transliteration of the Hebrew *Ish*.</note>, in which word there are two letters of the divinity, namely א *aleph* and י *iod*. These imply that a man endowed with virtue is doubly divine: first by nature, by which he contains the image of God; and second by virtue, by which he contains the likeness. According to this mystery, virtue can be defined thus: Virtue is an operation that likens a man to God and deifies him. 

Another thing to be observed in this word אָדָם **Adam** is that there are two "four-fold" letters: namely ד *dalet*, which signifies four, and ם *mem*, which signifies forty. From these they imply that man is composed of two <term>quadratures<note>The "four-fold" nature refers to the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) or the four humors.</note></term>, and is infused with a certain divinity, denoted by the letter א *aleph*. This is shown clearly enough in those words: *God made man from the dust of the earth* <note>original: "Fecit Deus hominem pulverem de terra." Refers to Genesis 2:7.</note>—for which we have "from the slime of the earth"—and *He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.* 

In this, three things are touched upon: dust, earth, and breath. For "earth" is one of the four lower elements, and עָפָר **Aphar**, which we call "dust"—or better, "atoms"—indicates a more subtle body suitable for the spirit, as is known to those who are learned. That divine "breath," however, is infused into us; which our thinkers call the "higher portion" of the soul.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
From this breath, together with our animal nature (as <term>Plotinus<note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whose ideas on the soul's ascent to the "One" heavily influenced Christian mysticism.</note></term> prefers), the rational soul buds forth. But when, by means of virtue, the whole man is led back from this double quadrature to that divine state and passes into God, then he changes the square and elementary letter into a mark of divinity; and he leads back the other square letter, with a great mystery, to the "triple-hundred" denoted by the letter ש *shin*, the third letter of the word signifying "man." 

To explain myself briefly: through the virtues and other means of purification, the animal and earthly man is made spiritual and heavenly, according to that saying of the <margin>Paul</margin> Apostle: *The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is from heaven, heavenly.* And again: *Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:47-49.</note>

This transition from the earthly man to the heavenly occurs through the four-fold virtues, as if by four steps: through the **civil** (or **moral**) virtues, through the **purifying** virtues, the **heroic** (or soul-cleansing) virtues, and the **exemplary** virtues.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
Plotinus and others treat these most extensively. But we, gathering the main points briefly, say: that man labors in the **moral** or **civil** virtues; he prevails in the **purifying** virtues; he rejoices in the **heroic** virtues; and he shines and attains divinity in the **exemplary** virtues. And although there is labor in the first three kinds of virtues, according to what he says...

Author's Book

<margin>Paul</margin> Paul the Apostle to Timothy: *Labor like a good soldier of Christ.* <note>original: "Labora ſicut bonus miles chriſti"</note> Especially in civil and moral matters, labor is a struggle unredeemed by any of the pleasure found in other, better virtues. Hence, he everywhere preaches to those new to the way of the virtues that the path of these virtues is arduous and difficult.

<margin>Basil</margin> Therefore, **Basil** says: *The way of virtue is rough at first, and almost impassable, full of continuous sweat and labors.* <note>referring to St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father.</note>

<margin>Lactantius</margin> For which reason, great strength is required for the hardship of grasping it; nor is it easy for one who desires it to ascend to its summit. And **Lactantius** says: *To the supreme peak of the good, one arrives only with the greatest difficulty and labor.* Nevertheless, when a man begins to be purified, he always prevails; and as the spirit is strengthened, he feels the path of virtues becoming lighter day by day.

<margin>Paul</margin> And this is what the Apostle says: *When I am weak, then I am strong.* <note>2 Corinthians 12:10.</note> For he does not speak of bodily weakness—from which I have never seen anyone become stronger—but he means: "When I am weakened in my **animal part** <note>the lower, instinctual nature of a human being</note>, debilitating it by the austerity of life and curbing lust by the love of virtues, then I am made stronger in the spiritual part." Because virtue, which was a whole divided into eight equal portions, is found on both sides as four. If indeed one part is weakened by half, two portions are added to the four of the other part, and it is made three times stronger.

<margin>The same</margin> Nor should it be doubted that the Apostle was not speaking of physical weakness, since from the words he prefixes, it is easily inferred what the discourse was about. For he says: 
> I take pleasure in my infirmities, in insults, in necessities, in distresses, in persecutions for Christ: 

all of these look toward the suppression of the **animal man** rather than bodily weakness. And these are the true <term>purgative virtues<note>The 'virtutes purgatoriae' are the initial stage of moral development where the soul is 'cleansed' of earthly attachments and passions.</note></term>, which diminish lust and strengthen the spirit.

<margin>Plotinus</margin> Hence **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher whose ideas deeply influenced Christian mysticism.</note>, discussing these same purgative virtues most excellently, says: 
> It is the role of this virtue to take away pain; or if it cannot, to ensure it is borne moderately; and because he does not grieve at the same time, the pain is lessened. Let it remove anger from the midst as much as possible, if it can be done entirely. If not: let the better man not be angry at the same time. He will certainly take care that the anger belongs to the 'other' <note>the lower self</note>. Furthermore, let it expel fear, fearing nothing. He will undoubtedly have no desire for shameful things, nor for sexual pleasures. But if he does have them, let them be natural only, I suppose, so that they do not have an unconsidered impulse. For altogether, the <term>Phantasia<note>The 'imagination' or the faculty that produces mental images; Plotinus argues it must be kept 'pure' from worldly distractions.</note></term> will be pure from all these things, wishing to make the irrational part pure so that it is not even moved, or at least minimally. And let its commotions be immediately stilled by the proximity of reason, just as if someone approaching a wise man perceives something from him by that very proximity, or becomes like him, or stands in such awe that he dares do nothing which a good man does not dare. 

Therefore, a man purified from lust, so that he no longer says: 
> I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin; <note>Romans 7:23.</note>

but instead says: 
> I chastise my body and bring it into servitude. <note>1 Corinthians 9:27.</note>

Then, released from that most unhappy bond, he rejoices even in whatever adversity occurs, which harms the purified man very little; instead, he hates the flesh, which he has already subdued into servitude as a most cruel enemy. Hence...

So the Apostles, having been purified and strengthened by that **holy breath** <note>original: "sancto flamine," referring to the Holy Spirit at Pentecost</note>, went out rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were considered worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus. <margin>Paul</margin> And Paul says to the Colossians: *Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you.* <margin>Peter</margin> And Peter: *Rejoice, sharing in the sufferings of Christ.* And this is true **heroic virtue** <note>a term used in moral philosophy and theology to describe excellence that goes far beyond normal human capacity</note>: to rejoice and be glad in every adversity inflicted upon the body and upon our animal enemy—the more bitter the better. And we must rejoice to such an extent that we consider it a down payment and a pledge of blessedness. <margin>CHRIST</margin> It is to this end that Christ speaks when He says:
*Blessed are the poor in spirit*—those fasting from the desires of lower things—*for theirs is the kingdom of heaven*, and the delight in celestial and divine things. *Blessed are the meek*, the gentle—namely, those who give offense to no one, having extinguished or at least suppressed the impulse of anger and revenge which is in the flesh and the blood "crying out from the earth" <note>a reference to the blood of Abel crying from the ground in Genesis</note>, that is, from this earthly body. *For they shall possess the land*, namely the **land of the living** <note>a common medieval metaphor for Heaven or the spiritual realm, contrasted with the physical "earth"</note>, from which the wicked and the defiled are expelled. *Blessed are those who mourn*, whether from the adversities of their neighbors or because they are indignant at the prolonged stay in this most miserable worldly valley, in which the purified person now lives impatiently, always aspiring toward the things above, having shaken off the heaviness that pulls one down to the depths. *Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice.* 

See how excellently these steps of perfection follow one another! The purified man abstains from the desire for lower things; hence, envying no one and desiring nothing, he becomes mild. Afterward, feeling compassion and mourning for the evil of others, he is saddened, as well as by the extension of this stay in "prison" <note>referring to the physical body as a prison for the soul</note>. From this, he hungers and thirsts for the justice of God and for all things above, by which he may truly be satisfied. Afterward, he becomes a benefactor to his neighbor and, kindled with true **charity** <note>from "caritas," meaning a selfless, divine love</note>, he wishes to draw everyone with him. Thus follows: *Blessed are the merciful*, the compassionate, and the pious toward their neighbor, *for they shall obtain mercy* and piety. Finally, those perfectly purified—or rather, adorned with purity and cleanliness—are introduced into the presence of the King. Thus follows: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* They shall see Him, therefore, united and in harmony with Him, in perfect peace and every kind of tranquility that we obtain from peace. Concerning this, it is added: *Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.* Now raised to a sublime rank and fortified by perfect charity (which "casts out fear"), they, intrepid and secure, dare to take on every difficult thing. They endure all things with a glad heart, having already attained the kingdom of heaven which—as the **Supreme Truth** <note>Christ</note> teaches—is within us. <margin>THE SAME</margin> Here He says: *Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.* 

These people, therefore, are **deified** <note>the process of *theosis* or becoming "god-like" through union with God’s grace</note> through exemplary virtues and shine for others. I would not dare to assert that men are able to reach the state of deity <margin>John</margin> unless John taught me in plain speech, saying: *He gave them power to become children of God.* Moreover, they shine <margin>CHRIST</margin> according to that word of the Supreme Truth: *Let your light shine before men, so that you may be seen by them.* For a candle or a lit lamp is not put under a basket, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. Indeed, that man is a lit and shining lamp who, having now been made perfect, has ascended to the highest peak of virtue, just

From here, therefore, we must seek out for ourselves the sweetest songs, of which it is said: <margin>David</margin> *How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey to my mouth!* <note>original: "Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua super mel ori meo"</note> And again: *The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves: more desirable than gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.* For they are right and harmonious in themselves, and thus they gladden the heart and illuminate the eyes; they so delight the whole man that he is blessed who dwells in them. ## Chapter XIV.

<margin>The same</margin>
**T**he Law and Holy Scripture indeed make one blessed; it converts souls and grants wisdom to the little ones, provided that one meditates on the laws within it and is admitted like a clean animal chewing the cud <note>In medieval and Renaissance scriptural study, "chewing the cud" (rumination) was a common metaphor for deep, repetitive meditation on the word of God</note>, which is offered as a sacrifice to God through the study of Holy Scripture. Hence, in the Davidic song, he is proclaimed blessed who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. <margin>The same</margin> And in another song: *Blessed are they who search His testimonies.* This he not only praises but observes, when he says: *My eyes anticipated the dawn,* or *my eyes anticipated the watches of the night, that I might meditate on your words.* <margin>Deuteronomy</margin> And this is what is commanded in the repetition of the law <note>The book of Deuteronomy, whose name literally means "Second Law" or "Repetition of the Law"</note>: *The words which I command you today shall be in your heart; and you shall meditate on them sitting in your house, and walking on the journey, and sleeping and rising; and you shall bind them so that they may never move from before your eyes.* They are not, to be sure, to be bound with a linen or silk thread—as the superstitious observers of the law were accustomed to do <note>A reference to the literal wearing of phylacteries (tefillin), which the author contrasts with a spiritual "binding" of the mind</note>—but with a firm tenacity of the mind, so that you may always have that from which you are moved and led to the sweetest harmony, which is contained in them in many ways—indeed, in every way. For there all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. From there we can meditate so that we may sing not only of the *wandering moon and the labors of the sun* <note>original: "errantem lunam, solisq̃ labores" — a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, used here to represent the study of the natural cosmos</note>; of which the latter, like a rooster, makes the whole heaven pregnant, while the former, like a womb <note>original: "matrix"</note>, receives the effects from all the stars and unfolds them to us. Rather, we meditate so that we may cause the melody of the whole machine of the universe to resound—the melody of the guests, of the archetype, of its Maker, and of all things together. For all things are accustomed to sing in wonderful ways in Scripture, provided we know how to search it out; and it is granted to us that, with unveiled face, we may behold the glory of the Lord contained within it, proceeding from glory to glory, until by the grace of God we reach the fountain of light that is otherwise inaccessible to our own strength. Hence, the one meditating in Scripture itself is judged blessed not only in the Davidic hymns, but also by Plato, who says in the *Phaedrus*: <margin>Plato</margin> *He who rightly uses divine meditations, and is always initiated into the perfect mysteries, alone truly becomes perfect. Separated from human pursuits and clinging to divine ones, he is criticized by the multitude as if he were out of his mind; but being full of God, he is hidden from the multitude.*

And that which the common people judge to be wealth, he deems the ultimate poverty: hence, impatient with these lower things—because he has tasted the heavenly—he sighs for them and prays anxiously for them.

->He makes melody through prayer.<-
->Chapter XV.<-

<margin>Proclus</margin>
**S**ince, therefore, he recognizes his own poverty, he procures the necessary things and asks for that which he still lacks. For since we are all parts of the whole, we lack the whole: as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who greatly influenced Christian theology</note> teaches from the sources of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a student of Plotinus and a major figure in Neoplatonism</note> and other wise men. And since the health and preservation of every nature truly depends on its conversion <note>original: "conversione" — in this context, the Neoplatonic concept of 'epistrophe' or the soul turning back toward its divine origin</note> to its own totality, he who desires to possess virtue must insist on prayers and frequently supplicate, so that He who contains all virtue in Himself and is the highest good might infuse it. For He is the cause of every goodness, existing not only through a certain series and succession, but producing all things immediately—even, if you will, matter itself. Nor is divinity removed or distant from anyone, but is present to all equally, since everything exists by the gift of God. Nor is anything outside of God, since He embraces and encompasses all things. And whatever we imagine to be <margin>Iamblichus</margin> outside of God is utterly nothing. Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher known for his focus on theurgy (ritual) and prayer</note> adds that the necessity of prayer is beyond all expectation: because all things are produced and guarded by the Gods <note>original: "a Diis" — though the author is writing in a Christian context, he uses the plural used by his Neoplatonic sources to refer to divine powers or emanations</note> at the command of the Highest. Therefore, he who desires to be saved must pray to those who save, from whom things cannot be separated. For everything born, if torn from its parents and root, immediately slips away into non-being and destruction; especially those things which, although they have proceeded into themselves, nevertheless remain in the parent: just as all created things are, which begin from God and end in God Himself, according to the perfecting Trinity <note>original: "perfectricem trinitatem" — the triad of remaining, proceeding, and returning, which the author aligns with the Christian Trinity</note>, by which they proceed from God, exist in themselves, and tend toward God Himself. For all created things complete a certain circle (as <margin>Proclus</margin> Proclus pursues from the mind of Plato), beginning from God and ending in God Himself, like the line of a circle, which closes where it begins. But in order for them to return, they need the favor of those from whom they proceeded. Favor, however, is obtained through prayers, the purpose of which is to persuade both the Angels and even God, so that He (namely, the Highest) may command, and they may guard with perpetual protection, and lead the soul back to that place from which we came. For what (he asks) is each thing without its ascent and return to God, and without the harmony which they call sympathy <term>sympathia: the belief that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" together in a shared cosmic harmony</term>? And although prayer is necessary for all, it is especially so for upright men, since it is a certain application and conjunction of them to God. For like is naturally born to be entwined and joined with like; and the upright and whole man is like God. Hence, he must be entwined with Him to obtain help, by which he may be drawn away from the blind prison and the bonds of the body, in which he lives as a pilgrim far from Him whom he resembles and to whom he comes to be united. And just as children led away from their parents pray because they are driven by impulse until they return to them: so it is necessary for us, removed and separated from the true Father of all, to pray to Him and supplicate Him that we may be led back. Hence the <margin>Academics</margin> Academics <note>Followers of the Platonic Academy</note> do not...

XVII
<header>OF THE THIRD SONG</header>

Some used to call those "orphans" who, lacking both parents, neglected to turn toward the superior and divine nature through orations and prayers. Therefore, among the various nations of men, whoever claimed any reputation for themselves under the guidance of virtue exercised themselves in the study of prayers and orations: as with the 
<margin>Brahmans.
Magi.
Theologians.
Chaldeans.</margin> 
Brahmans among the Indians, the Magi among the Persians, the theologians among the Greeks, and the Chaldeans among the Assyrians. These groups established the festivals of the Gods and the hidden mysteries, venerating them with prayers. How much more should this be done by us, for whom the gate of heaven has now been unbarred? Moreover, however many well-composed voices of the soul there may be, or intense thoughts directed toward God to moderate our needs or to obtain certain gifts, these are so many sweetest melodies offered to God, beyond the praises and hymns which we frequently pay in His honor. 

Regarding the best way to sing those 
<margin>Proclus</margin> 
melodies, Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher whose works on prayer and the soul's ascent were often harmonized with Christian thought by later scholars.</note> also provides the most exact instructions. The first of these is the **knowledge** of the divine orders which the one who prays approaches; for one cannot approach properly and swiftly if they are ignorant of their properties. For this reason, the oracle <note>Likely a reference to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text of late antiquity highly regarded by Neoplatonists.</note> (or divine responses) commands that the first thing in the sacred worship of God be a "kindled notion of fire." We do not doubt that this was taken from 
<margin>Leviticus</margin> 
Mosaic institutions, for in Leviticus, at the command of the highest oracle, it is prescribed: *The fire on my altar shall burn always.* 

After this, the **kinship** and affinity we have to God Himself holds the second place, according to an all-encompassing sincerity in us, a purification, and a faithfulness in those things committed to us—in 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> 
accordance with what the Greatest Teacher says: *He who does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister, and mother.* 

The third in the order is **contact**, according to which we touch the divine essence with the very highest peak of the soul <note>original: "supremo capite" — referring to the 'flower of the intellect,' the highest point of human consciousness in Neoplatonic thought</note> and, leaning toward it, we find our support. In this sense (as I believe), 
<margin>John</margin> 
John says: *That which we have heard, and seen, and touched concerning the word of life.* 

In the fourth place follows **application** (or "adhesion"), for so the 
<margin>David</margin> 
oracle calls it. This we also have expressly in the Davidic song, where it is said: *But for me, to adhere to God is good.* And in the oracle: *The mortal adhering to the fire will have the light of divinity.* This provides us with great communion and a clearer participation in the divine light, leading us there through a similarity of character and intense affection. 

The last stage is **union**, which places that "one" <note>original: "unum illud" — the 'One' within the soul that corresponds to the Divine One</note> which is in the soul into the unity of God; it makes us stable, reducing us into a single act. According to this state, we are not our own, but God's, remaining in the divine light and encircled by Him in a ring. And this is the highest end of true prayers: that it joins the "turning" <note>original: "conversionem" or epistrophe, the soul's return to its source</note> itself to the "abiding" <note>original: "mansioni" or mone, the state of remaining within the divine essence</note> and stabilizes everything that proceeds from the one God back into the One. This is also the true and perfected harmony, which only an upright and truly good person can possess. This is also the easy and most swift path to a happy and blessed life, as we are elevated by prayers and ascend into God.

i iii

# One is introduced by contemplation. Chapter XVI.

<margin>Richard</margin>
**I**ndeed, when we ask in prayer, we do not yet possess what we desire; but after the prayer has been heard, and once the wished-for gift is obtained, we are introduced to the innermost chambers <note>Latin: *penetralia*, referring to the most private or sacred parts of a temple or home</note> where it is permitted to gaze upon those eternal spectacles with the full delight of the soul. And this is true contemplation, just as Richard <note>Richard of St. Victor (d. 1173), a major mystical theologian</note> well defines it in *The Mystical Ark*, saying: "Contemplation is the free insight of the mind into the spectacles of wisdom, suspended in wonder." For the Lord, when knocked upon by prayers, sometimes opens one of the many chambers; having entered it, the person sees with enlightened eyes the sights of divine wisdom which are most hidden from the common crowd. And because they extend into infinity, the mind of the viewer—unable to penetrate all things—remains suspended in wonder. For (as it is said in 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus</margin>
Ecclesiasticus <note>Sirach 43:30–32</note>): "Exalt the Lord as much as you can, for He is greater than all praise. For who shall magnify Him as He is? Many things greater than these are hidden; for they see but few of His works." Even the blessed, though they see Him as He is, do not see Him as *great* as He is; for He is infinite, while they
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
have determined limits to their own power. Hence Isaiah, speaking familiarly with God Himself, says: "Truly You are a hidden God." He is hidden, indeed, and yet open: for God is in all things, and thus open to all; and He is in Himself as if covered in an abyss of His own darkness, and so remains hidden from all, as is said in 
<margin>David</margin>
the Davidic song <note>Psalm 18:11</note>: "He made darkness His hiding place; His pavilion round about Him was dark waters in the clouds of the air." Behold how He is covered by darkness, by a pavilion, and by dark waters. And sometimes, when the obstacles are broken through, He appears open and manifest; wherefore it follows: "At the brightness that was before Him the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Highest gave His voice," making Himself manifest to whom and when He willed. He does this not only in this vast machinery of the world, but also when dealing with an individual human; sometimes He hides His face from them and says: "No man shall see me and live." At other times He speaks face to face, acting with great 
<margin>The same (David)</margin>
familiarity. Wherefore the Royal Prophet prayed, saying: "Show Your face, and we shall be saved." 
<margin>Job</margin>
God shows us this face especially in prayer, as Job says of the God who approaches: "He shall pray to God, and He will be favorable to him; and he shall see His face with joy." 
<margin>Plato</margin>
Therefore, man returns to God through prayer. (Arriving there, as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*, he stops his horses and enters the chamber of the banquet, where he feeds on ambrosia and drinks nectar.) This ambrosia is that manna of which it is said: "I will give him hidden manna, which no one knows except him who receives it." 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
And that nectar is what the Heavenly Teacher spoke of in the Gospel: "I will drink it new with you in My Father’s house." 
<margin>Plato</margin>
For this (Plato continues) is the life of the Gods and of happy men: that, having turned back toward God in a circular motion, they are fed by His food, and having returned into Him, they find rest. 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
For the movement is "straight" (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, who described the "divine names" and the soul's movements</note> pleases) when it goes from God into creatures; but it is a "circular" reflection, or return, when the creature goes back into God, which occurs when the course of life is completed...

# OF THE THIRD SONG.
<meta>Catchword: [deter]mines</meta>

sometimes not yet fully released from the body. And this is given to a person when, with the veil removed and with an unveiled face, he gazes upon the glory of the Lord, ascending from brightness to brightness <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18</note>; and this is true contemplation. For that thinking which occurs through riddles <note>Latin: *ænigmata*; a reference to "seeing through a glass darkly" (1 Corinthians 13:12)</note> or images is "speculation" or a kind of discourse. But that which occurs concerning God immediately, as if in a clear mirror, is "contemplation," as Augustine rightly believes. Therefore, Rachel—whose name is interpreted as "seeing the Principle" or "seeing God"—is most appropriately used to represent the contemplative life or mind. She does not look through riddles nor through created things, but gazes upon God himself, the Principle in whom all things shine back. And this is the "best portion" <note>A reference to Mary in Luke 10:42, traditionally the symbol of the contemplative life, as opposed to Martha's active life</note>; indeed, it is the goal and the fulfillment of the entire race that we await.
<margin>Philippians</margin>
Philip, filled with some heavenly light, aspired to this when he said: *Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.* <note>John 14:8</note> And because the Father and the Son are the same, he [Jesus] responded here by saying: *Philip, he who sees me, also sees my Father,* because whatever shines in one, also glows most fully in the other.

->One is united by love.<-

### Chapter XVII.

**T**herefore, the mind, placed before the mirror of divine brightness, also feels a fiery heat which follows from that reflecting light. Because of this, the soul melts, dissolves, and is finally fused into one with God himself, who enlightens it. Those "know-it-alls" <note>Latin: *scioli*; a dismissive term for those with superficial knowledge</note> do not stand in the way of this truth, even though they wish to bind Him—who is free from all laws—to the laws of lower mathematics. They foolishly say that there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite, and consequently, there can be no union. Furthermore, they argue that since God is most simple <note>In theology, "simplicity" means God is not made of parts</note>, He admits no union or mixture. But He is one and most simple in a way perhaps better than the sun, which is singular in all the illuminated places of the entire world. And although the sun, illuminating and warming all things, admits no mixture, much less does He, who is most simple, pervading all things and transforming all things into Himself according to His will. This is no wonder; for if this lowly fire here below, in burning wood, converts that wood into itself while suffering no mixture, much more so does that 
<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
fire—of which it is said in Deuteronomy: *God is a consuming fire* <note>Deuteronomy 4:24</note>—convert those whom He ignites into Himself without any mixture. For a "consuming" fire, by its fiery and vital power, converts food into the nature of the eater. Nor is a "proportion" of quantity or power required by the First Cause from those subjects of every law. For that First Cause, which is of such infinite power and so exceeds the proportion of all lower things, nevertheless extends even to the smallest thing to be produced. He also unites to Himself at His will things which He exceeds infinitely. For what in lower things is a "proportion of greater inequality" in an actor, in the First Cause is an all-encompassing transcendence. Yet the First Cause itself is the actor, according to [what] is deter[mined]... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "deter," likely leading to "determined by itself."</note>

It then argues that the soul can be fused with God through divine love, refuting mathematical objections by using the metaphors of the sun's light and a consuming fire.</summary>

## THE SIXTH TONE.

<margin>Theology</margin> [deter]mined power <note>This completes the word "determined" from the previous page.</note>: because He acts freely (as all our theology proclaims) <margin>Philosophy</margin> and not according to an absolute necessity of power, as those falsely assert who think that God acts by necessity. Therefore, the law of proportion holds in those things which are of a determined power, and not in the most excellent Agent, who exceeds all natural force; at whose nod all things are present—both before they exist, so that they may be made, and after they are made, so that they may be led back into Him again. Man, however, is most capable of this, for he is born by his very nature to be united [with God], provided that the force of love intercedes, which joins the lover with the beloved and makes <margin>Paul</margin> two—I will not say into one flesh—but into one spirit, as Paul says: *He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him.* <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note> This union occurs not only through love and affection <margin>John</margin>, of which it is said: *God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him.* <note>1 John 4:16</note> But it also occurs through a transformation, which happens through ecstasy and a certain departure of the mind.

-> He is transformed by ecstasy and departure. <-
-> Chapter XVIII. <-

<margin>Paul</margin> **N**ot content then (as some are) to raise man only to union with God, we shall attempt to lead him to a further and final step: namely, to the transformation of the body into spirit, and of the spirit into God. Concerning the former, the Apostle says: *We look for the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humility, configured to the body of his glory.* <note>Philippians 3:20–21</note> And what kind of reformation this will be, he declares elsewhere when he says: <margin>John</margin> *What is sown as an animal body shall rise a spiritual body.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:44</note> Concerning the latter, the Evangelist says: *He gave them power to become sons of God,* specifically while men are transformed into that same image which is the Son of God. This transformation occurs through a departure of the mind and a certain ecstasy, <margin>Hebrews</margin> which the Hebrews call the <term>death of the kiss<gloss>original: "mors osculi"; a mystical concept where the soul is so overwhelmed by divine love that it "dies" to the physical world to be united with God</gloss></term>, concerning <margin>David</margin> which it is said in the Davidic song: *Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* <note>Psalm 116:15</note> <margin>Song of Songs</margin> For one dies in the departure of the mind through that kiss of which the Wise Man says in the Song of Songs: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* <note>Song of Songs 1:2</note> For a man existing in the departure of the mind dies to the body, so that his life then barely lives, nor is it sustained by its protection—although the body is by no means destitute of the soul's life-giving power. The soul, leaning upon God in that departure, is united to God by a certain kiss, delighted by such sweetness in Him that, forgetting all external things and even the body itself, it leaves the body living but deprived of its senses and <margin>Paul</margin> half-dead. Paul explains this when he says: *You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ.* <note>Colossians 3:3</note> Who so receives the soul itself and unites it with himself, that it lives by the life of Christ rather than its own, as <margin>The same</margin> the Apostle says again: *I live now, not I, but Christ lives in me.* <note>Galatians 2:20</note> But since this transformation occurs not only through the illumination of the mind itself, but also through uniting love—which is a certain divine fire, melting, uniting, and transforming—I have thought it appropriate to issue a specific "Song" about this, which we shall subjoin to this one.

<page-num>LXIX</page-num>
->THE SEVENTH TONE<-

# WHETHER THE RESURRECTION IS POSSIBLE.
## CHAPTER ONE.

That **supreme Architect**, whose most sweet spirit is the creator of all arts, just as He brought forth the highest harmony into His work, and disposes and moderates it with tranquility: so at last He shall lead it to a perfect and completed concert, by a more fortunate and perfect fate. This shall be when all the noisy and dissonant matter—which by its own nature tends toward dissolution—is laid aside, and **man**, the most finished work of God, shall be fitted together with the Architect by perfect measures <note>original: "modulis," referring to musical intervals or rhythmic units</note>, so that he may forever return to Him due and fitting praises. For indeed, we lay aside that dissonant and harsh matter through death, so that we may take it up again changed for a better fate; and at some time, by a certain most vehement power of the spirit, we may be changed for the better. 

<margin>Enoch, Elijah, Moses</margin>
This occurred beforehand to **Enoch**, who walked with God and was seen no more—that is, in a flesh that was passible <note>subject to suffering or feeling</note> and liable to corruption. This was also achieved by **Elijah**, who was carried up in a fiery chariot. So too **Moses**, whose face, while he still lived among men, so shone from his divine fellowship that the children of Israel could not gaze upon it because of the brightness radiating from it. This was a most evident sign of a body already transformed for the better. Hence, he did not see corruption, nor was he found among men, nor was he left to the power of the devil like other corpses; but he was 
<margin>Paul</margin>
transformed into the nature of the spirit, according to that saying of the Apostle: *It is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body.* <note>Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:44</note> Therefore, it is also hinted by Thaddeus <note>referring to the Epistle of Jude, often attributed to Jude Thaddeus</note> that he was brought back into the jurisdiction of **Michael**, who is appointed as Prince over all souls and spirits to be received. And this is that dispute and altercation which is said by the same author to have taken place with the devil concerning the body of Moses. 

But since this transformation has been granted to very few, we must therefore come to that harmony through the laying down of this tabernacle <note>A common biblical metaphor for the human body</note> and the fiery power of the **Supreme Architect** in the work of resurrection. 
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
**Ambrose** touches upon this in some way when he says: *Let those who have tasted the first fruits of the resurrection make known to you how He has again fitted together the organ of the body, which had been pulled apart, into its former state of nerves; or rather, how He has led it to something better with sweeter measures and such great fitness that it may never again be dissolved, but without any gap, may bless and praise the Creator of all with continuous songs.* 

But before we describe this concert, those poisonous doubts must be removed from the minds of men, which infect the healing food of truth. These things must be ruminated upon by us with continuous meditation regarding our state and end. For the whole life of a wise and happy man is a meditation, not on the death of the body and the dissolution of this our tabernacle, but on the **death of the saints**, which is *precious in the sight of the Lord* <note>Psalm 116:15</note>; through which we live to God, and, transformed into a better fate, begin to taste that blessedness which we expect. Hence we have seen fit to set forth first how this resurrection and transformation is both possible and true. Here indeed, I cannot help but wonder at many who grant so much faith to one asserting the impossible—

It cites the biblical examples of Enoch, Elijah, and Moses as evidence that physical matter can be transformed into a higher, incorruptible state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument for the resurrection of the body. The previous page ended with the examples of Enoch, Elijah, and Moses as precedents for bodily transformation. This page transitions into "natural theology," using examples from the biological world (spontaneous generation, plant cycles, and mythical creatures) to prove that life returning from death is a common law of nature established by God.</meta>

->CANTICLE THREE<-

[...it is unbelievable] that what has been once destroyed could return again, since we daily prove these returns, repeated many times in most things, now under another, now under the same specific form <note>In medieval philosophy, "form" refers to the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing—for humans, the soul is the "form" of the body</note>. For from the body of a bull, beaten with clubs, enclosed in a small chamber, and buried in the earth, in a few—that is, twenty—days, more or less, bees are generated <note>This refers to the ancient belief in "bugonia," where bees were thought to be spontaneously generated from the carcasses of oxen</note>. From a horse's carcass, however, beetles arise; but from the bodies of any animals whatever, various worms arise, so that what was just now the matter of an ox or a horse becomes a bee or a wasp. 

And quite often the same specific form is restored. For lettuce, cabbage, wild thyme, parsley, and such things produced from the earth, through their seminal power, are again dissolved into the earth, the seed being reserved, in which the power remains; by which, with the earth, they produce the same things again, so that every year they seem to rise again. Yet they are not strictly said to "rise again" <note>in the theological sense of resurrection</note>, because the same individual form is not judged to return, since the form of the aforementioned things is judged to be corruptible. But if the form were to remain, I do not see why the same thing could not return which was once dissolved. 

Since, therefore, the human form and soul (as all truly wise men assert and the truth of the matter is) always persevere uncorrupted, it follows beyond all contradiction that when it is reunited to its matter, it constitutes the same thing that was there before. Nor should any difficulty arise concerning a certain (as they say) "third entity," for that is either nothing, or if it is something, I do not see why it could not return if it belongs to the essence of man. But if it is an accident <note>a non-essential quality that can change without destroying the subject</note>, even if it does not return, it does not prevent the same man from returning. Although in the resurrection there occurs not only a repeated union of separated parts, but also a certain transformation into a better state, just as a dead seed turns into a plant. 

Therefore God, in order to slaughter such hesitation and incredulity regarding the resurrection, has offered many daily experiments of nature for us to contemplate. For He commanded the earth to bring forth very many living creatures and innumerable plants, and He trained it to yield its interest <note>original: "foenus," literally a dividend or interest on a loan, here meaning the cycle of growth and harvest</note>, so that when it is commanded to produce the dead, it will not be disturbed by the novelty of the command. For if it brings forth living bodies that had been dissolved, it will no longer seem new to it if it restores human corpses to be reunited with the form that remained. 

The Phoenix also, the famous bird of Arabia, lives over five hundred years, and when it reaches old age, having collected twigs of spices into a funeral pyre and turning toward the sun, it procures a voluntary fire for itself by the clapping of its wings, so that it might come back to life rather than die. For from its burned flesh (as **Ambrose** reports) or from the marrow (as **Pliny** asserts)
<margin>Ambrose
Pliny</margin>
a most sweet worm comes forth, which, putting out wings, is formed into the same bird. Nor should it be thought a wonder if from dust, mud, and the plants that sprouted from them, or from the carcasses of animals or fish that devoured human bodies, these same tabernacles of men <note>a metaphor for the physical body</note> are restored, since from the hardest stone <note>original: "osse," literally "bone," referring here to the hard pit of a fruit</note> of an apricot, but especially of a Date, where the nucleus is thin, a tree takes its beginning of birth; and through repeated cycles, a tree is produced again from these "bones." 

The worms called <term>bombyces: silkworms</term>, which make silk, once their work is finished, are shut up and enclosed in the cocoon itself (if I may call it that), as if in a prison or a cave.

It emphasizes that since the human soul is incorruptible, God can easily reunite it with physical matter just as He does in the cycles of nature.</summary>
