<page-num>70</page-num>
<header>THE SEVENTH TONE</header>

<margin>Theologians, Hebrews, Plato, Paul. The same.</margin>
Afterward, they are changed into butterflies, which produce eggs as if they were nurseries; these, warmed at a set time, break out again into those same worms. According to the more secret Theologians, the restoration of man is not different from these. They claim that a man’s bone—which they call the <term>Luz <note>Hebrew: לוז. In Jewish tradition, this is a tiny, indestructible bone, often identified as the coccyx or a bone in the skull, from which the entire body will be regrown at the resurrection.</note></term>—is about the size of a peeled chickpea and is subject to no fire and no corruption, remaining always unharmed. From this bone (as they say), the whole animal body sprouts forth again, just like a plant from a seed. Once this is taken up again by the same spirit and the soul—which the Hebrews themselves call <term>Neshamah <note>Hebrew: נשמה (Neshamah). This refers to the "breath of life" or the highest part of the soul, distinguished from the mere animal life-force.</note></term>—man is established as a higher and spiritual being. 

Just as the lower man is constituted by reason and discourse along with our animal nature (or with a celestial body, as the followers of Plato prefer), so this heavy and corruptible body will be transformed according to the opinion of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul, particularly 1 Corinthians 15:44: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body."</note>. For the dregs of the body and its coarser matter are not part of the true substance of man, as these thinkers believe. We can prove this from what happens in the transformations performed by craftsmen, where we see the entire substance, spirit, and life of a thing reduced into a small amount of matter—liquid, rare, and free from the dreg-like portion. In the same way, leaving behind what is animal and dreg-like, that which is spiritual shall rise (as the Apostle says), which is sufficient for the integrity of man. Indeed, man is to return fortified by a far better lot, transformed into an Angel and into the very Son of God.

->Chapter II. Whether the Resurrection occurred.<-

<margin>The same, Thomas. CHRIST</margin>
**B**ut whether any resurrection of men has actually occurred, since it is a matter of historical fact, cannot be proven except by witnesses and the evidence of the event. Indeed, we have many who testify that Christ rose from the dead and gave pledges of his true resurrection. For he showed himself visible not only to the Apostles and the women, but also to five hundred brothers at once or more, as Paul reports. He also showed himself to many who were present when he ascended into heaven—not without the wonder of those watching—and further, he showed himself as tangible and impassible <note>In theology, "impassible" means incapable of suffering or feeling pain, a quality attributed to resurrected bodies.</note> to Thomas. This occurred when he fearlessly offered his wounds to be touched, without any fear of pain arising from the touching of those very wounds. 

From this arose that cry of Thomas, born of the greatest reason, in which he said: *My Lord and my God.* "Now," he says, "I have known you as a faithful guarantor and patron, while you demonstrate the reward promised to faithful soldiers for the labors and death endured for love of you. Now I know you as God, since you have changed this mortal and suffering body into one immortal and beyond suffering, and this as a pledge that our bodies shall also be changed. I gather this from the fact that I touch this recent wound of yours with my fingers (as you commanded), yet it causes you no new pain at all. Because only God can perform such things, I confess you, who have done this, as my God." Heavenly spirits also testified to the resurrection of Christ himself, saying to the women: *Jesus, whom you seek, is not here; he has risen and goes before you into Galilee.* But lest the testimony of the Angels become known to us only through the report of the women, the same Angels addressed the astonished crowd with these words as Christ was ascending.

<header>OF THE THIRD SONG.</header>

## OF THE THIRD SONG.

"Men of Galilee, why do you stand wondering, looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in the flesh—that is, in a body already glorified—to judge the world, and to give that same glory to you, just as you saw him ascend into heaven already glorified." <note>This is a paraphrase of Acts 1:11, the address of the angels to the Apostles after the Ascension.</note> The Apostles, witnessing this along with the other deeds performed by Christ as they had seen them, proved it not only with words but with many miracles, and finally by the risk of their very lives. And to remove every suspicion of recklessness or fraud that might be attributed to the Apostles from this testimony, 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Paul wisely argues, saying: "Unless Christ had risen, and provided for us the way to resurrection, we would be more miserable than all other creatures," <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 15:19.</note> which enjoy the delights suited to them. For just as brute animals do, so the unbelieving man basely nurtures his lower appetite. The true Christian, however, abstains from all such things, so that he may enjoy those goods which have been prepared for the happy soul—whether separated from the body or joined with that same body, perhaps granted a better state. Hence, the Apostles and all evangelical men, who abstain from all pleasures so that they may receive that incorruptible crown, would truly be more miserable than all other creatures (which at least enjoy some pleasure) unless they were to obtain that very resurrection promised to them, to be enjoyed most fully by the whole man. Nor does this truth possess little strength, as it is accepted by all who are not 
depraved, is asserted by every law, and is expected by all—unless there be some so defiled by such great and numerous crimes that they persuade themselves there is no future life, no tribunal, and no judge for such great wickedness. For "horrid crimes" (as 
<margin>Hierocles</margin>
Hierocles <note>Hierocles of Alexandria (5th century AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher known for his commentary on the Golden Verses of Pythagoras.</note> says) "take away all faith, all God, and finally every judge from the minds of those who are blinded." The resurrection, I say, is asserted by every law, since not only do Christians confess it, but also the Muhammadans and the Hebrews. For the foremost of the 
<margin>Muhammadans. Hebrews.</margin>
Hebrews, who were called Pharisees—that is, "separated" and "set apart" from the common crowd—asserted this beyond any doubt. Hence Paul did not blush to profess himself a Pharisee, 
<margin>Paul</margin>
and to accept their own dogma concerning the resurrection of the dead. For he says: "I am a Pharisee, and the son of Pharisees; and I am being judged concerning the resurrection." <note>Acts 23:6.</note> Indeed, the Pharisees were anciently the truly religious among the Hebrews, called "separated" from the common people from the word <term>Paraz <note>original: "פרש" (Parash), a Hebrew root meaning to separate or distinguish.</note></term>, which means "he separated." However, when their spirit and fervor waned (as so often happens), they began to mingle with the crowds, committing things that were not lawful. But when Christ, the true Pharisee—utterly separated from the world and everything in it—rebuked them as being guilty against their own profession and name, they then rose up against the teacher of truth, for truth usually breeds hatred by common law. Those among the Hebrews themselves who think rightly profess the resurrection, expect the world to come, and celebrate it in many volumes, greatly magnifying those who have a solicitous concern for the world to come. Nor shall I bring forward what Muhammad asserts in his theology concerning the resurrection, since he stole every truth he professes from the Mosaic or Evangelical law. Yet I have thought it opportune to cite his sect, since at present the whole human race is divided into these three principal sects: the Hebrew, [the Christian, and the Islamic].

...one may see the matter divided between the Christian and the Muslim <term>Mahumeticā</term><note>The author uses the Latin term for followers of Muhammad to show that even non-Christian religions acknowledge a form of resurrection.</note> faiths, so that all may understand that there is no religion or dogma that does not profess and teach this truth concerning the resurrection.

### Whether the future resurrection can be proven by reasons. Chapter III.

<margin>Plato</margin>
**A**ND although (according to Plato) divine matters should rather be accepted through oracles than investigated by human ingenuity or proved by reasons, nevertheless, since these oracles themselves teach nothing dissonant, nothing that is not in agreement with nature, I judge it not incongruous to examine the harmony of these divinely revealed things with our reason and intellect. This kind of knowing is, to me, most elegant: when a truth accords with the intellect, which is fed by truth alone and delights in it, provided that the intellect remains purified. For a darkened mind cannot receive the light of truth, as John says: *And the darkness did not comprehend it.* <note>original: "Et tenebrę eam nō cōprehēderūt" from John 1:5.</note>
<margin>John</margin>

<margin>Paul</margin>
Dealing then with purified minds, let us propose that the soul is immortal, as not only the laws assert but all truly wise men profess; and reason persuades us that the soul must follow that end which it cannot possibly attain in this earthly pilgrimage, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> wisely says: *As long as we are in this body, we are on a pilgrimage away from the Lord.* <note>original: "Quādiu sumus in hoc corpore, pegrinamur a Dñio" from 2 Corinthians 5:6.</note> Moreover, the soul is a partaker of divine and eternal light, just like an Angel. For God himself (as John says) was the true light, which enlightens every man: <note>John 1:9</note> specifically that light which is the Word and the splendor of the Father; which even the Angels (as Augustine says) approach as if to the fountain of life.
<margin>John, Augustine</margin>
And (to proceed further) everyone who is a partaker of something senses the nature of that in which he partakes. For the eye, which is capable of receiving this sensible light, is judged to be of the same nature as light, even if one person sees less and another more, or one more sharply and another more dimly. It is no different with hearing and the other powers. Therefore, man will not be a stranger to the nature of the Angel and of God, since all (though in varying degrees) enjoy the same light. And since those beings are incorruptible and immortal, the soul will undoubtedly also be immortal, since it has communion with them. This is especially true because the soul itself draws its origin immediately, along with the Angel, from that immutable and eternal Parent, who—whatever He produced immediately and without any other aid—undoubtedly produced it eternal, as Plato teaches and Plotinus confirms. 
<margin>Plato, Plotinus</margin>
For He produced the heaven and the earth, which stands forever, and man as to his soul, and the "great dragons" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:21. <margin>Theologians, CHRIST</margin>

By the same law of these things, either universals (if they are indeed real things) are everlasting because they were produced immediately and without any intervening cause. Therefore, this soul is immortal and perpetual, so that it may perpetually enjoy the eternal God, having been made a partaker of Him; in whose company—though presently a pilgrim—and even if the soul sometimes falls away through negligence and does not receive Him fully and purely, nevertheless in itself...

# ->OF THE THIRD SONG<-

[The soul] possesses certain seeds <note>original: "seminaria"; a term used in both biology and Stoic/Neoplatonic philosophy to describe the latent potential for growth or restoration.</note> from which, with the favor of the supreme Sun itself, it can restore and recall its suppressed powers until it achieves its perfect likeness, image, and consummated union. Since the soul cannot do this entirely while it is a pilgrim <note>A common metaphor for the soul's temporary stay on Earth.</note> and clothed in this heavy mass of the body, it is necessary that its body be transformed and configured to the body of that clarity—He who gave the beginning to resurrection and life so that the soul may enjoy His full company. For He will make the transformed body like a seed growing into a vigorous plant, a companion and a dish <note>original: "ferculum"; literally a tray or course of a meal, suggesting the resurrected body becomes part of the divine banquet.</note> of the Prince of blessedness himself, just as He was made living bread and offered to us as food. And this is that mutual banquet of which the Food and Guest Himself speaks in the Apocalypse, saying: *I will sup with him, and he with me.* <note>original: "Cœnabo cū eo, & ipſe mecū" from Revelation 3:20.</note> 
<margin>Apocalypse</margin>
Indeed, He will eat me as living bread and hidden manna, by which He will be continually sustained. I, however, will be delighted by that better life, marked and made similar to Him; to whom I, the resurrection and the life, will provide that better life continuously. Nor should we labor here in bringing forth passages of Holy Scripture, since the same faith should be granted to a single passage as to many, given that every one of them flows from the unmixed and infallible fountain of truth. 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Paul, who saw the secrets of God and in whose breast Christ resounds, having been taught these things by the Master in the gymnasium of truth <note>A metaphor for the school or place of spiritual and intellectual training.</note>, brings them forth: *Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.* <note>original: "Ecce myſteriū uobis dico..." from 1 Corinthians 15:51-53.</note> Behold how clearly he reveals the secret and the manner of the resurrection, with which all agree who are educated in the same academy <note>Likely referring to the "School of Christ" or the community of Christian scholars.</note>. Nor are there lacking those who think the resurrection can be proven from the stars, if it were demonstrated that the aspects and locations of the planets were the same as when the world was first crafted; and that those surfaces upon which the stars revolve were not "incommensurable" (like the diagonal of a square to its side), but symmetrical, so that all things might finally meet just as they were. However, this is nothing <note>The author dismisses this astrological theory, known as the "Great Year," which suggests history repeats when stars return to their original positions.</note>, since the universal resurrection of the dead does not require the exact same condition of the stars that the world held when it was created in the beginning; for then human bodies were not yet fabricated, nor was the union of souls made with them, but occurred through many successive cycles of years. Therefore, this truth concerning the resurrection must be sought only from Him who will bring it about according to His will, and who gave man the means to rise again, just as He gave to plants and certain animals the means (as we have said) to be renewed in their own seasons. From these things alone (beyond what the oracles say) can we conjecture about the resurrection.

But although he recounts many things of this kind, he mentions nothing regarding the time except in those words which he brought in at the end, saying: *Amen I say to you, that this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.* <note>Matthew 24:34. This verse has long been a point of debate for scholars trying to reconcile the "generation" of Christ's time with the delayed Second Coming.</note> This word is quite obscure, as it can be understood in different ways. For we can interpret **this generation** as the "human race." But would it not have been superfluous to say of the human race that "this generation shall not pass away" until those things which must be carried out within that very generation are completed? There is also "generation" as the common life of a man, but in that sense, the sentence has no place at all: since the life of man from the time of the flood onward has been confined within the space of one hundred and twenty years—and already one thousand five hundred and more years have flowed by since that warning. Nor can that word be interpreted as the "great life" of man, which was established from the beginning to be extended up to a **millennium** <term>millenarium: a period of one thousand years</term>; for no mortal ever reached that limit (not without a sacred mystery), though some came very close to it, such as Adam, Methuselah, and others. For Adam lived nine hundred and thirty years; the other [Methuselah] lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years. Indeed, even this generation or life falls short of the time that has passed since those words were spoken.

Nor could it be understood as an **age** <term>sæculum: a Latin term that can mean a generation, a century, or a vast epoch of time</term>, because an "age" is sometimes taken for the common span of a life, like that which we read in Exodus: *And he shall be a servant for an age,* <note>Exodus 21:6. In this context, it refers to a slave serving for the duration of his life.</note> until he has completed the span of his life. And sometimes an "age" is extended even to a millennium of years, beyond which limit (as the Hebrews assert) it can by no means be prolonged. Hence (unless I am mistaken), by **this generation** the Savior understands the third part of the world's fluctuating course. For (as we can conjecture from other significant passages) the labor of the human generation will be consummated in six thousand years, but in the seventh, it shall rest—just as the Supreme Architect fashioned the world in six days and rested on the seventh. <note>This "Millennial" theory posits that because God created the world in six days, human history will last 6,000 years (six "Days" of 1,000 years each) before a final Sabbath rest.</note>

Nor do we unsuitably match the millennia of years with as many days, because among the more mystical theologians, a millennium of years is often computed as a day, according to that hymn of David: *For a thousand years in your sight are as a day of yesterday which has passed.* <note>Psalm 90:4</note> The sixfold pattern of labor and the seventh of rest, both in days and in years, is corroborated by divine law. For six days of the week are granted by law for performing works; but the seventh is dedicated to rest. And likewise, six years having been granted for cultivating the fields, in the seventh, rest is proclaimed for both the field and the farmer, as we read in Exodus. <note>Exodus 23:10-11, describing the Sabbatical year for the land.</note> It is no wonder, therefore, if after the human race has labored for six thousand years through various hardships and diverse agitations procured by **Satan** (that is, the Adversary), it shall rest in the seventh millennium, as the beloved Apostle of Christ describes in the **Apocalypse** <term>Apocalypsi: The Book of Revelation</term>. And this after that same Satan and our adversary—who is the ancient serpent—has first been bound: so that he may not seduce or disturb the nations in that happy millennium, but that men may be true priests of Christ, dedicating themselves to God, so that they may reign already in that...

To achieve these things, however, the Craftsman <note>Latin: *opifex*, referring to God as the master builder of the universe.</note> took up created things as co-workers, or as instruments, commanding the earth to bring forth green plants, and the waters to teem with life, and to deliver a living soul according to its kind, and the other things that follow. And although the sacred words <note>The Holy Scriptures.</note> may seem to testify only concerning the resurrection of man and his restoration to his first and highest parent, nevertheless, if anyone weighs well the words of the highest Truth, he will clearly perceive that all things are to be renewed. For he says: *Heaven and earth shall pass away.* <note>Matthew 24:35.</note> Nor (as I believe) will they make any "passing away" except, perhaps, into a 

<margin>CHRIST</margin>

better lot. For to "pass away" is not to perish, but to change place, state, or some condition. Therefore, the movable heavens shall pass away to a state of rest, toward which all motion tends. And the always-changeable earth shall pass to that state where it may perhaps receive the quality of a "land of the living." And men, in whom all things are contained, shall pass into an Angelic and divine nature, so that the words of the celestial oracle recently cited may truly have their place: 

<margin>Revelation</margin>

*Behold, I make all things new.* <note>Revelation 21:5.</note> To be sure, the human condition had been renewed in the first coming of the Redeemer by signs, sacraments, the law, worship, and all the preparatory means toward a perfect, complete, and evident renewal. But in the second and more famous coming, that renewal will be consummated, in which it will appear what the new sacraments, what the new signs, and the new rites have accomplished. The Author, therefore, of this resurrection and universal innovation will be God, three and one, by whose command all these things shall be done. But it is rightly ascribed particularly to him who is the Principle of resurrection, and who, rising first, provided the way for the rest to rise. 

<margin>Paul</margin>

Truly, the executors shall be the Angels and ministers of God himself, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul.</note> relates in plain speech, saying: *The Lord himself, at a command (namely, his own), and with the voice of the Archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven. And the dead who are in Christ will rise first.* <note>1 Thessalonians 4:16.</note> In like manner, Christ also—from whom Paul had learned—explains the same in the Gospel titled 

<margin>Matthew</margin>

according to Matthew, when he says: *They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and he will gather his elect from the four winds, from the heights of the heavens even unto their bounds.* <note>Matthew 24:30-31.</note>

For we often read that Angels spoke in the person of God: so much so that the command and the speech are brought forth by an Angel...

And yet he ascribes it to God. Hence, when the precept of God and Christ concerning the raising of the dead shall be spread abroad through the Angels, they themselves will be like trumpets, carrying not only the voice, but the power of God Himself to raise the corpses, or to clothe the souls once again. The trumpet, therefore, will be angelic, because the Angel will carry the voice and command; but it will be of God, who will command and breathe into it, or give a signal through the Angels (as some believe) or bring about some effect through them, whatever it may be. And he is rightly called a trumpet, who conveys the voice of God to the ears of men like a certain channel. And just as trumpets, receiving breath and life from the trumpeter, stir the horses to move the camp, kindle men for war, and invite the soldiers to receive a gift and to all the celebrated acts of military service—so the Angels, receiving the voice and power together with the command from God the Prince, will stir the "horses" of our bodies, together with their riders <note>A metaphor for the soul inhabiting the body.</note>, to that terrible examination, to enter new lodgings, and to receive rewards for things well done.

->What the future change of bodies shall be. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IX.<-

<margin>The same Theology</margin>
**W**hen this trumpet sounds, a most great thing shall happen, but especially the transformation of our bodies, as the Apostle says: *For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible: and we shall be changed.* <note>original: "Canet enim tuba, & mortui resurgent incorrupti: & nos immutabimur"; from 1 Corinthians 15:52.</note> However, to those wishing to inquire how and with what kind of body the dead shall rise, the Apostle responds, saying: *You fool, you who do not believe* <note>original: "Insipiens tu, qui non credis"</note> or perhaps do not understand: Do you not see how the dead shall rise and be changed? And observe what you sow: you do not commit to the furrows the body that is to be, but a bare grain of wheat, or of some other plant; but God gives it a body just as He wills: and to each of the seeds its own body. So to every human being to be raised, He will give a body suitable to his state; and whatever that body shall be, it will be a true body (even if the body of the blessed is to be celestial, incapable of suffering, and glorious, while that of the reprobate shall be capable of suffering and heavy) just as both the earthly body and the celestial body are each a true body. It is true, he says, but it is incorruptible flesh, and bones that cannot be diminished, yet a body that is palpable and visible at will. For he entered among the eleven disciples while the doors were closed, which could in no way have happened unless that body were able to be thinned at will, like wind and spirit. Again, he can present himself as large or small at will, and without any <term>circumscription of place<gloss>the physical limitation of occupying a specific volume of space</gloss></term> / as happens in the <term>Sacrament of the Altar<gloss>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</gloss></term>. All the wise scholars approve of this, though some think it happens through a miracle, by removing the relationship of the parts to the location while the relationship of those same parts to the whole remains. But (unless I am mistaken) this occurs from the nature of the spirit into which the one rising has been transformed. Therefore, the change of corruptible human bodies will be into the nature of celestial bodies and spirits.

For if the flesh or the <term>animal body<gloss>the physical body governed by the lower soul or "anima"</gloss></term> wins: it bestows a heaviness upon the spirit and the rational soul, so that it descends to the lowest parts of the world. It also wraps it in darkness, so that it can no longer perceive that divine light in whose brightness well-ordered souls rejoice. Moreover, it renders that soul <term>passible<gloss>subject to suffering and external influence</gloss></term>, which of itself was not able to be saddened, just as it could not weave or spin; so much so that it suffers even from physical fire. Finally, it provides a thickness along with its own weight, so that it can by no means depart from the infernal dwellings, but, enslaved to perpetual chains and prisons, it may lie forever in the lowest part of the world, always weighed down by the heavy burden prepared by its own crimes. But if the spirit prevails, it will bestow its own laws, and these better ones (which theologians call <term>endowments<gloss>original: "dotes"; the four supernatural qualities of the resurrected body</gloss></term>), upon our lesser part, according to that Apostolic word: 
<margin>Paul the Theologian</margin>
*But when this mortal shall have put on immortality, and this corruptible shall have put on incorruption* <note>1 Corinthians 15:54</note>. Following upon this immortality are agility, subtlety, clarity, and all the endowments which they attribute to glorified bodies, which bodies are said to "put on" by an appropriate term. For just as our body puts on a garment of another nature to cover its nakedness and defend itself from the cold, in like manner the body itself puts on the condition of another and better nature, so that, immune from labor and any sufferings whatsoever, it may always rejoice in a better lot. The body shall therefore be made **agile** and light, so that it can easily ascend to the highest heaven. It shall be **subtle**, so that it may be able to penetrate all things. It shall be **bright** and shining like a spark, or rather like a star, so that it may be a worthy inhabitant of the region of light and splendor. It shall also be **impassible**, so that it feels nothing that might hinder its beatitude and that full joy. Finally, it shall be **immortal**, so that it may enjoy those eternal joys forever.

...treating these matters in a certain way, they say that to each soul will be restored not a confused or foreign body, but its own which it had before, so that consequently, for the struggles of the present life, the flesh may be crowned as chaste alongside its soul, or punished as unchaste. 

<margin>Rufinus</margin>To express this more clearly, Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and theologian famous for translating Greek Church Fathers into Latin.</note> says that in his own church, where it is commonly held in the Creed <note>original: "symbolo"; the "symbol" refers to the formal statement of faith or Apostles' Creed.</note> as "the resurrection of the flesh," it was added "of *this* flesh," or the resurrection of *those* people: undoubtedly referring to the body held by the one who makes the profession of faith, with the sign of the cross placed upon their forehead. 

Others, however, cry out on the contrary and say: "How can the flesh, which is dissolved by rot, or turned to dust, or even swallowed in the deep of the sea and scattered by the waves, be collected again and joined into one, and a man's body be repaired from it? How, again, can the same flesh, which is now corruptible and dissoluble, be suddenly or after some time incorruptible, immortal, and entirely immune from all change: since the corruptible and the incorruptible (as they say) differ by more than just their kind?" 

The first of these objections is easily solved if one looks to the majesty of the supreme Creator and Governor. For divine power is not so narrow or weak that it cannot collect the scattered dust of each person's flesh into its proper reckoning and repair it. For we see that mortal ingenuity searches out various veins of metals in the depths of the earth, where the industrious eye of the craftsman sees gold, while the unskilled person thinks it is merely earth. Why, then, shall we doubt to grant this power to Him who made man, when he who was made by Him can achieve so much? And since mortal ingenuity can detect that there is a specific vein for gold, another for silver, one far different for bronze, and distinct ones for iron and lead, all hidden within the appearance of the earth, shall divine power not be thought able to find and distinguish the specific essence <note>original: "sensum"; here meaning the unique material identity or "feel" of each person's remains.</note> of each one's flesh? And can He not collect it into one, if it seems scattered, through the power of His own fire, just as miners of those same metals collect the tiniest particles with this common fire that we use?

But as for the second objection—whether the form of the incorruptible body, now converted into the nature of a spirit, will be the same as the corruptible form it has here—we ought not to assert this easily. It does not seem that the form subject to corruption is the same as that which is entirely free from all change. 

<margin>Paul</margin>This is especially true as the Apostle says: *We look for the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility, shaped to the body of his glory* <note>Philippians 3:20-21</note>. By these words (if one understands them rightly), the Apostle implies that another form and another figure of the body is to be resumed by those who are raised, just as he says elsewhere: "because we shall be changed, because it will rise spiritual, because this corruptible will put on incorruption," and because a <term>new sprouting<gloss>original: "pullulatio"; a botanical metaphor for the way a plant rises from a seed</gloss></term> will arise from the sown body. For the form of the sown grain is one thing, and the form of that which sprouts is another. For the former dies, and remains dead in the earth; but the latter grows green and lives. So too the body that shall rise will take up a life that remains forever. Therefore, we shall be raised with flesh and body, which sprouts from that which dies de-

### Chapter XII. Which hair is not destined to perish.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
But since sacred scripture makes mention of hairs, something must also be briefly examined concerning them. For Christ says: *The hairs of your head are all numbered.* <note>Matthew 10:30</note> Regarding these words, Jerome says: "They mock the ecclesiastical understanding in this place, those who deny the resurrection of the flesh: as if we were saying that even the hairs that were numbered and all those cut off by a barber are to rise again; for the Savior did not say: 'All the hairs of your head are to be saved,' but 'they are numbered.'" Where there is a number, the <term>scientia numeri</term> <note>original: "scientia numeri"; meaning the precise knowledge or accounting of a quantity</note> is demonstrated, not the preservation of that same number. By these words, Jerome seems to refute the idea that we will take up our hairs again. But what shall we say to that which is found in the Gospel according to Luke: *A hair of your head shall not perish*? <note>Luke 21:18</note> Therefore (unless I am mistaken), Christ is not speaking of these hairs which, being cut off, are cast away or consumed by fire; but of better hairs, which are commended in the <term>Nazarites</term> <note>original: "Nazareis"; individuals consecrated to God by a vow which included not cutting their hair</note> and are forbidden to be cut off. In these hairs resided the power of the Holy Spirit to lay low the foreigners, as Origen rightly perceives. For those hairs are the virtues of the soul
<margin>Origen</margin>
and the manifold senses, which were produced from the superior part of the mind, the "head" of the Apostles. For this reason, for the Nazarites and others close to God, not only was cutting forbidden, but even that a razor should come upon their head, as we read concerning Samuel, Samson, and others: because the thoughts of the righteous are not to be cut away, but are to be preserved. For whatever the righteous do shall prosper, and their leaf does not fall. But every work of sinners, every word, and every thought, being evil, ought to be cut away and removed. Hence in Deuteronomy it is commanded: that if any woman from the foreigners—that is, from the errors of the gentiles—is led captive, she should shave her hair; or as the literal truth of this passage has it, *she shall shave the hair of her head and clip her nails* <note>Deuteronomy 21:12</note>; so that nothing of her gentility or error remains when she is joined with a true Israelite. In Isaiah also, after the Prophet prophesied concerning the conception
<margin>Deuteronomy</margin>
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
and birth of the <term>Alma</term> <note>original: "Almæ"; Hebrew for a young woman or virgin, referencing the prophecy of the Virgin Birth</note>, he adds: *In that day the Lord shall shave with a hired razor those who are across the river, by the King of the Assyrians: the head, and the hairs of the feet, and the entire beard,* <note>Isaiah 7:20</note> clearly signifying that in the time of the Messiah, all things which belonged to idolatry and error ought to be cut away from the gentiles coming to the faith. And this is done by the "hired razor" through the merit of the Redeemer, by whom all things which belong to sin and error were shaved away. Therefore, the hairs of sin...

->Chapter XIII. In which members we shall rejoice.<-

**E**ven if works or thoughts are understood through the hair, we must also examine what all the members of this body will be like when they are transformed into a spiritual nature. Nor could I imagine that they will be feet that stumble against a stone, or knees that are weakened by fasting or excessive bending. Nor will they be hands that are made weary and rough from labor and hard tools. Nor a tongue that is sometimes loosed into idle and scurrilous words. Nor eyes that must be restrained lest they look upon vanity. Nor ears that, by receiving fables and lascivious songs, admit death into the inner chambers. Nor a mouth that, by indulging the belly too much, receives superfluous and harmful food. Nor a heart from which sometimes come evil thoughts, thefts, murders, and many crimes. But we shall receive (without any doubt) better and harmonious members, through which, without any interruption and without dissonance, we shall pay continuous and most sweet praises to the Creator. They say these affections are so well-shod <note>The author uses the metaphor of being "shod" or wearing shoes to mean being spiritually protected and prepared.</note> that they cannot be tripped or harmed by any evil object thrown in their way; they are directed toward the highest good itself, toward which they will hasten in an eternal and most joyful course. The legs indeed will be like columns of *shesh* <note>original Hebrew: שש; this word can mean "six," "fine linen," or "alabaster/white marble"</note>, which our translation renders as "marble," though it is more often interpreted as "fine linen." If, however, we wish to <term>theologize</term> <note>To reason or interpret through the lens of mystical theology and divine principles.</note> according to numbers, <margin>Plato</margin> the word *shesh* itself yields the number 6 in the higher numbering system; or according to common numbering, it represents the number six multiplied by a hundred. The meaning is this: The legs—that is, the strengths and virtues of the affections which carry us—will be perfect. This is denoted by the number six, which is the first "perfect number" <note>In ancient mathematics, a perfect number is one that equals the sum of its divisors; 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.</note>. To each of these six, a hundredfold corresponds, of which it is said: *You shall receive a hundredfold*; from this, the number 600 arises.

And these virtues are founded upon golden bases—that is, affections set aflame with divine clarity. This is so we may understand that a mystery is signaled there: not only of the virtues brought to completion through the perfect number six, but also the reward corresponding to them through the hundred. The belly, moreover, is aptly called a "heap of wheat," hedged about with roses or lilies, as our translation says; this agrees well with the golden feet. For wheat, which is crushed and gathered into one to <margin>CHRIST. Paul. Augustine.</margin> make bread, signifies the joining and union of the faithful gathered together in charity. As Christ wished to suggest (with Paul and Augustine interpreting) when he gave us his own body—the great sign of charity—under the appearance of bread as food: so that he might not only bind us <margin>Paul</margin> to one another, but also unite us with himself. This food of charity, the best of all, ought to be hedged with fragrant roses—for which our version uses "lilies"—so that we may say with the Apostle: *We are the good odor of Christ.* <note>2 Corinthians 2:15</note> The hands also—that is, the virtues of action—will be golden, filled with the same charity as the feet of the affections. They are full of hyacinths—that is, the gems of the merits of Christ, without which our works are worth nothing. The throat, indeed—that is, the <term>instrument</term> <note>original Latin: *organum*</note> for expressing thought—will be most sweet, so that it may always return harmonious praises to God.

The neck is like the Tower of David built with battlements: a tower which was not built for David out of bricks, or hewn stones, or marble—since that most holy King, the true type and particular ancestor of the Messiah (to whom a special promise was made), never put his trust in such things. <margin>David</margin> Rather, God Himself was David's tower, refuge, and bulwark; of whom he frequently repeats in the Psalms, saying: *God is our refuge and strength*; and again: *The Lord is my firmament, and my refuge, and my deliverer.* And again: *My protector, and the horn of my salvation.* And this is what follows:

God is a shield hanging and looming over the tower itself, to protect and defend: for this reason, it is poorly translated as "they hang from it" <note>Referring to Song of Solomon 4:4, "whereon there hang a thousand bucklers." The author argues the shield is God Himself, who protects from above.</note>; for God does not depend on another, but on Himself. He is the true shield, most perfectly protecting all who hope in Him: from which it follows that He is all the armor of the brave. 

Truly the nose shall be like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. By "the nose," the vigor of the spirit and the righteous impulse of anger are understood, which must be upright and strong, like a tower. Furthermore, it must look not against God, or a neighbor, or some good thing, but against Damascus—which is interpreted as "drinking blood," "the kiss of blood," and "offering blood" <note>Damascus was often etymologically linked in medieval thought to *dam* (Hebrew for blood). The author uses this to symbolize worldly corruption.</note>. And these (unless I am mistaken) signify nothing other than the kingdom of the world, the flesh, and the blood with its most wicked troops, which are the concupiscence <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Strong sensory desire or lust, particularly that which leads to sin.</note> of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. 

For what is "drinking blood" but the greedy man, who sucks the secondary blood of the poor, the lowly, and the orphans? And what is "the kiss of blood" but the concupiscence of the flesh, where there are mutual kisses and embraces according to the flesh and blood? And what is "offering blood" but pride, haughtiness, and ambition, for the sake of which such immense blood is shed daily?

<margin>CHRIST. Paul, John. CHRIST.</margin>
Against these evil works there must be indignation and zeal, so that it may be said with Christ: *I bear witness of the world, that its works are evil* <note>original: "Ego testimonium perhibeo de mundo, quia opera eius mala sunt." John 7:7</note>. And again with Paul: *To me the world is crucified, and I to the world* <note>original: "Mihi mundus crucifixus est, & ego mundo." Galatians 6:14</note>. Otherwise, unless one rises up against the world, but wishes to be its friend (as John witnesses), he is established as an enemy of God. 

Finally, the eyes shall be those of doves—namely, filled with the required simplicity, according to that Gospel saying: *If your eye is simple, your whole body will be bright* <note>original: "Si oculus tuus simplex fuerit, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit." Matthew 6:22</note>. For every work is built upon the intention, just as a column is built upon a base, and a wall upon a foundation. These, therefore, are the future members of our body to be changed into the nature of the spirit, according to which it will use the members and organs not of the inner man, but of the outer man.

## Chapter XIV.

<margin>Cleanthes. Cicero.</margin>
Now, above we have revealed that fire is found to be manifold, or that the same fire is distributed and varied in different things by different marks, as Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher; his views on the "vital heat" are preserved in the works of Cicero.</note> discusses at great length in the writings of Cicero <note>Likely referring to Cicero’s *De Natura Deorum* (On the Nature of the Gods), Book II.</note>. For there is this external fire which we use; and there is fire in stones, which we strike out by the blow and clash of steel. There is also fire in the earth, which smokes when dug up and heats the water in deep wells, especially in winter times for the reason that it contains a heat implanted in the earth. In the same way, we prove that heat is mixed into water: because the ground hardens when the north winds and other cold forces are applied, and in turn, the same ground liquefies when warmed and melts from the heat. The seas also, when tossed by winds, grow warm in such a way that it can easily be understood that heat is enclosed within those great waters. We also see the air grow hot many times. ## By what peculiar fire the wicked are to be burned. Chapter 15.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**T**hat the wicked are tortured by fire, and are to be tortured, almost all confess and agree with the Supreme Truth <note>i.e., Jesus Christ.</note> when He says:
> Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire and burn.
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
In that fire, surely, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For that fire was not ordained by God for our destruction, nor will anyone be tortured by it unless he has kindled it himself, as we may learn from the oracle of Isaiah saying:
> Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled: from my hand this has been done to you; you lie in sorrows.
The Prophet touches upon both points: that it is done by God, and that we ourselves kindle that fire. For although it is prepared by God, no one will be tortured by it unless he kindles it with the fuel of his sins, as <margin>Origen</margin> Origen rightly perceives. For just as we kindle fiery fevers in the body by harmful foods and immoderate labors, so we kindle fiery torments in the soul and in the body (when they shall be united) from the superfluity of evil works and crooked affections. The abundance of these, gathered within a person, boils up in its own time for the punishment and penalty of those who <margin>Pythagoras</margin> kindled it. And thus (to follow the Pythagorean doctrine), that fire which, when expanded and shining through, brings bliss to him who has a heart expanded in the way of God’s commandments; so the fire is constricted by the evil disposition of those who have a constricted heart, hardened toward the good like a stone or a smith's anvil, and rendered dark. For they themselves, darkened by the monstrosity of their crimes, <margin>A most excellent comparison</margin> are unable to receive the divine light. It becomes obscure and agonizing, just as the same sun or fire hardens or melts according to the variety of the subjects receiving that light and heat. This doctrine of the same fire both blessing and tormenting is not foreign to the sacred utterances. For that fire which in <margin>Deuteronomy</margin> Deuteronomy is called "devouring"—and consequently blessing and <margin>Exodus</margin> transforming—is the same fire which in Exodus gave the fiery law in a visible flame.

<margin>Isaiah</margin> And he who makes his Angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire, is described in Isaiah <note>Psalm 104:4 and Isaiah 66:15–16.</note> as a rebuking, judging, and punishing flame. ### How the wicked are to be tortured. Chapter 16.

<margin>Gregory</margin> **S**ince we have said enough concerning the agonizing fire, we must now run through how the wicked are to be tortured by that fire. This presents no small difficulty, if we presuppose that this fire is corporeal—that is, physical—(as is the common opinion) and that our souls, as well as evil <term>intelligences</term> <note>A technical term used in medieval philosophy to describe purely spiritual beings like angels or demons.</note>, are entirely removed from the body. This topic occurs to us as more difficult because it has many and various critics. For <margin>Gregory</margin> Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a foundational theologian for the Middle Ages.</note>, quickly resolving the matter, judges that this fire tortures the wicked as an instrument of divine justice. But how it acts as an instrument—and whether it inflicts torment from its own nature, or is guided by another (just as a saw or a hammer is guided to cutting or striking the wicked)—he left for posterity to explain. Truly, it is a wonder how Gregory faltered in a matter of this kind, since elsewhere he asserts that Angels and demons possess bodies, though so thin and refined that in comparison to our bodies they are called <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Bodiless; lacking physical matter.</note>. Therefore, regarding this business, there ought to have been no difficulty for him.

<margin>Theologians</margin> Among the more recent theologians, however, some are of the opinion that wicked spirits and souls are tortured by that physical fire as if by an object most disproportionate and vehemently distressing to them. Just as the sight of a horrid serpent is distressing to us, this is especially so because they are held down and thrust into that fire by God, whom they hate and who is most hostile to them, and they are unable to escape its presence. <margin>Academics</margin> The Academics <note>Followers of the Platonic school of philosophy, who often held that all created spirits have some form of subtle body.</note>, however, are more easily explained by this difficulty, since they all (as they say) run with one accord to this opinion: that all evil demons are corporeal. <margin>Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, Augustine</margin> With them agree Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, and the ancient doctors generally. Even Augustine does not disagree, who, in rendering the reason why evil spirits can divine the future <margin>Why evil spirits divine.</margin> in his work *On Genesis*, says: "Because they flourish with more subtle bodies." And in what follows, he says: "Demons are aerial and fiery animals." Because these are active elements, they do not dissolve like earthy and watery animals. Nor are there lacking those who say that not only the demons themselves, but even all Angels...

angels and souls separated from the earthly body possess ethereal bodies. If
<margin>Paul</margin> however, we wish to enter the school of Paul—who was instructed in the third heaven <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where St. Paul describes being "caught up to the third heaven."</note>—we will easily untie these knots. For here he teaches that the war between the spirit and the flesh is declared by this law: that whoever wins gives their properties and gifts to the defeated, and the defeated puts on the nature of the victor. Therefore, concerning those over whom the spirit has emerged victorious, he says: *When this mortal body has put on immortality.* And likewise: *What is sown as a natural body rises as a spiritual body.* <note>original: "Seminatur quod animale: surgit quod spirituale." From 1 Corinthians 15:44.</note> And by this same discipline of opposites, a soul defeated by the flesh and the body will put on "heaviness," so that it descends to the lower parts; it will receive those "bad gifts" of the body, by which it suffers from corporeal fire as if it were a body itself. Just as the soul, having put on the nature of the body, will be tortured by corporeal fire, so the body, putting on the nature of the spirit, will receive blessedness together with the soul from him who was called by Moses the "God of spirits." <note>original: "Deus spirituum." <margin>Moses, Origen, Academics</margin> Another kind of punishment for the damned is assigned by Origen and the ancient Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of Plato’s Academy; here, the author links Platonic thought on the soul's harmony with Christian theology.</note> as arising from the disorder and confusion of those parts which ought to be orderly and harmonious. For just as we feel the general torture of immense pain when the limbs of the body are loosened and its own joints are pulled apart, so when the soul is found outside of that order or harmony for which it was created by God—to act well and to perceive usefully—it will suffer punishment and penalty from that very disorder and confusion. 
<margin>Augustine</margin> This is according to that saying of Augustine: *You have commanded, Lord—and so it is—that every disordered mind should be its own punishment.* <note>original: "Iussisti Domine... ut omnis inordinatus animus sibi poena sit." From Augustine’s Confessions, Book 1, Chapter 12.</note> And concerning this torment resulting from the soul’s disorder within itself and with God (with whom it ought always to be in harmony), many things are said, not only by Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and many other Catholic doctors, but also by
<margin>Cicero</margin> outsiders like Proclus, Hierocles, and many others. Among them, Cicero, in his speech against Catiline, says: *Do not your iniquities run to meet you like furies?* <note>original: "Nonne iniquitates tuae quasi furiae tibi occurrunt?" Referring to the psychological "furies" of a guilty conscience.</note> 
<margin>Jeremiah, Isaiah</margin> The Prophets likewise assert this. *Know and see,* says Jeremiah, *that it is an evil and bitter thing for you to have forsaken the Lord.* <note>Jeremiah 2:19.</note> And Isaiah: *The heart of the wicked is like a boiling sea, which can never rest, but its waves overflow into trampling and grief; for there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.* <note>Isaiah 57:20–21.</note> See how the Prophet describes the punishments of the wicked resulting from disorder and the deprivation of peace, which is the "tranquility of order." <note>original: "tranquillitas ordinis," a classic Augustinian definition of peace.</note> Therefore, a soul that does not feel the structure of its rational movements to be in harmony with itself must necessarily undergo penalty and torture, and feel the punishment of its own discord, inconstancy, and disorder. 

Those authors we mentioned above describe another reason for torment: that it is generated from an "evil idol." <note>original: "ex malo idolo." In this context, "idol" refers to a mental image or "phantasm" of past sins stored in the memory.</note> For the mind, or our soul, receiving into its memory those things of which it impressed certain signs and forms upon itself when it was sinning, will see a certain "history" of its crimes set before its eyes. And then the conscience itself will be driven by its own stings, with 
<margin>Paul</margin> thoughts (as the Apostle says) *accusing one another.* <note>Romans 2:15.</note> From this, certain torments will be generated from those very worst affections; hence it will be tortured by the flame of an evil fire, of a distorted love, and of indignation against itself, or by the fires of envy; or it will be consumed by an insane sadness.

Because some (while they are still able to apply a remedy) cannot bear [their suffering], they undergo a voluntary death <note>That is, they commit suicide to escape earthly misery.</note> to avoid it, thinking it more tolerable to die than to endure those torments. Yet, they unfortunately pass from a torment that could easily be removed to eternal punishment, deceived by their own folly and an evil spirit.

There, a spiritual fire burns and tortures them from within, but does not consume them. <margin>The wicked shall be tormented by a double fire: spiritual in the soul and corporeal in the body</margin> A fire is also applied to the body, torturing it perpetually; and this is by the just judgment of God. For just as iron and fire <note>referring to cautery or surgical tools</note> are applied to the limbs of the body when they are so diseased that they cannot be healed, so fire is applied to punish wicked souls and bodies alike. These were once members of the **great ecclesiastical body** <note>original: "magni corporis ecclesiastici." This refers to the "Body of Christ," the theological concept of the community of the Church.</note>, but they were so overwhelmed by the enormity of various crimes that they could not be healed. Fire is applied so that they may always burn, yet be unable to infect or trouble the other members.

## Resolution of the difficulty concerning this fire. Chapter XVII.

Because we have implied through what was said above that this fire which tortures the wicked is sometimes corporeal, and at other times that it is the same fire—restricted and dark—which, when expanded, makes the good blessed and joyful, it is appropriate to explain more clearly what kind of fire it is. Since almost everyone asserts that it is corporeal, it would be difficult to depart from the common opinion. However, if we wish to follow the popular opinion and not disagree that it is corporeal, how can it be the same spiritual fire that blesses souls and a corporeal fire that afflicts bodies? <margin>Paul</margin> The Apostle solves this controversy, saying to the Corinthians: *There are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.* <note>original: "Diuisiones operationū sunt, idē autē Deus..." From 1 Corinthians 12:6.</note> Just as the same soul performs all functions in all the limbs of the body. Therefore, let no one say that Paul speaks there only of spiritual and internal operation. For He who fills not only the minds of men, but the whole heaven and earth, works all things in them, and in everything contained within them. It is no wonder, then, if the Judge of all also punishes the guilty in hell: either torturing them by His power, or by a presence that is unsuitable to their "infected eyes." This causes them greater pain than the brightest light causes to eyes that are bleary, swollen, or otherwise damaged. Or perhaps He punishes by withdrawing from them His kind influence, by which all things are filled with goodness, leaving them in their own evil disorder without any cooling comfort. And thus, He who is the source of resurrection and joy for those who are well-disposed, is the source of ruin and punishment for those in a bad state. <margin>Ezekiel</margin> This is what Ezekiel claims to have seen: the Lord appearing like **electrum** <note>original: "electri." This refers to a precious alloy of gold and silver, or a glowing amber-like substance described in the vision of Ezekiel 1:27.</note> shining from the waist up, but from the waist down in the figure of glowing fire. Truly, it is the Lord who, filling heaven and earth, sits in heaven gladdening the good; but on earth (which is His footstool), holding feet of white-hot fire, He tortures and torments those who are earthly and distanced from heavenly things. And unless Holy Scripture taught me this, I would in no way presume to utter it: that the same Lord now...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of divine fire, transitioning from its role as a punishment to its role as a purifying and beatifying force. It uses the authority of the Prophet Joel, King David, Origen, and the Apostle Paul to reconcile the physical and spiritual aspects of eternal fire.</meta>

<page-num>LXXXI, 1</page-num>

### OF THE THIRD SONG.

<note>The header refers to the "Canticle of Canticles" or a specific section of the author's work divided by "songs."</note>

[It] is light, and a **beatifying fire** <note>original: "ignis beatificans," fire that brings the state of supreme blessedness</note>, making the righteous shine like stars and like sparks of fire. Now, therefore, it is a **refining fire**, purging the sons of Levi <note>A reference to Malachi 3:3, where God purifies the priesthood like gold and silver.</note>. Now, indeed, it is a fire consuming the wood and the straw which we have poorly built <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:12–15, where life's works are tested by fire.</note>. 
<margin>Joel</margin> And it devours and destroys (as Joel says) the "beauties of the wilderness"—that is, whatever works seem glorious but are performed by those who are deserted by grace and heavenly influence. 
<margin>The same</margin> And now it is a torturing and burning fire. Regarding this, Joel says again: *A devouring fire goes before his face, and behind him a parching flame.* <note>Joel 2:3</note> The sense of these words is this: To those who are worthy to see his face, He himself is a consuming fire, transforming them into himself, as we touched on above. But to those who are left behind in the delight of "posterior" <note>That is, "lower" or "outward" things as opposed to the "face" or "inward" presence of God.</note>—that is, inferior—affections, He is a parching and agonizing flame. This happens either through the fire itself (which is perfect in its own nature), just as occurs with those who are physically ill, for whom light, wine, meat, and similar bodily goods are harmful. 
<margin>David</margin> Or, He does this through his ministers, whom He makes (as the prophet testifies) a burning fire <note>Psalm 104:4: "He makes... his ministers a flaming fire."</note>, though for the good this fire results in joy, and for the wicked, in torment. Or likewise, He may do this through some physical thing fashioned for the torture of the wicked, so as to satisfy those who argue that that fire is corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note>. Whether it is physical or not, God knows; 
<margin>Origen</margin> but it is well-proven to be invisible by Origen, based on the 
<margin>Paul</margin> Apostolic teaching. He says: "That fire is of such a substance that, being invisible itself, it burns visible things." As the Apostle says: *For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.* <note>2 Corinthians 4:18</note> If, therefore, that fire by which those who depart from God are punished is eternal, it must also be invisible, since according to the Apostolic view, only invisible things are eternal. 
<margin>Origen</margin> Do not wonder (as Origen continues) that fire is invisible and agonizing, since you cannot see the heat that enters bodies, yet it causes no small agony to those who are severely afflicted by it. This agonizing fire is therefore of a different kind than the one we use in common life; yet that supreme torture is compared to our fire, since nothing among us is more painful than this visible fire. If we wish to avoid this eternal agony, let us take care that there is no "eternal evil disposition" within us. Instead, let us cultivate that disposition by which we can receive that supreme fire as joy—or at least as the consumption of our "wood and straw" and the purging of our dross. Thus, we may become **beautiful vessels of pure gold**, to be placed in the heavenly wedding and those blessed and eternal dwellings.

<summary>This page explores the multi-faceted nature of divine fire, explaining that the same "fire" of God acts as a reward for the holy, a purification for the imperfect, and a torment for the wicked, while arguing for its invisible, eternal nature.</summary>

<page-num>LXXXII</page-num>
<header>THE EIGHTH TONE.</header>
<sig>l ii</sig>

### ON THE SWEETEST HARMONIES, AND THAT ETERNAL PAUSE IN ATTAINED BEATITUDE. THE EIGHTH TONE. <note>In the system of Gregorian modes, the eighth tone (Hypomixolydian) is the final one. Symbolically, the "eighth day" represents the resurrection and eternity, following the seven days of the week.</note>

Applying the finishing touch to this final song of the newest canticle, we shall imitate the most excellent musicians to the best of our ability; they always strive to render the final harmony even sweeter. Sometimes they draw out such sweetness that, were they not subject to the movements of time and weakened by the fatigue of labor, they would extend the song forever. But lasting as long as they can, now with continuous and now with changing turns, they do not cease from the egg to the apples <note>original: "ab ovo usque ad pomum," a Latin idiom meaning from the beginning of a meal to the end, or from start to finish.</note>. But the supreme **Arch-Musician** <note>original: "Archimuseus," a title for God as the ultimate composer of the universe.</note>, whose song we attempt to describe, since He both exceeds time and rejoices in eternity, now distributes and divides His songs throughout time, and now leads them toward eternity itself. For He has subjected this harmonic machine (by I know not what marvelous craftsmanship) both to temporal succession and released it from time itself. For all these elementary things are generated by daily and yearly successions. The heavens, too, are moved in time, or (to speak more correctly) being moved, they generate time itself.

<margin>David</margin>
The earth, nonetheless, stands forever, and the heavens will never fail from their being, even though—as the Psalmist sings—they shall grow old <note>original: "pibunt," likely a contraction or error for "peribunt" (they shall perish) or "veterascent" (they shall grow old), referencing Psalm 102:26.</note> in regard to their motion and influence.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
He also completed the sweeter harmony of redemption in a few (I will not say months, but) days; yet a plenteous redemption remains with Him forever, and its eternal fruit remains. *If anyone,* says the Redeemer, *eats of this bread* offered for your <term>redemption</term> <note>The act of being saved from sin or error.</note>, *he shall live forever*, enjoying the fruit of that same eternal redemption. He also wished to lead the sweetest song of union from merits acquired through time, and He determined to draw all people toward eternity itself with perpetual rewards, making them co-eternal with Himself.

<margin>Orpheus. Amphion.</margin>
Hence He will release from temporal succession all those whom, having been lifted up from the earth, He has drawn to Himself by a better harmonic force than **Orpheus** or **Amphion** <note>In Greek mythology, Orpheus and Amphion were musicians so skilled that their music could move stones, tame wild beasts, and influence the gods.</note>, placing them in those most harmonious dwellings where (if we believe **Augustine**, who was once enticed by such sweetness) even the numbers and bodily harmonies now hidden will be seen to resound together with other singers in the public praises of the **Artificer** <note>A term for God as the Great Builder or Creator.</note> and of that highest beauty.

<margin>Ezekiel. John.</margin>
Therefore, those heavenly scribes of both Testaments, **Ezekiel** and **John**, described those dwellings with the most exact figures and the most harmonious measures and divisions, just as the Holy Spirit taught them. Truly, Ezekiel describes only the measures of the structure, the arrangement, the divisions for the twelve tribes, the sacrifices, and the name of the city. But John, a member of the Lord's household admitted to the more secret inner chambers, brings forth sweeter songs. Both of them, however, are so clouded by darkness that unless the supreme Sun thins that density with His heat and expels the shadows with His light, one cannot even hear what they say...

<header>OF THE THIRD SONG.</header>

## OF THE THIRD SONG.

Nor shall we be able to see in any way what they describe and measure; for they hand down things of this kind wrapped in sensible riddles <note>original: "enigmatibus," referring to symbols or metaphors that represent spiritual truths through physical things</note>, either so that from these things which the mind already knows, it may be able to rise toward the unknown, and behold invisible things through such sensible ones; or because words have not yet been granted—neither to us who hear nor to those who speak—by which those things can be expressed. Just as those who have seen these things themselves openly affirm, it is not permitted for a man to speak of them. Or perhaps it is because the mind, still weighed down by the burden of the bodily mass, is unable to ascend to these heights; as <margin>Isaiah, Paul</margin> Isaiah and Paul agree: **"Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him."** <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 2:9 and Isaiah 64:4.</note> Therefore, if we do not fully unfold those mysteries, you will grant us pardon; for those things must be treated which transcend our every talent, escape every memory, and surpass all eloquence. Nevertheless, relying on a single aid, we shall approach this most arduous work, since we have guides to whom God has laid these things open. As the same Paul adds: <margin>The same Isaiah</margin> **"But God has revealed these things to us through His Spirit."** Hence Isaiah speaks more cautiously, saying: **"Eye has not seen a God besides thee, who has prepared such things for those who wait for thee."** Therefore, following these divine guides immediately, and as much as the supreme light shall have illuminated our eyes, we will explain in our own words those things which they have folded into their riddles. We shall follow especially the more secret and fuller songs of John, who, resting upon the inspired <note>original: "pegaseo," literally "Pegasean," a reference to the winged horse of the Muses, here used to denote divine poetic inspiration</note> breast of Christ between the two peaks of the divine and human nature, was so drenched in light and filled with such divine fury <note>In the Renaissance sense, "furore" refers to a state of divine inspiration or poetic madness</note> that he easily emerged as the prophet of divine things. Later, led away by the divine spirit from the island of Patmos to the supramundane continent, having been taught now by an Angel, now by the supreme Lead-Singer <note>original: "concentore," meaning one who sings in harmony with others</note> Jesus Christ, and now by various figures sounding all around him, he delivered to us those perfected songs. Running to and fro with wondrous craftsmanship, now ascending, now descending, according to the full laws of music, he left no melody of the supramundane instrument nor any voice of musical distribution untouched. For musicians distinguish the whole harmony discovered by them through twenty degrees <note>A reference to the twenty notes of the medieval musical scale, often mapped onto the "Guidonian Hand" as a mnemonic device</note>, which they have placed upon the hand so that practice might be easier and memory more tenacious. John touches just as many modules <note>musical measures or intervals</note> in which the entire supracelestial harmony is perfected. And he does this under the figure of a city, which is set forth as a celestial lyre, in which, when all these voices are tempered and touched by the supreme **Chief Musician** <note>original: "Archimuseo"</note>, that consonance which transcends all others is perfected. <margin>Dionysius</margin> **"All things rejoice,"** says Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian mystical philosopher</note>, **"when the Father moves them."** For the Son has been made the instrument <note>original: "organum"</note> of God, since within Him exist the Ideas of all created things; and in Him all things are arranged like pipes <note>original: "fistulae"</note>, so that if anyone does not remain in Him, he can bring forth nothing useful or harmonious. The breath <note>original: "flatus"</note>, however, is the Spirit who fills all things, as it is said <margin>Wisdom</margin> in the Book of Wisdom: **"The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and this, which contains all things, has knowledge of the voice."** But the Father is the first and the primary mover of all, most especially in that supernal city, in which all things correspond to Him like pipes, strings, or musical modules. Explaining these modules and dividing them into harmonies, we shall follow John; and with him, we shall make Ezekiel agree to the best of our abilities.

<page-num>LXXXI</page-num>
<header>OF THE THIRD SONG</header>

## FIRST MOVEMENT / SUBJECT MATTER.

->Why that city is said to be built of gold.<-

<margin>First Accord.</margin>

**J**ohn, therefore, establishing the foundation of the heavenly Building, describes it as composed of gold and precious stones. For gold is used not only as <term>stone-glue</term> <note>original: "lithocolla"; a substance used to cement or overlay stones in fine masonry.</note> for covering the walls, but as the cement and binding for the stones, and for the <term>small joints</term> <note>original: "carpusculis"; literally "little wrists," referring here to the structural hinges or connecting points.</note> and nails that hold the building together. And what is wondrous is that this gold does not obscure the brilliance of the precious stones, since it enjoys a perfect transparency. Hence our <term>composer</term> <note>original: "concinnator"; literally "one who joins things fitly," here referring to the author or the divine architect.</note> says <term>that</term> <note>original: "qp", a Latin abbreviation for "quod".</note> the gold itself is like pure glass. The precious stones, however, serve for the foundation, the gates, and the entire structure of the walls: so that both the stones and the glue are of the highest value for that most precious dwelling, and are incorruptible for those eternal mansions. And entering the inner sanctuaries—as far as is lawful and permitted by the <term>Master of the Muses</term> <note>original: "Archimusæo"; a title likely referring to the Holy Spirit or God as the conductor of divine harmony.</note>—we shall run through the mysteries and the more secret symphonies described under the figure of precious stones and of gold, which signifies life, according to that saying of the wise man: *Before the golden fillet runs down* <margin>Solomon</margin> <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 12:6, where the "golden bowl" or "cord" represents the fragility of life.</note>. This fillet, or golden thread, signifies true life. To do this, we must examine the properties and nature of gold and of the stones themselves. For gold is beautiful and comely; hence it is named, as it were, <term>auron</term> <note>Greek: αὖρον.</note> (as some prefer), or from <term>aura</term> <note>Latin for breeze or air, but here used for its connotation of "gleam" or "radiance".</note>, which signifies splendor. Although Hippocrates <margin>Hippocrates</margin> thought it was named after its inventor, <term>Augeias</term> <note>Greek: Αὐγίῳ.</note>. For it is beautiful, and it makes other things beautiful—yet not all things (as Hippias <margin>Hippias</margin> had once mistakenly said), but only those for which gold itself is fitting. Among all metals and liquids, it is of the most perfect value. It is also by its very nature most stable, so that even when stretched into the thinnest foils, it is not broken. For in our times, one hundred and twenty-four foils, each four fingers wide on both sides, are drawn from a single gold <term>denarius</term> <note>A standard unit of weight/currency.</note>, whereas the ancients could only stretch it to seventy. Furthermore, it is most tenacious despite its yielding nature; for it gives way to the one striking or folding it, yet it is never consumed by fire, nor by rust, nor by verdigris, nor by the juices of vinegar and salt (the masters of all things), nor even by sublimated arsenic, which (as Albert <margin>Albertus</margin> <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus, the medieval scholar-saint known for his work on alchemy and minerals.</note> testifies) consumes all other metals. Nor does any part of it waste away that might eventually diminish its quality or weight, nor does it lose its components of its own accord. This is Pliny's <margin>Pliny</margin> most elegant reason for its high value: <term>that</term> <note>original: "qp".</note> use wears it away the least. And it is indeed a wonder that it is in no way harmed by the fiercest fire, the consumer of all things, even though it is melted by it; rather, the more often it burns, the purer and more perfect it becomes. For this reason it is called <term>refined gold</term> <note>original: "obrizum"; gold tested and purified by fire.</note>, because having been frequently heated and scorched by fire, it is not consumed but rendered most pure. Its benefits, moreover...

Many properties of gold are recounted by experts. It is an enemy to every <term>distemper</term> <note>original: "distemperamēto"; an imbalance of the bodily humors.</note>, perhaps because of its own balanced temperament, in which it rejoices above all other metals; or perhaps because of a certain <term>Phoebian power</term> <note>original: "ui quadam phœbea"; referring to Phoebus Apollo, the sun god. Gold, therefore, is the divine or spiritual life, or rather **Charity** <note>original: "charitas"; meaning "love" in the highest, most selfless sense.</note>, which provides life. By it, all those guests and fellow-singers are decorated, made to shine, made beautiful, live, and are enriched. If you lack this, listen to the Master of the Muses saying:

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
> I advise you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so that you may become rich. <note>original: "Suadeo tibi emere a me aurum ignitū, ut locuplex fias"; a reference to Revelation 3:18.</note>

This is said to those hurrying toward those mansions; for those who enter without that garment, which is called the wedding garment, are most shamefully expelled. For all those guests must be dressed in this golden garment of charity, according to that prophetic saying: *In gilded clothing.* This golden charity was most burning in the Martyrs and all the saints; relying upon it, Paul said with great constancy:

<margin>The Psalm of Paul</margin>
> Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or persecution, or the sword? Charity also yields to the one who strikes, tortures, and tears it apart, as that famous herald of charity says again:

<margin>The Same</margin>
