It yields, therefore, because in those patient souls filled with charity, no murmur resounds, and no complaint. Yet it is most tenacious: so that it loses nothing of itself through rubbing or striking; rather, it grows stronger in such conditions. It is not eaten away by the rust of sin, nor by the <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "ærugine"; the green crust that forms on copper or brass, here used as a metaphor for malice.</note> of malice, nor by the "juice" of salt and vinegar—that is, of human or diabolical cunning—nor by anything else, no matter how sharply it bites. It stands invincible against the fire of trouble and the divine fire: indeed, it is perfected in the former, while in the latter it is increased and receives growth. For that highest Divine Fire exposes his beloved ones to the fire of hardships, so that they may be tested like gold in the furnace and the melting pot. Once purified by that fire, they may radiate and shine in the eternal mansions, where the guests burn and shine openly like <term>pure gold</term> <note>original: "aurum obrizum"; the highest quality of refined gold.</note>. However, this gold of charity melts, not so that it might fall from its perfection or rank, but so that it may be <term>refined</term> <note>original: "conflatū"; cast together or fused.</note> alongside other metals—or rather, with the refining fire itself—so that we may discourse on it in its proper place (God willing). Indeed, in its operation and virtue, it gladdens the heart, because nothing truly joyful can be had without charity. We can learn this from the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>, who, having lost that charity, was saddened and proclaimed himself afflicted, bent over, decaying, and full of trouble, so much so that he could in no way rejoice. <margin>Paul</margin>

This garment, of both the walls and the guests, is not meant for covering: since there is nothing defiled, nothing vulnerable, and nothing shameful that ought to be covered lest it seem ugly, be tormented by cold, or be overwhelmed with shame. Therefore, this garment will be an ornament that does not hide, but is transparent, so that nothing beautiful is concealed where no envy exists; nothing shameful is covered when all baseness has ceased. For all things will be open to every fellow citizen, so that each one burns with the love of his companion, rejoices in beauty, and shouts for joy with the most harmonious fibers of all their members.

### Why the Walls are made of Jasper.

<margin>John</margin>
**T**he structure of all the walls (says our lead singer John <note>Referring to the Apostle John’s vision of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21.</note>) was of Jasper: which the wise celebrate exceedingly. For 
<margin>Aaron, Pliny, Albert</margin>
Aaron, Pliny, Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a philosopher and scientist known for his work on minerals.</note>, and other more recent authors who write about stones, hand down that up to seventeen kinds of Jasper are found—although Albert mentions only ten. This one excels in utility, while the other excels in price. The city itself is constructed so that it is gathered from both sexes, so that they may bring forth the praises of Him who is (as Mercury says) most full of the fecundity of both sexes.
<margin>Mercury</margin> <note>original: "Mercurius"; refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary sage whom Renaissance scholars believed predicted Christian truths. He described God as containing both masculine and feminine principles.</note>
And its beauty very elegantly represents the beauty of all those citizens and those fiery stones: for in the presence of the highest beauty, nothing ought to stand unless it is beautiful and fitting. Moreover, its precious variety designates the royal pomp of that most beautiful city, which is clothed in a variety of many precious things. For a Cherub differs from a Seraph; a Virtue differs from a Power; and an Angel from an Archangel. 
<margin>Paul</margin>

<margin>The Apostle</margin> <note>referring to St. Paul</note>
nor can they be numbered among the children of God who follow the appetite of flesh and blood. And what is more suitable to those singers than this stone, which makes one chaste? For if (by Christ’s testimony) the pure in heart shall see God, those who do not have a pure heart ought not to see Him. 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>

<margin>The Apostle</margin>
having once been carried up to behold that dwelling. All heavenly things (even the walls) favor them; therefore they are described as being constructed from Jasper, which both favors the singers and puts hostile phantasms to flight.

# VOLUME EIGHT LXXXVIII

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
...deals with his birth in the beginning, his preaching and miracles in the middle, and his passion, death, and resurrection at the end. It also possesses properties shared with the **Jasper** stone itself. It is said of this stone that it provides strength for spiritual matters and, when set in gold, resists the terrors of the night. Furthermore, when crushed and stuffed with the hairs of a donkey <note>This refers to an ancient and medieval belief found in "lapidaries" (books about the magical properties of gems) that certain preparations of stones could ward off demons.</note>, it is said to terrify and drive away demons. From what source do we have a greater power for strengthening spiritual things than from the **Gospel**, provided its doctrine is "set in the gold" of charity? In this way, we do not only resist the night terrors brought by the powers of darkness, but we even strike terror into them—just as the Prince <note>Referring to Christ.</note> promised in the Gospel, saying: *Behold, I have given you the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.* <note>original: "Ecce dedi uobis potestatē calcandi super serpentes, & scorpiones, & super omnem uirtutē inimici" — Luke 10:19.</note> This power is granted when one has "penetrated the hairs of the donkey." This may perhaps seem like a superstition to someone who does not understand the nature of things; however, let us leave the stone and its secrets to the more profound philosophers, and let us examine how the power of the Gospel is "stuffed with donkey hair." This is easy to know if we understand why Christ ordered the donkey and the foal to be untied on Palm Sunday, so that he might enter Jerusalem sitting upon them while the crowds and children applauded, spreading their garments and 

<margin>Zechariah</margin>
olive branches—as had been prescribed through a great mystery by the oracle of **Zechariah**. <note>A reference to Zechariah 9:9, "Rejoice greatly, O daughter Zion... your king comes to you... riding on a donkey."</note> And why did Abraham, the father of mercy, ride only upon donkeys (as we read)?

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
For here, the donkey signifies mercy and piety, as is clear from the "inverted letters" in the ancient Hebrew language. For <term>חמר</term> <note>original: "chamor" — donkey.</note> means donkey, but if the letter **R** is placed first to say <term>רחם</term> <note>original: "racham" — to have mercy or compassion.</note>, it signifies piety or mercy. This denotes that Christ then began to exercise his supreme work of mercy by redeeming the human race. Therefore, those ancient fathers, aware of these mysteries, established that this mystery should be celebrated with a yearly memorial.

The **Beryl**, which aids against enemies and lawsuits, renders a person 

<margin>Bartholomew</margin>
mild in character and provides a good wit. It represents **Bartholomew**, who in Albania of Greater Armenia <note>This refers to Caucasian Albania, an ancient kingdom in the eastern Caucasus, often associated with Bartholomew's martyrdom in hagiography.</note> prevailed so greatly against the enemies of the human race that the demons, bound by Bartholomew’s chains, could no longer give any oracular responses. He rendered the Aonian peoples and the untamed Bactrians <note>Central Asian tribes.</note> mild, giving them a more refined wit for perceiving the mysteries of the Gospel.

<margin>Simon</margin>
The **Topaz**, gleaming with a golden-green hue, makes boiling water lukewarm if it is cast into it (as clear experience has proven) and heals various infirmities. It represents **Simon the Zealot**, who, burning with zeal for God, shone with the "paleness of golden charity" combined with the "greenness of good works." By the power granted to him, he tempered the "feverish" Egyptians who were in service to Mammon and the worship of the devil. He did this by moistening them with the refreshing preaching of the Gospel, cleansing them and kindling them with celestial fire—the complete opposite of the devilish fire—and he healed them of the infirmities of both soul and body.

<margin>Thomas</margin>
But through the **Chrysoprase**, which comes from India and is rare, can we not understand with clear light **Thomas**? He preached in India, rare and alone, where no other of the Apostles reached. This stone, which delights in the paleness of gold, represents Thomas himself, glowing with charity; inflamed by this, he [urged] the others...

->### OF THE THIRD CANTICLE.<-

The Apostle shed his life and blood for the love of Christ and the salvation of mankind. This stone is also said to correspond with the **Chrysolite**, by which we previously declared that the charity of **John** is signified. Does the **Jacinth**, whose chief virtue is to grant the grace of obtaining what is asked for without any refusal, not fit <margin>James the Great</margin> **James the Great** to a tee? He grants such grace to men for obtaining their requests from the Prince <note>Referring to Christ.</note> that people flock to his remains at **Compostela** <note>Santiago de Compostela in Spain, one of the most famous pilgrimage sites in the medieval world.</note> from every direction—not only in ancient times, but even more so in our own day. Thus, it can easily be proven that he has opened the ears of divine mercy and obtained the grace of petition for those who ask; for there is no other Saint visited with such great frequency. 

Let us see if the **Amethyst**, to which it is given by heaven (as they say) to make the sterile fertile, to extinguish drunkenness, and to restrain the malice of poison, matches <margin>Philip</margin> **Philip**. Indeed, he made the sterile eunuch <note>The Ethiopian Eunuch, though traditionally converted by Philip the Evangelist, the medieval tradition often conflated him with Philip the Apostle.</note> fertile in the vineyard of the Lord. Later, he extinguished the "drunkenness" of the **Scythians**; for they were drunk on blood and vices, but he healed them through holy preaching and power granted from heaven. After this, he restrained the poison of the **Ebionites** <note>A Jewish-Christian sect. The author claims here they believed Christ's body was a "phantom," a view usually called Docetism.</note> which was being offered throughout all of Asia; for these men asserted that Christ did not take on a true body, but a phantasmal one. 

And because an entrance is made into that holy city through any of these virtues—or through the grace and favor of these leaders—as if through a gate, the twelve gates are also said to be erected from these same stones. This was done so that these heavenly splendors might shine like divine powers both in the foundations and in the gates, and that they might harmonize with those twelve splendors and presiding intelligences <note>Refers to the angels or spiritual forces governing the celestial spheres.</note> whose names are also said to be written or carved upon the gates. They correspond to the twelve figurative and true tribes, whose names are likewise told to be written on those same gates. 

With beautifully increasing numbers, the **Angels**, the **Apostles**, and the **Chosen Tribes** sing together sweetly in alternating parts. Singing as if in certain "antitheses" <note>A musical term for counterpoint or opposing voices in a choir.</note> and responding in song to the praise and glory of the **Supreme Maker**, they continually increase. Hence our fellow-singer **John** often repeats that those twelve tribes, and those specifically marked, sang with untiring voices before the Throne of God and the Lamb—sometimes singing songs that were clear and public, and at other times more secret songs, which no one could sing except those rejoicing in that purity and marked with that character. May the **Supreme Prince**, by his grace and the intercession of so many singing in harmony, deign to lead us to that melody; for indeed, we waste away with weariness and sorrow at this prolonged exile <note>original: "Incolatus... prolongati." A common liturgical reference to Psalm 120:5, "Woe is me, that my sojourn is prolonged."</note>.

### Digression: From where do stones derive their power? &emsp; &emsp; Harmony IV.

Not without wonder do mortals, however wise they may be, contemplate the admirable virtues of stones. From where does the **Magnet** <note>The lodestone.</note> draw iron? Why does the **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas."</note> by its presence take away the power of the magnet? Why does the **Apistos** stone <note>A legendary stone mentioned in ancient lapidaries that, once lit, is almost impossible to extinguish.</note>, once set on fire, never or hardly ever go out? From where also do the **Balagius** <note>A type of ruby or spinel.</note>, the **Jet** <note>original: "Gagates."</note>, and almost all precious stones, when rubbed, attract straw? **Amber**, or **Electrum** (as the Greeks call it), attracts not only straw, but even leaves and the fringes of garments.

<margin>
Authors who treat of stones
</margin>
...concerning the virtues of stones by **Bocus**, **Aaron**, **Thetel**, **Zenotemis**, **Zoroaster**, and **Hermes**. **Euantes** the king of the Arabs, **Dioscorides**, **Joseph**, **Arnold**, and many others. **Zacharias** the Babylonian, writing to **Mithridates**, also says: Great power and human fates reside within stones. But from where these powers come requires a deeper investigation. **Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>, not departing from his own senses and qualities, was of the opinion that these powers come from the elements, or the qualities of the elements composing the stones themselves. This cannot possibly stand, since qualities are of the same species, yet the operations of stones are proven to agree neither in species nor in genus. Therefore the **Academics** <note>Followers of Plato.</note>, climbing higher, attributed these things to the "formative ideas" that rule them; **Hermes**, however, to the stars; **Avicenna** to the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, these were celestial spirits or angels that governed the movement of the heavens.</note>; and **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a famous 13th-century scientist and theologian.</note> reduces such operations to the "specific forms" of things. And though these wise men seem to oppose one another, yet if the matter is weighed well, none of them is far from the truth, provided their words are understood correctly: for diverse causes often agree in the same effect. For **God** in the first place, as the fountain and origin of all virtues, grants the "seal of Ideas" to His ministers; the **Intelligences**, as faithful executors, mark the things entrusted to them with no other seal than that royal one; the **Heavens**, as instruments, prepare the matter for receiving...

<margin>
Plato
</margin>

For the Maker does not need them as if they were co-helpers, but He has them as ministers, just as a Royal and Imperial Majesty requires. Yet the Supreme Moderator has committed such power to them over the things entrusted to them, so that all the virtue of stones, herbs, metals, and such things comes from those presiding Intelligences, as several wise men assert.

Therefore, the form and power of stones agree with the **Idea**, with the governing intelligences <note>In this context, "intelligences" refer to angelic beings or celestial spirits believed to guide the movement of the planets.</note>, with the disposing aspects of the heavens, and with the corresponding complexions of the elements disposed by the influxes of the heavens, by which the elements themselves are arranged. ### What the True Matter of the Heavenly City Is. Conclusion V.

<margin>The Peripatetics, Averroes, Aristotle</margin>
**S**ince we have so far treated those things which were described under enigmas by the prophets concerning the matter of heaven, it remains for us to say something about the true matter of the heavenly city: concerning which there is no small controversy—whether there is matter in heaven or not—and if there is, what kind it is. For some of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "covered walkways" where they studied.</note> (especially **Averroes** <note>A famous 12th-century Islamic commentator on Aristotle.</note>) seem to assert that there is no matter there, because matter exists in the potentiality of contradiction <note>The capacity for a thing to be one way and then its opposite (e.g., hot then cold).</note>, and for diverse forms: from which it would seem that heaven would be subject to corruption, since that matter could receive another form. **Aristotle**, truly in his usual manner in this as in other most difficult things, briefly and obscurely barely touches upon it. Hence the opinion left by them is quite doubtful: since he neither proved the incorruptibility of heaven, but only held it as an opinion; nor did he determine whether a form can be given to matter that so quiets its appetite that it seeks no further form. Nor did they prove whether the matter of heaven is of the same nature as the matter of lower and transmutable <note>Changeable or subject to decay.</note> things. <margin>Themistius, Simplicius, Avicenna, Philosophy, Theology</margin> **Themistius**, **Simplicius**, **Avicenna**, and many other distinguished philosophers, along with our **Theologians**, run with full speed to this opinion, and in many places testify that there is matter in heaven. Which Aristotle also implies, saying: *He who says this heaven, says matter* <note>original: "Qui dicit hoc coelum, dicit materiam"</note>, through which it may be seen that heaven receives the principle of individuation <note>The philosophical quality that makes an object a distinct, individual thing.</note>. Whence the greater difficulty is to discern what that matter of the celestial bodies is, rather than if there is matter in them: because they do not seem to have the conditions of things composed of this matter subject to transmutation, generation, and corruption. <margin>Albert</margin> Whence **Albertus Magnus**, following his Peripatetics, says that matter is in heaven, but it differs from that of transmutable things by an <term>equivocal reason</term> <note>Meaning the word "matter" is used for both, but it refers to two fundamentally different types of substance.</note>. <margin>Moses</margin> This can also be easily conjectured from Holy Scripture: For when **Moses** described the matter of things, although he relates that both the matter of heaven and of earth were created on the same day, yet he distinguishes one from the other separately, saying: *In the Beginning God created the heaven and the earth*, that is, the matter of heaven and the matter of earth, as we have declared above: which perhaps some not ineptly call the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; the quintessence or aether, a substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>: since it is distinct from the matter of the four elements which are continually changeable and transmut...

They confirm this from the etymology of the word in their own language, in which the heavens are called **שמים** (*shamayim*): where the last three letters, **מים** (*mayim*), signify "waters" without controversy. The first two, however, are **אש** (*esh*)—turning the **ש** (*shin*) into **ס** (*samekh*) according to their rules—signifying "fire." When joined together, those five letters signify "fire and water"; they assert the naming of the heavens is derived from these as their component parts. But since they possess a certain stability so that they may support the "waters above," <note>A reference to Genesis 1:7, where God separates the waters above the firmament from those below.</note> they also seem to participate in earth; and also in air, so that respiration can occur there. <margin>Zoroaster, Cleanthes, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle</margin>

## SECOND MEASURE: DISPOSITION.
### On the general partitioning of Ezekiel and John. Conclusion 1.

Touching upon the second <term>measure</term><note>The author uses "modulus" (measure/module), a term from music and architecture, to describe the proportions of his "harmonic city."</note> of our <term>harmonic city</term>,<note>A concept linking the architectural layout of the New Jerusalem with musical harmony and divine order.</note> we shall sound forth the reason why it is seen to be partitioned in different ways by Ezekiel and John. For Ezekiel, in his first partitioning, divides the structure into a temple, a city, and the entire promised region. He divides this into twelve parts for the twelve tribes, with twelve gates. Furthermore, he divides the temple into vestibules, chambers, courts, treasuries, porticos, the holy of holies, and other parts for the <margin>John</margin> kitchen and specific uses. John, however, excludes the temple entirely: *I saw no temple in it,* he says. Most harmoniously and aptly, Ezekiel, in describing the buildings of the <term>figurative family</term>,<note>The "figurative family" refers to the Old Testament Israelites, whose physical laws and structures were seen by Christian theologians as "figures" or shadows of spiritual truths to come.</note> includes a temple as necessary for prayer and the making of sacrifices. But John sketches the house and city of the Christian assembly, who do not require another temple because they themselves have already been built into the temple of God, according to the teaching of the Apostle. Therefore, Christ said to that Samaritan woman: *The time is coming, and is now here, <margin>CHRIST</margin> when the true worshipers will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in the temple, but in spirit and truth.* And thus we, having been purified here on our way, are made into the temple of God, receiving Him through piety, purity, and good works, just as the Host Himself promises, saying: *If anyone keeps my word, my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.* How much more shall we ourselves be the temple when we are received into those eternal tabernacles, with an open gaze, face to face, and enjoying mutual familiarity as citizens of that heavenly city? For now we receive God as a guest in our home, but then we shall be received by Him; regarding which John follows: *For the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb.* This refers to that city and the assembly of the blessed ascending there. He also describes the gates through which entry is open to all, provided they are willing to hear the One inviting them. He likewise describes its splendor, by which all are illuminated, as well as the river of living water and the tree of life in the midst of its street, to sustain the life of those dwelling there forever. He also tells of the throne of the Lamb, who is to reign in it perpetually with His co-heirs.

<margin>Baruch</margin>

As Pliny and several other wise men excellently put it, those who think they can measure the heavens are filled with an insane madness. Nevertheless, 
<margin>John</margin>
our John <note>The Apostle John, author of Revelation.</note> seems to encompass it within a few <term>stadia</term><note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>. He says: *And he measured the city with a golden reed for twelve thousand stadia for each of the four sides,* completing the whole city at forty-eight thousand stadia, which is six thousand <term>miles</term><note>The author is likely using the Roman mile (mille passus), which is slightly shorter than a modern mile.</note>. Ezekiel, however, measures it as four thousand five hundred <term>reeds</term><note>A biblical unit of length, often cited as six cubits.</note> on each side, which when calculated amounts to eighteen thousand reeds. According to 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
Jerome, this is forty-four thousand, three hundred and forty Roman paces, more or less; but in Venetian paces, it is thirty-one thousand, five hundred and forty. For a Roman pace (as Jerome accepts it) contains fifteen <term>palms</term><note>A "palm" was a hand-breadth, a common small unit of measure.</note> or a little less, while a Venetian pace contains exactly twenty palms; thus the latter is a quarter larger than the former. A reed, moreover, contains thirty-seven palms—that is, six <term>cubits</term><note>The distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> and a palm—for a cubit is completed by six palms. Therefore, the total circuit will amount to thirty-one thousand five hundred paces, more or less, if the measurement is made in Venetian paces. 

Nor should anyone be amazed if John found the circuit of that city to be six thousand miles, while it is described by Ezekiel as being about thirty-one miles. This is because this New City, built by Christ as a bride adorned for her husband, ought to be as much greater than the ancient Israelite one as the Christian reality is greater than its figurative precursor, which was contained within the tiny Promised Land. John also measures the height of the walls as one hundred and forty-four cubits, and all these things with a golden reed, "by the measure of a man, which is that of an Angel"; <note>Quoting Revelation 21:17, suggesting the measurements have a mystical, non-physical meaning.</note> and these things perhaps (God willing) we shall explain in their proper place. 

But now let us proceed regarding its magnitude, in comparison to which the dimensions described—indeed, the circuit of the entire earth, which is thirty thousand miles—is considered as nothing, or like a grain of millet compared to a huge mountain, where no proportion can be found. Indeed, reason does not allow that for so majestic a kingdom the city should be so narrow, or that so many thousands of the elect, with that great multitude from every tribe and every nation which no one could number, should be received in such humble lodgings. Therefore, if we wish to explain Ezekiel and John, we must necessarily leave behind this 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
literal number. For Sacred Scripture (as Augustine rightly feels) and the 
<margin>Pythagoreans</margin>
<margin>Academics</margin>
Pythagoreans and the Academics <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note> care little for that literal count, intending instead the proportion resulting from it, which they call the "natural" or "formal" number, and pointing toward the divine and the <term>sacraments</term><note>Here meaning "mysteries" or "sacred signs" encoded in the text.</note> emanating therefrom. By observing this, we can easily reconcile Ezekiel and John with other wise men who write about the im-

For the explanation of this, it must be noted that the <term>millenary number</term><note>The number 1,000.</note> pertains to the ultimate completion, since it is the cube and the "solid" of the <term>completed number</term><note>The number 10 (denarius), considered the "perfect" base in Pythagorean and medieval numerology.</note>, which is ten; beyond which no further number is given, but rather a repetition of the preceding numbers. Nor can a number be expanded beyond a "solid," which grows into length, breadth, and depth. Therefore, this number signifies the consummate perfection of that dwelling. 
<margin>The same [is found in] John</margin>
For this reason, Ezekiel measures the city, the temple, and the space of the entire region by thousands of reeds; and John measures the same city by twelve thousand golden <term>rods</term><note>Or "staves" (virgis), used as measuring tools in Revelation 21.</note>. <margin>Daniel</margin>
Through thousands, and thousands of thousands, Daniel also enumerates the army of the hosts of Angels. That this millenary number is multiplied here by eighteen pertains to the guests: who are divided into nine choirs of Angels, and into as many choirs of men, who are to be placed among those Angelic ones. For each person will fly to that order or assembly of Angels whose nature and office they carried out 
<margin>Gregory</margin>

By this number, the Wise men and Judges of the people were comprised in that figurative family [of Israel], and just as many disciples in the true army of Christ, according to the number of the

# THE EIGHTH TONE.

## XCII

<margin>Plato</margin> And all foundations, whether in man-made, natural, moral, or divine things, are square: as we have touched upon elsewhere. Hence, Plato said that the first foundations of this cosmic machine were cast by the Supreme Architect in a fourfold manner, so that it might be solid. For solid things (as he says) are joined not by one, but by two means, between which there is a corresponding proportion, just as between fire and air, air and water, this and earth, and again between earth and fire. The Maker of the world bound these together with such wondrous harmony that they cannot be dissolved by anyone except the one who bound them. So that the sacred city—firm and harmonious, and full of mysteries—might be divided, He partitions it by the square number, which is solid and harmonious. For in that number, all musical harmony seems to be contained. In the <term>quaternary</term><note>The number four, which in Pythagorean thought was the root of all things and contained the ratios for all musical intervals.</note>, one finds the ratios of double, triple, <term>sesquialtera</term><note>A ratio of 3:2, which produces the musical interval of a fifth.</note>, and <term>sesquitertia</term><note>A ratio of 4:3, which produces the musical interval of a fourth.</note>. From these result the <term>diapason</term><note>An octave.</note>, the <term>bisdiapason</term><note>A double octave.</note>, the <term>diapente</term><note>A musical fifth.</note>, and the <term>diatessaron</term><note>A musical fourth.</note>, and even the <term>tone</term><note>A whole step.</note>, if four is taken with three and one, which yield eight, and again 4, 3, and 2, which make 9; from which number to 8 there is a <term>sesquioctave</term><note>A ratio of 9:8, defining the whole tone.</note> proportion, which creates the tone. Thus, all harmony results from it. 

But so that it might be even more harmonious, the great four-lettered name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note> resonates within it, with one letter presiding over and influencing each corner, according to what is found in the words of 
<margin>Chronicles</margin> the book of Chronicles: "I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be in it." Stirred by the influence of this most sweet name, the inhabitants continually praise that name of God, as the Royal 
<margin>David</margin> Singer <note>referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> says: "Praise the name of the Lord, let the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth and for evermore." Therefore, in that city, the morning stars and all the sons of God praise its Maker; the twenty-four elders praise Him, as do the hundred and forty-four thousand who have His name and His Father’s name written on their foreheads. Finally, the whole multitude continually praises the Lord with the drum and dance, with strings and the organ, 
<margin>The same</margin> with cymbals and trumpets—as the same Royal Singer concludes at the end of his hymns, saying: "Let every spirit praise the Lord," or as the Hebrew truth better has it: **Let every breath praise the Lord** <note>original: "כל הנשמה תהלל יה col anessama tehalel iah"</note>. Translating this word-for-word, we say: Let every <term>anessama</term><note>A Latinized form of the Hebrew word 'Neshamah,' meaning soul or breath.</note> (that is, a soul purified and made superior or divine) praise <term>Iah</term><note>A shortened form of the divine name Yahweh.</note>, which is the name signifying the divine essence, which the blessed are led to behold. We have used a roundabout way of speaking here because we do not have names that precisely express the meanings of those words, *Iah* and *anessama*.

# OF THE THIRD SONG

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
The sum of all sacred things is enclosed in that most exalted Trinity; and the Trinity is contained within the <term>quaternary</term><note>The number four, symbolizing the material world and the four corners of the earth.</note>. From these, when led one into the other <note>i.e., three multiplied by four</note>, there arises the number twelve, according to which all those heavenly things are distributed: the marked tribes of the chosen families, the stones of the foundation, the presiding Angels, and the gates through which entry is made. For it is necessary for us to enter that kingdom through the Holy Trinity, as the Prince of that kingdom himself says: <note>original: "Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua... et spiritu sancto"</note> "Unless one is born again of water—that is, the Son (as we have declared elsewhere)—and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." But neither can anyone come to the Son, nor be reborn through him, unless the Heavenly Father has drawn him. See, therefore, how the entry into the heavenly kingdom is opened through these ternary <note>threefold</note> gates of the most Holy Trinity.

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
And for this reason, the Savior commands those being initiated to be baptized and sealed <note>original: "in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti"</note> "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." From whichever quarter of the world we wish to enter there, we must pass through these three gates: whether we enter from the East of adolescence, or from the South of youth and vigor; whether from the West of old age, or from the North of decrepitude. Or let the entry be made from the East of sublime goodness, or from the South of piety and mercy, or from the North of the fear of divine judgment, or from the West of kindly condescension; one always enters the fourfold city through the threefold gates. Now, twelve Angels are said to preside over these gates, because no one in the <term>church militant</term><note>The Christian church on earth, seen as engaged in spiritual warfare.</note> receives the faith of the most Holy Trinity except through the ministry of a priest—<margin>Malachi</margin>who is called by Malachi "the Angel of the Lord of hosts." Nor does one enter through the gates of the most Holy Trinity into the <term>kingdom of the triumphant</term><note>The church in heaven, having achieved victory over sin and death.</note> without the ministry of Angels, <margin>CHRIST</margin>as the Supreme Emperor teaches when he says the soul of Lazarus was led into the bosom of Abraham. And if the soul of the righteous man was carried by angelic ministry to that lower place where Abraham, the father of faith, presided, how much more ought souls be carried by the ministers of the Most High God to the bosom of the Eternal Father? This is especially true since the passage is made through the gates of the most Holy Trinity. There are also twelve Angels presiding over the twelve gates, they themselves being distributed by the number twelve, by which many heavenly things are counted: both the families of the chosen in each church, and their leaders. <margin>THE SAME</margin>Hence, not without reason did the Emperor of the heavenly host indicate that they were divided by the twelvefold number when he said to Peter: "Do you not think that I can pray to my Father, and he will even now furnish me with more than twelve legions of Angels?"

A legion at that time was composed of ten cohorts and held six thousand one hundred infantry, and seven hundred thirty cavalry. However, in the time of <term>Varro</term><note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note>, it consisted of only three thousand; at other times, it was enclosed by other numbers of soldiers, although it is commonly believed to be fixed at six thousand six hundred and sixty-six, with no difference made between cavalry and infantry. But lest anyone believe the number of Angels was completed in those twelve legions, He added, not without reason, "more than twelve." For these, distributed through many legions, reach <margin>Daniel</margin>(as Daniel says) unto a thousand thousands and ten hundred times a thousand, who all with one mouth and a harmonious voice, together with the other guests, continually praise the Prince of the city.

*What streets are there. Harmony 4.*

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**T**he streets are those places frequented by citizens and peoples, and where magistrates are accustomed to reside. Those of that supernal city are described as being made of gold, which signifies charity, as we have explained above. And this is so it may be understood that the gathering of all guests should shine in the love of God and neighbor, according to the sign given by the Prince, who says: 
<margin>John</margin>
> "By this shall men know that you are my disciples, and citizens of the world-transcending city: if you have love one for another." <note>original: "In hoc cognoscent homines, qđ eritis mei discipuli... si dilectionem habueritis ad invicem." Reference to John 13:35.</note>

In the middle of this street (says John), the Tree of Life was placed; and from each side of that same tree, the river of life was flowing: so that we might understand the guests to be filled not only with charity, but also with wisdom, which is denoted by the river of living water: 
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
according to that which is held in the book of Wisdom: *And the water of wholesome wisdom has given him to drink.* <note>Reference to Sirach 15:3.</note> This wisdom is most excellently said to abound and flow in the streets, as the Wise Man says: 
> "Wisdom preaches abroad; in the streets she utters her voice; she cries out at the head of the crowds." <note>Proverbs 1:20-21.</note>

I believe this was done for a twofold reason: the first is so that everyone may perceive that wisdom is to be shared with anyone, provided they wish to receive it, as Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure often cited by Renaissance scholars as a "pagan prophet" of Christian truths.</note> says when discourse with his son: 
<margin>Mercury</margin>
> "God filled a wide mixing-bowl with wisdom, and sent a herald commanding that whoever wished to receive the Mind—which is true wisdom—should immerse himself in this vessel." <note>A reference to the "Crater" or "Mixing-Bowl" from the *Corpus Hermeticum*, Libellus IV.</note>

The other reason is to persuade the magistrates, who chiefly dwell in the streets, that they ought to be entirely drenched in divine wisdom. So also, those who possess the more prominent places in that higher city are thought to be filled with greater wisdom and charity. And these are far more excellent than worldly citizens, because the tree of life is present for them, from which they continually pluck the fruits of life and live in perpetual happiness. Indeed, unless they diligently frequent these streets so that they may rejoice through charity in the gathering of their neighbors and enjoy the presence of the Prince—whence they might be continually kindled by a better love—they, falling away from the fountain of all good and beauty, are defiled and fail, full of ignominy: as 
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
Jeremiah says, lamenting in the Book of Lamentations: 
> "Their face is become blacker than coals, they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has cleaved to their bones." <note>Lamentations 4:8.</note>

It has withered, <term>namely</term> <note>original: "videlz," an abbreviation for "videlicet."</note> without the river of living water, and has become like dry wood to be burned in perpetual fire.

<margin>Jerome</margin>

Following, therefore, the true interpretation according to the mind of the prophet, we say that the measurement was not 37 palms, as our translation sounds, but 42: and by a most hidden sacrament, of which we shall report only that which the divine oracles permit. For the work is brought together by the palm and the hand, or the fingers: and this is under the auspices of the forty-second number, by which God went out into His work and measures all things: as is a common saying among the wise.

After these things, he measures the suburbs—that is, those external things belonging to man—through which entrance is made for God to reach us, and for us to reach God, and for our union with Him. Finally, he comes to the first fruits or tithes, namely <term>good works <note>original: "bona opera"</note></term> which we offer to God, which must be measured: so that a reward fitting for them may be a good and pressed-down measure, given in proportion. For "with the same measure," (says the <margin>CHRIST</margin> Prince of all), "with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you," <note>Reference to Matthew 7:2 and Luke 6:38.</note> yet according to a geometric proportion, each thing being repaid a hundredfold out of the greatest liberality of God. Thus, most beautifully, He who seeks tithes returns them to us in a thousandfold <term>parting-gifts <note>original: "apophoretis," a Greek term for gifts given to guests to take home.</note></term>, as will be clear to one calculating from the hundredfold retribution of the Gospel. Or let us say, that tithes received by God progress from simple numbers to the thousands; for when the grace of God is added (to which the number "thousand" is attributed), those things which were previously "tens" <note>original: "denaria"</note> become ten thousand, and so with the rest.

It must also be noted that at the end of the vision he measures by "thousand-fold" measures, whereas before he measured by the unit, by ten, and by twenty-five. Nor should it be overlooked that he measured the thresholds of the gate with one reed, and a little later he adds that the threshold of the gate is ten cubits. The prophet, being not ignorant of the <term>mysteries <note>original: "sacramentorum"</note></term>, was describing all these things with the same mystical meaning. For the measurement of all things is made through "one," which denotes the beginning, and through "ten," which is the fulfillment of all simple numbers: because the remuneration and reward of all is He who is the beginning and the end; and from this, the first fruits and tithes are justly owed to Him.

Then he passes from ten to a hundred, assigning the distance between gate and gate by hundreds of cubits: because the reward of those who enter through one gate differs by a hundredfold multiplication from those who enter through another. And yet he arrives at the thousand—namely the cube of the completed number ten—in which he closes and consumes every measurement, even if he does not fully express it. On the contrary, he frankly admits that he is submerged in such a deep sea; for when he came to the east, where the origin of all measurements lies, he says that the waters were overflowing greatly from the right side (whence come mercy, grace, and all gifts), denoting that those things imparted to us by the Giver of all good things are so great that we cannot comprehend them. And he said that the man coming from the east (where the fountain of all good resides, communicated through the power of the <term>right hand <note>The "right hand of God" traditionally symbolizes divine power and mercy.</note></term>) measured a thousand cubits with a cord: and the said waters reached up to the ankles. And he measured another thousand, and behold, the waters reached the knees. And he measured another thousand, and he was led through the water up to the <term>loins <note>original: "rhenes," literally "kidneys" or "reins," symbolizing the seat of strength or desire.</note></term>.

But when the measurer proceeded further, the waters grew so much that he could not cross; for the waters were too deep. Indeed, to report something of the secrets (which may nonetheless be spoken), as long as the measurer was measuring those things which belong to the <term>natural man <note>original: "animalis hominis," referring to the physical/soulish man as opposed to the spiritual man.</note></term>—whether they be ankles, knees, or loins—he was able to cross the depth of the water of wisdom, by which man himself is disposed and measured. But when he proceeded further, namely to those things which pertain to the **inner man**, further passage was not granted to him. Since these things are so great that the Prophet’s shoulders sank under the weight, much less can our [shoulders bear them]...

->On the measurement of first fruits or tithes. Conclusion II.<-

<margin>Exodus</margin>
**I** think that the measurements by which the Prophet measures the first fruits—or, to speak more accurately, the tithes to be offered—should not be overlooked. These are called <term>contribution <note>original Hebrew: "תרומה" (*terumah*), referring to a "heave offering" or gift set apart for God.</note></term> in Hebrew, as we read most fully in the book of Exodus. For the Prophet says: "And by the border of Judah, from the east side even unto the west side, shall be the first fruits which you shall set apart: twenty-five thousand reeds in length and breadth, just as each individual part, from the east to the sea, as in other quarters; whether in length or breadth, so that the whole circuit is one hundred thousand." I will not say "reeds," because "reed" is not found here in the Hebrew text, even though it is in our translation by choice, and not according to the attached mystery. For here, the reward is measured by a hundred, with which those who offer the true first fruits of their body—preserved purely and modestly—to God are remunerated. 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
For these (as Jerome pleases) are crowned with the number one hundred, which by the Prophet is multiplied by a thousand (a number always attributed to God), so that the divine reward may be understood as corresponding to the work pleasing to God. But the first fruits of the other tribes are measured by twenty-five thousand on the north side and as many on the south side; but from the east side ten thousand, and from the west as many, which when brought together make seventy thousand. The root of this number is seven—the number of remission <note>The number seven is historically associated with the Sabbath and the Year of Jubilee, symbolizing forgiveness and rest.</note>—which when multiplied by ten (the number of completion) and again by the divine thousand, denotes the works, offerings, and rewards of the penitent, who expect remissions from the true Seven; afterwards, the reward for completed works is supported by the ten through the divine thousand. Hence, those who cannot dedicate themselves with the royal Tribe of Judah—inasmuch as they have been sufficiently treacherous and rebellious—should at least offer the oblations of the penitent through the hands of a priest. And not just any priest, who might pollute the offering rather than present it, but through the hands of those who are of the sons of <term>Zadok <note>Zadok was a High Priest during the reigns of David and Solomon; his name means "Just" or "Righteous."</note></term>, which is interpreted as "the Just."

Furthermore, the prophet continues much regarding the measurements, number, and site of the suburbs and their borders, and concerning the measures of oil and other things which were to be offered in sacrifice. We leave these to be explained by those who interpret the literal text; for we have only sketched out those things which we judge, through a certain <term>type <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person, object, or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note></term>, to belong to the measurement of the heavenly city in which we are blessed.

->On the measurement of this city according to John.<- Conclusion III.

<margin>John</margin> **T**he measurement of John seems to differ considerably from that of Ezekiel: For the latter [Ezekiel] measures with a wooden reed those things which belong to the figurative family, not yet freed from the burdens of stones, wood, and straw. But John describes the merits of the Blessed and the structure of that city which we explained above as being woven from gold and precious stones; therefore, it is rightly said to be measured with a golden reed. However, he does not express how great the measurement is, because those things which are measured cannot be determined, since the glory of the Blessed revolves around an infinite and endless object, continually filling those who receive it according to their capacity; and that place is immense, with no measurement that is truly terminable. Nevertheless, with his reed, he traces that perimeter to twelve thousand stadia, and the walls by twelve squared cubits—namely, one hundred and forty-four thousand—running through both in some way with a great mystery. Therefore, he says that he who spoke with him was measuring with the measure of a man, which is that of an Angel; but how great it is, he does not declare even in this place. Yet in saying that it is the "measure of a man" and "measure of an Angel," he hints at the reward in which both are made blessed. Since that [reward] is God (as we have said), His measure can neither be bounded nor expressed. Yet the measure of an Angel and a man is said to be the same because it is given in the same portion, provided that their capacity and merits require it. Therefore, with that measure, the Angel who spoke with him measured the city at twelve thousand stadia, which is laid out as a square,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical architecture, moving from Ezekiel’s vision of the earthly temple to Saint John’s vision of the New Jerusalem in the Book of Revelation. ### OF THE THIRD SONG

And its height is as great as its width, since these relate to one another equally. And he measured its walls as one hundred forty-four cubits. Many things occur here which bring no small difficulty: and first, how the city can be equal in width and height when the width is said to be twelve thousand stadia, but the height is only 144 cubits. How also is it to be understood that it is "built in a square"? Does it mean that each side is twelve thousand stadia, and the whole circuit is forty-eight thousand stadia? Or is it that the whole circuit is completed in twelve thousand stadia, with each side extending to only 3,000 stadia? And what, moreover, are these stadia and cubits in relation to that heavenly and divine city measured with that golden reed, whose length was said to be unending? To these objections, as the Lord deigns to assist, we will provide a satisfying answer.

If we wish to preserve the literal sense, we will say regarding the first point that there is one height for the walls and another height for the city itself. For the walls are completed in 144 cubits, as the text very clearly opens; but the height of the city, which <margin>John</margin> John says is placed upon a great and high mountain, has a measure from the root of the mountain to the top of the walls of those twelve thousand stadia—a mystery soon to be declared.

But that city is square (says John) and "set in a square": which (in my judgment) is understood such that each side of the city is twelve thousand stadia, and the whole circuit is four times twelve thousand, which makes forty-eight thousand. It is not from a "squared number," as some who are deceived by the letter wring from the text, concluding the circuit to be 144,000 stadia. That would not be an equilateral square (as they think) but only a squaring of numbers, omitting the thousands, in which the mystery of this measurement chiefly consists. For if twelve thousand stadia are squared by area, 144 million <note>original: "144 millena millia." In the mathematics of this period, 12,000 multiplied by 12,000 equals 144,000,000.</note> stadia will result. But if they say the whole circuit is twelve thousand, and each side only three thousand stadia: then if it is squared, it yields exactly nine million.

This measurement certainly will not be that of the city of Jerusalem in which <margin>Josephus</margin> Christ suffered, since that city—according to the testimony of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works are the primary source for the dimensions of historical Jerusalem.</note>—is enclosed by thirty-five stadia. Rather, it is the measurement of the city in which He now reigns, which is distributed into thousands and thousands and twelve thousands: so that it might be accommodating and fit for the twelve thousand sealed from each tribe, and for the twelve families, both figuratively and in the true army of the Supreme Emperor. 

This should also correspond to the great four-letter name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four Hebrew letters YHWH (יהוה).</note> inscribed in it, so that it may be joined together by its power, as we shall say shortly. It ought to be square, just like the four-letter name, yet with a roundness, just as any letter of the same name signifies a "circular" and "spherical" number. For the first letter <note>The Hebrew letter Yod (י) has the numerical value of 10.</note> contains the number ten; the second and fourth <note>The Hebrew letter He (ה) has the value of 5.</note>, five; and the third <note>The Hebrew letter Vav (ו) has the value of 6.</note>, six. Each of these is a circular number. <note>In mystical mathematics, "circular" numbers are those whose powers always end in the same digit (e.g., 5x5=25, 6x6=36). Here, the author links the geometry of the New Jerusalem to the numerology of God's name.</note> The whole name, however, is reduced to the number twelve through the "revolution" which the <margin>Hebrews</margin> Hebrews call *tzeruf* <note>original: "siruph." *Tzeruf* is a Kabbalistic method of permuting and recombining letters to reveal hidden meanings.</note>, as we have said elsewhere: according to which revolutions it is set before the twelve signs <note>Referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac or the twelve tribes of Israel as celestial divisions.</note> by which the whole heavenly circuit and that celestial city is divided.

# THE EIGHTH TONE

Indeed, the number twelve <note>original: *duodenarius*</note> is reduced to our thousand, which is peculiar to God, to whom both "thousand" and "aleph" <note>the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which also signifies the number 1,000</note>—signifying that very thousand—are attributed. Furthermore, the width, length, and height are equal: for whatever is in God is neither greater nor lesser, but always equal. Nor is there true width or length in that divinity, which is everywhere spherical; hence those measurements, by a certain likeness and mystery, are said to be squared, so that they may correspond to the four-letter name <note>the Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew</note>. It remains now to be declared why that city is measured in cubits or stadia. And here we say briefly: that we do not have other words at hand by which divine things might be more suitably explained than these of ours, which are most fitting for the things we wish to express. Therefore, not without mystery are both the Ark of Noah and the Tabernacle of the Covenant said to be measured in cubits; and the massive building of the supernal city is said to be measured in stadia. These measurements were then in use and appropriate for measuring those structures; but ascending to allegory, let us hear how well and harmoniously the rewards and the place of rewards are measured by cubits and stadia. For the cubit <note>a unit of measure based on the length of the forearm</note> signifies the arm and hand together, by which we distribute and perform a good work outwardly. A stadium <note>a Greek unit of distance approximately 600 feet</note>, however, is finished (as they say) by a Herculean race in a single breath; hence by this stadium all possible affection in us is signified, by which we are carried toward God as if by feet. For in the sacred utterances, "feet" always mystically designate affection. And these must be of a strong, great, and vigorous soul, carried along by a single breath—that is, by a single intention. But by the cubit, arm, and hand, the work to be rewarded is understood. And since the reward and glory of that supernal city correspond to the work and affection by geometric proportion, therefore things pertaining to that city and glory are said to be measured in cubits and stadia. But what those cubits and stadia themselves are is not expressed, because those celestial things cannot be bounded by our number, although they are said to be commensurate with our works and affections by geometric proportion. Both of which <margin>CHRIST</margin> Christ, the Prince of that city, explains in the Gospel, saying: "You shall receive a hundred for one"—behold the geometric proportion—"and you shall possess eternal life"—behold the unending measure. Because affections and works, when sprinkled with accepting grace and embraced by the charity of God, smell of God himself; and therefore they rejoice in that divine thousand. And through it they are multiplied as many times as the divine name itself—from which is all virtue—is turned over.

## FOURTH MODULE: STRUCTURE.
### Who built it. First Harmony.

<margin>*John*</margin>
**W**HO built this city and our harmonious dwelling, most full of every harmony and joy, John declares clearly enough when he says: "I saw the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband." And so the city itself descends from heaven, along with its *Calotechnius* <note>from the Greek *kalos* (good/beautiful) and *technes* (craftsman): a Good Architect</note>, that is, its good Architect, maker, and decorator; so that receiving us into it, He might lead us back to heaven itself.

For John speaks of that building woven from living stones, just as the Church sings: *Blessed City Jerusalem, called a vision of peace* <note>original: "Vrbs beata Ierusalẽ dicta pacis uisio"; a famous 7th or 8th-century Latin hymn used for the dedication of a church</note>, which is constructed in the heavens from living stones and joined with Angels as a bridal companion. It was certainly prepared in the mind of the Craftsman from the very first constitution of the world, as it says in the Gospel: *Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world* <note>Matthew 25:34</note>.

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
For the Supreme Architect prepared a triple lodging for the human guest: One is that celestial kingdom and the mansions of the Blessed. The second is this mundane world for our pilgrimage; from its most elegantly arranged state, we can easily conjecture how great and of what quality that mansion is which He has prepared for our eternal stay. The third is this one, constructed upon the foundation which is Christ, and upon the twelve Apostolic foundations, composed of living stones and measured with the measurements of Ezekiel and John, which we touched upon above. And so great is the harmony of these three that we can infer one from the other, provided we understand well the nature and arrangement of each building. While this one we now inhabit is dreg-filled and the lowest, and that one toward which we strive is purified and most exquisite, the middle one—under whose auspices we hasten toward the supernal—is spiritual. It is the house and city of the Church, within whose bosom or embrace we must be contained if we wish to ascend to the celestial and supernal. For these buildings are similar, constructed by the same Craftsman, and each bears His image according to its capacity. Hence there is a symbol and likeness between them, through which by examining one, we can also understand the others. Nor was there any other builder of these structures except He of whom it is said: *For he is the craftsman of all, having all power, overseeing all.*

## How, and by what glue this building is compacted and united. Consideration II.

All things composed of many parts that come together into one must be glued together either by art, by nature, or by a divine mystery. For stones in a house are connected by <term>stone-glue</term> <note>original: "lithocolla"; a mixture of marble dust and lime used as a strong cement</note>, lime, and iron or bronze clamps into which lead is poured. Woods, however, are joined by nails, or by glues made of cheese, fish, or bull-hide—which is considered the most perfect. Bones in the human body are bound together by nerves, flesh, and skin. And sometimes stones and diverse bodies are not merely glued, but united by a certain natural force, such as two trees through grafting, or oysters with stones by a more hidden power of nature. I have even seen human bodies turned to stone and so united with stones that they appeared to have become a single, <term>homogeneous</term> <note>uniform or consistent throughout</note> body. And because the force of nature is stronger than art, it binds more strongly. But since divine power is the strongest of all, it not only connects but unites. And this is the power of His holy and great name, of which it is said: *O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth* <note>Psalm 8:1</note>; namely in both the superior and inferior worlds, binding, connecting, and uniting all parts and their members together. In the likeness of this in Jerusalem...

### Why the names of both the Apostles and the Tribes are engraved in the foundations, but the names of the Angels in the gates. Third Conclusion.

<margin>CHRIST, Exodus, Luke, Isaiah, Malachi</margin>
**A**nd although the names of all the elect are engraved in that holy city, as the supreme Truth proclaims <note>original: "perhibet"; literally "offers" or "testifies"</note> saying: *Your names are written in heaven* <note>Luke 10:20</note>. And though each one has the name of Jesus and the name of his Father written on the forehead, so that their connection might be perfect. Nevertheless, the names of the Apostles and the Tribes are said to be inscribed specifically in the foundations, and the names of the Angels in the gates. This inscription does not only refer to the characters <note>the literal letters or shapes</note>, for this would be of little moment, but to the hidden power that thrives in the names themselves, according to which names were imposed upon the elect by Him who said: *I know you by name* <note>Exodus 33:12</note>. Truly, concerning a few people, God has expressed a name which "the mouth of the Lord has named"; even if He calls by name all the stars, and the humans signified by the stars, which are also written in the heavens, and according to those names we shall be named there. 

Nevertheless, we have the explained names of certain individuals imposed upon them by God, such as Abraham, Isaac, Israel, Jedidiah <note>the name given to Solomon by the prophet Nathan</note>, John, and Jesus. For Abraham was previously called **Abram**, but by God’s command (as we read in the book of Genesis) he was called **Abraham** with the addition of the letter **He** <note>Hebrew: ה</note>, which signifies five in number. This number five, added to the prior name—which is written thus **אברם** <note>Abram</note> and signifies 243 in number—constitutes the name written thus **אברהם** <note>Abraham</note> and yields the number 248. This is the same number of bones in the human body and the number of affirmative commandments <note>A reference to Jewish Gematria, where the 248 affirmative laws of the Torah correspond to the parts of the body</note>. Therefore, in the same place, when He wished to adapt the name by adding the **He** (ה), which signifies five, He begins: *Walk before me, and be perfect* <note>Genesis 17:1</note>, namely in the virtues and my commandments signified by the bones. 

This number five (as He immediately introduces) He took away from **Sarah** <note>Hebrew: שרה</note>, who was previously called **Sarai** <note>Hebrew: שרי</note>. Her original name signifies 510 in number (a mystery to be declared elsewhere), but she remained with only 505. And just as here the number was removed from the woman and added to the man, so in our first parents it was taken from the man and given to the woman, who was formed from a rib taken from the man. Hence Adam fell, and here Abraham was perfected before God. Let us proceed no further here than is permitted. 

**Isaac** <note>original: "Izahac"</note> also was so named by his father Abraham, alluding to the mystery of Sarah’s laughter at the message of the Angels; he saw how the boy ought to be the laughter and joy of his father, just as Ishmael was a burden and a nuisance; for which reason Ishmael was cast out from his paternal house along with his mother by God’s command. Jacob received the name **Israel** from the Angel with whom he wrestled, which means "Prince" or "Heir of God." And because he prevailed with the great Prince of God, he was made both a Father and a Prince of the people campaigning under the true God. But also John...

### FIFTH MEASURE: ADORNMENT.
A symbolic description of adornment according to Ezekiel. First Harmony.

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>

Whence it follows: *because you were perfect in my beauty, which I had put upon you, says the Lord.* And because the prophet first prophesies concerning the synagogue, in which many were rebellious, he therefore adds the complaints which God himself makes concerning the fornications, debaucheries, adulteries, and idolatries perpetrated by that ungrateful people. For this reason, their disgrace is judged as more grievous than the crime of Gomorrah and Sodom. Nor can we express any further adornment in our own words.

## SIXTH MODULE: LIGHT.
### What light is in general. First Harmony.

<margin>Iamblichus</margin>
After the ornament of the city, light is treated quite fittingly; by it the ornaments themselves may be seen, and those looking on may delight in him from whom they receive all good things. For just as (as the Phoenicians teach in their theology, as reported by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated "Chaldean" and "Phoenician" wisdom into his theology.</note>) we receive all bodily goods from the light of the sun without any intermediary, or from the planets and stars to which that Phoebean light <note>original: *lux phæbea*; Phoebus is a classical name for the sun god Apollo.</note> 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
is communicated: so in the heavenly city, whatever good those citizens have, they receive from the Father of Lights and from that Sun who says: *I am the light of the world:* 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Or from the higher minds, who, obtaining stronger illuminations from the supreme light, afterward illuminate the lower ones; as Dionysius, privy to those secrets, hands down. However, since I have decided to say something about this light, I shudder at the first glance: because what offers itself to me is the darkest of all things, which indeed the more it shines, the more it is drawn together by a darker gloom and enveloped in a thicker cloud; so that eyes not well-purified are struck rather than enlightened. Hence that supreme light spoke to Solomon, the Prophets, and to Moses himself in the darkness, until their 
<margin>Exodus 34</margin>
eyes, shaken free from lower darkness, could endure the light itself. Whence Moses, at last freed from bodily impediments and transcending the darkness, saw the supreme light and the Good itself face to face: from which his face 
<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
shone so greatly that the children of Israel could not look intently upon his face (as Paul says) because of the splendor of his countenance. For descending from the mountain, he had a shining face from the divine company; although our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> has "horned." This error arose from the similarity of the word. For the Hebrews call one who is shining *qaran* <note>original: קרן (*qaran*); the author is correcting the famous mistranslation where the Hebrew word for "shining" or "sending out rays" was mistaken for "horns" (*qeren*), leading to centuries of art depicting Moses with horns.</note>.

### THE EIGHTH TONE ###

...and "horn" <note>original: קֶרֶן *qeren*</note> is written with the same letters, but with different vowel points. <note>In Hebrew, the word *qeren* can mean both a "horn" and a "ray of light." This philological point explains why Moses was often depicted with horns in art—a mistranslation of the "rays of light" emanating from his face.</note> But let us return to our subject. There are many who cannot bear that light, just as it was with the common people; thus it is necessary that a veil be placed between them. Otherwise, offended by their own darkness and unable to grasp that light, they utter many ravings when they presume to speak of it. For some say, and think they prove, that light is not a substance, because it occasionally "happens" to something <term>accidental property|In Aristotelian logic, an 'accident' is a quality that isn't essential to a thing's nature, like a person's hair color.</term> and because it cannot be the specific form of any [other] form. These views are childish, <margin>Peripatetics</margin> and bound by the laws of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on physical observation and logic.</note>. For we have it from our John: *that life was the light of men.* Since life is called light, it follows that light itself is a <margin>Augustine, Plotinus</margin> substance, just as life is. We also have it from Augustine, from the great Plotinus, <margin>Aristotle</margin> and from Aristotle himself in his second discourse *On the Soul*, that this light which is perceived by the <margin>Plato</margin> eyes is a certain bodily form. This light (Plato says), once the matter of heaven and earth was produced, the Creator immediately commanded to appear, so that it might enliven, distinguish, and illuminate all things, lest everything remain confused rather than distinct. For this light is so bright that it makes all things shine, yet so obscure that nothing is more difficult to perceive. In speaking of it, we do not go further than what has been shown by the light itself. For light is a radiant spirit, or a spiritual splendor, or a divine fire, illuminating and enlivening all things. But this visible light is a certain spiritual, sudden, and most wide-reaching emanation—an outflowing that does not diminish its source—bestowing upon lower things those benefits which it receives from the supreme light. No further discourse is given in general concerning light, which is both the clearest and the most obscure of all things.

->What the begotten light is. Conclusion II.<-

**B**ut since we must discourse on the light illuminating the city which we are describing, it is necessary to speak of the *begotten light*, by which the city is illuminated, as John says: *And its lamp was the Lamb.* Indeed, he abstains with the highest reverence from the *unbegotten light*; <margin>We also</margin> he instructs us not to presume to speak of it until we have received the *begotten*, from which we may learn of the *unbegotten*. This unbegotten light no one has seen nor known, except him to whom the Son and the begotten light have wished to reveal it. This, therefore, is the splendor emanating from the paternal <margin>Paul</margin> light, and from the Father of lights, if Paul teaches the Hebrews rightly, saying: *Who, since he is the splendor of the Father.* Thus, the begotten light is the Word, proceeding from the unbegotten light. <margin>Mercury</margin> This is called by Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom many mystical and "hermetic" texts were attributed.</note> the "shining word"; by Paul the "splendor and glory <margin>Plato</margin> of the Father"; by Plato the "sun" and "first son of the supernal light." Who, when he lived among men, <margin>CHRIST</margin> testified to this often: *I am the light of the world.* And: *Behold me in me and through me, expecting no other light in which you might see either me or my origin—that paternal light. Once you depart from this, you will immediately grope in the darkness.* Therefore, receive this light and walk in it while you have the light itself, because in this light alone shall you see light. This is the light of which he said...

# OF THE THIRD SONG

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Isaiah, reporting future things as if they were already past, says: *The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light.* <note>original: "Populus qui sedebat in tenebris vidit lucem magnam" — quoting Isaiah 9:2.</note> Elsewhere, inspired by a prophetic fury, he cried out: *Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.* <note>original: "Surge, illuminare Jerusalem..." — quoting Isaiah 60:1.</note> For this glory of the Lord is no other light than that which once rose in the world, having been begotten by the Father from eternity. This begotten light, together with the unbegotten, "brought forth the Artificer Mind," says 
<margin>Mercurius</margin>
Mercurius <note>Mercurius refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary ancient figure whose writings—the Hermetica—were believed by Renaissance scholars to contain "pagan" prophecies of Christian truths.</note>; that is, to speak in our own way, it produced the Holy Spirit, the artisan of all things. For this is the heat which, proceeding from light and splendor, is itself also light. For those three most Holy Persons are like three rays existing in one splendor, 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
as Dionysius teaches <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian who wrote extensively about the "Divine Darkness" and hierarchies of light.</note>; yet these rays are not confused with one another. We see proof of this in three physical lamps: we see a "trinity" in the shadows cast by those lights, yet a unity exists because they produce a single light and a single splendor. However, the example falls short, because the splendor of those physical lamps increases the total light when multiplied—as their boundaries end, one increases the light of the other. But those supramundane, infinite rays cannot be increased; nevertheless, they communicate their infinite light to lower things as much as they please. They are distinguished in "shadows"—that is, in the effects produced by them—since from the Father of Lights we have our *being*, from the Son our *intellect*, and from the Spirit our *warmth and love*. They are also distinguished among themselves as light, splendor, and heat, which 
<margin>The Logicians</margin>
are nonetheless the same in substance. This is not a "qualitative" splendor or heat (as the logicians say <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "quality" is an accidental property rather than the essential nature of a thing.</note>), but rather an essential light, splendor, and heat. These things subsist through themselves without being contained in a body or emanating from a body; such is that divine light, splendor, and heat of which we speak, from which all life and all things emanate. 
<margin>John</margin>
John explained this light in a few words, as is the custom of those who are closest to the light itself. For just as light is more intense and less scattered the closer it is to the source that shines and spreads it, and the more remote it is, the more it is scattered and less intense; in the same way, those who teach and spread this light understand it more intensely and explain it in fewer words the closer they have approached it. But those further from the light and its teaching, since they do not know well how to express what they do not well perceive, 
<margin>The same</margin>
multiply words and entangle their listeners and readers. John, therefore, being closest to that Illuminator and reclining upon His breast <note>A reference to the "Beloved Disciple" in John 13:23, traditionally identified as John the Evangelist.</note>, received an intense and concentrated light, and so he explained it from himself in few words. But we, who are much further distant from that light and who deal with those sitting in the lower seats, must necessarily explain that same light to our inferiors with more words, just as we receive it through many rays. Yet we follow those things which we have learned from John, who was admitted to the inner chambers of light—truths handed down in few but most sweet harmonies, concerning both 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
the light itself and those things which have emanated from it, and continue to emanate.

But for the sake of the many different things that receive it, it is made manifold. And the further it descends, the more rays it is seen to have...
