Embracing all these things, John says in a single word: *Everything that was made was life in him.* <note>original: "Omne quod factum est in ipso uita erat" — a common medieval reading of John 1:3-4.</note> Augustine says this is "creating life" indeed. And immediately he adds: that this life was the light from which all things were made, which he calls the "Word" <note>original: "uerbum" — the Logos.</note> by another name. There are also those who think that what was prescribed by Moses—*let there be light* <note>original: "fiat lux" — Genesis 1:3.</note>—refers to the Angels, as if they were the first lights emanating from God. Through these, as if through pieces of glass (as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians and the philosophy of Pythagoras.</note> brings forth from the Pythagorean workshop), that supreme light transmits its radiance into the other lower things. Let them be as if they were <term>transparent media</term> <note>original: "diaphana" — substances that allow light to pass through.</note>; the higher Angels, being the first intermediaries, receive the light itself, by which they illuminate all the lower ones in their respective degrees, as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic who organized the celestial hierarchy of angels.</note> pleases. Each of the lowest things, however, is illuminated through a medium or media suitable to itself, to which they also correspond, as we touched upon above. 

Each man, moreover, receives that portion of light whose nature belongs to the medium to which he is exposed, or with which he is connected. For if the soul emanates from that supreme light through the Seraphic <note>The Seraphim are the highest order of angels, associated with fire, love, and light.</note> intelligences, it is made seraphic; and it strives to arrive at the seraphic mansions (under the auspices of nature, but primarily with God favoring and drawing it). But if the soul receives the splendor of knowledge through the Cherubic <note>The Cherubim are the second order of angels, associated with divine wisdom and the contemplation of God.</note> minds, having been made a familiar of that light, it busies itself with reaching the cherubic seats. It has already put on the nature of that light through the light piercing through it; and let the same be said of any other orders. For just as light passing through glass of various colors also spreads out different-colored rays—red, for instance, through red; green through green; white through white; and so on—in the same way the intellect or soul puts on that nature through whose transparency it passes. Nor is the <term>transparent medium</term> of spiritual light the air, but spirit and intelligence, which can receive and transmit that light.

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
And of these things, perhaps, the Greatest Master speaks when he says: *Their angels always see the face of the Father.* <note>original: "Angeli eorum semper uident faciem Patris" — quoting Matthew 18:10.</note> And who are "their angels" if not those assigned to their protection? And how are they suitably assigned unless they have some symbol or likeness in common with those to whom they are destined? But since we have already equated all lower things with the heavens, and the heavens with the Angels, and the Angels with that supreme light, we can easily understand how all these things emanate from that same light.

-> How light illuminates. Conclusion 4. <-

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
**T**hat light in the divine mind surpasses all intelligence: so much so that things are contained there which are hidden even from the highest Seraphim, as Dionysius says. However, when diffused into Angelic minds and received according to the nature of the receiving intelligence, it is divided into various grades; nevertheless, all these are above the boundaries of reason. But when sent down into the minds of men, it is rational. This light is manifold, either according to 
<margin>Peripatetics</margin>

<margin>Theologians</margin>
who divides to each person as He wills: as perhaps the true theologians wish to say, and better. 
<margin>Solomon</margin>
Hence Solomon says: *From the beginning I was allotted a good soul.* <note>original: "A principio sortitus sum animam bonam" — an adaptation of Wisdom of Solomon 8:19.</note>

This light next descends to the <term>Imagination</term> <note>original: "Phantasiam" — in this context, the mental faculty that bridges the gap between raw sensory data and higher intellectual thought.</note> / above the sense alone: to which it finally arrives, especially to the sense of the eyes, which are the lamps of this <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "huius parui mundi" — literally "this small world," a common Renaissance term for the human being as a reflection of the greater universe.</note>. And 
<margin>Orpheus, Plotinus, Proclus</margin>this happens through this same visible light being spread abroad, which Orpheus, Plotinus, and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who saw the universe as a series of emanations from a single source.</note> thought was a certain vision of the deities / through the rays of the celestial eyes, and a spirit seeing all things: and which is seen by all. It descends further to transparent bodies / such as flowers / and the beauties of colors / so that bodies might be seen: For color (as they thought) 
<margin>Plotinus</margin>is <term>opaque light</term> <note>original: "lux est opaca" — the theory that color is light that has been "thickened" or "shadowed" by matter.</note>. <margin>Pythagoras, Plato</margin>are generated / it effects this. But in the center (as pleases Pythagoras and the Platonics) the rays become strongest, collected into a narrow space: so much so that the earth there, being dry and devoid of moisture, is easily ignited and thinned: so that through passages it belches out heat, and sometimes fires: and there the light is ignited into a <term>dark fire</term> <note>original: "caliginosum ignem" — a fire that burns without providing light, often associated with the center of the earth or the underworld.</note> without splendor, just as in heaven, where it is spread out, it is the clearest light devoid of burning. Nor is it a wonder if this most noble light is manifold: since even the soul itself is a ray of light (as certain Platonists teach) or an effect 
<margin>Mercury</margin>of light (as <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus, a collection of texts on philosophy, magic, and theology.</note> says); in the heart it gives life, in the brain it understands, in the eyes it sees, in the ears it hears, in the tongue it speaks, in the feet it walks, in the stomach it nourishes, and it descends even to the lowest operations. Therefore, the light known best in the Father of Lights is true light: In the Son, the exuberance of goodness itself, and the illuminating splendor: In the Holy Spirit, a burning brightness: In the Angels, shining intelligence and infused joy: In humans / the clear discourse of reason and the knowledge of divine things: In the celestial bodies, visible splendor / abundance of life / and effective propagation: In fire, a certain vital vigor infused from the heavens: In transparent bodies / color and shining beauty: In opaque bodies / a certain beneficial and generating power: In the center, truly / a certain agonizing and boiling heat: so much so that all things feel the benefit of light according to their capacity. And 
<margin>The same (Mercury)</margin>although humans (as Mercury teaches) proceed from life and light into the soul and mind, and receiving soul from life and mind from light, yet being voluntarily enveloped in darkness they lose the mind: and sometimes the soul: and being thrust into <term>Tartarean prisons</term> <note>original: "tartareis carceribus" — referencing Tartarus, the deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment.</note>, they experience the agonizing fire in the boiling center, but the beneficial light not at all: therefore they are said to be sent to the "outer darkness," having become themselves darkness inside and out in most miserable darkness. Other living creatures receive only this light which is perceived by corporeal eyes: but the better light not at all. Also, most humans existing in this <term>pilgrimage</term> <note>original: "peregrinatione" — referring to the human life on earth as a temporary journey toward the divine.</note> admit "lunar light" (that is, the discourse of reason), closing their eyes to the light 
<margin>John</margin>of the true sun, of whom John [says]: *The light came into the world, and men loved darkness more than light: because their works were evil* and darkened. Nor 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>did they strive to purge the eye: so that not only Christ, but Plotinus teaches 
<margin>Pythagoras, Stoics, Academics, Hierocles</margin>in his [book] *On Beauty*. common eyes <note>original: "uulgares oculi"</note> can [hardly] endure the rays of divinity. Yet there exist even among men, though they are few, those who strive to hear the herald's voice of the Prince of Light, by which it is said: *While you have the light, believe in the light*; *Walk while you have the light*; *I am the light of the world*: namely, manifesting myself to those willing to receive me. For the divine light offers itself to be beheld, without which we cannot see divine things: because (as <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher who merged Neoplatonism with theology.</note> says) it is only permitted to ascend to celestial things as far as the ray of divine eloquence deigns to insinuate itself. Moreover, he not only insinuates himself, but even invites us, taking pity on us who received a small portion of light from the beginning: and this has been covered over by the thickest gloom of this body: so that we can in no way grasp either the supreme light, nor that very modest portion granted to us, unless our eye is illuminated by that same light, and we are purged by constant study. Doing this, with that same light continually favoring us, we are made **sons of light** together with the **Angels of light**: who (as <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential Church Father.</note> rightly feels) approaching that true light as if to the fountain of life, consult it continually. Therefore, in men and Angels who follow that light, the character of light is imprinted, of which the Prophet says: *The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed or lifted up over us.* <note>A reference to Psalm 4:6.</note> These sons of light are also made sons of God, as John says: *But as many as received him* (that is, that same light of which he spoke above) *he gave them power to become the sons of God.* But to those who would not admit that light, <term>Job</term> says: *They were rebels against the light*, and were made into darkness: whose head in that rebellion is called, and was made, the prince of darkness: into whose service <note>original: "stipendium"</note> all those who have been darkened enter, who neglect to receive that light which illuminates every man: because he who acts wickedly hates the light, by the testimony of our John. Yet they are not entirely removed from that light: since they still receive the benefit of light by which they live. For we have two primary benefits from light: One is **life**, by which we live. The other is **light**, or luster, by which life itself can be seen. Therefore, those who are in darkness live, but do not know: for the light remains in the darkness, as the divine <term>Platonists</term> <note>Philosophers following the tradition of Plato, often emphasizing the spiritual over the material.</note> say, asserting some divine thing I know not what. Just as cold relates to heat, and whiteness to blackness, so darkness relates to light: But in blackness there is a tiny bit of white, and in cold a little heat; so also in darkness there is a modest light, by which they may live, but not by which they may understand: But leaving darkness aside, let us return to the light.

### How light itself ignites and awakens. -> Conclusion V. <-

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
<insert>H</insert>owever, this light does not only illuminate, but also ignites: and by its splendor—separating, thinning, and heating (as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> says)—it separates the pure from the impure, the good from the evil, the beautiful from the deformed: destroying and consuming the latter, while perfecting the former. But there is a difference between light and heat: For light remains in the one who is illuminating, yet shining through and penetrating the object illuminated: Heat, however, passing into the thing heated, becomes mingled with it.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine light, shifting from how humans perceive it to the specific roles of the Son (as Light) and the Holy Spirit (as Heat). It builds on the previous page's mention of how this light descends from the celestial realm to illuminate and "warm" the human soul.</meta>

### OF THE THIRD SONG ###

<margin>Paul</margin>
Hence the Holy Spirit—whose nature is to warm—is said to dwell within us and to be mingled with us more so than the Son, who is properly called Light. For the Son taught and illuminated the Apostles, and then ascended into the heavens. But the Spirit, being sent and destined by this Light, descends by entering within, inflaming, and remaining, so that he is made one and the same spirit with those whom he inflames—or rather, they become the same with him. And even if the Son ascended to the heavens, he does not abandon us; instead, he is with us until the end of the age, giving life and illuminating us. Yet the Son is not said to be "poured out" within us in the same way as the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle <note>Paul, in Romans 5:5</note> says: *The charity of God is poured out in your hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us.* We can confirm this through the image of the sun, which is a sufficiently clear likeness <note>original: "simulachro"</note> of God: its light illuminates us, but it is not "poured out" into us like heat is. For once the sun recedes, or a person moves away from it, or a window is closed, the light no longer provides its brilliance; yet the "poured out" heat remains for a time. So too does charity <note>Divine love</note> remain in our hearts, even if that Light is not actively illuminating us in that moment. Therefore, that Light—which in its solitary nature is entirely set apart from us—stirs us through the Son (acting as rays) and the Holy Spirit (acting as heat). This light stirred those ancient fathers through that enigmatic <note>original: "ænigmaticū̄"; referring to the symbolic or veiled truths of the Old Testament</note> splendor; yet that was the Son and the Wisdom of God wrapped in riddles and figures. Afterward, appearing in the flesh, he stirred us with clear light, according to that word of the Apostle:
<margin>The same <note>Paul</note></margin>
> God, who at many times and in various ways spoke in times past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things (as pertains to his humanity), through whom also he made the worlds (as pertains to his divinity).

<margin>The same</margin>
Paul continues: *Who, being the brightness of the Father's glory.* Behold, therefore, that this light and brightness is the Son of God, who taught and stirred the ancient fathers through various riddles, and finally demonstrated himself in a clearer light. But in the fatherland <note>Heaven</note>, the Light will be fully open to all, and continuous, without any interval, overshadowing, or hiding beneath dark cloaks. And for this reason, 
<margin>John</margin>
John says: *And there was no night there, because the Lamb was its lamp.* <note>Revelation 21:23</note> This is why the 
<margin>David</margin>
Prophet <note>King David</note> once entreated for that stirring which happens in this earthly pilgrimage, saying: *Stir up my glory, stir up the psaltery and harp.* Where we usually have: "Arise, my glory, arise psaltery and harp," the word <term>Hur</term> <note>Hebrew: עור</note> actually signifies "to stir" or "to waken," not "to arise." He prays, therefore, to that begotten Light—which was the <term>psaltery</term> <note>A stringed instrument; here representing the Old Testament</note> of the Old Testament and the evangelical harp, and the glory of all things—that it might stir him; for we cannot be stirred from any other source, nor do we have any other light that can awaken us.

->How this light amplifies and expands. Conclusion VII.<-

<margin>M</margin> Indeed, wondrous is this light, which at first offered itself in a veiled manner; but as soon as it begins to illuminate my eyes, it leads me into such spacious chambers, and so charms me by piercing the eye of my mind, that I am unable to depart from it—even though I cannot fully grasp even the smallest portion of it. For into its greatness...

# EIGHTH MODE #

[...with its] magnitude expands my heart, so that I cannot draw back; rather, I am compelled with loose reins to run into the path of its rays, when it has expanded my heart and my mind. It is no wonder that this light amplifies and expands; for the color white, which is a kind of opaque light (as we touched upon above), scatters and expands. And the purer this bodily light is, the more it stretches its visual rays out into width, length, and breadth. But that [divine] light is always most pure—so much so that the more our inner eye <note>The "inner eye" refers to the "oculus mentis" or the eye of the mind/soul, a common medieval concept for spiritual perception.</note> receives it, the more it is purified. Hence the wise, who have cleansed their inner eye through faith and doctrine, see more than the common people. And the simple who are purified see more than those entangled in the doctrines and cleverness of men, as the 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
true light itself says: *I confess to you, Lord Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones.* <note>Matthew 11:25</note> Furthermore, the Prophets, having a purer eye of the mind, saw more than the wise of this 
<margin>THE SAME</margin>
world. For those who are truly purified gaze into the pure splendor of light, as that same highest light says: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* <note>Matthew 5:8</note>

The vision of this light is followed by joy, as that same light says: *These things I have spoken to you*—namely, by illuminating you—*so that my joy may be in you, and your joy may be full.* <note>John 15:11</note> Nor can anyone feel this joy who is deprived of that light, as that good old man 
<margin>Tobias</margin>
Tobias used to say: *What kind of joy can I have, when I do not see the light of heaven?* <note>Tobit 5:12. In the Vulgate, Tobias (Tobit) speaks of his blindness as a lack of joy.</note> By this light, therefore, the heart and intellect of Solomon were expanded, so that he might look upon natural things and discourse *from the cedar of 
<margin>Moses Paul</margin>
Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall.* <note>1 Kings 4:33. Solomon was legendary for his encyclopedic knowledge of nature.</note> Expanded by this, Moses gave the law of most divine wisdom. Expanded by this, Paul saw the secrets of God which it is not permitted for man to speak. By this, all the Prophets saw not only hidden things, but those things which were done in times long past, and those which 
<margin>Benedict Francis</margin>
were to be done much later. By this, Benedict, Francis, and many others whose eyes were illuminated, saw things absent and remote from bodily sight. Finally, we, the blessed, hope to be expanded in this perfect amplitude, where we shall behold everything we wish for with a clear and open gaze.

->How this light gladdens and makes one blessed. Conclusion VII.<-

<margin>John</margin>
**F**inally, this most holy light gladdens and makes blessed those things which it has already given life, illuminated, roused, and expanded. For those things which shine and are illuminated "laugh," just as those things which lie in darkness mourn. And since there is no night in that most Blessed Kingdom, there is no sorrow or horror there; wherefore our divine John, attesting to this, says: *And there was no night there, because the Lamb was its lamp.* <note>Revelation 22:5/21:23</note> And as much as that celestial and divine light is more excellent than ours, so much more joy does it bring to the mind that beholds it. Indeed, our eyes rejoice in this solar light; our soul and the spirit itself rejoice, as if in a light most familiar to it, from which spirit and life—most similar to light—emanate.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Eighth Mode," specifically focusing on the joyful and transformative effects of divine light on the soul and body. It transitions from the previous discussion of the "pure in heart" seeing God to how this light creates a cosmic harmony among the blessed in heaven.</meta>

->OF THE THIRD CANTICLE<-

<margin>Mercury</margin>
The Father of all (says Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure in late antiquity whose writings—the *Hermetica*—were often cited by Renaissance theologians to show that even ancient "pagans" understood divine truths.</note>), existing as intellect, life, and brightness, created man in his own likeness, making him a participant in light and life. Therefore, when man returns to the light that is his kin, he rejoices much more than a man who, after wandering for a long time, returns to his own longed-for homeland. Our spirit and mind are so friendly toward light, and so delighted when bathed in it, that when the soul rejoices, it seems to emit light itself: just as the spirit is glad within, it smiles outwardly on the face and shines with a certain exhilaration. Even the eyes shine, for they are the most friendly to light; in that joyful laughter, they perform a circular motion like the heavens and dilate. In those who mourn, however, the eyes are on the contrary constricted and darkened, fixed as if in a center of darkness. For we rejoice in this light as if in the poured-out laughter of heaven. If indeed that light were seen in the Angels (as has happened to some), we would rejoice much more. In that supreme light, however, the blessed rejoice so much that their overflowing joy transforms the body itself into a heavenly nature, making it glorious, lucid, and clear. For the eyes of all the blessed—both of the body and of the mind—having been converted into the nature of light, become transparent and shining; with a mere gaze, they imprint rays of intelligence upon their companions, flashing between one another in that meeting of sight. And this occurs as that supreme light shines so abundantly and happily in all, just as this Sun shines among the stars. Indeed, it is much more, for the "stars" of the blessed shall cross over into the nature of that Sun, as the
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Savior says: *The righteous shall shine like the Sun in the sight of their Father.* <note>Matthew 13:43</note> From this, a better and more harmonious music and joy is born there than that which arises in the heavens from the consonant distance and most orderly motions of the stars, which smile together from the proper meeting of their rays. For those concurrent rays of the blessed in the supreme light produce a sweeter melody. Furthermore, those citizens laugh and rejoice in the light itself, which illuminates all things, however diverse; for having been made "children of light," they are converted in mind and body into that same light. All things grow beautiful in that light, which is so fair that, having put all deformity to flight, it brings a miraculous delight to those who behold and receive it. The blessed, therefore—sometimes in that "beginning light" <note>original: *luce inceptiva* (likely meaning the light as it first emanates or as perceived in the creation)</note> dispersed into many things, and sometimes in the "morning light" collected in the Word <note>The "Word" refers to Christ as the Logos. St. Augustine and others used the terms "morning" and "evening" knowledge to describe how angels see things either in God (the Word) or in themselves.</note>—behold all forms collected there in sweetest concord. Now turning themselves to that One shining in the "midday light," they draw from there also that which makes them glad, perceiving in that light the source from which all things grow beautiful and harmonious; they see the source of color, flavor, scent, life, and the harmony and agreement of all things. Their eyes, thus turned toward that midday light, are so absorbed that those who were previously "heavenly" then become "divine," having drunk the nectar of divine pleasure. Therefore, nothing remains for them to desire, because having been admitted to those inner sanctums, they are thoroughly intoxicated by the abundance of that light which immediately fills everything in that kingdom. And this is what Peter says:
<margin>Peter</margin>
*He has called us into his admirable light* <note>1 Peter 2:9</note>—a light which was first diffused into the Son, who is the splendor of the Father; then into the man Christ, the Prince of the whole city [of God]; then into the God-like Queen <note>A reference to the Virgin Mary.</note>, in whom it glows more splendidly than in all others. It passes then to the Angelic choirs arranged in their proper order, down to the lowest mansion of that heavenly city, so that all in it, seeing the Father of lights, may praise and glorify Him forever.

# THE THIRD MEASURE: THE DIVISION.
## How that heavenly house and family is divided. First Harmony.

<margin>John, Ezekiel</margin>
We are most fully taught by John and Ezekiel that the city and heavenly commonwealth is divided into many parts. They describe now the foundations, now the gates, now the streets, now the suburbs, now the temple, and now the <term>treasuries</term> <note>original: *gazophylatia*, referring to the storage chambers for sacred offerings or riches within the Temple complex.</note> into which that structure is partitioned.
<margin>Paul</margin>
In the same way, Paul openly testifies that the guests are divided into many ranks, saying: In the church—which is this holy city we are describing—He first appointed some to be Apostles, then Prophets, others Evangelists, others Pastors and Teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the building up of the body of Christ. To these ranks correspond distinct portions, dwellings, and seats, distinguished by their rewards, as Christ says:
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
> In my Father's house there are many mansions.

Since these are hidden from us, and Christ remained silent as to for whom they are prepared by the eternal Father—indeed, He even confessed it was not His to distribute them, but they are given to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father Himself—we too shall respect this with silence, except insofar as the Son Himself deigned to reveal it to the Prophets and His close followers. We shall follow those who treat such matters, considering first that if in this earthly house there is a manifold division into diverse seats for guests and quarters for travelers, we must think no differently of the blessed and heavenly kingdom, from which, without doubt, these lower things emanate. There, then, are the eternal mansions for all who do not succeed one another over time, but dwell together, having already been admitted as heavenly citizens and members of the household of God. Some are assessors and judges; others are souls of the bride and the queen; still others are <term>concubines</term> and young maidens <note>The author is using allegorical language from the Song of Solomon (6:8) to describe different levels of intimacy or "rank" in the soul's relationship with God.</note> in a mystery more sublime than these sensible words sound. The rest are distributed into so many ranks that I would by no means dare to pursue the full sequence of the matter. However, we shall add a few excerpts here and there from those who have been taught by divine oracles.

### On the Merkavah, or the Tribunal of God, according to the Hebrews. Conclusion III.

<margin>Abraham</margin> There exists also in the theology of the Hebrews the tribunal of God, which they call the <term>Merkavah</term> <note>Hebrew: *Merkavah* meaning "Chariot," referring to the divine throne-chariot seen in the visions of the prophet Ezekiel.</note> after Ezekiel, and which we find in various places of Scripture, but it is explained by the Doctors [of the law] especially in the <term>Book of Formation</term> <note>referring to the *Sefer Yetzirah*, an early and influential work of Jewish mysticism.</note>, which is attributed to Abraham. They say that to this tribunal belong the <term>Ophannim</term> <note>Hebrew: "Wheels"; a class of angels described as wheels within wheels covered in eyes.</note>, the Seraphim, the ministering Angels, and the <term>Holy Living Creatures</term> <note>Hebrew: *Chayot HaKodesh*, the four beings that support the divine throne.</note>. Because these are not in common use among us Latins, there is no doubt they will seem foreign—not to say foolish—to some, because they savor of nothing trivial or common. Yet I do not think one should desist from this path, but rather I shall gather some things worth knowing, beyond those we touched upon above. 

They say, therefore, that the Ophannim are the Angels whose care it is to arrange the matter of things so that form can be introduced. For matter does not arrange itself, since it has no active power; therefore, it is necessary that it be arranged by an external force. They say the Seraphim, however, are the "heating virtues" from whom life and form are supplied. The ministering Angels are indeed of many kinds, just as the ministries entrusted to them are many. But the Holy Living Creatures are four in number, as recorded harmoniously by Ezekiel and John:

<margin>Jerome</margin> the lion, namely the calf (or ox), the eagle, and the man. Although different men have perceived different things regarding these in the allegorical and moral sense (as Jerome recites in a long series in his commentary on Ezekiel), we, interpreting the <term>anagogical sense</term> <note>The "anagogical" or "mystical" sense of scripture deals with how earthly events or figures point toward the eternal and heavenly glory.</note>, will follow the ancient Fathers. We say that these four are, as it were, the kings of the four kinds of animals. For among the herds and domestic animals, the ox is King; among the wild beasts, the lion; among the birds, the eagle; and among all rational beings, the man—who even

<margin>Paul</margin> holds the principality over the Angels, even in both sexes. For in the male sex, Christ exceeds them, as Paul says: *He was made so much better than the Angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.* <note>original: "Tanto melior Angelis effectus quanto differentius prae illis nomen hereditauit." (Hebrews 1:4)</note> In the female sex, indeed, stands she who is said to be exalted above all the choirs of Angels. To these [humans] it was more particularly said (as it pleases some wise men)—even before man was formed from the earth and Eve was drawn from his rib: *Rule over the fish of the sea* and the other creatures. <note>Genesis 1:28</note> 

But for what purpose are the lion, the ox, and the eagle in that tribunal? I say that if all things emanate from Him, must they not all have their image and "idea" in Him, and be written in the account book of the most high God? For just as in the accounting books of kings and good rulers all things are noted down—both men and cities, and

<margin>David</margin> revenues, and whatever pertains to the kingdom—so too in the book of God (as the Prophet says) *all shall be written.* <note>Psalm 139:16</note> And lest it be argued that only men are written there, he preceded this by saying: *My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in*

<margin>Jerome</margin> *secret: your eyes saw my unformed substance.* <note>original: "Non est occultatum os meum a te, quod fecisti in occulto: Imperfectum meum uiderunt oculi tui." (Psalm 139:15-16)</note> Regarding this, Jerome says: even the elements from which man is composed, God knows before he is formed, and all...

# MODULE EIGHT / THE GUESTS
## How many guests there are of that city. First Harmony.

<margin>John</margin>
<margin>GOD</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
<margin>Daniel</margin>
Beyond the triune and unique supreme Prince and the Queen, it is impossible to define how many guests there are in that lodging who sing together there forever in praise of the Prince; as John says: *I saw a great multitude, which no one could number.* <note>Revelation 7:9</note> And concerning the seed of Abraham, which is for the most part to be saved, God said to Abraham himself: *Number the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be.* <note>Genesis 15:5</note> This seed indeed comes forth from Isaac, who was born (as Paul says) not according to the flesh of the handmaid, but of the free woman, according to the spirit through the promise, which things are spoken through allegory. <note>Galatians 4:22-31</note> Yet this number (as Dionysius says) <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, who argued that the number of angels surpasses all human calculation</note> transcends the capacity of human calculation and is known to Him alone who numbers all the hairs of the head. Nevertheless, some think they have discovered the number of Angels, and consequently of those who are saved (whom they believe to be as many as the Angels). For they say that in any of the nine choirs, there are as many legions as the legion itself contains units when the number of the legion is squared. Now, a legion contains (as they say) six thousand, six hundred and sixty-six. If this number is squared and multiplied by itself, it yields:
->4 4 4 3 5 5 5 6<-
which is forty-four million, four hundred and thirty-five thousand, five hundred and fifty-six. But the total collected from all nine choirs would be:

## NINTH MEASURE / NUPTIAL MATTERS.
### How and when the marriage between God and the soul was initiated.
### First Harmony.

**F**or indeed, the sacrament of marriage is so great that as soon as the perfect structure of the world was finished and its own High Priest <note>original: *Antistite*. This likely refers to Adam as the steward of creation, or God as the one presiding over the world.</note> was led into it, the nuptials were immediately celebrated. This marriage was proclaimed by God for our first parents. For the Architect, placing the final hand upon his work, decreed to give a helper to the man already made, who would stand before him; concerning which our text has: *He made a helper like unto him.* <note>A reference to Genesis 2:18.</note> Hence, having cast a deep sleep upon Adam, He took one of his ribs, and forming it into a woman, brought her to Adam and assigned her as a wife, so that the human race—from the application of the active to the passive—might feel its own harmony <note>original: *concinnium*, meaning a pleasing arrangement or musical fitness.</note> and rejoice in a fecundity all the more celebrated than that of the other living creatures, just as man is better than they. Adam himself received this woman, formed from the man's rib, saying: *Bone now of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife.*

<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
<margin>Hosea</margin>
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Reciting these words, Paul adds to the Ephesians: *This is a great sacrament, I speak in Christ and the church.* <note>Ephesians 5:32. Paul interprets the marriage of Adam and Eve as a "mystery" or "sacrament" pointing toward the union of Christ and the Church.</note> And just as Sacred Scripture, having described the creation, deals first with marriage, it ends in the same way with the sacrament of nuptials; as John says toward the very end of his most celebrated and final vision, while reporting the persona of the exulting blessed ones: *Let us rejoice and exult, because the marriage of the Lamb has come.* <note>Revelation 19:7.</note> And again: *Blessed are they who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb.* Even the Prince and Lord of that city, while he lived among humans, compared the kingdom of heaven and the summit of all human affairs to nuptials. Since, therefore, the most celebrated nuptials of all are conducted there, let us see who is the bridegroom, who is the bride, with what wedding song, with what guests, by what contract, and under what auspices they are celebrated. The Bridegroom, there is no doubt, is He who says through Hosea: *I will betroth thee to me in faith, and thou shalt know that I am the Lord.* <note>Hosea 2:20.</note> This Bridegroom is more clearly expressed in the Gospel by He Himself, when He says: *The kingdom of heaven is like a King who made a marriage for his son.* <note>Matthew 22:2.</note> Now, the Son of the highest King of all ages is Christ, and He is a King himself, for He received the scepter from the Father long ago. The Bride, however, is any soul consenting to this contract; and consequently, the entire church and assembly of the faithful is the bride—certainly not a superfluous or troublesome one to such a bridegroom, for he will never be lacking in those things which are required for those nuptials.

# OF THE THIRD SONG

<margin>John</margin>
For "from his fullness," says John, "we have all received"—all things, that is, which are necessary in this and other affairs. <note>The author quotes John 1:16, "From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace," to establish that Christ is the source of all spiritual needs.</note> For if he paid the debt for all the children of Adam, if he earned grace and glory for all, if he covers the nakedness of all, and if he regenerates everyone (for he himself is the father of all), he can also betroth all souls and give them the means to conceive and bring forth the fruit of good works. As the 
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>David</margin>
Apostle says: *God is able to make all grace abound in you, so that you may abound in every good work,* just as it is written: *He has scattered, he has given to the poor; his justice remains forever.* <note>The author combines 2 Corinthians 9:8 and Psalm 112:9 (attributed here to David) to show that divine generosity enables human virtue.</note> Furthermore, *He who supplies seed to the sower will also provide bread to eat, and will increase the growth of the fruits of your justice, so that you may be enriched in all things.* Therefore, no one should refuse such a groom on the grounds that he cannot provide for so many brides. For he is rich in all these riches, which do not decrease when shared; he is powerful in that virtue which is not exhausted when communicated to many—just as neither the light nor the power of the sun is diminished by being shared with many things or by making all lower things fertile.

And because a marriage is initiated, contracted, ratified, and consummated, we shall first see how and when it took its beginning. These nuptials were initiated through the Holy Spirit when, at his dictation, God invited us so many times through the Prophets to this contract. This is 
<margin>Hosea</margin>
seen clearly in Hosea: *I will betroth you to me forever; I will betroth you to me in justice and judgment, in mercy and in compassion.* <note>Hosea 2:19.</note> Regarding this, the Hebrew text has וּבְרַחֲמִים <note>original: *u-be-rahamim*</note>, which we can translate as "in tender loves" or "acts of piety." For under the Law, the severe groom betrothed in judgment and justice; but in the Messiah, showing himself most kind, he betrothed in mercy, piety, grace, and all the blessings signified by that word *rahamim*. 
<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
And through Ezekiel, inspired by the divine spirit, he says: *And I swore to you, and entered into a covenant with you, and you became mine*—namely, as a bride. This happens through the "consent" <note>term: *consensus* — In medieval law, the mutual consent of both parties was the essential element that made a marriage valid.</note> which every soul easily gives, since by its very nature it hungers for the happiness wrapped up in these nuptials. 

You have, therefore, how these nuptials were initiated, to which he first invited the Angels. Yet many of them were found unworthy; wherefore he ordered them to be expelled as rebels and rash ones. He also invited all human beings, but most of them—submerging themselves in foolish, cheap, and almost beastly things—were not unjustly rejected as unworthy of such a great partnership and left to wallow in the filth and mud of pleasures. Therefore, with these ones cast out, he called others to the wedding through "nomenclators" <note>term: *nomenclatores* — Originally Roman officials who whispered names to candidates; here used for messengers or heralds who announce the wedding guests.</note> and messengers: the Angels, the Prophets, and the Apostles. All of them, solicitous for our salvation, invite whomever they find in the streets, at the exits, or at the crossroads and meeting points of the world to those nuptials.

<header>THE EIGHTH TONE</header>

# THE EIGHTH TONE

<margin><unclear>Jesus</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>Augustine(?)</unclear></margin>
<margin>David</margin>
Marriage is contracted through words of the present <note>original: "uerba de præsenti." In medieval law, these were vows that created an immediate, legal marriage, as opposed to "words of the future," which were merely an engagement.</note> between spouses who consent on the spot. This differs from betrothals, which are made through words of the future, often arranged by parents, intermediaries, or various sponsors while the spouses are still minors. These children, once they reach adulthood, frequently rescind such agreements. In contrast, the marriage between Christ and the soul is initiated by the Prophets but is fully contracted through "words of the present" during baptism. This occurs when the one to be baptized asks for faith and offers full consent, through which a living marriage is contracted. And because it is customary for the couple to join their right hands, this is represented by the visible water in which the person is immersed, accompanied by the spoken word; from these, a sensible sign of this contract is provided. Just as it is common to say in a physical marriage, "I take you as mine," so it is said here: "I renounce the devil, the world, and its vanities, so that I may cling entirely to my spouse, Christ." He also confirmed this kind of marriage with an oath,

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
according to the words of Ezekiel: *And I swore to you, and entered into my covenant with you, says the Lord; and you became my bride.* <note>Ezekiel 16:8</note> But when did this happen? Hear what follows: *And I washed you with water and cleaned your blood from you, and I anointed you with oil.* <note>Ezekiel 16:9</note> All these things take place in baptism. There is no doubt that the Prophet speaks of this under the figure of a symbolic bride who was herself washed with water—though not with that perfect water with which we are washed. We are joined to Christ in baptism by a bond and an indissoluble treaty, which no one is ever permitted to break, nor can they, without committing express adultery. Truly, He has never repudiated a wife, even if He long ago divorced that ungrateful, formerly most chaste spouse, the Synagogue. We see this prefigured in the story of Vashti, <note>Queen Vashti was the first wife of King Ahasuerus in the Book of Esther; she was deposed for refusing the King's command.</note> who earned a decree of divorce by despising the King’s command. From this, a custom had also grown strong (though supported by law) that marriages were frequently dissolved. This is by no means granted to Christians,

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
to whom it was said by the groom: *I am with you always, even to the end of the age,* <note>Matthew 28:20</note> never to be repudiated. Even if you commit a thousand adulteries, though not without punishment, the marriage remains indissoluble with the whole Church. 

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
Every shameless soul will rightly pay the penalty for adultery when she is expelled by perpetual separation from the groom, who says: *Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire.* <note>Matthew 25:41</note> Therefore, this universal bride, which is called the Catholic Church, will never be repudiated. However, if any particular soul is rejected, another will be brought in so that the full number that concludes this wedding gathering may be complete. For it was predicted in Job:

<margin>John</margin>
*God will shatter many, and make others stand in their place.* <note>Job 34:24</note> And in the Apocalypse: *Hold fast to what you have, lest another receive your crown.* <note>Revelation 3:11</note> Nor are these souls repudiated by the groom unless they themselves despise coming to the most happy nuptials—either by rejecting them or by neglecting to be present, as is said in the Gospel: *And those who had been invited were not worthy.* <note>Matthew 22:8</note> Thus others are brought in so that the wedding may be filled. The groom persists in this purpose: that he shall have this congregation as a bride, repudiating no one of that congregation except those who have voluntarily despised coming or remaining. As for the former bride, he repudiated her for this very reason.

<header>OF THE THIRD SONG</header>

...so that he admits no one from that assembly to the wedding, unless he flees into the bosom of this new bride, having become a Christian. And to return to the sacrament <note>The word "sacrament" here refers to a holy mystery or sign.</note> of our first parents: the wife of the first-created man was called a "woman" <note>original: "virago." In the Latin Vulgate (Genesis 2:23), Adam calls Eve *virago* because she was taken from "man" (*vir*). The author is making a linguistic connection between the origin of the first woman and the origin of the Church.</note>, because she was taken from the man. Likewise, this assembly is called "Christian," because it is taken from Christ. The first was taken 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
from the rib of the man, and this one from the side of Christ: from which (as Augustine says) all the sacraments flowed forth, especially baptism, which received its power from that blood and water—or from that which the blood and water represented. And since this wife is formed in baptism, we can rightly say that she was extracted from the side of the sleeping Christ <note>A common medieval trope: as Eve was created while Adam slept, the Church was born from Christ's side as he "slept" in death on the Cross.</note>. And just as those two, and all married persons (as the Gospel testifies), come together into one flesh, so Christ and his bride—whether the universal Church or the individual soul—come together into one spirit, 
<margin>Paul</margin>
as Paul says: *He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him.* <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note>

## How it is Ratified. Conclusion III.

**F**leshly marriage is confirmed and held as valid before a priest, who stands as the witness and minister of that sacrament. In the same way, this spiritual betrothal is ratified before a Bishop, from whom we receive the sacrament (as they say) of Confirmation: for it confirms the covenant and the oath taken in baptism. It is also called the sacrament of chrism <note>The "chrism" is the holy oil used for anointing.</note>, because the recipient is anointed with a particular "unction of divinity." The wedding covenant contracted in baptism is also confirmed and ratified whenever we receive the sacrament of confession or the Eucharist, or whenever we are gifted with any other favor from Christ the groom. But we receive the *true* confirmation when we are so solidified in the grace of God that we remain in it through the course of this life; for this reason, no 
<margin>David</margin>
future divorce need be feared by us. The Prophet desired this confirmation when he said: *And confirm me with a Principal Spirit* <note>Psalm 51:12. The author is exploring the specific meaning of the Hebrew word used here.</note>; or a "voluntary," "liberal," "noble," or "generous" spirit. For that is what <term>nedib</term> <gloss>נדיב: noble or generous</gloss> signifies, which we have translated as "Principal." The Prophet also, foreseeing those things which the groom was going to do with his bride, the Church, prays and says: *Confirm this, O God, which you have worked in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem*—either this lower Jerusalem, where he celebrated this contract on the Cross and confirmed it by the pouring out of the Holy Spirit, or in the Jerusalem above, where these most celebrated weddings (and all others) are completed, as 
<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Christ says: *What God has joined, let no man separate.* If God, therefore, brings about 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
these unions and matrimonial bonds, they happen in heaven where he himself dwells. Whence we ask to be confirmed (as Jerome says) because we are weak.

## How it is Consummated. Conclusion IV.

**W**e finally consummate this spiritual marriage when we carry out in good works what we have promised. In this consummation, there occurs a conception and a birth. But because these things cannot happen without the bride being pregnant, Isaiah therefore says: *From your face, O Lord, we have conceived* <note>Isaiah 26:18</note>, just as women rightly conceive from the face of their husbands.

### TENTH MODULUS / SUSTENANCE

-> What Bread is prepared in this banquet. First Harmony. <-

**G**od, whose works are perfect, like the best Craftsman, fashioned all things very well: and in their various degrees, perfect. Hence, the best Provider (as we said above) prepared food and drink for the sustaining of both parts of man <note>The "inner" spiritual man and the "outer" physical man.</note>: lest perhaps, lacking protection from that same highest Creator who heaped countless benefits upon man, he should fail. Moreover, he prepared these many kinds of feasts to take away boredom: And what is wondrous, for the natural man he prepared a unique food, namely bread, which would never bring nausea. Also a unique drink, sustaining, giving life, and bringing joy, which is wine, from its <note>original: "phœbea natura," literally "nature of Phoebus [the Sun]," referring to how the sun ripens the grapes.</note> sun-warmed nature always bestowing its quality, unless the person receiving it is poorly disposed, or more is taken than was appropriate. Likewise, for the spiritual man, he prepared food under the appearance and name of bread, for which no food of nature is held more suitable, to which it could be compared and by which it could be named. Therefore that heavenly <term>ambrosia<explanation>In Greek mythology, the food of the gods; used here to describe the Eucharist or divine grace.</explanation></term>, and the 

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
most sweet manna, now hidden, but then revealed—a food truly filled with every sweetness—he called "bread," saying: "I am the living Bread who [came down] from heaven" <note>John 6:51. The text here breaks off as the author quotes Christ.</note>.

"I have descended; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever." <note>original: "descendi, si quis manducauerit ex hoc pane, uiuet in æternum." A reference to John 6:51.</note> How beautifully and how fittingly is the bread of life prepared as sustenance and for the life of the members of Christ: so that they may live by the spirit and by the life of Christ; so that what the Apostle says may follow: <margin>Paul</margin> "We are all one body and one bread, we who participate in one bread and one chalice." <note>1 Corinthians 10:17</note> For just as one bread is composed of many grains, so from many members of the faithful is formed the one body of Christ, <margin>CHRIST</margin> all of it living by the life of Christ—indeed, by that life which is Christ. Therefore he said: "He who eats this bread will live forever." And again: "He who eats me, he himself shall live because of me." <note>John 6:57</note> And just as nothing is better, nothing easier, and nothing more suitably transformed into our own body than bread; in the same way, so that we might be transformed into Christ, this food is given to us. He who eats it does not change the food into himself, but he himself <margin>Augustine</margin> is changed into the food he has eaten <note>original: "mutatur in cibũ manducatũ." This reflects a famous passage from St. Augustine's Confessions (7.10), where Christ tells him: "You will not change me into you, like the food of your flesh; but you will be changed into me."</note> (as Augustine says), so that he may live in him. He who wishes to live, therefore, has a place where he may live and a source from which he may live: let him believe, let him approach, let him eat; let him be incorporated, being transformed and gifted with a new life, so that at last he may eat that new food and drink the new wine. Those who have tasted these shall thereafter be subject to neither physical nor spiritual death. And that is the true bread of life, and the true hidden <term>manna<explanation>Referring to the miraculous "bread from heaven" provided to the Israelites in the desert; here it signifies the secret, interior sweetness of the Eucharist.</explanation></term>, which no one knows except him who receives it: for which reason he cannot be taught about it by another, but only by experience and the taste provided by the Author of Grace.

### Regarding the Wine. Conclusion II.

<margin>CHRIST</margin> **I**ndeed, at the Last Supper he offered us a wonderful wine: yet promising better in our resounding kingdom and at the heavenly nuptials, when he says: "From now on I will no longer drink of this fruit of the vine until 그날 [that day] when I drink it new in the kingdom <margin>THE SAME</margin> of my Father." <note>Matthew 26:29</note> Since, therefore, we are speaking of that kingdom and of those nuptials, we must also explain what that wine is which is promised to be given there. Wine is indeed pressed from the grape and born of the vine: nor can it come from any other vine except from that one of which he said: "I am the true vine." <note>John 15:1</note> And it is prepared in those heavenly nuptials which were prefigured by those wedding feasts <note>The Wedding at Cana (John 2:1-11).</note> in which the heavenly Bridegroom, first showing himself to be above man and above the order of nature, turned water into wine immediately and by command alone—something which nature does only over an interval of time and through the required means. Therefore, lest those nuptials (which he had determined to consecrate as a <term>sacrament<explanation>An outward sign of an inward grace; here, the earthly wedding is a sign of the spiritual union between Christ and the Church.</explanation></term> of the true nuptials) should be passed gloomily and tastelessly without wine, the most pious Mother, <margin>The Blessed Virgin</margin> voluntarily taking pity on human weakness and poverty, said to her Son, the true vine: "They have no wine." But since Jesus was present not at his own true nuptials, but at another's as a guest, <margin>CHRIST</margin> he therefore said: "What is that to me and to you, woman? Since these are not our nuptials. My hour has not yet come," namely the hour in which the true nuptials would be prepared for me, the true bridegroom. However, the Mother, caring also for these figurative [nuptials] and solicitous for them with maternal authority, and being aware of the will of her Son, said to the servants: "Whatever he tells you, do it." And the Evangelist says, not being himself unaware of the secret...

<margin>Jerome</margin>

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>

And to this corresponds the most bitter wine of divine judgment,

<margin>David</margin>

And *he distilled it*, or made it overflow (for which our translation has *he poured it out*). Malice overflows and continues to overflow upon the head of the one who commits evil, as divine justice decrees. Nevertheless, *all the sinners of the earth shall drink the dregs thereof.* For the good taste the wine of divine justice, but the sinners and the impious drink the dregs. But let us return to those who drink the good wine here, so that they may be refreshed by the better and heavenly wine. Therefore, the wine we ought to drink here is twofold: namely, of **charity** and of **wisdom**. Not, certainly, of that superior wisdom which in Holy Scripture is called "milk," as we have explained elsewhere—which is given to the few—but wine, which is given to many. ## THE EIGHTH TONE.

...so that we may be transformed into the flesh and body of Christ, and be made "two in one flesh," so that the true Adam may say of us: *This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.* <note>original: "Os nunc de ossibus meis, & caro de carne mea." A reference to Genesis 2:23, here applied to the mystical union between Christ (the "New Adam") and the Church or the individual soul.</note> We eat this bread, therefore, so that we might be transformed into the body and flesh of Christ, since we receive his doctrine—which is the bread of life and understanding, and the water of saving wisdom—and also when we duly eat the very body of Christ. But this growth <term>vegetatio: literally "vegetation" or "vital growth," referring to how the soul is nourished and flourishes like a plant</term> and transformation does not happen through anything else unless that fire of the Holy Spirit and of love is present, by which the food is "cooked" before we receive it. This ensures we do not receive it out of habit, or hypocrisy, or any other crooked motive, but with sincere love and affection. By this same fire, we "cook" and digest the food we have received.

<margin>Academics, Epicureans, Dionysius</margin>
For then a true transformation will be effected in us through the fire of love, which (as the Academics, the Epicureans, but most especially our Dionysius teach) transforms the lover into the beloved. <note>The author refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian, who argued that divine love (eros) draws the soul out of itself and unites it with God.</note>

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
Therefore, the flesh specifically prepared for the heavenly wedding is the flesh of our spouse, the immaculate Lamb sacrificed for the life of the world. And besides this flesh, in the Gospel, where those heavenly weddings are discussed, mention is made of certain other "meats" by the spouse, who says: *My bulls and fattened cattle are killed* <note>original: "Tauri mei, & altilia occisa." From Matthew 22:4.</note>; that is, the greatness of teachings

<margin>Jerome</margin>
is represented by the bulls (as Jerome feels), and the depth of God's doctrine by the fattened cattle. But

<margin>The Hebrews</margin>
the wise Hebrews say that God prepares for the righteous at the feast a bull, a bird, and a fish—the first of which Christ mentions. For the "bull" is our animal nature, which was purged by the royal bull; the "bird" is that highest portion of the soul which, in flying, always seeks the heights (interpreted elsewhere as an Eagle by Jerome). The "fish," however, which is nourished in the waters, is the middle spirit, or our rational part, which is nourished and takes delight in the waters of wisdom and doctrine. And all these things are prepared in

<margin>Revelation</margin>
that feast to be eaten by the spouse and the guests, just as he himself says in the Book of Revelation: *I will dine with him, and he with me.* <note>original: "Cœnabo secū, & ipsi mecū." From Revelation 3:20.</note> He truly delights to dine with us, not because he needs our good things, but so that by eating he may change us into himself, so that we may be made one and the same with him, having been "eaten" by him, digested, and grown into his own body.

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
Ezekiel touches upon the fish, saying: *Their fish shall be of many kinds, like the fish of the great sea* <note>original: "Plurimæ species erūt pisces eius, sicut pisces maris magni." From Ezekiel 47:10.</note>; for they shall be manifold—I will not say only in species, but in the various types of these fish, that is, of spirits and rational souls. These spirits are taken to that feast to be united together with the spouse. Christ did not name these fish in that prepared feast [of the Gospel parable], but after the resurrection, having taken on the nature and condition of a spirit, he wished to eat of them, also distributing them to the disciples, as John relates, saying:

<margin>John</margin>
*Jesus took the bread, and gave it to them, and the fish likewise.* <note>John 21:13.</note> But Luke also says:

<margin>Luke</margin>
*And when he had eaten a piece of broiled fish, and a honeycomb, taking the remains he gave them to them, saying: These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you.* <note>Luke 24:42-44.</note> Therefore, this "fish" which Jesus ate after the resurrection is different from those born in the sea, since (by Christ's own testimony) its "remains" are the words that he himself had spoken with them while he was in human form. For spiritual words are the remains of his very spirit, which we ought to preserve with much greater reverence than the physical relics of the saints, in which their spirits once dwelt.

->How great is the abundance and sweetness of the foods. Discourse V.<-

## ELEVENTH MODULE: THE INSTRUMENTS.
### Concerning the first instrument, which is the celestial sphere. First Harmony.

We have already sufficiently explained with what harmony the celestial spheres resound. But let us add this: those concerts of the heavens, as they ascend, resound throughout that entire heavenly hall where the performers are—namely, their <term>Intelligences: in medieval cosmology, these were the angelic beings responsible for moving and guiding the planets and stars</term> who govern them, and who stand (as we have said) always before the throne of God.
<margin>Plato</margin>
And these, like the Sirens (as Plato says), sitting upon those orbs, make their melody resound everywhere. But he makes them especially sonorous, of whom Orpheus said:
<margin>Orpheus</margin>
> You temper the heaven like a tuneful lyre. <note>original: "Tu coelum quasi canorā citharā tēperas." A reference to the Orphic Hymns, viewing God as a divine musician tuning the universe.</note>

And that place is so tempered by harmonic proportions that it renders the voices of those singing there far more sonorous than theaters or stages built with musical proportions so that spectators might more easily perceive the voices of the actors or performers. Whether they recited comedies on the proscenium <term>proscenium: the area of a theater stage in front of the curtain</term> or upon those platforms, or whatever else they related: so that just as they were seen by everyone—both those in the orchestra and those sitting in the periphery of the semi-circle—so their voices were heard in perfect consonance, with resonant vessels <note>This refers to the "acoustic jars" or echeia described by the Roman architect Vitruvius, which were placed in theaters to amplify and clarify the voices of actors.</note> fitted here and there with wondrous skill to facilitate the harmonic voices. For art cannot surpass nature; rather, it imitates it, though by a long distance. Therefore, the concert of the heavens is better than the structures and instruments produced by human skill. But it must be held beyond all ambiguity that among all the works of the supreme Craftsman, the most beautiful and sweet is that in which His throne resides.

As <margin>Augustine</margin> says, David, being learned in songs of this kind, loved musical harmony not with a common pleasure, but with faithful love and reverence. ### Concerning the second instrument, which is the human tongue. Section II.

<margin>Avicenna</margin> **O**nce the place for singing has been assigned and ordered, the tongue is necessary to emit the voice, and to make it sonorous through its intermediary instruments, which are the throat, the palate, the teeth, the lips, the gullet, the lungs, and the windpipe—which they call the *trachea*: and above all the chest muscles, which receive the beginning of this motion from the soul, as is held by <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina, a 10th-century Persian physician and philosopher whose works on anatomy were standard in European universities</note> and by others who write on the arrangement of the body. This tongue, even though corporeal, will exert itself in the praise of the Prince, as the Holy Spirit testifies in <margin>David</margin> David, who says: *The high praises of God are in their throats.* For no articulated and sonorous voice resonates in the throat except by the movement of the tongue: for this tongue has been restored to all the bodies that have risen or will rise, or will be restored along with all their windpipes and instruments in a much better harmony than anyone has had or could have in this <term>pilgrimage</term> <note>A common term for earthly life, viewed as a temporary journey toward the true home in heaven</note>. For just as all members that were deformed, distorted, or missing will be repaired and perfected, so that everyone meets the highest Prince (as the <margin>Paul</margin> Apostle says) *as a perfect man.* In the same way, the voice that was previously dissonant and jarring, or the tongue that was stammering, will be restored as polished and most harmonious, so that nothing foul, nothing unseemly, and nothing discordant will be seen there.

<margin>Physicists</margin> But because two mediums for forming voice and sound seem to be granted by nature (as those who treat natural things say, namely air and water, for sound is made in these elements, though more aptly in air), it must be seen what water or what air exists in that super-celestial region in which the voice can be established. This is difficult to define by those who admit elements only in the lower regions—those which are below the sphere of the moon. But those who acknowledge elements even in the higher regions (as was touched upon above) will determine this matter more easily. For there are waters, about which the <margin>David</margin> most wise philosopher David said: *And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.* <margin>Moses</margin> Moses had previously taught this same thing: namely, that there are waters divided above the globe of the heavens from those that are below it. And we have already said that some of the heavens are watery and <margin>Astronomy</margin> others airy. For if the ninth heaven (which astronomers call the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Mover," the outermost moving sphere in the medieval model of the universe</note> and some call the Crystalline) is watery, following the order of the elements we shall say the higher heaven...

### <margin>Conclusion 3.</margin> Concerning the Third Instrument, which is our body.

<margin>Augustine</margin> **W**e have previously revealed that the human body is ordered with the most perfect harmony <term>harmonia</term> <note>the fitting together of parts in a balanced whole</note>, so much so that in no other body is it better or sweeter. This harmony, Augustine says, exists not only in those parts which are visible on the outside, adapted to their numbers and measures, but also in those parts to which the human eye does not reach, conducted with such great numerosity and consonance that no one has been able to find it, however diligent the investigation of the anatomists <term>anatomicorum</term> <note>the early scientists who studied bodily structure via dissection</note> has been. 
<margin>Boethius</margin> Regarding this, Boethius also says: "That liveliness of reason in the body is mixed by a certain fitting together, just as a harmony <term>concentus</term> of low and high voices tends toward a single consonance." This arrangement a man feels better than he understands, according to 
<margin>Zoroaster</margin> that saying of Zoroaster: "A man exults because of the harmony he feels within himself." And what is more to be admired is that the human body does not only have consonance among its members and humors <note>the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—once thought to control health</note> with one another, and between the soul and the governing spirit, but also between divine and supra-mundane <note>realms above the physical world</note> things. Hence, by a very great mystery <term>sacramento</term>, there are given as many affirmative precepts in the Mosaic Law as there are bones in the human body—namely, two hundred and forty-eight—and as many negative precepts as there are nerves in the same body: which are, not without cause, three hundred and sixty-five, by which number the days and nights of the year are comprised. These joined together grow to six hundred and thirteen. These joined together make 612. And that "one" which results from them brings the number to 613. This indeed, according to the doctrine of those who theologize through numbers, denotes with a great mystery that the fullness of judgment 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> contained under the name *Elohim* was given to Jesus, who said: "For the Father judges no one"—namely, after this transfer of judgment was made—"but has given all judgment to the Son." ### Concerning the Fourth Instrument, namely the Angelic tongue. Conclusion 4.

<margin>Paul</margin>
**A**mong those harmonies are also the Angelic spirits, about whom we might indeed doubt whether they speak with a tongue and praise the Maker together, unless Paul—instructed in that heavenly school and in whose heart Christ resounds—said: "If I speak in the tongues of men and of Angels." <note>1 Corinthians 13:1</note> Therefore, Angels have their own tongue, by which they speak both with each other and with us; not indeed by a vocal sound, but by producing a new concept in those to whom they speak, which is better than if an audible voice were expressed. However, that instrument through which a person makes known to another the things that are bubbling in the mind, whatever kind of instrument it may be, is called a "tongue":
<margin>Plato</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Which (as Plato says and Aristotle agrees) was given so that under its guidance we might express those things which we have conceived in our mind. I also think it should by no means be passed over that by our fleshy tongue we administer a double food: bodily food for ourselves, and spiritual food for others.
<margin>M. Varro</margin>
Regarding the first administration, Marcus Varro says that the tongue (*lingua*) is so called as if it were a "binder of food" <note>original: "ligans cibum". Varro was a Roman scholar known for his etymologies, or histories of words.</note>; for it rolls the food around and offers it to the teeth to be ground; afterwards, gathering it into a ball, it sends it down into the belly. Regarding the second, it is clear that through the tongue we provide others with the food of the word of God. And what a human does with a sensible voice, an Angel accomplishes by impressing a concept. Hence, just as John <note>John the Baptist</note> was called a "voice," so the Apostles and preachers, in that they manifest the hidden word of God, are called "tongues"; indeed, even the Holy Spirit, who moves the tongue and provides the abundance of speaking, wished to appear in tongues of fire. <note>Acts 2:3, describing the event of Pentecost.</note> How the Angels may be "tongues" and speak, although it is hidden just as the Angels themselves are, we can still perceive in some way by noticing how each person speaks. For if someone is far away, he requires a louder shout; but if he is made very near, he speaks in a whisper into the listener's ear. And if he could be joined with the listener's mind and spirit, he would need no sound at all, but his speech, conceived in the mind, would glide into the listener with no sound at all. This indeed happens to souls departed from the body, to Angels, and to demons; for it is certain that all these speak (for the most part) without noise and wage many-sided hidden wars against us. For just as the air, when light is present, receiving colors and forms, carries them into those things which can naturally receive such things; which colors mirrors, by receiving them, represent as images to those looking in. So the demonic bodies (as some assert) transmit those forms, figures, and concepts which they receive from the Imagination or the thinking power into our very soul, instilling many enticements in us...

### Concerning Angelic and blessed minds, which are themselves resounding instruments. Conclusion 5.

**P**ost-conversion <note>The Latin 'Postq̄' (Postquam) begins the sentence: 'After, therefore...'</note> therefore, since the speech of that heavenly country is conducted by the mind rather than by sound, those minds themselves will be certain reverberating instruments of a sweeter harmony than those produced by vocal sound. We can infer this consonance from those things which we prove by continuous experience: for when people perceive a harmony of concepts between those speaking, a certain delight filled with sweetness rises up from that consonance. Likewise, horror, weariness, displeasure, and pain are felt from the dissonance of voices—and especially of souls—so much so that the very odor of hell is sensed from such things. Therefore, in that supramundane <term>supramundane|Beyond or above the physical world.</term> chamber, where there is the highest concord of all minds—divine, human, and angelic—toward one another and all with the Prince <note>Referring to God as the 'Prince' or Ruler of the Heavenly City.</note> Himself, a supreme joy will be conceived. <margin>Augustine</margin> Augustine considers and asserts this to be the cause of beatitude <note>blessedness or perfect happiness.</note>, which consists in a consonant adherence to God, just as the cause of misery is dissonance from Him. And this is the true consonance, namely of the mind, compared to which every vocal harmony—whether made through natural instruments or those that are external and crafted by art—is abandoned, as if in favor of the principal instrument of all praises. Therefore, the minds of all the blessed sing the praises of the Creator first and foremost with their own high-sounding voice: for we can contemplate more and higher things in the mind than we can express with the mouth. Nor is any melody more pleasing to the Prince than the concord of the mind, in which He Himself is most greatly delighted...

->On the state that provides sound to all these instruments, which is the Holy Spirit and the divine Word. Conclusion 6.<-

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
**O**f the previously described instruments, none would resonate unless the Divine Word and the power of the Holy Spirit were present. For if He provides the power of speaking before earthly Princes, should He not much more provide it to those who sing praises before the Supreme Prince? For we have it from Christ, who is the faithful witness, in the Gospel according to Matthew: *When you stand before Kings and Governors, do not think about how or what you should speak, for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in you.* Nor can we have a harmony of mind with God, from which truth may spring and grow together, unless He who said, *I am the truth* <note>original: "Ego sum ueritas"</note> provides us with this concord and truth. Hence, of the one who first rebelled and disagreed with that harmony, it was said: *He was a murderer* <note>original: "homicida"</note>—or a killer of himself—*because from the beginning he did not stand in the truth.* Therefore, once this harmony is held—which arises from true concord with God through the fountain of truth—a most sweet and delightful love rises up. Hence that wise man
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
said: *O Lord, how good and sweet is your spirit in all things.* And again: *For the holy spirit of understanding is sweet.* Therefore Paul, when he teaches that we should show ourselves
<margin>Paul</margin>
pleasing to God, says: *In sweetness and in the Holy Spirit.* For he connects sweetness with the Holy Spirit, as if the latter cannot be had without the former. For where the Holy Spirit is, there is sweetness; and where there is sweetness and true joy, there is the Holy Spirit; and where the Holy Spirit is, there is the Word leading the way to the Spirit Himself. Both provide life, both provide breath and power; yet one overflows more into the intellect through truth, and the other more into the will through love.

Here, Augustine is of the opinion that all those instruments refer to the manner of bringing forth divine praises, saying: "The Saints are said to sing divine praises mystically upon all musical instruments. In the **trumpet**, they show the most excellent clarity of praise. In the **psaltery** and the **lyre**, God is praised through celestial and terrestrial things—He who made heaven and earth; for the psaltery resonates from above, while the lyre sounds from below. The **drum** <note>original: "tympanum"</note> is made from dried and firm skin, so that it may signify the firmness of those offering praise. The **organ**, although it is said to sound through pipes by means of breaths and bellows, is nevertheless a general name for all musical vessels, so that it may denote manifold praise. Truly the **cymbals**, which sound by being touched, represent our lips, which emit sound by a certain striking against one another." But Cassiodorus interprets those instruments differently, saying: "Let the **trumpet** sound for the King; let the **psaltery** sing to God; let the **lyre** with the others sound for the Spouse—with the 'others,' I say, which sound through the tension of strings. Let the **organ**, built like a tower with various pipes, resonate for our Leader and the Victor."

<margin>The same (Paul)</margin>

For it should be noted that this word *anessama* is not in common use; but Scripture uses it with great mystery when God infused the soul into man, and at the end of the hymns, where man is stirred up to return perfect praise to God.
