For just as the world (according to the testimony of the Pythagorean Dorilaus) is the instrument of God, so the body is the instrument of the soul; its nerves, muscles, bones, and all arteries are called sometimes the pipes and sometimes the **strings** of this bodily organ. These strings are called in Hebrew <term>מינים</term> (*minim*), which we, interpreting them properly, could call "species" or "kinds"—namely, the kinds of manifold internal arteries. All of these the divine Harpist <note>David</note> stirs up elsewhere along with the soul to the praise of the Prince, saying: *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me* (or all my internal parts), *bless His holy name.*

# TWELFTH MODULE: WEDDING SONGS.

### Who sings the Wedding Songs. ->The First Harmony.<-

**H**aving prepared all the musical instruments, it remains for the **wedding song** <note>original: "epithalamium," a song or poem written for a bride on her way to the marital chamber.</note> to be sung, which is a sacred hymn celebrated at marriages. No one can produce these songs appropriately unless they have as leaders those who have been instructed by the supreme Arch-musician and the teacher of this sacrament. Among the sacred volumes, there are certain wedding songs and harmonies which, because of their excellence, are called the **Song of Songs** <note>The biblical Book of Solomon.</note>, celebrated by Solomon but dictated by the Holy Spirit. However, they were not received into the Holy Canon, nor inserted into the number of the twenty-four books of life, unless they were first examined and approved by the prophet Isaiah, as I have been able to gather from trustworthy and most celebrated authors. For among the ancient Fathers, nothing was held as authentic unless it emanated from the workshop of the divine Prophets, who would bring all sayings and opinions to the scale of divine mysteries and carefully weigh how much truth they contained. Hence, we receive these wedding songs as divine (both because they were published by Solomon, who was at one time filled with the divine spirit, and because they were sifted and approved by Isaiah, that most eminent Prophet), and we shall imitate them in those harmonies which we perform concerning divine matters and heavenly glory. But because the harmony of those poems regarding their meter could not be preserved in our translation, I wished to sing those things contained in those hymns in our own meters. And so, we shall first harmonize the wedding song of the **bride** (that is, of the soul thinking rightly about God and clinging to Him). Secondly, the wedding song of the **groom** for a bride who is well-initiated and already joined to him. Thirdly, concerning the marriage, mutual love, and marital affections. But since the things sung here are wrapped in so many and such great riddles and metaphors that what they say can scarcely be perceived, I have wished to open the meanings of these poems, at least somewhat, with certain small notes.

# EIGHTH TONE.

## Wedding Song for the Bride.
<note>original: "Epithalamiū in Sponsam." An epithalamium is a poem or song written specifically for a bride on her way to the marital chamber. In this context, it refers to the mystical marriage between the soul and God, or Christ and the Church, using the language of the biblical Song of Solomon.</note>

<margin>a</margin> Sweet daughters of Jerusalem, who
Wander here and there through shining fountains
And pleasant meadows, you who are skilled
At weaving flowers.

<margin>b</margin> If any of you, I pray, while walking
Should see my friend, be mindful
To tell him how great are the sorrows I suffer
For love of him.

<margin>c</margin> For that friend of mine is white,
And at the same time splashed with a red color,
Such that no other could be chosen
From ten thousand.

<margin>d</margin> His head is gold, and the hair
On his crown is like the foliage of a palm;
All his locks are black,
Vying with the ancient raven.

<margin>e</margin> His bright eye matches the doves
Which are accustomed to fly by glittering rivers,
Resting on snowy wings
In the clear air.

<margin>f</margin> Such is the appearance of his cheeks,
Like garden beds where there are fragrances,
Which early summer paints and varies
With a thousand flowers.

<margin>g</margin> His lips compete with snowy lilies,
And surpass roses with a cheerful redness;
The breath of his mouth exhales
A scent like myrrh.

<margin>h</margin> His hands are of a rounded shape,
His fingers seem smoothed by a lathe:
They glitter equally with gold
And with hyacinths <note>original: "hyacinthis." In older texts, this often refers to the jacinth stone or blue sapphire rather than the flower.</note>.

<margin>i</margin> His belly is smooth and at the same time
Reflective, and the plates of polished ivory shine
After they have undergone the strikes
Of the skilled iron tool.

<margin>k</margin> His legs surpass marble cut from the
Parian ridge, like straight columns
Upon which gold sustains itself,
Leaning above.

---

**a** She asks the daughters of Jerusalem, her companions, who are now nourished in the pleasant meadows of the paradise of delights, having drunk from that fountain which divided into four heads to irrigate the whole earth <note>A reference to the Garden of Eden described in Genesis 2:10.</note>; they gather the sweetest flowers of the affections and the fruits of good works.

**b** And adjuring these women, she seeks that they might indicate something of her beloved, without whom it is most grievous for her to remain: for he withdraws himself from the traveler according to his custom. For if the bridegroom were to comfort the soul with continuous visitation, he would make her blessed while she was still proceeding on her way, which is by no means appropriate for her <note>The author suggests that spiritual "dryness" or the absence of God is necessary for the soul's growth during its earthly journey.</note>.

**c** The signs of who the bridegroom is are these: he is "white" because of his most perfect innocence, found in no other; and "red" because of the love by which he gave up his life and all things for his beloved. "Chosen from thousands" refers to the completion of the number ten <note>original: "denarii numeri." The author is using numerology where ten represents perfection or divinity.</note>, which is a number fitting for God, to denote the sublime perfection and divinity of the chosen bridegroom himself.

**d** His head is compared to gold, the most perfect among all metals. But the beauty of his hair is rightly equated to the order of a palm tree, or rather the heart of the palm <note>original: "cerebro ipsius palmae." Literally "the brain of the palm," referring to the tender, vital core or "heart" of the tree.</note>, to denote the virtue of the hair; when it is torn out, strength is lost, as we read concerning Samson. Indeed, if that "brain" is torn out, the tree undoubtedly dies. In color, he is likened to the Raven, which is (if we follow the theology of the Hebrews) among the most excellent birds, reaching a measure of lofty strength; not without cause is it said in the 146th Psalm and the Gospel: *God feeds the young of the ravens that call upon him.*

**e** And although in strong constancy he is likened to the raven which possesses much lofty strength, the eye of his intention is nevertheless like a pure dove; for as one prudent and wise, she is deservedly said to reside above the most full floods of the water of saving wisdom.

**f** The cheeks of the modesty required in a bride are like beds of aromatics planted by perfumers, because of the fragrance of chastity and virtues; they are round, however, because of their capacity for divine influences.

**g** His lips are like roses dripping the first myrrh, or that which flows spontaneously, through which are understood disciplined words <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the interpretation of the bridegroom's speech.</note>.

a ¶ The Bride is called beautiful, just like the heavenly Jerusalem, toward which she strives as one who possesses its symbol. Thus "Jerusalem" figures both the city above and the individual Bride, or the collection of all Brides, which descends from heaven like a bride adorned for her husband; nor did he have anything more fitting to compare his friend to. b She who is thus beautiful is nevertheless terrible to the enemy because of her modesty and the fortification of her virtues and spiritual gifts, like the battle lines of a camp. c He prays she turn her eyes away, in the manner of one who charms, since he takes too much pride [in her], so that the Groom may delight in the sight of such a Bride. d The hair is like flocks of goats—not those goats given to the lot of Azazel <note>original: "Azazel." Referring to the "scapegoat" of Leviticus 16:8</note>, or those who will be placed on the left hand for judgment; but those who were placed from Gilead <note>original: "Gilahad." The commentator links this to the Hebrew "Gal-Ed," meaning "Heap of Testimony"</note>; that is, those who are placed before the Lord as a heap of testimony. For a "good goat" and "numbered hairs" are the same thing, and can be considered by the same Hebrew term. e The ivory teeth are the innocent and the pure, like sheep ascending from the washing. f The cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate...

**g** Your navel is not yet torn from the mother’s womb: just like a most capacious turned bowl for receiving celestial nourishment: just as an infant is nourished through the navel by blood cooked in the mother’s veins.
**h** The belly is like wheat—from which the best of all food is made—it is not yet put forth, just as a chick has not yet emerged from the shell of the egg: for it nourishes the child conceived in the mother’s womb by the Deific <note>God-making or divine</note> seed, with the nourishment of the grace of baptismal seed, until the born infant begins to desire milk, and finally solid food: which food, since it tastes of the scent of the celestial seed to the recently conceived, is therefore said to be hedged about with roses.
</margin>

---

<margin>
**i** He compared the navel to a bowl, and the belly to wheat and roses: but let it not be thought to be something according to the flesh: he equates the breasts to the fawns of high-dwelling stags, which the Lord prepares for our benefit, so that from there He might reveal dense and hidden things: just as happened to the prophets of old from whom those breasts flowed.
**k** The queens are sixty in number, a total reached through the complete ten and the first perfect six, denoting good works. But the concubines and mistresses—<term>that is,</term> the affections for celestial things, which expel animal affections—are gathered from the eight of justice and the complete ten into eighty. But of the young maidens—<term>that is,</term> of the hidden and newly budding affections—there is no number: for <term>halamot</term> <note>original: עלמות</note> signifies both young girls and hidden things.
**l** The body having been described through appropriate metaphors, the soul also, proceeding by its due steps, is first pictured as the dawn of natural light: afterwards as the moon of the Law, which was full in the days of David and Solomon: finally as the sun of the Gospel doctrine and faith, which never fails at the request of Christ. By which perfection, the gifted soul is made mistress of all things, both terrible and terrifying to the enemies of the human race, just as the standards of prevailing camps terrify enemy battle lines.
**m** She who is thus well-established is also said to descend into the garden of nuts, so that a certain kind of fall may be described, from which no bride is entirely free: because all have turned aside.
</margin>

<margin>...and any man, however just, falls because of him who committed no sin, but bore the sins of others <note>A reference to Christ taking on human sin</note>. Therefore he is said to descend—not indeed falling himself, but liberating those who fall from the bitterness and hardness of the shells of the "nut of sin." This nut also contains a good kernel, provided that by the grace and merit of Christ, the bitter and hard shell is immediately destroyed and broken, because where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.</margin>

<margin>n</margin> Finding the Bride in a fallen state, he calls her back from it, saying: "Return, return, Shulammite"—that is, the "pacified one," made perfect by my merits and established as a victor over enemies. Thus she is to be applauded, following what comes next: "What do you see in the Shulammite, but the dances of the camps?"—no longer of those still at war, but of those dancing for joy.

<margin>o</margin> Thus, having been raised up and fitted with proper conduct and affections, all who look upon her and recognize her fortunate state are led to such admiration that they say: "How beautiful are the steps of your affections and works in sandals"—by which the feet are clearly protected so they are not struck by a "bad stone" <note>An obstacle or temptation</note>, O daughter of the Prince: for she is called both Bride and Daughter.

<margin>a</margin> The <term>affection</term> <note>Latin: *affectus*—the inner disposition or emotional movement of the soul toward God</note> of the true celestial marriage is expressed in every possible way through mystical words. First, reciprocal love is declared when each is shown to be solicitous for the other, while they receive each other in mutual love and "between the breasts"—not indeed feminine ones, but those better ones from which milk is offered; he who drinks this milk knows how to reject evil and choose good.

<margin>b</margin> Nourished by this milk, both burn with a common love: for the "Breasts" in the Archetype <note>The divine original or heavenly pattern</note> are flowing springs of prophetic waters. They are also the books of the Law <note>The first five books of the Bible, the Torah</note> providing us with the true milk of wisdom.

<margin>c</margin> One reaches these breasts to suckle through a kiss, in which the soul, dying to the world, lives for God alone, content with that milk which is far better than all the wine of the wisdom of lower, worldly things. Truly, at times we even flee to the wine from those same breasts, of which it is also said: "your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine."

<margin>d</margin> Therefore, once the kiss is given and the milk is drunk, he leads her to the mother’s chamber—not indeed of this lower and mortal mother, but rather of that better one who is called the "mother of children, rejoicing and glad," namely in the most fertile offspring from which we must be reborn if we wish to enter the kingdom of heaven. Of her, the Apostle says: "That Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother." Into her chamber are led those who have received the true kiss and sucked that good milk.

<margin>e</margin> There also, the soul having been introduced drinks pure wine and the nectar of love seasoned with the juice of pomegranates—that is, of true charity—so that she may be preserved from the intoxication of a wanton and crooked love.

<margin>f</margin> Thus, the spouses, glowing with that love, come to mutual and holy embraces through the "arms" of virtues and good deeds, which are customary to be shared among true friends.

<margin>g</margin> In this embrace, the "left hand" and everything pertaining to it are placed beneath the head and reason, just as it had once been commanded: "Your appetite shall be beneath you," which follows the blood and its nature; which also in the Archetype...

# THE EIGHTH TONE

...takes its influence. But the right hand of love—and of all favorable and soothing influences—rejoices in the embrace. These two feelings, namely Fear and Love, usually flourish in lovers: Love so that the soul may grow warm and make progress, and Fear so that it may be careful not to offend, lest the beloved be moved to anger. However, Fear must always be subject to Love.

<margin>h</margin> Embraced, connected, and joined by this love, and having now reached their goal, both must lie down and rest upon those beautiful and fragrant coverings, the marriage beds of the true heavenly union. To this, the Bride condescends to sing: *In peace I will sleep and rest in the selfsame.* <note>Original: "In pace in idipsum dormiam & requiescam," a reference to Psalm 4:8, often used in liturgy to signify spiritual rest.</note>

<margin>i</margin> So that they may rest securely, those chambers and beds are surrounded by sixty brave men—not just any men, but from the strongest of Israel, meaning those who serve God in the warfare of the heavenly host. They are chosen in the number of sixty, derived from the number six <note>The number six was considered a "perfect number" in medieval numerology because its factors (1, 2, 3) add up to itself.</note> and the complete number ten, to signify the total perfection of these guardians. They all hold swords, like those of whom it is said: *My sword is drunk in heaven.* <note>Isaiah 34:5.</note> They are trained for war and for that service in which Michael the Archangel fought against the dragon. Each of these soldiers, according to custom, keeps a sword upon his thigh <term>מפחד בלילות</term> <note>Hebrew: mi-pahad ba-leilot</note> <gloss>against the fear of the night</gloss>, which is to say, they defend against the powers of darkness. These powers usually try to terrify us during the "night" of both time and sin. From these terrors, the guardians protect those resting in those tabernacles of trust and security, so that they are troubled by no fear.

<margin>k</margin> In this security, the soul rests so peacefully in the one from whom she received a kiss, that in that deep sleep she is transformed into the very thing in which she rests, and becomes one and the same spirit with him.

<margin>l</margin> Therefore, when the soul is elevated in that sleep and ascends into God, all her companions are adjured not to wake her, nor to make her stir from her rest, until the Spirit who seized her allows that sleep to end. This is especially true since the Spirit "breathes where it wills"; it is not in the power of the receiver, but of the one breathing and coming. Therefore, the soul must be cherished until the Spirit departs. And because the Bride becomes more beautiful during these embraces and this sleep than natural progress or human judgment can produce, those looking at her say in wonder: *Who is she that ascends from the desert*—meaning from this lower world—*like a pillar of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and all the powders of the perfumer?* <note>Song of Songs 3:6.</note> These scents are usually found in the garden of delight, which the Bride had now entered. 

I chose to use these Songs to cast a shadow over the divine mysteries contained in the Song of Songs, rather than trying to perform even the smallest part of their actual meaning. For they deal with the divine marriage, and in describing such things, all the sharpness of human wit grows dull. Thus, looking upon the immense ocean of divine things on one hand, and weighing the weakness of our own strength on the other, I judged this task to be quite beyond me. I felt I must not rashly depart from that sentiment of Saint Paul, in which all the wise of our religion especially agree: that the good things God has prepared for those who love Him are so great that no eye has ever seen them, nor ear heard them, nor have they entered into the heart of man. Much less could anyone, with however learned a pen, encompass those things which pertain to the happiness and dignity of this marriage. 

Nevertheless, so that the mystery might not remain entirely untouched, I wished to extract these odes from the Song of Songs itself, where King Solomon, "The Peaceful One," inspired by divine power, seems to have actually entered into this marriage rather than merely sensing it beforehand. I have aimed for brevity, lest I reveal the King's secrets too widely. For although it is difficult, as I said, to treat such a matter, I might have been able to say something—with God’s guidance—especially if I were speaking only among the "perfect" who eat solid food. I remember what Origen <note>A 3rd-century theologian who wrote famous allegorical commentaries on the Song of Songs.</note> thought of this; so much so that the words of Virgil might be applied here quite fittingly:

Through various accidents, through so many hazards of things
->We tend toward Latium, where the fates show quiet seats.<-
<note>A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.204-205). The author compares the spiritual journey to Aeneas's quest for a peaceful home.</note>

For those who wish to approach the Song of Songs must first travel through every other song contained in the Scriptures. First, they must depart from Egypt; having departed, they must cross the Red Sea so that they can sing the first Song. Then they must walk spiritually through the vast and uncultivated wilderness, until they arrive at the...

# OF THE THIRD SONG

...the well which the kings dug, so that they might offer another Song to the Lord in that same place. When they have proposed to take up that most famous Song of Moses, *Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth*, <note>original: "Attende cœlum & loquar / Audiat terra uerba oris mei," from Deuteronomy 32:1. In the medieval tradition, this song was seen as a foundational prayer of witness.</note> they should gather at that shore bordering the holy land, so that they may sing a song of this kind on the banks of the Jordan. After the other songs found in the sacred volumes have been sung harmoniously and sweetly, let them then ascend to higher things, so that they may sing this most hidden Song with the bridegroom. 

Undoubtedly, it must be established in the mind that they will encounter the most exquisite monsters, and they must strike them down with Herculean greatness of soul <note>The author uses "Herculean magnanimity" to describe the immense spiritual strength needed to overcome worldly temptations, likening the soul's struggle to the Labors of Hercules.</note> if they wish to earn the most August and sublime marriage. This will be easily achieved if they strive with the greatest zeal to avoid the snares of pleasure and, having defeated the portents of their disturbances, devote themselves to total peace of mind. Thus, they may be more ardently inflamed by "spiritual desire" (as Origen asserts); <note>Origen was an early Christian scholar who famously interpreted the Song of Songs as an allegory for the love between God and the soul.</note> indeed, this Love or desire coming from God winds its way into those hearts which—having expelled the love of the flesh and despised riches, flesh, blood, and all such things, and even heaven itself (for all these shall pass away)—have surrendered their mind and soul to this holy and divine love. Since no one can be possessed by two loves, let us yield to this love, under whose auspices that divine marriage is celebrated, about which no further speech is permitted at this present time.

# THE THIRTEENTH MEASURE
## THE TRIUMPH.

->What constitutes a just fight. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; First Harmony<-

<margin>David</margin>
<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
A noble and glorious Triumph first requires an equal fight and a beautiful victory. A fight is equal and "just" when there is a legitimate reason for fighting, and even when the war has been previously declared. Likewise, it requires the authority of a Prince, whose role it is to decree war and ensure it is fought by right, and not for the sake of evil vengeance. It is manifest that our Emperor, Christ, had a just cause in the war he took up against the enemy of the human race. This is because that most cruel plunderer, that ancient serpent who is the devil, was holding the human race itself under a most harsh and horrible yoke of slavery—a race he had subjected through many kinds of deceit and fraud. Therefore, Christ, fighting against him with truth, piety, and even zeal for divine honor and the salvation of souls, was most just in his war. 

And lest the enemy (though he be wicked) should have any just complaint, war was declared upon him through the ancient Fathers and prophets, to whom this task was entrusted as if they were <term>fecials</term>. <note>In ancient Rome, "fecials" (fetiales) were priests who acted as ambassadors, ensuring that wars were declared according to religious and legal ritual to make them "just."</note> Among these, the Royal prophet of God, acting as a most solemn Herald, proclaimed: *He shall deliver the poor from the mighty, and the poor who had no helper.* <note>Psalm 72:12.</note> Indeed, the Prince himself publicly protested, saying: *Now shall the prince of this world be cast out, because I am about to join battle with him.* <note>John 12:31.</note> And what is more, the enemy himself attacked him while he was fasting in the desert. Truly, he held the authority for warring from the Father, who destined him for this battle, commanding that he should defeat the enemy by his wounds, just as...

<margin>Isaiah</margin> God had spoken through Isaiah:
> Because of the sins of my people, I have struck him

(that is, I delivered him up to be struck and wounded). For in this new kind of battle, victory was to be won through wounds. In this war, no fraud or deceit intervened, nor any wicked spirit of vengeance; rather, it was the piety of liberating those unjustly oppressed. Therefore, he fought with truth against the lying enemy; he fought with zeal against the envious; with goodness against the malevolent and wicked; and with gentleness against the proud. All the soldiers of Christ, who received his wages <note>The "wages" or "stipend" refers to the spiritual grace and commitment made during the sacrament of Baptism.</note> in baptism, must diligently gird themselves for this same battle, just as Michael, the guardian of souls, had done against that same enemy, as John relates, saying:
<margin>John</margin>
> Michael and his angels fought with the dragon.

He had undertaken this battle for Christ the Prince, and by the same laws by which Christ himself fought. For the Evangelist says that when the woman (namely the <term>Deifera</term> Virgin <note>original: "uirgo Deifera," meaning "God-bearing Virgin" or the Mother of God.</note>)—clothed with the sun, that is, with divine light, having the moon (the synagogue, as it were) under her feet, and crowned with twelve stars (that is, that divine, heavenly, and Apostolic group of twelve of which we spoke above)—was seen and shown in heaven to be bringing forth her first and only-begotten son, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron, and who would give blessedness to all. That ancient serpent and dragon, who is the devil, puffed up with excessive audacity, refused to receive blessedness from the Christ who was to be born of the Virgin. Instead, swelling with pride, he said:
<margin>Same</margin>
> I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God <note>original: "In coelũ conscendam super astra Dei," quoting Isaiah 14:13, which was traditionally attributed to the fall of Lucifer.</note> (that is, above the saints) I will exalt my throne: I will set my seat in the north, as if standing in opposition to him who comes from the south.

And rightly he turns toward the north, from whence all evil is spread, and from whence comes every ruin and fall. Against him, Michael and his angels rose up for Christ, taking up that decree sung by the divine choir-leader <note>The "divine choir-leader" refers to King David as the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>:
<margin>David</margin>
> And let all his angels adore him.

They all took up war against the dragon for Christ and for the laws of Christ. For the serpent fought with defiance, while these fought with obedience; he with hate, they with love; he with envy, they with zeal; he with pride, they with piety. He presumed upon his own strength, while they were supported by divine virtue. By this justice and by this favor, Michael and his army prevailed against the dragon and his followers, even to their total extermination and irrevocable expulsion from that kingdom in which Christ, the King of Peace, reigns in peace. Therefore, the defeated and cast-out dragon directed a triple battle-line against us, which are the portents of the world, of which the dragon has been made prince and tyrant.
<margin>John</margin> John mentions these lines in his epistle, and they are now known to all: namely, the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. <note>These three categories—lust, greed, and pride—were considered the "triple temptation" of the world in medieval theology.</note>
<margin>Same</margin> And this is what the same John pursues in the Apocalypse:
> And the dragon was angry and went to make war with the rest, who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ.

And a little later:
> And it was given to him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them,

unless Christ had prepared the victory for us, by whose favor he is many times defeated by us.

### **Concerning the Great Victory won by Christ for himself and for his soldiers.**

->Harmony II<-

<margin>CHRIST</margin>
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
In this war, our Emperor Christ was so victorious that the enemy could not inflict even the smallest loss or wound upon him; hence he joyfully declares: *For the Prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing.* <note>original: "Venit enim Princeps mūdi huius, & in me non habet quicquam." Quoting John 14:30.</note> The entire praise for this victory must be ascribed to him alone, who fought with the enemy by himself, just as it had been spoken in the prophecy of Isaiah: *I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me.* <note>original: "Torcular calcaui solus, & de gentibus nō est uir mecum." Isaiah 63:3. The "winepress" is a common medieval image for the Passion, where Christ is crushed like grapes to produce the wine of salvation.</note> And for this reason, when Peter wanted to rush at the enemies with a drawn sword, Christ said: *Put your sword into its sheath; do you not think that I could ask my Father, and he would provide me with more than twelve legions of Angels? But I do not wish it, because I must enter this fight alone.* Hence, not without the wonder of those listening and those considering it attentively, he cried out to the Father in the midst of the conflict: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>Matthew 27:46.</note>—namely, leaving him alone in the <term>duel</term> <note>The text frames the Crucifixion as a "duellum" or judicial combat between Christ and the Devil.</note> with the most bitter enemy.

<margin>Paul</margin>

This refers to a legal document or "I.O.U." that represented humanity's debt of sin to the Law or the Devil.</note> of the decree that was against us; and he took it out of the midst, fastening it to the cross. Stripping the principalities and powers, he led them away confidently, triumphing over them openly in himself.* Did Paul not here expose and explain the mystery and the order of the entire war, and the victory of Christ over the adversary of the human race? For he shows why Christ fought: so that he might rescue us from death (that is, from the angel of death) and from sin, by remitting the debts for which we were liable and enslaved, destroying the bond which we had made for the devil through our evil-working hands. And he shows that Christ paid the debt through the cross, enriching us with the spoils of the principalities and powers of darkness. Finally, he concludes that Christ gained this victory and triumph through himself alone, for which reason he was most deservedly glorified. But as far as it concerns us, he fought alone so that we alone should be the ones redeemed, as Ambrose discusses in a long series

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
in his book *On the Patriarchs*. And he did not procure this victory only for himself, but for all of us, showing his magnificence in this: which the Apostle relates in plain speech, saying: *But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord,* provided that we are willing to serve faithfully as soldiers against that same Prince of the world and of darkness, and against his evil persuasions and battle lines. Many have done this, considering all earthly things as if they were dung <note>A reference to Philippians 3:8.</note> so that they might rush into the battle line, surrendered in obedience to the laws and strengths, lest the pride or arrogance of <term>Asmodeus</term> <note>A demon mentioned in the Book of Tobit, here representing the spiritual forces of pride or lust.</note> find a place where he might inflict some wound. Indeed, he submitted the whole world to his own authority, as Paul said to the Ephesians: *The Father placed him at his right hand in the heavenly places above all principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the future: and he subjected all things under his feet.* <note>original: "Pater cōstituit eū ad dexterā suā in cœlestibus supra oēm principatū... & omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius." quoting Ephesians 1:20-22.</note> Into which glory he entered by fighting, especially in his passion, as he himself testified in the gospel titled according to Luke, saying: *It behooved Christ to suffer, and so enter into his glory.* <note>original: "Oportuit Christum pati, & ita intrare in gloriā suā." quoting Luke 24:26.</note> Thus he began to triumph on the day when, redeeming captives, he rose glorious; but he perfected the triumph when he ascended to his kingdom with solemn preparation, as the church sings: *The triumph of grace is given, climbing the tribunal of the right hand.* <note>original: "Datur triūphus gratię, scandēs tribunal dexteræ."</note> For he ascended in the chariot of his glorified body, drawn by four white horses—that is, by the four <term>endowments</term> <note>In medieval theology, the "endowments" (dotes) are the four qualities of a resurrected, glorified body: agility, subtlety, impassibility, and clarity.</note> of the glorified body. That which was corruptible was made incorruptible, so that he might persevere in eternal glory. But what was dark was turned into light, just as on the day of his transfiguration his face shone like the sun: for he must be filled with light if he wishes to stand before the Father of lights, with whom there is no overshadowing. And finally, he rose from a physical state and ascended as a spiritual being, opening the way and providing the manner by which all might rise with these same endowments and arrive at the blessed kingdom. ### On the various triumphs of the leaders after Christ’s departure. Cohort IV.

Although the victory over the whole world was won by Christ in his own blood, to whom praise and glory is owed by all; nevertheless, by his command and favor, others have triumphed (especially the twelve Apostolic princes) over the twelve parts of the world, through the power of the Holy Spirit with which he had filled them. Therefore, they are called the governors of the twelve tribes, in which (as we have said) the whole human race is included. Nor was Paul excluded, who labored more than all of them: for he himself also (as is evident) triumphed with them over many cities and provinces, which he brought under the dominion of Christ: namely over Antioch, Seleucia, Rhodes, Perga, Pamphylia, and Cilicia; likewise over Phrygia, Philippi, Macedonia, and the Corinthians, the Thessalonians, the Athenians, and the Ephesians, and over many islands of Greece. Over Italy also and Spain—to which regions (as we have said) he carried the name of the Lord Jesus—a triumph must be especially decorated for Paul himself. But for Peter, over Rome, which [is the head] of this world...

It is also called a **prize**, promised, as is evident, to those running for the reward. Therefore, this reward (by whatever name it is called) is a good that never fails, nor is it diminished by being shared. Nor, because it is shared more with one than another, does it leave room for envy in the one who has less, since all rejoice together in the glory and the good of their fellow heirs. For those who were found to be envious <note>Referring to the fallen angels or the unrepentant who begrudge the salvation of others.</note> were irrevocably expelled from that fellowship and the sharing of that reward.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of divine rewards, shifting from the general concept of God as a "prize" to the specific nature of Divine Beauty. The author uses linguistic analysis of Hebrew terms and the lives of the Patriarchs to explain how God's glory is manifested.</meta>

-># OF THE THIRD CANTICLE<-

...beautiful to the sight, delightful to the senses, sweet to the taste, and perfectly proportioned to all powers, with the addition of a pact of perpetual possession. For God is that Beauty, from which all beautiful things are made, as the **Platonists** <margin>Plato</margin> <margin>Dionysius</margin> <margin>Hierotheus</margin> rightly perceive, along with **Dionysius** and **Hierotheus** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite and his teacher Hierotheus were influential mystical theologians who blended Christian thought with Neoplatonism.</note>, who say: That just as each thing is called "good" because it participates in the highest good, and "a being" because it participates in the highest being, so too is a thing "beautiful" by participation in the **First Beauty**. This beauty is called sometimes *Iaphit* <note>original Hebrew: יָפִית; meaning beautiful or fair.</note>, sometimes *Hadar* <note>original Hebrew: הָדָר; meaning splendor or ornament.</note>, and sometimes *Tipheret* <note>original Hebrew: תִּפְאֶרֶת; meaning glory or beauty, often associated with the heart or sun in mystical traditions.</note>. These differ if we carefully weigh the power of the words. For *Iaphit* signifies true beauty coming from within. But *Hadar* indicates a decorative beauty in outward appearance, dress, ornament, and manners. However, *Tipheret* signifies beauty itself and intrinsic majesty resulting in a certain glory and visible triumph.

For it is called *Iaphit* in the forty-fourth Psalm <margin>Psalm</margin>, where we have the translation: *Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.* <note>Psalm 45:2 in modern numbering.</note> For in Hebrew it is held as *iaph iaphita mibne adam* <note>original: יָפְיָפִיתָ מִבְּנֵי אָדָם</note>. Translating this word for word, we would say: *Beautiful with beauty from—or above—the sons of Adam.* We find *Hadar* in the ninety-fifth Psalm, where it says: *Praise and beauty are in his sight*, while the Hebrew has *hod ve hadar lepanau* <note>original: הוֹד וְהָדָר לְפָנָיו; usually translated as "splendor and majesty are before him."</note>. We also find *Tipheret* in the same place: *strength and beauty are in his sanctuary* <note>original: עֹז וְתִפְאֶרֶת בְּמִקְדָּשׁוֹ</note>, that is, power and beauty in his sanctuary. In our version we have: *holiness and magnificence in his sanctification.* These three terms are found in many other places.

But it should be noted that the majesty and beauty called *Tipheret* is sometimes represented by **light**; whence the one dwelling in it says: *I am the light of the world.* Sometimes it is represented by the **sun**, according to that word of the Psalmist: *In the sun he set his tabernacle.* <margin>Genesis</margin> For **Abraham** had stretched his tabernacle toward the south, in which he progressed greatly. <margin>Ibid.</margin> **Isaac** also was greatly enriched there, which is hinted at in the passage: *Isaac sowed in that land and found in that same year a hundredfold.* However, the **Hebrew Truth** <note>original: "veritas hebraica" — a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as the ultimate authority.</note> says: *He found in that year a hundred barleys, and the Lord blessed him, and the man became great; and he went on progressing and growing until he became very great.* 

**Jerome** <margin>Jerome</margin> <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> wonders how he could be made so great simply through finding "a hundred barleys." The truth is that he progressed in that **northern influence** indicated by the word *seharim* <note>original: שְׂעֹרִים</note>, which signifies both "barleys" and many other things. <note>In mystical thought, the "North" often represents the quality of Judgment or Strength (Gevurah), and the word for barleys is related to the word for "gate" or "measure."</note> **Jacob**, however, fixed his tabernacle in the middle, where *Tipheret* is—that is, beauty and the **Supramundane Sun**. Concerning this tabernacle, or tabernacles, <margin>Numbers</margin> it is said in the Book of Numbers: *How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob, and your tabernacles, O Israel.* <note>Numbers 24:5.</note> Therefore, it is the same to say: *Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men*; *He was the true light illuminating all*; *In the sun he placed his tabernacle*; *He shall reign in the house of Jacob forever*; and many similar things which agree, as is known to those who understand what is conveyed through such mysteries.

<summary>This page analyzes the mystical nature of Divine Beauty through three Hebrew terms (Iaphit, Hadar, and Tipheret) and interprets the lives of the Patriarchs as allegories for different spiritual influences.</summary>

God is therefore beautiful: he is our reward and our object, and consequently he is delightful to the internal sense through his divinity, and to the external sense through his assumed humanity. Peter David</margin> <note>A reference to John 10:9, where Christ describes himself as the door to salvation and "pasture."</note> He is also sweet and pleasant to the taste, as Peter says: *If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.* <note>1 Peter 2:3.</note> And David says in the psalm: *The Lord is sweet to all.* <note>Psalm 145:9.</note> Finally, he is perfectly proportioned to all our faculties, even though he is infinite and exceeds all faculties; for by that very excess he does not destroy us, but rather grants as much as the capacity of the receiving power can hold. This is the true joy that results from proportion and harmony. This joy, this pleasantness, this sweetness, and finally this full happiness would be as nothing, in a sense, were it not for the continuous security of the one possessing it. Therefore our Supreme Commander <note>original: *Summus Imperator*; a title for Christ emphasizing his absolute authority.</note>, so that he might make us certain that this joy would never be lost, said to the disciples and consequently to everyone: *Your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no one shall take from you.* <note>John 16:22.</note>

#### On the Extensive Empire of the Prince. First Harmony.

<margin>Paul</margin>

# OF THE THIRD CANTICLE

...[David] served under Saul; and because of his well-deserved and famous deeds, he was indeed very dear to the people, but hated by Saul and watched with many ambushes. He reached the point where he thought he must yield to envy, preferring to serve <note>original: "allophylis"; usually referring to the Philistines in biblical Latin.</note> foreigners rather than an envious king. And after he began to reign, he reigned for seven years restricted to his single tribe of Judah. This is shown to us as an example, so that no one may be saddened if they do not immediately obtain a promised kingdom. However, this royal scepter lasted in the tribe of Judah, either under the name of king or leader, until Christ. When he arrived, <margin>Genesis</margin> it was by no means taken away (even though the oracle says: *Until the Messiah comes*); instead, under him, it was changed for the better, since he was the King of Kings, and for all of us he acquired that kingdom which is truly real and eternal. Therefore, to Pilate asking if <margin>CHRIST.</margin> he were a King, he replied: *You say it, because I am a king: but my kingdom is not of this world,* but has a super-worldly root in the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original divine blueprint or "first form" in the mind of God.</note>, descending from which I have brought the kingdom with me. This is mysteriously hinted at in this name יהודה, **Judah**, from whose truly royal lineage I am born. In this name are contained all the letters of the great four-letter name, or <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew: YHWH.</note>, with the letter ד <term>dalet</term> <note>The fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note> placed between them, which signifies the number four. From this, it is implied that the divinity and royal majesty contained in the **Tetragrammaton** was found in the condition of a fourfold human body, composed of the four elements. Since, therefore, that sacred four-letter name belongs to the Messiah, and he was a true man, we easily understand him to be the true super-worldly King, and of the true tribe of Judah—though for the time of his pilgrimage, he remained hidden in a fourfold human body. But now he reigns with royal pomp on the heavenly throne, with which he will appear even to mortals in his second coming, of which he himself says: *When the Son of Man comes* <margin>The Same</margin> *in the seat of his majesty with his Angels:* And again: *All shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.*

-> By what right the Empire of this Prince is just. <-

<margin>Conclusion 2.</margin> **S**ed since one may take up imperial or royal dignity by a twofold right—namely, by inheritance and by just war—I believe we must see how Christ our Emperor claims that empire for himself not by tyranny, but by both rights. For he had a hereditary right to it, since he was the son of the Supreme Prince, with whom he had also fashioned all things that were subjected to him, <margin>Paul</margin> as Paul, the revealer of secrets, said: *Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages.* But this would have been a small thing for his justice, unless by merit and military skill (yet in a just war) he had acquired that noble empire once again. For the kingdom is set forth like a prize for those running or fighting, for those who have conquered in the <note>original: "agone"; the Greek-derived word for a struggle or athletic contest.</note> struggle of this mortal life. For the course of life itself is like a gymnastic race, through which anyone can arrive at either a prize or a punishment. As for the battle, a war has been declared against vices and hellish enemies, as we explained above. In this battle, all who fight are troubled and distressed, according to that <margin>The Same</margin> Apostolic word: *We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations.*

# SIXTEENTH MODULE / PEACE.
### What Peace is.
### First Harmony.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**P**eace indeed (as Augustine rightly perceives) is the "tranquility of order" <note>original: "tranquillitas ordinis" — This is a famous definition from St. Augustine’s *City of God* (Book 19, Chapter 13).</note>: which order is the arrangement of things, whether equal or unequal, assigning to each its own place. For when all things are properly ordered, tranquility and peace follow. Since peace is manifold, it is explained by many definitions.
Peace of the body is the ordered composition of its parts, which is called health. Peace of the irrational soul <note>The "irrational soul" refers to the part of the human psyche shared with animals, governed by instincts and appetites rather than logic.</note> is the ordered and quieted appetite. Peace of the soul and body is the ordered life, the harmonious union, and the consistent operation of both.
However, the peace of the rational part is ordered knowledge and the total agreement of the choice [of the will]. And this is that most happy "gathering of two or three" <note>A reference to Matthew 18:20, interpreted here as internal psychological harmony.</note> in which the King of Peace promises to dwell: namely, when our animal nature agrees with reason, reason with the will, and the will with reason. From this follows true peace with God, which is the pure observation of the law and the manifested will of God. Not only does the properly tempered mind become a temple of God, but whoever is thus composed will be heard immediately in whatever they ask for, because they do not differ in any way from what God has ordained. For such a person, the yoke of God and Christ is sweet and delightful. And in such a state, the hymn has its place which the 
<margin>Angels</margin>
Angels sang at the birth of the Prince of Peace, saying: *And on earth peace to men of good will* <note>Luke 2:14</note>—to those, namely, who have a will in concord with reason and with God. Indeed, these are deemed worthy to ascend to that peace of God which surpasses all understanding, and to reach the heavenly and sublime...

### THIRD SONG
<meta>catchword: Only indeed</meta>
<note>Translator's note: The manuscript shows water damage and dark staining on the left edge, but the text is legible.</note>

<margin>Job</margin> I recall that city in which (according to the author Job) God created such concord that the city was called a vision and the enjoyment of peace. And because no one can reach this kingdom of peace except the peacemakers, its Prince commands his ministers that wherever they may go, they should carry and announce peace. 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> When he departed from them, he left this peace to be preserved by a right of testament, saying: *My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.* <note>John 14:27</note> He who neglects to observe this testament shall in no way be able to reach the inheritance of peace; for one who is discordant (even in the slightest degree) should not and cannot be admitted to the harmonic concert and song-like sweetness. So too, those who serve the smallest sin or are slaves to pleasure in any part cannot arrive at the kingdom, since they are servants of sin; nor can they reach that peace which is defined by certain wise men as the **tranquil liberty of the soul**.

->By Whom Peace is Given. Consideration II.<-

<margin>The Church</margin> **B**ut since no one can be free from sin without God, so too can no one enjoy peace or make progress in it without God. Hence the Church prays: *Give to us that peace which the world cannot give.* <note>A phrase from the "Dona Nobis Pacem" in the Mass</note> For the dwellings of the world are threefold: the heavenly, the hellish, and the middle. There is the heavenly lodging, which is most harmoniously ordered and filled with full peace. There is the lowest, where no order, no rest, and no peace exists, but "everlasting horror dwells," as Job says. <note>Job 10:22</note> Then there is the middle dwelling, mixed of both, in which man is first placed; a fork in the road is set before him, and he is continually invited toward the extreme lodgings. But one runs easily to the hellish dwellings with loose reins, no bit, and no moderation; no order is observed, but everything is prepared for lawlessness. Therefore, the <term>descent to the underworld<note>original: "descensus averni," a classical reference to the easy path to the realm of the dead in Virgil's Aeneid</note></term> is very easy. Mortals slip into it without help, so separated from themselves and from God the Ordainer—and so out of tune—that they can never again possess any peace or tranquility. Those who truly strive for the heavenly dwellings and the higher airs undertake a difficult and arduous journey, so much so that it cannot be fully accomplished without the divine power, as the 
<margin>CHRIST</margin> infallible Truth testifies, saying: *Without me you can do nothing.* <note>John 15:5</note> For just as an instrument needs a <term>musician<note>original: "modulatore," one who sets the measure, tunes, or plays an instrument</note></term> to adjust the <note>original: "fibras," literally fibers, referring to gut strings</note> strings or pipes and make them harmonious, and then plays them with the proper resonance, so too we—as instruments (and hopefully good ones)—need a musician to adjust our strings and pipes. These strings are undoubtedly the soul and the body: our animal nature and our spirit: the higher part and the lower: the will and the reason. Finally, he brings all these things into harmony with God himself. For who pours a harmonious soul into a prepared body but God? Who connects those two things which seem completely discordant—namely, body and soul—with such harmony that the soul utterly shuns the dissolution of the body? Who will be able, or has ever been able, to fit our mind together with the divine? Who strikes the divine will with a fitting <term>plectrum<note>a small tool or pick used to pluck the strings of an instrument like a lute or lyre</note></term> so that it produces that sound which our own soul might approach, and not in vain?

### EIGHTH TONE

<margin>Paul</margin> This is achieved by Him of whom the Apostle says: <note>original: "Deus est, qui operatur in nobis & uelle, & perficere"</note> *It is God who works in us both the will and the performance:* And again: <note>original: "Idem uero Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus"</note> *It is the same God who works all things in all.* Therefore, by Him is given peace and the concord of the soul with the body. From Him comes the way the "animal man" <note>The "animalis homo" or "natural man" refers to human nature driven by physical instincts rather than spiritual grace.</note> is subjected to the spirit. From Him comes the fitting together of human minds with one another, because it is He who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house. From the same comes the correspondence of our mind with the divine. From this source, therefore, is the fitting together of instruments; from this comes a sonorous and harmonious operation; from this comes tranquility, peace, sweetness, and every good thing.

->How Sweet and Harmonious is that Peace. Consideration III.<-

<margin>David</margin> **A**s peace is so sweet and joyful, some wise men say that in nature nothing more excellent can be imagined, and nothing sweeter. For true peace is the tranquility of the mind, the simplicity of the heart, the bond of love, the connection of charity, the solace of the State, and the joy of homes; it is familiar to Angels, an enemy to demons, pleasing to God above all things, and is the concord of all things. And where there is concord, there is harmony; there is sweetness, and there is joy. Hence the Prophet sings: <note>original: "Ecce q̄ bonum & q̄ iucundum, habitare fratres in unum"</note> *Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell as one.* <note>Psalm 133:1</note> These "brothers" are clearly the soul and the body when they are in concord, or men together, or a man and his guardian Angel. For then God and Christ (whose name in the songs is called an ointment or oil poured out) is spread over those who thus assemble, sprinkling all things with the sweetest scent and fragrance. From this follows: *Like the ointment on the head,* namely Christ, *which descended onto the beard,* specifically the beard of Aaron the great high priest; because through the hands of priests, divine gifts of grace <note>original: "charismata"</note> are administered to the people. This ointment therefore descends even to the hem of the garment—the garment that Christ, our Anointed One, prepared and wove for us to cover the sins of all. He pours the ointment over this garment so that he might also heal the wounds of all. There is also this divine influx upon those living together in peace, *like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon the mountain of Sion.* For dew is a heavenly influx—indeed, a divine one—in which Isaac blessed both his sons, saying: *In the dew of heaven shall be your blessing.* <note>Genesis 27:28</note> For it descends from heaven through the place indicated as Hermon, which is interpreted as the "curse of sorrow"; <note>The author uses a traditional medieval etymology for "Hermon."</note> and this dew descends upon Mount Sion, that is, upon those who are placed upon the watchtower <note>The author follows the common etymology where "Sion" means "watchtower."</note> and in the governance of others, <margin>Theologians</margin> for "Sion" denotes a watchtower. But if we wish to imitate the more secret theologians, the dew which in Hebrew is called <term>Tal</term> <note>Hebrew: טל. The author is likely referring to the Gematria (numerical value) of the word, which equals 39, the same as the phrase "The Lord is One" (YHVH Echad).</note> carries, by way of numbers, the surname of the great hidden Name from which all things flow. And thus by "ointment" it is indicated that we have an influx of the Name, which is properly "ointment poured out"; and by "dew" an influx of the surname; so much so, that nothing is lacking to those living together in peace and unity. <margin>David</margin> And explaining more clearly, the prophet adds: *Because there the Lord commanded blessing, and life forevermore.* But what is life, if not eternal happiness? And what is blessing, but the gift by which we reach that very happiness?

# SEVENTEENTH MODULE: UNION.

->On the Union of the Blessed with God. A Unique Harmony.<-

<margin>CHRIST.</margin>
**F**rom the most sacred paternal storehouses, Jesus the Son of God, being about to depart from here, had given a pledge of His greatest love toward us; He also granted this memorial, hidden from almost all human minds, saying: <note>original: "Pater sancte serva eos in nomine tuo, quos dedisti mihi: ut sint unum, sicut & nos"</note> *Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given to me: that they may be one, just as we are.* And again: *I do not pray for these only, whom I have sent to preach—namely the Apostles—but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, and that they themselves may be one in us.* <note>John 17:11, 20-21</note> By these words, He not only explains our future union with God, but also hints at the manner of it when He says: *Just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you.*

<margin>The same from Plotinus</margin>
When Plotinus wished to treat this union—he being the most eminent reporter of the hidden doctrine of Plato, or rather of the divine wisdom imbibed by Plato to the extent that the prophets had offered it—he said: <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; here the author suggests Plato learned from Hebrew prophets, a common Renaissance belief.</note> "The institution of such mysteries indicates that it is forbidden to reveal them to men not yet initiated and purified." Hence, because Parmenides said that "all things are one," the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, often contrasted here with the more "mystical" followers of Plato and Parmenides.</note> mock him—though they themselves are the ones to be laughed at, because they argue against everything that Parmenides did *not* say; meanwhile, what he actually said, they have left entirely untouched, firm on its own feet, and unshaken.

<margin>Parmenides. Peripatetics.</margin>
<margin>Simplicius.</margin>
Simplicius says that Aristotle argues against the words, but not against the meanings of Parmenides, who spoke divinely and above the boundaries of natural philosophy—to which Aristotle was devoted in his *Physics*. For all things proceeded from the One, and for them to be these same things, it is necessary for them to participate in that One. And just as all things proceeded from the One into the "many," so all things that tend to return into that One from which they proceeded find it necessary to strip away the "multitude" <note>In Neoplatonism, "multitude" refers to the fragmented, material world of many things, as opposed to the divine Unity.</note> which pertains to the imagination, discourse, and the senses.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>The same from CHRIST.</margin>
It was through these [senses] alone that Aristotle proceeded; therefore, it is no wonder if he did not arrive at the One. And just as there is trouble and distraction of the soul concerning "many things" (according to the testimony of infallible Truth), so there is collection and rest concerning the "One." For He said: <note>original: "Martha turbaris erga plurima, porro unum est necessarium"</note> *Martha, you are troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary* <note>Luke 10:41-42</note>—namely, the One in whom all things are held together, so that those seeking rest and happiness need not wander among the many.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Hence Augustine most excellently says: *Why do you wander, little man, among many things? Seek the one good, in which are all goods, and it is enough.* But it is one thing to seek the One, and to tend toward that One, and quite another to *be made* one. Furthermore, nearly all wise men affirm that the One is necessary, toward which all ought to tend. But how those tending into...

### EIGHTH TONE.

Few or none have explained how that "one" and "He" are made the same thing, which is indeed difficult to explain: for it is held among those most hidden secrets <note>original: "arcana reconditissima"</note> which it is not permitted for a man to speak, except only to those who have experienced this union themselves, either through action or at least through contemplation.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
For he is (says Plotinus, bringing forth something from the inner workshop <note>original: "officina core"</note> of those who have proved it) the seer himself along with that which is seen; not two, but one; as if it were not properly something seen, but something united. He is moreover himself "one," having no difference toward himself, nor again regarding other things. For in him who sees in this way, nothing is moved—not anger, nor the appetite of anything lower—since he has already advanced to the heights. But neither is there reason, nor a certain intelligence, nor even himself at all—if it is right to say this. But as if snatched away, or entirely occupied by God, he is now established in a certain safe withdrawal, in a tranquil state, and utterly immobile. He does not deviate from his own essence in any way, nor even turn back toward himself, since he rests completely in that which he sees, and as if he himself has already become that state.

<margin>Paul</margin>
For to this point Paul had come while still a pilgrim (as I believe) when he said: *I live, yet now not I, but Christ lives in me.* <note>Galatians 2:20</note> He who, having been snatched up <note>raptus</note> into God at one time, testifies that he saw things which it is not permitted for a man to speak. But he himself and others come to this more beautifully and happily when they have already reached the finish line of the race, and have been joined by a firm clinging to that One toward which they had always stretched: concerning whom the same Paul says:

<margin>The same theologian</margin>
*He who clings to God is made one spirit with Him.* <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note> For our theologians say that Blessedness <note>Beatitudo</note> consists in the vision and enjoyment <term>fruitio|The joyful possession or use of a thing for its own sake, specifically the soul's delight in God.</term> of God, and the firm holding of that happiness, and they proceed no further.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
However, from the Gospel, as well as from Plotinus and other wise men, we hold that one also arrives at a union with God through being seen and loved. 

<margin>The same Dionysius</margin>
For if the seer becomes the same as that which is seen (as Plotinus recently said), the lover becomes one with the beloved even more beautifully and effectively, as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note> and many wise men say: that love is a uniting power <note>virtus uniens</note> joining the lover with the beloved. Climbing higher, just as the power of speculation or contemplation strips away the "many" if it must contemplate the "One," so also the effective power and all other progressive forces finally proceed from the many into the one, just as they proceeded from the one into the many: by which path the perfect <term>diapason|A musical term for the octave; here used to signify the most complete and perfect harmony possible.</term> and consummate harmony is conducted. They certainly strive to reach that One,

<margin>Plato</margin>
which (as Plato teaches in the *Parmenides*) is that from which all things come, which is outside all things, and in all things, and toward which all things tend: so that it is the first and most known, the beginning and the end, as the sacred letters testify in many places. But if by their very nature all things tend toward that, they shall finally arrive at it, lest that inborn appetite be in vain. Nor shall they cease to be what they are from that point, since they are united with a better thing and changed into something better, living more happily now that their end has been achieved.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
"For this," says Plotinus, "is the life of Gods and of divine and happy men: to utterly neglect the lower pleasures which consist in the 'many,' and the flight of the alone to the Alone." <note>original: "fuga solius ad solum." This is the famous concluding phrase of Plotinus's Enneads, describing the soul's ultimate mystical ascent.</note> For the thought of this hour rests entirely upon that coupling.

But as to how one arrives at it, since he does not leave it untouched, we also...

### HAPPINESS.

->Who is Happy and Blessed. First Harmony.<-

<margin>Augustine. Plato</margin>
Moreover, who should be considered happy and blessed? Augustine defines it saying: *He is blessed who has whatever he wants.* <note>Augustine, *De Trinitate*</note> Plato, however, in the *Philebus*, is not far off when he says: *He is blessed who lacks nothing.* But in the *Euthydemus*, he agrees with Augustine, saying: *Happiness is the attainment of things according to one's wishes.* But no one possesses all the things he desires unless he adheres to and is united with the source of all goods, from which he can draw all things at his pleasure. Therefore, he is blessed and happy who is united with God, in whom he sees all things, possesses all things, and enjoys all things in a better lot than he would perceive in their own kind; although the vision of those things is not denied,
<margin>Augustine</margin>
which is called by Augustine "evening knowledge" <note>term: uespertina (evening knowledge), an Augustinian term for the soul's knowledge of created things in themselves, contrasted with "morning knowledge" (matutina), which is knowing things through God.</note>, nor is their enjoyment denied...

# EIGHTH TONE.

...we have declared, provided that all things are referred back to God in that relationship and harmony which is fitting. From their agreement, the great glory of the Creator is perceived, which vibrates and shines in creatures, which eyes well <margin>Isaiah</margin> illuminated contemplate, like those Seraphim who (as Isaiah relates) sang: *Holy, holy, holy Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory.* <note>original: "Sanctus sanctus sanctus Dominus Deus exercituum, plena est omnis terra gloria eius." See Isaiah 6:3.</note> If this glory shines in created things, it shines much more happily in the Creator himself, whose <margin>GOD</margin> vision is given to those who, dead to the world and to themselves, live for God alone, who says: *No man shall see me and live.* <note>Exodus 33:20.</note> It is necessary, therefore, if anyone wishes to be happy, that he die the death of the righteous, either through a total separation from the body and vice versa, like all the blessed whose souls have reached that heavenly glory; or through a transformation of the body into a better lot, as we read of Elijah who was translated in a fiery chariot, his body already changed into the nature of a spirit; and like Enoch, who walked with God in soul and body, and was no longer seen by bodily eyes; and like many others whose bodies rose with Christ and entered the holy city, happy together with Him; or by a migration from the body for a time, like Paul in his rapture; Moses, who saw the Lord face to face; Isaiah, who saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up; and not a few others, whom it would be too long to recount, if not impossible.

<margin>Conclusion II.</margin>
->In what Happiness consists.<-

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**A**lthough in the first volume we brought forward many opinions of those who wished to define in what happiness and blessedness consist, here however, determining the matter resolutely and conclusively, we say: that happiness cannot exist except in God, and not in any external things, as Aristotle wisely decrees in his *Politics* <note>Aristotle, *Politics* 1323b. The author argues that God is the exemplar of happiness because He is self-sufficient.</note> saying: With God as witness, happiness is not in external things, because He himself is happy, and uses no external things. Here <margin>Cicero</margin> Cicero falls, struck by his own battering ram, while he places the blessed life in a vacancy <note>term: vacatione (exemption or leisure); Cicero often associated the happy life with *otium* or freedom from public business, which the author argues must be redirected toward God.</note> from all things, which must be placed in God alone. Nevertheless, progress toward God <margin>Paul</margin> is sometimes made through creatures, as Paul says: *The invisible things of God, through those things which have been made, are understood and perceived from the creation of the world.* <note>Romans 1:20.</note> From which, turning back again to created things while seeing God, they contemplate the glory of the Maker in them, feeling the wonderful harmonies resulting from both. This turning toward created things is in no way unfortunate, since it does not happen by turning away from God, from whom they never depart, continually contemplating Him in created things. Now, therefore, they are delighted by the vision of God himself (which is called the **midday vision**), now they perceive creatures in Him by the **morning vision**, and now they behold Him in creatures by the <margin>Augustine</margin> **evening vision**, as Augustine discusses at length and clearly in his commentary on Genesis. <note>term: uisione matutina / uespertina (morning/evening vision). ->CANTICI TERTII.<-

# OF THE THIRD SONG.

...we [stated]: <note>The word "eimus" likely completes "ante-diximus" (we said before) from the previous page.</note> that people are sometimes released from bodily laws and senses, whether through ecstasy or through rapture, and are led to a certain place which is sometimes called the paradise of delights, sometimes the third heaven <note>A reference to the experience of St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:2.</note>, and sometimes the breasts and bosom of the Archetype <term>Archetype: The divine original or the Mind of God, which serves as the model for all creation.</term>: where, as if in a place of higher learning, they are clearly taught about those things which they had previously learned only through images. For they discern judgments concerning consequences and future events, which they had previously conceived only in part, as if through a mirror or in a riddle. <note>original: "per speculum & in ænigmate." Paul</margin> <note>original: "Ubi sum ego, illic & minister meus erit." There, the blessed understand the causes of things, which the highest Truth does not hide from his beloved sons and faithful servants. There they perceive not only what each star does, where it is located, and why it is separated from another by such a great distance, but also which intelligence <note>The angelic "Intelligences" believed to move the planetary spheres.</note> presides over each constellation; and from what place in the Archetype it receives that influence which flows into the stars and, through them, into the lower world. Then, living now in pure splendor, the soul understands the meaning of the Priest, the Levite, and their various orders; and what the cycles of jubilees, weeks, years, feasts, and holidays actually signify, as well as the reasons for all the sacrifices—things which were ordained in the most deeply hidden mystery for the purification and expiation of souls. Furthermore, they understand the various types of leprosy and their cleansing, and the laws concerning bodily discharges. They see why the hunchbacked, the ruptured, the maimed, those with a crooked or too large or flat nose, the cross-eyed, or those defiled by any shameful blemish are kept away from the altar. <note>These are physical requirements for priests found in Leviticus 21:18–20, here interpreted as having deeper mystical significance.</note> They also recognize the Angelic minds, or those intelligences separated from the one supreme Mind: and which virtues and powers are good and which are evil; which are favorable and which are contrary. They behold the nature of souls and where each one comes from; what its essence is, its degree of perfection, and its measure of grace and gifts. They see the diversity of animals and wild beasts, and why each is divided into so many species. Nor will it be hidden by what logic certain wondrous powers are associated with certain roots or herbs, while other herbs or roots drive them away. Furthermore, they understand the things that happen to men—that they do not occur by chance or accident, but by a reason so carefully examined and so lofty, that not even the number of hairs on the heads of the saints (or perhaps all men) is overlooked; and by the logic of whose providence everything is brought forth, down to the two sparrows sold for a penny, <note>original: "duos passeres / qui asse ueneunt." See Matthew 10:29.</note> whether those sparrows are understood spiritually or according to the literal word. by the authority of absolution, the resurrection of the dead, and things of this sort: so that we may be carried toward the **perfect doctrine** among the perfect, which is to be shared only with those who have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit. In this doctrine, we treat the heavenly gift, the **hidden manna**, and the "better" word of God—namely, that which is concealed and shared with the perfect—and the powers of the world to come. To which (with God’s help) when we have arrived, then we shall see, even while still as pilgrims, at least in part, those things which are hidden. But if, having been released from the body, we are carried into God, then that which is "in part" is done away with, for the "perfect" has then been attained, in which we are fully blessed. 

However, whether the soul, once released from this bodily mass, immediately reaches the goal and limit where it is finally destined to come, or whether it still makes progress, there are varying opinions among the wise. <margin>Theologians</margin> For the more recent theologians follow the former opinion. <margin>Origen, Celsus</margin> But Origen—and other wise men with him—thinks that the blessed still make progress, as he says in a long discourse arguing against Celsus: "When the saints reach the heavenly places, then they shall know more fully and perfectly than they did during their pilgrimage." In this knowledge, the rational nature will grow through individual stages—not as it grew in the flesh, or in the body and soul during this life, but the mind and understanding, having been increased, are led to perfect knowledge, a mind now fully initiated. It will by no means be hindered by these carnal senses in the future, but increased by intellectual growth, and with every veil always removed, it will behold the causes of things clearly (so to speak) **face to face**. There, it will first enjoy that perfection by which it ascends into Him, and thereafter that perfection in which it remains. It shall have foods to feed upon, namely **theorems** <note>original: "theoremata"; here meaning objects of intellectual contemplation or divine truths</note> and the understanding of things, and the reasons for causes. 

For just as our bodies in this life, by the protection of food, continually grow and are fully perfected while we are still in our youthful years; <margin><unclear>D...guA</unclear></margin> but when nature, with its proper outlines, has led them to their full height, we then use food no longer to grow, but to live and be preserved in life through nourishment. In the same way, I believe that the mind, even when it has come to perfection, nevertheless feeds upon and uses its own proper and suitable foods in that measure in which nothing should be lacking, nor anything be in excess. In all these things, this "food" is to be understood as **theory** <term>theory: from the Greek *theoria*, meaning divine contemplation or spiritual vision</term> and the understanding of God, having its own proper measures suitable to this nature which was made and created. These measures must be observed by each individual who begins to see God and to understand through purity of heart. 

Certainly, in my judgment, the Apostle wished to indicate this progress to us where, after <margin>Paul / CHRIST</margin> he discussed the ascent on high and the "captivity led captive" by Christ, and the ranks distributed in the church—by which some were made Apostles, others Evangelists, others Teachers, and so forth—he added: **Until we all meet in the unity of faith, and in the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ**, <note>Ephesians 4:13</note> so that we are no longer children tossed to and fro, and carried about by every wind of doctrine.
