<page-num>CXXXII</page-num>
<header>OF THE THIRD CANTICLE</header>

The doctors of the church commonly hold—and we are with the church and with Christ—that we are here and everywhere. Yet it seems to some (unless this is contrary to the truth) that those who adhere to the Infinite always draw from Him that by which they may grow, until they become the same with Him, as we noted above. Then, having attained the perfect portion through which they grow, they rest in peace in that very state. For (as they say), if anything foul and unclean is found, it is clear that those who have completed their life’s course have a place in which they may be purged <note>A reference to Purgatory or a state of cleansing before entering heaven.</note> before they come to that illuminating and perfecting light. This is so that the person, being defiled and weak, is not struck down by its brilliance. Thus, the eye must be accustomed before it fixes its gaze on that most full light. As Plotinus <margin>Plotinus</margin> <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was a major Greek-speaking philosopher of the Neoplatonic school, whose ideas deeply influenced early Christian mysticism.</note> says: an eye infected with filth, not yet well-cleansed or weak, if it is directed toward a most bright spectacle, will immediately grow dark. For it is necessary that the one who is to see be made akin and similar to the thing seen before they are admitted to viewing it. For neither would the eye ever see the sun unless it were made sun-like; nor, again, will the soul behold beauty itself and God unless it were made beautiful and divine; nor will it receive the light unless it were made luminous and clear.

Hence Solomon <margin>Solomon</margin> says in Proverbs: "The path of the righteous is like a shining light that goes forth," <note>original: "Semita iustorum sicut lux splendet uadens"</note> or progresses and shines until the perfect day. Hence it says of the most blessed Christ: "But the child grew and became strong, full of wisdom." And again: "And Jesus progressed in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men." <note>These are references to the Gospel of Luke 2:40 and 2:52, which describe the human growth of Jesus.</note> Nor should it be said that He progressed only in appearance (for this would accuse the Scripture of falsehood), since the Scripture itself says that He progressed in wisdom, not merely in appearance, nor only in the estimation of men. Nor is the problem well-solved by the one who says He progressed in "experience," for it says in that same place that He progressed in wisdom. Indeed, Scripture never speaks incongruously, except by the fault of a translator. Therefore, that man [Christ] also progressed even when united with God, just as He also merited grace until that fullness to which the Father had preordained Him. 

The righteous also grow until the perfect day, which is the "noon," or the **southern vision** <margin>Augustine</margin> <note>original: "visio meridionalis." St. Augustine used this term to describe the clear, direct vision of God enjoyed by the angels and the blessed, compared to the "evening" or "morning" knowledge of earthly life.</note> so named by Augustine, when the blessed one clearly beholds God face to face as He is. In this vision there is infinite breadth, just as the object seen is infinite. Nor should those who hold this opinion consider it inconvenient that for the blessed there is both a "state" and "progress." The "state" is such that none of them can fall away in any way; but the "progress" is when they become ever more intimate with God, until they are made the same with Him. Hence even the Angels (as Peter <margin>Peter</margin> says) "desire to look into God." <note>1 Peter 1:12.</note> For they desire what they do not yet have; yet they do not desire in vain, for otherwise they would be cheated of their desire and would grieve, which is contrary to the nature of blessedness. They seem, therefore, to obtain at some point what they do not have, although they are blessed. 

Or, if it is asserted (as theologians <margin>Theologians</margin> commonly feel) that the blessed, once introduced to that vision, are found at a goal already fixed, so that they do not progress further or become more intimate with God, since they are already perfectly blessed once introduced there. But however it may be, perfect happiness is given to those who have already arrived at the final goal of their progress, and at the full measure according to their capacity, so that they can contain no more. And this is what is said <margin>CHRIST</margin>: "Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full." <note>John 16:24.</note>

# MOVEMENT 19. ALL GOODNESS.

## What goodness is, which is called the highest and true good. A Unique Harmony.

<margin>Trismegistus</margin>
**S**INCE no discussion can be held regarding that which is not subject to the senses or to composite reasonings—because it is most simple—therefore a simple discourse must be made about it, taught by the divine light alone, just as the truly wise instruct us. For Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic combination of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth; he was considered a source of ancient wisdom by Renaissance scholars.</note>, being indeed bathed in that light, says: God is the good itself, and nothing else besides the good; all other things are separate from the very nature of the good. The body and the soul, since they are finite, have no place in which they may contain the good, because the good is as vast as the existence that rules all things—both bodily and incorporeal, sensible and intelligible—and is itself that which exists above all existence. 

<margin>Dionysius. CHRIST.</margin>
Take care, therefore, lest you ever call anything else "good." For that would be a profane error, according to what the Highest Teacher says: *No one is good, except God alone.* <note>Mark 10:18. The "Highest Teacher" refers to Christ.</note> Nor should it be said that God is anything other than the good alone, for you would fall into the same impiety. And because the good is not understood by everyone, 

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
for that reason God, who is the good itself, is not known by everyone; but because of ignorance, both gods and men are called "good." Therefore Christ, rebuking the one who had said to him, *Good Master*, said: *Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God.* <note>Matthew 19:17.</note> This is meant in an absolute and proper sense; 

<margin>THE SAME</margin>
alternatively, someone can be good through participation <note>The philosophical concept where a created thing shares in a quality (like goodness or beauty) that belongs perfectly and essentially to God.</note>, just as the same Teacher, knowing that he participated most excellently in that goodness according to his humanity, said elsewhere: *I am the good shepherd.* <note>John 10:11.</note> Indeed, he openly confessed that the Father had given him all things; whence in that which he was as a man, he was not good of himself—which belongs only to God, of whom the Prophet 

<margin>David</margin>
says: *Give praise to the Lord, for He is good.* <note>Psalm 106:1. The "Prophet" refers to King David.</note> According to which goodness, no one (says Mercurius <note>Another name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note>) can be good, nor become so. Whoever, therefore, is honored for goodness, let it be in that which he has received from God. 

<margin>Mercurius. Paul.</margin>
Hence Paul cries out to everyone, saying: *What do you have that you have not received?* <note>1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> Since, therefore, all things receive from God and give nothing, and He Himself provides all things and receives nothing, therefore He alone is good. For the good one extends all things and receives nothing; but man and all things along with him receive everything and give nothing; therefore none of these can be called "good." Christ, therefore, in that he had received all things from the Father, did not wish to be called "good"; but in that which he gave, he performed the office of the good. God is therefore all goodness and the highest good, receiving nothing—because He has no need of any of our goods—but giving to all 

<margin>David</margin>
so that they may be good, just as the divine harpist <note>King David, traditionally credited with the Psalms.</note> sings, saying: *When you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness.* <note>Psalm 104:28.</note> And this is true humility, and true knowledge of oneself: to understand that one is pure nothingness, and to have received all things from God, and to be what they are from this source, since one only exists insofar as God pours Himself into them. And he who participates more in God is better, since God is the good itself; and he is more beautiful, since God is beauty itself. For this is (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential 5th-6th century Christian Neoplatonist.</note> and the Academics <note>Followers of the Platonic Academy.</note> teach) true beauty: 

<margin>Dionysius. Academics.</margin>
namely, to participate in the highest beauty; and true goodness, to participate in the highest.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>...goodness, just as He is truly being, insofar as a thing participates in that which exists by itself and is the highest being, as is most commonly held in all the schools. For (as the same Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works blended Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine.</note> says) because God is substantial goodness, He extends His goodness to all existing things, just as the sun by its very existence illuminates everything that can participate in its light. Therefore, the Highest Good, through its own essence, sends out rays of total goodness to all existing things by a certain measure and miraculous proportion. Not <margin>The same</margin>differently does he say of the "Beautiful" a little later: For the Beautiful itself—which is above beauty, always and in every part existing—is the cause of the beauty of all things. This "Beautiful" brings about the harmonies, friendships, and fellowships of all things; and all things belong to this Beautiful as their effective cause and their end. It is also the exemplar <note>original: "exemplar"; the perfect pattern or model in the mind of God.</note> and the goal <note>original: "meta"</note> toward which all things are defined. And the Beautiful and the Good are the same, which all things desire, and to which all things are related, because there is nothing in the substances of things that does not participate in some way in the Beautiful and the Good. And since He is the primary and immeasurable source from which all things desire to receive, therefore all things (as <margin>Theodore</margin>the great Theodore says in the works of Proclus <note>Theodore of Asine, a Neoplatonic philosopher cited by Proclus in his commentaries.</note>) pray, except for the First Himself; for all things are in need. And while they recognize that they must receive from Him those things which they lack, they ask Him. Hence the Highest Teacher, Christ, taught <margin>CHRIST.</margin>us to direct our prayer to the Father, from whom every best gift and every perfect gift comes, when He said: *When you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven.* And we must always pray until the measure of the gifts prepared for us is fulfilled, and until our joy is full. For then nothing remains that we can seek for ourselves; rather, out of charity, they pour out prayers for others, so that they might attain what we have already achieved. And therefore <margin>John</margin>(as John testifies) the Saints pray, as does the Son of God himself: *If anyone sins,* he says, *we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the propitiation for our sins, and for the sins of the whole world.* <note>1 John 2:1-2.</note> Paul supports this, <margin>Paul</margin>saying: *Jesus entered into heaven itself, to appear before the face of God for us,* and as a true mediator, he might lead all things back into the Highest Good to the same degree that they had fallen away from Him, so that they might become one with Him through a true union, just as they were in the exemplar and in the Archetype <term>Archetype: the original pattern or "blueprint" of all things existing in the divine mind before creation.</term> of the Good.

He becomes so much a part of it that, having forgotten all external things and being separated from them all, he has no one with whom he can speak; he converses only with Him for whom speech is not required, since He beholds all things. Furthermore, he beholds and delights in these things which, even if he wished to express them, he could not. From this point, therefore, one must be silent, except insofar as he manifests something to those below—according to the capacity of the recipients and for their benefit—at the command of the Prince. As
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Dionysius says concerning the Angels: they are the announcers of the divine silence, acting like clear lights that interpret that which is hidden in secret. That divine silence—or that which must be kept silent—is indeed that goodness, beauty, and light so eminent that it cannot be manifested in words; rather, it is perceived in that same light
<margin>The Psalms</margin>
which is manifested only to eyes that are well-illuminated. Therefore the Psalmist says:
> *In your light we shall see light.*

In this light are seen the secrets and hidden things
<margin>Paul</margin>
of God, which (as Paul testifies) it is not permitted for man to speak. Therefore, the field of speaking about such things is open to no one more than the ignorant. For if no one can perceive those things unless he is caught up in an ecstasy of the mind <term>excess of the mind <gloss>original: "excessus mentis," a state of mystical rapture where the mind "goes out" of its normal function</gloss></term>, or transformed into that same image which is the Son of God, how, I ask, shall those who are not lifted up or transformed explain them? Thus, even those who have seen them through an ecstasy of the mind must remain silent.
<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
For when Jeremiah (as we said recently) was discussing the solitary man who is lifted up into God, he added, according to the Hebrew truth: <note>original: "veritatem hebraicam"; a term used by scholars like St. Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as a more authentic source than the Greek or Latin translations.</note>
> *He shall sit, for the burden is upon himself.*

For a great burden has been placed upon the shoulders of those to whom the secrets of the Prince have been entrusted: namely, that they be faithful and remain silent. Hence, when Isaiah
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
saw in an ecstasy of the mind those things which were to come in the time of the Messiah, being unable to contain what was bubbling up in his mind, he said:
> *When the Lord shall be glorified—namely through the Messiah—they shall exult from the sea, that is, from the most high, from whence He shall come,*

just as it is said through another prophet:
<margin>David</margin>
> *Your ways are in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps shall not be known,*

meaning, by the natural light of reason. Therefore,
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Isaiah follows:
> *But in the lights, or the splendors (for which we have "in doctrines"), they shall glorify the Lord: for in the islands of the sea is the name of the Lord Israel; from the ends, or from the wings of the earth, we have heard praises, which are to come to you, O Just One:*

for which we have "the glory of the Just One."
<margin>The Septuagint</margin>
But the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> interpret that <gloss>where</gloss> as "appearance," but properly it signifies something "pleasant" and "excellent." The sense is: Excellent praise and pleasantness shall be to the Just One—that is, the Messiah, who alone was found just among mortals. But when he saw that he had spoken too openly, he immediately added:
> *My secret is mine, my secret is mine: Woe is me! because I have spoken so openly.*

Afterwards, he turned his discourse to another matter...

<page-num>LXXXX</page-num>
<header>### OF THE THIRD CANTICLE</header>

...turns aside. The Psalmist also hints at this in silence, saying: *I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you* <margin>Psalm</margin> <note>Psalm 119:11. The author interprets "hiding" the word as an act of mystical silence.</note>. To hide is to be silent. But how alien it is to the duty of a good man to <term>make public</term> <note>original: "propalare"; to reveal or broadcast secrets.</note> divine secrets, Hermes <margin>Hermes</margin> <note>original: "Mercurius"; the author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage believed by Renaissance scholars to be a contemporary of Moses and a teacher of divine wisdom.</note> declares in his address to Asclepius, when he says: "It is the mark of an irreligious mind to publish to the consciousness of the many a treatise filled with the full majesty of the divinity," because profound words and the mysteries of God become too cheap in weak minds. Therefore, the Greatest Teacher <margin>CHRIST</margin> said: *Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine* <note>Matthew 7:6</note>, namely by <term>making public</term> the most precious secrets of God to those who are unworthy and incapable. Add to this that sometimes, out of reverence (as Hermes says), silence provides a fertile pregnancy of truth, so that one who has preserved those secrets with reverence may speak all the more effectively and sublimely in his own place, just as he has been a more faithful servant in concealing them. Furthermore, those who praise the ineffable through silence are found to be more acceptable than those who bring forth something unworthily, stained by the falsehood that is contrary to true praise. Thus, the soul—with its senses closed, which take pleasure in colors, smells, tastes, sounds, and physical sensations, and with the wandering of reason closed, whose food and nourishment is truth and the knowledge of lower things—is gathered entirely in the <term>apex of the mind</term> <note>original: "mentis apice"; a technical term in mystical theology referring to the highest faculty of the soul, which transcends rational thought to touch the divine.</note>, whose nourishment is supramundane light. It is silent to others, and speaks only to Him who is the highest and only Good; in leisure, it offers praises. Let us also (as far as it is permitted to reveal) pay a hymn to God, the best and greatest.

-> Hymn to be offered in silence to God alone with a pure and elevated mind. <-

> **T**o you, holy Lord and supreme King of all things, praise is owed, which no one can fully pay, since you are immense, eternal, and ineffable. Whence, if not worthy praise, yet as much as is permitted to me and as much as my strength allows—indeed, as much as you, speaking within me, shall command—I will return it. You are enclosed by no limit, circumscribed by no reason, and accessible to no one; containing all things in yourself and existing as the cause of all things. And if you exist in all things, you are nevertheless so far removed from all things that the human mind can neither speak nor think of you, except insofar as your light has flooded it. You are indeed the Father of all, pure and inaccessible light, a profound spring, the hidden Creator whom no one knows except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him. You are the Fountain of Wisdom from which all things come, and the Eternal Word supporting all things, a hidden dwelling within things: being, life, foundation, and the beginning and end of all things. You are holy, blessed, God Most High himself, the seal, the form, the spirit, the bond, and the life of the world. You are great and highly to be praised, and of your greatness there is no end. In that immense goodness with which you built the world, you also preserve all things, and with your arm you protect all. You are the rising sun from which all light gleams and every good arises. You are powerful, and who resists you? Searching the <term>reins</term> <note>original: "rhenes"; literally "kidneys." In biblical and medieval thought, the kidneys were considered the seat of a person's most secret emotions and desires.</note> and hearts, you render to each according to his works with a just and most holy judgment, permitting nothing to go unpunished. Yours is <margin>XXI</margin> beauty, truth, and life, the measure and the mind that rules, a shining mirror, in—

<page-num>CXXXVI</page-num>
<header>THE EIGHTH TONE</header>

...through whom all things become clear: and the most beautiful light, by which all things become beautiful: Munificent and pious in all things, slow to anger and of great mercy: To You, what was, what is, and what is to come are the same. For in You is the present life and the age to come: in which both every time and every limit are concluded, because You are the end of all things. You are the true God, ascending without motion to Your own sublimity, and descending to us and to even the lowest things, like a <term>foundation</term> <note>original: "basis"; used here in the architectural sense of a pedestal or base that supports a structure.</note> that sustains all things, and You exist as the beauty of all. You are the living God, the life of the world, the author of the covenant, the tree of knowledge, the truth, and the seal of the world, the fountain of soul and form, the peace of all, the union, and the bond <note>original: "vinculum"; a common Neoplatonic term for the force that holds the universe together.</note> of all things. You are the King of the universe, the Prince of the world, its justice and its rule, the God of the elect and their guardian, as well as the all-seeing eye, the habitation and most holy guest within us, transferring Yourself into holy souls, so that by transforming them into Your own image You may lead them back to that place from which they came, and they may be able to do all things with You. 

And let him who is wise understand these things, because this is the <term>hidden manna</term> <note>original: "mana absconditum"; a reference to Revelation 2:17, symbolizing secret spiritual nourishment known only to the initiate.</note> which no one knows except he who receives it. Therefore, it is permitted to speak of such things very little. For these are not perceived by the vocal hearing, but by that eternal light by which those utterances are conceived, which must be hidden in the heart, lest like unfaithful and unworthy praisers we sin before the King, whose <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "sacramentum"; here used in the older sense of a sacred secret or mystery rather than a church rite.</note> it is good to hide. We cannot reveal it because it is ineffable. Therefore, since words are not sufficient, He must be praised with silence, with a pure and fervent heart; for "in silence and in hope shall be our strength," as the <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: "oraculum"; referring to Isaiah 30:15.</note> says. With which that saying of Jeremiah most greatly agrees: "It is good to wait in silence until, seeing Him face to face as He is," our true tongue may break forth into due praises, just as it is also written: "They who dwell in Your house shall praise You forever and ever." Amen. <note>Psalm 84:4.</note>
